docs.snippet: A Han model chariot: thirty spokes share one hub, and the wheel turns because the hub is empty.

docs.title: Night-Shining White
docs.snippet: The emperor's horse strains against its post, eyes rolling. One who stands on tiptoe is not steady.

docs.title: Mirror with Deities, Chariot, and the White Tiger
docs.snippet: A Han bronze mirror: its polished face is gone, but its back shows the cosmos. Can you clean the dark mirror so that no stain remains?

docs.title: Pictorial Stone: Queen Mother of the West, Chariot, Hunt
docs.snippet: A carved Han stone in three balanced bands: deities, a chariot, a hunt. The Way of heaven is like stretching a bow: lower the high, raise the low.

docs.title: Shide (from the pair Hanshan and Shide)
docs.snippet: Shide, the ragged temple sweeper, looks like a fool. Chapter 41 says the bright Way seems dark and the purest white seems soiled.

docs.title: The Sound of Spring in a Lonely Valley
docs.snippet: Hongren's valley is pale and still, with a thin stream running down its centre. The valley spirit does not die.

docs.title: Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains (detail)
docs.snippet: Huang Gongwang's long scroll of quiet hills shows people living by the river. I do nothing, and the people transform themselves.

docs.title: Auspicious Cranes
docs.snippet: Cranes circle the palace gate in a painting from Emperor Huizong's court, a sign of good fortune. Fifteen years later his dynasty fell.

docs.title: Listening to the Qin (detail)
docs.snippet: Under a pine, a man plays the qin while two officials listen. Music and good food make travellers stop; the Way has no flavour.

docs.title: Bi Disc
docs.snippet: A jade bi disc, a treasure offered to heaven. Better than jade and fine horses is to sit still and offer the Way.

docs.title: Cong
docs.snippet: The cong is round inside and square outside, a joining of heaven and earth. Everything that attains the One is whole.

docs.title: Seeking the Dao in the Autumn Mountains
docs.snippet: Juran's title says it all: seeking the Dao in the autumn mountains. Find the small hut in the fold of the hills.

docs.title: A Deep Valley Conceals a Monk's Home
docs.snippet: Kuncan hides a monk's house deep in the folds of the mountain. Find it, and notice how much the valley protects it.

docs.title: Laozi Riding an Ox (Paintings after Ancient Masters)
docs.snippet: Laozi rides slowly past bamboo on his ox. I have three things to treasure: tenderness, spareness, and not daring to go ahead of the world.

docs.title: Laozi Riding an Ox
docs.snippet: Zhang Lu's Laozi rides away on his ox, looking up from his book. True words are not beautiful; beautiful words are not true.

docs.title: A Solitary Temple Amid Clearing Peaks
docs.snippet: The great peak behind the temple has stood for ages. It lasts because it does not live for itself.

docs.title: Returning Herdsman in Snow
docs.snippet: A herdsman rides home on his buffalo through snow. Show plainness, embrace the uncarved block, have few desires.

docs.title: Five Horses (first section)
docs.snippet: Li Gonglin's horse stands calmly with its groom. When the world has the Way, horses fertilise the fields.

docs.title: Wind in Pines Among a Myriad Valleys
docs.snippet: Li Tang fills the scroll with pines and valleys. Know the male, keep to the female; be a valley for the world.

docs.title: Immortal in Splashed Ink
docs.snippet: Liang Kai's immortal stumbles forward, belly out, eyes squinting. Everyone else is bright; I alone am dull.

docs.title: Li Bai Strolling and Chanting
docs.snippet: The poet Li Bai, who had both favour and disgrace at court, walks off alone. Liang Kai needs only a few lines.

docs.title: Fish Swimming amid Falling Flowers (detail)
docs.snippet: Goldfish turn and drift among the plants. Govern a great state as you cook a small fish: gently, and not too much stirring.

docs.title: Listening to the Wind in the Pines
docs.snippet: A scholar sits under a pine and listens to the wind. Without going out the door, one can know the world.

docs.title: Waves of the Autumn Flood (Water Album)
docs.snippet: Ma Yuan's autumn water spreads in endless small waves. Nothing in the world is softer than water, yet nothing is better at wearing down the hard.

docs.title: Clouds Rising from the Green Sea (Water Album)
docs.snippet: Long swells of the sea under rising mist. Rivers and seas rule a hundred valleys because they lie lower.

docs.title: Walking on a Mountain Path in Spring
docs.snippet: Ma Yuan's scholar strolls along a spring path. A good walker leaves no tracks.

docs.title: Boundless Expanse of the Yangzi (Water Album)
docs.snippet: Ma Yuan's waves fill the whole leaf with a soft, even net. Water benefits all things and does not compete.

docs.title: Scholar Viewing a Waterfall
docs.snippet: A scholar watches a waterfall pour through the rocks. The softest thing in the world rides over the hardest.

docs.title: The Yellow River Breaches Its Course (Water Album)
docs.snippet: Ma Yuan's Yellow River throws up foam and spray. A whirlwind does not last all morning.

docs.title: Jar with Spiral Designs
docs.snippet: A potter shaped this jar more than five thousand years ago. The clay makes the walls; the empty inside makes it useful.

docs.title: Calligraphy in Cursive Script
docs.snippet: Mi Fu's cursive looks careless and spills across the page. The greatest skill seems clumsy.

docs.title: Cloudy Mountains
docs.snippet: These hills, attributed to Mi Youren, are only half there; mist takes away their edges. Look for the place where ink stops and nothing begins.

docs.title: Dragon (from Dragon and Tiger)
docs.snippet: This dragon, attributed to Muqi, comes and goes in the clouds. The Way is elusive and vague, and yet within it there is an image.

docs.title: Tiger (from Dragon and Tiger)
docs.snippet: This tiger, attributed to Muqi, crouches in the grass. One who cares well for life meets no tiger on the road.

docs.title: The Rongxi Studio
docs.snippet: Ni Zan paints an empty pavilion between two shores. Attain the summit of emptiness; hold fast to stillness.

docs.title: Ox and Herdsman Both Forgotten (Ten Oxherding Pictures, no. 8)
docs.snippet: The eighth of the Ten Oxherding Pictures is an empty circle. In pursuing the Way, one loses a little every day.

docs.title: The Peach Blossom Spring
docs.snippet: A fisherman finds a hidden valley where people have lived in peace for centuries. Small country, few people.

docs.title: Circle, Triangle, Square
docs.snippet: Sengai's square, triangle and circle lean on each other. Each shape is clear only because the others are next to it.

docs.title: Splashed-Ink Landscape
docs.snippet: Sesshū's splashed ink barely forms a picture. Look at it and you do not quite see it.

docs.title: Huike Offering His Arm to Bodhidharma
docs.snippet: Huike cuts off his arm to show Bodhidharma he is sincere. To know not-knowing: the highest.

docs.title: Autumn and Winter Landscapes
docs.snippet: In Sesshū's winter landscape a sharp line of cliff cuts down through cold air. The ancient masters were careful, as if crossing a winter stream.

docs.title: Landscape with Man Crossing a Bridge
docs.snippet: A man crosses a little bridge toward his cottage, a boy with a qin behind him. Do not crowd people's dwellings; do not weary their lives.

docs.title: Returning Home (album leaf)
docs.snippet: Shitao's traveller sits in a small boat on blank water, going home. Know the child; return to the mother.

docs.title: Dunhuang Star Chart (north polar region)
docs.snippet: A Tang dynasty star chart from Dunhuang maps the sky around the pole. Heaven's net is vast; its mesh is wide, yet nothing slips through.

docs.title: Children at Play in an Autumn Garden
docs.snippet: Two children bend over their game in an autumn garden, in a painting attributed to Su Hanchen. One who holds virtue fully is like a newborn child.

docs.title: Children at Play (album leaf)
docs.snippet: Two small children play beside a flowering plant, one reaching toward a butterfly. Can you soften your breath and become like a child?

docs.title: River Chart of Heaven and Earth
docs.snippet: One of the earliest printed yin-yang swirls, from about 1370. Returning is the movement of the Way.

docs.title: Pine Trees (left screen)
docs.snippet: Tōhaku's pines appear and disappear in fog. The Way does nothing, yet nothing is left undone.

docs.title: Ge Zhichuan Moving His Dwelling
docs.snippet: The Daoist Ge Hong moves his family into the mountains, leaving office behind. When the work is done, step back.

docs.title: A Thousand Li of Rivers and Mountains (detail)
docs.snippet: Wang Ximeng's blue and green peaks are dazzling. Laozi warns that the five colours can blind the eye.

docs.title: Solitary Walker in Autumn
docs.snippet: A lone figure walks under bare autumn trees. A journey of a thousand li begins beneath your feet.

docs.title: The Seven Junipers
docs.snippet: Wen Zhengming's ancient junipers are twisted and knotted. Bent, they stay whole.

docs.title: Old Trees by a Cold Waterfall
docs.snippet: Old trees twist beside a cold waterfall. Living things are soft and supple; dead things are hard and dry.

docs.title: Fisherman
docs.snippet: A fisherman floats on calm water, far from court. Which is dearer, fame or your life?

docs.title: Twin Pines
docs.snippet: Two old pines stand together, deeply rooted. What is well planted cannot be uprooted.

docs.title: Pure and Remote View of Streams and Mountains (detail)
docs.snippet: This scroll, attributed to Xia Gui, leaves most of the paper blank. The empty space works like the bellows in this chapter: it gives, and it is never used up.

docs.title: Twelve Views from a Thatched Hut (detail)
docs.snippet: Xia Gui puts a few trees and tiny figures on a low bank and leaves the rest as mist. Nothing here asks for attention.

docs.title: Fishermen's Evening Song (detail)
docs.snippet: Fishermen work the river under huge peaks. No ruler appears; the people live their lives and say, "We did this ourselves."

docs.title: Emperor Taizong Receiving the Tibetan Envoy
docs.snippet: The Tang emperor receives an envoy from Tibet. A great state should be like the low place where rivers meet.

docs.title: Yin Xi, Keeper of the Pass
docs.snippet: Yin Xi, the keeper of the pass, reads the book Laozi left behind. Notice that he holds the text, but the author is gone.

docs.title: Man and Horse
docs.snippet: A groom stands calmly beside his horse. Misfortune is what fortune leans on; fortune is where misfortune hides.

docs.title: The Pleasures of Fishes (detail)
docs.snippet: Zhou Dongqing's carp turn among water plants, free and at ease. One who knows does not speak.

docs.title: Kitchen Scene with a Butcher
docs.snippet: A kitchen relief, said to be Han, of a butcher at the carcass. What has no substance enters where there is no gap.

docs.title: Laozi on His Buffalo, Followed by a Disciple
docs.snippet: Laozi on his buffalo, a boy with a gourd beside him. Those who know me are few; and so I am precious.

docs.title: Spring Plowing (Landscape Album in Various Styles)
docs.snippet: Farmhouses sit among willows on a quiet river delta in spring. “Empty the heart, fill the belly.”

docs.title: Ding Ware Bowl of the Xing Type with Bi-Disc Foot
docs.snippet: A plain white bowl from the Gongxian kilns, made for drinking tea. “Dao is an empty bowl. Use it, and perhaps it does not fill.”

docs.title: Dog
docs.snippet: A glazed clay dog from the Eastern Han, with its head up and its mouth open. “They treat the ten thousand things as straw dogs.”

docs.title: Yoro Waterfall in Mino Province (Tour of the Waterfalls in Various Provinces)
docs.snippet: Hokusai’s Yoro Falls drops straight down to the low pool, where travellers stop to rest. “It stays in the place the crowd hates, and so it is near to Dao.”

docs.title: Windy Landscape with Sailboat
docs.snippet: A retired official’s small house by the water faces one distant sail. “The work carried through, the body steps back: the Way of heaven.”

docs.title: Old Trees by a Wintry Brook
docs.snippet: Wen Zhengming painted these bare old trees over a cold stream in his eighties. “Wary, as if crossing a river in winter.”

docs.title: Returning Home
docs.snippet: A small boat comes home to a pavilion below a pine and jagged cliffs. “Each go home again to the root.”

docs.title: River Village: Fisherman’s Joy
docs.snippet: On Zhao Mengfu’s round fan, fishermen work a flat river below blue hills. “The hundred families all say: ‘We are so of ourselves.’”

docs.title: Budai
docs.snippet: Budai, the wandering monk with a cloth sack, grins below a long inscription. “Mine is the heart of a fool!”

docs.title: River Village in a Rainstorm
docs.snippet: Wind and slanting rain lash a river village in Lu Wenying’s scroll. “A sudden rain does not last the day.”

docs.title: Streams and Mountains without End (detail)
docs.snippet: In this detail of a long silk handscroll, hills and streams run on past both edges. “Great means passing on. Passing on means far. Far means turning back.”

docs.title: Snow Landscape
docs.snippet: Buson’s snow covers mountains, trees, and a small scholar’s retreat, and no path shows. “Good walking leaves no rut or footprint.”

docs.title: Playing the Qin in a Secluded Valley
docs.snippet: Wen Zhengming’s deep ravine gathers cliffs, pines, and falling water into one long valley. “Be the valley of all under heaven.”

docs.title: Square Wine Container (Fangyou)
docs.snippet: A Shang bronze ritual vessel for wine, cast with crested birds. “All under heaven is a spirit vessel. It cannot be worked on.”

docs.title: Ceremonial Dagger-Axe with Animal Masks (Ge)
docs.snippet: A Shang jade blade in the shape of a bronze weapon, made for ceremony. “Fruit, and no forcing.”

docs.title: Sword
docs.snippet: A plain bronze sword from the Han dynasty, its blade dulled by age. “Weapons are tools of ill omen, not a gentleman’s tools.”

docs.title: River and Mountains on a Clear Autumn Day (detail)
docs.snippet: Dong Qichang’s folded hills run down toward open water. “A likeness for Dao in all under heaven: streams and valleys, and the River and the sea.”

docs.title: Poet and Recluse Hanshan
docs.snippet: The hermit poet Hanshan stands alone in a loose robe, his hair wild. “One who knows the self is bright.”

docs.title: Nine Dragon Pool
docs.snippet: Mei Qing’s waterfall at Huangshan bends left and right through nine pools. “The great Dao floods, oh: it can go left and right.”

docs.title: Tea Bowl (Jian ware)
docs.snippet: A Song tea bowl from Fujian with a dark glaze called hare’s fur. “The Dao, as it comes out of the mouth: bland! It has no flavor.”

docs.title: A Pair of Carp
docs.snippet: Two carp turn in deep water in a Korean ink painting. “Fish must not slip out of the deep.”

docs.title: Scholar Reclining and Watching Rising Clouds
docs.snippet: Ma Lin’s scholar lies by the water and watches clouds rise out of empty space. “Having is born from not-having.”

docs.title: Haboku (Flung-ink) Landscape
docs.snippet: Shūgetsu’s flung ink makes a landscape out of blots and a few quick strokes. “The great image is without shape.”

docs.title: Mirror with Images of Daoist Deities
docs.snippet: The back of an Eastern Han bronze mirror: one knob at the centre, then rings of deities and beasts. “The Dao gives birth to one. One gives birth to two.”

docs.title: Gazing at a Waterfall
docs.snippet: Two men on a terrace watch a thin waterfall pour through mist. “The softest thing under heaven gallops over the hardest thing under heaven.”

docs.title: The Hermit Xu You Resting by a Stream
docs.snippet: Xu You, who refused a throne, rests by a stream under cliffs and pines. “Know enough: no disgrace. Know to stop: no danger.”

docs.title: Crackle-glazed Bowl
docs.snippet: A Korean celadon bowl, its green glaze crazed with fine cracks. “Great completion seems chipped; its use does not wear out.”

docs.title: Farming and Herding Buffalo in Summer
docs.snippet: Farmers and water buffalo work the fields by a summer river. “When the world has Dao, running horses are turned back to dung the fields.”

docs.title: Scholar Reading in a Thatched Hut by a Waterfall (Paintings after Ancient Masters)
docs.snippet: In Chen Hongshou’s album leaf, a scholar sits in a thatched hut under a great pine. “Without going out of the door, know the world.”

docs.title: Covered Jar (Hu)
docs.snippet: A Warring States bronze jar, gilded and inlaid with silver swirls. “Glutted with drink and food, with goods in surplus.”

docs.title: Water Village (detail)
docs.snippet: A quiet village on low marshland, from Wen Boren’s handscroll. “Tend it in the village: its de then lasts.”

docs.title: Playing with an Infant
docs.snippet: Two women play with a small child in a Qing colour woodblock print. “One who holds de within, thick and deep, is like a red child.”

docs.title: Bodhidharma
docs.snippet: Unkei Eii’s Bodhidharma looks out in silence, wrapped in a few broad strokes of robe. “One who knows does not speak.”

docs.title: Returning Peasants in a Spring Evening
docs.snippet: Farmers walk home past bare trees at the start of the farming year. “I have no business, and the people grow rich of themselves.”

docs.title: Old Pine Tree (detail)
docs.snippet: Wen Zhengming’s old pine twists across the scroll, bent but deeply rooted. “This is called deep roots and a firm taproot.”

docs.title: Tripod Cauldron (Ding)
docs.snippet: A Shang bronze ding, a cooking vessel for offerings of grain and meat. “Ruling a great state is like the cooking of a small fish.”

docs.title: Traveling in Autumn Mountains (Landscape Album in Various Styles)
docs.snippet: A traveller on a donkey and his porter set out under autumn trees. “A journey of a thousand li begins under the foot.”

docs.title: Fishermen-Hermits in Stream and Mountain
docs.snippet: Zhao Yong’s fishermen sit low in their boats between two shores. “The River and the sea can be kings of the hundred valleys.”

docs.title: Monk Mending Clothes in the Morning Sun
docs.snippet: A monk holds his old robe up to the morning light and mends it. “The second is spareness.”

docs.title: Dagger-Axe (Ge)
docs.snippet: A bronze dagger-axe from the Shang, its blade worn green and silver. “I do not dare to advance an inch; I go back a foot.”

docs.title: Farmer Returning Home in Autumn
docs.snippet: Buson’s farmer shoos a crow from his grain while his buffalo wades the stream. “The people starve. Those above them eat so much in grain tax.”

docs.title: Bamboo in the Wind
docs.snippet: The monk Puming painted bamboo that bends in the wind and does not break. “The soft and weak are the company of life.”

docs.title: Waterfall and Rocks
docs.snippet: In Tsubaki Chinzan’s album leaf, a waterfall cuts down through folded cliffs. “Under heaven nothing is softer and weaker than water.”

docs.title: New Year’s Day in a Village at Stone Lake
docs.snippet: Guests come to a village farmhouse to greet the elders on New Year’s Day. “Their homes at rest, their customs a joy.”

docs.title: Poem by Wang Wei in the Cursive Script Style
docs.snippet: Emperor Lizong wrote out ten characters from a poem by Wang Wei on this round fan. “Words to trust are not beautiful.”

docs.title: Peach Blossom Spring
docs.snippet: A hidden valley of farms and blossom, reached through a cave. Though there are boats and carts, there is no occasion to ride them.

docs.title: The Wheelwright's Hand
docs.snippet: The hand gets it and the heart answers. The mouth cannot say it. Yet there is a knack in there.

docs.title: Words Run Out
docs.snippet: Writing does not exhaust speech. Speech does not exhaust meaning.

docs.title: The Gate of Illusion
docs.snippet: When false is taken for true, true is also false. Where nothing is made into something, something turns back to nothing.

docs.title: Born and Dying Together
docs.snippet: At the moment of birth, dying. At the moment of dying, birth. At the moment of yes, no.

docs.title: The Void as the Way
docs.snippet: Take the void as the Way, and see the Way as void.

docs.title: Straw Dogs, Before and After
docs.snippet: Before the straw dogs are set out, they lie in a basket, wrapped in embroidered cloth.

docs.title: The Clean White Ground
docs.snippet: It is just like birds that fly to the wood when the food is gone. What is left is a wide white ground, truly clean.

docs.title: The Field That Bears
docs.snippet: How complete is the source in Kun! The ten thousand things take their birth from it, and it follows and receives heaven.

docs.title: Set Out Last, Arrive First
docs.snippet: Set out after the other and arrive before the other. This is to know the plan of the crooked and the straight.

docs.title: Water Takes the Vessel's Shape
docs.snippet: Water follows the square or round vessel. It becomes one drop, and it becomes the wide blue sea.

docs.title: The Army Shaped Like Water
docs.snippet: The form of an army is like water. Water in its course avoids the high and hurries to the low.

docs.title: Water in the Pit
docs.snippet: Water flows on and does not fill up. It goes through danger and stays true.

docs.title: The Moon When Full
docs.snippet: The moon when full will wane. Water when full will spill.

docs.title: The Dragon Too High
docs.snippet: The dragon that has gone too high has regret. What is full cannot last.

docs.title: The Fasting of the Heart
docs.snippet: The breath is what is empty and waits for things. Only the Dao gathers in emptiness.

docs.title: Polishing the Mirror
docs.snippet: Polish the two hearts, mind and will. Sharpen the two eyes, the seeing-into and the looking-at.

docs.title: The Use of the Useless
docs.snippet: All people know the use of the useful. No one knows the use of the useless.

docs.title: Knowing What Is Not There
docs.snippet: Know the place where something is, and so know the place where nothing is. This is the void.

docs.title: The Back of the Mirror
docs.snippet: On no account look into the front. Look only into its back.

docs.title: A Puff of Smoke
docs.snippet: Wait for the time when I have turned into a puff of light smoke, and one breath of wind blows it away.

docs.title: Two Ways of Seeing
docs.snippet: Make the eye that sees into things strong and the eye that looks at things weak. See the far as near, and the near as far.

docs.title: If You Heard It, That Is Not It
docs.snippet: The Dao cannot be heard; what is heard is not it. The Dao cannot be seen; what is seen is not it.

docs.title: The Still-Water Mirror
docs.snippet: No one uses running water as a mirror. People use still water.

docs.title: Subtle to the Point of No Form
docs.snippet: Subtle, subtle, to the point of having no form! Spirit-like, spirit-like, to the point of having no sound!

docs.title: The Heart of Heaven and Earth
docs.snippet: In Return, does one not see the heart of heaven and earth?

docs.title: Back to the Great Waste
docs.snippet: Vast and dim, vast and dim: going home to that Great Waste.

docs.title: As If It Did Not Come from Him
docs.snippet: His work covers the world, yet it seems not to come from him. His changing reaches all things, yet the people do not lean on him.

docs.title: Fish on Dry Land
docs.snippet: They breathe damp on each other and wet each other with spit. Better to forget each other in the rivers and lakes.

docs.title: The Minister Who Dies for a Name
docs.snippet: There must first be a muddled ruler before he can protest.

docs.title: When the Sages Are Cut Off
docs.snippet: So cut off the sage and throw away knowledge, and the great robbers will stop.

docs.title: Baoyu Continues the Zhuangzi
docs.snippet: Burn the Flower, scatter the Musk, and then the women's rooms will keep their good advice to themselves.

docs.title: The Useless Boy
docs.snippet: For no cause he hunts for sorrow and seeks out regret. At times he seems a fool, at times like a madman.

docs.title: The One Stone Left Over
docs.snippet: It alone was without talent and not fit to be chosen.

docs.title: Zhuang Zhou and the Butterfly
docs.snippet: Between Zhou and the butterfly there must be some division. This is called the changing of things.

docs.title: The Straight Tree Is Cut First
docs.snippet: The straight tree is felled first. The sweet well is drained first.

docs.title: The Inchworm Bends
docs.snippet: The inchworm draws itself in so that it can stretch out. Dragons and snakes lie hidden in winter so that they keep their bodies whole.

docs.title: The Sun at Noon
docs.snippet: The sun at noon begins to slant. The moon when full begins to be eaten away. Heaven and earth fill and empty, growing and fading with the seasons.

docs.title: Walk as You Always Walk
docs.snippet: In footwork, the step may be large or small, slow or quick, as the case requires, but it is always like ordinary walking.

docs.title: What 'Natural' Means
docs.snippet: It is what heaven has of itself. It is not something brought about by human effort.

docs.title: Not Still When Still, Not Fast When Fast
docs.snippet: Even when all is quiet, the heart is not quiet. However fast things move, the heart is not fast at all.

docs.title: The Master Carpenter Wastes Nothing
docs.snippet: Wood that is strong, even if it has knots, even if it is warped ... he looks at closely and puts to use.

docs.title: Cook Ding Follows the Grain
docs.snippet: Knowing by the senses stops, and the spirit's own impulse moves, following the grain that heaven gave.

docs.title: The Stone Before It Was Clever
docs.snippet: But after the smelting made your spirit awake, you went among people to look for right and wrong.

docs.title: The Carpenter's Crime
docs.snippet: To wreck the uncarved wood in order to make vessels: this is the crime of the craftsman.

docs.title: Schemes Run to the End
docs.snippet: Too clever, working every device to the end; the reckoning turned and took your own dear life.

docs.title: Winning Without the Battle
docs.snippet: To make the other side's army yield without a battle is the best of the best.

docs.title: The Sword Swung Hard
docs.snippet: A sword swung with a 'strong' heart is a bad thing. With roughness alone it is hard to win.

docs.title: The Dead Do Not Come Back
docs.snippet: A state that has perished cannot be made to exist again. The dead cannot be brought back to life.

docs.title: The Root Is to Surpass
docs.snippet: The warrior's way of practicing strategy takes as its root, in every matter, being better than others.

docs.title: A Few Words Carved
docs.snippet: Only it still has no real merit. A few characters must be carved on it too.

docs.title: Know the Other, Know Yourself
docs.snippet: Know the other and know yourself, and in a hundred battles there is no danger.

docs.title: Beat Yesterday's Self
docs.snippet: Think: today I beat the self of yesterday; tomorrow I beat one less skilled; later I beat one more skilled.

docs.title: Lower Still
docs.snippet: 'How can it be still worse?' He said: 'It is in the shit and piss.'

docs.title: Friendship Plain as Water
docs.snippet: The friendship of the noble is plain like water. The friendship of the small is sweet like new wine.

docs.title: Able, Show Unable
docs.snippet: When able, show them you are unable. When using your force, show them you are not using it.

docs.title: The Sage as Sharp Tool
docs.snippet: Those sages are the sharp tools of the world. They are not something to hold up to the world's light.

docs.title: Down the Ladder
docs.snippet: Kindness can be put on. Right conduct can be chipped away. In rites, people deceive each other.

docs.title: More Flower Than Fruit
docs.snippet: Of the two, flower and fruit, there is less fruit than flower.

docs.title: Clear by Not Doing
docs.snippet: Heaven does nothing, and by this it is clear. Earth does nothing, and by this it is at rest.

docs.title: No Plain Without a Slope
docs.snippet: There is no level ground without a slope. There is no going without a return.

docs.title: A Stance That Is No Stance
docs.snippet: This is the principle called: there is a stance, and there is no stance.

docs.title: Yin and Yang Are One Word
docs.snippet: When yang is used up it becomes yin. When yin is used up it becomes yang.

docs.title: One Yin, One Yang
docs.snippet: One yin, one yang: this is called the Dao.

docs.title: What Has No Thickness
docs.snippet: Those joints have gaps, and the knife's edge has no thickness. What has no thickness enters where there is a gap.

docs.title: Only Fame They Can't Forget
docs.snippet: All people know it is good to be an immortal. Only fame and rank they cannot forget.

docs.title: Tail in the Mud
docs.snippet: Or would it rather be alive and drag its tail in the mud?

docs.title: The Master Looks Slow
docs.snippet: What a master does looks unhurried, and yet no beat is missed.

docs.title: Too Late to Draw Back the Hand
docs.snippet: With plenty stored behind you, you forget to draw back your hand. With no road left before your eyes, you think of turning round.

docs.title: One Branch, One Bellyful
docs.snippet: The wren nests in the deep forest and uses no more than one branch. The mole drinks at the river and takes no more than a bellyful.

docs.title: From One, Know Ten Thousand
docs.snippet: To know ten thousand things by means of one: this is the principle of strategy.

docs.title: Knowledge Must Come from People
docs.snippet: It cannot be had from ghosts and spirits ... it must be had from people, those who know the enemy's true state.

docs.title: Sitting and Forgetting
docs.snippet: Let the limbs and body drop, dismiss hearing and sight, part from form, leave knowing behind, and be one with the great passage. This is called sitting and forgetting.

docs.title: A Thousand Days to Forge
docs.snippet: Take a thousand days of practice as the forging, and ten thousand days of practice as the tempering.

docs.title: Good Means Over
docs.snippet: If it is not over, it is not good. If you want it good, it has to be over.

docs.title: The Heart Used Like a Mirror
docs.snippet: The perfected person uses the heart like a mirror. It does not see things off and does not go out to meet them. It answers and does not store.

docs.title: Not Only the Warrior Dies Well
docs.snippet: People seem to think that the warrior is simply one devoted to the way called dying.

docs.title: The Iron Threshold
docs.snippet: Though you have an iron threshold to last a thousand years, in the end you need one earth dumpling.

docs.title: Seven Holes for Hundun
docs.snippet: Each day they bored one opening. On the seventh day Hundun died.

docs.title: Nothing Hidden
docs.snippet: In this way of battle, what should one hide, and what should one reveal?

docs.title: The Baby Grips All Day
docs.snippet: It grips all day and the hand does not cramp. Its de is all of one piece.

docs.title: What Good Is an Infant?
docs.snippet: What is so good about that newborn? Only that it has no knowing, no learning, no greed, and no dread.

docs.title: Get the Meaning, Forget the Words
docs.snippet: Words are there for the meaning. Get the meaning and forget the words.

docs.title: No Place to Stand
docs.snippet: When nothing can be called proof, that is the ground to stand on.

docs.title: The Straight and the Surprise
docs.snippet: In all fighting, meet them with the straight, and win with the surprise.

docs.title: Yesterday's Coat, Today's Robe

docs.title: Gain and Harm Mixed
docs.snippet: So the thinking of the wise always mixes gain and harm.

docs.title: What Is Full Flows to the Low
docs.snippet: Heaven's way lessens what is full and adds to what is modest. Earth's way changes what is full and flows toward what is modest.

docs.title: No Name for Wisdom, No Credit for Courage
docs.snippet: So the victories of one good at war bring no name for wisdom and no credit for courage.

docs.title: One Step at a Time
docs.snippet: Even a road of a thousand ri is walked one step at a time.

docs.title: Frost Underfoot
docs.snippet: Treading on frost. Hard ice is coming.

docs.title: All Rivers Go Home to It
docs.snippet: Of all the waters under heaven, none is greater than the sea. The ten thousand rivers go home to it.

docs.title: First in Uselessness
docs.snippet: In all the world, first in having no ability. From old times to now, without equal in being good for nothing.

docs.title: Soldiers as One's Own Children
docs.snippet: Look on the troops as infants, and so you can go with them into the deep ravine.

docs.title: No Army Raised in Anger
docs.snippet: A ruler must not raise an army out of anger. A general must not give battle out of resentment.

docs.title: The Wooden Rooster
docs.snippet: Look at it from a distance and it is like a rooster of wood. Its de is complete.

docs.title: Letting Go of the Hilt
docs.snippet: There is a spirit of winning with no sword. There is also a spirit of not winning with the sword.

docs.title: First, Be Unbeatable
docs.snippet: First make yourself impossible to defeat, and so wait for the enemy to become possible to defeat.

docs.title: The Initiative Comes First
docs.snippet: The thing called the initiative is the first matter of strategy.

docs.title: Rags Outside, Jade Inside
docs.snippet: The monk had a scabby head and bare feet. The Daoist was lame, with wild hair. Both were raving like madmen.

docs.title: Easy to Know, Simple to Follow
docs.snippet: What is easy is easy to know. What is simple is easy to follow.

docs.title: Not Every Blank Is the Void
docs.snippet: To take the state of not understanding things for the void: that is not the true void.

docs.title: The Fixed Hand Is a Dead Hand
docs.snippet: To be fixed in place is the dead hand. Not to be fixed is the living hand.

docs.title: Decrease in Its Season
docs.snippet: Decreasing and increasing, filling and emptying: these go along with the time.

docs.title: Water That Moves Stones
docs.snippet: The rush of surging water reaches the point where it floats stones along. This is force of position.

docs.title: The Swimmer at Lüliang
docs.snippet: I follow the way of the water and do not set up anything private against it.

docs.title: The Gardener Refuses the Machine
docs.snippet: Where there are machines there will be machine business. Where there is machine business there will be a machine heart.

docs.title: The Passage, Quoted
docs.snippet: The sounds of roosters and dogs reach from one to the other, and the people grow old and die without going back and forth.

docs.title: The Village Built for Show
docs.snippet: It is plain to see that it was bored out and twisted into shape by human effort.

docs.title: Pages of Wild Words
docs.snippet: Pages full of wild talk, a handful of bitter tears. All say the author is a fool. Who can tell the taste inside?

docs.title: Shuowen Jiezi
docs.snippet: China's first great character dictionary, finished by Xu Shen around 100 CE.

docs.title: Xu Shen
docs.snippet: Han-dynasty scholar (c. 58–c. 147 CE) who wrote the Shuowen Jiezi.

docs.title: Duan Yucai
docs.snippet: Qing scholar (1735–1815) whose commentary on the Shuowen is the classic study of it.

docs.title: Wang Bi
docs.snippet: A brilliant young philosopher (226–249 CE) whose edition and commentary of the Laozi became the standard text.

docs.title: Heshang Gong
docs.snippet: “The Old Man by the River” — a legendary sage credited with an early Laozi commentary focused on the body and long life.

docs.title: Mawangdui silk texts
docs.snippet: Two manuscripts of the Laozi on silk, buried in 168 BCE and found in 1973 at Mawangdui, Changsha.

docs.title: Guodian bamboo slips
docs.snippet: The oldest known Laozi material: bamboo slips from a tomb of about 300 BCE, found in 1993 in Hubei.

docs.title: Beida bamboo Laozi
docs.snippet: A nearly complete Han-dynasty bamboo Laozi, bought by Peking University (Beida) in 2009.

docs.title: Fu Yi
docs.snippet: Tang scholar (555–639) who edited an “ancient text” of the Laozi said to come from a tomb.

docs.title: received text
docs.snippet: The version of a classic handed down by copying and printing, as opposed to manuscripts dug up from tombs.

docs.title: Warring States
docs.snippet: The age of China's wars of unification, about 475–221 BCE — the world in which the Laozi took shape.

docs.title: Zhou dynasty
docs.snippet: The long dynasty (c. 1046–256 BCE) whose ritual order collapsed into the Warring States.

docs.title: Han dynasty
docs.snippet: The empire of 206 BCE–220 CE that fixed the classics, made the first dictionaries, and buried the Mawangdui silk.

docs.title: Qin
docs.snippet: The western state that conquered all others in 221 BCE and founded the first empire.

docs.title: oracle-bone script
docs.snippet: The oldest Chinese writing (c. 1250–1050 BCE): questions to the spirits cut into turtle shells and ox bones.

docs.title: bronze script
docs.snippet: Writing cast into ritual bronze vessels, from the late Shang through the Zhou (c. 1200–200 BCE).

docs.title: seal script
docs.snippet: The formal script of Qin and Han — even, curving lines — still used today on name seals.

docs.title: clerical script
docs.snippet: The flat, broad script of Han clerks, where the brush first shows its own swells and flicks.

docs.title: regular script
docs.snippet: The standard, carefully separated script used since about the 3rd century CE — the form printed in books today.

docs.title: running script
docs.snippet: A semi-cursive hand: regular script written fast, strokes linking within a character.

docs.title: cursive script
docs.snippet: “Grass script”: the fastest, most abbreviated hand, where whole characters become a few loops.

docs.title: radical
docs.snippet: The component under which a character is filed in a dictionary, often hinting at its meaning.

docs.title: phonetic component
docs.snippet: The part of a character that hints at its sound rather than its meaning.

docs.title: Old Chinese
docs.snippet: The spoken language of the Zhou period, very different in sound from modern Mandarin.

docs.title: pinyin
docs.snippet: The standard way of writing Mandarin sounds in the Latin alphabet, with marks for the four tones.

docs.title: Unihan
docs.snippet: The Unicode Consortium's database of Chinese characters: readings, short definitions, variants.

docs.title: James Legge
docs.snippet: Scottish missionary and Oxford's first professor of Chinese (1815–1897); his 1891 Laozi is shown under each passage.

docs.title: Sacred Books of the East
docs.snippet: A 50-volume series (1879–1910) edited by Max Müller translating Asian scriptures into English.

docs.title: Zhuangzi
docs.snippet: The second great Daoist classic (4th–3rd c. BCE): stories, jokes, and dialogues by Zhuang Zhou and his school.

docs.title: Sunzi
docs.snippet: The classic of strategy, traditionally credited to Sun Wu (6th–5th c. BCE).

docs.title: Han Feizi
docs.snippet: The great Legalist book (3rd c. BCE); its chapters Jie Lao and Yu Lao are the oldest surviving commentary on the Laozi.

docs.title: Analects
docs.snippet: The sayings of Confucius (551–479 BCE) and his students.

docs.title: Mencius
docs.snippet: Confucian thinker (c. 372–289 BCE) who argued human nature is good.

docs.title: Xunzi
docs.snippet: Confucian thinker (3rd c. BCE) who argued human nature must be shaped by ritual and learning.

docs.title: Yijing
docs.snippet: The Book of Changes: an ancient divination manual of 64 six-line figures (hexagrams).

docs.title: Taixuan jing
docs.snippet: Yang Xiong's “Classic of Great Mystery” (c. 2 BCE), built on 81 tetragrams of four lines.

docs.title: tetragram
docs.snippet: A figure of four stacked lines, each solid, broken once, or broken twice — 81 in all.

docs.title: Zuozhuan
docs.snippet: A great narrative history of the Spring and Autumn period (722–468 BCE).

docs.title: Shiji
docs.snippet: Sima Qian's history of China up to about 100 BCE; it contains the earliest biography of Laozi.

docs.title: Book of Odes
docs.snippet: The oldest Chinese poetry anthology: 305 songs, about 1000–600 BCE.

docs.title: Liji
docs.snippet: The Record of Rites: Han compilation on ritual, mourning, family, and government.

docs.title: Huainanzi
docs.snippet: A Han encyclopaedia of Daoist-flavoured statecraft and cosmology, presented in 139 BCE.

docs.title: Guanzi / Neiye
docs.snippet: Neiye (“Inward Training”), a chapter of the Guanzi, is perhaps the oldest Chinese text on meditation and breath.

docs.title: Dao
docs.snippet: Literally a road or way; also “to speak” and “to lead.” The book's central, unnamable word.

docs.title: de
docs.snippet: The power or charisma that comes from being in accord with Dao — “virtue” in the old sense of a plant's virtue.

docs.title: wu wei
docs.snippet: Literally “no doing”: acting without forcing, so that things go of themselves.

docs.title: sage
docs.snippet: 聖人, the person of full attunement — in the Laozi usually a ruler.

docs.title: ten thousand things
docs.snippet: 萬物: everything that exists — all beings and things.

docs.title: Jicheng
docs.snippet: The 2014 complete edition of the Mawangdui silk and slip manuscripts, with new photographs and transcriptions.

docs.title: Zhao Mengfu
docs.snippet: Yuan-dynasty painter and calligrapher (1254–1322) who copied the whole Daodejing in small regular script in 1316.

docs.title: Wang Xizhi
docs.snippet: The “Sage of Calligraphy” (303–361 CE), master of running script.

docs.title: Miyamoto Musashi
docs.snippet: Japanese swordsman and painter (c. 1584–1645), author of the Book of Five Rings (五輪書).

docs.title: Dream of the Red Chamber
docs.snippet: Cao Xueqin's 18th-century novel, the greatest in Chinese, framed by a magic stone and Daoist and Buddhist wanderers.

text: 1 · dark, and darker still. a way that can be told as a way / is not the constant dao. / a name that can be given as a name / is not the constant name. / nameless: the beginning of heaven and earth. / named: the mother of the ten thousand things. / so: always without wanting, / to watch its fineness; / always with wanting, / to watch its edges. / these two come out together / and differ in name. / alike, call them dark. / dark, and darker still: / the gate of all fineness. four moves. first, two matched lines that turn on a pun: a way that can be told as a way is not the constant dao, and a name that can be named is not the constant name. second, two lines on origin: without name, a beginning; with name, a mother. third, two lines on looking: without wanting you watch the fine first stir of things, and with wanting you watch their borders. fourth, the knot is tied: the two come out of one place under two names, and the place is called 玄, the dark of deep dye. the last word is 門, a gate. two pairs of line-ends rhymed in the old language. nothing in the passage is abstract in chinese. it has a road, a mouth in the dark, a mother, a border patrol, a dye vat, and a door. the passage was not always the first page. the passage does not ask you to give up words or desire. it shows two modes of one mind and says they are twins. in one mode you name, want, and see edges; this mode lets you eat, build, and keep promises. in the other mode the wanting rests and the world shows its fine grain, before it divides into things for you. most contemplative schools rank the second above the first. this text does not: 同出, they come out together. the practice is not to stay in one mode. the practice is to know which mode you are in, and to feel the common source below both. when the text names that source “dark”, it removes the name at once. no higher world stands behind this one. there is this one, seen to the bottom. a leader works with names all day: roles, goals, plans, the story of what the team is. the passage does not say names are bad. it says no name is constant. the strategy document is a way that can be told; the living situation is not the document. a leader who forgets this defends the plan against the facts. the lines on wanting give a second tool. when you want a result, you see edges: deadlines, rivals, limits, who is in and who is out. that sight is necessary. but the first sign of change in a group or a market is often small and has no name yet, and a mind that wants nothing for a moment is the one that notices it. in the text’s own time, this was advice for people who ruled by names. later daoist practice reads the two looking-lines as instruction for sitting. 無欲: let the breath settle until the body stops reaching for the next thing; then watch the fine beginnings of breath, sensation, and thought. 有欲: when intention rises, watch where it goes and where it stops. the body knows this difference well. a hand that wants to grab feels the surface of a thing. a hand that only rests on a thing feels its weight, warmth, and pulse. martial arts teach the same: a fighter full of the wish to strike sees only the target and its edge, and misses the small shift of weight that comes before the opponent moves. wanting is of the belly and the breath before it is of the mind. stand at a river. you can name it, map it, and measure its banks; these are its edges. you cannot step into the name. the water you saw a moment ago is gone, and the river is still there: this is what 常 means, and why “eternal” is the wrong word for it. the world in this passage is not built by a maker. it has a beginning and a mother, so it is born and reared like a living thing. its source is dark as soil and deep water are dark: seeds open there. the older word for constancy in this line, 恆, was written with the moon, which keeps faith by changing each night. once today, look at one ordinary thing twice. first, name it and say to yourself what it is for: “cup, for coffee”. notice how quickly the name closes the looking. then look again for three slow breaths without the name and without a use for it. let color, weight, light, and small flaws come to you. you do not need to feel wonder. at the end, do not rank the two looks. the cup that holds coffee and the cup with no name came out together. if you like, read legge’s rhymed version of the looking-lines afterwards and see where he adds a “must”.

one word, three times in six. the first line has six characters, and three of them are 道. the first is a noun: a way, a road. the second is a verb. as a verb 道 can mean “to speak, to tell”; an old song in the book of odes says of palace gossip 不可道也, “it cannot be told”. it can also mean “to lead along a road” (the analects uses it for guiding a state). the third 道 is the noun again, now with 常 in front of it. so the line hears itself: a way that can be way-ed is not the constant way. english must pick “told” or “walked” or “followed”. the chinese picks nothing. the line also does what it describes: it names dao and, in the same breath, takes the name back. which verb did you hear first?

道: a head on a road. the shuowen jiezi, the first chinese dictionary (about 100 ce), defines 道 as 所行道也: “that on which one walks”. its parts are 辶, the sign for walking, and 首, a head. a common reading is a person who goes forward on a road; some see a leader, since the same word, written 導, means “to guide”. read such pictures lightly. the plain fact is enough: before 道 was a mystery it was a road, and a road exists because feet go over it. we leave dao in chinese because each english word is too small. “way” is closest. the chinese has no “the”, no capital letter, and no singular or plural; our second line adds the first two, because english cannot do without them.

constant is not “eternal”. 常 means regular, lasting, usual: a thing you can rely on, like the return of spring. english versions often say “eternal” or even “absolute”, with a capital. those words bring a second world with them: plato’s forms beyond change, or the god of the missionaries who stands outside time. the chinese word does not leave this world. it also does not say “unchanging”. a river is constant, and it is never the same water. note one more thing. in line 5 the same character comes back as a plain adverb, “always”: 常無欲. the text uses its great word for dao and for a daily habit in one breath. see the older word 恆 for what stood here before.

an emperor’s name in the first line. the mawangdui silk texts, buried in 168 bce and found in 1973, do not read 常 here. they read 恆 (heng): 非恆道也. the reason for the change is a taboo. the personal name of emperor wen of han (ruled 180–157 bce) was liu heng, 劉恆, and a subject could not write the ruler’s name. the silk texts were copied before the rule took full hold: text b already avoids 邦, the name of the first han emperor, and still writes 恆. scribes put 常 in its place, and the replacement stayed for two thousand years. the two words are close, but 恆 has its own picture. the shuowen says its ancient form contained the moon, and quotes the book of odes: 如月之恆, “like the moon’s steady waxing”. that is constancy as the moon has it: never still, and never late. the first line of this book about what cannot be named was itself changed because of a name.

an age that fought over names. this line entered a real quarrel. in the warring states period (5th–3rd century bce), names were politics. confucius said that government must start with 正名, “making names correct”: a ruler must be a ruler, a father a father. the debaters later called the school of names (名家) argued that “a white horse is not a horse”. the legalists built a method of rule on it: give each officer a title (名), then punish any gap between the title and the result. against all of this, the laozi says in six characters that no name holds for good. is that a withdrawal from politics, or the sharpest political statement in the debate?

名: a mouth in the dark. 名 is built from 夕, evening, and 口, a mouth. the shuowen explains: 夕者，冥也。冥不相見，故以口自名. “evening is darkness. in the dark people cannot see each other, so each one says a name with the mouth.” a name, in this picture, is what we call out when sight fails. it is useful, even kind. it is also proof that we stand in the dark. the same pattern as the first line returns: the noun 名, the verb 名, then 常名. keep this picture until the last lines of the passage, where the text itself gives a name, and the name it gives is dark.

where does the comma go?. classical chinese had no punctuation. each reader put in the pauses. the oldest commentators, wang bi among them, read 無名 and 有名 as units: “the nameless” and “the named”. some song dynasty readers, wang anshi and sima guang among them, cut after the first character: 無，名天地之始. then 名 becomes a verb, and the line says: “nothing names the beginning of heaven and earth. something names the ten thousand things’ mother.” in the first reading the subject is naming. in the second the subject is 無 and 有, not-having and having, the pair that the book returns to in passages 2, 11, and 40. the same cut is possible two lines later. english must choose. can you keep both in mind for one breath?

beginning and mother. two words for origin stand side by side, and both contain 女, woman. for 始, “beginning”, the shuowen says 女之初也, “the first of a woman”. for 母 it says the graph shows a woman who holds a child; “some say it shows the breasts”. the text has no father-creator and no craftsman who stands apart from the work. things are not made. they are born and then reared. wang bi keeps the two words apart: 始 is the first moment, before form; 母 is the long care after it. this mother returns in passages 20, 25, 52, and 59. what changes in your sense of the world if its origin is still here and still feeds it?

ten thousand things, twice. 萬物, “the ten thousand things”, is the usual chinese term for all that exists. 萬 is the largest common number; it means “too many to count”. the word 物 is a thing or a creature: an ox, a stone, a person, an event. note that there is no word “universe” here, no single container. the world is a crowd. the received text sets “heaven and earth” in the nameless line and “the ten thousand things” in the named line, and many readers built a two-step cosmology on the difference. the mawangdui silk texts read 萬物 in both lines: nameless, the beginning of the ten thousand things; named, their mother. in that version the same crowd is seen two ways, and there are no two stages.

wanting, in the body. 欲 is appetite. its parts are 欠, an open mouth that breathes out, and 谷, which gives the sound. it is the want of food, sex, gain, rank. modern versions that say “expectation” or “intention” move the word from the belly up into the head. the surprise is in the second half: 常有欲, “always with wanting”, is also a way to see. the text does not call it an error. as with the naming lines, a second cut is possible: 常無，欲以觀其妙, “in constant nothing, wish to watch its fineness”. the mawangdui silk texts add a particle that closes the question for their version: 恆無欲也, with the pause after 欲. sit for a moment. what do you see differently when you want nothing from that which is in front of you?

觀: to watch as a bird watches. 觀 is not a glance. the shuowen defines it as 諦視, “to look with full attention”. its parts are 見, to see, and 雚, a water bird (the stork), which mainly gives the sound; many readers also like the picture of a heron that stands in the shallows, still and awake. later the word named a watchtower, and then a daoist temple (guan): a place to look out from. try the two kinds of watching that the lines describe. take any object near you. first look at it as a thing you could use, buy, fix, or move; you will see its edges and its price. then let the wanting drop for three breaths and look again. do not decide which view is true.

wang bi on 妙. wang bi (226–249 ce) wrote his commentary before he was twenty-four. on this word he says: 妙者，微之極也。萬物始於微而後成，始於無而後生。 “妙 is the far limit of the minute. the ten thousand things begin in the minute and then are completed; they begin in nothing and then are born.” so 妙 is not “mystery” in the sense of a locked room. it is fineness: the first stir of a thing, too small to hold. the mawangdui silk texts write the word as 眇, with the eye radical: so small that the eye strains. the later graph 妙 is written with 女 (woman) and 少 (few, young). english “wonder” keeps the feeling and loses the smallness. “subtle” keeps the smallness and loses the delight.

徼: the patrolled border. 徼 (jiao) is a rare word and readers have never agreed on it. the shuowen glosses it 循也, “to go along, to patrol”. from that comes the sense “frontier”: the line that guards walk. wang bi takes it as 歸終, “the return and the end”: where a thing arrives when it is complete. so desire sees outlines, limits, results. other scholars have proposed that the graph stands for 皦, “bright, clear”, or 竅, “an opening”. the mawangdui silk texts read 其所噭, which is also disputed. our “edges” follows the frontier sense that grew from the shuowen’s “patrol”. wang bi’s comment on this line already quotes the thought of passage 11: 凡有之為利，必以無為用, “whatever gain there is in having, it must take not-having as its use”. note the fit with a state at war: a ruler who wants something looks at the map and sees borders. what do you see first in a room: the things, or the lines between them?

which two?. 此兩者, “these two”. the text does not say which. wang bi answers 兩者，始與母也: beginning and mother. others say the nameless and the named; or 無 and 有; or the fineness and the edges; or the two ways of watching. each answer is defensible, and the sentence works for all of them. the important words are 同出, “come out together”. 出 is to step out of a door, to be born. the pair is not a high thing and a low thing, or a real thing and an illusion. they are twins with two names. this is the line that resists a dualistic reading most plainly. dualism wants one side to win. here the text gives both sides one source, and then gives that source a name that is almost not a name.

玄: the dyer’s dark. the shuowen defines 玄 as 幽遠也, “hidden and far”, and then gives a color: 黑而有赤色者為玄, “black with red in it is called 玄”. it is the color that cloth takes when it goes into the dye vat again and again, and the color of the sky before dawn. the dark here is depth. it is not evil, and it is not ignorance; the western pair of light as good and dark as bad does not apply. english versions say “mystery” or “profound” and lose the color. later the word named a whole movement: 玄學, “dark learning”, the philosophy of wang bi’s generation. look at a night sky or deep water. is the dark there empty?

why say it twice. the text has just named the unnameable: it called the source “dark”. wang bi sees the trap and reads the next phrase as the escape: 若定乎一玄，則是名則失之遠矣。故曰玄之又玄也。 “if you settled on one ‘dark’, that would be a name, and you would miss it by far. so the text says: dark, and again dark.” the second 玄 removes the first. the phrase is a method, and tang dynasty daoists made it one. they called their school 重玄, “twofold dark”: first let go of having and not-having, then let go of the letting go. grammar helps the reading: 玄之 can be heard as a verb, “to darken it”. darken it, and darken it again.

門: two leaves that swing. 門 is a picture that you can still see: two door leaves on their posts. the shuowen says 从二戶，象形, “from two door leaves; a picture”. the passage ends at a gate, and it does not end with a definition. a gate is the one part of a wall that is not wall. it is useful because it is empty, as passage 11 will say of doors and windows. a gate also works in two directions: things come out, and you may go in. this is the first gate in the book. others follow: the gate of the dark female (6), the gates of heaven that open and close (10), the gates you are told to shut (52, 56). is the gate at the end of the passage, or was the whole passage the gate?

legge’s victorian door. james legge was a scottish missionary in hong kong and later the first professor of chinese at oxford. his 1891 version is honest work, and you can see its frame. he gives 常 two words, “enduring and unchanging”, the usual attributes of god in a sermon. he adds “(conceived of as)” in brackets before the nameless and the named: a careful scholar’s sign that the english needs more than the chinese gives. he puts the desire lines in rhyme, with “we must be found” without desire. that turns a description of two ways to see into a moral duty, and makes desire the thing that keeps us at the “outer fringe”. his “mystery” has a capital m. compare his text with the characters. where does the chinese say “must”?

not always page one. we read this passage as the grand opening. for early readers it was not always the opening. the oldest long commentary, in the han feizi (3rd century bce), starts with what is now passage 38. both mawangdui silk texts do the same: the part on 德 comes first, and this passage stands in the middle of the book, at the start of the second part. the guodian bamboo slips (about 300 bce), the oldest laozi material found so far, do not contain this passage at all. the order that we know, with dao before de, was fixed by the han. so the famous first line may have been met first as a turn in the middle of a roll. does the passage read differently as a hinge and not as a front door?

rhymes you cannot hear now. the passage was made to be heard. in the sound system that scholars reconstruct for old chinese, 始 (beginning) and 母 (mother) end in the same rhyme, the group that the tradition calls 之. so do 妙 (fineness) and 徼 (edges), in the group called 宵. each pair of opposed ideas is tied by sound: the beginning with its mother, the fine with the border. modern mandarin has lost the first rhyme (shi, mu) and kept the second (miao, jiao). much of the laozi is rhymed in this way, and rhyme was one means to hold a text in memory before it was fixed in writing. when two words rhyme, the ear takes them as a pair before the mind decides how they differ. say miao and jiao aloud. do the two kinds of watching sound like enemies?

無 and 有: twins, not rivals. the passage is built on one pair in three forms: 無名 and 有名, 無欲 and 有欲, 妙 and 徼. nameless and named. without wanting and with wanting. the fine stir and the edge. each time the text gives both sides a task. the nameless is a beginning; the named is a mother. without wanting, one watches fineness; with wanting, one watches edges. then it says 同出: these two come out together. a one-sided reading makes the nameless the true world and the named a fall from it, and then makes wanting the enemy. the characters do not rank them. 常 stands before both kinds of watching. a person who saw no edges could not cross a road. passage 2 says it in four words: 有無相生, having and not-having give birth to each other. which of the two ways of watching do you trust less?

a thing that can be named is not the constant thing; every name leaves something out.. a thing that can be named is not the constant thing; every name leaves something out. is that true in your experience? think of one thing you know well that no word for it has caught. where did you learn to trust names: at school, at work, from a parent who wanted things said clearly? or where did you learn to distrust them? take the other side for a while: an exact name is a gift, and what cannot be said clearly is not yet known. what do you notice in yourself when you hold that? which person do you judge more: the one who defines everything, or the one who says it cannot be put in words? what might that judgment show you?

seeing without wanting and seeing with wanting come from one source, and neither is the false one.. seeing without wanting and seeing with wanting come from one source, and neither is the false one. do you agree, or do you hold one of the two to be the real seeing? recall a time when wanting something made you see it more exactly. recall a time when wanting made you blind. which memory comes faster? suppose the opposite: desire spoils sight, and a mind must be free of wanting before it sees truly. stay with that for some breaths. what in you is relieved, and what objects? if you were taught that wanting is a fault, who taught you? if you were taught that wanting is the engine of a life, who taught you that? what would change in one ordinary day if you ranked neither?

玄 the dyer’s dark. start with the colour. the shuowen says 黑而有赤色者為玄: black with red in it. dyers got that colour by many dips in the vat, and the lower part of the character, 幺, is commonly explained as a small twist of silk thread; the same shape, doubled and given a tail, makes 糸, the silk radical in 紅 (red), 綠 (green), and 紛 (tangle). the early bronze forms look like such a twist, though scholars do not all agree on what they show. above the thread the shuowen sees a cover: a thing hidden. so the parts say “thread” and “covered”, and the word says dark, deep, far. now look at its family. two of them side by side make 玆, “black” in the shuowen; a look-alike with grass above, 茲, was borrowed for “this, here”. add 弓, a bow, and you get 弦, a bowstring or the string of an instrument: the thread sense is plain there. add 目, an eye, and you get 眩, dizzy: the eye goes dark. the shuowen, with a quotation from the huainanzi, even reads 畜, to rear animals, as 玄 over 田, a field; modern scholars doubt this. the laozi uses 玄 for the one source of having and not-having. the word is a colour before it is an idea. can you think of the idea and still see the colour? five strokes. watch the first two: a dot, then a level line under it. that is the lid, and a good hand sets the dot right over the centre so that the whole character hangs from it. strokes three and four are each one movement with a turn in it: down to the left, then a sharp return to the right. the brush presses, lifts at the corner, and presses again; together they make the twist of thread. the fifth stroke is a single dot at the lower right that stops the character from falling over. that dot has a history. the kangxi emperor’s personal name was 玄燁, and for the rest of the qing dynasty printers and writers left the last dot out, or wrote 元 in place of the character. a book can be dated by it.

道 a head on the road. two parts. on the right and above is 首, a head: it is one picture of a head. the shuowen says the top strokes show hair; the lower part, now written 自, is the face. 首 also means “first” and “chief”. around the left and bottom is 辶, the walking sign. in its full old form, 辵, it joins 彳, half of the crossroads 行, with 止, a foot: movement on a road. you meet it in 進 (advance), 退 (withdraw), 遠 (far), 近 (near), 通 (go through), 迷 (go astray). so 道 is a head that goes along a road, as the shuowen says: 所行道也, “that on which one walks”. some bronze forms set the head inside a full crossroads, 行, with a foot or a hand; scholars read them in more than one way, so take the “leader” story lightly. see how the meaning grew. first a road. then a way to do a thing, a craft’s method. then to lead someone along (later written with a hand added below: 導, to guide). then to speak, to lay a matter out. last, the course of everything that is. the first line of the book uses two of these senses against each other. trace the character with a finger: the head must be finished before the road is drawn. which of the two carries the other? twelve strokes. watch the order: the head 首 is written first, complete, and the walking sign comes last, although it sits on the left. the road is laid under a traveller who is already there. in the head, the two small opening strokes lean toward each other; then a long horizontal; then a short tick down to the left; then the narrow box with its inner lines evenly spaced. the walking sign begins with a dot, bends, and ends in the long final stroke that runs under the whole character. calligraphers call this a level 捺 and give it “one wave, three bends”: press in, travel, press harder, release to a point. it is the boat that the head rides in. zhao mengfu wrote the whole book in small regular script in 1316, and the story goes that wang xizhi once copied it out for a daoist priest in return for a flock of geese.

名 a mouth at dusk. above is 夕, evening. 夕 began as the same picture as 月, the moon: a crescent. the two graphs were later kept apart by one stroke, so that 夕 is a moon that has only just risen. below is 口, a mouth; a plain square now, a curved open mouth in the oldest writing. the oracle-bone form of 名 already has these two parts. the shuowen tells the story: 冥不相見，故以口自名, “in the dark people cannot see each other, so each says a name with the mouth”. not all modern scholars accept this as the origin, but no one has given a better picture. look at the cousins of each part. with 夕: 夜 (night), 外 (outside; commonly explained by divination done at evening), 多 (many: written as two 夕, as the shuowen says, though the oracle-bone forms are commonly read as two pieces of meat), 夢 (dream, with 夕 at the foot). with 口: 言 (speech), 告 (announce), 問 (ask: a mouth in a gate), 命 (command). 名 and 命 were close in sound and sense: the shuowen defines 名 as 自命, “to command oneself”, to give oneself a call. in modern mandarin 名 also sounds the same as 明, bright. in the old language the two did not rhyme, so this is only a lucky accident. a name, then, is a small light for the dark. and the dark itself, 玄, is the name that the passage gives at its end. six strokes, three and three. 夕 first: a short falling stroke to the left; then a longer stroke that goes right, turns, and sweeps down to the left in one movement; then a dot inside, the stroke that keeps evening apart from the moon. 口 next: left side down; then top and right side in a single stroke with a corner; then the base, which closes the box. watch the corner in the fifth stroke: the brush stops, sets its shoulder, and comes down. the art is in the fit. the long sweep of 夕 needs room at the lower left, so the mouth sits a little to the right and takes the weight. in running script the dot and the mouth often join in one loop, and you can still read it.

2 · each makes the other. all under heaven know the beautiful as beautiful: / there, already, is the ugly. / all know the good as good: / there, already, is the not-good. / so having and not-having give birth to each other, / hard and easy complete each other, / long and short measure each other, / high and low lean toward each other, / tune and sound answer each other, / before and after follow each other. / for this reason the sage / stays in the work of not-forcing / and walks the teaching without words. / the ten thousand things rise, and are not refused. / giving life, not owning; / acting, not leaning on it; / the work done, not dwelling in it. / only by not dwelling in it / does it not leave. the passage has two halves joined by 是以, “for this reason”. the first half is about knowing. when a whole realm knows the beautiful as beautiful, the ugly is there already; the same holds for good and not-good. then come six pairs, each with its own verb: having and not-having give birth, hard and easy complete, long and short measure, high and low lean, tune and sound answer, before and after follow. the second half is about conduct. the sage stays in work that is not forced and practices a teaching without words. things rise and are not refused. then three short refusals: not owning, not leaning, not dwelling. the close is a rhyme of stay and leave. the first half describes how the mind makes a world. before a judgment there is a face, a sound, a day. with “beautiful”, a line is drawn, and the other side of the line appears at the same instant. wang bi says the two sides have one root. a contemplative reader can test this directly. watch a liking arise, and see that a disliking came with it, as the back of a hand comes with the palm. the passage does not tell you to stop judging. that would be one more judgment: “judging is bad”. it shows a person who works among the pairs and does not move into either side. things rise and are not refused. this is non-preference, and it is not cold. it is the condition for meeting each thing as it is. what a leader names as excellent, the group learns to see as a ladder, and each ladder has a bottom. praise one kind of person in public and you have also made a second kind. the passage does not say to have no standards. it asks you to see what your standards make. the second half is a way to work. stay in the work and do not force it. teach by conduct, since people copy what you do. let people and projects rise, and do not claim that you began them. do the job and do not lean on it afterwards as a debt that others owe you. the first readers knew the risk of merit at a court. the text gives a fact, and it does not give a tactic: what you do not occupy does not leave. a body knows the six pairs without thought. a step forward needs a foot that stays back. a breath in is the shape of the breath out. in push-hands and in dance, hard and soft complete each other: a partner feels heavy only against your lightness. try the last lines in a movement you know well: a lift, a stroke, a stretch. do it, and at the end do not hold the finish. the habit is to sit down in the end position, to show it or to feel it. let it pass into the next movement. teachers of movement know the wordless teaching well. a student takes the teacher’s rhythm from the teacher’s body long before the explanation is understood. a hillside is one thing. people stand on it and say “high” and “low”, and the two words lean toward each other, as the slope does. a valley is the low part of a mountain, and the mountain is the high part of a valley. nothing in the land takes a side. spring does not announce its work, and the passage borrows that manner: the ten thousand things rise, and no one makes a speech. a tree gives life to fruit and does not own it. a river carves a canyon and does not stay to look. heaven, said confucius, does not talk; the seasons run. the sage of this passage acts as that pattern acts: work goes on, and no owner stands beside it. try the one “as” exercise today. or take the last lines alone. choose one piece of work that you will finish this week. decide before you start that you will not mention it afterwards and will not look for who noticed. then do it as well as you can. this is harder than it sounds, and the difficulty is the lesson: you will feel the wish to lean on the finished thing. you do not need to fight that wish. watch it rise, and let it be not refused and not obeyed. after a week, ask the passage’s question. did the work leave?

天下: all under heaven. 天下 is “under heaven”. it is not “the world” as a globe, and it is not “the universe”. it is a political word: the whole civilized realm that the zhou king once held under heaven’s mandate. by the fourth century bce that realm was in pieces. seven large states fought for it, and each court had its own experts who told the ruler what was fine and what was right. so the first line is not a remark about private taste. it describes a public event: a whole realm agrees on a standard. standards of this kind came from courts, in dress, in music, in conduct, and people were ranked by them. read the line again with a court in mind. who gains when all under heaven know what beauty is?

to know a thing “as”. the grammar is 知美之為美: “know the beautiful’s being-beautiful”. the weight is on 知, to know, and on 為, to count as. the line does not say that beauty causes ugliness, as one pole of a magnet needs the other. it says that an act of mind does it: when everyone knows beauty as beauty, the ugly is already there. 斯 means “at that point”. 已 means “done, already”, and some read it as only a final particle. english must give the sentence a verb, and each choice is a theory: “is”, “arises”, “becomes”. we write “there, already, is”, and add nothing more. legge put “(the idea of)” in brackets four times. is the ugly thing made at that moment, or only its name?

美: a fat sheep. 美 is 羊, a sheep, over 大, big. the shuowen defines it with a word of the mouth: 甘也, “sweet, good to taste”. it explains: 羊在六畜主給膳也, “among the six farm animals the sheep is the chief one for the table”. so the first chinese “beautiful” was a taste before it was a sight. greek and latin words for beauty mostly belong to the eye and to form. this one belongs to the offering table and the feast. the shuowen then adds a sentence that fits this passage: 美與善同意, “美 and 善 share one idea”. the good also has a sheep in it. the two words that open the passage are a pair in the script itself. see the first plate for the brushwork.

惡: ugly, not “evil”. 惡 has two readings. as e it is the opposite of 美: ugly, foul, coarse, bad in quality. as wu it is a verb: to hate, to find repulsive. the shuowen says only 過也, “a fault, a going too far”, from 心, the heart. english “evil” brings a different world: a force against god, a stain on the soul. nothing in this line has that weight. the pair is closer to “fine and foul”. note also that the two readings are one thought. the ugly is what people hate. wang bi uses the character both ways in a single sentence. the second pair is plainer still: 善 and 不善, “good” and “not good”. the text does not use a separate word for the bad. why might that be?

善: the sheep again. the old form of 善 is 譱: a sheep, 羊, between two 言, “speech”. the shuowen defines it as 吉也, “lucky, auspicious”, and says: 此與義美同意, “this shares one idea with 義 and 美”. all three carry the sheep: 美 beauty, 善 the good, 義 right conduct. the sheep was the animal of the offering, and the shuowen glosses 羊 itself as 祥, “good omen”. 善 is not only moral. it also means “good at”: skilled, fit for the task. passage 8 uses it nine times in that way. legge took the skill sense here and wrote “the skill of the skilful”. most readers take the moral sense, as a partner to beauty. english must choose. the chinese holds worth, luck, and skill in one word.

wang bi: one root, one gate. wang bi comments: 美者，人心之所進樂也；惡者，人心之所惡疾也。 “the beautiful is what the human heart moves toward and enjoys. the ugly is what the human heart hates and is sick of.” he does not put beauty in the object. he puts it in the heart’s movement. then: 喜怒同根，是非同門，故不可得偏舉也。 “delight and anger have one root. right and wrong have one gate. so you cannot lift up one side alone.” the picture is physical: two branches on one root, two leaves of one gate. pull at one and the other moves. on the sage’s work he adds five characters: 自然已足，為則敗也, “what is so of itself is already enough; work at it and you ruin it.”

有無: having and not-having. 有無 is a set pair in this book: what is there and what is not there. passage 11 shows it with a wheel, a pot, and a room. philosophy in english says “being and non-being”, words from greek ontology that sound like two great abstract realms. 有 is first “to have”, and 無 “to not have”. a poor family 無; a full barn 有. here the two 相生, “give birth to each other”. passage 40 seems to disagree: 有生於無, “having is born from not-having”, one direction only. the two lines do different work. passage 40 tells an order of origin. this line stands in a list about how people know things in pairs. in that list, neither comes first: a person learns “there is” and “there is not” together.

six pairs, six different verbs. the six lines are often read as one law of “opposites”. look at the verbs. having and not-having 生, give birth. hard and easy 成, complete, as a task is hard only beside an easy one. long and short measure or shape. high and low lean. tune and sound 和, answer in song. before and after 隨, follow, like people on a road. birth, craft, measure, slope, music, walking: six relations from six parts of life. the lines also rhyme. in the old rhyme groups, 生, 成, and 傾 belong to one group (耕), and 和 and 隨 to another (歌). so the list was made to be said aloud and remembered. one word breaks the first rhyme, and the silk texts are reported to repair it.

較 or 形: measure or shape. the pinned text has 長短相較, “long and short compare with each other”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 長短之相形也, “long and short give each other shape”; the graph on the silk is 刑, a loan for 形. many scholars think that 形 is the older word, for two reasons. it rhymes with 生 and 成 (the 耕 rhyme group), and 較 does not. and legge’s english fits it: his line says that the two “fashion out the one the figure of the other”. 形 is a strong word. it says that “long” has no outline until something short stands beside it. they are also reported to end the list with two characters that the received text lacks: 恆也, “this is constant”. the six pairs are then called a lasting pattern, with the word that passage 1 uses for the lasting dao.

傾 or 盈: lean or fill. 高下相傾: high and low “lean” toward each other, as a slope is one thing with a top and a foot. the shuowen defines 傾 as 仄也, “slanted”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 盈, “to fill”: high and low fill each other, as water runs from the high place and fills the low one. a common explanation of the change is a taboo. the personal name of the second han emperor was liu ying, 劉盈, and scribes of the han avoided his character. the same custom removed 恆 (the name of emperor wen) from many texts and put 常 in its place. so a ruler’s name may have changed a line about high and low. we keep 傾, the pinned text. both pictures are of one hillside.
