音 and 聲: two kinds of sound. english has one pair here with no clear line between its halves: “sound and voice”, “note and tone”. the chinese pair is exact. 聲 is sound as it comes: a cry, a struck stone, a voice. 音 is sound with order in it. the shuowen says of 音: 生於心，有節於外，謂之音, “born in the heart, given measure outside: this is called 音”. the record of music in the liji says the same in four words: 聲成文謂之音, “sound that forms a pattern is called 音”. the verb is 和, read he: to answer a singer, to join in. so the line pictures raw sound and shaped music in a call and response. neither is the better one. a tune is made of sounds, and a sound is heard as high or low only inside a tune.

聖人: the one who hears. this is the first 聖人 in the book. we write “the sage”, and the word needs a warning. it is not a saint: no church, no miracles, no life after death. it is not only a wise person with good sayings. the character 聖 has an ear, 耳, and a mouth, 口; the part below them is commonly explained as a standing person. the shuowen defines it as 通也: “to pass through, to be open all the way”. a 聖人 is a person through whom things pass with no block: one who hears well, and whose speech and conduct then fit. in this period the word also had a political sense. the 聖人 were the ancient kings who set the world in order. so the sentence is partly about rule. the chinese has no “he” and no “she”.

無為: the first not-forcing. 無為 appears here for the first time. word for word it is “without doing”. it is not laziness, and it is not a rule to sit still. the line itself blocks that reading: the sage 處…事, “takes a place in work”. there is work, 事, and the sage stays in it. what is absent is 為 in the strong sense: to make a thing be what it is not, to push a result, to act for show. wang bi gives the reason: things are already enough as they are. english has no single verb for this. “non-action” sounds like a strike. “effortless action” sounds like a sales promise. we write “not-forcing” and leave the question open. think of a task you do best when you stop pushing it. what stops, and what goes on?

a teaching with no words. 不言之教 comes again in passage 43, where the text says that few under heaven reach it. the age was full of talk. persuaders went from court to court and lived by argument. against that noise, more than one school pointed to silence. confucius says in the analects: 天何言哉, “does heaven speak? the four seasons run, the hundred things are born. does heaven speak?” the word 教 helps too. the shuowen defines it: 上所施下所效也, “what those above give out and those below copy”. teaching in early china was first a model that people copied. it was not first a lecture. so a teaching without words is not a riddle. it is the common case: children copy what parents do. what do the people near you learn from what you do not say?

不辭 or 弗始: refuse, speak, or begin. 萬物作焉而不辭. 作 is “to rise, to stir”: the shuowen says 起也, “to get up”. 辭 has two common senses. one is “to decline, to turn away”. then the line says that the sage refuses none of the things that rise; our rendering takes this sense, and our english passive hides who does the refusing. the other sense is “words”: things rise and the sage makes no speech about it, which fits the wordless teaching one line before. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to have a third reading: 萬物作而弗始, “the ten thousand things rise, and (the sage) does not begin them”. 辭 and 始 were near in sound, in one old rhyme group (之). they are also reported to lack the clause 生而不有 at this place. silk a is damaged here, and the reading rests on silk b. all three readings agree on one point. the things rise by themselves.

恃: a heart that leans. 恃 is 忄, the heart, beside 寺, which gives the sound. the shuowen defines it in one word: 賴也, “to depend on, to lean on”. some translations make this a line about hope: to act and expect nothing back. the chinese has a different picture. to 恃 a thing is to put your weight on it: a general 恃 his walls, a minister 恃 the ruler’s favor, and a person 恃 a past success. the line says: do the work, and do not then stand on it. do not use the finished act as a prop, a claim, or a right. the danger in 恃 is not hope for a reward later. it is the weight you put now on what you did before. on what past act do you lean most?

功: merit that a court counts. 功 is not any work. the shuowen defines it: 以勞定國也, “to settle the state by toil”. it is merit: service that a ruler records and pays for. in the warring states this was a new and sharp system. old noble families lost ground, and men rose by counted merit. the state of qin, under shang yang, gave ranks for enemy heads taken in battle. a minister with great 功 was also a danger to his lord, and many such ministers were killed after their success. so 功成而弗居 had a plain sense for its first readers: when the merit is complete, do not settle in it. passage 9 says it again: the work is done, the person steps back. the text does not say that modesty will be rewarded.

居 and 去: stay and leave. 夫唯弗居，是以不去. the last two lines end on 居 and 去. 居 now means “to dwell”. the shuowen gives an older and plainer sense: 蹲也, “to squat”, to get down on the heels and stay. 去 is “to leave”. the two words are opposites, and they rhyme: both belong to the old 魚 rhyme group, and in mandarin they are still ju and qu. the negatives differ too. 弗 is commonly explained as 不 with an object inside it: “does not dwell in it”. then 不去: “it does not leave”. what is the “it”? most readers say the 功, the merit. a thing you never sat down in cannot be taken from you. wang bi says: 使功在己，則功不可久也, “make the merit sit in yourself, and the merit cannot last”. some modern readers make this a method to keep credit. the text states a fact about holding. it makes no promise.

legge’s brackets. legge read the first half as a theory of ideas, and he showed his hand honestly. he put “(the idea of)” in brackets four times: people have “(the idea of) what ugliness is”; existence and non-existence give birth to “(the idea of)” each other. the brackets are his own words, and he marks them. his reading is fair to 知, to know. but it makes the passage safe. if only ideas are at stake, the world stays in order and only the mind is confused. the chinese does not separate the two so cleanly. legge also gave the sage a “his”, made the wordless teaching “his instructions”, and turned the last two lines into a rhymed english couplet about “power”. the chinese has no word for power there.

catch one “as”. today, catch one moment when you know a thing as good or as fine: a face, a piece of work, a plan, your own conduct. do not stop the judgment. look to its other side. what did that judgment just make less fine? who became plain when one person became beautiful? then try the second half of the passage with one small job. do it well. when it is done, say nothing about it and do not check who saw. later in the day, ask if the work has left you. the passage says that it does not.

相: pairs that make each other. this passage is the book’s plainest statement of how opposites work. the word 相, “each other”, stands in all six lines. neither side comes first. long is long beside short. a step is “before” because another step is “after”. the opening lines apply this to value: when all know 美 as 美, 惡 is there too. a one-sided reading takes this as a warning against beauty and goodness, or as a claim that nothing is better than anything. the text says neither. it says that a judgment has two ends, and that a person who picks up one end picks up the other. the sage’s conduct follows from this: 弗居, do not dwell at either end, because each end turns. passage 58 gives the turn: 正復為奇，善復為妖, the straight becomes the crooked again, and the good becomes the ominous again. where did one of your own “goods” turn?

when everyone knows the beautiful as beautiful, the ugly is already there; one judgment makes both.. when everyone knows the beautiful as beautiful, the ugly is already there; one judgment makes both. does this match what you have seen? name one standard of beauty or goodness in your world, and say what it pushed to the other side. which side of such a line were you placed on when you were young? how does that place still shape what you praise? hold the other view for a minute: some things are simply good, and to see them as good harms no one. what rises in you: ease, doubt, anger? what do you call ugly or not-good in others with the most force? could it be the back of something you need to be seen as?

hard and easy, high and low, before and after make each other; neither side stands alone.. hard and easy, high and low, before and after make each other; neither side stands alone. test it on one thing you call hard. hard beside what? hard for whom? think of a low time in your life that later held up a high one. did you see it then, or afterwards? now take the opposite: some things are hard in themselves, some people are ahead in fact, and the comparison adds nothing. how does that feel to hold? which comfort do you lean on more: that all is relative, or that there are fixed measures? what does each one protect you from?

work that is done and not claimed does not leave the one who did it.. work that is done and not claimed does not leave the one who did it. do you believe it? or has unclaimed work of yours simply gone to someone else? where does your need for credit come from? think of the first time you were passed over, or the first time you were praised. try the other side: say what you did and stand in it, or it will be lost. hold that fully. what thoughts and feelings come with it? both views can be lived. which one have you lived, and what has it cost?

美 the big sheep. cover the lower half with a finger. what remains is 羊, a sheep, with its tail cut short. the shuowen calls 羊 a picture: 象頭角足尾之形, “it shows head, horns, feet, and tail”. the two small strokes at the top are the horns. now cover the top half. the lower part is 大, “big”, and 大 is a person seen from the front with arms and legs spread; the shuowen says 大象人形, “大 shows the human form”. the shuowen joins the parts in a cook’s way: a big sheep is 甘, sweet in the mouth, because the sheep is the first animal for the table. many modern scholars explain the oldest forms in another way, as a person who wears a headdress of horns or plumes; the question is open. both explanations keep beauty close to the feast and the rite. now look for the sheep’s cousins. 善, the good, was once written 譱, a sheep between two words. 義, right conduct, is a sheep over 我. 祥, good omen, is a sheep beside an altar, and 養, to feed and raise, is a sheep over food; in 養 the shuowen takes the sheep as the sound (从食羊聲), and it says the same of 祥 (从示，羊聲). in a culture of herds and offerings, the sheep carried what was good. english “beautiful” goes to the eye. 美 goes first to the tongue, and passage 12 will warn about the five flavors. nine strokes. first the horns: a dot that falls to the right, then a short stroke that falls to the left; they lean toward each other. then a horizontal, a second horizontal, and the vertical that runs down through both. then a third horizontal. watch this sixth stroke: it is the longest line in the character, and the others are measured against it. then the top line of 大, a little shorter. stroke eight sweeps down to the left and thins to a point. stroke nine, the 捺, travels down to the right, presses, and lifts. these last two strokes open like a robe and carry the four level lines above them. four horizontals in a stack are a test: the white bands between them must be even, and no two lines the same length. in clerical script only one stroke in a character may have the flared “goose tail”.

教 teaching has no mouth. look for a mouth in this character. there is none: no 口, no 言. on the right is 攵, the side form of 攴. the shuowen defines 攴 as 小擊也, “to strike lightly”, and its old form is a hand, 又, that holds a rod. on the left, the modern shape is the same as 孝, “care for parents”, an old person carried on a child, 子, and the shuowen reads it so: 从攴从孝. many modern scholars read the early forms in another way: crossed marks, 爻, above a child, the same parts that stand inside 學, “to learn”. then the whole is a child, something to copy, and a hand with a rod. the shuowen’s definition says nothing of talk: 上所施下所效也, “what those above give out and those below copy”. now look at the family of the rod-hand. 牧, to herd: an ox and the rod; the shuowen says 養牛人也, “one who raises cattle”. 政, to govern: 正, “straight”, and the rod. 攻, to attack. 效, to copy. herding, ruling, attacking, and teaching share one hand. that is the usual teaching of the age, and this passage asks for another kind: 不言之教, a teaching with no words. read the character once more. words were not in it. the sage also puts down the rod. eleven strokes, left part first. a short horizontal, a vertical through it, and a longer horizontal below: the same start as 土. stroke four is the surprise: a long diagonal that falls from the upper right, crosses the vertical, and runs far to the lower left. it ties the top to the child below. then 子 in three strokes: a short horizontal that turns back, the curved vertical with its hook, and a last stroke that rises to the right. a horizontal would stop the eye; a rising stroke hands the eye to the right part. then 攵: a falling stroke, a short horizontal, a long stroke that falls to the left, and last the 捺 to the lower right. watch that last stroke cross the one before it. the right part must not push the left; the writer makes the left narrow and tall, so that the rod-hand has room to swing.

3 · empty heart, full belly. not exalting the worthy / keeps the people from contending. / not prizing goods hard to get / keeps the people from turning thief. / not showing what can be desired / keeps the people’s heart from disorder. / for this reason, the sage’s way of ordering: / empty the heart, fill the belly, / weaken the will, strengthen the bones. / always keep the people without knowing, without wanting. / keep the clever ones from daring to act. / act by not-forcing, / and nothing is left unordered. three causes come first, each with the same shape: a thing not done above, and a trouble that does not arise below. no exalting of the worthy, and no contending. no prizing of rare goods, and no thieves. no showing of the desirable, and no disorder in the heart. then the sage’s way of ordering, in four body words: heart, belly, will, bones. two are emptied or weakened, and two are filled or made strong. then two hard lines about knowing and about those who know. the close is three characters, 為無為, and a double negative. the verb 使, “to cause, to keep”, appears five times. the passage is about what causes what in a state. read with 其 as one’s own, the passage is a map of attention. the first stanza names three movements that pull a person out of place: comparing oneself with those who are ranked higher, wanting what is rare, and looking at what stirs desire. the second stanza gives the correction as a shift of weight inside the body. attention leaves the planning heart and the reaching will, and settles in the belly and the bones, which do not scheme. this is not a rejection of thought. it is a change of the place from which a person lives. “without knowing, without wanting” then describes a moment that everyone has had: full, quiet, and with no opinion. the clever one inside does not dare to start. order is what remains. what the top prizes, the whole house fights for. a leader who makes heroes makes rivals in the same act. a leader who displays rewards also teaches people to watch the rewards and not the work. the passage puts the cause of contention and theft at the top; it does not put it in bad character below. wang bi keeps this practical: give the task to the able person, and do not add glory larger than the task. the second half is harder, and a leader should read it with care. “keep them without knowing” was used by states to keep people small, and that history is real. the better test is to apply the four lines to oneself first. a leader with a quiet heart and a soft will stirs less. that may be the whole method. the stanza is a posture. every internal art in china teaches some form of it: the chest empty, the belly full; intention light, structure strong. if the upper body is full of effort and the will is tight, the breath is high and the stance is easy to topple. let the heart area soften and the breath drop, and the belly fills by itself. then the bones carry the weight, and the muscles do less. try it now, seated: release the chest, breathe low, feel the sitting bones and the spine hold you. the shuowen calls bone the kernel of the flesh. a body that rests on its kernel has no need for a tense will. that is a small case of acting by not-forcing. a forest has no prizes. no tree is set above the others by an authority, and so there is no race that all must run; each grows toward the light that it has. animals take what the belly needs, and the belly has a limit. stores of rare goods are a human thing, and where they pile up, guards and thieves appear together. the word for order in this passage is written with water, and the old model for order was a river given its channel. water in a good channel needs no command. the first stanza says: do not build the dams of rank, rarity, and display. the last says: then things settle, as silt settles in still water. 亂, the tangle, and the untangling were once one word. try the one-day practice with the four body lines. or work with the first stanza for a week. notice each time you rank a person as above or below you in worth: that is 尚賢 in small form. notice each time you want a thing mostly because it is hard to get. notice what you put on show, and for whom. do not correct anything. at the end of the week, ask what in your life has the structure of this passage: a prize set up, hands that pull, and a heart in a tangle.

尚賢: a slogan of the mohists. 尚賢, “exalt the worthy”, was a party slogan. three chapters of the mozi have it as their title. mozi (fifth century bce) attacked rule by noble birth and asked rulers to raise able men from any class: 有能則舉之, “if a man has ability, raise him”. confucians asked for nearly the same; the analects says 舉賢才, “raise the worthy and able”. rulers listened, because states that hired talent won wars. courts competed for advisers, and able men went from state to state and sold their plans. so the first three characters of this passage reject the main reform idea of the age. wang bi softens the point: use the able, he says, but why glorify them? the first plate shows what was inside the word 賢.

爭: two hands, one thing. the shuowen defines 爭 in one word: 引也, “to pull”. the graph is commonly explained as two hands that pull at one object from opposite sides. that is the whole idea of contention in this book: one prize, two hands. the sentence gives the cause. a court sets one kind of person above the rest, the prize now exists, and hands reach for it. passage 2 said the same of beauty and the good: to name the high thing is to make the low one. the word returns often. water does not 爭 (passage 8). the sage does not 爭, and so no one under heaven can 爭 with the sage (passages 22 and 66). the last line of the whole book ends on it: 為而不爭, to act and not contend.

goods hard to get. 難得之貨: goods that are hard to obtain. in the warring states these were jade, pearls, rhinoceros horn, fine bronzes, and horses from the steppe: things from far away that courts used to show rank. the best-known case is the jade disc of mr he. about 283 bce the king of qin offered fifteen walled cities for it to the weaker state of zhao, and both courts expected a trick. a stone had become worth more than cities because kings prized it. the phrase returns in passage 12, where such goods “hinder a person’s walk”, and in passage 64, where the sage does not prize them. the text does not blame the thief first. it looks at the 貴, the prizing, and prizing starts at the top. what makes a thing “hard to get” in your world: the thing, or the wanting?

盜: one who drools at a dish. the shuowen explains 盜 as a small scene. the definition: 私利物也, “to take private gain from things”. then the parts: 从㳄，㳄欲皿者, “from 㳄: one who drools and wants the dish”. 㳄 is water beside a person with an open mouth, and the shuowen calls it 慕欲口液也, “the mouth-water of longing”. below is 皿, a food dish. so a thief, in the script, is a mouth that waters in front of another’s bowl. that fits the sentence well. the line does not treat theft as a kind of person. it treats theft as a result: goods are prized and shown, and mouths water. in classical usage 盜 is the one who takes by stealth; the violent bandit is 賊. the second plate takes the character apart.

見: to see, or to show. 見 is “to see”, read jian. the same graph, read xian, is “to appear, to show”; later writers used 現 for that sense. so 不見可欲 has two readings. one: do not display the things that can be desired. this is advice to those who own such things, and first to the court. two: do not look at what can be desired. this is advice for one’s own eyes. legge chose the first and added an object: “not to show them”. our “showing” follows the same reading, because the first two lines are also about what a ruler does in public. but keep the second one in mind. it turns the sentence from policy to practice, and the next lines can turn the same way. 可欲 is exact too: “what can be wanted”. the desire is not yet there.

心: heart, not “mind”. 心 is a picture of the heart, the organ in the chest. early china did not put thought in the head and feeling in the breast. one organ did both. mencius says: 心之官則思, “the office of the heart is to think”. so translators write “mind”, or “heart-mind”. “mind” alone brings a western split: a thinking part above, a body below. this passage does not have that split. it sets the heart beside the belly, the will beside the bones, as four parts of one body. note a detail of the text: mawangdui silk b is reported to have no 心 in the third sentence (silk a is damaged here). it reads 使民不亂, “keeps the people from disorder”. the received text moved the disorder inside. which is first, do you think: disorder in the heart or disorder in the streets?

亂 and 治: one word defines the other. the passage runs from 亂, disorder, to 治, order, in its last word. now read the shuowen on 亂. the definition is one character: 治也, “to put in order”. the dictionary defines disorder by its opposite. the graph is commonly explained as two hands at work on tangled silk on a frame. the tangle and the untangling are one picture. the oldest texts use 亂 in both senses. king wu of zhou says in a line that the analects quotes: 予有亂臣十人, “i have ten ministers who 亂”, and it means ten ministers who govern well. so the two poles of this passage were once one word. passage 2 said that opposites give birth to each other. here the script agrees. is the act of ordering already a kind of disorder?

治: order, written with water. 治 has 氵, water, on the left. the shuowen lists it only as the name of a river. the sense “to govern” is commonly explained from the control of water: to dredge channels and guide a flood. the founding story of chinese rule is such a story. yu the great did not dam the flood, as his father did and failed. he cut channels and led the water to the sea. the same word means to treat an illness. so 聖人之治 is “the sage’s ordering”, and the word carries a method inside it: order comes when you give things their channel. english “govern” comes from a greek word for steering a ship; “rule” comes from a straight stick. note the aim also. the passage wants 治, a state of order. it does not speak of progress.

whose heart, whose belly?. 虛其心，實其腹，弱其志，強其骨. each line has 其: “their”, “its”, or “one’s own”. english must choose, and the choice decides the passage. if 其 is the people, as legge takes it, the lines are a policy: keep subjects simple, fed, without ambition, and strong for work. rulers did read it so, and the legalists built harder versions; the reader should feel that edge and not explain it away. if 其 is the sage, the lines are self-cultivation. the old heshang gong commentary says that the sage orders the state as the sage orders the body, and reads the four lines as care of the self: remove cravings, hold to the one, be soft and yielding, guard the essence so that the bones are firm. we write “the heart”, “the belly”, to leave 其 open. read the stanza twice, once each way.

wang bi: what knows and what does not. wang bi comments: 心懷智而腹懷食，虛有智而實無知也。 “the heart holds cleverness and the belly holds food. empty the part that has cleverness; fill the part that has no knowing.” and: 骨無知以幹，志生事以亂。 “bones know nothing, and so they serve as the trunk. the will breeds affairs, and so it makes disorder.” he sorts the four body words into two kinds. heart and will scheme. belly and bones only hold a person up. on the first line he is careful: 賢，猶能也, “worthy means able”, and 唯能是任，尚也曷為, “give the task to the able, and that is all; why exalt them?” he does not ask a ruler to refuse talent. he objects to the glory, 榮過其任, “honor that is larger than the office”.

腹: a real belly. modern versions often make the belly a symbol: a “center”, a “core”. first it is a belly, and the line is about grain. the shuowen defines 腹 as 厚也, “the thick part”. every school knew that order depends on food. the guanzi says: 倉廩實則知禮節, “when the granaries are full, the people know ritual and restraint”. it uses the verb of our line, 實, to fill. the belly has a second quality: it knows “enough”. the eye can always want one more thing; a belly gets full and stops. passage 12 makes this the sage’s rule: 為腹不為目, “for the belly, not for the eye”. later breath practice placed the body’s center below the navel and read this line as a direction for attention. both readings need a real body. when did you last feel plainly, in the body, that you had enough?

志: why weaken the will?. 志 is the heart, 心, under a part that the shuowen takes as 之, “to go”: a heart on its way to something. the shuowen defines it as 意也, “intention”. it is aim, purpose, ambition. for confucius it is a good word: 吾十有五而志于學, “at fifteen i set my 志 on learning”. a man of the 士 class was praised for having 志. the modern west agrees: a strong will is a virtue, and a weak will is a failure of character. so 弱其志 sounds wrong to almost every reader, then and now. wang bi’s answer is short: the will breeds affairs. an aim makes a person bend each day toward one point, and it makes rivals. 弱 here is “to make pliant”; the shuowen pictures it as a thing that bends. what would you keep, if your strongest aim became a little softer?

骨: the pit of the fruit. the shuowen defines bone with a picture from fruit: 肉之覈也, “the kernel of the flesh”. 覈 is the hard stone inside a peach or a plum. flesh is the soft part that the world sees and that spoils; bone is the pit that holds the form. the four lines of the stanza go inward in this way. heart and will are the parts that reach out and plan. belly and bones are the parts that stay. wang bi says bones “know nothing” and for that reason can be the trunk of a person. in the reading as policy, strong bones are strong farmers and soldiers. in the reading as practice, they are a frame that carries you with less effort from the will. the third plate shows the character, which has a skull and flesh in it.

無知無欲: “ignorance”?. 常使民無知無欲: “always keep the people without knowing, without wanting”. this is the hardest line in the passage, and it has a dark history. passage 65 says that the old masters of dao did not make the people bright; they kept them 愚, simple. in 213 bce the qin state burned books to keep the people from using the past against the present. a reader may fairly ask if this line helped. there is another side. 知 in early texts is also the word for cleverness and scheming, later written 智; the next line uses that graph. the knowing that the passage fears is the kind that passage 2 showed: to know beauty as beauty and so make the ugly. and the speaker claims the same simplicity: 我愚人之心也哉, “mine is the heart of a fool” (passage 20). do not settle this too quickly.

those who know do not dare. 使夫智者不敢為也: “keep those clever ones from daring to act”. 夫 here is a pointing word, “those”, and it has a cold sound. the first readers could name such men: the travelling persuaders who sold plans for alliance and war to any court that paid. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read the end of the passage differently: 使夫知不敢，弗為而已，則无不治矣. this is commonly divided as: “keep those who know from daring; simply do not act, and then nothing is left unordered”. there the last sentence is plain, 弗為, “do not do it”. the received text has the paradox 為無為, “do the not-doing”. the silk copies are older than any copy of the received text. the received reading gave the tradition one of its best-known phrases.

為無為: a verb that eats itself. three characters, and the first and third are the same: 為無為. the first 為 is a verb, “do”. its object is 無為, “not-doing”, the term that passage 2 introduced. so the phrase is “do not-doing”, or “act without acting”. it is not a statement that nothing happens. the grammar keeps an act and removes the forcing from it. passage 63 extends the pattern: 為無為，事無事，味無味, “do not-doing, work at no-work, taste the tasteless”. the result clause has a double negative: 無不治, “nothing is not in order”. chinese likes this form; it is stronger than a plain “all”. english wants to resolve the paradox with an adverb such as “effortlessly”. the chinese gives no adverb. it gives the same word twice with a “without” between.

legge: “(tries to)”. legge translates the hard reading and then softens it with a bracket. his sage “empties their minds, fills their bellies, weakens their wills, and strengthens their bones”: “their” each time, so the lines are policy on the people. then: “he constantly (tries to) keep them without knowledge and without desire”. the words in brackets are his. the chinese has 常使, “always causes”. a victorian scholar who believed in schools and missions could not easily praise a ruler who keeps people without knowledge, and the bracket shows that. he also writes “minds” for 心 and “men of superior ability” for 賢, which removes the moral side of that word. his plain “their” has one merit. it does not hide the reading that rulers in china in fact used.

one day for the belly. for one day, take the four lines as directions for your own body. empty the heart: at three set times, stop and drop the plan that you are turning over; it will come back by itself. fill the belly: eat one plain meal slowly and stop at the point of enough. weaken the will: choose one thing that you are pushing, and for today only, do not push it. strengthen the bones: walk, carry something, stand well. in the evening, ask two questions. did anything fall into disorder because you pushed less? and what did you not look at today, because you did not go where it was shown?

虛 and 實, 弱 and 強: both in one body. four lines use two pairs: 虛 empty and 實 full, 弱 pliant and 強 strong. the text does not choose one side of either pair. it gives each side a place. the heart is emptied and the belly is filled. the will is made pliant and the bones are made strong. a reader who knows later passages may expect “empty is good, full is bad” or “weak is good, strong is bad”. this stanza does not allow that: 實 and 強 are things that the sage brings about. the question is where each one sits. a full heart on an empty belly makes disorder; so does a hard will on weak bones. the placing also turns with time. a belly that is filled past its need becomes the dulled mouth of passage 12, and a heart that is held empty by force is one more aim. what in you is full where it could be empty, and empty where it could be full?

when no one is held up as worthy, people do not contend; the prize makes the fight.. when no one is held up as worthy, people do not contend; the prize makes the fight. is this what you have seen in the families, schools, or teams that you know? were you a child who won prizes, or one who watched others win them? what did that teach you about your worth? take the opposite side: honor given to the able lifts everyone, and a group with no praise goes slack. stay there for a while. what do you feel? which side do you defend at once? what might you lose if the other were also true?

a will made pliant and a heart made empty bring order; a fed belly and strong bones are enough.. a will made pliant and a heart made empty bring order; a fed belly and strong bones are enough. do you agree that a softer aim could leave you better off? answer before you make the answer polite. what was said in your home about ambition, and about people who lacked it? now hold the opposite: a strong will is the best thing you have, and without it nothing in your life would stand. what arises? rulers have used this passage to keep people small. has someone who gained from it told you to want less? does that memory color how you read the line? which do you fear more in yourself, the driven one or the one with no drive?

盜 a mouth that waters. this character is a short story in two floors. upstairs, on the left, three drops: 氵, water. beside them is 欠. the shuowen describes 欠 as 張口气悟也, an open mouth with breath that goes out, and says the graph shows breath rising from a person: a yawn. a person with a wide-open mouth, and water beside it: together they make 㳄, which the shuowen defines as 慕欲口液也, “the mouth-water of longing”. drool. downstairs is 皿, a dish; the shuowen calls it 飯食之用器也, “a vessel used for food”, and says it is a picture. now put the floors together, as the shuowen does: 㳄欲皿者, “one who drools and wants the dish”. that is a thief. the open mouth 欠 has a family, and in each member the shuowen takes it as the meaning: 欲, to desire, which stands in this same sentence; 歌, to sing; 吹, to blow. the drool has one more cousin: 羨, envy, defined as 貪欲也, “greedy wanting”. in the simplified form 盗 the water has lost a drop, and the top reads as 次, “next”. the picture is gone. the passage makes the same point as the old graph: the dish is shown first, and then the mouth waters. twelve strokes. the water comes first: a dot, a second dot below it, and a third stroke that flicks up to the right, toward the open mouth. then 欠 in four strokes: a short stroke that falls left, a horizontal that hooks back, and then the two legs of a person, one that falls left and one, the 捺, that sweeps right. the whole upper floor must stay shallow and wide; it is a lid. then the dish: a short vertical on the left, the top and right side in one turning stroke, two short verticals inside. watch the last stroke. it is the base line of the dish, and it runs the full width of the character, far past the walls of the dish on both sides. it is the longest stroke of the twelve. the drooling mouth above is light and busy; the dish below is calm and wide.

賢 a servant, a hand, a shell. three parts. at the bottom is 貝, a cowrie shell. the shuowen tells its history: 古者貨貝而寶龜, “the ancients used shells as money and treasured tortoise shell”, and adds that qin ended shell money. so 貝 in a character means value. count the shells in the first sentence of this passage: 賢, worth; 貴, to prize; 貨, goods. three of its key words carry money inside them. at the top left is 臣, a servant or minister. the shuowen says it shows 屈服之形, “the form of one who bends and submits”; modern scholars commonly explain the early graph as an eye turned on end, the eye of one who looks up at a lord. at the top right is 又, a hand. hand and servant together make 臤, which the shuowen defines as 堅也, “firm”, and of which it says: 古文以爲賢字, “the old script used this for 賢”. so the older word was a firm, capable servant, and the shell was added later. the shuowen’s definition of 賢 is 多才也, “much ability”; some editions read 多財, “much wealth”, and the shell fits that. the english “worthy” happens to carry the same double sense: worth as merit, and worth as price. the passage distrusts a court that sets such men high. the character itself is an able servant with pay. fifteen strokes, in three blocks: 臣, then 又, then 貝. 臣 has an order that surprises students. the top horizontal comes first, then a short vertical, the small box in the middle with its turning stroke, a horizontal, another short vertical. the long left side comes last, as stroke six: it falls the whole height and turns along the bottom, and closes the servant in. 又 is two strokes: a horizontal that turns and falls left, then a 捺 that crosses it. now the top is finished, and it must sit level, two blocks side by side. below, 貝 is tall and narrow: left side, top and right side, two short lines inside, the bottom line, and then two small legs, one that falls left and a last dot to the right. the shell stands on those two legs, and the two blocks above rest on the shell.

骨 the kernel of the flesh. the lower half is easy: it is the shape that looks like 月, “moon”. when this shape stands at the bottom or the side of a body word, it is nearly always 肉, flesh, in its short form. the shuowen calls 肉 a picture of a cut of meat. you know it from 腹, belly, in this passage, and from 肝, liver, and 胃, stomach. the upper half is 冎. the shuowen’s entry is grim: 剔人肉置其骨也, “to strip off a person’s flesh and leave the bone”, and it adds 頭隆骨也, “the domed bone of the head”. so the top is bare bone, and the bottom is flesh. the shuowen joins them, 从冎有肉, “bone that has flesh”, and gives a definition from the fruit bowl: 肉之覈也, “the kernel of the flesh”. bone is to the body what the stone is to a peach. cousins: 體, the body as a whole, is 骨 with a sound part; the shuowen counts it as “the twelve parts together”. 滑, slippery, is water beside 骨, where the shuowen takes 骨 as the sound. and this character names the oldest chinese writing that we have. the shang kings cut their questions into ox shoulder blades and turtle shells: 甲骨文, “shell and bone script”. 強其骨: the passage asks for strength in the part that lasts and knows nothing. nine strokes. the bare bone on top takes three: a short vertical on the left, then the top and the right side in one turning stroke, and a small inner corner. keep this part narrow. strokes four and five make a cover: a short dot on the left, then a wide horizontal that ends in a hook at the right. watch that fifth stroke. it is the widest line of the character, like shoulders, and the head sits in the middle of it. then the flesh below, four strokes: the left side, the top and right side with a hook at the foot, and two short horizontals inside that touch the left wall and do not reach the right. the form is a tall column: narrow head, broad shoulders, straight trunk. calligraphers use this same word for good writing. strokes with firm inner strength have 骨, and soft, fat strokes have only flesh.

4 · the bowl that does not fill. dao is an empty bowl. / use it, and perhaps it does not fill. / a deep pool, ah, / it seems the ancestor of the ten thousand things. / blunting what is sharp, / untying what is tangled, / tempering the light, / joining the dust. / sunk and still, ah, / it seems, perhaps, to be there. / i do not know whose child it is. / it looks like the forebear of the high god. the passage gives three pictures and one confession. a hollow bowl that you can use and not fill. a deep pool in a river, which seems to be the ancestor of the ten thousand things. then four short strokes with no subject: blunt the point, untie the knot, tune the light, be joining the dust. then water again, sunk and still, where something seems, perhaps, to be. then the confession: i do not know whose child this is; it looks older than di. three of the key words are written with water: 沖, 淵, 湛. the passage starts on a table, goes down into a river, down into dust, and ends before the high god. every step goes lower or earlier. none goes up. the usual picture of the sacred is fullness: more light, more presence, more certainty. this passage reverses each one. dao is a hollow. its depth is that of a pool. it is not a height. it tunes its light down to the room and joins the dust. even its existence is given with a “perhaps”. for the contemplative reader this is exact reporting. when the mind is quiet, what remains is not a bright object. it is a clear, still capacity, hard to point at, in which sounds and thoughts appear and do not fill it. the four middle lines then describe what happens in that stillness, with no one who does it: sharp reactions lose their point, knots come loose. the proverb made from this passage says that such a person looks ordinary. wang bi opens with a rule for anyone who carries responsibility: a person whose capacity is the size of the job cannot hold the job. you need unused room. the leader who is full of plans, opinions, and self has nowhere to put what the team brings. the four lines add a style. blunt the edge: do not win each point. untie the tangle: disputes are knots, and knots are untied, not cut. tune the light: let your ability raise the room and not shame it. join the dust: stay in the common work. this has a strategic side, and sunzi would know it; a force with no sharp point gives the enemy nothing to strike. but the passage does not promise a reward. the speaker ends with “i do not know”, which is also a thing a leader can say. feel the first line in the breath. the lungs are a vessel that works only because it does not stay full. at the end of the out-breath there is a hollow, and the next breath comes into it without your effort: 沖, empty and surging. the four lines are a good scan for a body that holds too much. where is something sharp: the jaw, the eyes, the tone of voice? let it go blunt. where is a tangle: the shoulders, the belly? let it loosen; do not pull at it. internal martial arts use the same order. a hard, pointed force is easy to meet and turn. a body that is sunk and still, with weight low like water in a pool, has no edge for the other person to find. a river explains the whole passage. its bed is a hollow, and for that reason water runs in it and is not used up. in its bends are pools where the current circles and the old fish stay. it blunts each sharp stone it carries and makes sand. it takes up silt and dust and is not harmed; when it slows, it clears, still and deep, and you can almost see the bottom. no one asks whose child a river is. the text also calls dao an ancestor, a kin word: stones, deer, and people sit in one family line. and dust in chinese is drawn as the earth that running deer raise. the lowest thing in the passage is a trace of life. try the bowl practice after a meal. or try this in a conversation today. find one moment where you have a sharp point ready: a correction, a clever answer, a proof that you are right. let it go blunt. say less than you could. then watch what the other person does with the space. you are not being weak, and you are not using a trick. you are testing the first line of the passage: use an empty thing, and see if it runs out. afterwards, ask the question that the text asks about its four subjectless lines: who did that?

dao, described by a cup. we leave 道 as dao. the word is first a road (see passage 1), and “way” is its nearest english. this passage gives it no definition. it gives it a kitchen object, then a pool, then dust. western philosophy tends to explain a first principle with the highest things it has: light, mind, the good, a king. this text goes down, to low and common things. note also the grammar of the first clause, 道沖: two words, “dao, empty”. it has no “is” and no “like”. english must add one or the other, and each adds a claim. our “bowl” is also an addition; it comes from the old reading 盅. legge chose “is (like)”, with the second word in brackets. which do you hear: a statement, or a comparison?

沖: water in the middle. 沖 is 氵, water, beside 中, the middle. the shuowen defines it as 涌搖也, “to well up and rock”: water that surges. that is the common sense of the word, and it is active. here the old readers take it as another word, 盅: the hollow of a vessel. both senses are alive in the book. passage 42 speaks of 沖氣, breaths that surge together and make harmony; passage 45 says 大盈若沖, “great fullness seems empty”. so this one character holds a vessel that waits and water that moves. an emptiness that surges is not a dead space. before you tap on, look at the character again: where is the water, and where is the middle?

the shuowen quotes this line. under a different character, 盅 (zhong), the shuowen jiezi says: 器虛也, “the emptiness of a vessel”. then it quotes this exact line as its example: 《老子》曰：道盅而用之. so about 100 ce a copy of the laozi was in use that wrote the word with 皿, a dish, below 中. the fu yi “ancient text” edition, put together in the tang from old manuscripts, also reads 盅. the received text writes 沖, with water. the two graphs sounded alike, and scribes exchanged them. the result is good luck for readers: the line means a bowl, and it looks like water. “empty” in english has no picture. it is a bare adjective, and often a sad one. the chinese word is a dish with space in it.

或: the first “perhaps”. 或 means “perhaps, it may be, some”. it is a word of doubt, and it stands at the center of the first line: use it, and perhaps it does not fill. many translations remove it, because a line about dao should sound certain. there is also a textual reason for doubt about the doubt. wang bi’s own comment paraphrases with 又, “again”: 又復不盈, “again and again it does not fill”. one of the mawangdui silk texts reads 有弗盈, where 有 is commonly taken as that same 又. so the line may once have said “again” and not “perhaps”. we keep 或, because it is the pinned text and because the rest of the passage hedges too. which speaker do you trust more: one who is sure, or one who says “perhaps”?

does not fill, or does not run out?. 不盈 is literally “not full”. the clause can go two ways. one: however much you pour in, the bowl does not fill; its capacity has no end. two: however much you take out, it is not used up; some commentators read 盈 here as “reach a limit”, close to 窮, “exhaust”. passage 45 supports the pair of ideas: 大盈若沖，其用不窮, “great fullness seems empty; its use does not run out”. legge found a third way and made it a warning: we must “be on our guard against all fulness”. the chinese has no “we” and no “must”. in english, a cup is for filling, and an empty cup is a lack. here the cup is good because it stays unfilled. wang bi explains why.

wang bi: fill it and it spills. wang bi comments: 沖而用之，用乃不能窮，滿以造實，實來則溢。 “empty, and so used: then the use cannot be exhausted. fill it to make it solid, and when the solid comes, it spills.” he begins with a political picture: a person whose capacity is the size of one household cannot keep a household whole, and a person whose capacity is the size of one state cannot complete a state. to carry a thing you need more room than the thing. of the four middle lines he writes: 銳挫而無損…其體同塵而不渝其真, “its edge is blunted and it takes no harm … its body is one with the dust and its trueness does not change”. for him the lines describe dao itself. they are not rules for us.

淵: the pool that turns. the shuowen defines 淵 as 回水也, “water that turns back on itself”, and reads the old graph as a picture: 左右，岸也。中象水皃, “left and right are the banks; the middle shows the look of water”. it is the deep place in a river where the current slows and circles, and where the big fish stay. passage 36 says: fish should not leave the 淵. english “abyss” comes with dread, from the greek for “bottomless” and from the first verses of genesis. 淵 has no dread. it is depth that feeds. confucius’s best student had this word in his name: yan yuan. the line moves from a bowl on a table to a pool in a river: the same emptiness, larger. what lives in the still part of your own day?

ancestor, not “source”. 宗 is a roof, 宀, over an altar, 示. the shuowen: 尊祖廟也, “the shrine where the ancestors are honored”. from the shrine the word came to mean the founding ancestor and the main line of a clan. translations that say “source” or “origin” make a kinship word into a physics word. in early china the ancestor was not a past cause. the ancestor was present: fed with offerings, asked for advice, able to bless or harm. to call dao the 宗 of the ten thousand things says that everything that exists is one clan, and that dao is the one at the head of the family table. notice also who is included. the text does not say “ancestor of people”. stones, deer, and rivers are kin.

a passage that will not swear. count the hedges. 或, perhaps. 似, seems. 似或, seems-perhaps, two doubts in a row. 象, looks like. then, plainly: 吾不知, “i do not know”. in forty-two characters about the first principle of everything, the speaker refuses five times to be sure. the particle 兮 (xi) adds to the tone. it has no meaning. it is a held breath in a sung line, common in the songs of the southern state of chu; the mawangdui silk texts write it 呵. we give it as “ah”. modern versions often delete all of this and give a calm definition. the chinese sounds like a person who looks into deep water and reports what may be there. is the doubt weakness in the speaker, or accuracy about the subject?

four lines that live twice. 挫其銳，解其紛，和其光，同其塵. these twelve characters come again, word for word, in passage 56, where they describe a person who knows and does not speak. many modern scholars think that they belong there and were copied into this passage by mistake: without them the pool line and the still-water line join cleanly. if it was a mistake, it is very old. the mawangdui silk texts (before 168 bce) already have the lines in both places. the guodian bamboo slips have passage 56 with the lines (in a different order, and with some different graphs), and do not contain this passage at all. we keep them, as the pinned text does. in 56 the lines are about a sage. here, with no subject, they may be about dao. read them both ways.

whose sharpness?. each of the four lines has the same form: a verb, then 其, then a noun. 其 is “its” or “their” or “one’s”, and the lines have no subject. so who blunts, and whose edge? three readings exist. dao blunts its own edge: it has power and does not cut. dao blunts the edges of things: time rounds every stone. or a person does it: the lines are practice. our “-ing” forms try to leave the subject open, as the chinese does. legge chose the third reading and added a subject. 銳 is the point of a blade or the tip of an army; 紛 is a snarl of silk thread. the first two lines can also be heard as statecraft: weapons made dull, disputes untied. see the note on their second home.

“we should” and “god”. legge was a missionary before he was a professor, and this passage shows it in two places. for the four subjectless lines he writes “we should blunt our sharp points … we should attemper our brightness”. the chinese has no “we” and no “should”. a description of how dao moves has become a short sermon on humility. then the last line: for 帝 he writes “god”, with the capital letter. this was a position in a long fight. protestant missionaries in china argued for decades over which chinese word should translate “god” in the bible, and legge held that the 帝 of the old classics was the true god, known to the early chinese. so his last line says, with visible discomfort, that the tao “might appear to have been before god”.

和: to tune the light. 和其光 is often given as “dim its light” or “soften its glare”. the verb is more interesting. 和 is the great word for harmony, and it began in sound. the shuowen: 相譍也, “to answer one another”, as one voice answers another in a song. it is also what a cook does with flavors: blends them so that none stands out. so the light is not put out. it is tuned to the room, as a singer matches a choir. the light does not become less. it stops being separate. the next line uses 同, “same”. early ethics set these two words against each other: confucius says that the noble person 和而不同, harmonizes and does not make the same. the laozi uses both, one after the other. english has no verb that does this to light. “temper” is our nearest: to bring to the right mix. think of a person you know who is brilliant and does not make others feel dull. what do they do with their light?

塵: what the deer kick up. the modern graph 塵 is a deer, 鹿, over earth, 土. the older form in the shuowen has three deer over earth, and the definition is a small poem: 鹿行揚土也, “deer run and the earth rises”. dust, then, is not dirt in a corner. it is the sign that living things have passed. in later chinese the word came to stand for the whole busy human world: 紅塵, “red dust”, is the life of the city and its desires. 同 is “same” and “together”. 同其塵 says: to be the same as its dust, to be in it with everything else. western religion mostly puts the holy above the dust and tells us to rise. this line goes the other way. see what the phrase became.

和光同塵: a proverb’s long life. the third and fourth lines were pressed into a four-character saying, 和光同塵, that every educated chinese reader knows. it names a way to live: to have light and not show it, to stay in the common world and not stand apart. it fit the old ideal that the greatest hermit does not hide in the mountains. a jin dynasty poem says the small hermit hides in the hills and the great hermit hides in the court and the market. chinese buddhists then took the phrase for the bodhisattva, who tempers a buddha’s radiance to live among suffering beings. in japan, as wako dojin, it explained how buddhas appear as local gods. the phrase can also be an insult: one who goes along with a corrupt age. how do you tell the two apart?

湛: under the surface. the shuowen defines 湛 with one word: 沒也, “submerged”; in that sense the graph was also read chen, the same word as 沈, to sink. from there the senses spread: deep, soaked through, still, clear. it is water again, the third water word in the passage after 沖 and 淵, and the calmest. the clause that follows is a wonder of hedging: 似或存, “seems, perhaps, to remain”. 存 means to be there, to persist, to be kept alive. legge heard permanence here, “as if it would ever so continue”. the plainer sense is a thing seen under water: you think it is there, the light moves, and you are not sure. dao does not show itself as a bright fact. it is like a stone on the bed of a clear pool. when did you last know a thing was present though you could not point to it?

whose child?. 吾不知誰之子: “i do not know whose child it is.” in a society built on lineage, to explain a thing was to give its descent. a man was the son of someone; a state was founded by someone; a king was 天子, the son of heaven. the speaker has just called dao the ancestor of everything, and now asks the family question about the ancestor itself, and has no answer. 子 is “child”; it often means “son”, and legge wrote “son”, but the word does not require it. this is the first “i” (吾) in the book. it appears in order to say “i do not know”. the greek tradition would ask “what is its cause?”. the chinese asks “who is its parent?”. the family words run through the whole passage: 宗, ancestor; 子, child; and in the last line 先, forebear. what changes when the question is about family?

象: an elephant’s bones. 象 is a picture of an elephant. the shuowen describes the animal: 長鼻牙，南越大獸, “long nose and tusks, a great beast of the far south”. the same graph means “image” and “to seem”. the han feizi, in the oldest commentary on the laozi, explains how: 人希見生象也，而得死象之骨，案其圖以想其生也. “people seldom see a living elephant. they find the bones of a dead one, and from that pattern they imagine the living one. so whatever people picture in the mind is called 象.” elephants once lived in north china and withdrew south as the forests fell. so the last line carries a quiet joke on itself. 象帝之先: we have only bones and a guess. wang bi reads it simply as 似, “seems”. some read it as a noun: “an image of what came before di”.

older than the god of kings. 帝, di, was the high god of the shang dynasty (to about 1046 bce). shang kings asked di through oracle bones for rain, harvest, and victory. the zhou, who overthrew the shang, joined di to their own heaven (天) and claimed heaven’s mandate; the king was heaven’s son. wang bi’s gloss is short: 帝，天帝也, “di is the lord of heaven”. so di was not only a religious idea. di was the top of the chain that made kings lawful. to say, even with a “seems”, that dao is older than di puts a nameless, childless emptiness above the source of royal right. in the fourth century bce, with the zhou house in ruins and seven states each calling its ruler “king”, that was a bold line. in 221 bce the first emperor took 帝 into his own title.

wash one bowl. after a meal today, wash one bowl or cup by hand, slowly. when it is clean and dry, hold it for a moment before you put it away. look into it. the part that you paid for is the wall. the part that you use is the room inside, and the meal did not use it up. now turn the same look on yourself for three breaths. after a day of use, is there a part of you that is still empty, still able to receive? do not try to make that part larger. see only that it is there. the passage says “perhaps” at this point, and you may say it too. the bowl returns in passage 11, with a wheel and a house.

沖 and 盈: empty and full. 沖 is the hollow of the bowl, and 盈 is fullness. the line sets them against each other and joins them through 用, use. the bowl is of use because it is empty, and the use does not fill it. english hears “empty” as a lack. the text here prefers the empty side, and it helps to ask what the preference is for. it answers a world that counted full things: full halls, full titles, the full vessel of passage 9. it does not say that fullness is bad. passage 45 puts the two words in one line, 大盈若沖: great fullness is like emptiness. passage 22 says 窪則盈: the hollow place is filled. so the empty side turns too. a bowl is emptied to be filled and filled to be emptied. the four lines that follow hold more pairs: sharp and blunt, tangled and loose, light and dust. which do you defend more, your fullness or your room?

the empty bowl is the useful one; use does not fill it, and so it does not run out.. the empty bowl is the useful one; use does not fill it, and so it does not run out. where in your life has this been true: a room, a silence, a free hour that gave more than a full one? how do you feel in front of an empty thing: a blank day, a pause in talk, an account at zero? where did that feeling begin? take the other side: a full store is safety, and emptiness is what happens to people who did not prepare. hold that as true for a minute. what comes up? which of the two sides sounds like a voice you know? whose voice is it?

the sharp point is blunted and the light is tuned down to the dust, and nothing is lost by it.. the sharp point is blunted and the light is tuned down to the dust, and nothing is lost by it. do you agree that nothing is lost? think of a time when you held back a sharp answer. what did you learn early about being bright in a room: that it was welcome, or that it had a price? now the opposite: a light is for shining and an edge is for cutting, and to dim them is a kind of lie. stay with that. what feelings and thoughts arrive? when someone else shines and does not hold back, what do you feel toward that person? what does it tell you about your own light?

沖 water at the centre. on the left, three drops: 氵, the short form of 水 when it stands at the side of a character. 水 itself is a picture of a current with spray on each side. every character in this passage that is about depth has it: 沖, 淵, 湛. count them in the chinese text. on the right is 中, the centre: a line through the middle of a space. the oldest forms of 中 show a pole with streamers, commonly explained as a flag set up at the centre of a camp or a field, where people gather; the detail is debated. the shuowen takes the two parts together, 从水中, and defines the word as water that wells up and rocks. its cousins by the right half are worth a look: 忠 is 中 over 心, the heart at its centre: loyalty. 仲 is a person in the middle: the second-born brother. and 盅, 中 over a dish, is the hollow of a vessel, the word that the old readers heard in this line. in modern chinese the short form 冲 has two drops and does heavy work: to rinse, to brew tea, to charge forward. so one sound holds a bowl that waits and water that moves. the line needs both: an emptiness that surges. seven strokes. the three drops come first, top to bottom, and no two are alike: the first falls, the second falls a little further left, and the third is not a drop at all but a flick upward to the right. watch that third stroke: it points at the place where the next part will begin, and it joins the two halves across the gap. then 中: left side, then top and right side in a single stroke, then the base. the last stroke is the vertical through the centre, from above the box to well below it. everything waits for it. a writer may end it in a point, the “hanging needle”, or in a rounded stop, the “dropping dew”. in running script the three drops become one line that hooks, like water that has started to move.

象 the elephant in the mind. this is a whole animal, turned on its side over three thousand years. the oracle-bone form is one of the clearest pictures in early writing: a side view with a long curved trunk, a heavy body, and a tail. stand the animal on its tail and you have the modern form: the trunk and head at the top, the body in the middle, the legs and tail in the strokes that fan out below. the shuowen still describes it as a picture: 象耳牙四足之形, “it shows the ears, tusks, and four feet”. elephants lived in the yellow river plain in the shang. the character 為, “to do, to make”, is commonly explained from its early form as a hand that leads an elephant: work. then the animals withdrew to the south, and the word did a strange thing. the han feizi says that people who found the bones of a dead elephant pictured the living one from them, and so every mental picture came to be called 象. add a person, and you get 像: a portrait, a statue, a likeness. in chinese chess, 象棋, the elephant still walks the board. in the last line here, 象 is a verb: it looks like, it seems. dao is given as a guess from the bones. eleven strokes in the form that the app writes (some standards count twelve). follow the animal from the top. strokes one and two make the small bent cap that was the trunk and head. three to five make the flat box, wider than it is tall. stroke six starts inside the box and falls a long way down to the left. then stroke seven, the spine: it curves down through the centre and ends in a hook. two more strokes fall away to the left of it, like legs. stroke ten is a short one on the right side that meets the spine. the last stroke is the long 捺 that sweeps to the lower right. watch it: the brush presses down as it travels and then lifts to a point. it is the counterweight for every stroke on the left. in clerical script it carries the flared “goose tail”, and the beast seems to walk.

塵 deer over earth. two pictures, one on the other. on top is 鹿, a deer. the oracle-bone form shows the animal from the side with branched antlers, a large eye, and legs; in the modern form the antlers and head are the upper part, and the two 匕 shapes at the foot are what is left of the legs. below is 土, earth: commonly explained as a lump of soil on the ground line. the shuowen’s older form of the character has three deer on top, 麤, a herd, and the definition is a scene and not a gloss: 鹿行揚土也, “deer run and the earth rises”. so dust is the track that life leaves in the air. three of a thing is the usual way in the script to say “many”: 森 is a forest from three trees, 眾 a crowd from three people, and 品, three mouths, is a set of things to compare. the herd shrank to one deer because the full form was heavy to write. the mainland short form went further and is a new small poem: 尘, 小 over 土, “small earth”. 鹿 has cousins too: 麗, “beautiful”, is commonly explained as a deer with a fine pair of antlers above it (the shuowen takes the top part as the sound), and 慶, to celebrate, has a deer inside it, commonly explained as a deerskin brought as a gift. the line says 同其塵: be where the hooves are. fourteen strokes: the deer first, then the earth. the deer opens with a dot and a level line, and then a long stroke that falls away to the left and shelters all that comes after it. under that roof the strokes are many and close, and the writer must keep the white spaces between them even, or the animal turns into a blot. the two leg shapes at the bottom of the deer are kept short, to leave room. then the earth: a short horizontal, a vertical, and last a long horizontal. watch that last stroke. it is the ground line, and it should be the widest line in the character; a tall, crowded shape stands or falls on it. in cursive script the deer is cut down to a few turns of the wrist, and only the ground line stays the same.

5 · straw dogs and a bellows. heaven and earth are not humane: / they treat the ten thousand things as straw dogs. / the sage is not humane: / the sage treats the hundred families as straw dogs. / the space between heaven and earth: / is it not like a bellows? / empty, and it does not give way. / moved, and more comes out. / many words: again and again, the dead end. / better to keep to the middle. the passage has three pieces. first, two matched sentences: heaven and earth are not humane and treat all things as straw dogs; the sage is not humane and treats the hundred families so. second, a question about the space between heaven and earth: is it not like a smith’s bellows? two short lines answer: empty, and it does not give way; moved, and more comes out. third, a proverb: many words meet the dead end again and again, and it is better to keep to the middle. the last two pieces rhyme and the first does not; they may have been separate sayings. one image joins them: a thing with nothing at its centre. the first line removes a comfort: the wish that the world has a special regard for me. much suffering is a quarrel with that wish. “why did this happen to me?” has no answer in a world of straw dogs, and the question can then stop. this is not coldness. the straw dog is honored with full care in its hour. what is absent is clinging before and after. the bellows gives the positive side. awareness is like the gap between heaven and earth: it has nothing inside it, and for that reason sights and sounds keep coming out of it and it is not used up. thought and talk fill the space and bring a person to the wall. to keep the middle is to rest as the hollow, while the breath moves. a leader who has favorites has a court. graded warmth, more for the near and less for the far, is what 仁 meant in practice, and every organization knows its cost: people study the leader’s affections and stop studying the work. the first stanza asks for a care with no inner circle. it is hard, and it is easy to abuse; rulers have quoted it to excuse the use of people as material. the test is the zhuangzi’s picture: the straw dog receives full honor in its hour. the second and third parts are lighter advice. an office, a meeting, a team needs a hollow: room that is not filled by the leader’s views. and a leader who explains again and again runs out. say it once, and then guard the space. the chest and belly are a 橐籥, a bag and a pipe. the breath lines are exact anatomy. 虛而不屈: after a full out-breath the body is empty and it does not collapse; the frame holds its form. 動而愈出: the more freely the diaphragm moves, the more breath there is. a person who holds the chest full and tight has less air. singers, swimmers, and fighters all learn this. in partner work the same law holds: a body that is hollow in the centre and not stuffed with tension can give force again and again, and a rigid body gives it once. the last line also applies. much explaining of a movement brings a student to a dead end. the teacher shows it, and the student finds the middle in the body. a hawk takes a young hare. a late frost kills the blossom, and the same frost kills the pests. heaven and earth do not take the side of the hare or of the hawk, and because they take no side, both species go on. a world that favored one creature would soon have only that creature. so 不仁 is the condition of the ten thousand things. it is the reason there are ten thousand. the straw dog adds time: each leaf is fully a leaf in its season, and then it is litter, and the litter feeds the root. the bellows is the sky itself: the hollow between ground and cloud, where wind, weather, and breath move and are not used up. wang bi notes that the earth does not grow grass for the beasts. they eat it all the same. do the three bellows breaths once in the morning. then carry one question through the day: where do i act from favor? notice a small case, such as the person whose message you answer first, or the task you treat as beneath you. give the less favored one its full hour of care, as the rite gives the straw dog. and when the hour is over, for a task or a meeting or a mood, let it be over. in the evening, look back at your talk. where did many words bring you to the wall?

天地: the sky and the ground. 天地 is “heaven-earth”, two words used as one: the whole world, named by its roof and its floor. english “heaven” with a capital brings god, angels, and a place for the dead. english “nature” brings a thing that people stand outside and study. 天地 is neither. it is the sky that sends rain and seasons and the ground that carries and feeds, taken as one working pair. people live in the gap between the two. some modern readers make 天 the spiritual realm and 地 the material one. that split is western. in this text both are physical, and both are 自然, “so of themselves”. note what the line does with this pair. it does not say that heaven and earth are cruel. it says they lack one named human virtue.

不仁: an attack on the first virtue. 仁 was the highest word of the confucian school. confucius was asked about it more than about any other thing, and mencius told kings that a 仁 government would win the world with no need for war. the age also believed that heaven itself cared: heaven gave its mandate to good kings and took it from bad ones. so 天地不仁, four characters, strikes at two beliefs together: the school’s first virtue, and the idea of a cosmos with moral favorites. later passages go on with the attack: when the great dao is left, there is 仁 and duty (18); cut off 仁, and the people return to family love (19). the first readers heard a provocation. a translation that makes the line comfortable has lost it. see what the word holds.

仁: what kind of love?. 仁 is 人, a person, and 二, two. the shuowen defines it as 親也: “to be close, to treat as kin”. that is the centre of it. 仁 is warm, and it is graded: most for parents, then family, then neighbors, then strangers. the mohists attacked that grading and asked for equal care for all. english has no word of this shape. legge wrote “benevolent”, a word of victorian charity. “humane” keeps the 人, and we use it. “ruthless” goes too far, and “impartial” is too mild: it turns a shock into a compliment. the line says that the world has no inner circle. rain does not fall first on its own relatives. there is also an old medical sense: in the early medical books, 不仁 is numbness, a limb that does not feel. which do you hear in the line: no favorites, or no feeling?

straw dogs, before and after. a 芻狗 was a dog made of bound straw for use in a rite. the zhuangzi (chapter 14) tells its life. before the offering, the straw dogs are kept in a box and covered with embroidered cloth, and the priests fast before they handle them. after the offering: 行者踐其首脊, “people who pass tread on their heads and backs”, and the grass-cutters take them to burn for cooking. so the image is not simply “worthless things”. a straw dog is honored fully and discarded fully, and no one acts from love or from hate at either moment. the difference is time. each thing has its hour in the rite, and then the hour is over. heaven and earth treat the ten thousand things so: full care in the season, no clinging after. wang bi reads the two characters quite differently.

wang bi: grass, and dogs. wang bi does not mention the ritual object. he reads 芻 and 狗 as two things: 地不為獸生芻，而獸食芻；不為人生狗，而人食狗。 “the earth does not grow grass for the beasts, and the beasts eat grass. it does not produce dogs for people, and people eat dogs.” the point is that nothing is made for the sake of another thing, and yet each finds its use. on 仁 he is sharp: 仁者必造立施化，有恩有為, “the humane must make and set up, bestow and transform; they have favors and they have doing”. then: 物失其真, “things lose what is true in them”. care that arranges things damages them. heaven and earth 任自然, “leave it to what is so of itself”. most later readers prefer the straw dog of the rite. wang bi’s grass and dogs are still a fair picture of a world with no plan for you.

a sage with no kindness?. 聖人不仁 is harder than the first line. we accept that weather is indifferent. a ruler who treats the people as straw dogs sounds like a tyrant, and some rulers used the line so. but the book elsewhere gives the sage a strong care. passage 49: the sage treats all the people as children. passage 67: of the three things that the speaker holds most dear, the first is 慈, the love of a mother for a child. how do the two fit? 仁 in this period was a public virtue with a name: a ruler displayed it, graded it by rank and kin, and was praised for it. 慈 has no grades and no display. so the sage lacks the virtue that picks favorites, and keeps the care that does not. wang bi says only: 聖人與天地合其德, “the sage joins heaven and earth in their power”. can a person care fully and still not cling when the hour is past?

百姓: the hundred surnames. 百姓 is “the hundred clan names”. in early zhou only noble clans had a 姓, and the phrase meant the great families. by the warring states it had moved down and meant the common people in general. the shuowen explains 姓 as 人所生也, “that from which a person is born”, and the graph is a woman, 女, beside birth, 生. the image of the straw dog was close to fact for these people. the states of the time enrolled farmers by household for mass infantry armies. the shiji reports that after the battle of changping in 260 bce the army of qin killed some four hundred thousand men of zhao who had surrendered; the number is disputed, and the scale of such wars is not. a reader of that century knew very well how rulers used the hundred families. the line may be describing the sage. it may also be a bitter description of the age.

間: the gap in the door. 間 is a door, 門, with the sun, 日, in the opening. the older form of the character is 閒, with the moon, 月, and the shuowen defines that form in one word: 隟也, “a crack, a gap”. the picture is light that comes through the space between two door leaves. so 天地之間 is “the gap of heaven and earth”: the world as the opening between a sky-leaf and an earth-leaf. everything that lives is in that crack. english says “the universe”, a word for the total of things. the chinese phrase is about the room, and it does not count the contents. this is the thought of passage 11 again: the use of a house is in the part where there is nothing. here the house is the world.

橐籥: the smith’s bag and pipe. 橐 is a sack; the shuowen says 囊也, “a bag”. 籥 is a pipe. together they name the bellows of the early chinese foundry: a leather bag that is pressed and released, and a tube that carries the blast into the furnace. this was high technology. chinese smiths were casting iron by about the fifth century bce, long before europe, and cast iron needs a strong and steady blast. iron plowshares and iron weapons changed the wars of the age. so the image is not rustic. it comes from the workshop that armed the states. wang bi divides the word: 橐 is the bellows and 籥 is a musical pipe, and he says that both are hollow inside, with no feelings and no doing. he ends with the pipe: 若橐籥有意於為聲也，則不足以共吹者之求也, “if the bellows-pipe had a will of its own to make sound, it could not meet the need of the one who blows”. a bag with nothing in it gave the blast for a furnace. what does it give out?

不屈: does not bend, or does not run out. 屈 is first “to bend, to buckle”. on that reading, the bellows is empty and does not collapse: its hollow keeps its form, and that is why it can work. a second reading takes 屈 as “to be exhausted”, close to 竭. wang bi reads it so: 虛而不得窮屈, “empty, and it cannot be brought to an end”. then the line says that the emptiness is not used up, which is the claim of passage 4. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write the word with water, 淈; the shuowen gives one sense of that graph as 水出皃, “the look of water that comes out”. our “does not give way” tries to hold both: a thing gives way when it buckles, and a supply gives way when it fails. the line that follows chooses neither, and adds a fact: the more it moves, the more comes out.

three sayings in one passage. listen to the ends of the lines. 屈 and 出 rhyme; both belong to the old 物 rhyme group. 窮 and 中 rhyme; both belong to the 冬 group. the straw-dog lines have no such rhyme. the passage has three parts with three forms: a hard parallel statement, a rhymed riddle about a bellows, and a rhymed proverb about words. the oldest copy supports the idea that they were once apart. the guodian bamboo slips (about 300 bce) are reported to hold only the middle part, from 天地之間 to 動而愈出, with no straw dogs and no proverb. an editor joined them later. the join is good. all three parts say that the centre is empty: no favor in heaven, no stuffing in the bellows, no profit in many words. read the three parts once as one argument and once as three separate cards.

多言 or 多聞: talk, or learning. the pinned text has 多言, “many words”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 多聞數窮, “much hearing: again and again the dead end”. 聞 is “to hear”, and 多聞, “to have heard much”, was the usual praise for a learned man. the analects lists a friend who is 多聞 among the three useful kinds of friend. so the two readings have two targets. the received line warns the talker. the silk line warns the scholar: a person who is full of things heard comes to the end of them. the silk reading suits the bellows better. a bellows works because it is not stuffed; a head packed with learning has no draft. a book that is itself five thousand characters of teaching says this about learning. how do you read it there?

數窮: three ways to hit the wall. 窮 is the end of a road. the shuowen enters the older form 竆 and defines it as 極也, “the far limit”, with 穴, a cave, as its meaning part. in the modern graph a body, 身, stands under the cave roof with a bow, 弓, beside it; the shuowen takes the part under the roof as the sound. the word also means “poor”: a person with no way out. 數 before it has three readings. as shuo it is “often, again and again”: the talker meets the wall each time. many scholars read it as 速, “quickly”: much talk, a quick end. as shu it is “number, count, lot”, and wang bi writes 必窮之數也, “this is the reckoning that must end in exhaustion”. we give the first. english must choose one. the chinese reader may hold all three.
