守中: which middle?. 不如守中: “not as good as keeping the 中”. modern versions say “stay centered”, which makes 中 a calm state of the self. the passage gives a nearer sense. 中 is “the inside”, and the thing just described is a bellows, whose work is done by its hollow inside. to 守中 is to guard that hollow: do not stuff it with words. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 守於中, “keep to the within”. some scholars connect 中 here with 沖, the empty bowl of passage 4; the two graphs differ only by the water. it is not the 中 of the confucian zhongyong, the mean between too much and too little. and it is not a rule of silence. a bellows moves and gives a great deal. it gives because it does not try to hold anything.

legge softens the blow. legge could not let heaven be simply “not benevolent”. he wrote that heaven and earth “do not act from (the impulse of) any wish to be benevolent”. the brackets are his addition, and so is “any wish”. the line now says only that heaven has no motive of kindness, and a reader may still think that its acts are kind. for a missionary, a heaven without benevolence was close to a denial of providence. his “dogs of grass” is exact and plain. at the close he turns to rhyme and pads the line: “your inner being guard, and keep it free.” the chinese is four characters, 不如守中, with no “your”, no “being”, and no “free”. his “inner being” is the start of the long english habit to read 中 as a private self.

three breaths as a bellows. sit or stand. put one hand on the lower ribs. breathe out fully and wait. do not pull the next breath in; let the ribs open by themselves, as a pressed bag opens when the hand lets go. do this three times. the chest is a 橐籥: a bag and a pipe. it gives most when it is emptied well, and it never needs to be held full. then take the last line into the day. in one conversation, notice the moment when you have said enough and feel the wish to add more. stop there. keep the hollow. see if the other person fills it, or if the silence does the work.

虛 and 動: empty and moving. the bellows lines hold two pairs. 虛 and 動: empty and moved. 屈 and 出: giving way and coming out. a bellows is not a still void. it works by a cycle: it opens and is empty, it is pressed and gives air, and it opens again. the emptiness makes the movement possible, and the movement renews the emptiness. a reading that keeps 虛 alone makes the passage praise stillness and silence. a reading that keeps 動 alone makes it praise output. the last lines do rank: many words are “not as good as” keeping the middle. the preference is aimed at a habit, the mouth that keeps pushing when the bag has no air. it is not a rule against speech; the passage itself is speech. the first lines work the same way. 不仁 is not cruelty set above kindness. it is care that has no favorite. when does your silence give, and when does it hold back?

heaven and earth have no favorites, and the sage has none; each thing gets its hour and is let go.. heaven and earth have no favorites, and the sage has none; each thing gets its hour and is let go. can you accept this, or does something in you ask to be the exception? think of when you first learned that the world would not make a special case of you. how old were you? what did you decide then? hold the opposite: love means having favorites, and a care that is the same for all is no care. what moves in you when you take that side? whom do you treat as a straw dog after its hour? who has treated you so? which is harder for you: to be let go, or to let go?

many words reach a dead end; guarding the empty middle gives more than filling it.. many words reach a dead end; guarding the empty middle gives more than filling it. is that your experience of your own talk? in the house where you grew up, who talked and who kept quiet? which of them had the power? take the other side: what is not said is lost, and silence leaves people alone with their guesses. stay with it. what do you notice? when is your silence a hollow that gives, and when is it a wall? how can you tell the two apart from the inside?

芻 two bundles of cut grass. most characters are built from a meaning part and a sound part. this one is a pure picture, and the shuowen says so: 象包束艸之形, “it shows the form of grass wrapped in bundles”. look at the top half. the outer stroke that wraps from above and down the right side is 勹, the form used in 包, “to wrap”. inside it is 屮, a single sprout: a stem with a blade on each side. the shuowen builds its word for grass, 艸, from two of these sprouts, and the short form 艹 stands on top of nearly every plant name. now look at the bottom half. it is the same shape again. the character is one bundle on another: a stack. the shuowen’s definition is 刈艸也, “cut grass”: fodder for animals, and the material of the straw dog. in its cousins the bundle gives the sound, and a new part gives the meaning. the shuowen says so of two: 雛, a chick, has a bird, 隹; 趨, to hurry, has running feet. the later character 皺, a wrinkle, has skin. the simplified form 刍 keeps the wrap and reduces the grass to a small hook. the plain word for hay is at the head of the hardest sentence in the book. the thing itself is light, bound by hand, made for one day, and burned in the kitchen the next. ten strokes, and the lesson is in the count: five strokes, then the same five again. first a short stroke that falls to the left. second, the wrap: a horizontal that turns the corner, runs down the right side, and ends in a hook. third, inside, a short vertical that turns along the bottom, like the left half of a cup. fourth, a short vertical for the right side of the cup. fifth, the stem of the sprout, which falls through the middle and leans left. then the brush moves down and does it all once more. the danger is plain: two equal halves look like a ladder. watch how the lower bundle is set a little wider and a little heavier, so that it can carry the upper one. the two hooks should not be twins; the lower one is firmer.

仁 a person and the number two. four strokes hold the word that confucius cared for most. on the left is 亻, the form of 人, a person, when it stands at the side: a person seen from the side, one stroke for the body and one for the arm or leg. on the right is 二, two. the shuowen reads the parts together, 从人从二, and defines the word as 親也, “to be close, to treat as kin”. the usual teaching is simple: 仁 is what there is between two people. one person alone cannot have it. some scholars explain the two lines differently, as a mark of repetition in early script; the shuowen’s reading is the one that the tradition used. bamboo texts found at guodian are reported to write the word in another way, with a body, 身, above a heart, 心: care felt in one’s own person. cousins by the left side are easy to find: 信, a person and speech, to stand by one’s word; 休, a person by a tree, to rest; 伐, a person and a dagger-axe, to attack. the shuowen takes each of these as two meanings joined. so the script itself says that 仁 belongs to pairs and to kin. this passage says that heaven and earth are not a pair with anyone. they do not stand at one person’s side. four strokes. the first falls from the upper right to the lower left, long and light at its end. the second is the vertical; it starts under the middle of the first stroke and stands straight. these two make the person, tall and narrow. then the two horizontals. the upper one is short and sits high. watch the last stroke: the lower horizontal is much longer, it rises a little to the right, and it ends with a firm press. a character with so few strokes has nowhere to hide. each stroke is fully seen, and the white space between the two level lines is as much a part of the writing as the ink. in the small-script copies of the daodejing, such as zhao mengfu’s of 1316, the simple characters like this one give the page its room to breathe among the dense ones.

狗 the dog that knocks. chinese has two words for a dog, and they are made in two ways. 犬 is a picture. the shuowen quotes confucius on it: 視犬之字如畫狗也, “look at the character 犬: it is like a drawing of a dog”. 狗 is the other kind of character. the left side, 犭, is that same 犬 pressed thin to stand at the side, and it gives the meaning: an animal of the dog kind. the right side, 句, gives the sound; alone it means “bent, a hook”, and the shuowen defines it as 曲也, “curved”. then the shuowen quotes confucius once more, with a pun as an explanation: 狗，叩也。叩气吠以守, “狗 is 叩, to knock: it knocks out its breath in barks and keeps guard”. old glossaries add that 狗 was the young or small dog and 犬 the general word. in this passage the dog is made of straw, and its work is in the rite. dogs were real offerings too. the shuowen says under 獻, “to offer”, which has a 犬 in it, that the dog of the ancestral temple had a special name and that a fat dog was chosen to offer. wang bi adds a plain fact: people ate dogs. so the animal in 芻狗 was guard, food, and gift to the ancestors, and here it is a thing of straw that stands in for all three. eight strokes. the dog radical takes three. first a short stroke that falls to the left. second, the spine: it starts at the top, curves down in a long bow, and ends with a hook to the left. watch this stroke; it gives the whole left side its spring. third, a stroke that falls left from the middle of the spine, like a leg. then 句 in five: a falling stroke on the left; then the long wrapping stroke, a horizontal that turns, drops, and hooks inward; and inside that wrap a small mouth, 口, in three strokes, closed by its base line last. the mouth must sit high and to the left inside the wrap, with white space below it. the left side is all curve and the right side is all corner. in running script the three strokes of the animal are often made as one linked motion.

6 · the valley spirit. the valley spirit does not die. / this is called the dark female. / the gate of the dark female: / this is called the root of heaven and earth. / thin as silk floss, it seems to be there. / use it: it does not wear out. six short lines, all in rhyme. the first names a thing: the valley spirit, which does not die. the second gives it another name, the dark female, with the word for a cow or a mare. the third and fourth go to her gate, and call it the root of heaven and earth. the fifth says how it is present: fine as silk floss, and only as if there. the sixth says what happens when it is used: it does not wear out. the images run from land to animal to body to plant to thread. each is low, open, or fine. the passage has no ruler, no sage, and no advice. it only names. the contemplative traditions of china took this as a direct pointer. what in experience is like the open middle of a valley? wang bi says: the part of the valley that is not valley. in a mind, that is the open awareness in which thoughts and sounds appear. it has no form and no shadow, and it opposes nothing. thoughts are born and die in it, and it does not die with them. it is dark in the exact sense: it cannot be looked at, because it is the looking. it seems barely there, thin as floss, and attention can use it all day and not use it up. the passage calls this a mother. the comparison is with birth. it is not with a mirror or a void: what appears comes out of it, as young come from a dam. the passage gives no advice on rule, and a reader should not force one from it. its picture of power is still worth a leader’s time. the strong thing here is low, open, and productive. it is not high, full, or commanding. a valley gathers water, and it does not chase the water. the people in a group who are like this are often not the visible ones: the person to whom others bring problems, the one whose room is always open. much comes out of them, and they do not seem to tire. the common picture of the “passive” feminine hides this kind of strength, and organizations often fail to see it for that reason. passage 66 draws the political conclusion: the sea is king of the valleys because it lies below them. the heshang gong reading makes the whole passage a breathing lesson, and it works. the nose and mouth are gates. the breath goes in and out fine and unbroken. the breather does not force it, and so it does not tire. internal martial arts add the pelvis: the body’s own valley, the low basin from which legs and spine both grow. a fighter or dancer who moves from there has a root. a person who moves from the chest and shoulders is a tree with no base. try to stand with the weight low, knees soft, and the breath in the belly, and let someone push lightly on your shoulder. the valley does not push back. the push runs down into the ground, like water that has found the low place. walk into a real valley. the ridge is dry, windy, and bright, and little grows there. all the water of both slopes runs to the bottom. there the soil is deep and dark, and the springs come out: water half seen, as the shuowen says. the first farm villages of north china stood in such places, along the streams of the loess country. the valley does none of this by effort. it is lower, and things come. the other images are from the same countryside: the cow or mare that drops her young each spring, the root under the tree, the floss pulled from the silkworm’s cocoon. passage 39 has a line that this passage explains: the valley, when it holds to the one, is full. try the floss breath for five minutes. then use the passage as a question for one day: where is the valley in this? in a room, it is the empty middle that people cross. in a talk, it is the listening. in a piece of work, it is the open time before you know what to do. find it, and for once do not fill it. see what comes out.

谷: water half seen. the shuowen defines 谷 by what a valley does: 泉出通川爲谷, “where a spring comes out and runs through to a river, that is a valley”. then it reads the graph: 从水半見，出於口, “from water half seen, as it comes out of an opening”. so the valley in this book is not first a view between two mountains. it is a low, open place with water in it. because it is low, the water comes to it. because it is empty, there is room for a river, for fields, for villages. passage 66 says that rivers and seas are kings of the hundred valleys because they lie below them. passage 28 tells a person to be the valley of the world. both mawangdui silk copies are reported to write the word 浴, with water at its side. in english, a valley is often a place of sorrow or of shadow. here it is the place where life gathers. see the first plate.

神: a spirit, plainly. 神 is a religious word. it has 示, the altar, on its left, and the shuowen defines it as 天神，引出萬物者也: “the spirits of heaven, which draw out the ten thousand things”. it names the gods and spirits that received offerings: spirits of mountains, rivers, grain, and the dead. people of the warring states made offerings to the spirits of real valleys and streams. so 谷神, “valley spirit”, would not sound abstract. it would sound like the god of a place. some modern versions avoid the word and make the god into a “mystery”. the text then does a strange thing with this god. it gives it no temple and no name. it says only that it does not die, and calls it a female animal. is 谷神 one thing, “the spirit of the valley”, or two, “the valley and the spirit”: emptiness and its power? the two characters allow both. wang bi and the heshang gong commentary each go a different way.

wang bi: the valley’s empty middle. wang bi comments: 谷神，谷中央無谷也。 “the valley spirit is the middle of the valley, where there is no valley.” that is: not the slopes, which are something, but the open part between them, which is nothing. he goes on: 無形無影，無逆無違，處卑不動，守靜不衰。 “no form, no shadow; nothing it opposes, nothing it goes against. it stays low and does not move; it keeps still and does not decline.” and on the hedge in line five: 欲言存邪，則不見其形，欲言亡邪，萬物以之生。 “you want to say it is there? you do not see its form. you want to say it is not there? the ten thousand things are born by it.” for him the passage is one more picture of 無, the not-having of passage 11.

another reading: “feed the spirit”. the heshang gong commentary, the other great early commentary, reads the first word as a verb. 谷，養也: “谷 means to nourish”. the graph 谷 was often used for 穀, grain, which the shuowen calls 百穀之緫名, “the general name of the hundred grains”; grain feeds. on this reading the line is an instruction: 人能養神則不死, “a person who can nourish the spirit does not die”. the spirit is then the spirits that live in the organs of the body. the dark and the female become the nose and the mouth, the two gates where the breath of heaven and the food of earth go in. the passage turns into a manual of breathing: long, fine, unbroken, never forced. daoist practice read it so for two thousand years. the two readings, valley and body, do not cancel each other. the body has valleys too.

不死: “does not die”, not “immortal”. 不死 is two plain words: “not die”. the shuowen defines 死 with a water word: 澌也，人所離也, “to run dry; that from which people part”. “immortal” in english belongs to gods and souls, and it suggests a being that lives forever. the line says less, and something stranger. a valley’s open middle was never a living thing. it cannot be killed, as a hole cannot be broken. fill the valley with a landslide, and the emptiness has only moved. the age wanted a different kind of deathlessness. kings of qi and yan, and later the first emperor of qin, sent ships to look for islands of immortals and a drug of 不死. this passage was read in support of such hopes. what it says is that the thing that does not die is the low, empty one.

玄: dark, not “mysterious”. 玄 is a color. the shuowen says 幽遠也, “hidden and far”, and then 黑而有赤色者爲玄, “black with red in it is called 玄”: the dark of the sky before dawn, or of cloth dyed many times. passage 1 used it for the place where the named and the nameless are one: 玄之又玄，眾妙之門, “dark, and darker still: the gate of all wonders”. note that passage 1 ends on a gate, and this passage has a gate also. english versions like “mysterious” or “subtle” here. those are words about the knower: a thing is mysterious to someone. 玄 is about the thing: deep enough that light does not come back out. a womb is dark in this plain sense. so is the soil around a seed. what grows in your life only where it is dark?

牝: the mother of the herd. 牝 is not the word for a woman; that is 女. it has 牛, an ox, on the left, and the shuowen defines it as 畜母也, “the mother among farm animals”: a cow, a mare, a ewe. its partner is 牡, 畜父也, the sire. the shuowen adds a line from the book of changes: 畜牝牛，吉, “to keep cows: good fortune”. so 玄牝 is “the dark dam”. the word is from the farmyard, about breeding and birth, and the first readers heard that. english versions say “the mysterious female” or “the subtle feminine” and make her an idea. the chinese chose an animal. the same word returns in passage 61: the 牝 always overcomes the 牡 by stillness. why might a text about the first principle prefer the word for a cow to the word for a goddess? see the second plate.

not the “passive feminine”. western readers have often used this passage for a list: the feminine is passive, receptive, quiet, and dao is like that. the list comes from europe. look at what the 牝 does here. she is the one from whose gate heaven and earth come. nothing in the book is more productive. she is called low, still, and dark, and those are the conditions of her power. they are not a weakness that the text excuses. note also what is absent. the passage has no male partner, no father, no seed from above. later chinese thought likes balanced pairs, yin with yang; the laozi names yin and yang only once (42). its picture of origin here is a mother alone. the zhou world passed power, names, and ancestors through fathers. this text puts a nameless dam under all of it.

門: the gate of birth. 玄牝之門, “the gate of the dark female”, is a body image, and it is plain: the opening through which the young are born. 門 is a picture of a door with two leaves. the victorian translators could not write this. legge gives “its gate, from which at first they issued forth”, in verse, and calls her “the female mystery”. many modern versions say “gateway” and move on to cosmology. the image deserves a pause. a gate is not a wall and not a road. it is an opening that things pass through in one direction, and nothing stays in it. the book has three such gates: the gate of all wonders (1), this birth gate (6), and the gate of heaven that opens and closes (10). each is a place where what was not seen comes into view.

根: a root is not a “source”. 根 has 木, a tree, on the left. the shuowen defines it as 木株也, “the base of a tree, the stump with its roots”. translations often write “source” or “origin”. those are words for a spring or a starting point: you leave them behind. a root is not behind. it is under the tree now, in the dark, and it feeds the tree at this moment; cut it and the tree dies today. so 天地根 says that heaven and earth are growing things, and that the gate of the dark female is below them now, alive. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write 天地之根, with the same sense. passage 16 gives the practice that goes with the image: all things flourish, and each returns to its 根. the third plate looks at the character.

緜緜: silk floss. 緜 is silk. the shuowen builds it from 系, a thread that hangs, and 帛, silk cloth, and defines it as 聮微也, “joined and fine”. it is the loose floss drawn out from cocoons: so fine that one fibre can hardly be seen, and yet it does not break and has no joints. silk was china’s own craft, and every household knew this material by touch. doubled, 緜緜 is a sound-picture of something that goes on and on, very thin. the book of songs uses it for a line of gourds on a vine and for a family that does not end. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to add the sung particle 呵 after it, as in passage 4. our “thin as silk floss” keeps the object. english “continuous” or “everlasting” keeps the idea and loses the thread.

若存: as if it were there. 若 is “as if”. 存 is “to be there, to remain”. so 若存 is a hedge: it seems to be present. passage 4 hedged in the same place and nearly the same words: 似或存, “it seems, perhaps, to be there”. english versions often remove the doubt and write “it is always present” or “ever-existing”. the chinese does not say that. a thread of floss is a good picture of the reason. you know it is there because something is held by it. you cannot quite see it. wang bi states the two sides: say “it exists” and you find no form; say “it does not exist” and all things are born from it. the text stays between yes and no. the speaker of this book does not claim to see more than can be seen.

不勤: not toil, or not used up. 勤 is commonly “to toil, to work hard”; the shuowen says 勞也, “labor”. on that reading the line says: use it, and there is no strain. wang bi reads it so: 用而不勞也, “used, and not wearied”. most modern scholars take 勤 here as a loan for a word that means “to be exhausted”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write the word 堇, with no “strength” part, which shows only that the graph was not fixed. then the line says: use it, and it is not used up. the grammar matters. in both readings the thing that does not tire or run out is the valley spirit. some versions turn the line into a promise to the user: act with dao, and your work will cost you no effort. that is not what the six characters say.

a chant in six lines. every line of this passage ends on a rhyme. 死 and 牝 close the first two lines; they belong to one old rhyme group (脂). then 門, 根, 存, and 勤 close the next four; all belong to the 文 group. the lines are short, mostly four characters. two of them use the same frame, 是謂, “this is called”. it is a chant, and it is easy to learn by heart. many scholars think that this is older verse, taken into the book, and one early book gives it another source. that would explain its manner. the passage does not argue, and it has no “therefore” and no sage. it names a thing three times, each name stranger than the last, and then says how it feels to the touch. read the chinese aloud with the pinyin: si, pin; men, gen, cun, qin. the modern sounds have moved. 牝 had two old readings: one rhymed with 死, and the other gave the modern pin. the second set of four can still be heard.

from a book of the yellow emperor?. the liezi, a daoist book of uncertain date, quotes these six lines whole. it does not give them to laozi. it introduces them with 黃帝書曰, “the book of the yellow emperor says”. the yellow emperor was the legendary first ruler. in the fourth to second centuries bce many texts on rule, medicine, and long life were written under his name, and “huang-lao”, yellow emperor and laozi together, was the name of a school that advised the early han court. so these lines may have gone about as a separate verse before any laozi book existed, or two traditions may have claimed them. either way, the passage reminds us what the daodejing is: a collection. sayings from several sources stand side by side in it, and this may be among the oldest.

legge in rhyme. legge saw that the passage is verse, and he made english verse of it. the price was padding. “the valley spirit dies not, aye the same”: the last three words are his. “the female mystery thus do we name”: 牝, a female animal, has become a “mystery”, and the adjective 玄 has become the noun. the last line is the furthest from the text: “used gently, and without the touch of pain.” the chinese is 用之不勤, “use it; it does not wear out”. there is no “gently” and no “pain”; they came with the rhyme. his first line is his best. “dies not” is closer to 不死 than the “immortal” of many later versions.

breathe like floss. sit with the back straight and the belly loose. let the breath become quiet through the nose, and make it fine: so fine that a feather held under the nose would not move. do not hold it and do not push it. let it be long and unbroken, like floss drawn from a cocoon. that is 緜緜. after a few minutes, see if you can say that you are breathing, or only that breathing seems to be there: 若存. then notice that this fine breath costs nothing and does not run out. the old breath teachers took the whole passage as this one exercise. if you prefer the valley to the body, go to a low place with water in it, and sit there.

牝 and 牡: the half that is not named. every image here has a partner that the passage leaves out. 牝, the female animal, implies 牡, the male. 谷, the valley, implies the ridge. 玄, dark, implies bright. 若存, “seems to be there”, stands between present and gone. the text names the low, dark, female side and is silent on the other. that is a choice, and it has a target: a zhou world that honored the high, the bright, and the father’s line. the passage corrects the count. it does not make one sex passive and it does not make the other bad. a valley has no meaning without slopes, and its water comes down from the ridge. passage 28 keeps both in one line, 知其雄，守其雌: know the male, keep to the female. and the favored side turns. passage 39 says that a valley with nothing to fill it would run dry. the low place is low so that it can be filled. which half of this pair does your own world leave unnamed?

what is low, open, and barely there does not die, and use does not wear it out.. what is low, open, and barely there does not die, and use does not wear it out. do you believe that? name something in your life that has lasted in this way. what were you taught about people who are low and open: that they are strong, or that they are used? now the other side: what lasts is what stands up, takes a shape, and defends it. hold that for a while. what do you feel in the body? which of the two do you admire in public, and which do you rely on in private?

the root of heaven and earth is a dark female gate; origin is a birth and not a command.. the root of heaven and earth is a dark female gate; origin is a birth and not a command. how does that picture of origin sit beside the one you were given as a child? what do the words “dark” and “female” each carry for you? which of those meanings did you choose, and which were handed to you? take the picture that the passage leaves out: a bright maker who speaks, and it is so. what feelings come with that one? one picture may feel like home and the other foreign. why might that be, and what in your life rests on it?

谷 water comes out of an opening. the character has three layers. at the top, two small strokes lean away from each other. under them are two longer strokes of the same kind, like a roof. at the bottom is a square, 口, which means a mouth or any opening. the shuowen explains the upper four strokes as water, drawn only in part: 从水半見，出於口, “from water half seen, as it comes out of an opening”. a spring comes out of the ground between two slopes; the definition is 泉出通川爲谷, “where a spring comes out and runs through to a river”. many teachers explain the top differently, as the lines of two hillsides that fall toward a gorge mouth. both explanations draw the same place. compare 泉, a spring, and 川, a river, which is three lines of running water. 谷 has cousins that keep it as a sound part, and the shuowen says so of each: 欲, to desire, is 谷 beside 欠, an open mouth, 从欠谷聲; 浴, to bathe, adds water; 俗, custom, adds a person. in this book the valley is the first teacher. it is low and empty, and so the water comes. 谷神 is the spirit of such a place. mainland simplified script also uses this graph for 穀, grain, and that brings back by chance the old reading “to nourish”. seven strokes. the top pair comes first: a short stroke that falls to the left, then a short one that falls to the right. they do not touch. then the second pair, in the same order and much longer: a stroke that sweeps down to the left, and then the 捺, which travels down to the right, presses, and lifts to a point. watch how these two meet at the top and spread wide, wider than anything else in the character. they are the slopes, and they shelter the mouth below. the mouth takes three strokes: left side, then top and right side in one turn, then the base. it is small and sits in the centre under the peak. the whole shape is a triangle on a small box. regular script made the four upper strokes into separate marks. in seal script they are curved lines, and they look like running water.

牝 the cow, and a small spoon. on the left is 牛, an ox, made narrow to stand at the side. the shuowen calls 牛 大牲也, “the great sacrificial animal”, and says the graph shows the horns and head. the usual explanation is a head seen from the front: two horns that curve up, and a line for the face. as a side part it marks cattle and the things of cattle: 牧, to herd; 物, “thing”, whose first sense is commonly explained as a kind of ox; 特, a bull; 犧 and 牲, animals for offering. on the right is 匕. the shuowen gives 匕 two senses: a person turned round, and a spoon for taking up rice. in 牝 it says only that 匕 is the sound: 从牛匕聲. some modern scholars think that 匕 was itself an old sign for “female” in the names of animals; this is debated. the partner word is 牡, the male: 牛 with 土, which the shuowen also takes as sound. the pair 牝牡 is the common classical way to say “female and male” of beasts, and it stands in passage 55. shang diviners wrote of offerings of so many 牝 and 牡. so the word that this passage chose for the mother of heaven and earth comes from the herd book. 玄牝 is the dark dam. six strokes. the ox takes four. first a short stroke that falls to the left, then a horizontal that starts from it. third, the long vertical, which runs the full height. then the fourth stroke. in the full character 牛 this is a level line; here, at the side, it rises to the right. watch it: the tip points at the right half and gives it room. then 匕 in two strokes. the fifth is a short stroke that falls to the left, from right to left, and touches the stem of the next. the sixth is the great one: it comes straight down, bends, runs along the bottom to the right, and flicks upward at the end. this last stroke is longer than all the rest and carries the character like a cradle. left side tall and tight, right side open and round.

根 a tree, and an eye that will not yield. the left side is 木, a tree. it is one of the clearest pictures in the script: a trunk, a line for the branches, and two strokes below for the roots. so the roots are already in the meaning part. two characters are made from that picture by one added mark. 本, the root or base, is a tree with a short line across the foot of the trunk. 末, the tip, is a tree with a long line across the top. 根 is made the other way, with a sound part: 从木艮聲. the right side, 艮, is worth a look of its own. the shuowen defines it as 很也, “defiant”, and reads it as 匕 and 目: eyes that measure each other and do not give way, 不相下也. in the book of changes, 艮 is the trigram of the mountain and of keeping still. its sound family is large, and the shuowen marks each as a sound-compound: 限, a limit or threshold; 恨, resentment; 眼, the eye. a root is the still part of a tree. it holds while the top moves, and the chinese word keeps that still, stubborn 艮 in it. the shuowen defines 根 as 木株也, the base of the tree. the passage says that the gate of the dark female is this for heaven and earth: the part below, unmoved, which feeds the rest. ten strokes. the tree first, in four: the horizontal, the long vertical through it, a stroke that falls to the left, and then a dot. in the free-standing 木 the fourth stroke is a long sweep to the right. at the side it is cut down to a dot, so that it does not push into the right half. calligraphers call this yielding, 避讓. then 艮 in six: the top and right side of the eye in one turning stroke, two short horizontals inside, and then stroke eight, a long vertical on the left that turns at the foot and rises to the right. then a short stroke that falls to the left, and last the 捺, long, pressed, and lifted. watch the last stroke: it reaches under the right side, as a root reaches under a tree. the left half is narrow and high, and the right half spreads at the foot.

7 · the body put behind. heaven is long, earth is lasting. / what makes heaven and earth able to be long and lasting? / they do not live for themselves. / so they are able to live long. / for this reason the sage / puts the body behind, and the body is in front; / puts the body outside, and the body is kept. / is it not because the sage is without the private? / so the private is brought to completion. the passage has two parts joined by 是以, “for this reason”. the first part is about heaven and earth. they are long and lasting, and the text asks why. the answer is one clause: they do not live for themselves. so they live long. the second part applies this to the sage in two matched lines. the sage puts the body behind, and the body is in front. the sage puts the body outside, and the body remains. the close is a question with its answer built in: is it not by having nothing private that the private is completed? the passage uses very few words, many times. each key word comes back in a reversed position. the strongest sense of “me” is a sense of the body as mine: this skin to protect, this place in the line to hold. the passage calls the guarding 私, a ring drawn round oneself. contemplative practice often finds what the passage reports. when the guarding relaxes, the body is still here. it is more here: it breathes more easily, and it is felt more fully, because attention is no longer spent on defense. to outside the body is not to despise it. it is to stop standing over it as an owner. then “the private is completed” has a plain sense. what is most one’s own was never the fence. a caution belongs here too: this cannot be done as a tactic, because the one who uses the tactic is the fence. people follow those who do not seem to need the front place. that is an old observation, and passage 66 states it of kings. a leader whose first concern is position turns each decision into a move in a private game, and others feel it at once. a leader who puts the body behind gives the team no rival at the top, and, as wang bi says, things come home to such a person. but read the warning before you use this. humility as a technique is quickly seen through, and it is rightly resented. the first readers also heard a matter of survival: the ministers who stood in front were the ones who died. the text’s only model is the sky and the ground, which give all day and keep no account. 身 is the body, and the lines can be done as movement. in partner arts, the person who pushes the body forward to win gives the other a target and a handle. the one who keeps the body back, behind the hands and behind the moment, cannot be found, and arrives first. fencers and boxers know it as distance. taiji players know it as not leading with the chest. 外其身 has a body sense too: treat the body as outside, and do not fuss over it or tense it to protect it. a tense body is hurt more easily in a fall than a loose one. and the first stanza describes good breathing. the lungs do not keep the air for themselves, and for that reason there is always more. the sky holds no rain back for its own use, and the ground does not eat its own harvest. everything that heaven and earth have goes through them to other things. that is why they are still here: there is nothing in them to use up. a thing that lives for itself is a store, and stores run out or are robbed. a thing that passes life on is a channel. in a forest, the oldest presences are of this kind: the soil, the watercourse, the fungus threads under the ground that feed all the roots. the showy individual lives a season. the passage’s word for the self-serving is 私, written with the grain plant: a share of the harvest fenced off. the fenced share is the part that spoils. try the door practice for a day. or work with the first stanza alone. choose one thing that you have and tend to keep for yourself: knowledge, a contact, time, credit, a good tool. for one week let it pass through you to others, with no account kept. do not expect a return; that would be the old habit in a new form. at the end of the week, look at the thing itself. is there less of it, or has it lasted better because it moved?

長 and 久: not “eternal”. 天長地久: four characters, two matched pairs. 長 is “long”, first of things in space and then of time; the shuowen defines it as 久遠也, “lasting and far”. 久 is “for a long time”. many versions write “heaven is eternal, earth everlasting”. “eternal” is a word from greek and christian thought: outside time, with no beginning and no end. the chinese words are modest. they say that the sky has gone on for a long time and the ground has held for a long time. they are words that a farmer could use of an old tree. other passages even say that heaven and earth are not permanent: a storm does not last a morning (23). the phrase 天長地久 had a long life of its own in poems of love and loss. what lasts, in your experience, and what kind of thing is it?

不自生: two readings. 不自生 is “not self-live”. 自 can mean “for oneself” or “by oneself”, and 生 can mean “to live” or “to give life”. so there are two readings. one: heaven and earth do not live for themselves. rain and soil go to the ten thousand things; the sky keeps nothing. this is the usual reading, and ours. two: heaven and earth do not give themselves life; they do not strive to add to their own being. on this reading the line looks ahead to passage 50, where people die early because they “feed life too thickly”. wang bi takes the first reading and adds the cause: to live for oneself is to compete. our “for themselves” adds a preposition that the chinese lacks. notice the logic of the stanza. the chinese gives one reason for their long life, and it is a “not”.

wang bi: things come home. wang bi comments on heaven and earth: 自生則與物爭，不自生則物歸也。 “if they lived for themselves, they would contend with things. they do not live for themselves, and so things come home to them.” 歸 is the word for going back to where one belongs: a bride to her husband’s house, a traveller to the village, water to the sea. wang bi’s reason is practical. it is not a moral reason. a thing that takes for itself is one more competitor; a thing that does not is a place to return to. on the sage he writes: 無私者，無為於身也。 “to be without the private is to do no forcing on behalf of one’s own person.” he joins the 無為 of passage 2 to the body: the sage does not work at the self.

長生: what the phrase became. 長生, “long life”, is a simple phrase here. it became the name of the great project of religious daoism: 長生不老, “long life and no old age”. from the qin and han on, masters of methods taught breathing, diet, sexual arts, and above all alchemy, and they read the laozi as their scripture. emperors paid for the search. the first emperor sent ships to find immortals. several tang emperors died of elixirs made with mercury and lead. the irony is strong when the phrase is read in its place. this passage says that heaven and earth live long because they do not live for themselves. the elixir-takers wanted long life for themselves, with great effort. passage 59 uses the fuller phrase 長生久視, “long life and lasting sight”, and ties it to deep roots. it does not tie it to a drug.

a passage made of repeats. count the repeated words. 長 comes three times, 久 twice, 生 twice, 身 four times, 私 twice, and 能, “able”, three times. the whole passage has forty-nine characters, and it is built from a small set that turns round. the argument is made by the turns. 自生, “live for self”, becomes 長生, “live long”, with one character changed. 後其身 becomes 身先: the same 身 moves from the end of one phrase to the head of the next, and the body goes from behind to in front on the page. 無私 becomes 成其私. english style avoids repeated words and reaches for a synonym each time. that habit destroys this text. we keep “body” four times and “private” twice. there is one more detail: the shuowen says that 能 was first the name of a strong animal like a bear, and passage 10 will ask 能 six times.

身: the body, the person. 身 is the body. the shuowen says 象人之身, “it shows a person’s body”, and early forms are commonly explained as a figure in side view with a round belly. from “body” it came to mean one’s own person, one’s life, oneself. english versions usually write “self”: the sage “puts himself last”. that brings in a western inner self, an “i” inside that owns a body. classical chinese does not make that cut at this place. the 身 is the living person, the one who can be fed, promoted, hurt, and killed. so 後其身 is concrete: to put one’s own skin behind. and 身存 is concrete: the body survives. we write “the body” throughout, and the same in passage 13, where the whole argument turns on this word. where do you feel “self” when you say the word: in the head, in the chest, or in the whole frame?

後 and 先: two kinds of feet. both words are about walking. the shuowen defines 先 as 前進也, “to go forward”, and builds it from a person and 之, “to go”; the top part is commonly explained as a foot. a foot above a person: one who has stepped ahead. 後 it defines as 遲也, “slow, late”; its parts are a road-step 彳, a thread 幺, and a trailing foot 夊, and it is commonly explained as a foot held back by a cord. in this line both are positions in a column of people: the rear and the front. an ancestor is a 先人, “one who went ahead”. passage 66 says the same thing of rulers: to stand before the people, put your body behind them. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write an old form of 退, “to draw back”, for 後 here; some editions print the graph as 芮. that is a stronger act than “to put behind”. it is the last word of passage 9.

外其身: the body as an outside thing. 外 is “outside”, and here it is a verb: “to outside the body”. english has no such verb. it can mean to treat one’s own person as an outer thing, of no more concern than a stranger’s; legge has it well: “treats his person as if it were foreign to him”. it can also mean to leave the body out of the count when one decides what to do. the zhuangzi uses the same verb for stages of practice: after three days a student could 外天下, put the world outside; after seven, put things outside; after nine, 外生, put life itself outside. so the phrase became a term of meditation. in this passage the result is the surprise: the body that is put outside is the body that remains. the third plate shows where the character 外 comes from, and it is not what you expect.

身存: to stay alive at court. 存 is “to survive”. its usual partner is 亡, “to perish”, and the pair 存亡 was the urgent word of the age: states were being destroyed one after another, and their ministers with them. for a member of the 士 class who served a ruler, 身存 was not a figure of speech. shang yang made qin strong and was torn apart by chariots in 338 bce. wu qi reformed chu and was shot full of arrows at his king’s funeral. han fei went to qin and died in prison there. each had put his body in front. many sayings of the laozi can be read as advice from those who watched such careers: do not stand in the first rank, and the body stays whole. the passage gives heaven and earth as the model. its first readers also knew the names of the dead.

私: my grain. 私 has 禾, a grain plant, on the left, and the shuowen’s definition is a surprise: 禾也, “grain”. it adds that in the north the owner of the grain was called 私主人. the right side, 厶, has its own entry, with a quotation from han fei: 自營爲厶, “to draw a circle round oneself is 厶”. and under 公, “public”, the shuowen quotes him again: 背厶爲公, “to turn one’s back on 厶 is 公”. so the private is a ring drawn round a share of the harvest. mencius describes the old ideal of the fields in these terms: eight families each farmed a 私 plot and worked the lord’s 公 plot together. in the warring states, 私 was a hard political word: private armies, private interest against the ruler. 無私 was praise for an official. see the first plate.

無私 … 成其私. 非以其無私邪，故能成其私. the line is a question that expects “yes”: “is it not because of the sage’s having no 私?” then: “so the sage can complete the sage’s 私.” the same word ends both halves, once denied and once fulfilled. english versions often change the second one to “fulfilment” or “true self”, and so remove the scandal. the chinese keeps the bare word. what is the 私 that is completed? the lines above have said it: the body in front, the body kept. it may also mean more: what is most a person’s own comes to fullness only when the person stops guarding it. 成 is the word for a thing that ripens, as in 功成, the work done. our rendering drops the possessive 其 and does not say whose private it is. the text does not explain how this works. should it?

a paradox, or a trick?. a reader can take the passage as a method: step back in order to get ahead; look selfless in order to gain. chinese critics saw this early. legalist writers used the laozi as a handbook of rule by concealment; the han feizi has two chapters that explain it. later confucians, zhu xi among them, accused laozi of cunning for lines like this one and like passage 36: to take, first give. the charge has a clear answer in the text. the model is heaven and earth, and they have no plan. a sky that sent rain “in order to” last longer is not what the first lines describe. and a person who puts the body behind as a tactic has not put it behind; the 私 is still in front, watching. the passage describes what happens. it cannot be used as a lever. or can it?

legge, careful here. legge is at his best in this passage. he does not write “eternal”. he writes “heaven is long-enduring and earth continues long”, clumsy and correct. for 不自生 he gives both senses with a comma: they “do not live of, or for, themselves”: “of” for self-born, “for” for self-serving. for 外其身 he finds “as if it were foreign to him”. his frame shows in small ways. the sage is “he”, with “his own person”. and the last line becomes a matter of “personal and private ends” that are “realised”, the language of victorian moral accounts: unselfishness pays. the chinese says 成其私, and 成 is to ripen or complete. it is not a word for a payment. still, a reader with no chinese gets nearer to this passage with legge than with many later versions.

go through the door last. take the line in its most literal sense for one day. 後其身: put the body behind. at each door, let the others go through first. in a queue, do not look for the faster line. in a talk, let your point wait until the others have spoken. do it with the body, and do not make a show of it or tell anyone. notice what the body does when it is put behind: often a small protest, a tightness, a fear of being left out. that protest is the 私, the ring drawn round oneself. then notice what else happens. did you lose anything that mattered? were you, at the end of the day, less present, or more?

後 and 先: behind turns to front. three pairs carry the second half: 後 and 先, behind and in front; 外 and 存, put outside and kept; 無私 and 私, without the private and the private. in each line the first word turns into the second. the text does not say that behind is good and front is bad. the body does come to the front, and the private is brought to completion; the passage does not hide that or regret it. a one-sided reading can go two ways. one makes self-denial the goal and stops at 後. the other makes 後 a lever to get 先. both freeze a movement. if behind turns into front, then front is also a place that turns. a sage who arrives in front and settles there is now a person who stands in front, and the first stanza has said what lasts: that which does not live for itself. where are you in front now, and how did you come there?

the one who puts the self behind comes to the front; the one who sets it aside is kept.. the one who puts the self behind comes to the front; the one who sets it aside is kept. has this happened to you? or have you stepped back and simply been left behind? who showed you how to stand in a line, at a table, in a family? did that person go first or last? hold the opposite: no one will put you forward if you do not, and those who step back are forgotten. what rises when you take that as true? when you do step back, is some part of you watching for the reward? what happens when you see that part?

heaven and earth last because they do not live for themselves; what is passed on is not used up.. heaven and earth last because they do not live for themselves; what is passed on is not used up. do you agree? look at one thing you have given freely and one thing you have guarded. where does your sense of “mine” come from: a time of too little, a thing that was taken, a rule of the house? now take the other side: fill your own store first, because those who do not are drained by others. stay with it. what thoughts follow? what do you think of people who look after themselves first? is there any envy in that opinion?

私 a ring round the grain. left side first. 禾 is a grain plant, most likely millet, the staple of north china. the shuowen builds it from 木, a plant, with an added stroke at the top that shows the hanging ear: 象其穗, “it pictures the ear of grain”. look at the first stroke of the character: it lies nearly flat and droops to the left, a ripe head that bends the stalk. 禾 stands in many words of the harvest and of what the harvest pays for: 秋, autumn; 稅, tax; 租, rent; 和, harmony, which the shuowen takes as a sound-compound; and 利, profit, which by its modern parts is a grain plant and a knife. the right side is 厶. it now looks like a small triangle that does not close. the shuowen quotes han fei on it: 自營爲厶, “to circle round oneself is 厶”. the same source gives the opposite: 公, “public”, is 八 over 厶, and 八 means “to turn the back”: 背厶爲公. put the two sides together. the shuowen says flatly that 私 means grain, 禾也, and that 厶 is the sound. the picture that readers have always seen in it is still there: a ring drawn round one’s own share of the crop. english “private” comes from a latin word for “set apart, deprived”. the chinese word began in a field. the passage asks what happens to a person who does not draw the ring. seven strokes. the grain plant takes five. first the flat stroke at the top, written from right to left with a slight droop. then a horizontal, and the vertical through it. fourth, a stroke that falls to the left from the crossing. fifth, a dot on the right; in the free-standing 禾 this is a long sweep, and here it is cut short to make room. then 厶 in two strokes. the sixth starts high, falls to the lower left, and then turns back to the right along the bottom: one stroke with one sharp corner. watch it. the brush must stop and gather at the corner and then set off again. the last stroke is a long dot at the right that leans in and does not quite close the triangle. so the ring that han fei described is left open by the brush. the left half is tall and upright; the right half sits a little lower.

久 held from behind. three strokes, and an odd story. the shuowen explains 久 as a picture: 象人兩脛後有距也, “it shows a person’s two shins with something set against them from behind”. its first words are 以後灸之: to apply heat from behind, with the word 灸, the burning of moxa on the skin. the shuowen defines 灸 as 灼也, “to burn”, with fire, 火, as the meaning and 久 as the sound. so many scholars take 久 to be the first way of writing 灸: a person treated with burning herb at the back of the legs. the treatment is slow, and the herb must stay in place a long time. on this account the graph was borrowed for the word “a long time”, and fire was added below to keep the old sense. the shuowen then quotes a line from the rites of zhou, in which a craftsman 久 a piece of wood against a wall, that is, props it and leaves it, to see how it bends. both uses share one idea: a thing held in place and left. that is a good picture of what “lasting” means in this book. it is not eternity above time. it is staying put. 天長地久: the sky is long, the ground stays. a modern cousin by sound is 玖, a dark jade, used as the formal numeral nine. three strokes, and each one is different. the first is short: it starts at the top and falls to the lower left. the second starts near the top of the first, goes a short way to the right, turns, and then makes a long sweep down to the left. watch this stroke. it is the longest of the three; the brush presses at the turn and then thins as it travels, and ends in a fine point. the third is the 捺. it starts from the middle of the second stroke and runs down to the right, pressing as it goes, and lifts at the end. the two long strokes spread like legs, and the character stands on them. simple characters are the hard ones. with three strokes there is nothing to cover a weak line, and the open space between the legs must feel calm. its three strokes are among the eight that students learn from the character 永.

外 a divination at dusk. left and right are both old pictures. on the left is 夕, evening. the shuowen says 从月半見, “from the moon, half seen”: it is 月 with a stroke missing, the moon as it first shows at dusk. on the right is 卜, to divine. the shuowen calls it a picture of the scorching of a tortoise shell, 象灸龜之形, and gives a second account: 象龜兆之從橫也, the crack lines that run down and across. shang diviners read such cracks, and the graph keeps their shape: a long line and a short branch. the word is thought to imitate the sound of the shell as it cracked. now the shuowen’s account of 外. the definition is 遠也, “far”. the reason: 卜尚平旦，今夕卜，於事外矣. “divination values the early morning. now to divine in the evening is to be outside the matter.” the right time to ask the spirits was dawn. a crack made at night was off the record, beside the point: outside. modern scholars doubt the explanation and often take one part as the sound; the shuowen’s story is the one that readers knew for two thousand years. so “outside” in chinese began as a matter of timing and ritual, and not as a place. the phrase 外其身 gains from this. to “outside” the body is to treat it as not the matter in hand. five strokes. evening takes three. first a short stroke that falls to the left. second, a stroke that starts beside it, goes right a short way, turns, and sweeps down to the left, long and curved. third, a dot inside the curve; it must touch nothing. then divination, in two. stroke four is the long vertical, the tallest line of the character: it starts above everything else and comes straight down. watch where it stands: close to the left half, so that the two parts hold together. the last stroke is a dot that begins on the vertical, a little above its middle, and falls to the right. it is the branch of the crack. the left half leans and curves; the right half is one firm upright. writers let the dot at the right reach out a little, and it balances the long sweep on the left.

8 · water takes the low place. the highest good is like water. / water is good at benefiting the ten thousand things, and does not contend. / it stays in the place the crowd hates, / and so it is near to dao. / for a dwelling, the good is ground. / for the heart, the good is a deep pool. / for giving, the good is humaneness. / for words, the good is keeping faith. / for rule, the good is order. / for work, the good is ability. / for movement, the good is the right time. / only by not contending / is there no blame. the passage has three parts. first a statement and its reason: the highest good is like water, because water is good at benefiting all things, does not contend, and stays in the place people hate. for this it is near to dao, and only near. second, seven lines of three characters each, with 善 in the middle of every one: ground, depth, giving, faith, order, ability, season. they rhyme. third, a close that returns to the opening: only by not contending is there no blame. the word 善 is used nine times and never defined. the passage defines it by pointing at water. water has no shape of its own and no place that it insists on. for a contemplative reader this describes a mind that has stopped defending a position. such a mind goes where it is needed. it can stay with what people avoid: boredom, grief, the unlovely person, the low task. it does not need to rise above them. the second line of the seven is the centre: the heart is good when it is deep. a shallow heart splashes at each thing that falls into it. a deep one receives the same thing and stays still. the passage says that water is only near to dao, because water is still something. that is honest about practice too. a calm, yielding mind is close to the matter. it is not the matter itself. the passage reverses the usual map of an organization, where the good places are at the top. water goes to the low place, the work that nobody wants, and the text calls that place nearest to dao. a leader of this kind is useful to everyone and is in a contest with no one, and so has no enemies to manage. the seven lines are a short job description. take a position on solid ground. keep a deep heart. give as heaven gives, with no favorites. let your word be something that people can lean on. govern so that things find their own level. be competent. move at the right time. sunzi used the same water to teach how to win. this passage says nothing of winning. it says no blame. water is the master image of the soft arts. it sinks: the weight goes down to the feet and the low belly. it takes the shape of what it meets: the body does not set itself against a push but fits round it. it does not pull against force, and yet nothing wears stone as it does (passage 78). the seven lines can be read as movement instruction. 居善地: know your ground and stand on it well. 心善淵: keep the centre deep and quiet. 動善時: move at the right moment, neither before the opening nor after it. timing and not speed is what makes a throw or a strike work. try one walk today as water would walk: weight low, no hurry, round each thing in the way. follow one raindrop. it falls on a ridge and at once starts down. it does not choose the clean path; it goes into the soil, the ditch, the swamp, the places that people avoid. on the way it feeds each root that it passes and keeps nothing. where it stops, it becomes level: the only truly flat thing in a landscape is the surface of still water. in a deep bend of the river it turns slowly as a pool, and fish live there. it freezes and thaws by season. in time it reaches the sea, the lowest place of all, which for that reason receives every river. the whole passage is this journey, written as ethics. the text’s one reservation is exact: water is near to dao. begin with the glass of water. then take the hardest line of the passage into one day: stay in the place the crowd hates. find one such place within your reach. it may be the dull task that everyone leaves, the seat next to the person others avoid, or the role with no credit. go there on purpose and be useful, and do not mention it. watch for the wish to be seen as humble; that is one more way to contend. at night, ask what the low place gave you.

上善: nine times “good”. 善 appears nine times in fifty characters. it changes its part of speech as it goes. in 上善, “highest good”, it is a noun. in 水善利, “water is good at benefiting”, it is a verb of skill. in the seven short lines it stands in the middle of each, and readers do not agree on what it does there. english keeps “the good” (ethics) apart from “good at” (skill). chinese does not, and this passage depends on that. its goodness is a competence, like that of a good carpenter. 上 is plain too: “upper, top grade”. it is not the “supreme good” of western philosophy, a single highest thing that all else is measured by. the line says only this: if you want to see the best kind of good, look at how water behaves.

every school looked at water. water was the shared image of warring states thought, and each school used it differently. confucius stood by a river and said: 逝者如斯夫，不舍晝夜, “what passes is like this; it does not stop day or night.” mencius argued that human nature tends to good as water tends to go down. sunzi wrote that an army’s form is like water: it avoids the high and hurries to the low; it avoids the strong and strikes the empty. the guanzi calls water the blood and breath of the earth. and in the same tomb at guodian that held the oldest laozi slips, there was an unknown text that begins 太一生水, “the great one gives birth to water”. so this passage enters an argument that was already loud. what does it see in water that the others did not stress? the low place, and the lack of a fight.

water that benefits, water that drowns. 善利萬物: water is good at being of use to all things. the first readers knew this as state policy. the kingdoms of the time were built on water works. about 256 bce the qin governor li bing divided the min river at dujiangyan, with no dam, and made the chengdu plain a granary. in 246 bce the zheng guo canal watered the land north of the wei river. these two works fed the armies that conquered the rest of china. the same age used water as a weapon. in 453 bce the lord of zhi turned a river onto the city of jinyang, and in 225 bce a qin general broke the dykes and drowned daliang, the capital of wei. the passage speaks only of the first kind of water. its readers had seen both.

不爭 or 有靜: no contest, or stillness. the pinned text says that water benefits all things 而不爭, “and does not contend”. the two mawangdui silk copies are reported to differ. silk a has 而有靜, “and has stillness”, and ends the passage with 夫唯不靜. silk b has 而有爭 and ends with 夫唯不爭. so silk a writes 靜 in both places where silk b writes 爭. the two words sounded alike, and most scholars take the 靜 of silk a as a loan for 爭. both copies have 有, “has”, where the received text has 不, “not”, and that difference is not resolved. if 靜 is taken as written, the sentence changes its colour: water gives to all things, and it is quiet. 爭 is two hands on one object; the shuowen defines it as 引也, “to pull”. water has no hands. pour it between two people who are pulling at a thing, and it goes round both. see the second plate.

the place the crowd hates. 眾人之所惡: “what the many hate”. 惡 is read wu here, the verb: to loathe. the place is the low one. wang bi says it in three characters: 人惡卑也, “people hate what is low”. low ground is where the dirty water goes: the ditch, the marsh, the foot of the wall. the social sense is exact, and a confucian text states it with the same image and the opposite advice. the analects records: 君子惡居下流，天下之惡皆歸焉, “the noble person hates to dwell downstream, for all the filth of the world collects there”. that is the voice of a class that lived by reputation and rank. this passage answers it directly. the downstream place, where everything unwanted arrives, is the place nearest to dao. whom do you see there, in your own city?

wang bi: why only “near”. 故幾於道: “so it is near to dao”. the text does not say that water is dao. wang bi explains the gap in four characters: 道無水有，故曰幾也。 “dao is not-having and water is having; so it says ‘near’.” water is still a thing. it has a form, even if the form is borrowed from each vessel; dao has none. the word 幾 is worth a look. the shuowen gives it two senses, 微也 and 殆也: “minute” and “on the edge of danger”. it is the word for the first faint sign of a change, the point just before a thing happens. so 幾於道 is “at the very edge of dao”. water is the last visible thing before the invisible one. the passage is careful: it is praise that knows its limit.

seven lines with no subject. 居善地 is three words: “dwell, good, ground”. the other six lines have the same form. there is no subject and no connecting word. three readings exist. one: water is still the subject, and the lines describe it: in its dwelling it is good at ground, in its heart it is good at depth. two: the subject is a person, and the lines are a rule: for a dwelling, what is good is the ground. three: a causative: the one who dwells makes the ground good. our rendering takes the second and keeps it flat. english forces “for” and “is”; the chinese has neither. some modern versions make the lines a list of values for a successful life. read them once with water as the subject of each. the list is then one picture: a thing that lies low, runs deep, gives, keeps its word, levels, does its work, and moves in season.

心善淵: a heart like a pool. 淵 is the deep place in a river where the water turns slowly; the shuowen calls it 回水, “water that turns back”. passage 4 used it for dao: “a deep pool, it seems the ancestor of the ten thousand things”. here the heart is to be like that. a pool is not empty and it is not stormy. it is deep enough that what falls into it does not splash out again. legge wrote “abysmal stillness”, and the adjective now sounds like a mistake; the “abyss” behind it has a dread that 淵 lacks. notice that the chinese says 心, the heart, and gives it a water word. if the seven lines describe water, then this line gives water a heart. if they describe a person, it gives a person a riverbed. which is the image, and which is the thing?

與善仁 or 予善天. the pinned line is 與善仁. 與 can mean “to give” or “to be with, to associate”. so: “in giving, the good is 仁, humaneness”, or “in company, the good is the humane”. legge took the second and wrote “with the virtuous”. the line is strange in this book. passage 5 says that heaven and earth are not 仁, and passages 18 and 19 treat 仁 as a sign of decline. mawangdui silk b is reported to have a different line: 予善天, “in giving, the good is heaven”; silk a is damaged at the last word. 予 is plainly “to give”. on this reading water gives as heaven gives: to all, with no choice of who receives. that fits passage 5 exactly. many scholars think that a later hand changed 天 to 仁 and made the line more confucian. we keep the pinned text, and we render 與 as “giving” because of the silk reading.

信: a person and a word. 信 is 人, a person, beside 言, speech. the shuowen defines it as 誠也, “sincere, real”, and marks it as a character made by joining two meanings. a person standing by a word: to be 信 is to be someone whose saying and doing are the same. it is more than “sincerity”, which is a feeling. it is closer to “reliable”, and it also means the trust that others then give. the laozi values it and worries about it: “when trust is not enough, there is no trust in return” (17); “true words are not beautiful, beautiful words are not true” (81). water has its own kind of 信. it always runs down. it always finds its level. it shows a face as it is. how many of your words today could a person lean on?

正善治: water as the level. 正 is “straight, upright”. early texts often write it for 政, “to govern”, and most readers take the line so: in government, the good is order. confucius made a famous pun on the pair: 政者，正也, “to govern is to set straight”. now the shuowen’s definition of water: 水，凖也, “water is the level”. builders in china found the horizontal with a trough of water, and the modern word for “standard” is still 水準, “water level”. water is the one thing that makes itself perfectly even with no command. and 治, “order”, is written with the water radical; passage 3 told the story of flood control behind it. so in this line three water ideas meet: the straight, the level, and the channelled. order here is the evenness of a pond when the wind stops. no rule imposes it.

時: time as season. 時 has the sun, 日, on the left. the shuowen defines it as 四時也, “the four seasons”. that is the first sense of “time” in chinese: a time for a thing, as there is a time to plant. it is not first an empty line on which events are placed. from it came 時 as “the right moment”, a main virtue in every school. mencius gave confucius his highest title with this word: 聖之時者, “the sage who was timely”. farmers, generals, and ministers all lived by it. 動善時 says: in moving, the good is the season. water is the example again. it freezes in winter and runs in spring; it waits behind a stone and goes when the level rises. it is never early. see the third plate.

the seven lines are a song. each of the seven lines has three characters, with 善 in the middle each time. the last words rhyme in two sets. 淵, 仁, and 信 belong to one old rhyme group (真); the silk reading 天 belongs to it also. then 治, 能, and 時 belong to another group (之), and the last word of the passage, 尤, joins them. only the first line, 地, stands outside. so the list was made for the ear: a drum beat of three, the same word in the centre seven times, and two runs of rhyme. in mandarin the rhymes are mostly lost. read the lines aloud all the same: ju shan di, xin shan yuan. the fixed middle word works like the water of the passage. it does not move, and everything else is arranged round it.

無尤: no blame. 尤 is “fault”, “blame”, and also “resentment”: the grudge that others hold against a person. 無尤 is close to phrases in the book of changes, where a line of a hexagram is judged “no blame”. so the close of the passage sounds like a verdict from divination. the logic is simple. blame and grudge need a contest: a winner whom the loser can resent, a claim that can be called false. a thing that does not pull against anyone leaves no loser. the text does not say that such a person is praised. it says there is no 尤. compare the close of passage 2: only by not dwelling in the work does the work not leave. the form is the same: 夫唯不…, “only by not…”. the book states many of its results in this way, as an absence.

legge’s “excellence”. legge writes “excellence” for 善 throughout: “the highest excellence is like (that of) water.” it is a fair choice, because it keeps skill and worth together. his brackets then show a problem with the seven lines. he must add nouns: “(the suitability of) the place”, “(the conduct of) affairs”, “(the initiation of) any movement”. the chinese gives one bare word each time. for the heart he has “abysmal stillness”. for 與善仁 he has associations “with the virtuous”, a victorian rule about the company one keeps. his list has six items for the seven lines; the line on words and faith has no clause of its own. at the close he adds a whole situation: one “does not wrangle (about his low position)”. the text says only 不爭.

pour a glass of water. pour water slowly from a jug into a glass and watch it. it goes down. it takes the shape of the glass at once and keeps no shape of its own. it finds its level and becomes still. it does not argue with the glass. then drink it; it benefits you and asks for nothing. now carry one of the seven lines for the day. choose 動善時: in moving, the right time. before you speak in a meeting, send a message, or start a task, ask one question: is this the season for it? wait if it is not. water behind a stone is not weak. it is early, and it knows it.

上 and 下: the highest goes lowest. the first word is 上, “highest”, and the image that follows goes to the lowest ground. that is the passage’s pair: 上 and 下, high and low, with 爭 and 不爭, contending and not contending, beside it. the crowd puts the good at the top and hates the bottom. the text does not turn the ladder over and make low the new high. it shows one movement: water is “highest” in worth because it goes down and serves there. take away the going down, and nothing is left of the height. the preference for the low place answers a class that lived by rank. it is not a rule that low is good at all times. water also drowns, and the rain that reaches the sea rises again as cloud. not contending turns too: passage 66 says that no one in the world can contend with one who does not contend. is your not-contending a going down, or a quiet way to be above?

the best kind of good is like water: it serves everything and settles in the place people despise.. the best kind of good is like water: it serves everything and settles in the place people despise. do you agree that the despised place is near to the best? or does that sound like a story told to people who are kept low? which places and tasks did your family look down on? which of them do you still avoid? hold the opposite: good work rises, and the top is where a person can do the most. what do you feel when you take that side? think of someone you know in a low place. do you see water there, or failure? what decides it?

one who does not contend draws no blame.. one who does not contend draws no blame. is that true in your life? when has not contending kept you clear, and when has it cost you? what did a fight mean where you grew up: danger, sport, love, shame? take the other side: some things are worth a fight, and one who will not contend lets other people decide. stay with that. what arises? is your own not-contending a strength, or is it a fear with a good name? how would you know?

in movement, the good lies in the right time, not in speed or force.. in movement, the good lies in the right time, not in speed or force. where have you seen timing do what effort could not? are you by habit early or late? whose pace did you learn? suppose instead that waiting for the right moment is an excuse, and that the one who moves first makes the moment. what does that stir in you? what are you waiting on now? is it a season, or is it a fear?

水 a current, and what it levels. this is a picture, and you can still see it. the centre stroke is the main current. the strokes at the sides are smaller streams or the broken water at the edge of the flow. the shuowen reads it so: 象眾水並流, “it shows many waters running side by side”. compare 川, a river, which is three lines of current with no breaks. before the picture, the shuowen gives a one-word definition that every reader of this passage should know: 凖也, “the level”. water is what makes things even; the shuowen defines the related word 準 as 平也, “flat”. it then adds the cosmology of its own time: water is the phase of the north. when 水 stands at the left of another character it shrinks to three drops, 氵, and in that form it is the most common meaning part in the script. you have met it in 沖, 淵, and 湛 in passage 4, and in 治, “order”, in passage 3. at the bottom of a character it can take another form, as in 泰. its cousins by picture are worth learning together: 冰, ice, is water with two extra dots, by its modern parts; 永, “long, lasting”, looks like water with a dot and a bend on top and is commonly explained as a picture of long flowing streams. 上善若水: the best good is like this four-stroke current. four strokes. the first is the centre: a vertical that comes straight down and ends in a hook that flicks up to the left. everything hangs on it, so it must be truly upright. the second stroke is on the left: a short line to the right that turns and falls away to the lower left. it does not touch the centre stroke. then the right side, in two. the third stroke is a short one that falls to the left and meets the centre. the fourth is the 捺: it starts at the same meeting point and sweeps down to the right, pressing and then lifting. watch the difference between the two sides: the left hangs free, the right is joined. in cursive script the four strokes become one line that swings left and right like a stream over stones. in seal script the whole form is a set of curves that still look like water.

爭 two hands and one thing. the shuowen’s whole definition is one word: 引也, “to pull”. the usual explanation of the graph is a tug-of-war. at the top is a hand that reaches down: the form 爫, a short version of 爪, a hand or claw seen from above. in the lower part is another hand, the form that is written 又 when it stands alone and that here has become a shape like 彐. between the two hands, and through the lower one, runs a long hooked line: the thing that both are pulling. the shuowen says the character comes from 𠬪, a graph of two hands, one above and one below, with an added stroke. so the idea of contention in chinese is concrete and symmetrical: one object, two grips, opposite directions. it has no word in it for anger or for right and wrong. its cousins, in which the shuowen marks 爭 as the sound, keep the pull in other materials: 箏, the zither, whose strings are stretched tight; 諍, to remonstrate, a pull made with words; 淨, clean; 靜, stillness. the last is the surprise: the word for quiet contains the word for struggle, and silk a is reported to write 靜 for 爭 in this passage. the simplified form 争 has lost the upper hand’s fingers. water does not contend, and water has no hands. eight strokes. the upper hand takes four: a flat stroke written from right to left, then two dots, then a short stroke that falls to the left. these are the fingers, and they should spread like a small fan. then the lower hand: stroke five is a horizontal that turns the corner and comes down the right side. stroke six is the long horizontal through the middle; it sticks out on both sides and is the widest line of the character. stroke seven closes the bottom. then the last stroke: a vertical that starts at the top of the lower hand, runs down through all three horizontals, and ends in a hook to the left. watch it. it is the rope, and it is written last, after both hands are in place. if it leans, the whole contest falls over. the top is light and open, the middle is wide, and the hook at the foot is sharp.
