時 the sun’s seasons. on the left is 日, the sun. in the oldest script it is a circle with a mark inside; brush and chisel made it a rectangle. as a meaning part it gives light and time: 明, bright; 早, early; 昏, dusk; 春, spring. on the right is 寺. in this character the shuowen takes 寺 only as the sound: 从日寺聲. alone, 寺 was a government office in the han, and later it became the common word for a buddhist temple. an old form of 時 is commonly cited that has no 寺 at all: 旹, with 之, “to go”, above the sun. that older form is a small sentence: the sun goes. the shuowen’s definition is 四時也, “the four seasons”. so the first chinese word for time is a word about the sky and the farm: the sun’s position decides what work is due. the sound part has a family, and each is marked as a sound-compound in the shuowen: 詩, a poem, has speech; 持, to hold, has a hand; 恃, to lean on, has a heart, and you met it in passage 2. 持 opens passage 9. in modern chinese 時間, “time-gap”, is clock time, a term fixed in the modern period. the line here needs the old sense: 動善時, move in season. the simplified form 时 keeps the sun and a hand. ten strokes. the sun first, in four: the left side, then the top and right side in one turn, then the short line in the middle, then the base. as a left part it is narrow and is set a little high. then 寺 in six. a short horizontal, a vertical through it, and then stroke seven, a long horizontal. watch it: it is the widest line of the right half, and it lies level with the middle of the sun. below it comes one more horizontal, shorter. stroke nine is the vertical with a hook at its foot; it stands to the right of centre. the last stroke is a dot in the angle of the hook. the left part is small and still. the right part is tall, with three level lines at different lengths and a hook at the foot.

9 · full to the brim. hold it and fill it to the brim: / better to have stopped. / hammer it and sharpen it: / it cannot be kept for long. / gold and jade fill the hall: / no one can guard them. / rich, high in rank, and proud: / this is to hand oneself one’s own ruin. / the work carried through, the body steps back: / the way of heaven. five pairs of lines. a vessel held and filled to the top: better to have stopped. a blade hammered and sharpened: it does not keep. a hall full of bronze and jade: no one can guard it. wealth and rank with pride: a ruin left to oneself. then the fifth pair, which is shorter: the work carried through, the body steps back; this is the way of heaven. the first four are warnings and the last is the alternative. the passage moves from small to large: cup, blade, hall, career. each case reaches a peak, and the text places the danger exactly at the peak. the mind has its own brim. it holds a good state and tries to add to it: a calm sitting that i want to make calmer, an insight that i sharpen into a doctrine. the effort to fill is the thing that spills it. the blade is the same in thought: an idea honed too far turns brittle and breaks on the first hard fact. the fourth case is the subtle one. rich in understanding, high in the regard of others, and proud of it: that pride is how a person hands themselves their own ruin. the last line gives the practice. let each thing complete, and step back from it at once: the breath, the thought, the good deed. do not stay to own it. the sky does this every evening. the passage is plain advice for anyone with power, and history has tested it. do not fill every hour, every budget, every role to the top; an organization at the brim has no room for the next thing and spills at a touch. do not grind a team or a strategy to the last degree of sharpness; what is keenest fails first. do not build a show of wealth that then needs guards. and know the last step. when the work is carried through, step back. fan li left and lived; wen zhong stayed and died. some modern readers make this a tactic: leave at the top and go on to something greater. the text has no “next”. its model is a season, which finishes and does not ask what it gets. the body knows this passage well. a lung filled to the very top cannot do anything but hold; the useful breath stops short of full. a muscle at full stretch or full tension has no reserve, and that is where it tears. good posture is never the extreme of straightness. in martial practice a strike that is driven to its last inch leaves the fighter fixed at the end of it, with nothing to draw back; the teaching is to complete the technique and withdraw the body in the same motion. 身退 is literal there. even the blade is literal: a working edge is ground to a sound angle, and a razor edge is kept for razors. find the place in your own training where you always add one repetition too many. the sky’s way is easy to observe. the sun is highest at noon, and from that moment it goes down. the moon is full for one night. a river in flood is at its greatest just before it breaks its bank and loses itself in the fields. the fruit that hangs longest is the one that rots on the branch. nothing in nature holds a peak, and nothing tries. each season brings its work to completion and moves on: spring does not stay to see the harvest. human beings are the creatures that try to stay at noon. the passage does not call this a sin. it notes, with four examples, that it does not work. do the full cup walk once, with real water. then choose one of the four cases for a week. the cup: leave a margin in each day, and do not fill it. the blade: stop improving one thing that is already good enough. the hall: give away or put out of sight one thing that you keep mainly so that it can be seen. the tall horse: notice 驕 each time it rises, in the voice or the back of the neck. and once this week, finish something and leave the room before anyone can say that it was good.

the vessel that tips over. 持 is to hold a thing in the hands; 盈 is to fill a vessel to the top. the first readers may have thought of a real object. the xunzi tells that confucius visited the temple of duke huan of lu and saw a 欹器, a tilting vessel that hung by the ruler’s seat as a warning. he had his students pour water into it: 虛則欹，中則正，滿則覆, “empty, it leans; half full, it stands straight; full, it turns over”. confucius sighed: is there anything that is full and does not overturn? so the image of this line was a known teaching tool, and the two schools shared it. even without the device, the picture is plain. carry a cup filled to the brim across a room. every step is a risk, and all your attention goes to the cup.

盈: a full dish, a good bargain. the shuowen defines 盈 as 滿器也, “a full vessel”. the lower part is 皿, a dish. the upper part is 夃, and the shuowen’s note on it is a piece of market talk: 秦以市買多得爲夃, “in qin, to get much when you buy at market is called 夃”. a dish, and a great deal got: full. the word is one of the keys of the book, and nearly always with a warning. dao is used and does not fill (4). those who keep this dao do not wish to be full (15). the hollow becomes full (22). great fullness seems empty (45). a chinese reader hears the moon in the word also: 盈 is the usual term for the moon when it is full, just before it wanes. see the first plate.

不如其已: stop when?. 已 is “to stop” and “to be done”. 不如其已 is “not as good as its stopping”. english must decide when the stop comes. one reading: stop in time, before the brim. a second: it were better to have left off altogether, and never to have filled. wang bi takes a hard line and reads the second: a person who holds on to power and merit and then adds more is worse off than a person with no merit at all. our “better to have stopped” leans the same way. note what the line does not say. it does not say that a full cup is wicked. it says that a full cup must be held, and that holding it is worse than rest. the measure is practical: how much of your day goes to carrying something level?

揣 and 梲: forge it, or feel it. the second line has two problem words. 揣: the shuowen gives 量也, “to measure”, and then 一曰捶之, “another sense: to hammer it”. 梲 in the pinned text is a wooden staff, which makes no sense here. mawangdui silk a is reported to read 銳, “sharp”. silk b is reported to have 鍛而允之, with 鍛, “to forge”, and 允 as a loan for 銳. wang bi’s own comment uses 銳 too, so his copy had it; 梲 is a scribe’s slip that stayed in the printed editions. with “hammer” and “sharpen”, the line is about a blade: beat it thin, grind it keen, and the edge will not last. legge took the other sense of 揣 and wrote of one who keeps “feeling a point that has been sharpened”. some modern versions follow him and make the line about a probing mind. the smith’s reading has the older support. a very fine edge is the first part of a tool to chip.

wang bi: the force of the situation. on the blade, wang bi writes: 既揣末令尖，又銳之令利，勢必摧衂。 “you have hammered the tip to a point, and then you sharpen it more to make it keen: by the force of the situation it must snap.” his word 勢 is the term of the strategists for the way a situation leans, as water leans downhill. he uses it twice in this passage; of the full vessel he says 勢必傾危, “it must tip into danger”. so the ruin is not a punishment. it is in the shape of the thing. on the last line he looks at the sky: 四時更運，功成則移。 “the four seasons turn one after another; when the work is done, it moves on.” summer does not stay to be thanked. that is all he says about the way of heaven here.

the sharpest states. the age knew blades well. the southern states of wu and yue made the best bronze swords in the world; one, with the name of king goujian of yue on it, was found in 1965 with its edge still keen. the same states are the classic case of this line. wu sharpened itself for a generation, broke its great neighbor chu, marched north to claim leadership of all the lords, and was wiped out by yue in 473 bce. later the state of qin made itself the keenest weapon of all: every farmer a soldier, every rank earned by enemy heads. it conquered all the other states by 221 bce, and its dynasty lasted fifteen years. 不可長保: “it cannot be kept for long”. the line is about a tool. the first readers could put the names of states to it.

gold and jade in the hall. 金 in this period is metal in general and bronze above all; the shuowen calls it 五色金, “the metals of five colors”, with yellow gold as their chief. 玉 is jade, the stone of rank and ritual. 堂 is the raised main hall of a great house, where guests were received and wealth was shown. tombs of the time show what such a hall held: that of marquis yi of zeng (about 433 bce) contained some ten tons of bronze. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 金玉盈室, “fill the room”, with 盈 again; 滿 is commonly explained as a han replacement, to avoid the personal name of emperor hui, liu ying. the phrase then had a strange later life. 金玉滿堂 is today a new year blessing, painted on red paper: may gold and jade fill your hall. the warning was cut off, and the wish was kept.

驕: a very tall horse. 驕 has a horse, 馬, on the left. the shuowen’s definition is a measurement: 馬高六尺爲驕, “a horse six chi high is called 驕”. the right side, 喬, gives the sound, and the shuowen defines it as 高而曲也, “tall and curved”, like a great tree. so pride, in chinese, is first a big, spirited horse that is hard to hold. english has the same picture by chance: to be “on a high horse”. the horse was the status animal of the age. it pulled the war chariot, and cavalry was new in china in the fourth century bce. 富貴 is the standard pair for worldly success: wealth, and rank at court. confucius grants that all people want these two. the line does not attack them. it adds the third word, 而驕, “and proud”, and the ruin comes from that. see the second plate.

咎: ruin that you leave to yourself. 咎 is a word from divination. in the book of changes, line after line ends with 无咎, “no blame, no harm”. the shuowen defines it as 災也, “calamity”, and takes it apart: 从人从各, a person and 各, and 各者，相違也, “各 means to be at odds with each other”. a person at cross purposes: harm. the verb before it is the sharp part. 遺, read wei, is “to hand on, to leave as a gift or a legacy”. parents 遺 land and goods to their children. so 自遺其咎 is “to bequeath one’s ruin to oneself”. no enemy is needed, and no judge in heaven. the proud person is both the one who leaves the estate and the heir. our “to hand oneself” supplies “oneself” for 自, as english requires. see the third plate.

功遂身退: four words, or six. the pinned text has four characters: 功遂身退, “the work carried through, the body steps back”. many later editions have six: 功成名遂身退, “the work done, the name achieved, the body steps back”. legge’s edition was of that kind, and he translates the name: “when the work is done, and one’s name is becoming distinguished”. the shorter form is the older. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to have 述 for 遂 and an old form of 退, which some editions print as 芮. the guodian bamboo slips, the oldest copy, also hold this passage, and are reported to have the short form. so “name” was added. the addition is telling: later readers wanted fame to be secured before the retreat. in the old text nothing is secured. the work goes through, and the person goes back.

those who stepped back, and those who stayed. every educated chinese reader hears names in this line. fan li helped king goujian of yue destroy wu in 473 bce. then he left at once, and wrote to his colleague wen zhong: when the birds are gone, the good bow is put away; when the hare is dead, the hound is cooked. wen zhong stayed, and the king sent him a sword to die by. three centuries later zhang liang planned the victories that founded the han, declined a great fief, and retired to study the arts of long life. han xin, the general who won the battles, stayed near power and was executed in 196 bce. the saying 功成身退 became a proverb from these lives. note 身 again: it is the body that steps back, the same body that passage 7 put behind.

天之道: the sky’s way. 天之道 is “the way of heaven”, and 天 is first the sky. the meaning is given by things that anyone can watch. the book of changes says: 日中則昃，月盈則食, “the sun at noon begins to decline; the moon when full begins to be eaten away”. it uses 盈, the first verb of this passage. some versions turn 天 into “nature” with a capital letter, a modern idea, or suggest a providence that rewards the humble. the text has neither. it does not promise that the one who steps back will rise again, or will move on to greater things. the step back is the end of the sentence. summer finishes and goes. this is the first 天之道 in the book; the phrase returns in passages 73, 77, 79, and 81, each time as a pattern that people can match or resist.

four pairs and a verdict. the passage is built like a set of proverbs. four pairs of four-character lines come first: a case, then its result. the fifth pair breaks the pattern: four characters, then only three, 天之道, and the passage stops short, as its subject does. the end words rhyme. 保, 守, 咎, and 道 all belong to one old rhyme group (幽), and 已 at the end of the first pair is close to it. the four cases also move in an order: a cup, a blade, a hall, a person. that is from a thing held in two hands to a whole life at court. each case has the same shape. something is brought to its extreme, 盈 or 銳 or 滿 or 驕, and the extreme is the turning point. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to add the particle 也 to several lines, which slows them into prose.

legge’s “obscurity”. legge turns the first line round to make it clear: “it is better to leave a vessel unfilled, than to attempt to carry it when it is full.” the sense is right, and “carry” is a good word for 持. for the second line he takes 揣 as “feeling” a point. the last sentence shows his frame: “to withdraw into obscurity is the way of heaven”. “into obscurity” is his addition. the chinese says 身退, the body steps back, and does not say where to. a victorian reader knew that phrase from the lives of statesmen who retired to their estates. he also capitalizes “heaven”, and for his readers that word was close to “god’s will”. the chinese 天 here is the sky with its seasons.

carry a full cup. fill a cup with water to the very brim and carry it from one room to another. feel what the body does: the breath held, the eyes fixed, the slow steps, the grip. that is 持而盈之. now pour a third of it out and carry it again. walk normally. look around. then ask where in your life you are carrying a full cup: a schedule with no gap, an account that must not drop, a reputation that must be kept level. you do not need to empty it. find one place today where you can stop a little before the brim: one task not added, one more point not made, one helping not taken.

盈 and 退: the peak turns. each case sets a rise beside its end: 盈 full and 已 stopped, sharp and broken, a full hall and a lost one, 功遂 and 身退, the work carried through and the body stepping back. the passage does not condemn the rise. a cup is filled, a blade is ground, and the work is carried through; 遂 is success. its claim is about the peak: the full point is where the turn begins, as with the sun at noon. so the text favors stopping short and stepping back. the preference is a correction for people who can only add, and the courts of the time were full of them. it is not praise of the empty cup or of work left undone: 功遂 comes first, and 身退 follows. stepping back also turns. winter is where spring starts, and a retreat that is held as a merit becomes one more thing to be proud of. what are you still filling that was full some time ago?

filling a thing to the brim is worse than stopping; the full point is where the loss begins.. filling a thing to the brim is worse than stopping; the full point is where the loss begins. do you agree? where have you added one thing too many? what does “enough” mean in your history? was there a time of too little, and is that time still filling the cup? hold the other view: go to the limit, because half measures are how people hide from their own capacity. what do you feel as you hold it? which do you judge more in others, the one who overreaches or the one who stops early? why that one?

when the work is carried through, stepping back is the way of heaven.. when the work is carried through, stepping back is the way of heaven. have you done this? have you stayed too long somewhere? what would you be if you left the thing you are known for? notice the first answer that comes. take the opposite: the one who built it should stay and tend it, and leaving is a kind of desertion. stay with that side. what arises? which is nearer to your fear: to hold on and be pushed out, or to step back and not be missed?

盈 a dish with too much in it. start from the bottom. 皿 is a dish; you met it in 盜, the thief, in passage 3. the shuowen calls it a vessel for food and a picture. many vessel words stand on it: 盆, a basin; 盤, a tray; 盛, to fill a vessel, to be abundant; 盡, to use up, which the shuowen defines as 器中空也, “the vessel is empty”, the exact opposite of this character; and 盅, the hollow of a cup, the word behind the first line of passage 4. now the top. the shuowen reads the upper part as 夃 and gives it a note from the market: in the speech of qin, 夃 was to buy and come away with a great deal. as written today, the top looks like 乃 with 又, a hand, inside it. a dish, and much got: the shuowen’s definition of the whole is 滿器也, “a vessel that is full”. compare the two words for “full” in this passage. 盈 is full as a vessel is full: up to the rim, with a rim that can be passed. 滿, with water at its side, the shuowen defines as 盈溢也: full and running over. the book keeps coming back to 盈, because a brim is a turning point. the moon is 盈 for one night. the first line of this passage puts such a dish in two hands. nine strokes. the first is the hardest: one long stroke that goes right, turns down, steps right again, turns down once more, and ends in a hook. it makes the outer frame of the top in a single movement, and the brush must gather at each corner. the second stroke falls to the left from the top of the frame. strokes three and four are the small hand inside: a short line that turns and falls left, and a stroke that crosses it to the right. then the dish, in five: a short left side, the top and right side in one turn, two short verticals inside, and last the base. watch the base line. it is the longest and steadiest stroke, far wider than the dish walls, and it holds up the busy top as a table holds a full bowl. if the top is too large, the character looks ready to spill.

驕 six feet at the shoulder. the left half is a horse. the shuowen calls 馬 a picture, 象馬頭髦尾四足之形: “it shows the head, the mane, the tail, and the four feet”. turn your head to the left and you can find them: the three level lines are the mane that flies back from the neck, the long hooked stroke is the back and tail, and the four dots are the feet. the shuowen’s gloss on the animal is two strong words: 怒也，武也, “fierce, martial”. the horse was the engine of war. dozens of characters once sorted horses by color, age, and size, and this is one of them: 馬高六尺爲驕, “a horse six chi tall is a 驕”. six chi of the time is nearly a metre and forty, a big animal. the right half, 喬, gives the sound and helps the sense. the shuowen defines it as 高而曲也, “tall and curved”, and quotes a line of the book of songs about tall trees. it stands in 橋, a bridge, the tall curved thing of wood, and in 僑, a person who lives away from home; in both the shuowen takes it as the sound. so 驕 is a tall, high-headed horse, and then the manner of a person who is like one: proud. the simplified form 骄 has thinned the horse to three strokes and kept the tall tree. twenty-two strokes. the horse takes ten. a horizontal, the left vertical, two more horizontals, and the centre vertical: this is the head and mane. stroke six is the long one: across, down, and a hook back to the left; it is the back and the tail, and it wraps the four dots that come next. the dots are the feet. the first leans to the left, and the other three lean to the right. then 喬 in twelve. a flat stroke from right to left, a horizontal, and two long strokes that fall left and right: this top spreads like a tree. under it a small mouth in three strokes: left side, top and right side, base. then a frame in two: a left vertical, and a stroke across the top and down the right side with a hook. inside it a second small mouth, in the same three strokes. the two long falling strokes are the widest part.

咎 at cross purposes. the shuowen says this character is made of a person, 人, and the character 各. look for them. 各 is the top left part, 夂, with the 口 at the bottom: the person has been pushed into the upper right corner, where it is written as a vertical with a short stroke, and it splits 各 into two floors. first 各 itself. 夂 is a foot that points downward, a foot that arrives or drags. 口 is a mouth. the shuowen explains: 夊者，有行而止之，不相聽也, “one walks and another stops him; they do not listen to each other”, and so it defines 各 as 異辭, “words that differ”. the common modern sense of 各 is “each”: each on a separate road. scholars who work on the oldest forms commonly explain 各 another way, as a foot that arrives at a dwelling, the first way of writing 格, “to come”. now add the person. 从人从各…相違也: a person, and being at odds. the shuowen’s definition is 災也, “calamity”. harm is what comes when a person and the turn of things go separate ways. cousins with 各 as the sound, each so marked in the shuowen: 客, a guest, under a roof; 格, a tall tree, later a frame; 洛, the luo river. 路, a road, has a foot beside 各, and there the shuowen joins the two as meanings. the diviner’s verdict 无咎, “no harm”, was the best that most lines of the changes could promise. this passage describes people who write their own verdict. eight strokes. the foot at the top left takes three: a short stroke that falls to the left; a second that starts beside it, goes right a little, and then falls left; and a long 捺 that crosses both and runs down to the right. watch this third stroke. it is the longest in the character, and it shelters the mouth below like a roof with one long eave. then the person in the upper right, in two: a vertical, and a short stroke out from its side. they are small and stand in the space that the long 捺 leaves open. then the mouth, in three: left side, top and right side, base. the mouth is centred under the meeting point of the strokes above. the whole is a little off balance on purpose. the top leans left, the long stroke pulls right, and the small square at the bottom holds them.

10 · six questions. carrying the bodily soul, holding the one in the arms: / can there be no parting? / gathering the breath to the utmost softness: / can one be as an infant? / washing clean the dark mirror: / can it be without a flaw? / caring for the state, ordering the people: / can it be without cleverness? / heaven’s gate opens and shuts: / can one take the hen’s part? / bright and clear, reaching the four quarters: / can it be without forcing? / giving them life, rearing them. / giving life, not owning; / acting, not leaning on it; / raising, not ruling: / this is called the dark power. the passage has two parts. the first is six questions, each a four-character practice followed by “can…?”. carry the bodily soul and hold the one: can there be no parting? gather the breath to full softness: can there be an infant? wash the dark mirror: can it be spotless? care for the state: can it be done with no cleverness? heaven’s gate swings: can it be met as the hen meets things? see to the four quarters: can it be with no forcing? the second part is five lines that also stand in passage 51: give life and rear, and do not own, do not lean, do not carve up. this is named the dark power. the order runs from the soul outward to the world. these are the oldest instructions for inner practice in the chinese record, and they are given as questions. that form is the teaching. a command would produce effort, and each of these states is lost by effort. the body-soul and the wandering soul come together when attention rests in the body. the breath becomes whole, and the person soft as a newborn, when the breath is no longer managed. the mirror is clean when wiping stops. then the passage turns outward with no break: the same quality that sits on the mat is asked to govern a state and to meet the opening and shutting of the gate. it allows no private calm that ends at the door. the final lines describe what such a person is to others: a source that does not sign its work. the fourth and sixth questions are for anyone with authority. can you care for the people in your charge without cleverness, that is, with no technique for managing them and no hidden calculation? can you see the whole field clearly and still not force it? wang bi’s definition of cleverness is a fair description of much modern management. the fifth question is about crisis. when the gate swings, in a reorganization, a death, or a sudden opening, can you respond and not crow? the closing lines set the standard: bring things to life, feed them, raise them, and do not treat them as yours to carve. the word for this kind of leader’s power is dark. its sign is that people cannot say who did it. read as body instruction, the first three lines are a complete session. one: collect yourself into the body; hold it as one thing, and do not leave. two: gather the breath low and whole and let softness spread to its limit. internal martial arts repeat this line as a rule. an infant’s body is the model: no held tension, and for that reason a grip that surprises adults and a fall that does no harm. 柔 is green wood, which bends and is not broken. three: clear the attention until it reflects what comes and adds nothing. then the fifth line becomes a skill of timing. a gate opens and shuts, in a partner’s guard or in one’s own breathing, and the body follows it and does not lead. the six questions are a training plan. each image is taken from a living thing that is not yet hardened. an infant with the skull still open. a green branch that bends. a hen on her eggs, who does nothing that can be seen and gives the eggs the one thing they need. animals reared in a field. the mirror, too, was at first a basin of still water. against these stand the words that the passage refuses: to part, to be flawed, to scheme, to force, to carve. nature in this passage is not scenery. it is the early state of each thing, before stiffness, and the questions ask if a grown person, or a state, can live from that state again. the last lines add how the earth itself behaves: it brings forth, it feeds, and it does not hold title. use the ten-minute sitting with the first three questions. then take one outward question into the day. for a parent or a teacher: 長而不宰, raise and do not rule. find one decision that you usually make for someone in your care, and let them make it. for anyone who leads: once today, when you see clearly what should be done, do not force it. state what you see, and wait. at night, put the passage’s own form to yourself. ask, and do not judge: can there be softness here?

six times 能 … 乎. the first part is six questions on one frame: four characters that name a practice, then 能 … 乎, “can … ?”. the chinese has no “you”. it does not say who is asked, and it does not say that the answer is yes. legge made the first three into statements about a “he”; many modern versions write “can you…?”. both are additions. we mostly write “can there be” and “can it be”, and twice english forces “one”. this is stiff, and it keeps the question open to anyone, the speaker too. the six run in an order: the soul, the breath, the mirror of the mind, then the state, the gate, and knowledge of the four quarters. the first three face inward and the last three outward. the word 能 has a surprise in it. the shuowen says that it was first the name of an animal like a bear. see the second plate.

載: a hard first word. the first character has troubled readers for two thousand years. 載 is “to load, to carry, to ride in a carriage”. wang bi glosses it 猶處也, “like ‘to dwell in’”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write 戴, “to wear on the head”. a poem in the songs of chu, the “far roaming”, has nearly the same words in a journey to the sky: 載營魄而登霞兮, “carrying the bodily soul, i climb the rose clouds”. so the phrase may come from the language of spirit-travel in the south. others take 載 as an opening particle with no meaning. an old proposal even moves it to the end of passage 9 as an exclamation. we write “carrying”. the image that results is good: a person is something that carries a soul, as a cart carries a load, and the load can fall off.

魄 and 魂: two souls. early china gave a person two souls. the shuowen defines them as a pair: 魄，陰神也, “the 魄 is the yin spirit”; 魂，陽气也, “the 魂 is the yang breath”. a speech in the zuozhuan, given to the statesman zichan in 535 bce, says that the 魄 comes first, with the first shaping of a human being, and the 魂 after it. the 魄 belongs to the body, the senses, and the bones. the 魂 is light, and it wanders in dreams. at death they part: the 魂 rises, and the 魄 goes into the ground with the corpse. families climbed to the roof with the dead person’s robe and called the 魂 to come back. 營魄 is read by the heshang gong commentary as these two souls together. so the first question is exact: can the two be held as one, and not part? parting is the definition of death. english “soul” is single and immortal, and it cannot carry this.

抱一: to hold the one in the arms. 抱 is what the arms do: to hug, to hold a child against the chest. 一 is “one”. english versions write “embrace oneness” or “cling to unity”, and the phrase turns into an idea. the chinese is a posture. something is held close to the body with both arms, and it is single. what is the one? the book leaves it open. passage 42 says that dao gives birth to one. passage 39 lists what has “got the one”: heaven is clear by it, earth is at rest by it, the valley is full by it. passage 22 says that the sage holds the one and becomes the pattern for the world. here, in a line about two souls, it is also plainly “one thing, not two”. the image comes back in the next question, where the one who holds becomes the infant who is held.

專氣: the breath gathered. this line is the clearest sign that the passage is about a trained practice. a text of the same period, the “inward training” (neiye) in the guanzi, has the phrase 摶氣如神，萬物備存, “gather the breath like a spirit, and the ten thousand things are all there”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write our line with that same verb: 摶氣至柔. 摶 is to roll loose stuff into a ball with the hands. the received 專 means “single, undivided”, and the shuowen notes that it was also the name of the whorl of a spindle, the weight that twists loose fibre into one thread. both verbs say the same thing: scattered breath is made one. so there were teachers in the fourth century bce who taught people to sit, to make the breath whole, and to become soft. the laozi asks about that work. it does not explain it.

氣: breath, not “energy”. 氣 is first what you can see on a cold morning: breath, steam, mist. the simple graph 气 is commonly explained as a picture of thin layers of vapor. the fuller graph has 米, rice, under it; the shuowen says that this form was first a word for grain given to guests, with 气 as its sound. from breath the word grew: weather, the mood of a person, the fine stuff of which all things are made, thick in a stone and thin in a spirit. mencius spoke of a 氣 like a flood that fills the space between heaven and earth. modern english writes “energy”, a word from physics. 氣 is material; it can be gathered, spoiled, or lost, and you can feel it move. in this line the plain sense is enough. it is the breath in the nose and belly.

柔: wood that bends. 柔 has 木, a tree, at the bottom, and the shuowen defines it by wood: 木曲直也, “wood that can be bent and made straight”. it is the quality of a green branch. a dry stick snaps. so “soft” here is not “weak” and not “mushy”. it is “alive and able to bend”. passage 76 says so plainly: people at birth are 柔 and weak, and at death hard and stiff; plants alive are 柔 and tender, and dead are dry. “so the hard and stiff are companions of death, and the 柔 and weak are companions of life.” 致柔 is “to bring softness to its furthest point”. that is a strange aim in an age of iron, when every state wanted hardness. it is also a strange aim for a modern person, who is told to be strong. what in you is still green wood?

嬰兒: a necklace and an open skull. the two characters for “infant” are both pictures of tenderness. the shuowen defines 嬰 as 頸飾也, “an ornament for the neck”: a woman, 女, with two shells, 賏, above her, and it says the shells are a string. the usual explanation of the later sense is that a baby is what a mother wears at her neck and breast. 兒 is 孺子, “a small child”, and the shuowen reads the top of the graph as the head 象小兒頭囟未合, “with the fontanelle not yet closed”: the soft gap in a newborn’s skull. the infant is the book’s image of full power. it has made no distinctions yet (20). its bones are weak, and its grip is firm; it cries all day and is not hoarse (55). the grammar here is bold: 能嬰兒乎, “can (one) infant?”. the noun is used as a verb. see the first plate.

玄覽 or 玄鑒: the dark mirror. the pinned text has 玄覽, “dark looking”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write 玄監 or 玄藍, which editors read as 玄鑒, “dark mirror”, and most scholars now read the line so. the two graphs are kin: both are built on 監, which the shuowen defines as 臨下也, “to look down from above”, and which is commonly explained as a person who bends over a basin of water. the first mirror was that basin. the shuowen still defines 鑑 as 大盆也, “a large basin”. later mirrors were discs of polished bronze, and they needed constant cleaning. so: wash the dark mirror, and can it be without a spot? the mirror is the heart. the zhuangzi says that the perfect person uses the heart like a mirror. a thousand years later the same image was at the centre of a famous chan dispute: one monk wrote that the mind is a mirror to be wiped all the time, and huineng answered that there is no mirror and nowhere for dust to land.

wang bi: what cleverness is. the fourth question asks if the state can be cared for 無知, “without knowing”. wang bi shows which knowing is meant: 任術以求成，運數以求匿者，智也。 “to rely on technique in order to get results, to work calculations in order to find what is hidden: that is cleverness.” he names the two words that the legalist advisers used for their craft, 術, technique, and 數, calculation. then: 治國無以智，猶棄智也, “to order a state and not use cleverness is like the ‘discard cleverness’ of passage 19”. his wording, 無以智, agrees with mawangdui silk b, which is reported to read 能毋以知乎, “can it be without the use of cleverness?” (silk a is damaged here). the silk text is reported to have that same question a second time, in the sixth place, where the pinned text has 無為. other old editions exchange the two endings. the three versions agree on the pair: a ruler who can see everything, and who does not scheme and does not force.

愛國: not yet “patriotism”. in modern chinese 愛國 is “to love one’s country”, patriotism, and a reader today cannot help hearing it. in this line it is a ruler’s task. 愛 is “to cherish, to be sparing with, to take care of”. 國 is a state of the time. the graph shows the idea: an outer wall, 囗, round 或, which is commonly explained as a weapon, 戈, guarding an enclosed place. a 國 was first the walled capital, then the lands it held. the shuowen glosses it with the other word for a state: 邦也. that other word has a history. 邦 was the personal name of the first han emperor, liu bang, and han scribes replaced it with 國 in book after book. mawangdui silk b is reported to give this line in another order, with the people first: 愛民, “care for the people”, and then the state; silk a is damaged here. legge’s text had that order also.

天門: which gate of heaven?. 天門開闔: “heaven’s gate opens and shuts”. 闔 is a door leaf, and also “to shut”. three readings are old. for wang bi it is the gate that all the world passes through, and its opening and shutting are 治亂之際, “the turns between order and disorder”: the great changes of the times. for the heshang gong commentary, in the body, it is the nostrils, which open and shut with each breath. for the zhuangzi, heaven’s gate is the place where things come out of nothing and go back. the line fits each. it also completes a set: the gate of all wonders (1), the gate of the dark female (6), and now this one, which moves. one detail of the text is political. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 啓 for “open”. 啓 was the name of emperor jing of han, and later copies changed it to 開.

雌: the hen. 雌 has a bird, 隹, on its right, and the shuowen defines it as 鳥母也, “the mother bird”. chinese has separate words for the sexes of birds, 雌 and 雄, and of beasts, 牝 and 牡; passage 6 used the beast word. the cock crows and struts, and the hen sits. wang bi explains with a term from music: 雌應而不倡, “the hen answers and does not lead the song”, and 因而不為, “follows along and does not force”. so when the gate swings, in a crisis of the state or in a single breath, can one take the part that responds? passage 28 says: know the cock, keep to the hen. legge wrote “as a female bird”, which is exact. some old copies read 無雌, “without the hen”, and that reverses the sense. most scholars treat it as a slip, and the silk texts are reported to have 為雌.

lines that live in two places. the last five lines come again in passage 51, and there they have a subject: dao gives them life, and de rears them. many scholars think that passage 51 is their home and that they were copied here; without them the passage ends on its sixth question. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to have them in both places, and in this place to lack 為而不恃, “acting, not leaning on it”, which stands also in passage 2. 畜 is a farm word again: to feed and keep animals. the shuowen quotes a saying about the graph: 玄田爲畜, “‘dark’ and ‘field’ make 畜”, and the top of the character is in fact 玄, the word that this passage uses twice. with no subject here, the lines can describe dao, or the ruler of the fourth question, or a parent. read after the six questions, they sound like an answer.

宰: the one who carves. 長而不宰. 長, read zhang, is “to make grow” and “to be the elder, the head”. 宰 is the hard word. the shuowen defines it with a scene: 辠人在屋下執事者, “a convict who does service under a roof”, from 宀, a roof, and 辛, which it glosses as “crime”. a bound servant in a great house became the steward who ran the house. one of his duties was to cut up the meat of the sacrifice and share it out, and so 宰 means “to butcher”. a steward who shares out meat shares out power: 宰 became the title of the highest ministers, and later 宰相 is the chancellor of the empire. so 不宰 is “does not carve it up, does not dispose of it as master”. english “not ruling” is pale. see the third plate.

玄德: power in the dark. 德, de, is often translated “virtue”. that is right only in the old sense, as when one speaks of the virtue of a herb: the power by which a thing does what it does. in early china it was above all the quality of a good king, which drew people to him with no force. 玄 is “dark”. so 玄德 is a power that works and is not seen: no owner shows, and no credit is taken. wang bi says it best: 有德而不知其主，出乎幽冥, “there is the power, and no one knows its master; it comes out of the dark”. “mysterious virtue” gives the wrong tone twice. the phrase returns in passages 51 and 65. it had an odd fame later: liu bei, the hero-king of the three kingdoms, had xuande as his public name.

legge answers the questions. legge makes the first three questions into promises: “when the intelligent and animal souls are held together in one embrace, they can be kept from separating.” the 乎, the question mark, is gone, and the reader is told that the method works. his terms for the two souls are from european psychology, a rational part and an animal part; the chinese 魂 and 魄 are not ranked so. for the mirror he had the reading 覽 and wrote “the most mysterious sights (of his imagination)”, which makes the thing to be cleaned into bad visions. in the last three he keeps the questions, with a “he”. and at the end he adds a subject in brackets, “(the tao) produces (all things)”, from passage 51. each choice is defensible. together they turn six open questions into a doctrine.

sit with the first three. sit down for ten minutes with the first three questions, in order. first: feel the body as one weight on the seat, and let attention stay inside it. when it leaves, that is 離, parting. come back, and do not scold. second: let the breath become even and fine, and with each out-breath let one part soften: the jaw, the shoulders, the belly. ask how an infant would lie here. third: look at what passes through the mind as marks on a mirror. you do not need to scrub. see that the mirror itself is dark and clear behind them. do not answer the questions. they are in the text as questions, and the practice is to keep asking.

開 and 闔, 雌 and 雄: the gate does both. the fifth question has one pair in plain view, 開 and 闔, open and shut, and one pair with a half missing: 雌, the hen, with no 雄, the cock. the gate does both things by turns, and neither is the right one. breath comes and goes; times of order and disorder come and go. then the question asks for one part: can one be the hen, who answers? the text prefers that part here, and the reason is practical. a person who has to lead each swing of the gate fights half of its movement. the preference does not rank female over male or rest over action. passage 28 gives the whole of it: 知其雄，守其雌, know the cock, keep to the hen. the one who keeps to the hen knows how to crow. the other questions work the same way: 柔 is asked of a body that has bones, and 無為 of a mind that is 明白, bright and clear. when the gate last swung in your life, which part did you take?

the breath can be gathered to full softness, as in an infant, and that softness is whole, not weak.. the breath can be gathered to full softness, as in an infant, and that softness is whole, not weak. do you agree that softness can be strength? where have you seen it hold, and where have you seen it fail? when did you learn to harden: at what age, after what event? what did the hardness protect? now hold the opposite: an adult needs a firm shape, and softness is for those whom others guard. what happens in your chest and jaw as you hold that? what do you feel toward very soft people? what do you feel toward very hard ones? which feeling is stronger?

to give life and to raise, without owning or ruling, is the deepest kind of power.. to give life and to raise, without owning or ruling, is the deepest kind of power. is that how you were raised? is it how you raise, teach, or lead? think of something you made, or someone you helped to grow. where do you still hold title? take the other side: what you bring to life is your charge, and to drop the reins is neglect. stay with it a while. what comes? which have you met more in your life, the hand that held too tight or the hand that was absent? how does that decide which side you defend?

when the gate opens and shuts, one can take the part that answers and does not lead.. when the gate opens and shuts, one can take the part that answers and does not lead. in a sudden change, do you move first, or do you respond? is that a choice? who led and who followed in the pairs you watched as a child? what did you conclude from them? hold the opposite: someone has to crow, and waiting to respond leaves the first move to others. what thoughts and feelings does that raise? what would it cost you to take the other part once this week?

嬰 shells at a woman’s neck. the top is two of the same thing: 貝, a cowrie shell, twice. you met 貝 in passage 3, where it stood for money in 賢, 貴, and 貨. two shells side by side make 賏, and the shuowen defines that as 頸飾也, “an ornament for the neck”: shells on a string. under them is 女, a woman. the early graph of 女 is commonly explained as a figure who kneels with the hands crossed in front. the shuowen joins the parts, 从女、賏, and says 賏，其連也: the shells are the string. so 嬰 is first a necklace on a woman, and as a verb, “to wear round the neck, to wind round”. how did it come to mean a baby? the common explanation is the place where a baby is carried: at the neck and breast, with its arms round the mother like a string of shells. some scholars say that the word for “infant” only borrowed this graph for its sound. the cousins keep the necklace as the sound (the shuowen says so of 纓 and 鸚), and each has a clear meaning part: 櫻, the cherry, with a tree; 纓, a cap-string or tassel, with silk; 鸚, the parrot, with a bird. in this passage the word is a verb: 能嬰兒乎, “can one infant?”. recall the line before it: 抱一, hold the one in the arms. the holder and the held change places. seventeen strokes, and the first fourteen are one shape written twice. each shell is seven: the left side, the top and right side in one turn, two short lines inside, the base line, and then two small legs, one that falls left and one dot to the right. write the left shell, then the right. they must stay small and a little narrow, and they must not be exact copies; the right one is often a touch larger. then the woman, in three. stroke fifteen falls to the left, turns, and runs down to the right. sixteen falls from the right, crosses it, and sweeps left. watch the last stroke: a long horizontal through the crossing of the two, the widest line of the character. it is the shoulders that carry the necklace. many strokes on top and three below: the three must be strong and open, or the character falls forward.

能 the bear behind “can”. this common word, “can”, is a picture of an animal. the shuowen’s entry begins 熊屬, “of the bear kind”, and adds 足似鹿, “its feet are like a deer’s”. look at the modern form with that in mind. the two matching shapes on the right, each like 匕, are the paws. the lower left, which looks like 月, is 肉, flesh: the body. the small part at the upper left is commonly explained as the head, with its open mouth; the shuowen takes it as the sound. then the shuowen explains how a bear came to mean ability: 能獸堅中，故稱賢能, “the 能 beast is solid inside, and so worthy people are called 能”. strength gave the name to power in general: to be able. later the word was used so much for “can” that the animal needed a new graph. fire dots were added below, and the result is 熊, the bear of today; the shuowen says of it 山居，冬蟄, “it lives in the hills and sleeps the winter away”. english has a like story: “can” once meant “to know how”. now read the six questions again. each asks 能, and under each one there is a large, quiet animal that is solid inside. the passage asks about that kind of ability. cleverness is not meant. ten strokes, in four small blocks. upper left, two strokes: one that falls to the left and turns back to the right, then a dot. lower left, the body, in four: the left side, the top and right side with a hook at the foot, and two short lines inside. then the paws on the right, two strokes each, and the upper paw comes first. stroke seven is a short one that falls to the left. stroke eight comes down, bends, and runs right with a flick upward. nine and ten repeat the pair below. watch the two paws: they must not be the same. the upper one is kept small and tight, and the lower one opens wider and ends with a longer hook, so that the character stands on it. the left half is closed and upright. the right half has two curves, one above the other.

宰 a convict under a roof. two parts, one above the other. the top is 宀, a roof: a dot for the ridge and a line that comes down on each side. it marks buildings and what is inside them: 家, a household; 室, a room; 宮, a palace; 守, to keep a post, from passage 5. below it is 辛. today 辛 means “bitter, harsh”. the shuowen glosses its core as 辠, “crime”, and modern scholars commonly explain the early form as a chisel or blade for marking the faces of convicts and slaves. its family is dark, and the shuowen is plain about it. 辠, the old graph for crime, is 辛 with a nose, and the first emperor replaced it with 罪 because it looked too much like his title 皇. 童, now “child”, was once a male slave, and 妾 a female one; in both, the top is a short form of this blade. so 宰 is a marked person who serves under a roof: 辠人在屋下執事者. such servants ran great houses. one of them cut and shared the sacrificial meat, and the word came to mean “to butcher”; another kept the accounts, and the word came to mean “steward”, then “minister”. confucius’s student zai wo carried it as a family name. in 長而不宰 all the layers sound together: to be head of a house and not to carve it up as its master. ten strokes. the roof takes three: the dot at the top centre, a short stroke at the left end, and then a horizontal that runs right and ends in a hook. the roof must be wide, wider than most of what is below, because it has to cover. then 辛 in seven. a dot, a horizontal, and two small strokes that lean toward each other: these four are the top of the blade and look like 立. then stroke eight. watch it: a long horizontal, as wide as the roof itself, and the main level line of the lower part. under it comes a shorter horizontal, and last the vertical, which starts at the long line and comes straight down to a point. that last stroke is called a hanging needle. three level lines of three lengths stand on one needle, and the needle must be exactly upright.

11 · thirty spokes, one hub. thirty spokes share one hub. / right at its nothing / is the use of the cart. / knead clay to make a vessel. / right at its nothing / is the use of the vessel. / cut doors and windows to make a room. / right at its nothing / is the use of the room. / so: having it gives the gain; / not having it gives the use. three workshops. a wheelwright sets thirty spokes into one hub, and the cart works at the hole for the axle. a potter kneads clay into a vessel, and the vessel works at its hollow. a builder cuts doors and windows to make a room, and the room works where the wall is absent. after each one the same refrain, 當其無: right at its nothing. then a two-line summary: having makes the gain, not-having makes the use. the examples grow: a thing that carries you, a thing that holds your food, a thing that holds you. the passage has no dao, no sage, and no advice. you could read it aloud in a workshop as a plain fact, and all three craftsmen would agree with it. the fourth vessel is not named: the one who reads. old practice traditions take the room as the heart-mind and the door and windows as the senses. a mind is of use where it has room. one that is packed with opinions, plans, and commentary on itself is like a pot filled with clay; it has much substance and no place to receive. the passage does not tell you to empty yourself by force. in every example the emptiness is already present and already at work; someone made it with care, and it does not need to be defended. the contemplative step is only to notice it: the gap between two thoughts, the silence in which a sound appears. 有 and 無 are not enemies here. they make one pot. the hub is the center of the wheel and it does not push the spokes. it holds a place open, and the axle turns in that place. read 共 with its second sense and the picture is a court: thirty face one, and the one is empty at the center. a leader who fills the center with their own voice, will, and presence leaves no room for the axle. wang bi says it in a line: the hub commands thirty spokes because its nothing can receive. this is a real kind of influence, and the strategists of the time knew it. but do not turn it into a trick, an absence staged to pull others in. in the passage the emptiness is not a tactic. it is how the wheel is built. the couplet also warns managers who count only 利: that which you can measure is half of that which works. your body is built like the three examples. the joints work at their gaps: a hip or shoulder turns because the socket has space. the lungs, the mouth, the stomach, the heart’s chambers, the ear canal: each works at its hollow. stand and let your weight sink. find the center of the turning, low in the belly. chinese movement arts treat that place as a hub, and the limbs as spokes. power that goes through a still, open center is whole. power from a clenched center breaks at the joints. then breathe out fully and wait. the pause at the bottom of the breath is 無. you do not make the next breath. it comes into the room that you left for it. a valley is land with something missing, and for that reason water, soil, and villages collect there. a nest, a burrow, a hollow tree, a tidal pool, the cells of a honeycomb: living things build with walls and live in the gaps. soil is fertile when half of it is pore space for air and water; packed soil has the same minerals and grows little. a forest needs its clearings. time has the same structure: the fallow year, the winter, the night. thirty spokes were read as the days of a month that turn around a still center. the book’s other great hollows are near this passage: the valley spirit (6), the bellows between heaven and earth (5), the empty bowl of passage 4. do the five-minute count of nothings today. then choose one container in your life that has become solid: a shelf, a calendar day, a bag, an evening. do not empty it as a project of self-improvement. take out one thing and leave the space open for a day. see what the space is used for. in the terms of the last couplet: you already know the 利 of that which you removed. find out the 用 of the gap. painters call this leaving white.

thirty spokes, thirty days. why thirty? the number was a standard of the craft, and it had a meaning. the kaogongji, an early manual of the state workshops, lists what each part of a chariot stands for. the square body is like the earth; the round canopy is like heaven; and 輪輻三十，以象日月也, “the wheel has thirty spokes, in the likeness of sun and moon”: the thirty days in which sun and moon meet again. the bronze model chariots found beside the first emperor’s tomb have thirty-spoke wheels; other excavated wheels have fewer or more. so the first image is also a month. thirty days go around a center that is no day at all. what is the hub of your month?

共: to share, or to bow toward. 共 is “together, in common”: thirty spokes have one hub in common. the same graph was also used for the word now written 拱 (gong): to fold the hands in respect, to surround and face a center. the analects uses it in a famous line about rule by 德: the ruler is like the north star, which keeps its place while 眾星共之, “all the stars turn toward it”. many readers hear that sense here: thirty spokes pay court to one hub. then the wheel is a small picture of a state, and the center that everything faces is the one part with nothing in it. the mawangdui silk texts read 同, “same, together”, which supports the plainer sense (see their other differences). english “share” gives the first meaning and loses the bow.

轂: where the spokes gather. the shuowen defines 轂 as 輻所湊也, “that on which the spokes converge”. the graph has 車, cart, at its foot, which marks it as a part of a vehicle. a hub was a short, thick cylinder of hard wood. the wheelwright cut a ring of mortises around its outside for the spokes, and bored a hole through its center for the axle. the hole is the 無 of the line. without it the wheel is a fine wooden disc that cannot turn on anything. note the order of work: the hole is not left over. it is bored with as much care as the spokes are cut, to an exact size. the emptiness in this passage is always a made and measured one.

當其無有: where is the comma?. 當 means “to be exactly at, to match, to face”. 當其無 is “right at its not-having”: at the very point where the hub has nothing. the refrain comes three times and each time the next word is 有: 無 and 有 touch, with only a pause between them. where is the pause? the usual reading, which we follow, is 當其無，有車之用: “at its nothing, there is the cart’s use”. another reading, argued by the qing scholar bi yuan among others, moves the comma: 當其無有，車之用. here 無有 is one word, “that which has nothing”, as in passage 43, where 無有 enters a place that has no gap. the line then says: “right at its emptiness is the cart’s use”. the sense is nearly the same; the hole still has the credit. we lose only the turn from 無 to 有 across the pause. the chinese reader sees both cuts at once.

the cart is a war machine. 車 can be any wheeled vehicle, but in this period the fine spoked wheel belonged above all to the chariot. states were ranked by chariots: a “state of a thousand chariots” was a middle power, and a “state of ten thousand chariots” a great one. the chariot was the most complex object that a workshop made, and rulers measured their strength by it. so the first image in a passage about nothing comes from the arms industry of the time. a reader at a warring states court would hear it so: the strength of your army turns on a hole. the shuowen says the graph is a picture, 象形: a vehicle seen from above, with a body between two wheels on one axle.

埏埴: hands in wet clay. both characters have 土, earth, at the left. 埴 is the material: the shuowen says 黏土也, “sticky earth”, potter’s clay. 埏 (shan here) is the act. the old heshang gong commentary glosses the pair: 埏，和也；埴，土也, “埏 is to blend; 埴 is earth”: to work clay with water until it is even. some editions write 挻, with the hand radical. it is a set phrase of the craft. the confucian thinker xunzi uses the same two words for the opposite lesson: 陶人埏埴而為器, “the potter kneads clay and makes a vessel”, and so, he says, goodness is made by effort and is not inborn. xunzi looks at the potter’s hands. the laozi looks at the space between them.

器: a vessel, a tool, a person. 器 is a pot or bowl, and from that any made thing with a function: a tool, a weapon, a ritual bronze. english must choose “vessel” or “utensil” or “instrument”. the chinese word then goes one step further, to people. a person of ability is a 器. confucius says 君子不器, “the noble person is not a vessel”: not a specialist with one use. the laozi plays on the word often: when the uncarved block is split, it becomes vessels (28); the world is a spirit vessel that cannot be handled (29); the great vessel is completed late (41). so the pot in this line is never only a pot. if a person is a vessel, what is the person’s 無?

戶 and 牖: half a gate, a hole in a wall. 戶 is a door of one leaf. the shuowen: 半門曰戶, “half a 門 is called 戶”; look at 門 and you can see the two halves. 牖 is a window in a wall; the shuowen says 穿壁以木為交窻也, “pierce the wall and set crossed wood in it as a window”. the verb is 鑿, to chisel. walls were made of rammed earth, and in the loess country of the north whole rooms are still dug out of the hillside. built or dug, the room becomes a room by removal: you cut openings into solid earth. door and window return in passage 47: 不出戶，知天下；不窺牖，見天道, “without going out of the door, know the world; without looking out of the window, see heaven’s way”. confucius asked: who can go out except by the door?

室: the dictionary says “full”. 室 is the inner room of a house: a roof, 宀, over 至, “to arrive”. the shuowen explains it with a pun on a word of like sound: 室，實也, “a room is that which is full, solid”, and adds 至，所止也, “to arrive: the place where one stops”. a room, for the dictionary, is the place that you arrive at and fill with your life. the laozi line says the opposite thing about the same object: the use of the room is where it has nothing. the two do not contradict each other. a room can be filled because it is empty, and a room packed to the door is a store. look around the room that you are in now. how much of it is air?

有: to have, not “being”. 有 means “to have” and “there is”. chinese uses one verb for both: “the table has a cup” and “there is a cup on the table” are the same sentence. the shuowen ties the graph to 月, the moon; many modern scholars instead see a hand, 又, that holds a piece of meat. western philosophy translates 有 and 無 as “being” and “non-being”, and the capitals bring in greek questions about what is ultimately real. the chinese pair is nearer to the hand: what is there to hold, and what is not. in this passage 有 does two jobs. in the refrain it is “there is”. in the last lines it is a noun, “the having of it”. passage 2 has already said it: 有無相生, having and not-having give birth to each other.

無: the dancer who became “nothing”. the early form of 無 is widely explained as a dancer with long tassels or plumes in each hand; it is the first form of 舞, “to dance”. the graph was then borrowed for a word of like sound that means “not have”, and the dancer was given feet (舞) to keep her own word. the shuowen records the sense simply: 亡也, “to be without”. so 無 is first a verb, the opposite of 有: not-having. it is not “the void” and not “nothingness” with a capital, an abyss that western thought tends to fear. here it is specific and local: 其無, “its nothing”, the hole of this hub, the hollow of this pot. each thing has its own. we do not claim that the dancer is in the meaning. but it is good to know she is in the picture.

利: a blade in the grain. 利 is 禾, a stalk of grain, beside 刂, a knife. the shuowen defines it as 銛也, “sharp”, and the common explanation of the picture is a blade that cuts the crop. from “sharp” come the senses “smooth, favorable”, and from the harvest come “gain, profit, advantage”. it was a fighting word. the mohists made 利, benefit to all, the test of each policy. mencius opened his book against it: 王何必曰利, “why must your majesty say ‘profit’?” the laozi does not attack the word here. it gives the word a place: the 利 of a thing is in its substance, in that which you can own, count, sell, and tax. then it asks where the other value is.

利 and 用: two words where english blurs. the last couplet sets two words against each other, and english has trouble, because “use”, “benefit”, “advantage”, and “utility” run together. 利 is the gain that a thing gives as a possession: the clay has a price, the wall can be measured, the wheel can be bought. 用 is function: the thing at work. the shuowen defines 用 as 可施行也, “that which can be put into practice”; its early form is disputed. the couplet says that substance gives you a thing to have, and the nothing in it gives you a thing that works. neither is put down: 以為, “serves as”, is used for both, and 之, “it”, points back at the thing: having it, not having it. 利 is also plain serviceability: wood, clay, and wall give you a thing to work with. modern life counts 利 very well and has few measures for 用. legge struggled here; see his brackets. see also wang bi’s tighter version.

wang bi: gain leans on nothing. on the hub wang bi writes: 轂所以能統三十輻者，無也，以其無能受物之故. “that by which the hub can command thirty spokes is its nothing; it is because its nothing can receive things.” his sentence ends 故能以實統眾, “so it can, by the solid, command the many”; some editors correct 實, “solid”, to 寡, “few”: the few command the many. on the close he writes: 木埴壁之所以成三者，而皆以無為用也。言無者，有之所以為利，皆賴無以為用也。 “wood, clay, and wall are that from which the three are made, and all three take nothing as their use. what this says of nothing is: that by which having serves as gain leans, in each case, on nothing for its use.” his verb is 賴, to lean on, to depend. for wang bi the two halves are not equal: 無 is the root.

legge’s brackets. legge’s version of this passage is careful and full of brackets, and each bracket shows a place where the english needed help. he adds “(for the axle)” after the empty space, and “(from the walls)” and “(within)” for the room: he explains the pictures and does not trust them alone. in the last line he writes “(positive) existence” for 有, the vocabulary of 19th-century philosophy, and gives 利 as “profitable adaptation” and 用 as “(actual) usefulness”. you can see him try to hold the two words apart with adjectives. for 車 he writes “the wheel”, and so narrows the whole vehicle to one part. his “nave” for the hub is the old english word, and his room is an “apartment”. read his sentence aloud, then the chinese count: 有之以為利，無之以為用 is ten characters, five and five.

what the arts did with it. this short passage had a long life in the chinese arts. ink painters speak of 留白, “to leave white”: the unpainted paper is mist, water, sky, or distance, and it is composed with as much care as the brushwork. garden builders set a window in a wall to frame a view, so that the window does the work of a painting. players of the qin, the old zither, give weight to the fading of a note and to the silence after it. in each case the passage’s point holds: the empty part is not a remainder. it is where the work is used. look at a page of this app. the characters are 有. what lets you read them?

count the nothings. for five minutes today, look at made things and find the 無 in each. the cup: its hollow. the key: the cuts in its edge. the flute or the guitar: the bore, the sound hole. the shoe, the pocket, the bag. the doorway that you walk through, which you have never touched. then widen the view. a week: the day with no meetings. a conversation: the pause in which the other person thinks. music: the rest. do not make more emptiness yet. only notice how much of what you use each day is the part that is not there, and that someone made it with care, to an exact size.

the silk texts: a room that is never built. the mawangdui silk texts differ from the received passage in small ways that show how the text moved. they write “thirty” as one graph, 卅. they read 同 where we have 共. in the potter’s line they say 有埴器之用, “there is the clay vessel’s use”: the material is named again beside the hollow. in the builder’s line they have no 以為室, “to make a room”: you cut door and window, and right at their nothing is the room’s use. that shorter line is sharper. door and window are themselves the nothing, and the sentence never builds the room at all. the received text made the three examples match. which do you prefer: three even verses, or the older, uneven ones? this passage is not among the guodian bamboo slips.

有 and 無: wall and room. the passage ends on the pair that passage 2 set first in its list: 有 and 無, having and not-having, here joined to 利 and 用, gain and use. each example needs both. the hole in the hub is a hole because thirty spokes and a rim stand round it. the hollow of the pot has the shape that the clay gives it. cut away all of the wall and there is no room; there is weather. so the nothing here is a made nothing. it depends on the something as much as the something depends on it. readers who love this passage often turn it into praise of emptiness alone. the last couplet does not. it gives each side its own work with the same two words, 以為. the stress falls on 無 because the eye misses it; people count spokes and clay. the turn is plain in any kitchen: the hollow is for filling, and the full pot is emptied again. which do you trust more, what you have or the room you keep?

a thing works at its empty place; what is there gives gain, and what is not there gives use.. a thing works at its empty place; what is there gives gain, and what is not there gives use. do you agree? find one case in your day where the gap did the work. how do you count your own worth: by what you have and can show, or by the room you give? where did that way of counting begin? take the opposite for a while: what is there is what counts, and an empty space is a waste that someone should fill. what do you notice as you hold it? which do you fill first when you are uneasy: your time, your rooms, or a silence? what is the unease about?

the useful emptiness is a made one: it needs the spokes, the clay, and the wall around it.. the useful emptiness is a made one: it needs the spokes, the clay, and the wall around it. is that right, in your view? or is the best emptiness one with nothing round it? think of the structures in your life: rules, routines, walls. did you learn to see them as a cage, or as the thing that makes a room? now hold the other side: every wall is a loss of space, and freedom is to have none. stay with that. what feelings come? do you lean toward building walls or toward taking them down? what does each one protect you from?

無 the dancer who became “nothing”. the story of this character is a loan. the early form is widely explained as a person seen from the front, arms out, with a tassel, plume, or branch that hangs from each hand: a dancer in a rite. that graph wrote the word “dance”. the word “to not have” sounded nearly the same and had no picture, since you cannot draw a lack. so scribes borrowed the dancer for it. in time the borrowed sense took the graph over, and the dance was given a pair of feet at the bottom to make a character for itself: 舞. set the two side by side, 無 and 舞, and you can see the same upper body. the four dots at the foot of the modern 無 look like 灬, the form of fire in 熱 and 煮, but they are not fire here; they are what the brush made of the lower part of the figure. other ways to write the word are older in the laozi itself: the guodian slips mostly use 亡, “gone”, and the short form 无, now the mainland standard, is already listed in the shuowen as a 奇字, a variant form of the ancient script. in this passage 無 is exact and local: the bore of a hub, the hollow of a pot. a character with twelve strokes, the fullest on the line, says “nothing”. the dance has gone out of it and the dancer is still there. twelve strokes, in three bands. the top begins with a short stroke that falls to the left, then two horizontals, then four verticals, then a long horizontal beneath them. together they make a kind of fence. the discipline is in the spacing: the four verticals stand at even distances, and the gaps between them are as much a part of the character as the ink. the bottom band is four dots, written from left to right. watch them: each dot leans a different way, the first to the left and the last to the right, with the two in the middle as a bridge, so that the row reads as one movement and holds up the fence. in cursive script the whole character is reduced to a few loops. zen calligraphers in china and japan have written this one character alone on a sheet, again and again, for centuries.

車 a chariot seen from above. turn the character on its side in your mind. the box in the middle is the body of the vehicle, where the driver stands. the horizontal lines above and below it are the two wheels, seen edge-on. the long vertical through everything is the axle. this is a plan view, drawn as if by a bird, and the shuowen calls it 象形, a picture. oracle-bone and bronze forms are richer: many show two round wheels with spokes, the axle, the pole, and the yoke for the horses, and no two are quite alike. the regular script kept the least that is needed. as a part of other characters, 車 marks things that roll: 輪 (wheel), 軸 (axle), 輻 (spoke) and 轂 (hub) from this passage, 載 (to carry), 輕 (light: at first, a light cart), 軍 (army: the shuowen explains it as chariots in a ring, a camp; the top was at first 勹, “to wrap”), and 庫, a chariot under a roof: an armoury, a store. it is also a piece in chinese chess, where it moves like the rook. now read the line again with the picture in view: thirty spokes share one hub, and the use of the cart is at the hole. in the character, the stroke for the axle goes through the centre of every other part. seven strokes. a horizontal first: the upper wheel. then the box: left side, then top and right in one stroke with a corner, then two short lines, one inside and one that closes it. then a longer horizontal: the lower wheel, and the widest line in the character. the seventh stroke is the vertical through the middle, from top to bottom. watch it. all that is written before it is a stack of level lines with nothing to hold them, and this one stroke joins them and makes them stand; it must be straight and exactly central. the writer makes the axle last, and the wheelwright bores the hub for it with most care. in cursive script the box and its lines became a few quick turns, and that cursive shape was later fixed in print as the short form 车.

器 four mouths and a dog. count the squares: four 口, two above and two below. in the middle is 犬, a dog. the shuowen reads the scene simply: 象器之口，犬所以守之, “it shows the mouths of vessels, and a dog is that which guards them”. the four mouths are openings of pots or bronzes set out in rows; the bronze forms of the character already have four mouths around an animal. modern scholars doubt the guard-dog story, and some think the middle was at first a different shape, so hold it as the dictionary’s reading. the square 口 is the busiest part in the script. alone, a mouth. three in a stack, 品: goods, grades, to taste. four, 㗊, the shuowen’s heading for this very character: many mouths. with 犬 below two mouths, 哭: to wail. 犬 itself is a dog seen from the side, and it has become 大, a person with arms out, plus one dot; as a side part it is written 犭, as in 狗 (dog) and 狐 (fox). the meaning grew from pot to tool to ritual bronze to a person of ability; see the note on 器. what you see in the character is the lesson of the passage: each of its four corners is an opening. the ink only draws the rims. sixteen strokes, in three layers: two mouths, the dog, two mouths. each 口 takes three strokes: left side, then top and right side together, then the base. four boxes of one size would be dead, so a good hand makes the upper pair a little smaller and tighter, and lets the lower pair spread to carry the weight. between them the dog opens out: a long horizontal that reaches past the boxes on both sides, then a stroke that falls to the left and a stroke that falls to the right, like a roof over the lower pair, and its one dot. watch the white inside the four mouths. in a well-written 器 the four hollows are the same size and shine like windows. the brush makes the walls and the paper makes the use.

12 · for the belly, not the eye. the five colors make a person’s eye blind. / the five notes make a person’s ear deaf. / the five flavors make a person’s mouth go wrong. / galloping and hunting make a person’s heart break out in madness. / goods hard to get make a person’s walk stumble. / for this reason the sage / is for the belly, not for the eye, / and so leaves that and takes this. five lines of one pattern, then a conclusion. the five colors make the eye blind. the five notes make the ear deaf. the five flavors make the mouth go wrong. the horse hunt makes the heart break out in madness. rare goods harm a person’s walk. each line names a pleasure of the great houses, an organ, and the ruin of that organ’s own work. then the sage’s choice in six characters: for the belly, not for the eye. the last four characters are a formula that the book uses three times: leave that, take this. the passage has no word for sin or for virtue. it describes damage, and then a preference. attention has two directions. it can go out through the eye to what is over there: the next sight, the next thing to want. or it can rest in what is here: breath, weight, the felt inside of the body, which the passage calls the belly. the first has no end, and it thins a person out; this is the real sense of the five ruins. a mind fed on strong impressions loses the fine ones, and silence starts to seem empty. the passage does not teach contempt for the senses. a sense that is not flooded is sharper. after a day of quiet, one birdcall is vivid. the practice is a change of master. let the organ that knows “enough” decide, and the eye, the ear, and the mouth recover their own offices. read with the mawangdui frame, this is advice on what a ruler should want for a people and from a court. a state that runs on display, with ever finer goods, louder ceremony, and the excitement of the chase, trains everyone in it to look outward and to want more. it then finds that no one can see or hear plain things, such as a quiet report of bad news. the leader’s own case comes first. a person who is led by the eye is, in wang bi’s word, drafted by things: prestige projects, rare acquisitions, the hunt for the next win. “for the belly” is a hard and humble test for any plan: does this feed people, or does it only look good? the passage leaves that and takes this. each sense has a working range, and training respects it. a musician protects the ear, and a cook rests the tongue. an archer knows that the eye strains and blurs when it fixes too hard on the target. the line on the hunt is exact about arousal: speed and the chase bring a state in which the heart bolts and fine control is lost. fighters call it losing the centre. the remedy in every internal art is the one given here: bring attention down from the eyes to the belly. breathe there, move from there, and let the eyes be soft and wide and not grasping. the gaze that is not chasing sees more of the field. try a walk with the attention held low, behind the navel. an animal in its own setting is led by the belly. a deer eats until it is full and then lies down and chews;
