a wolf that has fed does not hunt for sport. its senses stay keen, because they are used at their natural level: the ear turns at a twig. human courts invented the things in this passage: color made into a system, sound made into bells by the ton, flavor made into an art, the hunt made into a parade, and stones made precious. these are nature raised to a pitch that no creature’s organs were made for. the result is given in animal terms: the heart of the rider becomes a mad dog. “take this”, 此, is in the shuowen a foot that has stopped. it is the creature at rest in its place. have one plain meal with the eye off duty. then choose one of the five for a week and lower its volume. colors: fewer screens after dark. notes: one journey a day with no sound in the ears. flavors: three days with no added sweetness. the hunt: one day with no race against the clock. rare goods: one week in which you buy nothing that you want mainly because it is hard to get. at the end, test the sense that you rested. see what a plain thing looks, sounds, or tastes like now.

五色: the five correct colors. “the five colors” is not a loose phrase for “many colors”. it is a set: blue-green, red, yellow, white, and black, the five that ritual counted as pure. court robes, banners, lacquer, and the painted earth of altars used them by rule, and a rank could be read from them. in the third century bce the thinker zou yan and others tied each color to a direction, a season, a metal or element, and a dynasty, and new rulers chose their color to show their right to rule. the word 色 has its own history. the shuowen defines it as 顔气也, “the air of the face”: the color that comes and goes in a person’s look. from there it means beauty, and desire. so the first line is about the eye at court. it names a complete, official, costly display.

who had all five?. five colors, five notes, five flavors: three ordered systems, and each belonged to the rich. the five notes are the scale of court music, played on sets of bronze bells that only a lord could cast. the five flavors, sour, bitter, sweet, pungent, and salty, are the art of the palace cook. then come the horse hunt and the rare goods. a farmer of the time ate millet, wore undyed hemp, and heard a drum at the harvest. so the passage is not about the human senses in general. it is a description of how rulers lived, and the first critics of that life were the mohists, who wrote a whole chapter “against music” on the cost of bells and feasts to the people. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to make the frame plain: they add “in the sage’s rule” before the last line. the zhuangzi has its own form of the list.

令: the colors give the order. the verb in all five lines is 令. the shuowen defines it as 發號也, “to issue a command”, and that is its first sense: an order from above. it then came to mean “to cause”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to use the plainer 使, “to make, to cause”, in each line. with 令 the lines have an edge that english “make” does not keep: the five colors command the eye, and the eye obeys. the person in the line is 人, “a person, people”, with no “you” and no “men”; our “a person’s” follows that. note also that the object is each time a single organ and its function. the colors do not blind “the mind”. they blind 目, the eye. the harm is put exactly where the pleasure enters. what gives your eye its orders in the course of a day?

盲: the eye that is gone. 盲 is 亡 above 目. 目 is the eye, a picture turned on its side. 亡 means “gone, lost”; the shuowen defines it as 逃也, “to flee”. the shuowen takes 亡 here as the sound and defines the whole word: 目無牟子, “an eye with no pupil”. sound and sense agree: the seeing part of the eye has left. the line does not say that colors are bad. it says something that the body confirms. stare at a bright thing and you see less afterwards; live among strong stimuli and you stop seeing plain ones. the blindness here is a loss of fineness. a person who has had every color cannot see grey. passage 35 gives the opposite case: dao has no flavor, and you look at it and there is not enough to see, and its use does not run out. see the first plate.

聾: a dragon over the ear. 聾 is an ear, 耳, under a dragon, 龍. the shuowen says that the dragon gives only the sound, long, and it defines the word plainly: 無聞也, “to hear nothing”. still, generations of readers have seen the picture, and it is hard not to: a roar so great that the ear under it is finished. the music in question was very loud. a set of sixty-five bronze bells was found in the tomb of marquis yi of zeng (about 433 bce); the tomb also held stone chimes, drums, and pipes, enough for an ensemble of twenty or more. the shuowen’s gloss on the ear is worth setting beside the line: 主聽也, “it is in charge of listening”. an ear has an office. the five notes, when there are too many of them, put it out of office. see the second plate.

爽: a word with two faces. 爽 is the surprise of the passage. the shuowen defines it as 明也, “bright, clear”, and that is its usual sense: a clear dawn, a brisk wind. in modern speech it is the word for a thing that feels great. here it means the reverse. wang bi glosses it: 爽，差失也, “爽 is to miss, to go wrong”, and adds 失口之用, “the mouth loses its function”. a palate that has had every flavor can no longer taste. classical chinese has several words like this, with two opposite senses; passage 3 showed another, 亂, which is both “tangle” and “to set in order”. the effect on a reader is a small shock: five flavors make the mouth 爽, and for an instant the line says “bright”, and then it says “ruined”. the pleasure and the damage are one word.

the royal hunt. 馳騁畋獵 is four characters of speed. 馳 is “to drive hard” and 騁 “to gallop straight”; both are written with the horse. 畋 is to hunt across open fields, and the shuowen gives its base sense as 平田也, “to level a field”; 獵, with the dog radical, is 放獵逐禽, “to loose the hounds and chase game”. this was the sport of kings and lords. a great hunt used chariots, beaters, and nets over miles of country, and it served also as a drill for war. it was a known political sore. mencius told king xuan of qi that his people saw the royal park, forty li square, as a trap in the middle of the state, because to kill a deer in it was punished like murder. farmers’ fields lay under the hooves. the line says what the hunt does to the hunter.

發狂: the heart shoots off. 狂 has the dog radical, and the shuowen’s definition is blunt: 狾犬也, “a mad dog”. the word then covers every kind of wildness in people: frenzy, mania, and also the free, bold manner that confucius half admired in certain students. 發 is an archer’s word. the shuowen glosses it as the release of an arrow from the bow. so 心發狂 is close to “the heart lets fly, like a mad dog”. look at the animals in this one line. two characters with the horse, one with the hound, and then the hunter’s own heart with the dog in it. the chase turns the rider into one of the pack. english versions say that the hunt will “derange the mind”. the chinese is not about a mind and not about reason. it is 心, the heart, and the heart bolts.

行妨: a walk that is harmed. 難得之貨, “goods hard to get”, comes from passage 3, where a ruler who does not prize them has no thieves. here the harm is to the one who wants them: 令人行妨. 妨 is “to harm, to get in the way of”; the shuowen says 害也. 行 is “to walk”, and then “conduct”, the way a person goes through life; the shuowen defines it as 人之步趨, “a person’s walking and hurrying”. wang bi keeps the road: 塞人正路, such goods “block a person’s straight path”. legge moralized it: men’s conduct “will to evil change”. the chinese has no “evil”. it has a picture of someone who cannot walk straight, because something rare is in view and the feet turn toward it. this is the only one of the five lines that names no sense organ. the harm has moved from an organ to a whole life’s direction.

another order, and four more words. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to give the five lines in a different order: colors, the hunt, rare goods, flavors, notes. the received text is tidier. it puts the three “fives” together, eye, ear, mouth, and then the two larger cases. an editor has clearly arranged it. the silk order has a reason of sound: 盲, 狂, 妨, and 爽 belong to one old rhyme group (陽), and it puts these four together, with the unrhymed 聾 last. silk a is also reported to write 明, “bright”, for 盲 in the first line. the silk texts are also reported to have four more characters before the last line: 是以聖人之治也, “for this reason, in the sage’s ordering”. that is the phrase of passage 3, where the sage’s ordering fills bellies. with it, the last line is a policy of a ruler toward a people. without it, as in the pinned text, it reads as one person’s rule of life. which did you assume?

wang bi: fed by things, or drafted by them. 為腹不為目: “for the belly, not for the eye”. 為, read wei, is “to act on behalf of”. wang bi explains the pair in a sentence that is often quoted: 為腹者以物養己，為目者以物役己。 “one who is for the belly uses things to nourish the self. one who is for the eye uses things to press the self into service.” 役 is the word for forced labor and frontier duty; the shuowen defines it as 戍邊, “to guard the border”. so the eye makes a person a conscript of things. he says of the first lines: the ear, eye, mouth, and heart each have a nature to follow, and when they are used against that nature they are hurt; 故曰盲、聾、爽、狂也, “and so it says blind, deaf, spoiled, mad”. the four ruins are one event: a sense that is pushed past its own measure.

not “control of the senses”. western readers easily hear an old sermon here: the senses deceive, the flesh is weak, turn from the body to the spirit. the passage says nothing like that. its remedy for the eye is not the soul. its remedy is 腹, the belly, the most bodily part of the body. the contrast is between two ways in which a body meets the world. the eye reaches out to things at a distance, and it has no “enough”; it can always take one more look. the belly takes in what is near, and it knows exactly when it is full. passage 3 said that the sage fills the bellies. later breath practice put the centre of attention in the lower belly, and read this line as a direction for sitting. the text does not ask anyone to see less. it asks which organ gives the orders.

去彼取此: that and this. 故去彼取此, “so: leave that, take this”, is a set formula. it closes passages 38 and 72 also. the four characters are two verbs and two pointing words, and the shuowen shows that each pointing word has a movement inside it. 彼, “that”, has the road-step 彳 and is glossed 往, “to go toward”. 此, “this”, has 止, a foot at rest, and is glossed 止也, “to stop”. that is where one must go; this is where the foot already stands. the eye lives in 彼: its objects are over there. the belly is 此: here, inside. the verb 取, “to take”, holds one more thing, and it is grim. the graph is a hand on an ear. see the third plate. the formula gives no reasons. it is a gesture, like a hand that points down. what is “this”, where you are now?

the same list in the zhuangzi. the zhuangzi has a near twin of this passage. chapter 12 lists five ways to lose one’s inborn nature: 五色亂目, “the five colors confuse the eye”, so that it does not see clearly; the five sounds confuse the ear; the five smells assault the nose; 五味濁口, “the five flavors foul the mouth”; and fifth, likes and dislikes unsettle the heart. its word for the mouth’s damage includes our 爽. so the list was common property among the thinkers who distrusted court culture, and each shaped it. the zhuangzi keeps five senses and ends with the heart’s preferences. the laozi drops smell, adds the hunt and rare goods, and so leans toward the life of a ruler. the zhuangzi ends with a diagnosis: “these are all harms to life.” the laozi ends with a choice of belly over eye.

legge’s verse and his brackets. legge put the five lines into rhymed english: “colour’s five hues from th’ eyes their sight will take”. the form is close to the feel of the chinese, which is five hammer blows. the cost is at the end of the stanza, where rare objects, “sought for, men’s conduct will to evil change”. “evil” is his; the chinese 妨 is “to hinder, to harm”. in the prose that follows he explains by brackets: the sage seeks to satisfy “(the craving of) the belly, and not the (insatiable longing of the) eyes”. the brackets hold a good reading, the same as wang bi’s, and they also show how bare the original is: 為腹不為目, six characters, with no craving and no longing in them. he adds “he” for the sage, as always.

one plain meal. eat one meal today with the eye off duty. put away the screen and the page. choose plain food: rice or bread, one vegetable, water. eat slowly, and give your attention to the mouth and the belly. notice how much taste there is in plain food when nothing strong has come before it; that is a mouth that is not 爽 in the bad sense. notice the moment when the belly says “enough”. it is quiet, and it is easy to miss if the eye is busy. stop there. for the rest of the day, each time you reach for something, ask one question from the last line: is this for the eye, or for the belly?

腹 and 目, 此 and 彼: belly and eye. two pairs close the passage: 腹 and 目, belly and eye, and 此 and 彼, this and that. they are inside and outside, near and far, enough and more. the text takes a side: for the belly, not for the eye. ask what the preference is for. the five lines describe courts where sights, sounds, tastes, and the hunt were pushed past what an organ can bear. against that excess the belly is the correction. it is not a verdict on eyes. the sage is not asked to see less, and the “this” of 取此 is found by looking. the belly side also turns. the five flavors enter by the mouth and end in the belly, so a life lived for the belly alone has its own line in this list. and the belly empties: its “enough” lasts some hours. a reader who makes the inner good and the outer bad has moved the craving indoors. what does your eye want that your belly has not asked for?

too much color, sound, and flavor does not feed the senses; it blinds, deafens, and dulls them.. too much color, sound, and flavor does not feed the senses; it blinds, deafens, and dulls them. do you agree? what does a plain thing taste or look like to you now? where you grew up, was pleasure treated as a danger or as a right? how does that sit in you today? take the opposite: the senses grow by rich use, and a life kept plain is a life kept small. hold that for a minute. what arises? do you judge people who enjoy a great deal, or people who refuse to? what might the judgment guard?

the sage lives for the belly and not the eye: for what is here and enough, not for what is over there.. the sage lives for the belly and not the eye: for what is here and enough, not for what is over there. which one runs your day, the belly or the eye? how do you know? what were you taught to look toward: a place, a rank, a kind of life that was somewhere else? who pointed? now hold the other side: looking outward is how a person grows, and one who is content with enough has stopped. what do you feel when you take that as true? is your “enough” a fullness, or is it a limit that someone set for you? why would the difference matter?

盲 gone, over an eye. start with the lower part, 目, the eye. in the oldest script it is an eye as you would draw it: a long oval lying on its side with the pupil in the middle. when writing went onto narrow bamboo strips, wide shapes were turned upright, and the eye now stands on end; the two inner lines are what remains of the pupil. the shuowen says 人眼，象形: “the human eye; a picture”. turned eyes are in many characters: 見, to see, is an eye on legs; 相, to look closely, is an eye beside a tree; 眉, the eyebrow, has a brow drawn above it. now the upper part, 亡. the shuowen defines it as 逃也, “to flee”, and it means “gone, lost, dead”; in the oldest laozi manuscripts it is the common way to write 無, “to not have”. put together: 目無牟子, “an eye with no pupil”. the shuowen takes 亡 as the sound, and the sound part also tells the story. its cousins do the same. 忘, to forget, is 亡 over a heart: the shuowen says 从心从亡. 望, to gaze into the distance, the shuowen explains from 亡 too: someone has fled abroad, and you look for his return. modern 忙, busy, is a heart beside 亡. blind, forgetful, busy: an eye, a heart, a heart, each with “gone” written on it. the first line says that the five colors do this to the eye. eight strokes. 亡 takes three. first a dot at the top centre. second, a long horizontal; watch it, for it is the widest line of the character and covers the eye like a lid or a brim. third, a stroke that comes down on the left and turns to the right along the bottom: a short upright and a level foot. then the eye in five: the left side, the top and right side in one turning stroke, two short lines inside, and the base to close it. the eye must be narrow and upright, set under the middle of the long line, with even white spaces between its four level strokes. the top is wide and open, and the bottom is tall and shut. in seal script the eye still has curved lids; clerical script squared it off. a blind eye and a seeing eye are written with the same five strokes. only the top part differs.

聾 the dragon and the ear. top and bottom. the bottom is 耳, the ear, a picture of the outer ear with its folds; the shuowen says 主聽也，象形, “it is in charge of listening; a picture”. you have seen the ear in 聖, the sage, the one who hears, and in 聲, sound, and it will come back in 取 in the third plate. the top is 龍, the dragon, one of the grand characters of the script. the shuowen’s entry on it is a small poem: 鱗蟲之長, “chief of the scaled creatures”; 能幽能明，能細能巨, “it can be dark or bright, tiny or vast”; 春分而登天，秋分而潛淵, “at the spring equinox it climbs the sky, and at the autumn equinox it sinks into the deep pool”. the left half of 龍 as now written looks like 立 over 月, and the right half is the curling body; the oracle-bone form is commonly explained as a serpent with a crowned head and a wide mouth. in 聾 the shuowen says the dragon is only the sound: 从耳龍聲. the same sound part stands in 籠, a cage of bamboo, and in 寵, favor, where a dragon is under a roof; that character opens passage 13. readers have always enjoyed the accident here: a dragon on top of an ear. the five notes of the court were a roar of bronze, and under them the ear stopped work. twenty-two strokes: sixteen for the dragon and six for the ear. the dragon is written in two columns. left column: a dot, a horizontal, two small strokes that lean together, and a longer horizontal; then below it the shape like 月, in four strokes. right column: a short horizontal, a stroke that comes down, turns right, and turns down again, another short horizontal, and then stroke thirteen, the body: it falls, bends to the right, and hooks up. three short horizontals go inside its curve, like scales. all sixteen strokes must stay in the upper two thirds and must be kept thin. then the ear: a horizontal, a short vertical on the left, a long vertical on the right, two short lines inside, and last a long horizontal across the foot. watch that last stroke. it is the widest line in the character, and the whole dragon stands on it.

取 a hand on an ear. this is among the most common verbs in chinese, “to take”, and it holds a battlefield. the left side is 耳, an ear, made narrow. the right side is 又, a right hand: the shuowen calls 又 a hand, and its old form shows three fingers and a wrist. a hand that reaches for an ear. the shuowen explains why: 捕取也, “to capture and take”, and then it quotes the rites of zhou: 獲者取左耳, “the one who makes a kill or a capture takes the left ear”. soldiers cut the left ears from the enemy dead and brought them in to be counted; hunters did the same with game. the shuowen adds a line from an old military code about carrying in the tally of ears. rewards were paid on the count. so “to take” is first to take a trophy. the cousins soften with time: 娶, to take a wife, is 取 over a woman; 最, “most”, is commonly explained with 取 under a cover; 趣, to hasten toward, has running feet beside it, and there the shuowen takes 取 as the sound. now read the end of the passage: 去彼取此. the text has just said what the five notes do to the ear. its last verb has a severed ear in it, and the sage uses that verb for the gentlest of acts: to take what is here. eight strokes. the ear takes six. a horizontal at the top; a short vertical down from its left end; then the long vertical on the right, which runs the full height. two short horizontals go between the uprights. stroke six is the foot of the ear. in the free-standing 耳 it is a level line; here, at the left of a character, it rises to the right and reaches out past the long vertical. watch it: it starts far to the left, and its tip leads the eye across to the hand. then the hand in two strokes. stroke seven is a horizontal that turns and sweeps down to the left, long and fast. stroke eight is the 捺: it starts inside the angle, crosses the falling stroke, and presses out to the lower right. the ear is upright and narrow. the hand is all diagonals, and its last stroke reaches under and steadies both halves.

13 · favor startles like disgrace. favor and disgrace: like a start of fear. / honor great trouble as the body. / what is meant by “favor and disgrace: like a start of fear”? / favor makes the lower one. / getting it: like a start of fear. / losing it: like a start of fear. / this is meant by “favor and disgrace: like a start of fear”. / what is meant by “honor great trouble as the body”? / the reason i have great trouble / is that i have a body. / if i came to have no body, / what trouble would i have? / so: the body honored as all under heaven: / with such a one all under heaven can be lodged. / the body cherished as all under heaven: / to such a one all under heaven can be entrusted. the passage quotes two old sayings and explains each. first: favor and disgrace are both like a start of fear. the reason: favor makes one the lower; to get it is a fright and to lose it is a fright. second: honor great trouble as the body. the reason is given in the first person: i have great trouble because i have a body, and with no body there would be none. then a conclusion in two matched lines: the person who honors and cherishes the body as all under heaven is the one with whom all under heaven can be lodged. the key word is 身, the body, six times. the last lines can be read in two opposite ways, and the oldest copies choose one. praise and blame feel like opposites. the passage says that they are one movement: a jolt in a creature that is watching its position. any honest observer can confirm this. the lift at praise and the drop at blame have the same root, and the one who enjoys the first has agreed to suffer the second. the text names the root as “having a body”, a thing that can be raised and lowered. it does not tell anyone to hate the body or to leave it. its last lines speak of cherishing the body more than the world. the two fit. when what a person is no longer depends on the court’s opinion, the body is simply cared for, as one cares for a guest. that person is hard to frighten and hard to buy. the first half is a warning about any system that runs on favor: promotions, rankings, the regard of the powerful. such favor makes the receiver the lower one, and people who live by it stop telling the truth. the story of the peach is the classic case. a leader should ask what the people below must do to keep favor, and how much of their attention it takes. the second half is a test for those who are given power, and the oldest text makes it sharper than later ethics liked. do not hand the realm to the one who is eager to give everything for it. hand it to the one who will not trade a living body for any prize. such a person will not spend other people’s bodies either. the realm is then lodged. it is not owned. 驚 is a body event: a horse’s shy. notice where praise and blame land in you: the stomach, the throat, the skin of the face. a trained body learns to receive that jolt and let it pass through, as a rider sits a nervous horse; the centre stays low and the breath goes on. the last lines are a principle of training as well. the one who cherishes the body does not sacrifice it to a result: no victory is worth the injury, and no title is worth the joint. athletes who last are the ones who refuse to trade the body for the prize. teachers of the old arts said the same about students: give the art to the one who will not hurt himself or others to get it. use the day of watching the jolt. then try a harder version for a week. each time you receive favor, ask who is above you at that moment, and what you now have to lose. each time you give praise, notice that you have taken the higher seat. and once in the week, take the closing lines literally: do one thing that honors the body over the world’s demand. sleep when the work says stay. eat when the meeting says wait. see if you are less fit to be trusted afterwards, or more.

a commentary inside the text. this passage has a form that the reader has not met before. it opens with two short sayings. then it asks 何謂, “what is meant by…?”, quotes the first saying again, explains it, and closes with 是謂, “this is what is meant”. then it does the same for the second. that is the form of a teacher who explains an old text to students. so the two opening lines were most likely proverbs older than the passage, and what follows is an early commentary that became part of the book. the guodian bamboo slips (about 300 bce) are reported to hold this passage already in this form. the daodejing is thus a book that had begun to explain itself before it was complete. it also means that the explanation is one reader’s view of the sayings. the sayings are older, and they are harder.

寵: a dragon under the roof. 寵 is a roof, 宀, over a dragon, 龍. the shuowen takes the dragon as the sound and defines the word as 尊居也, “to dwell in honor”. the usual sense is favor that comes down from a superior: a ruler’s 寵 for a minister, a lord’s for a concubine, and today an owner’s for a pet, 寵物. the word is never used between equals. that is the key to the passage. english “favor” and “honor” can be earned and owned. 寵 cannot. it lives in the one who gives it, and it can be withdrawn in an hour. the opposite, 辱, is disgrace done to a person from above. the pair names the two things that a court can do to a man. the saying then puts one verdict on both: 若驚, like a start of fear. see the second plate.

the half-eaten peach. the han feizi tells the story that every chinese reader connects with 寵. mi zixia was the favorite of the lord of wei. once he walked with the lord in an orchard, bit into a peach, found it sweet, and gave the lord the rest. “how he loves me,” said the lord; “he forgets his own mouth and thinks of mine.” years later mi zixia’s looks had faded and the favor with them. he gave some offence, and the lord said: “this is the man who once fed me his leftover peach.” han fei’s comment is cold: the act had not changed; love had turned to hate. under 寵 a thing is a virtue, and when 寵 is gone the same thing is a crime. courts of the warring states were made of such changes. who decides, in your world, if your peach is sweet?

寵為下: three texts. the explanation begins 寵為下, “favor is (or makes) the lower”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read the line with one more particle, 之, and to write 寵 with the graph 弄. the thought is compressed. favor is a thing that only a superior can give, so to receive it is to be confirmed as the one below. this is why getting it is as alarming as losing it: the person who is given favor now has something to lose, and a master to watch. some later editions tried to mend the line. they read 寵為上，辱為下, “favor is the high thing, disgrace the low”, which is flat common sense and ruins the point. legge’s edition had a form of this, and he wrote: “disgrace is being in a low position (after the enjoyment of favour).” the older text is the stranger one. it calls favor itself the low position.

驚: a horse takes fright. 驚 has a horse, 馬, at the bottom, and the shuowen defines it by the animal: 馬駭也, “a horse takes fright”. a horse that shies does not think. the whole body jumps before any thought, the head goes up, the eyes show white. that is the word chosen for what favor and disgrace do to a person. english “alarm” and “anxiety” are states of mind. this is a jolt in the body. the grammar leaves one thing open. 若 is usually “like”: favor and disgrace are like a fright. some read it as “then” or as the old pronoun “you”: “with favor or disgrace, you start”. our rendering keeps “like”. note the horse family in these passages: the tall horse of pride in passage 9, the gallop of the hunt in 12, and now the horse that shies. the age thought with its horses.

辱: to miss the plowing. the shuowen explains 辱, disgrace, with a law of the fields. the graph is 寸, a hand, under 辰. and 辰者，農之時也: “辰 is the farmers’ season”, the star and the month that mark the time to plow. then: 失耕時，於封畺上戮之也, “one who missed the time of plowing was punished at the boundary mound”. the punishment was public, at the edge of the fields, where all could see. so disgrace in chinese is at root an exposure before the community for failing the season. english “disgrace” is the loss of grace, a word from court and church. “shame” is nearer. modern scholars read the old graph differently, as a hand with a farm tool, and doubt the story of the law. the shuowen’s story is still the one that readers knew. see the first plate.

貴大患若身: a line that will not parse. the second saying is five characters: 貴 value, 大患 great trouble, 若 like, 身 body. read straight, it says “value great trouble as you value the body”, and no one finds that easy. there are at least three ways out. one: the words are in an unusual order, and the sense is “value the body as you would take a great trouble seriously”. two: the heshang gong commentary glosses 貴 as “to fear” and 若 as “to reach”: fear the great trouble that reaches the body. three: 若身 is “is like the body”, and the saying is an equation: what people prize and their great trouble are both the body. the explanation in the text goes with the third: i have great trouble because i have a body. we keep the bare order and write “honor”. a proverb is allowed to be dark. which reading does your own life support?

患: a heart on a skewer. 患 is 心, the heart, with 串 above it: two objects run through by one line, as meat is strung on a stick. the shuowen says the heart has something that “pierces” it from above, 从心上貫吅, and defines the word as 憂也, “worry, grief”. the word covers both the outer event and the inner state: a calamity, an illness, and the worry about them. 大患, “great trouble”, is the kind that threatens a life: disaster, punishment, death. wang bi says that here it means glory and favor themselves, because “where life is made thick, one enters the ground of death”. the text’s own answer is simpler and goes deeper: the great trouble is the fact of having something that can be hurt. see the third plate.

吾: the speaker says “i”. four times in three short lines the text says 吾, “i”. the shuowen defines the word plainly: 我，自稱也, “‘i’: what one calls oneself”. the speaker of the daodejing seldom appears. when this voice says “i”, it is to confess a limit: “i do not know whose child it is” (4); “i alone am dull” (20). here it says: i have great trouble, because i have a body. the line is not addressed to “you”. it makes no accusation, and it does not say that people in general are too attached. english versions that write “we” or “you” lose the tone. a teacher is explaining a proverb, and at the hard point the teacher stops quoting and speaks in the first person. read the three lines aloud as your own words. are they true?

無身: to have no body. 及吾無身，吾有何患: “if it came to my having no body, what trouble would i have?” 身 is the body, the living person, as in passage 7. the line can be a dry remark: no body, no pain; the dead have no worries. it can be a state reached in practice. the zhuangzi describes “sitting and forgetting”: 墮肢體，黜聰明, “let the limbs and body drop away, dismiss hearing and sight”. chinese buddhists later heard their own teaching of no-self in the line and quoted it often. and it can mean what passage 7 meant: not to hold the body as a private possession. english versions write “selfless”, a moral word about generous people. the chinese is stranger and more physical. it says “no body”. it does not say that this is good, and it does not say how. it asks a question.

yang zhu and the worth of a body. the last lines belong to a debate. yang zhu, a thinker of the fourth century bce, taught 貴生, “value life”: one’s own living body is worth more than any thing outside it, a throne included. mencius attacked him: yang would not pull out one hair to benefit the world. but the school had a serious political point, and stories carried it. prince sou of yue fled to a cave because three kings before him had been murdered; the people smoked him out and made him king, and the comment is that they wanted exactly him, because a man who will not harm his life for a state will not waste lives. on this reading the lines say: only a person who values the body above the empire is safe to be given the empire. wang bi reads them so, and so do the oldest copies.

one small word: 於. the pinned text has 貴以身為天下, which can be read in two opposite ways, because 為 can be “to treat as” (wei) or “for the sake of” (wei). reading a: “who values the body as the world”: the person who holds the body as dear as the whole realm. reading b: “who values giving the body for the world”: the person who devotes the self to all. b is the reading of public service, and many versions prefer it; legge’s “honouring it as he honours his own person” is close to it. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to settle the question for their own time. in the first of the two lines they read 貴為身於為天下, with the comparative 於: “who values acting for the body more than acting for the world”. the zhuangzi quotes both lines with 於. so the early text says a, and strongly. our rendering keeps the open form of the pinned text.

寄 and 託: each defines the other. the two closing lines differ in two places only: 貴 and 愛 at the head, 寄 and 託 at the end. look up the last pair in the shuowen. 寄，託也. 託，寄也. each is defined by the other; the dictionary treats them as one idea. 寄 has a roof: to lodge, as a traveller lodges for the night. 託 has speech, 言: to commit a thing to someone by word. some versions make the two lines into two different outcomes. they are a pair, and their order was not fixed: wang bi’s own comment has 託 under the first line and 寄 under the second. the choice of verbs matters more than the difference between them. the text does not say that such a person can “rule” or “own” all under heaven. the realm is lodged with a person, as a guest is, or left in trust. passage 29 says why: the world is a sacred vessel, and it cannot be held.

wang bi: nothing to trade the body for. wang bi begins with a law of courts: 寵必有辱，榮必有患。 “favor always has disgrace in it; glory always has trouble in it.” the two are one coin. on the closing lines he explains the two verbs. 貴: 無以易其身，故曰貴也, “there is nothing for which this person would exchange the body; so it says ‘honor’”. 愛: 無物可以損其身，故曰愛也, “no thing can be allowed to diminish the body; so it says ‘cherish’”. then his conclusion: 不以寵辱榮患損易其身，然後乃可以天下付之也。 “one who does not let favor and disgrace, glory and trouble, diminish or change the person: only then can the world be handed to such a one.” for wang bi the body here is a person’s integrity. a ruler who can be bought with favor or frightened by disgrace will sell the realm.

legge on “the body (which i call myself)”. legge’s first line smooths the saying: “favour and disgrace would seem equally to be feared.” the horse is gone; 驚 has become a reasonable fear. in the middle he does something of interest. for 為吾有身 he writes “my having the body (which i call myself)”. the bracket is a small piece of western philosophy: there is a body, and there is a “myself”, and the speaker is said to confuse them. the chinese has one word, 身, and does not divide it. for the close he takes the public-service reading: “he who would administer the kingdom, honouring it as he honours his own person, may be employed to govern it”. the realm is the thing honored. in the oldest texts the body is the thing honored, and more than the realm.

watch the jolt. for one day, watch for the start of fear. it comes when you are praised: a message of thanks, a number that went up, a warm word from someone above you. it comes when you are slighted. both arrive first in the body: a lift or a drop in the chest, heat in the face, a quick breath. that is 驚, the horse’s shy. do not correct it. mark it only: “favor”, or “disgrace”, and notice that the jolt is the same animal each time. then ask the passage’s question at that moment: what in me can be raised and lowered by this? at night, count. was it praise or blame that made the horse jump more often?

寵 and 辱, 得 and 失: one jolt. the passage holds two pairs in one hand: 寵 and 辱, favor and disgrace, and 得 and 失, getting and losing. the common view ranks them: favor is good to get, and disgrace is the thing to avoid. the text does not rank them. it gives one answer to both, 若驚, and it uses the same four words for getting and for losing. the reason is that each side holds the other. favor can be lost, so the one who has it already fears disgrace; and only a person who has been raised can be thrown down. a reader could turn this around and say that favor is bad and that disgrace is the honest state. that is also a ranking, and the text does not make it. a third pair comes later: 有身 and 無身, to have a body and to have none. the speaker imagines no body and no trouble, and then ends with the body honored and cherished. the passage keeps both.

favor and disgrace are one shock, and to receive favor already puts you below the giver.. favor and disgrace are one shock, and to receive favor already puts you below the giver. is that true in your life? think of the last praise that mattered to you, and of who gave it. where did you learn to want favor: from a parent, a teacher, a first employer? what did it cost to keep? now hold the other view for a few minutes: praise is a plain gift, and to enjoy it binds you to nothing. what do you feel as you hold it? which view do you defend more quickly, and what does that speed tell you?

a person who cherishes the body more than the world is the one who can be trusted with the world.. a person who cherishes the body more than the world is the one who can be trusted with the world. do you trust such a person, or do you trust the one who gives everything for the cause? what do you think of people who guard their sleep, their health, their time? if you judge them, what is the judgment made of? take the opposite side: a great task deserves the whole body, and to hold back is small. stay with that. what rises: pride, tiredness, a memory? where has each side been true in what you have lived, and why might you need to know which one runs you?

辱 a hand under the plowing star. two parts, upper and lower. the lower part is 寸. it is a hand, 又, with one small mark at the wrist; the shuowen says the mark shows the place one inch from the hand where the pulse beats, and so 寸 means an inch. in other characters it often stands for a hand that acts by rule: 守, to keep a post; 寺, an office; 封, to mark a boundary. the upper part is 辰. today it is the fifth of the twelve time signs, and the “dragon” of the animal years. the shuowen ties it to spring: 三月，陽气動，靁電振，民農時也, “the third month: the yang breath stirs, thunder and lightning shake, it is the people’s time to farm”. modern scholars commonly explain the early graph as a farm tool, a blade of clam shell for cutting and weeding, and its family supports the farm sense. 農, farming, has 辰 at the bottom. 晨, early morning, is the sun over 辰. 震, thunder, is rain over 辰, and the shuowen defines 辰 itself by that word. so the shuowen reads 辱 as a judgment at the season: a hand of law under the farming star, on the one who missed the plowing. passage 8 said that the good in movement is 時, the right time. here is the old word for the person who failed it, shown at the field’s edge. the passage says that favor is as much a fright as this. ten strokes. 辰 takes seven. a short horizontal at the top; then a stroke that starts under its left end and falls far down to the left, like the wall of a cliff. inside the angle come two more horizontals, the second longer. stroke five is a vertical that turns at the foot and flicks up to the right. six is a short stroke that falls to the left, and seven is the 捺, which runs to the lower right. these last two open like a small skirt. then 寸 in three. stroke eight is the long horizontal. watch it: it is the widest line of the character, and the whole of 辰 rests on it. stroke nine is the vertical with a hook at the foot, and it stands right of centre. the last is a dot in the angle. the upper part leans left and spreads; the hand below stands straight, and its dot is small.

寵 the dragon indoors. you met the dragon, 龍, in the last passage, on top of an ear. here it is under a roof. 宀 is the roof: a ridge dot and two eaves. it shelters people and their goods in dozens of characters: 家, a household, with a pig under it; 安, peace, with a woman; 定, to settle; 宿, to lodge for a night; and 寄, to lodge, in the last lines of this passage. the shuowen says of 寵 that the roof is the meaning and the dragon is the sound, and it defines the word as 尊居也, “to dwell in honor”. readers have long seen more in it. the dragon is the greatest of creatures; the shuowen says it can be dark or bright, small or vast, and that it climbs the sky in spring. put it under a roof and it is kept: honored, fed, and no longer free. the word is used for a ruler’s favorite minister, for a favorite consort, and in modern chinese for a pet. that fits what the passage says about favor: it makes the lower one. the simplified form 宠 keeps the roof and writes the dragon in five strokes. set 寵 beside 聾 from passage 12: the same dragon makes an ear deaf and makes a house proud. in both, the shuowen says, it is only a sound. the first saying treats the honored dwelling as a place of alarm. nineteen strokes: three for the roof and sixteen for the dragon. the roof comes first: a dot at the top centre, a short stroke at the left end, and a horizontal that runs to the right and hooks down. it must be wide enough to cover everything below. then the dragon, in two columns, as in 聾. left column: a dot, a horizontal, two small strokes, a longer horizontal, and under them the shape like 月 in four strokes. right column: a short horizontal, a stroke that comes down, steps to the right, and turns down again, another short horizontal, and then stroke sixteen. watch it: the long body of the dragon, which falls, bends, runs to the right, and flicks up. three short horizontals go inside its curve. the roof is one broad sweep, and the dragon is many small moves packed close. the writer keeps the dragon’s strokes thin, so that the animal fits under the eaves.

患 strung through the heart. the lower part is 心, the heart. it is a picture of the organ; the old script is commonly explained as showing its chambers, and in the modern form there are three dots and one curved stroke that holds them like a bowl. as a meaning part it marks every movement of feeling and thought: 志, aim; 忘, to forget; 恃, to lean on; 惡, to hate; 慈, a mother’s love. the upper part is 串. it is two small boxes with one line through both, and it means things strung on a cord or a stick: a string of coins, meat on a skewer. street stalls today sell skewered food under this same name. the shuowen describes the upper part of 患 as two mouths, 吅, pierced through, and says the heart has this above it: 从心上貫吅. its definition is 憂也, “worry”. so the character is a heart with something run through it. the same word names the outer disaster and the inner grief: 患 is a calamity, an illness (a patient is a 患者), and the fear of both. the passage speaks of 大患, great trouble, and gives its cause in four characters: 為吾有身, “because i have a body”. a thing that can be strung can be hurt. the speaker does not complain about this. the speaker reports it. eleven strokes. the skewer first, in seven. the upper box takes three: left side, top and right side in one turn, and the base. the lower box takes three in the same way, and it is made a little wider than the upper one. then stroke seven: one vertical that starts above the upper box and runs down through both. watch it. it must pass through the exact middle of each box, and it stops before it reaches the heart. then the heart in four. a dot at the left that leans outward. then the long curved stroke: it starts low on the left, sweeps along the bottom, and ends in a hook that points up and back. then two dots, one above the curve and one at the far right. the three dots must look at each other, like three people in a talk. the top is straight and stiff, and the heart below is round and open.

14 · the lead thread. looked at, not seen: its name is level. / listened to, not heard: its name is sparse. / grasped at, not got: its name is minute. / these three cannot be questioned to the end, / so they blend and are one. / above, it is not bright; / below, it is not dark. / a cord, on and on, it cannot be named; / it goes back to where there is no thing. / this is called the shape of no shape, / the image of no thing. / this is called dim and flickering. / go to meet it: its head is not seen. / follow it: its back is not seen. / hold the way of old / to drive what there is now. / to be able to know the old beginning: / this is called the lead thread of dao. three tries and three names. the eye looks and does not see; the ear listens and does not hear; the hand hunts and does not get. the names are not “invisible, inaudible, intangible”. they are level, sparse, minute. the three cannot be cross-examined, so they are one. then the one is described by what it lacks: no bright top, no dark underside, no name, no head, no back. in the middle is a cord that runs on and on, back to where there is no thing. then the turn. with no warning the passage gives an instruction from the stable yard: grip the old way and drive what is here now. it ends with a thread from the silk room. so the pictures are a law court, a rope, a chariot, and a skein of silk. the silk manuscripts are reported to differ in some details. the passage reads like a report from sitting practice. attention goes out through each sense and comes back with nothing. do not treat that as a defeat. the three blanks turn out to be one blank, and it has a quality: even, thin, fine. wang bi says the names are taken from “the not-knowing of my ear, eye, and body”. then comes 惚恍, the state in which a thing is neither there nor absent. the text says you cannot meet it or follow it: it has no front, so it is not ahead of you as a goal, and no back, so it is not behind you as a loss. a thing that is not in front and not behind is here. the last lines keep the mind from floating away. they put reins in the hands. the final couplet is the part that rulers read. hold the way of old; drive what is here now. the verb is a driver’s verb. a driver feels the team through the reins, looks far down the road, and corrects early and lightly; one who fights the horses turns the car over. that is different from “control of the present situation”, and the difference is practical. the object, 今之有, is plain: the affairs that exist today. what is held is not a plan. it is something that cannot be named and that you learned from long before your own case. the silk texts make this sharper, or reverse it: they are reported to say “the way of now”. a leader may ask each morning which one is in the hands: a habit copied from the past, or a hold on that which does not change when times change. the body knows the three failures as skills. a good archer does not stare at the target; the gaze goes level and wide. a good listener in a fight or a dance does not wait for a loud signal; the attention goes thin, to the sparse sound. in push-hands, the taiji partner exercise, the hand that grabs gets nothing, because the other person is no longer there; the hand that stays light feels the smallest shift. then the charioteer: stand as if you hold reins. the elbows are down, the wrists are alive, and the hands are closed but not tight. the grip, 執, is firm at the centre and soft at the edge. you can try it on a steering wheel or the handles of a bicycle. where do you hold harder than the road needs? look for 繩繩 outside: a river seen from a bridge, with no first water and no last. a year, in which no day is the day when spring starts. morning twilight, when you cannot say at which moment it stopped being dark. the largest processes have no bright top and no dark underside, no front edge to meet and no rear to follow. you are in them. but the passage does not leave you with a blur. a weaver can find the lead end of a tangled skein, and then the whole of it comes free without a knot. each continuous thing has such a place where a hand can begin. in a watershed it is the spring. in a tree it is the root. passage 16 goes there next. do the three-sense sitting once: eyes level, ears thin, hand fine. then use the last lines on one real matter today. before you act on it, ask the weaver’s question: where is the head of this thread? most tangles get worse because we pull at the middle, where the knot is most visible. trace the matter back one step, and one step more, to the old beginning of it. then take hold there, lightly, as one holds reins. if you want a reward afterwards, read how a missionary found a ball of thread in the last line: legge’s “clue”. and if you want a warning about what readers bring to a text, read what a paris professor heard in the three names.

three names that are not “invisible, inaudible, intangible”. most english versions give the three names as the three failures: invisible, inaudible, intangible. the chinese words say something else. 夷 is level, flat: ground with no feature for the eye to catch. the shuowen defines it 平也, “level”. 希 is sparse: sound so thin that the ear finds no pattern. 微 is minute. so the text does not name what the senses lack. it names a quality on the other side: too even to see, too thin to hear, too fine to hold. wang bi says where the names come from: 更以我耳目體不知為名, “it is named from the not-knowing of my ear, eye, and body”. the capitals in our rendering are an english habit; chinese has none. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to exchange two of the names. the same three sounds also started a strange european theory.

希: the thin word that returns. 希 is “sparse, far apart”: the sense now written 稀, with the grain sign added, which the shuowen defines as 䟽也, “thinly spaced”, like seedlings set wide. the shuowen has no entry of its own for 希. the laozi likes this word for sound. passage 41 says 大音希聲, “the great note has sparse sound”. passage 23 opens 希言自然, “sparse speech is natural”. so when the text says here that what the ear cannot hear is called 希, a reader of the whole book hears an echo: the thinnest sound is the greatest one. the three names also chime. in the old rhyme groups 希 and 微 are in one group (微), and 夷 is in the group next to it (脂). mandarin still keeps a shadow of it: yi, xi, wei.

搏: the hand that hunts. 搏 has the hand sign, 扌, at the left. the shuowen defines it 索持也: “to search for and seize”. it is the word for a hawk that strikes, or for a fighter who grapples. it is not a gentle touch. so the third line is stronger than “touch it and do not feel it”. the hand goes out to catch, and closes on nothing. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to have a softer verb, 捪, which the shuowen glosses 撫也, “to stroke”: a palm that passes over a surface and finds none. try both now. close your hand fast on the air. then pass your palm slowly through it. which failure teaches more?

微: to walk unseen. the shuowen defines 微 as 隱行也, “to go in concealment”. its left part is 彳, the sign for a road or a step. the first sense is movement that no one notices: to travel in disguise, to slip past a guard. from this come “hidden”, “slight”, “minute”, and today the prefix “micro-”. the shuowen’s example is from an age of coups: 白公其徒微之, “the followers of the lord of bai hid him”. so the third name, like the verb before it, comes from a world of pursuit and escape. the hand hunts; the thing walks past unseen. this word opened the book’s account of fineness in passage 1, where wang bi explains 妙 as “the far limit of 微”. it returns in the next passage as the first word for the masters of old.

詰: the interrogation fails. 詰 is a word from the law court. the shuowen says only 問也, “to question”, but in the texts of the period it means to press, to cross-examine, to demand an account: an officer questions a suspect, a ruler calls a minister to answer. warring states courts were full of this. the debaters pressed each term until it broke, and the legalist state matched each name against the result. the line says that this method stops here: 不可致詰, the three “cannot be brought to full questioning”. they give no further answers. english “cannot be analyzed” makes it a matter of logic. the chinese picture is a witness who cannot be made to speak. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write 至計, “reckoned to the end”: there the failed tool is the count, and not the question.

who blends them?. 故混而為一: “so, blended, they are (or: are made) one”. the line has no subject. legge supplies “we blend them together and obtain the one”, as if unity were a result of our thinking. but the grammar allows the plainer sense: the three were never apart. eye, ear, and hand each made a separate report of failure, and the three reports are about one thing. 混 is a water word. the shuowen defines it 豐流也, “an abundant flow”: streams that run together until you cannot tell them apart. it is not “confusion”. passage 25 uses the same word for the origin: 有物混成, “there is a thing, blended and complete”. note 為一, “to be one” or “to make one”. chinese does not force the choice. english does, and we chose “are”.

a thing with no bright side. each visible thing has a lit side and a shadow. the top of a hill is bright and its foot is dim; the sun rises bright and sets dark. the line denies both: 其上不皦，其下不昧. 皦 is the white of polished stone; the shuowen says 玉石之白也. 昧 is the dark, or the grey before dawn. so this is not a light above the world, as heaven is in much western religion, and not a depth below it. it gives no direction in which to look up. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to begin the line with two more characters: 一者, “as for the one”. there the sentence is plainly about the unity of the line before, and the passage becomes a portrait of one single thing. some english versions turn above and below into rising and setting. the chinese has only the two space words: 上, 下.

繩繩: cord, cord. 繩 is a cord or rope; the shuowen says 索也. doubled, 繩繩 is a sound-picture of what continues without a break, as a rope is paid out hand over hand. the book of odes uses it for a line of descendants that does not end. commentators also heard a second sense, “without edge or measure”. the carpenter’s inked cord, 繩, was the standard tool for a straight line, and from it came the verb “to correct, to measure”; here the measuring cord itself cannot be measured or named. keep the cord in mind. the passage ends with another thread, 紀. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 尋尋呵. 尋 is the span of two arms held out; so there the image is fathom after fathom. in both versions, something is measured by the body and has no end. english “endless” keeps the idea and loses the hands.

無物 is “no thing”, not “nothingness”. 復歸於無物: it “again returns to no-thing”. 物 is a thing among things: a creature, an object, an event, each with a shape and a name. 無物 is the state in which there is not yet any such item. english “nothingness” makes this an abyss, and the western ear then hears either despair or a mystic void. the chinese is modest. it says only that the cord, if you follow it back, leads to a place with no separate things in it. then the text refuses to stop there, and adds a shape and an image. note 復歸, “to return again”. this verb pair is one of the book’s signatures; in passage 16 each thing 復歸其根, “returns to its root”, and in passage 28 the return is to the infant and to the uncarved wood.

wang bi: say it is not there? say it is there?. 無狀之狀，無物之象: “the shape of no shape, the image of no thing”. the phrase does not cancel itself. it holds two facts together. wang bi sets them out as two questions: 欲言無邪，而物由以成。欲言有邪，而不見其形。 “do you wish to say it is not there? but things come to completion through it. do you wish to say it is there? but its form is not seen.” this is the logic of the whole passage. it is easy to compare it with the “negative theology” of the west, which says only what god is not. use care with that. here nothing stands outside the world. the text does not deny that the way is present; it denies that the way is an item. 狀 is outer shape (the shuowen: 犬形也, “the form of a dog”). 象 is the likeness that the mind holds.

惚恍: a word made of sound. 惚恍 (hu huang) is not two ideas joined. it is one two-syllable word of a kind that chinese has many of: both halves begin with the same sound, and the meaning is in the pair, as in english “shilly-shally” or “flicker”. such words were written with any graphs of the right sound; other editions write this one with other graphs, such as 忽 and 怳, and the heart sign 忄 in both received characters only tells you it is a state of mind. the sense is: there and not there, as a thing seen at dusk. wang bi glosses it in six characters: 不可得而定也, “it cannot be got hold of and fixed”. passage 21 turns the word around, 恍惚, and looks inside it: “within it there is an image”. it is a word of experience. sitters know this state. do you?

the way of old, or the way of now?. the received text says 執古之道，以御今之有: hold the way of old to drive what there is now. both mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 執今之道: “hold the way of now to drive what there is now”. one character is different and the politics are reversed. the received line fits the common belief of the age that the old kings had the pattern, a belief the confucians taught and that the laozi shares in other places (passages 15 and 65 both begin “those of old who were good at…”). the reported silk line is nearer to the legalists, who said that a ruler must fit the present and not copy the past. both versions agree on the next line: by this, the old beginning can be known. so even the reported silk line reaches the origin, but it reaches it from here. which direction do you trust more: from the past to now, or from now to the root?

御 is to drive, not to control. 御 is the charioteer’s verb. the shuowen defines it in three characters: 使馬也, “to make the horses go”. modern versions say “manage”, “master”, or “control” the present, and the picture becomes an office. the chinese reader sees a driver who stands in a light car behind two or four horses, with the reins gathered in the hands. a driver does not push the horses and cannot overpower them. the reins carry the feel of each mouth to the hands, and small movements go back. the odes praise a driver whose reins are “like silk bands”. charioteering was one of the six arts that a gentleman learned, beside archery, writing, and music. and see the verb before it: 執, to grip. “i shall take up driving,” says confucius, 吾執御矣, with the same two words. what you hold is the way. what you drive is what is there.

今之有: “the there-is of now”. 今之有 is three small words: “now’s having”, the there-is of the present. wang bi gives it one of his shortest glosses: 有，有其事, “有 means: there are its affairs”. so the phrase is concrete. it is the business in front of you, the things that exist today and need a response. english versions say “the realities of the present” or “the present reality”; that makes one large abstract object, where the chinese has only the plain verb “to have” used as a noun. wang bi then explains the hold on the old way: 雖今古不同，時移俗易，故莫不由乎此以成其治者也. “though present and past differ, though times move and customs change, none has brought about order except through this.” times change, he says. the thing that is formless and nameless does not.

紀: find the end of the thread. 紀 has the silk sign, 糸, at the left. the shuowen defines it 絲別也: “to sort silk threads apart”. old commentators explain the craft. a cocoon or a tangled skein is useless until you find the head of the thread; that lead end is the 紀, and when you have it, the whole skein follows. from this the word came to mean a guiding rule, a record in order (the “annals” of a king are his 紀), and a cycle of years. so 道紀 is not “the essence of dao”, a thing inside it. it is the end of the thread: the place where a hand can take hold of what no hand can seize. the passage that began with a hand that closed on nothing ends with a thread to hold. it is the second cord in the passage; the first was 繩繩. legge, to his credit, found an english word for it.

the paris professor who heard “jehovah”. in 1823 jean-pierre abel-remusat, the first professor of chinese in europe, published a study of laozi in paris. he looked at the three names, which he read i, hi, wei, and proposed that together they wrote the hebrew name of god, ihv: jehovah. laozi, he thought, must have learned it from the west. the idea was not new: jesuit “figurists” of the century before, premare and foucquet among them, had looked for the trinity and the name of god in this passage, as they looked for noah in the chinese classics. his student stanislas julien rejected it in 1842, and legge rejected it again in 1891; it is wrong on the sounds, the grammar, and the history. but it shows the first frame through which the west read this book: as a lost fragment of the bible. the three words mean level, sparse, and minute.

legge’s capitals, and his one fine word. legge’s frame shows in his capitals: “the one”, “the semblance of the invisible”, “its front”, “its back”. a capital letter makes a title, and a title suggests a person. he adds “we” again and again in a passage that has no subject at all, and gives 夷 as “the equable”, a word for a calm temper. but see his last phrase: “(unwinding) the clue of tao”. “clue” is the old english “clew”, a ball of thread; the greek hero theseus used one to find his way out of the labyrinth, and from that story the word got its modern sense. legge knew this. for 紀, the lead thread of the silk, he found the one english word that is also a thread. most later versions say “essence” and lose it.

the silk texts and the order of the senses. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to give the three names in another order: looked at and not seen, 名之曰微, “name it minute”; stroked and not got, 名之曰夷, “name it level”. that fits the senses well. a thing too small escapes the eye, and a surface with no grain escapes the palm. the received text has the two the other way around: level for the eye, minute for the hand. that also works: the eye needs contrast, and the fingers cannot hold a thing that is too fine. they are also reported to write 名之曰, “name it, saying…”, with an object: an act of naming is done, three times, and the next lines then say that it cannot be named. they put the last two lines in the reverse order too: follow it first, then meet it. this passage is not among the guodian bamboo slips.

let three senses fail. sit where it is quiet. first the eyes: look at a plain wall or the open sky, with no point to rest on. stay until the looking has no object. that evenness is 夷. then the ears: listen for the faintest sound in the room, and then for what is between the sounds. that thinness is 希. then the hand: rub thumb and finger together more and more lightly, until you cannot say if they touch. that fineness is 微. do not look for a result. the passage says the three are one, and that they do not answer questions. give it two minutes. then stand up and take hold of the first thing you must do today, in the way that a driver takes up the reins.

pairs with no line between them. this passage names five pairs. it uses four of them to say what is absent: 上 and 下, above and below; 皦 and 昧, bright and dark; 首 and 後, head and back; 迎 and 隨, to meet and to follow. in things, each side of such a pair marks off the other: a top is bright because an underside is dark, and a front is a front because there is a back. here the top is not bright and the underside is not dark, so there is no line where one side stops and the other starts. the fifth pair is 古 and 今, old and now, and the text treats it otherwise. it keeps both sides and gives each a verb: the old is held, and the now is driven. a reader who takes one side hears “the old is better”, or, with the reported silk reading, “the now is all that counts”. but reins with no team move nothing, and a team with no reins has no driver. which of the two do your hands neglect?

to handle what is here now, take hold of the way of old and find where the matter began.. to handle what is here now, take hold of the way of old and find where the matter began. do you agree that the beginning of a thing is the place to take hold of it? name one case where that worked, or failed. how do you stand toward the old: do you lean on it, or push away from it? whose voice do you hear in that? try the reverse, which the silk copies are reported to give: hold the way of now, and let the past go. what loosens in you, and what protests? what does your preference for old or new protect you from having to face?

what matters most cannot be seen, heard, or held, and no questioning brings it to an account.. what matters most cannot be seen, heard, or held, and no questioning brings it to an account. do you believe that? or do you hold that what is real can, in the end, be measured and named? recall a time when you could not name a thing and it frightened you, or a time when it was a relief. what made the difference? now take the other side fully: what cannot be shown or tested is not there. stay with that for a while. what feelings come, and what do you lose or gain? which side do you look down on in other people, and what might that side know?

紀 the head of the thread. begin at the left. 糸 is silk; the shuowen says 細絲也。象束絲之形, “fine silk; it pictures a bound skein”. you can still see it: two twists, one on the other, and three short ends below. each character that carries it has to do with thread: 線 (thread), 紙 (paper, first made of silk waste), 經 (the warp of a loom, and so a classic text: the 經 in 道德經), 繩 (the cord of this passage), 終 (the end, at first of a thread), 絕 (to cut off), 繼 (to join on). on the right is 己, which gives the sound ji. alone 己 means “oneself”. many scholars think its early form was itself a picture of a cord used to bind or to keep things in order, so that 紀 is the old word with silk added to make it clear; the shuowen has a different account, and reads 己 as a sign of the calendar. so take the cord as “commonly explained”. the shuowen’s definition of 紀 is 絲別也: to sort silk, to find each thread’s end. see its cousins. 統, which the shuowen defines with this very word (紀也), is the thread-head that gathers a whole cocoon, and so “to unite, to command”. 綱 is the head-rope of a net. together, 綱紀 means the order of a state. and 記, with 言 (speech) in place of silk, is to put things in order in words: to record. 道紀 is the end of the way that a hand can find. nine strokes: six for the silk, three for 己. the silk begins with two strokes of one kind: each goes down to the left, then turns and returns to the right. they make the two twists; the second is a little larger than the first. the third stroke is a dot that closes the lower twist. strokes four, five, and six are three more dots in a row beneath: the loose ends. on the left side of a character they are written small and rise toward the right, to hand the eye on. then 己. the seventh stroke goes right and turns down. the eighth is a short level line that closes the top. watch the ninth: it goes down, bends, runs along the base, and ends in a hook that turns up. it is the longest stroke in the character, and it is drawn like a thread laid out on a table.

御 the driver’s hands. three parts, set side by side. at the left is 彳, a step or a road; it is the left half of 行, which first pictured a crossroads. you saw it in 微, “to walk unseen”, and it is in 往 (to go), 徐 (to walk slowly), 復 (to return), and 德, the inner power of this book’s title. the middle and the right, taken together, are 卸. the shuowen defines 卸 as 舍車解馬也: “to leave the car and loose the horses”, to unharness. it still means “to unload”. so for the shuowen, 御 is the whole work of the road: to harness, to drive, to unharness; its definition is 使馬也, “to make the horses go”. the oracle-bone form is debated; some see a kneeling person, the 卩 at the right, with a rope or a whip. another old way to write the word needs no debate: 馭, a horse 馬 and a hand 又. now see how the word rose. the one who drove the king’s car stood beside the king. so 御 came to mean “to attend the ruler”, then “of the ruler”: an imperial thing was 御. japanese still puts it before a word as a mark of respect. the zhuangzi gave it wings: the sage liezi 御風而行, “drove the wind and went”. in this passage the team is what there is now. twelve strokes, in three columns: three, seven, two. the road first: a short stroke that falls to the left, a longer one under it, then a vertical. the middle column is the busy one. a falling stroke, two level strokes, and a vertical through them: this top looks like 午. below it come a short level tick, a short vertical, and a base line that rises to the right, toward the last part. then 卩: one stroke that goes right, turns down, and hooks back; and the twelfth stroke, a long vertical, the tallest line in the character. watch that last one. a good hand lets it fall well below the rest, like a whip held down, or a driver who stands. the middle must stay narrow, or the three columns pull apart; calligraphers say that such a character must “give way” inside, each part with less room than it would take alone.

15 · crossing winter water. those of old who were good at being officers / were fine, subtle, dark, open all the way, / too deep to be marked. / just because they cannot be marked, / a likeness of them, made by force: / wary, as if crossing a river in winter. / watchful, as if in fear of neighbours on four sides. / grave, as if holding a formal bearing. / loosening, like ice about to melt. / solid, like uncarved wood. / wide, like a valley. / blended, like muddy water. / who can, muddy, through stillness, slowly come clear? / who can, at rest, through long movement, slowly come alive? / whoever keeps this way does not want to be full. / just because not full: / able to be worn, and not newly finished. the passage has three parts. first, a confession: the good officers of old were too deep to be marked, so a portrait can only be forced. second, the portrait itself: seven lines, each with an exclamation (兮) and the word 若, “as if”. wary at a winter ford. watchful, with enemies on four sides. grave. loosening like ice. solid like uncarved wood. wide like a valley. blended like mud. the seven move from tight to loose and from the person out to the landscape. the first two lines begin with the two halves of one word for doubt. third, two questions about mud and rest, and a close about not being full. the similes rhyme in sets, and the last line is uncertain in each edition. no line says what the masters knew or did. we get only how they looked. read the seven similes as states of attention, in the order in which they come in a long sitting. first care: each breath is a step on ice. then wide awareness in each direction, as if a sound might come from any side. then the upright body, formal, a guest in the house of the present moment. then the hold lets go. then plain, thick presence, without a carved self to show; then space; then a state with no clear edge between this and that. and then the question that each sitter knows: who can let the mud settle? the grammar is the teaching. stillness is the means, 以靜, and slowly is the pace. you do not clear the water. you stop stirring. then the second question keeps the practice from going dead: out of the rest, by long and gentle movement, life starts again. the first reader was an adviser or officer in a dangerous court, and the portrait is partly a manual for survival: do not be easy to file; test the ice; watch all four borders; behave as a guest where others think they own the hall. that reading is fair, and the strategists made use of it. but the second half goes past it. a group in crisis is muddy water. the leader’s reflex is to stir: one more meeting, one more reorganisation, one more message. the text asks who is able to hold still until it clears, and then who is able to start movement again before stillness turns into stagnation. both are hard, and they are opposite skills. the close gives the condition for both: not full. a leader who is full of answers has no room to wait, and one who must look new each quarter cannot afford to look worn. the first image is a lesson in stepping. on river ice you do not commit your weight; you set the foot down empty, feel, and then pour the weight in. taiji teachers describe the same step with a line from the classics of their art: “walk like a cat”. 豫 the elephant does it with four tons. try ten steps this way across a room. the fourth image is the other half: 渙, the thaw. hold a fist for a slow breath, and then let it open by its own weight, not by a decision. the portrait asks for both at once, structure and melt: grave like a guest, loose like spring ice. the questions are in the breath too. after the out-breath, wait. the body is at rest, 安. the next breath starts itself, slowly. each image is from a northern year. the river freezes; a traveller tests it. spring comes and the ice goes soft at the edge. a log lies with its bark on. a valley stands open and takes whatever runs down to it. the yellow river carries more silt than any other great river on earth, and people who lived beside it knew muddy water well: in a still pond it clears, and the silt it leaves is the richest soil of the plain. so mud is not dirt in this passage. it is water and earth that are not yet sorted, with a field inside. a marsh, an estuary, a flood plain in spring: the most fertile places are the least clear. then long, slow movement, and things grow. where did you last see clear water? what was under it? make the jar of muddy water and leave it in view for a day. or take the smaller form: when you next feel the urge to fix a confused matter at once, wait for the length of ten slow breaths and do nothing to it. note the pace at which things settle when you do not help. then read legge’s seven adjectives and choose the one that you fear most: shrinking, irresolute, grave, evanescent, unpretentious, vacant, dull. for one conversation today, permit yourself to be that. see what the other person does with the room that you leave. the first simile has a famous cousin in the confucian books, if you want to compare two kinds of care. and the opening four words connect this portrait to the first page of the book.

士: the class that served and wandered. the 士 were at first the lowest rank of the zhou nobility: men trained to drive a chariot, shoot, and keep the rites, in service to a lord. when the old order broke in the warring states, they became a class with skills to sell: officers, clerks, envoys, strategists, teachers. they went from court to court, and rulers competed for them. confucius, mozi, sunzi, and mencius were all 士. so the line is addressed to a profession, and its reader is a man who must advise a dangerous king and stay alive. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 善為道者, “good at practising the way”, as passage 65 does; the guodian bamboo slips are reported to read 士. legge shows both in a bracket: “masters (of the tao)”. english has no word for 士. “knight” has the horse and the rank; “scholar” has the book; “officer” has the service.

four words, each one a door. 微妙玄通: four characters with no grammar between them, and each one was used earlier in the book. 微 is the “minute” of passage 14, that which the hand cannot get; its first sense is to walk unseen. 妙 and 玄 are the fineness and the dark of passage 1. 通 is new: the shuowen defines it 達也, “to reach through”, and its walking sign, 辶, shows a road with no block on it. so the masters are described with the same words as the way: you cannot see them, for the same reasons. english must add “and” or commas and a verb. the chinese only sets four stones in a row. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 玄達 for the last pair; 達 is the shuowen’s own gloss for 通, so the sense is the same.

識: to know, or to put on record. 識 is not the general word for knowing, which is 知. it is to recognise a thing when you meet it again, to mark it, to keep it in mind. the shuowen gives 知也, “to know”, as its second sense, and the graph has 言, speech, at the left: knowledge that can be said. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write 志, a word that also means “to record, to note down”. so 深不可識 is “too deep to be marked”: they leave nothing by which a person, or an office, could file them. for a wandering officer in a state that kept registers of its people, that is a practical skill and a spiritual one in the same breath. english “unfathomable” keeps the depth and loses the record. who has a file on you, and what could never be in it?

a portrait under protest. 故強為之容: “so, forced, make them a 容”. 容 is the look of a person: the face, the bearing, and so a likeness of them. 強 (read qiang) is “against the grain, with effort”. the speaker says: this cannot be done, and i do it anyway, badly. the chinese has no “i”; english versions add it, and our line avoids it at some cost to ease. passage 25 has the same confession about the way itself, and there the “i” is written: 吾不知其名…強為之名曰大, “i do not know its name… forced to name it, i say ‘great’”. what follows is honest about its own method. there are seven lines, and each one has 若, “as if, like”. not one of them says what the masters are. wang bi notes it: 凡此諸若，皆言其容象不可得而形名也, “all these ‘likes’ say that their look cannot be given a form and a name”.

豫: the elephant at the bank. the right side of 豫 is 象, an elephant. the shuowen’s definition is a surprise: 象之大者, “a large kind of elephant”; and it adds one scholar’s remark, 不害於物, “it does no harm to other creatures”. elephants lived in north china in early times, and old tradition says the great beast is careful: it tests the ground before it puts its weight down. from this, readers explained the sense “wary, to hesitate”. the word also means “to prepare beforehand” and “to be at ease”. wang bi reads the image from the outside: 豫然若欲度、若不欲度，其情不可得見之貌也. “as if they wished to cross, as if they did not wish to cross: the look of one whose feelings cannot be seen.” so the caution is real, and it is also a kind of cover. this word is half of a pair; see the other animal.
