猶豫: a word cut in two. the first two portraits begin with 豫 and 猶. put together, 猶豫 is the common chinese word for “to hesitate”, in use from the warring states until today. the poet has split one word and set a half at the head of each line. the shuowen calls 猶 an animal, 玃屬, “of the ape kind”, and notes that in the far west the word meant a puppy. a sixth-century scholar, yan zhitui, tells the lore: a dog runs ahead of its master, waits, and runs back; or a timid beast climbs a tree at each sound and comes down again. modern linguists think the stories came later. for them 猶豫 is a two-syllable sound word, like 惚恍 in the passage before, and the animals are only the borrowed graphs. both facts are worth having. the reader of chinese sees an ape and an elephant, and hears one word for doubt.

thin ice: a shared image. to cross a northern river in winter is to walk on ice that may not hold, or to wade in water cold enough to kill. the book of odes has the same fear: 戰戰兢兢，如臨深淵，如履薄冰, “in fear and trembling, as if at the edge of a deep pool, as if treading on thin ice”. the confucians loved that line. the dying disciple zengzi quotes it in the analects as the sum of a careful life: now, he says, i know i have come through. so the laozi’s first portrait uses a picture that its rivals also used. the difference is in what the care protects. for zengzi it guards the body that his parents gave him, and his good name. here it has no stated object. it is how one moves when one does not assume that the surface will hold.

neighbours on four sides. 畏四鄰 was not a figure of speech in the fourth century bce. the states of the central plain, wei and han above all, had an enemy on each border and were called “ground of war on four sides”. wang bi reads the image as a siege: 四鄰合攻中央之主，猶然不知所趣向者也, “the four neighbours join to attack the lord at the centre, who, in two minds, does not know which way to turn”. the word 鄰 also has a smaller scale. the shuowen says 五家爲鄰, “five households make a 鄰”. in qin, the reforms of shang yang (from 356 bce) bound households in groups of five and ten that had to report each other’s crimes, or share the punishment. so a neighbour could be an informer. look at 畏, fear: the shuowen says it shows 鬼頭而虎爪, “a ghost’s head and a tiger’s claws”.

容 or 客: a face or a guest. our pinned text reads 儼兮其若容: grave, “as if a (formal) bearing”. most other editions read 客, a guest: grave, like one who is a guest in another’s house. the mawangdui silk texts and the older guodian slips are reported to read the same. the two graphs differ by a few strokes under the same roof, 宀. the guest is almost surely the older reading, and the proof is in the sound. the similes rhyme in sets. 客 and 釋 (melt) end alike in the old rhyme group 鐸, as 樸, 谷, and 濁 below them all end in the group 屋. 容 belongs to a different group and breaks the pair. a copyist’s eye may have caught 容 from four lines above. we render the text as it stands. but keep the guest in mind: a person who does not own the room, touches nothing without leave, and watches the host.

渙: the moment before the thaw. after three images of care, the fourth lets go. 渙 is a water word; the shuowen defines it as flowing and scattering. it is also the name of hexagram 59 in the book of changes, wind over water, which the tradition reads as the breaking up of what was rigid, as river ice breaks up in spring. 釋 is “to untie, to release”. the image is exact about time: 將釋, “about to melt”. the ice is still ice, but its edges are wet and its hold is gone. the portrait so far has been tight: wary, watchful, grave. this line says the same person is on the point of flowing. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write 淩澤 here, usually read as the same “ice that melts”. think of someone whom you know to be both very careful and very soft. is that one quality or two?

樸: wood before the knife. this is the first time the book uses one of its main images. 樸 has 木, a tree, at the left. the shuowen defines it in two characters: 木素也, “wood in its plain state”, a log or block that no tool has shaped. 素 in that gloss is undyed silk; the two words are a pair, and passage 19 sets them side by side. uncarved wood is not yet a bowl, a wheel, or an idol. it can become any of them, and when it becomes one, it loses the rest. passage 28 says so: when the 樸 is split, it becomes vessels. english “simplicity” makes it a virtue and “the uncarved block” a slogan. here it is only a comparison for a person: 敦, thick and solid, with the bark on. the image returns in passages 19, 28, 32, 37, and 57.

muddy as praise. the last simile is a shock in its own culture. 清, clear, was the word for a pure man, and 濁, muddy, for a corrupt age. a famous song says: when the canglang river is clear, i wash my hat-strings in it; when it is muddy, i wash my feet. mencius quotes it, and in the songs of chu a fisherman sings it to the exiled minister qu yuan, who chose to drown and not to soil himself. the fisherman’s question to him was: when the whole world is muddy, why not stir the mud and ride the wave? the laozi stands with the fisherman, and goes further. its masters are 混, undivided, and look like mud. the next lines say what the mud is for. the shuowen cannot help here: for it, 濁 is first the name of a river.

wang bi: two questions and why they are hard. the two lines are built alike: who can, in state a, by means b, slowly reach c? muddy, through stillness, clear. at rest, through long movement, alive. note that the second undoes the first. the place of 久, “long”, is open: “long at rest”, or “through long movement”. stillness is not the end; when the water is clear and settled, movement must start again or nothing grows. wang bi sets them in a row of three: 夫晦以理物則得明，濁以靜物則得清，安以動物則得生，此自然之道也。 “use the dim to order things and you get light; use the muddy to still things and you get the clear; use rest to move things and you get life. this is the way of what is so of itself.” then: 孰能者，言其難也, “‘who can’ says that it is hard”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to have no “who can”. there the lines are statements.

徐: at walking pace. the word that both questions share is 徐. the shuowen defines it 安行也: “to walk at ease”. its left side is 彳, the step. so “slowly” here is a pace of the legs. it is not delay, and it is not the slowness of a clerk. wang bi adds a gloss of his own: 徐者，詳慎也, “徐 means careful and attentive”. english “gradually” is a word about a graph; 徐 is a word about a body that does not hurry. it is the speed at which mud sinks and at which a seed comes up, and no effort makes either one faster. modern life treats this speed as a fault. note which of today’s tasks, if any, you did at the pace of a walk.

盈: full to the brim. 盈 has 皿, a dish, at its foot. the shuowen says 滿器也: “to fill a vessel”. it is fullness of the exact kind that comes just before a spill, and wang bi’s whole comment is four characters: 盈必溢也, “what is full must overflow”. the book returns to this vessel often. the way is an empty bowl that use does not fill (4). to hold a thing and fill it is worse than to stop in time (9). great fullness seems empty (45). legge writes “full (of themselves)”, and so turns a fact about cups into a sermon against pride. the chinese is wider than that. full of plans, of goods, of certainty, of virtue: each of these leaves no room for the next thing. what in you is at the brim?

a last line that no edition settles. the received line is 故能蔽不新成. 蔽 is “to cover”, and wang bi glosses it so: 蔽，覆蓋也. read that way the sense is “able to stay covered, and not be newly finished”. most readers since take 蔽 as a loan for 敝, a worn-out garment; the shuowen gives 敗衣, “ruined clothing”, as one sense of 敝. then: “able to be worn, and not newly finished”. both mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 是以能敝而不成: “so able to be worn and not complete”, with no “new” at all. other editions turn the line around, 敝而新成, “worn and then made new”, close to passage 22: 敝則新, “worn, then new”. so the tradition gives three endings: to refuse renewal, to refuse completion, or to be renewed. all three agree on the first half. one who is not full can afford to be worn. 成 is “finished, perfected”, and each version keeps that word. our rendering keeps the received words.

legge’s masters look weak. read legge’s adjectives in a row: “shrinking”, “irresolute”, “grave”, “evanescent”, “unpretentious”, “vacant”, “dull”. to a victorian reader that is the portrait of a poor character; a gentleman was resolute and bright. legge is not wrong about the words. he is faithful, and the faithfulness shows how far the passage is from his own ideal of a man. he also adds a host for the guest, “(in awe of his host)”, and people for the fear, “all around them”: the war of four borders has become shyness in company. in the questions he answers before the text does: “let it be still, and it will gradually become clear.” the chinese asks who can. it does not say “let it”. which of his seven adjectives would you least like to have said about you? start there.

a jar of muddy water. fill a glass jar with water and stir in a spoon of soil. set it where you will pass it during the day. do nothing to it. you cannot clear it by any act: to filter it with a finger, to shake it, to watch it with impatience, all keep it brown. in an hour the top is lighter. by evening there is clear water over a floor of silt. nothing was removed; the mud is all still in the jar, and it has found its place. then do the second half, which people forget. pour the clear water on a plant. rest, then long movement, then life. the next time your mind is thick with a problem, remember which one you are in: the stirring, the settling, or the pouring.

濁 and 清, 靜 and 動: the second question undoes the first. the two questions hold two pairs: 濁 and 清, muddy and clear, and 靜 and 動, stillness and movement. it is easy to read them as a ranking: clear is the goal, and stillness is the way to it. but the second question starts where the first one ends, and it goes the other way. what is at rest comes alive through movement. so stillness clears the mud, and then movement stirs the settled water into life, which is muddy again. neither state is the end. the portrait says the same: the masters are grave and loosening, solid and wide, and their last likeness is 濁, mud. the passage does favor one thing, 不盈, not to be full. that preference is aimed at an age that wanted each cup at the brim. it is not a rule to stay empty. the one who is not full can be worn, and passage 22 says that the worn is what becomes new. when did stillness last serve you, and when movement?

confusion clears by itself when it is left still; to stir it in order to fix it keeps it muddy.. confusion clears by itself when it is left still; to stir it in order to fix it keeps it muddy. has this been true for you? recall one tangle that cleared when you left it, and one that got worse. what happens in you when a matter is unclear and you do nothing? what do you fear will be said of you? the passage itself gives the other side: what is at rest comes alive through movement. take that as the main truth for a few minutes. what changes in the body? do you trust stillness or action more, and who taught you that trust?

the one who does not want to be full can stay worn and unfinished, and that is a strength.. the one who does not want to be full can stay worn and unfinished, and that is a strength. do you agree, or does “unfinished” sound like failure to you? where did you learn that a person must look complete, new, on top of things? what happened to those who did not? hold the opposite: fullness is good, and a life should be filled to the brim while there is time. what does that view wake in you? when you see someone who is content to look worn, what do you feel? what does the feeling say about you?

豫 an elephant tests the ice. start at the right, with 象. it is one of the clearest pictures left in the script. the shuowen describes the animal as if for someone who has not seen one: 長鼻牙，南越大獸, “long nose and tusks, a great beast of the far south”, and says the graph shows its ears, tusks, and four feet. turn the character a quarter to the left in your mind: the top is the head and trunk, the box is the body, and the strokes that sweep away below are legs and tail. elephants are named on the oracle bones of the north; the climate was warmer then. by the time of the laozi the animal was gone from the north, and people knew it from its bones and from pictures. the han feizi says that this is why 象 came to mean “image”: men got the bones of a dead elephant and from them pictured the living one. that is the 象 of the passage before this: the image of no thing. now the left side. 予 means “to give”; the shuowen says it pictures a thing handed over. here it gives only its sound. together they wrote the name of a large elephant, says the shuowen, and then a set of states of mind: wary, prepared, and also at ease, glad. 豫 is the name of hexagram 16 and the old one-word name of henan. how did one word get both “hesitate” and “delight”? perhaps both are what a great body does when it does not hurry. fifteen strokes: four for 予, eleven for the elephant. 予 first: a level stroke that turns back down to the left; a dot; a second level stroke that ends in a hook; then a vertical that hooks to the left at its foot. the elephant begins with a short falling stroke and a level one that turns down to the left: the head. then the flat box of the body: left side, top and right side in one stroke, and the line that closes it. now watch strokes ten to fifteen. a falling stroke; then the long curved stroke with a hook, the spine of the right side; then two more falling strokes under the first, on the left of the spine; then a short falling stroke on its right; and last a stroke that presses out to the lower right. strokes ten, twelve, and thirteen are parallel, and calligraphers warn against making them equal. they fan out like legs.

涉 two feet, one stream. left: 氵, three drops, the short form of 水, water. right: 步, a step. and 步 is itself two pictures. its top is 止, which was a drawing of a foot, with the toes up (it now means “to stop”). its bottom is the same foot turned the other way. the shuowen says exactly that: 从止𣥂相背, “from a foot and its mirror image, back to back”. left foot, right foot: one pace. so 涉 is water and two feet. the oracle-bone form is commonly described as even plainer: a stream that runs through the middle, with one footprint on each side of it. the shuowen lists the word under a fuller graph with the water written twice, and defines it 徒行厲水也, “to cross water on foot”. that is the first sense: to wade, with no boat and no bridge. then the meaning spread, as it does: to pass through (涉世, to go through the world), to have experience of, to be involved in (干涉, to interfere; 涉及, to touch upon). see the foot in its other homes: 正 (straight; commonly explained as a foot that marches on a town), 足 (the foot and leg), 走 (to run), 武 (commonly explained as a foot and a spear: to go to war), and in 辶, the walking sign of 道. the first portrait of the passage is a winter crossing. in the character one foot is still on the near bank. ten strokes: three, four, three. the water is two dots and a stroke that flicks upward; the flick points at the place where the right side begins, and in running script the three join in one wave. the upper foot, 止: a vertical; a short level stroke to its right; a short vertical at the left; and a long level base. that base is the bank, and it is the widest line in the character. under it the second foot: a vertical in the centre, a dot to the left of it, and then the tenth stroke, a long sweep down to the left. watch that last stroke; it is the leg that reaches out for the far side, and its slow thinning to a point is the whole movement of the word. note what is absent: the lower part looks like 少, “few”, but it has no dot on the right.

16 · home to the root. reach emptiness: the limit. / keep stillness: held firm. / the ten thousand things rise side by side; / i, by this, watch the return. / now things, thick and teeming, / each go home again to the root. / going home to the root is called stillness. / this is called reporting back on the charge. / to report back on the charge is called the constant. / to know the constant is called bright. / not to know the constant: / wild rising, ill-omened. / know the constant: room for all. / room for all, then even-handed. / even-handed, then whole. / whole, then heaven. / heaven, then dao. / dao, then lasting. / until the body goes under, no danger. two lines of instruction, then a report, then a chain. the instruction: bring emptiness to its limit and keep stillness firm. the report, in the first person: the ten thousand things rise side by side, and i watch them return. they are thick and teeming, and each one goes home to its root. then a run of definitions, each joined to the last: home at the root is stillness; stillness is the charge reported back; that is the constant; to know it is brightness; not to know it is a pit. the chain at the end has seven links with 乃, “and then”: room, even-handed, whole, heaven, dao, lasting. the last line is about the death of the body. the plain pictures are a bare hill, a slow horse, a herb, a bride, an envoy, a window with moonlight, and a trap. this is the nearest thing in the book to a meditation instruction, and it had a living context. the two verbs matter: 致, to bring a thing to its end, and 守, to guard. emptiness is reached; stillness is kept. then the text does not describe a blank. it describes a world in full motion, seen from a still place. that is the point that is easy to miss. the practice is not to stop things from rising. it is to see the whole arc of each one, the return as well as the rise. a mind that sees only risings is always behind: each new thing seems to need an answer. a mind that sees returns can let most things finish by themselves. wang bi makes stillness the ground and movement the visitor. and the end is honest: the body goes under too, and that also is a way home. the last chain is the political part. it starts in knowledge, not in will: know the constant, and you have room. a leader who knows that fashions, crises, rivals, and enthusiasms all rise and return does not need to crush each one, or to join each one. from room comes 公: even-handedness, the public interest, the quality of a true lord. the legalists got 公 by law and fear, with each private tie cut. here it comes from width. then the edition matters. if the next link is 王, king, as in every old copy, the passage tells a ruler how to deserve the title. if it is 全, whole, it tells anyone. the warning in the middle is for planners: 妄作凶. action that assumes the present trend will go on, with no knowledge of the return, is the pit in the road. 致虛極: breathe out fully and do not hurry the next breath. for a moment the chest is an empty hill. 守靜篤: 篤 is the tread of a heavy horse, so let the weight of the body go down through the seat or the feet, slow and firm. then watch the return in the breath itself. each in-breath is a rising, and each out-breath goes home. the standing practice of the chinese movement arts is called 站樁, “to stand like a post”, and its teachers speak of the legs as roots. a tree is still at the root and moves at the leaves. most of us live the other way: busy at the centre, and stiff at the edges. stand for two minutes and reverse it. where is the root of your standing? go to a deciduous wood at the end of autumn. all summer the trees sent matter up and out: leaves beyond counting, 芸芸. now the sugars have gone down into the roots, and the leaves lie on the ground over them, where fungi and worms turn them into next year’s soil. nothing has gone wrong. the wood is as alive as in june, and the life is at the root, in the dark, and still. the hexagram of return marks the solstice, when this stillness is deepest and the light has already turned. water does it too: rain, river, sea, cloud. so does each body. the text asks you to know this as a fact of the same order as gravity, and it says that people who plan as if growth had no return fall into a pit. take five minutes to watch one thing go home. then carry the question into the day: of the things that rose in you this morning, a worry, an anger, a wish to buy something, which have already returned without your help? count them at night. most people find that nearly all of them did. that count is a small piece of the constant, and to see it is a small piece of 明. one more exercise, for a larger scale. name one thing in your life or work that is now in its return: it grew, and now it goes back to the root. ask whether you still treat it as if it must rise. legge read stillness as a thing to guard “with unwearying vigour”. try it without the vigour.

虛: an empty hill. the shuowen’s entry for 虛 has nothing abstract in it. it says 大丘也, “a great mound”, and then gives a lesson on land: nine men make a well-field, four well-fields a town, four towns a 丘, and 丘謂之虛, “a hill-district is called a 虛”. the word was used for a wide, bare height, and for the site where a city used to be: the ruins of the shang capital are still called 殷虛 (now written 殷墟). so the picture behind “emptiness” is open ground with wind over it, where things once stood and may stand again. it is not a vacuum, and not the “void” that western thought fears. passage 5 called the space between heaven and earth 虛 and compared it to a bellows: empty, and never used up. english “vacancy”, legge’s word, sounds like a room to let.

靜 is stillness, not “harmony” and not “peace”. 靜 is the opposite of 動, movement. it is what muddy water does in the passage before this one: it stops, and so clears. modern versions often soften the word to “peace”, “tranquillity”, “serenity”, or “harmony”, which are pleasant feelings. 靜 is not a feeling. it is a physical fact that you can check: is it moving or not? the shuowen’s gloss is unexpected: 審也, “to examine closely”. the dictionary connects stillness with exact sight; a thing that keeps still can be looked at, and one who keeps still can look. the passage makes the same connection four lines later, when it calls knowledge of the constant bright. 靜 was also a term of the meditation teachers of the age; see the school in qi. it is the practice word of this passage. keep it hard and plain.

six characters, and no agreement on the last. 致虛極，守靜篤 is two matched lines of three. 極 is the ridgepole of a house, and so the highest point. 篤 is “solid, in earnest”; the shuowen’s picture is 馬行頓遟, “a horse that walks with heavy, slow steps”. the grammar is open: “reach the limit of emptiness”, or “reach emptiness, to the limit”. wang bi takes the second word of each line as the object: 言致虛物之極，篤守靜物之真正也, “this says: reach the limit of empty things; firmly keep the true rightness of still things”. the excavated texts differ. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to end each line with 也, as statements: 至虛極也. their last word is reported not to be 篤, and scholars dispute the graph. the guodian bamboo slips are reported to read 守中，篤也, “keep the centre: firm”. there 中, the centre, stands in the place of 靜, stillness. is stillness a centre for you, or an edge?

作 twice: to rise, and to rise wildly. 作 is “to get up, to start”; the shuowen says 起也, “to rise”. in line 3 the ten thousand things 並作, rise side by side: seeds come up, people get out of bed, plans begin. nine lines later the word returns in a darker phrase, 妄作, wild rising. it is one verb. the rising of things is not a fault; the text watches it with interest. the fault is to rise with no knowledge of the return. english needs two words, “arise” and “act”, and so the echo is lost. the lines were built for the ear in other ways too. in the old rhyme groups 篤 and 復 end alike (覺); so do 芸 and 根 (文), 靜 and 命 (耕), 常 and 明 (陽), 容 and 公 (東). each step of the argument is tied to the next by sound.

復: the hexagram of midwinter. a reader of the time knew 復 as the name of a figure in the book of changes, the twenty-fourth hexagram. it has five broken lines, and one whole line that enters at the bottom: thunder under the earth. the tradition matched it to the month of the winter solstice, when the dark is at its limit and the light starts to come back, though nothing can yet be seen above ground. an old comment on the figure says: 復其見天地之心乎, “in return, do we not see the heart of heaven and earth?” the verb in our line, 觀, “to watch”, is the name of another hexagram, the twentieth. so 吾以觀復 has the sound of a diviner at work. but here no stalks are counted. the “i” of the text only keeps empty and still, and watches where each thing goes. the shuowen defines 復 as 往來也: “to go and to come”.

wang bi: movement starts in stillness. on the line “i watch the return” wang bi writes: 以虛靜觀其反復。凡有起於虛，動起於靜，故萬物雖並動作，卒復歸於虛靜，是物之極篤也。 “by emptiness and stillness, watch their turning back. all that there is arises from emptiness; movement arises from stillness. so although the ten thousand things move and rise together, in the end they go back to empty stillness. this is the limit and the firmness of things.” for him, stillness is not one of two equal partners. it is the ground, and movement is a visit away from it. he said the same about the hexagram: when movement stops in the earth, the heart of heaven and earth is seen. later confucian thinkers objected that the heart of heaven and earth is life and motion. watch your own breath for a minute. which seems the base to you: the moving, or the pause?

芸芸: a plant that dies and lives again. 芸 has the grass sign, 艹, on top. the shuowen says it is a herb, like alfalfa, and then quotes a line that fits this passage almost too well: 芸艸可以死復生, “the 芸 plant can die and come to life again”. the word in that quotation is 復, the “return” of our passage. doubled, 芸芸 is a sound-picture of dense growth: leaves beyond counting. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write 雲雲, “cloud on cloud”, and read 天物, “the things of heaven”; the guodian slips are reported to have 天道員員, “heaven’s way goes round and round”. so one line has three pictures in three old copies: herbs, clouds, a wheel. the guodian text of this passage is reported to stop at this line. later chinese joined it to a buddhist term for the crowd of living beings: 芸芸眾生. look at a hedge or a lawn in june. each leaf in that crowd, the line says, has a way home.

歸: the bride goes home. english “return” can mean defeat: to go back, to lose ground. 歸 does not. the shuowen defines it 女嫁也, “a woman goes to be married”. in the old view a bride did not leave home. she went to the house where she belonged from then on, and the book of odes sings of it: 之子于歸, “this girl goes to her home”. so 歸 is to arrive where one belongs: soldiers 歸 from a campaign, rivers 歸 to the sea, and the dead were called 歸人, “those who have gone home”. 根 is the foot of a tree; the shuowen says 木株也, the stock. put the two together. in autumn the sap goes down and the leaves fall on the roots and feed them. the text does not call that a loss. it calls it a homecoming, and gives it the name stillness.

復命: fate, or a report to one’s lord?. 命 is a mouth, 口, and an order, 令. the shuowen says 使也, “to cause, to send on a task”. from “command” came “the mandate of heaven”, 天命, by which a house rules, and then “what heaven gives each creature”: its nature and its span of life. english versions say “returning to destiny” or “to fate”. those words suggest a future fixed in advance by gods or stars. 命 is a charge that was given, not a script. and 復命 was a plain phrase of court life. an envoy who was sent out with orders came back when the work was done and reported to his lord; the analects uses the phrase so. legge heard it: he writes of a “reporting” that things have “fulfilled their appointed end”. each thing was sent out with a charge: to be this leaf, this life. at the root it hands the charge back. what were you sent out to do?

the constant is the return itself. passage 1 used 常 as an adjective: the constant dao, the constant name. here it stands alone as a noun and has a definition: 復命曰常. to go back to the root and hand in the charge: that is called the constant. so the constant is not an object behind the world, and capital-letter words such as “the eternal” are poor english for it. nothing in this passage is outside time. what is constant is a movement: out and back, rise and return, as regular as the year. wang bi describes it by what it lacks: 常之為物，不偏不彰，無皦昧之狀，溫涼之象. “the constant, as a thing, does not lean and does not show; it has no bright or dark shape, no warm or cool image.” his “bright or dark” quotes passage 14. if the only constant thing is that all things go home, is that sad to you, or a relief?

明: light enough to see by. 明 is written with 日, the sun, beside 月, the moon. the shuowen enters it in an older form, 朙, with a window in place of the sun, and defines it 照也, “to shine on, to light up”: moonlight that comes in at a window. english versions say “enlightenment” or “insight”, and each brings its own history: the buddha’s awakening, the european age of reason, a flash in the mind. 明 is plainer. it is enough light to see what is in the room. in this passage it is defined: to know that things return is to be 明. passage 33 says 自知者明, “one who knows oneself is 明”; passage 52 says 見小曰明, “to see the small is called 明”. the opposite here is not darkness, which this book respects. it is 妄: action with no ground under it.

凶: the pit in the path. 不知常，妄作凶. six characters, with no “if” and no “then”. 妄 is “wild, baseless”; the shuowen says 亂也, “disorder”, and the graph has 亡, “lost”, in it. 作 is the rising of line 3. 凶 is the diviner’s verdict, the opposite of 吉, “auspicious”, and it is cut on thousands of oracle bones. the shuowen explains the graph as a trap: 象地穿交陷其中也, “it pictures a hole in the ground, and a thing that has fallen into it”. so the line is a small scene. one who does not know that things return starts up blindly, and walks into a pit. it is not a threat of punishment; there is no judge in it. a person who expects summer to last, a state that expects to grow each year, will meet the hole that was always in the road. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to repeat a word: 不知常，妄；妄作，凶.

容 again: from a face to a valley. in passage 15, 容 was the look of a person: a likeness, a bearing. here the same graph is a verb: to hold, to have room for. the shuowen gives this sense first: 盛也, “to contain, as a vessel does”. and it reads the graph as 宀, a roof, over 谷, a valley: a sheltered hollow that takes in what comes. the two senses are one in chinese. a face is that which holds a person’s feelings, and a large-minded person has a large “capacity”. wang bi glosses the line 無所不包通也: “there is nothing that it does not wrap and pass through”. legge needs two nouns, “capacity and forbearance”. note the logic. one who knows that each thing returns has no need to push any of them out. tolerance here is not a moral effort. it is what is left when the fear of things goes.

公: the back turned on the private. 公 is a political word. the shuowen defines it 平分也, “to share out evenly”, and explains the graph with a quotation from the legalist han fei: 背厶爲公, “to turn the back on the private is 公”. the lower part, 厶, is the old way to write 私, private interest; the upper part, 八, is read as two strokes that turn away from each other. in han fei’s state, 公 and 私 are enemies: each private loyalty to family, friend, or teacher is a theft from the ruler’s order. the same graph is the title “duke”, the lord of a state. so a warring states reader hears three things in 容乃公: fair, public, and lordly. the laozi comes to 公 by a road that han fei did not take. no law forces it and no private tie is broken. it follows from room for all.

whole, or king?. our pinned text reads 公乃全，全乃天: “even-handed, then whole; whole, then heaven”. this is a modern correction. every old transmitted edition reads 王, king: 公乃王，王乃天, “even-handed, then a king; a king, then heaven”, and the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read the same. legge follows it with “a kingliness of character”. scholars of the twentieth century proposed 全 for two reasons. wang bi’s own comment on the line does not speak of a king: it says 無所不周普, “there is nothing that it does not reach all round”, which explains “whole” well. and they held that 全 makes a nearer rhyme with 天, the next link. the shuowen’s entry for 王 has the han view of a king: three level strokes for heaven, earth, and humankind, and one line that joins them. with 王 the passage is advice to a ruler. with 全 it is open to any person. the evidence of the copies is for “king”. which chain would you rather climb?

沒身: when the body goes under. 沒 is a water word. the shuowen says 沈也, “to sink”. 沒身 is “until the body sinks”: to the end of life. the passage that began with rising ends with going under, and looks at it calmly. 不殆 is “no danger”; the shuowen glosses 殆 as 危也, “peril”. this is not a promise that one will not die. it says that the whole length of the road, the end included, has no pit in it. wang bi’s comment is his longest here: 無之為物，水火不能害，金石不能殘。用之於心則虎兕無所投其齒角，兵戈無所容其鋒刃. “nothingness, as a thing: water and fire cannot harm it, metal and stone cannot break it. use it in the heart, and tiger and rhinoceros find no place for tooth and horn, and weapons no place for their edge.” he borrows the beasts from passage 50. the same four characters come again in passage 52.

stillness had teachers. 虛 and 靜 were technical terms before they were poetry. in the fourth century bce the state of qi paid scholars of each school to live and debate near the ji gate of its capital. a group of texts linked to that circle and kept in the collection called guanzi teaches a method: sit with the body upright, calm the breath, empty the heart of likes and dislikes, and a fine vital essence will come to rest in you. the best known of them is the “inward training” (內業). its words are the words of this passage: 靜, 虛, 守, the still heart as a “lodging place”. so the first two lines were instructions that a student of the time could follow, with a teacher and a posture. the same texts say that a ruler who can do this will order the state without effort. in that age the practice and the politics were not separate.

legge guards stillness “with unwearying vigour”. legge’s first sentence shows a victorian at work on a word that he does not trust. stillness, he writes, is to be “guarded with unwearying vigour”: effort and energy, the virtues of his own age, are brought in to keep watch over their opposite. emptiness is “(the state of) vacancy”. he helps the plants with a bracket, “(in the vegetable world)”, which is right about the image and limits it to botany. at the end he promises that one “is exempt from all danger of decay”, where the chinese says only until the body goes under, no danger: decay is not denied in the text. but he also hears things that later versions miss. his “reporting that they have fulfilled their appointed end” keeps the court sense of 復命, and his “regular, unchanging rule” for 常 has the word “regular” in it.

watch one thing go home. sit upright for five minutes. do not try to empty the mind; that is one more rising. let things rise as they wish: a sound, an itch, a plan, a memory. your one task is the second half of each. each of them, if you do not feed it, goes back. the sound ends. the itch fades. the plan runs out of words. watch for the place where each one goes, as you would watch where a bird lands. you will find that you seldom see it; attention jumps to the next rising before the last has gone home. after some days it gets easier. the passage says that this watching has a result that is not mystical at all: room. what returns by itself does not need to be pushed away.

作 and 復, 動 and 靜: one arc. the pairs here are 作 and 復, rising and return, and with them 動 and 靜, movement and stillness. the passage leans to one side. it tells the reader to keep stillness, and it calls the return “the constant”. wang bi makes that lean a rank: stillness is the ground. the text itself is more even. the things rise 並, side by side, and no line blames them for it. what it calls ill-omened is 妄作, rising that does not know the return. so the lean is a correction. people see risings easily and miss returns, and the passage points to the half that they miss. the favored side turns too. a root is where the next shoot starts, and the hexagram of return shows one light line that already comes back under five dark ones. a stillness that refused to rise again would also fail to know the constant. which half of the arc do you see less often?

each thing that rises goes home to its root, and to know this is to see clearly.. each thing that rises goes home to its root, and to know this is to see clearly. do you hold this as a fact, or only as a comfort? what in your life has not come back to its root? think of a thing that you built and that is now going down. what did you learn, early, about endings? take the opposite view: growth can go on, and what returns to the root has failed. stay with it. what does it promise you, and what does it ask? is the return sad to you or a relief, and what past loss speaks in that answer?

stillness is the home state, and rising and action are a journey out from it.. stillness is the home state, and rising and action are a journey out from it. does that match what you feel? when you are still, are you at home, or are you waiting? what were you told as a child about sitting still, and about being busy? which of the two earned love? later thinkers answered that the heart of heaven and earth is life and motion, and that stillness is a pause in it. take their side for a few minutes. what do you notice? which do you call other people more often: lazy, or restless? could that word point at a part of you that you do not let live?

action that does not know the return is blind, and it ends in harm.. action that does not know the return is blind, and it ends in harm. do you agree? find one plan of yours that assumes that the present trend will hold. when you act fast and far, what are you afraid will happen if you wait? the other side says: one who waits to know the whole arc does not act at all, and boldness opens roads. what in you agrees? what has each side cost you so far, and which cost do you prefer not to count?

根 a tree, and an eye that looks back. the left side is 木, a tree, and it is a drawing: a trunk, a line of branches across it, and two roots that spread at the foot. three small additions to that drawing make three words that chinese children learn together. a mark at the foot of the tree is 本, the root, and so “origin, basis”. a mark at the top is 末, the tip, “the last and least”. a mark through the middle, in the shuowen’s account, is 朱, the red heartwood. our character is the other, later word for root, and it is made in the usual way: 木 for the meaning, with a second part for the sound. that second part is 艮 (gen). it is worth a look for its own sake. the shuowen explains it as 匕 and 目, an eye and a person turned around: “eyes that glare at each other, and neither gives way”. its sense is “stubborn, to stop”. in the book of changes 艮 is the name of the trigram of the mountain, whose quality is keeping still. no one planned this; 艮 is in 根 for its sound. but the reader’s eye sees a tree and a stillness, in the character for the place that things go home to. cousins by the same sound part: 很 (stubborn; now “very”), 限 (a limit), 恨 (a grudge), 眼 (the eye), 銀 (silver), 跟 (the heel; to follow). the laozi comes back to the root in passages 6, 26, and 59. ten strokes: four for the tree, six for 艮. the tree: a level stroke; a vertical through it; then a stroke that falls to the left; and a fourth that would be a long sweep to the right if the tree stood alone. here it is cut down to a dot. this is a rule of the regular script: a part at the left gives way and pulls in its right arm, so that the two halves do not strike each other. then 艮: a stroke that goes right and turns down; two short level strokes inside; then a long vertical that turns at its foot and flicks up to the right. watch the last two: a short stroke that falls to the left, and then the long stroke that presses out to the lower right. that final one is the only wide gesture in the character, and it runs low and far, like a root just under the ground.

靜 stillness, with a tug-of-war inside. two parts, and each has two parts more. on the left is 青, the colour of living plants: blue-green. the shuowen calls it 東方色也, “the colour of the east”, and reads the graph as 生 over 丹. 生 is a sprout that comes out of the ground. 丹 is the red mineral cinnabar, in its pit; it stands here for mineral colour in general. so 青 is “the colour of that which grows”. you know its family: 清 (clear water), 晴 (clear sky), 精 (fine, pure rice; essence), 情 (feeling), 請 (to ask). on the right is 爭, to contend. the shuowen glosses it 引也, “to pull”, and its seal form is commonly explained as two hands, one above and one below, that pull at one thing. the laozi uses this word for what the sage and water do not do: 不爭. so the character for stillness contains the character for struggle. the shuowen says that 爭 gives only the sound, and that is surely right. still, each reader of chinese sees it there, and it is a true picture of an hour of sitting: clear green on one side, and a tug-of-war on the other. the shuowen’s meaning for the whole is 審也, “to examine closely”. a short form, 静, is used today on the mainland and in japan. passage 45 says 清靜為天下正: “clear and still, the measure of the world”. both of its key words have 青 in them. sixteen strokes, eight and eight. 青 first: two level strokes, a vertical through them, and a longer level stroke that is the ground under the sprout. below it, the form that looks like 月: a vertical; a stroke that goes right, turns down, and hooks; and two short level strokes inside. then 爭: a flat stroke that falls to the left; two dots; a short falling stroke. these four are the upper hand. next, a level stroke that turns down; a long level stroke that crosses out to the right; one more level stroke below. watch the sixteenth stroke: a vertical with a hook that goes down through all three, and joins them as a hand closes. each half has many level lines. the skill is to keep them evenly spaced and not quite parallel, so that the two halves of the character are still and do not look frozen.

17 · we did it ourselves. the highest: those below know there is one. / next: one they hold dear and praise. / next: one they fear. / next: one they scorn. / trust not enough, there: / no trust, there. / far off: how costly the words! / the work done, the task carried through, / the hundred families all say: / “we are so of ourselves.” a ladder of four rungs, told from below. of the highest, the people know only that someone is there. the next is loved and praised. the next is feared. the last is scorned. then one line that explains the fall, with the same word twice: where trust is short, there is no trust. then a portrait of the first ruler in three strokes: far off, or wary (the copies differ); sparing with words; and absent from the sentence that reports the success. the last line is spoken by the hundred families, and it is the first place in the book where the people speak: “we are so of ourselves.” the passage has no sage and no dao in it. it is a short theory of government in forty-four characters, and in the oldest copy it is the first half of a longer piece. read the four rulers as four ways in which the mind governs itself. in the last, you scorn your own resolutions: you make rules and break them and think less of yourself each time. in the third, you rule yourself by fear: of failure, of shame, of the voice that scolds. in the second, you rule by self-praise and the pleasure of being good; it works, and it needs an audience. in the first, there is direction and almost no ruler: you eat when hungry and work when it is time, and the day gets done. contemplative practice often gets stuck on the second rung, in love with its own virtue. the trust line applies inside as well. a mind that does not trust the body sets a guard on it, and the body learns to cheat. what in you already runs of itself, if you let it? this is the passage that leaders quote, and it is easy to quote wrongly. it does not say: hide your power so that it works better. that is the reading of han fei, who took much from this book and made the ruler’s invisibility a method of control. in the text, the people’s last sentence is true. they did do it. the ruler’s work was of another kind: to keep trust whole, to speak rarely so that words kept their value, and to stay out of the account of the success. note where the popular leader stands: second. to be loved and praised is good, and it moves the people’s eyes upward and away from their own work. wang bi’s test is the health of a body: the organ that works well is not felt. which rung does your team’s talk about you put you on? a good teacher of movement shows this passage with the hands. the worst kind of correction pushes a student’s limb into place; the student resists, or learns nothing. better is the firm instruction that the student obeys from fear of doing wrong. better again is warm praise. best is a touch so light, or a change in the task so small, that the student’s body finds the line and the student says: i felt it myself. the same holds for your own body. you can force the breath to slow, and it will fight you; you can coax it; or you can make room and let it settle of itself. the first way is tiring, and it also breaks trust between you and the animal that you are. sit for a minute and do not manage the breath at all. no one governs a forest, and yet it is in order. a wolf pack or a herd has leaders, but mostly they lead by where they walk and when they stop, without display. the sun does the largest work on earth and issues no instruction; an old man in a story could sing that he owed it nothing. the word that the people use in the last line, 自然, later became the chinese word for nature, and this passage shows why: nature is the great case of work done with no credit claimed. a gardener knows the first rung. you do not make a plant grow. you see to the soil, the water, and the light, and stand back; and the plant, if it could speak, would say that it grew by itself. it would be right. do the one act of help with no credit today, and listen for “i did it myself”. then try the passage on your speech. for one meeting or one family meal, price your words high: say half as much as usual, and see whether the others say more. if you lead anything, write down the last three things your group did well, and ask of each one: could they tell that story without my name in it? if you want to see how hard this passage is for a language like english, read legge’s seven brackets. and if you want the oldest and shortest form of the ideal, read the song of the old man who beat the ground.

太上: the best, the oldest, and later a god. 太上 is “greatest” and “above”. it can be a rank: the best kind of ruler, with three worse kinds after it. wang bi reads it so: 太上，謂大人也。大人在上，故曰太上, “太上 means the great person. the great person is above, so the text says ‘the greatest above’.” it can also be a time: “in highest antiquity”, with 其次 as “the next age”. legge chose that, and then the four lines are a history of decline, which the next passage continues. the chinese does not need to choose, because in the thought of the age the oldest was the best. english must choose; our “the highest” leans to rank. the phrase had a third life. when laozi was made a god in the han and after, his title was 太上老君, “the old lord, most high”. a phrase for a ruler whom nobody notices became the name of a deity on an altar.

“know there is one”, or “do not know”?. 下知有之: “those below know that there is one”, and no more. wang bi adds two words, 而已, “and that is all”. many later editions change one graph, 下 to 不: 不知有之, “they do not know that there is one”. legge used such a text. the sense is more extreme and has pleased many readers: the best government is one that people cannot even find. but the old copies agree against it. both mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 下知有之, and the guodian bamboo slips are reported to read the same. the older line is also the more exact. the people are not fooled, and the ruler does not hide. they know that someone is there, as you know that a house has a foundation. they have no reason to think about it. note 之, “it, him, her, them”: the chinese gives the ruler no gender and no number. our “one” is as near as english allows.

loved and praised: only second place. 親 is the word for kin, and as a verb “to hold close as family”; the shuowen glosses it 至也, “to come right up to”. 譽 is praise spoken aloud. a ruler whom the people love as a parent and praise in songs was the confucian ideal. mencius told kings that their task was to be “father and mother to the people”. the laozi puts this ruler second. wang bi explains what has been lost: 不能以無為居事，不言為教，立善行施，使下得親而譽之也. “unable to manage affairs by not-forcing and to teach without words, this one sets up the good and hands out favours, and so gives those below something to love and praise.” the fault is small, and it is visible: the people now look up. their attention has moved from their own lives to the person at the top. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 親譽之, with no “and”.

feared: the legalist state. the third ruler is the one that the age was building. in qin and elsewhere, ministers such as shang yang ruled by published law, heavy penalties, and rewards for informers. han fei gave the theory: the ruler holds “two handles”, punishment and favour, and people must dread the first. wang bi describes the step down: 不復能以恩仁令物，而賴威權也, “no longer able to move creatures by kindness and humaneness, this one leans on awe and power”. european readers will think of machiavelli, who asked in 1513 whether it is better for a prince to be loved or feared, and chose fear as the safer of the two. the laozi has the same pair and the opposite order: loved is second, feared is third. and it puts both below a kind of ruler that machiavelli’s question does not allow for.

侮: the last rung. 侮 is a person, 亻, beside a sound part. the shuowen glosses it with one hard word: 傷也, “to wound”. it is contempt that is shown: to insult, to bully, to make sport of. so at the bottom the direction turns around. three lines told what those below feel about the one above: they know, they love, they fear. now those below do the wounding. wang bi says how a state arrives here: 不能法以正齊民，而以智治國，下知避之，其令不從. “unable to keep the people level by law and uprightness, this one rules the state by cleverness. those below know how to slip past it, and the orders are not followed.” rule by cleverness teaches the people to be clever. fear lasts while the police are efficient. after that it turns to jokes, and then to open scorn. where the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 其下, “the lowest”, the received text has a third “next”.

信: a person beside their word. 信 is 亻, a person, and 言, speech. the shuowen calls it a joined-meaning graph, 會意, and defines it 誠也: “true, sincere”. it is the state in which what a person says and what is so are one thing. english must divide it. “trust” is what i give you. “trustworthiness” is what you have. “good faith” is how we deal. “truth” is a quality of a statement. “faith” in english also means religious belief, which 信 does not mean in this period. all of them are 信. the word was a political tool. a commander proved a border treaty with a 信, a tally split in two halves; a letter is still a 信 in modern chinese. shang yang, it is told, began his reforms by paying a man a great sum to carry a pole across the market, only to show that the state’s word would be kept.

whose trust is short?. 信不足焉，有不信焉. eight characters, and 信 twice, with no person named. word for word: “trust not enough in it; there is not-trust in it”. who lacks, and who answers? one reading: the ruler is not worthy of trust, and so the people do not trust. another: the ruler does not trust the people enough, with laws for each case and a watcher at each door, and so the people become untrustworthy. the grammar permits both, and they are two halves of one circle. legge fills the gaps with three brackets, “(in the tao)”, “(in the rulers)”, “(in the people)”, and so decides each question that the chinese left open. the first 焉 can also be read as “then”, at the head of the second half; the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write 案 there, with that sense. the whole line returns, word for word, in passage 23. in your own house or work: where did the lack of trust start?

悠 or 猶: far off, or wary. the received text opens the last part with 悠兮: “far, long, unhurried”, the word for a distant view or a slow river. the shuowen’s gloss for 悠 is 憂也, “care, sorrow”; the sense “far” is from old songs such as 悠悠蒼天, “far, far, the blue heaven”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write 猶呵. that is the 猶 of passage 15, where the masters were “watchful, as if in fear of neighbours on four sides”, half of the word for hesitation. legge’s base text had it too; he writes “how irresolute did those (earliest rulers) appear”. so there are two portraits of the best ruler at the moment of speech. in one, the ruler is far away and at ease. in the other, the ruler weighs each word like a person on thin ice. both lead to the same act: few words. which of the two do you see when you think of someone whose rare words carry weight?

貴言: words priced high. 貴 has 貝, a cowrie shell, at its foot. cowries were early money, and the shuowen defines the word 物不賤也, “of goods: not cheap”. so 貴言 is “to treat words as costly”. you do not spend a costly thing often. the phrase is a merchant’s way to say “speaks little”. it belongs to a line of sayings on speech that runs through the book: the sage practises 不言之教, “the teaching without words” (2); 多言數窮, “many words are soon used up” (5); 希言自然, “sparse words are natural” (23); 知者不言, “one who knows does not speak” (56). remember the setting. a warring states government spoke all the time: edicts, law codes, proclamations read out in each district, slogans for war. the best ruler in this passage issues almost none. what would your own words be worth if you priced them as high?

功: the credit that nobody claims. 功成事遂: “the 功 is complete, the task has gone through”. 功 is 工, work, with 力, strength, and the shuowen’s definition is political: 以勞定國也, “to settle the state by toil”. it is achievement that earns a name, a rank, a reward; armies kept ledgers of 功 by heads taken. english “success” or “work” loses the question that the word always carries: to whom is it credited? the book answers the same way each time. 功成而弗居, “the work is done and one does not dwell in it” (2). 功遂身退, “the work goes through, the person steps back” (9). here the sentence has no subject at all. the grammar itself does what the ruler does: the doer is absent from the sentence about the deed. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to reverse the pairs, 成功遂事, with no change of sense.

百姓: who had a name. 百姓 is “the hundred clan-names”. in early zhou texts the phrase means the great families: only nobles had a 姓, and commoners had none. by the warring states the old nobility had lost its hold, family names spread downward, and 百姓 came to mean the common people, as it does today. the laozi stands at the turn; in passage 5 heaven and the sage treat the 百姓 as straw dogs, and in passage 49 the heart of the 百姓 is the sage’s heart. the word 姓 has a story of its own. it is written 女, woman, and 生, to be born, and the shuowen says 人所生也: “that from which a person is born”. it adds a legend: the holy mothers of old conceived by the touch of heaven. several of the oldest clan names are written with 女: 姬, 姜, 姚. a name, in this graph, comes from the mother.

自然: “self-so”, and not yet “nature”. this is the first time the book says 自然, and it puts the word in the mouths of farmers. 自 is “self” or “from itself”. 然 is “so, thus”. together: “so of itself”, “self-so”. it is a description of how a thing happened, and you could say it of a river or of a habit. in modern chinese 自然 is the noun “nature”, and english versions often carry that back: “we are natural”, “it happened naturally”. the noun came later. here nothing called nature exists as a realm apart from people. there is one more open point. 謂我自然 can be “say: we are so of ourselves”, the usual reading, or “say of me: self-so”, where “me” is the ruler. we follow the first; wang bi’s comment supports it. the word returns in passages 23, 25, 51, and 64, and in 25 it is the last thing that even dao follows.

wang bi: they do not know how it came to be so. wang bi describes the best ruler in words from passage 2: 居無為之事，行不言之教，不以形立物，故功成事遂，而百姓不知其所以然也。 “this one manages affairs by not-forcing and practises the teaching without words, and does not use outward forms to set things up. so the work is done and the task goes through, and the hundred families do not know that by which it came to be so.” his last four characters, 其所以然, “that by which it is so”, play on 自然. the people say “self-so” because the cause is not visible to them. is that a deception? wang bi thinks not, and gives a reason from the body in his comment on the trust line: 御體失性，則疾病生, “drive the body against its nature and sickness is born”. a body in health does not notice its own organs. the people are right about what they did.

the old man who beat the ground. chinese tradition has a small story that could stand as a picture for this passage. in the time of the sage-king yao, the land was at peace. an old man by the road “struck the ground”, 擊壤 (some old sources say this was a game played with two pieces of wood), and sang: 日出而作，日入而息，鑿井而飲，耕田而食，帝力於我何有哉. “sun comes up, i work. sun goes down, i rest. i dig a well and drink. i plough a field and eat. the emperor’s power: what is that to me?” the story is told as the highest praise of yao. he ruled so well that a subject could think he owed him nothing. the song is preserved in han and later books, and nobody knows its real age. the old man is not ungrateful, and he is not wrong. he is the evidence. how would you measure a leader, if the best result is that no one thinks to thank them?

one poem cut in two. we read 17 and 18 as two passages. the oldest copy does not. on the guodian bamboo slips, of about 300 bce, the text of this passage runs on with no break into the next, joined by 故, “and so”: …the hundred families say, we are so of ourselves; and so, when the great dao falls to ruin, there are humaneness and right conduct. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to keep that 故 at the head of passage 18. read together, the four rulers are four ages. first no one notices rule. then rulers are loved, and the teachers of virtue appear. then they are feared, and the law-makers appear. then they are scorned. the chapter division was added in the han. passage 38 tells the same decline at full length, as a ladder of five rungs.

legge: seven brackets in a short passage. count legge’s brackets: “(the people)”, “(their rulers)”, “(in the tao)”, “(in the rulers)”, “(in the people)”, “(earliest rulers)”, “(by their reticence)”. seven of them, for a chinese text of forty-odd characters. each one is honest; he marks what he adds. together they show how much an english sentence needs that the chinese does not give: a subject, an object, an owner for each feeling. two of his choices came from his base text: “did not know” (不知) and “irresolute” (猶). one came from his calling: 信 becomes “faith (in the tao)”, a word from the pulpit, and the breakdown of trust between ruler and people becomes a failure of belief. but his last line is good: “we are as we are, of ourselves!” he kept 自然 as a plain phrase. he did not make it “nature”.

help so that they say “we did it”. choose one thing today in which you have some power over another person: a child with homework, a colleague with a problem, a friend who asks for advice. before you act, place yourself on the ladder. do you want to be thanked? that is the second rung. do you want to be obeyed? that is the third. then try the first. do the smallest thing that removes the obstacle, a question in place of an answer, or a tool left within reach, and say little. afterwards listen to how they tell it. if they say “i worked it out”, do not correct them. notice the small ache of not being credited. that ache is the exact price of the first rung, and the passage says the price is worth paying.

上 and 下: the highest weighs least. the first line sets 上 beside 下: the highest, and those below. here the text does rank: 其次, “next”, three times. but see what it ranks. each step down is a ruler who weighs more on those below: first love and praise, then fear, then scorn. the highest is the one whose height is felt least, so that the people say “we”. above and below make each other, and the trust line shows it: what the top does not give, the bottom does not return. love and scorn look like opposites. both are a people that looks up and judges, and the ladder shows one becoming the other. a one-sided reading makes the top rung a technique: be unseen, and control more. that was han fei’s use of it. the preference for the light hand corrects rulers who wished to be loved or feared. the favored side turns too: a ruler who is so far off that trust runs short is already on the way down the ladder.

the best leader is hardly noticed, and the people take the finished work as their own.. the best leader is hardly noticed, and the people take the finished work as their own. do you believe this of leaders you have known? who was the best, and how much did you notice them? when your own work is not credited, what happens in you? where did you learn what credit means? take the opposite view: people need a leader whom they can see, love, and thank, and a hidden one leaves them alone. what in you welcomes that view? which do you want more: to be useful, or to be known as useful? what makes that question hard to answer?

where trust is not given in full, no trust comes back.. where trust is not given in full, no trust comes back. is this how it has gone for you? recall one person who trusted you before you had earned it. whom do you watch closely, and what do you expect to find? where does that expectation come from? hold the other side: trust must be earned, and to give it early is careless. stay with it a while. what does it protect? what did you become when you were trusted too little? and when you were trusted more than you had earned? which side fits what you have lived, and where does the other side still have a point?

信 a person stands by their word. two parts, and both are easy to read. on the left is 亻, the side form of 人, a person. 人 began as a figure in profile, bent a little forward, with one arm down; as a side part it stands up straight in two strokes. on the right is 言, speech. look at its foot: 口, a mouth. above the mouth are four strokes. the shuowen treats the top as a sound part, and it gives a fine distinction in its definition: 直言曰言，論難曰語, “to speak straight out is 言; to argue a matter is 語”. the oracle-bone form of 言 is variously explained: older accounts see a tongue or a flute that rises from the mouth, and many scholars now see 辛, a chisel-like blade, set over 口. put them together: a person, and words. the shuowen calls 信 a joined-meaning graph, 會意, and it is one of the dictionary’s own model cases of that class. its sense is that the person and the word do not come apart. see what else 言 makes: 語 (talk), 誠 (sincere: words made complete, 成), 記 (a record), 譽 (the praise of this passage), and 謂, “to say”, in the last line. see 亻 at work too: 仁 (humane: a person and two), 伐 (to attack: a person and a halberd), 侮 (to scorn), 休 (to rest: a person by a tree). the passage uses 信 twice in eight characters, and the second use is the echo of the first: your word, and then what comes back. nine strokes: two for the person, seven for the words. the person is a stroke that falls to the left, and a vertical that starts under its middle. the vertical must be plumb; a 信 with a leaning person does not persuade. then 言. a dot on top, like a first breath. then a long level stroke. this is the widest line in the character, and it reaches left over the person’s shoulder. then two shorter level strokes. watch these three lines and the gaps between them: they are a stack of spoken lines, and a good hand makes each a different length, with even space between, so that they do not look like a ladder. last, the mouth: left side; top and right side in one stroke with a square corner; and the base, which closes it. in running script the three level strokes often become a dot and a wave, and the mouth one loop.

姓 born of a woman. 女 on the left, 生 on the right. 女 is a woman. the shuowen says only 象形, “a picture”, and the old forms are commonly described as a figure who kneels with the arms crossed in front. 生 is a picture too, and the shuowen reads it so: 象艸木生出土上, “it shows a plant that comes up out of the soil”. the level line at the foot is the ground and the rest is the shoot. it means to be born, to grow, to be alive, and it is raw, fresh, a student (學生), a lifetime (一生). set a woman beside a birth and you have 姓: the name that tells from whom you were born. the shuowen defines it 人所生也 and says that 生 gives both sense and sound. some of the oldest clan names keep the woman in the graph itself: 姬, the name of the zhou royal house; 姜, the house of qi; 姚 and 姒, the names given to the lines of the sage-kings shun and yu. scholars have long seen in this a memory of descent traced through mothers; that is a theory, and the graphs are the fact. a second word for a family name, 氏, marked a branch, a fief, or an office, and was held by men. in time the two merged. so the hundred families who speak at the end of the passage carry, in the word for them, a woman and a sprout. the laozi’s own word for the source is 母, mother. eight strokes: three and five. 女 has an order that surprises learners. the first stroke goes down to the left, turns, and runs down to the right: one bent line. the second falls to the left across it. the third is the level stroke, written last, and as a left-hand part it is short and rises a little toward 生. then 生: a short falling stroke at the upper left; a level stroke; a second level stroke; the vertical through the centre; and the long base line, the ground. watch the three level lines of 生. the second is a little shorter than the first, and the last is the widest stroke in the character; the shoot stands on it. the woman must give room: her right side stays narrow, and 生 does not touch her. in clerical script, the script of the han stone inscriptions, the base of 生 ends in a flared tail.

18 · after the house falls. the great dao falls to ruin: / there are humaneness and right conduct. / cleverness and wit come out: / there is the great fabrication. / the six kin are out of tune: / there are devoted children and tender parents. / state and house are dark and disordered: / there are loyal ministers. four pairs, each of two short lines. a loss, and then 有, “there is”. the great road collapses: there are humaneness and right conduct. cleverness comes out: there is great fabrication. the family is out of tune: there are devoted children and tender parents. the state and the great houses are dark and tangled: there are loyal ministers. the scale moves from the whole world, through the mind and the family, to the court. three of the four things that appear are virtues that every school praised. the second pair is the odd one, since its result is a vice; the oldest copy is reported not to have it. no line has a verb of cause, and none has a word of blame; see cause, or sign?. twenty-six characters. everything else is tone, and the tone depends on one particle that the received text dropped. bring the passage inside one life. when ease in the body is lost, there are diets and regimes. when sleep is lost, there is the science of sleep. when a friendship has gone out of tune, there are careful messages and remembered birthdays. each of these is good, and each is a sign. the contemplative point is not to tear down the remedies; a person in the ruins needs a shelter. it is to see them as remedies, and to look now and then at what they stand in for. wang bi’s fish say it best. on dry ground the fish wet each other with their spit, and this is kind. in water they do not think of each other at all. the practice is not to become indifferent. it is to find the water. which of your disciplines would you forget, if you were well? a rule for diagnosis: read the slogans of an organisation as a map of its injuries. where “trust” is a stated value, trust was short. where teamwork is praised each week, people do not help each other without it. where a few heroic employees save each project at midnight, the structure is dark and tangled, and the heroes are its loyal ministers; the better the firm, the fewer the heroes. the second pair is a warning to those who design controls. each clever system of measures and audits teaches a cleverer evasion, and the result is a great fabrication: numbers made for the measurer. the passage offers no technique in reply. it only asks you to look under the virtue for the roof that fell. the confucians told the same history and concluded that rites and duties are what we have, so we must keep them well. that is an honest answer too. a wolf does not practise devotion to its young, and a tree does not show loyalty to the forest. things in a living system do what the system needs, and nobody names it. names come with breakdown. we spoke little of “clean air” before the smoke, or of “biodiversity” before the losses; a river has no “water quality” until it is fouled. conservation, like 孝, is a virtue of the ruins: real, needed, and a sign. the zhuangzi’s picture is exact. fish on the mud of a pond that has dried keep each other wet, and it would be better for them to forget each other in a lake. the passage does not tell us to stop wetting the fish. it asks where the water went. what do you now protect with effort that once needed no protection? do the day of noticing: each time a virtue is named, ask what fell. then try the reverse, which is harder and more cheerful. find one place in your life where nothing is named because nothing is wrong: a friendship in which nobody keeps count, a task that you do well and never mention, a street where neighbours help and have no word for it. that is what the great dao looks like when the roof is still on. it is easy to miss, because it makes no claim on your attention. last, read the passage once in the usual way and once with the question-word: “how can there be…?” note which reading you want to be true. for the long form of the same story, see the ladder in passage 38, and for a victorian’s sharp tongue, legge.

the confucians told the same story. 大道 is first “the great road”: the highway, wide and level, that passage 53 says people leave for the side paths. the idea that a great dao was once in use and then lost was common ground in early china. a famous confucian text, the “evolution of rites”, says it in almost the same words: 大道之行也，天下為公, “when the great dao was walked, the world was shared by all”. people then cared for each other’s parents and children, and doors were not shut at night. then: 今大道既隱，天下為家, “now the great dao is hidden, and the world is family property”; and so, it says, the kings made rites and duties to hold things together. the confucian author calls the result “the lesser peace”, and is grateful for it. the laozi tells the same history and is not grateful. is a splint a good thing?

廢: the roof comes down. 廢 has 广 at the top and left, the sign for a building open on one side: a hall, a shed. the shuowen’s definition is a picture: 屋頓也, “a house that collapses”. from it come the common senses: to fall out of use, to abandon, to abolish, to depose a ruler; a 廢人 is a person who is crippled or useless. so the first line does not say that the way was rejected by a decision, or that people sinned against it. it says a structure that everyone lived in fell down through neglect, as a house does when nobody keeps the roof. what follows in the passage is what people build in the ruins. english “declined” or “was forgotten” has no roof in it. the dao itself does not fall, as other passages make plain. the 大道 here is the road, the shared way of living.

one small word that could turn the passage around. the received text says only 有: “there is”. the older copies have a word before it in each line. mawangdui silk text a writes 案有, and silk text b and the guodian bamboo slips write 安有: 安有仁義, 安有大偽, 安有孝茲. 安 is ambiguous. it can mean “then, and so”: the way falls, and then there is humaneness. that is the sense of the received text, and the 案 of silk text a supports it. but 安 is also the common question word “how? where?”. then the lines say: “when the great dao has fallen, how can there be humaneness and right conduct? when the six kin are out of tune, how can there be devoted children?” that reading does not attack the virtues at all. it says they need the way as their ground. most scholars choose “then”, and the mocking tone of the received version depends on it. but the oldest copies leave the door open. read the passage aloud both ways.

仁: a person and two. 仁 is 亻, a person, and 二, two. the shuowen defines it with one word: 親也, “closeness, kinship”. it is the quality that exists between two people: fellow-feeling, the sense that the other is a person as i am. confucius made it the centre of his teaching and refused to define it; asked what it was, he once said 愛人, “to care for people”. the first english translators, missionaries all, chose “benevolence”, a word of the eighteenth-century pulpit that means good will from above. later versions say “humaneness” or “humanity”, which is nearer. the laozi is hard on the word in more than one place. passage 5 says heaven and earth are 不仁, not humane, and treat all things as straw dogs. passage 38 puts 仁 two steps below the way. it is not that kindness is bad. the question is why it had to be named.

義 is not “righteousness”. 義 is to do what is fitting in one’s place: a minister’s duty to his lord, a friend’s to a friend, a soldier’s to die where he stands. the shuowen defines it 己之威儀也, “one’s own dignified bearing”: it begins as how a person of rank carries himself. the graph is 羊, a sheep, over 我, “i”. english “righteousness” is a word of the king james bible, and brings in a god who judges and a sinner who is made right. 義 has no god in it. it is social, and it can be seen. mencius, in the fourth century bce, joined it with 仁 as a fixed pair, 仁義, and opened his book with it: a king, he says, needs only these two. so when this line names the pair, it names the slogan of a school that was alive and in competition for the ear of kings.

智慧: not yet “wisdom”. in modern chinese, 智慧 is the word for wisdom, and a wise old person has it. that is mostly the work of buddhism, which chose 智慧 centuries later to translate prajna, the insight that frees. in this line the two words are nearer to “cleverness and wit”. 智 is knowing-how, intelligence as a tool; the old texts often write it with the plain graph 知, as mawangdui silk text a does here. 慧 is quickness; the shuowen glosses it 儇也, “nimble, sharp”. the warring states prized such people. courts kept debaters, strategists, and persuaders who could argue either side by evening. wang bi explains the line as an arms race: 行術用明，以察姦偽；趣覩形見，物知避之. “use technique and sharp sight to search out fraud, and your aims show and your forms are seen, and creatures know how to slip past.” each clever control teaches a cleverer evasion. the guodian slips are reported to lack this line.

偽: a person plus “to make”. 偽 is 亻, a person, beside 為, to do or to make. the simplest reading of the parts is “what a person makes”: the made thing, as against what grows. the shuowen, which writes the graph in its fuller form 僞, gives the dark sense: 詐也, “deceit”. both senses were alive. a generation or two after this text, the confucian xunzi used the word with pride. human nature is bad, he wrote, and 其善者偽也: “what is good in people is 偽”, made by effort, as a potter makes a pot from clay. for xunzi culture is artifice, and artifice is our glory. the laozi sees the same fact and does not rejoice. note the echo inside the graph: 為 is the word in 無為, not-forcing. 偽 is 為 with a person added. english “hypocrisy” gives only the bad half. what of your own goodness is made, and what grew?

wang bi: fish on dry ground. wang bi names the six kin: 六親，父子兄弟夫婦也, “father and son, elder and younger brother, husband and wife”. then he gives the logic of the whole passage: 甚美之名生於大惡，所謂美惡同門. “the names of great beauty are born from great ugliness; as the saying goes, beauty and ugliness come from one gate.” 若六親自和，國家自治，則孝慈忠臣不知其所在矣. “if the six kin were in tune of themselves, and state and house in order of themselves, no one would know where the devoted child and the loyal minister were to be found.” he ends with fish, from a story in the zhuangzi. when the spring dries up, the fish lie together on the ground and wet each other with their spit. that is a touching sight, and the zhuangzi says 不如, “it is not as good as”, to forget each other in the rivers and lakes. wang bi’s sentence as it has come down seems to have lost a word, but the sense is clear: the virtue of mutual wetting is born when the water is gone.

the famous son needs a terrible father. 孝 is what a child owes to parents, and 慈 is the tender care that goes down from parent to child. the model of 孝 for all later china was the sage-king shun. his father, the blind old man, with his stepmother and half-brother, tried again and again to kill him: they set fire to a barn while he was on its roof and filled in a well while he was at its bottom. shun survived each time and served them with more devotion than before. the story proves the line. without a murderous father, shun is one more good son whose name no one records. the laozi does not despise the feelings. passage 67 calls 慈 the first of the three things that it treasures, and passage 19 says that when the slogans are dropped the people will 復孝慈, return to devotion and care. the passage objects to the name, the fame, and the need.

國家: two levels of power, both in trouble. in modern chinese 國家 is one word: “country, nation”. in this line it is two. a 國 was the walled domain of a ruling lord; the graph has a wall, 囗, around it. a 家 was the “house” of a great minister: a hereditary line with its own lands, towns, and troops. the story of the age was the war of the houses on the states. in jin, the strongest state of the north, three ministerial houses destroyed their rivals in 453 bce and cut the state in three; the king recognised them as lords in 403, the date from which the warring states period is often counted. in qi a minister’s house took the throne. so “loyal ministers” was a bitter phrase. mawangdui silk text a and the guodian slips read 邦家. 邦 is the older word for a state, and it was the personal name of the first han emperor, liu bang. silk text b, copied a little later, already avoids it and writes 國家.
