亂: a word that means its opposite. 昏 is dusk. the shuowen says 日冥也, “the sun goes dark”, and reads the graph as the sun, 日, gone down below. a state at dusk is one where nobody can see clearly: who holds power, what the law is, whom to believe. 亂 is disorder, revolt, a tangle. here the shuowen has a surprise: it defines 亂 as 治也, “to put in order”. the same word could mean the mess and the work of setting it right, and the classics use it both ways; ministers who brought order are called 亂臣 in one old text. the early graph is commonly explained as two hands at work on a tangle of silk on a frame. one picture, two readings: the tangle, or the untangling. it fits the passage very well. each remedy in these four lines arrives together with the disorder, and from a distance they are hard to tell apart.

loyal ministers die young. each reader of the time could name the loyal ministers, and each one of them was a corpse. bi gan protested against the cruelties of the last shang king, who said, “i hear that a sage’s heart has seven openings”, and had him cut open to see. wu zixu warned the king of wu against the state of yue, was ordered to kill himself, and asked that his eyes be hung on the city gate to watch the yue army march in; it did. the fame of the 忠臣 is a measure of how bad the court is. under a good ruler the same man gives the same advice, is listened to, and is forgotten. both mawangdui silk texts read 貞臣, “steadfast ministers”, and the guodian slips are reported to read 正臣, “upright ministers”. 忠 was not yet the fixed slogan that it became when the empire made loyalty its first virtue.

cause, or sign?. four times the passage says a, and then 有 b: “there is b”. it never says “because” or “therefore”, and it never says that b is bad. english versions often add a verb that decides the matter: virtue “arises”, hypocrisy “ensues”, as legge has it. the bare chinese permits at least three attitudes. first, satire: your prized virtues are symptoms of rot. second, diagnosis with no blame: when the body is sick, there is medicine, and one does not hate the medicine; one only wishes not to need it. third, with the older particle read as a question, a defence of the root: without the way, how could the virtues exist at all? the passage is twenty-six characters long. it gives the pairs and leaves the verdict to the reader. what you hear in it will depend a good deal on how you feel about the virtues that you were taught as a child.

the middle of a longer fall. this passage is not a separate poem. in the oldest copy, the guodian slips, it is the end of passage 17, joined on by “and so”: first the four ranks of rulers, from the unnoticed to the scorned, and then these lines as the result. the book also gives the same history a third time and in full. passage 38 says: 失道而後德，失德而後仁，失仁而後義，失義而後禮. “lose the way, and after that comes inner power; lose inner power, and then humaneness; lose humaneness, and then right conduct; lose right conduct, and then ritual.” and ritual, it adds, is the thin edge of loyalty and trust, and the start of disorder. passage 19 then proposes the cure. read 17, 18, and 19 in one sitting. they are one argument: how rule went wrong, what grew in the ruins, and what to drop.

legge: virtue “came into vogue”. legge gives 仁義 as “benevolence and righteousness”, the pair that he and other missionary translators fixed for a century, and that still colours how english readers hear confucius: as a preacher. then he does something sharper than he perhaps meant to. the virtues, he writes, “came into vogue”. vogue is a word for hats. it makes the two great confucian virtues a fashion, and so gives the satirical reading more bite than the chinese 有, “there are”, has by itself. he glosses 道 in a bracket as “(way or method)”, a sign that he was not sure the word here meant what it meant in passage 1. he renders 國家 “the states and clans”, and so keeps the two levels that “the nation” loses. and for 孝慈 he has only “filial sons”; the tender parents are gone, and with them the other half of the bond.

where a virtue is on the wall. for one day, notice where a virtue is named aloud or in print. a company puts “integrity” on the wall of the lobby. a family says often how close it is. a person tells you that they are “a very honest person”. a government names a ministry for truth, or harmony. do not judge; only ask the passage’s question in each case: what fell down here, that this had to be said? then turn the question on yourself. which of your own virtues do you mention most often, or most enjoy being praised for? what would be in its place if the ground under it were whole? the answer is not always shameful. sometimes the named virtue is a good splint on a real break. it is still worth knowing where the break is.

ruin and virtue arrive together. each couplet is a pair: 廢 and 仁義, ruin and the virtues; 不和 and 孝慈, discord and devotion; 昏亂 and 忠, disorder and loyalty. passage 2 gives the rule: when all know the beautiful as beautiful, there is already the ugly. this is the same rule from the other side. the named virtue is seen only against its lack, and the lack calls it out. two one-sided readings are common. one says that the virtues are simply good, and it misses what they stand on. the other says that they are false, and the text does not say that. its preference is for the state before the names, when kin were in tune and no one called it devotion. that preference answers schools that offered more virtue as the cure. and the favored side turns as well: the passage begins with the great dao in ruins. the unnamed order did not hold. out of the ruin come the virtues, and passage 19 says that the people can go back.

named virtues appear when something whole has broken; talk of duty and loyalty is a sign of loss.. named virtues appear when something whole has broken; talk of duty and loyalty is a sign of loss. do you agree? look at the virtues that are praised most where you work or live. what had gone wrong first? which virtue were you praised for as a child? what was missing in the house, that this virtue was needed? now take the confucian side: the break is a fact, and the virtues are what holds people together after it. hold that with respect. what do you feel toward your own disciplines? does it sting to see a virtue of yours as a splint? why might the sting be worth a look?

when cleverness comes forward, pretending on a large scale comes with it.. when cleverness comes forward, pretending on a large scale comes with it. have you seen this: a clever rule, and then a cleverer way around it? were you on one side, or on both? what do you feel about your own cleverness: pride, distrust, need? when did it first serve you? take the opposite: wit is how people lift each other out of hardship, and plain dealing with no skill leaves them poor. what comes up? where are you clever in place of honest, and what would the honest version cost?

孝 the old one on the child’s back. the top is what is left of 老, “old”. the shuowen reads 老 as a person with hair that has changed, 言須髮變白也: “it says that beard and hair turn white”; the oracle-bone form is commonly described as a bent figure with long hair who leans on a stick. in 孝 the lower part of 老 is cut away, and in the space is 子, a child. the shuowen says how to read the two: 子承老也, “the child bears up the old”. 承 is to receive from above, to carry, to continue. so the picture is a young person under an old one: a child who carries a parent on the back, or one who holds an elder up by the arm. the definition is 善事父母者, “one who serves father and mother well”. now see the same top in other places. 考, the shuowen’s partner word for 老, is a dead father, and then “to examine”. and look at 教, to teach: its left side has 子 at its foot too, under the sign 爻; the right side is a hand with a rod. in 孝 the child holds up the old. in 教 the old stand over the child. the two graphs between them hold the whole confucian family. in later china, 孝 was law as well as feeling: an unfilial son could be put to death. the passage says that the word becomes famous when families fail. in the graph there is no fame. there is only one generation with its back under another. seven strokes: four above, three below. a short level stroke; a short vertical through it; then a long level stroke, the beam that the whole character hangs from. the fourth stroke is the one to watch. it starts above the beam, cuts through it, and sweeps far down to the left: it is the old person’s bent back, and the longest line in the character. in its shelter sits 子: a level stroke that turns back with a small hook; a curved vertical that ends in a hook to the left; and the child’s arms, one level line across. the child must sit a little to the right of centre, under the place where the beam and the long sweep cross, so that it seems to carry the weight. if the last level stroke is too long, the child pushes the elder away. if it is too short, the elder falls.

義 a sheep above a weapon. the top is 羊, a sheep or goat, seen from the front: two horns, and a face with lines across it. in the script the sheep is a sign of good things: 美 (beautiful) is a sheep over 大, big; 善 (good) has it on top; 祥 (auspicious) has it at the side; 養 (to nourish) has it over 食, food. flocks were wealth, and the sheep was an animal of sacrifice. the bottom is 我, the word for “i, we”. but 我 did not begin as a pronoun. its early forms are commonly explained as a picture of a weapon, an axe with a toothed blade, and the shuowen still sees 戈, the dagger-axe, in it and records a view that it was an old word for “to kill”. the graph was borrowed for the sound of “i”. so 義 is a sheep over a weapon, or a sheep over “me”. scholars read it as sacrifice properly done, or as a fine display on a ceremonial arm; the shuowen’s definition, 己之威儀也, “one’s own dignified bearing”, points to display. its meaning grew from bearing to what is fitting, and to duty. a 義士 is a man who dies for a cause; in modern words it is “justice” (正義) and “meaning” (意義). the mainland short form, 义, keeps nothing of the picture. read the passage’s second line again with the old graph in view: when the great road is gone, there are bearing and sacrifice. thirteen strokes: six for the sheep, seven for 我. the horns first: a dot to the right and a short stroke to the left, which lean toward each other. then two level strokes, a short vertical through them, and a third level stroke, longer, which is the floor of the upper part. the sheep has no tail here; its vertical stops at that floor. then 我: a flat stroke that falls to the left; a long level stroke; a vertical with a hook; a short stroke that rises to the right. now watch the eleventh stroke, the long slanting hook. it starts high, crosses the level stroke, runs down to the lower right, and flicks up. it is the shaft of the weapon and the backbone of the character. then a falling stroke across its lower part, and a dot high on the right. the sheep is balanced on the point where the shaft and the level stroke cross.

臣 the eye that looks down. this is a whole character with no separate parts, and the shuowen calls it a picture: 象屈服之形, “it shows the form of one who bends in submission”. its definition is two words, 牽也, “to be led, as by a rope”, and then 事君也, “to serve a lord”. modern scholars read the old forms otherwise, and their account is widely accepted: it is an eye. compare 目, the eye, which is the same drawing set upright and squared. in 臣 the eye is turned on end, as it looks when the head is bowed, or when one looks up from the ground. the earliest 臣 were captives and bondsmen. by the zhou the word meant anyone who served a lord, up to the chief minister, and a man said 臣 for “i” when he spoke to his king. the eye appears in two other graphs that are worth knowing. 臥, to lie down, is a person beside it. 監, to oversee, is commonly explained as a person with a large eye who bends over a basin of water: at first, to look at one’s own face. its descendant 鑑 means a mirror. so the same eye that submits is also the eye that inspects. the passage’s last word joins it with 忠, a heart, 心, under 中, the centre: a 忠臣 is a heart held centred, and an eye held low. the line says when you will hear of such a person. six strokes. a level stroke on top. a short vertical down from it at the centre. then a stroke that goes right and turns down: the top and right side of the inner box. a level stroke that closes the box below. a second short vertical, from the box to the base. watch the sixth and last stroke. it starts at the upper left, comes straight down the whole left side, turns the corner, and runs along the bottom to the right: one long line that takes more ink than the other five together. it is the frame, and it is written last, so that the hand must judge the height and the width of everything from the inside first. the right side stays open; the two inner openings face the reader like a pupil. some schools of writing teach a different order, with the left side first.

19 · undyed silk, uncarved wood. cut off sagehood, throw away cleverness: / the people gain a hundredfold. / cut off humaneness, throw away right conduct: / the people go back to devotion and tender care. / cut off skill, throw away profit: / robbers and bandits, there are none. / these three, as ornament, are not enough. / so let there be something to fasten to: / show the undyed silk, / hold the uncarved wood; / less of what is private, fewer wants. three hammer blows, and then a quiet close. each blow has the same form: cut off x, throw away y, and a result for the people. cut sagehood and cleverness: the people gain a hundredfold. cut humaneness and right conduct: they go back to family feeling. cut skill and profit: no robbers. then the text comments on itself, which it seldom does: these three, as ornament or as wording, are not enough, so here is something to belong to. the something is two images and two measures: undyed silk, uncarved wood, less that is private, fewer wants. the pictures are all from the workshop: a knife on a thread, a child in a basket, a pattern in cloth, white silk, a log. the oldest copy is reported to aim the first blows at other targets, and the passage may have one more line. read the six things to be cut as six ways in which a person builds a self to show. i am wise; i am sharp. i am kind; i do my duty. i am skilled; i do well. each is good, as wang bi admits, and each is a dye. the passage does not ask what you should be in place of these. it asks what the cloth was before it went into the vat. 素 and 樸 are not achievements, and you cannot acquire them; they are what is there when the acquiring stops. so the practice has two motions, as the passage does. first the cut, which is quick. then something for the arms to hold, since a mind that has only dropped things will pick up the next shiny one. the close is kind: less, not none. who are you before you are good at anything? a ruler of the time heard advice from three sides. confucians: be a sage, teach humaneness and duty. strategists and debaters: be clever. economic advisers: promote crafts and trade. the passage cuts all three, and its test is one thing only, three times: what happens to 民, the people. that is the part to keep. a programme is judged by what it does to those below, and not by how wise, good, or skilled it makes those above look. the zhuangzi’s essay adds the cynical corollary: moral language is the first thing that a usurper steals. in an organisation, look for the three dyes: the cult of the brilliant founder, the values on the wall, the bonus scheme that makes people look at each other’s bowls. the passage also knows that a ban alone leaves a hole. what plain thing would your people hold if the slogans went? no river is wise and no forest is virtuous. plain things in nature are not poor: a block of oak has every bowl and beam in it, and white silk can take any colour. carving and dyeing are choices that cannot be reversed. for this reason the craft images are exact where “simplicity” is vague. a 樸 is not a small or humble thing; it is a thing with its possibilities intact. ecology has the same thought. a meadow that nobody has “improved” holds more kinds of life than a lawn. an old tree that foresters call over-mature is a city for birds and insects. to show the plain in a landscape is to leave some of it with no finish. where near you is there ground that has not been dyed? take one plain thing today and stay with it for a minute. then choose one of the three pairs for a week. cleverness: in one meeting or talk, do not make the smart remark. virtue: do one kind act that nobody can find out about. skill and profit: do one thing that you are good at, slowly and badly, as a beginner, for no result. each time, see what is under the thing that you put down. it may be only awkwardness at first. the passage says that under it is something to hold with both arms. if the first line still troubles you, read how the oldest copy puts it and why the book would cut its own hero. and see what happened when a victorian tried to rhyme the ending.

絕: a knife on the thread. the first word of the passage, used three times, is a weaver’s word. the shuowen defines 絕 as 斷絲也, “to cut silk thread”, and reads the graph as 糸, silk, with 刀, a knife, and 卩. to 絕 is to sever a line that was continuous: a thread, a road, a family with no heir, a friendship. it is sudden and final; a cut thread is not “reduced”. passage 14 ended with a thread to follow, the lead thread of dao; this passage begins with threads to cut. the partner verb, 棄, is as hard. english “renounce”, “give up”, or “abandon” are words of the will and the conscience. the chinese verbs are acts of the hand. note also what is cut. in each pair it is the thing that the schools of the age praised most.

棄: the abandoned child. 棄 is one of the darkest pictures in the script. the shuowen defines it 捐也, “to cast off”, and takes it apart: two hands at the bottom push a winnowing basket, and at the top is 𠫓, which it explains as 逆子也, “a child head-down”: a new-born. the graph shows an infant carried out in a basket to be exposed. this was done. the founder of the zhou people, lord millet, was named 棄, “the abandoned”: his mother left him three times, in a lane, in a wood, and on ice, and oxen, woodcutters, and birds kept him alive. so the word that the passage uses for cleverness, right conduct, and profit is the word for the hardest thing a parent can do. the line just after it speaks of 孝慈, the care between parent and child. was that placed there by chance?

the book cuts off its own hero. 聖 is the 聖人, the sage, who is the model in more than twenty passages of this book. here the text says: cut it off. readers have felt the shock for two thousand years. one answer: what is cut is the title and the cult, the “sage-kings” whom confucians and mohists held up to rulers as a standard. the shuowen defines 聖 as 通也, “to pass through, to understand through”, and puts it under 耳, the ear: at root it is a way of hearing, and a way of hearing cannot be an office. wang bi takes the plainest line: 聖智，才之善也, “sagehood and cleverness are the best of talents”, and still the text cuts them. the other answer is that this line is not the oldest form of the passage. a later follower took the line as far as it would go. would the sage of the other passages mind?

the oldest copy does not attack the sage. in 1993 bamboo slips with parts of the laozi were found in a tomb at guodian, closed about 300 bce. their text of this passage is reported to differ in two of the three pairs, and in the order. first: 絕智棄辯, “cut off cleverness, throw away debate”, and the people gain a hundredfold. second: “cut off skill, throw away profit”, as in our third pair. third, in place of “cut off humaneness, throw away right conduct”: two graphs that scholars read as 絕偽棄詐 or 絕偽棄慮, “cut off artifice, throw away deceit (or scheming)”, and the people go back to family feeling. in that version nothing is said against 聖, 仁, or 義. the targets are the debaters and the schemers, whom confucians disliked too. if the reading is right, the attack on confucian virtue was written in later. both mawangdui silk texts, copied about 200 bce, already have it: silk text b reads 絕聖棄知 and 絕仁棄義. we render the received text. it has a quieter ancestor.

利 twice: gain for the people, profit to discard. the same character stands in line 2 and in line 5, with opposite signs. 民利百倍: the people’s 利 is a hundred times greater. 絕巧棄利: throw 利 away. english hides the clash with two words, “benefit” and “profit”. in chinese it is plain to see, and it is the point. 利 is the sharp edge of a blade and the yield of a harvest: advantage. the mohists made 利, the benefit of all, the test of each policy; the legalists built the state on the fact that each person runs after 利. the passage separates what the schools ran together. when each one chases advantage, the sum is loss. when the chase is dropped, the people are better off, and the text measures the result with a trader’s figure: a hundredfold. passage 11 has the same word in its last couplet, set against 用, use.

the cure for the last passage’s illness. this line answers passage 18, which said: when the great road falls to ruin, there are 仁 and 義; when the six kin are out of tune, there are 孝 and 慈. now the text proposes to cut the first pair, and promises that the people will 復, go back to, the second. so the book does not want less family feeling. it claims that devotion and tender care are there before the teaching, and that the teaching covers them. a child loves its parents before it knows the word 孝. add a public standard, with praise for those who meet it and shame for those who fail, and the same child begins to perform. mencius, the great defender of 仁義, would agree with half of this: he also held that the feeling comes first, and gave the case of anyone who sees a small child about to fall into a well. the two differ on what naming does to the feeling.

巧 and 利: the workshop and the market. 巧 is a craftsman’s skill; the shuowen says 技也, “technique”, and the graph has 工, the carpenter’s square. with 利, profit, it names the two new forces of the age. iron tools and coined money spread through the states after about 500 bce. cities grew, and with them workshops for lacquer, bronze inlay, and silk, and merchants who became richer than lords; one of them, lu buwei, made himself chief minister of qin. fine goods were the visible sign of the change, and the laozi speaks of them in other places: “goods hard to come by make a person’s conduct go wrong” (12). the link to robbers is practical. passage 3 says: do not prize rare goods, and the people will not steal. a thing that is made to be envied has, in a sense, already made its thief.

盜: one who drools over a dish. the shuowen’s entry for 盜 is almost a joke. the definition is 私利物也, “to take a thing for private gain”. then the parts: the lower half is 皿, a dish. the upper half is an old graph for spittle, written with water and an open mouth; and the dictionary says 㳄欲皿者, “one who drools with desire for the dish”. a robber, in this graph, is first a person who looks at someone else’s bowl with a wet mouth. 賊 is the harder word; it has 戈, a dagger-axe, in it, and means one who does armed harm: a bandit, a rebel, an assassin. so 盜賊 covers the range from want to violence. note where the shuowen puts the origin: in 欲, wanting, the last word of this passage. the cure at the end, 寡欲, fewer wants, is aimed at the mouth above the dish.

“steal a hook, and die; steal a state, and be a lord”. a chapter of the zhuangzi called “rifling trunks” quotes this passage and turns it into the fiercest political essay of early china. you tie your trunk with strong cords against thieves, it says; then a great thief comes, lifts the whole trunk, and is only afraid that the cords may break. sagely laws are those cords. its example was recent history. in 481 bce the tian family murdered the lord of qi and took the state, and with it all the rites, measures, and moral teaching that the sages had made for qi, which then protected the thieves. 竊鉤者誅，竊國者為諸侯: “one who steals a belt-hook is put to death; one who steals a state becomes a feudal lord”. and at a lord’s gate, it adds, there is always 仁義. its conclusion borrows our first line: 絕聖棄知，大盜乃止, “cut off sagehood, throw away cleverness, and the great robbers will stop”.

文: pattern, ornament, text, culture. 此三者以為文不足 is a hard clause, and all turns on 文. the shuowen defines 文 as 錯畫也, “crossed lines”: a pattern, as in woven cloth or a tattoo. from pattern come ornament, a written character, a text, and “culture” itself; confucius called the heritage of zhou 斯文, “this culture”. at least three readings stand. one: “these three statements, as wording, are not enough”; the three bans are too bare. wang bi reads it so. two: “these three [sagehood, humaneness, skill] are mere ornament, and do not suffice” to govern. three: “these three, held as doctrine, fall short”. our “as ornament” keeps the ambiguity between one and two. in each reading the next step is the same: the passage sees that to cut is not enough, and offers something to hold. it is a thread image once more: after the knife of 絕, the pattern of 文, and then plain silk.

wang bi: a ban needs a home. 故令有所屬: “so cause there to be a place to belong”. 屬 (zhu here) is to join on, to attach; the shuowen says 連也, “to connect”, and oddly files it under 尾, the tail: what follows on behind a body. wang bi explains why the turn is needed. he grants that the three things cut off are goods: 聖智，才之善也。仁義，人之善也。巧利，用之善也。 “sagehood and cleverness are the best of talent. humaneness and right conduct are the best of persons. skill and profit are the best of utility.” 而直云絕，文甚不足，不令之有所屬，無以見其指. “but to say only ‘cut off’ is very insufficient as a statement; unless they are given something to attach to, there is no way to show what is pointed at.” a person told only what to drop has empty hands, and empty hands pick up the next thing. so the passage ends with four positive acts. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to say 此三言也, “these three sayings”, which supports his reading.

素: silk before the dye. the shuowen defines 素 as 白緻繒也: “white, close-woven silk”. it is cloth as it comes from the loom, before any colour, and so “plain”, “basic”, “what a thing is to begin with”; today it is the word for a chemical element and for a diet with no meat. the age thought with this image. mozi, it is told, saw silk being dyed and sighed: put it in blue and it is blue, put it in yellow and it is yellow; one must be careful what one is dipped in. confucius, asked about a line of verse, said 繪事後素, “the painting comes after the plain ground”, and his student saw that rites, too, come second. so the schools agreed that there is a ground. the laozi says: show it. the verb 見 has two readings. as xian it is “to show, to let be seen”; as jian it is “to look at”. we chose “show”. the other is “keep the plain in sight”.

抱樸: the phrase that became a man’s name. 樸 is wood before the knife; the shuowen glosses it 木素也, “the 素 of wood”, so the dictionary itself ties the two images of this line together: silk before dye, wood before carving. the verb is 抱, to hold in the arms against the chest, as one carries a child or a bundle. it is a verb of the whole body. passage 10 and passage 22 use it for 抱一, “to hold the one”. six hundred years later, about 320 ce, a scholar from the south named ge hong took this phrase for his name and for the title of his book: 抱朴子, “the master who holds the uncarved wood”. the book is a main source for chinese alchemy and the search for long life, with recipes for elixirs of cinnabar and gold. the plain block had by then become the emblem of a learned and complex religion. what are your arms around, most of the day?

less and fewer, not none. 少私寡欲: “make the private small, make wants few”. after three total verbs, cut and throw away, the positive programme is modest. it does not say 無私, no self-interest, or 無欲, no desire, though both phrases exist in this book (7, 1). it says 少 and 寡: less, fewer. english versions with “selflessness” or the ascetic “eschew lusts” of legge’s verse make it a harder and more christian demand than it is. 私 is what is one’s own, as against 公, the common. the shuowen says it was at first a word for grain, and the right-hand part, 厶, is the old graph for “private”, which han fei explained as a line that curls around itself. 欲 is appetite; see the drooling mouth. the measure is practical: a household can have its own share and its wants, in a size that needs no robbers to supply it and attracts none.

where does the passage end?. the next passage begins with four characters, 絕學無憂: “cut off learning: no worry”. many scholars think they belong here, as the last line of this passage. the verb is the 絕 that opens each of the three pairs above. the form fits: 少私寡欲 and 絕學無憂 are two lines of four. and the mawangdui silk texts, which have no chapter breaks, are reported to run straight on from one to the other. the oldest evidence points the other way. on the guodian slips this passage is reported to stand in one bundle and to end at 少私寡欲, and 絕學亡憂 opens the text of passage 20 in another bundle. so about 300 bce the line already belonged with what follows. if a later reader hears it here too, the list of things to cut grows to seven, and ends with the one that a reader of books least expects. you are, at this moment, in the act of 學.

legge breaks into verse. in the first half legge adds a subject and a mood: “if we could renounce our sageness”. the chinese has no “if”, no “we”, and no “our”; it gives an order, or states a law. with “we… our” he makes it a confession by the ruling class, which is a fair reading, and with “if we could” a sigh, which is his own. then, at the hard clause on 文, he does something unusual: he changes to rhymed verse, four lines that end “eschew”. he read the close of the passage as a rhymed saying, and tried to show it. the cost is high. 素 and 樸, the silk and the wood, become “simple views, and courses plain and true”, and the two craft images vanish. 欲 becomes “lusts”, a word from the english bible. compare the chinese: eight characters, two things held in the hands, two things made smaller.

one thing with no finish on it. find one thing today that is 素 or 樸: a thing with no finish on it. a board with no paint. a bowl of plain rice. a wall with nothing on it. tap water. a sentence with no adjective. give it one full minute of attention, and note the small restlessness that asks for more: colour, salt, a picture, a clever phrase. that restlessness is 欲 in its mildest form. do not fight it. then try the two verbs on yourself, in the passage’s own modest measure. 少私: once today, when you would say “my”, see if the sentence works without it. 寡欲: when you next want to buy or add something, wait one day. the passage does not ask for a monk. it asks for less, and promises that less will not feel like loss once the hands are around something plain.

文 and 素: pattern and the plain. the pair is 文 and 素: the worked pattern and the undyed cloth, and beside it the carved vessel and 樸, the uncarved wood. the passage takes the side of the plain, three times, with a knife. but see what the plain is in these images. 素 is silk that will take any dye, and 樸 is wood that can become any vessel. each is defined by the work that it has not yet had. pattern needs a ground, and a ground is plain only next to a pattern. the analects holds the pair level: 文質彬彬, pattern and substance in balance, make the noble person. the laozi leans, and the lean is a correction to courts where display had become a trade. it is not a rule for all time, and the close says less, not none. the favored side also turns: passage 28 says 樸散則為器, “the uncarved wood is split up, and then there are vessels”. what in you is ground, and what is pattern?

if the claims to wisdom, goodness, and skill are dropped, people gain, and return to natural care.. if the claims to wisdom, goodness, and skill are dropped, people gain, and return to natural care. do you think people are kind and honest without being taught to be? what have you seen that says yes, and what says no? what would be left of you if you could not call yourself wise, good, or capable? which of the three is hardest to put down? hold the other view: without teaching, ideals, and skill, people turn rough and poor. stay there. whose voice is that, and is it wrong? which view did your upbringing rest on, and how has it shaped what you expect from others?

the plain state, undyed and uncarved, with few wants, is enough to hold on to.. the plain state, undyed and uncarved, with few wants, is enough to hold on to. is plain enough for you? where do you feel that it is, and where not? what have you added to yourself so that others would value you? what were you afraid they would see under it? take the side of pattern: a person is made by cultivation, and the raw state is only a start. what feelings and thoughts come as you hold that? what do you feel when you meet someone plain and unpolished? and someone finely finished? what do those two reactions show about what you have accepted in yourself?

素 silk as it leaves the loom. look at the bottom first: 糸, the silk sign, a skein with two twists and loose ends. you have seen it on the left side of 絕, where a knife is beside it. here it stands at the foot, full size. the top of the character has three level strokes and a vertical. the shuowen explains it as 𠂹, an old graph for a thing that hangs down, and says 取其澤也, “it is chosen for the sheen”: fine raw silk that hangs in smooth, glossy folds. the definition is plain: 白緻繒也, white, close-woven silk. now see how far a word can go from a bolt of cloth. undyed, so “white”: mourning clothes were of 素. not coloured, so “plain”: 樸素 is “simple and unadorned”, a pair made of the two images of this passage. not yet worked, so “the base material”: 元素 is a chemical element, 因素 a factor, 要素 an essential. with no meat or strong flavour: 素食, the food of buddhist monks. as usual: 素來, “all along, in the ordinary way”. old texts speak of a “plain king”, 素王, a person who has the worth of a ruler and no throne; later ages gave that title to confucius. one more cousin: 索, a rope, looks alike and is also made of 糸. the passage sets 素 against 文, pattern. before a pattern there must be cloth. ten strokes: four above, six below. a level stroke; a second level stroke; a vertical through both; then the third level stroke, the longest, on which the top rests. keep the three level lines apart by even gaps; the vertical does not go below the third. then the silk. two strokes of one kind, each down to the left and then back to the right: the two twists, the lower one wider. a dot closes the second twist. now watch the last three strokes, which are different from the silk sign when it stands at the left: a vertical in the centre that ends in a small hook, then a dot to the left of it, and a dot to the right. they are the loose ends of the skein, and they stand like three small feet. the whole character is tall and narrow in the waist, with the widest line just above the middle.

棄 two hands, a basket, a child. read this character from the top down, as the shuowen does. the top four strokes are 𠫓. it is 子, a child, written upside down; the shuowen says 逆子也, “a child reversed”, and the same form is in 育, to give birth and to rear, and in 流, to flow, where it is commonly explained as a child that comes out with the waters. under the child is a shape with crossed lines, which the shuowen reads as a winnowing basket with a handle, the kind used to toss grain and to carry out rubbish. at the bottom, in the old forms, are two hands, 廾; the regular script has changed them and the basket’s foot into a shape that looks like 木, a tree. oracle-bone forms of the graph are commonly described in the same way: two hands, a basket, a child with drops around it. so the whole is: to carry a new-born out in a basket. the meaning is “to discard”, and it has not softened: 放棄 is to give up, 拋棄 to forsake, 棄權 to waive a right. the short form 弃, with only the child and the two hands, is very old; the shuowen records it as the ancient-script form, and it is the mainland standard today. the founder of the zhou people had this word for his name. the passage uses it for cleverness, right conduct, and profit: things, it suggests, that their parents will find hard to leave. twelve strokes, in three levels. the child first: a dot; a level stroke; then a stroke that goes down to the left and turns back to the right; and a last dot. then the basket: a long level stroke, the widest line in the character; two short verticals that start above it and cut down through it; and a short level stroke that joins them. then the lower part: a level stroke; a long vertical, drawn downward from above the basket through all the level strokes to the foot; and the last two strokes, one that falls to the left and one that presses out to the right. watch that final pair. they spread wide, like arms that hold the load away from the body. the danger in this character is weight at the top. a good hand keeps the child light and lets the two long level lines and the final pair carry the whole.

盜 a wet mouth over a dish. three parts, and the shuowen reads them as a little scene. at the upper left are three drops, 氵, water. beside them is 欠. this is a person with the mouth wide open: it means to yawn, to breathe out, to lack, and it is the right side of 欲, desire, and of 歌 (to sing), 吹 (to blow), 飲 (to drink). water and an open mouth together are 㳄, the old graph for spittle, the word now written 涎. under both is 皿, a dish. you know it from 盈, full, and 盤 (a tray), 盆 (a basin), 盡 (used up; commonly explained as a hand that scrubs an empty dish). so: one who drools over a dish. the shuowen says exactly this, 㳄欲皿者, and defines the word as 私利物也, to make a thing one’s private gain. in classical chinese 盜 is the robber and 賊 the one who does violence; in the modern language they have nearly changed places, and 盜 is the thief. it is a good graph for the passage’s argument about where robbers come from. the dish is someone else’s. the crime in the picture has not yet happened; there is only the mouth, and the water in it. the mainland short form, 盗, writes 次 on top: the spittle has lost a drop. twelve strokes: three, four, five. the water: a dot, a second dot, and a stroke that flicks up to the right. then 欠: a short stroke that falls to the left; a level stroke that ends in a hook; then the person below, a long stroke that falls to the left and one that presses out to the right. these two must be kept short and flat, because they have a dish under them. then 皿: left side; a stroke for the top and right side; two short verticals inside; and the long base line. watch the twelfth stroke. it is the widest line in the character, and it runs out past both sides of the dish like a table. all that is above leans over it. in a well-written 盜 the upper half is a little too large and a little too far forward for comfort. that is right for this word.

20 · not yet laughed. cut off learning: no worry. / “yes, sir” and “yeah”: / how far apart are they? / good and foul: / how far apart are they? / what people fear / cannot be left unfeared. / waste land, and no end to it yet! / the crowd is merry, merry, / as at the feast of the great sacrifice, / as on a terrace climbed in spring. / i alone am still, no sign yet, / like an infant that has not yet laughed; / drooping, drooping, as with no home to go to. / the crowd all have more than enough; / i alone seem to have lost it. / mine is the heart of a fool! / murky, murky. / common people are bright, bright; / i alone am dusk, dusk. / common people are sharp, sharp; / i alone am shut, shut. / swaying, like the sea; / a high wind, as with no place to stop. / the crowd all have their use; / i alone am a block, like a borderer. / i alone differ from the others, / and prize the mother who feeds. a slogan, three sharp questions, and then the longest “i” in the book. the slogan: cut off learning, no worry. the questions: how far is “yes, sir” from “yeah”? good from foul? and must one fear what people fear? then an outcry at a waste with no end. the rest is a set of contrasts between the crowd and “i alone”. they are at the sacrifice feast and on the spring terrace; i am an infant that has not yet laughed, a stray. they have surplus; i have lost it. they are bright and sharp; i am dusk and shut. they have a use; i am a block from the border. two lines break the list with size: the sea, the high wind. the last line gives the one thing that the speaker has: the mother who feeds. books on the contemplative life seldom admit this passage’s subject: the path can feel like loss. the others have plans, tastes, opinions, a place at the table; the one who has let the sorting stop has, for a time, a blank where the personality was. the text does not hurry to console. it lets the speaker be listless, left behind, a fool. yet look at the images chosen. an infant before its first laugh is not sad; it is prior to the social face. the sea is the lowest and the largest thing. dusk is when the eyes rest. each lack is also a description of the way from passage 14: no sign, no shape, no name. the final line is not a reward that comes later. the infant is at the breast the whole time. what feeds you when you produce nothing? read it first as a mirror of group life, which has changed little. careers are made of the correct yes, given in the correct tone to the correct rank. a group’s good and bad are often its likes and dislikes with a moral name. fears are caught from others. and everyone must have a use, a role that can be stated in a line. a leader should know how much of an organisation’s energy goes into this theatre, and that the people who decline to shine in it look, from the stage, like blockheads from the border. some of them are the only ones in touch with what feeds the place. passage 58 applies the same words to government: a sharp-eyed administration makes a broken people. there is a warning for the leader’s own person too, in the reported silk version of one line: whoever is feared must fear. the crowd in the passage is seasonal: it feasts in spring and climbs up to look at the green. the speaker’s images are older than seasons. the sea does not have a spring; it sways. the wind high up has no place to stop and needs none. waste land, which a farmer hates, is where everything that is not a crop lives. an infant is the nearest thing in human life to an animal’s way of being: fed, and without a plan. much of nature is murky and unsorted by a clerk’s standard, a swamp, a thicket, a tidal flat, and those are the places with the most life in them. the passage’s last word is 母. each wild thing is at that breast, and has no surplus stored. where in you is there still some land that nobody tills? try ten minutes of being dim at the feast. then, in private, take the three questions as real ones. write down two answers that you give with different degrees of “yes”, and ask what the difference protects. write one thing that you call bad, and ask how far it is from its opposite on a day when you are tired. write one fear that you hold because those around you hold it. do not resolve anything. then read the passage aloud, slowly, with weight on each “i alone”, and see which line you would rather not say. that line is yours. for company on the road, there is the story of confucius at the city gate, and the poet who said “i alone” the other way round. for the victorian view of a fool, see legge.

學 is not “knowledge”. 學 in this age was a definite thing: a young man’s training in the rites, the odes, the documents, and correct speech, under a master, with a post at court as its aim. the analects begins with it: “to learn, and at due times to practise it: is that not a pleasure?” the shuowen, under the fuller graph 斆, defines it 覺悟也, “to awaken”, and reads one part as a cover over a child who is 尚矇, “still in the dark”. so learning is the removal of a cover. this line says: cut it, and worry ends. passage 48 gives the reason: in learning one adds each day, in the way one takes away each day. it is not praise of ignorance. it is a question about a system that makes people anxious to be correct, and the next lines test that system’s first lessons: the right word for “yes”, and the line between good and bad. many scholars place this line at the end of passage 19.

a line between two passages. 絕學無憂 has the verb of the three bans in passage 19: cut off sagehood, cut off humaneness, cut off skill. many editors move the line there, as a fourth 絕 or as a partner to 少私寡欲, and the mawangdui silk texts, which have no chapter breaks, are reported to run the two together. the older guodian slips are reported to decide for the place it has here. they have the first lines of this passage as a separate piece, in a different bundle from passage 19, and that piece opens with 絕學亡憂. both places make sense. as the end of 19 the line is the last of the public bans. as the start of 20 it is the door to the most private passage in the book: after the programme, the cost. a person who does cut off the learning of the age no longer shares its “yes”, its good and bad, its feasts. what follows is how that feels. read the line once as a slogan, and once as the first words of a confession.

唯 and 阿: two ways to say yes. both words are sounds, written with borrowed graphs. 唯 (wei) is the quick, respectful “yes!”; the shuowen defines it 諾也, “assent”. the ritual books lay down that when a father or a teacher calls, one answers 唯 and rises at once; the slower 諾 is not respectful enough. 阿 (e) is a lazier sound, a drawled “yeah” or “uh-huh”; as a verb the word came to mean “to fawn, to go along with”. a boy was beaten for the wrong one. learning, 學, began here: with the exact syllable owed to each rank. the line asks how far apart the two really are. the mawangdui silk texts and the guodian slips are reported to write 訶 for the second word. many scholars take that as one more way to write 阿. read by its own sense it is an angry shout; the shuowen says 大言而怒也. then the question is larger: between a superior’s roar and an inferior’s “yes, sir”, how much distance is there? how many kinds do you have, and who taught them to you?

good and foul, or fair and foul. the received text asks about 善 and 惡: good and bad. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 美與惡: the beautiful and the ugly. wang bi’s own comment has 美惡 too, so his text may once have read like the reported silk text. 惡 (e here) covers both: it is what one turns away from, and read wu the same graph is the verb “to hate”. that reading joins this line to passage 2, where the world knows the beautiful as beautiful and so there is ugliness; the pair there is 美 and 惡. note that the line is a question and not an answer. it does not say that good and bad are the same. it asks 相去若何, “how far from each other?”, of a society that was quite sure of the distance. english “evil” would make the question a scandal. the chinese word is nearer to “foul”.

a line that can be read three ways. 人之所畏，不可不畏: “what people fear cannot be not-feared”. is it meant? one reading is plain: i am no hero; what others dread, i must dread too. wang bi takes it so: 人之所畏，吾亦畏焉, “what people fear, i fear also”. a second reading hears a sigh: the fears of the crowd cannot be escaped, however small the differences that they guard. the third is the reported reading of the mawangdui silk texts and the guodian slips, with two more words: 人之所畏，亦不可以不畏人. “one whom people fear must, for that reason, fear people.” that is a warning to a ruler, of a kind found all through the book: the feared lord of passage 17 lives in fear. the received line may be this one with its last word lost. we render the received words and keep the tone open. our “left unfeared” adds nothing, but english cannot keep the bare double “not”.

荒 and 未央: a waste with no centre. 荒 has grass, 艹, on top. the shuowen says 蕪也, “overgrown”, and adds: “some say, grass that drowns the land”. it is a field that nobody tills: wild, wide, a famine year. 央 is the middle; the shuowen shows a person, 大, inside a frame, and gives a second sense, 久也, “long-lasting”. 未央 is “not yet at the middle”, and so “far from over”. the han emperors liked the phrase and named their great palace at chang’an 未央宮, the palace of no ending. the line is an outcry, and readers have disagreed about its object for two thousand years. is it the way that is so vast? the folly of the crowd? the distance between the speaker and the others? wang bi chose the last: 歎與俗相返之遠也, “a sigh at how far he has turned from the common way”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write 朢, to gaze into the distance.

the great sacrifice and the spring terrace. 太牢 is the highest grade of offering in the state cult: an ox, a sheep, and a pig together. 牢 is the pen where the beasts were kept and fattened; the shuowen says 養牛馬圈也, and the graph is an ox, 牛, under a cover. after the rite the meat was shared out, so a 太牢 was the best feast that a person could attend, by invitation of a lord. the terrace is the other great pleasure. rulers of the age competed to build 臺, high platforms of rammed earth with halls on top; the shuowen defines 臺 as a lookout, “four-square and high”. in spring people climbed up to see the new green, and spring outings were the time of courtship. so the crowd’s happiness is public, seasonal, and paid for by the court. wang bi is sour about it: they are 惑於榮利, “dazed by glory and profit”. the speaker has no place at the table.

我獨: “i alone”, six times. the book has no proper names, no places, and no dates, and for the most part no speaker. here a voice says 我, “i”, and says 我獨, “i alone”, six times. nobody knows whose voice it is, and the lines were made to be spoken by anyone who has stood outside a feast. a reader of the time would hear a second voice behind it. the poet qu yuan, a minister of chu who was slandered and sent away, has the most famous “i alone” in chinese: 舉世皆濁我獨清，眾人皆醉我獨醒, “the whole world is muddy and i alone am clear; all are drunk and i alone am sober”. he drowned himself. the speaker of this passage says the reverse: all are bright, i alone am dim. it is the same loneliness with the pride taken out. the shuowen’s gloss for 獨 is odd and exact: sheep make a flock, and a dog goes alone.

孩: the first laugh, and the name. in modern chinese 孩 is “a child”. here it is a verb: of a baby, to laugh. the shuowen enters it as the old-script form of 咳 and defines that as 小兒笑也, “an infant’s laugh”. 嬰兒 is the child still at the breast. so 嬰兒之未孩 is a baby in its first weeks, before the first social smile, when its face has no answer for a face. wang bi: 如嬰兒之未能孩也, “like an infant not yet able to laugh”. there is a second layer. the ritual books describe how a child received its name: at the end of the third month the mother brought it to the father, who took its right hand and named it with a laugh; the text uses this same word, and the old commentators take it as the father’s fond chuckle to the child. so a child that has “not yet laughed” is, perhaps, one that has no name yet. the speaker compares the self to a thing before its name: the 無名 of passage 1, as a face.

a stray dog: the same was said of confucius. 儽儽 is a sound-picture of a thing that hangs down: the shuowen says 垂皃, “the look of drooping”, and adds “some say: slack, weary”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write the word 纍. with that graph the phrase has a famous twin. the historian sima qian tells that confucius once lost his disciples at the gate of a foreign city and stood there by himself. a local man described him to them: a tall stranger, 纍纍若喪家之狗, “forlorn as the dog of a house in mourning”, a dog that nobody feeds. when they told confucius, he laughed and said: that is right, that is right! so the two great teachers of china share one image of themselves: worn out, at a gate, with nowhere to 歸. in passage 16 each thing 歸, goes home, to its root. here the one who knows it looks like one who has no home.

餘 and 遺: surplus and loss. 眾人皆有餘: the crowd all 有餘, “have a surplus”. 餘 has the food sign, 飠, and the shuowen glosses it 饒也, “plenty”: more on the table than can be eaten. wang bi takes it inwardly: 眾人無不有懷有志，盈溢胸心, “each of the crowd has aims and ambitions that fill the breast and spill over”. against this, 我獨若遺. 遺 is to leave a thing behind or to be left behind; the shuowen says “to lose”. english must choose: “i alone seem to have lost everything”, “seem left out”, “seem forgotten”, “seem in want”. the chinese keeps all four. note 若, “seem”. the speaker reports how it looks, and perhaps how it feels, and does not say that it is so. passage 77 gives the other side: heaven’s way takes from those with surplus. have you ever been the one person at a table with nothing to show?

愚: a monkey’s heart. 愚 is 禺 over 心, the heart. the shuowen defines 愚 as 戇也, “simple, thick”, and explains the upper part: 禺，猴屬，獸之愚者, “禺 is of the monkey kind, the simple one among beasts”. so the fool’s heart is an ape’s heart: it follows what is in front of it and keeps no accounts. the speaker claims it with an exclamation. wang bi describes this heart: 心無所別析，意無所好欲, “the heart makes no distinctions and divisions; the mind has no likes and wants”. that is the point of the word here. it is not a low score on a test. it is a mind that has stopped sorting. the book uses 愚 once more, in passage 65, where rulers of old did not make the people clever but kept them 愚. that line has a harsh history. here the word is applied to nobody but “me”.

doubled words: the music of the middle. the centre of the passage is built of doubled syllables: 熙熙, 儽儽, 沌沌, 昭昭, 昏昏, 察察, 悶悶. chinese uses such pairs as english uses “pitter-patter”: they paint a state by sound, and they cannot be translated word for word. our “bright, bright… dusk, dusk” keeps the form at some cost to natural english. 昭 is full daylight; the shuowen says 日明也. 昏 is the sun gone down. 察 is to look into each corner, as an inspector does. 悶 is a heart, 心, inside a gate, 門: shut in, close, dull. the two sets return in passage 58 as a theory of government: 其政悶悶，其民淳淳；其政察察，其民缺缺. “when the government is shut and dull, the people are whole. when the government is sharp-eyed, the people are broken.” so the speaker’s private dimness is the same quality that the book asks of a state.

the sea: heaven’s pool. after the long list of lacks, two images of size. 澹 is what water does in a wide basin; the shuowen says 水搖也, “water that sways”. 飂 is 高風也, “wind high up”, the kind that moves clouds and is not felt on the ground. the sea, for people of the inland plain, was a thing heard of more than seen. the shuowen defines 海 with awe: 天池也，以納百川者, “heaven’s pool, that which takes in the hundred rivers”. it is the lowest place, and so the greatest; passage 66 says rivers and seas are kings of the valleys because they are good at being below. the grammar leaves open who is like the sea: no subject is given. many versions say “they” or “it”. wang bi and most readers give the lines to the speaker, and so do we. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write 忽呵 for the sea and 朢呵 for the wind.

wang bi: everyone has a use. 眾人皆有以. 以 is one of the commonest small words in chinese: “by means of, in order to”. here it stands as a noun, and wang bi explains: 以，用也。皆欲有所施用也. “以 means use. all of them want to have something to which they can be applied.” each person in the crowd has a function, a career, a reason. it is the 用 of passage 11 turned on people: a person as a vessel with a purpose. his long comment on the first line makes the same point with birds: 燕雀有匹，鳩鴿有仇…自然已足，益之則憂. “swallows and sparrows have their mates, doves and pigeons their partners… what is so of itself is already enough; add to it and there is worry.” then: 續鳧之足，何異截鶴之脛, “to lengthen a duck’s legs: how is that different from cutting short a crane’s?” the image is from the zhuangzi. learning, for him, is leg-lengthening.

頑 and 鄙: a block from the border. 頑 has 頁, a head, in it, and the shuowen’s gloss is a carpenter’s word: a thick, whole block of wood that has not been split. a 頑 person is a blockhead: nothing goes in. it is close kin to 樸, the uncarved wood of passages 15 and 19. 鄙 is a unit of the map; the shuowen says 五酇爲鄙, five hundred households in the outer lands of a state. people of the capital used it for all that was rustic: bad accent, plain food, no knowledge of the rites. “border” was a charged word. the states of the centre looked down on chu in the south and qin in the west as half-barbarian, and tradition says that laozi was a man of chu. the speaker takes the insult as a title. legge writes “a rude borderer”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 頑以悝, with a different last word.

食母: fed by the mother. the last two characters are a puzzle. 食 read shi is “to eat, food”; read si it is “to feed”. so 食母 can be “the mother who feeds”, “to feed on the mother”, or “to be fed by the mother”. it was also a set term: the ritual books say that the son of a great officer has a 食母, a wet nurse. each reading keeps the body: milk, a breast, a mouth. wang bi: 食母，生之本也, “the feeding mother is the root of life”. legge adds “(the tao)” in a bracket, which is right and is not in the text. the passage has been about an infant since its middle: one that has not yet laughed and has nowhere to go home to. now the infant says what it has that the feasters lack. they eat the sacrifice. it is at the breast. the mother appears in passages 1, 25, 52, and 59. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to say 吾欲: “i wish to be different”.

legge and the “stupid man”. legge turns the opening into a rhymed riddle and decides its sense with two brackets: “the (ready) ‘yes,’ and (flattering) ‘yea’”. then he does well with the lament, because victorian english had a register for melancholy: “listless and still”, “dejected and forlorn”, “as if i had no home to go to”. but the fool troubles him. “my mind is that of a stupid man; i am in a state of chaos” is a diagnosis. the chinese is a cry of recognition with two particles of feeling, 也哉. and for the infant he reaches for theory: “my desires having as yet given no indication of their presence”. the text says 未兆, “no sign yet”, and says nothing of desires. he hears a moral psychology where the chinese has a baby’s blank face. his “nursing-mother” for 食母 is exact and warm.

be dim at the feast. the next time you are in a bright room, a party, a meeting, a feed on a screen where each person shines, try the speaker’s place for ten minutes. do not perform, and do not withdraw in pride either; the passage has no pride in it. let the face rest, like a face before its first smile. have no opinion ready. if someone asks what you do, try an answer with no use in it. notice the fear that comes: of being taken for a fool, a block, a person from nowhere. the passage names each of those fears and puts “i” in front of it. then find the last line in your own body. under the wish to shine there is something that is fed without effort: breath comes in, and you did not earn it. stay there for three breaths.

昭 and 昏: the crowd’s light, the speaker’s dusk. the passage is built of pairs. at the start are 唯 and 阿, 善 and 惡, and the text asks how far apart the two sides are. then come the crowd and the “i”: 昭昭 and 昏昏, bright and dusk; 察察 and 悶悶, sharp and shut; 有餘 and 遺, surplus and loss. the speaker stands on the dim side each time, and a reader may take this as a rank: dull is good, bright is bad. the tone does not allow it. the speaker does not boast; the words are 若, “as if”, and a cry: a fool’s heart! brightness and dusk are also one day, and each comes out of the other. the lean to dusk answers an age that prized the sharp eye and the correct answer. it is a correction. a dimness that is worn as a badge is one more way to shine, and passage 24 has a word for that: 自見. where are you bright by habit, and what rests in you at dusk?

good and bad, like a polite yes and a rude one, stand closer together than people say.. good and bad, like a polite yes and a rude one, stand closer together than people say. do you agree, or does the thought alarm you? where does the alarm sit? think of a thing that you once called bad and now do not. what moved: the thing, or you? hold the opposite firmly: there is a real line between good and bad, and to blur it does harm. what do you feel as you hold it: safety, heat, relief? whom do you judge most sharply, and how far is that person from you on a tired day?

to be dim, unsure, and without a use, while others shine, can be a way to stay near the source.. to be dim, unsure, and without a use, while others shine, can be a way to stay near the source. does this ring true, or does it sound like an excuse? what in your own history makes it sound so? recall a time when everyone around you was sure and merry and you were not. what did you conclude about yourself then? take the crowd’s side: brightness, sharpness, and a place at the feast are good, and the one who stands apart is only afraid. stay with that. what answers in you? which do you hide more: your dullness, or your shine? from whom?

what other people fear cannot simply be left unfeared.. what other people fear cannot simply be left unfeared. do you agree that you must share the fears of those around you? name one that you carry and did not choose. who would be hurt or angry if you put that fear down? hold the opposite: a fear that is only borrowed can be handed back today. what do you notice in the body as you think it? what does the borrowed fear give you that you might not want to lose?

孩 a baby’s first laugh. left side: 子, a child. it is a picture, and one of the easiest to see once you are told: a large head, two arms out, and one line for body and legs: a wrapped baby, it is commonly said. the shuowen says 象形. as a word 子 is son, child, seed, and a title of respect: the 子 in 老子 and 孔子 is “master”. right side: 亥. it gives the sound; as a word it is the last of the twelve calendar branches, the pig of the animal cycle. the surprise is the meaning of the whole. today 孩子 is the everyday word for “child”, and 孩 alone feels like a noun. in the shuowen it is a verb, the old-script way to write 咳: 小兒笑也, “a small child laughs”. in that other form the laugh is written with 口, a mouth; in ours it is written with the child. the two graphs went two ways. 咳 kept the mouth and came to mean “to cough”. 孩 kept the child and became the child: the name of the one who laughs took the place of the laugh. the passage uses it in the first sense: an infant that has not yet laughed, and so, by the old rite, has not yet been named. cousins with 子: 好 (a woman and a child: good, to love), 字 (a child under a roof: to give a name, a written character), 孫 (grandchild: a child and a thread), 學 (learning: a child under a cover), 孝 (the child who carries the old). nine strokes: three and six. 子 as a left-hand part: a level stroke that turns sharply down to the left; then a curved vertical with a hook at its foot; then the arms. when 子 stands alone the arms are a level line. here they are written as a stroke that rises to the right, and it stops short, so as not to enter the other half. then 亥: a dot on top; a level stroke under it; then a stroke that goes down to the left, turns, and comes back; then two strokes that fall to the left, the first long and the second shorter, under it; and a last stroke that presses down to the right. watch strokes six to nine. they hang from the level line one below the other like a child’s mobile, and the final stroke, low on the right, is the counterweight that keeps the whole character from tipping toward the child.

獨 the dog that walks alone. on the left is 犭, the side form of 犬, a dog. 犬 is 大 with a dot; the old forms are a dog drawn on end, with a lean body and a curled tail. as a side part it marks animals, mostly the wild and wilful ones: 狗 (dog), 狼 (wolf), 狐 (fox), 猴 (monkey), 猶 (the ape of passage 15), 獵 (to hunt), 狂 (mad), and 狀, “shape”, which the shuowen defines as “the form of a dog”. on the right is 蜀. alone it is the old name of sichuan; the shuowen explains it as a grub in the mallow plant, with 目 for its head and 虫, a creature, below. here it gives the sound. now the definition, one of the dictionary’s best: 犬相得而鬬也, “dogs, when they come together, fight”, and then a proverb: 羊爲羣，犬爲獨也, “sheep make a flock; a dog makes one alone”. the graph for a flock, 羣, has 羊, a sheep, in it; the graph for alone has the dog. so to be 獨 is not to be abandoned. it is to be the kind of animal that does not herd. the word has an honoured place in chinese ethics. the confucian classics ask a person to be watchful when 獨, alone and unobserved, and passage 25 of this book says that the way 獨立, “stands alone”, and does not change. the speaker of this passage says 我獨 six times. the short form is 独: the dog, and only the 虫. sixteen strokes: three for the dog, thirteen for 蜀. the dog: a short stroke that falls to the left; a long curved stroke that bends outward and ends in a hook; and a second falling stroke across its lower part. keep it lean, with the curve like a back. then the flat eye on top of the right side: a short vertical; a stroke that goes right and turns down; two short verticals inside; and the line that closes it. under the eye, a falling stroke, and then a long stroke that goes right, turns, comes down, and hooks inward: it wraps the last part like an arm. inside the wrap is 虫: a small box of three strokes, a vertical through it, a rising stroke at the foot, and a final dot. watch the wrapping stroke. it decides the width of the whole right side, and the small creature must sit inside it with room to spare.

21 · inside the haze. the look of great de: / it is dao alone that it walks behind. / dao, as a thing: / only flickering, only dim. / dim! flickering! / within it there is an image. / flickering! dim! / within it there is a thing. / deep! dark! / within it there is essence. / this essence is very real; / within it there is a proof. / from now back to the old, / its name has not gone away, / and by it the fathers of all pass in review. / how do i know the shape of the fathers of all? / by this. the passage has a frame and a descent. the frame: great de has one look, which is that it follows dao; and dao, if you take it as a thing, is only haze. then the descent, in four steps, each introduced by cries of 兮 and each with the same phrase, 其中有, “within it there is”. in the dim and flickering: an image. in the flickering and dim: a thing. in the deep dark: essence. in the essence, which is very real: a proof. the close turns to time and knowledge. from now back to the old its name has stayed; by it the fathers of all things are reviewed, as at a gate; and the speaker knows them by this. the rhymes tie each found thing to its haze. the pictures are two walkers, a cave, a waning moon, polished rice, a token, and a gate. passage 14 said what the way is not: not seen, not heard, not held. this passage is its partner, and it says what is found if one does not turn away from the blur. that is the whole discipline: to remain in a state that the ordinary mind leaves at once, because it has no object. the text reports that the state is not empty. it has layers, and they come in an order: a pattern, something definite, a fine living essence, and at the centre a thing as plain as a kept promise. 恍惚 and 窈冥 later became names for stages of trance, and 精 was what the still heart collects. but the passage does not ask you to believe a map. its last words are a method: by this. and its first line says how the one who knows will look from outside: like a follower, with no face of their own. chinese medicine and the arts of long life took their vocabulary from lines like these. 精 is the body’s stored essence, the finest product of food and breath, and the seed; it is kept low in the belly, and guarded. in the later scheme, essence is refined into breath-energy and breath-energy into spirit. you need not hold that theory to feel the passage in the body. sit and let the gaze go soft, neither fixed nor closed; that is 恍惚 for the eyes. let attention drop down and back, as if into a cave behind the navel. the belly is dark to the mind; we seldom visit it. rest there, and notice whether there is something alive and warm that is not a thought. the old teachers said: that is real, and it can be relied on. it was there before you looked. at first light there is a quarter of an hour when the world is 恍惚: you cannot say if that dark mass is a hill or a cloud. then come shapes, then things, a tree, a wall. morning repeats each day the order of this passage. so does the growth of an embryo, where pattern is laid down before any organ; so does a pond in spring, cloudy with what will be frogs. the source of things is not clear and bright, with a blueprint. it is turbid, and full. the moon in 冥 wanes toward the dark, and from the dark comes back; farmers planted by it. and 精 is first of all seed-grain: the small, dense, picked part of last year’s harvest that holds next year’s. inside the least showy thing in the barn is the most real one. it keeps its word each spring. use the one-minute-longer exercise once today, on a real question. then take the frame of the passage into an ordinary hour. de has no look except that it follows. choose one activity, to cook, to walk, to listen to someone, and for its length let yourself be only the follower: of the heat in the pan, of the slope of the path, of the other person’s words. do not lead. afterwards ask what was reliable in it, what was 信. if you like to see how a mind of another age met this chant, read legge’s sixteen rhymed lines, and then go back to the four-character lines of the chinese. for the question of whether dao can be called a thing at all, give yourself a quiet minute, and for the fathers that file through the gate, another.

孔: great, or hollow?. 孔 is first a hole, an opening that goes through; the shuowen says 通也, “to pass through”. from early times it was also used for “very, great”, and the old heshang gong commentary reads it so here: 孔，大也, great de. wang bi takes the first sense and builds his reading on it: 孔，空也，惟以空為德，然後乃能動作從道. “孔 is hollow. only one who takes hollowness as de is then able, in each movement, to follow dao.” so for him the line says that power is a kind of emptiness, as the hub and the pot of passage 11 work at their hollow. the grammar bears both. we render “great” and keep the hole here. there is an accident too. 孔 is the family name of confucius, and for a reader of chinese 孔德 looks, for a moment, like “the virtue of kong”. nothing suggests that the author meant it.

德 meets 道. this is the first line, in the order that we now read, where the two words of the book’s title stand together, and it states their relation in four characters: 德 follows 道, and nothing else. 德 is the hardest word in the book to bring into english. “virtue” was right in the old sense of “the virtue of a herb”, its power to act, from latin virtus, strength. today it means moral goodness, and that is what the laozi says appears when the way is lost (passage 38). 德 is what a thing has got from the way: its own way of being effective, with no effort to be so. a person of 德 changes a room by entering it. the shuowen glosses the word 升也, “to rise”. we leave de in chinese, as we leave dao. legge writes “active force”, which is not bad.

容, a third time. the same character has now stood at an important place in three passages. in 15 the speaker was forced to draw a 容, a likeness, of the old masters, who were too deep to know. in 16, knowledge of the constant gave 容, room for all things. here it is the 容 of de. which sense? “the look, the outward bearing” fits passage 15: once more something inward shows a face. “the content, what it holds” fits the shuowen’s definition, 盛也, and wang bi’s hollow. a third sense, “movement, behaviour”, is used by some commentators. chinese readers feel no need to choose; a face is what holds and shows a person. the line says that all one can see of de, its whole expression, is a following. it has no look of its own. think of someone’s face while they listen with full attention. what is its expression?

從: one person behind another. the old way to write this word is 从: two persons, one after the other. the mainland short form has gone back to it. the full graph adds the signs for a road and a foot, and the shuowen defines it 隨行也, “to walk after”. it is the verb for a servant behind a master, a soldier behind a flag, a river that keeps to its bed. the line’s grammar is emphatic. 惟道是從 puts the object first and marks it: “it is dao, only that, which it follows”. the pattern is known from oaths and commands in the old documents. so de does not consult anything else: no rule, no model, no ruler’s wish, no idea of the good. legge reverses the picture; in his verse the forces “from tao come”, like water out of a source. the chinese has two walkers on a road, and the one in front cannot be clearly seen.

is dao a thing?. 道之為物 is a bold phrase. 物 is the ordinary word for a thing, a creature, an item in the world; the shuowen even ties it to cattle: 牛爲大物, “the ox is a big thing”. the book has said that dao returns to “no thing” (14). now it says: dao, 為物, “taken as a thing”. the usual reading is a kind of trial. suppose you treat it as an object and look straight at it: what do you get? haze. a second reading takes 為 as “to make”: “dao, in its making of things”. then the lines that follow are a cosmogony, the steps by which things come out of the blur. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to have only 道之物, “dao’s thing” or “the thing that is dao”, which favours the first. wang bi gives the lines to both at once: 以無形始物，不繫成物, “with no form it begins things; with no tie it completes them”.

恍惚, turned and turned back. passage 14 called the way 惚恍 and stopped there: it cannot be fixed. this passage takes the word and enters it. first it is split, 惟恍惟惚, “only 恍, only 惚”. then it is said in both orders, 惚兮恍兮 and 恍兮惚兮, each with the sigh 兮. the turning is not ornament. it makes the rhymes. in the old rhyme groups 恍 ends like 象, image (the group 陽), and 惚 ends like 物, thing (the group 物). further on, 冥 ends like 精 (耕), and 真 like 信 (真). so each thing that is found rhymes with the haze in which it is found. the ear learns, before the mind does, that the image is not hidden behind the dimness. it is the same sound. in later chinese 恍惚 became a term for trance, and today it means “in a daze”. wang bi calls it 無形不繫之歎, “a sigh at the formless and untied”.

image before thing. the order is exact: first 象, then 物. in the thought of the time an image comes before a formed thing. a commentary attached to the book of changes says 在天成象，在地成形: “in heaven, images take shape; on earth, forms take shape”. a 象 is a pattern not yet solid: the figure of a constellation, the look of the sky before rain, the six lines of a hexagram. passage 14 spoke of “the image of no thing”; passage 35 will call the way “the great image”; passage 41 says that this great image is without shape. so the first thing that shows in the haze is a pattern, and after it a thing that can be pointed at. a person who waits for an idea knows this order. something has a shape before it has any content. legge’s things “crouch” in the way, like animals in a thicket. that is his rhyme’s doing, and it is rather good.

窈 and 冥: a cave and a dying moon. for the third step the passage changes its word for the dark, as if it had gone further in. 窈 has 穴, a cave, on top; the shuowen says 深遠也, “deep and far”: the back of a cavern, where the light of the mouth does not reach. 冥 is “the dark”, and the shuowen’s account of the graph is a small poem of the calendar: the sun counts ten, and 十六日而月始虧幽也, “on the sixteenth day the moon begins to wane toward darkness”. the same word names the world of the dead. wang bi: 窈、冥，深遠之歎，深遠不可得而見。然而萬物由之. “窈 and 冥 are sighs at the deep and far, too deep and far to see. and yet the ten thousand things come by way of it.” the dark here is like the 玄 of passage 1: depth, not evil. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write the first word 幽, “hidden”.

精: the finest grain. 精 has 米, husked rice, at the left. the shuowen defines it 擇也, “to pick out”: grain that has been sorted and polished until only the best is left. from that it means the fine part of anything, its concentrated life: spirit, energy, and also seed, semen. the meditation teachers of qi made it a technical term. the “inward training” opens: 凡物之精，此則為生，下生五穀，上為列星. “the 精 of all things: it is this that makes life. below, it brings forth the five grains; above, it becomes the ranked stars.” stored in a person’s breast, it goes on, this makes a sage, and a still heart is the lodging to which it comes. so when this passage finds 精 inside the dark, a reader of the time hears a claim about practice and the body, not only about the cosmos. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write 請, a loan graph for the same word. english “essence” is abstract; 精 can be eaten.

真: real, and not “true”. this is the first time the book says 真. english versions give “true”, “truth”, “reality”. in western thought truth belongs first to statements: a sentence is true if it fits the facts. 真 is not about sentences. it is said of things: real gold, a real pearl, the genuine article and not a copy. so 其精甚真 is “this essence is very real”: not thinned, not faked. scholars have long noted an odd fact: the graph 真 does not occur in the confucian five classics. by the han the word belonged to the adepts: the shuowen defines it as 僊人變形而登天也, “an immortal who changes form and rises to heaven”. it is a word of this book and of the zhuangzi, where the 真人, the “real person”, is the highest human type, and it later became the ordinary daoist title for an adept. the passage has just compared the way to haze. now it uses its strongest word for the genuine about what is inside the haze. which do you trust more: what is clear, or what is real?

信: something that can be tested. the fourth and last thing found is 信, the word of passage 17: trust, good faith, words that hold. a 信 was also an object: a token or seal that proved a message was genuine. wang bi reads it in that sense: 信，信驗也, “信 means proof by trial”. and he says when the proof comes: 物反窈冥，則真精之極得，萬物之性定. “when things turn back to the deep dark, the utmost of the real essence is attained, and the natures of the ten thousand things are settled.” this is a strong claim, and it is not a call to faith. the text says that in the innermost part of what cannot be seen or named there is something that keeps its word: it can be relied on, and tried, like the return of the seasons. english “faith” would make it belief without evidence. 信 here is the evidence. what in your experience has never once failed to arrive?
