from now back to the old. our text reads 自今及古, “from the present to antiquity”. many printed editions read 自古及今, “from antiquity to the present”, the usual order of the phrase in chinese, and wang bi’s own comment quotes it that way. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to have “from now to the old”, and the rhyme proves that they are right: 古 must end the line to rhyme with 去 and 甫, all in the old group 魚. a copyist changed the strange order to the common one. the difference is one of method. “from antiquity to now” is the view of a historian who starts at the origin. “from now back” starts here: you take hold in the present and trace toward the beginning, as passage 14, in the silk version, held “the way of now”. then 其名不去, “its name does not leave”. but it has no name! wang bi: 無名則是其名也, “namelessness is its name”.

閱: the count at the gate. 閱 has 門, a gate, around it. the shuowen’s definition is a scene: 具數於門中也, “to count off the full number in the gateway”. goods were checked at the gate of a storehouse, and troops were mustered and counted as they filed through the gate of a camp; 閱兵 is still the chinese for a military review. so 以閱眾甫 has a picture in it. the speaker stands at a gate, and the origins of all things march through one at a time and are counted. today 閱 is “to read”: the eye passes the characters in review. english “observe” or “see” loses the gate and the file. and the gate is not a chance image in this book. passage 1 ended at “the gate of all fineness”, and passage 6 has the gate of the dark female. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 順, “to go along with”, where we have 閱.

眾甫: the fathers of all. 甫 is rare as a plain word. the shuowen calls it 男子美稱也, “a term of honour for a man”, and says the graph contains 父, father, which also gives its sound. men of rank had it in their formal names. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write the simpler graph: 眾父, “the fathers of the many”. wang bi glosses 眾甫，物之始也, “the beginnings of things”. so the phrase means the origins from which each kind of thing comes, pictured as a line of ancestors. this is notable in a book whose word for the source is “mother” (1, 20, 25, 52). the mother is one, and feeds. the fathers are many, and are counted at a gate. legge took the dictionary’s “beautiful term” another way and wrote “all the beauties of existing things”, which is a mistake that produced a lovely phrase. our “fathers of all” follows the reported silk reading.

以此: “by this”. the passage ends with a question and a two-word answer. 吾何以知…? “how do i know…?” 以此: “by this”. the same exchange closes an argument in passage 54 and opens one in passage 57. what is “this”? wang bi says: 此上之所云也, “what was said above”: the account just given. others say: this way; or this present moment, since the line before began from “now”; or this body and heart, in which the haze, the image, and the essence can be found by anyone who is still. the word is a pointer with no noun, and the open hand is the answer. the knowledge claimed in this passage is not from a book or a teacher, and not “from antiquity”. note the “i”, 吾, which enters only here. legge fills the pointer with a bracket: “by this (nature of the tao)”. when you say “this”, with nothing after it, where does your attention go?

legge in rhyme: “all right”. legge saw that this passage is a rhymed chant, and he was almost alone among early translators in trying to show it. he put it into sixteen lines of english verse with four beats. the attempt deserves respect, and the result shows what rhyme costs. to rhyme with “touch” the forms of things must “crouch”. to rhyme with “sight” he needs a filler: “there are their semblances, all right.” the haze becomes a matter of two senses, “our sight it flies, our touch as well”, borrowed from passage 14; 恍惚 says nothing of sight or touch. 精 is “essences”, plural, which makes it a set of platonic kinds. and 信, the token that can be tried, becomes “the truth… of what, when seen, shall then be told”. read his poem aloud for its swing. then read the chinese line 其中有信 and count: four characters.

stay in the haze one minute longer. the passage describes a sequence, and you can test it on a small scale. choose a question to which you do not know the answer: what to write, what a person meant, what you feel about a thing. sit with it, and do not reach for the first clear thought. that first clear thought is usually an old one. let the matter be dim and unfixed. after a while there is often a vague shape, a leaning: an image. do not grab it. then something more definite, a thing you could name. stay one minute longer than is comfortable, in the deep part, and see whether there is a sense that this is real, and that it holds when you lean on it. then get up and act on it. the method of the passage is in its last two words: not by report, by this.

the haze and the thing: 無 and 有. the pair is not named, but each couplet turns on it: 恍惚, the haze where nothing is definite, and 有, “there is”. passage 14 followed the same matter back to 無物, “no thing”. this passage says 其中有物, “within it there is a thing”. the two do not conflict. they are the two sides that passage 2 joins: 有無相生, there-is and there-is-not bring each other forth. read one side alone, and dao is a blank, and the practice is to empty the mind and stop. read the other side alone, and dao is an object, a highest being with a clear shape. the text gives neither. the image, the thing, the essence, and the proof are found inside the dimness, and they do not end it: the haze is how they are there. even the words turn: 恍惚 becomes 惚恍 and comes back. which do you trust more easily: what is clear, or what is dim and does not fail?

inside what is dim and dark there is something very real, and it can be trusted.. inside what is dim and dark there is something very real, and it can be trusted. have you found this? recall something sure that came out of a time when you saw nothing clearly. how long can you stay in not knowing before you reach for an answer? what did unclear times mean in your family? take the other side: what is clear and can be shown is to be trusted, and haze hides error. hold it for a while. what does it guard you against? which side feels like home, and which like a threat? what has each one kept from you?

the greatest power has no face of its own; it follows the way and nothing else.. the greatest power has no face of its own; it follows the way and nothing else. do you agree that the strongest way to act is to follow? where have you seen it work, and where have you seen it fail? what do you think of followers? if the word carries shame for you, where was that learned? now hold the opposite: power is to set the direction, and one who follows has given up their part. what rises in you? in which part of your life do you lead where you could follow, or follow where you are asked to lead?

精 rice, picked and polished. the left side is 米. it is rice or millet with the husk off, and the shuowen calls it a picture: 象禾實之形, “it shows the seeds of the grain”. the usual explanation of the drawing is a threshing stick or a sieve in the middle, with grains above and below. you find it in 粉 (flour, powder), 粥 (rice gruel), and in 氣, breath-energy, where steam rises over cooking rice. the right side is 青, the blue-green of growing things: a sprout, 生, over a pit of mineral colour, 丹. you met it in 靜, stillness, in passage 16. here it gives the sound, and it also lends a sense; its whole family leans toward “clear, fine”. 清 is clear water. 晴 is a clear sky. 睛 is the clear part of the eye, the pupil. 情 is what the heart truly feels. 請 is a courteous request; the mawangdui scribes are reported to have written that graph for 精 in this very line. and 精 is clear rice: the shuowen defines it 擇也, “to pick out”, the best grain sorted from the rest and polished white. then the word rose. the fine part of anything is its 精: the spirit of wine, the essence of a text, a skilled hand (精巧), a person’s vital force (精神, essence and spirit: “mind”, “vigour”), the seed of a man. a sprite or a goblin is a 精 too: a thing so concentrated that it has woken up. the passage finds 精 in the dark and says it is very real. fourteen strokes: six for the rice, eight for 青. the rice: a dot at the upper left and a short stroke at the upper right, which lean in toward each other; a level stroke; a long vertical through it; then a stroke that falls to the left. the sixth stroke would be a long sweep to the right if 米 stood alone. as a left-hand part it shrinks to a dot, so that the grain does not push into the other half. then 青: two level strokes; a vertical through them; a third, longer level stroke. below, the form like 月: a vertical; a stroke that goes right, turns down, and hooks; and two small level strokes inside. watch the two verticals, the one through the rice and the one in the top of 青. they are the two masts of the character, and they must be parallel.

孔 the swallow that brings a child. only four strokes, and the shuowen has a whole spring festival in them. the left side is 子, a child. the right side, a single bent line, is not a hook or a number. the shuowen says it is 𠃉, a picture of a swallow in flight, and explains: 𠃉，請子之候鳥也。𠃉至而得子，嘉美之也。 “the swallow is the bird of the season at which one prays for children. the swallow comes and a child is got; this is cause for joy and praise.” swallows return to north china at the spring equinox, and on that day the king offered sacrifice to the divine matchmaker and asked for sons. so the dictionary reads 孔 as swallow plus child: a happy passage, a thing that came through. its definition is 通也, “to go through”, and it adds that men of old named 嘉, “excellent”, took the formal name 子孔. modern scholars read the bronze forms otherwise: a child with a mark at the head, perhaps the soft spot of an infant’s skull, or a child at the breast; either way a small opening. the word’s ordinary sense is “hole”: 鼻孔 is a nostril, 毛孔 a pore. its old sense “very, great” is the one usually read in this passage. and it is the surname of confucius, 孔子, master kong, whose descendants still carry it. in this line, the look of de is 孔: great, and gone through. four strokes. the child takes three, as in 孩 of the passage before: a level stroke that turns back sharply to the left; a curved vertical with a hook at the foot; and the arms, written as a stroke that rises to the right. the fourth stroke is the whole right side, and you should watch it from start to end. the brush goes down, bends at the bottom in a round corner with no stop, runs to the right along the base, and then turns up into a tall hook. calligraphers name it the “floating goose” stroke. it is one of the hardest in the script, because it must change direction twice and keep the same strength; the turn is made with the wrist, and the hook is pushed up, not flicked. in a good 孔 the space between the child and that curve is wide and clean: the hole in the character.

22 · bent, then whole. bent, then whole. / crooked, then straight. / hollow, then full. / worn, then new. / few, then gain. / many, then bewildered. / so the sage holds the one in the arms / and is the measure for all under heaven. / not self-showing, and so bright. / not self-approving, and so plain to see. / not self-praising, and so there is merit. / not self-proud, and so lasting. / just because of no contending, / no one under heaven can contend with such a one. / what the ancients called “bent, then whole”: / how could it be empty words? / truly whole, and all comes home. six sayings of three characters each, with 則, “then”, as the hinge: bent, whole; crooked, straight; hollow, full; worn, new; few, gain; many, bewildered. the pictures are a tree or a bow, a warped board, a dip in a field, a rag and fresh-cut wood. then 是以, “so”, and a portrait: the sage holds the one and is a measure for the world. four lines say what such a person does not do, each with 自, “self”: show, approve, praise, be proud. each not-doing gets the very thing that the doing wanted. then the book’s great phrase, 不爭. the end comes back to the first line and names it as a saying of the ancients; so the passage is a small sermon on a proverb, and it closes with one word for going home. the four 自 lines are a precise list of what the self does all day: it shows itself, it holds itself right, it praises itself, it admires itself. contemplatives of every tradition have made such lists. the laozi’s point is less moral than most. it does not say that the self is bad. it says that these four acts take what is whole and make it many, and that with many comes bewilderment. to hold the one is the same instruction from the other side: arms that are full of one thing cannot pick up four others. note the first saying again in this light. to be bent is to have given up the straight line of one’s own will, and what follows is not loss. it is 全, nothing missing. when you stop holding yourself right, what is it that is suddenly intact? this is leadership by standing as a measure and not by pushing. the four lines are practical. a leader who displays is watched less closely than one who does not, since people look hardest for what is not shown to them. one who is always right teaches others to stop reporting facts. one who claims the credit finds that there is less of it each year; in passage 17 the people said, “we did it ourselves”. one who is proud does not last. the strategists knew the military form of the first line: give ground, keep the force whole. and 不爭 is not weakness in a negotiator. the person with no position to defend for its own sake cannot be cornered. a caution from mencius belongs here too: to bend oneself for advantage is a trade, and the text does not offer a trade. every martial art of china teaches the first line with the spine and the knees. a straight, locked limb breaks; a bent one stores force, like a drawn bow. in push-hands, when a partner pushes, you do not push back and you do not collapse: you curve, the force goes past, and you are still on your feet, whole. the teachers call it 捨己從人, “give up yourself and follow the other”, which is 不爭 as a skill of the joints. the hollow is the chest that sinks so that the breath can fill the belly. and to hold the one is a posture known to every student of standing practice: the arms rounded in front of the chest as if around a tree or a large ball. stand like that for two minutes. what do the arms learn that a list of four virtues cannot teach? grass bends in a gale and the oak comes down. a river keeps no straight course and so arrives at the sea. the dip in the field holds the pond, and the pond holds the frogs. a forest burns, and the worn-out wood becomes ash for seedlings; the graph for “new” has an axe in it. the inchworm draws itself into a hoop in order to go forward. none of these is a strategy. the grass does not bend to win. that is the difference between the old proverb and a clever reading of it: in nature the bending and the wholeness are one event, and not a price and a reward. even the first word says so. 曲, in the dictionary’s picture, is a vessel that is curved so that it can hold. the straight is in the list as well: it is what the crooked becomes. try the one deliberate bend today. then take the saying that fits your season. if you are being forced to give way, 曲則全: ask what stays whole if you do. if you have been wronged, 枉則直: ask whether you need to be straightened today. if you feel empty, 窪則盈: a low place is where things collect. if you are worn out, 敝則新. if you are bewildered, count how many things you are holding, and put down all but one. the ancients, the text says, did not speak empty words. for the close of the passage and its three ways home, read the note on the last six characters. for a victorian sermon made out of four mechanical facts, read legge.

曲: the curve that receives. 曲 is a bend: a curved line, a river’s turn, a corner of a room, and later a tune, since a melody bends. the shuowen calls it a picture: 象器曲受物之形, “it shows a vessel, curved, that takes things in”. so the first word already has the logic of the line in it. a curve is a form that can receive. 全 is “whole, intact”, and in the fourth century bce the word had a hard edge. to 全 one’s body or one’s life, in an age of conscription and mutilating punishments, was to reach old age with all one’s limbs. the followers of yang zhu made 全生, “keeping life whole”, a teaching. the image most readers supply is a tree: the bent one is not cut for timber and lives. the zhuangzi tells that story at length. english “yield and overcome” adds a victory. the chinese says only: bent, and so, whole.

a commentary on an old saying. the last lines say what the passage is: 古之所謂曲則全者, “that which the ancients called ‘bent, then whole’”. the first line is a quotation. it was a proverb before it was scripture, and the passage is an early commentary on it, perhaps the oldest we have on any line of this book. the form is that of folk wisdom the world over: a, 則, b, three syllables, easy to remember. the first six lines may all be old sayings, strung together. three of them rhyme in the old language: 直, 得, and 惑 all end in the group 職. then 是以, “for this reason”, opens the commentary. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to quote the saying without its middle word, 曲全, as a title, and end with a plain question, 幾語才, read as “how could it be mere talk?” this passage is not on the guodian slips.

枉: “bend a foot to straighten eight”. 枉 is a carpenter’s word; the shuowen says 衺曲也, “slanting and bent”, of wood. of people it means crooked, or wronged by a crooked judge. its opposite, 直, the shuowen explains as 正見, “to see straight on”: ten, 十, and an eye, 目. the pair was moral currency. confucius said: raise the straight and set them over the crooked, and the people will follow. and a proverb of the diplomats ran 枉尺而直尋, “bend one foot to make eight feet straight”: give way a little, flatter a bad king, and you may do great good. a disciple put it to mencius, who refused with scorn: no one who bent himself ever made another straight. the laozi’s line sounds like the diplomats’ proverb, but it makes no bargain. it does not say “bend in order to”. a commentary on the changes has the natural form of the same thought: the inchworm draws itself in, and so stretches out.

窪: the dip in the ground. 窪 is a low place in the land. its top is 穴, a cave or pit, and under it is the water word 洼, which the shuowen defines 深池也, “a deep pool”. after rain, every dip in a field has water in it and every rise is dry. the line is a fact of drainage before it is a moral. 盈 is the brim-fullness of passage 15, where the one who keeps the way does not wish for it. here it comes unasked, to the place that is lowest. the book returns to this ground often. water is good because it stays in the places that people dislike (8). the great state is the low reach of a river (61). rivers and seas are kings of the hundred valleys because they are good at being below them (66). in a meeting or a family, who is the low place where things collect?

新: “new” began with an axe. 敝 is a garment worn to rags; the shuowen gives 敗衣, “ruined clothing”, as one of its senses. 新 is “new”, and its history is a surprise. the right side is 斤, an axe. the shuowen defines the word 取木也: “to get wood”, to fell and split it. it is the first way to write 薪, firewood. the sense “new” was attached to the graph early: fresh-cut wood is white and wet, and it is the opposite of a thing worn dark with use. so the line holds a rag and a fresh log. passage 15 ended on this pair, in a line that no edition settles: “able to be worn, and not made new”. here the saying is plain: what is worn out is what gets renewed. nobody replaces a coat that still looks good. what in your life is kept from renewal because it is not yet shabby enough?

wang bi: the tree and its root. 少則得，多則惑. 得 is “to get”; the shuowen says 行有所得也, “to walk and come upon something”. 惑 is a heart, 心, under 或, “perhaps, either”: a mind among too many maybes. the line gives no object. few what? legge supplies “(desires)”. wang bi leaves it open and gives an image: 自然之道亦猶樹也，轉多轉遠其根，轉少轉得其本。 “the way of what is so of itself is like a tree. the more there is, the farther from the root; the less, the nearer one gets to the trunk.” twigs are many and the trunk is one. 多則遠其真，故曰惑也: “with much, one is far from what is real, and so the text says ‘bewildered’.” he then defines the one of the next line as 少之極也, “the limit of few”. the mathematics is simple. if you keep on making few fewer, you arrive at one.

聖人: not a saint. we write “the sage” for 聖人, and the word needs a warning each time. it is not a saint: no holiness, no miracles, no reward in another world. it is not only a wise man: the chinese has no “man” in it, and no gender; 人 is “person”. the graph 聖 has an ear, 耳, and a mouth, 口: one who hears well and so speaks to the point; the shuowen glosses it 通, “to pass through”. in this book the 聖人 is most often a ruler, or what a ruler should be: a person who governs by being in tune and not by force. passage 19 said to cut off 聖 as a title. here the figure returns, and is defined by four things that such a person does not do. english forces a pronoun on the lines that follow. we wrote “such a one”; legge writes “he”.

抱一 or 執一: embrace it, or grip it. 抱 is to hold in both arms against the chest, as one carries a child; passage 19 used it for the uncarved wood, and passage 10 asks, “can you hold the one and not let it go?” 一 is “one”: the unity before things are told apart, which passage 39 says heaven got and so is clear, and earth got and so is settled. legge narrows it in a bracket, “the one thing (of humility)”, which makes a cosmic term into a christian virtue. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to have another verb: 執一, “grips the one”. 執 is the firm hold of a hand on a tool or a rein; it was used in passage 14 for the hold on the way of old. “grip the one” was a slogan of rulership in other texts of the time: the lord holds one principle, and the many affairs sort themselves. the received text has made the hold softer. which do you do with what matters most to you?

式 or 牧: a measure, or a herdsman. in the received text the sage is 天下式, “the 式 of all under heaven”. 式 has 工, the carpenter’s square, in it, and the shuowen says 法也, “a standard”: the pattern piece that other pieces are cut from. wang bi: 式，猶則之也, “式 is, so to speak, to take as one’s rule”. the same word named the diviner’s cosmic board of the han, a square earth-plate with a round heaven-plate that turned on a pivot; some readers think of that here, though it cannot be shown. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to have a different picture: 天下牧, “the herdsman of all under heaven”. 牧 is a hand with a stick beside an ox; the shuowen says 養牛人也, “one who tends cattle”. it was a title of regional governors. a measure does nothing, and others match themselves to it. a herdsman walks behind the herd. both are quiet ways to lead. they are not the same.

four times “self”. four lines, each of the form 不自 x 故 y: “not self-x, so y”. 自見 (read xian): to show oneself. 自是: to “this” oneself, to hold oneself right. 自伐: to boast. 自矜: to be proud. the play is that each result is what the self-act was after. one who shows off wants to be 明, clearly seen; it is the one who does not who is. the first line is a pun on light: 見 is “to be seen” and 明 is “bright”. english must turn each 自 phrase into a noun, “self-display”, or add a person. the chinese has only the small word 自, which was first a picture of a nose: the place people point to when they mean “me”. passage 24 has the same four in the positive: “one who shows himself is not bright…”. in the mawangdui silk texts, that passage is reported to come just before this one. the last result, 長, has two readings: chang, “to last”, as we render it, or zhang, “to grow, to be chief”, which wang bi and legge prefer.

伐 and 矜: the boaster’s weapons. the two words for bragging in these lines are both arms. 伐 is 亻, a person, and 戈, a dagger-axe; the shuowen says 擊也。从人持戈, “to strike; a person who holds a halberd”. old forms are commonly described with the blade across the person’s neck. it means to attack a state, to fell a tree, and, as here, to trumpet one’s own deeds: self-praise as a military campaign. 矜 has 矛, a spear, at its left, and the shuowen defines it in three words: 矛柄也, “the shaft of a spear”. from something held stiffly upright came “to hold oneself high”; the same graph also means “to pity”. so a reader of chinese sees a halberd and a spear in the two lines about pride, and then, two lines on, 不爭, no contending. a war-word hides in the english too: we “blow our own trumpet”.

不爭 is not passivity. 爭 is two hands that pull at one thing; the shuowen says 引也, “to pull”. 不爭 is “not to pull against”. english versions say “does not compete”, “does not strive”, “does not quarrel”, and the victorian ear hears a meek person who lets others win. the line that follows is not meek: 天下莫能與之爭, “no one under heaven is able to contend with such a one”. the same sentence closes passage 66. the logic is that of a tug-of-war: it takes two to pull a rope. a person with no self to show, justify, praise, or admire has left nothing at the other end to pull on. the phrase is one of the book’s signatures. water benefits all things and does not contend (8). the good warrior is not warlike; this is called the power of not-contending (68). the way of the sage is to act and not contend (81): the last words of the book.

全 in the war manuals. 全 was a term of strategy. sunzi’s chapter on attack by plan opens: 凡用兵之法，全國為上，破國次之, “in the method of war, to take a state whole is best; to break it is second”. and so down the scale: an army whole is better than an army broken, a company, a squad. the best general wins with nothing destroyed on either side. the laozi and the sunzi come from one world, and the proverb “bent, then whole” would be at home in either: the commander who gives ground keeps the force intact. but notice the difference of aim. in sunzi wholeness is the best way to win. in this passage winning is not mentioned. the whole thing is one’s own life and person, and the last line does not say “and so conquers”. it says 歸, “comes home”.

誠全而歸之: three ways home. the last six characters are open. 誠 is “truly, in fact”; the shuowen glosses it 信也. 全 is whole. 歸 is to go home, or to give back. 之 is “it” or “to it”. one reading: “truly, wholeness goes home to such a one”: all things come to the person who bends. a second: “truly whole, one returns to it”, to the way, or to the root, as in passage 16. a third hears an echo that a reader of the time could not miss. a saying kept in the ritual books runs: 父母全而生之，子全而歸之，可謂孝矣, “father and mother bore you whole; to give yourself back whole may be called devotion”. that is 全而歸之, word for word. then the line says: keep whole what you were given, body and nature, and hand it back unbroken at the end. our “all comes home” leans to the first and leaves the door open.

legge: “the partial becomes complete”. legge renders 曲 as “the partial”: a corner, a fragment. that is a real sense of the word, and with it the first line becomes a statement about parts and wholes that sounds like the philosophy of his century. he loses the bent tree. in the fifth line he supplies an object twice, “(desires)”, where the chinese has none. he glosses the one as “(of humility)”. and the four 自 lines become a list of a gentleman’s faults: “self-display”, “self-assertion”, “self-boasting”, “self-complacency”. these are good victorian words, and each one has a moral frown in it that the chinese lacks. the chinese lines give effects. they do not say that boasting is wicked; they say that it does not work. read the four english words again as plain mechanics, with no sermon in them. which of them costs you the most effort in a day?

bend once on purpose. today, in one exchange where you are sure that you are right, bend. do not pretend to agree. only decline to pull: do not show, justify, list what you have done, or wait to be admired. say what you see once, plainly, and stop. then watch what the other person does when there is nothing to pull against. often their own position, with no opponent, straightens or falls of itself. feel also what it costs in the body: a heat in the chest, a wish to add one more sentence. that wish is the 自 of the four lines. in the evening, ask whether you came out of the exchange more whole or less. the saying is a claim that can be tested. it was a proverb long before it was scripture, and proverbs are kept because they work.

則: the hinge turns both ways. six pairs stand in six lines: 曲 and 全, 枉 and 直, 窪 and 盈, 敝 and 新, 少 and 得, 多 and 惑. the chinese joins each with 則, “then”. it does not say “better than”, and it does not say “in order to”. five lines begin on the low side and reach the high one. the sixth goes the other way: much, then bewildered. so the list is not a rule that the low side wins. it is 反者道之動 (passage 40): turning back is how dao moves. the passage does lean to the low side, and the reason is plain. most people reach for the whole, the straight, and the full at once, and the old saying corrects that reach. the whole and the full are not blamed; they are what arrives. and they turn in their time, as the sixth line shows. one who bends as a trick, to win later, has kept one half of the pair. where are you now on the curve: filling, or full?

what bends stays whole; to yield is how a thing comes through intact.. what bends stays whole; to yield is how a thing comes through intact. is that your experience? recall one time when you gave way and stayed whole, and one when you gave way and lost yourself. what did bending mean where you grew up: wisdom, weakness, survival? take the side of the straight: some things must not bend, and a person who yields each time has no shape. hold that view. what in you stands up? how do you tell a bend from a collapse in your own body? why does the difference matter to you now?

the one who does not display, justify, or praise the self is the one who is seen and lasts.. the one who does not display, justify, or praise the self is the one who is seen and lasts. do you believe that? or have you seen that the ones who show themselves get the place? when did you first learn to speak up for yourself, or to keep silent? what was the price of each? hold the opposite: if you do not show your work, no one will, and silence is a kind of pride. what feelings does that bring? what do you feel toward people who promote themselves with ease? what might they carry for you?

with few things there is gain; with many there is confusion.. with few things there is gain; with many there is confusion. does more confuse you, or feed you? look at your shelves, your plans, your days. what does the wish for more stand in for? when was there too little? take the other side: plenty is life, and to hold few things is fear dressed as wisdom. stay with it. what do you notice? which side would those who know you best say that you live on?

曲 a vessel made to hold. most characters are built from two or three parts. this one is a single picture, and the shuowen gives it its own section of the dictionary. its account: 象器曲受物之形, “it shows the form of a vessel, curved, that receives things”. then a second opinion: 或說曲，蠶薄也, “some say 曲 is a silkworm tray”, the shallow frame of woven bamboo on which the worms were fed mulberry leaves. either way, it is a made thing with bent sides and compartments. the early forms are commonly described as a bent line, or a bent object with marks inside it, like a carpenter’s curved rule. from “bent” the word spread in every direction. a bend in a river: 河曲. a corner, a secluded place. what is not straight in a moral sense: 曲解 is to twist someone’s meaning; 委曲 is a wrong one swallows. the inner turns of the heart: 心曲. and music: a 曲 is a tune, a song, since a melody goes up and down; 歌曲 is “a song”, and a whole kind of chinese opera is 曲. in the short script it also writes the word for wine leaven. its family by sound and shape is small. 典, the classic books on a stand, and 農, farming, have a top that looks like 曲 in print, but they come from other pictures: similar shape only. read the first line with the dictionary’s picture: the bent thing is the one that can take something in. six strokes. the left wall first: a vertical. then the top and the right wall in one stroke, which goes across, turns, and comes down. so far it is an open box, like 冂. the third stroke is the level line across the middle. then the two inner verticals, left one first: watch them. they start above the top of the box and go down through it, so that two small horns stand up from the roof; these are what make 曲 different from 田, a field, and 由, “from”. the sixth stroke closes the bottom. the frame should be a little wider than it is tall, and the two inner verticals must be evenly spaced between the walls, with the six small cells equal. a character whose name means “bent” is made entirely of straight lines and right angles. the curve is only in what it means.

伐 a man with a halberd. left: 亻, a person. right: 戈, the dagger-axe, the standard weapon of the bronze age in china. it was a blade set at a right angle on a long shaft, used to hook and slash from a chariot. the character still shows it: the long slanted stroke is the shaft, the level stroke is the blade, and the small strokes are the tassel and the butt. the shuowen reads the pair simply: 从人持戈, “a person who holds a halberd”, and defines it 擊也, “to strike”. in many oracle-bone forms, as scholars commonly describe them, the blade lies across the person’s neck: a beheading. the word’s first use is war: 征伐, a punitive campaign; a lord 伐 a neighbour state with drums. then to cut down: 伐木 is to fell trees, and the book of odes has a song of that name with the sound of the axe in it. then, by a turn that tells you something about boasting, “to brag of one’s deeds”: 自伐, to make a campaign of oneself. see 戈 in other graphs: 戰 (battle), 戒 (to guard: two hands on a halberd), 武 (martial), 我 (i: at first a toothed axe), and 國, a state, which has a halberd inside its wall. the passage says: not self-praising, and so there is merit. in the graph the merit and the weapon are still one thing. the line asks you to put the second down. six strokes: two and four. the person: a stroke that falls to the left, and a vertical from under its middle. then the halberd. a level stroke that rises a little to the right: the blade. then the fourth stroke, which you should watch: the long slanted hook. it starts high, above the blade, crosses it, sweeps down to the lower right in a slow curve, and ends in a hook that flicks straight up. it is the longest stroke and it gives the character its lean; calligraphers say it must be like a bow at full draw, bent and strong. the fifth stroke falls to the left across the lower shaft. the sixth is a dot at the upper right, placed high, which balances the hook below. the person stands close and upright, a little short, so that the weapon reaches over the head.

23 · a squall before noon. sparse words: so of itself. / so a whirlwind does not last the morning; / a sudden rain does not last the day. / who makes these? heaven and earth. / heaven and earth, even they, cannot keep it up; / how much less, then, people? / so, of those who make dao their work: / the one of dao is at one with dao, / the one of de is at one with de, / the one of loss is at one with loss. / at one with dao: dao too is glad to get them. / at one with de: de too is glad to get them. / at one with loss: loss too is glad to get them. / trust not enough, there: / no trust, there. one line of four characters, then weather, then a table of three rows. the line: sparse words, so of itself. the weather: a whirlwind is over before noon and a cloudburst before night; heaven and earth make them and cannot make them last; so how could people? then the table. those who make the way their work are of three kinds, the one of dao, the one of de, and the one of loss, and each becomes the same as its object. a second table repeats the three and adds that each object is glad to get them. a line about trust, borrowed from passage 17, ends it. the silk texts are reported to be shorter. the pictures are few and strong: a turning wind, a horse at a gallop, drums on a stand, a hand that lets go. the passage makes two observations about the inner life. first, intensity does not last. the mind has its whirlwinds: bursts of resolve, of rage, of rapture in meditation. they feel like the real thing because they are loud. the text points out that even heaven cannot keep a storm up until noon, and asks how you could. what lasts is of the other kind: thin, even, with almost no taste. second, you become what you do. this is not a doctrine of positive thought. it is closer to the fact that a hand takes the shape of its tool. give your hours to the way and you grow like it; give them to loss, to grievance, to counting what is gone, and that also takes you in, and gladly. no one judges. there is only the question of what you are practising now. the first lesson is about the style of rule. government by storm, the campaign, the purge, the hundred-day push, the daily announcement, has the force of heaven and earth behind it for a morning. the passage was read, after the fall of qin, as an exact forecast. a leader’s words follow the same law: few, and they are heard; a flood, and people take shelter and wait. the second lesson is about culture. a group becomes the same as what it works at. if its hours go to the craft, it comes to resemble the craft. if they go to covering losses, assigning blame, and explaining, it becomes a company of loss, and loss is glad to have it. the trust line at the end is the feedback loop in one sentence. which weather do you make: the kind people talk about, or the kind that fills wells? strong emotion is weather in the body, and the body cannot sustain it: the surge of a rage or a fright is spent in a minute or two, unless thought stirs it up again. athletes know the same law from the other side. a sprint is a cloudburst: it is splendid, and over. the work that builds a body is the long, easy, repeated kind that nobody watches. breath shows both. a forced deep breath is a small squall. the ordinary breath, thin and even, sparse as the first line says, has gone on since you were born. in your next hard effort, find the pace that you could keep up all day. that pace is 自然. the passage is good meteorology. the energy of a thunderstorm is spent in an hour, because it uses up the difference in heat that made it. a drizzle can go on for days. floods carve a valley in one afternoon, and the valley is then shaped for ten thousand years by water that hardly seems to move. it is good ecology too: the fast-growing weed is the first to die, and the slow oak stands longer. even heaven and earth obey this, the text says: there is no power in the world that can do the violent thing for long. the old belief read storms as heaven’s anger. this passage reads them as heaven’s brief exception. for the han dictionary, steady wind was the breath that wakes the insects in spring. what in the land around you was made by the slow water? two exercises. first, let one squall pass today without a word, and then say the single sentence that remains. second, keep a rough account of one day by the hour. at night, read it as the passage would: this is what i worked at. do not judge the list. ask only what you are becoming the same as. if the answer includes some hours of loss, note that the text says so calmly, and that the older copies say it more plainly still. for the long view, read how an empire that governed like a storm lasted fifteen years. and if you would like to see four characters grow into thirteen words, read legge’s first sentence, and then say the chinese aloud: xi yan zi ran.

wang bi: words with no taste. four characters, with no subject and no verb between the halves: 希言, 自然. 希 is the word of passage 14: “listened to, not heard: its name is sparse”. wang bi starts there: 聽之不聞名曰希. then he quotes passage 35, where the way, put into words, is 淡兮其無味, “flat, with no taste”, and concludes: 然則無味不足聽之言，乃是自然之至言也. “so then: words that have no taste and are not enough for the ear, these are the utmost words of the self-so.” for him the line is about the kind of speech that the way has. the usual reading is about quantity: to speak seldom is natural. the book has said it before. the best ruler holds words dear (17). many words are soon used up (5). the sage teaches without words (2). the weather lines that follow give the proof. nature has loud speeches, and they are short.

自然, the second time. in passage 17 the people said 我自然, “we are so of ourselves”. here the word stands with no speaker. 自 is “self, of itself”; 然 is “so”. it is still a description and not yet a noun: english “nature” with a capital, a realm of trees and weather set against the human world, is a later meaning, and the modern chinese word for nature was made from this phrase. so “nature says few words” reads a later idea into the line. and yet the text goes at once to wind and rain, and one can see how the later meaning grew: weather is the plainest case of what is “so of itself”, since nobody commands it. legge writes of one “obeying the spontaneity of his nature”, which turns two syllables into a victorian theory of character. try the plain sense on your own speech. which of today’s words came of themselves, and which were pushed?

飄風: the wind that turns. 飄 is not any wind. the shuowen defines it 回風也, “a wind that turns back on itself”: a whirlwind, a squall. in the book of odes it is the wind of bad times: 飄風發發, “the whirlwind roars”, sings a man who cannot go home to bury his parents. for the plain word 風 the shuowen has one of its long entries. it names eight winds, one for each direction, each with its season, and then says 風動蟲生, “when the wind stirs, insects are born”; that, it explains, is why the graph for wind has 虫, a creeping creature, inside it. wind, for the han, is what wakes living things. a steady seasonal wind does that work all year. the whirlwind is the opposite kind: it has great force, turns in a circle, and is gone before noon. 終朝 is “to the end of the morning”.

驟雨: rain at a gallop. 驟 has 馬, a horse, at its left, and the shuowen defines it 馬疾步也: “a horse’s fast pace”. rain that 驟 is rain that arrives at a gallop: a cloudburst. so the couplet has a turning wind and a running horse in it. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 暴雨, “violent rain”, with a word that is also used of a cruel ruler, as english says “a violent man”. wang bi sums up the two images in six characters: 言暴疾美興不長也, “this says that what rises violent, fast, and splendid does not last long”. his word 美, “fine, splendid”, is worth a second look. a cloudburst is impressive. people stop to watch it, and talk about it afterwards. the slow rain that fills the wells gets no comment at all. which kind of effort do you admire more in yourself?

heaven and earth are not almighty. 孰為此者？天地. “who makes these? heaven and earth.” a reader formed by the bible expects the answer “god”, and expects that what god does can last as long as god wills. the text says: even heaven and earth 不能久, “are not able to make it last”. they are the largest things there are, and they have limits. no will stands behind the storm, and no anger. this seems to conflict with passage 7, which says 天長地久, “heaven is long-lived and earth lasting”. the two fit. heaven and earth themselves endure, says passage 7, because they do not live for themselves. what does not endure is their violence. a storm is the one thing they do by force, and it is the one thing they cannot keep up. the last clause then turns to us: 而況於人乎, “and how much less, then, people?”

when storms were messages. in the old zhou religion a great storm was speech. heaven, 天, watched the king, and showed its displeasure by signs. one of the old documents tells that when the young king cheng doubted his loyal uncle, the duke of zhou, heaven sent thunder and a wind that flattened the ripe grain and tore up great trees; the king opened a sealed coffer, found proof of the duke’s loyalty, and wept, and the wind turned and the grain stood up again. court experts read such signs all through the warring states and the han. this passage uses the same pair, wind and rain, and takes the message out. the storm is short because storms are short. if it teaches anything, it teaches by being what it is. that is one of the quiet revolutions of this book. heaven still does things here. it no longer scolds.

the state that ruled like a storm. for the first readers, “people” who try to make violence last meant rulers above all. the states of the time were driven hard: mass levies, forced labour on walls and canals, new laws each season, campaigns each year. the state that drove hardest was qin. in 221 bce it conquered all the others, and its king took the title first emperor and announced that his house would rule for ten thousand generations. it ruled for fifteen years. the han thinkers who came after, lu jia and jia yi among them, wrote essays on why qin fell so fast, and their answer was this passage’s answer: it never ceased to use force. the early han court then governed for some decades by a policy of rest that it took from this book. the first line applies too. qin’s government spoke without end, in edicts carved on stone.

從事: on the job, not “believing”. 從事於道者 is “one who 從事 in dao”. 從 is to follow, the verb that passage 21 used for de behind dao. 事 is work, service, a post; the shuowen says 職也, “an office, a duty”. the compound is ordinary chinese, then and now, for being occupied with something: a person 從事 farming, or trade, or teaching. modern popular versions often turn the next lines into a law of belief: you become what you think. the text says nothing of thought or belief. it speaks of what a person does all day, as a craft is done, and says that a person comes to be the same as that. one knot remains. the received line says 道者 twice, and so seems to make all three kinds, even the one of loss, workers at the way. many scholars take the second 道者 as a copyist’s repeat; the mawangdui silk texts are reported to lack it. then there are three parallel cases, and the worker at the way is only the first. what is your work, in fact?

同: the same as, together with. 同 is “same” and “together”. the shuowen defines it 合會也: “to join, to meet”. chinese has no separate phrase for “to become one with”, which in english has a mystical ring. 同於道 is only “same-with dao”: of one kind with it, in its company, not to be told apart from it. the word was used in passage 1 for the two that “come out together”, 同出, and it will be used in passage 56 for 玄同, “the dark sameness”, when the edges are blunted and the dust is shared. here the surprise is that the pattern does not stop at the good cases. there is sameness with the way, sameness with de, and, by the very same grammar, sameness with loss. the text does not threaten. it reports that a person is in the company of what that person practises. wang bi’s phrase for it is 與道同體, “of one body with the way”.

德 and 得: power and getting. 德, inner power, and 得, “to get”, were near-homophones, and early writers defined one by the other: 德 is what a thing has got from the way. the passage plays on the pair. after “the one of 德” it sets “the one of 失”, loss, and the true opposite of loss is not virtue. it is gain. wang bi’s copy seems to have had 得 outright, since his comment reads: 得，少也，少則得，故曰得也, “得 is fewness; ‘few, then gain’; so the text says 得”. he quotes passage 22. and he glosses 失 as 累多, “to pile up much”: the “many, then bewildered” of the same passage. so for him the three kinds of people are: those of the way, those who get by having little, and those who lose by having much. english cannot keep the echo. our rendering keeps de and trusts this note.

失: what slips from the hand. 失 is often given as “failure” here, a word from the language of careers. the chinese is “loss”. the shuowen files 失 under 手, the hand, and defines it 縱也, “to let go”: a thing that slips out of the grip. it is the verb of passage 38’s ladder: 失道而後德, “the way is lost, and after that comes de”; lose de, and then humaneness; and so on down. so “the one of loss” is a person whose daily business is that ladder: more and more means, and less and less of the thing. the cool justice of the line is that such a person is not cast out. they too arrive at sameness, and have company. loss is a place where one can live, and many do. the sentence has no pity and no blame in it. is there a loss that you have made your work?

is the way “glad”?. the received text says three times 樂得之, “is glad to get them”. 樂 (le) is joy; read yue the same graph is music, and the shuowen explains it as drums on a wooden stand. a way that is glad looks like a person, and readers who want a loving god in this book have used the line. the mawangdui silk texts are reported not to have it. their reported reading is: 同於德者，道亦德之；同於失者，道亦失之. “those at one with de, the way also ‘de’s them (or: gets them); those at one with loss, the way also loses them.” there is no gladness there, and the subject in both halves is the way. that older form is harder and more exact: what you practise toward the way, the way does to you. the warm verb of the received text is a later hand. we render the received words; read them with the silk in mind.

the trust line, again. 信不足焉，有不信焉 stood in passage 17, where it explained how rulers fall from being unnoticed to being scorned. here it comes back word for word, and it does not fit so well. the mawangdui silk texts are reported not to have it in this passage, and many editors think a copyist added it from memory. wang bi had it and gave it a sense: 忠信不足於下，焉有不信焉, “when loyalty and trust toward those below are not enough, then there is distrust”. he reads the first 焉 as “then”, at the head of the second clause. if the line belongs, it gives the rule of the passage in the smallest space. trust is like the three samenesses: what you bring is what meets you. one who works at distrust finds that distrust, too, is glad to get them. is that a law of nature, or of people? the passage does not separate the two.

legge makes it a matter of agreement. legge’s first sentence needs thirteen words for four characters: “abstaining from speech marks him who is obeying the spontaneity of his nature.” it has a “him”, a duty (“abstaining”), and a master to obey. for the storm he adds a judgment in a bracket: heaven and earth’s “(spasmodic) actings”. the middle of the passage he reads as social life. for him 同 is “agree with”: those who pursue the way “agree with him in it”, and even those who fail “agree with him where they fail”. the picture is of a teacher and three sorts of company, and it ends in “the happiness of attaining”. that is a possible reading of 同, and a kind one. but the chinese has no “him” at the centre. it says that each person comes to be the same as that person’s own work. in the last line he again makes 信 “faith”.

let the squall pass. the next time a strong feeling rises, anger, panic, a flood of certainty, treat it as weather. say to yourself: a whirlwind does not last the morning. do not act and do not speak for the length of the squall; in the body it is often no more than a minute or two, if you do not feed it with words. watch it turn and thin. then say the one sentence that is still true when it has gone; that is your sparse word. for the second half of the passage, ask at the end of the day: what did i 從事, work at, today, hour by hour? not what i believe or intend. whatever the answer, you are a little more the same as that thing tonight than you were this morning. the passage adds, with no unkindness, that it is glad to have you.

the squall and the long day. the first pair is the violent and the lasting: 飄風 and 驟雨 on one side, 久 on the other; and with it, a flood of words and 希言, sparse words. the text leans to the sparse and the lasting. the lean is a correction to rule by storm, and to the belief that force shows strength. but the storm is not blamed. heaven and earth make it, and it ends of itself; it is 自然 too. the line is also wider than a rule that the gentle lasts. 天地尚不能久 names no object: it is open whether heaven and earth cannot make the storm last, or cannot make any one state last. on the second reading the quiet day ends as well, and its heat builds the next squall. the two are one weather. a one-sided reading forbids the raised voice. the passage says that a raised voice is short. when was a squall the true thing for you, and when did you try to hold one past noon?

得 and 失: getting and loss in one grammar. the second pair is 得 and 失, to get and to lose, and with it 德, which sounds like 得. most teaching ranks them: get the way, and avoid loss. the passage sets three rows in one grammar and uses 得 for loss too: 失亦樂得之, “loss too is glad to get them”. so a getting is inside each loss, and the one of loss is not cast out. the reverse is also in the book: passage 38 opens with 上德不德, the highest de does not act as de, and so has de. a one-sided reading makes the third row a threat, a place of punishment for those who fail. the text has no blame in it. it does have a direction: the one who works at dao is named first, and the trust line warns of what follows a lack. but it reports the three as one law of likeness. what have you got from a loss that you did not choose?

what is forced and violent cannot last; what is sparse and quiet is the natural way.. what is forced and violent cannot last; what is sparse and quiet is the natural way. do you agree? think of your own strong efforts and outbursts. what did they leave? how was intensity treated in your home: admired, feared, punished? how do you treat it in yourself? take the opposite view: the squall clears the air, and some things are done in a burst or not at all. hold it for a time. what does your body say? do you trust your quiet hours or your intense ones more? what has that trust built?

a person becomes the same as what they work at, and even loss welcomes those who serve it.. a person becomes the same as what they work at, and even loss welcomes those who serve it. is it true that you are what you do each day? what have this year’s hours made of you? is there a loss or a grievance that you tend like a job? what would you be without it? now take the other side: a person is more than their habits, and can stand apart from what they do. what hope, or what excuse, is in that? which side do you use when you look at others, and which when you look at yourself?

然 dog meat over a fire. the plainest word in the book’s most famous phrase has a kitchen in it. take the character apart from the bottom. the four dots, 灬, are fire: this is the form that 火 takes at the foot of a character, as in 熱 (hot), 煮 (to boil), 烈 (fierce), 照 (to shine on). the upper part is 肰, and the shuowen defines that with no fuss: 犬肉也, “dog meat”. it is itself two pictures: at the left a slanted form of 肉, meat (the same form that is written 月 at the side of 肌, muscle, and 肥, fat), and at the right 犬, a dog. dog was ordinary food in early china, and a sacrificial animal. so: meat of a dog, over a fire. the shuowen’s definition of the whole is one word, 燒也, “to burn, to roast”. how did “to burn” come to mean “so, thus, yes”? by loan. the spoken word for “so” sounded the same and had no picture, as is usual for grammar words, and scribes borrowed this graph for it. the borrowed sense took the character over, and the first meaning was given a second fire at the side to mark it: 燃, to burn, which is still the word. now the graph is in a great part of the language: 然後 (after that), 雖然 (although), 當然 (of course), 忽然 (suddenly), and 自然, “self-so”. as with 無, the dancer, in passage 11, we do not claim that the roast is in the meaning. it is in the picture. twelve strokes: four for the meat, four for the dog, four for the fire. the meat: a stroke that falls to the left; a level stroke that turns and falls to the left under it; then two dots inside. it leans, as if hung up. the dog: a level stroke; a long stroke that falls to the left through it; a stroke that presses out to the right, kept short here, because the fire is beneath; and the dot at the upper right. then the four dots, from left to right. watch them: the first leans to the left, the next two are small and nearly upright, and the fourth leans to the right and is the heaviest. a good hand makes them flicker and keeps them on one line. the whole upper part must sit close over them, so that the flames reach it. in cursive script the four dots become one level wave.

自 the nose you point to. the shuowen’s entry is four characters long: 鼻也。象鼻形。 “the nose. it shows the shape of a nose.” the oracle-bone forms are commonly described so too: a nose seen from the front, with the bridge and the two wings, and lines for the creases. this graph was first the word for “nose”. it came to mean “self” by a gesture: in china a person who says “me” points a finger at the nose, where a european points at the chest. the pointing became the meaning, and the borrowed sense took the character over. the nose was then given a new graph with a sound part added below: 鼻, in which you can still see 自 on top. the pattern is that of 然 and 燃. two senses grew from “self”. one is reflexive: 自知 is to know oneself, 自勝 to overcome oneself, and the four faults of passage 22 are all 自: 自見, 自是, 自伐, 自矜. the other is “from”, the point where a thing starts: 自古, “from of old”; passage 21 had 自今及古. put the two together and you have the sense in 自然: so from itself, with its own nose as the starting point and no other cause to point at. a near look-alike is 目, the eye, with one stroke fewer; 白, white, is close too. similar shapes only: the pictures are different. and 息, the breath, is 自 over 心: nose and heart. six strokes. first a short stroke that falls to the left, at the top: small, and set a little left of centre. it is the one stroke that makes this character 自 and not 目. then the left wall, a vertical. then the top and right wall in one stroke, with a square shoulder at the turn. then two short level strokes inside, which touch the left wall and stop just short of the right. last, the base, which closes the frame. the frame is tall and narrow, and its two long sides should lean very slightly toward each other at the bottom, as a face does. the art is in the three white spaces inside: they must be equal. the seal-script form is rounder and shows the nose more plainly. watch the order: the walls are built, the inside is filled, and only then is the door shut.

風 the insect in the wind. wind cannot be drawn, so the script had to borrow. the oracle bones use the graph of a great bird, the phoenix, 鳳, for the word “wind”; the two words sounded alike, and perhaps the bird’s wings were felt to make the wind. that bird is the ancestor of our character, and the outer frame of 風 is its last trace: the same frame, 凡, stands around 鳳. inside, where the phoenix has 鳥, a bird, the wind has 虫, a creeping creature. the shuowen explains: 風動蟲生。故蟲八日而化. “when the wind stirs, insects are born; and so insects take eight days to transform.” it then says the frame, 凡, gives the sound. so the han saw in this graph the spring wind and the first insects that wake in it. the eight days answer to the eight winds of the eight directions, which the dictionary lists by name. the word spread far. 風 is the air of a place and so its customs: 風俗. it is a style: 風格. it is news that travels: 風聞. the first part of the book of odes is the 國風, “the airs of the states”, folk songs by which a ruler could feel how the wind blew among the people. with 水 it is 風水, wind and water: the art of siting a house. the passage sets the turning wind against all of that. the squall wakes nothing, and is gone by noon. nine strokes: frame, then inside. the first stroke falls from the top to the lower left in a long, slow curve. the second is the one to watch. it goes across the top, turns, comes down the right side with a slight inward bow, and ends in a hook that kicks up and out. it is like the great hook of 孔 in passage 21, but it leans, and the frame it makes must be wide at the foot, like a sail. then the inside: a short falling stroke under the roof; then 虫: a small vertical, a stroke for the top and side of its box, a level stroke that closes it, a vertical through the box, a stroke that rises at its foot, and a last dot. the creature sits in the middle, with air on each side. in cursive script the inside is often one twist and the frame one sweep: the character looks blown.

24 · on tiptoe. one on tiptoe does not stand. / one at full stride does not walk. / one who shows the self is not bright. / one who calls the self right is not plain to see. / one who boasts has no merit. / one who is stiff with pride does not last. / in the dao these are called / leftover food, a wart on the walk. / creatures, it seems, loathe them. / so one who has the dao does not stay there. the passage is a list with a verdict. two lines show a body that overreaches: heels up, and it does not stand; legs wide, and it does not walk. four lines then show a self that overreaches, each one with 自 at the front: shown, approved, praised, admired. each gets the result opposite to its aim. then the verdict, in the dao: these are scraps of a meal and a growth that hangs on. the last line reports a feeling, creatures loathe them, and a choice: the one with the dao does not live there. the vocabulary is physical throughout: a heel, a foot, a nose, a halberd, a spear shaft, cold food, a wart. the silk copies are reported to start with a different word and to place the passage next to its twin. each of the four middle lines names an extra movement of the mind. something is done, and then a second motion turns back to look at the doer: see me, i am right, i did that, how fine i am. the text calls this second motion leftover food. the meal was good. the scraps are what stay on the table when the meal is over and no one clears it. so the teaching here is not “have no self” and not “think less of yourself”. it is narrower: do not add the extra. wang bi notes that the merit was real before the boast. notice also that the text gives the overreaching self a place inside the dao. it is not cast out. it is only seen as what it is, and then one does not make a home there. the text speaks of one person and the way; it has no group in it. yet it was heard by men who had to sell themselves to rulers, and it applies wherever people are chosen and promoted. the four 自 lines describe what display costs the one who displays. the person who works at being seen has less attention left to see with. the person who must be right cannot be read by others, because the position covers the person. credit that is claimed by its owner stops being credit. authority that is held stiffly does not grow. a leader can use this as a test of the self, not of others: when i describe my part in a result, does the room move toward me or away? creatures notice before they have words for it. the first two lines are instruction in balance. on the toes, the base of support shrinks to a few square inches and the whole body must work to hold it. at full stride, the weight is caught between two feet and neither can lift. every art of movement that came out of china teaches the opposite of both: the heel down, the step no longer than lets the back foot leave the ground freely, the weight complete on one leg before the other moves. a fighter on the toes can be pushed over. a fighter in too wide a stance cannot turn. if the silk texts’ word is read as breath, the same rule applies inside: breath pushed out by force does not settle. height and reach are bought with stability. try it for one minute. take one conversation today in which you would normally mention something you did well. do the work of the conversation and leave the mention out. do not replace it with a hint, and do not be modest in a way that asks for a reply; that is the same campaign with a different weapon. afterwards, notice what happened to the wish to be seen. did it press, like heels that want to rise? did it pass? notice also whether the thing you did well is any smaller because you did not name it. wang bi’s reading of the leftover food says that it is not. if the body helps, stand on tiptoe first and remember the feeling.

企: a person above a foot. the shuowen defines 企 in three characters: 舉踵也, “to lift the heels”. the graph sets 人, a person, on top of 止, a foot. the shuowen calls 止 the sound part; many modern scholars also see a picture, a person drawn with the foot made large. read the picture lightly. the word is clear without it: you go up on the toes to see farther or to be seen. from that came the later sense “to long for, to look out for”. a modern word carries the picture into every office: 企業, “enterprise”, a compound made in japan in the nineteenth century and taken back into chinese. the first line of the passage is a joke that the body understands. you are taller on tiptoe. are you standing?

跨: the foot that wants too much. 跨 has 足, the foot, on the left. on the right is 夸, which gives the sound. the shuowen defines 跨 as 渡也, “to cross over”: the long step over a ditch. it defines 夸 by itself as 奢也, “extravagant”, and the same 夸 later means “to brag”. so the character puts a foot beside a boast. the word covers a long stride and also a straddle, with one leg on each side of a thing. in both positions the legs are as far apart as they can go, and the next step is not possible. some english versions turn the line into a moral fault. the chinese only shows a body that has taken up too much ground. this line is reported absent from the silk copies.

the silk texts: a cook, or a breath. mawangdui silk text a is reported to open the passage with a different word: 炊者不立; text b is damaged at this point. the silk version is reported to have no line about the stride at all. 炊 is “to cook with fire”; the shuowen says its sound part is a short form of 吹, “to blow”. scholars disagree about what the copyist meant. some take 炊 as a loan graph for 企, so the sense stays “tiptoe”. others read it as 吹: one who puffs, who blows the breath out hard, does not stand firm. in that reading the first image is about breath, and it fits the breath exercises that other warring states texts describe. we cannot settle it. notice only that the oldest copy we have of this line, as reported, gives one image where the received text gives two. did a later hand add the stride to make a pair?

four times 自. four lines begin with 自, “self”. the shuowen says that 自 is a picture of a nose: 鼻也，象鼻形. the usual explanation is that a person points at the nose to say “me”. in each line the self is both the one who acts and the thing acted on: self-shown, self-approved, self-praised, self-admired. the first verb, 見, is read xian here, “to make seen”; the same graph read jian is “to see”. so the line has a quiet turn: the person who works to be seen does not see well, and is not 明, bright. three of the four end-words (明, 彰, 長) belong to one old rhyme group, the one the tradition calls 陽. so does 行, the end-word of the stride line and of the last image. passage 22 has the same four lines the other way round.

是: “this is it”. 是 is the common word for “this”. from “this” came “this is so”, “right”, and much later the verb “to be”. 自是 is to say “this is it” about oneself: my view, my side, my way is the right one. the opposite word is 非, “not this, wrong”, and the debaters of the warring states filled whole books with 是 and 非. the result that the line promises is 不彰. the shuowen explains 彰 as 文彰, a pattern that shows up clearly, like the figure on a cloth. english “self-righteous” carries a religious tone that the chinese lacks. the line does not say that the person is a sinner. it says that the person’s true pattern cannot be seen, because the person stands in front of it.

伐: to boast is to attack. the shuowen defines 伐 as 擊也, “to strike”, and reads the graph as 从人持戈, “a person who holds a halberd”. it is the usual word for a military campaign against a state. the same word means “to boast of one’s merit”. in the analects, yan hui wishes 無伐善, “not to boast of what i am good at”, and confucius praises a general who covered the retreat and did not boast: 孟之反不伐. so 自伐 can be heard two ways. the plain sense is “to praise oneself”. the picture says “to attack oneself”. the line then finishes the joke: 無功, “no merit”. 功 is the word for an achievement in war or in public work. the boast is a campaign, and the campaign wins nothing.

矜: the spear shaft. the shuowen gives 矜 a hard first meaning: 矛柄也, “the shaft of a spear”. its left part is 矛, the spear; 今 gives the sound. how the word came to mean “proud” is not certain. some early readers link the senses through stiffness: the person who holds the self upright and rigid, like a pole. treat that link as a memory aid, not as proven history. the same graph also means “to pity” and “to be careful”, so the old language heard pride and pity as neighbours: both look down from a height. note the weapons in two lines that follow each other. 伐 holds a halberd. 矜 holds a spear. the passage does not speak of war, yet its words for self-praise come armed. passage 30 uses both words again, about real armies.

長: to last, to grow, to lead. one graph, two readings. read chang, 長 is “long” in space or time: the proud one does not last. read zhang, it is “to grow”, “the elder”, “the chief”: the proud one does not grow, or does not become the head of others. the shuowen’s gloss is 久遠也, “long-lasting and far”. passage 22 says the reverse in the same words: 不自矜故長. english must take one sense. we chose “last”, because the passage began with two positions that cannot be held for long. the other sense stays true to the picture: a plant that stands on tiptoe has stopped growing at the root. which reading fits the proud people you have known?

half of a pair. in the received book this passage stands two places after passage 22, which gives the same four lines in the positive: not self-shown, so bright; not self-approved, so plain to see; no boast, so there is merit; no pride, so it lasts. in the mawangdui silk texts, as reported, the order is different. this passage comes directly before passage 22. read in that order, the two are one lesson: first the four ways that fail, then the four that work, with the words 明, 彰, 功, 長 as the hinge. the silk texts are also reported to set the lines in another order: the line on 自視, “looking at oneself” (with 章 written for 彰), comes first, then 自見者不明. someone later moved the passages apart. read 22 after this one and see if the two halves close.

“in the dao”: where is the speaker?. 其在道也 is four plain words and a pause mark: “these, in dao”. english wants more: “from the point of view of the way”, “for those who follow the way”, “judged by the way”. each of these adds a judge or a follower. the chinese adds neither. 在 means “to be located in”. the line puts tiptoe, stride, display, and boast inside the dao for a moment and asks what they are there. the answer is two things from a kitchen and a body. note that the text does not say these things are outside the dao, or against it. they have a place in it: the place of scraps and warts. for the untranslated word, see passage 1.

wang bi: the end of a feast. wang bi explains the two images with a man from history: 若郤至之行，盛饌之餘也。本雖美，更可薉也。本雖有功而自伐之，故更為肬贅者也。 “it is like the conduct of xi zhi, or like what is left of a rich feast. the dish was fine at first; now it is only filth. there was real merit at first; he boasted of it himself, and so it turned into a wart and a growth.” xi zhi was a noble of the state of jin. in 575 bce he fought well at yanling, where jin beat chu. then he went to the zhou court and praised his own part in the victory. a zhou minister said that he would not live long. the next year the duke of jin had him killed. wang bi’s point is exact: the merit was real. the boast is what spoiled it.

贅: a pawned thing, a wart. 贅 has 貝, the cowrie shell that was early money, at the bottom. the shuowen says: 以物質錢, “to give a thing in pledge for coins”, and adds that the shell shows it must be bought back. a pawned thing is yours and not yours; it hangs on. from this came “a thing attached that has no use”, and the word for a growth on the skin: the shuowen glosses 肬, wart, as 贅也. the second word, 行, is “conduct” or “a walk”. many commentators read it as 形, “the body”: “a wart on the body”; legge does the same. we kept 行, because the passage began with one who 不行, cannot walk, and so it ends with a walk that has a growth on it. the two images are chosen to disgust. why does the text want the reader to feel it in the stomach?

who loathes?. 物或惡之. 物 is any being or creature. 或 is “some” or “perhaps”. 惡, read wu, is “to hate, to find foul”; the shuowen’s first sense for the graph is 過也, “a fault”. so: “beings, some of them, hate these.” this is a statement about feeling. it is not a law of nature and not a command from heaven, and 物 cannot mean “law”. the small word 或 is honest: perhaps not every creature turns away. the text points to something you can test. a dog moves off from a person who pushes at it. a room goes quiet around a boaster. the same sentence returns in passage 31, where the things that creatures loathe are weapons. what does it mean that the book uses one sentence for bragging and for war?

not a place to live. 處 (chu) is to stop and stay in a place. the old form 処 shows this in the shuowen: 止也。得几而止, “to stop: to find a stool and stop”. the one who has the dao may pass through pride and display like anyone else. the text says only that such a person does not settle there. the book likes this verb: the sage “stays in” the work of not-forcing (passage 2), and water “stays in” the places that people hate (passage 8). the mawangdui silk texts are reported to end the line differently: 故有欲者弗居, “so one who has wants does not dwell there”. readers have not agreed on 欲. some take it as a loan for 裕, “one who has plenty”; some read it as it stands, “even one with wants”; some think it a copyist’s slip. the same closing sentence, in both versions, ends the first part of passage 31.

an age of self-recommendation. the passage is not about vanity in general. it was written into a job market. in the warring states period the old noble houses were falling, and a new class of trained men without land, the 士, travelled from court to court to sell advice. a man had to make himself seen. the most famous case is mao sui: in 257 bce, with handan under siege, this unknown retainer put himself forward for an embassy to chu and compared himself to an awl in a bag whose point would show. the phrase 毛遂自薦, “mao sui recommends himself”, is still used. in such a world, 自見, 自是, 自伐, and 自矜 were career skills. the laozi tells the same men that the skill defeats itself. was that advice naive, or did it describe what the rulers had already learned to distrust?

legge: merit that others must allow. legge keeps the bodily images. he has the tiptoes, and for 贅 he writes “a tumour on the body”, so he reads 行 as 形. his frame shows in the four middle lines. for 無功 he writes that the boaster “does not find his merit acknowledged”, and for 不長 that the proud one “has no superiority allowed to him”. both verbs put the loss in the opinion of other people. that is the moral world of a victorian gentleman, where reputation is the court. the chinese is shorter and harder: 無功, “there is no merit”. the boast does not hide the merit from others. it undoes it. compare the two. is merit a thing that others grant, or a thing that display can spoil at the source?

one minute on the toes. do what the first line says. stand with bare feet and rise onto the toes. stay there for one minute. notice the calves, the small corrections at the ankle, the breath that goes shallow, the eyes that fix on a point. you are taller, and all your attention is spent on not falling. now come down. let the heels take the weight. notice how much of the room comes back. then take three steps as long as your legs allow, and feel how each one stops you. the passage asks you to remember these two states in the body. later in the day, when you speak about your own work, ask which of the two states you are in.

reach and root: the more that becomes less. the pairs here are implied: 企 and 立, to rise on the toes and to stand; 跨 and 行, to straddle and to walk; and under them 餘, the extra, and what is enough. each line takes a wish to its limit and reports the opposite result. more height: no standing. more stride: no walking. more show: less light. this is the turn of passage 40, seen in a body. it is not a rule that low is good and high is bad. the text does not blame standing, walking, brightness, or merit; these are the things that it wants to keep. and a person rises on the toes to reach a shelf, and that is no fault. the fault is to stay there. the preference is for the plain stance, as a correction to an age of self-display. it turns too: a heel that does not lift does not walk, and a modesty that is shown is one more boast. where do you stand on the toes from habit?

the one who strains to be taller or to go faster loses the footing that standing and walking need.. the one who strains to be taller or to go faster loses the footing that standing and walking need. where are you on tiptoe now? is it true there that you do not stand? who first asked you to be taller than you were? what happened when you were not? take the other side: no one grows without a stretch, and to stay flat on the heels is to stay small. hold that for a time. what does it stir? how do you know, in your own case, a stretch from a strain?

to show, justify, and praise the self is leftover food: an extra that others turn away from.. to show, justify, and praise the self is leftover food: an extra that others turn away from. do you agree that people turn from display? or have you seen them drawn to it? what do you feel when someone boasts? is there a boast of your own that you hold back with effort? now the opposite: to speak well of your work is honest, and to hide it is a false modesty. stay with that. what eases, and what tightens? which have you been punished for more: showing too much, or showing too little? how does that still steer you?
