企 heels off the ground. two parts, one above the other. on top is 人, a person. the shuowen says that 人 shows 臂脛之形, “the shape of arm and leg”: a figure seen from the side, bent a little forward. below is 止. today 止 means “to stop”. in the oldest writing it is a foot; its early forms are commonly read as a footprint with the toes spread. the shuowen defines 企 as 舉踵也, “to lift the heels”, and calls 止 the sound part; many scholars see the picture too. a person, and under the person nothing except a foot: that is tiptoe. now meet the family of 止. two feet, one above the other, make 步, a pace; the shuowen says 从止𣥂相背, a foot and its mirror image. a foot under a line makes 正, “straight, correct”; the shuowen reads it as 一以止, a line at which one stops, and a common modern explanation is a foot that marches at a target. a foot with a round shape above it makes 足, the whole foot and lower leg; the shuowen says 从止、口. and a foot beside a halberd makes 武, “martial”; the shuowen quotes king zhuang of chu: 止戈爲武, “to stop the halberds is 武”. many scholars think the king made a pun. one small graph can say “go” and “stop”. a foot does both. which one does it do in 企? six strokes. the first is a long stroke that falls to the left from the top centre. the second starts just under the tip of the first and falls to the right; the brush presses as it travels and lifts at the end. these two make the person, spread wide like a roof. the third stroke is a vertical line under the peak. the fourth is a short horizontal that leaves the vertical to the right. the fifth is a short vertical on the left. the sixth is the long horizontal that closes the base; all the weight of the character comes down on it. watch the proportion as it is written: the two falling strokes must end lower than the top of the foot, or the person floats off. in seal script the person stands whole on top of the foot. the regular script opened the legs into a canopy.

伐 a person with a halberd. here the person stands at the left, in the narrow form 亻 that 人 takes when it shares a square. at the right is 戈, the dagger-axe: a bronze blade tied across the top of a long shaft, the common weapon of shang and zhou foot soldiers. the shuowen calls it 平頭𢧢, “the flat-headed halberd”, and says the graph is a picture. for 伐 it gives 擊也。从人持戈, “to strike; a person who holds a halberd”. in the oracle-bone forms, as they are commonly described, the blade lies across the person’s neck, so the first sense may have been “to behead”; take this as the usual account and not as certain. from “strike” came “to send an army against a state”, “to cut down a tree”, and “to boast of one’s merit”. look at the halberd’s family. the shuowen reads 戒, “to guard”, as two hands that hold a halberd: 从廾持戈. 或, the old graph for a state or domain, is a halberd that guards a walled place; the shuowen says 邦也, and this passage uses the same graph as the small word “some”. 我, “i”, has a halberd in it too; the shuowen includes 从戈 in its account, and modern scholars commonly explain the graph as a toothed weapon borrowed for the sound. the word for “i” and the word for “boast” both carry a blade. the passage puts 自 in front of 伐 and lets the reader look. six strokes. first a short stroke that falls to the left. second a vertical that starts from the middle of the first: together they are the standing person, and they stay narrow. the third stroke is a horizontal that rises a little as it goes right; it is the cross-blade. now watch the fourth stroke, because the character lives in it: a long slanting line that begins at the upper left of the halberd, cuts down across the horizontal to the lower right, and ends in a hook that flicks upward. it must be one confident movement; a slow hand makes it tremble. the fifth stroke falls to the left through the lower part of the slanting line. the sixth is a dot at the upper right, set last, like the tassel on the weapon. the person is upright and still. the halberd leans and moves. good writing keeps a clear gap between them.

25 · so of itself. there is a thing, formed in one blur, / born before heaven and earth. / soundless, empty, / it stands alone and does not change, / goes all round and is not in danger. / it can be taken as mother of all under heaven. / i do not know its name. / i style it “dao”. / forced to make a name for it, i say “great”. / great means passing on. / passing on means far. / far means turning back. / so dao is great, heaven is great, / earth is great, the king too is great. / within the borders there are four greats, / and the king holds one of those seats. / a person takes earth as the rule. / earth takes heaven as the rule. / heaven takes dao as the rule. / dao takes as its rule what is so of itself. five moves. first a report: there is a thing, whole and unsorted, alive before heaven and earth, soundless and empty, alone, in motion, fit to be called a mother. second, a scene of naming, and it is a scene of manners: the speaker does not know the true name, offers a polite second name, “dao”, and then, under pressure, a describing name, “great”. third, the describing name runs away from the speaker: great, gone, far, back. fourth, a count: four great things inside the borders, one of them the king. fifth, a ladder of models from a person up to the dao, which ends in two characters that mean “so of itself”. the speaker says 吾, “i”, in the naming lines: the one who names stands inside the passage. two lines of the usual text are reported missing or different in the excavated copies. the first lines can be read as a report from stillness. before the mind sorts the world into heaven and earth, self and other, there is something whole, without sound or content, that does not come and go with thoughts. it stands by itself. the passage then shows the mind’s next move with great honesty: it wants a name. the speaker gives one and marks it as a courtesy, gives a second and marks it as forced. this is a way to hold any name for what is deepest: use it, and know that you chose it. the final line removes the last support. if the dao had a model above it, practice would be imitation of that model. it has none. what is left is to be so of oneself, which cannot be done on purpose. the thing in the first line is not a god that made the world. the text gives the ruler a seat among the four greats and, in the same breath, three teachers. the 法 of the last stanza was the keyword of the legalists, who taught kings to issue standards and enforce them. here the direction is reversed: the one at the top is the one who takes a model. a person learns from the ground: what it bears, what it grows, where water runs. the ground keeps to the sky’s seasons. the chain ends in a source that imposes no shape and is square in the square. for anyone who leads a family or a team the test is practical. when i set a rule, am i pressing my shape on the thing, or did i first learn its shape? the title 王 was cheap in those years. the passage gives it worth on one condition. it is tempting to read the end as “follow nature”, and the temptation is half right. a person takes the earth as the rule: this is concrete. soil, slope, water table, and season decide what will grow, and a farmer who goes against them loses the crop. the earth in turn keeps to heaven: light, warmth, rain, the turning year. but the last step is not to a bigger nature. it is to 自然, which in this text is not a place or a set of living things. it is the way each of them is what it is with no one making it so. the river does not follow a law of rivers. it runs. the middle of the passage adds the motion: what is great goes out, goes far, and turns back, as water leaves the sea and comes home to it. try the speaker’s two sentences on something you think you know well: a person you love, your work, yourself. first say honestly: “i do not know its name.” wait and see if that is true. then give it a name on purpose, aloud, and hear it as a style-name: a polite handle for use in company, not the thing. then one more, forced, and notice the small strain in forcing it. for the rest of the day, when you use any big word (love, success, god, the market), remember that someone once gave it as a courtesy title. if you want a second exercise, look at one thing that is so of itself, such as a child asleep or rain on a window, and ask what rule it is following.

a thing? formed how?. 有物混成. 有物 is as plain as chinese can be: “there is a thing”, a something. the book that says dao cannot be named here calls it by the humblest noun it has, the one used for an ox or a pot. 混 has the water sign. the shuowen glosses it 豐流也, “a full, abundant flow”: many waters that run as one, so “mixed, not sorted”. passage 14 uses it of three things that “blend and are one”, and passage 15 of muddy water. 成 is “to be completed”. so: a thing that is whole while nothing in it has yet been told apart. english “chaos” brings in the greek gap or a disorder that a god must tame. this blur needs no taming. our “it” in the next lines is also an english need; the chinese has no pronoun there. the excavated copies are reported to read the first words differently.

what the excavated copies lack. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 有物昆成, with the plain graph 昆 for 混. the guodian bamboo slips, about a century older, are reported to write a graph that many scholars read as 狀, “shape, appearance”: “there is a shape, formed in a blur”. if that is right, the oldest known copy avoids even the word “thing”. two more differences are reported for the silk texts. they have no line 周行而不殆, “goes all round and is not in danger”; the thing only stands alone and does not change. and they say 可以為天地母, “mother of heaven and earth”, where the received text says “of all under heaven”. the guodian slips are reported to lack the circling line too, and to read 天下母 as the received text does. so the circling motion that many readers treat as the heart of the passage may be a later addition. does the passage need it?

born, not eternal, and not a maker. 先天地生: “before heaven and earth, born”. the verb is 生, which the shuowen explains with a picture: 象艸木生出土上, “it shows grass and trees that come up out of the soil”. the thing in this line does not make heaven and earth, as a craftsman makes a table. it does not stand outside time, as the god of the catechism does. it is born, or it lives, earlier. a reader raised on genesis looks for a creator and a first day. the line gives a birth with no parent named, and wang bi says so: 不知其誰之子, “one does not know whose child it is”, which are the words of passage 4. two lines later the thing that was born is itself called a mother. what kind of origin is born and gives birth?

wang bi on 寂 and 寥. two words, each followed by the sigh 兮, a particle of old song. 寂 is without sound. 寥 is without things: wide and deserted. both are written under 宀, a roof, as if silence and emptiness were first known in a house. wang bi takes the pair as one statement: 寂寥，無形體也, “soundless and empty: it has no form and no body”. he moves from the senses to the logic: what cannot be heard or met has no shape for a name to fix on. mawangdui silk text b is reported to write the words with other graphs, 繡呵繆呵, which shows that scribes wrote them down by sound. later, chinese buddhists chose 寂 to translate the stillness of nirvana. so when you read 寂 in a zen text, you are hearing this line.

獨: the dog, not the sheep. 獨, “alone”, has the dog sign 犭 at the left. the shuowen’s explanation is one of its best: 羊爲羣，犬爲獨也, “sheep make a flock; the dog makes ‘alone’”. a sheep by itself is lost. a dog by itself is complete. so 獨 is not loneliness. it is the state of having no partner and needing none; wang bi says 無物之匹, “no thing is its match”. 立 is “to stand”, and the shuowen sees a person, 大, on a line that is the ground. passage 24 began with one who rises on the toes and 不立, does not stand. here is the thing that does stand: alone, on nothing, and it does not change. later the phrase 獨立 became the modern chinese word for political independence.

round, or everywhere? danger, or tired?. 周行而不殆 holds two choices. 周 can mean “in a circle”, a full circuit that comes back, or “all over, to every place”; the shuowen’s gloss is 密也, “close, with no gap”. wang bi takes the second sense: 周行無所不至, “it goes all round and there is no place it does not reach”. 殆 is “danger” in the shuowen, 危也, and that is how we render it: a thing that goes everywhere and is not at risk. many readers take the graph as 怠, “to grow slack, to tire”: it goes round and does not weary. the first reading pictures a traveller who cannot be harmed. the second pictures a motion with no friction. the line is reported absent from the excavated copies, so the choice may be between two later readers. which would you want to be true of the mother of the world?

a mother, by permission. 可以為天下母: “it can be taken as the mother of all under heaven”. note the caution. the text does not say “it is the mother”. 可以為 is “may be regarded as, can serve as”. the speaker offers a likeness and marks it as one. the shuowen says the graph 母 shows a woman who holds a child, or the breasts. as in passages 1, 20, 52, and 59, the origin is a mother who rears, and no father, lord, or judge is named. 天下, “all under heaven”, was the political word for the whole known world, the thing that kings fought to own. the line gives that world a mother before it gives it a king. what does a mother do for a grown child that a ruler cannot?

名 and 字: two names for one person. a man of the zhou elite had two names. his 名 was given in infancy and was used by his parents, his ruler, and himself. at about twenty he went through the capping rite, and then he received a 字, a public name; the book of rites says 冠而字之, “he is capped and given a style-name”. from then on, other people used the 字. to use an adult’s 名 was rude; a ruler’s 名 could not be written at all. confucius had the 名 qiu and the 字 zhongni. so the speaker’s two sentences are exact manners. “i do not know its 名”: the true, private name is not mine to know. “i give it the 字 dao”: here is a polite name for use in company. wang bi: 名以定形，字以稱可言, “a name fixes a form; a style-name designates what can be spoken of”. dao is a courtesy title.

強: an insect lends its name to force. 強, read qiang here, is “by force, against the grain”. the shuowen gives the graph a surprise for its first meaning: 蚚也, an insect, usually taken as a grain weevil; that is why 虫 sits in it. the word “strong” had a graph of its own, 彊, defined as 弓有力也, “the bow has power”. scribes borrowed the easier insect graph for the bow word, and it stayed. the speaker has just refused to give a name, and now gives one under pressure. passage 15 does the same with the old masters: 強為之容, “forced to make a likeness of them”. elsewhere in the book 強 is what the dao is not: stiff, violent, close to death (30, 55, 76). to name the dao is, by the text’s own word, a small act of violence. did you feel the speaker wince?

逝: the river and the dead. the shuowen defines 逝 as 往也, “to go away”. it has the walking sign 辶. it is the word that confucius used when he stood by a stream: 逝者如斯夫，不舍晝夜, “what passes on is like this; it does not stop by day or night”. it is also a quiet word for death; modern chinese still says 逝世, “to pass from the world”. english versions that say “flowing” or “continuing” keep the river and drop the loss. the text says that the great thing does not stay to be admired. wang bi: 不守一大體而已, “it does not just guard one great body”. greatness here is not size that sits still. it is a leaving. the mawangdui copies are reported to write the word as 筮, a sound-loan. can a thing be great and not remain?

a chain of three links. 大曰逝，逝曰遠，遠曰反. each line ends with the word that starts the next, so the sentence walks: great, gone; gone, far; far, back. 曰 is “to say, to be called”. the speaker is still naming, and each name gives way to another. the last link is 反. the shuowen glosses it 覆也, “to turn over”, as a hand turns. it is both “to return” and “to reverse”; passage 40 will say 反者道之動, “turning back is the motion of dao”. the chain is not a circle drawn on paper. it is what happens to anything that goes far enough: at the limit it is on its way back. the form recurs in the last four lines, where each line hands its final word to the next line as a subject. read the three steps aloud and feel where the turn comes.

the king, or the human?. the received text says 王亦大, “the king too is great”. the last stanza then starts with 人, a person. there is old evidence for that. the shuowen, about 100 ce, explains the graph 大 by quoting this passage as 天大，地大，人亦大: “heaven is great, earth is great, the human too is great”. but the guodian slips, four centuries older, are reported to read 王亦大, and the mawangdui silk texts likewise. so 王 is the oldest reading that we can see, and 人 is an early, humane correction, or a parallel tradition. the shuowen’s entry for 王 builds a bridge with a saying of dong zhongshu: 三者，天、地、人也，而參通之者，王也, “the three strokes are heaven, earth, and the human, and the one who joins them through is the king”. wang bi builds the same bridge: the king is 人之主, “the lord of humans”. is the fourth great thing one man, or the kind?

borders, and too many kings. 域 is a territory with limits. its core is the old graph 或, which the shuowen explains as a state: 邦也。从囗从戈，以守一, “a domain: an enclosure, and a halberd that guards the ground”. mawangdui silk text b is reported to write 國中, “within the state”. so the cosmos in this line is drawn as a guarded country, and in it “the king has a seat”. when the passage took shape, the word 王 had lost its old weight. for centuries only the zhou son of heaven was king. chu took the title early, and then in 334 bce the rulers of wei and qi recognised each other as kings, and by 323 bce most of the great states had one. a reader of that time knew several men called 王, all at war. the text allows the king one seat in four, and then sets over him three things to learn from.

one sentence, two ways to cut it. the usual cut is four clauses of three characters: 人法地，地法天，天法道，道法自然. each object becomes the next subject, like the chain of great, gone, far, back. a tang dynasty reader, li yue, cut the same characters another way, with 人 as the only subject: 人法地地，法天天，法道道，法自然. “a person takes as rule the earth’s way of being earth, heaven’s way of being heaven, dao’s way of being dao: the rule of the so-of-itself.” few have followed him, yet his cut shows something. in the standard reading the human is three steps from the source and must go up a ladder. in li yue’s reading the human learns one thing from every level directly. the characters allow both. note also that the stanza says 人, not 王: whoever the fourth great one was, the one who learns is any person.

法: a model, before it is a law. 法 is used here as a verb: to take something as one’s pattern. the old noun covers a carpenter’s standard, a method, a model to copy, and a penal law. in the same century the thinkers later called 法家, the legalists, made 法 the written statute that a ruler fixes and enforces with punishment. this stanza takes their word and turns it. here no one issues the 法. each level looks at the next and shapes itself after it. wang bi explains the verb as 不違, “not to go against”: 人不違地，乃得全安, “people do not go against the earth, and so get full safety”. english “law” brings a lawgiver and a penalty; “follows” brings obedience. a potter who “takes the wheel as the rule” is nearer. see the plate for the strange beast inside the old graph.

自然 is not “nature”. the last two characters are the most discussed in the book. 自 is “self, from itself”. 然 is “so, thus”. together: “so of itself”, what is as it is without being made so. in modern chinese 自然 is the noun “nature”, and many english versions end the passage with “tao follows nature”; legge did not. that makes a fifth thing above the dao, which the passage has just denied by counting four. the early commentators saw the trap. heshang gong: 道性自然，無所法也, “the character of dao is to be so of itself; there is nothing it takes as a rule”. wang bi: 自然者，無稱之言，窮極之辭也, “‘so of itself’ is a word for what has no designation, an expression for the last limit”. the ladder of models ends on a step that is not a step. the dao’s rule is its own way of being. what in you is so of itself?

in the square, square. wang bi gives the last line a concrete test: 在方而法方，在圓而法圓，於自然無所違也. “in what is square, it takes the square as rule; in what is round, it takes the round as rule; it goes against the so-of-itself in nothing.” the dao has no shape of its own to press on things. it is square in the square thing and round in the round thing. read this way, the line reverses the direction that a reader expects. one expects the highest term to give the pattern and all the rest to copy it. wang bi’s dao copies: it lets each thing be the model for what the dao does there. he then adds the order of worth that runs through the whole chain: 用智不及無知, “to use cleverness does not come up to not-knowing”. who is the model in a room: the one who shapes, or the one who fits?

legge’s brackets and capitals. legge is careful here, and his care shows his frame. he writes “the (sage) king”, with a bracket that turns any ruler into a moral one; the chinese says only 王. he gives 域中 as “in the universe”, a word from astronomy for a word that means a guarded territory. he calls the first name “the great”, with capitals, as english writes a title of god. and his last stanza begins “man takes his law from the earth”: 人 becomes “man”, male and singular, and 法 becomes “law”. his final sentence is his best: “the law of the tao is its being what it is.” he did not write “nature”. a reader who knows exodus 3:14 may hear an echo of it; we cannot say that legge intended one. do you hear it?

遠 and 反: far, and back. the chain ends on a pair: 遠, far, and 反, to turn back. a common reading ranks them. going out is loss, and the return is the cure. the chinese does not say that. it joins the two with 曰, “is called”: far is called turning back. the going is not a mistake that the return corrects; it is how the great shows that it is great, 逝. without the going out there is nothing to come back, and a return that stays at home has not returned from anywhere. the first stanza holds the same two sides in one line: it stands alone and it goes all round. stillness and travel are both said of one thing. a reader who keeps only the return makes dao a place to hide in. a reader who keeps only the going has a road with no turn. where are you on the chain today?

whatever goes far enough is already on its way back.. whatever goes far enough is already on its way back. is this true of anything you have lived: a journey, a quarrel, an ambition, a time away from someone? if it sounds true, where did you learn to trust the turn? if it sounds false, what did you once go far from and not come back to? hold the other view for a while: some roads go one way, and what is gone is gone. what do you feel in the body as you hold it? one view comforts and one is hard. which is which for you, and what does that say about what you want to be true?

the deepest rule is what is so of itself; nothing stands above it to give it orders.. the deepest rule is what is so of itself; nothing stands above it to give it orders. do you agree that things go best by their own nature, with no outside rule? where do you see it, and where do you doubt it? who or what did you take as your rule when you were young: a parent, a book, a god, a boss? what did that teach you about your own nature? take the opposite: a person left to what is so of itself goes wrong, and needs a model to follow. stay with it for a minute. what comes up? is there a part of you that you do not let be “so of itself”? what do you fear it would do?

字 a child under a roof. two parts. on top is 宀, a roof. the shuowen calls it 交覆深屋, “a deep house with crossed coverings”, and says it is a picture: the dot is the ridge and the two sides fall away. under it is 子, a child; the shuowen says 象形, a picture, and the usual account is a baby with a large head and wrapped legs. a child under a roof: the shuowen’s gloss for 字 is 乳也, “to suckle, to bear and nurse”. the first sense is to bring up young in the house. then the word bred. in his postface xu shen says that the first writing was simple pictures, called 文, and that when these were joined, the results were called 字: 字者，言孳乳而寖多也, “字 means that they are born and nursed and grow many”. written characters are the children of pictures. that is why 字 means “a written character” today. the style-name is a third growth: a name born from the first name when the child is grown. look at the roof’s family in this passage. 寂 (soundless) and 寥 (empty) both sit under it. elsewhere 安, “peace”, is a woman under a roof; the shuowen says 从女在宀下. 家, “household”, is a pig under a roof. 宗, “ancestral line”, is an altar under a roof. so the name “dao” is, in its graph, a thing born and reared in a house. whose house? six strokes. the first is a dot at the top centre; set it firmly, because the roof hangs from it. the second is a short stroke at the left edge that leans down and out to the left. the third is the roof beam: a horizontal that runs to the right edge and ends in a small hook turned down and back. now the child. the fourth stroke is a short horizontal that turns at once into a slant down to the left. the fifth is the spine: a vertical with a slight bow that ends in a hook to the upper left. the sixth is the long horizontal that crosses the spine; these are the child’s arms, and they reach wider than the roof. in good regular script the roof is kept flat and small so that the arms can be the widest line. in running script the last three strokes are often written in one turning movement.

大 a person, arms out. three strokes, and one of the oldest pictures in the script: a person seen from the front, arms held out, legs apart. to show “big”, the makers of the script drew an adult who takes up room. the shuowen explains the graph by quoting this very passage, in a form that differs from ours by one word: 天大，地大，人亦大。故大象人形, “heaven is great, earth is great, the human too is great; so 大 pictures the human form”. see the note on king and human. compare 人, the person seen from the side, small and bent. chinese has two people: one in profile who works and walks, one face-on who is great. now add to the figure. a line under the feet gives 立, to stand; the shuowen says 从大立一之上. a stroke through the top gives 夫, a grown man; the shuowen sees a hairpin: 一以象簪也. a line above the head gives 天, heaven or sky; the shuowen says 顛也。至高無上。从一大, “the crown of the head; the highest, with nothing above; from 一 and 大”. so three of the four greats are tied to this figure: 大 itself, 天 above it, and 人 beside it. when the speaker is forced to name the dao and says “大”, the word that comes out is, in its graph, a human body opened as wide as it will go. is that a failure of the name, or its point? three strokes. the first is the horizontal, the arms; it rises very slightly to the right and is not long. the second begins well above the horizontal at the centre, comes straight down through it, and then curves away to the lower left, growing thin to a point. the third starts where the second crosses the horizontal, or just below, and falls to the right: the brush presses more and more, then lifts off in a level tail. watch the legs as they are written. the left one is quick and light. the right one is slow and heavy, and it must end a little lower than the left or the figure tips over. teachers give this character to beginners because it has nowhere to hide: three strokes, and each shows the hand that made it.

法 water, and a beast that left. today the graph is 氵, water, and 去, “to go away”. the old full form is 灋, and it has a third part between them. the shuowen explains each: 刑也。平之如水，从水；𢊁，所以觸不直者；去之，从去. “punishment. it makes level as water does, so it has water. the beast is that which butts the one who is not straight. it drives that one away, so it has 去.” the beast, written 廌 in modern print, is the one-horned animal of legend that was led into the court of the judge gao yao and struck the guilty party with its horn. so the first picture of law in chinese is level water, a judging animal, and removal. later scribes dropped the beast and kept water and “go”. the shorter graph was easier to write, and it also happens to say something gentler: the way water goes. this passage uses 法 as a verb for taking a model, and it is fair to notice that a model is level, like the surface of water in a builder’s trough. cousins by the water sign in this passage: 混, the blur of the first line. cousin by 去: the shuowen reads 去 as 人相違也, “people who turn from each other”, with 大, the open figure of the other plate, on top. the old graph judged and expelled. the laozi asks its reader to copy the earth. eight strokes. the first three are the water sign at the left: a dot, a second dot under it, and then a short stroke that flicks up to the right. the three do not line up; they make a shallow curve that opens toward the right side. then 去. the fourth stroke is a short horizontal. the fifth is a vertical that comes down through it. the sixth is a long horizontal under them, the widest line in the character. the seventh starts under the long line, slants down to the left, and turns sharply to the right. the eighth is a dot that closes the turn. the upward flick of the third stroke points at the start of the fourth, so the brush crosses the gap in the air as if still on the paper. in seal script you can see the full 灋 with the beast in place; the short form won in the scripts that came after.

26 · the baggage wagons. heavy is the root of light. / still is the lord of restless. / so the sage travels the whole day / and does not leave the baggage wagons. / though there are splendid towers, / rests at ease, clear of them. / how can the lord of ten thousand chariots / take the body lightly before all under heaven? / light: the root is lost. / restless: the lord is lost. two axioms, one picture, one question, two verdicts. the axioms pair heavy with light and still with restless, and give the first of each pair a title: root and lord. the picture is a march: someone travels all day and stays with the supply wagons; there are towers or sights on the way, and the traveller rests in private, over and past them. the question turns to the top of the warring states world, the lord of ten thousand chariots, and asks how such a man can make his own person light. the verdicts repeat the opening words as losses. the silk copies are reported to call the traveller a gentleman, not a sage, and the first reader on record applied it to a king who abdicated. nearly every key word has a chariot or a tree in it. read the lord as the mind and the passage is about attention. there is a part of experience that is quick and bright: plans, alarms, news, the next thing. there is a part that is slow and has weight: the breath, the seat, the felt sense of being here. the text does not tell the quick part to stop. the traveller travels all day. it says where the quick part gets its life. stillness, in the old sense, is close looking, and what looks closely is not carried off by each fine tower. wang bi’s phrase is the instruction: the sights do not pass through the heart. they are seen. notice the order in the last couplet. lightness loses the root first. restlessness loses the lord second. one forgets the body, and then no one is in charge. the first known commentator took this as a rule for kings, and he had a body in the case. his reading still works for anyone who holds a seat that others depend on. the 輜重 of a leader is what is slow and unglamorous and feeds everyone: the cash, the people who keep the records, the promises already made, the leader’s own health and presence. the light chariot is the exciting side venture, the conference, the war of words. the passage does not forbid travel. it says: go with the wagons. its last question is about the leader’s own person. a founder who treats sleep, family, and attention as things to burn is, in these terms, 輕: the weight has gone out of the centre. and the variants of the last couplet list what goes next: the body, the best people, the seat. every art of balance knows the first line. a potter centres the clay before raising a wall. a rider sits heavy and has light hands. in the internal martial arts the teaching is nearly a quotation: sink the weight to the feet and the lower belly, and then the arms can be quick; if the weight rises to the chest, the hands are fast and have nothing behind them. even the script agrees: the shuowen makes 動, “to move”, from 力, strength, and 重, the heavy, which gives the sound. the second line is about the nervous system. 躁 has a foot in it: the leg that jigs under the table, the urge to get up. stillness “lords” it not by force. it is simply what is there when the feet stop. what does not move lets the rest move. today, name your baggage wagons. write down three slow, heavy things that everything else in your life eats from: perhaps sleep, one relationship, one piece of long work, the state of your accounts. then look at the day’s plan and mark each item w, for wagon, or c, for light chariot. no blame goes with c; the text allows a full day of travel. only check one thing at evening: did you leave the wagons out of sight at any point? if a splendid tower comes up in the day (an offer, a quarrel, a bright piece of news), try wang bi’s test. see it fully, and notice whether it passes through the heart or stays outside. then go back to the carts.

a passage on wheels. the passage plays on two words, and both run on wheels. 重 is “heavy”, and so “weighty, serious, important”. it comes twice: as the idea in line 1, and four lines later inside 輜重, the army’s word for its baggage, which is just “the heavy things”. 輕 is “light”, and so “quick, careless, cheap”. it comes three times. the shuowen gives its first meaning: 輕車也, “a light chariot”, the fast vehicle of an attack. the graph has 車, a chariot, at its left. so does 輜, the supply wagon. the lord at the end is counted in 乘, chariots. english must use “gravity”, “baggage”, “frivolous”, and “light”, four words with no visible link. in chinese the reader watches a light chariot leave the heavy wagons. what in your day is the wagon, and what is the fast chariot?

根 and 本: two words for root. the first line says 根. the last lines say 本. both are written with 木, a tree. the shuowen glosses 根 as 木株也, the stock of a tree. for 本 it says 木下曰本。从木，一在其下: “what is below the tree is called 本; a tree with a line at its foot”. you can still see the mark: 本 is 木 with one short stroke across the base of the trunk. english versions often say “foundation”. that is a mason’s word: a thing that men lay, dead and flat. a root is alive, out of sight, and it feeds what stands on it. the claim of line 1 is therefore a claim about plants. the light parts of a tree, leaf and blossom, hold on only because of the heavy, dark part. the root returns in passages 6, 16, and 59.

still is not passive. 靜 is usually “still, quiet”. the shuowen’s gloss is a surprise: 審也, “to examine closely”. in that old sense the word is not a blank. it is the steadiness of someone who looks with care. its opposite here is 躁. the left part of 躁 is 足, a foot; the shuowen lists the word in an older form, 趮, with the running sign 走, and glosses it 疾也, “hasty”. so the pair is not rest against motion. the sage of the next lines travels all day. the pair is the settled against the hurried: feet that go because there is somewhere to go, and feet that cannot stop. english “stillness” suggests a pond, or a person who does nothing, and legge’s version makes the other side simply “movement”. can you move for a whole day and be 靜?

君: the same lord, twice. the shuowen explains 君 as 尊也。从尹。發號，故从口: “the honoured one. from 尹; he issues commands, so it has a mouth.” 尹 is a hand that holds a staff, “one who has the business in his grip”. a lord is a hand of office and a mouth that gives orders. the word opens and closes the passage. in line 1 it is a figure of speech: stillness is the lord of restlessness, as a mind is lord of its limbs. in the last line it is a fact: 失君, “the lord is lost”. wang bi reads it as the throne: 失君，為失君位也, “to lose the lord is to lose the lord’s seat”. the grammar allows a second sense too: the restless man loses his own inner ruler. the two losses are stated in one phrase. which comes first?

wang bi: what does not move. wang bi gives the first line a short physics: 凡物輕不能載重，小不能鎮大。不行者使行，不動者制動。 “in all things the light cannot carry the heavy, and the small cannot hold down the great. what does not travel makes things travel; what does not move governs movement.” a reader who knows aristotle will think of the unmoved mover, the first cause that stands outside the world and starts it. that is not the picture here. wang bi’s still thing is inside the moving one, as a root is in a tree, an axle in a wheel, a keel under a sail. it does not start the motion from far off. it is what lets the motion be motion and not a fall. for his last phrase the plain examples are the best: a door turns on a hinge that stays in its place.

the sage, or the gentleman?. the received text says 聖人, the sage. the shuowen glosses 聖 as 通也, “to get through, to be open”; the graph has an ear, 耳, and the common form adds a mouth, 口. the sage of this book is not a saint and not only a wise man. it is a person whose hearing is open and who rules by that attunement. the mawangdui silk texts are reported not to have the word here. they read 是以君子眾日行，不離亓甾重 (眾 is a sound-loan for 終): “so the gentleman travels all day and does not leave his baggage wagons”. the han feizi, in the third century bce, quotes the line with 君子 too. 君子, “the lord’s son”, is the confucian term for a man of rank and conduct. in the laozi of the silk copies, as reported, it comes only here and in passage 31, the two passages about a march. so the older wording, if the reports hold, is social and plain: an officer on a road.

輜重: what an army eats. 輜重 is a soldier’s term. 輜 is a covered wagon; the shuowen describes its body, closed in front and behind. with 重, “the heavy”, it names the supply train: grain, tents, spare weapons, tools. warring states armies were mass armies of conscript farmers, and they lived or died by these slow carts. sunzi puts it in three short clauses: 軍無輜重則亡，無糧食則亡，無委積則亡, “an army without its baggage train is lost; without grain it is lost; without stores it is lost”. his chapter is about the temptation to race ahead for an advantage with light troops and leave the wagons. the men who first heard the laozi knew what that had cost. so the image is not “keep your possessions”. it is a commander who rides with the carts through a long day, and is not drawn off by anything faster. one famous king did leave them.

the king who left his wagons. the oldest reading of this passage that we have is a case from politics. the han feizi says: 邦者，人君之輜重也, “the state is the baggage train of a ruler”. its example is king wuling of zhao, the man who put his army into trousers and on horseback. in 299 bce, at the height of his success, he gave the throne to a young son, took the title “lord father”, and went off to campaign and to travel. four years later a struggle between his sons broke out. he was shut in his palace at shaqiu by the winning party and starved to death. han fei’s verdict uses the words of the passage: he was lord of ten thousand chariots and made his own person light before the world. “to be without position is called light; to leave one’s seat is called restless.” this reading is narrow. it is also what the lines meant to the first people who quoted them.

fine sights, towers, or a camp?. 榮觀 can be read three ways. read guan, 觀 is “a sight”: glorious views that tempt the traveller to stop and look. read guan, it is a watchtower or a high terrace, the showpiece of a palace. the shuowen supports the building: one of its senses for 榮 is 屋梠之兩頭起者, “the two ends of the eaves that turn up”. we chose towers, since warring states rulers competed in such terraces. the third reading comes from the mawangdui silk texts, which are reported to write 唯有環官 (text a has 又 for 有; 唯 is the usual early loan for 雖, “although”). some scholars take 環官 as a sound-loan for 榮觀 itself. others take it as 環館, a walled lodging, a guarded stop on the road; then the couplet is about the traveller’s nights, and has no splendour in it. this is not settled. in every reading the sage is near something that could hold the attention, and it does not.

燕: at ease like a swallow. the graph 燕 is a swallow. the shuowen calls it 玄鳥, “the dark bird”, and says the graph is a picture. early writers also used it for a word of the same sound that means “at ease, at leisure”, later written 宴; the analects describes confucius 燕居, “when he was at home and at ease”. 處 is to stay in a place. so 燕處 is to rest in private, off duty. english “at ease” cannot show the bird, and we did not add it to the rendering, because the sense here is the borrowed one. yet the reader of chinese sees a swallow on the page, one line after the upturned eaves where swallows build. the bird makes its nest of mud in great halls and takes no interest in the hall. the text may not intend the picture. it is there on the page.

超然: a leap, not another world. 超 is “to leap over”; the shuowen says 跳也, and the graph has 走, to run. 然 makes it a manner: “leapingly”, in the way of one who is over and past. later chinese uses 超然 for a detached person. western languages reach for “transcendent”, and that word carries a second, higher realm, as in plato or in christian teaching. nothing here leaves the road. the sage is beside the towers, in the same dust, with the wagons. wang bi’s gloss is the most exact: 不以經心也, “does not let them pass through the heart”. the sights are seen, and they do not pass through. the mawangdui texts are reported to write 昭若, “clear and bright”, a different quality: not above the sights, but unclouded by them. which describes your best hours better: above, or clear?

ten thousand chariots. 乘, read sheng, is the unit that counted a state’s power: one war chariot with four horses, its crew, and the foot soldiers who went with it. in the old zhou order, ten thousand chariots was the nominal force of the son of heaven alone; a great lord had a thousand. by the fourth century bce the seven large states were each called 萬乘之國, and mencius opens his book with the phrase. so 萬乘之主 names the handful of men who could destroy a country, in the language of an arms count. the mawangdui texts are reported to say 萬乘之王, “king”. note the humble word in our text. 主 is “master”; the shuowen says the graph is first 鐙中火主, the flame in the middle of a lamp. one small steady flame, and around it ten thousand chariots. what happens to the room when the flame jumps about?

以身輕天下: three readings. five characters: “by-means-of body, light, all-under-heaven”. 身 is the body and the person as one thing; the shuowen says it pictures the human trunk. first reading: the lord behaves lightly, in his own person, in front of the world. second: he treats the world lightly for the sake of his own pleasures. third: he holds his own person to be lighter than the world, and so spends it. the mawangdui texts are reported to add one word, 以身巠於天下, which favours the first and third. the third fits passage 13, where only one who values the body as the world can be trusted with the world. our line keeps the first and third. it says “the body” with no owner, as the chinese does. is your body part of your work, or the cost of it?

lose the root, or lose the ministers?. our text ends 輕則失本, “light, and the root is lost”. wang bi explains: 失本，為喪身也, “to lose the root is to lose one’s own person”. so for him the root is the body of the line before. other old copies close the couplet differently. the heshang gong text and the quotation in the han feizi read 失臣, “loses the ministers”: a light ruler is deserted by his officers, a restless one loses the throne. that version is pure statecraft, and it makes a neat social pair, 臣 below and 君 above. some editions read 失根, which repeats the “root” of line 1 exactly. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 失本, as ours does. the three variants show three ages asking what a ruler stands on: his body, his men, or his roots.

legge’s “gravity”. legge begins “gravity is the root of lightness”. in 1891 “gravity” was a word of character as much as of physics: the sober bearing expected of a victorian man in office. his version follows that sense. the sage is “a wise prince”. the towers are “brilliant prospects”, a phrase that can mean a career as well as a view. the question becomes how a lord should “carry himself” before the kingdom, and 躁, the restless feet, becomes “active movement”, as if any action were the fault. he adds “(in his proper place)” in brackets. he does keep the “baggage waggons”. but the english reader receives a lesson in deportment. what the chinese puts in a root, a cart, and a body, he puts in manners. where in the chinese is a “proper place”?

重 and 輕, 靜 and 躁: root and leaf. two pairs open the passage: 重 heavy and 輕 light, 靜 still and 躁 restless. the text does favor one side. it calls heavy the root and still the lord. but a root is the root of something, and a lord rules someone. the line does not say “be heavy, not light”. it says where the light gets its hold. the sage of the next lines travels the whole day; the wagons are for the march, and they do not replace it. the preference answers courts that prized the fast chariot and the fine view and forgot the supply train. it is not a rule for all time. the heavy side turns too: wagons with no march are a store that rots, and a root with no leaf is dead wood. is your weight today a root, or is it a load?

the light and quick live off the heavy and slow, and are lost when they leave it.. the light and quick live off the heavy and slow, and are lost when they leave it. do you agree? name one time when speed cost you your footing, and one time when it did not. where did you learn your answer: from a parent who was steady, or one who was not, or from a time when you were weighed down? now hold the other side: weight is the trap, and lightness keeps a person alive and able to leave. what feelings come with that? which do you judge more in other people, the heavy or the restless? what might that judgment say about you?

a person can be among fine sights and honours and remain clear of them.. a person can be among fine sights and honours and remain clear of them. is that true in your life, or do the fine things get into you? give one honest case. what is your own splendid tower: praise, a view, a screen, a place at a table? when did it first take hold of you? take the opposite view: to stay clear is a kind of coldness, and a full life means to be moved and carried off at times. what rises in you as you hold that? why might it matter to know which of the two you live by?

重 a person under a load. the modern graph looks like a stack of lines on a pole, and it hides a picture. the shuowen’s gloss is 厚也, “thick”, and its analysis is 从壬東聲: the part 壬 with 東 for the sound. bronze inscriptions, as they are commonly described, show more: a standing person fused with a bundle, 東, which may also give the sound. many modern scholars explain 東 as a sack tied at both ends; the shuowen records another view, the sun, 日, seen in a tree, 木. either way, 東 was borrowed for the word “east”. so read the strokes of 重 as person plus pack, with the ground at the bottom. heavy is what a carrier feels. see what the script built on it. 動, “to move”: the shuowen says 从力重聲, strength beside the heavy. 量, “to measure”: 稱輕重也, “to weigh light and heavy”, with a short form of 重 below. 種, “seed”, puts grain beside it. the same graph read chong means “again, in layers”, one load on another. and in this passage the army’s word for its baggage is just this character after the word for wagon. the text says that the heavy is a root. the graph says that the heavy is a thing a person carries all day. which do you know better? nine strokes. the first is a short, flat stroke at the top that falls to the left. the second is a long horizontal under it. the third is a short vertical on the left, the side of the box. the fourth is a horizontal that turns down to make the top and right side of the box. the fifth is a short horizontal inside the box. the sixth is a short horizontal that closes it. the seventh is the spine: one long vertical from above the box, down through it, to the lower lines. the eighth is a short horizontal that crosses the spine. the ninth is the long base. so six horizontals are stacked on one upright. the task is spacing: the gaps between the lines must look even, and the second and ninth strokes must be the two widest, like a carrying pole and the ground. a crooked spine makes the load slide.

燕 the dark bird in four pieces. the shuowen draws this bird in eleven characters: 玄鳥也。籋口，布翄，枝尾。象形. “the dark bird. a mouth like pincers, wings spread, a forked tail. a picture.” you can find each piece. the top, 廿, is the open beak. the 口 in the middle is the body. the two halves of 北, split to the left and the right of the body, are the wings. the four dots at the bottom are the tail. those dots look like the fire sign 灬 in 然 or 熱, and they are not fire. the shuowen says so in its entry for the fish: 魚尾與燕尾相似, “the fish’s tail and the swallow’s tail are alike”. regular script uses the same four dots for the legs of 馬, a horse, and the feet of 鳥, a bird. the dark bird has old duties. an ode says that heaven sent the dark bird down to give birth to the house of shang. the northern state of yan, one of the seven powers of the warring states, was written with this graph, read yan; its capital stood where beijing is now. and by sound-loan the swallow wrote the word for ease and leisure, which the shuowen lists as 宴 and glosses 安也, “at peace”. a swallow nests under the eaves of the hall and is at home there, while the business of the hall goes on below. the passage asks a ruler for the same. sixteen strokes, built from the top down and from the centre out. the first is the long horizontal of the beak. the second and third are two short verticals that cross it. the fourth is a short horizontal that joins their feet. then the body: the fifth stroke is its left side, the sixth is the top and right side in one turn, the seventh closes it. then the left wing: the eighth is a vertical, the ninth a short horizontal that touches it, the tenth a stroke that rises to the right. then the right wing: the eleventh is a short stroke that falls to the left, the twelfth a vertical that bends to the right and ends in an upward hook. last, the four dots of the tail, from left to right: the thirteenth leans left, and the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth lean right. the wings must stay level with each other, or the bird banks. in cursive script the whole tail is one wavy line.

27 · no rut, no footprint. good walking leaves no rut or footprint. / good speaking has no flaw to blame. / good counting uses no tally rods. / good shutting has no bar or bolt, / and it cannot be opened. / good tying has no cord or binding, / and it cannot be undone. / so the sage is always good at coming to people’s aid, / and so there is no discarded person; / always good at coming to the aid of things, / and so there is no discarded thing. / this is called light under a robe. / so the good person is the not-good person’s teacher. / the not-good person is the good person’s material. / not to prize the teacher, not to care for the material: / however clever, greatly lost. / this is called the fine crux. three parts. first, five trades, each in one line: travel, speech, reckoning, door-making, binding. each is said to be good when its usual tool or trace is absent: no rut, no blemish, no rods, no bar, no rope. the last two add a boast: and yet no one can open it or untie it. second, 是以, “and so”: the sage has the same kind of skill with people and with things, and the result is stated as an absence too: no one and nothing thrown away. this gets a name, 襲明. third, a pair: teacher and material, each owed something, and a warning that cleverness does not help the one who forgets it. this also gets a name, 要妙. wang bi reads the whole first part as one rule. the five skills describe action that comes from fit and not from force. when attention is whole, a thing is done and nothing is left over: no track of self-regard, no after-thought to defend, no tally of who owes whom. the contemplative traditions call this many things; this passage calls it light under a robe, clarity that does not need to be seen. the second half turns the same eye inward. each person holds a good one and a not-good one. if the part that sees clearly despises the part that fails, the result is “greatly lost”, with all one’s cleverness intact. the failed part is the material. it is what practice is made of. the text asks for two feelings, in order: respect for what teaches, and affection for what is taught. no part is put out in the basket. wang bi’s comment turns this into a question about systems: rejects are made by standards. any organisation that ranks people creates a bottom rank and then has to decide what to do with it. the passage offers another picture of a group: someone good at a thing, someone not yet good at it, and a bond between them that runs both ways. the one who knows is owed honour. the one who does not know is owed care, and is also the reason the first one has a function at all. the five opening lines apply to management directly. a team that needs many bolts (approvals, contracts, surveillance) is showing that its doors do not fit. a bond that holds without a cord is slower to make and cannot be ordered. in the silk copies, as reported, even the good person needs a teacher. watch someone who is truly good at a physical craft: a mason, a cook, a calligrapher. the movement is small and nothing is corrected afterwards. the beginner leaves marks everywhere: chips, spills, strokes gone over twice. skill in the body is the removal of the extra motion, until the act leaves no rut. the door lines can be felt in a joint. a well-set shoulder or hip is closed by its own shape and needs no clenched muscle to hold it; a clenched one is a bolt, and it can be forced. the tying line is known to anyone who has learned a real knot: the good one holds by its form and comes apart when you want, and the bad one is a tangle with much rope in it. good at is first a thing that hands know. choose one small task today and do it so that it leaves no trace of you: wash a cup and put it away, close a matter with one clear sentence, return a borrowed thing in better order than you got it. do not mention it to anyone. that is the first stanza. for the second, look for one discarded thing in your house or your work (a tool, a draft, a plant, a person who has been written off) and ask what it would take to bring it back into use; do one step of that. for the third, name privately one person who is your teacher and one who is your material. ask if you prize the first and hold the second dear. if the second answer is no, the text has a word for your position.

善, eleven times. the passage uses one word eleven times, and the word changes under the reader’s eyes. in the first five lines 善 means “good at”: skilled at walking, at speech, at counting, at shutting, at tying. in the middle it is the sage’s skill with people. in the last stanza it has become “the good person” and “the not-good person”, which sounds moral. english has two words, “skilled” and “good”, and must change horses in the middle. chinese does not. the old graph, 譱, has a sheep, 羊, between two 言, “speech”; the shuowen glosses it 吉也, “auspicious”, and says that it has the same idea as 義, right, and 美, fine. so goodness here is closer to a craft that turns out well than to obedience to a rule. if “good” and “good at it” were one word for you, whom would you call good?

轍 and 迹: wheel and foot. two kinds of trace. 轍 has 車, a chariot; the shuowen says 車迹也, “the track of a cart”. 迹 has the walking sign; the shuowen says 步處也, “the place of a step”. so 行 in this line covers riding and walking. in the warring states period ruts were a practical matter: the carts of different states are said to have had different axle widths, each wearing its own grooves into the roads, and in 221 bce the first emperor ordered one gauge for all carts. a rut records every earlier traveller and forces the next one into the same line. wang bi explains how one could leave none: 順自然而行，不造不始, “travel in accord with what is so of itself; do not make, do not initiate”. the line does not say that the good traveller hides the tracks. there are none. what have you done that left no groove for the next person to fall into?

speech that cannot be punished. 瑕 is written with 玉, jade: it is a flaw or stain in the stone. 讁 is written with 言, speech; the shuowen lists it in the form 謫 and glosses it 罰也, “to punish”. so the line pairs a blemish with its penalty. this was not a figure of speech for the first readers. a travelling adviser lived by his tongue at courts where one wrong phrase could end a career or a life. the han feizi has a whole essay, “the difficulties of persuasion”, on how a speaker dies: he touches the ruler’s secret, or praises the wrong man, or is right too early. good speech, in this line, is not eloquence. it offers no edge for blame to catch on. the mawangdui copies are reported to write 瑕適, a sound-loan for the same word. can you say a true thing so that it leaves nothing to seize?

counting rods. before the abacus, chinese arithmetic was done with small rods laid out on a mat or table. both 籌 and 策 have 竹, bamboo, on top. the shuowen describes the tool under another graph, 筭: 長六寸。計歷數者, “six inches long; that with which one calculates the calendar and numbers”, and adds that because the rods are always handled, 弄, there are no mistakes. the rods stood upright for units and lay flat for tens, in turn, so the system was already decimal and positional. 策 also names the yarrow stalks that were counted out to consult the book of changes. so the tool was used both to reckon and to divine. wang bi says of the good counter: 因物之數，不假形也, “follows the number that things themselves have, and borrows no outward form”. think of a shepherd who knows that one is missing without counting. what do you know that way?

關 and 楗: the bar and the pin. a chinese gate was locked from inside with wood. the shuowen defines 關 as 以木橫持門戶也, “a timber set across to hold the door leaves”, and 楗 as 限門也, the piece that stops the door. for 閉, “to shut”, it explains the small shape inside the gate as 所以歫門也, “that which blocks the door”. the silk copies are reported to say 不可啟 where ours says 不可開: 啟 was the personal name of emperor jing of han (ruled 157–141 bce), and later copyists could not write it. the word 關 grew: from a door bar to a fortified pass on a frontier, where a state shut out its neighbours. legend places the birth of this book at such a pass. sima qian tells that the keeper of the pass asked the old man who was leaving the country to write down his teaching first. a book about doors that need no bar was, in the story, written at a barred gate.

約: a knot, a treaty. 繩 is a rope. 約 is “to wind round and bind”; the shuowen says 纏束也, and both graphs have 糸, silk thread. but 約 was also the daily word for a sworn agreement between states, and 結, “to tie”, was the verb for making one. the fourth century bce was full of such knots. states swore covenants over the blood of a sacrificed animal, formed the “vertical” league against qin and the “horizontal” league with it, and broke them within a season. a reader of that time heard politics in this line: the good bond needs no oath and no hostage, and it holds. the zhuangzi has a close parallel: things in their constant state are bound together 不以纆索, “not by ropes”; and the mawangdui copies of our line are reported to write 纆約, with the same word for rope. what holds you to the people you would not leave?

wang bi: five skills, one rule. wang bi sums up the five opening lines in one sentence: 此五者皆言不造不施，因物之性，不以形制物也。 “these five all speak of not making and not applying: of following the nature of things, and not ruling things by forms.” 形 is outward shape: a visible device, a rule, a tool laid on from outside. the rut, the checked phrase, the rod, the bolt, and the cord are all 形. each is a sign that the work did not fit the thing and had to be held in place. the door that fits its frame does not need the bar. this is his reading of 無為 as craft, and it is close to the cook in the zhuangzi who cuts up an ox for nineteen years with one knife, because the blade goes where the gaps already are. where in your work is there a bolt that covers for a bad fit?

the sage as a craftsman. 聖人 is “the sage”, and the english word misleads. this is not a saint, who is holy, and not only a wise man, who knows much. the shuowen glosses 聖 as 通也, “open, getting through”, and the graph has an ear in it. in this passage the sage comes after five craftsmen, joined by 是以, “and so”: the sage is the sixth craftsman, and the material is people and things. note also 常, “always”. the mawangdui copies are reported to write 恆, the older word that a han taboo later removed (see passage 1). the sage’s skill is steady, like a trade that someone has practised for a lifetime. the text does not say that the sage loves everyone. it says that the sage is good at something. does that seem a lower claim to you, or a higher one?

救 is not “to save”. the shuowen defines 救 in one word: 止也, “to stop”. the right side of the graph, 攵, is a hand with a stick, a sign of action. to 救 is to step in and halt a harm: to put out a fire, relieve a besieged town, pull a child from a well. armies were sent to 救 an ally. english “save” carries a second meaning from the churches: to rescue a soul from sin for another life, and legge writes “saving men”. nothing here concerns souls. the sage’s skill is practical and present: no one is left in the ditch. and the object is not only people. the next line says 救物, to come to the aid of things: tools, animals, scraps, land. the mawangdui copies are reported to put it another way, with no second “always good at”: 而无棄人，物无棄財, “and no person is thrown away; among things, no goods are thrown away”.

棄: a child in a basket. the word for “discard” has a hard picture in it. the shuowen analyses 棄 as two hands, 廾, that push a winnowing basket to throw something out, and on top a part that it explains as 逆子也: “a child, upside down”. the oldest forms are commonly described the same way: an infant, a basket, two hands. to 棄 was first to expose a newborn. the founding ancestor of the zhou royal house was named for it. he was hou ji, lord millet, whose personal name was 棄, “the abandoned”: an ode tells how his mother left him in a lane, in a forest, and on ice, and each time oxen, woodcutters, or birds kept him alive. so when the text says 無棄人, “no discarded person”, the graph on the page is a baby that someone is throwing away. who, in your world, is in the basket?

wang bi: who makes the rejects?. wang bi asks how anyone comes to be discarded, and his answer is institutional: 聖人不立形名以檢於物，不造進向以殊棄不肖。 “the sage does not set up forms and names to check things against, and does not create goals to advance toward, by which the unworthy are singled out and discarded.” in his view the reject is produced by the standard. set up a title and a test, and at once some people are those who failed it. he then quotes passage 3: do not exalt the worthy, and the people do not contend. this is a direct answer to the legalist method of his text’s own time, 形名, “forms and names”, in which each officer was measured against his title. the sage in this reading does not rescue people one by one from the heap. the sage does not build the heap.

襲明: three readings of a rare phrase. no one is sure what 襲明 means. 襲 has 衣, a garment, under a dragon, 龍, which is short for the sound part 龖, two dragons. the shuowen’s gloss is 左衽袍, “a robe that closes to the left”: the dress of the dead, since the living closed their robes to the right. from that the word means to put one garment over another; then to inherit, to repeat, to follow; then to fall on an enemy from cover. so 襲明 may be light that is covered, as the good walker’s skill is; or light that is handed on, from teacher to pupil; or “to follow the light”. we chose the first, because the passage began with a skill that shows no trace. passage 52 has a sister phrase, 襲常. the mawangdui copies are reported to write 曳明 here, a graph that means “to trail, to draw along”; scholars differ on how to take it. which light do you trust more: shown, or worn under a robe?

whose teacher?. the received text makes a neat cross: the good person teaches the not-good; the not-good person is material for the good. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to say something else in the first half (text a is damaged here): 故善人，善人之師；不善人，善人之齎也. “so the good person is the good person’s teacher; the not-good person is the good person’s stock.” in that version both lines are about what the good person needs: a model, and material. no one is appointed to instruct the bad. this may be a copyist’s slip, or it may be the older thought, later tidied into a symmetry. the compound that later chinese made from the two words, 師資, came to mean a teacher, and then “teaching staff”. a phrase that once named two people on opposite sides of a lesson now names one side only. what was lost when the material dropped out of the word?

資: stock, capital, raw material. 資 has 貝, the cowrie shell of early money, at the bottom. the shuowen glosses it 貨也, “goods”. it is what a trader has to work with: stock, capital, supplies. wang bi explains it by a verb: 資，取也, “資 is to take from”. so the line is blunt. the not-good person is what the good person draws on, as a carpenter draws on timber. read one way, this is hard: people as material. read the other way, it is humble: a carpenter with no timber is not a carpenter, and the skilled have their skill only because the unskilled are there to be met. the next line settles the tone with the verb 愛, “to care for, to hold dear”. one does not hold dear a thing that one merely uses up. who has been your material, and did you care for them?

迷: lost on the road. 迷 has the walking sign 辶 round 米, which gives the sound. the shuowen glosses it with 或, here the old way to write 惑, “to be in doubt, led astray”. it is the word for a traveller who has lost the road. the silk copies are reported to write 大眯; the shuowen glosses 眯 as 艸入目中也, “grass has got into the eye”. the passage began with good walking that leaves no rut, and it ends with a clever person on foot and far off the way. the word before it is 智: knowledge, cleverness. in this book that word is usually a warning (passages 18, 19, 65). wang bi names the fault: 自任其智，不因物, “relies on his own cleverness and does not follow things”. the size word matters too: 大迷, “greatly lost”. a fool is lost in a small way and may ask. the clever person is lost at speed, and with a map. have you been lost like that?

要妙: the waist of the matter. 要 was first the waist. the shuowen says 身中也, “the middle of the body”, and describes the graph as a person with both hands at the waist; the body sense is now written 腰. the waist is where the body turns and where a belt gathers a robe, so 要 came to mean the point that holds the rest: the essential. 妙 is the fineness of passage 1, the first small stir of a thing. together: the fine point on which it all turns. the mawangdui copies are reported to write the two words in the other order, 眇要, with the eye-radical graph 眇, “so small that the eye strains”. and what is the crux? not the five skills, and not the rescue. the passage gives its name to the last pair: the teacher prized, the material held dear. the secret that it promises is a relation between two people.

legge and the “man of skill”. legge renders 善 as “skilful” all the way through, even at the end: “the man of skill is a master”. this is consistent, and it protects the english reader from a sermon about good and bad people. but see what he does with the two relations. the not-good one becomes “the helper of (the reputation of) him who has the skill”. the bracket turns the material into an audience: the unskilled make the skilled look good. and the warning line becomes a remark about a third party, an “(observer)” who “might greatly err about them”. the chinese has no observer and no reputation. it says that the one who fails to prize the teacher or to care for the material is lost. he also gives 襲明 as “hiding the light of his procedure”, which adds a method to a phrase that has none. why might a victorian need the bystander?

善 and 不善: each is made from the other. the last stanza sets two people side by side: 善人 and 不善人, the one good at it and the one not good at it. english hears a saint and a sinner, and then the lines rank them: one above to teach, one below to be worked on. the chinese ties them with two nouns, 師 and 資, and both nouns are debts. the not-good person needs a teacher. the good person needs material, and with no material there is no skill and no teacher. each is what the other is made from. the next line asks the same of both sides: 貴 the teacher, 愛 the material. and the pair moves. the pupil of today teaches later; a master of one craft is raw stock in the next. 不善 is “not good”, with 不; it is not “bad”. so the sage discards no one. in which room are you the material?

for one who is truly skilled at helping, no person and no thing is waste.. for one who is truly skilled at helping, no person and no thing is waste. do you believe that? think of a person you have written off, and ask it again. where did you learn who counts as waste: at school, at work, in your family? were you at some time the one set aside? hold the opposite for a time: some people and things must be let go, and to refuse is pride. what do you feel as you hold it? which view do you use on others, and which on yourself? are they the same?

the skilled and the unskilled need each other, and to despise either one is to be lost.. the skilled and the unskilled need each other, and to despise either one is to be lost. do you agree that the one who teaches needs the one who cannot yet do it? where have you seen it? whom do you find it hard to respect: those who know more than you, or those who know less? what in your past makes that side hard? now try the other view: the skilled owe nothing to the unskilled, and do best among their own kind. sit with it. what thoughts and feelings arrive? what does your reaction tell you about how you see your own skill?

good work leaves no track, and needs no lock or knot to hold it.. good work leaves no track, and needs no lock or knot to hold it. is this your experience of good work, your own or another person’s? how much do you need your work to be seen and signed? where does that need come from? take the opposite: a life should leave marks, and work that no one can trace is lost. hold that for a while and notice what it stirs. which of the two would you choose for your name after you are gone, and why?

師 the teacher is an army. this character means “teacher” in the passage, and it did not start there. the shuowen’s first words are a troop count: 二千五百人爲師, “two thousand five hundred men make a 師”. it is a division of the zhou army. the shuowen reads the two halves as 帀, “all round”, and 𠂤, and says that together they give 眾意, “the idea of a multitude”. 𠂤 is in its account a small mound; modern scholars debate what the early form shows, and in the oldest inscriptions 𠂤 alone already writes the word for an army in the field. follow the meaning as it grew. a host of men; then the capital, where the hosts are (京師); then the one who leads and trains a host, a master; then the master of any art: a music master, a teacher. the same thing happened to its cousin 官. the shuowen says of that graph: 𠂤猶眾也。此與師同意, “𠂤 is like ‘the many’; it has the same idea as 師”. an official is one who has charge of many under a roof. other cousins by 𠂤: 追, to pursue, and 歸, to return, where the shuowen takes it as the sound. so chinese remembers that teaching began as command of a crowd. this passage quietly changes the word: its 師 has one pupil, called material, and owes that pupil care. in passage 30 the same graph is back in armour: 師之所處, “where the army camps”, thorns grow. ten strokes. the left half first. stroke one is a short stroke at the top that falls to the left. stroke two is a long vertical from under it down the left edge. stroke three is a horizontal that turns down: the top and right side of a small upper box. stroke four is a horizontal that closes that box. stroke five turns in the same way to make a second box under the first, and stroke six closes it. now the right half. stroke seven is a horizontal across the top. stroke eight is a short vertical on the left of the lower part. stroke nine is a horizontal that turns down and ends in a hook to the left. stroke ten is the long vertical through the centre of the right half; it comes last and goes lowest, like a standard set in the ground. in seal script both halves are made of curved lines; the two small boxes are a product of the brush.

善 a sheep and what is said. at the top of 善 is a sheep, 羊: two horns, then three bars and an upright for the head and body. the shuowen says of 羊 that it shows 頭角足尾之形, “head, horns, feet, and tail”, and glosses the animal as 祥也, “a good omen”. the full old graph is 譱: the sheep stands between two 言, “speech”. the shuowen gives that pair as a word in its own right, 誩, 競言也, “speech in dispute”. what a sheep does between two parties who argue is not explained; a common account is that the sheep was the offering, or the sign of a lucky outcome, at a settlement. the shuowen says only 吉也, “auspicious”, and adds a key remark: 此與義美同意, “this has the same idea as 義 and 美”. so meet the family. 美, “beautiful, fine”: sheep over 大, a person face-on; the shuowen says 甘也, “sweet”, because the sheep is the chief of the six animals for the table. 義, “right, duty”: sheep over 我, “i”. 祥, “omen”: the altar sign beside a sheep. 養, “to feed, to rear”: food with a sheep for the sound. 羣, “flock”: the shuowen has 羊 under 君, a lord. the good, the fine, and the right all begin with one useful, mild animal. in the modern graph the two speeches have shrunk to a few strokes and a mouth. the word still means “good at” before it means “good”. twelve strokes. the first two are the horns: a dot that leans right, then a short stroke that leans left, tips apart, feet together. the third, fourth, and fifth are three horizontals; in a good hand the fifth is longer than the two above it. the sixth is the vertical that runs down through all three. the seventh and eighth repeat the horns in small: a dot and a short left-falling stroke, set under the sheep. the ninth is the longest horizontal in the character; everything above rests on it. then the mouth: the tenth stroke is its left side, the eleventh its top and right side in one turn, the twelfth the base that closes it. the danger is height. five horizontals and a box are stacked in one square, so each layer must be thin and the gaps even. in running script the lower horns and the long line fuse into one zigzag.

28 · keep to the hen. know the cock, keep to the hen: / be the ravine of all under heaven. / be the ravine of all under heaven, / and the constant de does not leave. / go back again to the infant. / know the white, keep to the black: / be the pattern of all under heaven. / be the pattern of all under heaven, / and the constant de does not go wrong. / go back again to what has no limit. / know honour, keep to disgrace: / be the valley of all under heaven, / and the constant de is then enough. / go back again to the uncarved wood. / uncarved wood, split up, becomes vessels. / the sage uses them and becomes chief of the officers. / so the great cutting does not sever. three stanzas on one frame, then a turn. frame: know x, keep to y; become a low or dim place for the whole world; the constant de behaves in a certain way; go home to something whole. first: cock and hen, the ravine, de that does not leave, the infant. second: white and black, the pattern, de that does not err, what has no limit. third: honour and disgrace, the valley, de that suffices, the plain wood. then the wood is split into vessels, the sage appears among officers, and a last line of four characters sets one knife against another. the pictures are a farmyard, a gully, a baby, soot, a roof beam, a field boundary, a log. the oldest witnesses order and count the stanzas differently. the three “keeps” describe where attention rests. one can be fully capable of assertion, clarity, and standing in the world, and let the centre of gravity stay with the receptive, the unlit, the unpraised. this is not self-denial. the text says 知: the strong pole is known, owned, available. but the one who lives at the bright pole must keep it bright, and that is work without end. the low place needs no upkeep. things come to it of themselves. each stanza then names what is found there, and the three names point one way: the infant before habits, the limitless before boundaries, the wood before the tool. it is the mind before it was cut into roles. the word for getting there is 歸, the word for going home. one does not build that state. one stops leaving it. the last three lines are about organisations, and they are realistic. wholeness gets divided; work needs roles, and a role makes a person into a vessel for one function. the text does not forbid it. it asks who is fit to stand over the vessels, and answers with the first three stanzas: the one who knows command and keeps to listening, who can stand in full view and keeps out of the glare, who has honours and is at ease when looked down on. such a person can divide work without dividing people, because that person is not defending a pole. the great cutting does not sever: departments that remain one cloth, a reorganisation that leaves no one outside. wang bi’s test is to take the heart of everyone under heaven as one’s own heart. the age that wrote this was inventing bureaucracy, and knew the cost. the infant is the body’s lesson here, and the book returns to it often. a baby is weak in every muscle and yet holds a finger with a grip that surprises, breathes with the whole belly, and falls without bracing. its skull has not closed. adult strength is mostly held tension: a body that has taken a fixed shape, a vessel. the internal arts of china read 知其雄，守其雌 as a rule of practice: have the strike, and stay in the yielding;
