know how to be hard, and remain soft enough to feel. the ravine is felt as a sinking: weight and breath go down and collect low, as water does. try to stand so that nothing in you is held up on purpose. what in the body still knows how to be unworked wood? take the third stanza, since it is the hardest. today there will be some small chance to be seen in a good light: to correct someone, to mention a success, to take the better seat. know it fully. notice that you could. then keep to the other place, once, without comment, and without the private glow of having been humble (that is the cock again). watch what the body does when no credit comes: the heat in the face, the wish to explain. that is 辱, felt at the edge of the field. stay one breath longer than is comfortable. the text makes a claim about that position: 常德乃足, the de is then enough. find out for yourself whether “enough” is the right word. if you want a gentler exercise, look at a page of writing and read the white.

know one, keep to the other. three stanzas use one frame: 知其 x，守其 y. 知 is to know, and in old usage also to be in charge of, to have mastery of. 守 is to guard a post; the shuowen glosses it 守官也, “to keep an office”, a hand of duty under a roof. so the frame does not say “choose y, reject x”. the person in these lines has the cock’s strength, the white, and the honour, and knows them from inside. then that person takes up a post at the other pole. a dualist reading wants a good side and a bad side. the text wants both in one person, with the weight set low. our verbs are commands, “know, keep”, because english needs a form; the chinese has no subject and no mood, and can as well be read “one who knows the cock and keeps to the hen is the ravine”.

雄 and 雌: father bird, mother bird. the text does not say “male and female” in the human words 男 and 女. it does not use 陰 and 陽, the later cosmic pair, which the book names only in passage 42. it uses farmyard words. both have 隹 at the right, the shuowen’s “general name for short-tailed birds”. the shuowen defines 雄 as 鳥父也, “the father of birds”, and 雌 as 鳥母也, “the mother of birds”: cock and hen. the same pair serves for any animal, and for “victor” and “loser” in war. so the line is not about the nature of men and women. it is about two ways an animal behaves: the cock who struts, crows, and fights on the wall, and the hen who sits low and still on the eggs. wang bi takes it more plainly yet: first and behind. which do you watch, in a yard, to learn where the next generation is?

谿 and 谷: ravine and valley. the first stanza ends in 谿 and the third in 谷. the shuowen separates them. 谷 is where a spring comes out and joins a river: 泉出通川爲谷, and the graph is “water half seen, coming out of a mouth”. 谿, which contains 谷, is 山瀆無所通者: “a mountain watercourse that leads through to nowhere”, a closed gully. both are low places, and low places receive: rain, soil, leaves, streams, without effort. the passage moves from the narrow, closed gully to the open valley, as water does when it goes downhill. the valley is one of the book’s standing images: the valley spirit that does not die (6), wide like a valley (15), the valleys that fill (39), the sea that is king of a hundred valleys because it lies below them (66). the lowest point of a landscape is the one place all its water has been.

wang bi: first and behind. wang bi removes sex from the first line: 雄，先之屬；雌，後之屬也。 “the cock is of the kind that goes first; the hen is of the kind that goes behind.” he then quotes passage 7: the sage puts the self behind and so is in front. on the two images he writes: 谿不求物而物自歸之，嬰兒不用智而合自然之智。 “the ravine does not seek things, and things come to it of themselves. the infant does not use cleverness, and fits the intelligence of what is so of itself.” the key word is 自, “of themselves”. nothing in the stanza is a technique for getting people to come. a ravine has no plan. if you lower yourself in order to gather others, you are, in wang bi’s terms, still using cleverness, and the cock is still in charge. is there a way to be low that is not a strategy?

德 is not “virtue”. we leave 德 as de. the usual english is “virtue”, which now means moral goodness, and to the victorians often meant chastity. the shuowen has two graphs for the word. for the older one, 悳, a heart under 直, “straight”, it says 外得於人，内得於己也: “outwardly, to get it with others; inwardly, to get it in oneself”. it plays on the sound of 得, “to get”: de is what a thing has got from the dao that makes it itself, and the hold it therefore has on others. the power of a herb to heal is its 德. so is the pull of a person whom others trust without knowing why. here it is called 常, constant, and the mawangdui copies are reported to write the older 恆 (see passage 1). three things are said of it: it does not leave, it does not go wrong, it is enough.

a third bird. 常德不離: the constant de “does not leave”. the graph for “leave”, 離, has the same bird sign, 隹, as the cock and the hen two lines above. the shuowen says that 離 was first a bird’s name: 黃倉庚也, the yellow oriole, whose song tells that the silkworms are hatching. the word “to depart” had no graph of its own and borrowed the oriole’s. so a reader of the first stanza sees three birds on the page: 雄, 雌, 離. the author did not plan this; the borrowing is far older than the book. but the eye takes it in. a cock, a hen, and a power that does not fly off. english can give the sense of each word and none of the flock. in passage 10 the same graph asks if body and spirit can hold to the one 無離, without parting.

復歸: to go home again. each stanza ends 復歸於, “again return to”. both words mean return. 復 is the shuowen’s 往來也, “to go and come”: the round trip. 歸 has a warmer first sense. the shuowen defines it 女嫁也, “a woman marries”: she goes to the house that will be hers. from that it means to go where one belongs, to come home; the dead are said to 歸. so the phrase is not “regress”. english “return to infancy” sounds like a loss of what was gained. in chinese, the infant, the limitless, and the uncarved wood are the home, and the adult years of display are the time away. wang bi links it to the motion of passage 40: 反者道之動, “turning back is how dao moves”. three returns, to three places. are they three homes or one?

嬰兒: a necklace, an open skull. two graphs, two pictures. 嬰 is 女, a woman, under two cowrie shells. the shuowen says 頸飾也, “a neck ornament”: shells strung round the neck. the word for a baby at the breast is commonly explained from this: the child hangs at the mother’s neck and chest like the necklace. 兒 is the child itself. the shuowen says the top of the graph shows 小兒頭囟未合, “a small child’s skull, the fontanelle not yet closed”. the infant in this book is a body before it is a symbol: soft bones and a firm grip, a cry all day without a hoarse throat (55), breath gathered until it is supple (10), no smile yet (20). the top of the head is still open. nothing has set. to “go back” there cannot mean to become ignorant; the one who returns knows the cock. what in you has not yet closed?

white and black are not good and evil. in english, white is innocence and black is sin; the pair comes loaded from the pulpit. none of that is in 白 and 黑. the shuowen defines 黑 as 火所熏之色也, “the colour that fire smokes on”: soot. white is the colour of plain silk and of daylight. so 白 is the clear, the evident, the seen; 黑 is the dim and unnoticed. to know the white and keep to the black is to see clearly and stay out of the glare. this black is kin to 玄, the dye-vat dark of passage 1, which is the book’s word for depth. painters and calligraphers quoted the line as 知白守黑, and it was later paired with a rule of their own art, 計白當黑, “reckon the white as black”: the blank paper is part of the character. the page you read now is the same. which carries the meaning, the ink or the space it leaves?

two stanzas, or three?. the oldest quotation of this passage has only two pairs. the last chapter of the zhuangzi cites lao dan: 知其雄，守其雌，為天下谿；知其白，守其辱，為天下谷. cock with hen, and then white with 辱, which can mean “soiled” as well as “disgraced”; passage 41 says 大白若辱, “great white seems soiled”. there is no black, no pattern, no limitless. some qing and modern scholars therefore judged the middle stanza a later insertion that split the old pair of white and soiled. the mawangdui silk texts complicate this. text b, the better preserved here, is reported to have all three stanzas, in another order: cock and hen; then 知亓白，守亓辱, with the valley and the uncarved wood; then 知亓白，守亓黑, with the pattern and the limitless. so if a stanza was added, it was added before 168 bce, and the silk copy still keeps “white” opposite “soiled”. our text’s “honour”, 榮, opposite “disgrace” looks like the last step in the tidying.

式: a pattern, perhaps a board. the shuowen glosses 式 with one word: 法也, the “model” of passage 25’s last lines; wang bi says 模則也, “a mould, a rule”. the graph has 工, the carpenter’s square. so the one who keeps to the dim becomes what others take their measure from, which is a paradox: the standard for the world is the one who stays out of sight. some scholars hear a more exact object. 式 is also the name of the diviner’s board, a square earth-plate with a round heaven-plate that turns on it, marked with the stars and the calendar signs; boards of this kind have been found in early han tombs. a person who is such an instrument does not decide. the heavens turn through it and the reading is true: 不忒, “it does not go wrong”. this second sense is possible and not proven for our line.

無極: no ridgepole. 極 is first a piece of a house. the shuowen says 棟也, “the ridgepole”: the highest beam, where the roof stops. from that it means the utmost point, a limit, a pole. 無極 is “without a limit”, and wang bi glosses it in three words: 不可窮也, “it cannot be exhausted”. in this passage the phrase is modest, one of three names for the place one returns to. thirteen centuries later it became one of the largest terms in chinese thought. the song philosopher zhou dunyi began his “explanation of the diagram of the supreme ultimate” with five characters, 無極而太極, “without limit, and yet the supreme limit”, and zhu xi built the cosmology of neo-confucianism on the phrase. his critics said that the first two words were daoist, and they pointed here. english versions that write “the infinite”, with a capital, bring in a term of theology. the chinese says that the roof has no top beam.

辱: shame at the edge of the field. the shuowen gives 辱 a farm story. the graph is 寸, a hand, under 辰, and 辰者，農之時也: “辰 is the farmers’ season”. then: 失耕時，於封畺上戮之也, “one who missed the time for ploughing was punished on the boundary mound of the fields”. disgrace, in this account, is public and exact: to be shamed in front of the village, at the border, for failing the season. modern scholars doubt the story and read 辰 as an old farm tool; either way the graph ties shame to the soil. the word also means “soiled, dark”, as in passage 41, and the oldest version of this line used it in that sense, opposite “white”. to 守其辱 is then to hold the place of the person on the mound: looked at and counted low. passage 13 says that favour and disgrace both make people start. who can stand there and not start?

樸: wood as it is. the shuowen defines 樸 as 木素也. 素 is plain silk before the dye; so, “wood in its plain state”: timber with the bark off and no tool mark on it. it is not a “block” waiting for a sculptor, and it is not “simplicity” as a style. it is material that could still become anything: a bowl, a wheel, a coffin, a god. each cut makes it one thing and ends the others. the image comes in passages 15, 19, 32, 37, and 57. wang bi glosses it 真也, “the real, the true”. the surprise of this passage is the next line: the wood is split, and the text does not mourn. a different graph, 朴, “tree bark” in the shuowen, is now used as the short form of 樸; the two are separate entries there. look at something made of wood near you. what else could it have been?

器: a vessel is one thing only. 樸散則為器: “the plain wood, dispersed, becomes vessels”. 散 is to scatter, to come apart. 器 is any made object with a use: a cup, a tool, a ritual bronze. the shuowen says 皿也, “a dish”, and describes the graph as the mouths of vessels with a dog to guard them. a vessel is good for one thing. that is its worth and its limit, and the age knew the word as a judgement on people. confucius said 君子不器, “the gentleman is not a vessel”: not a specialist, not a tool for another’s hand. a man could also be praised as a “great vessel”. here the word describes what happens when a whole society is cut up into trades, ranks, and offices. passage 29 will call the realm itself a 神器, a vessel of the spirits. what vessel have you been made into?

who uses whom?. 聖人用之則為官長 can be read three ways. first: the sage uses them, the vessels, and so becomes head of the officers: the one who is not a vessel directs those who are. second, with 之 as the plain wood: the sage uses the uncarved state and by that becomes the chief. third, with the sage as the one used: “when the sage is employed, he becomes chief of officers”; legge reads it so, and the mawangdui copies, which are reported to have no 之 (聖人用則為官長), allow it. wang bi takes a fourth path: 聖人因其分散，故為之立官長, “the sage follows their dispersal and so sets up officers and heads for them”. our line follows the first reading. for 聖人, “the sage”, see the note in passage 27: not a saint, and here plainly a ruler. the line turns the passage. what began as a teaching for one person at the low place is now about government.

the age that invented the office. 官 is an office and its holder; the shuowen says 史，事君也, a clerk who serves the ruler, and reads the graph as “the many” under a roof. 官長 is the head of such men. the term belongs to the great change of the warring states period. in the old zhou order, a state was run by noble kin who inherited their posts. from the fifth century bce, rulers replaced them with appointed, salaried men who could be moved and dismissed: clerks, magistrates, generals, each with a defined task. shen buhai in han and shang yang in qin made systems of it. the whole plain wood of a clan society was being split into 器, parts with functions. the laozi does not ask for the old nobles back. it accepts that there will be vessels and a chief, and it puts its condition in the last line: the cut that makes them must not sever.

大制不割: a cut that does not cut. both words have 刀, a knife. 制 is the shuowen’s 裁也, “to cut out”, as a tailor cuts cloth for a robe; hence to shape, to regulate, and the noun “institution, system”. 割 is 剥也, “to strip, to hack apart”, as a butcher divides a carcass; states “cut” land from each other with this word. so the line plays knife against knife: the great tailoring does not butcher. after the plain wood has been split into vessels, this is the one thing asked of the ruler’s cutting: that the pieces stay one cloth. wang bi: 大制者，以天下之心為心，故無割也, “the great cutting takes the heart of all under heaven as its heart, and so nothing is severed”. the mawangdui copies are reported to read 夫大制无割. passage 32 takes up the same word: 始制有名, “when the cutting starts, there are names”. what have you organised that came apart at the seams you made?

legge in rhyme: strength, feebleness, stains. legge put the three stanzas into rhymed verse, and the rhymes needed words that the chinese does not have. the cock and hen become “his manhood’s strength” and “his female feebleness”: a victorian doctrine of the sexes in six words, where the text has two farm birds and no “feeble”. the infant is “free from all stains”, which brings in the nursery of the saved soul. the limitless becomes “man’s first state”, a phrase with eden behind it. the black is “the pattern of humility”, a christian virtue. and 大制不割 becomes a promise that the sage in office “employs no violent measures”, which is mild good sense and loses the knife. read his first stanza beside the characters 雄 and 雌. where is the feebleness?

three pairs, and a weight on the light end. cock and hen, white and black, 榮 honour and 辱 disgrace: three pairs, and one frame for all three (see know one, keep to the other). the text does lean. it sets the post at the hen, the black, the disgrace. the lean answers a world in which each court ran after the first of each pair; it is a weight put on the light end of a scale. it does not make the low side good. honour and disgrace arise together: there is no low seat in a room with no high one, and passage 13 says that both make people start. and the low side turns. the valley fills. the uncarved wood is split into vessels three lines later. disgrace that is kept as a badge becomes a quiet honour, and the cock is back. what would it be to keep the low post and not be proud of it?

one can know strength fully and still choose to stay with the soft, low side.. one can know strength fully and still choose to stay with the soft, low side. do you think this can be done, or does a person who stays low lose the strength in time? which side were you taught to live on: the cock or the hen, the one who is seen or the one who gives way? who taught you? hold the reverse for a minute: know the soft, and keep to the strong. what changes in your chest and shoulders as you hold it? which of the two do you look down on in other people? what might that side of you want?

to stay in the place of disgrace, while knowing honour, makes a person whole and sufficient.. to stay in the place of disgrace, while knowing honour, makes a person whole and sufficient. does that ring true, or does it sound like an excuse for being treated badly? where do you draw the line? remember a time when you were shamed in front of others. what did you decide about yourself then, and do you still hold it? take the opposite view: honour is worth seeking, and a person should stand up and claim it. stay there. what feelings come? which side is more natural for you, and what has it cost you?

before roles and uses cut it, a person is whole, and can go back to that.. before roles and uses cut it, a person is whole, and can go back to that. do you believe there is such a state to go back to? what in your life suggests it? which roles have cut you into a useful shape? which of them did you choose? now take the other side: a person is made by the cutting, and with no role there is no one there. hold it and see what arises. why would it be worth knowing which of these you believe?

黑 soot at the smoke hole. the shuowen defines black by how it is made: 火所熏之色也, “the colour that fire smokes on”. its analysis: 从炎，上出𡆧。𡆧，古窻字, “from 炎, flames, which go up and out through 𡆧; 𡆧 is the old graph for a window”. so the picture is a hearth and the smoke hole above it, caked with soot. the four dots at the bottom of the modern graph are the fire, the same 灬 as in 然 and 熱 (and unlike the swallow’s tail of passage 26, which only looks the same). the box at the top with its two small marks is the sooty opening. modern scholars read the earliest forms in other ways, some as a person with a marked face, and the question is open; the shuowen’s chimney is the picture that chinese readers have learned for two thousand years. see what the script made from soot. 墨, ink: black over 土, earth; the shuowen says 書墨也, “ink for writing”. chinese ink is in fact lampblack or pine soot bound with glue and dried into a stick, so every character ever brushed is written in 黑. 點, a dot: 小黑也, “a small black”. 默, silent: a dog beside black; the shuowen says it is a dog that suddenly goes for a person, and later readers add: with no bark. 黨, a faction: 不鮮也, “not fresh, dim”. black in this family is quiet, hidden, and useful. it is what the passage says to keep. twelve strokes. the first is the left side of the box, a vertical. the second is the top and right side in one turn. the third and fourth are two small marks inside the box, a dot on the left and a short stroke that leans the other way on the right. the fifth is a horizontal that closes the box. the sixth is a vertical from inside the box down through its floor. the seventh is a short horizontal that crosses it. the eighth is a long horizontal, the widest line. then four dots from left to right: the ninth leans to the left, and the tenth, eleventh, and twelfth lean to the right, the last one the largest. the qing calligrapher deng shiru is quoted for a rule that was later linked with this passage: 計白當黑, “reckon the white as black”. look at the two small windows of white inside the box as it forms. if they are choked with ink, the character is dead.

辱 a hand under the farming season. the top part is 辰. the shuowen explains 辰 by the calendar: the third month, when the yang breath stirs, thunder shakes, and it is 民農時也, “the people’s time for farm work”; it is also the name of a group of stars that farmers watched. many modern scholars see in the early forms a tool, a blade of shell or stone for cutting weeds and grain; this is the common account and not a certainty. the signs agree in one thing: 辰 means work on the land at the right time. it is in 農, farming; 晨, early morning; 震, thunder; and it is the fifth of the twelve calendar signs, the one that later got the dragon. the bottom part is 寸, a hand with a mark at the wrist. the shuowen says the mark shows the pulse point, one inch from the hand, and 寸 is the word “inch”; in compound graphs it often stands for measure and rule, as in 守, to guard a post. now the shuowen’s story of the whole: 失耕時，於封畺上戮之也, “one who missed the time for ploughing was punished on the boundary mound”. the hand of the law, under the season. disgrace in this graph is not private guilt, the feeling of having sinned. it is a public fact about a farmer and a field. the passage asks the reader to know honour and to stand, by choice, on that mound. ten strokes. the first is a short horizontal at the top. the second starts under its left end and sweeps down to the left in a long curve; it is the wall of the character. the third is a short horizontal inside. the fourth is a longer horizontal under it. the fifth is a vertical that ends with a flick up to the right. the sixth is a short stroke that falls to the left. the seventh is a long stroke that falls to the right and ends in a level tail. these seven are 辰. now the hand. the eighth is a long horizontal that carries everything above it. the ninth is a vertical through its right part, ending in a hook to the left. the tenth is a dot in the angle on the left. the right-falling seventh stroke and the long eighth stroke compete for width; a good hand lets one be wide and holds the other back.

29 · the spirit vessel. wanting to take all under heaven and work on it: / i see that this will not succeed. / all under heaven is a spirit vessel. / it cannot be worked on. / who works on it ruins it. / who grips it loses it. / so with creatures: some go ahead, some follow; / some breathe warm, some blow cold; / some are strong, some thin; / some break, some fall. / so the sage puts away the extreme, / puts away the lavish, / puts away the grand. three parts. first a case and a verdict: someone is about to take the world and work on it; the speaker sees failure. the reason is a definition: the world is a vessel of the spirits. two short laws follow, each built as “who does x, loses by x”: the worker ruins, the gripper loses. second, a look at creatures in four pairs joined by 或: ahead and behind, warm breath and cold, strong and lean, broken and fallen. third, what the sage does about it: removes three kinds of excess, and nothing else. the verbs carry the picture: a hand on an ear, a hand leading an elephant, a stick against a shell, a prisoner in manacles. history supplied real vessels and a real taker. replace “all under heaven” with “my life” or “my mind” and the passage is unchanged. there is a wish to seize the whole of it and make it into what it should be. the speaker sees that this does not come off. experience is a thing put together by what has no form; one cannot find the joints. meditators know both laws from the cushion. work on the mind to make it calm, and it is spoiled. hold a good state, and it is gone. the middle stanza is what one actually finds when one stops: at times ahead, at times behind, warm, cold, strong, worn out. that is not failure of practice. it is the nature of the creature. what is left to do is small and exact: notice the too much, and put that down. the passage is addressed to a founder: someone with the means and the will to take a whole thing and reshape it. its warning is not that ambition is wicked. it is that a living whole, such as a people, a company, or a family, was not assembled by anyone’s hands and has no handle. plans that treat it as material break it; control that is tight enough to feel secure kills what was worth controlling. the middle lines are a lesson in staffing and in timing: some lead and some follow, and the same person is strong in one year and spent in the next. a design that needs everyone warm fails. the method on offer is wang bi’s 因: go by what is there. the leader’s own part is a subtraction, three removals, and every one of them begins at the top. the middle stanza is an ecologist’s sentence. among creatures some go in front and some behind: the herd has its lead animal and its stragglers. some breathe warm and some blow cold. some are sturdy and some are lean: every population has both. some are heaped up and some slide down: banks build and banks collapse. a manager of land who wants only the strong, the leading, and the standing will drain the marsh, cull the weak, straighten the river, and be surprised by the flood. the text’s word for the whole is 器, a made thing, and its maker cannot be found, so no one has the drawings. what can be done with such a thing is to learn its tendencies and go by them. the qin empire tried the other way. do the breath test first; it takes ten seconds and fixes the middle stanza in the body. then choose one thing you are trying to improve by force: a person, a habit, a piece of work that will not come right. for one day do nothing to it. do only what the last stanza says. ask the three questions in order. where is this too sweet, where am i getting too much comfort from it? where is it too wide, where am i showing off? where is it too smooth, where have i grown grand and careless? remove one excess, once. leave the thing itself alone. in the evening, look at your hand as the note on 執 suggests. then ask if the thing is in a worse state for a day without your work on it.

取: a hand on an ear. the verb for what the ambitious man wants to do is 取, “to take”. its parts are 耳, an ear, and 又, a hand. the shuowen explains: 捕取也, “to capture”, and quotes the rites of zhou: 獲者取左耳, “the one who makes a kill takes the left ear”. that line is about the royal hunt, where the left ear of each animal was cut for the tally. the shuowen then quotes the methods of the marshal, 載獻聝, “they carry in and present the cut ears”, and that is war: 聝 is its word for “to cut ears in battle”. so the common word “take” began as a count of the killed. 取天下, “to take all under heaven”, was the stated aim of every large state in the fourth and third centuries bce; the phrase returns in passages 48 and 57, where the world is taken only by having no business with it. the passage opens with a hand that reaches for an ear. whose?

為: to do, to make, to tamper. 為 is the most general verb of action in chinese: to do, to make, to act as, to manage. here it has an object, 之, “it”: to do things to the world, to work it as a craftsman works a piece. the line says that the world 不可為, cannot be treated so. this is the positive ground of the book’s famous 無為, wu wei, often put into english as “non-action”, which sounds like idleness. the text does not ask for a ruler who does nothing. it denies that the world is material for a project. the shuowen gives the graph, in its old form 爲, an odd first sense: 母猴也, “a female monkey”, a creature that is good with its claws. most modern scholars see in the oracle-bone form a hand that leads an elephant: the largest job of work the shang knew. either picture will serve. which things in your care are elephants, and which are not?

不得已: failure, or no rest?. 吾見其不得已. in passages 30 and 31 the three characters 不得已 are a fixed phrase: “to have no choice”, action taken only when it cannot be avoided. is this the same phrase? most readers say no. here 得 is the full verb “to get, to succeed”, and 已 is the particle that closes a statement: “i see that he will not get it, and that is that.” the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 弗得已, with a negative that implies an object: “will not get it”. a second reading is possible: 已 as “to stop”. then: “i see that he will get no rest.” the one who sets out to take and remake the world can never finish. we rendered the first and keep the second in mind, because both are true of the same man. the speaker says 吾見, “i see”. this is offered as an observation, not as a rule.

wang bi on 神器. 神 is a spirit, one of the unseen powers that received sacrifice; as a describing word it is “of the spirits, numinous”. 器 is a vessel (see passage 28). wang bi explains the pair: 神，無形無方也。器，合成也。無形以合，故謂之神器也。 “神 means without form and without fixed place. 器 means a thing put together. it is put together by what has no form; so it is called a spirit vessel.” the world is an assembled thing, he says, like a pot or a cart. but no one can find the maker or the joints, so it cannot be taken apart and rebuilt. english versions say “sacred” or “spiritual”. “sacred” suggests a rule against touching, with a god to enforce it. the chinese point is more practical: you cannot find where to put your hands. for the other thing a reader of that time heard in the words, see the nine tripods.

the nine tripods. for a warring states reader, the sacred vessels of the world were real bronzes. tradition said that the sage-king yu cast nine tripods from the metal of the nine provinces; the shuowen repeats it under 鼎: 昔禹收九牧之金，鑄鼎荊山之下. they passed from xia to shang to zhou, and to hold them was to hold the mandate. in 606 bce king zhuang of chu led his army to the zhou border and asked how heavy the tripods were. the zhou envoy answered 在德不在鼎: “it lies in de, not in the tripods”. “to ask about the tripods” still means to plot for the throne. in 307 bce king wu of qin, a strong man, tried to lift a great tripod on a visit to the zhou capital, broke his legs, and died. when qin ended the zhou house in the 250s bce, it carried the tripods off, and they were lost. 執者失之: who grips it loses it.

敗: to break the treasure. the shuowen defines 敗 as 毀也, “to wreck”, and reads the graph as 攴, a hand with a stick, beside 貝, a cowrie shell, the early form of wealth: 敗、賊皆从貝, “敗 and 賊 (robber) both have the shell”. some early forms are commonly described as a hand that strikes a bronze cauldron in place of the shell. either way, the picture is of something precious struck with a tool. the same word is the normal term for defeat in battle. so 為者敗之 is exact in two ways. the one who works on the world spoils it, as a clumsy hand breaks a pot. and the one who works on the world is beaten. the couplet 為者敗之，執者失之 comes again word for word in passage 64, with its remedy: the sage does not work on things and so does not ruin them, does not grip and so does not lose.

執: an arrest. 執 is “to hold in the hand”: a brush, a rein, a rule. the shuowen gives the older sense: 捕罪人也, “to arrest a criminal”. in its account the graph joins 丮, a kneeling person with both hands held out, and 㚔, which early forms show as wooden manacles. to grip, then, is to put the thing in shackles. wang bi sets it against another verb: 可通而不可執也, “it can be gone along with; it cannot be gripped”, because 物有往來, “things come and go”. a prisoner in fetters does not come and go. that is why the grip fails. what is held that hard is no longer the living thing one wanted. later chinese buddhists chose this word for “attachment”, the clinging that their teaching aims to end. look at your hand when you want something badly. is it open?

wang bi: follow, do not make. wang bi’s comment on the central lines gives the positive side of the warning: 萬物以自然為性，故可因而不可為也。 “the ten thousand things have what is so of itself as their nature. so they can be followed and cannot be made.” his key word is 因, to go by, to rely on, to take one’s lead from. the shuowen glosses it 就也, “to go to, to settle on”. a farmer does not make the wheat grow. he goes by its nature and by the season, and the work is hard. so 因 is not passivity. it is the kind of doing that starts from what is there. on the sage wang bi adds: 除其所以迷，去其所以惑, “he clears away what makes them lose the road and removes what confuses them”. the sage’s whole programme, in this reading, is removal.

the state that took it. the passage was tested within a century. from 230 to 221 bce the state of qin took all the others, one each year or two, and its king named himself first emperor. he then worked on the world as no one had: one script, one axle width, one law, one set of weights, a great wall, books burned, families moved by the hundred thousand. he died in 210 bce. by 206 bce his house was gone, destroyed by revolt in fifteen years. the thinkers of the next dynasty, the han, read the fall in the terms of this passage. jia yi’s essay “the faults of qin” says that qin took the world by force and could not change its ways to hold it. much of the early han court honoured the laozi and governed lightly for some sixty years. 為者敗之 was, for them, recent history.

或…或: some, or sometimes?. eight times the middle stanza says 或. the word means “some” and “at times”, so the four lines can be read across space or across time. across space: among creatures, some lead and some follow, some are strong and some are 羸 (the graph has a sheep in it; the shuowen says 瘦也, “lean”). the world is mixed, and a ruler who wants all of it one way must break half of it. across time: the one who goes ahead now will follow later; what is strong will be thin. then no state lasts, and the attempt to fix one is lost at the start. wang bi takes the second: 逆順反覆, “things go with and against, turn and turn back”. legge makes it a rhyme about fortune. the chinese gives no ranking in either case. it does not say that to lead is better than to follow.

warm breath, cold breath. 歔 and 吹 are both ways to breathe out. both graphs contain 欠, the shuowen’s sign for a yawn, breath that leaves an open mouth; for 吹 it says 出气也, “to send out breath”. the difference is in the lips. try it. hold your palm near your mouth and breathe out slowly with the mouth open, as if to fog a mirror: the air is warm. that is 歔. now purse the lips and blow hard, as on hot soup: the air is cool. that is 吹. the same lungs, the same breath, one moment apart. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to make the first word 炅, a graph read as “hot”: some heat, some blow. early breath training used exactly these named breaths; the zhuangzi lists 吹呴呼吸, “to blow, to breathe warm, to breathe out and in”. if one mouth holds both, what sense does it make to rule that all the world must be warm?

break and fall, or build and fall?. the first three pairs are opposites: ahead and behind, warm and cold, strong and thin. the fourth pair in our text is not. 挫 is to snap or crush (the shuowen: 摧也), and 隳 is to collapse; both are ruin. something has slipped. the heshang gong text reads 或載或隳, “some ride, some fall”, which restores the contrast. mawangdui silk text b is reported to have a third version, 或培或橢, where the second graph is taken as 墮: “some are banked up, some tumble down”. 培 is to heap earth at the foot of a wall or a plant. that gives the clearest pair of all, and it is a builder’s pair: walls go up, walls come down. our rendering keeps the received words. the older picture seems to be an earthwork under repair.

a sage who only removes. 聖人, “the sage”: not a saint, and not only a wise man. the graph 聖 has an ear, and the shuowen’s gloss is 通也, “open, getting through”. notice the place of the ear in this passage. it began with 取, a hand that seizes an ear. it ends with a person named for an ear that listens. and notice what this sage does. after a passage on the ruin that comes from doing, one expects to be told what to do. the text gives one verb, three times: 去, “to put away”. the sage has no programme for the world. the sage takes three things out of the way, and they are all in the sage’s own conduct, or the court’s. is there a project of yours that would go better if you only removed something?

three words for too much. 去甚，去奢，去泰. the three objects are near in sense, and each has its own picture in the shuowen. 甚 is 尤安樂也, “the height of ease and pleasure”; the graph joins 甘, sweet, with 匹, a mate. it is too much of what is pleasant. 奢 is 張也, “stretched out”, with 大, big, on top: display that spreads beyond its frame. 泰 is 滑也, “slippery, smooth”; it shows two hands and water, and came to mean great, grand, at ease to the point of arrogance. so: the over-sweet, the over-wide, the over-smooth. none of the three is a thing. each is a degree. the sage does not put away pleasure, wealth, or greatness. the sage puts away the “too”. mawangdui silk text b is reported to give the order 甚, 大, 楮, with the last two as sound-loans for 泰 and 奢. which of the three is yours?

terraces. 奢 was a political word. the rulers of the age competed in building. king ling of chu finished the zhanghua terrace in 535 bce and invited the other lords to admire it; six years later his army left him and he took his own life. the histories tell this as a lesson. every high terrace was made by farmers taken from the fields in the season of work, and paid for by the grain tax. the followers of mozi made “moderation in use” a whole doctrine and counted the cost of music, funerals, and palaces in hungry people. so 去奢 is not advice about personal taste. in its own world it meant: stop the works. the laozi comes back to it in passage 53, where the court is “very well swept” and the fields are “full of weeds”.

legge’s “active doing” and fortune’s wheel. legge writes that the kingdom “cannot be got by active doing”. he joins 取 and 為 into one idea, getting, and so the lines become advice on how not to win a crown. the chinese has two verbs: to take the world, and to work on it. he calls the world “a spirit-like thing”, careful and pale. then he puts the four pairs into rhyme: “what was in front is now behind; / what warmed anon we freezing find.” this is the wheel of fortune from european moral verse, the fall of the great. his last couplet adds a store in ruins that “mocks our toil”, and neither the store nor the mockery is in the text. for the three excesses he gives “excessive effort, extravagance, and easy indulgence”: the first reads the passage’s lesson back into 甚. where the chinese lists kinds of creature, he preaches on vanity.

four pairs, and what the sage removes. ahead and behind, warm breath and cold, 強 strong and 羸 thin, and a last pair that the editions give in more than one form (see the variants). the stanza names both sides of each and praises neither. this is its reply to the first stanza. to work on the world is to pick one side of each pair and try to make it stay: all leading, all warm, all strong. but the sides need each other. no one goes ahead unless someone follows, and “strong” is a word that needs a thinner thing beside it. they also change places (或 can mean “at times”). so the sage in the last lines does not remove the weak side or the strong side. the three things put away are all excess: the point where one side is pushed until it breaks into the other. which side of a pair are you trying to make permanent?

the world is a sacred vessel, and whoever tries to remake it ruins it.. the world is a sacred vessel, and whoever tries to remake it ruins it. do you agree? think of something that you or others tried to fix and made worse. then think of one that got better. where does your urge to fix things come from, or your urge to leave them alone? whose voice is in it? hold the opposite: the world is unfinished, and it is a duty to take hold of it and work. what do you feel as you take that side? is your answer different for the world, for other people, and for yourself? what explains the difference?

no one way of being suits all creatures, and each takes its turn at strong and weak.. no one way of being suits all creatures, and each takes its turn at strong and weak. do you accept this for the people near you, or do you want them to be one way? which side of a pair were you not allowed to be as a child: slow, weak, behind, cold? what happened to that side of you? try the other view: some ways of being are simply better, and people should be moved toward them. stay with it. what comes? when you are the thin one or the one behind, how do you treat yourself? why does that matter?

取 a hand on an ear. left side: 耳, an ear. the shuowen says 主聽也。象形, “it governs hearing; a picture”, and you can still see the outer rim and the folds. right side: 又, a hand. the shuowen: 手也。象形, and it adds that the hand is drawn with three fingers because “the many are shown by no more than three”. in early writing 又 is the right hand in profile, reaching. hand takes ear: 取. the shuowen’s citation makes the scene plain, an ear cut as proof of a kill. from the battlefield the word went everywhere: to fetch, to choose, to draw water, to take a wife. follow the hand first. 又 was borrowed for “again”. the hand is in 友, friend, which early forms write as two hands side by side; in 受, to receive, two hands with a thing between them; in 及, to reach, a hand that catches a person from behind. now follow 取 itself. put a woman below it: 娶, to take a wife; the shuowen says 取婦也. put a cap above: 最, which the shuowen explains as 犯而取也, “to rush in and seize”, and which now means “most”. and the ear by itself sits in 聖, the sage, and in 聞, to hear, an ear at a gate. the same ear is in the taker and in the listener. this passage begins with one and ends with the other. eight strokes. the ear first. stroke one is a horizontal across the top. stroke two is a vertical on the left. stroke three is a long vertical on the right, which runs lower than the rest of the ear. strokes four and five are two short marks inside, one above the other. stroke six starts at the far left, below the ear, and rises to the right; it crosses the foot of stroke two and touches stroke three. it rises because the brush is already on its way to the hand. stroke seven is a short horizontal that turns and falls to the left. stroke eight starts at the left under that turn, crosses the falling part of stroke seven, and runs down to the right, long, with pressure at the end. the ear is narrow and upright; the hand is wide and open. the hand must not crowd the ear: a clear channel of white stays between them.

神 an altar and a bolt of lightning. two parts. the left is 礻, the side form of 示. the shuowen says 天垂象，見吉凶，所以示人也, “heaven hangs down signs and shows good and ill fortune; by them it shows people”, and 示，神事也, “示 is the business of spirits”. modern scholars commonly explain the graph as an altar, a stand on which offerings were set; it is the sign of everything that concerns spirits and rites: 祭, sacrifice; 祖, ancestor; 福, blessing; 禮, ritual; 社, the altar of the soil. the right is 申. for 神 the shuowen says 天神，引出萬物者也。从示，申聲: “the spirits of heaven, which draw out the ten thousand things”, with 申 for the sound. it is more than a sound part: the shuowen glosses 申 itself as 神也. its early forms are commonly read as a fork of lightning; the shuowen keeps the trace under 電, lightning, which it analyses as 从雨从申, “rain and 申”. so a spirit, 神, is in its graph the bolt and the place where people answer it. it is power that arrives from where no one can see, and is not held. in old chinese usage 神 are many: the powers of rivers, mountains, grain, and the dead. the word is also what is quick and fine in a person: 精神, vital spirit. when the passage calls the world a 神器, it puts lightning beside a pot. nine strokes. the altar side takes four. the first is a dot at the top left. the second is a short horizontal that turns and falls to the left. the third is a vertical that starts on the falling part of the second stroke. the fourth is a small dot to the right of the vertical, tucked in close. then 申, in five. the fifth stroke is the left side of the box, a short vertical. the sixth is the top and right side in one turn. the seventh is the line across the middle. the eighth closes the box below. the ninth is the stroke to watch: one long vertical from above the box, straight down through its centre and far below it. this is the bolt. calligraphers call such an ending a “hanging needle” when it tapers to a point and a “dewdrop” when it ends rounded. everything else in the character is small so that this line can fall freely.

30 · fruit, and stop. one who assists a lord of people with dao / does not force all under heaven with weapons. / such business likes to come back. / where an army has camped, thorn and bramble grow. / after a great host there are sure to be years of hunger. / the good one bears fruit, and stops, / and does not dare take the strong place by it. / fruit, and no pride. / fruit, and no boast. / fruit, and no high horse. / fruit, because there was no choice. / fruit, and no forcing. / a creature at its full strength then grows old. / this is called not-dao. / what is not-dao is early finished. four parts. a rule for one profession: the one who serves a lord as his left hand by the dao does not make the world submit by arms, because that kind of business comes back. evidence from the fields: thorns where the army camped, and failed harvests after it. a code for the case in which force is used: get the fruit and stop; then five short lines, each “fruit, and…”, that take away the spear, the halberd, the tall horse, plead necessity, and forbid forcing. a law of bodies to close: what is driven to its prime grows old; this is not-dao, and it is soon over. the passage assumes that there will be armies. its age left no room to doubt it. every person has a lord to assist and weapons to hand. the lord is whatever one serves: an aim, a principle, the wish to be good. the weapons are will, anger, argument, discipline turned harsh. the passage says what happens when the aim is served by those means. the ground where the force camped grows thorns: a habit broken by violence leaves a waste where it stood, and something tough and unpleasant moves in. the middle stanza gives the alternative in the same domain, because sometimes one must act hard. do the thing until it has borne. then stop. no story of victory, no new opinion of oneself, no high horse. and check the claim of necessity honestly. the last law is about energy: a state of mind held at its peak by effort is already on its way down. the speaker stands where many readers stand: not the owner, but the one who advises. the first counsel is about means. a leader can usually get the next result by force: by threat, by a purge, by a price war, by pressure on the team. the adviser is asked to see the return: force teaches force, and the ground it crosses is poorer afterwards. the second counsel is about success, and it is rarer. when a hard action was truly needed and it worked, the danger starts. five lines list what to refuse: self-satisfaction, the public claim, the swagger, the reason found afterwards, and the use of this win to become the strong one. the military writers of the time said much the same. an organisation at its forced peak should be read as old. the passage reasons from fields and trees. an army is described as an ecological event: it settles on worked land, and the land’s response is succession, the tough thorny shrubs that take a disturbed and abandoned plot. then the harvest, which is what a year is, fails. the alternative is also a plant: 果, the fruit. a tree puts out blossom, sets fruit, ripens it, and is done; then it rests. it does not hold the fruit, and it does not treat the fruit as a reason to grow thorns. the last stanza is a law of organisms. growth that is driven hard and early to a maximum, like a forced bulb or a crop on too much manure, is followed quickly by decline. the plant that lasts is seldom at full stretch. find one result this week that you got by pushing: an argument won, a child or colleague made to comply, your own body driven through tiredness. go back and look at the ground where the force camped. what is growing there now: resentment, a flinch, a debt of sleep? that is the second stanza. then take the next task that does need firmness and try the code. before: ask if there is truly no other way. during: aim at the fruit only, the one outcome needed. after: stop at once. say nothing about it for a day. notice the pull to mention it, to stand a little taller, to press the advantage. each pull is one of the “and no…” lines. see which is strongest in you: the spear, the halberd, or the horse.

佐: the left hand. the word for “assist” is written 佐: a person, 亻, beside 左, “left”. the person was added late. the older way to write the word was 左 alone, and the shuowen defines that graph by the act: 手相左助也, “hands that help each other”. its parts are a left hand and 工, a tool, the carpenter’s square: the hand that holds the work steady while the right hand cuts. so a minister is a ruler’s left hand, and the two words “left” and “help” were one. the speaker of this passage does not address the lord. it speaks to, or about, the left hand: the adviser who has knowledge and no army of his own. passage 31, which follows, turns on left and right. which of your two hands holds things still?

the adviser’s trade. 人主, “lord of people”, is the warring states term for a ruler seen as an employer. the men who served such lords were mostly outsiders: trained, landless, hired for results. the quickest result was military, and several advisers made states strong by arms and paid for it. wu qi reformed the army of chu; when his king died in 381 bce the nobles shot him full of arrows. shang yang rebuilt qin for war; in 338 bce, under a new ruler, he was torn apart by chariots. so the first sentence is professional advice inside a dangerous profession, and the third sentence, “such business likes to come back”, had faces. the passage does not ask the adviser to leave. the verb is 佐, to assist. it asks what the left hand should refuse to hold.

兵: two hands on an axe. 兵 is the general word for arms. the shuowen says 械也, “implements”, and reads the graph as 从廾持斤，并力之皃: “two hands that hold an axe; the look of strength joined”. 斤 is an axe or adze, “for cutting wood” in the shuowen. you can still see the hands as the two legs at the bottom of the modern form. the word then moved from the tool to the man: 兵 came to mean the soldier, then troops, then war as such. sunzi’s book is the 兵法, “the method of 兵”. notice that the picture is not a sword or a spear. it is a woodsman’s tool gripped with both hands, a thing made for trees and turned on people. the same graph opens passage 31, where it is called a tool of ill omen.

強, three times. the passage is fenced by one word. line 2: do not 強 the world with weapons. middle: do not dare to 取強, “take strength”, where 取 is the trophy word of passage 29. last line of the list: 果而勿強, “fruit, and no forcing”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to end the list with a summary that makes the point outright: 是謂果而不強, “this is called fruit without force”. 強 is “strong”, “to force”, and “stiff”, and in this book it is often a symptom (see the note in passage 25 on the insect in its graph). the text does not oppose strength to weakness here. it opposes 強 to 果: forcing an outcome against letting an outcome ripen. both get results. only one of them, the last stanza says, has a long life.

wang bi: what comes back?. 其事好還 is four characters: “its affairs are fond of return”. the common reading is retaliation. the use of arms comes back on the user: the invaded invade, the son avenges the father. legge has “its proper return”. wang bi reads the line in a different direction: 為始者務欲立功生事，而有道者務欲還反無為，故云其事好還也。 “those who start things strive to set up merit and make business. those who have the dao strive to turn back to not-doing. so the text says: their business is fond of return.” for him 其 points to the adviser with the dao, and 還 is the homeward motion of the whole book, the 復歸 of passage 28. one reading is a warning and the other is a description of character. the grammar allows both, and both use the same picture: a thing that goes out and turns round.

the teacher comes back as an army. 師之所處: “where the 師 stays”. three passages ago 師 was the teacher whom the not-good person needs. here it is the older sense of the same graph, an army; the shuowen counts it at two thousand five hundred men. the next line has the larger unit, 軍, which the shuowen explains as 圜圍也, “an encirclement”, a camp ringed with chariots, 車. and the verb is 處, “to stay, to settle”, the word passage 24 used for what the one with the dao does not do among warts and leftovers. an army 處 on farmland as a household does, with fires, latrines, and horses, and then moves on. the line does not describe a battle. it describes the ground afterwards. what grows in a place after you have camped there?

荊棘: thorn country. two shrubs that take over abandoned fields. 棘 is the wild jujube; its graph is two thorns side by side (see the plate). 荊 is the chaste tree, a tough bush whose rods were used for flogging; the shuowen says 楚木也, “the tree of chu”, and under 楚 it says 一名荊也, “another name is 荊”. the great southern state of chu was also called jing: thorn-land. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write 楚棘 here. tradition makes laozi a man of chu, and the guodian slips, the oldest copy of this passage, came out of a chu tomb. so for its first readers the plant that follows an army had the name of their own country. in modern chinese 荊棘 still means hardship, and a “thorny” problem is 棘手, “thorns to the hand”.

a line the oldest copies lack. 大軍之後，必有凶年: “after a great host there are sure to be bad years”. 年 is in the shuowen’s old form “the grain is ripe”, so a year is a harvest, and a 凶年 is a harvest that fails. for 凶 the shuowen sees a pit in the ground that something has fallen into. the line is exact about cause: men and oxen taken from the fields, seed grain eaten, dikes unrepaired. but the mawangdui silk texts are reported not to have it; they go from the thorns straight to “the good one bears fruit”. the guodian slips are reported to lack it too, with the thorn line and the three closing lines on vigour and age. most scholars therefore take the famine sentence as an early reader’s comment that entered the text; wang bi’s note explains the thorns by “ruined and wasted fields” and does not quote the famine sentence. someone who had seen it added eight characters. they are true, and they stayed.

what war had become. in the old zhou world, war was a matter of nobles in chariots, a few thousand men, and a day’s fight with rules. by the fourth century bce the states had registered their whole farming populations, and they put conscript infantry into the field by the hundred thousand for campaigns of months or years. the histories give numbers that may be inflated and are still a measure of the horror: 240,000 heads taken by qin at yique in 293 bce; 400,000 men of zhao killed after their surrender at changping in 260 bce. mencius said of his own time: 爭地以戰，殺人盈野, “they fight for land, and the killed fill the fields”. every soldier was a farmer who was absent from a plot. that is why this passage counts the cost of war in weeds and harvests. its author did not need to mention the dead.

果: fruit on the tree. the shuowen defines 果 as 木實也, “the fruit of a tree”, and says the graph shows the shape of fruit on top of 木. from fruit came “result”, “outcome”; then “to carry through, resolute”; then the adverb “indeed, as it turned out”. wang bi glosses it here with 濟, “to bring across, to bring relief”: the good commander goes to settle the trouble, and that is all. our source has 善有果, with no 者; other old copies are reported to read 善者果, and “the good one” follows them and wang bi. most english versions say “achieves his purpose” or “wins” and lose the tree. the picture matters because of the next two words, 而已: “and stops”. a tree bears and is finished for the year. it does not press on to bear more in winter. the word then comes five more times, each with a thing to leave off: 果而, 果而, 果而, 果而, 果而. what have you carried to fruit and then kept working on?

驕: the tall horse. the third warning is 勿驕. the graph has 馬, a horse, and the shuowen gives the first sense with a measurement: 馬高六尺爲驕, “a horse six feet high is called 驕”. it quotes an ode about a team of such horses. a tall, spirited horse carries its head high and is hard to hold; from that the word came to mean “haughty”. english happens to own the same picture, and we used it: a proud person is on a high horse. now look at the three warnings as graphs. 矜 is in the shuowen a spear shaft. 伐 is a person with a halberd. 驕 is a warhorse. passage 24 used the first two of a civilian’s self-regard. here they are back in their own country: a commander after a victory, told to put down the spear, the halberd, and the horse that are inside his pride.

不得已: when there is no choice. 不得已 is, word for word, “not get to stop”: one cannot leave it undone. it is the phrase for action under necessity, and it is the nearest thing in the book to a rule for when arms may be used. it comes in passage 31 as well: weapons are used 不得已. the phrase does not say “when it is justified”. a justification is something one constructs. 不得已 is something one runs out of alternatives to. the zhuangzi makes it a discipline for all of life: to lodge in what cannot be helped and so feed what is central. legge gives “a matter of necessity”, which is fair. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to word the line differently, 果而毋得已居, and scholars do not agree on how to read it. ask of the last hard thing you did: had i truly no choice, or had i a reason?

壯 and 老: the prime, and after. 物壯則老: “a creature, at its prime, then grows old”. 壯 is the body at full power; the shuowen says only 大也, “big”. the book of rites gives it an age: 三十曰壯, “at thirty one is called 壯”. 老 is seventy in the shuowen, someone with hair and beard gone white: 言須髮變白也. the line can seem to call ageing a fault, and that cannot be meant; trees age. wang bi shows the sense by glossing 壯 as 武力暴興, “armed force that rises suddenly”, and quoting passage 23: a whirlwind does not last the morning. the fault is the forced peak. a thing pushed to its maximum has nowhere to go from there. the same three lines close passage 55, which is about an infant: the child is all vitality and no 壯, so the vitality does not run out. what in your life is being held at its peak by effort?

can anything be “not-dao”?. 是謂不道: “this is called not-dao”. dao is left in chinese (see passage 1): a way, the way things go. the phrase raises a real question. if dao is the course of everything, how can a thing be off it? passage 24 placed even boasting “in the dao”, as its scraps. the answer in this passage is practical and not metaphysical. nothing escapes the way things go; a forced peak is followed by a fall, and that fall is the way going on. what is 不道 is the conduct: it does not take the way as a way. it rows against the current, and the current remains in charge. so the text does not threaten punishment. it gives a forecast, in the next four characters. legge’s “not in accordance with the tao” makes it sound like a breach of regulations. is a river “not in accordance” with a swimmer who tires?

已, twice: stop, or be stopped. the passage uses 已 two times in the received text, and they answer each other. in the middle: 果而已, “fruit, and stop”. there 已 is a choice. the good commander ends the action when the result is in. at the end: 不道早已, “not-dao: early finished”. there 已 is what happens to the one who did not choose it. the mawangdui texts are reported to write the last phrase 蚤已, with a sound-loan for 早. the shuowen explains 早, “early”, as the sun, 日, over a sign it reads as armour: first light. so the forecast is not “destroyed”. it is quieter: over by morning. the whole ethic of the passage sits between the two uses of one small word. stop, or be stopped. in passage 29 the same graph ended the sentence about the man who would take the world.

the soldiers agreed. it would be easy to read this passage as a civilian’s protest. the military writers of the same centuries say much the same. sunzi: 夫兵久而國利者，未之有也, “there has never been a long war from which a state gained”. and: to win a hundred battles is not the best skill; to subdue the enemy’s force without a battle is. his book begins by calling war “the ground of death and life” for a state, a thing to be studied with dread. the laozi and the sunzi share a vocabulary, the same cool eye for costs, and the idea of a result with no display. they differ in the aim. sunzi wants to win cheaply. this passage wants the adviser to get the fruit and then, in its own words, to stop, and it applies the same law to the victor’s own strength.

legge’s “decisive blow”. legge turns 果 into a military act: “a skilful (commander) strikes a decisive blow, and stops.” he repeats “strikes” through the list. this is the idiom of a nineteenth-century campaign report. the chinese word is a fruit. it names what comes of the action, and it leaves open that the result might be reached with no blow at all. his 好還 is “sure to meet with its proper return”: “proper” makes the comeback a just reward, as if a judge were keeping accounts. and for 不道 he has “not in accordance with the tao”. still, he keeps the briars and the bad years plain. set his “strikes a decisive blow” beside 果. what does the reader of each picture expect the good commander to be doing?

壯 and 老: the peak and the slope. 壯 and 老, the prime and old age, look like a good state and a bad one. the line only joins them with 則, “then”: at the prime, then old. this is the turn that passage 25 called 反, and the second line of this passage has already named it: such business likes to come back. strength is not the fault, and age is not a punishment. one arises with the other; a peak is a place that has a slope on each side. what the text calls not-dao is 強, the attempt to hold the peak or to reach it early. its own preference, fruit and then a stop, is a correction for an age of armies. it is not a fixed rule either. fruit also falls and rots, and a stop that is made into a policy becomes one more thing to force. can you tell a ripe result from a forced one while it is in your hand?

force used on the world returns to the one who used it.. force used on the world returns to the one who used it. has this been true in your life? recall one time when you forced a result. what came back, and when? what did the people who raised you believe about force: that it works, or that it is paid for? which of them do you sound like? hold the opposite for a while: force settles things, and those who refuse to use it are used by others. what do you feel when you hold that? which of these two views would you not want others to know that you hold? why?

it is enough to get the result and stop, with no pride and no further gain taken.. it is enough to get the result and stop, with no pride and no further gain taken. do you agree that a result can be enough? when did you last stop at the result? what makes it hard for you to stop: a fear that the gain will not last, a wish to be seen, an old lack? now take the other side: a win should be pressed, and to stop early is to waste it. what thoughts and feelings arise? which does your body know better, the pressing or the stopping?

what is pushed to its full strength has already begun to decline.. what is pushed to its full strength has already begun to decline. is that what you have seen in careers, bodies, or groups that you know? are you afraid of your own peak, or of what comes after it? where did that fear begin? take the opposite: full strength is the point of a life, and to hold back is to live at half. what does that view wake in you? what would you do differently this year if you believed one side fully?

果 fruit at the top of the tree. start with 木, a tree: an upright trunk, a line for the branches, two strokes that fall away as roots. the chinese script makes many words by marking this one picture. a short line at the foot gives 本, root (passage 26). a line at the top gives 末, the tip; the shuowen says 木上曰末. a line through the middle gives 朱, which the shuowen calls a tree with a red heart. a hand above gives 采, to pick. a nest of birds above gives 巢. and a round thing on top gives 果: 木實也，象果形在木之上, “the fruit of a tree; it shows the shape of fruit on the tree”. the top part looks like 田, a field, in today’s writing. it is not a field. it is one large fruit, drawn round in the old script and squared by the brush; early forms, as commonly described, show several fruits on the branches. the word grew as fruit grows. first the thing you can eat. then any outcome: 結果, “to tie fruit”, is the modern word for a result. then the quality of a person who carries things through, 果敢, “resolute”. then the buddhist 因果, cause and fruit, the law that acts ripen. when this passage says 果而已, all of these are present, and the picture underneath them is a tree in autumn. it has done the year’s work. it is not proud of the pear. eight strokes. the fruit is written first, and it is not closed in the way that a box usually is. stroke one is its left side. stroke two is the top and right side in one turn. strokes three and four are two horizontals, one across the middle and one that closes the bottom. stroke five is the long horizontal of the tree, wider than the fruit. now watch stroke six: one vertical that starts inside the fruit at the top, comes down through its centre, crosses the long horizontal, and continues as the trunk. a single line is the core of the fruit and the trunk of the tree. stroke seven falls to the left from the crossing, and stroke eight falls to the right, heavier, with a level tail. the fruit must sit square and compact, and the two falling strokes must spread wide under it, or the tree looks top-heavy.

棘 thorn beside thorn. one part, written twice. the part is 朿, which the shuowen defines as 木芒也, “the awn of a tree”, a thorn, and calls a picture: a tree, 木, with spikes that stick out from the trunk. the shuowen adds 讀若刺, “read like 刺”, and 刺, to stab, is the thorn with a knife added. now the script does something clever with position. put two thorns one above the other and you have 棗, the jujube or chinese date, a thorny tree that grows tall: 从重朿, “from thorn stacked on thorn”. put two thorns side by side and you have 棘, the wild jujube that stays low and spreads in thickets: 小棗叢生者。从並朿, “the small jujube that grows in clumps; from thorn beside thorn”. up means height; across means a hedge. chinese often makes a word by doubling: 林, two trees, a wood; 炎, two fires, a blaze; 賏, two shells, a necklace; 誩, two speeches, a quarrel. other thorns in the script: 策, bamboo over 朿, the whip and the counting slip of passage 27. because 棘 makes a hedge that nothing passes, it was planted round prisons and examination halls, and the word still means a hard matter. in this passage it is what a camp leaves behind. a field is rows of one useful plant. a thicket is the same sign repeated with no room between. twelve strokes, six and six. the left thorn: stroke one is a short horizontal. stroke two is a short vertical at the left, under it. stroke three is a horizontal that turns down and hooks inward: with stroke two it makes the pair of spikes. stroke four is the long vertical through the middle. stroke five falls to the left from the crossing. stroke six is only a dot on the right. now the right thorn repeats the first five movements as strokes seven to eleven. but stroke twelve is a full stroke that falls to the right with a long tail. this is the lesson of the character. a regular-script character has only one such long right-falling stroke, so the left tree gives up its own and takes a dot. the two parts are the same in the dictionary and unequal on the page: the left one stands narrow and yields, and the right one finishes.

31 · victory as a funeral. fine weapons are tools of ill omen. / creatures, it seems, loathe them, / so one who has the dao does not stay with them. / the gentleman at home honours the left; / when weapons are used, honours the right. / weapons are tools of ill omen, / not a gentleman’s tools. / they are used when there is no choice, / and then calm and plain is best. / win, and do not find it beautiful. / one who finds it beautiful / delights in killing people. / one who delights in killing people / cannot get what the heart is set on in all under heaven. / glad occasions favour the left; / occasions of death favour the right. / the second general stands on the left, / the chief general on the right: / which says, they are placed as at a funeral. / when many people have been killed, / weep for them in grief and sorrow. / a battle won: / observe it with the rites of mourning. the passage has one long segment in the source, and it moves in five steps. a judgement: weapons are things of ill omen, loathed. a fact of etiquette: the gentleman honours the left at home and the right in war. a rule of use: only with no choice, and without relish. a warning about taste: victory must not be found beautiful, because that is to make music of killing, and such a person will not get the world. then the etiquette is explained: left is for glad things and right for death, and the generals stand in funeral order. last, two commands: weep, and keep the mourning rites for a victory. the source carries no wang bi commentary here. with 29 and 30 it makes one argument. the passage is about the inner posture of someone who must do harm. it does not pretend that such moments can always be avoided. it says what to guard in oneself when they come. first, no flavour: the act is done flat, with no savour of righteousness or skill. second, no aesthetics: one does not step back and admire it. third, grief, and grief for the other side. the text’s psychology is exact. the danger of force is not only what it does to the one struck. it is the pleasure, which grows, until a person needs the music. ritual mourning is the antidote the text knows: a set form that keeps the heart on what was lost, when the heart would like to celebrate. any win over another person, in a quarrel or a contest, can be met the same way. those who lead have weapons: the power to dismiss, to sue, to out-compete, to end a thing that people built. the passage grants that these are sometimes used and gives a strict code for it. they are not the leader’s proper tools, 非君子之器, and a leader known mainly for them has become one. they come out only when the alternatives have run out. they are used without heat. and afterwards there is no victory party. when a rival fails, when a restructuring “succeeds” and a hundred people have lost their work, the leader’s place is where the chief mourner stands. this is more than tact. the passage says that a leader who enjoys winning in this way will not gain the allegiance of the world, and history has a recorded case of a king who understood. left and right are in the body before they are in ritual. two hands: for most people the right is the hand that strikes, cuts, and writes, and the left is the hand that holds and steadies. the peaceful order honours the holding hand. war honours the striking hand, and the text calls that the order of death. the feeling it asks for is also bodily. 恬淡 is a state of the breath and the tongue: slow, with no taste in the mouth. a martial artist will recognise the instruction. train the strike fully; when it must be used, use it without anger, because anger makes the body stiff and the judgement poor; and feel no thrill afterwards, because the thrill is what brings a person back to fight again. the last lines put the body in hemp, wailing. think of the last time you won against someone: an argument, a negotiation, a game played hard, a decision that went your way and not theirs. recall the moment just after. was there a taste? that is 美. the practice has three parts. next time, before you use whatever weapon you have (rank, a sharp tongue, a better lawyer), ask the question from passage 30: is there truly no choice? if you go ahead, do it plain, with no flourish. and when you have won, take one minute alone for the other person’s loss. do not perform it for them. stand in it. a minute is not three years in hemp; it is the same rite in small. then notice whether you still want to tell someone about your victory.

“fine” weapons?. the received text begins 夫佳兵者. 佳 is “good, fine, handsome”; the shuowen says 善也. so: “fine weapons”, and readers have long found it odd, since the next lines condemn all weapons, not the good ones. the qing scholar wang niansun proposed that 佳 is a slip for a similar graph, 隹, an old way to write the particle 唯; the line then begins “now, weapons are…”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to support the simpler text: 夫兵者，不祥之器也, with no word in that place at all. we kept “fine”, because the pinned text has it, and because the mistake, if it is one, is a telling one. the weapons of the age were beautiful: see the king’s sword. and the passage goes on to forbid exactly this, to find war 美. did a copyist’s eye put the beauty in?

不祥: ill omen, not “evil”. 祥 is written with the altar sign and 羊, a sheep, the animal of offering; the shuowen glosses the sheep itself as 祥也, a good sign, and 祥 as 福也, “a blessing”. 祥 is what the spirits send to show that things stand well. 不祥 is its absence: unlucky, unblessed, a thing that should not be near the altar. the phrase is from the world of divination and taboo. it was used of an owl’s cry, of a comet, of a corpse. english “evil”, legge’s word, moves the phrase into morals and makes the weapon wicked. the chinese says something colder and more physical: a weapon is contaminated. it is the kind of object that one washes after touching. that is why the rest of the passage is about ritual: where to stand, how to weep. morals tell you whom to blame. ritual tells you what to do with a thing that cannot be made clean.

the same sentence as passage 24. 物或惡之，故有道者不處: “creatures, it seems, loathe them; so one who has the dao does not stay there.” these ten characters closed passage 24, word for word. there the loathed things were tiptoe, display, and boasting, called leftover food and warts. here they are weapons. the book files the brag and the blade under one sentence. the link is not forced. passage 24’s words for boasting were 伐, a person with a halberd, and 矜, a spear shaft; passage 30 forbade both to a commander. the mawangdui copies are reported to repeat the sentence in both places in their own form, 故有欲者弗居 (here in text b; text a is damaged). for the word 物 see passage 24: it is living things, and it cannot mean “law”. the honest small word is again 或, “perhaps, some”. not every creature turns from a weapon. some are drawn to it, and the next lines speak to them.

君子: a confucian in the laozi. 君子 is “the lord’s son”: first a man of noble birth, then, in the school of confucius, a man of noble conduct whatever his birth. english has used “gentleman” and “superior man”. it is the central figure of the analects and almost a stranger in this book, whose own figure is the sage. in the received text the word comes only in this passage, twice; the mawangdui copies are reported to have it in passage 26 as well, the other passage about a march. some scholars take that as a sign that this passage came from another hand or another circle. or the text here speaks to a class in its own terms: the officers were 君子 by birth and training, and the argument turns their code, with its fine sense of rank and ritual place, against their profession. the gentleman is known by where he sits. so: where does he sit in war?

left and right. the two graphs are two hands. 左 is a left hand over 工, a tool; 右 is a right hand over 口, a mouth; the shuowen glosses both with the idea of help. the right hand eats and strikes. in chinese ritual order, though, the left is the higher side. the ruler faced south; his left was the east, where the sun rises, the side of spring, growth, and what later thought called yang. his right was the west: sunset, autumn, killing frost, yin. so in peace the place of honour was on the left. death reversed the order, and the text says so: 吉事尚左，凶事尚右. even the clothes turned round: the shuowen records a robe for the dead that closes on the left, where the living close theirs to the right. the passage then makes its one observation. an army already uses the order of death. the commander stands on the right.

器, three times. 器 is a vessel, a tool, any made thing with a use (see passage 28). the passage says it three times. weapons are 不祥之器, tools of ill omen; again, 不祥之器; and 非君子之器, not a gentleman’s tools. a reader who knew the analects heard a famous sentence under the third: 君子不器, “the gentleman is not a vessel”, not a thing with one function. the laozi’s line goes further. there is a kind of tool the gentleman should not even own as his. and a person who takes up a tool whose one function is killing becomes that tool. two passages back, the world itself was a 神器, a vessel of the spirits, which cannot be worked on. so the three passages set vessel against vessel: the unlucky tool of bronze, and the sacred one that it is used to seize.

恬淡: calm, and thin in taste. 不得已而用之，恬淡為上. first the condition, 不得已, “no choice” (see passage 30). then the manner. 恬 is in the shuowen 安也, “at rest”. 淡 is 薄味也, “thin flavour”: water with very little in it. the pair names a temper without heat or relish. one does what must be done and tastes nothing in it. english “calm restraint” keeps the first word and loses the second, and the second is the laozi’s own: the dao when spoken is “thin, without taste” (35), and one should “taste what has no taste” (63). mawangdui silk text b is reported to have two other graphs here. the first is 銛, “sharp”; the second is hard to read, and editors have transcribed it as 龐 and as 襲. some take the pair as a loan for 恬淡, though only the first graph fits by sound; others read it literally, as a remark about sharp weapons. the matter is open. the received phrase fits what follows: a person who finds flavour in this work is the one the text fears.

the word is “beautiful”. 勝而不美: “win, and do not find it beautiful”. 美 is a sheep, 羊, over 大, a person; the shuowen says 甘也, “sweet”, and that it shares its idea with 善, good (see the plate in passage 27). it is the word for a handsome face, fine food, a splendid thing. translators often soften it to “do not rejoice” or “do not glorify”. the chinese is about the eye and the palate. war is beautiful: the ranks, the banners, the bronze, the clean arc of a campaign on a map. the line does not deny it. it forbids one to take it so, because of what the taste is a taste for. the mawangdui text is reported to make it a flat command: 勿美也, “do not find it beautiful”. when did you last admire something that was made to kill?
