the king’s sword. in 1965 archaeologists opened a chu tomb at wangshan in hubei and found a bronze sword in a lacquered scabbard. the blade is covered with a dark diamond pattern. the guard is inlaid with blue glass and turquoise. eight characters in the ornamental “bird script” say that goujian, king of yue, made it for his own use; he ruled from 496 to 465 bce. after twenty-four centuries the edge still cut. this is what 佳兵, “fine weapons”, were: the highest art of the bronze casters, objects that kings named, gave as state gifts, and took to the grave. halberd blades carried gold inlay; chariot fittings were works of sculpture. the laozi’s warning against the beauty of war was written among people who owned such things. it is addressed to connoisseurs.

樂: to make music of it. the graph in 樂殺人 is the graph for music. the shuowen defines 樂 as 五聲八音緫名, “the general name for the five notes and the eight kinds of instrument”, and says it pictures drums on a wooden stand. read yue, it is music. read le, it is joy, the feeling that music is. read as a verb, it is “to take delight in”. so “one who delights in killing people” is, in the eye, one who makes music of killing people. the two things were close in fact: armies advanced to drums and withdrew to bells, and a victory was reported with music in the ancestral temple. the text also uses the bluntest object it has. it does not say “war” or “the enemy”. it says 殺人, “to kill people”. a mourner, the analects says, 聞樂不樂: hears music and feels no joy. the passage will end there.

who can unite the world?. 不可以得志於天下: “cannot get the heart’s aim in all under heaven”. 志 is a heart, 心, with a sign for going on top: where the heart is headed. 得志於天下 was the set phrase for the great prize of the age, to bring the whole world under one rule. everyone knew that it would be done by someone, and soon. mencius was asked about it by king xiang of liang, about 318 bce: how can the world be settled? “by being made one.” who can make it one? 不嗜殺人者能一之: “one who has no taste for killing people can unite it.” the laozi says the same from the other side. both were wrong in the short run. in 221 bce the world was united by qin, the state that counted heads for promotion. qin held it for fifteen years. which run counts?

where the generals stand. 偏將軍 is the general “to the side”, the second in command. 上將軍 is the “upper general”, the commander. in any peacetime gathering the senior man would take the left. on campaign, the text reports, the order is turned: the junior on the left, the senior on the right. then it reads the custom: 言以喪禮處之, “this says that they are placed as at a funeral”. the top commander stands where the chief mourner stands. it is an observation about what armies already do, with a meaning drawn from it; the text does not invent a new rite. these lines were once doubted as a later note, partly because the titles sound like those of the late warring states and han. but the guodian bamboo slips, from about 300 bce, are reported to contain them, and the mawangdui silk texts are reported to have them too.

what a funeral asked. 喪禮, the rites of mourning, were the heaviest duty in zhou life. the mourners put on coarse undyed hemp. they wailed at fixed times. they ate thin gruel and gave up meat and wine. they left their offices. there was no music: on a day when he had wailed, the analects says, confucius did not sing. the chief mourner did not speak of his own affairs. to receive a victory this way means all of that. no feast, no songs, no report of merit at the temple; the commander in hemp, in the place of the son of the dead. elsewhere this book is hard on ritual: passage 38 calls 禮 the thin husk of loyalty and the start of disorder. there is no conflict. that passage attacks ritual used to rank and to compel. here ritual does its first work. it gives grief a form that a whole army can enter.

to weep, or to attend?. 以哀悲泣之. the three words of feeling are distinct in the shuowen. 哀 is 閔也, pity. 悲 is 痛也, pain. 泣 is 無聲出涕, “tears that come without sound”: silent weeping, as against 哭, the loud wail of the rite. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read differently: 殺人眾，以悲依立之. 依 is taken as a sound-loan for 哀, grief, and 立 as 莅, “to be present at, to preside over”, and many scholars think that the received 泣 is an old slip for it, since the two graphs are alike. then the line says: when many have been killed, attend them with grief; stand over the dead as one stands at a funeral. one version asks for tears. the other asks for presence. note who is mourned. the text says 殺人之眾, “the multitude of people killed”. it does not say “our dead”. in which version are you asked for more?

why wang bi is silent here. almost every passage of the received book carries wang bi’s commentary. this one has none. a song dynasty scholar, chao yuezhi, noted in 1115 that wang bi’s copy had no commentary here; from this it was inferred that wang bi doubted the passage. wang bi left no verdict of his own. later editors built on the inference. they noticed the doublets (“tools of ill omen” twice, “the rites of mourning” twice) and the explaining phrase 言, “this says”, and concluded that an old commentary had been copied into the text. some modern versions therefore cut the second half and print it as a note. the excavated texts have settled the main point. the mawangdui silk copies, buried in 168 bce, are reported to contain the passage with its funeral lines, and the guodian slips of about 300 bce to contain those lines too. the lines are four centuries older than wang bi. whatever their first source, they were in the laozi as early as we can see it, and they stay in our main text.

the king who refused a monument. there is a recorded case of the last lines. in 597 bce king zhuang of chu beat the army of jin at bi. an officer urged him to pile the enemy dead into a great mound, a 京觀, as victors did, “to show your descendants and keep the martial merit in memory”. the king refused. he said that the graph 武, “martial”, is made of 止 and 戈, “to stop the halberds”, and that true martial power forbids violence, puts away weapons, and gives the people rest. the men of jin, he said, had died loyal to their ruler’s orders; how could they be made a trophy? he sacrificed to the river, built a shrine to his ancestors to report the event, and went home. the shuowen quotes his words under 武. the same king had once asked the weight of the tripods.

one king, two stories. king zhuang of chu (ruled 613–591 bce) appears twice in the background of these passages. in 606 bce, young and rising, he marched to the zhou border and asked how heavy the nine tripods were: an open hint that he could carry off the sacred vessels of the realm (see passage 29). nine years later, after his greatest victory, he declined to raise a mound of enemy dead and spoke of stopping the halberds. the histories do not explain the change. they only record both. he is counted among the five great lords of the age. it is tempting to see in him the man whom passages 29 to 31 address: someone with the strength to take the world, who learned somewhere between the first story and the second what 果而已 means.

three passages, one argument. passages 29, 30, and 31 stand together and share their words. 29: the world is a spirit vessel, 神器; who works on it ruins it. 30: do not force the world with 兵; get the fruit and stop, 果而已; no pride, no boast. 31: 兵 are unlucky vessels, 不祥之器; victory is not beautiful; mourn. the phrase 不得已, “no choice”, comes in all three. so does 天下, “all under heaven”, as the thing that cannot be had this way: it cannot be taken (29), cannot be forced (30), and the killer cannot get his aim in it (31). read in order they move from the wish to conquer, to conduct in war, to conduct after war. in the mawangdui silk texts the three are reported to stand in this order too. read them once as a single piece. where does the argument turn from policy to grief?

legge’s “superior man” at war. legge writes “the superior man” for 君子, the phrase he used through all his confucian volumes, and so marks the word as foreign to this book. his weapons are “instruments of evil omen”: “evil” where the chinese says unlucky. he softens the centre. for 勝而不美 he gives “victory (by force of arms) is to him undesirable”, and the question of beauty is gone; to find it beautiful becomes “to consider this desirable”. but he does not flinch at the object: “to delight in the slaughter of men”. in the last sentence he adds one word in brackets: the victor has his place “(rightly)” according to the mourning rites. the chinese has no “rightly”. it does not argue that the rite is correct. it tells the victor where to stand. why might a victorian reader have needed the bracket?

left and right, glad and grim, win and mourn. the passage is built on 左 and 右, left and right, and on 吉 and 凶, the glad occasion and the occasion of death. neither side is the fixed seat of honour. at home the left is honoured; with weapons, the right. the ritual order turns with the occasion, and a person must know both orders to stand in the correct place. the last lines then join a third pair that the world keeps apart: 勝, to win, and 喪, to mourn. a one-sided reader takes the victory and leaves the funeral, or takes the grief and forbids all fighting. the text holds both. it grants that weapons are used when there is no choice, and it puts the victor in the mourner’s place. it prefers calm and plain because victors of that age raised monuments. calm also turns: with no grief in it, it is cold. which of your wins had a loss inside it?

a victory in which people were harmed should be met with mourning and not with joy.. a victory in which people were harmed should be met with mourning and not with joy. do you agree, even for a fight that had to be fought? think of a time when you won against someone. what did you feel in the first hour? what had you learned about winning as a child? hold the opposite view for a while: a hard win has earned its joy, and to mourn it dishonours the effort. what arises? is there a win of yours that you have not mourned, or a loss of another person that you enjoyed? why is that worth knowing?

weapons are unlucky tools, used when there is no choice and then without relish.. weapons are unlucky tools, used when there is no choice and then without relish. what are your weapons: rank, words, silence, money, anger? do you think of them as unlucky? when you say “i had no choice”, how often is it true? where did you learn to say it? take the other side: strength that is shown and enjoyed keeps the peace, and shame about it is weakness. stay with it. what do you notice? which do you fear more, your own force or your lack of it? what does the answer explain about how you act?

喪 weeping, and one who is gone. the shuowen reads this graph as two parts and one sentence: 亾也。从哭从亾, “to lose; from 哭, to wail, and 亾, gone”. 哭 it defines as 哀聲也, “the sound of grief”, and it has two mouths, 吅, at the top. 亾, now written 亡, is 逃也, “to flee”: in the shuowen’s account a person who goes into a hidden corner. mouths that cry out, and someone who is no longer there. you can still see the two mouths in the modern form, side by side under the cross at the top; the strokes below them are what remains of the rest. the oldest history is different and odder. oracle-bone forms, as scholars commonly describe them, show a tree with several mouths among its branches, and the tree is read as the mulberry, 桑, whose name sounded the same. so the first scribes wrote “loss” with a mulberry and added mouths, perhaps only to mark the word as something spoken or wailed; no one is certain. by the time of the shuowen the tree had been reshaped into weeping. the word has two readings. read sang, it is to lose: a state, an office, a life. read sang, it is the rites for the dead. the passage uses the second, twice, and means the first as well. a victory is a loss, and is to be given the rites of one. twelve strokes. stroke one is a short horizontal at the top. stroke two is a vertical that crosses it and comes down between the two mouths. strokes three, four, and five make the left mouth: its left side, then top and right side in one turn, then the base. strokes six, seven, and eight make the right mouth in the same way. keep the mouths small and level, like two eyes. stroke nine is the long horizontal under them, the widest line of the character. stroke ten is a vertical below it that ends with a flick up to the right. stroke eleven is a short stroke that falls to the left. stroke twelve is the long last stroke that falls to the right. the top half is square and still. the bottom half opens and leans, like a robe in movement. a good hand lets the final stroke run out slowly.

左 the hand that holds the work. two parts. the upper part, the horizontal and the long falling stroke, is what is left of a picture of a hand: the left hand, 𠂇, drawn with its fingers pointing right. the lower part is 工. 工 is a tool, most often explained as the carpenter’s square; it is the sign of skilled work, as in 巧, skill, and 式, pattern (passage 28). the shuowen’s gloss for 左 is not a direction at all: 手相左助也, “hands that help each other”. the left hand holds the square against the timber while the right hand marks and cuts. so “left” was first “to assist”, and when the graph was needed for the direction, the word “assist” was given a person at its side and written 佐: the verb of passage 30’s first line. now compare the twin. 右, right, is the other hand, 又, over 口, a mouth; the shuowen says 手口相助也, “hand and mouth help each other”. the right hand feeds. with a person added it is 佑, to protect. two hands, one with a tool and one with a mouth, and the script says that both of them help. chinese ritual gave the higher honour to the hand that steadies, and the passage builds on that: honour passes to the right hand only when there is killing to do. five strokes. the first is a horizontal, short, set high. the second begins above the horizontal, crosses it left of centre, and sweeps down to the lower left in one long curve; this stroke gives the character its lean. the third is the top horizontal of 工, short, tucked under the right half of the first stroke. the fourth is a short vertical. the fifth is the base horizontal, longer than the third, and it must reach far enough right to balance the sweep on the left. the stroke data used here writes 右 in the same order, horizontal first. many teachers of the older tradition, and the schools of japan, begin 右 with the falling stroke instead, and explain that the two hands faced opposite ways in the old script. write both and feel which hand each one is.

兵 both hands on the axe. the shuowen reads 兵 as 从廾持斤: two hands, 廾, that hold 斤. 斤 is an axe or adze; the shuowen says 斫木也, “for hewing wood”, and calls it a picture. in the modern graph the axe is the upper part and the two hands have become the long horizontal with the two short legs below it. the shuowen adds a phrase that is almost a comment on armies: 并力之皃, “the look of strength put together”. one sees the same two hands in 共, together; in 具, to make ready, hands that lift a vessel; in 戒, to stand guard, hands on a halberd; and in 弄, to handle, hands on a piece of jade. the axe is in 折, to break; in 新, new, first “to cut firewood”; and in 斧, the big axe. so the picture of 兵 is a workman’s grip. the word went from the tool to the man who carries it, and then to the whole business: weapon, soldier, army, war. english needs four words, and each time must decide whether a sentence is about objects or about people. the passage opens with the objects, “tools of ill omen”, and ends with the people. passage 30 said that where they camp, thorns grow. the graph does not show an enemy. it shows only the hands. seven strokes. the first is a flat stroke at the top that falls to the left, almost level. the second starts from its left end and comes down as a vertical. the third is a short horizontal that goes right from the middle of the second. the fourth is a short vertical that drops from the middle of the third. these four are the axe. the fifth is the long horizontal, the widest line: it touches the feet of both verticals. the sixth is a short stroke below it that falls to the left. the seventh is a firm dot or short stroke that falls to the right. the two legs do not touch each other or the line above; the gap is the open space between two wrists. in clerical script of the han the long horizontal is given the great flaring tail that marks that style.

32 · sweet dew. dao is constant, without name. / the uncarved wood, though small: / no one under heaven can make it a servant. / if lords and kings could keep to it, / the ten thousand things would come of themselves as guests. / heaven and earth join / and send down sweet dew. / the people, with no one’s order, / are evened of themselves. / when the cutting begins, there are names. / once the names are there, / it is time to know where to stop. / know where to stop, and so be out of danger. / a likeness for dao in all under heaven: / streams and valleys, and the river and the sea. four movements, each with its own image. first, wood: the dao has no name; the uncarved is small, and nothing can make a servant of it; if rulers kept to it, all things would come as guests. second, dew: sky and ground meet, sweet dew falls, and the people are even without a command. third, a knife: the first cut brings names, and with names comes the need to know where to stop. fourth, water: a likeness of streams and valleys and the river and the sea. one small word runs through the first two and into wang bi’s reading of the last: 自, “of themselves”. the passage continues the carving image of 28 and answers the three war passages before it: this is how things are won without arms. before thought divides experience there is something plain and featureless in awareness, and it is small: easy to miss, with nothing in it to grasp. the passage says that nothing can enlist it. fear cannot use it, and ambition cannot either, because it has no handle. when attention rests there, the many contents of the mind stop being enemies or tools and arrive as guests. then naming begins, as it must: this is anger, that is my plan, i am this kind of person. the cut makes names. the instruction is not to refuse names. it is to know where to stop: to name as far as is useful and not take the names for the wood. the last image is the direction of the whole practice. nothing is forced down to the sea. it was already going. the passage holds a complete theory of organisation in its third movement, and it is not against structure. when work is divided there must be titles, roles, and written rules. the skill it asks for is rare: to know where that should stop. past the stopping point, every new title makes a boundary to defend, and every new rule makes a wording to argue about, “the tip of an awl”. the first two movements say what the structure is for and what it cannot replace. people give real allegiance as guests, not as servants, to a centre that does not use them. and the fair share, the thing that most rules are written to secure, is pictured as dew: it falls evenly when nothing is in the way. a leader might ask of each rule: is this a channel, or an obstacle to the dew? read the images in their order and you have the water cycle. dew condenses out of the night air where sky and ground meet, and settles on every leaf without preference; the shuowen even calls the people “sprouts”. it gathers into streams in the valleys. the streams reach the river, the river reaches the sea, the “pool of heaven”, and from the sea the water goes up to come down again as dew. no part of this is commanded, and no part can be made a servant; people dam rivers, and the sea is not impressed. the passage sets one human act inside the cycle, the cut, and asks only that it know its limit: fields, ditches, and names, as far as needed. the uncarved wood is the forest that is still standing. take the third movement as an experiment in stopping. pick one thing today that you organise: your notes, a plan for the week, the rules in your house, the labels you put on a person you find difficult. you have already made cuts and given names. ask where the next cut would be one too many, and stop one short of it. leave one thing unsorted, one person undescribed. then try the first movement for a few minutes. sit, and look for what in your experience is plain and small and has no name yet. do not improve it. see if the thoughts that arrive can be received as guests: respected, and free to go. and tomorrow, early, go out and look at the dew before the sun takes it. see who got more.

where does the first sentence end?. the first seven characters are 道常無名樸雖小, and old books had no punctuation. our source cuts after 名: “dao is constant, without name. the uncarved wood, though small…”. a second cut is after 樸: 道常無名樸, “dao is constantly the nameless uncarved wood; though small…”. test the units against the rest of the book. passage 37 has the phrase 無名之樸, “the uncarved wood of the nameless”, so 無名 and 樸 do belong together in this author’s mind. wang bi keeps the first cut and joins them by sense: the uncarved 亦無名, “is also without name”. then there is 常. it may be the predicate, “dao is constant”, or the adverb, “dao is always nameless”. the mawangdui texts and the older guodian slips are reported to write the older word, 道恆无名. for dao left in chinese, and for the taboo that changed 恆 to 常, see passage 1. our line keeps the comma and both senses.

why “small”?. 樸 is plain timber before the tool; the shuowen says 木素也 (see passage 28). here it gets a surprising word: 小, “small”. one expects the source of all things to be called great, as in passage 25. the shuowen defines 小 as 物之微也, “the minute in things”. the uncarved is small because it has no features: nothing sticks out of it that the eye can catch, no size that a ruler can measure, no use that a buyer can price. wang bi says it is 近於無有, “near to not-having”. passage 34 will say outright that the dao “can be named among the small”. the same thing is the largest and the least. english “simplicity” makes it a quality one can admire and so removes the point. this is a piece of wood that no one looks at twice. what near you is like that?

臣: the one who is led. 臣 is the subject of a ruler: a minister, a servant, in the oldest texts a male slave. the shuowen’s first gloss is 牽也, “to be led”, as an ox is led on a rope, and then 事君也, “one who serves a lord”; the graph, it says, shows 屈服之形, “the form of one who bends and submits”. in the text 臣 is a verb: to make a subject of. nothing in the world can do that to the uncarved wood. the mawangdui silk texts and the guodian slips are reported to say 弗敢臣, “does not dare”; ours says 莫能臣, “is not able”. the first is awe. the second is plain fact: there is nothing on it to tie the rope to. for a reader at a warring states court the word had weight. every man there was some lord’s 臣 and said so when he spoke: “your servant”. here is one thing in the realm that is not.

wang bi: every talent is a handle. why can no one make a servant of the uncarved? wang bi answers with a list: 夫智者可以能臣也，勇者可以武使也，巧者可以事役也，力者可以重任也。 “the clever can be made servants through their ability. the brave can be used for war. the skilled can be set to tasks. the strong can be given heavy loads.” each gift is the place where a master takes hold. then: 樸之為物，憒然不偏，近於無有, “the uncarved, as a thing, is blank and leans no way; it is near to not-having”. it has no special excellence, so it cannot be employed. this is the vessel of passage 28 seen from the other side: to be carved into something useful is to get a handle. wang bi wrote as a young official in years when talented men at court were used and then killed. he knew what a handle was. by which of your talents are you held?

侯王: lords and kings. 侯 was a rank of the zhou nobility, a lord who held land from the king. 王 was the king, and for centuries there was one. the compound 侯王 belongs to a later world, in which the lords of the great states had taken the royal title themselves (see passage 25) and “lords and kings” had become a general word for those who rule. it comes in passages 32, 37, and 39, and in 32 and 37 in the same conditional: if they could keep to this. the sentence is a promise shaped like an offer. such men wanted 賓, the free allegiance of others, more than anything, and tried to get it by armies and covenants. the text says that it comes to the one who holds a small, plain thing that cannot be owned. it does not say that any of them had done so. 若, “if”, is the most political word in the line.

servant and guest. two court words answer each other. in line 3: 臣, a subject, one who is led. in line 5: 賓, a guest. the shuowen defines 賓 as 所敬也, “one who is treated with respect”, and the graph has 貝, the shell of a gift, under a roof. a guest comes freely, is honoured, and may leave. as a verb 賓 also meant to submit: the old texts call the distant peoples who sent envoys and gifts to the zhou court the zone of 賓服, “guest service”. so the line carries a political sense, “all things will offer allegiance”, in the language of hospitality. the contrast is the point. the uncarved cannot be made a 臣. the ruler who keeps to it receives the world as 賓. rule of this kind has guests and no servants. note also 自, “of themselves”: it comes here and again with the dew. no one sends for a guest of this kind.

sweet dew. dew was thought to come down from heaven in the night. 甘露, “sweet dew”, is the image of a blessing that needs no channel: heaven and earth 相合, “join with each other”, and it falls. the verb can also be heard as a union of male and female, which is how later daoists took it. the phrase had a long career. under the han, sweet dew on the palace trees was reported to the throne as an omen that heaven approved the reign, and emperor xuan named a reign period 甘露 (53–50 bce). so the image that this passage uses against rule by command became a tool of court ceremony. buddhist translators then chose 甘露 for the sanskrit amrta, the drink of deathlessness. the mawangdui texts are reported to write 以俞甘洛: 洛 is a sound-loan for 露, and 俞 is read as 輸, “to convey”, a different verb from our 降. in the passage it is still only dew: the one water that no dike or ditch directs.

民 and 令: sprouts, and a command. 民, “the people”, are the governed, those with no office. the shuowen gives the word a gentle gloss: 眾萌也, “the multitude of sprouts”. modern scholars read the earliest forms far more harshly, some as an eye that has been pierced, the mark of a slave; that is disputed. in the shuowen’s picture, the line needs no comment: dew, and sprouts. 令 is “to command”. the shuowen says 發號也, “to issue an order”, and the lower part of the graph is a person on the knees. the same definition, “issues orders”, was its account of 君, a lord (passage 26). so the line removes the central act of rule. 民莫之令: the people, and no one who commands them. it was the legalist claim that order exists only where 令 are issued and enforced. this line says that the most even order known falls every night with no decree.

均: even, to everyone. the shuowen defines 均 as 平徧也: “level, and reaching everywhere”. the graph has 土, earth: ground made flat. it is the word for equal shares of land or tax, and, written with metal, for the potter’s wheel, which makes clay even as it turns. so 自均 is “become even of themselves”. english versions that say “harmony” or “cooperation” turn a claim about fair shares into one about good feeling. the grammar leaves one thing open. what is evened? perhaps the dew: it falls on rich and poor fields alike. perhaps the people: with no orders, they level out among themselves. our line takes the second and lets you hear the first. passage 77 states the principle: the way of heaven takes from what has too much and adds to what has too little; the way of people does the reverse. dew does not look at the deed to the field.

始制: the first cut. 制 is the tailor’s and carpenter’s cut that makes a thing to pattern, and so “to institute” (see passage 28, which ended 大制不割, “the great cutting does not sever”). this line follows straight from it. the uncarved wood of line 2 now meets the knife: 始制有名, “at the first cutting, there are names”. a log has no name except “wood”. split it, and there is a bowl, a ladle, a wheel spoke, and each must be called something. wang bi reads the cut as the founding of government: 始制，謂樸散始為官長之時也, “‘the first cut’ means the time when the uncarved was dispersed and officers and heads first came to be”. the text does not say that this is a fall. 名亦既有, “the names are there now”: a fact. english “institutions” is correct and bloodless. the chinese word still has a blade in it.

names on bronze. 名 in this line is more than words. it is titles, ranks, and the written terms of law: what wang bi calls 名分, “names and portions”, which fix who is high and who is low. the age had a famous quarrel about it. in 536 bce zichan, chief minister of zheng, had the penal laws cast in bronze for all to read. shuxiang of jin wrote to protest: once the people know the text, they will stop looking to their betters and start arguing from the wording; 錐刀之末，將盡爭之, “they will contend over every tip of awl and knife”. wang bi uses that very phrase here: go past the needed names, and people 將爭錐刀之末. the laozi takes neither side of the old quarrel. it accepts the bronze and asks one thing of those who write on it: to know where to stop.

知止: to know the foot’s place. 止 is a foot. the shuowen calls it a base and says it was used for “foot”; its early forms are commonly read as a footprint (see the plate in passage 24, where a person on tiptoe is 企, a figure over this foot). a foot planted is a stop, so 止 is “to halt” and “the place where one halts”. 知止 is then to know where the foot goes down: how far the cutting, the naming, and the ranking should run, and no farther. the reward is 不殆, “no danger”, the phrase that passage 25 used of the dao as it goes round. passage 44 repeats the pair, and a confucian classic, the great learning, begins its account of the mind with the same two words: 知止而后有定, “know where to stop, and then there is steadiness”. the schools quarrelled over much and shared this. where today did you go one step past enough?

which side of the likeness is dao?. the last sentence is an open comparison, marked by 譬, “to liken”, and 猶, “is like”. its two halves are built alike: 道之在天下, “dao’s being in the world”, and 川谷之於江海, “streams and valleys in relation to river and sea”. most readers match dao with the sea: all things run to it as streams run down. wang bi reads it so, and thinks of the ruler who holds the dao. but the word order matches dao with the streams and the world with the sea: dao is in the world as the small waters are in the great, everywhere, feeding it, going toward it. then the dao is the small thing again, like the uncarved wood of line 2. the grammar does not decide, and perhaps the likeness is meant to run both ways, as water does in fact: the sea comes back as rain. legge decides, and adds “great”.

江 and 海: the river and heaven’s pool. in old chinese 江 is a proper name. it is the yangtze, as 河 is the yellow river; the shuowen describes its course from the mountains of shu to the sea. only later did the word mean any large river. so the picture is from the south, the country of chu, where every stream and marsh drains to one great water. 海, the sea, has one of the shuowen’s finest glosses: 天池也。以納百川者, “the pool of heaven: that which takes in the hundred rivers”. 川 is a stream in its channel, and 谷 the valley of passage 28. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to say 小浴, and the guodian slips 小谷, “small valleys”, for 川谷. the image returns in passage 66 with its reason given: river and sea are kings of the hundred valleys because they are good at lying below them. water does not obey the sea. it goes down.

wang bi: no summons, no seeking. on the last line wang bi writes: 川谷之求江與海，非江海召之，不召不求而自歸者。 “when streams and valleys make for the river and the sea, it is not that river and sea summon them. without summons and without seeking, they come home of themselves.” two negatives carry it. 不召: the sea sends no call. 不求: and in the end the streams are not seeking either. what looks like a pull from one side and a striving from the other is neither. it is the lie of the land. his verb is 歸, to go home (see passage 28). he then ties the three images of the passage together with the same word, 自: guests of themselves, evened of themselves, home of themselves. a ruler who sends out a summons has, by that act, shown that he is not the sea. who comes to you without being called?

legge’s brackets. legge opens with the dao “considered as unchanging”, a hedge of his own. then count his brackets; there are three. the world dares not deal with “(one embodying)” it as a minister: a person has been put in where the chinese has only the wood. heaven and earth unite “(under its guidance)”: a guide has been added to a line whose point is that no one directs. and “(men)” can know to rest in it. each bracket supplies an agent or an authority. his frame needs someone in charge, as a sermon does. he reads 始制有名 as “as soon as it proceeds to action, it has a name”, which loses the cut, and 知止 as “to rest in it”, which turns a limit into a refuge. he also makes the rivers and seas “great” and all things “submit themselves to him”. the guests have become subjects again.

無名 and 有名: the wood and the cut. the passage moves between 無名, without name, and 有名, having names; between the uncarved wood and the cut. it is easy to read the first as pure and the second as a fall. the text does not say so. the names “are there now”, as a fact, and it asks for 知止, to know where to stop. the two sides need each other. “nameless” is a name, and wood is called uncarved by someone who has seen a carved thing. they also turn into each other: the wood is cut into vessels, and streams with many names run to one sea. the lean toward the nameless answers an age that multiplied titles, ranks, and laws. it is not a rule against words. wood that is not cut holds no water, and people with no names cannot call each other. where does a name of yours serve, and where has it gone too far?

names and divisions are needed, and safety lies in knowing where to stop them.. names and divisions are needed, and safety lies in knowing where to stop them. do you agree that naming can go too far? where have you seen a name, a title, or a rule do harm? which names were put on you early: the clever one, the difficult one, the quiet one? how far do you still obey them? hold the opposite: more exact names bring more freedom, and what has no name cannot be cared for. what feelings and thoughts come? is there something in your life that you have named too much, or something that you refuse to name? why might that be?

with no order from anyone, people share out evenly of themselves.. with no order from anyone, people share out evenly of themselves. do you believe that? what have you seen that supports it, and what have you seen that does not? how much were you ordered as a child, and how much were you trusted? how does that shape what you expect of others now? now take the other view: with no one in command, the strong take the most, and order must be made. stay with it for a minute. what rises? which view do you apply to yourself: do you command yourself, or trust yourself? what would the other way feel like?

臣 the eye that looks down. the shuowen explains 臣 in three steps: 牽也, “to be led”; 事君也, “one who serves a lord”; 象屈服之形, “it shows the form of bending and submitting”. modern scholars, with the oracle-bone forms before them, commonly explain the graph as an eye, the same picture as 目, turned on its end. look at the two: 目 is an upright eye with two lines inside; 臣 has the same frame, opened at the right, with the inner strokes pushed sideways. an eye stood on its side is commonly taken as the eye of a person whose head is bowed: someone who looks up from below, or down at the ground. in the oldest texts 臣 is a male slave or captive; then a servant of the king; then any minister; then the humble word for “i” in front of a ruler. the shuowen’s own cousins fit the downcast eye. 臥, to lie down: 从人、臣，取其伏也, “a person and 臣; it takes the sense of lying prostrate”. 監, to look down on, to inspect: commonly explained as a person who bends over a basin of water, the first mirror. 臨, to look down from above, to preside. 宦, an official: 臣 under a roof. so chinese wrote “minister” with the eye of a prisoner. this passage says of the uncarved wood: nothing under heaven can 臣 it. it has no eye to lower. six strokes, and the order is a surprise. stroke one is the top horizontal. stroke two is a short vertical that hangs from it in the middle. stroke three is a horizontal that turns down: the top and right side of the small inner box. stroke four is a horizontal that closes that box below. stroke five is another short vertical, from the box down to the base. only then comes stroke six, the frame: one long line down the whole left side that turns at the foot and runs right along the bottom. the enclosing stroke is written last, although it stands at the left, so that the brush can fit it to what is already inside. the right side stays open. in seal script the eye is still a curve; the brush made it a set of shelves. keep the three horizontals of the interior evenly spaced, or the eye squints.

甘 a mouth that holds one thing. 甘 is one of the simplest and oldest signs of feeling in the script. the shuowen says: 美也。从口含一, “fine; from a mouth that holds 一”. the outer shape is 口, a mouth, drawn open with its top line run wide. the short stroke inside is a thing held on the tongue: not chewed, not swallowed, kept there because it is good. xu shen then adds three characters that a reader of this book will notice: 一，道也, “the one is 道”. commentators take him to mean the true taste, the “way” of flavour; he is not making a claim about the dao. still, the dictionary’s picture of sweetness is a mouth with the one in it. the family is small and pleasant. 甛, sweet (now written 甜): 甘 beside 舌, the tongue, “which knows sweetness”. 旨, fine flavour, and so the fine point of a text. 香, fragrant: the shuowen has millet over 甘. and 甚, “extreme”, one of the three things the sage puts away in passage 29: 甘 with a mate. sweet was the centre of the five flavours and belonged to earth and the middle. in this passage it describes dew: what heaven and earth give when they meet, with nothing added. passage 80 uses the word once more, as a verb, for people who “find their food sweet”. what do you hold in the mouth without wanting more? five strokes. the first is the long horizontal, written before anything hangs from it; it is the widest line. the second is the left vertical, which starts above the horizontal and crosses it. the third is the right vertical, the same on the other side. the fourth is the short horizontal inside: the thing in the mouth. it runs between the two walls. the fifth is the base that closes the mouth. two small points make the character. the verticals rise above the top line like the corners of a basket. and the inner stroke sits a little above the middle, so that the lower chamber is the larger: there is room in this mouth. in seal script the outline is one smooth curve, like a bowl seen from the side.

33 · dies and is not lost. one who knows others is clever. / one who knows the self is bright. / one who overcomes others has force. / one who overcomes the self is strong. / one who knows enough is rich. / one who walks on with effort has will. / one who does not lose the place lasts. / one who dies and is not lost has long life. eight short lines in one shape, each a new entry for a word that people prized. the first four are two pairs, and in each pair the object turns from others to oneself: to know others is cleverness, to know oneself is clear sight; to overcome others is force, to overcome oneself is strength. the last four stand alone: enough is wealth; forced walking is will; not to lose one’s place is to last; to die and not be lost is long life. the passage has no image from nature and no sage. it is the plainest in this part of the book. after three passages on war and one on rule, it turns to a single person, and takes the two great words of state policy, rich and strong, with it. the first two lines describe a turn of attention, and the whole contemplative life is in it. attention goes out by habit: it reads faces, weighs motives, predicts. that is 智, and it never has to stop, because other people are endless. turned round, the same attention finds its source. the text calls the result 明 and the shuowen draws that word as moonlight through a window: a quiet light, inside a room. the next pair applies it to struggle. the contest with others has winners; the contest in the chest ends in a person who is no longer divided. the rest follows as description. such a person knows enough, because the lack was the division. and the last line asks what in a person is not lost at death. it does not answer. it gives a word for it that means old age. the opening pair sets an order of work for anyone with authority. reading others is the daily craft: who is able, who is afraid, what the other side wants. the passage grants it a name and sets a second name beside it. a leader who has not looked at the self’s own fear and appetite will project them onto everyone, and the cleverness will serve them. so: the inward look, together with the look at people. the second pair is about power. force over others is real, and it is a stock that runs down and invites a greater force. command of oneself cannot be outbid; wang bi states it as a rule of direction. the fifth line is a rule for budgets and for ambition: an organisation or a person that cannot say “enough” is poor at any size. the state’s own slogan promised wealth and strength. this passage says where they are kept. later daoist practice read these lines as instruction for the body. 自勝: to be equal to oneself, to carry one’s own weight without strain; the old story says the man who won that war grew fat. 知足: the graph is a foot, and practice begins by feeling the feet as enough, the weight complete on them. 強行 is steady training, one step and then the next, and the caution in the word applies: effort that forces the breath or the joints builds will and not much else. 不失其所: keep the centre, low in the belly, the place that the weight and breath return to; a body that keeps it lasts. and the last line was the charter of the long-life arts. they sought 壽 in the body, and their best teachers said that it meant something the body could not hold. run the first pair as a timed exercise. for one conversation today, do what you usually do: read the other person. notice their mood, guess what they want. that is the first line, and you are probably good at it. in the next conversation, keep a part of the attention turned round. notice what you want from this person, where you tighten, when you stop listening and start preparing. do not fix anything. afterwards ask which conversation went better, and who was more visible to you in the second: they, or you. for the fifth line, take one thing you are trying to get more of, and say aloud the amount that would be enough. if you cannot name an amount, that is worth knowing. for the last line, there is nothing to do. read it again tomorrow.

知 and 智: one word, split. the first line has 知 at one end and 智 at the other. they are one word in two uses: 知 the verb, “to know”, and 智 the quality, “knowing, clever”. 智 is 知 with a mark added below to tell them apart, and early copyists often did not bother. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write the line 知人者知也: “one who knows others: knowing”. the effect is flat on purpose. to know people is to be knowing, and no more than that. the shuowen analyses 知 as 口, a mouth, and 矢, an arrow. later scholars explained: what one knows comes out of the mouth as fast as an arrow. that is cleverness: quick, aimed at a target outside, and useful; it was a paid skill. in this book 智 is rarely praise; passages 18, 19, 27, and 65 all distrust it. the line grants it and moves on.

not the greek “know thyself”. a western reader hears delphi in this line, and should be careful. the greek maxim first meant: know that you are a mortal and not a god; know your limit. later the west made self-knowledge an inventory of a thing called the self: its character, its motives, its soul. the chinese has no such thing here. 自 is not a noun. it is the reflexive word, in origin a picture of the nose, and it means “oneself” as the object of whatever verb comes next. 自知 is knowing, turned round. the same faculty that reads other people is pointed the other way, and the text gives it a different name, 明, as if it were a different light. wang bi says it is 超智之上, “above and beyond cleverness”. it does not gather more facts. it sees the one who gathers. we wrote “the self” because english needs an object, and it is too solid.

明: moonlight in a window. everyone learns 明 as 日, the sun, beside 月, the moon: two lights, so “bright”. that form is old. the shuowen’s main entry has another, 朙: 照也。从月从囧, “to shine on; from the moon and 囧”, and 囧 is a window with its lattice. moonlight that comes in at a window. the picture suits the laozi’s use better than a blaze of sun and moon together. 明 in this book is not brilliance. it is the kind of seeing that works in low light: “to know the constant is called 明” (16), “to see the small is called 明” (52). passage 24 said that one who shows the self is not 明. here one who knows the self is. it is the eye adjusted to the dark of passage 1. english “enlightened” is too loud, and it carries the eighteenth century with it. what can you see only when the lamp is out?

sunzi’s version. the age had another famous sentence on these two kinds of knowing. sunzi, on war: 知彼知己，百戰不殆, “know the other and know yourself, and in a hundred battles there is no danger”. for the strategist the two are equal parts of intelligence work: the enemy’s strength and your own, both counted before the fight. courts hired men for the first kind especially. reading people was a profession: the persuader studied a ruler’s wishes, and the ruler studied his ministers for signs of treason. the laozi takes the same pair and ranks it. knowledge of others is 智, the paid skill of the age. knowledge of oneself is of another order. sunzi’s reward for both is 不殆, “no danger”, a phrase this book also loves (passages 16, 32, 44). the laozi’s reward for the second is not safety in battle. it is light.

the war in the chest. 勝 is “to win, to overcome”. the shuowen gives an older sense: 任也, “to bear, to be equal to a load”, and the graph has 力, which it explains as a sinew. to 勝 a thing is first to be able to carry it. so 自勝 is to be equal to oneself. the han feizi explains the phrase with a story. zixia, a disciple of confucius, met zengzi, who asked why he had grown fat. he said: i won a war. at home i saw the right as the former kings held it, and i honoured it. outside i saw the pleasures of wealth and rank, and i honoured them too. the two fought in my chest and neither was winning, so i was thin. now the right has won, so i am fat. han fei concludes: 自勝之謂強. the body knew who had won.

強 as a good word?. in passage 30, 強 was the thing to avoid: do not force the world, do not take the strong place, and what reaches its forced prime grows old. passage 76 will call the stiff and strong “companions of death”. yet here, three passages later, 自勝者強 is praise. the two do not conflict; the book is redefining the word. it does the same in passage 52: 守柔曰強, “to keep to the soft is called strong”. strength pointed outward, at others, the text calls 有力, “having force”: a quantity that can be used up and met by a greater one. strength with nothing outside it to beat is 強 in the new sense. wang bi: 無物以損其力, “no thing can wear its force down”. english has one word, “strong”, for the bully and the oak. which did you mean the last time you used it of a person?

足: enough is a foot. 知足, “to know enough”. the word for “enough” is written with the graph for a foot, 足; the shuowen says 人之足也。在下, “a person’s foot; it is below”. the sense “sufficient” is usually explained as a loan for a word of the same sound, though some like to think of a thing that reaches its foot, its full measure. now set this beside the end of the passage before: 知止, “know where to stop”, where 止 is also a foot (see passage 32). the two phrases are a pair across the two passages, and passage 44 puts them in one line: 知足不辱，知止不殆, “know enough, no disgrace; know when to stop, no danger”. both say that the knowledge that matters is of a limit, and both write the limit with the part of the body that stands on the ground. the one on tiptoe in passage 24 knew neither.

“rich state, strong army”. 富 and 強 were the two most political words of the age. the reformers who rebuilt the warring states, shang yang in qin above all, had one programme, and later writers gave it four characters: 富國強兵, “enrich the state, strengthen the army”. wealth meant grain in the state’s granaries; strength meant conscripts in the field; and each fed the other. a ruler who heard 富 and 強 together heard policy. this passage takes both words and moves them inside one person. 強 is to overcome oneself. 富 is to know what is enough. it is a quiet act of theft from the vocabulary of the state. no granary can make a man rich in this sense, and no law can stop him from being so. the slogan had a long life: japan took it as the motto of its modernisation in the nineteenth century.

強行: praise, or a warning?. 強行者有志: “one who walks on with effort has will”. this is the one line of the eight that can be read against itself. wang bi reads it as praise: 勤能行之，其志必獲, “one who can walk it with diligence will surely gain the aim”. passage 41 supports him: the best student hears the dao and “walks it with diligence”. but look at the words. 強 as an adverb was the “forced” naming of passage 25, and passage 30 warned against 強 by name. 志, the heart’s aim, is what passage 3 says the sage weakens in people: 弱其志. on that reading, the line gives forced effort its due and no more: such a person has will. it does not say bright, or rich, or lasting. our rendering keeps the effort and the walking and does not decide. the line sits between “rich” and “lasts”. do you hear it as one of their company?

所: a place, from the sound of an axe. 所 is “place”, and it is one of the script’s odd borrowings. the shuowen defines it as 伐木聲也, “the sound of wood being chopped”, and quotes an ode: 伐木所所, “they fell the trees, suo, suo”. the graph has 斤, an axe, and 戶, a door, which gives the sound. the word for “place” had no picture and took this one. what place does the line mean? the text says only 其所, “its place”, or “one’s own”. legge makes it a station in society with duties. wang bi makes it a matter of measure: 量力而行, “gauge your strength and then walk”. body-practice readers take it as the centre, low in the belly, where breath and weight settle. the simplest sense may be best: the spot where a thing belongs, as a fish belongs in water (passage 36). the verb is 失, to let slip from the hand.

久 and 壽: two kinds of long. the last two lines end in two words for duration, and the shuowen ties them together: it defines 壽, long life, by the other word, 久也. 久 is “for a long time, to last”. its graph, the shuowen says, shows a person’s two legs with something that holds them from behind. to last is to be kept in place. 壽 is written with a short form of 老, old, on top: it is length of years in a body, the blessing that many bronze inscriptions ask of the ancestors first. the laozi uses the pair elsewhere: heaven and earth are 長 and 久 because they do not live for themselves (7); knowing when to halt leads to 長久 (44). the two lines step up: not losing the place, one lasts; and then the text goes one step past lasting.

亡 or 忘: not lost, or not forgotten?. the received text says 死而不亡. 亡 is “to be gone, to cease to exist”; the shuowen’s first sense is 逃也, “to flee”. so: one dies and is not gone. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 死不忘者壽也, with a heart under the same graph: 忘, “to forget”. one dies and is not forgotten. in early writing 亡 often stands for 忘, so the two texts may record one word, and a reader could take it either way. they point to different hopes. “not forgotten” is the hope of the zhou gentleman; a statesman of 549 bce defined “to die and not decay” as leaving behind virtue, deeds, or words. “not gone” is stranger. wang bi explains it by the dao that one lived by: 身沒而道猶存, “the body sinks away and the dao remains”. later daoist religion took it as the survival of a refined spirit. our “not lost” tries to leave both doors open.

壽 for the dead. 壽 means a long life in the body: many years, white hair, grandchildren. it is not “eternal life”, a phrase that brings the christian heaven, and it is not “immortality” in the greek sense of a soul that cannot die. that is what makes the last line a paradox in chinese and only a pious hope in english. the sentence gives the prize for staying alive to someone who has died. it says 死, “dies”, with no softening; the shuowen glosses the word as 澌, water that runs out, and as 人所離也, “what people part from”. the text does not deny the parting. it claims that something of the kind 壽, bodily and of this world, belongs to one who has parted. the first emperor sent ships to find the herb of deathlessness. this line had already told him where long life is found, and he would not have liked the first word.

wang bi: turned on oneself. wang bi reads the first four lines as one instruction about direction. 用其智於人，未若用其智於己也。用其力於人，未若用其力於己也。 “to use one’s cleverness on others is not as good as to use it on oneself. to use one’s force on others is not as good as to use it on oneself.” then the gain: 明用於己，則物無避焉；力用於己，則物無改焉, “when brightness is used on oneself, nothing evades it; when force is used on oneself, nothing alters it”. the ranking, 未若, is wang bi’s; the text only sets the two side by side. his claim is practical. other people can hide from your cleverness and resist your force. you cannot hide from your own clear sight, and force that is spent on yourself meets no opponent who will wear it down. he was about twenty when he wrote this, and he died at twenty-three. his commentary has lasted nearly eighteen centuries. see the last line of the passage.

a small dictionary. eight lines, and each has one shape: a description, the word 者, “the one who”, and a single term of value. the mawangdui copies are reported to close every line with 也, the particle of definition: 自知者，明也; 知足者，富也. it reads like a list of entries. the eight terms are the things that the age wanted: 智 cleverness, 明 clear sight, 力 force, 強 strength, 富 wealth, 志 will, 久 duration, 壽 long life. the passage does not reject one of them. it rewrites the entry for each. confucius called his programme 正名, “making names correct”; this is the laozi doing the same work its own way, and with a pattern. in the first four lines the object moves from others to oneself. in the last four the grasp loosens: enough, a place not lost, and a death. the first word of the passage is 知. the last is 壽.

legge’s “lot” and “position”. legge’s english is sound here, and two phrases show his century. 知足者富 becomes “he who is satisfied with his lot is rich”. a “lot” is what providence has assigned; the phrase belongs to the sermon that tells the poor to be content. the chinese says “knows enough”: a judgement that a person makes, of any amount. and 不失其所 becomes “does not fail in the requirements of his position”. 所, a place, has become a social station with duties attached, which one can fail. it is the ethics of a victorian household, upstairs and down. his first pair, “discerning” and “intelligent”, is hard to tell apart, so the step up from 智 to 明 is lost. he keeps the last line plain: “he who dies and yet does not perish, has longevity”, and “longevity” is exactly the right, bodily word. every line begins “he who”. the chinese 者 has no gender.

人 and 自: others and self. four lines turn on one pair: 人, others, and 自, self. to know others, to know the self; to overcome others, to overcome the self. many versions add a ranking: the second of each is the true one, and the first is a lesser thing. wang bi does this in his comment. the lines themselves give each side a name and stop: 智 and 明, 力 and 強. the two sides depend on each other. a self is known partly in the faces of others, and a person who watches the self alone has a small window. they also change places: the self that was overcome yesterday is one of the “others” today. the lean toward the inward answers an age that paid for the reading of rivals. it can turn as well: self-knowledge can become a mirror that no one else is let into. note the next pair too: enough, and walking on with effort. which do you trust less?

to know others is cleverness; to know the self is a different thing, a kind of light.. to know others is cleverness; to know the self is a different thing, a kind of light. which of the two are you more skilled at? how do you know? what made you a reader of other people: was it once needed for safety? and what did you avoid looking at in yourself? take the opposite: the self is known through others, and the inward look by itself deceives. hold that for a while. what do you feel? whose view of you do you most resist? what might it show?

the one who knows what is enough is the one who is rich.. the one who knows what is enough is the one who is rich. do you agree? when did you last feel that you had enough, and how long did it last? what did “enough” mean in the house where you grew up? was there a fear under it? the next line of the passage speaks for one who presses on with effort. take that side: wanting more is life, and “enough” is giving up. what arises as you hold it? which of the two do you judge in others, the content or the driven? what does that tell you?

something of a person is not lost at death, and that is the true long life.. something of a person is not lost at death, and that is the true long life. do you believe it? what do you think is not lost? where does your belief about death come from: a faith, a loss, a fear, a parent’s silence? hold the opposite: at death all of it ends, and a long life is a count of years. stay with it. what feelings come, and what thoughts? how does the side you take change the way you spend an ordinary day?

亡 a person gone into the corner. three strokes for the largest absence. the shuowen says 逃也。从人从乚: “to flee; from a person and 乚”, and 乚 is a bent line, a nook, a place to hide. a person has slipped into the corner and cannot be seen. that is the first sense: to run away, to be missing. then to lose a thing; then to be destroyed, as a state is; then to be dead. the oracle-bone forms are read in several other ways, and no account is agreed; the shuowen’s is the one the tradition taught. now see how much the script builds on the missing person. add a heart: 忘, to forget; the shuowen says 不識也, “not to recognise”, the mind’s thing gone. add an eye: 盲, blind; 目無牟子, “an eye with no pupil”. add wailing mouths: 喪, mourning (the plate in passage 31). and 望, to gaze into the distance, to hope: the shuowen explains it with a small story, 出亡在外，望其還也, “someone has fled and is abroad, and one looks out for the return”. even 無, the great “not-having” of this book, is glossed 亡也, and the oldest bamboo manuscripts often write 亡 where later copies have 無. so the word in the last line is not a dramatic word. it is the ordinary graph for a thing that is not where it was. the line says that one who dies is not, in that sense, missing. three strokes. the first is a dot at the top centre, pressed in and released. the second is a horizontal under it, long, rising a hair to the right. the third starts at the left under the horizontal, comes straight down, and then turns to run right along the bottom, in one movement with a firm corner. that is all. the corner is the nook where the person hid, and the brush must slow there: stop, set the tip, and go on. if the last stroke is too short, the character falls to the left; let its base run nearly as far right as the horizontal above. because there are so few strokes, the white space matters more than the ink. the character is mostly an open room with one wall and a floor. in running script the dot and the horizontal join, and the form is close to a single turning line.

知 an arrow and a mouth. left side: 矢, an arrow. the shuowen says the graph shows 鏑栝羽之形, “the shape of point, nock, and feathers”, and you can still find them: the top stroke is the head, the lines across are the shaft and its binding, and the two strokes that spread at the bottom are the fletching. right side: 口, a mouth; the shuowen says 人所以言食也, “that with which people speak and eat”. for the whole it gives only 詞也, “a word, an utterance”, and 从口从矢. why an arrow? the usual answer, from later commentators, is speed and aim: what is known is said at once and goes to the mark. another account takes 矢 mainly as a sound hint. either way, knowing was first something done with the mouth: to know a thing was to be able to say it. compare the first line of the book, where the dao that can be said is set aside. the arrow has a grim family: 矢 with a person is 侯, a lord, first the archery target; 矢 in a body is 疾, sickness; 矢 in the old form of 族, a clan, is the band that gathers under one banner with its arrows. put 日, the sun, or in old forms other marks, under 知 and you have 智, the word that this passage ranks second. knowledge of others flies outward to a target. the passage asks what happens when the archer turns the arrow round. eight strokes. the arrow first. stroke one is a short stroke at the top that falls to the left. stroke two is a short horizontal. stroke three is a longer horizontal below it. stroke four starts at the first horizontal, passes down through the second, and sweeps to the lower left: the shaft. stroke five would be a full right-falling stroke if the arrow stood alone; here it is cut to a dot, pressed and held, so that the arrow gives room to its neighbour. then the mouth. stroke six is its left side. stroke seven is the top and right side in one turn. stroke eight closes it. the mouth is set low, level with the foot of the arrow, not up beside its head. watch the gap between the dot and the mouth: it should be narrow and clean. the left side is all slant and movement, and the right is a still square.

富 a full jar under the roof. the top is 宀, a roof, the same one that covers the child in 字 (the plate in passage 25) and the woman in 安, peace. under it is 畐, which the shuowen treats here as the sound part. its early forms are commonly described as a jar with a narrow neck and a round belly, full to the top: the 一 is the lid or mouth, the 口 the neck, the 田 the belly, which has nothing to do with a field. a house with a full wine jar in it: 富. the shuowen’s gloss is 備也, “provided, complete”, and then 厚也, “thick”. wealth is first having everything needed, in store, under one’s own roof. the same jar fills other words. with the altar sign it is 福, blessing: the full jar set before the spirits. with cloth it is 幅, the full width of a bolt. with a knife it is 副, which the shuowen glosses 判也, “to split”: to cut the full thing in two, and so a second, a deputy. the opposite of 富 is as clear: 貧, poor, is 貝, a shell, under 分, to divide; 財分少也, “the goods divided and small”. so in the script a rich person is one whose jar is full, and a poor one is a person whose shells have been shared out. the passage adds a new entry: the rich one is whoever knows that the jar is full. the size of the jar is not mentioned. twelve strokes, from the roof down. stroke one is the dot at the peak. stroke two is a short stroke at the left that leans out to the left. stroke three is the roof line, a horizontal with a hook down at its right end. stroke four is a short horizontal under the roof: the lid. strokes five, six, and seven make the small mouth: left side, top and right side in one turn, and base. strokes eight and nine begin the belly: left side, then top and right side in one turn. stroke ten is the horizontal inside it. stroke eleven is the vertical inside it, crossing the last. stroke twelve closes the base. three boxes sit under one roof, so the danger is a tall, thin tower. keep the roof wide, the lid short, the neck narrow, and let the belly be the broadest of the three, as a jar is.

34 · the flood goes both ways. the great dao floods, oh: / it can go left and right. / the ten thousand things lean on it and live, / and it does not turn them away. / the work is complete; / it does not name it “mine”. / it clothes and feeds the ten thousand things / and does not act the lord. / always without wanting: / it can be named among the small. / the ten thousand things come home to it / and it does not act the lord: / it can be named great. / because to the end it does not make itself great, / it can complete its greatness. a river leaves its bed. the first line is that picture: the great dao floods and goes to both sides. then come seven short statements about how it behaves with the ten thousand things. they lean on it; it refuses none. the work is complete; it claims nothing. it clothes and feeds; it is no lord. then two names, small and great, for the same conduct. the verbs are verbs of a household: feed, clothe, come home. six times the passage says 不, “not”, and each 不 removes a mark of ownership: not refuse, not name, not lord, not lord again, not make itself great. the greatness of the last line is that which remains when each claim is taken away. look for the one who owns your attention. sights and sounds lean on awareness and appear in it; it turns none away, the pleasant and the unpleasant alike. it holds each one and puts no name of “mine” on it. thoughts come home to it when they end, and no master is found there to receive them. it is so little a thing that you can pass a whole life without notice of it: name it small. nothing that you have known was outside it: name it great. the passage does not ask you to become like this. it describes that which is the case before you do anything. the only error it names is 自為大, to make oneself great. the passage was read by men who wanted to be lords, in an age that paid for merit with rank and land. it tells them that the thing on which all depend keeps no accounts. a good parent, a good teacher, the person who maintains the system that no one sees: people lean on them and live, and the work has no signature. this is not modesty as a style. a leader who must be the host of each success makes all others into guests, and guests do not build the house. notice also the silk version, where the sage is named: greatness is completed by the one who does not act great. do not use the passage as a method to become great by a quiet road. the text says 終, “to the end”. on a flood plain the river is not the enemy of the field. it is the origin of the field. each flood leaves silt, and the silt is the soil that feeds the villages; the yellow river built the north china plain in this way and also drowned it many times. water goes left and right with no plan and feeds that which it touches. then all water goes home: the streams to the river, the river to the sea, the sea to cloud and rain. passage 32 gave the same picture: the dao in the world is like rivers and valleys that run to the sea. no part of the cycle is its lord. sunlight has the same manners. it lands on the leaf, the leaf lives, and no bill comes. try the unsigned act today. then, in the evening, do the reverse and count what came to you unsigned: who cooked, who built the road, whose patience held a meeting together. the passage has two movements and you can feel both in one day. in the first, things lean and are fed. in the second, things come home. note where in your day you were the one that leaned, and where you were the place to which a person returned, and if in that hour you needed to be the lord of it.

大道: a great road under water. 道 is first a road, and 大道 is the main road, the highway. passage 53 uses the phrase in that plain sense: 大道甚夷, “the great road is very level”, and people still prefer the side paths. we leave dao in chinese because “the way” with a capital sounds like a doctrine or a path to salvation. here the passage does a strange thing with the road. a road has edges and one direction. in the first line the road becomes a flood, and a flood has no edges and no direction. the picture cancels itself as you read it. what kind of road can you not step off?

氾: water over the banks. 氾 has 氵, water, at the left. the shuowen defines it with one word, 濫也, “to overflow”, and defines 濫 in turn as 氾也. the two make the compound 氾濫, a flood that leaves its bed. the word also means “to float, to drift” (also written 泛). so the line can be heard two ways: the dao spreads like flood water, or the dao drifts like a boat with no mooring. for the people of the yellow river plain, a flood was the great fear. mencius uses this exact word for the chaos before the sage-kings: 洪水橫流，氾濫於天下, “the great waters ran wild and flooded all under heaven”, until yu cut channels. the confucian hero puts water into channels. the laozi makes the unchanneled water its picture of the highest thing.

左右: both sides, and both helping hands. 其可左右 says, word for word, “it can left-right”. chinese nouns become verbs without a change of form, so the line is “it can go to the left and to the right”: flood water does not choose a side. a second sense is near. 左 and 右 were the first way to write two words for “help”, later written 佐 and 佑. the shuowen defines 左 as 手相左助也, “the hands help each other”, and 右 as 助也, “to help”. as a compound, 左右 also means the attendants who stand at each side of a ruler, and as a verb, “to steer, to have at one’s command”. the grammar permits a passive reading: “it can be turned left or right”, as water accepts each channel. which did the first hearers take: water that goes where it wants, or water that goes where it is led?

恃: the heart that leans. 恃 has 忄, the heart, at the left, and 寺 at the right for the sound. the shuowen says 賴也: to depend on, to lean on. it is a word with a moral risk. in most of its uses in early texts, to 恃 a thing is to presume on it: a state that leans on its walls, a minister who leans on favor. the laozi uses the word for the opposite virtue four times: 為而不恃, “to act and not lean on it” (2, 10, 51, 77). there the dao and the sage do not lean on their own work. here the direction turns. all things lean on the dao, and the dao permits it. the one that leans on nothing is the one that all can lean on. whom do you permit to lean?

不辭: does not refuse, or does not speak. 辭 has two families of meaning, and the line uses both. one is “words”: a speech, a statement, a plea in court. the shuowen starts there: 訟也, “to plead in a lawsuit”. the other is “to decline”: to refuse a gift or an office with polite words, and so to take one’s leave. with the second sense, the dao does not turn the things away; we render that. with the first, the dao gives life and says nothing about it: no speech, no claim, no instruction. passage 2 has almost the same line about the sage: 萬物作焉而不辭. a third reading is possible in the grammar: the things live and do not decline the gift. english must choose one. the chinese hearer gets a host who refuses no guest and makes no speech of welcome. legge chose the third reading and added a word.

功: merit was a currency. 功 is 工, work, with 力, strength. the shuowen gives it a political meaning: 以勞定國也, “to settle the state by one’s toil”. in the warring states this was not a soft word. the reforming states broke the old nobility of birth and paid for service. in qin, after the reforms of shang yang in the fourth century bce, a soldier rose through a ladder of ranks by counted achievements in battle, and land and servants came with each rank. 功 was written down, measured, and exchanged for a name and a holding. read 功成不名有 against that system: the work is complete, and no name is entered, and nothing is held. the line refuses the central transaction of its age. where is your work entered in a book?

不名有: three words that english must unpack. 不名有 is “not / name / have”. 名 is a verb, “to give a name, to claim by name”, and 有 is “having, possession”. the sense is: it does not call the result its property. some editors think that the line is damaged and should end with 不有, “and does not possess”, as in passages 2 and 51; the mawangdui silk texts are reported to have 弗名有 (see the silk version), so the odd phrase is old. a point about our english: the chinese has no “it” in these lines. from 萬物恃之 to the end no subject is written; 之 and 其 point back to the dao. english grammar forces a pronoun each time, and each “it” makes the dao more of a thing that stands apart and acts. read the lines again without the pronouns: “clothes, feeds, does not act the lord”. the verbs are there, and no one is there.

衣養: clothe, cover, or love. 衣 is a garment, and as a verb (read yi) “to put clothes on someone”. 養 has 食, food, in it: the shuowen says 供養也, “to provide for”. so 衣養 is to clothe and feed, the two daily acts of a parent. the word for “mother” does not occur in this passage, but these are the mother’s verbs; compare 貴食母, “to value the mother who feeds”, in passage 20. other old editions differ here. the heshang gong text reads 愛養, “loves and feeds”; the fu yi edition reads 衣被, “clothes and covers”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to have no such line at all. we keep the pinned text. notice what the plain version does: it makes the highest thing in the book do housework.

主: the flame in the lamp. 主 is “lord, master, owner”, and also “host”, the opposite of 客, guest. the shuowen explains the graph as a picture of a small thing: 鐙中火主也, “the flame in a lamp”. the dot at the top is the fire; the rest is commonly explained as the lamp and its stand. the character 炷, a wick, keeps that first sense. from the one point of light in a dark room came the head of the house, and from that the lord of a state. 不為主 is then “does not make itself the flame at the center”. the line comes two times. all things are fed, and no master appears; all things come home, and no host stands at the door to receive them. have you ever been given much by a person who did not make you a guest?

常無欲: who is without wanting?. three characters stand between two commas: “constant / without / desire”. they have no subject. most readers take the dao as the subject: it feeds all things and wants nothing back, so it can be classed with small things, which ask for little. wang bi takes the things as the subject: when the world has no wants, each thing is in its place and no giver is noticed. the same three characters open a line of passage 1: 常無欲，以觀其妙, “always without wanting, to see its subtlety”. some editors think that the words came into this passage from there. the silk texts are reported to read here: 則恆无欲也, “then it is constantly without wanting”, with 恆 for 常, because 恆 was the personal name of emperor wen of han and later copies avoided it.

小 and 大: two names for one thing. the passage gives the dao two names, and they are opposites. it asks for nothing and is not noticed: name it with the small. all things return to it and it does not rule them: name it great. the two clauses are built alike, 可名於小 and 可名為大, and each begins with 可, “can”; the small word after 名 differs, 於小, “classed among the small”, against 為大, “named as great”. both are names that are permitted, not names that are true. passage 25 said it directly: 強為之名曰大, “forced to name it, i say ‘great’”. passage 32 said 樸雖小, “the uncarved wood, though small”, and no one in the world can make it a subject. the shuowen entry for 大 reads 天大，地大，人亦大, “heaven is great, earth is great, the human is also great”; the graph is a person with arms out. 小 is commonly explained as three small grains. a thing that is correctly called by two opposite names has, in fact, no name.

歸: the bride goes home. 歸 is “to return”, but the shuowen defines it with a wedding: 女嫁也, “a woman marries”. a bride was said to 歸 when she went to the house of her husband: the book of songs sings 之子于歸，宜其室家, “this girl goes to her home; she will order well her house and family”. in the old view that house was her true home, and her arrival was a return. so the word is not “go back” in the sense of retreat. it is “to arrive where one belongs”. the dead also 歸: the shuowen defines a ghost, 鬼, as 人所歸爲鬼, “that which a person goes home as”. english “return” gives the direction and loses the house. “merge” loses both. the things in this line go home as a person does, and they find that the house has no master. see 主, the lord who is absent.

the silk texts: home two times, and a sage. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to give a shorter and different passage. it opens 道渢呵, without 大, and with a different water word. the lines on leaning and on clothing are absent. after 成功遂事而弗名有也, “it completes the work and follows the task through and does not name it ‘mine’”, the silk is reported to have 萬物歸焉而弗為主 two times: all things come home and it does not act the lord, so it can be named with the small; all things come home and it does not act the lord, so it can be named great. one fact, two names. then: 是以聖人之能成大也，以亓不為大也，故能成大, “thus the sage can complete greatness: because the sage does not act great, the sage can complete greatness”. our pinned text has no sage, and the last line is about the dao. many received editions have the sage. passage 63 says the same of the sage in almost the same words.

wang bi: they do not know where it came from. on the first line wang bi writes: 言道氾濫，無所不適，可左右上下周旋而用，則無所不至也. “this says that the dao floods over; there is no place that it does not reach. it can be used left and right, up and down, round and about; so there is no place where it does not arrive.” he adds up and down to left and right. on the small name: 萬物皆由道而生，既生而不知所由. “the ten thousand things all are born by way of the dao, and once born, they do not know by way of what.” for wang bi the smallness is this ignorance: the giver is so little felt that the gift seems to have no source. on the last line he only quotes passage 63: 為大於其細，圖難於其易, “do the great in its fine detail; plan the hard in its easy part”.

legge: obedience and a presiding lord. legge was a missionary, and his sentence for 不辭 shows it: all things depend on the dao, “not one refusing obedience to it”. the chinese has no word for obedience; he moved the refusal from the dao to the creatures and made it a matter of submission. for 歸 he adds a bracket: the things “return (to their root and disappear)”, a reading from passage 16, and death comes into a line that only speaks of home. for the second 不為主 he writes that the things “do not know that it is it which presides over their doing so”. the chinese says that it does not act the lord. legge’s english says that it does preside, in secret. a god who rules and is not seen is a christian idea. the line is harder than that: no one presides.
