one thing done, no name entered. today, do one useful thing for a person or a place and leave no mark of the giver. fill the kettle. fix the shared document. pay for the next person. then watch the mind for the next hour. it will want to mention the thing, or to be seen near it, or at least to tell itself a story about a generous person. this is 名有, to name it “mine”. do not fight the wish. only see how fast it comes. then think about what feeds you every day without a signature: the water system, the soil, the people who wrote the words you think with.

小 and 大: one act, seen from two sides. two pairs run through the passage: 小 small and 大 great, and lord and guest. the two names come from one act. the dao does not act the lord: seen from its lack of wanting, that is small; seen from all that comes home to it, that is great. so small is not the humble, good name, and great is not the proud, bad one. each is true from one side. the last line is often turned into a method: be modest, and you will be great. the chinese gives a reason, 以, and not a plan. a smallness that is worn to gain greatness is already 自為大, making oneself great. and the pair moves. that which is great because it holds all things is, for the same reason, plain and easy to overlook; that which is overlooked is what all things lean on. where in your work is the small thing the great one?

the greatest work feeds all things, claims nothing, and does not act the lord.. the greatest work feeds all things, claims nothing, and does not act the lord. do you agree that the largest work is done with no claim? who has done such work for you? how much do you need credit? remember a time when your work was not named. what did you feel, and where did you learn that feeling? take the opposite view: to claim your work is honest, and to hide it is a false modesty that lets others take it. hold that. what arises? which of the two do you dislike in others, the one who claims or the one who hides? why might that matter?

greatness is completed by the one who does not make itself great.. greatness is completed by the one who does not make itself great. is that true of the great people you have known in person? when you make yourself small, is it free, or is it a way to be safe or to be praised? how can you tell? now hold the other side: no one becomes great by accident, and a person must stand up and take their full size. what does your body do with that? which side clashes with what you were taught? what has that teaching given you, and what has it cost?

歸 a bride, a broom, a foot. this character has three parts, and the shuowen names each one: 从止，从婦省，𠂤聲, “from 止; from 婦, abbreviated; 𠂤 gives the sound”. start at the right. 帚 is a broom: a hand shape at the top and hanging cloth or bristles below. put 女, a woman, beside the broom and you have 婦, a wife; the shuowen says 从女持帚灑掃也, “a woman who holds a broom to sprinkle and sweep”. in 歸 the woman is left out and the broom stands for her: that is what 婦省, “婦 abbreviated”, means. at the lower left is 止. today it means “to stop”, but its early form is a footprint, and as a part of characters it means movement on foot: 步 (a step) is two of them. at the upper left is 𠂤, which the shuowen calls a small mound; here it is only the sound. so: a foot goes, and a wife is in it. the shuowen’s definition is 女嫁也, a woman marries. the oldest forms have only the mound and the broom, with no foot, and scholars do not agree on what they picture; hold the wedding as the dictionary’s reading. the short form 归 comes from quick handwriting; the foot is gone from it. in this passage the ten thousand things are the bride. they go to the house where they belong, and the text says twice that the house has no lord. eighteen strokes. the mound first: a short stroke that falls to the left, a vertical, a horizontal with a corner, a horizontal, a second horizontal with a corner, a horizontal. then the foot beneath it: a vertical, a short horizontal to its right, a second vertical at the left, and a base stroke that rises to the right, toward the broom. then the broom: a horizontal with a corner, a horizontal, a second horizontal; a dot, a horizontal with a hook that covers; a vertical, a horizontal with a corner and a hook, and last a long vertical through the cloth. watch stroke ten, the base of the foot. it lifts toward the right half and joins two columns into one character. the left side is narrow and stacked; the right is wider and hangs from the last vertical like cloth from a pole. in the cursive hands the whole left side becomes two quick strokes, and the short form 归 was made from that.

衣 a robe with its collar. 衣 is a picture, and you can still see it. the dot and the line at the top are the collar. below, the strokes cross as the two sides of a robe cross over the chest; a chinese robe closed left side over right, and to close it the other way was the mark of a foreigner. the shuowen explains the word by a pun, 衣，依也: “a garment is that which one leans on”, and 依 (to lean on, to depend) is 人, a person, beside 衣. it adds 上曰衣，下曰裳: “the upper piece is called 衣, the lower is called 裳”. its reading of the picture, 象覆二人之形, “it shows two people covered”, is not followed by most modern scholars, who see collar, sleeves, and crossed lapels. as a left-side part the character is written 衤, as in 被 (a cover) and 補 (to mend). look also at 初, “beginning”: 衣 with 刀, a knife. the shuowen says 裁衣之始也, “the start of the cutting of a garment”. to begin is to make the first cut in the cloth. in this passage 衣 is a verb: the dao clothes the ten thousand things. the pun of the dictionary agrees with the line before: the things lean, and that on which they lean is their coat. six strokes. a dot at the top. a horizontal under it, long, the shoulder line. third, from the middle of that line, a stroke that falls far to the left. fourth, a vertical that starts on the third stroke, goes down, and ends in a lift to the right; this small lift is the center of gravity. fifth, a short stroke that falls left, placed high on the right. sixth, the long stroke that falls to the right; it begins thin, swells, and ends in a flat tail. watch strokes three and six: they are the two hems of the robe and must open at the same angle, or the figure leans. in seal script the form is nearly symmetrical, a collar over two curved lapels. the clerical script broke the curves into these six separate strokes.

35 · bland beside the feast. hold the great image: / all under heaven goes toward it. / goes, and meets no harm: / rest, evenness, great ease. / music and cakes: / the passing guest stops. / the dao, as it comes out of the mouth: / bland! it has no flavor. / look at it: not enough to see. / listen to it: not enough to hear. / use it: not enough to end it. the passage has two halves that seem not to fit. the first is about power: hold the great image and the whole world moves toward it, unharmed, into three kinds of peace. the second is about dinner: music and cakes stop a traveler, but the dao in the mouth has no flavor, and eye and ear get too little from it. the join is the question of attraction. two things draw people. one draws by flavor, and the guest stops and later goes on. the other has no flavor at all, and all under heaven goes to it and stays whole. the first attraction is strong and short. the second is so weak that it cannot be sensed, and it does not run out. each experience that stops you has a flavor: pleasure, fear, a good idea, a mood. the one who tastes them has none. attention to a sound is not loud; the sight of red is not red. look for that which is aware and you find not enough to see: no color, no place, no edge. contemplatives of many schools report the first meeting with it as a disappointment. it is bland. the mind is a passing guest and goes back to the music. but a person can rest in that plainness for a whole life and not reach the end of it, and sights and sounds go to it and are not harmed by it. to hold it is not a grip. it is closer to not being bought by each cake. rulers of the time wanted exactly the first line: that all under heaven should go to them. most tried music and cakes: displays, rewards, promises, a strong flavor of some kind. it works, and the passage admits it; the guest does stop. but a guest who came for the feast leaves when a better table is laid. a leader who draws people by charm must supply more charm each year. the second way is poor in drama. the leader keeps to a thing with no particular quality, which wang bi calls “not cold, not warm, not cool”, and so excludes no one. people come and are not used. be careful with the later history of “great peace”: an image that is held with a shackle grip becomes a banner. taste belongs to the body, and the body knows this passage well. strong flavors, sugar and salt and fat, stop us as bait stops a fish; the food industry is a science of 餌. the staple foods of the long-lived are bland: rice, bread, water, tea. you can eat them every day because they do not shout. the same law holds in movement. a showy effort feels like something; an efficient movement feels like almost nothing, and teachers of the internal martial arts say that correct structure feels bland, even empty. breath is the clearest case. it has no flavor, you cannot see it, you hardly hear it, and you have used it since birth and not come to the end of it. do the water exercise. then make a list, in the evening, of what stopped you today as music and cakes stop a traveler: a headline, a snack, a message, a quarrel. no blame; the passage says plainly that this is what happens to guests. then make a second list, shorter and harder: the flavorless things that carried the day and that you did not notice. air, light, the floor, a person who was simply there. ask of each list: which of these could i use for forty years?

執: the grip of an arrest. 執 is a hard word for “hold”. the shuowen defines it as 捕罪人也, “to seize a criminal”, and the early forms are commonly explained as a person on the knees with both hands in a wooden shackle. from that came each firm grip: to hold a tool, a post, an opinion. the laozi mostly speaks against it: 執者失之, “the one who grips it loses it” (29 and 64). now it tells the reader to grip, and the thing to be gripped is an image with no shape. the hand closes on nothing. passage 14 has the same hard grammar: 執古之道, “hold the dao of old”, in the passage that says the dao cannot be seen, heard, or touched. how does a hand hold that which it cannot close around? perhaps only by not holding a different thing.

大象: image, emblem, elephant. 象 is the elephant; the shuowen describes its long nose and tusks. by the warring states the word also meant a likeness, the form by which an unseen thing is known. it became a technical term: the signs in the sky are 天象, and the figures of the book of changes are 象. english “image” suggests a picture in the mind, a thing that a person forms. passage 41 says that this one cannot be formed: 大象無形, “the great image has no shape”. so 大象 is a name for the dao: the pattern behind all patterns. wang bi calls it “the mother of heaven’s images”. a reader of chinese also sees, for a moment, the animal: “take hold of the great elephant”. the line does not mean that. but the largest land animal is in the word, and it is hard to hold.

天下往: people went on foot to a better state. 往 is “to go toward”. the shuowen glosses it with 之, “to go to”. most english versions write “comes”, from the viewpoint of the one who holds. the chinese stands with the people: they go. in the warring states this was a fact of policy. borders were open to farmers, and the strength of a state was its number of households. rulers competed for migrants. king hui of liang complains to mencius that he works hard for his people and yet his population does not grow. mencius answers that people go to a humane ruler 由水之就下, “as water goes downward”. the laozi agrees about the movement and removes the program. nothing is offered. the one at the center holds an image that has no shape, and the world walks toward it.

往而不害: who does not harm whom?. four characters: “go / and / not / harm”. classical chinese does not mark active and passive, and gives no object. three readings are in the line together. the people go and are not harmed; we render this one. the people go and do no harm, to each other or to the one they go to. or the going itself does no damage: the world moves and nothing breaks. wang bi keeps the third: the great image is formless and leans to no side, so all things can go and are not hindered. the shuowen defines 害 as 傷也, “to wound”, and says that the roof and the mouth in the graph show that harm starts with words in the house. legge and many others add “him” and “men”. the chinese has no persons here, only motion and no wound.

安平太: three words for peace, or two. three characters with no grammar between them. 安 is a woman under a roof: the shuowen says 靜也, “still”, 从女在宀下. it is the peace of being safe at home. 平 is “level”: ground with no high and low, a scale in balance, and so fairness. 太 is the same word as 泰: wide, at ease; it is the name of the hexagram in the book of changes where heaven and earth meet. so: safety, evenness, ease. english has one word, “peace”, and its root is a pact that ends a war. a second reading is old and serious. 安 is also a connecting word, “then, thereupon”. the line is then “they go and meet no harm; and so: even, and at great ease”, and 平太 is one compound. the same two words in the other order became a slogan with a long history.

太平: what the two words did later. 平 and 太 in this line, reversed, are 太平, “great peace”. in the han dynasty this became the name of the perfect age that a true ruler would bring. a long religious book, the taipingjing, the “scripture of great peace”, promised it. in 184 ce the yellow turban movement rose under that sign with hundreds of thousands of followers, and the wars that followed ended the han. seventeen centuries later a rebel state took the same name, the taiping heavenly kingdom (1851–1864), now with a christian vision; its war cost some twenty million lives. so the words of a line about a world that meets no harm were carried on the flags of two of the bloodiest risings in chinese history. each time, people held an image very tightly. was it the great image, or music and cakes?

樂: music, and joy. one graph writes two words: yue, “music”, and le, “joy, pleasure”. the confucian school made a doctrine of the pun: 樂者樂也, “music is joy”, says the record of music. the shuowen takes the graph as a picture of drums on a wooden stand: 象鼓鞞。木，虡也. here the word is yue, because it stands beside food as the second attraction of a feast. but the reader sees le too: pleasure and cakes. music was also statecraft. court music with bronze bells was a ruler’s display, and confucians held that correct music made correct people. the mohists wrote a whole chapter, “against music”, on its cost. the laozi does not argue. it only notes what music does to a person on the road: the person stops.

餌: cake, and bait. 餌 has 食, food, at the left. it is a cake of steamed rice or flour, a treat for a feast. it is also the usual word for bait: the thing on the hook, the thing in the trap. later, 餌 is the verb for “to lure” an enemy, and daoist texts use it for taking drugs of long life. the line gives the pleasant sense first: music and cakes, and the traveler stops, as any tired person does. the second sense arrives a moment later. the traveler has been caught. good smells and sounds are the hooks of the world, and the dao is described next as a thing with no smell and no sound: it has nothing to put on a hook. notice the fairness of this. the dao does not catch people. what stopped you on the road today?

過客: the one who is passing through. 客 is a guest, and also a stranger: a person who lodges in a house that is not theirs. the shuowen defines it as 寄也, “to lodge, to stay for a time”. the roads of the warring states were full of 客: traders, envoys, and the “guest-ministers” who went from court to court with advice to sell. great lords kept thousands of them at their tables, and fed them in grades. 過客 is a guest who is only passing. later chinese poetry took the phrase as a name for human life. li bai wrote: 夫天地者，萬物之逆旅也；光陰者，百代之過客也. “heaven and earth are the inn of the ten thousand things; time is the passing guest of a hundred generations.” read the line with that sense. each of us is on the way through, and each of us stops for music and cakes.

出口: out of the mouth that eats. 道之出口 is “the dao’s coming out of the mouth”: the dao as it is spoken. 道 itself can mean “to say”, as in the first line of the book, so the phrase is also “the saying, as it leaves the mouth”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 故道之出言也，曰淡呵亓無味也: “so when the dao puts out words, they are called bland: they have no flavor”. wang bi also paraphrases with 出言, “puts out words”. the received 口 is the stronger picture. the shuowen defines the mouth as 人所以言食也, “that with which a person speaks and eats”. one opening, two directions: cakes go in, words come out. the passage puts the dao in the traffic of the mouth and says that it has no taste. english “when it is spoken” loses the tongue.

淡: bland is a word of praise. the shuowen defines 淡 as 薄味也, “thin flavor”. in english, “bland”, “insipid”, and “tasteless” are complaints; legge wrote “insipid”. in chinese, 淡 became one of the highest words of praise. the zhuangzi says: 君子之交淡若水，小人之交甘若醴. “the friendship of noble people is bland like water; the friendship of small people is sweet like new wine.” water does not tire the tongue, so one can drink it for a lifetime. painters and poets later prized 平淡, the “even and bland”: pale ink, plain words, a style with nothing that seizes the eye. the laozi itself says 恬淡為上, “calm and bland is best” (31), and tells the reader to 味無味, “taste that which has no taste” (63). a strong flavor ends the appetite. what have you been able to return to every day without tiring of it?

不足: three times “not enough”. the last three lines have one frame: verb, 之, 不足, verb. look at it, not enough to see. listen to it, not enough to hear. the pairs are exact in chinese: 視 is to direct the eyes and 見 is to see something; 聽 is to give ear and 聞 is to hear something. the effort is made and the result does not come. passage 14 has the same pairs: 視之不見…聽之不聞, “look for it, not seen; listen for it, not heard”. 足 is a foot, and so “to have enough to stand on, to be worth”. the first two lines sound like a judgment against the dao: it is not worth a look. then the third line turns the same words around: use it, and the use is not enough to finish it. the lack in the first two lines was on the side of our eyes and ears. in the third it is on the side of our need. we are too small to exhaust it.

既: the meal is over. 既 usually means “already”. here it is a verb, “to finish, to come to the end of”. the shuowen enters the word under the older graph 旣 and defines it as 小食也, “a small meal”. the early form is commonly explained as a person who kneels at a food vessel and has turned the head away: the meal is over. if that is right, the last word of the passage goes back to the table where the passage began, with music and cakes. a feast is the thing that ends: the dishes are emptied and the guest goes on. the dao is the meal at which no one reaches the turn of the head. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 用之不可既也, “use it: it cannot be finished”, with 可, “can”, where the pinned text repeats 足, “enough”, for a third time. the book says the same in other pictures: 用之不勤, “use does not wear it out” (6); 用之或不盈, “use never fills it” (4).

wang bi: not cold, not warm, not cool. wang bi on the first line: 大象，天象之母也，不寒不溫不涼，故能包統萬物，無所犯傷，主若執之，則天下往也. “the great image is the mother of heaven’s images. it is not cold, not warm, not cool; so it can enfold and gather the ten thousand things and wound none. if a lord holds it, all under heaven goes to him.” an image that has one quality, such as heat, excludes the opposite quality. only an image with no quality can hold all. note his word 主, lord: for wang bi the line is advice to a ruler. on the second half he is honest about the audience: when people hear the words of the dao, 乃更不如樂與餌，應時感悅人心也, “they are in fact not equal to music and cakes, which at once move and please the human heart”.

legge: “to him who holds”. legge begins “to him who holds in his hands the great image (of the invisible tao), the whole world repairs.” the chinese has no “him”: 執大象 is a bare verb and its object, and we render it as an imperative only because english needs some form. his bracket explains the image before the reader can wonder at it. his people “resort to him, and receive no hurt”; see the open grammar of that line. for 餌 he writes “dainties”, a word from a victorian tea table, and he softens the last part with “though … seems”: the dao only seems insipid. the chinese does not say “seems”. it says 無味: it has no flavor. legge defends the dao against a charge of dullness. the text pleads guilty, and means it as praise.

drink plain water slowly. pour a glass of plain water at room temperature. drink it slowly, as you would taste a wine. for the first seconds the tongue looks for a flavor and reports that nothing is there: 無味. stay with it. after some moments the water has a coolness, a weight, a faint sweetness or a mineral edge. the tongue had to become quiet before it could find them. then notice the next thing that you taste after the water, and how loud it is. do the same once today with the ears: one minute of the plain sound of the room before you put on music.

味 and 無味: the feast and the plain. the pair is 味 and 無味, flavor and no flavor: the feast with music and cakes, and a dao that is bland. a moral reading makes the feast a temptation and the plain taste a virtue. the text makes no such charge. it reports two effects. flavor makes the guest stop, and the guest is one who will go on. that which has no flavor stops no one, and use does not end it. the two sides need each other: “bland” is a word for a tongue that has known flavor, and passage 63 says 味無味, to taste the tasteless, which is still a tasting. the preference is for what can be returned to, in an age of court display. it also turns. plainness that is praised and shown becomes a flavor, with its own guests. and some who stop for the music stay to hear what has no sound. what is your feast, and what is your water?

what draws us by flavor holds us for a while; what is plain cannot be used up.. what draws us by flavor holds us for a while; what is plain cannot be used up. do you agree? name something sweet that ended, and something plain that you still return to. what is the music and cake that stops you on your road? when did it first get that power? take the opposite: flavor is the point, and a life of plain water is a life not tasted. stay with it. what feelings arise? do you distrust pleasure, or do you distrust plainness? where might that come from?

to one who holds the great image all the world comes, and comes to no harm.. to one who holds the great image all the world comes, and comes to no harm. have you known a person or a place that people went toward and were not harmed? what was held there? what do you hold on to that draws people to you, or keeps them away? did you choose it? hold the other view: people come for what they can get, and one who draws a crowd will be harmed or do harm. what comes up? which view matches your own history with groups and leaders? why is that worth seeing?

淡 water beside two fires. read it from the left. 氵 is water: three drops, the form that 水 takes at the side of a character. to the right are two fires, one on the other. 火 is a flame with a spark at each side; doubled, it is 炎, and the shuowen says 火光上也。从重火, “the light of fire goes up; from fire, doubled”. today 炎 means blazing heat and inflammation. so the character for “bland” is water beside a blaze. it is tempting to tell a story from that: fire put out, flavor boiled away. the shuowen does not tell that story. it says 从水炎聲: water gives the meaning, and 炎 is there for its sound. its definition is 薄味也, thin flavor, as a broth with too much water. but the sound part gives the character a family, and the family is worth a look. put 言, speech, in place of the water, and you have 談, “to talk, to chat”, also 炎聲 in the shuowen. this passage is about the dao when it comes out of the mouth: its talk, 談, is 淡. in mandarin the two differ only in tone, tan and dan. that is the modern sound; but scholars of the old sounds also put both words in one rhyme group, and they name the group 談. the sense of 淡 grew from weak soup to pale colors, light ink, a quiet season of trade, and a calm heart: 淡泊, to want little. eleven strokes. water first: a dot, a second dot under it, then a stroke that rises from low left toward the fires. then the upper fire, in four strokes: a dot at the left, a short stroke at the right that falls left, the long stroke that falls to the left, and last a short dot where a long right-falling stroke would be. then the lower fire: a dot, a short stroke that falls left, the long left-falling stroke, and the final long stroke that falls to the right. watch stroke seven against stroke eleven. they are the same stroke of 火, but the upper fire draws its right leg in to a dot, and only the lower fire is given the full sweep. two full sweeps would fight; a good hand lets one flame yield. the third water stroke points up at the flames, and the white space between water and fire must stay open.

客 a foot arrives under a roof. the top part, 宀, is a roof; you can see the ridge and the two eaves. it marks things of the house: 家 (home: a roof over 豕, a pig), 安 (rest: a roof over 女, a woman; see three words for peace), 室 (a room), 寄 (to lodge), and 害, the harm of this passage, which the shuowen says begins with words under a roof. under the roof here is 各. the shuowen takes 各 as the sound of the character and defines the whole as 寄也, “one who lodges”. but 各 is not an empty sound. its lower part is 口, here commonly explained as the opening of a dwelling. its upper part, 夂, is the picture of a foot that points down, toward the viewer: someone is arriving. early inscriptions use 各 for the verb “to arrive”, later written 格. so 客 is: a foot comes to a door, under a roof. a guest. the same foot walks in 路 (road: 足 with 各). the mawangdui scribes are reported to have written this line as 過格止, with 格 for 客: they wrote the arrival and left the roof off. now see the word for “stops” at the end of the line: 止 is also a foot, the footprint that points up and away. the line begins with a foot that comes in and ends with a foot that rests. nine strokes. the roof takes three: a dot at the top center, a short dot at the left that leans down, and a horizontal that ends in a hook back to the left. the roof must be wide enough to cover all that follows. then the foot, 夂: a stroke that falls to the left; a short horizontal that turns and falls left in one movement; then a long stroke that falls to the right. watch this sixth stroke. it reaches out past the roof on the right, like a traveler’s leg in mid-step, and it is the one free line in the character. last the opening, 口: left side, top and right side in one stroke, then the base. keep the box small and directly under the crossing of the two long strokes, so that the foot seems to stand on the threshold.

36 · fish stay in the deep. what is to be drawn in / must first be stretched. / what is to be weakened / must first be made strong. / what is to be pulled down / must first be raised up. / what is to be taken / must first be given. / this is called the faint light. / soft and weak overcome hard and strong. / fish must not slip out of the deep. / the state’s sharp tools / must not be shown to people. four pairs with one frame: 將欲…之，必固…之. each pair sets a verb against its opposite: draw in and stretch, weaken and strengthen, pull down and raise, take and give. then a name for the knowledge of this: the faint light. then a statement with five characters and no particles: soft, weak overcome hard, strong. then two prohibitions, a fish and a state. the pictures are a lung, a bow, a house, a bird in the hand, green wood, a blade, deep water. nothing in the chinese says who acts. that silence is why the passage has two histories, one as a manual and one as a description of how the world turns. the text can carry both, and a careful reader keeps both open for as long as possible. watch a strong emotion. anger must reach its full stretch before it draws in; a craving is strongest in the moment before it lets go. to push against it at the top only strings the bow tighter. to know this, while the emotion is still loud, is a faint light. it does not feel like power. it is a small, quiet seeing that the peak is already a turn. the fish is the same lesson from the other side. attention lives in a depth that has no name. when it leaps out to be seen, to be a meditator, to be a person with insight, it is a fish in air. the sharp tool of the inner life is the one that you have no need to display, even to yourself. the readers were rulers and their advisers, and they knew the cases: gifts that opened roads for armies, allies who were fed until they burst. it is right to read the passage as a warning before reading it as a tool. when a rival gives you land, praise, or room to grow, ask what is being stretched. when an organization is at its largest and most admired, it is strung like a bow. the last line has two old readings and they still divide people who lead. han feizi: keep reward and punishment in your own hand and do not show how you decide. wang bi: the true tool is that no one feels a tool; a leader who must show the whip has lost. the debate over the code cast on bronze asks which secrecy serves the people. this passage can be read as an instruction in movement. to coil, first extend. a throw starts with the arm drawn back; a jump starts with a bend of the knees. chinese martial arts made a rule of the fourth pair: to take the opponent’s balance, first give the direction that the opponent wants. push, and the partner is not there; the force that was strong travels past its base and falls. this is soft and weak in the exact sense of the characters: wood that bends and returns. it is not limp. and the fish: power in the body lives low and deep, in the legs and the centre. shown early, in tense shoulders and a hard face, it is already out of the water. the four pairs are a description of each wave. water draws back from the beach before the breaker; the trough is the stored wave. the moon is full on the night that it begins to wane. a forest grows dense, and the fuel for the fire is laid; a population of deer rises, and the grass that will starve it is eaten. ecologists draw this as a loop of growth, peak, release, and renewal. none of it is a plot. the soft things win by time: roots split rock, water cuts a gorge, grass comes back after the hard frost has broken the hard ground. and each creature has its deep. take it from its element and admire it, and you have a specimen. do the breath exercise once today. then choose one of the two prohibitions for the day. the fish: find one good thing that lives in your depth, a plan not yet ripe, a kindness, a skill, and for today do not take it out to show. or the tools: notice each time you display a strength in order to control someone, a title, a fact, a sharp word. no rule against it. only see what the display did to the tool, and to the other person.

歙: a breath drawn in. the first verb of the passage is a breath. the shuowen defines 歙 as 縮鼻也, “to draw in through the nose”. its right side, 欠, is a person with the mouth open; it marks 吹 (to blow) and 飲 (to drink). its left side is 翕, which is 合, “to close”, over 羽, “feathers”: a bird that folds its wings. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write this simpler graph, 翕, in the line. so before any talk of states, the first pair is bodily: draw in, stretch out. lungs must be full before they can empty, and wings must be open before they can fold. no one plots this. legge saw the breath and built his whole first sentence on it. if you read the four pairs as breathing, does the passage still sound like a scheme?

張: to string the bow. 張 has 弓, a bow, at the left. the shuowen: 施弓弦也, “to put the string on a bow”. a bow of the time was kept unstrung, bent the wrong way, and it was strung only for use; to 張 it was to load it with force. from there the word went to each kind of stretching: to open a net, to spread a sheet, to make a show of strength. passage 77 uses the same picture for heaven’s way: 天之道，其猶張弓與, “the way of heaven is like the stringing of a bow”: the high end is pressed down and the low end is lifted. a bowyer knows that a bow kept strung grows weak. full stretch is the moment before the release. so the first pair has two pictures in it, a lung and a bow, and both say that the extreme is the turn.

固 or 姑: surely, or for a while. 固 is “firm, solid”; the shuowen says 四塞也, “closed on all four sides”. as an adverb it means “firmly, certainly”, and also “originally, already”. so 必固張之 can be “it must surely be stretched” or “it must already have been stretched”. the second is a remark about how things are and has no plotter in it. a third reading takes 固 as a loan for 姑, “for the time being”. this has an old witness. the han feizi and the zhanguoce both tell how a minister quoted the “documents of zhou” in the crisis before 453 bce; the wording here is that of the zhanguoce, and the han feizi has 予 for the last verb: 將欲敗之，必姑輔之；將欲取之，必姑與之. “to defeat him, first help him for a while; to take from him, first give to him for a while.” so a saying of this form was in circulation before the laozi, as statecraft. see the story. our “first” is a compromise between the three.

who does this? a plotter, or no one. the chinese lines are active and have no subject: “about to wish to shrink it, must firmly stretch it”. english needs a doer or a passive; we chose the passive, to leave the question open. the question is the oldest quarrel about this passage. one reading: a strategist speaks. to ruin an enemy, feed the enemy’s growth until it breaks. this is how the han feizi read it, and for that reading later confucians called the passage a craft of scheming and blamed the laozi for the cold statecraft of the legalists. the other reading: no one speaks of a method. the lines describe the course of things. that which shrinks has been at full stretch; the moon is full before it wanes; a power is at its peak just before it falls. passage 40 gives the law in five words: 反者道之動, “return is the movement of the dao”. on that reading the passage is a way of seeing, and its name is the faint light.

han feizi’s examples: jade, horses, and a bell. the han feizi, a legalist book of the third century bce, has the oldest surviving commentary on this passage, and it explains by cases. duke xian of jin wished to take the small state of yu, so he sent its ruler a jade disc and a team of fine horses; with the road thus opened he destroyed yu’s neighbor and then yu. zhi bo wished to take a hill state, so he sent it a wide cart as a gift (a second chapter of the book, “shuo lin”, tells the story with a great bell as the gift); the hill people cut a road to receive it, and his army came up the road. the text concludes: 故曰：將欲取之，必固與之, “so it is said: to take it, first give to it”. then zhi bo was himself destroyed in 453 bce by lords who had given him land. these were not parables. the readers of the early laozi knew the cases by name. does the passage teach the trick, or warn the one who receives the gift?

廢 and 興: a house falls, hands lift. the third pair is from building. 廢 has 广, a roof against a cliff, a building; the shuowen defines it as 屋頓也, “a house collapses”. from that came “to abolish” a law, “to depose” a ruler, “to waste” a field. 興 is defined 起也, “to rise”, and the shuowen reads the graph as 同力也, “strength joined”: hands on all sides that lift one thing together. it is the word for the rise of a dynasty. historians wrote of the 興 and 廢 of states as of a breath. passage 18 uses the first word without pity: 大道廢，有仁義, “the great dao is pulled down, and there are humaneness and rightness”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to have a different third pair; see the note on the state. a house must stand before it can fall. this is not policy. it is grammar.

奪 and 脫: one old word, used twice. 奪 is “to take by force”. the shuowen gives it a surprising first meaning: 手持隹失之也, “a hand holds a bird and loses it”. the word was at first “to lose from one’s grip”; a different graph, 敓, was “to seize by force”, 彊取也. the qing scholar duan yucai noted that the old sense of 奪 is the word later written 脫, “to slip free”. now read the passage again. in the fourth pair something is to be 奪, taken. three lines later the fish must not 脫, slip out. they are two branches of one word, and the sounds were close in old chinese; scholars put both in one rhyme group. the hand that seizes and the bird that gets away are in one syllable. whoever takes by force holds a thing that is already on the way out of the hand. see the plate for the bird.

微明: a light that is hardly there. 微 is “minute, faint, hidden”; the shuowen says 隱行也, “to walk concealed”. 明 is light, and in the laozi it is the word for true sight: 知常曰明, “to know the constant is called light” (16); 見小曰明, “to see the small is called light” (52). the two words pull against each other: a hidden brightness. three senses are possible. it is light on a faint thing: the sight that reads the turn while the bow is still at full stretch. or it is a faint light: an understanding that is dim, hard to state, easy to miss. or, for the strategist, it is a concealed insight: one sees and does not show that one sees. english versions that write “insight” make it a talent that a clever person has. the chinese is closer to the first grey before dawn. it is weak, and it is the only true information about the day.

柔弱: green wood, a bent bow. both words are pictures of bending. 柔 has 木, a tree, at the bottom; the shuowen says 木曲直也, “wood that can be bent and made straight”: green wood, a sapling. 弱 is defined as 橈也, “bent, curved”, and the shuowen sees in it two bent things with fine hairs; many now see two weak bows. neither word means “defeated”. they name that which gives under force and is not broken. passage 76 makes it a law of life: people and plants are 柔弱 at birth and stiff at death. english “weak” is a word for failure, and “soft” can be an insult. the laozi wants the offense. it does not say “flexible”, a word that a strong man can accept. it says weak. the silk texts are reported to have the short form 柔弱勝強, “soft and weak overcome the strong”. see also the other pair.

剛強: a knife and an insect. 剛 has 刂, a knife, at the right. the shuowen: 彊斷也, “to cut with force”. it is the hardness of an edge. it breaks other things, and at the end it chips. 強 has a stranger history. look at the 虫 in it: the shuowen defines 強 as 蚚也, a kind of insect, most likely a grain weevil. the true graph for “strong” was 彊, defined as 弓有力也, “a bow that has force”, and scribes borrowed the simpler insect graph for it. so the hard and strong of this line are a blade and a bow; these are weapons. the line is a military claim, and the military writers of the time agreed with it in part. sunzi: 兵者，詭道也…能而示之不能. “war is the way of deception: when able, show them that you are unable.” note his verb, 示, to show. it returns in the last line.

the zhuangzi quotes the fish. the last two lines were famous early. the zhuangzi quotes them exactly, with 故曰, “so it is said”, and adds an explanation that few expect: 彼聖人者，天下之利器也，非所以明天下也. “those sages are the sharp tools of the world; they are not things to light up the world with.” in that chapter the sage’s wisdom is a tool that great thieves steal together with the state, so wisdom itself must stay in the deep. the han feizi quotes the same lines and names a different tool. so within a century or so, two schools used one sentence for opposite ends: one to disarm the state, one to arm the ruler. each took the fish for itself. the fish is a plain fact: out of deep water it dies. what is the deep for a person? for a state? for an idea?

不可: cannot, or must not. 不可 is “not / possible, permitted”. it covers “cannot” and “must not”, and the two lines use the range. of the fish it is close to a fact of nature: a fish cannot leave the deep and live. of the state’s tools it is a rule: they must not be shown. the grammar is the same, so the rule borrows the force of the fact. the words do not say who takes the fish out. 脫 is “to slip off, to come away from”, as flesh from a bone or a hand from a sleeve; the fish may leap out itself, or be lifted. legge wrote “fishes should not be taken from the deep” and so made it a rule for fishermen. the chinese puts the fish first and gives it the verb. a line with a fish as subject is a warning to the fish. see 奪 and 脫.

國 was 邦: a banned name, and other changes. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 邦利器不可以示人: 邦, where our text has 國之. both words mean “state”; the shuowen defines each by the other. 邦 was the old word for a ruler’s domain. it was also the personal name of liu bang, founder of the han in 202 bce, and the name of an emperor could not be written. copyists changed 邦 to 國 through the whole book. the older of the two silk manuscripts is reported to write 邦 still, which is one sign that it was copied before or near the start of his reign. the silk texts are reported to differ in the pairs too. the third is 將欲去之，必固與之 and the fourth 將欲奪之，必固予之: “to remove it, first 與 it; to take from it, first give to it”. 與 can be “to give” or “to side with”, and some read it here as 舉, “to raise”; 予 is plain “give”. the editors of the received text made the pairs clearer.

利器: which tools?. 利器 is “sharp instruments”: 利 is a blade in the grain and 器 is any tool or weapon. the phrase means the best weapons, and then each decisive means of power. what are the state’s sharp tools? the han feizi answers: 賞罰者，邦之利器也，在君則制臣，在臣則勝君. “reward and punishment are the sharp tools of the state. in the ruler’s hands they control the ministers; in the ministers’ hands they overcome the ruler.” the ruler must not let others see how he decides, or they will use it. the deep, he says, is the ruler’s position of power. wang bi turns this over: for him, to rely on punishments is itself “to show”. passage 57 uses the phrase with open distrust: 民多利器，國家滋昬, “the more sharp tools the people have, the more the state is in the dark”. a third answer is in the zhuangzi.

示: an altar, and a display. 示 means “to show, to make known”. the graph is commonly explained as an altar or spirit tablet, and the shuowen defines it: 天垂象，見吉凶，所以示人也, “heaven hangs down its images and shows good and ill fortune: that by which it shows to people”. the dictionary’s last two words are the last two words of this passage, 示人. as a part of characters (written 礻 at the left) it marks sacred things: 神 (spirit), 祭 (sacrifice), 福 (blessing), 禮 (ritual). so “to show” is at root what the powers do when they reveal an omen. rulers showed too. a state displayed its bronze vessels and its chariots to envoys, and proclaimed its laws. in 536 bce the state of zheng cast its penal code on bronze tripods for all to read. a noble of jin wrote a famous letter of protest: if the people know the code, they will argue from the text and will not fear their superiors. that was a real dispute about tools shown to people. the line also asks a smaller question. what do you display, and what does display do to it?

wang bi: punishment is the display. wang bi accepts that the first half is a method, and limits it: 將欲除强梁，去暴亂，當以此四者。因物之性，令其自戮. “to remove the violent and end disorder, use these four. follow the nature of the thing and let it destroy itself.” on the tools he writes: 利器，利國之器也。唯因物之性，不假刑以理物，器不可覩，而物各得其所，則國之利器也。示人者，任刑也. “sharp tools are tools that profit the state. only follow the nature of things and do not borrow punishments to order them; the tool cannot be seen, and each thing gets its place: that is the state’s sharp tool. to show it to people is to rely on punishments.” this is a direct answer to han feizi. for the legalist the hidden tool is punishment. for wang bi, punishment is the fish on the bank.

legge: an inspiration and an expiration. legge begins: “when one is about to take an inspiration, he is sure to make a (previous) expiration.” he heard the breath in 歙, and this is to his credit; most translators write only “shrink”. he keeps the order of the chinese, aim first and prior step second. but he gives 張, “to stretch”, as the breath out, and the lungs do not stretch when they empty. in the next pairs his “one” and “he” become a schemer who will “weaken another” and “despoil another”: the persons are his additions. for the last line he writes “instruments for the profit of a state”. he took 利 as “profit”, as wang bi did, and so the blade is gone from 利器. his “should not be shown to the people” makes 人 the common people; the word is only “others, persons”, and may as well be rival states.

find the top of the breath. sit and breathe in slowly until the lungs are full. do not hold. at the top there is a point where the in-breath is complete and the out-breath has not started. notice that you do not decide the turn. fullness itself is the turn. do this five times. then look at one thing in your life that is now at full stretch: a workload, an argument, a success, a market. do not predict. only ask what the first small sign of the turn would be, and whether it is already there. that small sign is the faint light.

a win that also turns. the first eight lines are four pairs: drawn in and stretched, weak and strong, pulled down and raised, taken and given. each side comes by way of the other. then one line seems to end the game: 柔弱勝剛強, soft and weak overcome hard and strong. it has five characters, and none of them is “always”. read with the lines before it, it is one more turn and not a final score. that which has overcome is now the strong one, and the second pair applies to it next. the preference for the soft is a correction for states that trusted in walls and sharp tools. it names the side of the turn that the world of that time did not see: the faint light. if it is made into a fixed rule, “the weak win”, softness becomes a technique for winning, which is hardness with patience. what soft thing in you has become hard since it won?

what is at full stretch is about to draw in; what is raised highest is near its fall.. what is at full stretch is about to draw in; what is raised highest is near its fall. do you see this in your own life: a height that was already the start of a turn? when things go well, do you relax, or do you wait for the fall? where did you learn to expect it, or to not expect it? take the opposite: growth can go on, and to look for the fall is what brings it. hold that for a while. what do you feel? which side is hope for you and which is fear? what does that say about what you have lived?

the soft and weak overcome the hard and strong.. the soft and weak overcome the hard and strong. do you believe it? give one case from your life for it and one against. were you soft or hard as a child, and what did it get you? what did you decide then about weakness? hold the other side: the hard and strong prevail, and softness is what the losers call their loss. stay with it. what arises in you? if the soft side wins, does it stay soft? what happened to a softness of yours after it won?

some things keep their life in the deep, and are lost when they are shown.. some things keep their life in the deep, and are lost when they are shown. is there something of yours that lost its life when you showed it? what do you hide, and from whom? is it protection, or is it shame? take the opposite: what is hidden rots, and things become real when they are shared. hold it. what feelings and thoughts come? which do you resist more, to be seen or to stay unseen? why might that be useful to know?

奪 the bird that leaves the hand. three parts, from the top: 大, 隹, 寸. begin in the middle. 隹 is a bird; the shuowen calls it 鳥之短尾緫名也, “the general name for short-tailed birds”, and says it is a picture. you know it from 集 (to gather: a bird on a tree) and 雙 (a pair: two birds on a hand). on top is 大, a figure with arms out. the shuowen joins the two as 奞: 鳥張毛羽自奮也, “a bird spreads its feathers and rouses itself”, a bird at the moment of take-off. put that bird over 田, a field, and you have 奮, “to rise with force, to exert oneself”. at the bottom is 寸, “an inch”, which in compounds is a hand: 又, a hand, with a mark at the wrist. so the whole character is a hand under a bird that has opened its wings. the shuowen reads it: 手持隹失之也, “a hand holds a bird and loses it”. the first meaning was to lose one’s hold. later the graph was used for the opposite side of the same event: to snatch. both are true to the picture. something is taken away, and the character does not say if you are the hand or the one who takes the bird. in this passage, that which is to be 奪 must first be given. the short form is 夺: the bird is gone. fourteen strokes. first 大: a horizontal, a stroke that falls to the left, a stroke that falls to the right. these two open like a roof, or like wings, over all the rest. then the bird, eight strokes: a short stroke that falls left, a vertical, a dot, then three horizontals, then a vertical that goes down through them, and a last horizontal that closes the foot. then the hand: a long horizontal, a vertical with a hook at its end, and a dot. watch the two long horizontals, the first stroke and the twelfth. the top one is short and the lower one is the widest line of the character, a floor on which the bird stands. the right-falling stroke of 大 must not come down too far, or it presses the bird. in running script the bird’s horizontals join into one quick zigzag, as if it had begun to move.

魚 head, scales, and a tail of dots. this is one of the pictures that a child can read. the shuowen says 水蟲也。象形: “a water creature; a picture”. in the oracle-bone and bronze forms it is a whole fish, drawn upright with the mouth at the top: head, a body crossed with lines for scales, fins, and a forked tail. in the modern character the three zones are still there. the two strokes at the top are the head. the box with a cross, which looks like 田, a field, is the scaled body; it is not a field. the four dots at the bottom look like 灬, fire, as in 煮 (to boil); they are not fire. they are what the brush made of the forked tail. the shuowen adds a careful note: 魚尾與燕尾相似, “the tail of 魚 is like the tail of 燕, the swallow”. look at 燕: the same four dots, for the same reason. the short form 鱼 makes the tail a single line. as a part, 魚 marks water life: 鮮 (fresh: fish beside sheep), 鯉 (carp), 漁 (to fish: water added). the fish swims through early chinese thought. in the zhuangzi, fish forget each other in the rivers and lakes, as people forget each other in the dao. here it has one line: it must not leave the deep. on the page it stands upright in white paper, already out of the water, which the character does not draw. eleven strokes. the head: a short stroke that falls left, then a horizontal that turns and falls left. the body: the left side; the top and right side in one stroke; the horizontal inside; the vertical inside; then the base that closes the box. then the tail: four dots, written from left to right. watch the dots. the first leans to the left and is a little apart; the next three lean right, and the last is the heaviest. they must look like one motion of a tail and not like four stones. keep the body narrow and tall: a wide box makes a field, a tall one makes a fish. in seal script the tail is still a fork of two lines, and you can see the animal; the clerical script of the han cut it into dots.

37 · weighed down with plain wood. the dao is constant in not-doing, / and nothing is left undone. / if lords and kings can keep to it, / the ten thousand things will change of themselves. / changed, and wanting stirs: / i will weigh it down / with the nameless uncarved wood. / the nameless uncarved wood: / that too will be without wanting. / not wanting, and so still: / all under heaven will settle of itself. the passage has four moves. one: a statement about the dao, that it is constant in not-doing, with a second clause that the oldest copies lack. two: a condition. if lords and kings can keep to this, the things will change by themselves. three: a difficulty. after the change, wanting stirs, and a speaker says “i” and presses it with plain wood. four: a correction. the plain wood too must not be wanted; then stillness, and the world settles. 將, “will”, comes five times: the passage is a forecast, each step out of the last. and 自, “of itself”, stands at both ends. this is the last passage of the dao book, and it closes on a verb of rest. leave the mind alone and it changes of itself: it clears, it becomes inventive, it grows. then, out of that ease, wanting stirs: the wish to use the clarity, to keep it, to become someone who has it. each person who has sat quietly knows this moment. the passage does not say to cut the wanting off. it says to weigh it down with the thing that has no name, attention before it is shaped into a thought of “i want”. and then it adds the most exact line: do not want that either. a person who clings to plainness has a new possession. the stillness at the end is not produced. 不欲以靜: where wanting is absent, still is what is there. the addressees are rulers in a century of new kings, and the promise is large: keep to not-doing and things order themselves. the honest part is the middle. a leader gives a team room, the team flourishes, and with success come appetites: for growth, for projects, for status. the usual answers are new rules, new incentives, a reorganization: more 為. the passage answers with a weight that is not a rule: the leader’s own plainness, placed on the matter, with no name on it. and then the warning that makes this more than a technique: a leader who needs the team to be simple, who is attached to the result “they are calm”, has brought wanting back in at the top. wang bi says it in four characters: not to act the lord. a field left alone changes of itself. weeds come, then shrubs, then trees; no one directs the order. growth then makes its own pressure: each plant wants the light, and the stand becomes crowded. the forest does not answer with a law. the canopy closes, the floor becomes dim and cool, and the rush slows. the weight is only shade, a thing with no name. a pond does the same: stirred, it is brown; left, the silt goes down by its own weight and the water is clear and still. nothing has to make it settle. 自定 is exact for this: the mud settles of itself, and the stillness of the water is not a second thing added after. use the three-breath weight once today. in the evening, look for one place where you are trying to make a thing settle by more doing: a child’s mood, a discussion at work, your own sleep. ask what the muddy water would do if you stopped stirring. then, as the passage does, check the checker: is there a want inside your wish for calm? you do not have to remove it. see it, and let that too be plain wood.

無為: not “doing nothing”. 無為 is “without 為”, and 為 is a wide verb: to do, to make, to act as, to act for a purpose. the phrase does not mean idleness. a river does much and does not 為. the sense is: no action that is forced on things from outside, by a will with a plan. “non-action” sounds like a withdrawal; “inaction” sounds like a fault. we write “not-doing” and ask you to hear “not-forcing”. the line does not tell anyone to practice it. it says that the dao is so, 常, constantly. wang bi glosses the four characters with three: 順自然也, “it follows that which is so of itself”. notice that the pinned text divides the sentence after 為, in the middle of the paradox, as a breath divides it when it is read aloud.

the famous line may be late. 無為而無不為, “not-doing, and nothing is not done”, is one of the best-known sentences of the book. it also stands in passage 48. but the oldest copies do not have it here. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to open this passage with 道恆无名, “the dao is constantly nameless”, which is also the first line of passage 32, and they have no second clause. the guodian bamboo slips, a century or more older, are reported to read 道恆亡為也, “the dao constantly does not do”, and to stop there. so the oldest form of the line had not-doing and no promise that all will be done. the second clause adds a result, and a result can be taken as a method: do nothing in order to achieve all. read the passage once with the short line. is it poorer, or cleaner?

侯王: when every lord became a king. 侯 was a rank of the zhou order, a lord who held a state from the king; the word’s first meaning is an archery target, and the lords shot at one in the royal rite. 王 was the one king, the son of heaven. the shuowen defines it as 天下所歸往也, “the one to whom all under heaven goes home”, and quotes a han explanation of the graph: 三者，天、地、人也，而參通之者，王也, three lines for heaven, earth, and humankind, and the one who joins them is the king; many modern scholars see an axe blade, the tool of punishment. in the warring states the difference between the two ranks collapsed. in 344 bce the lord of wei took the royal title; in 334 wei and qi recognized each other as kings; in 323 five states, wei, han, zhao, yan, and zhongshan, recognized one another as kings. the phrase 侯王, “lords-and-kings”, belongs to this time: it addresses each man who has a state and an army. it occurs in passages 32, 37, and 39, and always with advice to hold still.

守: to keep a post. 守 is a roof, 宀, over 寸, a hand. the shuowen defines it as 守官也, “to keep an office”, and says that the 寸 stands for rule and measure. it is the word for a guard at a gate, a commander who holds a city, an official at his post. it is a military and administrative word, and passive only in appearance: the one who 守 does not attack, and does not leave. the laozi tells its reader to 守 several things: the center (5), stillness (16), the female, the black, the disgrace (28), the mother (52), the soft (52). here the object is 之, “it”: the dao, or its not-doing. the lord is asked to treat not-doing as a post. english “hold to” is close. “maintain”, which legge used, makes it a matter of upkeep.

自: the family of “by itself”. 自化 is “self-change”: to transform of one’s own accord. 自 is the word for “self” used as an adverb, and it marks the central idea of the book, 自然, “so of itself”. the passage begins and ends with it: the things will 自化, the world will 自定. passage 57 gives a list in the voice of a sage: i do not act, and the people 自化, change of themselves; i love stillness, and the people 自正, come right of themselves; i have no business, and they 自富, grow rich of themselves; i have no wants, and they 自樸, become plain wood of themselves. passage 32 adds 自賓, “make themselves guests”, and 自均, “share evenly of themselves”. in each case the ruler’s part is a negative and the people’s part has 自. versions that write “are transformed” or “are influenced” move the cause back to the ruler. the chinese gives the verb to the things.

化而欲作: wanting stirs, or they want to act. four characters, two readings. 欲 is “to want” and also the noun “desire”. 作 is “to rise, to start up”; the shuowen says 起也, “to get up”. so: “they change, and desire arises”. or: “they change, and want to act”, to make things, to start projects. the first reading sees a feeling. the second sees ambition: the things have grown, and now they wish to 為. wang bi says 作欲成也, “to stir is to want to achieve”. in both readings the trouble comes out of the success. the things were left alone, they flourished, and that which flourishes begins to want. the text does not treat this as a failure of the method. it expects it. who or what is it that stirs? 之, “it”, in the next line does not say: the things, the desire, or the heart of the lord himself.

吾: someone says “i”. most of the laozi has no speaker. here one appears: 吾, “i”. the shuowen: 我，自稱也, “i: what one calls oneself”. the sentence began with lords and kings in the third person, and now a first person will do the pressing. who is it? perhaps the ruler, in a line that he is to speak for himself. perhaps the teacher, who shows the ruler what he would do. perhaps the voice of the book, which speaks at times as one who has done the work: 吾以觀復, “by this i watch the return” (16). the change of person has a result that a reader of english can miss. the whole method depends on 自, things by themselves, and at the one point of difficulty an “i” comes in and acts. the passage sees the problem; see the next line.

鎮: a weight of metal. 鎮 has 金, metal, at the left. the shuowen defines it as 博壓也, “to press down broadly”. a 鎮 was a weight. people sat on mats, and bronze weights in the shapes of animals held the corners down; many have been found in han tombs. the king’s own jade tablet was the 鎮圭, and the zhouli names for each province a great mountain as its 鎮, the weight that holds the region in place. from this came the military sense, “to garrison, to hold down a district”, and the modern word for a market town. so the verb is not “to calm”. it is to put a heavy thing on something that lifts. now look at the weight that the speaker chooses: not bronze, not jade, not troops. a piece of plain wood with no name. can the lightest thing in the state hold the mat down? the mawangdui texts are reported to write a different graph here, which editors read as the same word.

樸: wood before the knife. 樸 has 木, tree, at the left. the shuowen: 木素也, “wood in its plain state”; 素 is undyed silk, so the gloss says: wood as silk is before the dye. it is timber that has not been cut into a vessel or a tool. it has no use yet, and so no name, because names in this book come with cutting: 始制有名, “when the cutting begins, there are names” (32), and 樸散則為器, “when the plain wood is split, it becomes vessels” (28). the phrase 無名之樸 joins the two ideas of passage 32, where the dao is “constantly nameless, plain wood”. english “simplicity” makes it a virtue or a lifestyle. the chinese is a block in a workshop that no one has yet marked. every finished thing was once this. it is not empty, as the hub is; it is full of that which it has not yet become.

夫亦將無欲: the cure must not be wanted. the phrase 無名之樸 is said two times, the second time alone, as a topic. then: 夫亦將無欲, “now that, too, will be without wanting”. what is “that”? one reading: the things, once pressed by plain wood, will also come to have no wants. a second and sharper reading: the plain wood itself must also not be wanted. the speaker has just used simplicity as a weight, and a ruler who wants simplicity, who makes it a policy and enforces it, has only a new desire with a good name. so the tool is put down in the next breath. the silk texts are reported to support a turn of this kind, though with other words: 夫將不辱，不辱以靜, “then there will be no disgrace; no disgrace, and so stillness”. have you ever wanted very much to be a person who wants little?

靜: stillness, with “contend” inside. 靜 is “still, quiet”. look at its right side: 爭, “to contend, to fight over”, the thing that the laozi most often says not to do. the shuowen says that 爭 is only the sound of the character and 青, the color of living plants and of clear sky, gives the sense; it defines 靜 as 審也, “to see exactly”. so the dictionary’s stillness is first a clearness, like water that lets you see the bottom when it stops moving. passage 15 asks: who can make the muddy water clear by stillness? passage 16 names the return to the root 靜. passage 45: 清靜為天下正, “clear and still is the standard of the world”. the grammar here is 不欲以靜: not-wanting, and by that, still. stillness is not made by an effort. it is that which remains when wanting stops. the struggle stays in the written character, held in place by the clear color beside it.

自定 or 自正; the world or heaven and earth. the pinned text ends 天下將自定, “all under heaven will settle of itself”. 定 is a roof over 正: the shuowen says 安也, “to be at rest”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to end 天地將自正: “heaven and earth will come right of themselves”. 正 is “straight, correct, a standard”. two changes, then. the verb goes from “come right” to “come to rest”, and these differ: a pendulum that stops has settled, and it need not be correct by any person’s rule. and the subject goes from the cosmos, 天地, to the political world, 天下. the silk ending is larger and stranger: the stillness of one who wants nothing puts heaven and earth in order. the guodian slips are reported to read 萬物將自定, “the ten thousand things will settle of themselves”, and, before it, 知足以靜, “to know what is enough, and so be still”.

the last line of the dao book. the received laozi has two parts. passages 1 to 37 are the 道經, the dao book; 38 to 81 are the 德經, the de book; and from the two comes the title 道德經. this passage is the last of the first part. its end answers the first passage: there, name and wanting appeared together (無名, 有名; 無欲, 有欲). here the two return together, as the nameless wood and the end of wanting, and the world is still. in the mawangdui silk manuscripts the order of the two parts is the reverse: the de part is first, and this passage is the last of the whole work. in the second silk manuscript each part ends with its own count: 3,041 characters after the 德 part, and 2,426 after the 道 part, that is, after this passage. if these were the final words of the book that you held, how would they sound?

wang bi: “not acting the lord”. wang bi’s notes here are very short. on 道常無為: 順自然也, “it follows that which is so of itself”. on 而無不為: 萬物無不由為以治以成之也, “of the ten thousand things, none is not governed and completed by way of this”; the copies read 由為, “by way of doing”, and editors take it as a slip for 由無為 or 由之. on the weight: 化而欲作，作欲成也。吾將鎮之無名之樸，不為主也. “they change and wanting stirs: to stir is to want to achieve. ‘i will weigh it down with the nameless uncarved wood’: that is, not to act the lord.” the last four characters are his whole account of the pressing. to press with plain wood is not a different kind of rule. it is the refusal to be the master of the result, the 不為主 of passage 34. on the absence of wanting he writes three characters: 無欲競也, “no wish to compete”.

legge: a bracket and a rhyme. legge writes that the dao “does nothing (for the sake of doing it)”. the bracket is his own, and it is a fair gloss of 無為; it also shows that he could not leave the bare words alone. for the middle of the passage he takes 欲 as the speaker’s own desire: “if this transformation became to me an object of desire, i would express the desire by the nameless simplicity.” this agrees with the sharper reading of the line on the cure, but the weight is gone: for 鎮, to press down, he has “express”. then he ends in verse, with rhymes on “name” and “aim”, “still” and “will”. the chinese of the close is not a song. it is two flat statements. a victorian reader expected scripture to rise at the end of a chapter. the laozi goes quiet.

a weight that is not a rule. the next time a want rises strongly today, to buy, to answer at once, to fix a person, do not obey it and do not fight it. put one plain thing on it. a plain thing has no name and no argument: the feeling of your feet on the floor, one slow breath out, a look at the grain of the table. stay for the time of three breaths. this is a small 鎮, a weight on the corner of the mat. then notice the second step of the passage. if you become proud of the method, or want to be good at it, put that down too.

作 and 靜: stirring and stillness. the passage runs on a pair: 作, to rise and stir, and 靜, to be still. it also shows that the two feed each other. not-doing lets the things change of themselves. the change brings wanting, and wanting stirs. the weight of plain wood brings stillness. then the world settles, and a settled world is the ground where things again change of themselves. so the passage is a circle, and 將, “will”, marks each turn of it. the text leans to the still side. the lean is a correction for lords and kings who answer each stir with more doing. it is not a verdict against movement: 化, change, is what the stillness allows. a reading that takes stillness as the goal and stirring as the fault makes the plain wood a thing to want, and the passage warns against that. where in your day does a calm already carry its next stir?

left without interference, things change and settle of themselves; stillness does more than control.. left without interference, things change and settle of themselves; stillness does more than control. is this true in your experience? name one thing that settled when you left it, and one that did not. when you step in to manage a thing, what do you fear will happen if you do not? whose voice taught you that fear? take the other side for a while: nothing comes right unless someone makes it right. what in you agrees at once, and what feels tired at the thought? which do you judge in other people, the one who controls or the one who lets things drift? what might that judgment protect?

even the wish to be plain and free of wanting is a wanting, and it too must be let go.. even the wish to be plain and free of wanting is a wanting, and it too must be let go. do you accept this, or does it seem to take away the one tool that you have? think of something good that you want to be: calm, simple, kind. how does the wanting feel in the body, and how is it different from the thing itself? hold the opposite: a strong wish for a good state is exactly what brings it. stay there for a minute. which memories support it? which view matches what you have lived? what would change in your days if the other one were true?

化 one person upright, one turned over. four strokes, two people. the left part, 亻, is 人, a person who stands, in the narrow form that it takes at the side of a character. the right part, written 匕 today, is not the spoon that it looks like. the shuowen lists it as a graph of its own, 𠤎, and says: 變也。从到人, “to change; from 人 turned upside down”. in the oracle-bone forms you can see it: two human figures, one head up and one head down. that is the whole idea: a thing becomes its other. the shuowen defines the full character as 教行也, “teaching takes effect”, the change that a good ruler works in the people. the laozi’s 自化, change of itself, takes the teacher out. chinese built a small family from two persons side by side, and the shuowen explains each: 从, one behind the other, “to follow”; 比, two close together, “to be close, to compare”; 北, 从二人相背, two back to back, which first meant “to turn the back” and then “north”, the side that one’s back is to when one faces the sun; and 化, one of the two overturned. 化 also gives its sound to 貨, goods, things that change hands. in the zhuangzi, 化 is the great word for death and birth: the 物化, the “change of things”, in which a man dreams that he is a butterfly. four strokes. first a stroke that falls to the left: the head and arm of the standing person. second a vertical under it: the body. third, on the right, a short stroke that falls to the left; it starts high and comes in toward the vertical. fourth, the long stroke: it goes down, turns at the bottom into a level run to the right, and ends in a hook that points up. watch the fourth stroke. it is the turned person, and it does all the movement in the character; the left side only stands and waits. the turn must be round and the hook quick. the third stroke crosses or touches the fourth near its top, and the point where they meet sets the balance. with so few strokes there is no place to hide a weak line.

自 the nose that means “self”. the shuowen is direct: 自，鼻也。象鼻形, “自 is the nose; it shows the shape of a nose”. the early forms are a nose seen from the front: the bridge, the two wings, the lines across. how did a nose come to mean “self”? the common explanation is a gesture: people in china point to their own nose, not to their chest, when they say “i”. when the graph was taken over by the words “self” and “from”, the nose got a new character, 鼻, with a sound part added below. the old nose still works inside other characters. 息, “breath, to rest”, is 自 over 心, the heart: the shuowen says 从心从自. 臭, “smell”, is 自 over 犬, a dog: the shuowen explains that the dog is the animal that follows a trail by its nose. the second meaning, “from”, is the nose again: the point from which one starts. now read 自化 and 自定 in this passage, and the great word 自然, “so of itself”. each has in it a face that points at itself. in chinese, the self of “by itself” is not a soul and not an ego. it is the place where the breath comes in. see the family of 自. six strokes. first a short stroke at the top that falls to the left. second, the left side, a vertical. third, the top and right side in one stroke, with a firm corner. fourth and fifth, two short horizontals inside, which touch the left side and do not reach the right. sixth, the base that closes the box. watch the first stroke: it is the only difference between this character and 目, the eye. it is small and it must be alive, set a little left of center, like the bridge of the nose above the face. the three inner spaces should be equal. the form has hardly changed since the seal script. the han clerks only made the round nose square.

38 · the fruit, not the flower. highest de is not “de”: / and so it has de. / lower de does not let go of de: / and so it has no de. / highest de does not act, / and has nothing it acts for. / lower de acts, / and has something it acts for. / highest humaneness acts, / and has nothing it acts for. / highest rightness acts, / and has something it acts for. / highest ritual acts, and when no one answers / it bares its arms and drags them. / so: lose the dao, and after that, de. / lose de, and after that, humaneness. / lose humaneness, and after that, rightness. / lose rightness, and after that, ritual. / now ritual is the thin part of loyalty and trust, / and the head of disorder. / foreknowledge is the flower of the dao, / and the beginning of folly. / so the full-grown one stays in the thick / and does not dwell in the thin; / stays in the fruit / and does not dwell in the flower. / so: leave that, take this. the passage has three parts. first a test. highest de does not act as de and has it; lower de holds on and has none. then a scale of grades by two questions: is there action, and is there a “for”? de: no action, no “for”. humaneness: action, no “for”. rightness: action and a “for”. ritual: action, no answer, and then force. second, the same four as a ladder of loss. third, two judgments and a choice. ritual is thin trust and first disorder; foreknowledge is flower and first folly. the grown person lives in the thick and the fruit. it is the longest passage so far, the most argued, and for early readers it was the first. the first line describes a fact of attention. the moment that you notice your own patience, it is a little less patience and a little more a picture of a patient person. highest de does not “de”: it does not turn and look at itself. lower de never lets go, and the grip is the loss. this cannot be made into a method, since to try not to notice one’s virtue is one more way of noticing it. the passage offers a direction and no technique: toward the thick, the fruit. in practice this is a preference for that which has no shine. the plain fact of a feeling, before the fine thought about it. the kind act, before the story of the kind self. the ladder is also a map of one moment: ease, then warmth, then “should”, then form, then force. each institution knows the ladder. a group begins with a shared sense that needs no words. when that weakens, it relies on good will between persons. when that weakens, on principles and fairness, with their accounts of who owes what. when that weakens, on procedure: the form to fill in, the code of conduct. and when the form gets no answer, on enforcement. the passage does not say that codes are useless. it says what they are evidence of. a leader who meets a loss of trust with more ceremony treats the thin place with paint. wang bi gives the working rule: one cannot produce good will by a demand for it; keep the mother and the child lives. note the warning on forecasting: the adviser who is paid to be right before the others is a flower. an orchard explains the end of the passage. blossom comes first, and it is the tree’s advertisement: color and scent for the bees, seen from far away. almost all of it falls. the fruit sets in the place where a flower was, grows slowly, hides in the leaves, and is dull green for most of its life. a grower who loves only the blossom gets a bad harvest; some trees are forced to flower so heavily that they break. the thick is here too: thick soil, a thick trunk, the thick rind that carries a fruit through the winter. nature does not despise the flower. it passes through it. the passage asks the reader to stay with the part of each process that feeds, and to look at the bright part as the tree does, as a stage. do the search for the “for” this evening. tomorrow, try one day of thick over thin in small things. in talk: say the plain fact and drop the phrase that would make you look good. at work: do the part that carries weight and will not be seen before the part that will be praised. with a friend: skip one form of politeness that has become a wall, and offer the thing behind it. if someone does not return a courtesy, notice the arm that begins to push up its sleeve.

德: not “virtue” as a rule of conduct. 德 is the second great word of the book, and english has no good match. it is the power that a thing has from the dao to be what it is: the potency of a seed, the hold that a person of character has on others without force. the old english “virtue” had this sense once, as in “the virtue of a herb”, and lost it; now “virtue” means good conduct by a moral code, and that is nearer to what this passage attacks. in early zhou bronzes, 德 is the charisma by which a king holds the mandate of heaven. the confucians made it moral excellence. the laozi takes it back toward power that is not owned. we leave it as de. the graph has a step, an eye that looks straight, and a heart; see the plate. legge chose “attributes of the tao”.

上德不德: de that does not “de”. four characters: “high / de / not / de”. the second 德 is a verb, and chinese lets a noun do this without a change of form. highest de does not “de”: it does not act the part, does not treat itself as de, does not hold on to de. then the turn: 是以有德, “for this reason it has de”. a second word sounds under the first. 德 and 得, “to get”, were close in sound and are in one old rhyme group, and early writers used them to explain each other. the shuowen defines the older graph 悳 as 外得於人，內得於己也, “to get it from others outside, to get it in oneself inside”. so a hearer also takes the line as: highest de does not get, and so it has. lower de does not let go, 不失, a grip that never opens, and so has none. which part of your goodness do you watch over?
