無以為: nothing to act for. the test in these lines is two small words, 以為. 以 is “by means of, for the sake of, with which”. 無以為 is “to have nothing by which, or for which, one acts”; 有以為 is “to have something”. most readers take it as purpose: an act with no end in view, against an act with an aim, a reason, an account to settle. a modern translator writes “motive”, and the reading is fair, but the word brings psychology in: hidden motives, an inner self to be examined. the chinese is plainer and is about the act. does this act lean on anything outside itself? another reading takes 以 as “means”: highest de has nothing with which to act, no tool and no program. the grades that follow use the test. humaneness acts and has no “for”. rightness acts and has one. ritual acts and gets no answer.

a line that the silk texts lack. 下德為之而有以為, “lower de acts and has something it acts for”, is in the pinned text. the mawangdui silk texts are reported not to have it. they go from highest de to highest humaneness with no line between. the han feizi, which comments on this passage in the third century bce, also does not quote it. the line is likely a later addition, made to give “lower de” a description to match its entry in the first stanza. it creates a small problem that readers have long noticed: its description is word for word the same as that of highest rightness, two lines below. without it, the list is a clean descent of four: de, humaneness, rightness, ritual; no-act and no-for, act and no-for, act and for, act and force. some received editions read 無以為 in this line, which only moves the duplication from rightness to humaneness. read the stanza once without the line.

仁: a person and two. 仁 is 人, a person, with 二, two. the shuowen: 親也。从人从二, “to be close; from person and two”. it is the feeling between one person and another, what makes a person human in company. confucius made it the center of his teaching and would not define it; he gave a new answer each time that a student asked. mencius said that it starts in the heart that cannot bear to see a child fall into a well. “benevolence” makes it the kindness of a superior; “philanthropy” makes it a gift of money. we write “humaneness”. note where the laozi puts it: one step below de, and still with no “for”. the passage does not mock humaneness. it says only that it comes when something older has been lost, as a family starts to speak of love when it is in trouble (18).

義: a sheep above “i”. 義 is 羊, a sheep, above 我, “i”; and 我 is at root a picture of a weapon with a toothed blade, borrowed for the pronoun. the shuowen defines the whole as 己之威儀也, “one’s own dignified bearing”: at first the correct look of a person in a rite, where the sheep is commonly explained as the offering or as a sign of the good, as it is in 善 and 美. from correct bearing came “what is fitting”, duty, justice. mencius paired it with 仁 as the two roots of the moral life, and for him one must choose 義 above life itself. in the laozi’s list it is the first grade that has a “for”. rightness judges; it divides right from wrong, and it acts because of something. “righteousness”, the usual english, adds a church tone that the word does not have. notice the “i” in the graph.

禮: the rites were the constitution. 禮 is first the rites of sacrifice; see the plate. by the time of the laozi it meant far more: the whole graded order of zhou society. who bows to whom, how many tripods a lord may use, how long one mourns a father, how an envoy is received. 禮 was the unwritten constitution of the old world, and the confucians were its experts. confucius said that to master oneself and return to ritual is humaneness. by the fourth century bce the forms were still performed while the lords broke each rule of rank; rulers who had no right to the title of king held royal rites. so the attack here has a target that was in plain view. “propriety” and “etiquette” make it a matter of manners. for the first readers it was the system that claimed to hold the world together, and the passage calls it the last thing left when the rest is gone.

攘臂而扔之: sleeves up. the one comic picture in the passage. 攘 has the hand at the left; the shuowen says 推也, “to push”. 攘臂 is to push the long sleeves of a robe up the arms, as a person does before a fight or hard work. 扔 today means “to throw away”. its old sense is different: the shuowen says 因也, here “to pull along, to drag”. so: ritual performs its bow, no one bows back, and it pushes up its sleeves and pulls people into line by the arm. a ceremony of respect ends as a scuffle. both verbs return together in passage 69: 攘無臂，扔無敵, “bare an arm that is not there, drag an enemy that is not there”. the joke is exact about how codes behave. a rule of courtesy that is not returned does not stay courteous. behind 禮 the next thing is punishment. when did you last enforce a politeness?

the ladder down, and who quoted it. four lines with one frame: 失 a 而後 b, “lose a, and after that, b”. dao, de, humaneness, rightness, ritual. the three lower steps are the confucian virtues in their standard order, so the list says to that school: your goods are real, and they are a record of loss. the grammar gives no subject and no tense. it can be a history, the decline of the world from an early age. it can be the course of one life, one marriage, one institution. the zhuangzi quotes the ladder word for word, introduced by 故曰, “so it is said”, and adds: 禮者，道之華而亂之首也, “ritual is the flower of the dao and the head of disorder”, with the two halves of our next stanza joined in one line. the mawangdui texts are reported to end each step with 而后, the same words. is the ladder a fall, or only an order of appearance?

薄 and 厚: thin and thick. the passage ends on two pairs of pictures, and the first is of thickness. 薄 is “thin”: a thin sheet, thin soup, thin feeling. 厚 is “thick”: the shuowen defines it by mountains, 山陵之厚也, “the thickness of hills”. to treat a person 厚 is to be generous to them; a 薄 person is mean and shallow. so 忠信之薄 is “the thin of loyalty and trust”: the place where the trust between people has worn thin, and a form is put there to cover the wear. 忠 is a heart, 心, with 中, “center”: a centered heart. 信 is a person beside 言, speech: the shuowen says 誠也, “sincere”, a person who stands by their word. where these are thick, no ceremony is needed; old friends do not bow. the silk texts are reported to write 泊 for the thin, a water word. legge has “attenuated form”. the chinese picture is nearer to thin soup.

亂: disorder, and to put in order. 亂 is “chaos, revolt, confusion”. the shuowen defines it with its opposite: 治也, “to put in order”. this is not a mistake. the left side of the graph is commonly explained as two hands at work on a tangle of silk thread on a frame, and the one picture gives both senses: the tangle, and the work of setting it right. classical texts use 亂 in both ways; a minister who “亂s” the state may be its destroyer or, in the oldest books, its able manager. so when the line calls ritual 亂之首, “the head of 亂”, the first meaning is clear: disorder begins here. a reader may hear the second for a moment: the first act of ordering. the two are one event. the hands go into the silk because it is tangled, and the handling is the sign that the natural order of the threads has been lost.

前識: the man who guessed the ox. 前識 is “knowledge ahead”: to know a thing before it shows. it was a prized skill, in diviners and in clever advisers. the han feizi explains the phrase with a story. zhan he sat with a student and an ox lowed outside the gate. the student said: a black ox with a white forehead. zhan he said: black, yes, but the white is on the horns. they sent to look. it was a black ox with its horns wrapped in white cloth. the han feizi’s comment: he wore out his spirit to reach what a simple child could learn by a walk to the gate. that is “the flower of the dao, the beginning of folly”. wang bi reads it as cleverness that runs ahead of others. the laozi praises a different early sight, the faint light of passage 36, which sees a thing while it is small. the difference is display: zhan he guesses in order to be right. see flower and fruit.

華 and 實: flower and fruit. 華 is a flower. the shuowen: 榮也, “a blossom”, and the graph is commonly explained as a picture of a plant in full bloom. the character 花 was made later for the plain sense, and 華 kept the grand ones: splendor, brilliance, and 華夏, the old name for the chinese cultural world, “the flowering”. 實 is fruit. the shuowen says 富也, “wealth”, a roof over strings of cowries; in plants it is the kernel, and from that come “solid, real, true”. the pair is from the orchard. the flower is early, bright, visible from the road, and falls in a week. the fruit is late, plain, and feeds. the passage does not say that flowers are false. a flower is a true part of the tree. it says where to stay. the faint light of passage 36 is a different thing from the “flower” of foreknowledge; it shows nothing. versions that write “luster” or “veneer” change an orchard into a furniture shop.

愚: a heart and a monkey. 愚 is “stupid, foolish”. its parts are 心, the heart, under 禺, and the shuowen explains: 禺，猴屬，獸之愚者, “禺 is a kind of monkey, the dull one among the beasts”. a monkey-heart. here the word is a plain insult: clever foresight is where folly starts. but a reader of the whole book must settle an apparent conflict, because elsewhere 愚 is praise. the speaker of passage 20 says 我愚人之心也哉, “mine is the heart of a fool”. passage 65 says that the ancients did not make the people bright; they kept them 愚. those lines use the word for a mind that is whole and not sharp, the uncarved wood. this line uses it for the confusion that comes from too much sharpness. the two meet. sharpness that is pushed far ends in the confused kind of dullness, and the whole mind begins in the plain kind. one word names both ends, so bright and dull are not two fixed camps.

大丈夫: the one who has come of age. the usual hero of the book is the 聖人, the sage. here, only here, it is the 大丈夫. 丈 is a measure of ten feet; 夫 is, in the shuowen, a person with a pin through the hair, 从大，一以象簪也: a male who has come of age and put his hair up. the shuowen adds that by zhou measure a man is eight feet tall, 故曰丈夫. so 丈夫 is a grown man, and 大丈夫 a “great grown man”, a person of full stature. the word is male, and it is the one place in this passage where we have turned from the chinese: “full-grown one” keeps the growth and drops the sex. mencius used the same term in a famous definition: wealth cannot corrupt him, poverty cannot move him, force cannot bend him. the laozi’s measure is quieter. maturity is a choice of where to live: in the thick, in the fruit.

the first page of the oldest book. this passage opens the second half of the received text, the 德經 or de book, named from its first line as the dao book is named from the first line of passage 1. in the mawangdui silk manuscripts, buried in 168 bce, the order of the halves is the reverse: de first, dao second. in those copies this was the first passage of the whole work, and a reader began with “highest de is not de”, not with “the dao that can be spoken”. the han feizi’s commentary also starts with this passage, and the peking university bamboo copy from the han is reported to call the de half the “upper” book. so for many early readers the laozi was first a book about power and its decay, and the dark sayings on the dao came after. the closing phrase 去彼取此, “leave that, take this”, also ends passages 12 and 72. which door would you choose to enter by?

wang bi: “de is to get”. wang bi’s note on this passage is the longest in his commentary, a small essay. it begins with the pun: 德者，得也。常得而無喪，利而無害，故以德為名焉。何以得德？由乎道也。何以盡德？以無為用. “de is to get. to get constantly and not lose, to gain and not harm: so ‘de’ is its name. by what does one get de? by way of the dao. by what does one bring de to the full? by taking nothing as its function.” of the person of highest de he says 不德其德, “does not de his de”, does not treat his power as power, and so 不求而得，不為而成, “gets without seeking, completes without doing”. of foreknowledge he says 前人而識也, “to know ahead of other people”: a contest. he follows a text that had the line on lower de and explains it at length. see also his image of mother and child.

wang bi: keep the mother to keep the child. at the end of his essay wang bi saves the confucian virtues from the ladder. he does not say that humaneness and rightness are bad. he says that they cannot be made by aiming at them: 仁德之厚，非用仁之所能也, “the thickness of humane de is not something that the use of humaneness can achieve”. his rule: 守母以存其子，崇本以舉其末, “keep the mother to preserve her child; honor the root to lift up the branch-tips”. and two exact sentences: 仁義，母之所生，非可以為母。形器，匠之所成，非可以為匠也. “humaneness and rightness are what the mother gives birth to; they cannot be made the mother. shaped vessels are what the craftsman completes; they cannot be made the craftsman.” wang bi was a young official at a confucian court, and this is his peace between the two schools. does it keep the edge of the passage, or blunt it?

legge: brackets, past tense, and attributes. legge’s version of the first stanza has more words in brackets than out of them: “(those who) possessed in highest degree the attributes (of the tao) did not (seek) to show them”. three choices are in this. he adds persons, “those who”, where the chinese speaks of de itself. he puts it all in the past, so that the passage becomes a history of a lost golden age; the chinese has no tense. and he renders 德 as “attributes”, a word from christian theology, where god has attributes. for 仁, 義, 禮 he gives “benevolence, righteousness, propriety”, the set that became standard in english for a century. for 忠 he found “leal-heartedness”, an old scots word, and for 前識 “swift apprehension”. his ritual “bared the arm and marched up to them”: he kept the sleeve and softened the drag.

find the “for”. choose three good acts from yesterday: a kind word, a duty done, a courtesy. for each, ask the question of the passage: was there a “for”? for thanks, for my picture of myself, for the rule, to be in the right? do not judge the answer. most human goodness has a “for”, and the passage ranks it and does not forbid it. then look for one act that had none, that was done before any reason appeared, as a hand goes out to steady a person who trips. notice how little you remember of it. that is how 上德 feels from inside: like nothing in particular.

厚/薄, 實/華: two pairs, one plant. the passage ends on two pairs: thick 厚 and thin 薄, fruit 實 and flower 華. the text chooses: stay in the thick, stay in the fruit. but look at what the pairs are. thick and thin are two places on one thing. flower and fruit are two times of one branch: the fruit sets where the flower was, and the seed in the fruit will flower again. so the choice is not good against evil. it says where to dwell, 處 and 居, at a court that lived on show, ceremony, and clever forecasts. the favored side turns too. fruit that is kept too long rots, and a plainness that is worn for others to see has become a flower. the first line says the same of de: the de that holds on to de is the lower kind. a reader who takes this passage as contempt for form misses the orchard. what flower in your life is on its way to fruit?

real goodness does not know itself as goodness; the virtue that keeps hold of itself is the lesser kind.. real goodness does not know itself as goodness; the virtue that keeps hold of itself is the lesser kind. do you agree? think of the kindest person that you know. do they know it? where did you learn to keep count of your own good acts, or to hide the count? who was watching then? now hold the opposite: virtue must be chosen, known, and practiced on purpose, or it is only luck of temperament. what rises in you as you hold that? which side do you defend more quickly? what would you lose if the other side were right?

rules and ceremony appear where trust has worn thin, and they are the first sign of disorder.. rules and ceremony appear where trust has worn thin, and they are the first sign of disorder. does this match what you have seen in a family, a team, or a country? recall a rule that you were grateful for. what was it holding together, and what had already been lost by then? take the other view: form is what makes trust possible, and people learn care by first practicing courtesy. which moments of your life speak for this? do you lean toward the people who keep the forms or toward the people who break them? what do you dislike in the other group, and is any of it in you?

a mature person stays with what is thick and feeds, and does not live in what is bright and shows.. a mature person stays with what is thick and feeds, and does not live in what is bright and shows. where do you agree, and where does this sound like a refusal of beauty? what in your life is flower: early, bright, made to be seen? do you feel shame or pleasure in it? suppose that the flower matters as much as the fruit, and that display is how living things find each other. stay with that. what changes in your picture of yourself? why does one of the two sit more easily with you? what did it cost you to prefer it?

德 a straight heart on the road. fifteen strokes, three ideas. at the left is 彳, the “step” sign, half of the crossroads picture 行; it marks movement on a road, as in 往 (to go) and 得 (to get). at the lower right is 心, the heart. between them, under a cross, is an eye turned on its side: 罒 is here a form of 目. the cross and the eye and the line below them are a slanted writing of 直, “straight”, which the shuowen explains as 正見也, “to see correctly”, with ten (十) and eye (目) in it. so the right side is 直 over 心, a straight heart, and that is an older character by itself: 悳. the shuowen defines 悳 as getting from others outside and getting in oneself inside. the left side adds the road. the shuowen defines the full character 德 with one word, 升也, “to rise, to go up”, and says that the right side is its sound. scholars of the bronze inscriptions find the graph first without the heart, an eye that looks straight ahead on a road; the heart was added in the western zhou. put it together as a teacher would: to walk with the eye straight and the heart in it. the line 上德不德 uses this character three times in eight characters. the short form 徳, common in japan, leaves out the one horizontal above the heart. fifteen strokes. the step sign: a short stroke that falls left, a longer one under it that falls left, then a vertical. on the right, the cross: a horizontal, then a short vertical through it. the eye on its side: a short vertical at the left, the top and right side in one stroke, two short verticals inside, and the base. then one horizontal, alone. then the heart: a dot at the left, the long hook that lies down and turns up at its end, a dot inside the curve, and a last dot at the right. watch stroke eleven, the single horizontal between eye and heart. it is the floor of the eye and the roof of the heart. then watch stroke thirteen, the lying hook: it must be wide and open, like a bowl, so that the upper parts can rest in it. look for it in zhao mengfu’s small-regular daodejing of 1316, where it returns many times in the second half of the scroll.

禮 an altar and a full vessel. the left side, 礻, is the narrow form of 示. it is commonly explained as an altar stone or a spirit tablet, and it marks what belongs to the gods and ancestors: 神 (spirit), 祖 (ancestor), 祭 (sacrifice), 福 (blessing), 祝 (to pray). the right side, 豊, is the older way to write the whole word; the shuowen says of it 行禮之器也, “a vessel for the performance of rites”, and 讀與禮同, “it is read like 禮”. look at its two layers. below is 豆, a food bowl on a high stem, with its lid: a real ritual vessel of bronze or pottery, later borrowed for the word “bean”. above, the part that now looks like 曲 is the offering in the bowl; many scholars see two strings of jade in the early forms. the near twin 豐, “abundant”, is the same bowl heaped full; the shuowen calls it 豆之豐滿者也. the shuowen defines the full character: 履也，所以事神致福也, “to tread a path; that by which one serves the spirits and brings blessing”. so 禮 is: at the altar, a bowl with precious things in it. the rite came first, and all the later meanings grew from it: the correct forms of court and family, courtesy, a gift (禮物). in this passage the full bowl is called the thin part of trust. the character stays generous: it shows only an offering. it does not show the arm that drags; the laozi adds that. seventeen strokes. the altar side takes four: a dot, a horizontal that turns and falls left, a vertical, and a small dot at the right of the vertical. then the offering, six strokes: the left side of the box, the top and right side, a horizontal inside, two verticals that rise through the top of the box like stalks, and the base. then the bowl, seven strokes: a horizontal lid, the small mouth in three strokes, a dot and a short left-falling stroke for the stem, and a long horizontal foot. watch the last stroke. it is the widest line on the right side, and it reaches left under the altar a little, so that the two halves stand on one floor. the right side has many horizontals, and they must not be of equal length or the vessel looks like a ladder. the song master mi fu wrote that a character needs a frame of bone, and flesh that wraps the sinew.

39 · common as stone. of old, these got the one: / heaven got the one, and so is clear. / earth got the one, and so is at rest. / spirits got the one, and so have power. / valleys got the one, and so are full. / the ten thousand things got the one, and so live. / lords and kings got the one, / and so became the true measure of all under heaven. / that is what brings them to it. / heaven, with nothing to make it clear, might well split. / earth, with nothing to keep it at rest, might well burst. / spirits, with nothing to give them power, might well give out. / valleys, with nothing to fill them, might well run dry. / the ten thousand things, with nothing to make them live, might well die out. / lords and kings, with nothing to keep them noble and high, might well fall. / so the noble has the lowly as its root; / the high has the low as its footing. / for this reason lords and kings name themselves / “the orphan”, “the lone one”, “the unfed”. / is this not to take the lowly as root? is it not? / so: count out the cart, and there is no cart. / no wish to be rare, rare as jade: / common, common as stone. the passage is built as a chant. six things got the one and each has its excellence: heaven clear, earth at rest, spirits potent, valleys full, all things alive, rulers true. six mirror lines say what each would suffer without it. then the argument: the noble has the lowly as its root, and the proof is in the mouths of kings, who call themselves orphans. last come a riddle about a cart and a choice between jade and stone. the movement is from the highest thing to the lowest: it begins with heaven and ends with a common rock. the one is never described. it is known only by what holds together when it is present. what makes an experience one? this moment has a sound, a color, a thought, a feeling in the chest. list them, and the list does not contain the fact that they are one moment, known together. that unity is not a seventh item. a mind that has it is clear and at rest with no effort toward clearness; wang bi says that heaven does not use clearness to be clear. a mind that works at being clear, at being calm, at being spiritual, is the sky that splits. the second half moves to the person. the part of you that wishes to be jade, noticed, rare, and fine, stands on something that has no rank at all: plain presence, as common as stone. that base is not a humiliation. it is the root. the passage speaks to rulers by title two times. first it flatters: they are in the list with heaven and earth. then it shows them the footing. a king is high, and high stands on low as a wall stands on rammed earth. this is engineering, and the ritual language of the court already confessed it. each organization can read the line directly: the executive floor stands on the people who answer the telephone, and when that footing is treated with contempt the wall cracks. the cart warns against rule by inventory: a leader can count the departments and miss the one thing that makes them a company. and jade: a leader who needs to chime as he walks, who needs the tokens of rank, has moved from the root to the branch-tips. an ecologist could have written the six lines. a clear sky, stable ground, valleys with water, the living things: each condition seems to stand by itself, and each one lasts only inside a whole. break the whole and the passage’s verbs become exact: the ground lets go, the springs run dry, species die out. the valley line is the purest case. a valley does not make its water. it is full because it is low and joined to all the slopes. in the same way, the tall tree stands on the mat of roots and fungi that no one sees. the passage’s last image goes to the commonest thing on the planet. soil is ground stone. jade is admired and inert. stone, broken and common, becomes the ground that things grow in. do the exercise of the cart with one thing today. then try the last line for an afternoon: no wish to be jade. in one meeting or one conversation, drop the small moves that are made to be found rare: the reference that shows what you know, the story in which you did well. be a stone among stones: useful, ordinary, part of the ground. notice if anything real was lost. notice also the opposite pose, the pride of the humble. the grammar of the line may refuse that one too.

得一: to get the one. 得 is “to get, to obtain”, a plain verb of possession, and 一 is the numeral one, a single stroke. 得一 is “got one”, “got the one”. the passage before this one played on 德, de, and 得, to get, words of nearly one sound; now the de book’s second passage says 得 seven times. to have de is to have got the one. what is the one? the book does not define it. the shuowen opens its whole dictionary with this character and a daoist sentence: 惟初太始，道立於一, “at the very first, the dao was set up in the one”. it is held, 抱一, in passages 10 and 22; the three things that cannot be seen, heard, or touched merge into it (14); the dao gives birth to it (42). it is the state of being whole and undivided, before two. versions that write “harmony with the one” keep two things, a self and a one, in a relation. the chinese says that heaven has it, as one has a thing. see wang bi on the number.

清 and 寧: clear water, a bowl under a roof. each line of the litany gives a thing its proper virtue in one word. heaven is 清. the shuowen: 朖也。澂水之皃, “bright; the look of water that has settled”. the word has water at the left: heaven’s clearness is described by a pond with the mud gone down. earth is 寧, “at rest”. the older graph for this word is 寍, and the shuowen reads it part by part: 安也。从宀，心在皿上。人之飲食器，所以安人. “peace. a roof, with a heart above a bowl. the vessels of people’s food and drink are that by which people are at peace.” peace is a heart with a full bowl under a roof. the pair became a formula. later imperial names used it: in the forbidden city of beijing the emperor’s residence is the palace of heavenly clarity, 乾清宮, and the empress’s is the palace of earthly rest, 坤寧宮.

神: the spirits are in the list. 神 are spirits: the gods of mountains and rivers, the powers of the soil and grain, the ancestors who receive offerings. the list goes heaven, earth, spirits, valleys, living things, rulers, and the spirits stand third, as real as the valleys. a modern version turns the word into “mind” and makes the passage a psychology. for the first readers the question was practical. a spirit that is 靈 answers: the rain comes, the oracle is correct, the sick person recovers. a spirit that has lost its power is a wooden tablet. the laozi is not a devout book; passage 60 says that when the dao is present in the world, 其鬼不神, “its ghosts have no spirit-power”. but it does not deny the spirits. it puts them inside the order of the one, with the same need as a valley. what gives a holy place its power, and where does it go?

靈: rain, mouths, and a dancer. 靈 is the power of a spirit to respond, and the word for a person or place through which it comes. the graph is a scene. at the top is 雨, rain. under it are three 口; the shuowen says of the upper part, 霝, 雨零也, “rain falls”, and takes the three shapes as large drops. at the bottom is 巫, the spirit-medium, of whom the shuowen says 以舞降神者也, “one who by dance brings the spirits down”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write only the top part, 霝. so the character holds its own test: a medium is 靈 when the rain comes. in the south, in the songs of chu, the possessed medium is herself called 靈. english has to choose “divine”, “numinous”, “efficacious”, or “soul”; a modern version says “inspired”. the chinese word is a power that is proved by an answer. see the plate.

谷: where the spring comes out. the shuowen defines 谷 as 泉出通川爲谷, “where a spring comes out and goes through to a river: that is a valley”, and it reads the graph as water half seen, 从水半見, that comes out of an opening, 口. a valley is first a watercourse. the valley is the laozi’s favorite land form: the valley spirit that does not die (6), “wide open, like a valley” (15), “be the valley of the world” (28), highest de is like a valley (41). each time it is praised for being empty and low. here, for once, it is 盈, full. the two do not conflict. a valley can be filled because it is hollow, and it is filled from above with no effort: all water comes down to it. the silk texts are reported to write the word as 浴, “to bathe”, the same graph with water added.

five lines or six. the pinned text has six that got the one: heaven, earth, spirits, valleys, the ten thousand things, lords and kings. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to have five. they have no line 萬物得一以生, and in the second list no line about the ten thousand things that die out. this is probably the older form. the five are great, particular powers, each with its own excellence. “the ten thousand things” is a different kind of member: it is the sum of all that there is, and it breaks the climb from heaven down to the ruler. a later editor likely added it for completeness, and to bring in the great word 生, “to live”. notice what the addition does to the lords and kings. in the list of five they are the last of the cosmic powers. in the list of six they come after everything.

貞: the word of the oracle bones. the ruler’s excellence is to be 天下貞, the 貞 of the world. the shuowen keeps the first meaning: 卜問也, “to ask by divination”. on the shang oracle bones this is the word that begins each question to the ancestors: the diviner “tests” a statement by fire on bone. from the true answer came the senses “firm, constant, correct”; it is one of the four first words of the book of changes. a ruler who is the world’s 貞 is that by which the world checks itself, a fixed point, like the crack that gives the answer. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write 正, “straight, a standard”, a plainer word with the same use. later 貞 was narrowed to the “chastity” of widows, and a reader must put that sense aside. the claim here is large: by the one, a king becomes a measure. without it, the passage says, he will fall.

其致之, and a second way to read the warnings. 其致之 is three characters: “that / brings about / it”. some editions add 一也: “what brings them to this is the one”. we keep the short form. the silk texts then open a different door. the received warnings say 天無以清將恐裂, “heaven, without that by which it is clear, might well split”. the mawangdui texts are reported to read 謂天毋已清將恐裂. the two small words 毋已 can be read as 無以, and then the sense is the same. but as written they say “without stopping”: “this means: if heaven were clear without end, it would split”. on that reading the second list does not describe a loss of the one. it describes excess: clearness that is pushed to its limit, a valley that must be full for ever, a king who must be noble and high without pause. then the turn to lowliness follows at once. scholars are divided, and both readings are old.

six ways to come apart. the second list has one frame and six verbs of ruin, and each verb fits its subject. heaven would 裂: the shuowen ties the word to cloth, 繒餘也, a torn remnant of silk; the sky rips like a sheet. earth would 發: the first sense is the release of an arrow, 䠶發也; the ground lets go, in a quake or a flood. spirits would 歇: the shuowen has 气越泄, “the breath leaks away”; a spirit runs out like air. valleys would 竭, run dry. living things would 滅; the graph has water and fire, and the shuowen says 盡也, “to be used up”. kings would 蹶: 僵也, “to fall stiff”, as a runner trips. all six verbs belong to one old rhyme group, which scholars name 月, and the frame 將恐, “will, one fears”, is repeated like a drum. this was written to be recited. read the six english lines aloud, quickly, and you have a little of it.

本 and 基: a root and a wall footing. the passage turns here from the cosmos to rank. the turn is prepared one line earlier: the kings’ excellence was 貞 in the first list, and in the mirror list it is 貴高, “noble and high”. now come two pictures from below ground. 本 is a tree, 木, with a mark at its foot; the shuowen says 木下曰本, “the lower part of a tree is called 本”. the same tree with a mark at the top is 末, the branch-tip. 基 has 土, earth: the shuowen says 牆始也, “the beginning of a wall”, the rammed footing on which the wall is raised. so 貴以賤為本 is not a moral remark that the great ought to be modest. it is a statement about structure. the noble stands on the lowly as a tree stands on its root: 貴 is “costly” and 賤 is “cheap”, and both have 貝, the cowrie, in them; rank is a price. a wall has no choice about its footing. the lords of the time lived on the grain, labor, and soldiers of people whom they did not see.

孤, 寡, 不穀: how kings said “i”. this is court history. a zhou ruler did not use the common words for “i” in formal speech. he said 寡人, “the person who lacks”, usually explained as “of little de”. in mourning or after a defeat he said 孤, “the orphan”; the shuowen defines it as 無父也, “without a father”, and a ruler normally came to his seat when his father died. 不穀 is frequent in the zuozhuan, most of all in the mouths of the kings of chu and of the zhou king. 穀 is grain, and by extension “good, well provided”, so the phrase is “the unfed” or “the not-good”. the histories are full of these words. they were formulas of ritual modesty, said by men with armies. the laozi takes the formula as evidence: at the top of the state, the language already admits what holds it up. the same three names return in passage 42 as “what people hate”. legge read the third one very differently.

數輿無輿: a cart, or praise. this line is one of the hard places of the book. the pinned text reads 致數輿無輿: “carry to the end the count of the cart: no cart”. 輿 is the box of a cart, and so a cart. list the parts, wheel, axle, box, pole, and no part is “cart”; the cart is the one thing that the count does not find. that fits the passage: take the one away and you have a heap. wang bi has this text. a buddhist book of later centuries, the questions of king milinda, makes the same point about a chariot and the self. other old editions read 譽, “praise”, a word of the same sound: 致數譽無譽, “the highest renown is to have no renown”, or “count up your praises and none is left”. the zhuangzi has 至譽無譽, “the utmost praise is no praise”. the silk texts are reported to write 與, which can stand for 輿 or 譽 and so does not decide.

琭琭, 珞珞: doubled words. classical chinese makes vivid words by saying a syllable two times. they work like “glitter” or “clatter”: they give the look, the sound, and the feel of a thing together, and they are hard to define. 琭琭 goes with jade and 珞珞 with stone, and old readers do not agree about what they say. the heshang gong commentary takes them as number: 琭琭 is “few”, as jade is rare and so is prized; 珞珞 (other texts write 落落) is “many”, as stones lie about and are cheap. others hear the materials: the fine ring of jade pieces, the dull knock of rocks. the silk texts are reported to write 祿祿 and 硌硌, different graphs for like sounds, which shows that scribes wrote these words by ear. our “rare, rare” and “common, common” keep the doubling and follow heshang gong. what would you call the sound of a person who has no need to be valued?

jade was rank that one could hear. jade was the most prized substance of early china. a noble wore jade pendants at the belt, and the ritual books say that their chime as he walked kept his pace correct. lords held jade tablets at court as tokens of their rank. a single disc could move states: in 283 bce the king of qin offered fifteen cities for the jade of mr. he, which belonged to zhao, and a minister of zhao became famous because he brought it home whole. so “not to wish to be like jade” is said against the main sign of nobility. the grammar leaves a question. 不欲 may govern both halves: no wish to be jade, and no wish to be stone, since both are poses. most readers supply “rather”: not jade, but stone. the chinese has no “rather”. passage 70 gives one more turn: the sage wears rough cloth and carries jade inside.

wang bi: use the one, not the clearness. on the first line wang bi writes: 昔，始也。一，數之始而物之極也. “‘of old’ is ‘at the beginning’. one is the beginning of number and the limit of things.” each thing got this one and so became itself; then 既成而舍以居成，居成則失其母, “once complete, it leaves the one and settles in its completeness; settled in completeness, it loses its mother”. that is the cause of the six disasters. his sharpest sentence is on heaven: 用一以致清耳，非用清以清也。守一則清不失，用清則恐裂也. “it uses the one to arrive at clearness; it does not use clearness to be clear. keep the one and clearness is not lost; use clearness and the split is to be feared.” a sky that tried to be clear would crack. on the end: 貴在其母，而母無貴形, “the worth is in the mother, and the mother has no form of worth”.

legge: rhymes, and a carriage with no nave. legge puts both lists into rhymed couplets: heaven is “bright and pure”, earth “firm and sure”. the chinese gives each thing one word; the rhyme needs two, so each virtue is doubled. he adds “(the tao)” after “the one”, an equation that the text does not make; passage 42 says that the dao gives birth to the one. his oddest choice is in the royal names. for 不穀 he writes “carriages without a nave”. this is not his own slip. he followed the heshang gong commentary, which reads 轂, the hub of a wheel, a graph that differs from 穀, grain, by one part: the king says that he cannot be the hub on which the spokes meet. modern scholars take that reading as a folk explanation. it is a suggestive one, since a cart comes two lines later and the hub is the empty center of passage 11. his kings rule by “moral sway”, a victorian phrase with no chinese behind it. he follows the cart reading of the hard line, with a long paraphrase.

a litany and its dark mirror. the form is the content here. six lines with one mould, x 得一以 y: only two characters change in each. then six lines that mirror them, x 無以 y 將恐 z. the first list goes down like steps, from the sky to one man on a throne. the second goes down the same steps and knocks each one away. the six end words of the first list, 清, 寧, 靈, 盈, 生, 貞, are all in one old rhyme group, which scholars name 耕. a hearer who knows the first list can predict the second, and that is the point: the mind feels the dependence before it is argued. this is the method of ritual chant and of the old court odes, and it is rare in the laozi, which more often speaks in couplets. after the twelve lines the prose changes to questions: “is it not? is it not so?” the teacher turns from the cosmos and looks at the king. count how many times the english must say “the one”. the chinese says 一, one stroke.

count out the cart. choose a thing that you are proud of or depend on: a team, a family, a skill, your own name. list its parts on paper, as many as you can. then ask where in the list the thing itself is. the team is not any member, the skill is not any single movement. what makes the parts one? you will not find it as an item, and without it the items are a heap. then do the second half of the passage. ask what low thing this high thing stands on: who cooks, who cleans, which dull routine, which people that no one names. write those down too. they are the 本, the root.

貴/賤, 高/下: the wall and its footing. two pairs stand here: noble 貴 and lowly 賤, high 高 and low 下. the chinese does not rank them. it relates them: one is root and footing of the other. no footing, no wall; and with no wall above it, a footing is only packed earth. passage 2 says it of the pair itself: 高下相傾, high and low lean on each other. the text does send kings toward the low side. that is a correction for men who looked only upward. it does not say that the low place is the better place. the low side turns as well. the humble titles show it: “the orphan” and “the lone one” were words that in practice only a ruler used, so the low name grew into a badge of the highest rank. a one-sided reading makes this passage praise of humility. it is a statement of how height is built, and a warning that each side can be worn as a pose, as the last line may say.

what is high stands on what is low, as a wall stands on its footing.. what is high stands on what is low, as a wall stands on its footing. is that how you see the high places in your own world? what are they standing on? where do you place yourself, among the high or among the low? when did you first learn where you belonged? take the reverse: the low depends on the high, and without those who lead and carry risk the base has no shape. what feelings come with that view? which side makes you angry or uneasy? what does the unease tell you about what you have lived?

there is no need to be rare like jade; to be common like stone is enough.. there is no need to be rare like jade; to be common like stone is enough. do you believe it? or is there a part of you that must be jade? who first told you that you were special, or that you were not? how does that voice still steer you? hold the opposite for a few breaths: each person has something rare, and to hide it is a waste. what rises: relief, pressure, grief? notice also the pride of being plain. do you know that pose in yourself, or in someone whom you judge?

each thing keeps its excellence only while it is joined to a whole; cut off, it breaks.. each thing keeps its excellence only while it is joined to a whole; cut off, it breaks. where have you seen this happen: a strength that failed when it stood alone? what whole do you depend on that you seldom name? what stops you from naming it? try the other side: a thing becomes itself only when it separates and stands alone. which periods of your life prove that? which do you trust more, belonging or independence? what happened that taught you so?

靈 rain, three drops, a dancer. this is one of the great pictures in the script. read it from the top down, in three floors. the top floor is 雨, rain: a sky line, a cloud that hangs from it, and four drops. you know it from 雲 (cloud), 雪 (snow), 電 (lightning), 雷 (thunder). the middle floor is three 口 in a row. they are not mouths here; the shuowen, in its entry for the two upper floors together, 霝, says 雨零也, “rain falls”, and takes them as big drops. others see three mouths that chant for rain. the bottom floor is 巫, a spirit-medium. the shuowen defines her: 女能事無形，以舞降神者也。象人兩褎舞形. “a woman who can serve the formless, and by dance brings the spirits down. it shows a person with two sleeves, dancing.” in the modern form you can see two small 人 at each side of a post, between a line above and a line below: heaven, earth, and the dancers between. so the whole character is a rain rite. the medium dances below; the drops come down above. if the rain comes, she is 靈, potent. the shuowen lists the character under jade, in an older form with 玉 at the bottom, 以玉事神, “one who serves the spirits with jade”, and gives 靈 as the variant with 巫. the short form 灵 is an old popular variant. in this passage the spirits got the one and so are 靈. the character says how people knew: it rained. twenty-four strokes. rain takes eight: a horizontal; a short stroke down at the left; a horizontal that hooks down at the right; a vertical in the middle; then four dots, two at each side of the vertical. then three small boxes from left to right, three strokes each: left side, top with right side, base. then the medium, seven strokes: a horizontal; a vertical post; a left-falling stroke and a dot for the person at the left; a left-falling stroke and a dot for the person at the right; and a long horizontal floor. watch the three boxes. they are the hardest part: equal in size, level, with equal gaps, and small enough that the character does not grow fat in the middle. the rain cover must be wide and flat and the last stroke the widest of all. a writer who gives each floor the same height makes a tower. the good hands press the top two floors and let the dancer have room.

玉 the king with a dot. three horizontal lines and one vertical through them: that was the whole character for jade in the old scripts, and the shuowen explains it: 象三玉之連，丨其貫也, “it shows three pieces of jade joined; the 丨 is the cord through them”. the trouble was that the character for king, 王, had come to look the same: three lines and a post. the tang editor li yangbing, quoted in the shuowen text, tells them apart by spacing: of 王 he says 中畫近上, “the middle line is near the top”, and of 玉, 三畫正均, “the three lines are exactly even”. later writers solved the problem with a dot at the lower right, and jade became 玉. but when jade is a part at the left of a character, it is still written with no dot, and looks like a king: 理 (to work jade along its veins, and so “pattern, reason”), 現 (to appear), 珍 (a treasure), 玩 (to play, first to turn jade in the hand). the two rare words of this passage, 琭 and 珞, have this side: they are jade words, though they seem to say “king”. that is a good accident for a passage that speaks to lords and kings and ends by refusing jade. the king, 王, is jade with the dot taken away. stone, 石, by contrast, is a rock under a cliff: the shuowen calls it 山石也, “mountain stone”. five strokes. a horizontal at the top. a second horizontal under it, shorter. then the vertical, from the middle of the first line down through the second. then the long base line, the widest stroke. last the dot, at the right, in the space between the second line and the base. watch the dot. it is one touch of the brush and it turns a king into a stone; it should lean and have a tail, like a seed, and it must not touch the vertical. keep the two spaces between the three lines equal: that evenness was the old sign of jade. in clerical script the base line has the long “silkworm head and goose tail” wave, and the character sits on it like a pendant on a cord.

40 · the way turns back. turning back is the movement of the dao. / weak is the use of the dao. / all under heaven, the ten thousand things / are born from having; / having is born from not-having. twenty-one characters; it is the shortest passage in the book. two twin lines and one sentence in two steps. the dao has a movement, and it is turning back. the dao has a way of working, and it is weak. then the things of the world: they are born from what is there, and what is there is born from what is not. no sage, no ruler, no advice, no “therefore”. the passage does not argue. it states, as a carpenter states that wood has a grain. notice also the order inside the last sentence. it goes backward: from the ten thousand things to having, from having to not-having. the sentence about origins is itself a return. follow a thought back. it is here, vivid, a thing that you have: 有. a moment ago it was not. where did it come from? look, and you find no place and no stuff, only a quiet that was there before it and is there after. that is not a mystical claim; it is what anyone finds who looks. the contemplative reading of 反 is this turn of attention, from the things that appear to that out of which they appear. it is weak work. force does not help; a mind that grabs at the source of thought produces one more thought. the turn happens when effort gives out. wang bi says that to keep having whole one goes back to not-having: the world is not lost in the quiet. it is seen to stand in it. each leader is trained to move forward and to be strong. the passage says that the deepest movement goes the other way and works by weakness. read it first as a description of what will happen in any case. a policy that is pushed to its extreme turns into its opposite; growth returns to its base; the thing at the top is on its way down. a leader who knows this plans for the return and does not fight it. read it second as a manner of acting. a force that lasts in an organization is often of the weak kind: listening, patience, the question that is asked and not the order that is given. these do not look like power, and that is why they are not resisted. do not make this a tactic, a show of softness to get one’s way. the line says that the dao works so. it does not offer a technique for winning. the body moves by return. a step is a fall that is caught; a jump begins with a bend downward; the arm goes back before the throw; the heart fills before it beats. each skilled movement has its 反, and beginners are known by the lack of it: they try to go straight to the target. the second line is the teaching of every soft art. strength that is used is local and soon spent. weakness, in the exact sense of a joint that gives and a muscle that is not held, lets the whole body act as one, and the ground does the work. try it with the breath: do not push the air out; let the ribs fall. the out-breath that is not forced goes further, and the in-breath arrives out of the pause with no help from you. all large motions in nature are returns. the planets go around; the seasons come back; water goes up as vapor and comes down as rain to the sea it left. a tree is the plainest text. the seed is almost nothing, the tree is a great having, and at the end the trunk goes back into soil, out of which seeds grow. and the working of all this is weak. no part of it uses force as a human engine does. roots advance by cells, rivers cut rock with soft water, and the light that drives the whole system arrives without weight. the picture in 生 is the last line seen in a field: a shoot, there, where yesterday nothing was to be seen. do the three turnings: a breath, a sound, a mood. then pick one place today where you would normally push: a door, a conversation, a problem at work. use half of the force that you planned, and look for the direction in which the thing already wants to return. tonight, read the four lines aloud in chinese if you can find a recording, or simply count them: five characters, five characters, seven, four. each line but the third is as short as a breath.

反: three words in one. 反 holds three senses, and english needs a word for each. one: to go back, to return home; this sense was later written 返. two: to turn over, to reverse, as a hand turns from palm to back; the shuowen gives this first: 覆也, “to turn over”. three: the opposite, contrary to. so the line says at once that the dao moves by return, that it moves by reversal into the opposite, and that it moves against the common direction. the book uses each: 遠曰反, “far means return” (25); 正言若反, “straight words seem their opposite” (78); dark de goes 與物反, “the other way from things” (65). a modern version chose “polarity”, which gives two fixed poles and no motion. 反 is a motion. we write “turning back” and lose the opposition. see also return in the book of changes. which of the three do you see most often in your own life?

動: strength on a heavy thing. 動 is 重, heavy, with 力, strength, at the right. the shuowen says that 重 is the sound, and defines the word as 作也, “to rise, to start up”; the same verb 作 named the wanting that stirs in passage 37. the parts make a fair picture: force applied to a weight. this is the only place where the book gives the dao a 動, a motion, as its own. in other passages the dao is still, and moving is what things do: 動善時, “in movement, the good is timing” (8); the bellows of heaven and earth, 動而愈出, “the more it moves, the more comes out” (5). and the motion that the dao is given here is no advance. each motion that we admire goes forward: progress, growth, a career. the one movement of the dao is the way back.

five characters, two times. the first two lines are twins. 反者道之動 and 弱者道之用: the frame x 者道之 y is fixed, and only the first and last characters change. 者 after a word makes it a topic, “that which turns back”, and 之 joins owner and thing owned, “the dao’s movement”. nothing says “is”. classical chinese sets two noun phrases side by side, and the equation is made by the reader’s mind. the frame makes a second equation that is not stated. 反 stands where 弱 stands, and 動 where 用 stands: turning back is a kind of weakness, and movement is a kind of use. the end words rhyme: 動 and 用 belong to one old rhyme group, which scholars name 東. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to add four particles, 反也者，道之動也, and the lines slow to the pace of a teacher who explains. the received text is as bare as a formula.

弱: the word should stay uncomfortable. 弱 is “weak”. the shuowen defines it as 橈也, “bent”; it is the weakness of that which gives under a load. it was not a good word in early china any more than it is now. states feared to be 弱, and the reformers of the time promised 富國強兵, a rich state and a strong army. to say that weakness is how the dao works is an offense against the whole program of the age. translators often help the reader here with “yielding”, “gentleness”, or “receptivity”, words that a strong person can accept as skills. the text does not help. it says that the dao has no force to apply: it does not push, win, or insist, and by this lack it does everything. water in passage 78 is the proof: nothing is weaker, and nothing that attacks the hard can beat it. where do you hide your weakness, and what does the hiding cost?

用: how it works, not what it is for. 用 is “use, function”: a thing at work. passage 11 found the 用 of a wheel, a pot, and a room at the place where each has nothing. passage 4 said that the dao is an empty bowl and that use does not fill it. now the 用 of the dao gets a name: weak. english “use” suggests a user with a purpose, as if someone took up the dao as a tool, and some versions make the line a method: be weak and you will succeed. the chinese says only that this is the manner of its working. later chinese philosophy made a great pair of 體 and 用, “body” and “function”: what a thing is and how it acts. wang bi, who began that way of speaking, comments here in six words: weak and soft go through everywhere and cannot be exhausted.

the silk texts: plainer, and in a different place. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 天下之物生於有，有生於无: “the things of the world”, with no “ten thousand”. wang bi also quotes the line as 天下之物, so 萬 seems to have entered after his time. the larger difference is position. in the silk manuscripts this passage does not stand between 39 and 41. it comes after passage 41 and directly before passage 42. read them in that order. passage 41 ends: the dao is hidden and nameless, and it alone is good at giving and completing. then these four lines: turning back, weakness, things from having, having from not-having. then passage 42: the dao gives birth to one, one to two, two to three, three to the ten thousand things. the account of origins runs without a break, and this short passage is its hinge. the received order cut the hinge out and set it alone, and there it looks like a riddle. see also the oldest reading of the last line.

生: a sprout comes out of the soil. the verb of the last two lines is 生, and it is a picture. the shuowen: 進也。象艸木生出土上, “to come forth; it shows grass and trees that grow out above the soil”. the word means to be born, to give birth, to grow, to live, and to be raw or fresh. english versions often write “produced”, “created”, or “came from”; legge has “sprang”. “produced” is a factory word. “created” brings in a maker who stands outside the work and a first moment of time. 生 has neither. a sprout is not made by the soil and is not apart from it; it is the soil’s own outward growth, and it goes on. so 有生於無 does not say that a nothing made a something long ago. it says that what is there grows, now, out of what is not there, as a shoot out of dark ground. see the plate.

有 and 無: not being and nothingness. 有 is “to have, there is”; 無 is “to not have, there is not”. as nouns they are “the having” and “the not-having”: what is present and what is absent. western philosophy translated them as being and non-being, and then read this line beside its own long quarrel. the greeks held that nothing comes from nothing. christian doctrine answered that god made the world out of nothing. both sides took “nothing” as absolute: no thing at all, a blank. the chinese 無 is not that. in passage 11 it is the hollow of a pot: an absence with a shape, which works. it is nearer to “the not-yet-formed”, or to the silence that a note comes out of. the line states no doctrine of creation. it points to the fact that each thing that is there stands in, and comes out of, what is not. does that fact need a beginning in time?

the quarrel over 無. this line caused one of the great debates of chinese thought, six centuries after it was written. wang bi and his circle, in the 240s ce, took it as the key to the book: 無 is the root of all that is, and the wise ruler goes back to it. their position was called 貴無, “to honor not-having”. two generations later the official pei wei wrote an essay against them, “in honor of having” (崇有論). he argued that pure not-having cannot give birth to anything, that things come about by themselves, and that the fashion for 無 gave idle aristocrats an excuse to neglect their duties. the commentator guo xiang then built a philosophy on the same point: there is no source behind things; each is self-born. both sides could quote the laozi. passage 2 says 有無相生, “having and not-having give birth to each other”. is that a different teaching from this line, or the same one seen from the side?

the guodian slips: one character less. the oldest copy of this passage is on the guodian bamboo slips, from a tomb of about 300 bce. its last line is reported to read 天下之物生於有，生於亡: “the things of the world are born from having, born from not-having”. the second 有 is not there, and 亡 is the old way to write 無. if the scribe wrote what he meant, the sense changes much. having and not-having are then two parents of things, side by side, as in passage 2, and not a chain in which one comes first. the priority of 無, on which wang bi built so much, would be a later reading. but scribes of that time marked a repeated character with a small sign, and such signs were easily lost in copying; many scholars think that this is a simple slip. one missing mark, and two philosophies. we cannot decide it, and the chinese reader now reads the line with both in view.

return in the book of changes. the idea of 反 was not the laozi’s alone. the book of changes has a hexagram named 復, “return”: five broken lines with one whole line that enters at the bottom. it stands for the winter solstice, the longest night, when the light turns and begins to come back. its judgment text says 反復其道，七日來復, “turning and returning on its way; in seven days comes the return”, and the old commentary adds 復其見天地之心乎, “in return, do we not see the heart of heaven and earth?” the laozi’s own word for it in passage 16 is 復: the ten thousand things rise together, and i watch their return. a later proverb made it a rule of prudence: 物極必反, “a thing at its limit must turn back”. the farmer, the diviner, and the strategist all used this. the laozi’s claim is larger: the turn is not one event among others. it is the only way that the dao moves.

wang bi: to keep having whole, go back to not-having. on the first line wang bi quotes the passage before: 高以下為基，貴以賤為本，有以無為用，此其反也. “the high has the low as its footing, the noble has the lowly as its root, having has not-having as its use: this is its ‘turning back’.” for him 反 is the dependence of each thing on its opposite. on weakness: 柔弱同通，不可窮極, “soft and weak alike go through, and cannot be brought to an end”. on the last line: 天下之物皆以有為生，有之所始，以無為本，將欲全有，必反於無也. “the things of the world all have their life as having. that from which having starts has not-having as its root. to keep having whole, one must turn back to not-having.” his final clause joins the last line to the first. the return of line one is the road from 有 to 無, and it is not a loss of the world. he says it is how the world is kept.

legge: a hymn stanza and a capital “it”. legge made the first two lines a rhymed quatrain in the metre of a hymn: the dao “by contraries proceeds”, and weakness “marks the course of tao’s mighty deeds”. the chinese has no “mighty” and no “deeds”; he could not leave weakness alone without a counterweight. in the last lines he writes that all things “sprang from it as existing (and named)” and that existence “sprang from it as non-existent (and not named)”. the capital “it” is the dao, which the chinese sentence does not mention: the line has only 有 and 無. he made the two into two states of one supreme subject, with brackets taken from passage 1. this protects the reader from the strange claim that having is born from not-having. it also makes the dao a thing that exists in two modes, close to a god who is before and in creation.

watch one thing turn. today, find the turning point in three ordinary things. a breath: follow the out-breath to its end and wait; do not pull the next breath in; see it start. a sound: ring a glass or a bell and listen until you cannot say if you still hear it. a mood: when irritation or delight is strong, notice the moment at which it is no longer growing. in each case look at what the next thing comes out of. the in-breath comes out of the empty pause, and the silence after the bell is where the next sound will appear. that is 有生於無 at the scale of a minute.

有/無 and 強/弱: does one side come first?. two pairs work in this passage. having 有 and not-having 無 are named. strong 強 is not named, but 弱, weak, calls it up. the last line seems to rank the first pair: things come from having, and having from not-having. passage 2 says something different: 有無相生, the two bear each other. the first line here settles it. if turning back is how the dao moves, then not-having is not a throne above having. it is the place that having returns to and leaves again; the oldest copy may even set the two side by side. the same holds for weak. the line calls weakness the use, 用, of the dao. it does not say that weak defeats strong for all time. a shoot is weak and grows hard; the hard tree falls and becomes soft soil. the text speaks for the weak side in an age that worshipped strength. the turning applies to the weak as well.

everything that goes far enough turns back; return is how the way moves.. everything that goes far enough turns back; return is how the way moves. do you see this in your life, or do you see lines that only go forward? think of something that is at its height now: a success, a bond, a strength. what do you feel when you picture its return? hold the opposite: some gains are permanent, and progress is real. what in you needs that to be true? which do you fear more, that things turn back or that they do not? where might that fear have begun?

the way does its work through weakness, not through force.. the way does its work through weakness, not through force. is this true in what you have seen, or is it a comfort for those without power? where do you hide your own weakness? who taught you that it had to be hidden? take the opposite side fully: strength gets things done, and weakness is used by others. stay with it. what memories arrive? what do you feel toward weak people, and toward strong ones? what do those feelings say about the part of you that you do not show?

what exists comes out of what does not exist.. what exists comes out of what does not exist. can you find this in experience: a thought, a mood, a meeting that came from nowhere? how do you feel about empty time, an empty room, a gap in talk? where did you learn to fill it, or to like it? now hold the opposite: something comes only from something, and an empty place gives nothing. what does that view make you do with your days? which view is closer to how you in fact live? is that the one you would choose?

反 a hand turns over. four strokes, and the shuowen sees two parts: 从又，厂反形. 又 is a hand. it is the lower right part, and you know it from 友 (friend: two hands) and 取 (to take: a hand at an ear). in the old scripts 又 is a right hand seen from the side, three fingers and a wrist. the other part is the line that covers the hand from the upper left, written like 厂, a cliff; the shuowen does not call it a cliff here. it says that it shows the shape of turning over, 反形, and it defines the whole as 覆也, “to turn over”. so the common explanation is a hand that flips something, or a hand that is itself turned, palm to back. from that one gesture come all the senses: to turn over, to turn round, to go back, the reverse side, the opposite, to rebel. the family is large. add the walking sign and you have 返, to go back by road; the shuowen says 从辵从反. the others take 反 for its sound, and it is fair to notice that some keep a turn in the sense: 販, to trade, defined as 買賤賣貴者, “one who buys cheap and sells dear”; 版, a board split from a log. in this passage the dao has one movement, and it is this small gesture: a hand turned over. it takes no force to turn a hand. that is the second line of the passage. four strokes. first a flat stroke at the top, written from right to left: the brush lands at the right, heavy, and thins as it goes left. second, a long stroke that begins under the left end of the first and falls down and away to the left. these two make the cover. third, the hand: a short horizontal that turns at its end and falls to the left, in one movement, through the space under the cover. fourth, a long stroke that falls to the right, crosses the third, and ends in a broad foot. watch the first stroke. it is the only one in the character that the brush writes against its usual direction, right to left: the character for turning back begins with a stroke that goes backward. then watch the crossing of strokes three and four; it should sit under the center of the top stroke, or the hand slides out from under its cover.

生 a sprout above the soil. the base line is the ground. the vertical is a stem that comes up out of it. the two upper horizontals and the small slanted stroke at the top left are leaves or branches. the shuowen reads it so: 象艸木生出土上, “it shows grass and trees that grow out above the soil”, and its definition is 進也, “to go forward, to come forth”. in the oracle-bone forms the picture is simpler still: a small plant with one pair of leaves on a line of earth. compare 土, earth: a base line, a vertical, one cross-line; a clod on the ground. 生 is 土 with more growth on top. from “sprout” the word spread to all that lives and begins: to be born, to bear, to grow, life, a living, raw, fresh, unfamiliar. a teacher is 先生, “born earlier”. as a part of other characters it gives sound and often sense. the shuowen explains 姓, a family name, as 人所生也, “that from which a person is born”: 女, a woman, with 生; many of the oldest clan names, such as 姬 and 姜, are written with 女. by its modern parts, 性, “inborn nature”, is 心, the heart, with 生; the shuowen takes 生 there as the sound. in this passage the verb comes two times: things are born from having, and having from not-having. keep the plant in mind. the white paper under the base line is not drawn, and the sprout stands on it. five strokes. first the short stroke at the upper left, which falls to the left. second, a horizontal that starts from the middle of it. third, a shorter horizontal below. fourth, the vertical, from above the first horizontal straight down through both. fifth, the base, the longest line. watch the three horizontals: they must be unequal, middle one shortest, base longest, and each one tilted up a little to the right, or the plant becomes a fence. the vertical must stand exactly on the middle of the base. the first stroke is the only one that leans, and it gives the character its life; write it too flat and the sprout wilts. in cursive script the whole character becomes one line with two loops, written in a single breath.

41 · if no one laughed. the highest scholar hears the dao / and works hard to walk it. / the middle scholar hears the dao: / now it is there, now it is gone. / the lowest scholar hears the dao / and laughs out loud at it. / no laughter: not enough to be the dao. / so the established sayings have it: / the bright way seems dim. / the way forward seems to go back. / the level way seems knotted. / highest de seems a valley. / great white seems soiled. / broad de seems not enough. / firm de seems slack. / plain truth seems to fade. / the great square has no corners. / the great vessel is late complete. / the great note is thin of sound. / the great image is without shape. / the dao is hidden, without name. / yet only the dao / is good at lending and at completing. three parts. first a scene with three scholars and three responses to one teaching: toil, wavering, loud laughter, and the remark that the laughter is required. second, a citation: twelve old sayings from the “established sayings”, eleven of four characters and one of five. eight say that a good thing seems its opposite: bright seems dim, level seems knotted, white seems soiled. four say that the great form of a thing lacks its mark: a square with no corners, a vessel not finished, a note with hardly a sound. third, a summary of two lines: the dao is hidden and unnamed, and it alone lends and completes. the twelve sayings explain the laughter. if the real thing can look like its opposite, then a sensible person, who judges by looks, must laugh. the three hearers are not three people. they are three moments of one mind, and they can come within an hour. there is the moment of plain recognition, when hearing and doing are one. there is the wavering, and it is honest: the thing in question does seem there and seem not there. and there is the laugh, the mind’s quick defense of what it already knows. the twelve sayings are a preparation for how the path will feel from inside. clarity will feel like dimness, since the old certainty is gone. progress will feel like retreat, since one has less to show. the even state will feel lumpy. if your practice feels like a steady rise in brightness and attainment, the passage suggests a question. the last line gives comfort that is not sweet: what you need is lent, not earned. a new and true idea in an organization gets the same three receptions, and a leader should expect all three and not count votes. a few people simply start to work in the new way. most hold it and drop it, by turns. some laugh in the meeting. the laugh is information: an idea at which no one laughs is probably the old idea in new words. the twelve sayings then describe how good leadership looks from outside, which is: not impressive. the clear direction looks vague. the solid person looks slack, because there is no display of effort. the capable institution has no sharp corners, and its best work makes little noise. be careful with the proverb about the great vessel. in its older form it does not promise a late success. it says that the greatest capacity stays unfinished. the sayings are observations before they are paradoxes. the light by which all things live is not seen as light; in full daylight no one notices the sun, and one sees by it. the level path over real ground winds and bumps; only a road forced through hills is straight. a valley is where the greatest fullness of water and soil collects, and it is the low place. the horizon of the sea is the edge of a shape too large to have corners. the deep background sounds of the world, wind and far water, are hardly sounds at all, and they contain all the others. and each living thing has its form on loan: the carbon, the water, the warmth are borrowed for a season and returned. no tree is ever a finished vessel. it grows until it falls. try the three hearers exercise with one line. a second exercise for the ears, from the great note: tonight, sit for three minutes and listen for the quietest sound that you can find, then for the one behind it. do not name them. find the level at which you cannot tell hearing from not hearing. that edge is 希. the sayings claim that it is not the absence of music. it is the largest note, the one in which no single note has yet shut out the others.

士: the men who went from court to court. the shuowen defines 士 by a pun, 事也, “one who serves, who does tasks”. 士 was the lowest rank of the old zhou nobility: men of good family with no land of their own, trained in arms, writing, and ritual. when the old order broke, they became a class for hire. a 士 of the fourth century bce could be a knight, a clerk, a strategist, or a traveling teacher; states competed for the best, and the king of qi kept hundreds of them in an academy at the jixia gate of his capital. they are the public of all the philosophers, and the first readers of this book. 上士, 中士, 下士 are also real titles: mencius lists “upper, middle, and lower 士” as the three lowest grades of office. the passage takes the grades of the civil service and sorts them again, by one test: what a man does when he hears the dao. english “scholar” gives the study and loses the sword and the job search.

勤: with toil, or only just. the received text says that the highest scholar 勤而行之, “toils and walks it”. the shuowen defines 勤 as 勞也, “to labor”. this is a surprise in a book of not-forcing: the best student is the one who works at it. the line agrees with passage 70, where the speaker says that his words are very easy to practice and no one in the world can practice them. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write 堇, a graph that has no strength sign, and the guodian bamboo slips are reported to read 堇能行於其中. many editors take 堇 as 勤 and see no difference. others read it as 僅, “barely”: the highest scholar hears the dao and is only just able to walk in it. that reading is humbler and may be older. even the best can hardly do it. which of the two is more true of your own practice?

若存若亡: the middle hearer. four characters: “as if / there / as if / gone”. 存 is to be present, to keep alive; 亡 is to be gone, to lose, to perish; the shuowen defines 亡 as 逃也, “to run away”. what is it that seems there and seems gone? the grammar permits three answers. the dao: to this hearer it seems now real and now not. the hearing: he seems to keep it and then to lose it; 亡 was also used to write 忘, to forget. the hearer himself: half present, half absent. the same words 若存 describe the dao in passage 6: 綿綿若存, “fine as a thread, it seems to be there”. so the middle scholar’s wavering is an accurate report: the dao is in fact a thing that seems there and seems not. the passage does not mock him. most readers of this book are him, on most days.

笑: the missing entry. the character for laughter has a hole in its history. in the shuowen jiezi the entry for 笑 says only 此字本闕, “this character was originally missing”: the editors of the tenth century found a gap and said so. they added what they could gather from older books, and the explanations do not agree. the modern form has ⺮, bamboo, above 夭, a figure that bends. the tang calligrapher li yangbing, in a note that the editors kept, explained it thus: bamboo in the wind bends like a person who laughs. nobody knows. the word here is 大笑, “great laughter”, and with 之 it has an object: he laughs at it. the lowest scholar is not dull. he is quick; he knows at once that this talk of weakness and of things that seem their opposites is absurd. see the plate, and see why the laugh is needed.

不笑不足以為道: the laugh is the proof. 不笑不足以為道: “not laughed at, not enough to count as the dao”. two negatives make a strict condition. the laughter of the lowest scholar is not a regrettable side effect. it is a mark of the real thing, as a hallmark is the mark of silver. if a teaching pleases everyone at first hearing, it has only told them what they already think. the line is also a joke at the expense of the book’s own audience, which was made of 士, and at the expense of the reader, who must now ask which of the three he is. the zhuangzi opens with the same structure: the cicada and the little dove laugh at the great bird that flies ninety thousand li. the small laugh at the great because they measure by themselves. but the laozi does not despise the one who laughs. it uses him. when did you last laugh at an idea that you later needed?

建言: a book that is lost. 建言有之 is “the 建言 has it”, the phrase with which a writer cites a source. wang bi glosses 建 as 立, “to set up”: “established sayings”, old maxims. other readers take 建言 as the title of a book, and if so, the book is lost and these twelve lines are all that remain of it. in both cases the laozi here shows what it is made of. it is not one author’s essay. it is a weave of proverbs, rhymed sayings, and comments on them, collected over a long time; the guodian slips of about 300 bce already have this passage, in a bundle with a few others. the twelve lines that follow have a different beat from the prose before them: four characters each, but for one of five, with rhyme. legge called their authors “the sentence-makers”. the voice of the book steps back and lets an older voice speak.

若 eight times, then 無. the twelve sayings fall into two groups by one small word. the first eight have 若, “seems like, is as if”: bright seems dim, forward seems back. these are statements about appearance. the way is in fact bright; it looks dim to the one who looks. the last four change the word. the great square has no (無) corners; the great vessel is late (晚) in completion; the great note is sparse (希) in sound; the great image is without (無) shape. these do not say “seems”. they say that the great form of a thing really lacks the mark by which we know the thing. so the list goes from “it will look wrong to you” to “it is not what you think it is”. rhyme crosses the divide. by the old rhyme groups the end words fall into four sets: 昧, 退, 纇; 谷, 辱, 足 (group 屋); 偷, 渝, 隅 (group 侯); and 成, 聲, 形 (group 耕), with 名 of the next line as a fourth. the silk texts are reported to write 如 for 若.
