昧: the grey before sunrise. 昧 has 日, the sun, at the left. the shuowen gives two senses. the first is in the compound 昧爽, 旦明也, “the light at daybreak”: the grey time when the sun is not yet up. the second: 一曰闇也, “some say: dark”. so the word is not black night. it is the dimness in which things can just be made out. 明, “bright”, at the head of the line, is the book’s word for true sight. 明道若昧, “the bright way seems dim”: to an eye used to lamps, real light looks like dusk. wang bi glosses the line with four words from passage 58: 光而不耀, “it has light and does not dazzle”. compare the faint light, 微明, of passage 36. the silk text is reported to write the last word with another graph, 費, which editors read in the same sense.

夷 and 纇: a level road, a knot in the silk. 夷 is “level, flat”: the shuowen says 平也. passage 53 uses it of the highway: 大道甚夷, “the great road is very level”, and people love the bypaths. 纇 is a weaver’s word. it has 糸, silk thread, at the left, and the shuowen defines it as 絲節也, “a knot in the silk”: the lump where a thread was joined or the raw silk was uneven. run a silk thread through your fingers and it catches there. so: the level way feels knotty. a road that follows the land is not flat like a ruled line; a mind that follows things is not smooth like a rule. wang bi explains: 大夷之道，因物之性，不執平以割物, “the greatly level way goes by the nature of things; it does not hold up a level and cut things to it”. a level that is forced on the ground is the true roughness.

辱: disgrace, and a dark stain. 大白若辱: “great white seems 辱”. the common meaning of 辱 is “disgrace, humiliation”. the shuowen gives it a farmer’s origin: 恥也。从寸在辰下。失耕時，於封畺上戮之也, “shame; a hand under 辰, the season sign: one who missed the time of plowing was punished at the boundary mound”. old commentators say that in this line the word means soiled, dark with dirt, the opposite of white; a shamed person is “blackened” in chinese as in english. both senses work together. the whitest thing looks stained; the purest person looks disgraced. passage 28 has the pair: know the white, keep to the black; know glory, keep to 辱, and be the valley of the world. and here the line before is “highest de seems a valley”. white silk, in fact, shows each mark; cloth that has been used and washed many times has a different whiteness. which would you trust?

偷 and 渝: slack, stolen, faded. two lines with hard last words. 建德若偷: 建 is “set up, firm”, and 偷 is “to steal”, and from that “furtive”, and also “careless, to take things easy”. so firm de looks like slackness, or like something done on the sly. the qing scholar yu yue read 建 as 健, “vigorous”: vigorous de seems lazy. wang bi writes 偷，匹也; commentators read 匹 as “ordinary, like a commoner”, and some suspect a copying error. english must choose one; we wrote “slack”, and “thief” is lost. a person of real power does not strain and does not announce the act; from outside this looks like idleness or stealth. 質真若渝: 質 is raw stuff, 真 is “true, genuine”, and 渝 is defined by the shuowen as 變汙也, “to change and become dirty”, as dye fades or runs. the genuine thing seems to change color. plastic flowers keep their red. real ones fade.

大方無隅: a square with no corners. 方 is a square, and by extension a region, a direction, a method, and uprightness of character: a 方 person is “square” in the good old sense, straight and exact. 隅 is a corner, the angle where two walls meet; it has the hill sign 阝 at the left. the earth itself was 方: “heaven is round, earth is square” was the common picture of the cosmos. now make the square great enough. you stand on a square earth and can find no corner; the edges are too far away to be edges for you. a person of the greatest uprightness is like that: no sharp angle on which others cut themselves. passage 58 says it of the sage: 方而不割, “square, and does not cut”. english “square” has lost the moral sense, so the paradox sounds like geometry only. in chinese it is also a remark about character: the truly straight person does not have an edge.

大器晚成: late, or never. this line is a living proverb in chinese, japanese, and korean: the great vessel is completed late; great talent ripens slowly. parents say it of slow children. the mawangdui silk text is reported not to say it. it reads 大器免成: the great vessel is spared completion, or escapes it. 晚 is 日, the sun, beside 免; the silk is reported to have the bare 免. a scribe may have written the sound part for the whole word, as scribes often did, and then nothing changes. but look at the three lines beside it: no corners, sparse sound, no shape. each one denies the defining mark. a vessel is defined by being finished, cut and fired to a form with one use; the greatest vessel is the one that is never closed into a final form. that agrees with the uncarved wood. the guodian slips are reported to have a third graph, 曼. the reading “late” comforts. the reading “never” does not. which do you want to be true of yourself?

大音希聲: the note with almost no sound. 音 is a musical tone; 聲 is sound that the ear receives. 希 is “sparse, rare”: passage 14 says 聽之不聞名曰希, “listen for it and do not hear it: its name is 希”. wang bi explains why the great note cannot sound: 有聲則有分，有分則不宮而商矣, “if there is sound there is division; with division, if it is not the note gong then it is the note shang”. any note that sounds is one note and so shuts out the rest of the scale. the zhuangzi says the same of a famous lute player: when zhao wen plays, something is completed and something is lost; when he does not play, nothing is lost. the idea shaped chinese music. the qin, the scholar’s zither, is played softly, with long fading tones, for the player alone. the poet tao yuanming is said to have kept a qin with no strings, and to have laid his hands on it when he was happy.

the silk text: three small differences at the end. in the mawangdui manuscripts this passage comes before passage 40, and the text has small differences that matter. where we have 大象無形, “the great image has no shape”, the silk is reported to have 天象无形, “the images of heaven have no shape”; 天 and 大 differ by one stroke, and the received reading agrees with passage 35. where we have 道隱無名, “the dao is hidden and without name”, the silk is reported to have a different second graph, which editors read as a word for “great” or “full”: the dao is vast and has no name. the received 隱, “hidden”, turned an abundance into a concealment. the shuowen defines 隱 as 蔽也, “to be screened”, as by a hill. and the last line has “begin” where we have “lend”. a hidden dao has to be searched for. a vast one is around you already and has no name, as water has none for a fish.

善貸且成: the dao lends. 貸 has 貝, the cowrie, money, under 代, “to take the place of”. it is the word for a loan. the shuowen defines it as 施也, “to give out”. so the last line says that the dao alone is good at lending and at bringing to completion. the picture is exact. a thing does not own its life or its shape. these are on loan, and the lender asks for no interest and does not name itself; in the end all is returned, the 反 of passage 40. wang bi writes: 貸之非唯供其乏而已，一貸之則足以永終其德. “its lending does not merely supply what is lacking; one loan is enough to bring the thing’s de to its lasting end.” the mawangdui silk text is reported to read 善始且善成, “good at beginning and good at completing”. that is smoother and loses the money. editors still disagree about which is older. what do you hold that you treat as owned and that is in fact lent?

wang bi: answers from other passages. wang bi’s notes on the twelve sayings are short, and most of them answer one line of the book with another. on the highest scholar he writes two words: 有志也, “he has resolve”. on “the way forward seems to go back” he quotes passage 7: 後其身而身先，外其身而身存, “put the self behind and the self is in front; put the self outside and the self remains”. on “highest de seems a valley”: 不德其德，無所懷也, “it does not treat its de as de; it holds nothing to its breast”. on “great white”: 知其白，守其黑，大白然後乃得, “know the white, keep to the black: only then is great white reached”. this is his method as a reader: the book explains itself. on the great image he repeats his argument about notes: 有形則有分，有分者不溫則炎，不炎則寒, “with shape there is division; a divided thing, if not warm, is hot; if not hot, cold”.

legge: twelve lines of victorian verse. legge calls the three hearers “scholars of the highest class”, “the middle class”, and “the lowest class”, which in 1891 sounded like a society and not like a civil service. for 建言 he has “the sentence-makers”. he then turns the twelve sayings into four rhymed triplets, and rhyme forces the sense. “great white seems soiled” becomes “its greatest beauty seems to offend the eyes”. “the great note is sparse in sound” becomes “loud is its sound, but never word it said”: a loud sound is the opposite of the chinese. “the great image has no shape” becomes “a semblance great, the shadow of a shade”, a phrase that sounds like shakespeare and brings in a world of illusions that the text does not have. the chinese sayings are four characters each, with one of five, and as plain as proverbs about weather.

three hearers in one day. take one line of the passage for the day; for example, “the way forward seems to go back”. watch for the three hearers in yourself. in the morning you may be the first: you see where it applies and you act on it. by noon you are the second: you have forgotten the line, then remember it, then doubt it. at some point you will be the third: the line will seem naive, or useless in the real world, and you will smile at it. note the exact moment of that smile and what you were protecting. do not correct any of the three. only see that all of them heard the same words.

明/昧, 進/退: what 若 does to a pair. eight sayings put a quality beside its opposite: bright 明 and dim 昧, forward 進 and back 退, level 夷 and knotted 纇, white 白 and soiled 辱. the joint is 若, “seems”. the word does not say that dim is the true bright, and it does not tell the reader to seek dimness. it says that the large form of one side has room for the look of the other. a way that could not seem dim would be a glare. an advance with no step back in it does not last a mile. so the pairs are not ranked; each side is seen through the other. the scene at the start makes the same point with people: there is a highest scholar and a lowest, and the laugh of the lowest is needed. a one-sided reading trusts only the bright look, or it learns to distrust that look and collects dim looks as proof of depth. both judge by looks. which look do you trust too fast?

a teaching that no one laughs at is not deep enough to be the way.. a teaching that no one laughs at is not deep enough to be the way. do you agree, or is this a way to make any strange idea safe from doubt? when did you last laugh at an idea? what was the laugh guarding? take the other side: what most sensible people laugh at is usually wrong. when has the laugh of the crowd saved you? are you more often the one who laughs or the one who is laughed at? what did each role teach you to hide?

the real thing often looks like its opposite: clarity seems dim, and progress seems like going back.. the real thing often looks like its opposite: clarity seems dim, and progress seems like going back. where has this been true for you? where has dim simply been dim? think of a time that felt like a retreat. who decided that it was a retreat: you, or the eyes of others? hold the plain view for a while: things are mostly what they look like, and a path that feels wrong is wrong. what do you feel as you hold it? which view do you use to judge your own life this year? what would the other view say about it?

the greatest capacity is slow to be finished, and may stay unfinished.. the greatest capacity is slow to be finished, and may stay unfinished. is this a truth for you, or an excuse that you have used? who set the clock by which you are early or late? do you still accept that clock? try the opposite: what is not finished in time is lost, and form needs a deadline. which of your works speak for that? what in you is still unfinished, and how do you feel when you say so aloud?

笑 the character with a gap in the dictionary. look at the two layers. on top is ⺮, the crown form of 竹, bamboo: two stalks, each with a pair of hanging leaves. the shuowen calls bamboo 冬生艸也, “a grass that lives through winter”, and says that the hanging parts are its leaf sheaths. as a top part it marks things made of bamboo: 筆 (a brush) and 簡 (a writing slip, as in the guodian slips). below is 夭. the shuowen says 屈也。从大，象形: “bent; from 大, a person; a picture”. it is 大, the figure with arms out, with the head tipped to one side. 夭 by itself means “young and supple”, and also “to die young”. so the modern character is: bamboo over a person who bends. why should that be laughter? the honest answer is in the note on the missing entry: the shuowen’s own explanation was lost, and the editors who restored the entry reported more than one form of the graph, one of them with 犬, a dog, below the bamboo. the explanation that people remember is a picture and not a proof: bamboo that bends and shakes in the wind looks like a person bent double. compare how the script writes the other feelings. 喜, joy, is a drum over a mouth; the shuowen says 樂也. 哭, to wail, is two mouths over a dog, 哀聲也, “the sound of grief”. laughter got the lightest materials: a hollow grass and a body that gives way. in this passage the lowest scholar laughs out loud. ten strokes. the bamboo crown has six: on the left a short stroke that falls left, a short horizontal, a dot; on the right the same three again. the two halves are twins, but the right one is written a little larger and its horizontal a little longer, so that the crown is not stiff. then the bent figure, four strokes: a flat stroke written from right to left, the tilted head; a horizontal, the arms; then a long stroke that falls to the left, and last a long stroke that falls to the right. watch stroke seven. it is the head that tips, and it must lean, or the figure stands straight and is only 天, heaven. the last two strokes open wide like legs set apart, and the whole character should feel a little unsteady on them, as a laughing person is. in cursive script the bamboo crown becomes two quick hooks, and the character looks like a face.

晚 the sun, and one who gets away. the left side is 日, the sun: a circle in the oldest writing, made square by the brush, with a mark in the middle. it measures time in many characters: 早 (early), 明 (bright), 昧, the dawn dimness of this passage, 時 (season, time). the right side is 免, “to escape, to be let off, to avoid”. the shuowen explains the whole as 莫也。从日免聲: “dusk; from the sun, with 免 for the sound”. its word for dusk, 莫, is a beautiful picture that it explains too: 从日在茻中, “the sun in the middle of the grasses”: the sun has gone down into the plants at the horizon. so 晚 is the late part of the day, and then “late” in general: a late guest, a late harvest, the last years of a life, 晚年. now the surprise. the right side, 免, has no entry of its own in the shuowen, like 笑. and 免 alone is what the silk manuscript has in this line: 大器免成, the great vessel is spared completion. take the sun away from “late” and you have “escapes”. the whole question of the famous proverb is inside this one character: was a sun added, or was a sun left out? by their modern parts, two more characters keep 免 in view: 勉, to strive, is 免 with 力, strength; 娩, to give birth, is 免 with 女. eleven strokes. the sun takes four: the left side; the top and right side in one stroke; the short line inside; the base. at the left of a character the sun is made narrow and is set a little high. then 免, seven strokes: a short stroke that falls left; a horizontal that turns and falls left; then a flat box in three strokes, left side, top with right side, and a line that closes it; then a long stroke that falls left from inside the box; and last the stroke that goes down, bends, runs to the right, and ends in a hook up. watch the last stroke. it is the leg of someone who runs: long, low, with the hook like a heel. it needs room, so the sun must stay small and high to leave the lower left open. in running script the last two strokes are often joined in one movement, a turn of the wrist.

42 · shade behind, sun before. the dao gives birth to one. / one gives birth to two. / two gives birth to three. / three gives birth to the ten thousand things. / the ten thousand things carry shade on the back / and hold sun in the arms; / the surging breath makes their accord. / what people hate / is to be orphaned, alone, unfed, / and kings and dukes take these as their titles. / so a thing may be lessened and so grow, / or grow and so be lessened. / what people teach, i teach too: / the hard and overbearing do not get their own death. / i will take this as father of the teaching. the passage opens with a count: the dao bears one, one two, two three, three all things. four short clauses with one verb; then the count stops, since after three there is only “many”. the second sentence turns from origin to structure: each thing has shade on its back and sun in its arms, and a breath that blends them. then, with no bridge, we are at court: kings name themselves with the words that people hate, and an observation is drawn, that a lessening may be a growing. last, the speaker cites a common proverb and names it father of the teaching. some hold that these are two passages. read as one, it goes from the largest thing that can be said to the smallest: from the birth of the world to how a bully dies. the count can be watched in experience. before a thought, awareness is not divided: no number fits it. then “here i am”: one. then “and there is that”: two, a knower and a known. then the relation between them, liking or fear or interest: three. from three the whole busy world unfolds in a second. wang bi saw that the first step is a word: to say “one” is already two. the way back is the 損 of the second half: less, and less. the middle lines describe the state of any living moment: it has a lit side that we show and hold, and a shaded side that we carry and do not see, and it is whole when breath moves freely between them. no part of this says to get rid of the shade. kings chose the worst words for their titles: orphan, alone, unfed. the passage reads the custom as a pattern of power. an organization that grows by adding, with more staff, more rules, more reach, is at some point lessened by the adding; one that cuts back to its root may grow. a leader who takes the low name and the blame is made larger, and one who takes each honor is made smaller, and the people around both of them can see it. then the proverb: the hard and overbearing end badly. each office has known such a person and has seen the end. the speaker claims no new wisdom. for a leader this may be the most useful line: the principle that you need is probably one that your grandmother said, and you have not yet made it the father of your practice. chinese medicine and the movement arts took their first map from this passage. the back of the body is its yin side in the passage’s own sense: it is carried, and turned from the light. the front is held open to the sun. stand and feel both. most people live in the front, in the face and chest and hands, and forget that half of the body is behind them. then the breath: a full breath widens the back as much as the chest, and when it does, front and back stop being two. that is 和, accord, as a physical fact. the last lines are also of the body. stiffness is 強梁, the strong beam: locked knees, a held jaw, force used against force. such a body is easy to break and wears out early. go to any hill at noon. the south slope is 陽: warm, dry, with one set of plants. the north slope is 陰: cool, mossy, with ferns and a different wood. one hill, two climates, and the ridge between them is not a wall. by evening the light has moved and the slopes have begun to change roles. life needs both: seeds sprout in the shade and fruit ripens in the sun. and between them moves air, warm rising from the lit side, cool sinking on the dark side; the wind on a mountain is this surging of two breaths. the count at the head of the passage is the same hill seen in time: one land, two slopes, the weather between them, and then all the living things. do the exercise of the shaded side once today. then choose one 損, one small lessening, and watch for the gain in it: say less in one meeting, own one thing less, leave one claim unmade. and remember one saying that your elders repeated, the kind that everyone knows and no one obeys. for a week, treat it as the speaker treats his proverb: as the father of the teaching.

生: gives birth, not “produces”. the verb comes four times in thirteen characters: 生. it is the picture of a sprout that comes out of soil, and it means to bear, to be born, to grow. legge and most english versions write “produced”, as of goods. but the passage is a line of births: each term comes out of the one before as a child from a parent, and remains of its substance. the book calls the dao a mother more than once: 可以為天下母, “it can be taken as the mother of the world” (25; compare 以為天下母 in 52). so the opening is nearer to a family record than to a formula. the chinese has no “the” before the numbers: 一 is “one” and “the one” together. and no tense: it does not say that this happened once, long ago. it can be read as happening now, in each thing, at each moment. see the old ways to count.

one, two, three: what the old readers said. the text does not say what the numbers are, and each age has filled them in. the huainanzi, a han book of the second century bce, quotes the line and explains: the dao begins in one; one alone does not give birth, so it divides into yin and yang; yin and yang join in accord and the ten thousand things are born. the heshang gong commentary is close: one is the first breath; two is yin and yang; three is the clear, the turbid, and the blended breaths, which become heaven, earth, and the human. wang bi gives no cosmology at all; he derives the numbers from the act of speaking. a modern reader has matched them to space-time, electric charge, and matter, and europe’s first readers had a map of their own. each map dates itself. the line survives them because it gives only a count, the oldest thing that people share: one, two, three, many. small children count that way.

the jesuits found the trinity here. when europe first read this passage, it read its own creed. a group of french jesuits at the qing court around 1700, called the figurists, held that the oldest chinese books kept traces of the first revelation to humankind. in 道生一，一生二，二生三 they saw the three persons of the christian trinity. a latin version of the laozi that reached london in 1788 was sent to prove this point. in 1823 the first professor of chinese in paris, abel-remusat, argued that three words of passage 14, 夷, 希, 微, spelled the hebrew name of god. legge, a missionary himself, rejected these readings, and his notes say so. but the habit remained in the vocabulary: “the one”, “the three”, “produced”, each with a capital or a tone of genesis. the chinese numbers are small words that a market trader uses. try the line as “way bears one, one bears two”.

陰 and 陽: two sides of one hill. before they were cosmic principles, 陰 and 陽 were words for landscape. both have the hill sign 阝 at the left. the shuowen defines 陰 as 闇也。水之南、山之北也: “dark; the south bank of a river, the north side of a mountain”, the side that the sun does not reach. it defines 陽 as 高、明也, “high and bright”. many chinese place names keep this: luoyang is the city on the sunny, north bank of the luo river. so the pair is one hill at one moment, with a lit slope and a shaded slope, and as the day goes on, each becomes the other. nothing here is “positive” and “negative”, male and female as fixed things, or good and evil. shade is not the enemy of the sun; it is what the sun makes when it meets a hill. this passage is the only place where the laozi names the pair. see the plate.

yin and yang appear only here. a reader who comes to the laozi from later daoism expects yin and yang on every page. they are in this one line, and nowhere else in the book. in the oldest texts the two words are plain: the book of songs uses them for the shady and sunny sides of hills and for cloud and sun. in the fourth and third centuries bce they became a theory. thinkers such as zou yan of qi, in the early third century bce, joined them to the “five phases” and made a system that explained seasons, medicine, and the rise and fall of dynasties; the han empire took this up as state doctrine. the laozi stands before that system or at its edge. its line is still close to the hill: things have a shaded back and a sunlit front. some scholars think that the line is a late addition to the book for this reason. the guodian slips do not have this passage.

負 and 抱: the back and the arms. the two verbs are of the body. 負 is to carry on the back, as a porter or a mother carries; from that, to turn one’s back on, to owe. the shuowen explains the graph as a person who guards cowries, 从人守貝, and so “to rely on”. 抱 has the hand at the left and 包, “to wrap”, at the right: to hold in the arms against the chest, as one holds a child. the laozi uses it for its dearest objects: 抱一, “hold the one” (10, 22); 抱樸, “hold the uncarved wood” (19). so each of the ten thousand things is given a body with a back and a front. on the back, shade; in the arms, sun. a chinese house was built in this posture, with its back wall to the north and its door to the south, and a ruler sat on his throne facing south. a plant also stands so. which way do you face?

沖氣 or 中氣: surging, empty, or middle. 沖氣以為和: “沖 breath, taken as the accord”. 沖 was the key word of passage 4, where the dao is 沖, and it has two senses that the tradition never fully separated: to surge and dash together, as waters meet; and to be empty, hollow. so 沖氣 is the breaths of shade and sun as they surge into each other, or it is the empty breath between the two, a third thing that lets them blend. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 中氣, “the middle breath”, which favors the second: there is a breath at the center. 和, “accord”, is at root a word of music: the shuowen says 相譍也, “to answer one another”, as one voice answers a second in a song. it is not sameness. two notes that are the same note make no accord. passage 55 says that to know this accord is to know the constant.

氣: breath, not “energy”. 氣 is one of the words that english cannot hold. its first meaning is vapor: mist over a field, steam, the breath that one sees on a cold morning. from that it is the air that we breathe, the weather, the temper of a person, the vigor of a body, the mood of an age, and, for chinese medicine and physics, the fine stuff of which all things are made and which moves between them. it is matter and force at once, and it is never apart from breathing. “energy” is a word of nineteenth-century physics; it has no moisture and no lungs. “spirit” is too holy. a modern version gives “influence”. the laozi uses the word only three times, and each time it is in a body: the infant gathers its 氣 and becomes soft (10); the heart that forces the 氣 is called violent (55); and here, where the breaths of shade and sun meet in each thing.

the royal names again. 孤, 寡, 不穀: “the orphan”, “the lone one”, “the unfed”. these are the three words that rulers used for “i”; passage 39 gave them as proof that the high rests on the low. here they come back with a different point. 人之所惡: these are the things that people hate. to be fatherless, to be without a mate, to be without grain: these are the plain disasters of a farming society, and the zhou texts list such people as the ones a good king must feed first. and the men at the top chose exactly these words as titles. the silk text is reported to say 以自名, “name themselves by them”. the passage takes it as a case of its law of loss and gain: a title that lessens makes its owner greater. it is also a quiet joke. no king was unfed.

損 and 益: two hexagrams. 損 is “to lessen”; the shuowen says 減也, “to reduce”, and the hand at the left takes something away. 益 is “to add, to increase”, and its graph is a picture that the shuowen reads: 饒也。从水、皿, “abundance; from water and a dish”: a vessel so full that the water stands above the rim. it is the first form of 溢, to overflow. the two words are also the names of two hexagrams that stand side by side in the book of changes, 損 and 益, numbers 41 and 42, and each is the other turned upside down. a han story says that confucius sighed each time that he read them, because he saw in them that an act meant to benefit a thing can harm it, and an act meant to harm can benefit. the line here says more than “gain and loss alternate”. with 或, “sometimes”, it says that a lessening can itself be the growing. passage 48 gives the practice: in learning, add each day; in the dao, 損, take away each day.

人之所教: the sage has no new doctrine. 人之所教，我亦教之: “what people teach, i also teach it”. after the grandest opening in the book, the speaker says that the lesson is not original. it is what everyone says. then a common saying is quoted. this is an unusual modesty for a philosopher of the age; each school claimed a doctrine that the others lacked. the claim here is the reverse: the truth is already in the proverbs of the people, and the teacher’s work is to take one of them seriously. wang bi reads the line with more edge: i do not force people to follow; i point to what is so, and those who go against it bring ill on themselves. the silk texts are reported to have a different and difficult wording, 夕議而教人, which editors read in several ways. what do the old sayings of your own family teach that you have not yet taken as a teaching?

強梁: the saying on the bronze man. 強梁者不得其死 was a proverb before it was in the laozi. 梁 is a roof beam or a bridge; 強梁 is a set phrase for a person who is stiff, forceful, and overbearing, perhaps “strong as a beam”, perhaps a loan for a different word; scholars are not sure. a han collection of stories, the shuoyuan, tells that confucius, on a visit to the ancestral temple of zhou, saw a bronze statue of a man with his mouth sealed three times, and an inscription on its back. one line of the inscription is 強梁者不得其死，好勝者必遇其敵: “the overbearing do not get their own death; those who love to win will meet their match”. the story is late, but the saying was plainly common property. the silk texts are reported to write 強良. the stiff beam is the one that cracks; compare passage 76, where the tree that is strong is the one that the axe finds.

不得其死: to “get one’s death”. 不得其死 is “not / get / their / death”. chinese treats a good death as a thing that a person gets, like an inheritance: to die in bed, of age, with one’s body whole and one’s children present. the violent do not get it. they die by the sword, by execution, on the road. confucius used the same phrase of his boldest student: “a man like you will not get his death”; and zilu did die in a fight, in a palace coup in 480 bce. english “die a natural death” is close but clinical. the chinese has a 其, “their own”: each person has a death that belongs to them, and force loses it. note the verb 得, “to get”, the word that passage 39 used for getting the one. heaven got the one and is clear. the overbearing do not even get their own end.

教父: the father of the teaching. 吾將以為教父: “i will take it as teaching-father”. 父 is the father, and so the head, the origin, the one with authority; the shuowen sees a hand that holds up a rod: 家長率教者, “the head of the house, who leads and teaches”. 教, to teach, is defined there as 上所施下所效也, “what those above give out and those below copy”. so the speaker takes a people’s proverb about violent men as the father of all his teaching: its first principle and its authority. this is striking in a book whose own images of origin are mothers. some editions read 學父, “father of learning”, as the silk texts are reported to do. english versions that write “the basis” or “my main teaching” lose the parent. in modern chinese 教父 has a new life: it is the word for a godfather at a christian baptism, and the title of a famous film about one.

two passages in one?. a reader feels a break after 沖氣以為和. the first part is cosmogony: numbers, shade and sun, breath. the second is about the titles of kings and a proverb on violent men. some scholars think that two separate pieces were joined here, and some move the second half to passage 39, where the royal names first appear. but the passage has its own logic. the first half says how each thing is made: of two that are opposed, in accord. the second half applies it: so what is low and hated gives greatness, and what is hard and strong loses even its death. in the mawangdui silk order this passage comes directly after our passage 40, which ends “having is born from not-having”; then 道生一 follows with no break. read 41, 40, 42 in that order once. the account of origins runs from the laughing scholar to the father of the teaching.

wang bi: the numbers come from speech. wang bi does not say that one is breath or that two is yin and yang. he asks how one can arrive at one at all: 何由致一，由於無也。由無乃一，一可謂無。已謂之一，豈得無言乎。有言有一，非二如何？有一有二，遂生乎三. “by what does one arrive at one? by nothing. from nothing, then, one; so one can be called nothing. but we have already called it ‘one’: how can there be no word? there is the word and there is the one: what is this, if not two? there is one and there is two, and so three is born.” the argument is from the zhuangzi. the moment that you say “all is one”, there is the one and the saying, and you have two. number is born from naming. then he draws the practical end: 愈多愈遠，損則近之, “the more, the farther; lessen, and you come near it”.

legge: “leave behind” and “go forward”. legge writes: “the tao produced one; one produced two”, the factory verb, in the past tense, with capitals. his next sentence changes the picture of the passage. all things “leave behind them the obscurity (out of which they have come), and go forward to embrace the brightness (into which they have emerged)”. for legge, shade and sun are a before and an after: creatures march out of the dark and into the light. this is a story of progress, and of salvation; a victorian missionary could hardly see it in a different way. the chinese has no motion in it. 負 is to carry: the things have the shade on their backs now, and keep it. for 沖氣 he gives “the breath of vacancy”, which is fair to one sense of 沖. and for 不穀 he again has “carriages without naves”, the hub reading that he took from the heshang gong commentary; see passage 39.

find your shaded side. stand outside on a clear day, or by a window, with the light on your face and chest. feel the warmth in front. then put your attention on your back: the cooler side, which you never see. you carry it everywhere. breathe in and out a few times and notice that the breath moves between the two, front and back, and makes them one body. then apply it. take one quality that you show, a sunny one: competence, cheer, patience. ask what its shaded side is, the thing that goes with it and stays behind you. do not turn around to fix it. the passage says only that you carry it, and that the accord is in the breath between.

陰/陽 and 損/益: neither side alone. the passage has two pairs. shade 陰 and sun 陽 are two sides of one hill: each thing carries one and holds the other. the text gives no rank. it gives a third thing, 和, accord, made by the breath that moves between the two. a thing with only sun is scorched; a thing with only shade does not ripen. later ages took sides: some made yang the noble half, and some readers make the laozi a book of yin. this line does neither. the second pair, less 損 and more 益, is written as a crossing: lessened and so grow, grow and so be lessened. the word 或, “in some cases”, keeps it from being a rule that less is more. each side is on its way to the other, as the slopes change with the hour. which side of yourself do you hold to the light, and which do you carry?

every thing carries a shaded side and holds a lit side, and is whole only when the two blend.. every thing carries a shaded side and holds a lit side, and is whole only when the two blend. do you accept this about yourself? what is on your lit side, and what do you carry behind? what did your family show in the light, and what did it keep in the shade? which did you inherit? take the opposite: a person should bring everything into the light, and what stays dark is a fault to remove. what rises as you hold that? which quality do you judge most quickly in others? could it be standing on your own shaded slope?

a thing may grow by being lessened, and may shrink by being added to.. a thing may grow by being lessened, and may shrink by being added to. where has a loss made you larger, or a gain made you smaller? where has it simply not been so? what are you adding to now? what do you fear would happen if you stopped? hold the common view for a minute: more is more, and loss is loss. what part of you is relieved to hear it said plainly? which side do your choices of the last year follow? is that the side that you say you believe?

the hard and overbearing do not come to a natural end.. the hard and overbearing do not come to a natural end. does life bear this out? think of the forceful people that you have known, and how it went for them. where are you the overbearing one? what are you protecting there? now suppose the opposite: the forceful take what they want and die content, and the mild are passed over. what do you feel: anger, envy, doubt? why might you need the proverb to be true? what would you do differently if it were not?

氣 vapor, and a gift of rice. two parts. on top and around the right side is 气: three thin lines that drift, the last with a long tail. this is the original character for vapor; the shuowen says 雲气也。象形, “cloud vapor; a picture”. in its oldest forms it is just three wavy strokes: mist that rises, cloud layers, breath in cold air. inside is 米, rice or millet in the grain; the shuowen says 粟實也。象禾實之形, “the kernels of grain; it shows their shape”: a stalk with seeds at each side. many teachers explain the whole as steam that rises from a pot of cooking rice, and it is a good picture to remember: breath as what food becomes. but the history is different, and more interesting. the shuowen defines 氣 as 饋客芻米也, “to present fodder and grain to guests”, and says 从米气聲: the rice gives the meaning and 气 only the sound. the character with the rice in it was first a word for a gift of provisions. scribes then borrowed it for the vapor word, and the gift word was given a new character with the food sign, 餼. so the grain came into “breath” by a loan. later daoists wrote the first, formless breath in a third way, 炁, commonly read as 无, nothing, above 灬, fire. and the short form used today, 气, has gone back to the three bare lines. in this passage the surging breath joins shade and sun. see also why “energy” will not do. ten strokes. the vapor first, in four: a short stroke that falls to the left; a horizontal from its middle; a second, shorter horizontal under it; then the great stroke of the character, a horizontal that turns down, sweeps in a long curve to the lower right, and ends in a hook that flicks up. then the grain, in six, tucked under the curve: a dot at the upper left, a short stroke at the upper right that falls left, a horizontal, a vertical through it, then a stroke that falls left and a last one that falls right, here pressed short into a long dot. watch stroke four. it is one of the longest single strokes in the regular script, and it must stay elastic along its whole curve, like a bent bow; a weak curve drops the rice on the floor. the grain sits a little left of center, sheltered. in the cursive hands the three vapor lines become one ribbon that falls and loops.

陽 the sunny side of the hill. the left part, 阝, is all that the brush has kept of 𨸏 (阜), a hill or a terraced slope; the old forms are a set of steps cut into a height. at the left of a character it means land that rises: 陵 (a mound), 降 (to come down: two feet that descend a hill), 隅 (a corner, from passage 41), 陰. the right part is 昜. its top is 日, the sun. under the sun is a line, and under that some slanting strokes that are commonly explained as rays that come down, or as the sun above an altar; the shuowen defines 昜 as 開也, “to open”, and lists it as a character by itself. with the hill at its side, the shuowen’s gloss is 高、明也, high and bright. the same right side gives its sound, and often its brightness, to 揚 (to lift, to spread), 湯 (hot water), and 場 (an open ground). now set 陰 beside it. same hill. on the right, 今 above 云, and 云 is the old picture of a cloud. so the pair is: a hill with the sun up, a hill under cloud. the short forms make it simpler still, and children learn them first: 阳 is hill and 日, sun; 阴 is hill and 月, moon. in all these forms the hill is the same hill. the passage says that each of the ten thousand things is such a hill, with one side to the light. eleven strokes. the hill takes two: first a stroke that goes right, turns back, and curls twice like an ear; then a long vertical that stands under its left edge. then the sun, four strokes: left side, top with right side, the line inside, the base. then a long horizontal under the sun, the widest line of the right half. then four more: a stroke that falls left; a horizontal that turns down and ends in a hook to the left; and inside that frame two strokes that fall left, side by side. watch the last two. they are parallel and must stay apart, like rays; if they touch, the light goes out of the character. the hill should be narrow and stand a little high, so that the sun on the right can be full. its long vertical ends in a point like a needle that hangs.

43 · no gap, and it enters. the softest thing under heaven / gallops over the hardest thing under heaven. / what has no substance enters where there is no gap. / by this i know that not-doing has its gain. / the teaching without words, / the gain of not-doing: / few under heaven reach them. three sentences. one: the softest gallops over the hardest. two: the no-thing enters the no-gap, and from this the speaker knows that not-doing adds something. three: the wordless teaching and the gain of not-doing are things that few reach. the passage climbs by degrees of softness. first something soft, like water, which still has body and still needs a way in. then something with no body at all, which needs no way in. then the human forms of that: a teaching with no words in it, a benefit with no deed in it. each step removes more, and the reach grows wider at each step. the pictures are a horse, a wall, and a shut gate. the passage does not name water. thoughts and feelings can be very hard: a fixed resentment, a belief about oneself, a fear with walls like a fortress. one can attack such a thing with a harder thing, an argument or an act of will, and then two hard things grind. attention is of a different kind. it has no substance; it does not push; it has no edge to catch on. and it goes into the hardest state where there is no gap, because it was never outside. to attend to anger from within the anger changes it more than any effort made against it. this is the gain of not-doing in its nearest form, and the passage is right that few reach it: the mind does not believe that something with no force can do anything. the hardest things in an organization are not its buildings. they are positions: a refusal, a rule that no one will bend, a person who has dug in. the usual reply is a harder position, and then the matter becomes a siege. the passage points to what in fact goes through hard things: trust, time, a question that is asked without an agenda, the example of how the leader behaves when no one is looking. none of these has an edge, so none meets resistance. that is the teaching without words at work. read the warning in the note on not-doing as well: this is no technique of light pressure. people feel a light hand that still steers. the gain comes when the hand is not there, and for that reason few reach it. breath is the plainest case of the first two lines. it is soft beyond any other thing in the body, and it goes everywhere in it; wang bi names it before water. in the movement arts the same law is a daily experience. a stiff partner can be moved; a truly soft one gives you nothing to push on, and your own force carries you past. the hands of a good bodyworker do not dig into a tight muscle. they rest on it and wait, and the hardness lets go from inside, as if something had gone in where there was no gap. try it on your own shoulder: do not press and do not rub. lay the hand there, let it be heavy and warm, breathe, and count to sixty. water finds each crack in a rock, and when it freezes it opens the crack: mountains come down in this way. a root tip is one of the softest tissues that there is, and it enters stone. wind has shaped whole deserts. these are the old examples and they all work through gaps and time; see the drip and the stone. the second line asks for an example that is stranger, something that needs no gap. warmth is one. it passes into the densest iron with no opening. gravity is one: it reaches the center of the earth through all that lies between. the softest influences in nature are the ones that nothing keeps out, and for the same reason no one notices them at work. do the wordless teaching once this week. a second exercise, for a hard thing of your own: choose one fixed difficulty, a tight place in the body or a matter that you have attacked many times. for today, add no force. bring to it only what is softest: attention, breath, time. do not look for a gap; the passage says that none is needed. in the evening, do not judge by whether the hard thing moved. ask whether something entered.

至柔: the softest what?. 天下之至柔 is “the utmost-soft of all under heaven”. 至 is “to arrive”, and so “the furthest point, the most”. the chinese names no thing: it is the softest, whatever that is. english needs a noun, and “thing” is our addition. what did the first readers supply? most say water, from passage 78: 天下莫柔弱於水, “nothing under heaven is softer and weaker than water”, and nothing surpasses it against the hard. wang bi says water and also breath. others say the dao itself. the text leaves the place open on purpose. a riddle that says “the softest” makes the reader search the whole world for it, and each answer, water, air, a root tip, patience, a mother’s voice, is tested against the second line. the word 柔 is green wood that bends: see passage 36. before you read on: what is the softest thing that you know, and what has it worn down?

馳騁: a full gallop. both characters have 馬, a horse, at the left. the shuowen defines 馳 as 大驅也, “to drive hard”, and 騁 as 直馳也, “to race straight ahead”. together they are a set phrase for horses at full speed, in a chase or a charge. it is one of the most violent verbs in the book, and it is given to the softest thing. the other place where it occurs is passage 12: 馳騁畋獵，令人心發狂, “the gallop and the hunt make the human heart go mad”. there the gallop is a vice of nobles. here the same word is taken from them and given to water. with an object, as here, 馳騁 can mean to ride a horse hard, and so to master; the hard thing is the horse, and the soft thing rides it. the silk texts add 於, “in, through”: the softest races through the hardest. english versions that write “overcomes” keep the result and lose the horse.

堅: armor, walls, and the horse. 堅 is “hard, solid”; the shuowen says 剛也, and the graph has 土, earth, at its base: ground that is packed hard, like the rammed-earth walls of every city of the time. in the language of war the word is fixed in a phrase: 堅甲利兵, “hard armor and sharp weapons”; mencius uses it for the armies of qin and chu. the hardest things under heaven, for a reader of 300 bce, were things that states made with great labor: walls, armor, bronze and iron. and the gallop was the newest power. in 307 bce king wuling of zhao ordered his army to wear the trousers of the steppe peoples and to shoot from horseback, and cavalry began to replace the chariot. so the line takes the two proudest pictures of the arms race, hardness and speed, and gives the victory to something with neither. sunzi had said that an army’s form should be like water. the laozi leaves the army out.

無有: that which is nothing. 無有 is two characters, “not-have / have”, and here they make one word: “that which has no having”, what has no substance, no bulk, no edge. it is not the 無 and 有 of passage 40 set side by side. passage 11 has a line where the same pair can be read as one word or as two, and the comma moves; here the grammar is clear, because 無有 is the subject of 入, “enters”. english must choose a noun: “the insubstantial”, “non-being”, “nothing”. each is heavier than the chinese. the line makes a claim that the first line did not. water is soft, but it is a thing; it needs a crack. now the text goes one step further than water. that which is no thing at all goes in where there is no crack at all. what is in the stone already, with no way in? space is. so is stillness.

間: moonlight in the gate. 間 is a gap, a space between. the older graph is 閒, and the shuowen explains it: 隟也。从門从月, “a crack; from gate and moon”. the two leaves of a gate are shut at night, and the moon is seen between them: so there is a crack. later the moon was changed to a sun, 間, and the moon form was kept for the word “leisure”, a gap in time. 無間 is then “no crack”: a gate so well made that no light shows. the zhuangzi has a famous use of the pair. cook ding explains why his knife is still sharp after nineteen years: the joints of the ox have gaps, and the blade has no thickness; 以無厚入有間, “with that which has no thickness, enter that which has a gap”. the laozi’s line asks for more. cook ding still needs a gap. here there is none, and that which has nothing goes in.

the drip that goes through stone. the idea that soft wears hard was common knowledge, and the han writers gave it its best-known pictures. mei cheng, in a letter of advice to a prince in the second century bce, wrote: 泰山之霤穿石, “the drip from mount tai goes through stone”, and the well rope cuts the wooden rim: water is no drill and rope is no saw; the slow rubbing does it. from this comes the later proverb 水滴石穿, “water drips, the stone is pierced”. those sayings are about time: the soft wears the hard down by patience. the passage itself does not mention time, and its verb is not “to drip”. it is “to gallop”. that is the strange part. it does not say that the soft slowly outlasts the hard. it says that the soft rides the hard at speed, now, as a rider on a horse. what soft thing moves you in that way: at once and with no force?

吾是以知: “by this i know”. 吾是以知 is “i / this / by / know”. the speaker says “i”, which is rare in the book, and gives the ground of a conviction: i looked at this, and from it i know. the same formula ends several passages as a question and answer: 吾何以知…以此, “how do i know? by this” (21, 54, 57). it is the manner of someone who reasons from what can be seen, and not of a prophet. no revelation is claimed and no ancient authority is cited. one watches water and stone and draws a conclusion about conduct. english versions often make the tone grander than it is. in chinese it is close to a remark at the riverside: look at that; so that is how it is. the conclusion is modest in form too: not “not-doing is supreme”, only that it 有益, has some gain in it.

益: increase, not “advantage”. 益 is a dish with water above the rim: more, increase, and so benefit. legge and others write “advantage”. but an advantage is a gain over someone, a word of contests, and with it the passage becomes a tip for winning: use the least effort and beat the rigid. 益 names no opponent. it says only that something is added, to all. passage 42 has just shown how the book thinks about the word: a thing may be lessened and so grow, or grow and so be lessened; and passage 48 sets 益 on the side of learning and its opposite, 損, on the side of the dao. so 無為之有益 has a turn in it: the practice of taking away, of not adding action, is the one that adds. a reader who takes the line as a method for profit has read the last word and missed the first two.

無為: not “the lightest touch”. 無為 is “without doing”: no action that is pressed on things from a private plan. this passage is often used to turn it into a principle of economy: when you must act, use the smallest force, as a small rudder turns a great ship. that is good advice, and it is not what the line says. a rudder is a tool of control in the hand of a pilot. the passage’s example has no pilot. that which enters where there is no gap does not push a little. it does not push. the benefit comes from the absence of the doer, not from the doer’s skill at being light. this is hard for a practical mind to hold, and the passage knows it: few reach it. see how passage 37 says it: the dao is constant in not-doing.

不言之教: the wordless teaching. the phrase comes two times in the laozi: here, and in passage 2, where the sage 行不言之教, “carries out the teaching that does not speak”. the shuowen defines 教 as what those above give out and those below copy, and what is copied is conduct, so the best teaching was always an example. but the laozi means more than “set a good example”. it distrusts the names themselves. a teaching in words divides the world into right and wrong before the student has looked at it. the idea ran through all later chinese thought. the zhuangzi repeats the phrase, and tells of wang tai, a man with one foot, who taught nothing and whose students went home full. confucius himself once said, 予欲無言, “i wish to say nothing: does heaven speak? the four seasons run and the hundred things are born.” the chan school of buddhism, a thousand years later, described itself as “a transmission outside the scriptures, not set up on written words”. and the book that says this is five thousand characters long.

希及: a hand that just catches up. 及 is “to reach, to come up with”. the shuowen: 逮也。从又从人, “to catch up with; from a hand and a person”. in the early forms a hand comes from behind and takes hold of a figure that walks ahead: caught. so 及之 is to come level with these two things, the teaching and the gain, as with someone on the road in front. 希 is “sparse, rare”, the word of the great note in passage 41. 天下希及之: under all of heaven, few catch up with them. the line is not a complaint, and it does not say “none”. it measures the distance. the wordless teaching and the gain of not-doing are close at hand and plain, and people walk past them toward something harder. the silk texts are reported to add 能, “are able”, and a final particle: few in the world are able to reach it.

the silk texts: small words of place. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to agree closely with the received passage and add three small words. they read 馳騁於天下之致堅, with 於, “in, through, upon”, after the gallop, and 致 for 至. they read 无有入於无間, again with 於: “that which has nothing enters into that which has no gap”. and the last line is 天下希能及之矣. the two 於 make the pictures a little more spatial: the soft moves in the hard, and the no-thing goes into the no-gap. without 於, as in our text, the first verb takes the hard thing as its direct object, and the sense leans toward “drives” or “rides”. this passage is not among the guodian slips. a related sentence is in the huainanzi, which praises water at length and then quotes these lines; so by the second century bce they were read as lines about water.

wang bi: breath and water. wang bi names two things for the softest: 氣無所不入，水無所不出於經. the second half of his sentence is damaged in the copies; textual critics think that 出於 strayed in from the line 出於無有，入於無間, as the huainanzi quotes it. the sense is: “breath: there is no place that it does not enter; water: there is no place that it does not pass through”. breath comes first. it is softer than water and it needs no channel. then, on the next line: 虛無柔弱，無所不通，無有不可窮，至柔不可折，以此推之，故知無為之有益也. “the empty, the not-having, the soft and weak: there is nothing that they do not go through. that which has nothing cannot be exhausted; the softest cannot be snapped. reason out from this, and so one knows that not-doing has gain.” a hard thing can be snapped and a full thing used up. what has no hardness and no content offers nothing to break and nothing to spend.

legge: “dashes against and overcomes”. for the one verb 馳騁 legge gives two: the softest thing “dashes against and overcomes the hardest”. the first is his picture of waves on rock; the second is the result, which the chinese does not state. the gallop itself is gone. for 無有 he writes “that which has no (substantial) existence”, and the bracket shows his care: he will not say that nothing enters, only that something thin does. for 無間 he has “no crevice”, which is exact. his 無為 is “doing nothing (with a purpose)”, the same bracket as in passage 37. and 益 is twice “advantage”; see the note on that word. his version is honest prose. what it cannot carry is the shock of the first line, where the softest thing does the most violent act in the vocabulary of a horse-riding nobility.

teach one thing without a word. today, pick one thing that you would normally explain or correct in someone: a child, a colleague, a friend. do not say it. do the thing yourself, plainly, where it can be seen, and add no look that means “notice this”. then leave it. the hard part is not the silence. it is the wish for a result that stays in the silence and pushes through it. see if you can let that go too, so that nothing presses on the other person, not even your hope. check in a week. you may find that what entered was something for which you had no words.

柔/堅: the rider needs the ground. the pair is soft 柔 and hard 堅, each at its extreme, 至. the verb between them is to gallop, and a gallop needs ground. the softest moves across the hardest, through it, over it. the hard is not destroyed in the line; it is the field of the ride. so the picture relates the two before it ranks them. the text does favor the soft. its age trusted walls, armor, and hard things, and the line corrects that trust. it does not state that the soft wins each time. the soft side turns too. water freezes and splits rock as a hard thing. the body is soft at birth and stiff at death, as passage 76 says. and softness that is used as a method to win has a hard aim inside it. a one-sided reading also misses the last line: few reach this, 希及之, because it is not a thing that force can get.

the softest thing moves freely through the hardest thing.. the softest thing moves freely through the hardest thing. have you seen this happen between people? have you also seen the soft simply crushed? what is the hardest thing in you? what has reached it, and what has only bounced off? take the other side: hard things yield only to harder things, and softness invites harm. where did life teach you that? which do you trust in a real conflict, your softness or your hardness? what does the untrusted one do while it waits?

not acting brings a real gain, and few people ever reach it.. not acting brings a real gain, and few people ever reach it. do you believe that doing nothing can add something? what is your evidence? how do you feel when you are not useful? whose approval did usefulness once buy? hold the opposite for a while: nothing is gained that is not worked for. notice what in you stands up straight at those words. which is harder for you, to act or to refrain? what does the harder one threaten?

the deepest teaching is given without words, by what a person is and does.. the deepest teaching is given without words, by what a person is and does. who taught you most without saying it? what exactly did you take from them? what do you teach the people near you by your conduct, apart from what you tell them? is there a gap that you would rather not see? try the reverse: what is not said clearly is not learned, and silence leaves people to guess. when did someone’s silence fail you? do you lean on words or away from them? what does each choice let you avoid?

間 light between two doors. the frame is 門, a gate: two door leaves that hang on posts, each with its panels. the shuowen calls it 从二戶。象形, “from two 戶, single doors; a picture”; the single door is in passage 11. inside the gate is 日, the sun. sunlight between the leaves of a gate: there is a crack. that is a gap, 間. the older form has a different light. it is 閒, with 月, the moon, in the gate, and the shuowen defines it as 隟也, “a crack”. xu kai, a commentator of the tenth century, explains the picture: a gate is shut at night, and if moonlight is seen through it, there is a gap. from a crack in a door the meaning spread to each kind of between: the space between two things, a room (one “between” of pillars), an interval of time, a spy (one who gets into the gap), and with a change of tone, “to separate”. the same gate holds other things too. 開, to open, is commonly explained as two hands that lift the bar; 閉, to shut, has the bar set. by their parts, 問, to ask, is a mouth at the gate, and 聞, to hear, is an ear at the gate; the shuowen takes the gate in both as the sound. this passage says 無間, no gap: a gate so well shut that neither sun nor moon shows. something enters in any case. now look at the character once more. the light is already inside it. twelve strokes. the left leaf of the gate: a vertical; then a horizontal with a corner that comes down a short way; then two short horizontals inside. the right leaf: a short vertical; then the great stroke, a horizontal with a corner that drops the full height of the character and ends in a hook to the left; then two short horizontals inside. then the sun, in the lower middle: left side, top with right side, the line inside, the base. watch the two long verticals, the first stroke and the sixth. they are the door posts and must be parallel and strong; the left one may stop a little short, and the right one, with its hook, goes lowest. the sun must hang free and touch neither post. that white space around it is the gap of the character. the cursive form reduced the gate to a dot and one sweeping line, and the short form 间 comes from it.

至 something comes down and lands. the bottom line is the ground; the shuowen says so: 从一，一猶地也, “from 一, and the 一 is like the earth”. what comes down to it? the shuowen sees a bird: 鳥飛从高下至地也, “a bird flies from on high down to the ground”. it then sets 至 beside 不, which it reads as a bird that flies up and does not come down: 不，上去；而至，下來也. many modern scholars read the early forms differently, as an arrow, point down, that has struck the earth. bird or arrow, the idea is one: arrival, the end of a flight. from “to arrive” comes “the furthest point”, and so the word that makes a superlative: 至柔, soft to the limit; 至堅, hard to the limit. the summer and winter solstices are 夏至 and 冬至, the “arrivals” of the sun at its extremes. as a part, 至 marks places where one comes to a stop. 到, to reach, adds 刀 for the sound. 室, a room, is a roof over 至, and 屋, a house, has it too; the shuowen remarks 室、屋皆从至: one arrives and stays. in this passage the word stands in both halves of the first line. the softest and the hardest are both arrivals at a limit, and the passage says which limit the other cannot keep out. six strokes. a horizontal at the top. second, one stroke with a sharp turn: it falls to the lower left, then bends and runs right, rising a little. third, a dot at the right, which closes the upper shape. fourth, a short horizontal. fifth, a vertical down through it. sixth, the long base line, the ground. watch the second stroke. it is the dive: the brush comes down, stops, and turns without lifting, and the angle must be clean. the lower part is 土, earth, and should be steady and wide; the top is narrower. do not let the base line be flat: it rises a little to the right and presses down at its end.

馳 a horse at speed. the left part is 馬, a horse, and the shuowen describes the picture: 象馬頭髦尾四足之形, “it shows the head, mane, tail, and four legs of a horse”. turn it a quarter in your mind. the three horizontal lines at the upper right are the mane that streams back from the neck. the long stroke that wraps around the bottom is the back and the tail. the four dots are the four legs. in the oracle-bone script the animal stands upright on its tail, with a great eye and a brush of mane; no two are drawn alike. the shuowen’s definition is two words of sound and character: 怒也。武也, “fierce; martial”. as a left-hand part, the horse marks its own world: 騎 (to ride), 駕 (to yoke), 驅 (to drive), 驚 (to startle: a horse that shies), 驕 (proud: a tall horse), and the two words of this passage, 馳 and 騁. the right part of 馳 is 也, which is here only the sound. the shuowen defines the whole as 大驅也, to drive hard. the short form 马 kept the outline and took out the mane and the legs; the four legs became one line. in this passage the rider of the horse is the softest thing under heaven. in the character, look at the legs: four dots that do not touch the ground. thirteen strokes. the horse takes ten. a horizontal at the top; a vertical at the left; two more horizontals, the mane; a second vertical through the mane; then the long stroke that runs right, turns down, and hooks: the back and tail. then the four dots inside the hook, written from left to right; the first leans left and the other three lean right. then 也, three strokes: a horizontal that rises, turns, and hooks; a tall vertical through it; and the long last stroke that goes down, bends, runs right under everything, and flicks up. watch the dots and the last stroke together. the dots are quick and light, hooves in the air; the last stroke of 也 is long and low, like the ground that goes past under them. as a left side, the horse is made narrow, and its dots are small and close.

44 · name or body. name or body: which is nearer? / body or goods: which counts for more? / gain or loss: which is the sickness? / so: extreme love must cost greatly; / much stored must be heavily lost. / know enough: no disgrace. / know to stop: no danger. / then it can last long. three questions of five characters each, all on one frame: a 與 b 孰 c, “a or b, which is more c?” name or body, which is nearer? body or goods, which is more? gain or loss, which is the sickness? the body stands in the first two and is the hinge between them. no answer is given. then two laws, each with 必, “must”: great love, great cost; much stored, heavy loss. then two short rules of four characters, built on two words for the foot: know enough, know to stop. the reward is stated last and it is modest: it can last. the passage has no dao, no heaven, and no sage. it is addressed to a person who has a name and a store, and something to lose. the questions do not work as rhetoric. ask them slowly and something moves. which is nearer, the name or the body? the name is made of other people’s thoughts; no one has ever met their own reputation. the body is here before the question is finished. yet most of a day’s worry goes to the first. the passage does not say that the name is bad. it asks about distance, and a person can check the distance directly. the same test applies to love. the line does not tell you to love less. it observes that 甚, the extreme degree, turns love into a grip, and that a grip is tiring to hold. know enough is then not a rule of restraint. it is what remains when the nearer thing is felt as nearer. a person who leads is paid in 名 and 貨: title and reward. the passage speaks to that person. in the courts of the time, disgrace and danger were concrete, and they came most often to those who had risen far and stored much. the warning still holds for a house, a company, a team. an organisation that loves one thing to the extreme, a product, a founder, a number, will pay any cost to keep it, and the cost appears elsewhere. wang bi names the mechanism: the loved thing stops moving. and the hoard, of cash, of data, of authority, brings the many who seek it. the skill of stopping is a hard one for the successful, because each earlier step past “enough” was rewarded. put the passage where it points: in the body. stand up. 足 and 止 are both feet. let the weight go down into the soles until the two feet are fully on the floor. this is the physical sense of “enough”: nothing leans forward to the next thing. in movement arts, the one who reaches too far gives away the centre, and the hand that grips hard cannot feel. extreme love of the win costs the balance: 甚愛必大費. try a slow reach for an object and stop at the point where the back foot would lift. that point is 知止. past it you are in 殆: you can be pulled. before it you can stay as long as you like. ask the three questions about one real thing today, and answer in writing. a message that you want to send to defend your name: name or body, which is nearer? a purchase, or an extra hour of paid work at night: body or goods, which counts for more? a gain that you have chased for a month: is the gain or the loss the sickness? then do the small exercise of stopping once. do not make a rule from it. the passage gives none; it gives questions, two observations, and the word enough.

名: a name is also a reputation. 名 is the plain word “name”. the shuowen explains the graph as 夕, evening, above 口, a mouth: in the dark people cannot see each other, so each one calls out who they are. in the warring states the word had grown large. 名 was a person’s reputation, and it was also rank and title, the name by which a court knew and paid a man. the wandering advisers of the time lived by it. a good name opened the gate of a ruler; a ruined one closed every gate. english must choose “name”, “fame”, or “reputation”. we keep “name” because the first line of the book uses the same word: the name that can be named. a name is a sound in the mouths of others. where is it kept?

身: the body, not “life”. the shuowen says of 身: 象人之身, “it pictures a person’s body”. the graph is commonly explained as a figure seen from the side with the trunk drawn large; some see a pregnant belly, and 身 still means “pregnancy” in the phrase 有身. the word covers the trunk, the whole body, and the person: 身 is how classical chinese says “oneself”. english translators often write “life” or “self” here, and both are too thin. the question is physical. fame is in the mouths of others, and this is in your skin. the book returns to the word often. passage 13 says that great trouble comes from having a 身, and then gives the world to the one who values the body as the world. passage 26 asks how a lord of ten thousand chariots can treat the body more lightly than the realm.

親: near, kin, dear. 親 is one word where english has three. it means near in space, it means parents and relatives, and it means dear. the shuowen defines it with one syllable: 至也, “it arrives”, it comes all the way to you. the graph has 見, to see, on the right: the people whom you see every day. so the first question does not ask which of the two is “better” or “more valuable”. it asks which is closer kin. the answer looks easy, and the text gives none. the question had a school behind it. in a court society the honest answer was often the name: men died to protect it, and families lived on it for generations. the question measures a distance. how far from you is your reputation, and how far is your hand?

貨: shells that change hands. 貨 is 貝, a cowrie shell, under 化, to change. the shuowen glosses it 財也, “wealth”, and treats 化 as the sound. under 貝 the same dictionary keeps a short history of money: 古者貨貝而寶龜, “the ancients used shells as goods and treasured tortoise shell”; the zhou had coins, and the qin ended the shell. cowries came from distant seas and are found in shang tombs. by the warring states, bronze money in the shapes of spades and knives moved between the states, and great merchants grew rich on salt and iron. 貨 is wealth in that form: things that can be carried, priced, and exchanged. the book is wary of it. passages 3, 12, and 64 all speak of 難得之貨, “rare goods, hard to come by”, and of what such goods do to people.

孰多: which is “more”?. 多 means “much, many”. here it is the measure: of body and goods, which is the greater amount? the word is exact for the topic. goods are the things that people count, and the line asks you to put the body on the same scale. a story told in the zhuangzi and in the lushi chunqiu makes the test concrete. master zihua asks a lord of han, who is at war over a strip of land: suppose a document said that whoever takes it gains the world and loses a hand. would you take it? the lord says no. then, says zihua, your two arms count for more than the world, and your body for more than your arms; and the land that you fight for counts for much less. we render “counts for more”; “is worth more” would also do.

得與亡: gain and loss of what?. the third question names no objects. 得 is to get and 亡 is to lose, or to be gone. gain of what, and loss of what? one reading takes the line alone: is it getting or losing that harms a person? common sense says loss, and the passage then argues that getting is the sickness. wang bi reads the line as the sum of the first two: to gain name and goods and to lose the body. a third reading reverses it: gain the body and lose the rest. the chinese holds all three, because it does not say whose gain it is. the rendering adds no objects. note the sound: 得 is said like 德, the “inner power” of the book’s title, and early texts often explain 德 as 得, “to get”. the word 亡 returns in the fifth line as the fate of the hoard.

病: sickness, not “worse”. 病 is illness. the shuowen: 疾加也, “a sickness that has grown heavy”. as a verb it means to make ill, to distress, to find fault with. many translations write “which is worse?” or “more harmful”, and the image is lost. the first two questions used words of measure: nearer, more. the third changes to medicine. it asks for a diagnosis. the answer is not obvious to the patient, because this sickness feels like health: the store grows, the name grows. passage 71 uses the word in the same way and makes a remedy from it: 病病, to be sick of the sickness, is to be free of it. the left and top part of the graph, 疒, marks illnesses; the shuowen explains it as a person who leans on a bed.

愛: to love and to grudge. 愛 has two old senses, and the line uses both. it is to love, to hold dear. it is also to be sparing with a thing, to grudge it. in the mencius a king sees an ox on its way to be killed for a rite and orders a sheep in its place. the people, mencius tells him, 皆以王為愛也: “all took your majesty to be stingy”. the word there is 愛. so 甚愛必大費 says: extreme love must cost greatly. it also says: the extreme miser must pay greatly. 費 is to spend and to waste; it has 貝, the cowrie, at its foot. english “attachment” brings in modern psychology, and “love” alone misses the miser. notice that the line has no object. it does not say love of what. is there a love that does not hold on?

多藏必厚亡: the storehouse and the tomb. 藏 is to store and to hide. the shuowen gives one word: 匿也, “to conceal”. a reader of the time would think of two places. one is the treasury. the states of this period fell one after another, and a full storehouse was a reason for an attack. the other place is the grave; 厚, “thick”, the word for the loss in this line, is also the usual word for a lavish burial, 厚葬. the rich were buried with bronzes, jade, lacquer, and silk, and tomb robbery was already an old trade. the heshang gong commentary reads the line across both: goods in the storehouse bring raiders in life, and goods in the grave bring diggers after death. there is an irony for us. this very line survives in its oldest copy because it was stored in a tomb at guodian, about 300 bce, and robbers had opened that tomb shortly before the archaeologists came in 1993. see the old copies.

知足: to know the foot. 足 is “foot”, and it is also “enough”. the two are one graph and one syllable; how the second sense came from the first is not settled. so 知足, “to know enough”, can be seen as “to know the foot”: to know where you stand. the phrase runs through the book. passage 33: 知足者富, “who knows enough is rich”. passage 46: 知足之足常足, “the enough of ‘know enough’ is always enough”, with three 足 in six characters. english “contentment” makes it a feeling. the chinese makes it knowledge: an accurate sense of a quantity. it is also not “settle for less”. the line does not say how much is enough. it says that there is such a point, and that it can be known. see the plate for 足.

足 and 止: two feet in two lines. look at the two characters together. 足 has 止 inside it: the shuowen analyses it as 从止、口, from 止 and 口. and 止, “to stop”, is commonly explained as the picture of a foot or footprint. the shuowen itself notes the link: 故以止爲足, “so 止 is used for the foot”. the couplet therefore puts a foot in each line. enough is a foot. stopping is a foot. the image under both is a person who stands still on the ground. the sound joins them too. in the old rhyme groups, 足 rhymes with 辱 in its own line, and 止 rhymes with 殆 in the next and with 久 at the close. mandarin still keeps the first pair, zu and ru; it has lost the second.

知止: the skill of stopping. passage 32 has the same promise: when names have been made, know to stop, and there is no danger. stopping sounds like the absence of a skill. try it today and see. stop a meal one bite before full. end a talk one sentence before the last point that you wanted to add. close the work when it is done and not when you are tired. in each case you will find a moment when enough has arrived, and a pull to go past it. the pull is the 甚 of the fourth line, “extreme, too much”. do not fight it. only learn to recognise the moment just before it. what does “enough” feel like in the body, one second before “more”?

辱: shamed at the edge of the field. 辱 is public disgrace. the shuowen explains the graph with a scene from the farming year: 从寸在辰下。失耕時，於封畺上戮之也, “from 寸 under 辰. one who missed the time of ploughing was punished on the boundary mound.” 辰, it adds, is 農之時, “the farmer’s season”. so the dictionary’s disgrace is the shame of bad timing, displayed where the neighbours could see. modern scholars read the picture in another way; see the plate. in either case 辱 is social: it is done to you in front of others. that fits the audience. a man at a warring states court could lose rank, be mutilated, or be killed with his kin when his name or his wealth grew too visible. the book pairs 辱 with 寵, favour, in passage 13: both arrive like a shock.
