殆: danger with bones in it. 殆 is “danger”; the shuowen says 危也. its left part is 歹, written 歺 in the dictionary: broken bone, the sign of death and harm. it stands in 死, to die, and in 殘, to maim. the right part, 台, gives the sound. the word is the usual one for mortal risk in the texts of the time. sunzi’s most famous line uses it: know the other and know yourself, and in a hundred battles there is no 殆. the laozi uses the same two words, 不殆, five times. once they describe the way itself, which goes round and is not imperilled (25). in the other four the cause of safety is not strength. it is a kind of knowing: to know the constant (16), to know to stop (32 and here), to know the mother’s child and keep to the mother (52).

可以長久: what lasts?. the last line has no subject. 可以 is “can thereby”; 長 is long and 久 is lasting. english wants to know who or what lasts: you, your life, your house, your state? the rendering says “it” and leaves the place open. read with the first line, the answer is the body: a long life. read at a court, it is the family line and the state. passage 7 gives the model: 天長地久, “heaven is long and earth is lasting”, and they last because they do not live for themselves. note the size of the promise. the passage does not offer wealth, peace of mind, or success. it offers two absences, no disgrace and no danger, and time. is that a small reward or a large one?

wang bi: things that cannot pass through. wang bi answers each question in one line. on the first: 尚名好高，其身必疏, “exalt the name and love height, and the body must grow distant.” on the second: 貪貨無厭，其身必少, “crave goods without limit, and the body must count for less.” his two adjectives, 疏 (distant) and 少 (less), are the exact opposites of 親 and 多. on the fourth and fifth lines: 甚愛不與物通，多藏不與物散，求之者多，攻之者眾，為物所病. “extreme love does not let things pass through; much storing does not let things disperse. those who seek it are many, and those who attack it are a crowd; one is made sick by things.” his verbs are 通, to flow through, and 散, to scatter. the fault for him is the blockage. a thing that is loved too much is taken out of circulation.

yang zhu and the party of the body. the first two questions sound like a school of the fourth century bce that later lost its books. its teacher was yang zhu. mencius attacks him in a famous line: yang would not pull out one hair to benefit the whole world. other sources are kinder. the huainanzi sums up his teaching as 全性保真，不以物累形: “keep your nature whole, protect what is genuine, and do not let things burden the body.” chapters of the lushi chunqiu with titles such as “value life” and “the self is weighty” argue the case in full. in a time when rulers spent bodies freely, in armies and in labour on walls, to say that one body outweighs goods and office was a political statement. the laozi shares the premise, and it was yang’s kind of question that legge turned into a hymn. its conclusion is different: it turns the care of the body into the test of who may hold the world (13).

legge sings it. legge saw that this passage rhymes, and he put it into english rhymed verse: dear, adhere, near; shame, blame. it was an honest attempt, and it shows the cost. the three questions of five characters each become seven lines. 身 becomes “life”, and the body goes. 病 becomes “sorrow and pain”, the language of a victorian hymn. for the fourth line he writes that the one who cleaves to fame “rejects what is more great”: he has supplied an object, fame, for a line that has none, and the double sense of 愛 goes too. the close, “long live shall he”, adds a “he” that the chinese does not have. read the chinese count aloud instead: five, five, five; then six and five; then four, four, four.

among the oldest lines we have. this passage is on the guodian bamboo slips, the oldest known copy of laozi material, buried about 300 bce. it is nearly the same as the text of five centuries later. the mawangdui silk texts, buried in 168 bce, are reported to differ in one small place: they have no 是故 before the fourth line and put 故, “so”, before 知足: 多藏必厚亡 故知足不辱. the conclusion is then drawn one step later: the cost and the loss are stated as facts, and the “so” belongs to the advice. the guodian slips are reported to read the fifth line with the two adjectives exchanged, “thick storing, much loss”. the sense is the same. the three questions have stood unchanged for some twenty-three centuries.

得/亡: the store and the loss arrive together. the passage asks about pairs and gives no answers: name or body, body or goods, getting 得 or losing 亡. then it shows how one side of the last pair makes the other. much stored, 多藏, and heavy loss, 厚亡, are one event seen at two times; a person with no store cannot lose it. extreme love and great cost are joined in the same way. so the text does not say that gain is bad and loss is good. it says that each is carried inside the other, and that 甚, “extreme”, is the point where the turn starts. the passage favors “enough” and “stop”. that is advice for those who have a name and a store, in courts where both were deadly. it turns as well: “enough” held as a rule is a new store, and a name for wanting little is still a name. what have you lost that left you with more?

your body is nearer to you than your name, and counts for more than your goods.. your body is nearer to you than your name, and counts for more than your goods. answer the passage’s question honestly: on an ordinary day, which do you serve first? when did you first learn that your name, your standing with others, could be lost? what did you start to do then? take the opposite: a good name outlasts the body, and some things are worth the body’s cost. what have you gladly spent yourself on? which side embarrasses you a little? why might that be the one to look at?

the more extreme the attachment, the greater the cost; the bigger the hoard, the heavier the loss.. the more extreme the attachment, the greater the cost; the bigger the hoard, the heavier the loss. do you agree, or does this sound like fear of loving anything fully? what do you hold most tightly? trace the grip back: what earlier loss does it remember? now hold the other view: only what you love without measure is worth having, and its cost is the proof. what feelings come? do you admire people who hold on or people who travel light? what do you say about the other kind when they are not present?

a person who knows what is enough, and when to stop, meets no disgrace and can last.. a person who knows what is enough, and when to stop, meets no disgrace and can last. has stopping in time ever protected you? has it ever cost you something that you still want? how do you know that you have had enough: of work, of food, of praise? is the signal in the body or in a rule? suppose the opposite: those who do not say “enough” are the ones who change things, and to last long is not the highest aim. stay with that. what stirs? which do you fear more, going too far or stopping too soon? where does that fear come from?

足 the foot that means “enough”. two parts, one above the other. the top is 口, which in most characters is a mouth. here it is not a mouth: it is commonly explained as what is left of the knee or the lower leg, a round shape in the old forms. the bottom is 止, and that is the foot itself. 止 alone is commonly explained as a footprint, the sole with its toes; it came to mean “to stop”, the place where the foot rests. the shuowen keeps both facts: 足 is 人之足也。在下。从止、口, “a person’s foot; it is below; from 止 and 口”. look for 止 in other characters and you find feet everywhere. 步, a step: the shuowen analyses it as two 止 turned opposite ways, left foot and right foot. 正, upright, has it at the base. as a side part, 足 is squeezed to 𧾷 and marks what legs do: 路 (road), 跪 (to kneel), 跳 (to jump), 踐 (to tread). then the second meaning: enough, sufficient, to be worth. no one is sure how the foot came to carry it. in this passage the pair is the whole teaching: 知足, 知止. a foot above a foot. the character for “enough” is a person who has come to a stand. seven strokes. the first three make 口: the left side down, then the top and the right side in one stroke with a corner, then the base. keep this box small and a little flat; it is the knee and not the main part. the fourth stroke is a vertical from the middle of the box’s base. the fifth is a short horizontal that goes out to the right from the middle of that vertical. the sixth is a stroke that falls to the left. watch the seventh: a long stroke that begins near the sixth, travels down to the right, presses, and lifts into a sharp tail. it runs far past the box on the right, and it is the ground on which the character stands. in seal script the lower part is still a clear 止. in cursive the bottom becomes one turning line.

辱 a hand and a hoe. the top is 辰 and the bottom is 寸. take the bottom first. 寸 is “inch”: the shuowen explains it as the spot one inch back from the hand where the pulse moves, and analyses it as 又, a hand, with one mark. in compounds it usually means only “hand”: 守 (to guard), 封 (to raise a boundary mound), 得 (to get), which stands in this passage. now the top. 辰 is today the fifth of the twelve branches and a word for a time or a star. the shuowen calls it 農之時, the farmer’s season. many modern scholars explain the old form as a farm tool, a hoe or a blade made from a large clam shell; the basis is the family of characters around it. 農, farming, has 辰 below. 蜃 is a great clam. 耨, to weed, has 辱 itself on the right. so 辱 is commonly explained as a hand that holds the hoe: to weed, to work the soil. how did it come to mean disgrace? the shuowen answers with its story of the late ploughman punished at the field’s edge. others think the word “shame” only borrowed the graph for its sound. this is disputed; hold both. its cousin 恥, shame, is glossed by the shuowen with this character: 恥，辱也. ten strokes: seven for 辰, three for 寸. 辰 begins with a horizontal, then a long stroke that falls to the left and makes a roof with it, like the cliff shape 厂. under that roof come two more horizontals, the second one longer. the fifth stroke goes down and flicks up to the right. the sixth is a short stroke to the left, and the seventh is a long one that falls to the right; let it reach wide. then 寸: a long horizontal, a vertical that ends in a hook to the left, and one dot. watch the eighth stroke, the horizontal of 寸. it is the widest line in the character and it carries the whole upper part like a tray. the weight above is to the right, and the hook and dot below answer it on the left.

45 · the clumsy master. great completion seems chipped; / its use does not wear out. / great fullness seems empty; / its use does not run dry. / great straightness seems bent; / its use does not settle. / great skill seems clumsy; / its use does not break off. / great eloquence seems tongue-tied; / its use does not miss. / restlessness beats cold; / stillness beats heat. / clear and still: / the measure of the world. five lines on one frame: 大 a 若 b, “great a seems b”, where b is the common opposite of a. completion and the chip; fullness and the hollow; straight and bent; skilled and clumsy; eloquent and tongue-tied. the order moves from things to a person: first two vessels, then a line, then a hand, then a mouth. after each comes a refrain on use. then the passage changes voice: two short facts about cold and heat, and a final line of six characters that names the measure of the world: clear and still. there is no “therefore” between the parts. the reader must find the link. one way: only a still, clear eye can see the five greats as great. we judge by finish. the complete thing should look complete, the full one full, the skilled one smooth. the five lines take this habit apart. they do not say that defects are good. they say that the largest form of a quality gives up the signs of that quality, because the signs are for an audience. skill that must look like skill is still partly display. straightness that must look straight is partly pride. turn this on the self. a person tries to appear whole, and guards the appearance. the passage suggests that wholeness is easier than that: it has room for a chip, and it does not need to be seen. clear and still is then the state of one who has stopped managing how they look. at a court of the time, men were chosen by their speeches. the passage warns the one who chooses. the smooth disputer, the plan with no visible weakness, the minister who is always seen to be upright: these are small completions. the great ones look worse at the interview. a leader also meets the lines from the other side. the work that lasts is often the work that does not advertise its skill, and a team can use an unfinished proposal more than a sealed one. the close, 清靜為天下正, was read as a policy: the still ruler sets the standard, and the early han tried it. do not make clumsiness a style. a staged stammer is one more kind of 巧. 躁勝寒，靜勝熱 is true in the skin. when you are cold, move: the large muscles make heat in a minute. when you are hot or angry, stop: sit, let the breath go long, and the heat leaves. the body already knows both medicines and when each applies. in movement arts the five lines are daily experience. the master’s form looks plain, even awkward, because nothing is added for show. the power that looks bent, with knees and elbows unlocked, is the power that does not break. the hand that seems empty can receive. beginners straighten, tighten, and finish each gesture. watch an old teacher walk across a room. what is missing from the walk? nothing in nature is finished in the way that a polished object is finished. a tree is always part dead wood. a river bank is always breaking. yet the forest and the river do not wear out, and a sealed, complete machine does. the spring is the plain case of great fullness: a hollow in the ground that gives water all year. the seasons give the closing lines. animals move in the cold and lie still in the heat of noon. muddy water becomes clear when nothing stirs it; this is the root picture of 清, and passage 15 asks who can make the muddy clear by stillness. do the exercise of one chip: leave one piece of work a little open, and see whether its use ends sooner or later. and use the two medicines once each today. when you are dull and cold, move for two minutes. when you are heated, in body or in an argument, be still for two minutes before the next word. notice which of the two you reach for by habit, and whether it is the right one for the weather.

大: “great” is not “very”. each of the five lines begins with 大, and english “great” makes it sound like praise or like size. in the laozi 大 is nearer to “whole, at full scale”. passage 25 uses it as a forced name for dao itself: 強為之名曰大, “if i must name it, i say ‘great’”. so 大成 is not a very big achievement. it is completion that has gone all the way, and the claim is that completion at that scale does not look like completion at ours. a small finished thing shows its finish: the edges are closed, the surface is polished. passage 41 has the same family of lines: 大器晚成, the great vessel is completed late; 大音希聲, the great tone is rarely heard. what would you have to change in yourself to see a great thing as great?

若: seems, or is like?. 若 is the hinge of every line, and it has two edges. it can mean “to seem”: the great completion only appears chipped, and the fault is in the eye of the viewer. it can also mean “to be like”: great completion is in fact like a chipped thing; it shares some real quality with it. english must choose “seems” or “resembles”, and the choice decides the teaching. with “seems”, the passage is about perception and about those who misjudge. with “is like”, it is about the nature of the great thing: it does keep a gap, and it does not seal itself. wang bi reads it the second way. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write 若 in the first two lines and then 如, a near synonym. we render “seems” and ask you to hear the other word under it.

缺: the pot with a piece gone. the shuowen defines 缺 in three characters: 器破也, “a vessel is broken”. the left part is 缶, an earthenware crock; the dictionary says that it held wine and that the people of qin beat it to keep time for their songs. the right part gives the sound and is shared with 決, to breach, and 玦, a jade ring made with a slot in it. from the chipped pot the word spread to any gap: a missing tooth, a vacant post, the dark part of the moon. so the first line holds a picture that english “imperfect” does not have: the most complete thing looks like a bowl with a chip in its rim. remember passage 11: a vessel is of use where it has nothing. the chip is one more opening.

其用不…: five ways not to end. in this text each of the five “greats” is followed by 其用不 and one verb: its use does not 弊, wear out like old cloth; does not 窮, come to the end of the road; does not 居, stay in one place; does not 輟, break off; does not 差, miss. the grammar is the same each time and the verb changes, so the refrain turns one idea in the light. the subject is 用, the working of a thing, the word that closed passage 11. the first refrain answers a fear. a chipped thing should be near its end. the line says that this one is not: the things that look complete are the things that wear out. only the first two refrains are in every old copy.

沖: empty, and welling up. this line repeats the vocabulary of passage 4: 道沖而用之或不盈, “dao is 沖; use it, and it does not fill”. the same three words are here: 沖, 用, 盈. the graph 沖 is water beside 中, the centre, and the shuowen defines it as 涌搖, “to well up and rock”: a moving, surging thing. the sense “empty” belongs to another graph, 盅, which the dictionary explains as 器虛也, “the vessel is empty”, and under that entry it quotes the laozi itself: 道盅而用之. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write 盅 in this line. if so, the han dictionary and the han manuscript agree: the word is the hollow of a bowl. the later graph adds water, and a reader of the received text sees both, an emptiness that moves. a spring looks like this. it is a hole in the ground, and it does not run dry.

屈: the animal with no tail. the shuowen entry for 屈 is a surprise: 無尾也, “to be without a tail”. the dictionary places it under 尾, tail, with 出 as the sound; the tail part was later worn down to the 尸 that we see. from “short-tailed, cut short” the word came to mean bent, curled up, and then made to yield: 屈服 is to submit, and 冤屈 is a wrong that one has had to swallow. so the line has a moral edge that “bent” does not show. great uprightness can look like giving way, even like accepting a wrong. passage 22 opens with the same thought, 曲則全, “bent, then whole”. commenting on passage 58, wang bi cites this line: the sage guides things with straightness and does not use straightness to make them boil.

three refrains that most copies lack. the chinese text pinned for this app gives all five lines a refrain. most editions do not. in the common received text, and in the copies of the wang bi text that most scholars print, only the first two lines have one; then come three bare lines: 大直若屈，大巧若拙，大辯若訥. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to have refrains for the first two only, and the guodian slips are reported to be the same. the three extra refrains, 其用不居, 其用不輟, 其用不差, are in no standard edition, and wang bi’s own commentary passes over them in silence. they are best held as a later expansion: a reader or editor completed the pattern. we render them because they are in our base text, and we mark them here. it is a small lesson in the passage’s own terms. someone found the text chipped and filled it in.

拙: clumsiness as an ideal. 拙 is the plain word for “not skilful”; the shuowen says 不巧也. this line gave it a second life. the zhuangzi quotes it, 故曰大巧若拙, after a call to break the compass and square and to break the fingers of the master craftsman. in the fifth century the poet tao yuanming left office and wrote that he would 守拙, “keep to clumsiness”, and go home to his fields. in the arts the word became praise. painters and potters looked for the awkward line that hides nothing. the calligrapher fu shan, in the seventeenth century, set it as a rule: 寧拙毋巧, “better clumsy than clever”. the target in each case is 巧, skill that shows itself and pleases at once. think of a thing that you own and have used for years. is it the clever one?

辯: the age of the disputers. 辯 is to argue a case. the graph shows the setting: 言, speech, between two 辛. the shuowen analyses its base, 辡, as two accused persons who bring suit against each other. the fourth and third centuries bce were the great age of this art. rulers kept halls of scholars, and men travelled from court to court to sell plans in set speeches. a group known as the 辯者, “disputers”, made paradox a profession: hui shi, and gongsun long with his white horse that is not a horse. even mencius had to defend himself: “do i love disputation? i cannot avoid it.” the last passage of the laozi answers them all: 善者不辯，辯者不善, “the good do not dispute; the disputers are not good”. a book of paradoxes here declines the contest.

訥: speech that stays inside. 訥 is 言, speech, beside 內, inside. the shuowen reads the two parts together: 言難也, “speech is hard”. the words are there, and they do not come out easily. this is one of the few virtues on which the laozi and confucius agree. the analects says that the noble person wishes to be 訥 in word and quick in deed, and that the firm, the resolute, the plain, and the 訥 are near to humaneness. english has no kind word for it. “stammering”, “inarticulate”, and “tongue-tied” all name a defect, and greek and roman culture made the orator a model of the complete man. here the model speaker is the one whose words come slowly. whom do you trust more: the one who answers at once, or the one who pauses?

cold and heat: plain sense, and a puzzle. 躁勝寒，靜勝熱. the plain reading is knowledge of the body. move about, stamp your feet, and you overcome cold. sit still, and you overcome heat. 躁 has 足, the foot, at its left: restless feet. but readers have long felt a difficulty. the first line gives 躁 a victory, and the next line gives rule to stillness; and passage 26 says 靜為躁君, “stillness is the lord of restlessness”. some modern editors therefore change the order of the words to 靜勝躁，寒勝熱: “stillness beats restlessness, cold beats heat”. no old copy has that order. the text can stand as it is. each of the two has its season, and the one who is clear and still can tell which season it is. wang bi reads it so, with one sharp addition.

清靜: two words that ruled an empire. 清 is water that has become clear; the shuowen says 澂水之皃, “the look of settled water”. 靜 is stillness. together they became the motto of a way to govern. in the first decades of the han, after the wars that ended qin, the minister cao can learned from a teacher of the laozi that 治道貴清靜而民自定: “the way of rule values clearness and stillness, and the people settle themselves”. he kept the laws of his predecessor and did little else, and the land recovered. the historian sima qian ends his life of laozi with the same pair: 清靜自正. later the words passed to religion. a short scripture of the tang period, the qingjing jing, is still chanted each day in daoist temples. english “purity” for 清, legge’s choice, is a moral word. the chinese is a pond when the mud has gone down.

為天下正: a standard, or a ruler?. 正 is “upright, correct”. the shuowen analyses it as 止, a foot, with a line that stops it. it is also the root of 政, government: “to govern is to set right”, confucius says, 政者正也. so the last line has a range. it can say that clearness and stillness are the world’s standard, the level by which things are judged. it can say that they set the world right. and it can say that the clear and still person becomes the head of the world, since 正 was also a word for a chief. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 可以為天下正, “can serve as”: there it is a person who qualifies. the guodian slips are reported to end with 定, “settled”. passage 57 opens with the word: 以正治國. we write “measure” and leave the ruler in this note.

wang bi: no single shape. wang bi explains each “great” with the same two words, 隨物, “in step with things”. on the first line: 隨物而成，不為一象，故若缺也. “it completes in step with things and does not make one single shape; so it is like a thing that lacks.” completion that fits each thing has no form of its own to show. on fullness: 隨物而與，無所愛矜, “it gives in step with things and grudges and vaunts nothing”. on skill: 因自然以成器，不造為異端, “it follows what is so of itself to complete the vessel and contrives nothing strange”. on the close he adds a limit to movement: 躁罷然後勝寒, “only when restlessness is spent does it overcome cold”, and a judgment: 靜則全物之真，躁則犯物之性, “stillness keeps whole what is genuine in things; restlessness violates their nature.”

legge turns it into modesty. legge again writes rhymed verse, and the rhyme leads him. his first line speaks of one “who thinks his great achievements poor”. the chinese has no person and no thinking: 大成若缺 is four words about how a great thing looks. legge has made it a rule of humble self-opinion, a virtue of his own church and century. the next lines become commands: “do thou what’s straight still crooked deem”. for 訥 he writes “a stammering scream”, and the scream is there only to rhyme with “seem”. at the close 清靜 becomes “purity and stillness”, and 正 becomes “the correct law”. purity and law are large words in a missionary’s english. the chinese has clear water, and a line that is straight.

the silk texts: great gain seems loss. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to have a different fifth “great”. after straightness and skill the collated text reads 大贏如㶧. 贏 is surplus, profit, the winnings of a merchant. the last graph is rare; editors read it as 絀, “to fall short, deficit”. the line is then: “great surplus is like shortfall”. it speaks of wealth, and it follows passage 44 well. the line on eloquence is absent there. the guodian slips are reported to have yet another set and order, with no line on eloquence. so the oldest copies do not agree on what the “greats” are; the pattern mattered more than the list. a reader could add one. what is yours? great kindness seems cold? great courage seems afraid?

leave one chip. take one piece of work today, a message, a plan, a drawing, a meal, and stop before the last round of polish. leave the join visible. then watch what the gap does. often the other person steps into it: they add the missing part, ask the question, finish the thought. a sealed thing can only be admired. in a conversation, try the same with 訥: when you know the clever reply, wait for three breaths, and say the plain one, or nothing. this is not a method to look humble. it is a test of the first line: does the use wear out sooner when the thing is left a little open?

躁/靜, 寒/熱: each has its season. five pairs open the passage, joined by “seems”: complete and chipped, full and empty, straight and bent, skilled and clumsy, eloquent and tongue-tied. then come two more, crossed: restless 躁 and still 靜, cold 寒 and hot 熱. here the text gives each side its work. movement answers cold. stillness answers heat. neither is the cure for all weather, and some editors have wished to change the line because it lets restlessness win once. the last line does lean to the still side: clear and still is the measure, 正. a measure is not a place to stay. it is the level from which a person can tell which season it is. stillness also turns: sit long enough and you are cold, and then the text itself says to move. a one-sided reading makes this passage a rule to be still, or a rule to look clumsy. what does the weather of today ask for?

what is truly complete looks flawed, and great skill looks clumsy.. what is truly complete looks flawed, and great skill looks clumsy. whom do you know who fits this? and where has a flaw simply been a flaw? how much of your effort goes to looking finished? who is the audience that you picture? take the opposite: excellence shows, and a polished surface is honest evidence of care. which of your own works say so? what do you feel in front of a clumsy person: impatience, tenderness, superiority? what does that say about your own unfinished places?

movement answers cold and stillness answers heat; each has its season, and a clear, still mind can tell which.. movement answers cold and stillness answers heat; each has its season, and a clear, still mind can tell which. which of the two do you reach for by habit when you are troubled? where did the habit start? was the other medicine not allowed, or not safe, in the house where you grew up? hold the view that the medicine you use less is the one that you need now. what objections come at once? do you agree that stillness is the measure? or is that the taste of a tired age, or of a tired person?

拙 a hand, and “out”. two parts side by side. on the left is 扌, the form that 手, hand, takes when it stands at the side of a character. it marks hundreds of actions of the hand: 打 (to strike), 持 (to hold), 推 (to push), 技 (craft). on the right is 出, “to go out”. the shuowen says that 出 only gives the sound here: 拙，不巧也。从手出聲, “not skilful; from hand, with 出 for the sound”. so we must not read a story into the pair. but look at what else is in this passage. 屈, “bent”, two lines above, has the same 出 for its sound, according to the same dictionary. the mawangdui silk text is reported to write that word as 詘, with 出 again. to the eye, bent and clumsy are relatives, and the two old words shared that sound-part and a final consonant. 出 itself is explained in two ways. the shuowen sees plants that push up and out. many modern scholars see a foot that steps out of a hollow; this is the common explanation today. and the opposite word, 巧, is 工, the carpenter’s square, with a sound part. the square is the tool of exact work. the skilled character has an instrument in it. the clumsy one has only a hand. eight strokes. the hand takes three: a short horizontal, a long vertical that ends in a small hook to the left, and a stroke that rises from lower left to upper right and cuts through the vertical. keep this side narrow. then 出, in five strokes. the fourth stroke goes down and turns to the right in one movement. the fifth is a short vertical that closes the right side. watch the sixth: one long vertical from the top through the middle to the lower level, and it must stand straight, because the whole right side hangs on it. the seventh is a second down-and-right turn, wider than the first, and the eighth closes it on the right. the lower tier is broader than the upper, like a tree with wide low branches. calligraphers prized this character’s meaning: a line with visible effort and no charm.

寒 a person in straw, on ice. this character is a small winter scene, and the shuowen describes it part by part: 从人在宀下，以茻薦覆之，下有仌. “a person is under a roof; grass is laid as bedding and cover; below there is ice.” take the parts in turn. 宀 at the top is the roof, as in 家 (roof over pig: a household) and 室 (room). in the seal form, a person stands in the middle, with four tufts of grass, 茻, around: the straw in which a poor household passed the winter. the regular script has pressed the person and the straw together into the middle section of level and upright lines, with two legs that spread below. at the bottom are two dots. they are 仌, which the shuowen defines as 凍也, “to freeze”, the shape of water that has set hard. the same two dots are in 冬, winter, and at the side of 冷 (cold), 冰 (ice), and 凍 (to freeze). so the dictionary’s entry for cold is one word, 凍, and the picture is a person who is doing what can be done about it. the passage gives the other remedy: 躁勝寒, move, and the cold gives way. twelve strokes. the roof is three: a dot at the top centre, a small stroke at the left edge, and a horizontal that ends in a hook down at the right. under it come two horizontals, then two verticals that cross them, then a longer horizontal that closes the frame below. space these evenly; this is the tight, warm middle of the character. then the form opens: the ninth stroke falls far to the left and the tenth far to the right, like the two sides of a thatched roof or a spread cloak. watch the last two strokes, the two dots under them. they are the ice. they sit in the open space at the bottom, one above the other, and each is pressed and lifted quickly. a heavy upper part, wide arms, and two small cold points below.

訥 words kept inside. left: 言, speech. right: 內, inside. the shuowen takes both parts as meaning: 言難也。从言从内, “speech is difficult; from 言 and from 內”. look first at 言. at its base is 口, a mouth; the lines above it are explained in different ways, and the shuowen calls the upper part a sound element. it defines the word with a distinction: 直言曰言，論難曰語, “to speak straight out is 言; to discuss and dispute is 語”. as a side part, 言 marks acts of speech: 語, 說, 論, 誠 (sincere: speech made complete), 信 with a person beside it (trust), and 辯, the disputation of this same line, where 言 stands between two litigants. now 內. the shuowen defines it as 入也, “to enter”, and adds 自外而入也, “from outside, to come in”: the part 入, enter, under a cover. add a mouth to it and you have 吶; add silk and you have 納, to take in. so 訥 is speech that has gone in, or has not yet come out. the line pairs it with 辯 on purpose. both have 言. in one, speech stands in the middle of a quarrel. in the other, it stays at home. eleven strokes. 言 takes seven: a dot, a long horizontal, two shorter horizontals, and then the mouth in three strokes: left side, top with right side, base. as a left-hand part it is written narrow, and its long horizontal reaches out only to the left, so that it does not strike the neighbour. 內 takes four. first the left vertical, then the top and right side in one stroke that ends in a hook. watch the tenth stroke: it starts above the frame, comes in through the top, and falls to the left; the last stroke leans to the right from its middle. the brush enters the box from outside. written so, with the left-falling stroke the higher one, the inner part is 人, a person. the shuowen explains the older 入, “to enter”, in which the right-falling stroke is the higher.

46 · war horses at the outskirts. when the world has dao, / running horses are turned back to dung the fields. / when the world has no dao, / war horses are born at the outskirts. / no calamity is greater than not to know enough; / no fault is greater than the wish to get. / so the enough of know-enough / is always enough. two pictures of the same animal, and then a diagnosis. when the world has the way, the running horses go back to the farm and the fields are dunged. when it has none, war horses are born on the open ground outside the wall. each picture is nine characters. no ruler is named and no battle is described; the horse alone shows the state of the world. then the cause, in two parallel lines of religious weight, 禍 and 咎: not to know enough, and the wish to get. then one line that turns on three 足. the move from the horses to the heart is made without a connecting word. the reader is left to see that the war at the 郊 and the wanting in the chest are one thing at two sizes. read the two pictures as states of one mind. in one, the fast energy is turned to the ground under the feet: the task at hand, the meal, the person in the room. in the other, the mind is on campaign, and even its tender parts are in harness; something that should be born in shelter is born at the front. the passage places the cause where a person can look at it. it is not “desire” as a large enemy. it is the precise movement of 欲得, the lean toward getting, which can be felt as it starts. and the remedy is not a victory over that movement. it is a kind of knowledge: the enough of know-enough. wang bi says it in four words: seek nothing outside. the passage is short, and it is one of the angriest in the book. it was written when rulers measured greatness in horses and land. its claim is direct: the wars come from the top, from one person’s inability to say “enough”, and han fei, no friend of soft rule, read it the same way. the test that it gives a leader is useful and hard. do not listen to what an organisation says about itself. look at where its fastest horses are. are the best people and the most money on the field that feeds everyone, or on a contest at the border? and look for the mare: the function that should be protected and is in the fight. a growth target with no “enough” in it will reach the 郊 in time. the first picture is a closed circle. the horse eats from the field, and its dung goes back to the field, and the field grows more. farmers of north china kept this circle with great care for three thousand years; manure was collected, stored, and valued. the second picture breaks the circle at each point. the grain goes to feed horses that grow nothing. the dung falls on the road. the foal is born where there is no stable and no pasture. a world with the way, in this passage, is not a paradise. it is a nutrient cycle that has not been cut. notice that the enough of the last line has the same shape: it is a circle that closes, and wanting is a line that runs outward. do the exercise of the fast horse today: name one strength that you keep for a contest, and turn one hour of it to the field. then test the last line in a small way. before a meal, a purchase, or the next check of a screen, ask a question of fact, not of morals: is there enough here already? do not answer “yes” by rule. look. sometimes there is not enough, and then you act. the line says only that the one who can know this has a supply that does not run out.

天下有道: the world “has” the way. 天下 is “under heaven”: the whole known world, the zhou realm and its states. 有道, “has the way”, was a common political phrase of the time, and it did not belong to the daoists. confucius uses it often. when the world has the way, he says, show yourself; when it does not, stay hidden. and: when the world has the way, rites, music, and campaigns of war come from the son of heaven alone. for such speakers 有道 means that the realm is in order and under right rule; 無道 means the age of usurpers. the laozi takes the phrase that everyone used and gives it one test only: look at the horses. english versions write that the dao “prevails”, a word of contest. the chinese verb is 有, to have, as a field has water.

走: to run. in modern chinese 走 means “to walk, to go”. in the classical language it means “to run”. the shuowen defines it as 趨也, “to hurry”, and analyses the graph as 夭 above 止: a foot, with a figure over it that the dictionary calls bent. many modern scholars see in the old form a person with swinging arms above a foot. so 走馬 are running horses: fast horses, bred and fed for speed. in this age such a horse had one main purpose. it pulled the war chariot, four to a team, or from the late fourth century carried a mounted archer; it also ran in the relay posts that took a ruler’s orders across the state. a fast horse ate grain that could feed people. to send it back to the farm is to turn the costliest machine of the state toward food.

卻: who turns the horses back?. 卻 is “to step back, to send back, to decline”. the line has no subject. it does not say “the ruler turns back the horses” or “people send them home”; the horses simply go the other way. english needs a subject or a passive, and we use the passive. the shuowen as we have it defines the word in a surprising way: 節欲也, “to restrain desire”. later editors doubted this text and corrected it to a sense of “hold back and withdraw”. take it as a curious chance, since this passage ends with a judgment on 欲, desire. it is still a good chance. the first act of a world that has the way is a step backward. the word for it is the same word that a dictionary could gloss as desire held in check.

以糞: four characters became a debate. 糞 is dung, and as a verb it is to manure a field. the line ends on it with no object: “turn back the running horses in order to 糞”. old readers fill the gap in three ways. the horses pull the plough and the manure carts. or the horses are kept for their dung. or, as wang bi has it, they are sent to 治田糞, “to work the fields and dung them”. the han feizi says that in such a world the relay posts are not used, so the fast horses go to the farm. all three agree on the direction: from the road to the soil. note the level of the image. the sign of a world in order is not music or jade. it is manure. some english translators softened the word. legge did not, and the chinese does not.

戎馬: the horse as an arms race. 戎 is weapons and war; the shuowen records it in an older graph and explains it as 戈, the dagger-axe, with 甲, armour. the same word named the peoples of the western frontier. 戎馬 are war horses. a state’s rank was counted in chariots, and each chariot needed four trained horses, a driver, an archer, and a spearman. in 307 bce king wuling of zhao ordered his army to wear the trousers of the steppe riders and to shoot from horseback; cavalry spread to all the great states, and the demand for horses grew again. good horses came from the northern border. to the people who paid the grain tax, a war horse was a visible measure of what the state took. the line after this one says where the measure ends.

生於郊: foals on the field of war. 生 is “to be born”. english versions often write that war horses are “bred” or “raised”, and the line becomes a note on stud farms. the oldest readers heard a harder thing. the han feizi, the first commentary that we have, says that when wars do not stop, the stallions run short and the mares must be sent to the army; so foals are born on campaign. a han text, the discourses on salt and iron, repeats it of its own time: mares enter the ranks, and the young are born on the battle ground. a mare in foal is the future of the herd, and here she is in harness at the front. passage 30 uses the same verb for the same grief: where an army has camped, thorns are born.

郊: not a suburb. a zhou city was a wall with the ruler’s house and the ancestral temple inside it. outside the wall lay the 郊: open land, fields, and beyond it the wilds. the shuowen gives a formal measure: 距國百里爲郊, “a hundred li from the capital is the 郊”. armies met there, since a state fought before its own walls or before the enemy’s. and at the 郊 the ruler made the great offering to heaven, which took its name from the place. so the word carries two things that the dictionary word “suburb” or “border” cannot: the place where the state faces heaven, and the place where it faces the enemy. the han feizi stresses a third: 郊 is near. the war is not at a far frontier. it has come to the edge of home.

禍 and 咎: words from the diviner’s table. both nouns come from religion. 禍 has 示 at its left, the altar sign that marks what concerns spirits: 神 (spirit), 福 (blessing), 祭 (offering). the shuowen defines 禍 as 害也，神不福也, “harm; the spirits do not bless”. 咎 is the word for blame in the book of changes, where the best that a line can often promise is 无咎, “no blame”. the shuowen defines it as 災也, “disaster”, and reads the graph as 人, a person, with 各, which it explains as 相違, “to go against each other”. in the older view, calamity came from heaven and the ancestors, and one asked a diviner for its cause. this passage keeps the words and moves the cause. it is inside: not to know enough, and to want to get. no altar is needed to find it.

欲得: wanting to get. two plain words: 欲, to want, and 得, to get. the fault is not in having, and not in getting as such. it is in the wish that leans forward to get. 得 is the same word that stood in the third question of passage 44, “gain or loss, which is the sickness?”, and this passage gives the answer. there is a sound in it as well. 得 was a homophone of 德, the “inner power” of the book’s title, and early writers explain one by the other: to have 德 is to have got something. passage 38 says that the highest 德 does not act as 德. here the same thought is put low and plain: the one who is bent on 得 has the greatest fault. the link from this private wish to the war horses is the whole argument of the passage. see also the missing line.

知足之足常足: three times enough. six characters, and three of them are 足. the first is inside a verb phrase: 知足, “to know enough”. the second is a noun: 之足, “the enough of” that. the third is the predicate: 常足, “is always enough”. so: the enough that consists in knowing what is enough is the enough that lasts. the line separates two kinds. one is the enough of quantity: the store is full. that kind does not hold, because the measure moves as the store grows. the other is the enough of knowing, and it does not depend on the store. english must use “contentment”, “sufficiency”, and “satisfaction” to follow the turns, and the echo is lost. in chinese the word strikes three times like a foot set down. 足 is also “foot”; see passage 44.

常 and 恆: an emperor’s name. our text says 常足, “constantly enough”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to say 恆足. the two words mean nearly the same, and the change has a known cause. the personal name of emperor wen of han, who came to the throne in 180 bce, was heng, 恆. a reigning emperor’s name could not be written, so scribes put 常 in its place through the whole book; the first line, 道可道非常道, was once 非恆道. the shuowen shows how odd the stand-in is. its entry for 常 reads 下帬也, “a lower garment”: the word was first a skirt. under 恆 it says 常也, and explains the graph as a heart and a boat between two banks. the steady word of the laozi was a boat that goes across and comes back.

the line that wang bi’s text lost. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to have three “none greater” lines, and the first is not in our text: 罪莫大於可欲, “no crime is greater than the desirable”, or “than to approve of desire”. then: 禍莫大於不知足，咎莫憯於欲得. the last has 憯, “painful”, where we have 大: no fault is more grievous. the heshang gong text and the han feizi have the three lines too, and the guodian slips are reported to have three, in another order and with other adjectives; they are also reported to lack the two lines on horses. the extra line sharpens the politics. 可欲 is the word of passage 3: do not display the desirable, and the people’s hearts are not troubled. the first crime is then not in the one who wants. it is in the one who sets up the object.

罪: a word rewritten by the first emperor. the word for “crime” in the older copies has its own story of power. the shuowen says that 罪 was first a bamboo net for fish: the top part is 网, a net. the word “crime” was written 辠, which the dictionary explains as 辛, bitter, with 自, the nose: an offender who wrinkles the nose in pain. then it adds: 秦以辠似皇字，改爲罪. “qin, because 辠 looked like the character 皇, ‘emperor’, changed it to 罪.” the first emperor had taken the new title 皇帝 in 221 bce, and he did not want the graph for “criminal” to look like his own. the state that won the wars of this passage by the largest use of war horses then corrected the dictionary. see the silk texts for the line.

wang bi: inside and outside. wang bi reads the two pictures with one pair of words, 內 and 外, inside and outside. on the first: 天下有道，知足知止，無求於外，各修其內而已. “when the world has the way, people know enough and know to stop; they seek nothing outside, and each simply tends what is within.” on the second: 貪欲無厭，不修其內，各求於外，故戎馬生於郊也. “craving without limit, they do not tend what is within, and each seeks outside; so war horses are born at the outskirts.” he joins this passage to the last lines of 44 with the words 知足知止. and he gives the horses a direction: the farm horse works inside the walls and fields, and the war horse is at the 郊, outside. war, for wang bi, is the outward form of a search that has left home.

the first commentator was a legalist. the oldest explanations of laozi lines that survive are two chapters of the han feizi, “explaining lao” and “illustrating lao”. han fei died in a qin prison in 233 bce. he was the great theorist of state power, and he read the laozi as a book for rulers. both chapters treat this passage. in one he draws the world without the way: attack follows attack, armies face each other for years, lice breed in the armour, swallows nest in the tents, and the soldiers do not come home. in the other he traces the cause step by step, from a ruler’s desire, to disordered thought, to calamity for the state. so the first reader on record already saw the link that the passage makes with one word, 故: the wish to get, and then the horses.

legge: guilt, ambition, contentment. legge translated a text with three lines, and his first is: “there is no guilt greater than to sanction ambition”. each noun is a choice. “guilt” is a state of the soul before a judge; 罪 is an offence against a law. “ambition” is one desire among many; 可欲 is anything that can be wanted. in the last line 知足之足 becomes “the sufficiency of contentment”, and the triple strike of 足 turns into two long latin words. “contentment” was a christian virtue of his day, the duty to accept one’s lot, and he writes “discontented with one’s lot” in the line before. the chinese has no lot. it has a quantity, enough, and the verb “to know”. for the horses he is exact, and he does not hide the dung.

find the fast horse. every life keeps some running horses: strength that is fed and trained for a contest. it may be the hours given to rivalry at work, the attention spent on a quarrel, the money held ready to win something. name one today. then ask the question of the first line: what would it mean to turn this back to the field? the same energy, on the thing that feeds you and the people near you. do one small act of that kind. then ask the second question, which is harder. is there a mare at the front? something that should be resting, growing, or bearing, a body, a child’s time, a friendship, that the contest has taken into service?

有道/無道: one horse, two uses. the passage is built on 有 and 無: the world has dao, the world has no dao. it does not picture two worlds. it pictures one animal. the same horse dungs the field or is born to war at the border. so the two states lie near each other, and one turns into the other when the wish to get moves. the second pair is enough 足 and not-enough 不足. the text clearly favors “enough”, and it speaks to rulers whose wanting filled the outskirts with war horses. but the last line does not rank a small store over a large one. it moves the measure from the store to the knowing. the favored side turns too: “enough” as a fixed rule can be a refusal to see real need, and a contentment that is announced is one more thing gained. a one-sided reading makes peace and war two kinds of people. where is your horse today?

the greatest disasters start from not knowing what is enough and from the wish to get.. the greatest disasters start from not knowing what is enough and from the wish to get. does this explain the conflicts that you know at close range: in a family, at work, in yourself? where is your own wish to get strongest? what lack, real or remembered, feeds it? take the opposite: wanting more is what built every good thing that we have, and contentment keeps people poor. what in you cheers at that? when you see greed in another person, what do you feel? is there a want of your own that you do not allow yourself?

enough is not an amount; it is a kind of knowing, and that knowing does not run out.. enough is not an amount; it is a kind of knowing, and that knowing does not run out. is that true for you, or does enough in fact depend on how much there is? recall a time when you had little and felt that it was enough, and a time when you had much and did not. what was different? hold the other side honestly: some people do not have enough, and to tell them that it is a matter of knowing is an insult. what does that do to the line? which statement would you defend at a dinner table? which one do you live by?

the state of a world shows in where its best energy is put: on the field or at the border.. the state of a world shows in where its best energy is put: on the field or at the border. where are your fast horses today? on what feeds you, or on a contest? who or what trained you for the contest? what did you fear would happen if you did not compete? suppose that the border must be guarded, and that a life with no fight in it is taken by others. what truth is in that for you? what would you have to trust in order to turn one horse back to the field?

馬 head, mane, tail, four legs. this is a drawing, and the shuowen tells you how to see it: 象馬頭髦尾四足之形, “it pictures the horse’s head, mane, tail, and four legs”. imagine the animal stood on its tail, nose up. the upper block is the head and neck; the level lines that stick out to the right are the mane. the long line that turns along the bottom and hooks is the back and the tail. the four dots are the four legs. oracle-bone and bronze forms are much more of a portrait, with a long face, an eye, and a brush of mane; they differ among themselves, so look at them in the links and do not trust one description. the dictionary’s definition is a pun on the sound: 馬，怒也，武也, “horse: fury; war”. for the han scholar the animal was first of all a thing of battle, as it is in this passage. as a part, 馬 marks its kind and what is done with it: 駒 (a colt; the shuowen says a horse of two years), 駕 (to yoke), 馳 (to gallop), 驚 (to startle, as a horse does), 驕 (a tall horse, and then “proud”). it also serves as a sound, in 媽 (mother) and 嗎, the modern question word. see running horses and war horses. ten strokes. first a horizontal at the top. second, the long vertical at the left: the line of the neck. third and fourth, two more horizontals, the mane. fifth, a vertical through the middle of the three horizontals. keep the three level lines evenly spaced and let them reach to the right; the left side is closed and the right side is open. watch the sixth stroke. it starts at the foot of the left vertical, runs to the right, turns the corner, comes down, and ends in a hook that points back to the left: one stroke for the back, the rump, and the tail. it makes a shelter, and the last four strokes, the dots, go underneath it from left to right. in cursive script the four legs became one line, and that form is the base of the short modern 马.

糞 what looks like rice and is not. read the modern character from the top and you get a pleasant error: 米, rice; 田, a field; 共, together. rice, field, shared: a farm. none of the three is what it seems. the shuowen has the word under an older graph and defines it as 棄除也, “to throw out, to clear away”. it explains the parts: two hands, 廾, push a kind of dustpan and throw out what is in it. then it quotes an authority, guan pu, on the top part: 似米而非米者，矢字, “that which is like 米 and is not 米 is the graph for excrement”. so the “rice” is waste; the “field” is the pan or basket; and “together” is the two hands at the bottom. the first sense is to sweep out the house or stable. the second sense is the thing that is swept out. the third is what a farmer does with it: to dress a field. that is the sense of 以糞 in this passage. one character holds the whole circle: the stable is cleaned, and the field is fed. two cousins by the hands: 共 itself, and 棄, “to abandon”, the first word of the shuowen’s definition, which the dictionary also explains with two hands and the same pan. seventeen strokes in three floors. the top floor is six strokes, written like 米: a dot at upper left, a short stroke at upper right that leans in, a horizontal, a vertical through it, then a stroke that falls to the left and one that falls to the right. the middle floor is the box, five strokes: left side; top and right side in one; the inner horizontal; the inner vertical; the base. the bottom floor is six strokes: a horizontal, two short verticals, a long horizontal, and two dots below that lean apart. watch the fifteenth stroke, the long horizontal near the bottom. it is the widest line in the character and the two hands carry everything on it. the danger is height. a good writer presses each floor flat, so that three characters’ worth of strokes fit in one square.

47 · without leaving the door. without going out of the door, / know the world. / without peeping through the window, / see heaven’s way. / the farther the going out, / the less the knowing. / so the sage / does not travel, and knows; / does not see, and names; / does not act, and completes. a person in a house. the first four lines are two matched pairs: not out of the door, know the world; not peeping from the window, see heaven’s way. the door leads to the human world and the window opens on the sky, so the pairs cover earth and heaven. then a general law in eight characters: the farther out, the less known. then 是以, “for this reason”, and the sage with three lines of one frame, 不 a 而 b, “not a, and yet b”: no travel and knowing, no seeing and naming, no doing and completion. the passage is short and has no images after the house. it does not explain how. its neighbours in the book supply that: passage 48 on the practice of loss, and 54 on knowing the world “by this”. the usual picture of knowing has an inside that lacks and an outside that has, and a trip between them. the passage reverses the direction and then removes the distance. what is to be known, the way things go, is fully at work at the place where you sit: in breath, in want, in the rise and fall of a mood. to go far for it is like searching the house for the glasses that are on your face. the han feizi’s reading is practical here. the senses are doors, and attention leaves by them all day. “not going out” does not mean that the eyes are shut. it means that someone is at home while they are open. then the last three lines are plain reports: the knowing is already present before the search begins. the first great readers were men of the state, and they heard a design: the centre stays at the centre. a leader who runs to every site and inspects every detail knows many things and loses the view of the whole; and the staff learn to wait for the visit. there is truth in that, and a danger in it, which the first emperor’s walled roads show. to stay in is not to wall oneself in. the passage praises the sage, who is an ear. a leader who does not travel must be a person to whom things can come: one who can hear bad news without punishing it. and the test of 不為而成 is concrete. when you were away, or silent, did the work complete itself? movement arts teach this passage in the first year. the beginner looks at the hands and the feet to know where they are, and the teacher says: do not look. feel. the body knows its own position without sight; the attention only has to stay in. when the eyes chase the opponent’s hand, the centre is lost and the response is late: 其出彌遠，其知彌少. when the attention rests low and wide, the other’s movement is felt as it starts. try it standing. close the eyes, and know where both hands are. know the room behind you by its sound. that is knowing without going. then open the eyes and keep the same knowing. the window is open now, and no one has leaned out of it. do the exercise of one room today, ten minutes with the door shut. then try the third line of the sage’s three in one small thing. choose a matter that you want to check on, push, or fix, a person’s work, a plant, a plan that is already under way, and for one day do not act on it. stay attentive to it; do not turn away. see whether it comes to completion and what your doing would have added. some things will need your hand. the practice is to find out which, by the test and not by the itch.

戶 and 牖: the room of passage 11. the door and the window have been in the book before. in passage 11 a room was made by cutting them: 鑿戶牖以為室, and the use of the room was where it had nothing. now someone is inside that room. 戶 is a door of one leaf; the shuowen says 半門曰戶, “half a 門 is called 戶”, and you can see one half of 門 in it. 牖 is a window in a wall. the shuowen entry for 牖 ends with a remark from an older scholar: 牖，所以見日, “the window is that through which one sees the sun”. so the second line is exact. people looked out of the 牖 to see the sky and to tell the hour and the season. the passage says that this too can be left. nothing in it calls the house a prison. it is the most ordinary room in the world.

知: what kind of knowing?. if 知 means “to have information”, the first line is false. no one learns the price of grain in qi by sitting at home. so the word must mean something else here, and english “know” does not help, because it covers facts, skills, and acquaintance alike. 知 in the laozi is most often recognition: to know enough (44), to know the constant (16), to know the male and keep to the female (28). it is knowing how a thing goes. the world, 天下, is then not a list of events. it is a pattern of rise and fall, want and war, mother and child, and the pattern is complete in a single house and a single body. passage 54 gives the method in two words. how do i know that the world is so? 以此, “by this”.

闚: a small look through a gap. the verb in the third line is not “to look”. it is 闚, to peep. the graph has 門, a gate, around 規; the shuowen defines it as 閃也, and it defines 閃 in turn as a person glimpsed in a gateway. many editions write the word with a different top, 窺: 穴, a hole, over the same 規, and that graph the shuowen glosses as 小視也, “a small look”. gate or hole, the sense is one: a narrow, partial, slightly furtive view. the word was also used for spying on a neighbour state. so the line carries a quiet judgment. a look out of the window at the sky is a look through a slit. the one who studies heaven by peeping gets a slit of heaven. what is your window? how wide is the view from a screen?

天道: the course of the sky. 天道 is “the way of heaven”, and in this period the first meaning was concrete: the paths of sun, moon, and planets, the turn of the seasons. court astronomers watched the sky each night, because the calendar and the omens of the state came from it. a statesman in the zuo zhuan answers such an expert with a famous line: 天道遠，人道邇, “heaven’s way is far, the human way is near”. the laozi uses it, as 天道 or 天之道, for a pattern that is seen above and holds below. it retires when the work is done (9). it does not contend and yet wins (73). it takes from what has surplus, like the bending of a bow (77). it has no favourites (79). it benefits and does not harm (81). “nature” is too green a word for this, and “heaven” with a capital is too near to a god.

彌遠: an age of travellers. 其出彌遠，其知彌少: eight characters in two halves that mirror each other, with 彌 … 彌, “the more … the more”. hear it in its century. learning then meant travel. a man of the shi class left home to find a teacher and then went from court to court to find a ruler. confucius spent some fourteen years on the roads between the states. mencius moved with a train of carts and followers. the strategists who sold alliances crossed the whole zhou world. to have gone far was a credential. against that whole economy of talent the line states an inverse law, strange to western ears, with no exception clause. it also turns on the word 出: the “going out” of the first line was through a door, and now it has a distance. wang bi gives a reason; the han feizi gives another.

聖人: the sage is an ear. we write “the sage” and must say what the word is not. 聖 is not “saint” or “holy”: no god stands behind it. it is not merely a wise old man. the shuowen defines 聖 in one word, 通也, “to pass through, to be open all the way”, and places it under 耳, the ear; the old forms are commonly explained as a person with a large ear, with a mouth beside it. a 聖人 is first a listener: a person whose hearing is so open that things reach them without a journey. in the texts of the time the word also means the ideal ruler, the one fit to hold the world. this passage shows why the ear matters. the eye must go to its object or peep through a gap. sound comes in through walls.

three old ways to read it. readers before the modern age understood these lines in three ways, and none of them is “intuition”. the first is the ruler’s reading. the lushi chunqiu, a book made for the court of qin about 239 bce, quotes the passage in a chapter on what a ruler should keep to: the lord stays still, and the ministers bring the realm to him. see the palace. the second is the reading of the body: the door and window are the senses. see the han feizi’s line. the third is wang bi’s: things have a source, and whoever holds the source knows the many. the three differ on what the house is: a palace, a body, a principle. they agree that 行, travel, adds nothing essential. which house do you read it in?

the ruler who does not come out. for the theorists of the state, a ruler who went to look for himself had already failed. he should sit at the centre and know through a system: reports, tallies, and officials who are checked against their words. the lushi chunqiu says that the one who has the way does not go out of the door and knows the world. in this reading the passage is a design for administration, and also for spying. the first emperor took it to an end that the text does not ask for. on the advice of a magician, the shiji tells, he joined his palaces with covered and walled roads so that no one knew where he was, and he put to death those who revealed it. he did not leave the door, and he came to know less and less. the line on distance has a second edge.

the doors and windows of the spirit. the han feizi explains this passage with a sentence that later daoists made their own: 空竅者，神明之戶牖也. “the openings of the body are the doors and windows of the spirit.” eyes and ears are spent on colours and sounds, it goes on, and the spirit is spent on outward show, until there is no master within. then even if fortune and ruin were as large as hills, one would not recognise them. so the 戶 and 牖 are the senses, and “not going out” is keeping the spirit at home in its house. passage 52 uses the same picture as an instruction: block the openings, shut the gates. read in this way, the line on distance describes attention. the farther attention runs from the body, the less there is at home to know anything.

名 or 明: to name, or to be clear. our text says 不見而名: does not see, and names. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to have 名 too. but the han feizi quotes the line with 明, “bright, clear, to understand”, and many editors prefer it: does not see, and is clear. the two words sounded alike and were often written for each other. 明 makes a simple series: know, understand, complete. 名 is the harder and richer word. to name a thing is to give it its place among things, and rulers and sages were those who fixed names. the book begins with the limits of the name (1) and says that when cutting begins there are names (32). here the sage can give the right name to a thing that is not in front of the eyes, because the name comes from the thing’s place in the pattern and not from its look.

不為而成: who completes what?. the last line is four characters: not, do, and, complete. 成 can be transitive, “completes things”, or intransitive, “things come to completion”. chinese does not mark the difference, and the line means both: the sage brings things to completion and things complete themselves. english “accomplishes” puts an achiever at the centre. the phrase is close kin to 無為, wu wei, “not-forcing”, which the next passage takes up in its most famous form: 無為而無不為. the silk texts are reported to write 弗為, a stronger negative that points at an object: does not work on it. note the order of the three lines. walking, then seeing, then doing: feet, eyes, hands. one by one the organs of effort are set down, and one by one the result is still there. wang bi explains the last in six words.

wang bi: many roads, one home. wang bi begins: 事有宗，而物有主，途雖殊而同歸也，慮雖百而其致一也. “affairs have an ancestor and things have a master. the roads differ, and they come home to one place; the thoughts are a hundred, and their end is one.” he borrows the image from the book of changes. if all roads come home, the one who stands at home has the end of every road. on the line about distance: 無在於一，而求之於眾也, “the nothing is in the one, and people seek it among the many”; 若其不知，出愈遠愈迷也, “if one does not know it, the farther out, the more lost”. and on the last line: 明物之性，因之而已, “be clear about the nature of things and simply follow it”. his knowing is not mystical. it is knowledge of a root, as one knows a family from its ancestor.

against the grain of “go and see”. western thought has given this passage a hard hearing, and it is useful to know why. the greek word that gave us “history” means inquiry by one who has gone and asked. modern science began with instruments and voyages: the telescope is a better window, and the ship takes the observer farther out. in that frame, 其出彌遠，其知彌少 sounds like a refusal to learn. but the passage does not rank the same kind of knowledge by another method. it separates two kinds. travel gives more items. it does not, by itself, give 知 of how things go, and a mind that is full of items can lose that. the two meet in an odd way: the great travellers often report that the main thing that they learned on the road was about home. legge may be a case.

legge, who went far out. legge adds four things in brackets, and each shows a worry. he writes that one understands “(all that takes place)” under the sky: he has taken 知 as information, and the claim becomes larger than the chinese. he writes “the farther that one goes out (from himself)”: here he has chosen the inward reading and put it into the text. the sages “got their knowledge”, in the past tense, as figures of old; the chinese has no tense. and they gave “their (right) names to things”. his last line, “without any purpose of doing so”, turns 不為 into absence of intention, a christian and kantian interest. there is some irony in the case. legge, a scot, sailed from britain in 1839, spent three decades based in malacca and hong kong, and knew more of the chinese classics than any european of his time.

the silk texts: “so as to know”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read: 不出於戶 以知天下 不窺於牖 以知天道. two things differ. first, each line has 以, “so as to, and by that”: not going out of the door is the means of knowing, and not only a condition under which one knows. second, the verb is 知 both times. our text has 見, “to see”, for heaven’s way; the silk has “know”. the received 見 makes a fine paradox, to see without looking, but it may be a later polish. in the third line the silk adds a particle, 其出也彌遠, which slows the phrase: “as for the going out: the farther …”. the quotations in the han feizi and the lushi chunqiu also have 於 and “know”. this passage is not among the guodian slips.

one room, ten minutes. sit in a room with the door shut and no screen. for ten minutes, take the room as the whole world, and look for the world’s patterns in it. something here is rising and something is wearing out. something was fought for; something was given. there is want in the room, yours, and there is enough. there is a thing that works because of what it lacks. when the ten minutes end, ask what you would have learned about how things go by reading the day’s news in the same time. do not conclude that news is useless. only weigh the two kinds of knowing. then, the next time you travel, notice what you carry with you that makes the new place look like every other place.

出/不出, 遠/少: a door has two sides. the pairs here are out 出 and not-out, far 遠 and little 少, travel 行 and knowing 知. the text takes a side with force: the farther out, the less known. it is a correction. its age counted miles as learning, and the line states the opposite to stop that count. yet the images are a door and a window, and each is a thing that joins inside and outside. a house with no door is a tomb. inside means something only because there is a world to know, and the passage begins with it: know the world, 知天下. so the two sides depend on each other. the favored side turns too. staying in can become a wall, a pride in not looking, a ruler who hears nothing. then the cure is the road. a one-sided reading makes this passage contempt for experience. it asks where the knowing happens, on any road or in any room. which do you run from: the journey or the room?

the world can be known without going out; the farther a person travels, the less that person knows.. the world can be known without going out; the farther a person travels, the less that person knows. do you agree? what have you learned by staying that you could not learn by going? what have journeys, new places, and new people given you? could you have found it at home? be exact. take the opposite for a while: we know only what we have gone out and met, and the one who stays home knows a small room. what do you feel? do you run toward the road or toward the room? what is the one that you avoid likely to show you?

some things come to completion without being acted on.. some things come to completion without being acted on. name one thing in your care now. would it complete itself without you? what does it mean about you if it would? notice the first feeling before you answer. hold the other side: things left alone decay, and care means showing up. where did you learn that, and from whose neglect? how do you tell the things that need your hand from the things that only draw your itch?

戶 half a gate. put 門 beside 戶. 門 is a gate with two leaves, each hung on its post; you can see the pair, left and right. the shuowen defines 門 as 从二戶, “made of two 戶”, and 戶 as 半門, “half a gate”. so 戶 is one leaf on one post: the door of a room or a small house, where 門 is the gate of a compound, a city, or a palace. the dictionary also gives a pun on the sound: 戶，護也, “a door is that which protects”. from the door came the household behind it. 戶 is still the unit by which china counts families, and in the warring states the new bureaucratic states registered their people by 戶 to tax them and to draft them. as a part, 戶 covers rooms and openings: 房, a side room; 扉, a door leaf; 啟 (to open) has it at the upper left. and 所, “place”, is 戶 with 斤, an axe; the shuowen says that 戶 only gives the sound there, and that the word first meant the sound of chopping wood. in this passage 戶 stands for the smallest boundary there is between a person and the world: one leaf of wood. the text does not say to bar it. it says that there is no need to pass it. four strokes, the fewest of any plate in these passages. first a short stroke at the top, written from upper left down to the right like a heavy dot: the top of the post. second, a horizontal that turns the corner and comes down a short way: the top and right edge of the leaf. third, a horizontal that closes the box below. watch the fourth stroke. it starts at the upper left corner of the box and falls in a long curve to the lower left, far below the rest, thin at the end. it is the post on which the leaf hangs, and it gives the character its lean. the small box sits high on the right, the long stroke sweeps low on the left, and the lower right is left empty. in 門 this same shape appears twice, face to face.

知 an arrow and a mouth. left: 矢, an arrow. right: 口, a mouth. the shuowen says that 矢 is a picture of the arrow of bow and crossbow, with its point, its notch, and its feathers. it then defines 知 in a way that surprises a beginner: 詞也。从口从矢, “a word of speech; from mouth and arrow”. the dictionary gives no story for the pair. the one that is now commonly repeated is credited to the tenth-century scholar xu kai, and the qing scholar duan yucai gave it its familiar wording: the one who knows a thing says it at once, and the word leaves the mouth as fast as an arrow. hold that as a later teaching aid; some scholars think that the arrow only gives the sound. the same graph also wrote the noun “wisdom, cleverness”, read zhi. later a 日 was added below for that sense, and the result is 智. the laozi is hard on 智 (passage 19 would discard it) and makes 知 its central verb, so the eye must watch which is meant. compare other characters where 口 stands beside a second part: 名, a mouth under the evening, a name called in the dark; 如, “to be like”. now look again at the passage. its knowing is the opposite of the fast arrow. the arrow goes out, far and straight. this 知 does not leave the house. eight strokes: five for the arrow and three for the mouth. the arrow begins with a short stroke that falls to the left, then a short horizontal beneath it, then a longer horizontal. the fourth stroke starts at the first horizontal, crosses the lower one, and falls away to the lower left. the fifth should be a long stroke to the lower right, but here it is held back to a dot, because the mouth is waiting on that side: a part yields when it has a neighbour. then 口: the left side, the top and right side in one stroke, and the base. watch where the mouth sits. it is not level with the top of the arrow; it hangs a little below the middle, small and square, so that the tall, leaning arrow and the low, still box balance each other.

48 · each day less. work at learning: each day more. / work at dao: each day less. / less, and again less, / until it comes to not-doing. / not doing, and nothing is left undone. / to take the world / is always by having no business. / once there is business, / unfit to take the world. two lines of four characters, alike but for two words: work at learning, each day more; work at the way, each day less. the second path is then followed down: less and again less, until one arrives at not-doing. then the line that the whole book is known for: 無為而無不為, not doing, and nothing not done. the second half changes the scale from a person to all under heaven. the world is taken by no-business; the one who has business is not sufficient to take it. the passage contains no image at all. it is made of nine common words, and one of them, 為, appears six times. the first line describes most of a life: more skills, more knowledge, more experience, more self. nothing in the passage says that this is wrong. it says that there is a second movement with the opposite sign, and that the way belongs to it. the practice is a subtraction, and it is exact about its end. the end is not emptiness as a prize. it is the point where the one who works upon things is no longer found; the text says arrive, as a bird arrives at the ground. what is left acts, and often acts well, because nothing stands between the situation and the response. yan hui’s report gives the feeling of it: he calls each loss a gain. the second loss guards against the last possession, the pride of the one who has let go. the second half was written for men who wanted to take the world, and it tells them that their wanting disqualifies them. read it for any place where one person has power over others. a leader with many projects gives the organisation much to do, and each project has a cost that the leader does not see. wang bi’s line is a good rule of management: where there is doing, something is missed. the leader who has taken off the personal plans, the wish to be seen acting, the favourite reforms, leaves room for what the work itself asks. this is not passivity, and it must not be used as a cover, as
