the legalists used it: a hidden will behind a show of stillness. the test is whether things are in fact not left undone. every physical skill is learned in two phases. in the first you add: positions, corrections, strength, rules. in the second you take away: the extra tension in the shoulder, the breath held at the hard part, the thought about the next step. a beginner’s movement is full of 為. a master’s movement has had things removed from it for thirty years, and looks like less. try it with one simple act, standing up from a chair. do it once as usual. then do it five more times, and each time find one effort that is not needed, and leave it out: the push of the hands, the forward jerk of the head. less, and again less. at some point the standing up does itself. keep the ledger of less for one week: each evening, one line on what you put down. and try the second half of the passage once. choose a matter in which you have power, at home or at work, and for one day have no business with it: no check, no advice, no improvement. stay present. see what is left undone at the end of the day, and what was done without you.

為: one verb, six times. the passage is built from the verb 為, which stands in it six times. 為學: to do learning. 為道: to do the way. 無為: not-doing. then 無為而無不為, with three more. english must change the word each time, “pursue”, “practise”, “act”, “do”, and the thread is cut. in chinese it is one thread, and it is pulled until it turns round on itself: the doing of the way is a daily loss that arrives at not-doing, and from not-doing nothing fails to be done. 為 is a strong verb. it means to make, to work on a thing, to act as, to govern. its old form is commonly explained as a hand that leads an elephant; see the plate. so the word that the passage takes apart is the word for work done on a large and living thing.

學: what “learning” meant. 學 was a programme with a content, and one school owned the word. for the followers of confucius it meant the odes and documents, the rites, music, and the long shaping of conduct by them. the analects opens with it: to learn and at due times to practise, is that not a pleasure? the xunzi opens with it too: 學不可以已, “learning must not stop”, and it goes on to praise accumulation: pile up earth and make a mountain. that is 日益, more each day, stated as an ideal. the laozi answers from outside the school. passage 20 says: cut off learning and there is no grief. passage 64 says that the sage learns to un-learn. the shuowen records the word under an older graph and glosses it 覺悟也, “to awaken”. the quarrel is over what wakes a person: more, or less.

益 and 損: the full dish and the hand. 益 is 皿, a dish, with water over it; the shuowen defines it as 饒也, “abundance”, 从水、皿. add the water sign again and you have 溢, to overflow. 損 is 扌, a hand, beside a part that gives the sound; the shuowen says 減也, “to reduce”. one word fills a vessel and the other takes away with the hand. readers of the time knew them as a pair from the book of changes, where sun and yi are two hexagrams side by side, the forty-first and the forty-second, each the other turned upside down. the lesson there is that they turn into each other: what is reduced below is added above. passage 42 has said the same: things are sometimes added to by being reduced, and reduced by being added to. here the pair is given to two ways of life.

為道: to do the way, or to hear it. dao, 道, the way, is left untranslated: it is a road, a method, a way of speaking, and the course of all things. 為道 is then an odd phrase. one can do learning. how does one “do” the course of things? the verb makes the way a practice, a thing worked at each day like a craft. the mawangdui silk text is reported to read differently: 聞道者日損, “the one who has heard the way loses each day”. that makes the loss a result and not a method. a person hears, and from then on things fall away. the same words open passage 41, where the best student hears the way and walks it. the guodian slips are reported to read 為道者, as our text does, and to say 學者, “the one who learns”, in the first line. both versions add 者: they speak of persons.

日損: less of what?. the text does not say what is lost. 損 has no object in the second line, and in the third only 之, “it”. english wants to fill the place, and each filling is a doctrine. legge writes “(his doing)”. the heshang gong commentary says that the loss is of passions and outward ornament. wang bi says that the aim is to go back to empty nothing. a modern reader thinks of opinions or possessions. the open object is better than any of these. whatever was added by the first way of life is what the second takes off: the stock of knowledge, the wish to add to it, the plans that knowledge makes, the self that owns the stock. notice also 日, “each day”. it is not a single renunciation. it is a small loss today, and another tomorrow.

損之又損: the second loss. 損之又損: “lose it, and again lose”. the frame is the same as in the last line of passage 1, 玄之又玄, “dark, and again dark”. the plain sense is persistence: reduce, and keep reducing. later daoist thinkers of the tang read the repetition as two different acts. the first loss removes what one holds: desires, views, doing. the second loss removes the one who is proud of having removed them: the holding on to emptiness, the project of reduction itself. without the second, the path of less becomes one more kind of gain, a store of renunciations. the word 又, “again”, is in origin a hand; the shuowen says 手也. the hand that takes away comes back once more, and the second time it takes itself.

無為: a place that is reached. 無為, wu wei, is “without 為”: not-doing, not-forcing. it does not mean idleness. 為 is purposeful work upon things, the act of one who has a plan and makes the world fit it; 無為 is the absence of that. this passage is the only place in the book that says how it comes about, and the verb matters: 以至於無為, “and so arrive at”. 至 is to reach a place. the shuowen explains the graph as a bird that flies down from a height and comes to the ground, the bottom line being the earth. so not-doing is not a technique that one applies. it is where one lands when enough has been taken off. one cannot decide to do it, because the deciding is 為. english “non-action” makes it sound like a kind of action with a minus sign.

無不為: two negatives, and who does it?. 無不為 is “there is nothing that is not done”. the grammar hides the doer. it can mean “and yet one does everything”, or “and yet everything gets done”. the second is nearer to the book: in passage 37 the way itself is described with these same six characters, and the ten thousand things then transform of themselves. the first reading had a long career in politics. legalist writers took it as a rule for the throne: the ruler does nothing, the ministers do everything, and the ruler holds them to account. that reading keeps a will at the centre, hidden. the passage has just spent three lines removing such a will. wang bi gives the logic in one line: where there is doing, something is missed.

取天下: the hand and the ear. 取 is “to take”, and its picture is plain: 耳, an ear, and 又, a hand. the shuowen explains it by a custom of war. it quotes the rites of zhou, 獲者取左耳, “the one who makes a capture takes the left ear”: ears were cut from the enemy dead and counted for reward. so 取天下 is the language of conquest, and in this century it was a real programme. each great state aimed to take all under heaven, and in 221 bce one did. the heshang gong commentary softens the word and glosses it as “to govern”. the book’s own use is sharper. passage 29: those who would take the world and work on it, i see that they do not succeed. passage 57: by no-business take the world. the prize of the age is offered to the one person who does not reach for it.

無事: no business. 無事 is a term of its own, and it is not the same as 無為 or as “no effort”. 事 is an affair, a task, a piece of business; as a verb it is to serve. the shuowen glosses it 職也, “an office, a duty”, and derives it from 史, the scribe: 事 is what an official has on his desk. a state full of 事 is a state of projects: surveys, levies, works, campaigns, laws. 無事 is the absence of these, and passage 57 gives the result: 我無事而民自富, “i have no business, and the people of themselves grow rich”. passage 63 makes it a practice, 事無事: serve no-business. modern english has the word “busy” as praise. what would it be to hold an office and to have nothing on the desk?

有事: “to have business” with a neighbour. 有事, “to have business”, had a special use in the speech of courts. the zuo zhuan says that the great affairs of a state are two, sacrifice and war. and when the ji family prepares to attack a small dependent territory, the analects reports it in these words: 季氏將有事於顓臾, “the ji are about to have business with zhuanyu”. confucius is angry with his students for allowing it. 有事 there is a polite word for a campaign. heard so, the last lines carry a pointed sense: whoever has such “business” is not sufficient to take the world. the words for “not sufficient” are 不足, the 足 of “enough” in passages 44 and 46. the one who cannot know enough is not enough.

wang bi: doing always misses something. wang bi’s notes here are very short. on learning: 務欲進其所能，益其所習, “the aim is to advance what one can do and to add to what one has practised”. on the way: 務欲反虛無也, “the aim is to go back to empty nothing”. his verb is 反, to return: the loss is a way home. on the central line: 有為則有所失，故無為乃無所不為也. “where there is doing, something is missed; so it is not-doing by which nothing is left undone.” any act selects, and what it does not select is neglected. only what does not select leaves nothing out. on the last lines he gives three notes of three or four characters. no-business: 動常因也, “movement always follows”. having business: 自己造也, “it is made out of oneself”. not sufficient: 失統本也, “the governing root is lost”.

yan hui “gains” by forgetting. the zhuangzi quotes these lines almost word for word, and it also tells a story that plays them out with the vocabulary reversed. yan hui, the best student of confucius, comes to his master and says: 回益矣, “i have gained”. how? “i have forgotten humaneness and duty.” good, says confucius, but not yet enough. another day: “i have gained. i have forgotten rites and music.” not yet enough. a third day: “i have gained. i sit and forget.” confucius is startled and asks what that is. yan hui describes limbs and mind let go. confucius asks to become his follower. the joke is in the word 益. each loss is reported as a gain, in the mouth of the school of learning. the phrase 坐忘, “to sit and forget”, became the name of a daoist practice.

legge’s seven brackets. legge needed seven brackets for forty-odd characters. the learner “(seeks)” to increase “(his knowledge)”; the follower of the tao “(seeks)” to diminish “(his doing)”. he has given the loss an object, and it is the object that makes the next line easy for him. then: till he arrives at doing nothing “(on purpose)”. the bracket turns 無為 into a matter of motive, a problem of the will that his own theology knew well. and at the end the world is got by “giving himself no trouble (with that end)”, a bracket that he uses twice. 取, the taker of ears, has become “gets as his own”. each addition is intelligent, and together they turn six uses of one verb into a paragraph of explanation. he also writes “he” throughout; the chinese has no person.

half a passage on bamboo. the guodian bamboo slips, about 300 bce, are reported to hold only the first half of this passage, down to “nothing is left undone”, and to write 亡 for 無 throughout. the lines on taking the world are not there. they may once have been a separate saying; passage 57 has a close relative of them. this matters for the reading. without the second half, the passage is about a person and a practice. with it, the practice becomes the qualification for rule. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to be damaged at this place. the collated text has both halves, with 恆 for 常, and adds a particle that slows the second line from the end: 及其有事也. on 聞道, “to hear the way”, in the silk, see the note on 為道.

a ledger of less. at the end of today, do not ask what you learned or got done. ask what you put down. one opinion that you did not defend. one piece of information that you did not look up. one plan that you let go. one improvement that you did not make to another person. write a single line. do this for a week and read the seven lines. the chinese word is 日損, a loss each day, and the scale is small on purpose. watch for the second loss too: if the list becomes a source of pride, lose the list.

益/損: two directions of one hand. more 益 and less 損 stand in two lines of the same form, and with them learning 學 and dao 道. the chinese sets them side by side. it does not say that learning is wrong or that less is better than more. each needs the other: a person can put down only what was picked up, and the long adding of a skill is what the later taking-away works on. the passage then follows the “less” side. that is the preference of a book written against an age of piled-up doctrine and busy rule. the less side turns as well, and the text shows it two times. less, and again less: the second loss is the loss of losing as a project. and at the end of less stands nothing left undone, which is the largest “more”. a one-sided reading makes a creed of subtraction. which do you count as progress: what you added, or what you put down?

learning grows by adding each day; the way is reached by putting something down each day.. learning grows by adding each day; the way is reached by putting something down each day. do both movements exist in your life? which has had more of your years? what do you hold that you would be afraid to put down: a skill, an opinion, a picture of yourself? what would you be without it? take the opposite: a person is what they have gathered, and to lose it is only loss. stay with that. what do you want to protect? do you count progress by what you added or by what you dropped? who gave you that way of counting?

when doing has been stripped away entirely, nothing is left undone.. when doing has been stripped away entirely, nothing is left undone. have you known a moment when a thing was done and you could not find the effort in it? what do you believe would fall apart if you stopped pushing? how do you know? now hold the plain objection: what is not done by someone stays undone. which duties in your life are truly of that kind? which of the two beliefs lets you rest, and which lets you feel needed? which do you need more?

those who meddle and keep busy are not fit to hold the world; it comes to the one with no agenda.. those who meddle and keep busy are not fit to hold the world; it comes to the one with no agenda. does this fit the leaders, parents, and teachers that you have known? what agenda do you carry into most rooms? when did it become yours? take the other side: those without a plan are steered by those with one. when did your lack of a plan cost you? what do you feel toward a person who wants nothing from you? trust, suspicion, discomfort?

取 a hand takes an ear. two parts, and both are parts of the body. on the left is 耳, an ear; the shuowen calls it a picture and says 主聽也, “it governs hearing”. on the right is 又, which is now the word “again” and was at first a right hand: 手也, says the shuowen, a hand drawn with three fingers. a hand at an ear. the dictionary explains the scene with two quotations from the old books of rites and war. one is 獲者取左耳, “the one who makes a capture takes the left ear”. the ears of the slain, or of game, were cut off, carried back, and counted. a nearby entry, 聝, is defined as 軍戰斷耳也, “in battle, to cut off ears”. so the ordinary verb “to take”, which a child learns in the first year, began on a battlefield. its family keeps the sense of seizure. 娶, to take a wife: the shuowen writes 取婦也, a woman under 取. 最, now “most”: the dictionary’s gloss is 犯而取也, “to attack and take”. in this passage the object of 取 is 天下, all under heaven. the text says that the world cannot be had by the hand that reaches for the ear. look once more at the left side. 耳 is also the first part of 聖, the sage, who listens. one hand cuts the ear off. the other way is to use it. eight strokes: six for the ear and two for the hand. the ear begins with a horizontal across the top. then the left vertical, short. then the right vertical, which is long and goes down past everything else: it is the spine of this side. two short horizontals follow inside, and the sixth stroke rises from the lower left up to the right and crosses the long vertical. as a left-hand part the ear is made narrow and its last stroke lifts toward the neighbour. then 又 in two strokes. the seventh goes to the right, turns sharply, and falls to the lower left. watch the eighth: it begins inside that angle, crosses it, and sweeps down to the right with growing pressure to a long, sharp end. that stroke is the reach of the hand, and it is the only expansive line in the character.

益 water over the dish. look at the bottom first. 皿 is a dish or shallow bowl seen from the side, on its foot; the shuowen calls it 飯食之用器, “a vessel used for food”, and a picture. it is the base of many vessel words: 盆 (a basin), 盤 (a tray), 盛 (to fill a vessel, and so “abundant”), 盈 (full; passage 45), and 盅, the empty bowl that the shuowen quotes from the laozi. now the top. in the modern form it looks like two dots, a line, and two legs. the shuowen tells you what it was: 从水、皿, “from water and dish”. the upper part is 水, water, laid on its side across the bowl. water above the rim: the vessel has more than it can hold. the dictionary’s gloss is 饒也, “abundance, more than enough”. when the graph came to be used mostly for “to add, benefit, more”, a second water was put at the left for the plain sense, and that is 溢, to overflow: 器滿也, “the vessel is full”. so 益 is a picture of the first line of this passage, and of its hidden cost. 日益, more each day, is water poured into a dish that is already full. passage 9 says of that: to hold and fill it is not as good as to stop. ten strokes. the top is five: a dot at upper left that leans in, a short stroke at upper right that leans in to meet it, then a horizontal under both. below the horizontal, a stroke falls to the left and a shorter one to the right; they must not touch each other. these five are the water. then the dish in five: the left side, then the top and right side in one stroke, then two short verticals inside, and last a long horizontal along the bottom. watch that tenth stroke. it is much wider than the dish that stands on it, and it gives the character a foot. keep the upper part light and open and the dish broad and low. if the top is heavy, the water looks ready to spill, which may be the truest way to write it.

為 the hand that leads an elephant. this is the verb “to do”, and its history is one of the surprises of the script. the shuowen writes it 爲 and gives an explanation that scholars no longer follow: 母猴也, “a female monkey”, with the top as its claw. inscriptions on bone and bronze, found long after the dictionary was written, are commonly read differently: a hand at the top, and under it an elephant, with trunk, body, and legs. a hand leads an elephant to work. elephants lived in north china in the shang period, and the shuowen’s own entry for 象 still describes the animal with care: long nose and tusks, a great beast of the far south, which bears young once in three years. by the time of this passage the animal was gone from the north, and few who wrote 為 thought of it. the picture is still exact for the word’s sense: to work upon a thing that is large, alive, and stronger than you, and to make it serve a purpose. that is the 為 that this passage removes, six uses of the same verb. 無為 does not let the elephant loose in the village. it takes away the hand at its trunk and the idea that the animal is for something. a related graph adds a person at the side: 偽, “made by people, artificial”, and in later use “false”. twelve strokes; the stroke data draw the form with the full claw at the top. first four small strokes: one that falls to the left, two dots, and one more short stroke that leans in from the right. they are the fingers of the hand. fifth, a long stroke that falls from under the claw to the lower left: the line of the trunk. then three strokes that each go right and turn down, one under the other, like steps; the third and largest ends in a hook. they are the body. last, four dots in a row inside the hook: the legs. watch the three turning strokes. each is wider than the one above, and the rhythm quickens as the brush descends. in running and cursive script the whole figure is reduced to two or three linked turns, and that habit of the brush is the source of the short form 为.

49 · the hundred clans’ heart. the sage has no constant heart: / the heart of the hundred clans is taken as heart. / the good, i am good to them. / the not good, i am good to them too. / de is good. / the true, i trust them. / the untrue, i trust them too. / de is trust. / the sage, in the world, draws breath in, / and for the world muddies the heart. / the hundred clans all fix ears and eyes. / the sage treats them all as infants. three parts. first, a definition in eleven characters: the sage has no constant heart and takes the heart of the hundred clans as heart. second, two matched triplets in the first person. the good and the not good receive the same goodness; the true and the untrue receive the same trust; each triplet closes with two characters, 德善, 德信. third, a portrait. in the world the sage draws the breath in and muddies the heart. the people fix their ears and eyes. the sage is to them all as to infants. the key grammatical fact is that 善 and 信 are used as verbs: “i good them”, “i trust them”. goodness in this passage is not a rank that people hold. it is something done to them. a constant heart is a set of standing judgments: these people are good, those are not; this one can be believed, that one cannot. it feels like character. the passage calls its absence the mark of the sage. without the standing list, each person is met as they come, and the goodness that is given does not wait for a reason. this is possible only if goodness is not a payment. if i am good to you because you are good, your badness can stop me, and you control my heart. the lines 德善, 德信, say where it comes from instead: from de, from what one is. the muddied heart is the same thing seen from inside. the sharp line between the worthy and the unworthy has gone soft, and nothing has been lost with it. read it as a text on government, as wang bi did. the usual ruler has a strong mind of his own and brings the people to it. he rewards the good, punishes the bad, trusts the proven, and watches the rest; and for that he needs eyes everywhere. wang bi describes the result exactly: the watched learn to watch back, the distrusted become skilled in deceit, and one mind is set against ten thousand. the sage’s way removes the contest. where nothing is spied on, nothing needs to hide. this does not mean that a leader has no judgment. it means that the judgment does not harden into a file on each person, and that trust is given first, because trust withheld is returned as distrust. the debate with confucius marks the risk: someone must still be fair to the good. 歙歙 is an instruction for the breath. sit, and take a slow breath in through the nose. on the in-breath the chest and belly receive; nothing is sent out; the face softens and the eyes stop reaching. stay a moment at the top. that is the sage’s posture in the world. most of the day is spent on the out-breath: speaking, pushing, declaring, judging. then try the next line. let the gaze go wide and a little unfocused, so that no one object is picked out. this is a muddied seeing, and with it you take in a whole room at once. meet the next person who comes in with that breath and that gaze, before the mind has said who they are. do the exercise of trust first with one person today. and for a morning, notice your constant heart at work: each time the mind says of someone “that is how they are”, note it, and add one word, “today”. see whether the heart of the people in front of you becomes easier to hear when your own verdict is less loud.

聖人: the one who rules by listening. “the sage” is our word for 聖人, and it needs a warning. a 聖人 is not a saint, and not only a wise person. the shuowen defines 聖 as 通也, “open all the way through”, and places it under 耳, the ear. in the political writing of this age the word names the ideal ruler: the one whose hearing is so open that the realm orders itself around them. this passage is the clearest portrait of such a person in the book, and it is drawn with negatives. no fixed heart. no list of the good and the bad. no sharp gaze. the sage here is defined by a relation to the 百姓, the people, and has no content apart from it.

無常心 or 恆無心. our text reads 無常心: “has no constant heart”: the mind is not fixed. the mawangdui silk text is reported to have two characters in a different order, with a different word for “constant”: 恆无心, “is constantly without heart”. the difference is real. in the received line, the sage has a heart, and it is not fixed; it moves with the people’s. in the silk line, the sage has no heart of their own at all, as a lasting state, and the people’s heart is the only one there. the received reading may come from the scribes’ change of 恆 to 常 (see passage 46) and a later shift of word order. the silk is also reported to say 百姓之心, with a particle that makes the phrase firmer: the heart that belongs to the hundred clans. which is harder to live: a mind that can change, or no mind of one’s own?

百姓: from the nobles to everyone. 百姓 is “the hundred clan names”. in early zhou only the nobility had a 姓, a clan name received from an ancestor, so the “hundred clans” were the great families who held office under the king. common people had no surname. during the warring states the old order broke down. states registered every household for tax and for the army, and surnames spread downward with the registers. by the time this text was fixed, 百姓 meant what it means in chinese today: ordinary people, everyone. so the phrase has a history of levelling inside it. the line says that the sage’s heart is taken from them. in a world where rulers consulted ministers, diviners, and ancestors, that is a strong claim. see the plate for 姓.

心: heart and mind are one organ. 心 is the heart, a picture of the organ; the shuowen says 在身之中, “it is in the middle of the body”. chinese thought placed thinking there too. 心 feels, wants, considers, and decides, so translators write “heart-mind”, or choose one half. english “mind” is too cool for this passage and “heart” is too soft. the split between a head that reasons and a heart that feels comes from greek and later european thought, and the chinese word does not have it. to take the people’s 心 as one’s own is then not to study their opinions, as a poll does, and not only to feel for them. it is to want and to think from where they are. mencius, of the same period, makes the 心 that cannot bear the suffering of others the root of all good rule.

善: good, and good at. 善 is “good”, and english hears a moral verdict. the chinese word is wider. it also means “good at”, skilled, fit for the purpose: passage 8 lists seven things that water is 善 at, and passage 27 speaks of the one who is 善 at walking and leaves no track. the shuowen writes the word in an older form with 羊, a sheep, in it and glosses it 吉也, “auspicious”; it notes that 義 and 美, right and beautiful, are made with the same sheep. so 善者 are the capable and decent, and 不善者 are those who are no good, at life or toward others. the verb use is the key. 善之 is “to good them”: to treat them as good and to be good to them. passage 27 gives the reason: the not-good person is the good person’s material.

吾: who says “i”?. the middle section says 吾, “i”, four times. this is rare in the book, which mostly speaks of “the sage” at a distance, and readers have asked who the “i” is: the author, the sage, the ruler who recites the text? the mawangdui silk text is reported to have no “i” at all. the collated text reads 善者善之，不善者亦善之: “the good are treated as good; the not good are also treated as good”. there the lines continue the description of the sage. the pronoun seems to be a later addition, and it changed the passage. with 吾, a description became a vow, and each reader who says the line aloud takes the vow. the rendering keeps the “i” of our base text. try the lines both ways. which one asks more of you?

德善: “de is good”, or “gets goodness”. two characters close each triplet: 德善, 德信. de, 德, is the “inner power” of the book’s title: the force of a person or thing that is true to its nature, which acts on others without pressure. read so, the lines say: de is good, de is trust; or, this is the goodness of de. but 德 was a homophone of 得, “to get”, and several old editions write 得 here: “and so goodness is got”, “and so trust is got”. then the lines state a result. the bad become good because someone treated them as good. legge translated that reading. the silk texts are reported to write 德善也. the two readings do not conflict as much as it seems. power of this kind is the capacity to get a result without forcing it. one word names the cause and the other the effect.

信: a person and their word. 信 is 亻, a person, beside 言, speech. the shuowen calls it a joined-meaning graph and glosses it 誠也, “real, sincere”. a 信 person is one whose word holds. as a verb it means to hold someone’s word as true: to trust, to believe. english divides these among “sincere”, “faithful”, “trust”, and “believe”; chinese has one word for the quality and the response to it. the hard line is the second. to trust the trustworthy is prudence. to trust the one who does not keep their word looks like folly. the book has prepared it. passages 17 and 23 say twice: 信不足焉，有不信焉, “where trust is not enough, there is no trust in return”. distrust is a thing that the one above gives first. see wang bi on what follows.

confucius heard this and said no. the idea of these lines was in the air, and the analects records an objection to it. someone asks confucius: 以德報怨，何如, “to repay injury with de, how is that?” the same phrase stands in passage 63 of the laozi. confucius replies: “then with what will you repay de? repay injury with uprightness, and repay de with de.” his point is justice. if the bad get the same as the good, the good are cheated and the measure is lost. the laozi’s sage has given up the measure on purpose: there is no fixed heart to keep the list. the question between them is still open in every school, court, and family. is equal goodness to the good and the bad a failure of justice, or the only thing that changes the bad?

歙歙: the breath drawn in. 歙 is a rare word. the shuowen defines it as 縮鼻也, “to draw in at the nose”: to inhale, to sniff in. the right side is 欠, which the dictionary explains as a person with breath rising from an open mouth, a yawn. passage 36 uses the word as the opposite of “to stretch out”: 將欲歙之，必固張之. doubled, 歙歙 describes a manner, and the sense must be found from the picture: breath held in, the self drawn together, nothing pushed out at the world. some read it as wary; some as without preference, taking all in alike. editions disagree on the graph here and several write words that mean “anxious”. the image of the received text is of the body. the sage’s way of being in the world is the in-breath: receiving, not issuing.

渾: the muddy heart, and hundun. 渾 is water that runs mingled; the shuowen gives 混流聲也, “the sound of a mixed current”. it means muddy, and also whole, not yet separated. passage 15 praises the old masters as 渾, like turbid water. 渾其心 is “to make the heart muddy”: to blur the sharp lines by which a mind sorts the world into good and bad, true and false. the zhuangzi tells a story about the word. the emperors of the north and south seas often met in the land of hundun, 渾沌, who treated them well. they saw that hundun lacked the seven openings by which people see, hear, eat, and breathe, and to repay the kindness they bored one opening each day. on the seventh day hundun died. put that beside the next line: the people fix ears and eyes.

注其耳目: at what do they look?. 注 is to pour; the shuowen says 灌也. the people “pour their ears and eyes”. the line does not say at what. one reading: at the sage. the people watch and listen to the one above, as subjects study a ruler for signs. the silk texts are reported to have 屬, “to fasten on”, which would support this. the other reading is wang bi’s: each of them uses their own hearing and sight, 各用聰明, sharply and busily, on their own affairs. in the first reading the sage is the calm centre of attention and does not use it. in the second the people are keen and the sage, alone, is not. the heshang gong text has this line; some old copies of the wang bi text lacked it. either way a contrast is drawn: focused senses below, and a muddied heart above.

孩之: three readings of the last word. 聖人皆孩之: “the sage 孩s them all”. 孩 is a noun made into a verb, and there are three ways to take it. first: treats them as infants, cares for them as a parent cares, without judging. second: makes infants of them, brings them back to the state of the newborn, which the book prizes (10, 28, 55); wang bi reads it so. third: 孩 has an older sense. the shuowen has the word 咳, defined as 小兒笑也, “a small child’s laugh”, and the received shuowen lists 孩 under it as the old-script form of the same word. passage 20 uses it so: an infant before its first smile. then the line can say that the sage smiles on them all, or is to them all as a laughing child. english “treats them as children” sounds like condescension. the chinese is warmer and stranger.

wang bi: one against ten thousand. at the last line wang bi writes one of the longest notes of his commentary, an essay against rule by surveillance. its core: 夫以明察物，物亦競以其明應之；以不信察物，物亦競以其不信應之. “if one examines people with sharp sight, they will compete to answer with their own sharpness. if one examines them with distrust, they will compete to answer with their distrust.” the ruler who relies on cleverness sets everyone’s cleverness against him: 己以一敵人，而人以千萬敵己也, “he is one against the others, and the others are thousands and tens of thousands against him”. multiply the nets of law and the punishments, he says, block the paths and raid the hidden dwellings, and 鳥亂於上，魚亂於下, “birds are in turmoil above and fish below”. his conclusion: 無所察焉，百姓何避, “where nothing is spied on, what would the people evade?” he also points to the ruler’s crown.

the crown that covered the eyes. in the same note wang bi points to the ruler’s ceremonial dress. if each thing has its source and each affair its master, he says, then 冕旒充目而不懼於欺，黈纊塞耳而無戚於慢: “the strings of the crown may fill the eyes with no fear of being deceived, and the yellow floss may stop the ears with no grief at being slighted”. the crown of a zhou or han ruler was a flat board with rows of jade beads that hung before and behind, in front of the face, and pads of yellow silk hung beside the ears. ritual writers explained them as a sign: the ruler should not see every fault or hear every word. so the highest person in the state wore, as regalia, a screen over the eyes and stoppers at the ears. what would it be to lead with such a crown on?

legge adds “(to me)”. legge writes: “to those who are good (to me), i am good; and to those who are not good (to me), i am also good”. the bracket narrows the line. 善者 are simply the good, and the not good; legge makes them people who treat the speaker well or badly, and the saying comes to resemble a text that he knew by heart: do good to them that hate you. the chinese is less personal and wider. for 信 he writes “sincere”, a virtue of the inner life, where the word is about whether a person’s word can be relied on. he follows the reading 得: “and thus (all) get to be good”. the sage has “an appearance of indecision”. and at the end the sage “deals with them all as his children”: a father, and a “his”, for 孩, which has neither.

trust first, once. choose one person today whom you have filed as 不信, not to be relied on, or 不善, no good. it may be a colleague, a relative, a stranger at a counter. for one meeting, set the file down. do not pretend that the past did not happen and do not hand over anything that you cannot afford to lose. only give them, for this hour, the same plain good treatment and the same assumption of honesty that you give to those whom you like. watch two things. watch them: wang bi says that people answer in the coin that they are offered. and watch yourself: notice how much effort the file took to carry, and what the in-breath feels like without it.

善 / 不善: one answer to both sides. the passage names two pairs: 善 and 不善, good and not good; 信 and 不信, true and untrue. notice how the second side is written. it has no word of its own. it is the first word with 不, “not”, in front. the two are one measure, and each needs the other to be seen; passage 2 says that when all know the good as good, the not good is already there. the sage does not deny the difference. the lines keep both names. what the sage does not do is answer in two ways. one response meets both sides. a one-sided reading makes this a rule, “be kind to bad people”, and keeps the list of who is bad. the text takes away the list, which is the constant heart. it also does not say that the not good stay so. a person turns.

goodness given to those who are not good is still goodness, and it does not wait for them to earn it.. goodness given to those who are not good is still goodness, and it does not wait for them to earn it. is this true in your experience, or does it sound like a way to be used? think of one person before you answer. who taught you that kindness has to be earned, or that it does not? what happened in your life that made the lesson stay? take the other side for a while: to be good to the not good wrongs the good, and people should get what they have shown. say it as your own view. what rises in you: relief, anger, shame? whom do you keep on your own list of the not good? what in them do you most refuse to find in yourself? which view has your life given you more evidence for? what would it cost you if the other one were right?

a fixed heart, with standing verdicts on people, hears less than a heart that takes its shape from others.. a fixed heart, with standing verdicts on people, hears less than a heart that takes its shape from others. do you agree, or do you count firm judgments as part of having character? recall a verdict on someone that you have held for years. when did you form it, and what was it protecting? now argue against the passage: a person with no fixed heart is a weathervane, and nobody can rely on them. hold that for a few minutes. what do you notice in the body and in the thoughts? which do you fear more in yourself: to be rigid, or to have no centre? what does that fear say about what you have lived?

姓 born of a woman. left: 女, a woman. right: 生, to be born. the shuowen takes both as meaning, and adds that 生 also gives the sound: 从女从生，生亦聲. its definition is direct: 姓，人所生也, “a clan name is that from which a person is born”. it then tells a myth: 古之神聖母，感天而生子，故稱天子. “the divine sage-mothers of antiquity were stirred by heaven and bore sons; hence the title son of heaven.” why should a family name, which passed from the father in historical china, be written with a woman? look at the oldest clan names themselves. 姬, the clan of the zhou kings. 姜, the clan of the lords of qi. 嬴, the clan of qin. 姒, the clan of the xia. each has 女 in it, and the shuowen ties the first two to the rivers where the founding ancestors lived. many scholars take this as a trace of a time when descent was counted through the mother; that is a common explanation and not a proven fact. 生 itself is a plant that comes up out of the soil: 象艸木生出土上, says the dictionary. so the word in 百姓, the people, is “woman” and “a shoot from the ground”. in a book that calls the way the mother of the world, it is the right word for those whose heart the sage takes. eight strokes: three for the woman, five for the shoot. 女 begins with a stroke that falls to the left, turns, and runs down to the right as a long dot. the second stroke falls to the left across it. the third is a horizontal; when 女 stands at the left of a character this last stroke rises toward the right and stops short, to leave room. then 生. a short stroke that falls to the left; a horizontal from it; a second horizontal below. watch the seventh stroke: the vertical, drawn from above the first horizontal down through both. it is the stem of the plant, and it must be straight. the eighth is the long base line, the ground, the widest stroke in the character. the woman leans a little toward the plant, and the plant stands upright.

孩 the child who laughs. left: 子, a child. right: 亥, which here gives the sound. 子 is a picture; the common explanation of the old form is an infant with a large head and arms held out, the legs wrapped in one line. it is in 好 (woman with child: good, to love), 字 (a child under a roof: to nurse, and later a written character), 學 (to learn), and 孫 (grandchild). 亥 is today the last of the twelve branches, the sign of the pig. the shuowen’s entry for it is odd and worth reading for this passage. it sees in the graph a man, a woman, and a curved line, and says of the curve: 象褢子咳咳之形, “it shows a child carried at the breast, going hai-hai”: the sound of a baby’s laugh. and the dictionary’s word for that laugh is 咳, 小兒笑也, written with a mouth; the received shuowen lists 孩, with a child in place of the mouth, as its old-script form. so the first sense of 孩 is not “a child”. it is the chuckle of a baby who has begun to know a face, at two or three months. passage 20 speaks of the infant 未孩, before its first smile. from the laugh came the one who laughs. read the last line again with the sound in it: 聖人皆孩之. nine strokes: three for the child, six for the right side. 子 is written first: a short horizontal that turns and falls to the left; then a vertical that curves slightly and ends in a hook; then the arms. in the full character 子 the arms are a level line. here, at the left side, the third stroke rises from lower left to upper right, so that it points to its neighbour. then 亥: a dot on top, a horizontal under it, and four strokes below. the sixth stroke falls left and turns back to the right. the seventh and eighth fall to the lower left, one under the other, like two steps. watch the ninth: a firm stroke to the lower right that ends the character and balances the three left-falling strokes before it. the child is narrow and upright; the right side is all movement.

信 a person stands by a word. left: 亻, the form that 人, a person, takes at the side of a character. right: 言, speech. the shuowen names this as a model case of the kind of character that joins two meanings to make a third: 信，誠也。从人从言。會意, “real, true; from person and speech; joined meaning”. a person, and what they said: 信 is the state in which the two agree. the pieces are familiar. 亻 marks human matters: 仁 (humane: a person and two), 位 (a place to stand), 伐 (to attack: a person and a dagger-axe). 言 has 口, a mouth, at its base. from “true to one’s word” came “to trust”, then a pledge or token that proves a message, and at last the modern sense “a letter”. for confucius 信 is one of the load-bearing words: a person without it, he says, is like a cart without the pin that joins the yoke to the pole. the laozi values it too, and distrusts fine speech: 信言不美，美言不信, “true words are not beautiful; beautiful words are not true” (81). this passage does something else with it. it makes 信 a gift that goes first, to the one who has not earned it. see the note on 信. nine strokes. the person takes two: a stroke that falls to the left, and a vertical that starts from the middle of it. keep it slim. then 言 in seven. a dot at the top. a long horizontal: the widest line of the character, and it reaches left almost to the person. two shorter horizontals below it, even and parallel. then the mouth in three strokes: left side, top with right side, base. watch the stack of three horizontals. if they are equal the character goes dead, so the first is long, the next two are short, and the spaces between them are the same. the mouth at the bottom is a little wider than the two short lines above it, and so the speech has a base to rest on.

50 · no place for the horn. out into life, in to death. / the followers of life: three in ten. / the followers of death: three in ten. / people who live, and in moving go to the death-ground: / also three in ten. / now why is this? / because they live life thickly. / it is said that one good at holding life / walks the land and does not meet rhinoceros or tiger, / enters an army and wears no armour or blade. / the rhinoceros has nowhere to thrust its horn, / the tiger nowhere to set its claw, / the blade nowhere to lodge its edge. / now why is this? / because they have no death-ground. the passage has two halves of the same shape: a statement, the question 夫何故, “now why is this?”, and an answer that begins 以其, “because they”. the first half opens with four bare words and then counts: followers of life, followers of death, and people who are alive and moving to the death-ground, each “ten have three”. why? they live life thickly. the second half is a report about one kind of person, good at holding life, drawn in three pairs of images: land and army; beast and weapon; and then horn, claw, and edge, each with nowhere to go. why? no death-ground. the first half is arithmetic, and the second is a picture. between them stands a missing number. the first half says that most movement is toward death, and that the cause is the effort to have more life. the grip on life is the death-ground. the second half then describes someone in whom the grip is absent, and the description is negative throughout: does not meet, does not wear, nowhere, nowhere, nowhere, none. nothing is said about what this person has. fear makes a place in the body and in the mind that harm can find. a person defends, and the defence marks where the wound will be. the one who holds life without clutching it gives the world’s horns nothing to push against. wang bi puts it in one clause: does not make life the thing to live for. the passage does not teach contempt for life. it teaches a lighter hold. martial arts in china have long used this passage, and in a physical sense. a strike needs a target that stays and resists. the skilled body does not stay: it turns, yields, and lets the force pass through empty space, so that the fist has nowhere to lodge. stiffness is the death-ground. a stiff arm can be broken and a rigid stance can be thrown. passage 76 says it: the hard and strong are followers of death. stand and let someone push your shoulder slowly. resist first: you become a thing that can be moved. then let the shoulder turn away under the hand while the feet stay. the push finds nothing. notice also the line on armour. the best armour was the hide of the very beast that one feared. read the census as a view of a court. three in ten thrive. three are finished. three are alive and busy, and each move takes them nearer the end, because they are trying so hard to secure themselves: more wealth, more allies, more guards. in a warring states court that last group was large, and its members died of what they had gathered. the term for where they go is military. for a person in office the lesson is concrete. each privilege that you defend and each rival whom you mark is a place where you can be struck. the official whom no one can hurt is the one who holds the post lightly and has taken nothing that must be hidden. there is no place in such a person for the horn. do the exercise of the place that braces: find, in the first second of a threat, where the body hardens, and breathe out through it. then make the passage’s count for your own day, in thirds. which of today’s movements were in life’s company? which in death’s? and which were the third kind, lively and well meant, and wearing you down? do not correct anything yet. the passage asks 夫何故, “why is this?”, before it says anything else, and that is the practice: to ask it.

出生入死: four words, three readings. out, life, in, death. the four characters have no grammar marks, and readers join them in different ways. one: to come out is to live, and to go in is to die; the oldest commentary, in the han feizi, says that a person’s beginning is called “coming out” and the end is called “going in”. out of what? the womb, the earth, the unseen. two: people come out into life and go into death, as a traveller passes through two gates. wang bi writes: out of the ground of life, into the ground of death. three: to leave life is to enter death; one step does both. in modern chinese the phrase is an idiom for facing mortal danger, “to go through fire”. the rendering keeps the bare four beats and adds only two small words.

徒: those who go on foot. 徒 has 彳, a step on the road, at its left, and 止, a foot, at the lower right. the shuowen lists it in an older graph and defines it 步行也, “to go on foot”. those who walked behind a chariot were the foot soldiers and the retinue, and so the word came to mean followers, companions, disciples, a kind of people. 生之徒 are “life’s followers”: those in life’s train. some scholars read the word as 途, “road”: the roads of life, the roads of death. the book supports “followers”. passage 76 uses the same two phrases and tells us who they are: 堅強者死之徒，柔弱者生之徒, “the hard and strong are followers of death; the soft and weak are followers of life”. death and life are pictured as two lords, each with a company on foot behind. whose company are you in today?

十有三: three in ten, or thirteen?. this is one of the old disputes of the book. 十有三 is, word for word, “ten have three”. in normal classical usage the phrase is a number: thirteen. confucius says 吾十有五而志于學, “at ten-and-five i set my heart on learning”, and no one reads that as five in ten. on that basis the earliest commentary reads thirteen here. wang bi reads it otherwise: 十有三，猶云十分有三分, “ten-have-three is like saying three parts in ten parts”. then the lines are a census. three people in ten follow life. three follow death. three more are alive and move toward death. we render wang bi’s reading, because our base text is his and because the count leads somewhere; see the tenth. the grammar is on the side of thirteen. english cannot write a phrase that is both.

thirteen: the limbs and the openings. the han feizi, about 240 bce, explains the number in this way. the body has four limbs and nine openings: two eyes, two ears, two nostrils, the mouth, and the two below. these thirteen are the great equipment of a person. in life, all thirteen belong to life; they are 生之徒, life’s followers, the same thirteen. at death, all thirteen turn and belong to death. and when a person lives and moves, each movement of the thirteen wears them toward the death-ground. the heshang gong commentary also counts thirteen, as nine openings and four “passes”, 九竅四關. in this reading the passage has no census of people. it is about one body and its doors, the same doors that passage 52 says to shut. the life-keeper is then the one whose thirteen do not carry them out to die.

three, three, three: where is the tenth?. if the count is by tenths, do the sum. three in ten for life, three for death, three who live and move toward death. that is nine. the passage never mentions the one who is left. then, with no link but the words “it is said”, it begins to describe a single person whom the horn and the blade do not find. many readers take that person as the missing tenth: the one in ten who belongs to no company. this may not be what the author counted; numbers in early texts are often round. but notice the form. the text does not write “and one in ten is the keeper of life”. it leaves a gap in the arithmetic, and the reader finds a person in it. the one who has no death-ground also has no line in the census.

死地: a term from the art of war. 死地, “death-ground”, is soldier’s language. the sunzi lists nine kinds of ground, and the last is this: 疾戰則存，不疾戰則亡者，為死地. “where you survive if you fight at once and perish if you do not, that is death-ground.” it is terrain with no way out: backs to a river, enemies in front. the sunzi gives the general a hard rule for it: throw your troops onto ground from which they cannot escape and they will live, because men who cannot run will fight. death-ground there is a tool that commanders use on their own soldiers. the laozi takes the term and turns it inward. most people, it says, carry themselves to such ground by their own movement, 動之死地. and one kind of person has no such place in them at all. the same verb, 投, “to throw”, is in both texts.

生生之厚: too thick a life. 以其生生之厚: “because of the thickness of their living of life”. the first 生 is a verb and the second its object: to live life, to feed life, to make a living of living. 厚 is “thick”; the shuowen defines it by mountains, 山陵之厚也. thick living is rich food, rich goods, and strong attachment to staying alive. the claim is a paradox with a plain core: those who work hardest to add to life are the ones who move toward death. passage 75 says it of rulers: the people take death lightly because those above seek 生之厚, and it ends: only the one who does not act for the sake of life is wiser than the one who prizes life. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to have a shorter answer, 以亓生生也, “because they live for life”. if so, there is no “thick”, and the striving itself is the cause.

蓋聞: “it is said”. the second half opens with 蓋聞, “now, [one] has heard”. it is a formula of report. the author does not say “i know” or “it is so”; the text marks what follows as something handed down, a saying about a kind of person. english translators, legge among them, supply “i have heard”, but the chinese has no “i”. the distance matters for how literally to take the tigers. a text that wished to promise magic could state it flatly. this one says: there is a report. it then asks its own question, 夫何故, “now why is this?”, and answers with a reason and not a miracle. the same question and the same form of answer close both halves of the passage. the first asks why people die early. the second asks why this one does not.

攝生: to hold life in the hand. 攝 has 扌, a hand, beside three ears, 聶, which give the sound. the shuowen defines it as 引持也, “to draw in and hold”. it is what you do with a robe when you gather its skirts to walk, and with an office when you hold it for another. 攝生 is then “to gather life in and hold it”: to keep it collected, not to add to it. that is the difference from the thick living of the line before. feeding life makes it large and exposed. holding it makes it compact. the phrase had a long future. it became a common term for the care of health, beside 養生, “to nourish life”, and a whole literature of breathing, diet, exercise, and sexual practice grew under those names. the zhuangzi is cool toward the bodily version: those who puff and stretch like bears and birds only to live long, it says, are people who nourish the form.

“does not meet” or “does not avoid”. our text says 陸行不遇兕虎: walking on land, does not meet rhinoceros or tiger. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 陵行不辟兕虎: walking in the hills, does not avoid them. two words differ. 陵, hills, is wilder than 陸, level land: it is where the animals are. and 辟, “to avoid, to step aside”, changes the claim. in the received line the beasts are simply not there; it sounds like luck or a charm. in that line the person takes no detour. the beasts may be there, and no precaution is taken. that fits the next line, where the person enters an army and wears no armour. both lines then describe the same thing: a person who has dropped the stance of defence. the received 不遇 would then be a later softening, by an editor who found “does not avoid” reckless.

兕: rhinoceros in the yellow river plain. the 兕 is a real animal, and scholars still argue which. the shuowen lists it under an old picture-graph and says 如野牛而青, “like a wild ox, and dark”; it keeps a separate entry for 犀, the two-horned rhinoceros “from beyond the southern border”. shang kings hunted 兕 and recorded the kills on oracle bones. some zoologists identify it as a wild buffalo; the traditional reading is rhinoceros. either way it was a large horned beast that charged. north china was warmer and wetter then, with elephants and rhinoceros in the river plains; by the warring states they survived mostly in the south. there is a link to the next line. armour was made of the hides of both animals. the kaogongji says that armour of 犀 hide lasts a hundred years and armour of 兕 hide two hundred, and a song of chu describes warriors who 被犀甲, “wear rhinoceros armour”. the beast and the armour in these two lines are one skin.

不被甲兵: wears none, or is touched by none. 被 is first a covering, a long coat for the night, and as a verb “to put on, to wear”. it also means “to be covered by” in the bad sense: to suffer, to be struck. so 入軍不被甲兵 has two readings. one: enters an army and does not put on armour or carry a weapon. two: enters an army and is not struck by armoured men and blades. 甲 is the armour and 兵 is the weapon; together they can also mean “troops”. the han feizi quotes the line with another verb, 不備, “does not make ready”, and explains: the sage has no heart to harm others, so no one harms the sage, and so no guard is kept. that supports the first reading, and we follow it. it is the stronger claim. the person is not well protected. the person is unprotected.

角, 爪, 刃: three pictures of a point. the three things that find no place are written with three of the simplest picture-characters. 角 is a horn; the shuowen says 獸角也。象形, “an animal’s horn; a picture”, and you can still see the curved tip and the rings. 爪 is a claw: 覆手曰爪, “a hand turned palm down is called 爪”, fingers pointing to the ground. 刃 is a blade’s edge: a knife, 刀, with one stroke added to mark the place that cuts; see the plate. horn, claw, and edge are nature’s weapon, the predator’s weapon, and the human weapon, in rising order of skill. each of the three verbs is also exact. the horn is 投, thrust or thrown. the claw is 措, set down, placed. the edge is 容, let in. each attack needs a place that receives it.

容: the body that gives no room. 兵無所容其刃: “the weapon has no place that 容 its edge”. 容 is to hold, to contain, to have room for. the shuowen glosses it 盛也, “to hold as a vessel holds”, and the graph has a roof, 宀, over 谷, a valley: a sheltered hollow. it is a warm word in this book. passage 16 says that to know the constant is 容, to be capacious, and that capacity leads to fairness and to kingliness. so the verb is chosen with some wit. the person in this passage, who has room for everything, has no room for a blade. think of how a blade works. it needs something that resists it, a firm surface to part. what would a person be like in whom an insult, a threat, or a loss found nothing firm to enter?

無死地: magic, or a way of being?. “because they have no death-ground.” later religion took the lines at face value. daoist adepts sought bodies that weapons could not cut, and handbooks gave charms for going into the mountains among tigers. the older commentators are sober. for the han feizi, the person has no wish to harm and so draws no harm. for wang bi, the person does not let desire burden the body, and so is not baited onto fatal ground. the zhuangzi offers a picture: a drunk man falls from a cart and is not killed, because he does not know that he is falling and nothing in him braces against the ground. on this view the death-ground is not a spot on the body. it is the place where a person is stiff with wanting to live. passage 55 says the same of the infant: it is not stung by wasps or seized by wild animals.

wang bi: the hawk and the sweet bait. wang bi’s note ends with a small fable. 夫蚖蟺以淵為淺，而鑿穴其中，鷹鸇以山為卑，而增巢其上. “the eels and water-lizards find the deep pool shallow and bore their holes in its bed; the hawks and falcons find the mountain low and build their nests above it.” no corded arrow can reach them and no net can arrive, he says; they may be said to live where there is no death-ground. 然而卒以甘餌，乃入於無生之地. “and yet in the end, through sweet bait, they enter the ground where there is no life.” is this not, he asks, the thickness of living? his conclusion is the key to his reading: 善攝生者無以生為生，故無死地也. “the one good at holding life does not make life the thing to live for, and so has no death-ground.” safety of position does not save the hawk. only the absence of the hook does.

legge: life “entrusted for a time”. legge follows wang bi’s count, “of every ten three”, and translates 徒 as “ministers”: ministers of life, ministers of death. that is a churchman’s word for a follower. the most telling phrase comes later. for 善攝生者, five characters, he writes: “he who is skilful in managing the life entrusted to him for a time”. entrusted by whom? the chinese has no giver and no loan. the idea that life is a trust from god, for which the holder must give account, is the doctrine of stewardship in which legge was raised, and here it has entered the text without a bracket. for 甲兵 he writes “buff coat or sharp weapon”: the leather coat of a seventeenth-century english soldier. his rhinoceros and tiger are left as they are.

find the place that braces. today, when something comes at you, a sharp remark, bad news, a car that cuts in, a demand, notice the body in the first second. somewhere it braces: the jaw, the belly, the chest. that hardening is a small 死地, a firm place offered to the horn. do not try to remove it by will. only find it, name it, and breathe out once through it. then see what the remark does when it has less to strike. separately, look at one way in which you live thickly: a comfort or a safeguard that has become heavy to maintain. ask whether it adds to your life or only to your exposure. the passage ranks nothing here. it only describes how its two kinds of people move.

生 / 死: two gates on one path. 生 and 死, life and death, stand with 出 and 入, out and in. the first four words do not set them against each other. they put them on one path: what comes out goes in. the count that follows treats both sides alike, three in ten for each, and then gives a third group who turn the first into the second by their own motion. the cause is not a love of death. it is too thick a life. so the passage does not rank life above death, and it does not praise death. it says that a hard grip on one side moves a person to the other. a one-sided reading hears a method to live longer. but one who holds life lightly in order to keep it has made a new grip. the text only says where death finds no ground.

people move toward death because they hold on to life too hard.. people move toward death because they hold on to life too hard. does this fit what you have seen, in yourself or in someone near you? give one case. where do you hold life most tightly: health, money, safety, plans? when did that grip begin, and what had just happened? try the opposite view: those who guard life with care are the ones who keep it, and a light hold is carelessness. stay with it. what thoughts defend it, and what feelings come with them? the passage offers a picture and no proof. what in your own history makes you want it to be true, or want it to be false?

a person who does not brace against harm gives harm no place to land.. a person who does not brace against harm gives harm no place to land. do you believe it? or do you think that harm falls where it falls, whatever a person is like inside? think of a time when you were hurt. was there a place in you that the blow found ready? this is a question, not a charge against yourself. take the other side: defence is wise, armour saves lives, and those who do not guard themselves are the first to be struck. hold that as true for a while. what is it like to stand there? what do you call people who seem unguarded: naive, lucky, or free? what does your word for them tell you? which view did the people who raised you live by? how much of your answer is theirs?

刃 the dot that points at the edge. begin with 刀, a knife. the shuowen calls it 兵也。象形, “a weapon; a picture”: the old forms show a handle and a curved blade. now add one small stroke on the blade, and you have 刃. the shuowen explains: 刀堅也。象刀有刃之形, “the hard part of the knife; it shows a knife that has an edge”. the added stroke is not a picture of anything. it is a pointer. it says: this part, here. chinese scholars call such characters 指事, “pointing at the matter”, and they are few and easy to love. 本, root, is 木, a tree, with a mark at its foot; the shuowen says 木下曰本, “the lower part of a tree is called 本”. 末, tip, is the same tree with the mark at the top. so 刃 is a knife with a finger on its sharpest place. it then serves as a sound in other characters. 忍, to endure: 刃 over 心, the heart, which the dictionary treats as sound only, though generations of readers have seen an edge held over a heart. in this passage the edge is the last of three points, and the one made by people. the text says that it finds no place to enter. the character itself is a mark that shows where the cut would be. three strokes. the first makes the body of the knife: it runs to the right, turns the corner, comes down with a slight lean to the left, and ends in a hook. the second starts under the middle of the first and falls in a long curve to the lower left; this is the cutting edge, and it should be slim and quick. watch the third stroke, the pointer. it is a single short mark set just beside the falling stroke, on the outside of the curve, close to it and not on it. press, and lift at once. if it is too large the character becomes clumsy, and if it drifts far from the blade it means nothing. the whole lesson of this small character is placement: one touch of the brush, in exactly the place that matters.

死 a person beside the bones. two parts. the left is 歹, which the shuowen writes 歺 and defines as 𠛱骨之殘也, “what remains of bones that have been stripped”: bare, broken bone. it marks death and damage in 殘 (to maim), 殃 (calamity), and 殆, the “danger” of passage 44. the right part looks like 匕, a spoon, but the shuowen is clear that it is a person: 从歺从人, “from bones and a person”. the common explanation of the early form is a living person who kneels or bows beside the remains of the dead. so the character for “to die” does not show the dying. it shows the mourner and what is left. the dictionary’s definition has the same view from outside: 死，澌也，人所離也, “to die is to run dry; it is what people part from”. put 死 between two tufts of grass and you have 葬, to bury, which the shuowen explains as the dead laid in thick grass with a mat beneath: 从死在茻中. in this passage the word comes five times, and twice in the term 死地, the ground of death. notice that the text never uses it for the life-keeper. of that person it says only 無死地: there is no such ground. six strokes. first a long horizontal across the top: a lid over the whole character. under it on the left, the bones in three strokes: a short stroke that falls to the left; then a stroke that goes a little to the right, turns, and falls far to the lower left; then one dot inside the angle. on the right, the person in two strokes: a short stroke that comes in from the right and leans down to the left, and then the last and largest stroke. watch it. it comes down, bends at the bottom, runs to the right along the ground, and ends in a hook that turns up. this sixth stroke gives the character its base and its only open curve. the two sides do not touch each other; a narrow channel of white runs down between the bones and the one who stays.

虎 the tiger with human feet. the shuowen gives the tiger a title: 山獸之君, “lord of the beasts of the mountains”. it then divides the character in two. the upper part is 虍, which the dictionary defines as 虎文也, “the stripes of the tiger”, and calls a picture. the lower part is two strokes. the standard traditional form writes them as 几; the shuowen saw the legs of a person, 儿, and says so plainly: 虎足象人足, “the tiger’s feet are like human feet”. modern scholars read the history differently. oracle-bone forms draw the whole animal on its side, with open jaws, a striped body, claws, and a long tail, and the regular script is what the brush made of that drawing, set upright; the “human feet” are the worn-down legs and tail. look at those early forms in the links. still, the dictionary’s remark is a good thing to hold beside this passage, which puts a person and a tiger on the same path. 虍 on its own makes the top of other characters, usually as a sound: 虛, empty; 處, to dwell; 慮, to think ahead. with 豸 or 犬 beside it the tiger becomes an adjective of ferocity. the tiger’s weapon here is 爪, the claw, a hand turned down, and the text says that it finds no place to set it. eight strokes. the stripes take the first six. a short vertical at the top centre. a short horizontal that goes out from it to the right. then a horizontal with a small hook at its right end, which covers what is below. fourth, a long stroke that starts at the left end of that cover and falls far down to the left: the back of the animal, and the longest line. inside, a short horizontal that rises a little, and a stroke that comes down through it and bends to the right. then the feet in two strokes: one that falls to the left, and one that begins with a short run to the right, turns down, bends, runs to the right again, and hooks upward. watch the last stroke. it must reach out past the upper part on the right, so that the heavy head has something to stand on.

51 · rearing without owning. dao gives them birth. / de rears them. / things give them shape. / circumstance completes them. / so the ten thousand things, every one, / honour dao and prize de. / the honour of dao, the prizing of de: / no one commands it; it is always so of itself. / so dao gives them birth, de rears them: / grows them, raises them, / settles them, ripens them, / shelters them, covers them. / gives birth and does not possess. / acts and does not lean on it. / leads and does not carve. / this is called dark de. the passage runs in four steps. first, four lines of three characters, each with a different subject and the same object, 之, “them”: the way gives birth, de rears, things shape, circumstance completes. second, the response of the creatures: all of them honour and prize the first two, and no one orders this; it is so of itself. third, the care is spelled out in six more verbs, in pairs. fourth, three lines of the form “a and not b”, a refrain of the book, and the name for all of it: dark de. the vocabulary is drawn from a farm and a great household: birth, livestock, the ox in “thing”, the wine jar of honour, the steward’s carving knife. the passage describes how you were made, and it is worth reading it in the first person. something gave me life, and i did not ask. something fed that life, each day, before i could notice. other creatures gave me my shape: parents, a language, a town. the time and place finished the work. at no point did the source send a bill. that is the meaning of dark: the giving left no signature. the usual self says the opposite, “my life, my work, my children”, and each “my” is a small act of 有, possession. the contemplative step is to feel how much is given without a claim on it, and then to try to give in the same way. the honour that the passage speaks of then arises of itself, and can be noticed: it is plain gratitude with no one in particular to thank. the three closing lines are the best short guide to parenthood, teaching, and the founding of anything. give it life and do not own it: the child, the student, the company is not yours. do the work and do not lean on having done it: no ledger of sacrifices. be the elder, 長, and do not carve: do not cut the other into the portions that you planned. the four lines at the head add realism. you are not the only maker. the thing that you lead is shaped by its peers and completed by its circumstances, and your part is the humble middle one, to feed it. the passage also says what such a leader receives: honour that no one commanded. honour that must be commanded is of another kind. this is one of the book’s most exact pictures of how living things come to be. a seed has life from its parent plant. the soil and rain feed it. its neighbours give it its form: a tree in a forest grows tall and narrow, and the same tree in a field grows wide. the slope, the wind, and the season complete it; that is 勢. no part of this process owns the tree. the sun does not send for it, and the soil keeps no account. ecology says the same in other words: an organism is born of its kind, fed by flows of energy, shaped by other organisms, and finished by its place. the herdsman’s word is a reminder that people can take part in this as keepers and not as owners. do the exercise of feeding one thing and taking no credit. then, once today, trace the four lines backward for a single object in your hand, a cup of tea or a loaf of bread. what circumstance completed it? what things gave it shape? what fed it as it grew? what gave it life? go as far back as you can. at the end of the chain there is no one to pay. that is where the passage says that honour comes of itself.

道生之: birth, not creation. dao, 道, the way, stays untranslated. here it is the subject of 生, and the choice of english verb decides a theology. 生 is “to give birth, to grow, to live”; the shuowen pictures it as a plant that comes up out of the soil. it is the verb of a mother and of a field. legge writes “produced”; others write “creates”, and a western reader then hears genesis: a maker who stands outside the work, plans it, speaks it into being, names it, and has dominion over it. each of those ideas is denied in this passage. the way has no plan or command, it does not possess what is born, and no one orders the honour that it receives. the next passage says outright what the verb implies: the world has a mother.

德: not “virtue”. de, 德, is the second word of the book’s title, and we leave it as it is. “virtue” is the usual english, and it misleads twice. the latin root is “manliness”, and the victorian sense is moral good conduct. 德 here is neither. it is the power that a thing has by being fully what it is: the share of the way that has become this creature and keeps it alive. wang bi defines the pair in one line: the way is that from which things come, and de is that which they get. he plays on the sound, since 德 and 得, “to get”, were said alike. so the first two lines divide one work. the way gives the birth, and de does the long feeding afterward. every creature has a de; a ruler’s de was the force that drew people without commands.

畜: de as a herdsman. 畜 is the word for livestock, and as a verb, read xu, it means to keep and feed animals. the shuowen says 田畜也, and quotes an older book for the picture: 玄田爲畜, “玄 and 田 make 畜”: a dark field. it is a farm word, with dung and fodder in it. english versions write “nourishes” or “nurtures”, which belong to the nursery. the chinese has put de in a pen with cattle, to feed them morning and evening through the winter. the same word was used of a lord who “keeps” his people, and of supporting one’s wife and children. note the thing that a herdsman does not do. he does not make the animal grow. he brings it to water and grass, and the growing is the animal’s own. see the plate.

物: the ox in “thing”. 物 is “thing”, and the english word is too dead for it. the graph has 牛, an ox, at its left. the shuowen explains: 萬物也。牛爲大物, “the ten thousand things; the ox is the great thing”, the largest creature that a farmer handles. so 物 are first of all creatures and kinds, the living variety of the world; 萬物, “the ten thousand things”, includes people. in the third line 物 is the subject: 物形之, “things give them shape”. how can things shape things? each creature gets its form from others of its kind and from what surrounds it: a calf from a cow, a pot from clay and a potter’s hands, a child from a family. the way gives life in general. the particular shape comes from the neighbours. with 畜 and 宰, this makes three words from the cattle yard in one passage.

勢: the word of generals and kings. 勢 has 力, strength, at its foot; the shuowen defines it as 盛力權也, “full force and weight of authority”. it was a technical term of the age. for the sunzi, which gives it a chapter, 勢 is the energy of a situation: 激水之疾，至於漂石者，勢也, “the rush of pent water that tumbles boulders along, that is 勢”. a good general does not ask courage of his men; he places them where the slope does the work. for the legalists, 勢 is the position of the throne: a dragon is strong because it rides the clouds, and a king because he sits where he sits. the laozi uses the word only here, and for something gentler: the season, the soil, the setting that brings a creature to completion. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 器, “vessel”, in its place: things shape them, and each is completed as a vessel.

尊 and 貴: a wine jar and a cowrie. the two verbs of honour are concrete objects. 尊 is a bronze wine vessel of the ancestral rites. the shuowen records the word in an older graph and defines it 酒器也, “a vessel for wine”, raised by two hands in offering; the modern form keeps one hand, 寸, under the jar. to 尊 someone is to lift the wine to them. 貴 has 貝, the cowrie shell of early money, at its base, and the shuowen’s gloss is 物不賤也, “a thing that is not cheap”. to 貴 is to hold at a high price. so the line says that all creatures offer wine to the way and hold de dear as treasure. these are the two forms of honour that a zhou noble knew: rite and wealth. and the next line says that in this case no one arranged the ceremony.

莫之命: honour that no king conferred. in the zhou world honour came from above by a formal act. the king gave a lord his rank in a ceremony at the ancestral temple; a scribe read the 命, the charge, and the lord cast the words in bronze for his descendants. 命 is that word: a command, a charge of office, and by extension fate, what heaven charges. the line says of the way’s honour that 莫之命, “no one charged it”. an old note printed with wang bi’s commentary records that other texts had 爵 here, and the mawangdui silk texts are reported to have it: 夫莫之爵也, “no one gave it rank”. 爵 is itself a wine vessel: the three-legged cup used at investiture, which the shuowen calls 禮器, “a vessel of the rites”, and so the word for noble rank. after the jar of 尊, the cup: and no hand holds it out.
