自然: “self-so”, not “nature”. 自然 is two words. 自 is “self”, and “from”; the shuowen says that the graph is a nose, 鼻也, and people in china still point to the nose to say “me”. 然 is “so, thus”; its first sense, says the shuowen, was “to burn”, and the fire is still at its foot. 自然 is “so from itself”: what a thing is and does when nothing outside makes it so. in modern chinese the word translates “nature”, and many english versions write “naturally” or “spontaneously” here. but the laozi has no noun “nature”, no green realm set apart from human affairs. it has a quality, and courts, rulers, and people can have it or lose it. the people say “we are so of ourselves” (17). the way models itself on the self-so (25). here the honour that creatures give is of that kind: no one ordered it.

six verbs, and whose they are. after “gives them birth” and “rears them” come six more verbs, each followed by 之, “them”: 長, to make grow; 育, to raise a child; 亭 and 毒; 蓋, to shelter with a roof or lid; 覆, to cover over. the heshang gong text and the standard editions of wang bi have 養, “to feed”, where our text has 蓋, a reading of the fu yi “old text” line. all are verbs of a parent, a farmer, or a nurse, in the order of a life, from growth to shelter, and perhaps to the covering of the grave. whose verbs are they? in our text the list follows 德畜之, so they read as the work of de. in the mawangdui silk texts, as reported, the word 德 is absent at this point: 道生之畜之長之遂之亭之毒之養之覆之. there the way itself does everything, in one breath of eight verbs. the rendering leaves the six without a subject, as the chinese does.

亭之毒之: a rest-house and a poison. two strange verbs stand in the middle of the list. 亭 is a pavilion or a post-station on a road; the shuowen says 民所安定也, “where people are made secure and settled”. 毒 is “poison”. to station them, to poison them? the old readers saw two ways through. one takes the words by sound: the heshang gong text writes 成之孰之, “completes them, ripens them”, and 亭毒 may be another spelling of that. the other keeps the graphs and their older senses: 亭 is to bring to rest, to give a fixed place; the shuowen’s first gloss for 毒 is 厚也, “thick”, before it speaks of a plant that harms people; a medicine is strong in that way, and so 毒 is “to bring to full strength”. both arrive near our “settles them, ripens them”. after this passage, 亭毒 became a literary word for the care that heaven gives to creatures. the poison in the list may be an accident of spelling, and it does make one think: what ripens a creature is strong stuff.

three lines that the book says three times. 生而不有，為而不恃，長而不宰. each line is “a, and not b”, where b is what usually follows from a. to give birth, and not to have: 有 is to own. to act, and not to 恃: the shuowen glosses 恃 as 賴也, to lean on, to count on, as one leans on a service done. to be the elder, and not to carve. these lines are a refrain. passage 2 has the first two, of the sage. passage 10 has all three with the same closing words, 是謂玄德, at the end of a set of questions on practice. here the subject is the way and its de. the repetition is the point: the same grammar describes the source of the world, the sage, and the person who sits and breathes. which of the three “and not” is hardest for you: not to own, not to count on thanks, or not to direct?

宰: the butcher who became prime minister. 宰 is the last verb, and it is a strong one. its first sense is to slaughter and carve up an animal. the 宰 of a great house was the steward who cut the meat of the sacrifice and shared it out by rank, and from that office came the title of the chief minister of a state. a story in the shiji shows the link. the young chen ping carved the meat at his village festival so evenly that the elders praised him. he sighed: let me 宰 the world, and it would be like this meat. he later became chancellor of han. so 長而不宰 is exact: to be the head, and not to cut the thing into portions and hand them out. passage 28 says the same: the great tailor does not cut. english “does not control” loses the knife. see the plate.

玄德: power that does not show. 玄 is a colour: the shuowen says black with red in it, the dark of deep water or of the sky before dawn, and so “remote, hard to see into”. 玄德 is de of that colour. english versions write “mysterious virtue” or “profound power”, and the phrase begins to sound occult. the passage has just defined it in plain terms. it is the power that gives birth and does not own, acts and does not lean on the act, leads and does not carve. it is dark because it leaves no mark of ownership: wang bi says that there is de and no one knows who is its master. the term returns in passages 10 and 65. it also had a life outside philosophy: the founder of the shu-han kingdom in the third century, liu bei, bore it as his courtesy name, xuande.

wang bi: from which, and what is got. wang bi turns the first four lines into four questions: 何由而生？道也；何得而畜？德也；何由而形？物也；何使而成？勢也. “from what are they born? the way. by getting what are they reared? de. from what do they take shape? things. what makes them complete? circumstance.” then his definitions: 道者，物之所由也。德者，物之所得也. “the way is that from which things come. de is that which things get.” the pun on 德 and 得 carries the philosophy: de is not an addition to a creature; it is what the creature has received. on the last line: 有德而不知其主也，出乎幽冥，是以謂之玄德也. “there is de, and its master is not known; it comes out of the dark and hidden. for this reason it is called dark de.”

legge: “outflowing operation”. legge could not write “virtue” for 德 in this passage, and what he wrote shows his frame: the tao’s “outflowing operation”. this is the language of emanation, a divine source whose energy flows out into creatures, and it comes from neoplatonic and christian theology. the honour that creatures pay is “not the result of any ordination”, a word of church and decree, “but always a spontaneous tribute”. for 玄德 he gives “its mysterious operation”. he supplies “(all things)” as the object and makes the tao the subject of every verb. the herdsman’s word 畜 becomes “nourished”, and 宰, the carver, becomes “exercises no control”. the translation is careful and reverent, and by its end a cattle yard has become a cathedral. he is right on one point of grammar: the subject of the last three lines is the way, not “you”.

what the silk texts change. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to differ from our text in four places that matter. for 勢 they have 器: “things shape them and vessels complete them”. for 命 they have 爵, rank. in the list of care they give all the verbs to the way and include 遂, “to bring through”, and 養, “to feed”; see the six verbs. and the three closing lines use 弗 where we have 不: 生而弗有也，為而弗恃也，長而弗宰也. 弗 is a negative that includes its object: does not own them, does not lean on them, does not carve them. the received 不 is more general and can be read as advice on character. the silk form keeps the eye on the creatures. this passage is not among the guodian slips.

feed one thing, and take no credit. choose one living thing that depends on you: a child, a plant, an animal, a junior colleague, a piece of work that is still growing. today, do one act of 畜 for it, plain feeding: water, a meal, time, the tool that it needs. then apply the three “and not”. do not speak of it as yours. do not mention what you did or wait for thanks. and do not decide for it what it should become. notice which of the three you break first, and how soon. the passage says that creatures honour what rears them without being told to. see whether that is true of the thing that you tend when you stop asking for it.

生 / 有: to give and to hold. each of the three lines joins two acts that people take as one: 生 and 有, to give birth and to own; 為 and 恃, to do and to count on it; 長 and 宰, to lead and to carve up. in common life the second follows the first as its pay. the refrain cuts the link with 不, and it keeps the first half. this matters. the text does not favour not-doing over doing. dao gives birth; de rears; six verbs of care follow. nor does it call all keeping bad: a herdsman keeps the herd. it describes a giving that is complete, because no claim is held back from it. a one-sided reading takes “does not possess” as the whole teaching and turns it into distance. then the birth and the rearing are lost. where in your work does the doing end and the claim begin?

to give life to a thing and to work for it gives no right to own it.. to give life to a thing and to work for it gives no right to own it. do you agree when it is your own child, your own work, your own idea? take the hardest case, not the easy one. where did you learn what a maker is owed? was there a ledger in your family, spoken or unspoken, of who had done what for whom? now hold the opposite: what i make is mine, and a claim on it is fair pay for the care i gave. stay there for a few minutes. what feelings come, and do they surprise you? is there someone whose claim on you still rests on what they once gave? how does that shape what you think here?

real honour arises of itself, and honour that has to be commanded is of another kind.. real honour arises of itself, and honour that has to be commanded is of another kind. is that so in your experience? think of someone you honour, and ask whether anyone told you to. when have you wanted thanks or respect and asked for it, openly or by a hint? what did you fear would happen if you did not ask? take the other view: people forget, and respect that is not required soon fades; a parent, a teacher, an office has to insist on it. hold it as true. what do you notice? which view matches the way you were raised, and which matches the way you now live? why might the gap be worth a look?

畜 the dark field. two parts, one above the other. the lower part is 田, a field. the shuowen says of it 樹穀曰田, “where grain is planted is called 田”, and reads the cross inside the square as the raised paths that divide the plots. you know it from 男, a man: 田 with 力, strength, the one who works the field. the upper part is 玄, “dark”, the same character that ends this passage in 玄德. the shuowen’s entry for 畜 is short. it defines the word as 田畜也 and then quotes: 玄田爲畜, “玄 and 田 make 畜”. a dark field. why dark? one old explanation is the black, rich soil of land that animals have grazed and dunged. modern scholars doubt the story; some see in the early form a cord or a gut above the field, since 玄 is related to 幺, a fine thread, and take the whole as tethered animals or stored produce. hold the dictionary’s reading as the traditional one. with the grass sign on top the same graph is 蓄, to store up. as a noun, read chu, it is livestock; the “six 畜” are horse, ox, sheep, pig, dog, and fowl. here it is the verb of de. the passage begins with de under a sign of darkness in a field and ends with dark de. the first character of the title, 玄, has been inside the herdsman’s word all along. ten strokes: five above and five below. the top is 玄, pressed flat. a dot; a long horizontal that reaches wider than the field below; then the thread in three strokes: one that falls to the left and turns back to the right, a second that does the same lower down, and a final dot. the two turns must be small and tight, like a twist of cord. then 田: the left side; the top and right side in one stroke; the inner horizontal; the inner vertical; and the base that closes the square. watch the second stroke, the long horizontal. it is the lid of the character. the field sits under its centre, a little narrower, so that the whole has the outline of a roofed granary. in seal script the upper part is written with rounded loops, like a twist of thread.

育 a child, head down. compare the top of this character with 子, a child. the shuowen says that the top is 子 turned upside down. it lists the inverted form as a graph of its own and defines it 不順忽出也。从到子, “to come out suddenly; an inverted 子”. the dictionary gives this a moral turn, an unruly son. modern scholars commonly read the picture more simply: a baby at the moment of birth, which comes into the world head first. the lower part is 月, which here is the form that 肉, flesh, takes inside characters; the shuowen treats it as the sound. the same inverted child is in 棄, to abandon: there the shuowen sees two hands that push a newborn out in a basket. and it is in 流, to flow, at the upper right. the dictionary’s definition of 育 is 養子使作善也, “to raise a child so that it does good”, with a quotation from the documents. so the word covers the whole span from the first minute to the grown person: to bear, to nurse, to bring up, to educate. in this passage it is the fourth thing done for the ten thousand creatures: 長之育之, grows them, raises them. every creature in the count was once in the position that this character draws. eight strokes: four for the child and four for the flesh. a dot at the top centre, then a horizontal. the third stroke falls to the left from the middle of the horizontal and turns back to the right; the fourth is a dot that closes the small triangle. these four strokes are the head-down infant, and they should be compact, wider than tall. then 月: a left stroke that comes down and curves slightly outward at the foot; the top and right side in one stroke that ends in a hook; and two short horizontals inside, which touch the left side and not the right. watch the proportion. the lower part is narrow and tall and stands under the centre of the wide top, so the character has the shape of a mushroom, or of a mother’s arms above a standing child.

宰 under the roof, a knife. the top is 宀, a roof, the sign of houses: 家, a household; 室, a room; 安, a woman under a roof, “at peace”. the bottom is 辛. the shuowen explains 辛 in several ways; in this entry it says 辛，辠也, “辛 is crime”, and many modern scholars take the old form as a chisel or a short blade, the tool that marked the faces of convicts. with that the dictionary reads the whole: 辠人在屋下執事者, “a convicted person who does service under a roof”. a household slave. the work of such a servant in a great house was the kitchen and the slaughter of animals for the rites, and 宰 came to mean to butcher and to carve. the one who cut and shared the sacrificial meat held a place of trust, and so the same word rose through the house: steward, head of the household staff, and at last the chief minister of a state. the history of the word is a history of power in three steps: a bound servant, a man with a knife, a ruler. the passage uses it for what the way does not do. it leads and does not 宰. for 辛 in another role, see 辯 in passage 45, where two of them are parties in a lawsuit. ten strokes. the roof first: a dot at the top centre, a short stroke at the left edge, and a horizontal that ends in a hook down at the right. then 辛 in seven strokes. a dot under the roof; a horizontal; then two small strokes that lean toward each other, a dot on the left and a short left-falling stroke on the right. next come two horizontals, and the first of them is the longest line in the character; it reaches out past the roof on both sides. watch the tenth stroke: a vertical that starts at the long horizontal and goes straight down through the last horizontal to a point. it is drawn last and it is the blade. it must hang plumb, with nothing beside it, and a good hand lets it thin toward the end like a needle.

52 · return to the mother. the world has a beginning, / taken as the world’s mother. / having got the mother, thereby know the child. / having known the child, go back and keep to the mother: / until the body sinks, no danger. / block the openings, / shut the gates: / to the end of life, no wearing out. / open the openings, / add to the business: / to the end of life, no rescue. / to see the small is called clear sight. / to keep to the soft is called strength. / use the light, / and go back again to the clear sight. / leave the body no calamity. / this is to practise the constant. three movements, each with the same shape. first: the world has a beginning, its mother; get the mother, know the child, and go back to keep the mother. second: two matched triplets on the openings and the gates. close them, and life is not worn out. open them and succeed in affairs, and life is beyond rescue. third: two definitions, of clear sight and of strength; then the light that is used and brought home. in each movement something goes out, child, business, light, and the instruction is the word 復, “again, back”, which appears twice. the close gives the whole a name: practising the constant. the passage begins with the mother of the world and ends inside one body, and it treats these as one subject. this is one of the book’s clearest texts on practice, and its instruction is a single gesture: return. attention is born from a quiet source, goes out through the senses into the world of things, and usually does not come back; it goes on to the next thing, and the next. the passage does not forbid the going out. it says: know the child, use the light. it adds the half that is forgotten. after knowing, come back to what knows. closing the gates is the same gesture made with the body. the fruit is described in negatives, not worn out, no danger, no calamity left behind, because what is gained is not a new experience. it is the end of a leak. the mother was never far. one was only facing the other way. for a person with responsibilities the second triplet is the uncomfortable one: 濟其事, to bring one’s affairs to success, is set on the side that ends past rescue. the text does not say that work is bad. it describes someone who is all outlet: every channel open, every matter answered, a life of pure response. such a person is effective for years and at the end is past help, because nothing was ever brought home. wang bi reads the lines on light as advice to a ruler: let your clarity guide people, and do not turn it on them as a searchlight. and 見小曰明 is a rule that any leader can use. the useful sight is of small things, early: the first sign of trouble, the quiet person, the detail before it has grown. 守柔曰強 is a fact of the body before it is a philosophy. the shuowen’s 柔 is green wood that bends, and its true “strong” is the bow. a joint that is held soft can take a load from any angle; a locked joint has one angle and then breaks. stand with knees and elbows a little bent and let someone press on your arm: the soft arm sends the force to the ground, and the stiff arm sends it to the shoulder. the gates have a bodily sense too. close the mouth and breathe through the nose. let the eyes rest. the energy that goes out all day in talk and looking stays in, and one finishes the hour less tired. that is 終身不勤 on the scale of an afternoon. the mother and child are literal in every field. a river is the child of its spring, and the water that reaches the sea comes back as rain. a tree sends out leaves, the leaves fall, and the tree feeds on them at the root; wang bi’s root and tip are a real tree. a bird flies out from the nest and returns at dusk. the character 習, to practise, is that bird, young, trying its wings again and again near home. the rhythm of all living things is out and back, and what only goes out, a stream cut off from its source, a branch off the tree, lasts for a short time. the passage asks a human life to keep the same rhythm that a day and a year already have. do the exercise of ten breaths with the gates shut, three times today, each before an ordinary task. in the evening, look back on the day for one case of 見小: a small thing that you noticed early. and look for one place where you went out and did not come home: an hour in which attention ran from thing to thing. do not scold yourself for it. only notice, at the end of that hour, how tired you were.

始: the beginning is written with a woman. 始 is “beginning”. its left part is 女, a woman, and the shuowen defines the word in a way that few readers expect: 女之初也, “the first of a woman”. commentators differ on what that means, a girl’s first stage of life or the first-born, and the right part, 台, gives the sound. so when the passage says that the world has a 始 and that it serves as the world’s 母, the two words are already kin on the page: both are built on 女. the first passage of the book set them side by side: what has no name is the 始 of heaven and earth; what has a name is the 母 of the ten thousand things. here the two are joined in one line. a beginning, in this language, is not a point on a line of time. it is nearer to a womb.

母: more than a figure of speech. the book calls the way “mother” five times: of the ten thousand things (1), the one on whom the speaker alone feeds (20), of the world (25, and here), and of the state (59). english readers tend to file this as a metaphor for “source” and move on. two frames get in the way. one is the father and creator of the bible, beside whom a cosmic mother sounds like a pagan goddess. the other is abstraction, which turns her into a “principle”. the chinese is neither. a mother is the one from whose body the child came, who is still alive, and to whom the child can go back. the whole passage rests on that last fact. one cannot return to a first cause. one can return to a mother. see the plate for 母.

mother first, then child. 既得其母，以知其子: “having got the mother, by that know the child”. the order goes against a habit of the modern mind. we expect to study the children, the many things, and to reason back to their source: from data to law. the line runs the other way. get the mother first, and the children are known through her. wang bi glosses the pair as root and branch-tip. then the passage adds a second step that is easy to miss: 既知其子，復守其母. having known the child, come back. knowledge of the world is allowed and even expected, and it is not the place to stay. who is the child? the ten thousand things; the world of affairs; and the reader, who is also a child of that mother.

守: “keeping” became a word for meditation. 守 is to guard, to keep watch, to hold a post. the graph is 宀, a roof, over 寸, a hand; the shuowen defines it as 守官也, to keep one’s office, and says that the hand stands for rule and measure. a sentry 守 a gate; an official 守 a city. the laozi turns the word inward and uses it often: keep to the centre (5), keep to stillness (16), know the male and keep to the female (28), keep to the soft (this passage). in the religious daoism of the han and after, 守 became a technical term. 守一, “guarding the one”, is one of the oldest names for meditation in china: the practitioner holds attention at one place as a guard holds a pass. this passage is among its sources. note 復, “again, back”: the keeping is a return.

沒身: until the body goes under. 沒 has water at its left, and the shuowen gives it one word: 沈也, “to sink”. it is used for a diver, for a thing that is covered by a flood, for the sun that goes down. 沒身 is then “until the body sinks from sight”: to the end of one’s life. english “all your life” or “to the end of your days” keeps the time and loses the water. 身 is the living body, as in passage 44. the promise, 不殆, “no danger”, is also from 44, and the full phrase 沒身不殆 closes passage 16. three times in this passage the measure is a lifetime: 沒身 once and 終身 twice. the text does not speak of what comes after. its horizon is the whole of one life in a body, with nothing left over.

兌: an opening, a mouth, a trigram. 兌 is a short word with a long reach. here it means an opening or hole; old commentators, and legge after them, read it as the mouth, or as all the openings of the head. the shuowen defines it as 說也, a word that covers “to speak” and “to be pleased”. and 兌 is the name of one of the eight trigrams of the changes, ☱, whose image is a lake and whose attributes include the mouth and tongue, speech, and joy. so a reader of the time heard several things in 塞其兌: stop the hole; shut the mouth; and close the channel of pleasure and exchange. in later chinese the word means “to exchange”, as money is exchanged. the opening is where things pass out and in. wang bi calls it the place where desires for affairs are born. see the plate.

塞其兌，閉其門: lines the book repeats. these six characters come again, word for word, in passage 56, where they lead on to “soften the glare” and “become one with the dust”. they are a formula, and they may be older than either passage; the guodian slips are reported to have this middle section and not the rest. 門, the gate, pairs with 兌 as a larger opening with a smaller. the han feizi called the body’s openings the doors and windows of the spirit (see passage 47), and later practice took the line as an instruction for sitting: lips closed, eyes lowered, hearing turned in, so that breath and attention do not leak away. it is not a rule to be deaf and dumb in daily life. it marks a direction. for some part of each day the traffic at the gates stops, and what is inside is no longer spent.

不勤: not “idle”. 勤 is toil; the shuowen says 勞也, and the graph has 力, strength, on the right. in modern chinese it is a virtue, “diligent”, and a hasty reader may take 終身不勤 as a reproach: a whole life without effort. the classical word names the cost, not the virtue: to labour until one is spent. 不勤 is “not worn out”. passage 6 uses it of the valley spirit: 用之不勤, “use it, and it is not exhausted”. so the line promises that the one who closes the openings will not be used up, to the end of life. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write 堇, which editors read as the same word. wang bi says: 無事永逸, “no business, and ease for good”. what in your day wears you out: the work, or the open gates?

濟其事: to ford, to succeed, to add. 濟 has water at its left. its root sense is to cross a river, and from that to get a thing across: to bring it off, to help, to supply what is lacking. 濟其事 is “to carry your affairs through” or “to add to your affairs”. in any other book of the age this is praise. a capable minister 濟 the business of the state. here it is the second half of a warning: open the openings, be effective in affairs, and to the end of life there is 不救, “no rescue”. 救 is to save, and also to stop a harm, as one stops a fire. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to end the line with another word, 棘, “thorns”, which editors explain in several ways. the passage does not offer a middle path between the two triplets. one closes and is not spent. the other opens and succeeds, and is past help.

曰明: a definition against common sense. 見小曰明: “to see the small is called 明”. the form a 曰 b, “a is called b”, is how the book defines its terms, and its definitions usually overturn the common use. common sense says that a clear eye sees great things and far. the text says: 明 is to see what is small, the first sign, the thing before it has grown. passage 36 calls this 微明, “the subtle light”; passage 64 tells us to act on a thing while it is not yet there. other definitions of 明 in the book: to know the constant (16, 55); to know oneself (33). the shuowen records the character in an older form, a moon beside a window. the modern form is sun and moon side by side. wang bi makes the line political: the work of rule is not in what is large.

強: “strong” is a borrowed insect. 守柔曰強: “to keep to the soft is called strong”. look up the two characters in the shuowen and each has a surprise. 柔, soft, is 木, wood, under 矛, a spear; the definition is 木曲直也, “wood that can be bent and straightened”. softness, for the dictionary, is not weakness. it is the quality of green wood that takes a curve and does not break. 強, strong, is defined as 蚚也: a kind of insect, with 虫 inside it. the word “strong” only borrowed this graph for its sound. the proper character for strength, says the dictionary, is 彊: 弓有力也, “a bow that has force”. so the two halves of the line are closer than they seem. the soft is the bendable wood, and true strength is the bow that is made of it. passage 76 says the rest: the living are soft, and the dead are stiff.

光 and 明: two lights. english has “light” and “brightness” and uses them loosely. the chinese line depends on a difference. 光 is light that goes out from a source: the shuowen explains the graph as 火在人上, “fire above a person”, a torch held up. 明 is the state of being lit and clear, the capacity itself. 用其光，復歸其明: use the beam, and then come home to the lamp. the same structure governs the first part of the passage: know the child, and go back to the mother. light that is sent out is a child of the clear state within. it may be used; attention may go out to the world. but a light that only shines outward is spent, and the book distrusts glare: soften the 光 (4, 56); be bright and do not dazzle (58). when you have finished looking at something, where does your attention go?

無遺身殃: nothing bad left behind. 遺 is to leave behind, to lose, to bequeath. 殃 is calamity; the shuowen glosses it with one word, 咎也, the “fault” of passage 46, and the graph has 歹, bare bone, at its left, like 殆 and 死. 無遺身殃 is “do not leave the body a calamity”, or “leave no calamity to yourself”. the verb suggests an inheritance. each act that sends the light out and does not bring it home leaves something for the body to receive later, as an heir receives a debt. the silk texts are reported to make the line a prohibition, with 毋, “do not”. passage 9 used the same verb of wealth and pride: 自遺其咎, they bequeath their own ruin. the line is modest, like the close of passage 44. it promises no bliss. it says that nothing bad is left for later.

習常 or 襲常: to practise it, or to wear it. our text ends 是為習常: “this is to 習 the constant”. 習 is to practise by repeating; the shuowen says 數飛也, “to fly again and again”, the fledgling at the edge of the nest. see the plate. the mawangdui silk texts, as reported, and several old editions write a different character of the same sound: 襲常. 襲 is a garment word. the shuowen defines it as a robe of a certain cut, and as a verb it means to put on a layer of clothing, to cover, and so to continue or inherit. 襲常 is then “to wear the constant”, to be clothed in it, or to carry it on. passage 27 has a sister phrase, 襲明, “to wear the light”. the two readings give two pictures of one thing. in one it is done again each day, like wing-beats. in the other it is worn next to the skin.

wang bi: do not leave the root to chase the tip. on mother and child: 母，本也；子，末也。得本以知末，不舍本以逐末也. “the mother is the root; the child is the branch-tip. get the root and by it know the tip; do not let go of the root to chase the tip.” 本 and 末 are his master terms, and each is a tree with a mark, at the foot and at the top. on the openings: 兌，事欲之所由生；門，事欲之所由從也. “the opening is that from which desires for affairs are born; the gate is that through which they go.” on the light, he reads as a statesman: 用其光 is 顯道以去民迷, “show the way, to remove the people’s confusion”, and 復歸其明 is 不明察也, “do not scrutinise with sharp sight”. the ruler’s light may guide. it must not be turned on the people as a lamp of inspection. compare his long note to passage 49.

legge supplies nostrils. legge begins with a bracket: “(the tao) which originated all under the sky”. the chinese has no subject, only “the world has a beginning”; he has added the cause and the verb of origin. for the openings he writes: “let him keep his mouth closed, and shut up the portals (of his nostrils)”. the nostrils are his own gloss. he had read of daoist breath control, and he puts it into the line as an odd rule of hygiene; later, the person with the open mouth “(spends his breath)”. the passage becomes advice on talking too much. at the end he changes to rhymed verse, bright, blight, sight, and takes the last phrase as “hides the unchanging from men’s sight”, which follows the reading 襲 in the sense “to cover”. his “children” are told what they “should be”: a moral word that the plain 知, “know”, does not have.

the old copies. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to agree with our text in structure and to differ in single words. the collated text has 啓, “to open”, for 開: a known case of the taboo on the name of emperor jing of han, liu qi, 啓, whose name later scribes avoided. it has 堇 for 勤 and 棘 for 救 (see the notes on those lines), 毋 for 無 in the line on calamity, and 襲常 at the end (see 習常). the guodian bamboo slips, a century and more older, are reported to contain only the six short lines on the openings, with the gate named first. if that is the older state, then the mother and child and the two lights were joined to the formula later, by an editor who saw that all three say one thing: go out, and come back.

shut the gates for ten breaths. sit. close the mouth and let the tongue rest. lower the eyes or close them. for ten slow breaths, let sounds come and do not go out to meet them; let thoughts of business come and do not add to them. that is all. then open the eyes and use them: look at one thing with full attention, a leaf, a face, a line of text. when you have seen it, do not go at once to the next thing. come back for one breath to the one who was looking. out, and home: the child, and the mother; the light, and the clear sight. do this three times today, at the start of three ordinary tasks. the passage calls the habit practising the constant.

柔 / 強: the soft that is called strong. 柔 and 強, soft and strong, are a pair that the book comes back to often. common speech sets them apart. this line joins them with 曰, “is called”: to keep to the soft is the strong. it does not say that soft is good and strong is bad. if it did, it could not use 強 as its word of praise. the shuowen’s pictures show how each holds the other: green wood that bends, and the bow that is made of it. the text leans toward the soft, and the lean is a correction. the age prized hard force, and the book points at what that age did not see. the soft side turns too. wood that bends and has no spring is no bow. and passage 55 uses the same form of line with 強 as a warning. which of the two sides do you trust less?

塞 / 開: shut and open, out and back. the middle lines set 塞 and 閉, to block and to shut, against 開, to open. the two results look like a verdict: shut is safe, and open is past rescue. read with the rest, they are two halves of one movement. the first lines say to know the child, and the later lines say to use the light. both are a going out, and the passage does not cancel them. it adds 復, “back”. an opening that can also close is a gate. the trouble named in the second triplet is an opening that has lost its other half. so the text favours the closing, because people do it less. closing turns as well. a gate that stays shut is a wall, and then the mother has no child to know. what do you open with ease, and what do you find hard to shut?

a life with every opening open wears out, and a life that returns to its source does not.. a life with every opening open wears out, and a life that returns to its source does not. do you agree? look at one recent week of your own before you answer. what do you believe about being available, busy, and quick to respond? whose approval did that belief first win you? hold the opposite for a while: life is for going out, and a person who shuts the gates has stopped living before the end. what comes with that thought: energy, guilt, a fear of missing something? when you are told to withdraw and rest, what in you objects? when you are told to engage more, what objects? which voice is older?

to keep to the soft is the real strength.. to keep to the soft is the real strength. has this been true in your life? name one time when yielding held, and one time when it did not. what were you taught about softness as a child, and by whom? was it a danger, a duty, or a gift? now take the plain opposite: strength is hardness, and the soft are pushed aside. believe it for a few minutes. what memories come up to support it? what do you feel toward people who are harder than you, and toward people who are softer? what do those feelings say about the side that you have not owned? why might it help to know which side you were given, and which side you chose?

母 the woman with two dots. start from 女, a woman. the shuowen calls 女 a picture, and the common explanation of the early form is a figure who kneels with her hands crossed in front. now put two dots inside the body of the figure, and you have 母. the shuowen says: 从女，象褱子形。一曰象乳子也. “from 女; it shows her holding a child. another view: it shows her suckling a child.” the second view is the one that most scholars follow: the two dots are the breasts. a mother, in this script, is a woman drawn as one who can feed. the dictionary’s definition is a pun on a word of like sound: 母，牧也, “a mother is one who tends”, the verb for a herdsman with cattle. passage 51 has just used the herdsman’s word, 畜, for what de does. take the two dots and join them into one stroke, and the graph is 毋, “do not”, a different word that borrowed the mother’s form. put 母 under a plant-like top and you have 每, “each”; put water beside that and you have 海, the sea. the laozi gives this character to the way itself. the passage says that there is a mother of the world, and that a person can go back and keep to her. the two dots say what for. five strokes. the first comes down on the left with a slight lean, turns at the bottom, and runs to the right: the left side and floor of the figure. the second starts at the top left, goes to the right, turns, comes down the right side, and ends in a hook that points inward. together these two make a leaning, open box. third, the upper dot. fourth, a long horizontal that passes through the whole box and out on both sides: the arms. fifth, the lower dot, under the horizontal. watch the two dots. they are not alike: each is pressed and lifted in the same direction, one above the line and one below, and they must sit on one slanting axis. the box leans to the right, the horizontal holds it level, and the dots give it a centre.

兌 the open mouth, and its family. three layers. at the bottom, 儿: the two legs of a person. in the middle, 口: a mouth. on top, two short strokes that part, like 八. the common explanation of the old form is a person with the mouth open and breath or words that spread out above it: someone who speaks, or laughs. the shuowen treats the upper part as a sound element and gives the meaning in one word: 說也. that word is itself the best commentary, because 說 is 兌 with 言, speech, at its side, and it has two readings. read shuo, it is to speak, to explain. read yue, it is to be pleased, later written 悅 with a heart. speech and pleasure: the two things that come out of an open mouth. the family is large, and the shuowen marks 兌 as the sound in each. 稅, with grain: a tax, what is drawn out of the harvest. 脫, with flesh: to shed, to slip off. 銳, with metal: a sharp point; passage 56 says to blunt it, straight after it says to block the 兌. something leaves or comes to a point in every one. so when the passage says 塞其兌, “block the opening”, the character shows what kind of opening: the one through which a person pours out. seven strokes. first the two small strokes at the top: a dot on the left that leans to the right, and a short stroke on the right that falls to the left, so that the two lean toward each other and do not touch. then the mouth in three strokes: left side, top and right side in one, base. keep it small and square under the two strokes. then the legs. the sixth stroke falls from under the mouth to the lower left. watch the seventh: it comes down, bends, runs out to the right, and ends in an upward hook. it is the longest stroke and it carries the character. the upper two layers are tight and the legs spread wide beneath them, like a person who stands with feet apart to call out.

習 wings, again and again. the top is 羽, feathers: two wings side by side, each with its quills. the shuowen calls it a picture of the long feathers of a bird. the bottom is written 白, “white”, in the modern form; scholars debate what it was at first, and some early forms seem to have a sun, 日, there. the shuowen’s definition is what matters: 習，數飛也, “to fly again and again”. a young bird at the edge of the nest beats its wings, lifts, drops back, and tries once more. an old calendar text says of the sixth month: 鷹乃學習, “the young hawks now learn and practise”, and those last two characters are the modern chinese word for “to study”. confucius opens the analects with the same pair: to learn, and at due times to 習 it. from flying practice came practice of any kind, then habit, custom, what one is used to. a related word of the same sound is 襲, to put on a garment, which other texts read here. in this passage the thing practised is 常, the constant: the going out and coming home of the mother and child, of the light and the clear sight. the image fits closely. a fledgling’s practice is a short flight that always ends back at the nest. eleven strokes: six for the wings, five for the base. each wing is three strokes: a horizontal that turns and comes straight down; then a dot inside, which points down to the right; then a second small stroke inside that rises to the right. write the left wing, then the right wing, and make them twins. they stand side by side at the top and take the full width. then the base: a short stroke that falls to the left from under the middle of the wings; the left side of the box; the top and right side in one stroke; a horizontal inside; and the bottom line. watch the four small strokes inside the wings. they are the quills. in each wing the dot and the rising stroke lean toward each other, and all four must be light and quick. the box below is narrower than the wings, as a body is narrower than a wingspan.

53 · the robbers’ boast. suppose i had a grain of knowledge / and walked on the great road: / only straying would i fear. / the great road is very level, / yet people love the shortcuts. / the court is very well swept; / the fields are very weedy; / the granaries are very empty. / patterned silks are worn, / sharp swords at the belt; / glutted with drink and food, / with goods in surplus. / this is called the robbers’ boast. / not the way, indeed! the passage has two parts and a cry. in the first, an “i” with a grain of knowledge walks the great road and fears only to stray; the road is level, and people prefer the shortcut. in the second, with no connecting word, the camera turns to a state. three lines with 甚, “very”: court swept, fields in weeds, granaries empty. four lines on persons, each of three or four characters: figured silk, sharp swords, too much food and drink, goods left over. then the verdict in four characters, 盜夸, and the cry, 非道也哉. the order of the list is exact: from the building, to the land, to the store, to the body of the courtier, its clothes, its weapon, and its stomach. the first part states a principle; the second shows where the shortcuts lead. the level road is hard to stay on for a strange reason: nothing is wrong with it. it is flat and open and has no drama. the mind loves a shortcut, a trick, a faster way to be someone, and each shortcut needs upkeep. read the second part as a picture of one person. the court is the self that others see, and it is kept very well swept. the fields are the plain, unseen sources of a life: rest, attention, honest work, the people who are close. the granary is what is in reserve. when all effort goes to the front, the fields go to weeds and the store runs down, and the person dresses the emptiness in pattern. the speaker’s fear in the third line is then precise. it is not a fear of enemies. it is a fear of one’s own turning aside. the reading for a leader is the literal one, and it should not be softened into a parable about organisations. the passage says that a ruling class that lives well while the farms fail is a band of thieves, and it says so in the language of law. any person who holds office can use its test, which needs no theory. look at three places. is the headquarters very fine? are the fields, the places where the real work is done, short of hands and care? are the reserves empty? if all three are “very”, the comforts at the top are not a reward. they are the missing grain. the han feizi adds the warning of the lead pipe: those below will play the tune that the top plays. 蕪 is what land does when it is left: grass and scrub return within a season, and in a few years the field is gone. a farm is a daily agreement between people and a piece of ground, and it lapses the moment the people are called away. the passage reads the health of a society from its land, as an ecologist reads a watershed: the state of the fields and of the stores tells the truth about the court, whatever the court says. there is also the image of the road. water takes the level way and reaches the sea. animals make paths that follow the ground. the great road of the passage is level in that sense. it goes where the land lets it go, and the shortcut is the line that someone in a hurry cut across the slope. do the exercise of the weedy field: name your swept court, your neglected field, and your empty store, and move one hour from the first to the second. then keep the third line in mind for a day as a single question, asked at each choice: is this the level road, or am i turning off because the turn looks quicker? you will not always know. the speaker of the passage does not claim to know much either: only a grain.

使我介然有知: a modest and ironic “i”. 使我 is “suppose i were made to”, a hypothesis. 介然 is the hard word. 介 is small, a mere particle, as in 纖介, a hair’s breadth; so 介然有知 is “to have knowledge in the smallest degree”. other readers take 介 as “firm, resolute”: if i had solid knowledge. the rendering follows the first, an old gloss recorded by lu deming; heshang gong reads the opposite, “great”, and wang bi simply repeats the word. the speaker is one of the rare “i” voices in the book, and the tone is dry. this “i” claims almost nothing: grant me a grain of sense, no more. then the passage shows what that grain is enough to see: a level road, people who leave it, and a court that eats the country. the implied judgment on those in power is sharp. they lack even this small amount.

大道: here the way is a road. 道 is first a road, and this passage is the place in the book where the first meaning is most alive. every key word of the opening is a road word. 行, to walk. 大道, the great road: the main highway, wide enough for carts. 夷, level. 徑, a footpath. and 施, on one reading, to veer off. a warring states reader knew such highways well; states built them for armies and grain, and footpaths ran off them across the fields. english must print “the way” with a capital, or “the road” without one, and each choice loses half. in chinese the speaker is on an actual road and on the way in the same four characters. the last line of the passage will play on the word once more: see 非道.

唯施是畏: fear of acting, or of straying. “only 施 is to be feared.” the grammar is emphatic: 唯 … 是 puts the object first. but what is 施? its common meanings are to apply, to carry out, to bestow, to display. wang bi reads it so, as 施為: the one thing to fear on the great road is to set things up and do them, wu wei stated from the other side. legge follows with “a boastful display”. the qing scholar wang niansun proposed that 施 stands here for 迤, “to go slanting”, a road that bends away: the fear is of leaving the highway. that fits the images before and after it, and we render “straying”. the two readings meet. in this book, to act with purpose upon the world is the main way to leave the road. the shuowen’s own entry for 施 is a flag that waves.

夷: level; and the people of the east. 夷 is “level, flat, smooth”. the shuowen says 平也, and then adds a second fact: 从大从弓。東方之人也, “from 大, a person, and 弓, a bow; the people of the east”. the same word named the non-zhou peoples of the eastern coast, drawn as a person with a bow, and it was later used for foreigners in general; nineteenth-century chinese documents used it of the british, who objected by treaty. how one graph serves both senses is not settled. in the laozi it is always the first: the way that is 夷, level, looks rough (41); what is looked at and not seen is named 夷 (14). a level road asks nothing of the walker. it has no climb, no view, and no interest. that may be why the next line follows. see the plate.

徑: the shortcut. 徑 is a path for feet. the shuowen says 步道也, “a walking path”: a track across the fields, too narrow for a cart, which saves distance. it had a moral colour in the speech of the time. a disciple of confucius praises an honest man in these words: 行不由徑, “when he walks he does not go by the shortcut”, and he never comes to my office except on public business. the shortcut is the private way, the clever way, the way that gets there first. so 民好徑 is not a remark on rural footpaths. people love the quicker path, and the great road, which is level and open to all, stands empty. who are the 民? the word is usually “the common people”; some editions have 人, “persons”, and what follows shows that those at court are meant most of all. the silk texts are reported to add a second 甚, “very much”, and to end the line with a different word, 解.

朝甚除: three lines, three “very”. 朝甚除，田甚蕪，倉甚虛. three lines of three characters with 甚, “very, too much”, in the middle of each; passage 29 says that the sage gets rid of 甚. 朝 is the court, the place of the morning audience. 除 is first the steps of a palace hall, says the shuowen, and as a verb “to clear, to sweep away”. wang bi takes it as praise turned sour: 朝，宮室也。除，潔好也, “the court means the palace buildings; 除 means clean and fine”. the palace is spotless, and the fields are in weeds. some later scholars read 除 as “corrupt, defiled”, which gives three evils in a row. the first reading is the sharper, because it makes a cause. wang bi states it: set up the one, and a crowd of harms is born. the labour and grain that keep the court swept are the labour and grain that are missing in the fields.

蕪: grass over nothing. 蕪 is 艹, grass, over 無. the shuowen glosses it 薉也, “choked with weeds”, and treats 無 as the sound. a reader of this book cannot help seeing more. 無 is the great word of the laozi: not-having, the nothing that makes the wheel, the pot, and the room of use (11). here it sits under the grass radical, and the nothing is of the other kind: a field in which nothing has been planted and where the wild growth has come back. why are the fields in weeds? in the warring states the answer was known to all. the men were away, on campaign or on labour service for walls, roads, and palaces, and they were away in the farming season. a weedy field in this passage is not a sign of lazy farmers. it is a sign of a busy state. see the plate.

虛: the book’s good word in a bad place. 虛, “empty”, is one of the laozi’s words of praise. empty the heart (3). the space between heaven and earth is empty and is not exhausted (5). reach the utmost emptiness (16). in this line it is used for an empty granary, and it means hunger. the book knows the difference between its two kinds of nothing, and it does not romanticise want. the hollow of a bowl is of use because the bowl is whole. a granary is of use when there is grain in it, and its emptiness in spring before the harvest is death for a village. the shuowen defines 虛 by an image of loss: 大丘也, “a great mound”, the word for an abandoned site, later written 墟, ruins. emptiness in the heart of a ruler fills the granaries. emptiness in the granaries comes from a ruler whose heart is full.

文綵: the cloth of rank. 文 is a pattern of crossed lines; the shuowen says 錯畫也。象交文. 綵 is silk of many colours. 文綵 are figured silks: woven or embroidered cloth with designs, the most labour-heavy product of the age. in a zhou court, pattern was law. rank fixed the colours and emblems that a person could wear, and a robe was read like a badge. the word 文 then grew to mean writing, culture, refinement, all that the school of confucius valued as the ornament that makes people civilised. so the line has two targets. the first is plain luxury: one robe took a household of women months to weave, while the farmers who fed them wore hemp. the second is 文 itself, pattern laid over an empty store. the silk texts are reported to write the simpler 采, “colours”.

帶利劍: the sword at the belt. the long sword was a new thing in this period. earlier nobles fought from chariots with the dagger-axe and the bow; a short bronze sword was a side weapon. in the warring states, bronze swords grew long and fine, iron ones appeared, and the sword became the personal weapon and the mark of a gentleman. the shuowen, which writes the word in a variant form, defines it by the custom in this line: 人所帶兵也, “the weapon that a person wears at the belt”. the shiji notes under the year 409 bce that the state of qin first ordered its officials to wear swords. 利 is “sharp”, the blade in the grain of passage 11. so the courtier of this passage is dressed in the latest style: figured silk, and at the waist an edge that is kept keen. against whom does a man at court need a sharp sword?

有餘: surplus, and whose it is. 厭 is to be sated, full past wanting; the same graph means “to be sick of”. 餘 is what is left over; the shuowen glosses it with 饒也, “abundance”, the word that it used for 益 in passage 48. 財貨有餘 is “wealth and goods in surplus”. a modern reader hears success: a surplus is good management. the laozi uses 有餘 as a technical term, and passage 77 shows it in motion. heaven’s way takes from those who have surplus and gives to those who have not enough, like the bending of a bow. the way of people does the reverse: 損不足以奉有餘, “it takes from those who lack, to offer to those who have surplus”. surplus, as passage 77 sees it, is somebody’s shortage, moved. the list in this passage runs from the empty granary to the full table in four lines, and the reader is left to connect the two.

盜夸 or 盜竽: a boast, or a pipe. our text names such people 盜夸. 盜 is a robber. 夸 is “extravagance”, 奢也 in the shuowen, and “to boast”: so “robber-braggarts”, or “the robbers’ boast”, theft that shows itself off. the han feizi has a different last word, 盜竽, and the mawangdui silk text is reported to agree. the 竽 was a large mouth-organ of reed pipes; the shuowen gives it thirty-six reeds. the han feizi explains. the 竽 is the leader among instruments: when it sounds first, bells and zithers follow, and when it sings, all the players join. so when great villains rise, the common people take up the tune, and small robbers answer. the court in its silks is the lead pipe of a band of thieves. the two graphs sounded alike. one image is of display. the other is of example: what the top does, the rest play.

非道也哉: robbers and the way. the passage ends on a cry of four characters: 非道也哉, “this is not the way, indeed!” read it aloud in modern chinese with the line before: dao kua … fei dao. 盜, robber, and 道, way, are the same syllable today, and the close sounds like “robbery … not dao”. was it a pun for the author? we must be careful. in the old rhyme groups the two words are neighbours and not twins: 道 belongs to the 幽 group and 盜 to the 宵 group, with the same kind of initial. so the first hearers had a near echo, which mandarin has since made exact. the surer music is the rhyme. 除, 蕪, 虛, 餘, and the final 夸 or 竽 all belong to one old group, 魚, so that the list of court, fields, granaries, and surplus strikes one sound five times, and 道 at the very end falls outside it.

the rulers are the thieves. this is the most direct social attack in the book, and it was a view shared across the schools. mencius says to a king’s face: there is fat meat in your kitchens and there are fat horses in your stables, the people have the look of hunger, and in the wilds lie the bodies of the starved; this is to lead beasts to eat people. the zhuangzi puts it in one line: the one who steals a belt-hook is executed, and the one who steals a state becomes a lord. the laozi’s own passage 75 gives the mechanism: the people starve because those above eat too much in taxes. the warring states court took grain, cloth, and labour from farming households to pay for armies and display. the text gives this the legal name. everyone knew that 盜 was a crime with a punishment.

wang bi: set up one thing, and harms are born. on the road: 言大道蕩然正平，而民猶尚舍之而不由，好從邪徑. “it says that the great road is broad, straight, and level, and still people leave it and do not go by it; they like to follow crooked paths.” on the three “very” lines he gives a sentence that could stand over the gate of any government office: 朝甚除，則田甚蕪，倉甚虛，設一而眾害生也. “when the court is very fine, the fields are very weedy and the granaries very empty: set up one thing, and a crowd of harms is born.” on the name: 凡物不以其道得之，則皆邪也，邪則盜也. “whatever is not got by its proper way is crooked, and what is crooked is robbery.” he adds a phrase for those in office: 竊位也, they have stolen their position. note his play on 道: to get a thing by its 道.

legge keeps the anger. legge’s first line is his own construction: “if i were suddenly to become known, and (put into a position to) conduct (a government) according to the great tao”. he has read 知 as “be known” and built a scene of a sage called to office; the chinese says only “had some knowledge and walked on the great road”. for 夷 he gives “level and easy”, and “easy” is an addition that makes the way a matter of comfort. for 徑 he has “by-ways”, which misses the point of the shortcut. but in the second half he is plain and strong. the people “pamper themselves in eating and drinking”, and “such (princes) may be called robbers and boasters”. his bracket names the target correctly. a victorian clergyman and oxford professor did not soften that line.

find the weedy field. apply the three lines to something that you help to run: a household, a team, your own week. first find the swept court: the part that is kept fine because it is seen, the front room, the report, the public face. then look for the field that pays for it. what basic work, the kind that feeds everything else, has gone to weeds while the front was polished? sleep, a friendship, the maintenance of a tool, the training of a new person. then look in the granary: what reserve is empty? do not fix all three. take one hour this week from the court and give it to the field. and notice your own shortcut: one place where you take the quick private path past a level public road.

虛 / 餘: the empty and the left over. two words in the list face each other: 虛, empty, for the granaries, and 餘, surplus, for the goods. with them stand the swept court and the weedy fields, and the level road and the shortcut. the lines put no “because” between them. they are set side by side, and the reader sees one fact with two faces: what is too much in one place is what is missing in the other. here the text does judge. it calls the result robbery. but look at what it judges. it is not fullness: a full granary is the health of a state. it is not emptiness: the book praises that word elsewhere. it is the holding of the two apart, so that nothing flows back. passage 77 shows the same pair in motion, as a bow that is bent: the high end comes down and the low end goes up.

the great road is level and plain, and people leave it because they love a shortcut.. the great road is level and plain, and people leave it because they love a shortcut. is this true of you? name one shortcut that you are on now. what drew you to it: hurry, a fear of being left behind, the wish to be seen as someone? where did that pull begin? take the opposite view: shortcuts are how anything new is found, and the level road is for those who lack nerve. hold it for a while. does some part of you cheer? what do you think of people who stay on the plain road, year after year? is there envy in the judgment, or contempt, or both?

great surplus beside empty granaries is a kind of theft, however lawful it looks.. great surplus beside empty granaries is a kind of theft, however lawful it looks. do you agree, or is this too hard on those who have much? where do you place yourself in the picture? what did your family say about wealth and about the people who had it? what did they say about those who had little? now argue the other side with full force: surplus is the fruit of work and skill, and it takes nothing from anyone. stay with it. then notice the body: does it relax or tighten? leave the state aside and look at one life, your own. is there a swept court in it that is paid for by a weedy field? what do you feel when you see it? which of the two views would be more costly for you to accept? why is that worth knowing?

盜 drooling over another’s dish. the modern short form, 盗, hides the picture; look at the full one. at the bottom is 皿, a dish, the same vessel that holds up 益 and 盈. on top is a rare character, 㳄, made of 氵, water, and 欠. you met 欠 in passage 49: a person with the mouth wide open, breath going out, a yawn. water beside an open mouth is saliva, and the shuowen defines 㳄 with care: 慕欲口液也, “the fluid of the mouth in longing and desire”. its entry for 盜 then joins the parts into a scene: 私利物也。从㳄，㳄欲皿者, “to take a thing for private gain; from 㳄: one who drools with desire for the dish”. a robber, for the dictionary, is not first a man with a knife. it is a person who stands with open mouth and wet lips over someone else’s bowl. the definition has two words that matter in this passage: 私, private, against the great road that is open to all, and 利, gain. the same 㳄 is the lower part of 羨, to envy, which the shuowen glosses 貪欲也, “greedy desire”. now read the list again: glutted with drink and food, with goods in surplus. the text calls these people by a character in which the wanting has not stopped. the dish is full and the mouth is still open. see 盜夸. twelve strokes in two floors. the upper floor is seven strokes in two parts. on the left, water in three: a dot, a second dot below it, and a third stroke that rises from lower left to upper right. on the right, the open-mouthed figure in four: a short stroke that falls to the left; a horizontal that ends in a downward hook; then a long stroke that falls to the left and a long one that falls to the right, like a person’s spread legs. the lower floor is the dish in five: the left side; the top and right side in one stroke; two short verticals inside; and the long base line. watch the twelfth stroke. it is the widest line of the character and it must run past both upper parts, because the whole leaning, hungry upper floor has to stand on it. keep the dish low and flat.

蕪 grass above the dancer. two parts. the top is 艹, the short form of 艸, grass: two small plants side by side. it marks plants of every kind: 草 (grass), 花 (flower), 茶 (tea), 葉 (leaf), and 藏, “to store”, from passage 44. the rest is 無, twelve strokes, the character that this book made famous. if you have read the plate at passage 11 you know its story: the early form is widely explained as a dancer with tassels in the hands; the graph was borrowed for the word “not have”, and the dance took a new character with feet, 舞. the shuowen says that in 蕪 it gives only the sound: 蕪，薉也。从艸無聲, “overgrown; from grass, with 無 for the sound”. both words were said alike, and both are still wu. but a sound-part is seldom chosen at random when a fitting one is at hand, and this one fits: a field with “nothing” in it, under grass. the word has a small family of ruin. 荒, “waste”, is glossed by the shuowen with this very character, 蕪也; 荒蕪 together is still the chinese for derelict land. the poet tao yuanming begins his most famous piece with the same fear: my fields and garden will go to 蕪; why not go home? in this passage the weedy fields are the middle term of three. the court takes, the granary lacks, and between them is this character. sixteen strokes: four for the grass and twelve for 無. the stroke data write the grass in its older, divided form: a short upright and a horizontal on the left, then a short upright and a horizontal on the right, two separate plants with a gap between. below them 無 begins: a short stroke that falls to the left, then a horizontal, then a long horizontal. four verticals follow, evenly spaced, and a long horizontal closes them underneath; this is the widest line of the character. last, four dots in a row, from left to right. watch the four verticals. they pass through the middle band like fence posts, and the white between them must be equal. the danger is height, since grass is set on top of a tall character. press the upper part down and keep the dots close under the long line.

夷 a person and a bow. the shuowen analyses this character as two pictures laid one over the other: 从大从弓, “from 大 and from 弓”. 大 is a person seen from the front with arms and legs spread; it means “big”, and you can find its top stroke, its arms, and its two legs here. 弓 is a bow, with its curved stave: the three bends in the middle of this character. a person who carries a bow. the dictionary adds: 東方之人也, “the people of the east”, the coastal peoples whom the zhou knew as archers. modern scholars do not all accept this analysis of the earliest forms, so take it as the han reading. the first definition that the shuowen gives is the other sense: 平也, “level”. how the archer and the level ground came to share a graph is not known; the simplest view is that one word borrowed the other’s character. the level sense makes its own family: 夷 as a verb is to flatten, to raze a city, to wipe out a clan; a calm sea is 夷. in the laozi the word belongs to the way. it is the name of what the eye cannot catch (14), and it is the quality of the great road here: 大道甚夷. hold the two senses together for a moment. the zhou drew the people at the edge of their world with this character, and the book uses it for the main highway. six strokes. first a horizontal across the top: the arms of the person. then the bow in three strokes: a horizontal that turns down at its right end; a second horizontal below it; and then a stroke that starts at the left, goes down, turns right, turns down again, and ends in a hook. these three must stack closely, like the folds of a stave. watch the fifth stroke. it starts above the first horizontal, passes down through all the bends of the bow, and sweeps away to the lower left; it is the body and one leg of the person, and it joins everything. the sixth stroke is the other leg: from the centre down to the right, pressed harder as it goes, with a long sharp tail. the two legs must spread wide, because the bow in the middle is narrow and needs a base.

54 · the sacrifice does not stop. what is well set up is not torn out. / what is well held in the arms does not slip away. / sons and grandsons bring the offerings, / and the line does not break. / tend it in the body: its de is then real. / tend it in the household: its de is then more than enough. / tend it in the village: its de then lasts. / tend it in the state: its de is then abundant. / tend it in all under heaven: its de then reaches everywhere. / so: by the body, look at the body. / by the household, look at the household. / by the village, look at the village. / by the state, look at the state. / by all under heaven, look at all under heaven. / how do i know that all under heaven is so? / by this. the passage has three parts. first, two short claims and their proof: a thing well set up is not torn out, a thing held in the arms does not slip, and the sign is that the sacrifices of the descendants go on without a gap. second, a ladder of five places: body, household, village, state, all under heaven. at each one the same act, 修, gives a different fruit of 德: real, ample, lasting, abundant, everywhere. in the old text each place rhymes with its fruit. third, the ladder again, now as a way of knowing: by each thing, look at that thing. then a question and a two-word answer. no sage is named, and no ruler. the speaker says 吾, “i”, once, to ask how “i” know. the order matters. the realm is last and the body is first, and the fruit of the first rung is the only one that is not a quantity: 真, real. the others, more than enough, lasting, abundant, wide, are sizes. they grow from the first, and a large thing that grows from an unreal root is only large. the second half is a discipline of attention. to look at the body by the body is to look without a second thing held up beside it: no ideal body, no other person’s body, no story. most looking is a comparison. this is the look before comparison. the answer 以此 points at that. the knowledge of “all under heaven” is not collected from far away. it is here, at the scale where you can check it. founders want to know how to make a thing that lasts. the first line uses their words, 建 and 拔, and the answer turns away from walls and armies to a table that is laid again each season: a thing lasts when those who come after choose to continue it. nobody can force that choice. the ladder then gives a rule that leaders break daily. each scale has its own 德 and must be seen as itself. a household is not a small state. a team is not a family, and a state is not a firm. other schools made the ladder a chain of command that runs outward from the ruler’s person. here nothing is pushed outward. wang bi adds the hardest part: look at the realm with the heart of its people, not with your own. a stance teaches the first line. stand with the feet under the hips and let the weight go down through the legs into the floor. a person who is “well set up” in this way is hard to pull off balance, and the reason is not stiffness. stiff legs give one handle to push on. then the second line: make a circle of the arms in front of the chest, as if around a large ball or a child, with the shoulders down. this is the shape of 抱. a grip of the fingers tires in a minute. a hold with the whole frame can last, because nothing in it is clenched. now look at the body by the body: feel it from inside for a few breaths, with no picture of how it should be. that is where 修之於身 begins. a tree that is not pulled out by the storm is one whose root took hold before its crown spread. wang bi says so in a line: the root first, the branch-tips after. the five fruits also follow growth as a farmer knows it. seed that is real, not empty husk. then a surplus over what the plant needs. then length of season. then a full ear: 豐 is the picture of a ritual vessel piled high. then spread over the whole field. and each scale in a living system has its own measure. a cell, an organ, a body, a herd, a valley: what is health for one is not health for another, and a part that grows by the rule of a different scale is a sickness in the whole. do the five looks once this week, slowly. then take the question of the first lines into one ordinary thing that you have set up: a habit, a friendship, a project, a rule in your home. ask of it: if i stopped pushing, would anyone lay this table again? if yes, it is well set up. if no, do not push harder. go down the ladder one rung, toward the body, and see what is not yet real there.

建 and 拔: to found, to storm. english versions make this a garden: a plant that is not uprooted. the chinese words are harder. 建 is to set a thing upright: a post, a banner, a house, and above all a state. to give a kinsman land and a title was 封建, “to enfeoff and set up”. the shuowen defines the word from the court: 立朝律也, “to establish the statutes of the court”. 拔 is to pull out by the root, and in the war records of the time it is the usual verb for the fall of a town: 拔城, “to pull out a city”. a reader in the warring states, where a state was “pulled out” every few years, heard a claim about politics in the first five words. there is a way to found a thing so that no army can take it. the passage then says where that foundation is, and the answer is not a wall. the agent is open too; see 者.

善建者: who, or what?. 者 turns the words before it into a noun: “the one that…”. 善建者 can be “the one who is good at setting up”, a person, or “that which is well set up”, a thing. chinese does not choose. our english has to, and we took the thing, because 不拔 fits a thing best: it “is not pulled out”. but hear the other reading as well. the good founder is not pulled out; the good embracer does not lose the grip. then the first two lines describe a person, and the third line gives that person descendants. the line also has no passive mark. 不拔 is only “not pull out”. english adds “is” and “what”. which do you hear first: the thing that stays, or the one who set it up?

抱: the arms of the book. 抱 is to put the arms around a thing and hold it to the chest. the character is 扌, hand, with 包, “to wrap”, which also gives the sound. this is a verb that the laozi loves. in passage 10 the question is whether a person can 抱一, hold the one in the arms, and not let go. in passage 19 the advice is 抱樸, hold the uncut wood. in passage 22 the sage holds the one and becomes a measure for the realm. in passage 42 the ten thousand things carry yin on the back and 抱陽, hold yang to the chest. so the verb here is not new. what is held is not named, and readers supply 道, or the one. the picture is a parent with a child. a thing that you grip with the fingers can be pulled away. what do you hold with the whole of the arms?

祭祀: feeding the dead. in early china a family did not end at death. the dead lived on as ancestors as long as their descendants gave them food and drink at fixed times: grain, meat, wine, set out before a tablet or a living stand-in. that is 祭祀. a line with no sons had no one to feed its dead, and that was the worst end. the same was true of a state. to destroy a ruling house fully was 絕祀, “to cut off its sacrifices”, and a decent conqueror did not do it: the zhou kings set up a descendant of the fallen shang house in the state of song so that the shang ancestors still ate. so “the sacrifices do not stop” is the chinese way to say “it lasts for ever”. it is not an abstract eternity. it is a table that someone lays again each season. the line also has 以, “by this”: by what was well set up, the descendants keep the rite. our english drops the word. see 輟 for the verb.

輟 or 絕: a pause or a cut. the received text says the sacrifices 不輟. 輟 has 車, cart, at its side. the shuowen explains it from a column of carts: 車小缺復合者, “carts with a small gap that close up again”. so 輟 is to pause, to leave a gap in a row. the silk texts are reported to read 子孫以祭祀不絕: 絕 is to cut a thread through, the word used for a line that dies out. the silk reading is the stronger word. the received reading is finer: not one small gap in the row, not one season missed. english must add an object. the chinese says only “not pause”, and it does not say what does not pause: the offerings, the sons, or the thing well set up. we wrote “the line does not break” and so chose for you. this passage is also among the guodian bamboo slips, the oldest laozi material found so far; they write the verb as 屯, which editors read as 輟.

修: not quite “cultivate”. 修 is always “cultivate” in english, and the word brings a field or a garden. the chinese picture is different. the shuowen says 飾也, “to adorn”: to dress, to trim, to brush clean. the three strokes at the lower right, 彡, are in characters for hair, feathers, and ornament. from there the word means to repair a wall, to put a road in order, to keep a tool fit. 修身, “to keep the person in order”, was a term that all the schools shared. so 修 is regular care of a thing that is already there. it is nearer to how a person keeps a boat than to how a person grows a crop. the object is only 之, “it”. readers take “it” as the dao, or as the thing well set up. the silk texts are reported to be shorter still: 修之身, “tend it, the body”, with no “in”.

身: the body that is the person. 身 is the trunk of the body, and it is also “self, person, one’s own life”. the shuowen says 躳也。象人之身, “the body; it shows a person’s trunk”. chinese does not split a person into a body and a self that owns it. english does, and translators of this line write “self”, “inner self”, “one’s person”. each of those moves the work into the mind. the chinese puts it in the flesh: breath, posture, appetite, sleep, what the hands do. the legalist han feizi read the line just so. in his chapter on the laozi he says 身以積精為德, “the body takes stored essence as its de”. the first place where a person can check if a teaching is real is a place that nobody else can see or fake. where in the body do you know that a thing is true?

德: what the tending yields. we leave 德 as “de”. “virtue” is the old english word for it, in the sense of “the virtue of a herb”: the power that a thing has because of what it is. the moral sense is later and narrower. in this passage 德 is plainly a yield. you tend, and the 德 of that place becomes real, then ample, then lasting, then abundant, then wide. it is the 德 of the body, of the household, of the village: 其, “its”, points each time to the scale and not to a ruler. han feizi counts it in plain goods: the body’s 德 is stored essence, the household’s is its property, and for village, state, and realm it is the people. 德 here is not a private merit that a person carries from place to place. each scale has its own.

真: a word the classics do not use. 真 means “real, genuine, not fake”. it is a common word now, so the surprise is easy to miss: scholars since gu yanwu in the 17th century have noted that 真 does not occur in the confucian five classics. it is a word of the daoist texts. the laozi has it three times (passages 21, 41, and here), and the zhuangzi makes a figure of it, the 真人, the “real person”. by the han the word was so tied to that world that the shuowen defines it thus: 僊人變形而登天也, “an immortal who changes form and rises to heaven”. that is a late, religious gloss, and we do not read it back into this line. but it shows the place of the word. the first fruit of tending the body is not goodness, and not health. it is to be real. what would it mean for your 德 to be fake?

鄉: those who eat together. 鄉 is the home district: a group of villages with its own elders, wine feasts, and archery meets. the early form of the character is commonly explained as two people who kneel face to face with a vessel of food between them. the same picture gave three words: 鄉, the community; 饗, to feast (the food radical 食 was added below); and 卿, a high minister, at first one who dined with the ruler. so a village, in the eye of the script, is the people who share a meal. the ladder of this passage is therefore a ladder of tables: the body that eats, the household at one hearth, the district at its feast, the state, the realm. the first rung and the third are joined by the offerings to the dead, which are also a meal. the shuowen enters the word under an older graph, 𨞰, and defines it from the side of the state: 民所封鄉也。嗇夫別治, “the district to which people are assigned; a 嗇夫 governs each”. that officer’s title is the farmer’s word of passage 59.
