國 was 邦: a broken rhyme. silk manuscript a is reported to read 修之邦，亓德乃豐; manuscript b, copied under the han taboo, has 國. 邦 is the older word for a state: land given by grant, with its lord. when liu bang founded the han dynasty in 202 bce, his personal name became taboo, and scribes changed 邦 to 國 in book after book. our received text carries that change. it cost a rhyme. in this stanza each scale rhymes with its fruit: 身 and 真 (the 真 group), 家 and 餘 (the 魚 group), 鄉 and 長 (the 陽 group), 天下 and 普 (the 魚 group again; the silk texts are reported to have 博 there, of the related 鐸 group). 邦 and 豐 belonged to the neighbouring 東 and 冬 groups, which early verse rhymes together. 國 rhymes with nothing here. so the old reader heard five matched pairs: the place and its result sound alike, as if one came out of the other. the emperor’s name removed one of the five.

天下: not “the world”. 天下 is “under heaven”: all that the sky covers. english says “the world” or “the empire”, and both miss. “the world” is a globe seen from outside. “empire” did not exist yet. 天下 is seen from the ground: the whole of the known, settled land with its many states, which had once had one king, the son of heaven, and now had none who mattered. for a warring states reader the word had a wound in it. who would join 天下 again, and by what means, was the question of the age. this passage answers in an odd way. it does not say how to take it. it says how to tend it and how to look at it, and it places it fifth in a row that starts at the body.

the same ladder in other hands. body, household, state, realm: the ladder was common property. mencius says 天下之本在國，國之本在家，家之本在身, “the root of the realm is in the state, of the state in the household, of the household in the person”. the “great learning” made it a program: the person is put in order, then the household is made even, then the state is governed, then the realm is at peace. there each step is a cause that pushes the next one. the laozi ladder has no “then”. each scale is tended where it is, and has its own fruit. the guanzi is nearer to our text and may share a source with it: 以家為家，以鄉為鄉，以國為國，以天下為天下, “treat the household as a household, the district as a district, the state as a state, the realm as the realm”. it adds a warning: run a district as if it were a household, and the district cannot be run.

觀: to look, not to judge. 觀 is to look long and with care. the shuowen says 諦視也, “to look at with close attention”. 以身觀身 is five plain words: “by body, look at body”. english wants more: whose body, and by what standard? three readings are old. one: by my own body i look at the bodies of others. two: by the body that is tended i look at the body that is not. three, and the plainest: look at a body as a body, on its own scale and by its own measure, and do not judge a village as if it were a family. the guanzi parallel supports the third. all three agree on what 觀 is not. it is not to plan, to picture an ideal, or to improve. later the same character, read guan, became the name for a daoist temple: a place for looking.

wang bi: with the people’s heart. on the first line wang bi writes: 固其根而後營其末，故不拔也, “make the root firm, and only after that see to the branch-tips; so it is not pulled out”. on the last rung he writes: 以天下百姓心觀天下之道也, “with the heart of the hundred families of the realm, look at the way of the realm”. the ruler does not look at the realm with a ruler’s heart. and on the closing answer: 察己以知之，不求於外也，所謂不出戶以知天下者也. “examine yourself and so know it; do not seek it outside. this is what is meant by: without going out of the door, know all under heaven.” he ties the passage to passage 47. for wang bi “this” is the self: what is true in the nearest case is true in the farthest, since 彼皆然也, “those others are all so too”.

以此: two words for an answer. the question is long and formal: 吾何以知天下然哉, “by what do i know that all under heaven is so?” the answer is two words: 以此, “by this”. the same question and the same answer close a section in passage 21 and open the proof in passage 57. 此 is the pointing word for what is near the speaker, as 彼 is for what is far. so what is “this”? the method just given: look at each thing as itself. or the body, the first rung, which is as near as a thing can be. or this that is in front of you now. wang bi takes it as the self. the silk texts are reported to write 然茲以此, where 茲 is a loan for the particle 哉 at the end of the question and not a part of the answer. legge adds a bracket. the chinese adds nothing, and the gesture is a finger that points down.

legge’s hymn. legge puts the first two stanzas into rhymed english verse, and the form changes the content. his opening has a “skilful planter”, in brackets the tao’s own, and by the third line a “shrine”. the grammar of a hymn has entered: a person, male, who is honoured. the chinese has no “his”. in the ladder he writes that the tao is “nursed within one’s self” and that the family gets “riches”. then he gives up verse, and the five looks become a flat report that “the effect will be seen” in each place: the act of looking is gone, and a result is put where it was. at the end he explains the two last words as “by this (method of observation)”. that is one fair reading. but the bracket closes a door that the text left open; see 以此.

one scale at a time. try the five looks as an exercise, and keep each one on its own scale. first the body: sit, and for two minutes only notice it as a body. is it tired, tight, hungry, at ease? do not explain it with your work or your family. then the household: think of your home at a normal hour, as if you stood in the doorway. what is its mood? do not judge it by how you feel. then one wider circle that you belong to: a street, a team, a town. each time, ask what this thing is like when you measure it only by itself. most trouble in judgment comes from a mix of scales: a company treated as a family, a family run as a state. what changes when you stop?

建 / 拔, 抱 / 脫: set up and torn out, held and lost. the first two lines are built on two pairs: 建 and 拔, to set up and to pull out; 抱 and 脫, to hold in the arms and to slip free. in common experience each first word calls up the second. what is set up can be pulled out, and what is held can get away. the harder the founding and the tighter the grip, the more this is so; the war records of the time are full of it. the lines do not deny the turn. they say 善, “well”: there is a way of setting up that gives the puller no hold, and a way of holding that does not make the thing struggle. the proof offered is not a wall. it is grandchildren who come of their own will. a one-sided reading hears “make it strong enough and it stays for ever”. the text has no “for ever”. it has a table that someone has to choose to lay again.

what is well set up lasts because those who come after choose to carry it on.. what is well set up lasts because those who come after choose to carry it on. do you agree? think of something that outlived its founder, and something that did not. what have you built by force of will that would stop if you stopped? what are you afraid would be shown if you let go? take the opposite: things last because they are defended, with rules, walls, and effort, and what is left to free choice is dropped. hold that as true for a while. what comes up? which did you inherit from your own family: a table that you were glad to lay again, or a duty that you carried? how does that colour your answer?

each thing is known by looking at it as itself: the body by the body, the state by the state.. each thing is known by looking at it as itself: the body by the body, the state by the state. is that how you look? or do you measure your body by another body, and your home by another home? where did the habit of comparing come from in your life? who was held up beside you? try the other view: nothing is known alone, and comparison is what shows a thing for what it is. stay with it. does it feel like clear sight, or like an old pressure? the passage puts the body first and the realm last. do you tend to start at the other end, with the world and its faults? what might that order spare you from seeing?

祭 a hand, a piece of meat, an altar. read this character as a small scene with three actors. at the top left is a tilted form that looks like 夕 with an extra dot. it is 肉, meat, in the squeezed shape that it takes inside other characters; you know it in a different squeezed shape as the 月 at the side of 肝 (liver) and 腸 (gut). at the top right is 又, a right hand, with its last stroke stretched out. below both is 示, the mark for all things that concern spirits. 示 is commonly explained as a picture of an altar stand or a spirit tablet, and it is the part that 神 (spirit), 福 (blessing), 禍 (disaster), 祀 (the round of offerings), and 禮 (rite) all share. so: a hand sets meat on the altar. the shuowen says just that: 祭祀也。从示，以手持肉, “to sacrifice; from 示, with a hand that holds meat”. the oldest forms are reported to be simpler, a piece of meat with drops beside it, and scholars differ on the details, so hold the early history lightly. cousins by sound: 察, “to examine”, in which the shuowen sees a roof 宀 over 祭, and 際, “border, meeting place”. the passage says that a thing well set up is known by this act, repeated without a gap. see the note on the rite. eleven strokes. the meat first, four strokes: a stroke that falls to the left, a horizontal that turns and falls to the left, then two dots inside. then the hand, two strokes: a horizontal that turns and falls to the left, and a long stroke that sweeps down to the right. watch that sixth stroke. with the second stroke of the meat it makes a wide roof, and all the rest of the character stands under it. then 示, five strokes: a short horizontal, a longer horizontal, a vertical with a hook, a dot to the left and a dot to the right. the two top parts lean toward each other like two people over a table. the altar must be narrow and upright below them, or the character falls open. in clerical script the sweep of the hand is the showpiece, flared like a wing.

孫 a child on a thread. 孫 is “grandson”, and with 子 before it, 子孫, it is “descendants”. it has two parts. on the left is 子, a child. the shuowen calls 子 a picture, 象形; the common explanation is an infant with a large head and arms out, the legs wrapped. on the right is 系, a thread that hangs from a hook or a hand: the top stroke, then the twisted silk 幺, then the loose ends 小. the shuowen reads the pair with care: 子之子曰孫。从子从系。系，續也, “the child of a child is called 孫. from 子 and from 系. 系 is to continue.” a grandchild is the child who continues the thread. the silk radical carries this idea in many words: 繼 (to succeed, to carry on), 續 (to continue), 絕 (to cut off: silk and a knife), 經 (the warp of a loom, then a classic text), 統 (the main thread, a ruling line). chinese speaks of a family as one line of thread, and of its end as a cut. now read the third line of the passage again. the silk texts are reported to say that the sacrifices are not 絕, not cut. the thread is in the grammar of the line and in this character both. ten strokes. 子 first, three strokes, written narrow because it is a left side: a horizontal that turns down in a short hook, then a vertical with a hook to the left, then a stroke that rises to the right. in the full character 子 this third stroke is a level horizontal; here it lifts, and it points at the thread. then 系, seven strokes: a short stroke that falls to the left on top; two strokes that fall left and turn back, like a folded cord; a dot; then a vertical with a hook, a dot on the left and a dot on the right. watch the two folds of the silk. they must be the same angle and stack exactly, and the vertical below must hang from their centre like a weight on a line. the simplified form 孙 keeps the child and cuts away all the silk but 小.

觀 the bird that watches. 觀 has twenty-five strokes and two parts. the right side is 見, “to see”: an eye, 目, on two legs. the eye is so large that the person under it is only legs. the left side is 雚 (guan), and the shuowen says it gives the sound: 从見雚聲. but look at what it draws. at the bottom is 隹, a short-tailed bird. above the bird are two 口, and above them a crest. 雚 is an old name for a water bird, commonly identified as a stork or heron, and the two “mouths” are often explained as its two wide eyes. we cannot prove that the scribes chose it for the picture; sound was their reason. still, a reader sees a tall bird that stands in shallow water without a move and looks. that is a good teacher for this verb. the same sound-part is in 歡 (joy), 勸 (to urge), and 權 (the weight of a scale, then power). 觀 is also the name of hexagram 20 of the changes, where it means both to look and to be looked at, like a tower. a gate tower was a 觀, and then a daoist temple. passage 1 has the same verb: 以觀其妙, “to look at its fine points”. twenty-five strokes. the left side takes eighteen. the crest, four strokes: a vertical, a horizontal, a vertical, a horizontal. two small mouths side by side, each in three: a vertical, a horizontal that turns down, a closing horizontal. then 隹, eight strokes: a stroke that falls left, a vertical, a dot, three horizontals, a vertical through their middle, and a last horizontal as the base. the right side, 見, takes seven: the eye in five (left side; top and right side in one stroke; two lines inside; the base), then a stroke that falls to the left and a last stroke that goes down, turns right, and ends in a hook up. that final hook is the only free line in the character. all the rest is packed tight, and the white inside must stay open. cursive script reduced it to a few turns, the source of the short form 观.

55 · the red child. one who holds de within, thick and deep, / is like a red child. / wasps, scorpions, vipers, snakes do not sting. / fierce beasts do not seize. / clawed birds do not strike. / bones weak, sinews soft, yet the grip is firm. / not yet knowing the joining of female and male, / yet fully roused: / essence at its peak. / howls all day and is not hoarse: / harmony at its peak. / knowing harmony is named the constant. / knowing the constant is named clear sight. / adding to life is named an omen. / the heart-mind driving the breath is named forcing. / a thing in its prime then grows old. / call this not the dao. / what is not the dao ends early. a newborn is described as a naturalist would describe it, by four facts. animals do not attack it. its bones are soft and its fist is tight. it knows nothing of sex and its body rises. it howls all day and is not hoarse. after the third fact comes a verdict: 精 at its peak. after the fourth: 和 at its peak. then four short definitions in the form “x is called y”, two that praise and two that warn, and the warning is easy to miss because 祥 and 強 look like good words. then a proverb that also ends passage 30. the first line says that all this is a likeness: the person who holds 德 within is “like” the red child. it does not say “is” one. the infant is not innocent in a moral sense, and the text does not say it is good. it is undivided. it has no second self that watches the first, so its grip has no doubt in it and its cry has no shame in it. each of the four facts is strength without a one who is strong. then the text names the adult disease with precision: 心使氣, the mind that takes command of the breath. the return to the infant is not a return to ignorance. a grown person cannot un-know. what can stop is the constant small act of command: the held belly, the managed face, the life that is added to. the text calls what is left 和, and to know it, 常. notice that the infant has 和 and does not know it. only the adult can “know harmony”. read the animals as politics for a moment. wasps, vipers, beasts, and raptors are what a court is made of. wang bi gives the rule: the one who does not trespass is not trespassed on. a person with no hidden aim offers nothing for an attack to hold. this is not a method to act harmless; a grown predator smells an act. the second half is for any organization. 壯, the peak year, the record quarter, the largest army, is the point at which age starts. a leader who drives the body of the group by will, 心使氣, gets force for a time and then an early end: 早已. the rulers of the time called their subjects 赤子 and promised to guard them like babies. the laozi turns it round: the ruler should be like the baby. this is the body chapter of the book. take its claims as instructions for the hands, belly, and voice. hands: soft bones, firm grip. in the arts of the sword, the brush, and the bow, teachers say the same: hold it as you would hold a small bird, fully, with no squeeze. belly: the breath of a baby moves low and nothing pulls it. voice: sound from the belly does not tear the throat. then the warning. 心使氣 is the athlete’s error: to push the breath, to grit through. it works, and it costs. many students of taijiquan hear a rule that comes from this line: use intent, do not use force, and do not drive the 氣. 精 is not made by effort. it is what remains when it is not wasted. see what later schools built on this. young things are soft. a shoot bends where the old branch cracks; passage 76 says it outright: the living are soft and weak, the dead hard and strong. a seedling has all the growth of the tree still in it, and in that sense the smallest form holds the most life. the curve that the last lines draw is the curve of every living thing: rise, peak, decline. the text does not say that the curve can be escaped. it says that to rush toward the peak is 不道, and that what does so ends early. a fruit tree forced to bear heavily for a few years is spent. the old growers thinned the fruit. to add to life is to take from it. today, three times, drop the general. stop where you are, put a hand low on the belly, and for five breaths give the breath no orders: not slow, not deep, not “right”. let it be short or rough if it is. see how hard it is to watch a breath and not manage it. that small urge to manage is 心使氣. then try the baby’s fist and the long “ah”. do not make a regimen of this. a regimen is 益生.

含: held in the mouth. 含 has 口, a mouth, at the bottom, and 今 above it for the sound. the shuowen says 嗛也, “to hold in the mouth”. it is the verb for a thing kept behind closed lips and not swallowed and not spoken: a sweet, a sip of water, a word that is not said. so 含德 is not “to have virtue” as a person has a medal. it is 德 kept in, unshown, as a baby’s strength is all inside. 厚 is “thick”; the shuowen explains it from the land, 山陵之厚也, “the thickness of hills”. the same verb named a funeral custom: a piece of jade, a 含, was put in the mouth of the dead. and the silk texts are reported to add 者 after 厚, which makes the subject plain: “the one who…”; our “one who” follows that, and our “thick and deep” is two words for the one word 厚. what do you hold in the mouth and not say?

赤子: why the child is red. 赤 is red: the shuowen calls it 南方色也, “the colour of the south”, the colour of fire. 赤子, “red child”, is the newborn. the tang scholar yan shigu gave the usual reason: a baby just born has no brows or hair yet, and its skin is red. 赤 also means “bare”: 赤手 is “bare-handed”, and to be 赤貧 is to be poor to the skin. so the word holds both facts of the first days: red, and with nothing on. english “infant” (latin: one who cannot speak) and “baby” do not have this colour. the book returns to this figure often, as 嬰兒: in passage 10 (can you gather the breath, be soft, be an infant?), in 20 (like an infant that has not yet smiled), in 28 (return to the infant). mencius knew the image too: the great person is one who has not lost 赤子之心, the heart of the red child.

why nothing stings: wang bi. is the infant protected by magic? later religion sometimes read the lines so, and passage 50 has a like claim about the rhinoceros and the tiger. wang bi’s answer is plain: 赤子無求無欲，不犯眾物，故毒蟲之物無犯之人也. “the red child seeks nothing and desires nothing, and does not trespass on the many things; so the creatures with poison do not trespass on such a person.” the verb is 犯, to cross a line, to offend. animals strike what threatens or what flees. the baby does neither. it is not a claim that a baby cannot be bitten. it is a picture of a being with no aggression in it for another aggression to meet. he goes on: 含德之厚者，不犯於物，故無物以損其全也, “one who holds de thickly does not trespass on things, so nothing has a way to harm their wholeness”. the silk texts and the guodian slips are reported to have two clauses where we have three: 蜂蠆虺蛇弗螫，攫鳥猛獸弗搏, with no 不據.

握固: the baby’s fist. put a finger in a newborn’s palm and the hand shuts on it, hard. doctors call it the grasp reflex. the text saw it 2,300 years ago and saw the paradox: the bones are weak, the sinews soft, and the grip is 固. the shuowen defines 固 as 四塞也, “shut on four sides”: the character is a wall 囗 around its sound-part 古. the strength of the hold does not come from hard muscle. it comes from a hand with no doubt in it. the zhuangzi quotes a version of these lines and adds: 終日握而手不掜, “it grips all day and the hand does not cramp”. later daoist breathing manuals made 握固 a technical term: a fist with the thumb folded inside under the four fingers, as a baby holds it, used in sitting practice to “keep the breath in”. try it for a minute. is it effort?

牝牡: words from the stable. the text does not say 男女, “man and woman”. it says 牝牡, and both characters have 牛, an ox, at the left. the shuowen defines them as 畜母也 and 畜父也: “the mother among livestock”, “the father among livestock”. these are a herdsman’s words for cow and bull, mare and stallion. 合 is “to join”, and for animals it is the plain word for mating. so the line speaks of sex as a farmer does, without shame and without romance. english versions move it up a register: “the union of male and female”, “the union of the sexes”. the chinese stays in the yard. 牝 is also one of the great words of this book: the dark female of passage 6, and the female that wins by stillness in passage 61. here the infant is before all that, before two.

全作: what the scribes covered. our text says 全作, “the whole rises”, and we wrote “fully roused”. it is an odd phrase, and the older texts show why. the silk texts are reported to read 未知牝牡之合而朘怒. 朘 (zui) is a baby boy’s penis (the shuowen has the graph 脧: 赤子陰也, “the sex of a red child”), and 怒 is “to swell with force”, the word for anger and also for a bud that bursts or a river in flood. so: “with no knowledge yet of how female and male join, its small member stands”. an erection with no desire and no object: the text points at it as proof that the life-force is full when the mind wants nothing. some received editions are reported to keep 朘作 or 峻作. wang bi’s text already had 全, and he explains it with care: 作，長也, “作 is to grow”; nothing harms the body, so it can 全長, “grow whole”. a rare graph was lost, or a blunt one was made polite. legge made it more polite still.

精: the picked grain. 精 has 米, husked grain, at the left; 青 gives the sound. the shuowen says only 擇也, “to select”: grain that has been picked over and polished, the best of the crop. from “the finest part” the word went to the finest part of anything: of a metal, of the breath, of a body. in the body 精 is the stuff of life at its most dense, and in particular it is semen. that is why this line follows the one before it. english “essence” has lost the body; it sounds like perfume or philosophy. “vitality” has no substance in it. 精 is a thing that a person has in a certain amount and can spend. texts of the same age, such as the “inward training” in the guanzi, tell the student how to store it. later it became the first of three “treasures”, with 氣 and 神, spirit.

號: a cry that does not hurt. 號 here is read hao: to howl, to wail. an adult who shouts for an hour is hoarse the next day. a baby can cry from morning to night and its voice is as strong at the end. why? the adult shouts from the throat, against a tight chest, with a purpose and with fear of how it sounds. the baby cries with the whole belly, and nothing in it resists the cry. the text names this 和之至, harmony at its peak: sound that does not fight its own body. the zhuangzi gives the same line with a small change: 終日嗥而嗌不嗄, “it howls all day and its throat is not hoarse”. watch a baby breathe if you can. the belly moves, and the shoulders do not. then put a hand on your own belly and say one long “ah”. where does it start?

和: not peace and quiet. the proof of 和 in this passage is a baby that screams all day. that should stop us if we hear “harmony” as calm, niceness, or the lack of conflict. 和 has 口, a mouth; the shuowen says 相譍也, “to answer one another”, as voices do in a song. early texts explain it from music and from the kitchen: different notes that answer, different tastes that blend in a broth. a cook does not get 和 with one taste. so 和 is a fit between parts that are different and all active. in the infant the parts are breath, voice, belly, and want, and they act as one. passage 42 says where this comes from: the ten thousand things carry yin and hold yang, and 沖氣以為和, the breaths blend and make 和. can a loud thing be in harmony? can a quiet thing be out of it?

常 and 明: a chain with a missing link. 知常曰明, “knowing the constant is named clear sight”, also stands in passage 16, where the constant is the return of each thing to its root. here a step is put before it: 知和曰常, “knowing harmony is named the constant”. the silk texts are reported to be shorter: 和曰常，知和曰明, “harmony is named the constant; knowing harmony is named clear sight”. that is cleaner logic, and it has no “knowing the constant” at all; the received text was perhaps made to match passage 16. where we have 常, older copies often have 恆; it was changed under a han emperor’s name taboo. wang bi describes the constant as a temperature: 不皦不昧，不溫不涼，此常也, “not glaring, not dim, not warm, not cool: this is the constant”. 明 is 日 and 月, sun and moon, in its modern form. it is the light that sees, not cleverness.

祥: a blessing that is a warning. this line and the next can be read as praise: “to increase life is auspicious; the mind that commands the breath is strong”. 祥 does usually mean a good sign, and it is on new year cards today; the shuowen, a han book, gives only that sense: 福也, “a blessing”. but the word is first a neutral one: any sign from heaven or earth. in the zuozhuan a duke sees meteors fall and asks: 是何祥也，吉凶焉在, “what omen is this? where is the good or ill fortune in it?” the old commentators all take it as an ill omen here, and the grammar agrees: these two lines lead straight to “a thing in its prime then grows old”. wang bi: 生不可益，益之則夭也, “life cannot be added to; add to it and you die young”. 益 is the picture of water over the brim of a dish. life is full already. tonics, regimens, ambition for more years: the text calls the wish itself a sign.

心使氣: against mencius. 心 is the heart, and in chinese the heart thinks: “heart-mind”. 氣 is breath, and also the energy that moves in a living body. 使 is to give orders, as a lord sends a servant. so 心使氣 is the mind in command of the breath and the energy: will-power. mencius, in the same century, praised exactly this. 夫志，氣之帥也, he says: “the will is the general of the 氣”, and he was proud of his own “flood-like 氣”, fed by right action. the laozi puts the general under suspicion. wang bi: 心宜無有，使氣則強, “the heart should have nothing in it; if it drives the breath, that is forcing”. this is a real quarrel between two schools about the body: do you train it by command, or by removing the commander? the baby is the laozi’s evidence. its breath is perfect and nobody is in charge of it.

強: one word, two values. 強 is “strong”, and the book uses it both ways. passage 33: one who overcomes the self is 強. passage 52: to keep to the soft is called 強. those are praise. but passage 30 says: get the result and do not 強, do not force. passage 42: the violent and 強 do not die a natural death. passage 76: the hard and 強 are the companions of death. here the form of the line, “x is called 強”, is the same as in passage 52, and only the content shows that the value has turned. english must pick “strength” or “forcing” and so hide the pun. a fact for the curious: the shuowen defines the graph 強 as an insect, 蚚也, a grain weevil; it has 虫 in it. the proper character for “strong” was 彊, which has a bow, 弓: 弓有力也, “a bow that has power”. scribes borrowed the weevil.

物壯則老: the same lines, a new place. the last three lines are also the last three lines of passage 30. there the subject is war: do not use arms to force the realm, for a campaign at its height is close to its fall. here the same words close a passage about a baby. 壯 is the full strength of an adult; the ritual books give it an age, 三十曰壯, “at thirty one is called 壯”. so the passage sets two bodies side by side. the infant: weak bones, and all its life ahead. the man of thirty at his peak: and the next word is 老, old. to push toward the peak is to push toward the far side of it. that is why it is 不道, “not the dao”. was the saying moved here from passage 30, or was it a proverb that both drew on? we do not know. does it change when the subject is your own body and not an army?

legge’s latin moment. legge was a victorian missionary, and this passage tested him. for the infant’s body he finds the phrase “its virile member may be excited”: latin words, a passive verb, and “may”. in truth his text only had 全作; the commentaries supplied the anatomy, and he followed them honestly. for 精 he writes “physical essence”, and for 德 “the attributes (of the tao)”: a term from christian theology, where god has attributes. then he turns the four sayings into a rhymed stanza with a “throne” for wisdom, and ends on a line that is almost all brackets: “(false) is the strength, (and o’er it we should mourn.)” only three words of that are in the chinese: 曰強, “is called 強”. he read the sense correctly, as a warning. but count the words that he needed to make a warning sound like one.

what later daoists did with the baby. this passage became a charter for the arts of long life. its words are their vocabulary: 精, 氣, 和, 握固. from the han onward, teachers of breathing and “guiding and pulling” exercises told students to breathe like an infant, low and soft. inner alchemy, from the tang and song, went further and spoke of an “infant” that the adept forms inside the body by refining 精 into 氣 and 氣 into spirit. there is an irony, and the tradition knew it. the passage also says 益生曰祥: to add to life is an ill omen. a school of life-extension took its texts from a passage that warns against the wish to extend life. the better teachers answered that the work is to stop spending, not to add. is there a difference between care for life and greed for it? where is the line in you?

弱 / 固: weak bones, firm grip. the line sets 弱 and 柔, weak and soft, beside 固, firm, and joins them with 而. that small word is “and” as much as “yet”; our “yet” leans on the surprise. in the infant the two are not at war. the grip is firm because nothing in the hand works against it. the passage then gives a second pair, 壯 and 老, prime and old age, and there one side becomes the other in three characters. the text does favour the soft and the young. the favour is a correction, to an age and to a reader that push toward the peak. it is not a rule that weak is good. the infant’s softness also turns: the child grows. and 強 is a word of praise in other passages. a one-sided reading would have you act weak. the text shows a state in which soft and firm have not yet come apart.

what is pushed to its peak grows old early.. what is pushed to its peak grows old early. do you believe it? where have you seen a person, a team, or a body reach its height and then fall fast? what in your past taught you to push for the peak? was there praise for it, or a fear of being ordinary? now take the other side: a life held back from its peak is a life not lived, and it is right to burn. say it as your own belief for a few minutes. what feelings come with it? which of the two do you hear as wisdom and which as an excuse? what would someone who knows you well say?

the effort to add to life, and to drive the breath by will, is a strain and not a strength.. the effort to add to life, and to drive the breath by will, is a strain and not a strength. does that match your experience of effort, training, and self-improvement? think of one regimen that you keep. what does it promise to protect you from? hold the opposite for a while: nothing good comes without will, and the body left to itself goes slack. what do you notice as you hold it: agreement, tiredness, pride? the infant in the passage has harmony and does not know it. do you trust anything in yourself that you did not make by effort? if not, when did that trust go? why might it matter which of these two views runs your day?

赤 a person over a fire. the shuowen takes this character apart in four words: 从大从火, “from 大 and from 火”. 大 is “big”, and the dictionary says that it is the shape of a human being: 天大，地大，人亦大。故大象人形, “heaven is great, earth is great, and the human is also great; so 大 shows a person’s form”. (that first phrase is a quotation from passage 25 of this book.) 火 is fire, a picture of flames. so 赤 is a person above a fire, or a great fire: the red of flame, the colour of the south and of summer. in the modern shape both parts are hard to see. the top has become a form like 土, and the fire below has opened into four strokes. a cousin makes it plain: 赫, “blazing, awesome”, is two 赤 side by side, and the shuowen calls it 火赤皃, “the look of fire-red”. chinese has several reds. 朱 is vermilion. 丹 is cinnabar, the red mineral of the alchemists. 紅, the usual word today, has the silk radical and was first a pale dyed red. 赤 is the oldest and the barest, and it also means bare: 赤手, bare-handed. a red child is a person with nothing on and nothing added, still warm from the fire. seven strokes. a short horizontal; a short vertical that crosses it; then a long horizontal, the widest line of the character. those three are what is left of the person. then the fire: a stroke that goes down and curves away to the left; a vertical with a hook; a dot on the left side that falls leftward; a dot on the right. watch strokes four and five. they are the two legs of the form and they must stand apart under the long horizontal like the legs of a stool, with the two dots outside them like sparks. in seal script the person and the flames are still clear, one above the other. in running script the four lower strokes are often written in one turning movement, and the fire seems to flicker.

氣 vapour, and a gift of rice. two parts: 气 above and around, 米 inside. start with 气. the shuowen: 雲气也。象形, “cloud vapour; a picture”. its early form is widely explained as three thin level lines, a picture of mist or cloud layers; to keep it apart from the number 三, the top line was bent up and the bottom line bent down, and that is the hook you see today. that was the first way to write “vapour, breath”. 米 is grain: the shuowen calls it 象禾實之形, a picture of the seeds of the crop. now the surprise. the shuowen does not define 氣 as breath at all. it says 饋客芻米也, “fodder and grain that are presented to a guest”. 氣 was the character for a gift of provisions, a word now written 餼. scribes then borrowed the fuller character for “breath”, and the plain 气 fell out of use for two thousand years, until the simplified script brought it back. people love to read 氣 as steam that rises from cooking rice, and as a memory aid it is perfect: breath is what food becomes. but it is a later reading of a loan. later daoists used a third graph, 炁, for the breath that a person has before birth. in this passage 氣 is what the baby has in full and the mind, when it drives it, is said to force. ten strokes. first 气, four strokes: a short stroke that falls to the left; a horizontal; a second, shorter horizontal; then the great stroke of the character, which goes right, turns, sweeps down in a long curve to the lower right, and ends with a hook upward. watch this fourth stroke. it makes a roof and a wall at once, and it must leave a room under it. then 米 goes into that room, six strokes: a dot at upper left, a dot at upper right that leans inward, a horizontal, a vertical through it, then a stroke that falls to the left and one that falls to the right. the grain should sit low and left, sheltered, and not touch the curve. in cursive hands the long hook is thrown out in one breath. calligraphers use this very word for the life of a line: a stroke has 氣 or it is dead.

號 a cry with a tiger in it. the baby howls, and the character for the howl has a tiger in it. on the left is 号. the shuowen gives it an entry of its own: 痛聲也。从口在丂上, “the sound of pain; a mouth 口 above 丂”, where 丂 is commonly explained as breath that tries to come out and is blocked. on the right is 虎, the tiger, 山獸之君, “lord of the mountain beasts”. the dictionary joins them without comment: 號，呼也。从号从虎, “to call out; from 号 and 虎”. so a cry of pain plus the roar of the largest animal that a chinese farmer could meet: a full-throated howl. the word then widened. to cry out a thing is to proclaim it, so 號 (read hao) came to mean an order, a signal, a title, a name that is called out, and at last a number: the modern 三號 is “number three”. the simplified script kept only the left half, 号. 虎 as a part gives its top, 虍, to other characters: 虐 (cruel), 慮 (to worry), 處 (to dwell). the passage chose the wild word on purpose. this is not the baby’s “voice”. it is the tiger in a body with soft bones, and it does not go hoarse. thirteen strokes. the left side takes five: the mouth in three (a vertical; a horizontal that turns down; a closing horizontal), then a horizontal below it, then one stroke that goes down, bends, and ends in a hook to the left. the right side, the tiger, takes eight. a short vertical and a short horizontal at the top. a horizontal that ends in a hook, like a brow. a long stroke that falls to the left: the tiger’s back, and the longest line of the character. a short horizontal and a bent stroke with a hook inside. then the two legs: a stroke that falls to the left, and a last stroke that goes down, turns right, and hooks up. the left half is small and held high; the tiger is tall and takes the weight. the two final hooks, one in each half, turn away from each other.

56 · one with the dust. one who knows does not speak. / one who speaks does not know. / stopping the openings, / shutting the gate, / blunting what is sharp, / untying what is divided, / tempering the light, / joining the dust: / this is called the dark sameness. / so: not to be got hold of and drawn close, / not to be got hold of and kept far; / not to be got hold of and given gain, / not to be got hold of and harmed; / not to be got hold of and raised high, / not to be got hold of and brought low. / so it is what all under heaven prizes. three movements. first a pair of mirror lines, four characters each, built from only four different words: 知者不言，言者不知. then six lines of three characters, all of one form: a verb, 其, a noun. stop the openings, shut the gate, blunt the point, untie the divisions, tune the light, be the same as the dust. they get a name, 玄同. then six more lines, again of one form: 不可得而 and a verb, in three pairs of opposites: near and far, gain and harm, high and low. then one line of result. four of the six verb lines also stand in passage 4, where they have no person near them. the grammar never says who does any of this. we kept that: our english has “-ing” forms and no “he”. why does the knower not speak? not from a rule of secrecy. speech needs a speaker who stands apart from the thing and points at it, and this knowing has no such distance in it; see the wheelwright. the six lines then describe how the distance closes. each takes away a way of standing apart: the mouth that comments, the senses that go out to fetch, the edge that needs to be right, the knots of mine and yours, the glare of being someone. what is left is called the dark sameness. it is not a union of two things, since the second thing is what was removed. the result is given only by negatives, and that is honest. from inside, nothing special is felt. from outside, a person cannot be got hold of. praise finds no one to inflate. blame finds no one to wound. the second half is a study of leverage. a court, a firm, or a family holds people by three ropes: closeness, reward and penalty, rank. wang bi gives the mechanism: whoever can be drawn in can be shut out. a leader who needs to be liked can be steered by anyone who withholds liking. an adviser who wants the next title cannot say the true thing. the passage does not tell you to be aloof; 不可得而疏 says that this one cannot be pushed away either. it describes a person who is fully present and is not for sale. the first half says how such a person looks in a meeting: the light is tuned to the room, and the point is off the blade. the loud ones are usually still learning. beware one misuse. a show of mystery in order to gain value is only a subtler price. in the body the six lines are familiar to anyone who has sat in stillness or stood in a martial stance. the mouth closes and the tongue rests. the eyes soften and the hearing widens: the gate is shut, and yet sound still comes in. then tension that has an edge, in the jaw, the hands, the brow, is let down. then the knots: the places where the breath does not pass. a body with no edge and no knot gives an opponent nothing to hold; in push-hands the skilled partner seems to be nowhere, and that is 不可得 in the flesh. the last two lines are about bearing. a trained person tends to shine. many good teachers look like nobody in particular: ordinary clothes, ordinary walk, one with the dust. choose one conversation today and take the first line into it as a test. when you notice the wish to show that you know, a correction, a better story, the right term, let one such moment pass in silence. watch what the wish does when it is not fed. does the knowing become less? then, afterwards, one of the three pairs: recall a recent word of praise and a recent word of blame, and find the place in the body where each took hold. that place is the handle. you need not remove it. only see that it is one handle, and that both pulled on it.

知: a mouth in the word for knowing. look at the character that says “know” in a line about not speaking. 知 is 矢, an arrow, beside 口, a mouth. the shuowen says 詞也。从口从矢: “a word of speech; from mouth and from arrow”. a common explanation of the pair is that one who knows a thing can say it as fast and as straight as an arrow flies. so the script itself holds that knowing shows in the mouth, and the line denies it in four characters. the oldest copy, the guodian bamboo slips, writes 智 here (in the script of chu that was the usual graph for the verb “to know”; 知 and 智 were kept apart only later), and adds an object: the one who knows it does not speak of it. 者 makes “the one who”. english must say “he”, “those”, or “one”; the chinese gives no number and no sex. is there a thing that you know and cannot say straight?

a book that says speakers do not know. the passage is made of words, and its first line says that the one who speaks does not know. the tang poet bai juyi made the joke that every reader makes: 言者不如知者默，此語吾聞於老君；若道老君是知者，緣何自著五千文. “‘one who speaks is not equal to one who knows and is silent’: i heard this from lord lao. if you say lord lao was one who knew, why did he himself write five thousand words?” there are old answers. one: 言 is talk that explains and argues, and the book does neither; it points. two: the line is about a moment, not a rule. while you are in the knowing, there is no speaker apart from it. three: the book admits the charge. its first line already said that the dao that can be told is not the constant dao. the text is not confused about its own position. it writes from inside the paradox and expects you to see it.

the wheelwright and the duke’s book. the zhuangzi quotes these two lines, and then tells a story to show what they mean. duke huan sits in his hall and reads. below the steps the wheelwright bian is at work on a wheel. he puts down his chisel and asks what the duke reads. “the words of the sages.” are they alive? “dead.” then what you read, says bian, is only the dregs of the men of old. the duke demands an explanation or his life. bian answers from his craft. if i cut the wheel too slowly, the chisel slides and does not hold. too fast, and it sticks. not slow, not fast: i get it in the hand and feel it in the heart. the mouth cannot say it. i cannot teach it to my own son, so at seventy i still make wheels. the knowing in the line is of this kind. it is not secret. it simply does not fit in a sentence.

兌: the opening. 兌 is an old and odd word. the shuowen defines it as 說也, and 說 here is both “to speak” and “to be pleased”; both words were written with that one graph. the character is commonly explained as a person, 儿, with a mouth, 口, and two strokes above the mouth: breath or words that come out. in the book of changes 兌 is one of the eight trigrams: the lake, joy, the youngest daughter, and, in the old list of body parts, 兌為口: “兌 is the mouth”. so 塞其兌 is first “stop the mouth”, which fits the lines before it. commentators widen it to all the openings through which a person leaks outward: mouth, eyes, ears, nose. the same two lines stand in passage 52, with a promise: do this, and to the end of your life you are not worn out. see the gate.

the gate: a sitting instruction. read as practice, the six lines are steps for sitting still, and their order makes sense. stop the openings: the mouth is shut, and the eyes and ears no longer go out to fetch things. shut the gate: 門 is the two-leaf gate of a house, and here the commentators take it as the gate of the senses and of desire. then the inside work. what is sharp in you, the wish to be right and to win, is filed down. what is knotted comes loose. the glare of self goes soft, and what is left is as plain as dust. note what the lines do not ask for. no visions, no special breath, no effort to feel one with all things. each verb removes or softens; none adds. try the first two for ten minutes: sit, close the mouth, lower the eyes, and let sounds come without going out to them.

兌 inside 銳: the mouth has a point. look at the last character of 塞其兌 and the last character of 挫其銳. the second is the first with 金, metal, added at its side: 銳 is a point of metal. the shuowen defines it as 芒也, “the awn”, the sharp beard on an ear of grain, and then any fine point: a blade tip, a quick mind, the front rank of an army (精銳, “picked and sharp”, is still the word for crack troops). 兌 gives the sound. but to the eye the opening and the edge are one graph in two forms, three lines apart. is that an accident? we cannot say that the author planned it. still, the reader sees a mouth turn into a weapon, and both are closed. sharp speech is the edge that most people carry. 挫 is to file or press down. it does not break the blade. it takes off the point.

分 or 紛: divisions or a tangle. our pinned text, wang bi’s, reads 解其分. 分 is a knife, 刀, that parts a thing in two, 八: to divide; and, read fen, a share, a lot, one’s allotted place. wang bi comments 除爭原也, “this removes the source of contention”: people fight over shares and ranks, so the divisions are untied. passage 4 and most other editions, and by report the silk texts, have 紛, with the silk radical: a snarl of thread, confusion. the two readings give two pictures, a cut and a knot, and 解 fits both. the shuowen explains 解 as 判也。从刀判牛角, “to part; a knife that parts the horn from an ox”. it is the verb for the cook in the zhuangzi who takes an ox apart at its joints and never dulls the blade. the silk texts and the guodian slips are reported to give the six lines in another order: light and dust come before sharpness and tangle.

wang bi on light and dust. wang bi glosses the first two lines of the passage in four characters each. the knower does not speak: 因自然也, “this follows what is so of itself”. the speaker does not know: 造事端也, “this makes the first threads of trouble”. then light and dust. on 和其光: 無所特顯，則物無所偏爭也. “where nothing is made to stand out, things have nothing to fight over on one side.” on 同其塵: 無所特賤，則物無所偏恥也. “where nothing is held especially low, things have nothing to be ashamed of on one side.” his reading is social and exact. brightness that is shown starts a contest. lowness that is marked starts shame. the sage does neither: does not shine above, does not look down. passage 4 has more on the two verbs, 和 and 同, and on the dust that deer kick up. whom does your light put in the shade?

同: a fighting word. 同, “same”, was a word that the schools fought over. confucius used it for the yes-man: the noble person harmonizes and does not make the same, 和而不同; the small person makes the same and does not harmonize. the mohists used it for the state. one of their core doctrines is 尚同, “to conform upward”: each rank takes its idea of right from the rank above, up to the son of heaven, so that the realm has one standard and no disputes. that is sameness by command, and the centralizing states of the age liked it. the laozi takes the same word and turns it down, not up: 同其塵, to be the same as the dust. this sameness has no standard, and nobody enforces it. nothing is made equal. a person stops holding the self apart. the shuowen defines 同 as 合會也, “to come together”. see 玄同.

玄同: not “mystical union”. 玄同 is two words: 玄, the dark colour of depth, and 同, same. english versions give “mysterious agreement” (that one is legge’s), “deep identity”, “mystic unity”. each brings in a western frame: a soul that unites with god, or a subject that identifies with an object. in those frames two things first exist apart and then join, and the joining is a high event. the chinese is plainer. 同 is a state that is left when the separating stops: the mouth is closed, the edge is off, the glare is gone. nothing is added. and 玄 says that this sameness cannot be seen from outside. a person in it looks like anyone else, and in that sense it is “dark”. the word 同 was a verb two lines before, “to be the same as the dust”, and is now a noun. what was an act has become a condition.

不可得而…: no handle. the same five characters come six times: 不可得而, and then a verb. word for word: “not-can-get-and”. 得 is to get, to get hold of; 而 joins it to the next act. so 不可得而親 is “cannot be got hold of and made close”. the pattern says more than “cannot be befriended”. it says that there is no place to take hold. you cannot get a grip on this one in order to do the next thing, whether the next thing is kind or cruel. two more points. the lines have no subject: it may be the person, or the dark sameness itself. our english keeps those six lines without a subject; only the closing line needs “it”. and the silk texts are reported to add 亦, “also”, to each second half: cannot be drawn close, and also cannot be kept far. wang bi explains why the two go together.

wang bi: what can be favoured can be dropped. on each pair wang bi writes one sentence of the same form. 可得而親，則可得而疏也: “if one can be got hold of and drawn close, then one can be got hold of and kept far”. if one can be benefited, one can be harmed. if one can be raised, one can be brought low. the logic is that of a handle. the same handle serves for both directions. a person who can be won by praise can be broken by blame; a person who needs the favour of the court is in the power of the court. this is not coldness. it is the end of being for sale. on the last line he writes 無物可以加之也, “there is nothing that can be put above this”, and also “nothing that can be added to it”: 加 means both.

three ways a court holds a man. the three pairs are a full list of the means by which a warring states ruler controlled people. 親 and 疏 are near and far: who is admitted to the inner circle and who is kept out. 親 is also “kin”, and courts ran on kinship. 利 and 害 are gain and harm. the legalists built a science on this pair: han feizi calls reward and punishment the “two handles”, 二柄, by which a ruler moves ministers as a driver moves a horse. 貴 and 賤 are high and low rank, with the salary and the dress that go with each. the men who read this book were mostly of the 士 class, educated men without land who lived by finding a patron. every one of them was held by these three ropes. the passage describes a person on whom none of the three works. to a ruler such a person is useless as a tool, and also the only adviser who is safe.

貴 and 賤: rank is a price. both characters stand on 貝, a cowrie shell. the shuowen records why: 古者貨貝而寶龜, “in antiquity shells were money and tortoise-shells were treasure”, until the qin replaced shells with coins. almost every character about wealth keeps the shell: 財 (wealth), 貨 (goods), 買 (buy), 賣 (sell), 貧 (poor). so 貴 and 賤 are first words of the market. the shuowen defines 賤 as 賈少也, “the price is low”, and 貴 as 物不賤也, “a thing that is not cheap”. only then are they “noble” and “base”, the ranks of people. chinese does not hide that honour is a price that others set on you. in english “dear” still has both senses and “cheap” has both. the lines say: on this one, no price can be set, high or low. what would it be to live outside the valuation, and not above it?

貴 twice: the turn in the last line. the line before the last says 不可得而貴: it cannot be made 貴. the last line says 故為天下貴: so it is 天下貴, the 貴 of all under heaven. the same word, one line apart, with the opposite result. this is how the book often closes: the thing refused comes back at a larger size. the one who cannot be priced high by anyone is prized by everyone. the first 貴 is an act done to a person: to raise in rank. the second is a state that nobody granted. english needs two words (“raised high”, “prizes”) and so the echo is lost. passage 62 ends with the same five characters, 故為天下貴, said there of the dao. that supports the reading that the hidden subject here is not only a person. do not read the last line as a reward. a person who did the six things in order to be prized would have a handle again.

legge’s nostrils. legge’s version shows a victorian reader at work with a text that leaves things out. the chinese of the first line is four characters. he adds “(the tao)”, “(care to)”, “(about it)”, and “(ever ready to)”: the knower now has a mood, and the speaker has a fault of character. for 塞其兌，閉其門 he writes that the sage will keep the mouth shut and close “the portals (of his nostrils)”. the nostrils come from later daoist breath lore, and they turn a general line about the senses into a breathing technique. 玄同 is “the mysterious agreement”, with capitals and in quotation marks, like the name of a treaty. and each line gets a subject, “he”, “(such an one)”. the effect is a portrait of a rare male adept. the chinese has six verbs with no owner, which any reader may try on.

親 / 疏, 利 / 害, 貴 / 賤: three pairs, no side taken. six lines, three pairs: 親 and 疏, close and far; 利 and 害, gain and harm; 貴 and 賤, high and low. the grammar gives each side the same words, 不可得而, so no side is set above its partner. that is the point of the form. most advice says how to get the first of each pair and avoid the second. the passage treats the two as one thing with two ends: whoever can be raised can be brought low. to want one side is to be open to the other. a one-sided reading takes the lines as praise of distance. but 疏, far, is one of the six, and it is refused like the rest. the last line then uses 貴 once more. what kind of “high” has no “low”? the first two lines hold a pair as well, 知 and 言; see the book that speaks.

one who knows does not speak, and one who speaks does not know.. one who knows does not speak, and one who speaks does not know. is this true of the people you have met? count the cases for and against. when do you speak in order to show that you know? what was it like, early in your life, not to be heard? take the opposite view: knowledge that is not spoken helps no one, and silence is often a hiding place. stay there. what do you feel about your own silences? do the talkers annoy you, or the silent ones? what might the annoyance point at in you?

a person who can be won by praise can be broken by blame; it is one handle.. a person who can be won by praise can be broken by blame; it is one handle. do you agree that the two go together? test it against one piece of praise that you still carry. whose good opinion did you most need when you were young? is the same need at work today, under another name? now hold the opposite: to need the regard of others is human, and a person whom nothing can reach is cold. believe that for a while. what does it protect, and what does it cost? which do you want more: to be free of the handle, or to be held by it? answer before you pick the answer that sounds wiser.

兌 a person who opens the mouth. three layers, from the bottom up. at the foot, two strokes: 儿, a pair of legs, the form that “person” takes at the bottom of a character (as in 兄, elder brother, and 見, to see). in the middle, 口, a mouth. on top, two short strokes that part like breath in cold air. the common explanation is a person whose mouth opens in speech or in a smile. the shuowen files it under 儿 and says 說也: that single word covers “to speak” and “to be glad”, and it calls the top part a sound element. now watch the family that grows from this root. add 言, words: 說, to speak, to explain, to persuade. add 忄, heart: 悅, to be glad. add 月, flesh: 脫, to shed, to slip off (it is in passage 54). add 禾, grain: 稅, the tax taken out of the harvest. add 金, metal: 銳, a sharp point, which stands three lines later in this passage. in all of them a thing comes out or comes off. in the book of changes 兌 is the trigram of the lake and of joy, and of the mouth. the passage says to stop it up. see the note on the opening: it is the mouth first, and then every place where a person leaks. seven strokes. first the two on top: a dot that leans down to the right, then a short stroke that falls to the left. they lean toward each other and do not touch. then the mouth, three strokes: a short vertical; a horizontal that turns down at the corner; a horizontal that closes the box. then the legs: a stroke that falls away to the left, and the last stroke, which goes down, bends to the right along the floor, and ends in a hook that flicks up. watch the seventh stroke. it is the longest and the only one with a curve, and it must reach out wider than the mouth so that the figure does not fall. this top is the 丷 form, as in 兑. older printed fonts open the two strokes outward like 八: 兌. both forms are old.

閉 a gate and its bar. the outside is 門, a gate. the shuowen calls it a picture, 从二戶，象形: “from two 戶”, two door-leaves that hang side by side, and you can still see them, each with its panel at the top. inside the gate stands 才. as a word 才 means “talent” or “just now”, but the shuowen says that here it is a thing: 才，所以歫門也, “才 is that with which the gate is held against entry”. it is the bar and its post: one line across, one down, one brace. so 閉 is a gate with the bar in place: 闔門也, “to shut the gate”. the gate is a small theatre in the script, and each thing set in it makes a scene. a mouth in the gate, 問: to ask. an ear, 聞: to hear. the sun seen through the crack, 間: a gap, between. a piece of wood, 閑: a barrier, and then leisure. a heart, 悶: stifled, dull (it comes twice in passage 58). and 開, to open: commonly explained as two hands that lift the bar. the book speaks of gates often: the gate of all subtleties (1), the gate of the dark female (6), the gates of heaven that open and shut (10). here the gate is yours. eleven strokes. the left leaf first, four strokes: a vertical; a horizontal that turns down; and two short horizontals inside. then the right leaf, four strokes: a vertical; a horizontal that turns and goes all the way down to end in a hook; two short horizontals inside. the two leaves must not be twins: the left is a little shorter, and the right has the long hooked side that carries the weight. then the bar, three strokes: a horizontal; a vertical with a hook to the left; a stroke that falls to the left from the crossing. watch where the bar is set. it hangs in the open space under the two panels, clear of both sides, so the white around it is even. the cursive hand wrote the whole gate as one hooked line and a dot, and that shorthand became the simplified 门.

貴 a shell under a basket. the lower part is 貝, a cowrie, the small glossy sea-shell that was used as money in the shang and early zhou. the shuowen calls it a picture and tells its history: shells were the currency, then came bronze coins, and 至秦廢貝行錢, “when the qin came, shells were ended and coins were used”. the currency changed and the script did not: the shell is still in 買 (to buy), 賣 (to sell), 財 (wealth), 貨 (goods), 賞 (to reward), 貧 (poor), 賤 (cheap, base), and 寶 (treasure). the upper part of 貴 is harder. the shuowen says that it gives the sound and that it is an old form of 蕢, a carrying basket. some modern scholars see two hands in the early form. we cannot settle it; what the modern eye sees is a small load above a shell. the meaning is clear in any case: 物不賤也, “a thing that is not cheap”. from a high price the word went to high rank, and then to the act of esteem: to 貴 a thing is to hold it dear. all three senses are at work in this passage, and the last line plays the first against the third. the noble are, in the script, the expensive. twelve strokes. the top takes five: a short vertical; a horizontal that turns down; a horizontal that closes the small box; a vertical that goes through the box from above; then a long horizontal below. that long fifth stroke is the beam of the character. watch it: all the upper part rests on it, and it reaches past the shell on both sides. then the shell, seven strokes: a vertical; a horizontal that turns down; two short horizontals inside; a horizontal that closes the box; and two small legs, one that falls to the left and one dot to the right. the shell is tall and narrow, with even white bands inside. the legs are short; they are the last trace of the shell’s opening. in running script the inner lines of the shell join into a single zigzag.

57 · more laws, more thieves. by the straight, govern a state. / by surprise, use arms. / by having no business, take all under heaven. / how do i know that it is so? by this. / the more bans and taboos under heaven, / the poorer the people. / the more sharp tools the people have, / the more the state and its house go dark. / the more craft and skill people have, / the more strange things arise. / the more laws and orders are displayed, / the more thieves and bandits there are. / so the sage says: / i do not force, and the people change of themselves. / i love stillness, and the people come straight of themselves. / i have no business, and the people grow rich of themselves. / i have no desire, and the people are of themselves uncut wood. three lines of one pattern: by x, do y. by the straight, govern a state. by surprise, use arms. by no business, take the realm. then a question, how do i know, and four pieces of evidence, each of the form “the more a, the more b”: bans and poverty, sharp tools and darkness, skill and strange things, displayed law and thieves. then a speech of four lines, each of the form “i not-x, and the people of themselves y”. the count is 3, 4, 4. the four results answer the four troubles, though not one to one. two words tie the ends together: 正 opens the passage as a method and returns in the speech as an outcome, and 無事 is in line three and again in the sage’s third sentence, where its fruit is that the people grow rich. read the state as a person and the ruler as the part of you that manages. the four proofs then describe a managed mind. many inner bans, and less life. many sharp tools of analysis, and less light. much technique, and a stream of strange products. many rules set up for yourself, and a growing habit of small theft from them. the speech of the sage is then an inner instruction, and it is in the first person for that reason. i do not force, and things change. i love stillness, and what was crooked comes straight. the hard part is the claim about cause: that much of the disorder you fight in yourself is a response to the fight. this cannot be believed in advance. it can be tested for an hour. the last word says what is found when the carving stops: wood. this is among the most political passages in the book, and it is easy to misuse. it has been read as a charter for small government, and as an argument against all rules. look at what it names: taboos, arms, published penalties, and above all the ruler’s own want and undertakings. its target is the restless top. the test for a leader is in the four “the more…” lines. when you add a rule, do you get the behaviour, or a new skill at evasion? when you launch one more initiative, who pays for it in hours? one government tried this and the granaries filled. note also the grammar of credit: “i do not… and the people of themselves…”. the sage claims the restraint and gives the result away. wang bi warns that even “being correct” is a way to start a war. a gardener who is always at work in the bed, staking, spraying, moving plants, gets weak plants and more pests. systems that live have their own ways to come level, and a constant push from outside sets off a constant push back. foresters learned that a wood where every small fire is put out builds up the fuel for a great one. farmers learned that each new poison breeds an insect that survives it: 奇物滋起. the four lines of the sage are how a good keeper of land talks. not “i leave it alone” as neglect, but: i do not force it, i disturb it little, i want little from it, and it grows rich of itself. the image at the end is the tree that was not cut: 樸. pick one small domain that you run: a team’s routine, a child’s evening, your own morning. find one rule in it that you have had to tighten more than once. for one week take the rule away, and take away your wish for the result as well, which is harder; that is 無欲. do not announce it. watch what the people, or you, do of themselves. if things get worse, put the rule back; the passage is an observation, and you are checking it. then ask the question of the first line about your usual method: am i governing here, or using arms?

正: the first word comes back. 正 is “straight, upright, correct, regular”. it was the word for good rule: 政, “government”, is 正 with a hand that holds a rod, and the shuowen defines the one by the other: 政，正也. confucius said the same to a minister: 政者，正也, “to govern is to make straight; if you lead by being straight, who will dare not to be?” so the first line sounds like common wisdom: rule by the correct. then the passage undoes it. the four proofs show what correction by decree produces. and at the end the people 自正, come straight of themselves, when the ruler loves stillness. the straightness that opened the passage as a tool returns as a result that nobody applied. wang bi heard the first line as a warning from the start, and legge half agreed. the next passage finishes the thought: 正復為奇, “the straight turns back into the strange”.

奇 and 正: terms of the generals. 正 and 奇 are a pair from the art of war. in sunzi’s chapter on force, 正 is the regular body of troops that meets the enemy head-on, and 奇 (qi) is the irregular force that strikes where nobody looks. 凡戰者，以正合，以奇勝: “in every battle, engage with the regular and win with the irregular.” he adds that the two give birth to each other, like a ring with no end. the same book says that war is 詭道, a way of deception. so the first two lines share out the pair: 正 for the state, 奇 for the army. a general or minister of the time would nod. the third line then steps outside the pair. the realm is taken by neither. note that the passage does not say “never use arms”. it says what arms are: the field of the crooked. the silk texts are reported to write 畸, an odd-shaped leftover field, and to open with 以正之邦 (manuscript a; 之 stands for 治).

無事: not “doing nothing”. 事 is work done in service: a task, an office, an affair of state. the shuowen says 職也, “a duty”. a state’s 事 were its undertakings, and an old saying names the greatest: 國之大事，在祀與戎, “the great affairs of a state are sacrifice and war”. to “have 事” with a neighbour was to be at war with it. add the palaces, walls, canals, and royal tours, each paid for with the forced labour of farmers. 無事 is a state with none of that on its hands: no campaigns, no projects. english “non-interference” makes it a theory, and “inaction” makes it laziness. it differs from 無為, which is about how one acts; 無事 is about how much is set going. passage 48 says it flatly: the realm is always taken by 無事, and one who 有事 is not fit to take it. passage 63 makes it a verb: 事無事, “serve no-business”.

取天下: the prize of the age. 取 is “to take”: its picture is a hand on an ear, a trophy of war (see the plate in passage 48). 取天下, “to take all under heaven”, is not a soft phrase. it was the open aim of every large state: to end the wars by being the last one left. soft translations, “win the world”, “gain the empire’s trust”, hide that. the laozi keeps the word of the conquerors and gives it an impossible method. history then ran a test. qin took all under heaven in 221 bce by the opposite way, with law, armies, and endless 事, and its dynasty fell in fifteen years. the han that followed began with rulers who admired this book. see what they did. is “take” still the right verb for what the third line describes? or does the method change the meaning of the prize?

when a government tried it. for about sixty years after 200 bce the han court favoured the teaching called huang-lao, “the yellow emperor and laozi”. the land was ruined by war. the chancellor cao can, a former general, took office and changed nothing that his predecessor had set up; when officials came with proposals he poured them wine until they forgot. the historian sima qian records the song that the people made: he kept it pure and still, and the people were at peace as one. under the emperors wen and jing taxes on land fell to a thirtieth, mutilating punishments were ended, and the granaries filled. sima qian also opens his chapter on harsh officials with lines from this book, among them 法令滋章，盜賊多有 (he writes 章 for 彰). it did not last; emperor wu chose war and state monopolies. but for two generations the last four lines were policy. did it work because of the teaching, or because the country was too tired for anything else?

以此: here “this” is a list. the question and its two-word answer also stand in passages 21 and 54. there 以此, “by this”, is left open. here it is followed at once by four observations, so “this” reads as “what follows”: look at the realm as it is. the speaker does not argue from a principle. the proof is four things that anyone at the time could see. the silk texts are reported to have the question and no 以此 at all: 吾何以知亓然也, and then 夫, “now,…”, and the list. so the answer may have been added here later, to match the other passages. the first-person 吾 is rare in the book. it marks the places where the text stops to say how it knows.

忌諱: the forbidden and the unsayable. two words for two kinds of “do not”. 忌 has 心, heart, below: the shuowen says 憎惡也, “to hate and shun”. it was used for things and days that brought bad luck: do not dig on this day, do not travel in that direction. 諱 has 言, speech: it is a word that must not be said, above all the personal name of a ruler or a father. a taboo on a name could change the text of books; this very book lost its word 邦 to the name of the first han emperor. together 忌諱 covers all that a state and its customs forbid. why would bans make people poor? a farmer who may not cut wood on the lord’s hill, fish his marsh, work on unlucky days, or speak of what goes wrong has fewer ways to live. count the things in your working day that are forbidden for reasons nobody can give.

利器: weapons, tools, or tricks?. 利 is “sharp” and also “profit” (a blade in the grain; see passage 11). 器 is any made tool. so 利器 is “sharp implements”, and readers differ on what they are. one: weapons. when the people are armed, the state is in the dark. two: clever devices, the new machines of an inventive age. three, wang bi’s: 凡所以利己之器也, “all means by which one profits oneself”. he then adds a hard line: 民强則國家弱, “when the people are strong, the state is weak”. that sounds like the legalist book of lord shang, which says the same and draws the opposite lesson: so weaken the people. passage 36 uses the phrase of the ruler: the 利器 of the state must not be shown to people. english must choose one reading. we kept “sharp tools”, which can still cut three ways. which did you hear first?

昬: the people inside the dark. 昬 is dusk: the hour when the sun has gone under. the usual form is 昏. the shuowen explains that form as the sun, 日, below a short form of 氐, “down”: 日冥也, “the sun grows dark”. then it adds four words: 一曰民聲, “one view: 民 gives the sound”. that second view is the form in our text: 民, “the people”, over 日. read the line again with that in the eye: 民多利器，國家滋昬. the word for the people stands at the head of the line and again inside its last character. the form with 民 was avoided in the tang, since 民 was in the personal name of the emperor taizong, li shimin; the qing scholar duan yucai held that the four words on 民 were added to the dictionary later. 國家 is two things, the ruler’s state and the great houses, and not yet the modern word “country”. the darkness is that of a mind as well as an evening: 昏 is also “confused, dazed”. the speaker of passage 20 uses it for the self: i alone am 昏.

奇 again: from tactic to gadget. the second line gave 奇 to the army: surprise. seven lines on it is back: 奇物, “strange things”. the age had many. iron was cast in moulds. the crossbow had a bronze trigger of several fitted parts. the mozi tells of an engineer who built a “cloud ladder” to storm a city wall. 伎巧 is the skill behind such things; the shuowen defines 巧 as 技也, “craft”, and its left side 工 is a carpenter’s square. the text does not say that skill is evil. it says what grows with it: novelties, and after them the wish for novelties. the silk texts are reported to read 人多知, “people have much knowledge”, in place of “craft and skill”. that widens the target from the workshop to the clever mind. the same word 奇 serves the general and the inventor: both make the thing that you did not expect.

法令滋彰: law put on show. 彰 is “bright, displayed, made plain”. in 536 bce the minister zichan of zheng had a penal code cast in bronze for all to see. the statesman shuxiang wrote to him in dismay: once the people know the written rule, they lose awe of their superiors and will argue over every point “down to the tip of an awl and a knife”. that quarrel ran through the next three centuries. the legalists won it in practice: shang yang’s laws in qin were published, exact, and merciless, and they made qin the strongest state. the line takes shuxiang’s side in eight characters, and adds a result: more thieves. a law creates its crime, and a displayed law teaches how to stand just outside it. there is a variant. the heshang gong edition reads 法物, and the silk texts are reported to agree; that commentary takes it as “fine things”: the more fine goods are shown, the more thieves. both readings share the verb: display.

盜 and 賊: the mouth that waters, the spear. the two words are not the same crime. 盜 is the thief who takes by stealth. the shuowen takes the character apart with humour: 从㳄，㳄欲皿者, “from 㳄, to drool: one who drools with desire over a dish”. the top is water beside an open mouth, and the bottom is 皿, a dish that belongs to another. theft begins as a look at a plate. 賊 has 戈, a dagger-axe, on its right, and the shuowen says 敗也, “to ruin”: this is the one who harms with force, a bandit or a rebel, and it is also a verb, to injure. (its left part still shows the shell 貝.) legal texts of the time kept the two apart: 盜 for property, 賊 for violence. so the line names the full range, from the hungry eye to the armed band, and puts the published law at the start of both.

聖人 says “i”. 聖人 is “the sage”, and the english word misleads. it is not a saint: no holiness or moral purity is meant. it is not a philosopher. the character 聖 has an ear, 耳, and a mouth, 口; the shuowen defines it as 通也, “to get through, to be open”: one who hears what is there and speaks in tune with it. in this book the 聖人 is usually a ruler, the ideal one. here the sage speaks, and that is rare. 我, “i”, comes four times. chinese does not need the pronoun, so its use is a stress: i, for my part. all four sentences have the same shape. the first half is a thing that the ruler does not do. the second half is a thing that the people do. the ruler does not take credit for the second half; 而 is only “and”. the silk texts are reported to introduce the lines as “the words of the sage”: a saying already old.

無為: without the forcing. 無為 is “not doing” by the characters: 無, to be without, and 為, to do, to make, to act as. the usual explanation of the early form of 為 is a hand that leads an elephant: work done on a large thing by will. so 無為 is not idleness. it is action without that hand: with no forcing, no scheme laid on top of how things go. we write “do not force”. “non-action” suggests a ruler asleep, and that reading has been used to mock the book for two thousand years. here 無為 is the first of four, and the other three explain it: love of stillness, no business, no desire. each one removes a pressure that comes from the top. the claim is an observation about cause: the people’s disorder was a response.

自: a nose that points at itself. four times the people do a thing 自: 自化, 自正, 自富, 自樸. 自 is “self” and “from”. the shuowen gives the picture: 鼻也。象鼻形, “the nose; it shows the shape of a nose”. a person in china points at the nose to say “me”, and the word for self took the picture. (the nose then needed a new character, 鼻, which keeps 自 on top.) put before a verb, 自 means that the act starts from the one who does it, with no push from outside. this is the grammar of the book’s great word 自然, “so of itself”, which english turns into “nature”. passage 17 gives the same scene from the people’s side: the work is done, and the hundred families all say: we are like this of ourselves. english “spontaneously” sounds sudden, and “naturally” sounds weak. the chinese is plain: from themselves.

無欲, or 欲不欲. the received text says 我無欲, “i am without desire”. the silk texts are reported to read 我欲不欲: “i desire not to desire”, or “i desire what is not desired”. the same phrase is in passage 64, where the sage 欲不欲 and does not prize rare goods. the silk reading is the more honest of the two. a ruler with no desire at all is hard to picture; a ruler whose one wish is to be free of the usual wishes is a person. wang bi explains why this line matters most: what the one above wants, the people run after. 欲 is want of every kind. the shuowen says 貪欲也, “greed”; the graph has 欠, a mouth wide open, beside 谷, valley, which gives the sound. a court that wants pearls sends divers down. a court that wants land sends farmers to die. what does the top of your house want, and who runs to get it?
