樸: wood before the knife. 樸 has 木, a tree, at the left. the shuowen defines it in two words: 木素也, “wood in its plain state”: timber that is felled and not yet cut into anything. it is a main image of the book, and “simplicity” loses it. in passage 15 the masters of old are solid like 樸. passage 19 says: show the undyed silk, hold the 樸 in your arms. in 28 the 樸 is split up and becomes tools, and the sage, who uses it whole, becomes chief of the officials. in 32 the dao is called nameless 樸, small, and nobody under heaven can make it a subject. in 37 it is what calms desire. so when the people “are 樸 of themselves”, it does not mean that they are simple-minded or poor. it means that they are not yet carved into the tools of a state: soldiers, taxpayers, informers. the last word of the passage is a piece of wood.

wang bi: the first line is a trap. most readers take line one as advice. wang bi does not. 以道治國則國平，以正治國則奇正起也: “govern the state by the dao and the state is level. govern the state by correctness and the irregular and the regular both arise.” to rule by 正 is to set up a standard and attack what departs from it, and that already is the logic of war. he goes on: 夫以道治國，崇本以息末；以正治國，立辟以攻末. “to govern by the dao is to honour the root and so let the branch-tips rest. to govern by correctness is to set up penalties and so attack the branch-tips.” the root is not established, the people have nowhere to turn, and so it must end in “surprise and arms”. on the last lines: 上之所欲，民從之速也, “what the one above desires, the people follow fast”. his summary of all four is his own motto: 崇本以息末.

legge’s “crafty dexterity”. legge gives 正 as “(measures of) correction”, which is close to wang bi’s sense. for 奇 he writes “crafty dexterity”, and he uses the same two words again for 伎巧, the people’s skills. so in his english the general’s surprise and the craftsman’s cleverness are one moral fault; the chinese has two different words, and neither is plainly a fault. for the third line he has the kingdom “made one’s own (only) by freedom from action and purpose”. “purpose” is his addition: a protestant conscience has entered, in which the will is the thing to examine. in the sage’s speech he writes “i will do nothing (of purpose)” and “i will manifest no ambition”. the chinese verbs have no future tense and no “will”. the sage does not make a resolution. the sage reports what is the case.

正 / 奇: the straight and the strange. 正 and 奇, the straight and the strange, or the regular and the surprise, are a pair from the art of war, and sunzi says that each gives birth to the other. the first two lines seem to rank them: the straight for the state, surprise for arms. the rest of the passage does not let the rank stand. the four proofs show the straight, when it is applied by decree, giving rise to the strange: 奇物, strange things, and thieves. then 正 comes back in this line as something that the people do of themselves. so the passage has two kinds of straight, one pressed on and one grown, and the first turns into its opposite. a one-sided reading takes the first line as plain advice, “govern by the correct”, and misses the turn. the next passage says it in four characters: 正復為奇. has a rule of yours bred the thing that it forbade?

the more rules and bans are set up, the more disorder they breed.. the more rules and bans are set up, the more disorder they breed. is this what you have seen, at work, at home, in yourself? give one case each way. how do you react to a rule, as the one who makes it and as the one who is under it? where did each reaction start? take the other side in full: people need firm rules, and without them the strong take from the weak. hold it as true for a while. what feelings arise, and what memories? which view suits your temper, and which view would you prefer not to look at? why is that useful to know?

when the one in charge stops forcing and wanting, people come right of themselves.. when the one in charge stops forcing and wanting, people come right of themselves. do you trust this? think of a time when you stepped back and it went well, and a time when it did not. what do you fear will happen if you stop managing? is that fear from an event, or from the voice of a person? now hold the opposite: left alone, people drift, and someone has to push. stay with it for a few minutes. does it feel like duty, like worry, or like a wish to matter? the sage in the passage wants nothing from the result. could you? what would you lose if the people did well and it was not your doing?

兵 two hands on an axe. the word means “weapon”, then “soldier”, then “war”, in that order of age. the shuowen sees the first sense in the shape: 械也。从廾持斤，并力之皃, “an implement; from two hands that hold an axe: the look of strength joined”. the top of the character is 斤, an axe. the dictionary calls 斤 a picture and says what it is for: 斫木也, “to chop wood”. it was a tool before it was a weapon, and it is in 析 (to split wood), 匠 (a carpenter: an axe in a box), and 新 (new; the shuowen says “to take wood”). it also became a unit of weight, the “catty”. the bottom of 兵 is what the brush made of 廾, two hands that reach up; the same two hands hold a dagger-axe in 戒, “to be on guard”, 从廾持戈. so a weapon, for the script, is a tool for wood in a tight grip. that is the history of weapons in one sign, and it is the worry of this passage: the people have many sharp tools, and a tool is a weapon when two hands decide so. sunzi’s book opens with this character: 兵者，國之大事, “war is the great affair of the state”. the second line here gives it its method. the book’s own verdict is in passage 31: arms are tools of ill omen. seven strokes. first a stroke at the top that falls from right to left, short and flat. then a vertical down the left side. then a short horizontal from that vertical to the right. then a second vertical, on the right. these four are the axe. the fifth stroke is a long horizontal under them all: the widest line, and the place where axe and hands meet. then the hands, now only two short strokes: one that falls to the left and one dot that falls to the right. watch the fifth stroke. if it is level and long, the character stands like a table on two feet. if it is short, the top falls over. in seal script two full hands are drawn under the axe. in clerical script the long horizontal ends in a heavy flare.

民 the many sprouts, or a blinded eye. 民 comes six times in this passage, more than any other word: “the people”, those who are ruled. the shuowen defines it in two characters: 眾萌也, “the many sprouts”. 萌 is a shoot of grass that has just come up, and the dictionary says so in its own entry: 艸芽也. the people are the countless small green things that come up of themselves, and that fits the end of the passage, where they change, come straight, and grow rich of themselves. then the shuowen adds that the graph follows the shape of the ancient script, and stops; it cannot explain the picture. modern scholars have looked at the bronze forms, and a view that is widely repeated, and disputed, is dark: an eye with a spike driven into it, a captive blinded in one eye and put to work. if that is right, 民 began as a word for slaves and widened to all subjects. the reader may hold both: the grass and the wound. 民 is not 人. 人 is any human being; 民 is the governed mass as a ruler sees it. watch the passage change from 民 to 人 in the line on craft and skill. the character gives its sound to 氓, a commoner, and in this passage it sits inside 昬, the word for dusk. in the tang it was an emperor’s name, and copyists wrote 人 in its place. five strokes, and each one is different. first a horizontal that turns down at the right: the top and right side of a small box. second, a short horizontal that closes the box below. third, a vertical on the left that runs down the whole height and ends in a flick up to the right. fourth, a longer horizontal that starts from that vertical, below the box, and reaches right. fifth, the long hook: it starts at the middle of the box’s base, slants down to the lower right across the fourth stroke, and ends with a hook that points up. watch the fifth stroke. it is the spine of the character, a bow drawn from corner to corner, and the brush must keep pressure through the whole curve and release only at the hook. the box at the top is small; if it is large the character looks like 尸.

正 a foot that stops at the line. five plain strokes. the lower four are 止, and the shuowen says of 止 that it came to be used for the foot: 故以止爲足. the stroke on top is 一, a line. the dictionary reads the two together: 正，是也。从止，一以止, “正 is ‘right’; from 止, with 一 as that at which it stops”. a foot that goes to the mark and stops there: on target, straight, correct. many modern scholars read the oldest forms in a harder way: the top was a small square, a walled town, and the foot marches on it. that is the first form of 征, “to go on a punitive campaign”, to correct a neighbour by force. we cannot settle the early form here. but both readings are in this passage. wang bi says that to rule by 正 is already to prepare for war. the family is large. 政, government, is 正 with a hand that holds a rod, and the shuowen defines the one by the other. 定, “settled”, is 正 under a roof: 从宀从正. 是, “this is so”, is 正 under the sun: 从日、正. 整 is “to put in order”. and since the character has exactly five strokes, chinese uses it to keep count: one stroke for each item, a full 正 for each five. the first word of the passage is a tally mark and a march. five strokes. a horizontal across the top. a vertical down from its middle. a short horizontal that goes right from the middle of that vertical. a short vertical on the left, which stands a little apart and does not touch the top line. then the long horizontal at the bottom, the widest stroke, which joins the feet of both verticals. watch the top and bottom lines. they are parallel, and the bottom one is longer; the whole character hangs between them like a frame. nothing in it leans, and for that reason a writer shows a slow, even hand here or shows nothing. beginners in regular script practise this character for its right angles. in running script the third and fourth strokes join in one small loop, and the foot begins to walk again.

58 · where disaster crouches. where the rule is muffled and dull, / the people are thick and whole. / where the rule is sharp-eyed, / the people are chipped and lacking. / disaster, ah: good fortune leans on it. / good fortune, ah: disaster crouches in it. / who knows where it ends? / there is no straight. / the straight turns back into the strange. / the good turns back into the uncanny. / the people’s bewilderment: / its days are long indeed. / so the sage is / square, and does not cut; / cornered, and does not wound; / straight, and does not push to the limit; / bright, and does not dazzle. three parts that seem at first to be three subjects. part one is politics, in four doubled words: a muffled rule and a whole people; a sharp-eyed rule and a chipped people. part two is fortune: disaster and blessing each hold the other; nobody knows the last turn; the straight turns strange and the good turns uncanny; people have long been lost. part three is four lines on form: square, cornered, straight, bright, each with a “but does not”. the link is the short line in the middle, 其無正. since no fixed “correct” holds, a rule that enforces the correct breaks its people, and a person who has a shape must take care that the shape does not cut. the passage is the second half of passage 57, and shares its key words: 正, 奇, 民. the two lines on fortune are often read as comfort: bad luck holds good luck. they are that. they are also a caution of the same weight: your good fortune has something crouched in it. taken together, they loosen the habit that runs most of a day, the instant sorting of each event into “for me” and “against me”. the text does not say that the sorting is wrong. it asks who knows the end. the mind that stops insisting on the verdict becomes a little 悶悶, less sharp, less sure, and in the terms of the first stanza, more whole. the same holds for the idea of oneself as good. 善復為妖: goodness that is held up and watched goes strange. the four last lines describe a character without that self-watching: it has form, and it does not use the form on anyone. the first stanza is a finding about measurement. a leader who inspects everything, who sets a metric for every act, gets people who are 缺缺: each one reduced to what is checked, and skilled at the gaps between the checks. a leader whose rule looks vague from outside may be the one whose people are 淳淳. this is not a defence of neglect. wang bi says the muffled rule ends in “great order”; the test is the people and not the look of the office. the middle lines warn reformers. a correction can become the next abuse, and a published virtue the next freak. do not give up on standards for that reason. hold them as the last four lines say: square and not cutting. and hold the lamp so that a lost person can see the road. do not point it into the person’s face. the four last lines are good instructions for posture and for touch. square: the frame is aligned, hips and shoulders level, and yet nothing in it is rigid enough to hurt on contact. cornered: the angles of the joints are exact, and their edges are padded with softness. straight: the spine is long, and it does not strain upward past ease; that is 不肆. bright: the eyes are awake, and they do not stare. in partner work the same four hold. a teacher’s correcting hand should have a clear shape and no cut in it. timing belongs to the middle lines: strength at its fullest is where the fall lies in wait, and the low point of a movement is where the rise leans. a fighter who loves the winning position is already in the next one. a river in flood is disaster to this year’s field and the source of next year’s soil; the yellow river built the plain that it drowns. a fire clears a wood and opens the seeds that only heat can open. a fat year breeds the many mouths of a hungry one. living systems do not have a “correct” state that stays. they have turning, 復, and what is called health is an ability to keep turning. the last four lines read well as a description of a mature landscape: old mountains are still mountains, and their edges are worn so that things can live on them. light at noon in the desert kills, and under leaves it feeds. 光而不燿 is the light of a forest floor. use the old man’s question for one day: how do i know? then look at one place where you are in charge of others, even slightly, and ask which of the two governments you run there. count your acts of checking in a day. remove one. do not announce the change, and give it a week before you judge it. see if the people there become, by a small degree, less chipped. then ask the old man’s question about that result as well.

悶悶: a heart behind a gate. 悶 is 心, a heart, inside 門, a gate. the shuowen says 懣也, “stifled, pent up”; today it is the word for a stuffy room and a low mood. said twice, 悶悶, it is a rule that seems shut in and slow: no bright policy, no clear voice. a reader of the time would call such a government stupid. the text takes the insult and wears it. it has done this before. in passage 20 the speaker says of the self: 俗人察察，我獨悶悶, “the common people are 察察, sharp-eyed; i alone am 悶悶”. the two doubled words of that line are the two doubled words of this passage. what passage 20 said of a person, this one says of a state. the dull ruler is the sage of passage 20 on a throne. wang bi describes it: no form, no name, no business, no policy that one can point to.

four doubled words. the first stanza is made of four doubled syllables: 悶悶, 淳淳, 察察, 缺缺. classical chinese doubles a word to describe a look or a mood, as english says “hush-hush” or “so-so”. the sound does half the work. in the old pronunciation 悶 and 淳 rhymed (both are in the 文 rhyme group): a low, closed, humming pair. 察 and 缺 also rhymed (the 月 group), and both ended in a stopped consonant: clipped and hard. so the calm state hums, and the watched state clicks. 淳 has the water radical; it is used of a liquid that is thick and not thinned, like the related word 醇, strong unmixed wine, and then of people who are honest and whole. flat english adjectives lose all of this, and legge tried rhyme in their place. our pairs, “muffled and dull”, “thick and whole”, are only a rough stand-in for one word said twice. the silk texts are reported to write the first two as 閔閔 and 屯屯: other graphs for like sounds.

察察: the state that sees everything. 察 is to look into, to inspect. the shuowen explains it as 覆也。从宀、祭: “to go over a thing; a roof above 祭, sacrifice”: the close check of an offering under the temple roof. doubled, it is a gaze that misses nothing. this was a policy with a name and a date. in qin, from 356 bce, lord shang put all households into groups of five and ten that answered for one another. one who did not report a crime in the group was cut in two at the waist. one who reported it got the same reward as a soldier who took an enemy’s head. wang bi sums up the method in three phrases: 立刑名，明賞罰，以檢姦偽, “set up punishments and titles, make rewards and penalties clear, and so check the false and the wicked”. the result, he says, is that the people 懷爭競, “carry rivalry in their hearts”. what does it do to you to be watched well?

缺缺: chipped pots. 缺 has 缶, an earthenware jar, at its left. the shuowen: 器破也, “a vessel is broken”: a chip in the rim, a piece gone. doubled, it is said of the people under a sharp-eyed rule. they are not whole. something has been knocked out of each one. other readers take the word as “wanting, needy” or as “cunning”: people who learn to slip through gaps. all three follow from the picture. the silk texts are reported to differ here in a way that matters: 亓正察察，亓邦夬夬 (so manuscript a; b has 國 for 邦), “where the rule is sharp-eyed, the state is 夬夬”. 夬 is “to split open, to breach”, the root of 缺 and of 決, a dyke that bursts. so in the older text the thing that breaks is the state. it is the same thought as passage 57: the state goes dark. the received text moved the damage to the people. both are true. which breaks first?

禍 and 福: both from the altar. look at the left side of both words: 礻, the short form of 示, the altar sign that marks things of the spirits. in early china good and bad fortune were not chance. they were sent: by ancestors who were fed or neglected, by heaven that was pleased or angry. 福 was the blessing asked for at the sacrifice; the meat from the altar, sent to kin after the rite, could itself be called 福. 禍 was what the spirits sent down in displeasure; the shuowen defines the one by the lack of the other: 害也，神不福也, “harm: the spirits do not bless”. so the common belief was moral and simple: do right, feed the dead, and get 福. the two lines here break that link without a word against the spirits. they only observe that the two are found in each other. 兮 is a breath in the line, the “ah” of a song; it marks this as verse and slows it. english “luck” is too light, and “blessing” and “curse” too churchly. see also the two verbs.

倚 and 伏: to lean, to crouch. the two verbs are body positions. 倚 is a person, 亻, who leans on a thing; the shuowen says 依也, “to rest against”. good fortune leans on disaster as on a door-post: take the post away and it falls. 伏 is a person beside 犬, a dog. the shuowen: 司也。从人从犬, “to keep watch; from person and dog”. it is the dog that lies low and waits, and the word for an ambush is still 埋伏. so disaster is not after good fortune, like a later stage. it is inside it now, flat on the ground and patient. there is a small thing for the eye as well: the sound-part of 倚 is 奇, the “strange” that the straight turns into three lines later. the grammar is exact: 福之所倚 is “that on which fortune leans”. each one is the place where the other is to be found.

the old man who lost his horse. the best-known comment on these lines is a story in the huainanzi, a han book of the second century bce. an old man who lived near the northern frontier lost his horse; it ran off into the land of the nomads. people came to console him. the old man said: how do you know that this is not good fortune? months later the horse came back with a fine nomad horse beside it. people came to congratulate. the old man said: how do you know that this is not disaster? the son rode the new horse, fell, and broke his thigh. people came to console. the old man said the same. a year later the nomads invaded; every able man took up the bow, and nine in ten died. the lame son lived. every chinese child knows the four-character form: 塞翁失馬, “the old man of the frontier loses a horse”. notice that the old man never says “this is good”. he only asks how they know.

極: the ridgepole. 極 has 木, wood, and the shuowen defines it as 棟也: “the ridgepole”, the highest beam of a house, where the two slopes of the roof meet. from “the top beam” the word came to mean the highest point, the farthest limit, the end of a road, and the pole of the sky. 孰知其極 is “who knows its 極?”: who knows the last turn, the point where disaster and fortune stop changing places and one of them is final? english “end” has only time in it and “limit” only space. 極 keeps the picture of a ridge: the line at which one slope becomes the other. the passage’s answer is that nobody stands there. the same phrase comes in the next passage in a good sense: of one who stores up 德, nobody knows the 極. have you ever been sure that a thing was the worst, or the best, and been wrong?

其無正: three readings, and wang bi’s. three characters, and no agreement. one: a statement. “there is no straight”: no fixed standard holds, since the next line says that the straight turns strange. we render this. two: a question, as some editions mark with a final particle: “is there then no standard?” three, wang bi’s. he takes 正 as 政, rule, which the silk texts are reported to write as 正 in line one, and he joins the phrase to the question before it: 言誰知善治之極乎！唯無可正舉，無可形名，悶悶然而天下大化，是其極也. “this says: who knows the utmost point of good government? only where there is no correcting that one can hold up, no form and name that one can give, where all is muffled and dull and yet the whole realm is transformed: that is its utmost point.” for him the line is not about fate at all. it names the best government: one with no 正 to show. which reading does the stanza before it support? and the stanza after?

復: turning, not poles. 復 is “to go back along the road”; the shuowen says 往來也, “to go and come”. it is one of the verbs that carry the thought of this book: all things rise, and i watch them 復 (16); return to the infant, to the uncut wood (28). here the turn is unwelcome. 正復為奇: the straight goes round and is the strange. this takes up the first lines of passage 57, where 正 was for the state and 奇 for the army; wang bi makes the link himself. western readers reach for “opposites” or “polarity”. those words draw two fixed ends with a line between. the chinese picture has no ends. it is a path that bends until it faces the other way, and the walker does not feel the bend. a reform hardens into a creed, and a cure into a habit. where on the curve are you now?

妖: a word from the omen books. 善, “good”, turns into 妖. english versions say “evil”, and that makes a moral pair that the chinese does not have here. 妖 is a term of omen lore. the zuozhuan defines it: 天反時為災，地反物為妖, “when heaven goes against the seasons, that is calamity; when earth goes against the nature of things, that is 妖”: a tree that flowers in winter, a hen that crows, a birth that is wrong. it is the uncanny, the thing out of its kind. later, with its woman radical 女, it named the bewitching spirits of popular tales, the fox that takes a girl’s shape; the silk texts are reported to write the word with no woman sign, as 訞. so the line says more than “good becomes bad”. goodness that is set up as a standard turns into a thing against nature. wang bi: 立善以和萬物，則便復有妖之患也, “set up the good in order to harmonize all things, and at once you have the trouble of 妖 again”. think of a virtue that you have seen go strange.

迷: lost on the road. 迷 has 辶, the sign of walking, the same that is in 道. its other part, 米, gives the sound. the shuowen glosses it 或也, where 或 stands for 惑, “to be in doubt, deluded”. the first sense is concrete: to lose the way, as a traveller does at a fork with no sign. so 人之迷 is not “the sin of man” and not “ignorance”. it is people who have lost the road, and since the road is the 道, the pun is built in. 其日固久, “its days are long indeed”: this did not start with us. the tone is odd for the book, almost a sigh. wang bi draws a mild rule from it: people have been lost for so long that you cannot hold them to account with “correct” and “good”. one who is lost needs a direction, not a verdict.

聖人: a sage the silk texts lack. 聖人 is “the sage”: not a saint and not a scholar, but one whose ear 耳 and mouth 口 are tuned to how things go, and in this book usually the ideal ruler. here the words may be a later guest. the silk texts are reported to read only 是以方而不割: “so: square and not cutting”, with no subject. then the four lines are not a portrait of a rare person. they are four rules of form that anyone may take up, or a description of the muffled government of line one. the received text gave the lines an owner. they are reported to differ in the four pairs too: 兼而不刺 (“not stabbing”) for 廉而不劌, and 直而不紲 for 直而不肆.

four words from the workshop. 方, 廉, 直, 光: square, corner, straight line, light. english versions turn them at once into morals: “upright”, “honest”, “principled”. in chinese they are first the terms of a carpenter and a jade-cutter, and each is paired with the harm that its shape can do. a square thing has edges that slice: 割, which the shuowen glosses 剥也, “to flay”. a corner can gash. a straight line can run on past its place. a light can blind. so each line says: have the form, and do not let the form injure. the moral sense is there, since 方 is also “correct” and 直 “honest”. but the picture comes first, and it is exact about the danger of each virtue. wang bi quotes passage 41: 大方無隅, “the great square has no corners”. how can a thing be square and have no corner that cuts?

廉而不劌: said of jade. 廉 is first a place in a building: the sharp edge of the raised platform on which a hall stands. the shuowen files it under 广, a building open at the front, and glosses it with a rare word for “side, edge”. from “edge” it became a quality of people: one with clean edges, who takes nothing that is not due; then “incorrupt”, the standard praise for an official. (today 廉 is also “low-priced”.) 劌 is to wound with a blade: 利傷也, “to hurt with sharpness”. the four characters 廉而不劌 are not found only here. in the record of rites, confucius explains why the noble person values jade, and lists its virtues. one is this: jade has edges, and they do not cut the hand, and that is its rightness. the shuowen says of jade, in like words, 銳廉而不技: its edge is keen and does not cut. so the line may be a saying of jade-workers that both schools used. pick up a stone that is worked and polished. the corner is exact, and it is safe.

肆: straight, and then too far. 肆 is to let a thing go out to its full length: to spread goods on a stall (it also means “a shop”), to lay out a body, to give free rein. of a person it is “unrestrained, reckless”. 直而不肆 is “straight, and not let loose”. straightness has a typical vice: it keeps going. an honest person says the true thing and then the next true thing, past the point of use, into the other’s wound. wang bi’s image is of water at the boil: one leads with straightness and does not 激沸, “stir to boiling”. he cites passage 45: 大直若屈, “great straightness seems bent”. the silk texts are reported to read 紲, a tether; the shuowen glosses that 系也, “to tie”. if that is the old reading, the sense may be “straight, yet not a leash on others”. english “straight” has lost the edge. is your honesty a line or a ray?

光而不燿: wang bi’s two lamps. 光 is light: the shuowen sees fire above a person, 从火在人上. 燿 is to blaze, to dazzle; 照也, “to shine on”. the line recalls 和其光, “temper the light”, of passages 4 and 56. wang bi’s comment here is among his best: 以光鑑其所以迷，不以光照求其隱慝也. “use the light to mirror that by which they went astray; do not use the light to shine into them and hunt out their hidden faults.” there are two ways to hold a lamp. one lights the road, so that a person who is lost can see where the wrong turn was. the other is turned on the person’s face. the second is the 察察 of the first stanza: inspection. so the last line of the passage answers its third. he ends with his motto: all this honours the root and lets the branch-tips rest; 不攻而使復之也, “without attack, it brings them back”.

legge’s couplets. legge turns the first stanza into four lines of rhymed english, in the manner of an 18th-century moral poem. 悶悶 becomes a government “that seems the most unwise”: the “seems” is his, and it saves the ruler’s honour at once. 察察 becomes “meddling, touching everything”: hands, where the chinese has eyes. the people’s two states are gone; in their place are “goodness” and “disappointment”. the doubled sounds, which carry the feeling, could not survive verse of this kind. for 其無正 he writes a full question with a “we”: “shall we then dispense with correction?” that follows wang bi’s sense of 正 as government, and it adds an anxious victorian voice that fears disorder. at the end he says the sage “allows himself no license” for 不肆. the line is now about self-control and private morals. the chinese is about not harming others with one’s straightness.

the old man’s question. for one day, use the question of the old man at the frontier. when a thing happens that you call bad, a delay, a refusal, a loss, do not correct the judgment. add a question after it: how do i know? do the same when a thing happens that you call good. the point is not to pretend that pain is pleasant or to stop caring about results. it is to notice how fast the verdict comes, and how little the verdict knows. then try one of the four last lines in a conversation where you are right. be square: hold your shape. and watch the edge: does it cut? if you see the other person flinch, you have found your 割.

禍 / 福: each inside the other. the passage is made of pairs: 悶悶 and 察察, dull rule and sharp rule; 禍 and 福, disaster and good fortune; 正 and 奇, straight and strange; 善 and 妖, good and uncanny. the middle pair shows how to read the others. its two lines are a mirror: each side is the place where the other leans or crouches. neither comes first. the comfort and the warning have the same weight, and a reading that keeps the comfort alone has cut the pair in half. the first stanza does favour one side, the dull rule over the sharp. read it by the middle lines. the favour is a correction to states that watched too much. it is not a fixed law, for the text says next that there is no fixed straight. dull rule turns too: it can go round into neglect. the four last lines then show a person who holds both sides: a shape, and no cut.

disaster carries good fortune in it, good fortune carries disaster, and nobody knows where the turning ends.. disaster carries good fortune in it, good fortune carries disaster, and nobody knows where the turning ends. does your life bear this out? name one loss that opened something, and one gain that cost you. how fast do you sort an event into good or bad? who taught you to be sure so quickly? take the opposite and hold it: some things are simply bad, some are simply good, and to blur them is a way to avoid grief or joy. what rises in you as you hold it? is there a loss that you would refuse to call anything but a loss? stay near that refusal for a moment. what does it guard?

close watching makes people smaller, and a looser hand leaves them whole.. close watching makes people smaller, and a looser hand leaves them whole. have you found this, as the one who watches and as the one who was watched? were you watched closely as a child, or left alone? what did that do to you, and what did you decide about it? now argue for the sharp eye: what is not checked is not done, and vague rule is neglect with a kind face. hold it as true. which part of you agrees at once? which side do you live by, and which do you criticise in others? are they the same side?

a person can have a firm shape and not use it to cut others.. a person can have a firm shape and not use it to cut others. do you think this is possible, or does every edge cut someone? recall a time when your being right wounded a person. what did you want in that moment? take the other view: to hold back the edge is dishonest, and truth has to cut. stay with it. what do you feel? which have you been more often: sharp, or shapeless? what would the other one have cost you?

伏 a person and a dog. six strokes, two parts, and no sound element: this is a character made only of meaning. on the left, 亻, a person standing, the side-form of 人. on the right, 犬, a dog. the shuowen says of 犬 that it is a picture, and quotes confucius: 視犬之字如畫狗也, “look at the character 犬: it is like a drawing of a dog”. in the modern form the dog has become 大, a person with arms out, plus one dot; the dot is what remains of the animal’s ear or tail. person plus dog gives 伏, and the shuowen’s definition is 司也, “to keep watch”. a person with a dog lies low and waits: a hunter in the grass, a guard at a door. the body posture is face down, flat, hidden. from it come all the later senses: to lie prostrate, to submit, to hide, to ambush (埋伏), and the hottest weeks of summer, the 三伏 or “three crouchings”, when the cool is said to lie hidden under the heat. in this passage disaster does the crouching. the script gives it a dog’s patience. there is a cousin with the same parts in another order of thought: 器, four mouths and a dog that guards vessels (passage 11). dogs in the script are mostly on watch. six strokes. the person: a stroke that falls to the left, then a vertical that starts under its middle. the dog: a horizontal; a long stroke that starts above the horizontal, crosses it, and falls away to the left; a long stroke that starts at the crossing and sweeps down to the right; and last the dot, high on the right, above the horizontal. watch the last three. the left-falling and right-falling strokes open like the two sides of a tent, and the right one must be the longer and heavier, pressed down at its end and then lifted. the dot goes in the empty space at the upper right and balances the tall person on the left. left side narrow and upright, right side wide and open: a still thing beside a thing ready to spring.

福 an altar and a full jar. this is among the most written characters in the chinese world. at the new year it hangs on doors in gold on red paper, and many households hang it upside down. on the left is 礻, the short form of 示, the sign for things of the spirits, commonly explained as an altar or a spirit tablet. the shuowen: 祐也。从示，畐聲, “help from above; from 示, with 畐 for the sound”. that 畐 on the right is, from top to bottom, a line, a mouth 口, a field 田. that modern look misleads. the part is commonly explained as a picture of a jar with a neck and a round, full belly: a vessel of wine. the same part is in 富, “rich”, a full jar under a roof 宀, which the shuowen glosses 備也, “fully supplied”, and in 幅, the width of a bolt of cloth. so 福 is a full vessel before the altar: the blessing that comes back from the spirits to those who feed them, or the wine that is offered. its partner 禍 has the same altar. two games are played with this character. it is hung head-down because 倒, “upside down”, sounds like 到, “has arrived”, in modern chinese: a homophone only. and the bat, 蝠, is painted as a sign of luck for the same kind of reason. the passage is less sure. under the full jar, it says, a dog is lying. thirteen strokes. the altar side, four: a dot; a horizontal that turns and falls to the left; a vertical; and a small dot on the right of the vertical. keep this side narrow, with the dot at the top well above the rest. the jar side, nine: a short horizontal, the lid; then the mouth in three strokes (a vertical, a horizontal that turns down, a closing horizontal); then the field in five (a vertical; a horizontal that turns down; a horizontal across the middle; a vertical down the middle; the closing base). watch the proportions of the right side. the mouth is small and the field is wide and square, so the jar has a neck and a belly. folk calligraphers write “a hundred 福”, one sheet with a hundred different forms of this one character, from seal script to wild cursive.

廉 the edge of the hall. the cover of this character is 广 (yan), a building seen from the side with one wall open; it marks halls and sheds, as in 庫 (armoury), 府 (office, treasury), 廟 (ancestral temple), and 庭 (courtyard). under it is 兼, which gives the sound. 兼 is worth a look in itself: the shuowen says 从又持秝, “a hand that holds two stalks of grain”, and so “to hold two at once, to combine” (it has a plate in passage 61). the shuowen puts 廉 among the buildings and explains it as the side or edge. in the ritual books it is the sharp border of the platform on which a hall stands, the line where the floor ends and the drop begins. guests of different rank stood nearer to it or farther from it. the meaning then moved from stone to character, as english moved “upright” and “square” from carpentry to persons. a 廉 person has a clean edge: takes nothing over the line. in the han, men were recommended for office as 孝廉, “filial and incorrupt”. the passage adds the craftsman’s warning: an edge that is exact need not cut. its phrase is also said of jade. thirteen strokes. the building, three: a dot on top; a horizontal; a long stroke that falls away to the left and makes the open wall. then 兼 beneath, ten: two short strokes at the top that lean toward each other; a horizontal; a horizontal that turns down at the right; two more horizontals, the upper one longer, across the whole of 兼; then two verticals that pass down through all the horizontals; and last a stroke that falls to the left and one that falls to the right, like two feet. watch the two long verticals, strokes ten and eleven. they are the two stalks of grain, and they must be parallel and evenly spaced, with the horizontals tied across them like a hand. the left-falling wall of 广 must be long enough to shelter the whole of 兼 and must not touch it.

59 · the farmer’s store. to order people and serve heaven, / nothing equals the farmer’s sparing. / only sparing: / this is called being ready early. / being ready early is called storing de in layers. / with de stored in layers, there is nothing that is not overcome. / with nothing not overcome, nobody knows the limit. / when nobody knows the limit, a state can be held. / with the mother of the state, it can last long. / this is called deep roots and a firm taproot: / the way of long life and lasting sight. one sentence of advice, a chain, and an image. the advice: for putting people in order and serving heaven, nothing is as good as 嗇, the farmer’s habit of storing and not spending. the chain: 嗇 is early readiness; that is 德 piled in layers; then nothing is too heavy; then nobody knows the limit; then a state can be held; and with the state’s mother, it lasts. the image: two kinds of root, deep and firm. the last phrase names the whole thing as a way of long life and lasting sight. the vocabulary is of the farm from end to end: the granary in 嗇, the grain stack in 積, the roots, and 長生, where 生 is at first a plant that comes up out of the soil. the passage never says what the person does. it says only what is kept. the dao is not named until the last word, and no sage appears. what is described is a quality of reserve. a person can meet each day at the edge of their strength, with all attention out on things, and seem very alive. or a person can live some distance back from the edge. han feizi says the second is stillness, and that it spends little. this is not withdrawal from life and not a cold heart. it is that there is more in the person than is in use. others feel it as depth: nobody finds the limit. from inside it is felt as time, as not being pressed. the mother in the chain suggests where the store comes from. a person does not make it. it is what feeds a person when the leaks are closed. passage 56 named the leaks: the mouth, the gates. read it as a rule for anything that you want to outlast you. the measure of an institution is not this year’s output. it is the depth of what it does not need to spend: money, yes, and also trust, trained people, goodwill, and unused capacity. a leader who runs at full stretch and uses each quarter all that the quarter gave has a known limit, and rivals and bad luck find it. the state without three years of grain is not a state. note the order of the chain: the store comes before the holding of the state. and note the last link. to “have the state” is not enough to last; one must have its mother, the thing that fed it at the start: a purpose, a people, a piece of land. wang bi’s farmer adds the method: remove the cause of blight, and do not pull at the crop. this passage is the root text for an old idea of health: a person is born with a store, and how fast it is spent is the main thing under one’s control. han feizi lists the leaks: eyes that strain, ears that strain, thought that never rests. the body lens is simple, then. end a practice session with something left. stop eating before full. sleep before you are wrecked. in the arts of movement the image of the last lines is used directly: sink the weight, let the root go down through the feet, and the upper body can be soft and free, as a crown moves in wind because the taproot holds. power that comes from the root is not felt as effort. and 久視: rest the eyes. look far and softly for a minute, as a farmer looks at weather. a tree grows down before it grows up; in a dry land the seedling’s root is many times longer than its shoot. animals that live long, the tortoise, the elephant, the whale, have slow hearts. seeds are the pure form of 嗇: a whole life held in store, spent only when the conditions are right, sometimes after centuries. a field that is cropped every year without rest gives less and less; one that lies fallow in turn can be farmed for a thousand years, and the fields of north china were. the passage sees no conflict between long life and full life. it observes that the things which last are the ones that keep more than they show: the taproot, and the roots that spread. do the exercise of the seed grain: name what you must not spend, in attention, in strength, and in one relationship. then choose one small act of early readiness for today: a thing done before it is needed, when it is still easy. mend the small tear. fill the tank at half. go to bed with one task undone and the strength for it saved.

治人: rule others, or order the person?. 治 is to put in order: first of water, as the hero yu did with the great flood, then of a state, then of an illness. 人 is “person, people”. so 治人 is “to govern people”, and that is how wang bi reads it: the line is advice to a ruler. the oldest comment on this passage, in the han feizi, splits the line another way. for it, 人 and 天 are two sides of one human being: 聰明睿智，天也；動靜思慮，人也, “keen hearing, clear sight, and wisdom are heaven; movement, rest, thought, and worry are the human”. then 治人事天 is: put your own activity in order and serve what you were born with. the classical language does not choose; one sentence holds a manual of rule and a manual of self-care. english must add an object for 治, and so must pick. legge picked the inner reading. we kept “people”, which can still be yourself.

事天: what it was to serve heaven. 事 is to serve, as a son serves a father or a minister a lord. 天 is the sky, and from the zhou conquest it was also the highest power, which gave the right to rule and took it away. only the king, the “son of heaven”, could offer the great sacrifice to it, on an open altar outside the capital. so 事天 was first a royal duty with a calendar. by the fourth century bce thinkers had turned it inward. mencius: to keep one’s heart and feed one’s nature is 所以事天也, “the way to serve heaven”. han feizi, as his reading of the line shows, takes heaven as the eyes, ears, and mind that a person receives at birth; to serve them is to not wear them out. the passage gives one answer for the altar and the body: 嗇. the christian phrase “serve god” brings in love and obedience to a person. neither is in 事天.

嗇: wheat into the granary. this is the key word, and english has no good one for it. the shuowen takes the character apart: 从來从㐭。來者，㐭而藏之。故田夫謂之嗇夫. “from 來 and 㐭. the 來 is put into the 㐭 and stored. so men of the fields are called 嗇夫.” 來 was first the word for wheat, and 㐭 is a granary. a farmer does not eat the seed grain. however hungry the winter, a part of the harvest is shut away, since next year is in it. that is 嗇: to not spend. our “the farmer’s” is added from this picture; the line has the one word. today the word means “stingy”, a vice. “frugality” and “moderation” make it a mild virtue of the middle class. the old sense is harder and more hopeful: restraint now, for the sake of life later. passage 67 has a different word, 儉, for the plain living that its speaker holds dear; do not confuse them. wang bi and han feizi each explain 嗇 in their own way.

wang bi: the farmer weeds. wang bi reads 嗇 as the farmer himself: 嗇，農夫. he then describes the work: 農人之治田，務去其殊類，歸於齊一也。全其自然，不急其荒病，除其所以荒病. “when a farmer puts a field in order, he works to remove what is of another kind and bring it back to one even kind. he keeps whole what it is of itself. he does not rush at its blight; he removes that by which it is blighted.” the picture is weeding, not storing. a good farmer does not pull at the crop to make it grow, and does not treat each sick leaf. he takes away the cause and leaves the plant to its nature. on 有國 he adds a hard line: 以有窮而莅國，非能有國也, “to preside over a state with what has a limit is not to be able to hold a state”. and the mother, for him, is what makes a state secure: root first, branches after.

han feizi: do not spend the spirit. the chapters “explaining laozi” in the han feizi, from the third century bce, are the oldest commentary on this book that we have, and this passage is one that they treat at length. their reading is about the body’s budget. 眾人之用神也躁，躁則多費，多費之謂侈。聖人之用神也靜，靜則少費，少費之謂嗇. “the many use their spirit in a restless way. restlessness spends much, and to spend much is called waste. the sage uses the spirit in a still way. stillness spends little, and to spend little is called 嗇.” eyes that look too hard go dim; ears that strain go dull; a mind that plans without end is confused. so one saves sight, hearing, and thought as a farmer saves grain. it is strange to find this in the book of the arch-legalist. it shows that before the laozi was a religion or a philosophy, it was read as a guide to care of the self and to rule, both at once.

早服: three readings of one word. 早 is “early”. 服 is the trouble. the shuowen gives 用也, “to use”, and a second sense, a horse in a chariot team. the word’s common senses are to wear, to submit to, to take on a task. so 早服 may be “to submit early” (to the dao), or “to take on the yoke early”. han feizi reads it as action before trouble shows: the sage complies with the pattern while the signs are still small. many scholars read 服 as 備, “ready, prepared”, the first transcription of the graph on the guodian slips (some palaeographers now read that graph as 服 itself); we follow that sense, which fits a farmer. others, with legge, change it to 復, “return”. the silk texts are reported to write 蚤服: 蚤 is “flea”, a common loan in old manuscripts for the like-sounding “early”. wang bi says only 早服，常也, “early 服 is the constant”. all agree on 早: the work is done before it is needed.

重積德: de as a harvest. 積 keeps the farmer’s image going. its left side is 禾, grain on the stalk, and the shuowen says 聚也, “to gather”: sheaves in a stack, grain in a heap. 重 is read chong here, “again, layer on layer”; read zhong it would be “heavily” or “to treat as weighty”. so 重積德 is to heap up 德 in layers, as a granary fills year after year. 德 is the power that a thing or person has from being what it is; we leave it as “de”. this passage treats it as a stock. it can be stored, and by implication it can be spent, on display, on quick results, on being admired. wang bi stresses the tempo: 不欲銳速, “one does not want it sharp and fast”. the confucian xunzi has a like phrase, 積善成德, “pile up good and 德 is formed”. there the stock is good deeds. here it is what is saved by not acting.

a chain of hooks. read the middle of the passage aloud in chinese and you hear a chain. each clause begins with the words that ended the one before: …早服；早服…重積德；重積德…無不克；無不克…莫知其極；莫知其極…有國；有國之母… chinese rhetoric calls the figure 頂真, “thimble”, or linked pearls. it is not decoration. it makes an argument in which no step can be skipped: thrift, readiness, a store of 德, nothing that defeats you, no visible limit, a state, the mother, long life. the form is the same as that of the famous chain in the “great learning”, which runs from the person to the realm. but notice what kind of chain this one is. nothing in it is an act upon others. each link is only a result of the link before, and the first link is a refusal to spend. what is the first link in your own chain?

克: to carry on the shoulder. 無不克 is “nothing not 克”, and versions say “nothing he cannot overcome”, “nothing is impossible”. that is the tone of a slogan, and the word is quieter. the shuowen defines 克 by one word: 肩也, “the shoulder”, to shoulder a load. the first sense is to be equal to a weight: to bear it, to be able. the sense “to conquer” comes from that: one who can carry the thing has mastered it. so the line says that a person with deep reserves is equal to whatever comes, as a full granary is equal to a bad year. it does not say that such a person goes out and wins. the double negative matters too. chinese says “nothing not borne”. it lists no victories. the next clause turns the same form on knowledge: nobody knows the limit.

莫知其極: the same phrase, turned. in the passage before this one, 孰知其極, “who knows its 極?”, was a question about disaster and good fortune: nobody can see where the turning ends. here the same words are praise: of one whose store is deep, 莫知其極, “nobody knows the limit”. 極 is the ridgepole of a house and so the highest point of anything. two senses work at once. others cannot find the bottom of this one’s reserves, and that is a real strength in a world of rivals; a state whose granaries are known to be empty is attacked. and the person does not reach the bottom either. wang bi comments in three words: 道無窮也, “the dao has no end”. a store that is drawn from the dao has no floor. compare a person whose limit everyone knows: how long they can listen, what makes them angry, the price. what does it do to you to deal with one whose limit you cannot find?

有國: holding a state in an age of famine and war. 有國, “to have a state”, was a set phrase; 有國者 are “those who hold states”, the rulers. in the warring states period to hold one was not a matter of course. states died. dozens were swallowed between 500 and 221 bce. what killed them was often not the lost battle. it was the lack of anything left after it. the record of rites states a rule of thumb: a state without nine years of stored grain is “not sufficient”; without six, it is “in danger”; without three, 國非其國也, “the state is not its state”. so the farmer’s word 嗇 at the top of the passage is exact for politics. the ruler who spends the people’s strength each year on wars and works has no depth. this passage sets the condition for holding a state: reserves so deep that nobody, enemy or friend, can find their end.

國之母: a state has a mother. after a chain of dry terms comes a body: 母, mother. the shuowen gives the picture two ways: 从女，象褱子形。一曰象乳子也, “from 女, woman; it shows her with a child in her arms. another view: it shows her giving suck.” the book uses this word for the dao itself. passage 1 calls the named the mother of the ten thousand things. there is a thing that may be taken as mother of all under heaven (25). passage 52 says: when you have the mother, you know the children; hold to the mother, and to the end of life you are not in danger. passage 20 ends: i alone prize the mother who feeds. translators write “the root principle” or “the foundation”, and the breast is gone. western political thought has founding fathers and a fatherland. here the thing that lets a state last is the thing that fed it. what fed the thing that you lead?

根 and 柢: two kinds of root. english has “root”, and the line seems to say it twice. chinese has two words. the shuowen glosses them almost alike: 根 is 木株也, “the stock of a tree”, and 柢 is 木根也, “the root of a tree”. han feizi, who knew his trees, tells them apart. a tree has spreading roots and a straight root. 柢 is the straight one: 木之所以建生也, “that by which the tree sets up its life”. the spreading roots are 木之所以持生也, “that by which the tree keeps up its life”. one anchors, and the others feed. so 深根固柢 is: let the feeding roots go deep and the anchor root hold firm. he applies it at once: 德 is the anchor, and income is the spreading root. the phrase became a common idiom, 根深柢固, and today it is mostly said of bad habits: “deep-rooted”. look at a tree in wind. what you see move is held by a part that you do not see.

長生久視: a phrase with a long future. 長生 is “long life”. 久視 is “to see for a long time”: to keep the eyes open, and so to stay alive. the four characters were probably a current phrase; a text of the third century bce says that every lord, wise or foolish, wants 長生久視. here the phrase is given a way, a 道, and the way is thrift and depth. later history took the phrase and ran. from the han, seekers of immortality made 長生 their goal: elixirs, breath arts, diets. 久視 was read as the clear eyesight of one who does not age, and in 700 ce the empress wu, who was old and ill, named a year of her reign 久視. the passage itself promises less and more. it does not say “not to die”. it says that a life or a state with roots lasts as long as its nature allows, and is not cut short by its own spending. is that enough?

legge’s “moderation”. legge renders 嗇 as “moderation”, the favourite virtue of his own century and class, and the farmer and the granary are gone. he follows the inner reading of the first line and makes it explicit with a bracket: “regulating the human (in our constitution)”. that is the han feizi’s reading in the dress of victorian physiology. for 早服 he reads 復 and writes “an early return (to man’s normal state)”: a small story of fall and recovery, which the chinese does not tell. 重積德 becomes “the repeated accumulation of the attributes (of the tao)”, and 無不克 “the subjugation (of every obstacle…)”: an empire’s word. at the end he gives 柢 as “flower stalks”, which no commentator supports; the old glosses all say root. his closing words keep the two verbs of the last phrase: enduring life is “long seen”. where his english is long, count the chinese: 治人事天莫若嗇 is seven characters.

find the seed grain. a farmer knows which sacks are for eating and which are seed. most of us do not know this about our own stores. take three: attention, strength, and good will. for each, ask: what part of this is seed grain, which i must not spend however great the need looks today? for attention it may be the first hour of the morning. for strength, the sleep before midnight. for good will with a person, the one thing that you do not say in anger. then look at yesterday. where did you eat seed? do not make a plan to be more productive with what you save. that would be to plant in order to spend more. 嗇 only asks that the store exists, and that you are ready early, before the bad year.

嗇 / 費: to store and to spend. the passage names one side: 嗇, to keep back. its partner is not named. han feizi supplies it: 費, to spend. the text plainly favours the keeping. ask what the favour is for. it speaks to rulers and to persons who run at the edge and use up people, grain, and spirit. for them the correction is to store. but the image is a farmer’s, and a farmer stores in order to sow. seed grain that is not put in the ground next spring is as lost as seed that is eaten. the store and the spending make one year between them. so the favoured side turns too: sparing that forgets its purpose is the miser’s vice, which is what 嗇 means in modern speech. a one-sided reading hears “hold back, always”. the passage says 早, early: keep now, so that there is something to give when the time comes.

the body, a life, and a state each have a finite store, and sparing it is the root of long life.. the body, a life, and a state each have a finite store, and sparing it is the root of long life. do you agree? where do you see it hold in your own body and days, and where not? if you hold this view, where might it come from in your past: a time of want, an illness, a tired parent, a fear of running out? if you reject it, what made holding back look like a small way to live? look at your shadow here. whom do you judge: the one who hoards strength, or the one who burns it? what might that judgment hide about you? now take the opposite view: the store grows when it is spent, and what is given out comes back. hold it for a while as if it were yours. notice the feelings and thoughts that arise, and do not correct them. which view sits with what you think, believe, or have lived, and which one clashes? why might it be of value to know that, whichever is true?

readiness comes from what was put by early, before any need could be seen.. readiness comes from what was put by early, before any need could be seen. is this how you live, or do you do your best work late and under pressure? what does last-minute strain give you: a thrill, a proof of worth, an excuse? when did it first serve you? hold the other side for a while: life cannot be prepared for, and those who store for tomorrow miss today. what does that view free in you, and what does it frighten? which side did the people around you live on when you were young? have you copied them, or run from them?

嗇 wheat in the granary. the character is a small diagram of a farm at the end of harvest: grain above, a storehouse below. the shuowen names both parts. the top is 來. today 來 means “to come”, but the dictionary says it was first a plant: 周所受瑞麥來麰, “the auspicious wheat and barley that the zhou received”, a picture of a stalk with its awns. wheat was a gift that “came” from heaven, 天所來也, and so, it says, the word for wheat was used for “to come”. (the plant then got a new character, 麥.) the bottom of 嗇 is 㐭 (lin), a granary: 穀所振入, “where the grain is brought in”. the dictionary adds that its box shows a building with a door and a window. in the modern form the granary has become 回, a box in a box. put together: 來者，㐭而藏之, “the wheat: one puts it in the granary and stores it”. hence 嗇夫, “granary men”, for farmers, and later for the village officers who kept the stores. add 禾, grain, and you have 穡, the harvest. add a sign for planks, and you have 牆, a wall: at first, it seems, the wall of the store. the word went from “store” to “sparing” to today’s “stingy”. the passage uses the old sense: the seed that is not eaten. thirteen strokes. watch the app draw the top: first the two small pairs, left and right, each a short stroke that falls leftward and a dot; then a short horizontal above them; then a vertical that comes down from the top through the middle; then the long horizontal that carries it all. these seven strokes are the wheat, and the long line under them is like the edge of the granary roof. then the store, six strokes: the left wall; the top and right wall in one stroke with a corner; then the inner box (a short vertical; a horizontal that turns down; a closing horizontal); and last the floor of the outer box. the inner box must sit in the centre with even white on all four sides. that white is the room for the grain. a crowded 回 makes the character look choked, and a wide one makes it look rich.

柢 the root that touches bottom. left side: 木, a tree. the shuowen’s entry for 木 already speaks of roots: 从屮，下象其根, “from a sprout, and the lower part shows its roots”. the middle line is the trunk; the two strokes that spread at the bottom are roots, not branches. two famous characters are made by a single mark on this tree. a mark at the foot gives 本, “root, origin”: 木下曰本. a mark at the top gives 末, “tip, end”: 木上曰末. wang bi’s whole philosophy uses that pair: honour the 本, let the 末 rest. right side: 氐 (di), which gives the sound and more than the sound. the shuowen explains it as 至也。从氏下箸一。一，地也: “to reach; a line set under 氏, and the line is the ground”. to reach the ground: bottom. every character with 氐 goes down: 低, “low” (下也); 底, “the bottom” of a well or a cup; 抵, “to push against, to arrive at”. so 柢 is the part of a tree that goes straight down until it touches bottom: the taproot. han feizi says that it is the root by which a tree “sets up its life”, and the passage asks that it be made 固, firm. the common word for root, 根, is beside it in the line: the roots that spread. nine strokes. the tree, four: a short horizontal; a vertical through it, tall, with no hook; a stroke that falls to the left from the crossing; and a dot on the right, short because it must make room. then 氐, five: a flat stroke at the top that is drawn from right to left; a vertical that goes down and flicks up to the right at its foot; a horizontal that starts from that vertical and goes right; then the long hook that leans down to the right and ends with a point upward; and last a dot at the very bottom. watch the final dot. it is the “ground line” of the old form, now only a touch of the brush under the hook, and it is the lowest point of the character. the long hook, stroke eight, gives the right side its force; the tree stands straight and lets it lean.

母 a woman with two dots. begin with 女, woman. the shuowen calls it a picture, and the usual explanation of the early form is a figure that kneels with the arms crossed in front. three strokes are left of it today. now add two dots inside the frame of the body. the shuowen reads them plainly: 从女，象褱子形。一曰象乳子也, “from 女; it shows her with a child in her arms. another view: it shows her suckling a child.” the second view is the one that most people hold: the two dots are the breasts. in the modern form the figure has been turned and squared, so that 母 looks like a box, but the dots are still there, and the line through the middle is the old arms. the dictionary’s one-word definition is 牧也, “to tend, to pasture”: a pun on the sound, and also a thought. a mother is one who feeds and herds. compare 毋, “do not”, which the shuowen derives from 女 with one line across: a mark of stopping. the mother is a sound-part in 每, “each”, and through it in 海, the sea, which the shuowen calls 天池也，以納百川者, “heaven’s pool, which takes in the hundred rivers”. in this book the mother is the dao as that which feeds. here she is the mother of the state. five strokes. first a stroke that goes down, leaning a little to the left, and then turns sharply to run rightward: the left side and the floor. second, a stroke that starts at the top, goes right, turns down, and ends in a hook to the left: the roof and the right side. the two make a leaning frame, a parallelogram and not a square. third, a dot in the upper half. fourth, the long horizontal, which crosses the whole frame and comes out on both sides. fifth, a dot in the lower half. watch the fourth stroke. it is the arms, and it must be long, level, and exactly between the dots. the lean of the frame gives the character life; written upright it is stiff. in cursive the two dots run together into one vertical line, and that form is close to how 毋 is written.

60 · a small fish in the pot. ruling a great state / is like the cooking of a small fish. / with the dao presiding over all under heaven, / its ghosts have no spirit-force. / it is not that its ghosts have no spirit-force: / their spirit-force does not harm people. / it is not that their spirit-force does not harm people: / the sage also does not harm people. / now the two do not harm each other, / so de crosses and comes home there. the passage has a famous first line and a strange remainder. line one is a likeness: a great state is ruled as a small fish is cooked. then the scene widens to all under heaven and to the unseen. with the dao over the realm, the ghosts lose their force; the text corrects itself twice, and comes to rest on harm: the spirits do not hurt people, and the sage “also” does not. the close says that the two do not harm each other, and so 德 comes home from both sides. the verb 傷, to wound, comes four times in forty-eight characters. that is the real subject. the fish, the ghosts, and the sage are three cases of one thing: a delicate body in the hands of a power that can ruin it by handling. read the realm as yourself, and the ghosts as your own dead: old fears, old griefs, wrongs that you did and that were done to you. they do not go away. the text is careful here. 非其鬼不神: it is not that they have no force. what changes is that the force does not wound. a memory can be present and not be a haunting. how? the passage gives one instruction, and it is the first line: do not keep turning it over. a mind that handles its ghosts, that checks them, argues with them, tries to drive them out, feeds them. a mind that the dao presides over, which is to say a mind that is not being run by a nervous manager, gives them a place to go home to. then the inner ruler, too, stops being a source of harm, and 德 has room to return. three lessons for one who runs anything large. first, the cook’s: the bigger and more delicate the thing, the lighter the hand that it asks for. reorganizations, new rules, and constant checks are stirring; han feizi counted their cost, and the people pay it. attention is not the same as handling. second, the ghosts. every institution has its unquiet dead: people who were wronged, old injuries that nobody names, fears that govern behaviour from the dark. a leader cannot abolish them by decree. where rule is fair and light, they lose their grip, and nobody needs to speak of them. third, wang bi’s: authority that is felt as authority is already in decline. count yourself, as the text does, among the things that can hurt people. that one word, 亦, “also”, is the best check on a ruler in the book. things that are small and whole are damaged by handling: a seedling that is dug up to see if the roots have grown, a nest that is visited too often, a pond that is stirred. ecologists have a hard-won rule that the first act of care is to stop the disturbance and wait. the passage then says a thing about fear in a landscape. where people live at war with a place, it is full of dangerous spirits: every forest and river has one that must be bought off. where they live well with it, the same forest is only a forest. its powers are still there, as the text insists, and they do not strike. both sides stop harming, and the good of each flows to the other. cook the fish, in the kitchen and then in one piece of work. and once this week, when an old ghost visits, a shame, a grudge, a dread, do not stir it. do not argue with it or push it out. give it a place: say what it is, let it sit, and turn back to what is in front of you. see if its force, which may remain, still wounds.

大國: the big powers. by the time this book took shape, seven large states had eaten the rest. each had a million or more people, a paid bureaucracy, and a conscript army. a ruler of such a state had tools that no earlier king had: population registers, written law, grain taxes, and ministers who offered plans to make the state rich and its army strong. the plans had a name, 變法, “to change the laws”, and the great reformers, li kui in wei, wu qi in chu, shang yang in qin, each turned a state upside down. so “how do you rule a great state?” was the question that every court asked, and the expected answer was a programme. the answer here is a kitchen image of seven characters. wang bi draws out the rule of scale in it: 其國彌大，而其主彌靜, “the larger the state, the stiller its lord”. more power calls for less handling.

烹: the cook and the cauldron. 烹 is to cook in a pot over fire: the four dots at the foot, 灬, are flames. cooking was a serious image of rule. the bronze cauldron, 鼎, was the emblem of a dynasty; to “ask the weight of the cauldrons” was to threaten the throne. the model minister of legend, yi yin, was a cook, who is said to have won the first shang king by a talk on how tastes are blended. to “blend the cauldron” stayed a phrase for a chief minister’s work. there was a dark side to the word. 烹 was also a punishment: a man could be boiled alive, and kings of the time did it to officials and envoys. every reader knew both pots. the line picks the gentlest dish possible. the state is in the pot either way. how hot is the fire, and how often does the hand go in? see the fish.

小鮮: do not gut, do not scale, do not stir. 鮮 is 魚, fish, beside 羊, sheep. it means fresh fish, and then “fresh” in general. the shuowen treats it as the name of one kind of fish from the far northeast, and says that the sheep side only gives the sound. a small fresh fish goes into the pot whole. the han commentary of heshang gong gives the cook’s rule: 烹小魚不去腸，不去鱗，不敢撓，恐其糜也. “when you cook small fish you do not take out the gut, you do not take off the scales, and you do not dare to stir, for fear that they turn to mush.” the skill is all in restraint: low heat, and patience. a cook who turns the fish again and again to check it serves a plate of flakes. note what the image does not say. the fish is still cooked. the fire is lit, and someone watches the pot. han feizi gave the first political reading.

han feizi: do not keep changing the law. the oldest comment on the line is by the legalist han feizi, and it is exact: 烹小鮮而數撓之，則賊其澤；治大國而數變法，則民苦之. “cook a small fish and stir it often, and you ruin its gloss. rule a great state and change the laws often, and the people suffer for it.” his point is about the cost of change. each time a craftsman changes trade, he says, work is lost; a state of many people that shifts its rules loses that much on a vast scale. so the ruler who has the way values stillness and does not alter the law lightly. this is a narrower lesson than the passage gives. han feizi wants firm law that is left alone; the laozi is not sure that the law should be there. but the two meet on one thing: the urge to adjust is itself the damage. how often do you stir? the line has had a modern career too.

the fish in a modern speech. the first line has had a second life in the west as a maxim of small government. in january 1988 president ronald reagan quoted it to congress in his yearly address, and added the lesson that one should not overdo it. it was perhaps the largest audience that a line of the laozi has had in one evening. the use was fair to han feizi’s reading and to the kitchen. it left out the rest of the passage. the chinese text goes straight from the pot to ghosts, spirits, and a sage who is counted among the things that can hurt people. a line about restraint in budgets was, in its own setting, the opening of a line of thought about religion, fear, and the state. what happens to a saying when only its first seven characters travel?

莅: to preside; the silk texts say “stand”. 莅 (also written 蒞) is a formal verb: to arrive at a place and look over it from above, as a lord comes to court or an official to a post. 以道莅天下 is, word for word, “by-dao-preside-all-under-heaven”. no subject is given. we wrote “with the dao presiding”, which makes the dao the one in the high seat; a version with “when a ruler uses the dao to oversee the world” is equally possible and adds a ruler. the silk texts are reported to read 立: 以道立天下. 立 is a person who stands on the ground, 从大立一之上, and it means “to set up, to establish”; it was also an early way to write 位, a position at court, and so “to take one’s place”. either way the picture is of where one stands in relation to the realm. the pot of the first line had a cook. this line asks who, or what, stands over the pot.

鬼: the dead who need a home. 鬼 are ghosts, and in early china that means the human dead. the shuowen defines the word by a pun: 人所歸爲鬼, “that which a person goes home to be is a 鬼”. the two words sounded alike: 鬼 and 歸, “to return”. a ghost with descendants was fed at the sacrifices and was at peace. a ghost with no one, or one who died by violence or injustice, was hungry and came back to haunt. in 535 bce the capital of zheng was in terror of the ghost of a murdered noble. the minister zichan gave the man’s son an office, so that the offerings could start again, and the hauntings stopped. he explained: 鬼有所歸，乃不為厲, “when a ghost has a place to go home to, it does not become a demon”. so ghosts were a political fact. a realm with many wronged dead is a haunted realm. now look at the last line of the passage: its verb is 歸.

不神: “spirit” as a verb. 其鬼不神 is four words: “its ghosts do not 神”. 神 is usually a noun: a spirit, a god, the higher powers of sky and mountain, as against 鬼, the dead. here it is a verb or an adjective: to be potent, to act with uncanny force, to work wonders. english has no such verb, and legge reached for latin. “its ghosts are not spiritual” is wrong, and “do not manifest” is thin. we wrote “have no spirit-force”. in the next line the same word is a noun: 其神, “their spirit-force”. english also divides the unseen into ghosts, spirits, gods, and god, with walls between. the chinese pair 鬼神 covers the whole range in two syllables, and a dead human can rise along it. the text does not ask if they exist. it says what they do under a certain kind of rule. the shuowen defines 神 as 天神，引出萬物者也, “the spirits of heaven, which draw out the ten thousand things”; its right side, 申, is commonly explained as lightning.

非…: a staircase of corrections. the middle of the passage moves by taking back what it has just said. a: the ghosts have no force. no, not a; rather b: their force does not harm people. no, not just b; rather c: the sage, too, does not harm people. 非 is “it is not that”. each step repeats the last clause in order to push off from it. the figure is a kind of chain, like the one in the passage before, but here every link is a correction. why write this way? it lets the text say a thing and decline to stand on it. the crude claim, “good rule makes ghosts powerless”, is the folk belief. the text touches it and moves on, twice, until it arrives where it wants to be: at the sage, and at harm. the ghosts were the door. by the third step the subject is what a ruler does to people.

傷人: how spirits hurt, how rulers hurt. 傷 is a wound; the shuowen says 創也, “a cut”. how do spirits wound people? in the belief of the time: by sickness, madness, bad harvests, floods, and deaths that have no clear cause. the cure was to find which spirit was offended and pay it with offerings, and a great part of the wealth of households and states went that way, until a later religion refused to pay. how does a sage, which here means a ruler, wound people? by punishments, wars, labour service, and taxes. the line puts the two in one list with the small word 亦, “also”. that is a bold step. the ruler stands beside the angry dead as a source of harm that falls on people from above. a state can be a haunting. in the same century the mohists argued the reverse: that belief in sharp-eyed ghosts who punish is good for order, and should be taught. which side would a ruler prefer?

聖人: a sage nobody notices. 聖人, “the sage”, is not a saint or a wise old man. in this book it is the ruler as the ruler should be: one who is tuned to how things go and governs by that. wang bi’s comment here shows what the title is worth: 神不傷人則不知神之為神…聖人不傷人則不知聖人之為聖也. “when the spirits do not harm people, people do not know that the spirits are spirits. when the sage does not harm people, people do not know that the sage is a sage.” power is noticed when it hurts. he goes on: 夫恃威網以使物者，治之衰也。使不知神聖之為神聖，道之極也. “to rely on a net of awe in order to drive things is rule in its decline. to bring it about that people do not know the spirits and the sages to be spirits and sages is the height of the way.” the best ghost is one that you never hear of. so is the best government.

兩: which two?. 夫兩不相傷: “now the two do not harm each other”. the text does not say which two, and readers have three answers. one: the spirits and the sage; neither harms people, and neither works against the other. that is wang bi’s. two: the spirits and the people; the dead and the living leave each other in peace. three: the ruler and the people; han feizi reads it so and says that the people then do not offend the law, and those above do not punish. the silk texts add fuel. they are reported to read 聖人亦弗傷也: “the sage also does not harm them”, with no 人, “people”, and the object left open. “them” could be the spirits. then the line says that the sage does not hurt the ghosts, and the ghosts do not hurt the sage’s people: a peace treaty between the visible and the unseen. 相 is “each other”, so the harm that stops goes both ways.

德: the last word is not “productivity”. 德 is left as “de”: the power and good that a thing has by being what it is. “virtue” makes it moral, and “power” makes it force. here it is close to “benefit” or “well-being”, but with its source kept: it is the good that flows where nothing blocks it. the passage does not say that the sage gives 德 to the people. no giver is named. it says that when harm stops on both sides, 德 comes. modern versions for managers write “energy” or “productivity” at this point. the word in the chinese is the one in the title of the book, and it arrives by itself, as the next note shows. han feizi glosses it from the people’s side: when those above and those below do not hurt each other, their 德 is heaped up together and all of it goes home to the people.

交歸: crossing, and going home. 交 is two things that cross. the shuowen’s entry is a small drawing in words: 交脛也。从大，象交形, “crossed shins; a person, 大, with the legs crossed”. from there: to meet, to exchange, on both sides, mutually. 歸 is to go home. the shuowen’s first sense is a wedding: 女嫁也, “a woman marries”: she goes to the house where she will belong. it is the verb for rivers that go to the sea, for the dead who go to the earth, and for people who give their loyalty to a ruler who deserves it. so 德交歸焉 is: “de, from both sides, comes home there”. 焉 is “there, to that place”. where? to the people, to the two that do not harm each other, or to the realm. and hear the pun from the note on ghosts: 鬼 was defined as 歸. the passage begins its second part with ghosts that have nowhere to go and ends with 德 that comes home.
