when daoists made it a rule. four hundred years later a new religion took this passage at its word. the way of the celestial masters began in sichuan in the second century ce. it held laozi to be a god, and it recited this book. its “pure covenant” with the unseen world, as a daoist of the fifth century sets it out, had two famous clauses: the gods do not eat or drink, and the master takes no money. that meant an end to the bloody and costly sacrifices by which villagers bought off dangerous spirits of the dead. the old ghosts were declared “stale”, without force. in their place were written petitions to an orderly heaven, and confession of faults. it is 其鬼不神 as church policy. later, the tang emperors, whose family name li was that of laozi, claimed him as an ancestor and wrote their own commentary on the book. so the passage about quiet ghosts became the charter of a church, and then the family scripture of a throne.

legge’s “manes”. for 鬼 legge writes “the manes of the departed”. manes is a latin word, the spirits of the dead in roman religion. a victorian scholar could say in latin, at a safe distance, a thing that in plain english, “ghosts”, would sound like superstition or like the holy ghost. for 神 he writes “spiritual energy”, a phrase of his century; and the ghosts do not “manifest” it, which is the language of the seance, then in fashion. he makes the sage “the ruling sage”, which is right, and has the 德 of both “converge in the virtue (of the tao)”, with the tao added in a bracket. his first line is plain and good, and it is the form in which the saying entered english. the missionary’s unease shows only where the dead come in. he translated the kitchen with ease and the religion with care.

cook the fish. do it for real once. buy a few small whole fish, or take any food that breaks easily: a soft egg, a ripe pear in syrup, a fillet. put it on low heat and cook it without touching it more than once. watch what your hand wants to do. it wants to lift, to check, to turn, to press. each of those is care, and each one harms. notice the difference between attention, which stays with the pot, and handling. then carry the two words into one thing that you are in charge of this week: a child’s homework, a colleague’s draft, a plant, your own mood. give it attention, and count your handlings. the cook of small fish is not absent. the cook stands at the stove the whole time.

大 / 小: the great handled as the small. the first line rests on 大 and 小, great and small, joined by 若, “is like”. the chinese does not rank them. it does not say that small is better, or that a great state is bad; it takes the great state as a fact. it says that the great thing is treated as one treats a small one. the pair crosses over: what is largest is, in the hand, easily broken, and the rough stirring that a big pot seems to allow is what ruins it. a second pair comes after: the seen and the unseen, people and ghosts, with the sage between. here too neither side defeats the other. the two stop harming each other, and the good goes both ways. a one-sided reading makes the first line a rule of doing little. but a cook does cook. there is fire, and attention, and a meal at the end.

a great thing is ruined by much handling and has to be treated like something small and delicate.. a great thing is ruined by much handling and has to be treated like something small and delicate. do you agree? name something that you spoiled by stirring, and something that failed because you left it. what makes it hard for you to leave a thing alone? what do you believe about yourself when you are not acting on it? take the opposite: big things need a firm and busy hand, and a light touch is a way to dodge the work. stay with that view. what comes: energy, dread, a sense of being needed? whose handling of you, when you were small, do you still feel? was it too much or too little? how does that shape your answer?

the old ghosts keep their force, yet under a quiet rule that force does no harm.. the old ghosts keep their force, yet under a quiet rule that force does no harm. is that true of your own ghosts: the old fears, griefs, and wrongs? has one of them been present and not hurt? how do you deal with them as a habit: argue, push out, feed, obey? where did you learn that way? now hold the other view: what haunts has to be faced and fought, and to let it sit is to let it rule. believe it for a few minutes. what happens in you? the passage counts the ruler among the things that can harm. in what way are you one of the things that can hurt the people near you? what makes that hard to look at?

鮮 fish and sheep. two animals side by side: 魚, a fish, and 羊, a sheep. start with the fish, since it is one of the clearest pictures left in the script. the shuowen says 水蟲也。象形, “a creature of the water; a picture”, and adds a detail that only a careful eye would give: 魚尾與燕尾相似, “the tail of the fish looks like the tail of the swallow”. read 魚 from the top: the head, then the body with its scales, drawn like 田, then the tail. the four dots at the bottom are that tail. they look like 灬, fire, and they are fire in 烹, the cooking word beside it in the passage, but here they are fins. 羊 is also a picture, and the shuowen quotes confucius on it: 牛羊之字以形舉也, “the characters for ox and sheep are raised from their shapes”: two horns on top, a face, a body line. the sheep is in many good words: 美 (beautiful), 善 (good), 義 (right), 養 (to feed), 祥 (a good sign). fish and mutton together make people think of a full table, and many readers explain 鮮, “fresh, delicious”, that way. the shuowen is cooler: 鮮 is the name of a certain fish, and the sheep half, short for 羴, three sheep, only marks the sound. hold the feast as a memory aid. read as xian the same character means “rare, few”. seventeen strokes: eleven for the fish, six for the sheep. the fish: a short stroke that falls to the left; a horizontal that turns and falls back to the left, which makes the head; then the body as a box with a cross (a left vertical; the top and right side in one stroke; a horizontal inside; a vertical inside; the closing base); then four dots in a row, the first leaning left and the other three leaning right. as a left-hand part the fish is tall and narrow, and its dots climb a little to the right to make room. the sheep: two small strokes at the top that lean toward each other, the horns; three horizontals, of which the third is the longest; and last a vertical through all three, straight down, ending in a point. watch that final vertical. it is the longest line in the character and hangs below the fish’s tail.

鬼 a person with a strange head. the shuowen’s entry is one of its best, since it gives a pun, a picture, and a warning in one line. the pun: 人所歸爲鬼, “what a person goes home to be is a 鬼”; 鬼 and 歸, “to return”, sounded alike. the picture: 从人，象鬼頭, “from 人, a person, and it shows a ghost’s head”. the top of the character, a large square head with a stroke above it, is a head that is not a living human’s: commonly explained as a mask, or the oversized head of a figure seen in fear. under it are the two legs of a person. the warning: 鬼陰气賊害，从厶, “the dark breath of ghosts harms by stealth, so it has 厶”. 厶 is the small hooked part at the lower right, the sign of what is private and crooked. a ghost, then, is a person, changed at the head, with a hidden hook. the character is a radical, and its family is the unseen side of a human being: 魂, the soul that rises like cloud (the shuowen: 陽气也); 魄, the soul that stays with the bones (陰神也); 魅, a spirit that charms; 魔, a demon, a character made much later for a buddhist word. beside them stand 醜, “ugly”, and 畏, “to fear”, which the shuowen explains as a ghost’s head with a tiger’s claws. the passage does not deny any of it. it says when the hook does not catch. nine strokes. a short stroke that falls to the left sits on top. then the head: a vertical on the left; a horizontal that turns down on the right; a horizontal inside; a horizontal that closes the box. the sixth stroke starts inside the head at the centre, comes down through the base, and curves away to the left: the first leg. the seventh starts under the head, goes down, bends to the right, runs along the floor, and hooks up: the second leg, and the longest stroke. then the hook of stealth, two strokes tucked above that long floor-line: a stroke that falls left and turns back right, and a dot. watch the seventh stroke. it must sweep far to the right to carry the 厶 on its back. in running script the head is closed in one turning stroke, and the hook of stealth becomes a single flick.

烹 an offering over the fire. the bottom is fire: 灬, the four-dot form that 火 takes under another part, as in 煮 (to boil), 熟 (cooked, ripe), 熱 (hot), and 然 (to burn; then “so”). the top is 亨. that part has a history of its own. the shuowen has no 烹 and no 亨; it has an older character, 亯, which it defines as 獻也, “to offer up”, and describes as 象進孰物形, “the shape of cooked things being presented”. it quotes the classic of filial piety: 祭則鬼亯之, “at the sacrifice, the ghosts enjoy it”. from that one old graph three modern ones came, by small changes of the brush: 享, to offer and to enjoy; 亨, the success that follows an offering that is accepted, a key word of the book of changes; and, with fire added, 烹, to cook. so the cooking word in the first line has an altar in its past. food was first cooked for the dead. that makes a bridge that the english reader cannot see: the pot of line one and the ghosts of line two belong to one scene, a sacrifice. the quotation in the dictionary even names them together. the same root has a cruel branch, since 烹 was also a way to execute. all of this is in the kitchen where the fish is cooking. eleven strokes. a dot on top, then a horizontal: the lid. then a small mouth in three strokes: a vertical; a horizontal that turns down; a closing horizontal. then the lower part of 亨 in two strokes: a horizontal that turns and falls to the left in a short hook, and a vertical that curves and ends in a hook to the left. then the fire, four dots from left to right: the first leans to the left, and the other three lean to the right, each a little larger than the one before. watch the dots. they must sit on one level line and be spread wider than everything above, so that the pot stands on its flames. keep the upper part narrow and tall. in running and cursive hands the four dots are often drawn as one wavy line, a single low flame, which is the right heat for a small fish.

61 · the great one below. a great state is the low reach of the river: / where all under heaven meets, / the female of all under heaven. / by stillness the female constantly gets the better of the male, / and by stillness takes the place below. / so a great state that puts itself below a small state / takes the small state. / a small state that puts itself below a great state / takes the great state. / so one goes low in order to take; / one goes low, and so takes. / a great state wants no more than to gather people in and feed them. / a small state wants no more than to enter and serve. / now both get what they want. / the great one ought to be the one below. an image, a rule, and a bargain. the image comes in three quick names for a great state: the low reach of a river, the meeting place of the world, the world’s female. that image is then explained: by stillness she is more than a match for the male, and she is below. the rule is drawn from it in two matched sentences: great below small takes the small; small below great takes, or is taken in by, the great. a summary marks the difference with two particles. then the bargain: the great wants to gather and feed people, the small wants to enter and serve, both get it, and the burden is assigned: the great should be below. the word 下 comes nine times. no dao, no sage, and no 德 are named. the passage talks to kings in their own terms: size, taking, and wanting. take the two states as two parts of a person: a strong part that manages, plans, and knows, and the many small parts that it would like to command, a mood, a fear, a tired body, a wish that does not fit. the usual way is conquest: the great part overrides the small. the passage offers a different relation. the strong part goes below: it becomes still and receives. a fear that is listened to from below comes in, as a stream comes to a river, and what was a border war becomes one water. the female image is exact here. receiving is an act, and it outlasts the act of pushing. nothing is given up. the great part still takes. but it takes by being the place where things arrive, and that is also what is meant by a mind that is large. the passage is realistic about power in a way that makes it useful. it does not ask the strong to become weak or to stop wanting. a great state, firm, or person wants to bring more people in and keep them; the passage says so without blame and then says how. the strong party that stands on its rank gets fear, and fear leaves when it can. the strong party that goes to the other, asks, serves first, and takes the lower chair gets what force cannot get: others who come of themselves. the burden is on the strong since only the strong have a choice; wang bi says why. there is a warning for the reader who likes this too much. lowness that is used as a technique, with stillness missing, is felt as a trick. the old code between great and small states failed at that point. the low place has its own strength. a wrestler, a judo player, and a taijiquan player all learn that the one whose centre is lower moves the one whose centre is higher. the lower hips take the other’s weight and turn it. but the passage gives the order of things, and it is stillness first: 以靜為下. a person who drops low with a restless mind is only crouching. sink by letting go, not by pressing down, and the weight goes to the feet by itself, as water goes to the low reach. then receive. in partner work, do not meet the push; be the place where it arrives, and it has nothing to stand on. the same holds for the voice in a quarrel: the one who speaks lower and slower, from stillness, is the one toward whom the talk begins to flow. every river system is this passage. small streams are high, fast, and loud. the great river is low, slow, and wide, and it is great only for that reason: it lies below all the others and they have nowhere else to go. the sea is the lowest of all and is never full. a delta, the lowest land, is the richest; the first cities were built on such ground. 下流 is also where the silt, the dead leaves, and the dirt of a whole country end up. the low place takes what nobody wants along with the water, and makes soil of it. in the script and in the book, the valley, the female, and the low water are one family of images. what they share is that they receive, and that what receives grows. do the exercise of the lower seat once today, in a meeting where you are the stronger. keep the order of the passage: become still first, then go low. afterwards ask two things. what came toward me that i did not pull? and did i do it in order to take, or did i do it and find that something was given?

下流: a word of shame, turned. 下流 is the lower course of a river, the place toward which everything in the valley runs. in the moral language of the time it was a bad place to be. a disciple of confucius says in the analects: 君子惡居下流，天下之惡皆歸焉. “the noble person hates to dwell in the low reach, for all the foulness under heaven comes to rest there.” his example is the last shang king: once a man is down, every crime is laid on him. in modern chinese 下流 still means “low, obscene”. the laozi takes this exact word and makes it the definition of greatness. the low reach is where the filth collects; it is also where the water collects, and the river is greatest at its mouth. the book has said it before: water is good because it stays where people hate to be (8); rivers and seas are kings of the hundred valleys because they are good at being below them (66). wang bi: the great state that sits low is where the whole realm flows.

交: confluence, and the other meaning. 交 is a crossing: the shuowen’s picture is a person with crossed legs. 天下之交 is the place where all under heaven crosses: a confluence of rivers, a junction of roads, a centre of dealings between states (邦交 is still “diplomatic relations”). the word has a second sense that every reader knew. 交 is also the joining of male and female, and the next line names the female. the two short lines are set side by side on purpose: the world’s meeting place, the world’s female. the silk texts are reported to give them in the other order, 天下之牝，天下之交也, female first and crossing second, which makes the link to the lines on female and male smoother. in the received order the geography comes first and the body second. english must choose “confluence” or “intercourse”. the chinese word is both a map and a bed.

牝: the female animal. 牝 has 牛, an ox, at its left, and the shuowen defines it as 畜母也, “the mother among livestock”: cow, mare, ewe. its partner 牡, “the father among livestock”, stands in the next line. these are a herdsman’s words. they are not 女 and 男, woman and man, and not the cosmic pair 陰 and 陽. english writers on this book like “the feminine” with a capital, and that brings in a 19th-century european idea of a soft, eternal, womanly principle. the chinese is an animal in a field at mating time. the book uses the word at key points: the valley spirit that does not die is called the dark 牝, and her gate is the root of heaven and earth (6); the infant does not yet know the joining of 牝 and 牡 (55). here a great state is told to be one. no ruler of the time, each a man with an army, could have liked the comparison.

以靜勝牡: the plain image, and wang bi. the image is of mating, and the text does not look away. the male moves, pursues, and is spent. the female is still and below, receives, and is not spent. 勝 is usually “to defeat”; the shuowen gives its root sense as 任也, “to bear, to be equal to”. so the female is more than a match for the male, and outlasts him, and her means is 靜, stillness. wang bi says it without a blush: 雄躁動貪欲，雌常以靜，故能勝雄也. “the male is restless, moves, and is greedy in desire. the female is constant in stillness, and so can overcome the male.” he adds: 以其靜復能為下，故物歸之也, “by her stillness she is, further, able to be below, and so things come home to her”. the silk texts are reported to give the reasoning in other words: 為亓靚也，故宜為下, “because of her stillness, it is fitting that she be below”. note that stillness comes first. the low place follows from it and is no trick of posture.

下: nine times. count the character 下 in this short passage: nine. it does five jobs. in 下流 it is an adjective, “lower”. in 天下, “under heaven”, it is part of the name of the world. in 以靜為下 and at the very end it is a noun: “the one below”. in 大國以下小國 it is a verb with an object, a use that english lacks: “a great state by under-ing a small state”. we wrote “puts itself below”. and in 下以取, 下而取 it is a verb alone: “to go low”. classical chinese lets a word change its part of speech without any change of form, and the passage uses that freedom to make one syllable sound through every line, like a low note held on a string. even the world is named by it: all that is under. by the last line, 大者宜為下, the ear has been taught where greatness goes.

取: the conqueror’s verb. 取 is “to take”, and its picture is a hand on a severed ear, a war trophy; the shuowen cites the army rule for it. 取國, “to take a state”, is in the chronicles the plain term for conquest. so the sentence says: by going below the small state, the great state takes it. this is hard speech, and soft versions (“wins its trust”, “gains its friendship”) mislead. the passage speaks to rulers who meant to swallow their neighbours, and it does not tell them to stop wanting it. it says that the armies are the wrong tool. some commentators ease the word by reading 取 as 聚, “to gather” (the two graphs are related: 取 gives 聚 its sound). the effect is the same either way: the small state ends inside the great one. but it enters as a river enters the sea, of itself. is that still conquest? what is the difference to the one who is taken?

取大國, or 取於大國. in our text the two sentences match: the great state 取 the small; the small state 取 the great. can a small state “take” a great one? it can win it, as a client wins a patron. but the silk texts are reported to have one more word: 小邦以下大邦，則取於大邦 (so manuscript a; b writes 國 for 邦). 於 after a verb marks the agent or the source: “is taken by the great state”, or “gets from the great state”. with 於 the two sentences are not a mirror. the great one takes; the small one is taken in. the received text dropped the small word, and then the second 取 had to bear two senses. wang bi, who had the shorter text, still read it the old way: 大國納之也, “the great state admits it”. english cannot use one verb for “take” and “be taken”. chinese can, and the lost 於 was the only sign of which was meant. see the next pair of lines.

以 and 而: two small words. 或下以取，或下而取. the two halves differ by one particle. 以 joins an act to its aim: “to go low in order to take”. 而 only joins two things in time or result: “to go low, and take”, or, if 取 is passive as in the reported silk reading, “to go low and so be taken in”. the first half is the great state. it has a choice and an aim; its lowness is policy. the second is the small state. it is low already, by its size; what it gets is a place. so the same act, 下, is a strategy in one case and a condition in the other, and the same verb, 取, is active in one and passive in the other. a whole theory of unequal relations is carried by 以 against 而. english has no way to do this in eight syllables. we gave “in order to” for 以 and “and so” for 而.

great and small: the diplomacy behind the passage. how great and small states should deal with each other was a set topic. the older code is stated in the zuozhuan: 禮也者，小事大，大字小之謂, “ritual means that the small serves the great, and the great cherishes the small”. the small sent tribute and troops, and the great gave protection, in theory. by the fourth century the great simply ate the small. mencius, asked by a king how to deal with neighbours, gave an answer close to this passage: only the humane can, being great, serve the small; only the wise can, being small, serve the great. he meant moral feeling. the laozi gives no moral. it gives a mechanism, water, and a body, the female. the old phrase 事大, “serve the great”, had a long later life: for five centuries it was the name of korea’s policy toward the ming and qing courts. the other half of the code, the duty of the great, was easier to forget.

兼畜: to bind sheaves, to keep a herd. two farm words for what a great state wants. 兼 is a hand that holds two stalks of grain at once: 从又持秝, says the shuowen. from “to hold two together” it became the word of the age for swallowing states: 兼并, annexation. the mohists used the same character for their ideal, 兼愛, care that takes in everyone. 畜 is livestock, and as a verb (xu) to rear and feed animals. it is the word for what the dao’s 德 does for all things in passage 51: 德畜之, “德 rears them”. so 兼畜人 is “to bring people together under one hand and feed them”. people are the herd. english softens it to “unite and nourish”, but the chinese is honest about power in a way that modern political speech is not. a governor was in fact called a 牧, a herdsman. the text does not sneer at the wish. it grants it: both get what they want.

入事人: to go in and serve. 入 is to enter: a door, a court, a sphere. 事 is to serve, as a minister serves a lord. 入事人 is “to enter and serve people”, that is, to come inside a greater power’s order and take a place in it. a small state had few other ways to live. it could not win a war against a great one, and neutrality between two great ones was a quick death; the chronicles are full of small states crushed between jin and chu. service bought survival, its ancestral temple kept, its lord left on his seat. the phrase 不過欲, “wants no more than”, is exact and a little dry. neither side has a noble aim. one wants more people; the other wants to go on existing. the passage builds on wants as they are. modern readers may hear “serve” as shame. in the old code it was the normal state of nearly everyone: son, wife, minister, and lesser lord.

大者宜為下: on whom the duty falls. the last line has five words: “great-one-fitting-be-below”. 宜 is “it is fitting, it suits, ought”. it is a mild word, the “ought” of a good fit and not of a command. why does the duty fall on the great? the small state is low already; its low place costs it nothing new and gains it little beyond its life. the great state has a choice, and its choice sets the terms for all. wang bi: 小國修下自全而已，不能令天下歸之，大國修下則天下歸之. “a small state that practises lowness only keeps itself whole; it cannot make all under heaven come to it. when a great state practises lowness, all under heaven comes to it.” the line is one of the few in the book that sounds like a plain political demand, and history has mostly ignored it. english “humble” is a feeling, and legge’s words are heavier still. 為下 is a position that one takes, like the lower seat at a table.

legge’s “condescending”. legge writes that a great state gains small states “by condescending” to them, and that small states win a great one “by abasing themselves”. both words are of his time. in victorian english “to condescend” was still praise: a superior steps down graciously, and stays a superior. “abasement” comes from the language of the pulpit, where the sinner abases himself before god. so his great state stoops from above, and his small state grovels. the chinese has one word for both acts, 下, with no moral colour: to be under. he also softens the first line with “(like)”, and calls stillness “(a sort of) abasement”. his female “overcomes the male by her stillness”, which is exact. he ends with “the great state must learn to abase itself”. “learn” is his. the text says only that it is fitting.

take the lower seat. in any meeting of two there is a greater and a smaller: by age, rank, money, knowledge, or need. find one meeting today in which you are the greater. then take the place below, in fact and not as a show. go to the other’s room. ask first, and wait through the answer. let the other set the time. sit lower if there are two chairs. keep still; that is the female’s method in this passage, and the low place comes from it. watch what flows toward you when you do not push. then notice the cases in which you are the smaller, and see the difference: there your low place is not a choice. the passage asks nothing of you there. what it asks, it asks of the one who could do otherwise.

大 and 小, 牝 and 牡: a pair needs both. three pairs run through the passage: great and small (大, 小), female and male (牝, 牡), above and below. the text does not sort them into good and bad. both states go low, both take, and both get what they want: 兩者各得其所欲. the female gets the better of the male, but the image is of mating, and it needs two. the preference for the low place is spoken to the great, who are high already. it corrects a world of states that pressed down on small neighbours. it is not a rule that low is good. the low place also turns: the river that takes in all streams becomes the great one, and then the duty to go below falls on it again. a reader who hears only “the low one wins” has made a new high place. what would it be to hold both ends?

when a strong party and a weaker one meet, it is the strong one that ought to take the lower place.. when a strong party and a weaker one meet, it is the strong one that ought to take the lower place. does this match what you have seen? think of one time when the stronger person went low, and one time when they did not. where did you learn how a strong person should carry themselves: from a parent, a boss, a team, a country? take the other side for a while: the strong should stand tall, and the small should come to them. what in you agrees? what feelings come with that? when someone with power over you acts humble, what do you first suspect? what does that suspicion say about your own use of the low place?

stillness that receives gets more, in the end, than movement that pursues.. stillness that receives gets more, in the end, than movement that pursues. is this true in your experience of love, work, or argument? name one case for it and one against. which role do you take by habit, the one who pursues or the one who waits? who showed you that role? now hold the opposite: what you do not go after, you do not get. stay with it for a minute. does it bring relief, hunger, or shame? the passage needs both the river and the streams that run to it. what do you judge in people who live on the side that is not yours?

two parties of unequal size can both get what they want, with neither one losing.. two parties of unequal size can both get what they want, with neither one losing. do you believe this, or do you expect that one side pays? where does that expectation come from? recall a bond in your life between unequal parties: parent and child, employer and worker. did both get what they wanted? take the view that every bargain has a loser. what does that view protect you from? what does it cost you? in that bond, were you the great one or the small one? would your answer change if you had stood in the other place?

兼 one hand, two stalks. the shuowen explains this character with a comparison, like a teacher who sets two things side by side. 兼持二禾，秉持一禾: “兼 holds two stalks of grain; 秉 holds one.” look at 秉 first: 禾, a grain plant with its bent head, and through its middle a hand, 又 in an old shape, that grips the stalk. it means “to grasp, to hold” a brush, a candle, power. now give the hand a second stalk. the shuowen: 从又持秝, “from a hand that holds 秝”, and 秝 is two 禾 side by side, grain planted in an even row. in the modern form of 兼 the two plants have run together: the two verticals in the middle are their stalks, the two small strokes on top are their heads, the two strokes at the foot are their roots, and the horizontal lines with a corner are the hand that binds them. to hold two as one: “both, at once, to combine”. the warring states gave the word its hard sense, 兼并, to swallow a neighbour, and the mohists its generous one, 兼愛, to care for all alike. a great state wants to 兼. add 言, speech, and you get 謙, “modest”, the name of a hexagram of the changes that shows a mountain placed under the earth: the high below the low. it is the cousin that this passage is about. add 广, a hall: 廉, the clean edge of passage 58. ten strokes. two short strokes at the top that lean toward each other: a dot on the left and a short fall to the left on the right. then a horizontal. then a horizontal that turns down at the right: the first part of the hand. then the long horizontal, the widest stroke, which crosses the whole character. then one more short horizontal below it. now the two stalks: two verticals side by side, drawn down through all the horizontals. then the roots: a stroke that falls to the left and a stroke that falls to the right. watch the two verticals. they are the heart of the meaning and must be twins: parallel, the same length, the same distance from the centre. if one is stronger, the hand holds one stalk and a shadow. the two last strokes spread wide and settle the weight.

畜 the dark field. top: 玄. bottom: 田, a field, which the shuowen calls a picture of plots with the paths that cross between them. the shuowen’s entry for 畜 is short and odd: 田畜也, “livestock of the fields”, and then a quotation from the huainanzi: 玄田爲畜, “dark field makes 畜”. that is an old teaching rhyme for the two parts. 玄 is the “dark” of the book’s first passage, and its picture is commonly explained as a twisted cord or a skein of silk. so some modern scholars see a rope above a field, a beast on a tether, and others see a different thing in the early forms; the origin is not settled. what is clear is the range of meaning. as a noun, read chu, it is the animals that people keep: ox, horse, sheep, pig, dog, fowl, the “six 畜”. as a verb, read xu, it is to rear them: to feed, to pen, to keep, to tame. from there it means to support a family, to keep retainers, and to store up; with the grass sign on top it is 蓄, “to save, to hoard”, which the shuowen glosses 積也. two hexagrams of the changes are named with it: “small taming” and “great taming”. in this book the verb is tender: the dao gives life to things, and 德 rears them (51). in this passage it is what a great state wants to do with people. both senses are true of a herd. ten strokes. the dark part first, five strokes: a dot; a horizontal; then two strokes of the same kind, each falling to the left and turning back to the right, one under the other like two twists of a cord; then a dot at the lower right that closes the twist. then the field, five strokes: the left side; the top and right side in one stroke with a corner; the horizontal inside; the vertical inside; and the base. watch the two folds of the cord. each is one movement of the brush, down-left and back, with the turn made by pressure and not by a lift. they must stack exactly, and the field must sit square under them, a little wider than the cord. a tall narrow field makes the character weak. a broad field holds the tether.

交 crossed legs. six strokes that the shuowen reads as a body: 交脛也。从大，象交形, “crossed shins; from 大, a person, and it shows the form of crossing”. 大 is the standing human with arms out. in 交 the upper part is still that figure, head and arms, and at the bottom the two legs do not stand apart as in 大. they cross, the left leg swinging right and the right leg swinging left. from a person with crossed legs the word took in everything that crosses: roads, rivers, glances, swords, and the dealings of people. to 交 is to hand over, to exchange, to make friends (交友), to conduct relations between states (外交 is “diplomacy” today), and to mate. the changes uses it for the largest crossing of all. its hexagram “peace” is drawn with earth above and heaven below, and the comment says 天地交而萬物通也, “heaven and earth cross, and the ten thousand things go through”. that hexagram is this passage as a diagram: the high one has gone below, and for that reason things flow. the family of 交 keeps the idea of two that meet: 郊, the outskirts where town and country meet, and where the king offered the great sacrifice; 校, a school; 較, to compare. the meeting place of all under heaven is a cross drawn on the map. six strokes. a dot on top. a horizontal under it. then two short strokes under the horizontal: one that falls to the left and one that falls to the right, like the character 八; these are what remains of the arms and the body. then the crossing itself: a long stroke that starts on the right side and falls to the left, and a last stroke that starts on the left side, crosses the fifth stroke, and sweeps out to the right with a pressed, flared end. watch the point where the last two strokes cross. it must lie exactly under the dot at the top, on the centre line. the two long strokes should open at the same angle, so the figure is balanced on its crossed legs. in cursive script the four lower strokes are written as one continuous knot.

62 · the inmost corner. dao is the inmost corner of the ten thousand things: / the good person’s treasure, / and what the person who is not good is kept safe by. / fine words can be traded; / honoured conduct can raise a person over others. / what is not good in a person: / what is there to throw away? / so when the son of heaven is set up / and the three dukes are installed, / though there be a disc of jade that fills both arms / sent ahead of a team of four horses, / it is not equal to sitting and offering this dao. / why did the ancients prize this dao? / did they not say: by it the one who seeks, gets, / and the one who has guilt goes free? / so it is what all under heaven prizes. the passage opens with a house and ends in a court. dao is the south-west corner, the innermost place, of all things. two kinds of people relate to it by two words of one sound: the good have it as treasure; the not-good are kept by it. then two dry remarks on the world’s currency, words that sell and conduct that lifts, and a question: what is there to throw away? the court scene follows: at the enthronement, better than jade and horses is to kneel and offer this dao. the close asks why the ancients prized it and answers with a saying: the seeker gets, the guilty go free. the vocabulary of value runs through all of it: 寶, 市, 尊, 璧, 貴. the passage sets each kind of worth beside the dao and finds it smaller. the contemplative centre is the question in the middle. a mind sorts without rest: this in me is good, that is not; this person is in, that one is out. the sorting feels like virtue. the passage says that the dao is the inner corner of all things, of the unsorted whole, and that the part you call not-good is not outside it. it is kept there. this does not mean that harm is good or that nothing should change. it means that change does not begin with throwing away. a fault that is pushed out comes back by the window. a fault that is given a place in the house can be seen, and what is seen can turn. the last lines name the two fruits. one who seeks, finds, since nothing was far. and one who carries guilt is let go, since the one place that could condemn did not. every group decides whom it keeps. a court of the time kept the well-spoken and the well-behaved, and the text says with some dryness that both are forms of money. a leader who keeps only the useful gets a market, not a household. the harder standard is in the first lines: a good house has a corner where those who have failed are still kept. that is not softness. the person who knows that they will not be thrown away can afford to tell the truth, and the one who expects the basket hides everything. then the gift. at the great occasions people bring the leader jade and horses: praise, results, presents. the rarest thing that an adviser can bring is none of these. it is plain counsel, offered from a low seat. and the rarest ruler is one who knows which gift is worth more. a forest keeps everything. the fallen tree, the dead leaf, the dung, the carcass: each has its place and its eaters, and the soil is made of what was dropped. nothing in a living system is thrown away, and the word “waste” has no meaning there. the oldest part of the wood is not the tall trees. it is the dark floor where all of it is taken back in, the 奧 of the place. or follow the silk reading: a watershed, in which every drop that falls, clean or foul, runs to the same low water and is received. the good seed and the bad both lie in one ground. the ground does not sort them. it keeps them, and what can grow, grows. ask the question of the thrown-away once, about one person and one part of yourself. then, the next time that you are about to bring someone a gift, of praise, of help, of a finished piece of work, consider the other gift: to sit down, be still, and offer the plain thing that you see. it costs less than jade, and it is given less often.

奧: the south-west corner. 奧 is a place in a house. the shuowen: 宛也。室之西南隅, “a recess; the south-west corner of the room”. an old chinese house faced south, with its door off-centre to the east, so the south-west corner was the deepest and darkest point, farthest from the door. that was the place of honour. the head of the family had his mat there, and the household sacrifices were set out there. the analects quotes a proverb about it: better to pay court to the stove than to the 奧, that is, to the one with real power in the kitchen than to the honoured one in the corner. from “inner corner” came the senses “deep, hidden, hard to fathom”; in japanese the same character is still “the interior” of a house. translators write “the mysterious” or “the storehouse”. the chinese is homelier: dao is the back corner of the house of all things, where the elders sit and where a child runs to hide. see wang bi and the other reading.

the silk texts: 注, where things pour. the silk texts are reported not to have 奧. they read 道者萬物之注也. 注 has the water radical, and the shuowen defines it as 灌也, “to pour into”: water that is led to one place. then the line says that dao is that toward which the ten thousand things pour, the low place where they collect. that is the picture of the passage before this one, where a great state is the low reach of a river. some scholars take 注 as a way to write 主, “lord, host”. which is the older image, the corner of the house or the gathering of waters? we cannot tell; the two graphs do not look alike, so this is not a slip of the brush. both images say “the place where things end up and are safe”. one is a room and the other is a sea. the received text chose the room, and with it a household, an altar, and a seat of honour.

wang bi: a word for shelter. wang bi glosses the key word in two short phrases: 奧，猶曖也。可得庇蔭之辭. “奧 is like ‘dim, shaded’. it is a term for a place where one can get cover and shade.” 庇蔭 is the shade of a roof or a tree over a person. so for him the first line is about protection: dao is that under which all things shelter. he then splits the two kinds of people by two verbs. for the good, it is a treasure: 寶以為用也, “they treasure it and so put it to use”. for the not-good, a refuge: 保以全也, “they are kept by it and so stay whole”. one uses it; the other is kept alive by it. on the close he writes that with it one who seeks gets and one who would be let off is let off: 無所而不施, “there is no place where it does not reach”. the shade falls on every head under the roof.

寶 and 保: one sound, two needs. the second and third lines end on the same syllable: 寶, treasure, and 保, to keep safe. they sounded alike in the old language too (both are in the 幽 rhyme group), and the lines rhyme on a pun. for the good person dao is a 寶: a thing of value that one has and uses. for the not-good person it is 所保: “that by which one is kept”. 保 is a person, 亻, beside a child; the shuowen says 養也, “to rear”, and the early form is commonly explained as an adult with an infant on the back. so the second word is not a possession at all. it is being carried. the silk texts are reported to write both lines with one graph, 葆, an old loan for 寶 and for 保 alike, which makes the pun an identity: what is the one’s treasure is the other’s keeper. english “treasure” and “refuge” share no sound. which of the two do you need today?

不善人: not “the wicked”. the text says 不善人, “not-good person”. english versions say “bad men”, “the wicked”, “sinners”. each adds a thing. chinese has strong words for evil, 惡 and 凶, and does not use them here. 不善 is only the lack of 善, and 善 in this book is as much “good at” as “morally good”: the one who is not good is the one who has not got it right, the unskilled. no devil stands behind such a person, and no fallen nature. passage 27 gives the relation between the two kinds: the good person teaches the not-good, and the not-good is the good person’s material; so the sage is always good at saving people, and nobody is thrown away. passage 49: to the not-good i am also good. this passage adds the ground for it. both live in one house, and its inner corner holds both.

美言可以市: where does the sentence end?. the text had no punctuation, and this line can be cut in two places. our pinned text cuts after 市: “fine words can be traded; honoured conduct can add to a person”. 市 is the market; the shuowen says 買賣所之也, “where buying and selling go”. the huainanzi, a han book, quotes the line with a different cut and one more word: 美言可以市尊，美行可以加人, “fine words can buy honour; fine conduct can raise one over others”. then 尊 belongs to the first half. either way the tone is debated. is this praise of the dao’s words, which outbid all goods, as wang bi says? or a cool remark on the world: speech is for sale, and good behaviour is a way to climb? passage 81 says that fine words are not trustworthy. we keep the cool reading. it makes the next line turn: if even words and deeds are currency, why would a person be thrown away?

加人 or 賀人. 加 is “to add”, and from that “to put on top of, to be above”. the shuowen gives the root sense as speech: 語相增加也, “to pile words on one another”; the character is 力, strength, beside 口, a mouth. 加人 is then “to be placed above others”, or “to add something to others”, to benefit them. the silk texts are reported to read 賀: 尊行可以賀人. 賀 is 加 with a cowrie shell, 貝, beneath, and the shuowen defines it as 以禮相奉慶也, “to present gifts to one another in ritual congratulation”. on that reading the line stays in the world of gifts and prepares the jade and horses that follow: fine words can be sold, and noble conduct can be given as a present. the received 加 is a simpler graph for a word of the same sound. the reader of the silk text hears, twice in one line, the sound of money changing hands.

何棄之有: a child named abandoned. 棄 is to throw away, and the plate for this passage shows what the shuowen saw in the character: two hands that push out a basket with a newborn in it. that was no figure of speech. unwanted infants were exposed in early china, as in greece and rome. the zhou people told that their own first ancestor, the lord of millet, was put out three times by his mother: in a lane, where oxen stepped around him; in a wood; and on ice, where birds covered him with their wings. he lived, and his name was 棄, abandoned. every zhou noble descended from a thrown-away child. so the question 何棄之有, “what throwing away is there?”, had weight. the grammar is a rhetorical form: 何 x 之有, “what x is there?”, meaning none. we render the open form. it leaves two readings: why throw the person away, and what is there in a person that could be thrown away?

立天子，置三公: an enthronement. the scene is the greatest day of the political year: a new king is set on the throne. 天子, “son of heaven”, was the title of the zhou king, who alone could sacrifice to heaven. 三公, “the three dukes”, are the three highest ministers; tradition names them grand tutor, grand preceptor, and grand protector. the silk texts are reported to read 三卿, “three ministers”. on such a day the lords of the states came or sent envoys, and every envoy brought gifts in a fixed order. by the time of this book the zhou king was a shadow, and seven rulers called themselves kings and planned to be the next son of heaven. a reader would see in this line the court that each of them hoped to hold. the text walks into that hall, among the jade and the horses, and names a better gift. wang bi takes the offices themselves as made for one purpose: to honour the practice of the dao.

拱璧 and 駟馬: jade first, then horses. a 璧 is a flat disc of jade with a round hole at its centre, the most solemn object in zhou gift-giving; the shuowen says 瑞玉圜也, “a round jade token”. 拱 is to bring the two arms round in front; a 拱璧 is a disc so large that it takes both arms to carry it. jade of that size was beyond price: in 283 bce the king of qin offered fifteen walled towns for one famous disc. 駟馬 is a team of four horses for a chariot; the shuowen defines 駟 as 一乘也, “one chariot’s team”. the word 先, “to go before”, is a term of protocol. gifts were presented in stages, and the lighter and finer one went in first, carried by hand, while the heavy one waited in the courtyard. so jade “precedes” horses. the line is exact about the ceremony, like a note in a court diary. then it says: 不如, “not as good as”.

坐進此道: two words with two readings. 坐 is “to sit”, and in a world with no chairs that is to kneel on a mat with the body upright. 進 is “to go forward”, and at court “to send up, to present” to a superior. so 坐進此道 has two readings. one: the envoy kneels in his place and offers, in place of jade, this dao: a word of counsel as the gift. we follow this; legge has “present on his knees”. two: 坐 as “without stirring, simply sitting”, and 進 as “to advance”: better than all gifts is to sit still and go forward in this dao. the first is a court scene. the second is the earliest hint of sitting practice as an offering, and later daoists read it so. the silk texts are reported to lack the last word: 不若坐而進此, “not as good as to sit and present this”. “this” may be the dao, or the very words that we are reading.

以求得: “seek and find”?. 求 is to seek, and 得 is to get. 以求得 is “by it, seek-get”: the one who seeks by means of it gets. wang bi: 以求則得求, “seek with it, and you get what is sought”. an english reader hears the gospel at once: seek, and ye shall find. legge heard it too, and wrote that the dao “could be got by seeking for it”, which turns the dao from the means into the prize. the likeness is real, and so is the difference. in the gospel a father gives to the one who asks. here nobody gives. the getting is an effect of where one stands, as one who goes into the inner corner of a house is out of the wind. mencius has a line in the same form about what is within a person: seek and you get it, let go and you lose it. the silk texts are reported to have 不謂 for 不曰, and 求以得 for 以求得: “is it not said…?” the saying was already old.

有罪以免: guilt, not sin. 罪 is an offence against the law or against a superior, and the state of one who has done it: guilt, liability to punishment. 免 is to get off, to be released, as a prisoner is let go or a tax is waived. 有罪以免: “those who have guilt, by it, go free”. when christian missionaries put the bible into chinese they chose 罪 for “sin”, and since then a western reader sees “sinners are forgiven” in this line. take the later sense away. in the warring states 罪 meant mutilation, forced labour, or death under codes that grew harsher each decade; the fear in the word was of the executioner. the line says that the dao is where the condemned are let off. it names no judge who pardons, no repentance, and no price paid. how does a person “go free” by the dao? the text does not explain. perhaps as in passage 27: nobody is thrown away. see the plate for the odd history of the character.

故為天下貴: the second time. the last five characters are also the last five of passage 56. there they followed a list of six things that cannot be done to a person: cannot be drawn close or kept far, helped or hurt, raised or lowered. here they follow two things that the dao does for anyone: the seeker gets, the guilty go free. the two endings explain each other. what cannot be priced is what all prize; and what all prize is what is open to all, the good and the not-good alike. 貴 comes twice in this last section. first as a verb with a history: “why did the ancients 貴 this dao?” then as the closing noun. between the two a jade worth fifteen towns has been set aside. the word 貴 has a cowrie shell in it, the old money. the passage has gone through the whole market, fine words for sale, honour, jade, horses, and ends on the one thing whose price is everyone’s regard.

legge and the stain of guilt. legge puts the first three lines into a rhymed triplet, and the third reads like a hymn: bad men it guards, and “doth their ill efface”. the chinese says only that they are kept; nothing is effaced. in the last section he writes that the guilty could escape “(from the stain of their guilt)” by it. the stain is his, in a bracket. it is the language of the christian doctrine of atonement, in which sin marks the soul and must be washed away. legge was a missionary for thirty years before he was a professor, and he spent his life looking in the chinese classics for signs of a knowledge of god. here he found a text that seemed to promise pardon, and his english leaned toward what he hoped to see. for 奧 he has “the most honoured place”, which is one true sense of the corner and loses the shelter.

whom have you thrown away?. sit for a few minutes with the question of the middle line: 何棄之有? first the people. bring to mind one person whom you have written off: a relative, a former friend, someone at work, a public figure. you need not like them or let them back in. only look for the act of throwing away, the moment when you put them in the basket and pushed. is the person in fact gone from the house of things? then turn it inward. what in yourself have you put out: a failure, a trait, a year of your life? the passage says that the dao is the corner of the house where this, too, is kept. nothing is asked of you there but to stop pushing the basket.

善 and 不善: one corner for both. the passage names a pair, the good person (善人) and the person who is not good (不善人), and then gives both the same root. dao is treasure to one and shelter to the other, and the two words, 寶 and 保, share one sound. the text does not say that the two people are the same. it also does not rank them and send one away. its question, 何棄之有, refuses the step from “not good” to “thrown out”. the close keeps both sides too: the seeker gets, and the guilty go free. a one-sided reading takes the passage as praise of the good, with some mercy added. but passage 2 says that when all know the good as good, the not-good is already there. each is known by the other. who would the good person be with no one to stand beside?

a person who is not good is still kept by the dao, and nothing in them calls for throwing away.. a person who is not good is still kept by the dao, and nothing in them calls for throwing away. do you agree? is there a person, or an act, that you hold to be past keeping? who was thrown away in the house or the school where you grew up? were you ever close to being that one? take the opposite view: some things must be cut off, and a group that keeps everyone protects no one. what rises in you when you hold that? what part of yourself have you put outside the door? what do you think of people who show that same part openly?

plain counsel offered from a low seat is worth more than the richest gift.. plain counsel offered from a low seat is worth more than the richest gift. when did someone last give you the plain thing they saw, and not a present or praise? how did you take it? what do you bring to people whose good opinion you want? what did you learn early about how to be welcome? hold the other side: a generous gift is love made visible, and plain talk is often cheap. is there truth in that for you? which is harder for you, to give the jade or to sit down and say what you see? why might that be worth knowing?

the one who seeks gets, and the one who carries guilt can go free.. the one who seeks gets, and the one who carries guilt can go free. do you believe that guilt can be let go with no payment? where did you learn what guilt costs? is there a fault of your own that you still hold? who would you be if it were let go? take the opposite: a debt must be paid, and to go free with no payment is unjust. stay with that. toward whom do you feel it most? do you allow others the release that you refuse yourself, or the reverse? what does the difference tell you?

棄 two hands, a basket, a child. this character is a scene, and the shuowen describes it stroke by stroke: 捐也。从廾推𠦒棄之，从𠫓。𠫓，逆子也. “to cast off. two hands push a winnowing-basket to throw it out; and it has 𠫓. 𠫓 is a child that goes against.” read the modern form from the top. the top part, a dot, a line, a fold, and a dot, is 𠫓. the shuowen explains that graph in its own entry as 从到子, “an upside-down 子”: the character for child, turned head down. that is how a baby comes into the world, and the same inverted child is in 育, “to rear”, and in 流, “to flow”. the middle part, with its crossed lines, is the basket, of the kind used to toss grain and carry rubbish. at the bottom, where the modern form has what looks like 木, were two hands, 廾, raised to push. a newborn, in a basket, in two hands, on its way out of the house. the dictionary’s gloss says the child is 逆, “contrary”: born wrong, or unfilial. the script kept the memory of a real practice; see the note on the child named abandoned. the simplified form 弃 shows it more clearly than the full one: the child on top, and two hands. the passage asks its question with this picture: 何棄之有? twelve strokes, in three tiers. the child, four strokes: a dot; a horizontal; a stroke that falls to the left and folds back to the right; and a dot that closes the fold. the basket, four strokes: a long horizontal, the widest line in the character; a short vertical on the left; a short vertical on the right; and a short horizontal that joins them below. the hands, now in the shape of a tree, four strokes: a long horizontal; a vertical that starts up inside the basket and comes down through it; a stroke that falls to the left; a stroke that falls to the right. watch the two long horizontals, strokes five and nine. the upper one carries the child and the lower one is the arms; they must be parallel, and the vertical between them ties basket to hands. the last two strokes spread wide, like arms at full stretch.

寶 under one roof: jade, a jar, and shells. twenty strokes and four parts: this character is a strongroom, and you can list what is in it. the roof is 宀, a house. under it on the left is 王, which is jade here, the old form of 玉, which the shuowen reads as 象三玉之連，丨其貫也, three jades joined, with the cord that goes through them; the dot that now marks 玉 was added later to keep it apart from 王, “king”. under the roof on the right is 缶, an earthenware jar. the shuowen says of it: 瓦器，所以盛酒, “a pottery vessel, for holding wine”, and adds that the people of qin beat on it to keep time when they sang. at the bottom is 貝, a cowrie shell: money. the shuowen lists them: 珍也。从宀从王从貝，缶聲, “precious things; from roof, jade, and shell, and 缶 gives the sound”. so the jar is there for its sound, but the eye counts it with the rest: jade for ritual, shells for trade, wine for the feast, all indoors. the simplified form 宝 keeps only the roof and the jade. now look at what the passage does with the word. it calls dao the treasure of the good, and a few lines later sets a great jade disc aside as the lesser gift. the character’s own first item is outbid. passage 67 uses the same word for the speaker’s three most valued things, and none of them is jade. twenty strokes: plan the space before the first one. the roof, three strokes: a dot at the top centre; a small stroke at the left end; a horizontal that ends in a hook at the right. make it wide; everything hangs under it. the jade, four strokes, on the left: horizontal, horizontal, a vertical through them, and a last horizontal that tilts up to the right. the jar, six strokes, on the right: a short stroke that falls left; two horizontals; a vertical through them; then the open box below, in two strokes. the shell, seven strokes, across the bottom: a vertical; a horizontal that turns down; two lines inside; the closing line; and two small feet. watch the middle tier. jade and jar must be the same height and stand close, so that the shell below can centre under both. in small regular script, writers treat this character as a test of even spacing.

罪 a fish-net, by order of the emperor. top: 罒, a net, the flat form of 网. the shuowen says that fuxi knotted the first one of cord, to fish with. bottom: 非, “is not, wrong”, which the dictionary derives from the two wings of a bird, spread back to back. a net over wrongdoing: the modern reader takes it as a picture of the law, and it is a good one. but the shuowen says that this is an accident of politics. its entry for 罪 reads: 捕魚竹网, “a bamboo net for catching fish”. that is all the character meant. the word “guilt, crime” had a character of its own, 辠: 自, a nose, above 辛, the sign of harsh punishment. the dictionary explains it as the offender who wrinkles the nose in bitter pain; many scholars think of the penalty of cutting off the nose. then: 秦以辠似皇字，改爲罪. “qin, since 辠 looked like the character 皇, changed it to 罪.” 皇 is “august”, the word that the first emperor had just taken for his new title. he did not want “crime” to look like “emperor”, so crime was moved to the fish-net. the passage was written before that decree, with the nose and the knife. its promise is that the one who has 罪 goes free. in the form that we read now, a fish gets out of a net. thirteen strokes. the net, five: a short vertical on the left; a horizontal that turns down on the right; two short verticals inside; and the closing horizontal. it is a wide, flat box with three even cells. then 非, eight, in two halves. the left half: a vertical that curves away to the left at its foot; two short horizontals drawn from the left into it; and a third that rises to the right. the right half: a straight vertical; then three short horizontals that go rightward from it. watch the two verticals. they stand back to back with a clear strip of white between, and the six short strokes stick out from them like the barbs of two feathers. the left vertical bends and the right one is straight. keep the net wider than the wings, so that it covers them.

63 · hard things begin easy. do the not-doing. / serve the no-business. / taste what has no taste. / great, small, many, few. / answer resentment with de. / plan for the hard while it is easy. / work on the great while it is fine as a thread. / the hard affairs under heaven must start from the easy. / the great affairs under heaven must start from the fine. / so the sage, to the end, does not do the great, / and so can complete what is great. / a light “yes” must be short on trust. / much that is called easy must bring much that is hard. / so even the sage treats it as hard, / and so, to the end, has nothing hard. the passage starts dark and ends plain. three riddling phrases: do the not-doing, serve the no-business, taste what has no taste. four words with no grammar: great, small, many, few. one hard saying: answer resentment with 德. then the tone changes to that of a manual. plan the hard at its easy stage; do the great at its thread stage; all hard and great affairs start so. the sage does nothing great and so completes the great. a light promise is not kept, and much “easy” brings much “hard”. the sage treats things as hard and so has no hardship. the second half may be read as a comment on the first: this is what 為無為 looks like in a working day. the oldest copy lacks most of that comment. the first three phrases describe an attention that is fully at work and adds nothing. to taste the tasteless is the clearest of them. most experience is thin: the walk to the door, the cup of water, the minute with nothing in it. a mind that is trained on strong flavours calls this “nothing” and goes to look for something. the practice is to stay and taste. then the small is no longer small: 大小, the small is treated as great. the line on resentment belongs here too. a grievance is easiest to meet when it is a thread, the first tightening in the chest, before it has a story and a history. at that stage it can be answered with something whole. the second half of the passage is this same skill seen from outside: one who feels the fine beginnings does not have to fight the great ends. institutions reward the one who solves the crisis and seldom see the one who made sure that there was none. the doctor in han feizi’s story is not thanked when the sickness is in the skin. this passage asks a leader to work in exactly that unrewarded place: to plan while the thing is easy, to act while it is a thread, and so to end a career with no great deeds to show. it gives two checks. the light yes: each quick promise to a client, a board, or a child is a debt taken on at the one moment when it could have been weighed. and the word “easy”: a team that calls many things easy is storing up hard ones. the cure is not worry. it is respect for small things, 猶難之, held as a habit by the person with the most skill in the room. in the body, the hard arises from the easy in a way that anyone can feel. a stiff back was once a slight holding in one place for many hours. a fall begins as a small lean that was not corrected. the skill of a mover is to notice at the thread stage: the first tightening, the first loss of root. in partner arts this is the whole game. the push that cannot be stopped at full force can be turned with one finger at its start, and a good player works only there, and looks as if nothing was done: 為無為. the same holds for training. do the simple form as if it were hard. those who find the basics easy stop looking at them, and their difficulties begin. and taste your food. plain rice, chewed slowly, becomes sweet. the great things of the land rise from fine ones. a canyon was a line of run-off. a reef is the work of animals the size of a grain. an oak begins as a root-hair that finds water. the same is true of ruin: the gully that takes a field starts as a wheel-rut, and the flood comes through the hole of an ant. a good farmer or forester walks the ground often and does very small things: a stone moved here, a channel opened with the heel, one seedling pulled. seen from far off, such a person does nothing, and the land is in order. water is the model of the first line. it has no taste and no shape, starts no great works, and completes them all. do the exercise of the thread with three things that weigh on you, and act only at the easy stage of each. then, once today, taste what has no taste: a glass of water, drunk slowly, as if it were a rare tea. and the next time that someone asks you for something, wait one breath before the “yes”. in that breath, feel the whole weight of what is asked.

為無為: a verb that eats its own negation. three phrases of three characters, all of one mould: a verb, then 無, then the same word as a noun. 為無為: “do not-doing”. 事無事: “serve no-service”. 味無味: “taste no-taste”. english wants to smooth this into “act without acting”, which makes 無為 an adverb, a manner. the chinese is odder. 無為 is the object: the thing that one does is not-doing. it is as if not-doing were a craft with its own work to be done, like a cook’s or a potter’s. the form also blocks a lazy reading. one who only stops has not done 為無為; the first 為 is still there, a real verb, in the place of command. we write “do the not-doing”. 無為 itself is “without forcing”: action that adds no scheme of its own to how things go. passage 3 ends with the same three characters and a result: then nothing is out of order.

事無事: work at having no work. 事 is service: a duty, a task, a state’s campaigns and projects. as a verb it is “to serve, to attend to”. 事無事 is “to make it your business to have no business”. passages 48 and 57 say that the realm is taken by 無事, and that the people grow rich when the ruler has none. here the phrase is turned into a job description. it answers a real objection. a minister who started nothing would be thought idle, and in fact it is hard, daily work to keep a calendar empty: to refuse the project that would win praise, to let the small trouble settle and not call a meeting. english “non-interference” names a policy. the chinese names a task, and its verb is the verb for serving a lord. whom, or what, does one serve in serving no-business?

味無味: the taste of water. 味 is a mouth, 口, beside 未. the shuowen defines it as 滋味也, “rich flavour”, and it explains the sound-part 未 by the same idea: 未，味也, the sixth month, when things have come to full flavour; 象木重枝葉也, “it shows a tree heavy with branches and leaves”. so the character for taste holds a tree at its ripest. the third phrase asks for the opposite: to taste 無味, that which has none. this is a real sense act. water, plain rice, clear broth have a taste, and a tongue that is used to salt and sugar cannot find it. passage 35 says of the dao: when it comes out of the mouth it is 淡, thin and flat, 無味. chinese painters, poets, and tea drinkers later made 淡 a high ideal. wang bi: 以恬淡為味, “take the calm and thin as your flavour”. drink a cup of plain water slowly today. what is there?

wang bi: where to live, how to teach, what to taste. on the first line wang bi writes: 以無為為居，以不言為教，以恬淡為味，治之極也. “to take not-forcing as one’s dwelling, wordlessness as one’s teaching, and the calm and thin as one’s flavour: this is the utmost of good order.” he turns three verbs into three places to stand: a home, a teaching, a diet. on “answer resentment with 德” he is cooler than most readers expect: 小怨則不足以報，大怨則天下之所欲誅，順天下之所同者，德也. “a small grievance is not worth an answer. a great one is what all under heaven wishes to see punished. to go along with that in which all under heaven is at one: this is 德.” he does not hear “love your enemy”. he hears: do not answer small wrongs at all, and in great ones do not act from private anger. on the end: if even one with a sage’s gifts treats the small and easy as hard, how much more should the rest of us.

大小多少: four words, no grammar. great, small, many, few. the four characters stand with no verb and no link, and nobody is sure how to read them. one: as verbs with objects. “treat the small as great and the few as many”: give small things the care that others keep for great ones. this fits the lines that follow, and legge took it. two: as a frame for the next line. “great or small, many or few”, whatever the size and number of the wrongs, answer with 德. three: as a bare observation. great comes from small, many from few. some scholars think that words have fallen out. the oldest copy has only 大小之, which supports the first reading, and a quite different continuation. we print them as they stand, and the reader must do what a chinese reader does: hold all three until the passage has been read to the end. which did your mind supply first?

the bamboo text: a passage half as long. this passage is among the guodian bamboo slips, buried about 300 bce, and it is much shorter there. after the three opening phrases the slips read 大小之 and then at once 多易必多難, “much easy, surely much hard”, and then to the sage who treats things as hard. all of the middle is missing: “answer resentment with 德”, the lines on planning the hard while it is easy, the sage who does not do great things, and the light promise. so either a scribe’s eye jumped from one 多 to another and dropped fifty characters, or the passage grew. in the second case, the famous line about resentment and the practical advice about small beginnings were added later, perhaps as an early comment on the four dark words. the silk texts, a century younger, are reported to have the long form already.

報怨以德: the line that confucius refused. 報 is to pay back in kind. 怨 is the bitterness of one who has been wronged, and it was a public matter. in the code of the time a son did not live under the same sky as his father’s killer, and feuds ran for generations between houses and between states. into that world the line says: pay back the grievance with 德. someone put this saying to confucius. his answer is on record: 何以報德？以直報怨，以德報德. “then with what will you repay 德? repay grievance with straightness, and repay 德 with 德.” he means justice: each gets what is due. the two sayings mark a real border between the schools. western readers hear the gospel here, and the likeness is there. but see how wang bi reads it, and passage 79: when a great grievance is settled, some of it is sure to remain, so the sage holds the creditor’s half of the tally and makes no claim.

圖: the dictionary quotes the line. 圖 is a border, 囗, around the part 啚. the shuowen’s definition is a surprise: 畫計難也。从囗从啚。啚，難意也. “to draw up plans for a difficulty. from 囗 and 啚; 啚 gives the idea of difficulty.” the verb 圖 and the word 難 are joined in the dictionary’s own gloss, just as they are in this line, 圖難於其易. xu shen may have had this very sentence in mind, or the two words went together in common speech. 圖 is to draw a thing out before one does it: a plan, a chart, a map. a map of a region was the standard gift of surrender; in 227 bce an assassin reached the king of qin by offering one with a dagger rolled inside. so 圖 is cool, forward-looking thought, and the line says when to use it: 於其易, “at its easy”, at the point in the life of the trouble when it is still easy. see the plate.

易 and 難: counting the pair. 難, hard, comes five times in this passage and 易, easy, four times, and the two change their parts of speech as they go. first they are states of a thing: its hard stage and its easy stage. then they are kinds of affairs: 難事. then verbs of attitude: 多易, “to call much easy”, and 難之, “to treat it as hard”. then a noun again at the close: 無難, “no difficulty”. the last four lines are a small machine built on this. to treat as easy brings the hard. to treat as hard brings no hard. english needs “difficult”, “difficulty”, “to find difficult”, “to make light of”, and the single thread is cut into four. one more thing is hidden from the english eye: 易 is also the word “change”, as in the book of changes. the stage at which a thing is easy is the stage at which it can still be changed.

細: thin as silk. 細 has 糸, a silk thread, at its left, and the shuowen says 微也, “minute”. it is not “small” in general, for which the text has 小. it is thin: a filament, a hair, a crack. the choice is exact. great things are said to start not as small copies of themselves but as threads: a single line that can be followed or cut with two fingers. the next passage gives the pictures: a tree that fills the arms grows from a tip as fine as down; a tower of nine storeys rises from a basket of earth. han feizi adds two that became proverbs: a dyke of a thousand measures is broken by the hole of an ant, and a house of a hundred feet burns from a spark in the chimney crack. see his story of the doctor. what in your life is a thread now?

the doctor who ran away. han feizi explains these lines with a story. the great physician bian que came before lord huan and said: you have a sickness in the pores of the skin; if it is not treated, it will go deeper. the lord said: i have no sickness. when the doctor had left, he added: doctors like to treat the healthy and take the credit. ten days later bian que said: it is in the flesh now. the lord did not reply. ten days later: it is in the stomach and gut. still no reply. after ten more days bian que saw the lord from a distance, turned, and ran. a man was sent to ask why. in the skin, he said, hot compresses reach it; in the flesh, needles; in the gut, a draught. now it is in the marrow, and that belongs to the master of fate. five days later the lord’s body began to ache. he sent for bian que, who had fled the state. the lord died.

聖人終不為大: the sage does nothing great. 聖人, “the sage”, is not a saint and not a genius. the character has an ear 耳 and a mouth 口; the sage is one who is attuned, and in this book usually one who rules by attunement. this line gives the trait a hard edge. 終不為大: “to the end, does not do the great”. 為大 can be “to do great things”, or “to act the great one”, or “to make oneself great”; all three are refused. the same sentence closes passage 34, where the dao clothes and feeds all things and never acts as their lord. a culture of heroes finds this strange. the founders and conquerors of the time were praised for 大事, great deeds. the sage has no great deeds, since each was done when it was a thread. nothing was left to grow great. the greatness is all in the result: 成其大. our english adds “what is” there; the chinese says only “complete its great”.

輕諾: the weight of a “yes”. 諾 is the word that one says to accept a request: “yes, i will”. it has 言, speech, at its left. 輕 is “light”; at first, as the shuowen says, a light chariot. a light 諾 is a yes that costs the speaker nothing at the moment when it is given. 寡信: “little trust”. 信 is a person, 人, beside 言, their word: to stand by what one said. the four characters 輕諾寡信 are still a common phrase. the ideal was the reverse. a saying about the chu general ji bu, a man known for keeping his word, ran a generation after this book: a hundred catties of gold are not worth one 諾 from ji bu. why does the line stand here? a promise is the smallest form of a large task. to say yes is easy, and it is the easy stage of the thing: the one point at which the whole weight could still be weighed. the light yes skips that point.

猶難之: even the sage. 猶 is “still, even so”. 難之 is 難 used as a verb with an object: “to hard it”, to regard it as hard. so 聖人猶難之 can be heard two ways. “even the sage treats it as hard”: if the sage does, who are you to be casual? wang bi reads it so. or “the sage still treats it as hard”: after all the skill, the respect for the thing has not worn off. both are meant. what is “it”? the text does not say: the task, the easy stage, each thing in turn. this is not anxiety. a good cook treats a knife as sharp every time, and for that reason is not cut. the last line then lands with a small smile: 故終無難矣, “and so, to the end, no difficulty”. the one who takes nothing lightly has a light life. the one who finds all things easy stores up trouble.

legge fills in the three phrases. the first line is nine characters. legge’s english for it runs to more than thirty words, since he explains each paradox away as he goes: to act “without (thinking of) acting”, to conduct affairs “without (feeling the) trouble of them”, to taste “without discerning any flavour”. in each case the chinese object, not-doing, no-business, no-taste, has become a state of mind in the doer. the shock of the grammar is gone. he begins with a bracket that tells the reader what kind of text this is: “(it is the way of the tao)”. for 報怨以德 he writes “to recompense injury with kindness”, and in his notes to the analects he had already weighed confucius’s answer against the teaching of christ, to the advantage of the latter. here 德 becomes “kindness”, a warm, personal word. the chinese word is cooler and larger: the power of a person who is whole.

find the thread. make a short list of three things that weigh on you. for each one, do not ask how to solve it. ask: where is this thing still a thread? a hard talk that you dread has an easy stage: one sentence, today, that opens it. a large piece of work has a first five minutes. a habit has the moment just before the hand moves. do only the thread, and do it with full care, as if it were the hard part; that is 猶難之. then look at your recent promises. find one “yes” that you gave lightly. it is still at its easy stage now, or it was last week. either carry it today or go back and take it up again honestly. notice that none of this is a great deed.

難 and 易: each is the other’s early form. passage 2 says that hard and easy complete each other, 難易相成. here the pair is shown in time. the hard thing was once easy, and the great thing was once fine as a thread. then the pair turns the other way: much that is taken as easy brings much that is hard, and what is treated as hard ends with nothing hard. so neither word is a fixed property of a task. each is a stage, and a way of meeting the stage. the text seems to favour the easy and the small. look again: the sage treats it as hard. the preference is for the early moment and for care, against an age that admired great deeds. it does not say “avoid what is hard”. the same holds for great and small, many and few, which stand with no verb between them. which side do you call your work?
