every hard affair starts as an easy one, and the time to work on it is then.. every hard affair starts as an easy one, and the time to work on it is then. does your own history agree? name one hard thing in your life and look for its easy stage. when trouble is still small, what do you do by habit: act, wait, or look away? who taught you that? take the other side: some things cannot be seen while they are small, and some hard things are worth meeting at full size. what in you likes that view? do you admire the person who solves the crisis more than the one who had none? what does that say about what you want to be seen doing?

resentment is to be answered with de, and not with a like return.. resentment is to be answered with de, and not with a like return. do you agree, or do you hold with the old objection: then with what do you answer kindness? think of a wrong done to you that you still carry. how did your family deal with wrongs: by return, by silence, by forgiving? hold the opposite for a minute: a wrong that is answered with good is a wrong rewarded. what feelings come, and toward whom? is your answer different when you are the one who did the wrong? what do you hope for then?

a quick yes is a weak promise, and calling many things easy brings many hard ones.. a quick yes is a weak promise, and calling many things easy brings many hard ones. is this true of you? recall your last quick yes and what became of it. what do you fear will happen if you pause before you agree? where does that fear come from? now take the other side: a ready yes is generosity, and a person who weighs every request is cold. which person were you taught to be? what do you think of people who often say “that is hard”? what might they see that you pass over?

圖 a map of the hard part. start with the frame. 囗 is an enclosure, a line that goes round; the shuowen says 回也, “to go around”, and it is the outer wall of 國, a state, and 園, a garden. inside the frame of 圖 is 啚 (bi). look at its parts: a small 口 on top, and below it a form that ends in 回. that lower form is the granary, 㐭, the same one that sits at the bottom of 嗇, the farmer’s word of passage 59. the shuowen’s entry for 啚 says so in one word: 嗇也, “to be sparing”, a place where grain is kept; the character was an early way to write 鄙, an outlying district with its stores. a border drawn round the settlements and granaries of the countryside: that is a map, and “map, chart, picture” is the main sense of 圖 to this day (地圖 is “map”; 圖書 is “charts and writings”, books). but the shuowen defines the word as an act of mind: 畫計難也, “to draw up plans for a difficulty”, and reads the inside part as a sign of that: 啚，難意也, “啚 gives the idea of difficulty”. a thing held tightly is hard to get. so the character is a plan drawn round the hard part. the passage says when to draw it: while the hard part is easy. later the word could also mean “to scheme, to covet” a neighbour’s land, since the one who draws your map wants your granaries. fourteen strokes, and the order teaches a rule of the script: build the house, fill it, then shut the door. first the left wall. then the top and the right wall in one stroke with a corner. the frame now stands open at the bottom. fill it: a small mouth in three strokes; then a short stroke that falls to the left, above a horizontal; then the granary, a box within a box, in six strokes (left side; top and right side; the inner mouth in three; the outer base). only then the fourteenth stroke: the long horizontal that closes the great frame. watch for that last stroke. until it is drawn, the map has no southern border. inside, keep the three tiers apart with thin bands of white, or the character goes black. the simplified form 图 puts a different part inside and has only eight strokes.

易 a lizard, or the sun and moon. the shuowen gives this small character two origins and does not choose. the first: 蜥易，蝘蜓，守宮也。象形. “the lizard, the gecko, the ‘palace guard’. a picture.” on this view 易 is the house lizard, head at the top (the part that looks like 日) and legs and tail below, and the word “change” is its gift, since such lizards were held to shift their colour through the day. the lizard itself was later written with an insect sign, 蜴. the second: 祕書說：日月爲易，象陰陽也. “the secret writings say: sun and moon make 易; it shows yin and yang.” here the top is 日, the sun, and the bottom is a form of 月, the moon: the two lights that take turns, the model of all change. modern scholars have a third account from the oldest forms, which we leave aside. both of the dictionary’s readings serve the two meanings of the word. 易 is “to change, to exchange”, as in the 易經, the book of changes. and 易 is “easy”. why should one word mean both? what changes readily is easy; what is fixed is hard, 難. this passage uses the easy sense four times, and its advice depends on the other sense: act on a thing at the stage when it can still change. in the market the same word is “to trade”: 貿易. eight strokes. the upper part is 日 in four: a vertical on the left; a horizontal that turns down on the right; a short horizontal inside; a horizontal that closes the box. make it flat and wide; it is a head, and it is not as tall as the sun written alone. the lower part is 勿 in four: a stroke that starts at the left under the box and falls to the left; then a horizontal that turns, sweeps down in a curve, and ends in a hook that points up and left; then two more strokes inside that curve, each falling to the left, each a little longer than the one before. watch the three strokes that fall to the left, numbers five, seven, and eight. they are parallel, like the legs of the lizard or rays of light, and the gaps between them must be even. the long hook, stroke six, wraps them like a tail.

味 a mouth and a full tree. left: 口, a mouth, the sign for all that goes in and out of it: 吃 (to eat), 喝 (to drink), 呼 and 吸 (to breathe out and in), 吹 (to blow), 唱 (to sing). right: 未 (wei), which gives the sound. but the shuowen says that the sound-part also gives the sense: 未，味也, “未 is flavour”. it ties 未 to the sixth month of the old calendar, high summer, when fruit and grain have taken on their taste, and it reads the shape as a tree: 象木重枝葉也, “it shows a tree with doubled branches and leaves”. compare 木, a tree, with 未: one more line across the top, a second tier of growth. a tree in full leaf, and a mouth beside it: 味. the same 未 is the common word “not yet”, and the eighth of the twelve branches that count hours and years. take care with its near twin 末, “the tip, the end”, in which the upper line is the longer one; passage 64 has it, in “the tip of a hair”. the meaning of 味 grew from the tongue to the mind: 意味 is “meaning”, 趣味 “interest”, and to 體味 a thing is to taste it with the whole body, to take it in slowly. that last use is close to the line here, taste what has no taste: the fullest character for flavour is turned on what has none. eight strokes. the mouth, three: a short vertical; a horizontal that turns down; a closing horizontal. as a left-hand part it is small and sits high, level with the upper half of the tree, and it must not grow to the full height. the tree, five: a short horizontal; a longer horizontal under it; a vertical through both, tall, with its top well above the first line; then a stroke that falls to the left and one that falls to the right from the crossing of the vertical and the second horizontal. watch the two horizontals. the upper one must be the shorter, or you have written 末 and changed the word. the two falling strokes spread wide and low and carry the small mouth as a branch carries a fruit. in running script the mouth is two quick dots and a turn.

64 · under the foot. what lies still is easy to hold. / what shows no sign yet is easy to plan for. / what is brittle is easy to break apart. / what is fine is easy to scatter. / act on it while it is not yet there. / order it while it is not yet in disorder. / a tree that fills the arms’ embrace / is born from the tip of a hair. / a terrace of nine tiers / rises from heaped earth. / a journey of a thousand li / begins under the foot. / who acts on it ruins it. / who grips it loses it. / so the sage does not force, and so ruins nothing; / does not grip, and so loses nothing. / people at their work / constantly ruin it when it is nearly done. / be as careful of the end as of the start: / then no work is ruined. / so the sage desires not to desire / and does not prize hard-to-get goods; / learns not to learn / and goes back to what the many pass by, / to assist the self-so of the ten thousand things, / and does not dare to act. the passage has two movements, and the oldest copies keep them apart. the first is about beginnings. four things are easy: to hold what is still, to plan for what shows no crack of a sign, to break the brittle, to scatter the fine. three pictures follow, and each sets a great thing beside its first state: tree and hair-tip, terrace and load of earth, journey and the ground under the foot. the second movement is about endings and about the hand: do not force, do not grip, give the end the care of the start. the close turns to the sage, who wants and studies in reverse, assists the self-so of all things, and dares no more than that. read the first lines as a description of the mind. a mood is easy to hold while it is at rest. an anger that has shown no sign yet is easy to meet; a breath is enough. later it is a tree, and two arms do not go around it. the contemplative skill here is not control. it is early seeing: to know the 幾, the first slight movement, as it rises. wang bi warns that a slight thing left alone gives birth to a great one. then the passage turns the same light on the one who watches. who acts on it ruins it: the hand that reaches in to fix the mind is one more movement of the mind. so the sage learns not to learn, and goes back to what was passed by. what in you is already so, with no help? a good leader in this passage is hard to see. problems are met when they are small enough to have no name, so no one records a rescue. this goes against the way that states and companies reward people: the one who puts out the fire is promoted, and the one in whose care no fire began is not noticed. the second half is a warning about grip. forms and names, targets and audits, produce skilled evasion. the last line gives the leader’s true work in one verb, 輔: to stand at the side of what people and things are already becoming, and to carry part of the load. do not make a method of it, a quiet way to keep control. the text says the helper does not dare. in the movement arts this passage is a rule of timing. a push is easy to turn at the moment it starts, when the partner’s weight has only begun to shift; a finger on the elbow is enough. the same push at full force needs strength against strength, and who grips loses. teachers of taijiquan quote this kind of line: the opponent has not moved, i do not move; the opponent moves slightly, and i have already moved. feel 足下 now. stand, and let the weight go down through the soles. each step begins from that pressure, before the leg lifts. then watch the end of a movement. most injuries and most spilled tea come in the last moment, when the mind has gone ahead and left the hand alone. an oak that two people cannot circle with their arms was a root tip finer than a hair, and at that stage a dry week could end it. growth in the passage runs upward and outward from almost nothing: hair-tip to trunk, basket to terrace, sole to road. the same law runs the other way. erosion begins as a line that a child’s finger could smooth; a flood begins as ice that starts to break upstream. gardeners know the first half of the passage: weed when the weed has two leaves. they also know the last line. no gardener makes a plant grow. the gardener assists a growth that is of itself: water, a stake at the side, and then hands off. do the last tenth today. then choose one of the three pictures and stay with it for a minute. for the tree: find the smallest living shoot near you and look at its tip. for the terrace: recall one large thing in your life and name its first load of earth. for the journey: stand still, feel the floor under both feet, and say where you are. do not start anything. the passage puts the beginning under the foot, and you are already standing on it.

兆: the crack on the shell. 未兆 is “not yet 兆”. the word comes from divination. a diviner of the shang and zhou courts put a hot point to a turtle shell or an ox bone. the shell cracked, and the diviner read the cracks as the answer. those cracks are 兆. the shuowen enters the word under a fuller graph, 𠧞, with the part 卜, and says 灼龜坼也: “the splits of a scorched turtle shell”. so the line does not say “before it begins”. it says: before the shell has cracked, while no sign can be read at all. the sage of this passage works earlier than the diviner. a diviner waits for the crack. what do you wait for before you act?

泮: ice that breaks up. the received text writes 泮. the shuowen knows this graph only as the name of a lords’ ceremonial hall with water on one side. here it writes a different word of the same sound: to break up, to come apart. the book of songs uses it for river ice in spring: 迨冰未泮, “while the ice has not yet broken up”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 判, “to split with a blade”, and add a particle to each phrase: 亓脆也，易判也. both words share the part 半, “half”. so the brittle thing in this line is perhaps thin ice. it also gives the passage a season: early spring, when one warm day decides. english must choose “break”, “melt”, or “split”. the chinese holds all three.

為, twice, in two senses. 為之於未有: “act on it at the not-yet-there”. eight lines later: 為者敗之, “who acts on it ruins it”. the verb is the same, 為. the first use is advice. the second is a warning. this is not a slip. the passage puts the two side by side on purpose. to 為 a thing that is already large and hard is to force it, and force meets force. to 為 a thing that has no form yet takes almost no force at all; a touch is enough. at the limit, the earliest action and no action are the same act. that limit is 無為. the rendering keeps “act” for both lines so that you can feel the turn. which of your present labours were once a thing that a touch could have settled?

毫末: the tip of an autumn hair. 毫 is the fine hair of an animal’s coat; the lower part of the graph is 毛, hair. 末 is the tip (see the plate). the set phrase is older than this passage. animals grow a new, very fine coat in autumn, and “the tip of an autumn hair”, 秋毫之末, was the standard example of the smallest thing that an eye can see. mencius uses it at a king’s court: a man whose sight can examine the tip of an autumn hair, and who does not see a cartload of firewood. a brush is also a 毫: its hairs are tied so that their tips meet in one point. the image of the line is exact. a tree too wide for two arms was once thinner than the thing you write with.

臺: how a terrace was made. a 臺 was a high platform of rammed earth with a hall or tower on it. the shuowen says 觀，四方而高者: “a lookout, four-sided and high”. in the warring states period, rulers competed in terraces as they competed in chariots. the method was slow. workers carried loose earth in baskets, tipped it between wooden boards, and beat it hard, one thin layer after another. 累 is “to pile, to add one on one”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 九成之臺，作於羸土; some scholars read their 羸 as a word for an earth basket, so that the terrace rises from one basketload. either way, the line names the labour of the many. a reader then knew who had carried the earth. the text praises no ruler for the height. it looks at the first load.

足下: not “a single step”. english knows this line as a proverb about a thousand miles and one step. the chinese has no step in it. 始於足下 is “begins at under-the-foot”: the ground on which you stand now, before any movement. a li was about four hundred metres, so the journey is some four hundred kilometres. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to have a different third image: 百仞之高，始於足下, “a height of a hundred 仞 begins under the foot”. a 仞 was a measure taken from the human body, about the height of a person. that older line continues the upward direction of the tree and the terrace. the received text turns it level, into a road. both keep the last two characters. the beginning is not in front of you. where are your feet?

為者敗之: a line that comes twice. 為者敗之，執者失之 also stands in passage 29, where the object is 天下, the world: a spirit vessel that no one can handle. here the object is any affair. the pair of verbs had a clear target in the 4th and 3rd centuries bce. the reforming states governed by written law and quotas, and by a method called 形名, “forms and names”, linked first with shen buhai of han and later with han fei: each office has a title, and each result is measured against it. wang bi names this method in his comment here: 形名執之, to “grip it with forms and names”, and he says the result is 巧辟滋作, “clever evasions multiply”. the more tightly a state grips, the more skill its people put into escape. the line is a remark on government and not only on character.

聖人: the one who hears. “sage” is the usual english, and it misleads in two ways. a 聖人 is not a saint: there is no holiness, no god who chooses, and no life after this one in the word. a 聖人 is also more than a wise old man. the shuowen defines 聖 as 通也, “open all the way through”, and files it under 耳, the ear; the graph also holds 口, a mouth: a person who hears well and whose speech fits what was heard. in the laozi the 聖人 is most often a ruler, or the pattern that a ruler should follow. in this passage the sage is defined by negatives: no forcing, no gripping, no prized goods, no daring. the ear comes before the mouth. notice how much of the passage is listening for things that make no sound yet.

無為: not “doing nothing”. 無為 is “without 為”. 為 is to make, to act on a thing, to work it into a shape that you have chosen. english “inaction” and “doing nothing” are wrong, because this passage has just ordered an action: 為之於未有. we write “does not force”. the sense is nearer to a carpenter who cuts with the grain, or a doctor who treats a fever on the first day. such work looks like little. the passage gives the reason in one small word, 故, “and so”: no forcing, and so no ruin. it is a claim about results and not a vow of passivity. the western habit is to honour the hero who saves a thing that is nearly lost. this text honours the person in whose care nothing was ever nearly lost. no one tells stories about that person.

幾: the edge of done. 幾成 is “nearly complete”. 幾 (ji) means “close to, on the verge”. it is also a noun: the first, smallest movement of a thing, the point at which it can still go either way. the appended statements of the book of changes say 幾者，動之微: “the 幾 is the slightness of a movement”. so this one character links the two halves of the passage. the first half looks at the 幾 of a beginning. the second half looks at the 幾 of an end, and says that people fail there. the mawangdui silk texts are reported not to have the word: 恆於亓成而敗之, “they always ruin it at its completion”. in both versions the cause is the same. attention arrives late and it leaves early. the cure is four characters: 慎終如始.

欲不欲: three words, two readings. 欲不欲 is verb, negative, verb or noun. reading one: “desires not-desiring”. the one desire that the sage keeps is to be free of desire. it is a small joke, and it is honest: the sage has not stopped wanting. reading two: “desires what is not desired”: the sage wants the things that other people leave. legge takes the second and adds “(other men)” in brackets. the next clause can support both: 不貴難得之貨, “does not hold dear the goods that are difficult to obtain”. that phrase is a refrain of the book. passage 3 says that it keeps the people from theft; passage 12 says that such goods make a person’s conduct go wrong. jade, pearls, rhinoceros horn: their value is their distance. english must fill the empty place after “not”. the chinese leaves it empty.

wang bi: what needs no learning. 學不學 has the same form as 欲不欲: “learns not-learning”, or “learns what is not learned”. wang bi reads it through 自然: 不學而能者，自然也，喻於不學者，過也. “what one can do without learning is the self-so. to go beyond what needs no learning is the fault.” his 喻 is usually read as 踰, “to overstep”. for him the 過 of the next line is this excess: the many have gone past the place where they could already walk, breathe, and care for a child, and they have added to it. the sage’s study is then a strange one. its course runs back. passage 48 gives the same rule in numbers: for learning, add each day; for the dao, take away each day.

過: to walk past, to go wrong. 過 has 辶, the sign of walking, and the shuowen defines it as 度也, “to cross, to pass”. from “to go past” the word grew a second sense: to go too far, and so a fault, an excess. 復 also has two senses: “to go back to” and “to restore, to make good”. so 復眾人之所過 has two full readings. one: the sage goes back to the place that the crowd walked past. the plain thing was beside the road, and everyone was in a hurry. two: the sage makes good the excesses of the crowd. we render the first, because 復 as “return” is the great verb of this book (16, 28). the second is wang bi’s. in chinese a mistake is a kind of overshoot. what did you pass today?

輔: the helper at the side. 輔 has 車, a cart, at the left. the old use of the word is for a pair of side pieces that were tied to a cart to strengthen it under a heavy load. a poem in the book of songs warns a ruler with the image: 其車既載，乃棄爾輔, “your cart is loaded, and now you throw away your props”. from the cart the word passed to people: a 輔 is a minister who supports a ruler and does not sit on the throne. the shuowen records another old sense, the jaw (see the plate). the choice of verb is the point of the line. the sage does not lead the ten thousand things, or improve them, or manage them. the sage is tied on at the side, takes some of the load, and the cart goes where it was going.

自然: self-so, not “nature”. in modern chinese 自然 is the word for “nature”, and translators often write “natural” here. in this text it is two words: 自, “self”, and 然, “so, thus”. a thing is 自然 when it is so of itself, with no one who makes it so. the shuowen gives each graph a first sense that surprises: 自 is 鼻也, the nose (people point at the nose to say “i”), and 然 is 燒也, “to burn”, borrowed for the word “thus”. “nature” in english is a place, or a system outside the human being. 自然 is not a place. it is a way of happening, and a person or a state can have it or lose it. here it is a noun with an owner: the self-so of the ten thousand things. see passages 17, 23, 25, and 51.

不敢: a sage who does not dare. the last three characters are 不敢為, “does not dare to act”. western ethics from the greeks on counts daring as a virtue, and a translator is tempted to soften the phrase. legge adds a bracket: the sage does not dare to act “with an ulterior purpose of his own”. the chinese has no such limit. 不敢 is a phrase of the book: in passage 3 the clever do not dare to act; in passage 67 the third treasure is not daring to stand ahead of the world; passage 73 says that courage in daring kills and courage in not-daring keeps alive. it is the language of a junior before a senior. the senior here is the self-so of things. the sage stands before a growing tree as a careful guest stands in another person’s house.

two texts, later joined. this passage reads as two parts, and the oldest evidence agrees. in the bamboo slips from guodian, buried about 300 bce, the part that ends at “begins under the foot” is reported as one unit, and the part from 為者敗之 to the end as another, in a different place. the second part is reported twice, in two bundles, with small differences of wording. the guodian copies are also reported to read 教不教, “teaches not-teaching”, for 學不學, and 弗能為, “cannot act”, for 不敢為. so in the oldest copies that we have, these were separate sayings. a later editor joined them, and the join is good: one saying about beginnings, one about endings. the mawangdui silk texts, about a century later, already have them as one. the book was not written in one sitting. it was gathered, as a terrace is, load by load.

wang bi: a nothing that is not held. wang bi does not let the first lines become advice to relax. he writes: 不可以無之故而不持，不可以微之故而弗散也。無而弗持則生有焉，微而不散則生大焉。 “one may not, because it is nothing yet, fail to hold it; one may not, because it is slight, fail to scatter it. a nothing that is not held gives birth to a something. a slight thing that is not scattered gives birth to a great thing.” on the people who fail near the end he writes three characters: 不慎終也, “they are not careful of the end”. his reading is strict. things are easy at the start, and for that reason the start asks for full attention. ease is the reason for care and not a release from it.

legge’s “ulterior purpose”. legge was a scottish missionary in hong kong, and later the first professor of chinese at oxford. a sacred book that warned against action troubled a victorian reader. so he repairs it with brackets. 為者敗之 becomes “he who acts (with an ulterior purpose) does harm”, and the last line ends “does not dare to act (with an ulterior purpose of his own)”. the brackets turn a claim about action into a claim about motive: action is good if the heart is pure. the chinese says nothing of motive. he also gives the tree a “sprout” where the text has a hair, and the journey “a single step” where the text has the ground under the foot. his version of 自然 is “natural development”, a word of his own century, the century of darwin.

the last tenth. choose one thing that you will finish today: a message, a meal, a repair, a talk with a child. notice the moment when you judge that it is nearly done. this is the 幾成 of the passage. watch what your attention does at that moment. it usually leaves and goes to the next thing. today, do the last tenth as you did the first: the same pace, the same care for small parts. wash the last dish as you washed the first. read the last line before you send. then try the other half. find one thing that has shown no sign yet: a tiredness in a friend’s voice, a small wrong sound in a machine. hold it now, while a hand is enough.

始 and 終: the start inside the end. the passage is built on beginning and end. its first half looks at beginnings: the hair-tip, the first load of earth, the ground under the foot. its second half looks at ends, where people ruin the work when it is nearly done. the sentence 慎終如始 joins them: be as careful of the end as of the start. it does not rank them. the start is noted as easy to work on, and the end is to be met as if it were a start. other pairs follow the same line. order is made inside not-yet-disorder (治, 亂). the great tree is in the small tip. acting and ruin, gripping and loss, are set side by side, and the sage’s not forcing is still a way of working: it assists. a reading that hears only “begin small” has kept half. a reading that hears only “do nothing” has kept less. where in your day does an end need a beginner’s care?

the one who acts on a thing ruins it, and the one who grips it loses it.. the one who acts on a thing ruins it, and the one who grips it loses it. where has this been true for you? where has it been false, and your grip kept something from harm? what are you gripping at present? what do you believe will happen if the hand opens? take the opposite: things left alone decay, and what you do not hold is taken. who in your past lived by that? did it serve them? what do you think of people who let things be: do they seem wise to you, or lazy? what might that judgment guard in you?

work is most often ruined when it is nearly done, so the end needs the care of the start.. work is most often ruined when it is nearly done, so the end needs the care of the start. is this your pattern? think of something that you spoiled, or dropped, in its last tenth. what happens in you when the end comes into view: hurry, boredom, fear that the finished thing will be judged? hold the other view: the start decides everything, and a good beginning carries itself home. which do you trust more, your starts or your finishes? is there something in your life that you keep nearly done? what would its completion ask of you?

the sage helps things be what they are of themselves and does not dare to do more.. the sage helps things be what they are of themselves and does not dare to do more. do you agree that the best help adds nothing of the helper’s own plan? think of a child, a student, or a garden in your care. who helped you in this way? who helped you by making you into something? how do you now see each of them? take the opposite: people and things need to be shaped, and to hold back is to fail them. stay with that. when has it been true? the text says “does not dare”. what is it that you do not dare: to act, or to stop acting?

末 a mark on the treetop. begin with 木, a tree: a trunk, a line for the branches, and two strokes that spread at the foot like roots. the script then makes new words by adding one mark to the tree, and the shuowen lists them almost as a set. put the mark at the top: 末, 木上曰末, “the top of a tree is called 末”: the tip, the end, the last and least part. put the mark at the foot: 本, 木下曰本, “the base of a tree is called 本”: the root, the origin, the thing that matters most. put it through the middle: 朱, which the shuowen calls 赤心木, “a tree with a red heart”: the colour vermilion. these are not pictures of things. the chinese name for such a graph is 指事, “to point at the matter”: the stroke is a finger that points. a fourth cousin looks almost the same: 未, “not yet”, the word that comes three times in the first lines of this passage. the shuowen explains it as a tree with a second layer of branches and leaves. in 末 the upper line is long. in 未 the upper line is short. the pair 本末, “root and tip”, became a common term of chinese thought for the main thing and the minor thing. this passage turns the pair over: the tip of a hair is where the great tree is born. five strokes. first a long horizontal, which is the pointing mark; press at the start, travel, and press again to close. second a shorter horizontal beneath it: the branches. watch these two, because their lengths are the whole identity of the character. if the first is shorter than the second, you have written 未. third the vertical, from above the top line down to the foot; it must stand straight, since everything hangs on it. fourth a stroke that falls to the left from the crossing, with the brush lifting as it goes, so that the end is a point. fifth a stroke that falls to the right, thin at first and then pressed wide before the final lift. the two falling strokes are the oldest part of the picture. in seal script they are curved roots. the clerical script of the han straightened them and gave the right one its heavy foot.

兆 cracks read as an answer. this character is a picture of something that happened by heat. in the divination of the shang kings, more than three thousand years ago, a hollow was cut in the back of a turtle shell or an ox shoulder blade. a hot point was put to the hollow. the front face split with a sharp sound, usually into a long crack and a short crack that branched from it. that branched shape is the character 卜 (bu), “to divine”, and its sound is perhaps the sound of the shell. the pattern of cracks as a whole was the 兆: the thing to be read. the shuowen calls 兆 a picture, 象形, and enters it under a fuller graph with 卜 beside it. the early forms are debated; the modern shape is commonly seen as two sets of cracks, back to back. the meaning grew from “crack” to “sign, omen” and then to “first trace of a thing to come”, as in 兆頭 or 預兆. much later it became a number, a million in one system and a million million in another, and on the mainland it is now the “mega” of megabytes: a count too large to see, written with the smallest sign. cousins that keep it for the sound: 跳, to jump; 逃, to flee; 桃, a peach. in this passage it is a verb with 未 before it: not yet cracked. the earliest chinese writing that we have is on those shells. six strokes, three on each side. on the left: a long stroke that curves down and to the left, then a dot, then a short stroke that rises to the right. on the right: a stroke that goes down, bends to the right, and ends in a hook that turns up; then a short stroke to the left, and last a dot. watch the two long strokes, the first and the fourth. they start close and lean apart, like a split that runs both ways from one point. the four small strokes branch from them, as the side cracks did. the writer should keep the middle open. on the bone itself, the questions and answers were cut with a knife beside the cracks: thin, straight lines, with no thick and thin. the brush gave the same graph its swelling curves a thousand years later.

輔 cart and cheek. two parts. at the left, 車: a cart seen from above, with a body, two wheels, and an axle. at the right, 甫, which gives the sound (the shuowen: 从車甫聲). the cart tells you the class of thing. a 輔 was a side piece lashed to a cart so that it could bear a heavy load; a poem warns the man who throws his props away when the cart is full. yet the shuowen defines the word with a part of the face: 人頰車也, “the cheek-frame of a person”, the jaw. the two senses meet in a proverb from the zuozhuan. in 655 bce the great state of jin asked the small state of yu for passage to attack its neighbour guo. a minister of yu objected: 輔車相依，脣亡齒寒, “prop and cart lean on each other; when the lips are gone, the teeth are cold”. readers have taken 輔車 there as cheek and jawbone and also as prop and cart. yu gave passage. jin destroyed guo, and on the way home it destroyed yu. so the word holds a whole idea of support: a thing at the side that carries load and does not steer. later it named the ministers at a ruler’s side. the right-hand part 甫 lends its sound to other words: 補, to mend; 捕, to catch; 浦, a riverbank. in the last line of this passage the sage is the 輔 of the ten thousand things. fourteen strokes: seven for 車, then seven for 甫. in 車: a horizontal; the left side of the box; the top and right side in one stroke with a corner; a short line inside; a line that closes the box; a long horizontal; and last the vertical through the centre. as a left-hand part the cart is made narrow, and its long horizontal slants up to the right to give way to its neighbour. in 甫: a horizontal; the left vertical of the frame; the top and right side in one stroke that ends in a hook; a short horizontal inside; a second short horizontal under it; a tall vertical through the middle; and at the end a dot at the upper right. watch the two central verticals, strokes seven and thirteen. they stand side by side like two poles. neither part leans on the other, and each helps the other stand.

65 · the great going-along. those of old, good at working the dao, / did not use it to brighten the people. / rather, they used it to make them simple. / the people are hard to govern / because their cleverness is much. / so: to govern a state by cleverness / is the state’s ruin. / not to govern a state by cleverness / is the state’s good fortune. / to know these two is also the pattern to check by. / to know the pattern always: / this is called dark de. / dark de is deep. it is far. / it turns back with things, / and only then arrives at the great going-along. the passage is an argument in three steps. first a claim about the old masters of the dao: they did not sharpen the people; they kept them simple. then a reason and a verdict in rhyme: much cleverness makes people hard to govern, so rule by cleverness is the state’s ruin, and rule without it is the state’s fortune. then the passage climbs. to know these two results is a standard; to keep the standard in mind always is dark de; and dark de is deep, far, and turned back, until it comes to the great going-along. the last word, 順, answers the first verb, 為: the work of the dao ends where nothing is worked against. take the state as the self, as many old readers did. then the people are the many movements of body and mind, and the ruler is the part that plans. a mind governed by cleverness is hard to live in. it watches itself, calculates its own moods, and makes rules for its own improvement; the moods learn the rules and go around them, as in wang bi’s spiral. the passage offers another way to keep house: 愚, the plain attention that the speaker of passage 20 claims, with nothing bright about it. this is not stupidity, and it is not a pose of innocence. it is knowing that does not turn into strategy. from there the last lines read as an experience: things turn back, and one goes with them. a system takes on the character of its head. when the person at the top is strategic with people, people become strategic in return, and soon each message has a second meaning. the passage calls that leader the state’s ruin, and the word fits: such a leader destroys trust, the common store. its remedy is not to give people less information. the burden falls on the one who governs: do not rule by technique. say what is the case, and make few rules. history is a warning here. the legalists took the first lines and built a state on them, and that state lasted fifteen years. if you find that this passage approves of you, read the fifth line again. 順 is a water word: its left side is a river. a stream does not compute its course. it goes down by the nearest way, and the valley that results is exact, the fit of water to land. things in nature also turn back: sap goes down in autumn, rivers return to the sea, the year comes round. the passage sets this going-with against 智, the faculty that finds short cuts. a straightened river is a clever thing: it moves water fast and floods the town below. engineers now put the bends back. the great going-along is not weakness before nature. it is what remains when the short cuts have been counted with all their costs. try one day without the angle. then, in the evening, apply the passage’s own standard, which has only two marks. think of one thing that you arranged cleverly this week and one that you left plain. in which did trust go down, as if something had been ruined? in which did something arrive that you did not plan, like a gift? the passage says that to know these two, always, is the whole pattern. you do not need a theory of it. you need to remember tomorrow what you saw today.

“those of old”: a later frame. the received text opens 古之善為道者, “those of old who were good at working the dao”. passage 15 opens with nearly the same words. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to begin differently: 故曰：為道者非以明民也, “so it is said: those who work the dao do not use it to brighten the people”. there is no “of old” and no “good at”. 故曰, “so it is said”, joins this passage to the end of passage 64, which stands before it in the silk texts too. the appeal to antiquity is then an editor’s frame. in the warring states period each school claimed the ancient kings for its own programme, and “the ancients did it” was the strongest argument that a writer had. the older line is plainer and takes no shelter in the past. it says: this is what the work is.

為道: the dao as a thing one does. we leave 道 as dao. the word is first a road, then a way of doing something, then the way that all things go. english “the way” with a capital suggests one fixed path and, to many ears, a religion. here the grammar helps: 為道 is “to do dao”, to work at it, as one works a craft. passage 48 uses the same two words: 為道日損, “for the work of the dao, each day take something away”. so the first line already tells you what kind of work this is. it is practice, and a practice that subtracts. the people of old in this line are not believers in a doctrine. they are skilled workers. what does a ruler look like whose skill is to take things away?

wang bi: what “bright” means here. 明 is sun and moon side by side: bright, clear, to see clearly. in this book it is nearly always praise. to know the constant is called 明 (16, 55); who knows the self is 明 (33). here it is a thing that the old masters refused to do to the people. wang bi explains both hard words in one sentence each: 明謂多見巧詐，蔽其樸也。愚謂無知守真，順自然也。 “明 means to see much and be skilled in tricks, which covers over their uncarved state. 愚 means to be without such knowing and to keep what is genuine, which goes along with the self-so.” so for him the 明 of this line is sharpness: the bright eye that sees every angle and every advantage. it is not the light of passage 16. the same graph names both.

愚: the hard line. 將以愚之: “they used it to make them 愚”. no reading makes this line comfortable, and we should not hide it. 愚 is “dull, simple, foolish”; the shuowen ties the graph to a monkey (see the plate). rulers have quoted this line to defend keeping people ignorant. two facts stand against that use. first, the speaker of the book claims the word for the self: 我愚人之心也哉, “mine is the heart of a 愚 person” (20). the people are to be as the sage already is. second, the next lines turn on the ruler: it is the ruler’s cleverness that ruins the state. english “ignorant” assumes that knowledge is light and its lack is darkness, the frame of the enlightenment. this text asks a question from outside that frame. is there a knowing that makes people worse at living together?

who used this line. “the people are hard to govern” was a practical problem in the 4th and 3rd centuries bce. the states were at war, and each needed farmers and soldiers who obeyed. the legalist answer was direct. the book of lord shang says 民弱國強，民強國弱: “when the people are weak the state is strong; when the people are strong the state is weak”. han fei, who wrote the first known comments on the laozi, served the same programme. in 213 bce the qin court burned the books of the schools; a han writer, jia yi, described the aim in this passage’s own word: 以愚黔首, “to make the black-haired people 愚”. the laozi was thus read as a manual for that policy. but look at what it forbids. shang yang ruled by exactly the 智 that this passage calls the state’s ruin.

智 or 知: to know a state. the received text writes 智 (zhi), “cleverness”. early manuscripts did not separate this graph from 知, “to know”; 智 is 知 with an added part. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read: 民之難治也，以亓知也。故以知知邦，邦之賊也；以不知知邦，邦之德也. two things stand out. the verb “govern” is also written 知: “to know a state by knowing”. and the reward is 德 where we have 福. silk a is reported to write the state as 邦; silk b and later copies have 國, because 邦 was the personal name of liu bang, the first han emperor, and could not be written. in this passage, then, 知 is knowing as technique: to see through people, to calculate them. passage 3 has the same target: 使夫智者不敢為也, “make the clever ones not dare to act”.

賊: harm with a weapon. modern 賊 means a thief. the classical word is stronger. the shuowen defines it as 敗也, “to ruin”, and gives its parts as 戈, a dagger-axe, with 則 for the sound. in the modern form you can still see 貝, a cowrie shell, at the left, and 戈 at the right. a 賊 is one who injures: a murderer, a bandit, a rebel, a traitor inside the walls. mencius used it for a king: 賊仁者謂之賊, “one who does violence to humaneness is called a 賊”, and such a man, he said, may be killed as a common fellow and not as a ruler. so 國之賊 is a hard charge. the ruler who governs by cleverness is not a poor manager. that ruler is the enemy inside the state. we write “ruin”; the chinese noun is the person who ruins.

賊 and 福: a rhyme you cannot hear. the two verdicts rhymed. in the old sound system 賊 and 福 belong to one rhyme group (the 職 group), and the mawangdui reading 德 is in the same group. mandarin has moved them apart: zei, fu, de. a warring states listener heard a couplet with a click at the end, like a proverb. 福 is the common word for good fortune; it is on red paper at every chinese new year. the shuowen defines it 祐也, “help from above”. its left part, 示, is the sign of an altar, so the fortune is first a thing received from ancestors and spirits and not a thing made. passage 58 says that fortune and disaster lean on each other. here the verdict is plain: one way of rule harms, and one is a gift. even so, the passage asks the reader to know both.

稽式 or 楷式. 式 is a model or standard; the shuowen says 法也, “a rule to follow”. the graph before it differs between editions. wang bi’s text has 稽, a verb for checking one thing against another, as a tally is checked, and wang bi glosses it as 同, “the same”: that which is the same in the present and the past. the heshang gong edition has 楷, “a model”, the word that later named the regular script, 楷書, the model hand. the shuowen knows 楷 only as a tree, said to grow on the grave of confucius. with 稽 the phrase is “the pattern to check by”; with 楷, “the model pattern”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to support 稽. in both, the claim is modest in form and large in content: the two results of rule, ruin and fortune, are the standard. no other is needed.

玄德: dark power. 德 is not “virtue” in the moral sense of the english word. it is the power that a thing or a person has from the dao: the quality by which a person affects others with no force. 玄 is a dark colour; the shuowen says 幽遠也, “hidden and far”, and adds: black with red in it. legge writes “mysterious excellence”, and the darkness turns into a puzzle to be solved. but 玄 is dark as deep water is dark: there is too much of it to see through. passages 10 and 51 define 玄德: to give life and not own, to act and not lean on it, to lead and not rule. here a fourth mark is added: to know the two patterns and not use cleverness. a later hero, liu bei, had 玄德 as his courtesy name.

與物反: against things, or back with them. 與物反矣 is four characters and two sentences. 反 means “to turn over, to turn back”. the shuowen has 覆也, “to turn upside down”. reading one: dark de is the reverse of things. it runs against what the world expects, as this whole passage does. legge takes this line, and makes the sage “opposite to others”. reading two: dark de returns, and 與物, “together with things”: it goes back and takes all things with it. wang bi takes this line in four characters: 反其真也, “it returns to their genuineness”. we render the second, because passage 40 makes 反 the movement of the dao itself, and there it is return. a chinese reader does not choose. the word that means “contrary” is the word that means “homeward”. in english these are two thoughts.

大順: not harmony, not obedience. 順 is a head beside a stream (see the plate): to go the way the water goes. english has no good word. “harmony” is taken; it belongs to 和, the blend of different notes. “obedience” and “conformity” make it submission to a master; legge ends the passage with “a great conformity to him”, and the chinese has no “him”. 順 is to move along the grain of a thing. its opposite is 逆, “to go against the current”. 大順 comes once in the laozi, as the last word of this passage. the zhuangzi echoes it in a sentence that holds all three hard words of the passage: 若愚若昏，是謂玄德，同乎大順, “as if simple, as if dim: this is called dark de, one with the great going-along”. what moves in your day when you stop rowing?

wang bi: the spiral of technique. wang bi’s longest comment here describes a spiral. a ruler uses clever technique to move the people: 以智術動民. then: 邪心既動，復以巧術防民之偽，民知其術，防隨而避之，思惟密巧，奸偽益滋。 “once their crooked hearts are stirred, he uses more skilful technique to guard against their falseness. the people learn his technique, and they avoid each guard as it comes. thought grows close and cunning, and deceit increases the more.” read it as a description of any system of rules and incentives. each new control teaches the controlled how the controller thinks. wang bi wrote in the 240s ce, at the court of wei, in the age of the three kingdoms, and he died at twenty-three. he had seen such a court from inside.

legge: “simple and ignorant”. legge renders 愚 with two words, “simple and ignorant”. the pair shows his difficulty. as a missionary and teacher he had given his life to the enlightenment of a people, in both senses of the english word, and his own version of the first line says that the ancients did not seek “to enlighten the people”. the sentence stands against his vocation. his notes to the passage try to limit the damage. he also adds “(of a governor)” after the “mysterious excellence”, which narrows 玄德 to an official’s merit, and he ends with “conformity to him”. the victorian frame is a school: a master, pupils, a lesson that is learned. the chinese last word has no master in it.

one day without the angle. cleverness in this passage is a specific habit: to look at a person and see what can be got, and how. for one day, in one relation, put it down. choose a person you often manage a little: a child, a colleague, a partner. do not arrange the words to get the result. do not hint. do not praise in order to move. say the plain thing, ask the plain question, and let the answer be what it is. notice the moment when the angle appears in your mind; it is quick and it feels like intelligence. notice also what the other person does when no technique is used on them. wang bi says that people learn the ruler’s method. what have the people near you learned from yours?

兩者: bright and simple, ruin and fortune. 兩者, “these two”, are the two ways of rule and their results: 賊 and 福, ruin and good fortune. behind them is a second pair, 明 and 愚, bright and simple, with 智, cleverness, on the bright side. the text takes a side here, and we do not hide it. but see what the preference is for. it answers an age in which rulers and advisers prized cunning, and each clever law bred a more clever evasion. it is not a rule that knowing is bad: this very line asks the ruler to 知, to know, both sides. elsewhere 明 is praised; to know the constant is called 明 (16). the favoured side also turns. simplicity that is ordered from above becomes a policy of ignorance, and that is one more piece of cleverness. passage 58 says that fortune and disaster lean on each other. the standard is to keep both in view.

to govern by cleverness ruins a state; to govern without it is the state’s good fortune.. to govern by cleverness ruins a state; to govern without it is the state’s good fortune. does your experience of leaders, parents, or teachers bear this out? give one case each way. when were you last clever with someone and not plain? what were you guarding? take the other side: a ruler with no cunning is eaten by those who have it. how much of your own cleverness comes from that fear? do you trust plain people more than clever ones, or less? where did you learn that?

people are easier to live with and to lead when they are simple than when they are sharp.. people are easier to live with and to lead when they are simple than when they are sharp. this line has been used to keep people ignorant. before you reject it or accept it, what is your first feeling on reading it? were you praised as a child for being bright? what did that praise ask you to give up? hold the opposite: light is good, and more knowing makes people more free. then hold the passage’s side. does one of them feel like home? is there a kind of knowing in you that makes you worse at living with others? is there a kind of simplicity that you look down on?

愚 a monkey over a heart. two parts, one above the other. at the foot is 心, the heart, which for the chinese is also the organ of thought; the shuowen says 在身之中, it is “in the middle of the body”. the heart at the foot of a graph marks a state of mind: 思 to think, 忘 to forget, 怒 anger, 慈 a parent’s love. above it is 禺. the shuowen says of 禺: 母猴屬。頭似鬼, “of the macaque kind; the head is like a ghost’s”. then, under 愚 itself: 戇也。从心从禺。禺，猴屬，獸之愚者, “simple-minded. from 心 and 禺. 禺 is of the monkey kind, the 愚 one among the animals”. so the dictionary reads the graph as a monkey’s mind. many modern scholars think that 禺 is here mostly for the sound, as it is in 遇, to meet; 偶, a pair, an image; 寓, to lodge; and 隅, a corner. hold both. the word’s history is kinder than its picture. chinese writers used 愚 for themselves as a polite “i”: 愚見, “my simple view”. a famous story tells of 愚公, old mr. simple, who began to dig away two mountains with baskets; the clever man who laughed at him has the name 智叟. in passage 20 the speaker of the laozi takes the word as a badge. thirteen strokes: nine for 禺, four for 心. first a small box, in three strokes: the left side; the top and right side with one corner; a horizontal inside. a fourth stroke closes it. next the lower frame: a vertical at the left, then the top and right side in one stroke that ends in a hook. the seventh stroke is a long vertical that starts at the top of the box, goes down through it, and ends inside the frame; watch it, because it ties the head to the body. then a short horizontal and a dot inside the frame. last the heart: a dot at the left; a long hook that lies almost flat; a dot above the hook; and a dot at its right. the upper part must be compact, so that the heart can spread wide beneath and carry it. in running script the three dots of the heart join into one wave.

順 a head beside a stream. at the left are three lines that fall side by side: 川, a river. the shuowen calls 川 water that 貫穿通流, “passes through and flows on”; the oldest forms are lines of current between two banks. at the right is 頁. the shuowen says 頭也, “the head”; the graph is a large head with its hair above a small body, and it marks parts of the head in 頭 (head), 頂 (crown), 額 (forehead), 顏 (face), and 頸 (neck). the shuowen lists 順 as a joint meaning, 从頁从巛, head and stream, and defines it 理也: to follow the lines in a thing, as a jade worker follows the veins of the stone. so the picture is a person who faces the way the water runs. two cousins take 川 for the sound, and both keep the idea: 訓, “to instruct”, with 言, speech, which the shuowen explains as 說教也; and 馴, “tame”, with 馬, a horse, of which the shuowen says 馬順也, “a horse that goes along”. the opposite word is 逆, to meet head-on, to go upstream. in confucian texts 順 often means a son’s or a subject’s obedience. this passage uses the same word with no superior in it: the great going-along has no one at the head of the stream. twelve strokes: three for the river, nine for the head. the river first: a stroke that curves down to the left, a short vertical, and a long vertical. they must not be parallel bars. the first leans, the second is short and waits, the third is the longest and straightest; together they should move like water. then 頁: a horizontal across the top; a short stroke that falls to the left under it; then a tall box in five strokes: left side, top and right side with one corner, two horizontals inside, and the base. last come two small strokes under the box, one to the left and one to the right, like feet. watch the white channels between the three river strokes. in seal script the three were curved and equal. the clerical and regular scripts made them unequal, and so gave the stream a direction.

66 · king of a hundred valleys. the river and the sea can be kings of the hundred valleys / because they are good at being below them. / so they can be kings of the hundred valleys. / so: to wish to be above the people / is to have to go below them in words. / to wish to be ahead of the people / is to have to put the body behind them. / so the sage stays above, and the people feel no weight; / stays in front, and the people take no harm. / so all under heaven are glad to push the sage forward / and do not tire. / because the sage does not contend, / no one under heaven can contend with the sage. the passage is one long sentence of cause. it starts with a map: the river and the sea lie lowest, so the streams of a hundred valleys run to them, and so they are kings. then it turns to people with the same logic: above by going below in speech, ahead by putting the body behind. then two results. the people do not feel the weight of the one above or take harm from the one in front, and the world is glad to push that person forward and does not tire. the last line gives the root: no contending. count the “so” and “because”: 所以, 以其, 故, 是以, 是以, 是以, 以其, 故. the grammar runs downhill, like the water. where is the sea in a person? it is the part that lies lower than each feeling and receives it. a thought comes down like a stream, loud in its own valley. if attention stands above it and judges, the thought finds a wall. if attention lies below, the thought arrives, is received, and is quiet. this is not humility as a virtue to be proud of. the sea makes no effort to be low; it is low, and so it is large. the question of the manuscripts matters here. if you go low in order to become great, you are a stream that is acting. the passage, in its oldest form, has no wish in it. it only says where the water goes. this is the book’s clearest picture of legitimate power, and it rests on a pun: the king is the one to whom people go. authority here is a measurement of flow. you can hold a title and have nothing run to you. the tests are concrete. words: who speaks first and longest, and who is heard. body: who eats first, who is paid first, who is safe first. weight: what your position costs the people under it. be careful with the line about wishing. a leader can learn humble speech as a tool, and people feel it within a week. the zhou kings called themselves orphans and went on with their wars. the body has to go behind as well. low is strong: every teacher of the fighting and moving arts says so. sink the weight, and a push has nothing high to catch; the one whose centre is lower takes the other’s balance. in pushing hands, the partner who does not pull or push back cannot be pulled or pushed, since force needs something to lean on. try it standing. soften the knees and let the breath go down to the belly. feel how the upper body becomes light when the lower body takes the weight; this is 處上而不重 in one’s own frame. then walk behind someone for a minute, at their pace, with no wish to pass. notice what the body does with the wish. water goes to the lowest place and keeps nothing back on the way. a watershed is a kingdom of this kind: each drop that falls on the slopes moves, by the nearest path, to one low line. the river does not send for it. the sea is the largest thing on the earth’s surface because it is the lowest; the shuowen calls 海 “heaven’s pool, that which takes in the hundred rivers”. and it gives back: the sea is where the rain comes from. the hundred valleys are fed by the king they feed. the passage asks us to read the human world as hydrology. where in your life do things arrive with no call from you? you are low there. go through the door last today, and speak after the others. in the evening, draw a small map. put yourself in the middle and mark the people around you. draw an arrow for each thing that came to you today with no demand from you: a question, a confidence, a child who sat down beside you. these are your valley streams. then mark the things that you had to pull toward yourself. the passage has a name for the pulling: 爭. do not correct anything yet. look at where the land slopes.

江: one river, in the south. in early chinese 江 is a proper name. it is the yangzi, the great river of the south, as 河 is the yellow river of the north. the shuowen defines it as a place on a map: 水。出蜀湔氐徼外崏山，入海, “a river; it comes out of the min mountains beyond the border of jiandi in shu, and enters the sea”. so the first word puts the passage in the wet south, the country of the state of chu, where tradition places laozi’s home. the yellow river of the northern plain was a danger held back by dikes. the yangzi was a wide, low gatherer of lakes and tributaries. passage 32 uses the same pair: the dao is to the world as 江海 are to the streams and valleys. english “rivers and seas” makes a general plural of it.

王: the one to whom all go. 王 is a king, and early chinese explained the word with a pun. 王 (wang) sounded like 往 (wang), “to go toward”. the shuowen makes it the definition: 王，天下所歸往也, “a king is the one to whom all under heaven turn and go”. the baihu tong says the same: 王者，往也. this is a theory of rule in one sound. a king is not the one who commands. a king is the place where people arrive of themselves. the passage is built on this pun and never states it. the streams of a hundred valleys go (往) to the river and the sea, so the river and the sea are their 王. water votes with its weight. in passage 35 the same verb returns: hold the great image, and 天下往, the world comes. see also what wang bi says of it.

谷: water half seen. 谷 is a valley with a stream in it. the shuowen: 泉出通川爲谷。从水半見，出於口. “where a spring comes out and goes through to a river, that is a 谷. from water half seen, as it comes out of an opening.” the upper strokes are the “half-seen water”; the 口 at the foot is the mouth of the valley. here 百谷 are the hundred valley streams, and “hundred” means all. the valley is one of the great images of the book: the valley spirit that does not die (6), wide like a valley (15), be the valley of the world (28), the highest de is like a valley (41). a valley is low and empty, and for that reason it receives. this passage goes one step down. below every valley there is a lower place still, and that place is king.

下 as a verb. english “below” is a preposition; it cannot do anything. in classical chinese a word of place becomes a verb when it stands in a verb’s position. 下之 is “to below them”: to take the lower place toward them. the passage does this four times in two lines: 上民, to above the people; 下之, to below them; 先民, to ahead the people; 後之, to behind them. position is treated as an act that one performs toward others. and 善, “good at”, makes the low place a skill, as one is good at swimming. other passages use the same verb: the great state is like the low reach of a river (61); one who is good at using people goes below them (68). in english, being under someone is a fact about rank. here it is something that one does well or badly.

欲: is the low place a trick?. the received line has no subject and one troubling word: 欲上民, “wishing to be above the people”. english must supply a subject, and our rendering avoids one with “to wish”. read coldly, the line is a technique: act low in order to rise. the manuscripts differ on this point. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to name the sage and keep the wish: 是以聖人之欲上民也，必以亓言下之. the guodian bamboo text, the oldest, is reported to have 在, “to be at”, where the others have 欲: the sage is in front of the people, and puts the body behind them. in that version nothing is wished for. it describes how a person who is already in front behaves. the river does not go low in order to be king. which version do you find in yourself?

以言下之: how kings spoke. “go below them in words” was a real custom of zhou rulers. a lord did not say “i” in public. he used a self-name that made him the lowest person present. passages 39 and 42 list the three: 孤, “the orphan”; 寡, “the bereft one”, the one with little; and 不穀, “the one without grain”, or “the unworthy”. these were the words that people most hated to be called, and the kings and lords took them as their titles. the custom is older than the laozi. the laozi takes it seriously, as something more than etiquette: the high has the low as its root (39). by the warring states the formulas were often empty; a king could say “this orphan” and then order a city destroyed. the passage asks for speech that goes down in fact. how do you speak to those you direct?

身: the body is the self. 以身後之 is “with the 身, to put oneself behind them”. 身 is first the body; the shuowen says 躳也。象人之身, “the torso; it pictures a person’s body”. the same graph means “oneself, in person”. chinese does not divide these. english “self” has become an inner thing, a mind that owns a body. in 身 the self is the body that stands in a place and can be put in front or behind. so the line is concrete: where do you stand when the group walks, eats, is paid, is in danger? passage 7 has the same move: the sage 後其身而身先, puts the body last and the body comes first. the pair in this passage is exact. words go low. the body goes behind. one without the other is a performance.

聖人: here, plainly a ruler. we write “the sage”, and the word needs care. a 聖人 is not a saint and not a hermit. the shuowen defines 聖 as 通也, “to pass through, to be open all the way”, and the graph has an ear, 耳, in it: one whose hearing reaches everything. in this passage the sage is a ruler with no disguise: 處上, “stays above”, 處前, “stays in front”. the text does not say that there should be no one above. it asks what kind of weight the one above puts on those below. chinese has no “he” or “she” in these lines, and we repeat “the sage” to avoid adding one. the final word of the rendering is therefore long in english. in chinese it is 之, a single syllable, “it” or “them”.

重: the weight of a ruler. 民不重: “the people do not 重”. 重 is “heavy”, and here it is a verb of feeling: they do not find the ruler heavy. the word is physical. a ruler sat above the people in fact: on a platform, in a carriage, on a litter that men carried. and a ruler was heavy in grain. passage 75 says it without ornament: the people starve since their rulers eat up too much in taxes. the usual phrase for harsh taxation was 重斂, “heavy collection”. so “above” and “weight” are one image, and the line is a test that can be measured: what does it cost those below to have you above them? the parallel line says 不害, “take no harm”, of the one in front. a leader in front can block the road and the view.

推: pushed forward, not elected. 推 is “to push”; the shuowen says 排也, “to push aside, to push along”, and the graph has a hand at the left. 樂推 is “glad to push forward”. modern translators are tempted to make it a word of voting, and the passage a foretaste of democracy; legge chose “exalt”. it is neither a ballot nor a divine right. it is the old chinese idea of how a true king is known: people move toward him. mencius tells it of shun. after the death of yao, the lords who came to court went to shun and not to yao’s son; people with lawsuits went to shun; singers sang of shun. no one chose. people pushed, as water goes, and the direction of the pushing was the mandate. notice the body in the image: hands on a back.

厭: full, pressed, weary. 不厭 is “do not tire of”. the word has a root in the stomach. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write it as 猒, and the shuowen defines 猒 as 飽也, “to have eaten one’s fill”. from “full” comes “to have had enough of, to be sick of”. the fuller graph 厭 adds 厂, a cliff, and the shuowen gives it a second word: 笮也, “to press down”. so the one graph holds weight and weariness together, and passage 72 will play on both: do not press, and they will not be weary. here the two senses are already near each other. the people do not feel the ruler as a weight, and they do not grow sick of the ruler. english “tire” loses the picture of a meal that goes on too long. how long is your welcome?

不爭: no pull on the rope. 爭 is usually “strive” or “compete”. the shuowen defines it with one word, 引也, “to pull”, and explains the graph as two hands on one object. to 爭 is a tug of war. then the last sentence is a fact of mechanics and not a moral: if one side does not pull, the other cannot pull against it. the sentence also stands in passage 22, word for word, and 不爭 runs through the book: water benefits all things and does not contend (8); heaven’s way does not contend and is good at winning (73); the book’s last words are 為而不爭 (81). the mawangdui silk texts are reported to make it a question: 非以亓无諍與, “is it not because there is no contention in them?” “non-competitive” in english suggests a weak player. here it names the one whom no one can play against.

legge’s “homage and tribute”. for 百谷王, three characters, legge writes that the rivers and seas “receive the homage and tribute of all the valley streams”. he explains the image before the reader can see it, and the explanation comes from a court: homage, tribute. the word “kings” appears only at the end of his sentence. he writes “the sage (ruler)” with a bracket, which is fair, and gives the sage “his words” and “his person”; the chinese has no pronoun. for 推 he has “delight to exalt him”, a verb from the english psalms. his version is not wrong. it is a british reading of monarchy: a sovereign who is gracious downward and is lifted up in return. the chinese picture is lower and wetter. water does not exalt the sea.

wang bi says nothing. wang bi left no comment on this passage. in the received edition of his commentary the text stands alone, as it does for passage 31. we do not know the reason: he may have thought it plain, or a comment may have been lost. his view can be found one passage later, where he explains why the one who does not dare to be first can lead: 唯後外其身，為物所歸, “only by putting the body behind and outside does one become that to which things turn”. his word 歸, “to turn toward, to come home to”, is the word of the king pun: a king is the one to whom all 歸往. so the silence here is not a disagreement. sometimes a commentator, too, takes the lower place.

go through the door last. take the two halves of the passage as two small experiments. words: in one meeting or one family talk today, speak after the others have spoken, and when you speak, say first what you heard. do not use the low voice as a method to win. only find out what you learn from that place. body: once today, put the body behind. go through the door last. serve yourself last. take the seat that no one wanted. these acts are small, and the body will tell you at once whether it holds a claim to the front. then ask the question of the passage about your own position, wherever you are above someone: do they feel the weight? you may have to ask them.

上 and 下, 先 and 後: the high place is kept. two pairs carry the passage: above and below (上, 下), ahead and behind (先, 後). it is easy to hear a rule in it: low is good, high is bad. the text does not say that. the sage 處上, stays above, and 處前, stays in front. the high place is not refused. what changes is the way to it and the weight of it: one comes to be above by going below, and then the people feel no weight. the image shows why the two sides need each other. with no valleys above them, the river and the sea have nothing to receive. with no low water, the valleys have nowhere to go. the preference for the low is spoken to those who are, or wish to be, above, in an age of kings who pressed down. the low place also turns: the one who goes below is pushed forward. then the question begins again.

rivers and seas rule the valleys because they lie below them; what is lowest receives the most.. rivers and seas rule the valleys because they lie below them; what is lowest receives the most. do you believe this of people as well as of water? who in your life receives much and demands little? what does “going low” mean in your history: safety, shame, good manners, defeat? take the other side: those who go low are stepped on, and the world goes to those who climb. which of your own experiences speak for that? the passage keeps the sage above and in front. are you more at ease in the high place or the low one? what do you think of people who prefer the other?

the one who does not contend is the one with whom no one can contend.. the one who does not contend is the one with whom no one can contend. is that so? recall a time when you did not pull back on the rope. what did the other person do? what did you learn about contests as a child: to win, to stay out, to let others win? hold the opposite for a while: what you do not fight for, you lose. where in your life is that the truer sentence? when you refuse to contend, is it from ease or from fear of losing? how do you tell the two apart in the body?

to be above people, one must speak from below them; to lead, one must put oneself behind.. to be above people, one must speak from below them; to lead, one must put oneself behind. does this read to you as wisdom or as technique? what makes the difference? think of a leader who spoke low and one who spoke high. under which did you feel less weight? take the plain opposite: a leader should stand in front and say so. what is honest in that view? have you gone low in order to rise? what did the people around you feel?

下 a line, and a mark under it. some things cannot be drawn. you can draw a tree or a horse; you cannot draw “below”. the early scribes solved this with a sign. they drew one long line as a base of reference and a short mark under it. that was 下; the shuowen’s entry reads 底也。指事, “the bottom; a pointing graph”. the same line with the mark over it was 上, “above”. xu shen, who wrote the shuowen around 100 ce, sorted all characters into six kinds, and for the kind called 指事, “pointing at the matter”, he gave exactly these two as his examples: 指事者，視而可識，察而見意，“上、下”是也. “a pointing graph: look, and it can be recognized; examine it, and the meaning shows. 上 and 下 are such.” later hands added the vertical stroke that joins the mark to the line. the pair still builds other graphs. a heart with 上 over it and a heart with 下 over it make the word 忐忑, “to be nervous”: the heart goes up and down. 卡, 上 set on 下, is a later graph for “stuck”, a thing that can go neither up nor down. in chinese grammar 下 is also an act: to descend, to dismount, to go under. this passage uses it so, twice: the river and the sea are good at 下. it is one of the simplest graphs in the script, and the passage makes it a king’s whole skill. three strokes. first the horizontal: the reference line, written left to right, with a firm start and a firm stop. in this character it is the roof, so it is the longest stroke. second the vertical, which starts at the middle of the horizontal and goes straight down; the brush lifts slowly, and the end may be a point, like a hanging needle. third the dot. it leaves the vertical on the right side, below the horizontal and close to it, and it falls to the right. watch this last stroke. it is the old mark, the one that means “under”; the vertical was added later to carry it. a master makes the dot touch the vertical or nearly touch, pressed down and then lifted off. with so few strokes there is no place to hide: the three must balance with the paper around them.

江 water and a carpenter’s tool. the left side is 氵, “three dots of water”, the short form of 水 that marks nearly every word for a liquid or a river. the right side is 工. the shuowen says of 工: 巧飾也。象人有規榘也, “skilled work; it shows a person with compass and square”. modern scholars commonly see a single tool, perhaps a square or a rammer. in 江 the tool has no meaning. it is there for its sound, and xu shen chose this very character, with 河, as his example of the most common kind of graph, 形聲, “form and sound”: one part gives the class, one part gives the pronunciation. “江、河”是也, he wrote. today 工 is gong and 江 is jiang, and the match is hard to hear. in the old language they were close; both belong to one old rhyme group (the 東 group). the same family includes 紅, red; 空, empty; 功, merit; 攻, to attack; and 項, the neck, which changed as 江 did. note what kind of word this is: a proper name. 江 was the one great river of the south. some linguists propose that the word itself came from a language of the southern peoples; that is a hypothesis. from this one graph and its northern partner 河, chinese built its general words for rivers. six strokes. the water first: a dot that falls to the right; a second dot under it, a little to the left; then a stroke that begins low and flicks up to the right. watch the third stroke: its tip points at the start of the next part, and so hands the movement across. then 工: a short horizontal, a vertical from its centre, and a long horizontal at the base. the lower horizontal is the longest line in the character. it runs under the water dots like a riverbed and holds both halves. the three dots must not stand in a straight column; they form a shallow curve that opens to the right. in running script the three become one continuous line with two turns, and in cursive the whole left side can be a single vertical flick.

67 · three things held dear. all under heaven say that my dao is great / and seems to take after nothing. / because it is great, it seems to take after nothing. / if it took after something, / how long it would have been small! / i have three things to treasure. / i hold them and keep them safe. / the first is tenderness. / the second is spareness. / the third is not daring to go ahead of the world. / tender, and so able to be brave. / sparing, and so able to be wide. / not daring to go ahead of the world, / and so able to be head of the finished vessels. / now: to let go of tenderness and take courage, / to let go of spareness and take width, / to let go of the rear and take the front: / that is death. / tenderness: fight with it and win; / defend with it and stand firm. / whom heaven will rescue, / it guards with tenderness. the passage opens with a complaint and an answer. the world says the speaker’s dao is great and takes after nothing. yes, says the speaker: anything that took after something would long since have been small. then comes the centre: three precious things, held and kept: tenderness, spareness, and a refusal to go first. each one produces its seeming opposite: tenderness gives courage, spareness gives width, the rear place gives the head’s place. then a warning in the same three steps: take the fruit with no root, and you are dead. the end returns to the first treasure alone and sets it in a war: it wins, it holds, and heaven posts it around those it would save. the three precious things are not rules. each is a way that attention can hold what comes before it. 慈 is to meet one’s own states as a mother meets a child: the fear, the dull morning, the failure are all hers, and she turns none of them out. 儉 is to spend little: fewer comments on experience, fewer plans laid over the present hour. the third is to let each moment arrive before the mind runs in front of it to say what it is. then the opening lines read differently. a self that is like something, that can be described and ranked, is small. what you are when you are compared with nothing has no size. the speaker holds that with open hands, and so it is called a treasure. every organization praises the right-hand column: courage, reach, leadership. this passage says that each one is an effect, and it names the causes. bold decisions that hold come from care for the people who will bear them. reach comes from restraint, as a firm that spends little can go far. and the front place is safe only for the one who did not seize it. the warning is the most practical line in the passage. a leader who lets go of the left-hand column and keeps the right is reckless, overextended, and self-promoting, and the text says that this ends in death: of the venture, or the state, or the person. the age that produced these lines proved it. the question for a team is always the same: brave from what? in a body the three precious things can be felt. tenderness is a soft
