chest and belly: the front of the body does not armour itself, and for that reason the back and legs can be strong. fighters know that a tight, angry body is slow; the one who protects something is quick and does not tire. spareness is economy of movement: no extra tension, no wasted step, the breath kept low. a master of any art looks as if little is done. not going first is timing: let the other move, and answer. the final lines give the martial result in two verbs: win and hold. stand for a moment as if a small child were asleep behind you. feel what that does to the feet. do the three checks of the practice note: a root for one brave act, one thing to use less of, one moment at the front to recall. then take the opening lines as a short meditation. sit, and finish the sentence “i am like…” five times, with whatever comes: like my father, like other people of my trade, like a tired person. each answer is true and each is small. then stop the sentence at “i am” and sit for one minute with no comparison. the world may call that good for nothing. the speaker of this passage calls it great.

我道: who says “i”?. most of the laozi has no speaker. here, and in passages 20 and 70, a voice says 我, “i”. we keep 道 as dao: it is a road, a way of doing, and the way all things go, and no english word holds the three. the received text has 我道大, “my dao is great”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to have no 道: 天下皆謂我大，不肖, “all under heaven say that i am great, and unlike”. that older line is odder and more personal. the world’s complaint is about the speaker: too large, and of no use, like nothing that people know. “my dao” makes it a remark about a teaching, and legge goes further and adds “(to other systems of teaching)”. who is the “i”? an old teacher, the sage as a type, or the dao itself. the text does not say. read it once in each voice.

不肖: the child who is unlike. 肖 is “to resemble”, and it is a family word. the shuowen: 骨肉相似也, “bone and flesh are alike”, and then 不似其先，故曰“不肖”也: “one who is not like his forebears is therefore called 不肖”. in everyday classical chinese 不肖 means “unworthy, good for nothing”: a son who does not take after the father. so the world’s remark has an edge that english loses. they say: your dao is great, and it is a worthless child that resembles no one. the speaker takes the insult and agrees. it is unlike because it is great. passage 4 has already said of the dao: 吾不知誰之子, “i do not know whose child it is”. there is one more turn. the sound part of 肖 is 小, “small”. to resemble is, in the graph itself, to be small.

wang bi: what can be compared is small. 久矣其細也夫 is an exclamation with the order turned round, and wang bi first puts it straight: 久矣其細，猶曰其細久矣, “‘long indeed, its smallness’ is the same as ‘its smallness would be of long standing’”. then he gives the reason in one line: 肖，則失其所以為大矣. “if it resembled, it would lose that by which it is great.” 細 is “fine, thin”; the graph has silk thread, 糸, at the left. a thing that is like another thing can be set beside it, measured, ranked, and given a use. that is what it means to be small. the same test works on a person. the parts of you that can be compared are the parts that can be ranked. what in you is like nothing?

三寶 before the buddhists. today 三寶 is known across east asia as a buddhist term: the three jewels, which are the buddha, the teaching, and the community. that use is later. when buddhist texts were put into chinese, from the 2nd century ce on, translators used this phrase, which chinese readers knew from the laozi. daoist religion later answered with its own three: the dao, the scriptures, the masters. in the warring states period the phrase meant something else again. mencius says: 諸侯之寶三：土地、人民、政事, “the treasures of a lord are three: land, people, and government”. that is a list of what a state owns. against it, this passage’s three are strange. not one of them is a possession. all three are ways of holding back. a ruler who heard 我有三寶 expected jade.

寶 and 保: treasure and keep. 我有三寶，持而保之. the noun 寶, “treasure”, and the verb 保, “to keep safe”, are the same sound, bao, and the chinese ear hears: “three bao; i hold them and bao them”. a treasure is that which is kept. the graph 寶 is a small storehouse. the shuowen lists its parts: 从宀从王从貝，缶聲, a roof 宀, jade (written 王 here), a cowrie shell 貝, which was early money, and 缶, a jar, for the sound. jade and shells under a roof: what a household guards. 保, in the shuowen, is 養也, “to nurture”, and its early form is commonly explained as a person with a child on the back. so even the verb for guarding these treasures is a word of child care. the treasures return in passage 69: 輕敵幾喪吾寶.

慈: love that goes downward. 慈 has no good english word. it is the love of a parent for a child, and above all of a mother: 慈母 is the set phrase. it runs downward, from the stronger to the weaker, and its partner is 孝, the child’s devotion, which runs upward (passages 18 and 19 name the pair). “compassion” is the usual choice, but that word came to 慈 later, when buddhists used it to translate their term for kindness to all beings. “mercy” assumes a judge who could punish. legge’s “gentleness” is a manner. 慈 is none of these. it is fierce: it feeds, carries, and stands in front. the book calls the dao the mother of the world (25, 52). the first treasure is to hold things as that mother does. we write “tenderness” and ask you to hear the mother in it.

儉: not “economy”. 儉 is to use little and hold much in. the shuowen says 約也, and 約 is “to wind round and tie”: a bundle bound tight. legge writes “economy”, a word of victorian household accounts. “moderation” brings aristotle’s mean between two extremes. “frugality” is nearer, but it sounds like saving money. 儉 is wider: few words, few wants, few orders, little display. confucius used the word of ritual: better sparing than lavish. wang bi explains the result: 節儉愛費，天下不匱，故能廣也, “sparing and careful of cost, so that the world does not run short; and so one can be wide”. this is the logic of a reservoir. that which is not spent is there when it is needed. passage 59 praises a different word, 嗇, the farmer’s care in storing grain. what do you spend that you do not notice?

a treasure made of “not”. the first two treasures have one character each. the third needs six: 不敢為天下先, “not daring to act as the front of all under heaven”. chinese had words for modesty and for yielding, and the text does not use them. it describes a refusal. and 不敢, “not dare”, is the phrase of a junior before a senior; it names a real fear, the kind that one has on thin ice. it is not a quiet opinion about one’s rank. the line does not say “be last”. it says: do not make yourself the first. the front is a place that others may push one into; see passage 66. in modern china the phrase lost its negative and became a slogan of reform: 敢為天下先, “dare to be the first under heaven”. two characters fewer, and a treasure thrown away. which do you hear more often?

勇: courage with a root. 慈故能勇: “tender, and so able to be brave”. the small word 故, “and so”, makes a claim about cause. courage is not a first thing. it grows from care, as a hen’s attack on a hawk grows from the chicks. the shuowen defines 勇 in one word: 气也, “it is breath”, the surge of energy in the body. the lower part of the graph is 力, strength. courage alone is only that surge. confucius made the same cut: the humane are sure to have courage, and the brave are not sure to be humane. passage 73 divides courage in two by its direction: courage in daring kills, and courage in not-daring keeps alive. english “brave” is praise with no conditions. here the question is always: brave from what?

成器長: chief of the vessels. 器 is a vessel, then any finished tool, then a person shaped for one use: an official. passage 28 gives the picture: when the uncarved wood is split, it becomes vessels, and the sage, using them, becomes 官長, head of the officials. so 成器長 is “head of the finished vessels”: the one who can lead all those who have a function, and who has no fixed function. legge turns the phrase round and makes the sage himself “a vessel of the highest honour”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 故能為成事長, “and so can be head of the completed affairs”, and han fei quotes the line in that form. in both, the logic is that of passage 66. the one who does not take the front is the one whom others will have at the front.

舍 … 且: a small word that english must fix. 今舍慈且勇: “now, let go of tenderness, 且 courage”. 舍 is 捨, “to throw away”. 且 is a small word with several jobs: “moreover”, “for the moment”, “and yet”. wang bi gives it a rare gloss: 且，猶取也, “且 is like 取, to take”. on his reading the line has two verbs, drop and take. others keep the common sense: “let go of tenderness and yet be brave”. the meaning is close in both. people want the fruit and cut the root. the word 今, “now, these days”, makes it a complaint about the speaker’s own age. no subject is named. it can be the rulers of the time, or anyone. we follow wang bi and write “take”, because it shows the hand that grabs.

死矣: three ambitions of the age. 死矣 is two syllables: “dead”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to be longer and no softer: 則必死矣, “then death is certain”. look at what was grabbed. 勇, courage, was the prized quality of the warring states: qin gave ranks of nobility for enemy heads, and lords kept swordsmen who died to show their daring. 廣, width, was state policy; to “widen the land” by taking a neighbour’s territory was the normal aim of a court. 先, to be first, was the dream of each king: to be hegemon and then sole ruler. the passage names the three ambitions of its time and calls each one a fruit cut from its root. it was written while those states were destroying one another. within about a century of the oldest copies, every one of them was gone.

wang bi: why the tender win. a line about love now speaks of battle, and this troubles readers who want the book to be gentle. the claim is practical. wang bi: 相慜而不避於難，故勝也, “they feel for one another and do not turn away from hardship; so they win”. an army whose members care for each other does not break. the strategists said the same from the commander’s side. the sunzi says: look on your soldiers as infants, and they will go with you into deep ravines; look on them as beloved sons, and they will die beside you. note the second half of the laozi line: 以守則固, “defend with it and stand firm”. the stress is on holding. a mother is the picture: she does not look for a fight, and nothing moves her from the door.

救 or 建: rescue, or set up. the received text says 天將救之，以慈衛之: “heaven will rescue them; with tenderness it guards them”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to read 天將建之，如以茲垣之: “heaven will set them up; it is as if it walled them round with 茲”. two things differ. 建 is “to establish, to set upright”, the word of passage 54, where that which is well established is not pulled up. and the verb for guarding is 垣, a wall of earth; the shuowen says 牆也, “a wall”. their 茲 is our 慈, written with no heart beneath it. in both versions heaven is not a god with a will. 天 is the sky and the order of things. the line can also be read the other way: the one whom heaven means to save is the one to whom it gives tenderness.

衛: guards who walk in a ring. 衛 is a military word. the shuowen, which writes it 衞, says 宿衞也, “the night guard”, and explains the outer part: 行，列衞也, “行 is the ranks of the guards”. look at the graph: the two halves of 行, a crossroads, stand at left and right, and the middle part is commonly explained as feet that go round a walled place. it is a picture of a patrol. the word named the troops around a ruler and a state in the central plain. so the last line is exact: tenderness is posted around a person like sentries at night. english “protect” is general. 衛 is a ring of living guards, and it is used here of the least warlike thing in the book. who stands guard around you, and around whom do you stand?

legge: gentleness, economy, shrinking. legge’s three are “gentleness”, “economy”, and “shrinking from taking precedence of others”. each is a virtue of a victorian christian household: a mild manner, careful accounts, and good behaviour at a door. they are not wrong, and they are small. 慈 becomes a temperament where the chinese has a mother’s force; 儉 becomes thrift; and the third becomes etiquette, with “shrinking” for 不敢. he then reads 成器長 as “a vessel of the highest honour”, which echoes “a vessel unto honour” in the letters of paul, and so brings the sage near the new testament. his first paragraph adds “systems of teaching” twice in brackets. a missionary and scholar of religions saw rival doctrines there. the chinese says only that the speaker is like nothing.

find the root of one brave act. take the three pairs as three checks, one for each part of a day. morning, courage: you will have to do one hard thing today, such as a refusal, a hard talk, or a risk. before it, ask what it protects. if you can name a person or a living thing that you care for, go on; the courage has its root. if you find only the wish to look strong, wait. midday, width: before you take on one more thing, look for one thing to use less of. evening, the front: recall a moment when you made yourself first, in a queue, in a talk, in credit for work. do not blame yourself. notice what it cost, and who felt it. the passage says of the three: 持而保之. they are kept by daily handling.

後 and 先, 慈 and 勇: root and fruit. the passage gives three pairs: tenderness and courage (慈, 勇), spareness and width (儉, 廣), the rear and the front (後, 先). they look like opposites, and a quick reader ranks them: tender good, brave bad. the text says a different thing. each first term produces the second: tender, 故, and so able to be brave. courage, width, and the head’s place are wanted, and they are reached. what the text calls death is to take the second with the first let go: the fruit cut from the root. so the preference is for an order, and not for one side. it answers an age that grabbed at the front. the favoured side also turns. tenderness goes out to fight in the last lines, and the one who stays behind becomes head. what of tenderness from which no courage grows? the text does not name it. but it is the root that bears which is treasured here.

courage that lasts grows out of tenderness; courage taken with no such root ends in death.. courage that lasts grows out of tenderness; courage taken with no such root ends in death. think of the bravest thing that you have done. what was it for? was care under it, or something else? were you taught that tenderness and courage go together, or that one must be given up for the other? by whom? hold the opposite: tenderness makes a person hesitate, and the brave act needs a hard heart. when have you believed that? which do you show more readily, the tender side or the brave one? what do you fear would happen if the other were seen?

the one who does not dare to go ahead of the world can become its head.. the one who does not dare to go ahead of the world can become its head. do you agree? where have you seen a person reach the front because they did not seize it? what is your own relation to being first: do you want it, avoid it, or deny that you want it? put the modern slogan in its place: dare to be first. stay with it. what does it wake up in you? if you hold back, is it this treasure, or is it fear in the treasure’s clothes? how would you know?

spending little is what makes it possible to reach far.. spending little is what makes it possible to reach far. is this true in your use of money, words, or strength? where has it failed? what did your family teach about spending and saving? did that come from want, from fear, or from choice? hold the other side: what is spent freely comes back, and a tight hand makes a small life. which side resists in you? what do you judge in people who spend in the way that you do not?

慈 the loving stone. at the foot is 心, the heart. above it is 兹. the shuowen gives 慈 as 愛也, “to love”, with 兹 as the sound, and it enters that sound part as 玆: 黑也。从二玄, “black; from two 玄”, two dark twists of thread, the shape 幺 that is also in 絲, silk. a separate entry, 茲, with grass on top, is 艸木多益, “plants and trees that grow more and more”; the two graphs merged in use. the same sound part is in 滋, to moisten, to nourish, and 孳, to breed, to bear young. so the family of 慈 is about increase and feeding, though the dictionary claims only the sound. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write the word in this passage with no heart, as plain 茲. the best cousin is a surprise. the modern word for a magnet is 磁石. early texts write it 慈石, “the loving stone”. the lushi chunqiu, about 240 bce, says 慈石召鐵, “the loving stone calls iron”, and a han commentator explains that the stone is the mother of iron and draws her child to her. a stone radical was put under it later to make 磁. this is the force that the first treasure names. it does not push or command. it draws, and what it draws comes home. our word “magnet” is only a greek place name. thirteen strokes. first a dot, then a short stroke that falls to the left: two small tips. third a long horizontal, which is the roof of the character. under it come the two threads, left then right. each thread is three strokes: a stroke that goes down to the left and turns back to the right; a second, larger one of the same kind; and a dot. watch the two threads: they are twins, and the right one is written a little larger and slightly higher. last comes the heart: a dot at the left, a long hook that lies almost flat and flicks up at its end, a dot inside the curve, and a dot at the right. the heart is the base, and it should be as wide as the roof. in clerical script the threads are small and round, and the heart spreads like a boat.

儉 many mouths, one voice. the left side is 亻, a standing person, the form that 人 takes at the side of a character. it tells you that the word is about human conduct. the right side is 僉. the shuowen says of 僉: 皆也。从亼从吅从从, “all, together. from 亼 (to gather), 吅 (two mouths), and 从 (two people)”. read it from the top: a roof-like sign of gathering, two mouths, two persons. several people speak as one: “all”. in 儉 this part gives the sound, and it gives the sound to a large family: 檢, to inspect (the mawangdui silk texts are reported to use this graph for the second treasure); 驗, to verify; 險, a narrow, dangerous pass; 劍, a sword; 臉, the face; and 斂, to gather in, to draw tight. scholars often note that 儉 and 斂 are close in sense as well as sound: both are a drawing-in. the shuowen defines 儉 as 約也, “to bind”. so one can read the character as a person who gathers many things into one and ties them. the opposite word is 奢, “lavish”, which the shuowen explains as 張也, “to stretch open”. one closes and one opens. confucius set the two side by side: in ritual, rather 儉 than 奢. the short form 俭 keeps the person and reduces the crowd to three small strokes. fifteen strokes. the person first: a stroke that falls to the left, then a vertical beneath it. then the right side, from the top. a long stroke falls to the left and a long stroke falls to the right; they meet at the peak and make the roof. a short horizontal sits under the peak. then the left mouth: left side; top and right side with one corner; base. then the right mouth, with the same three strokes in the same order. then the left small person: a stroke to the left, and a dot. then the right small person: a stroke to the left, and a last stroke to the right. watch the roof. its two strokes must reach wide enough to cover all that stands under them, the mouths and the persons. the lesson of the form is the lesson of the word: eleven small strokes are held in order by two.

先 a foot ahead of a person. the shuowen says: 前進也。从儿从之, “to go forward. from 儿 (a person) and 之 (to go)”. the lower two strokes, 儿, are a person’s legs. the upper part was 之, and in the oldest forms 之 is commonly explained as a foot on a line: a foot that sets out. so the early graph is a foot drawn above a person: someone whose foot has already gone, the one in front. from “ahead in space” came “ahead in time”: 先 is “earlier, former”. 先生, “born before”, is a teacher, and today the plain word for “mr.”. 先王 are the former kings. and 先 alone means forebears, the dead of the family: the shuowen’s own entry on 不肖 speaks of the child who is not like 其先. this gives the third treasure a second edge. 不敢為天下先 is not to dare to be the world’s forerunner, and also not to set oneself up as the world’s ancestor, the one from whom all must descend. the opposite word is 後, “behind, after”. the shuowen defines it 遲也, “late”, and lists its parts: 彳, a step; 幺, a thread; 夊, a foot that drags. a foot on a thread walks behind. in this passage the foot that goes ahead is the dangerous one, and the foot that comes after is safe. six strokes. first a short stroke that falls to the left. second a horizontal that starts from it. third a vertical through that horizontal, from above it to below. fourth a long horizontal: the ground line, and the widest stroke of the upper part. then the legs. the fifth stroke falls to the left in a long curve. the sixth goes down, bends to the right, runs along the base, and ends in a hook that turns up. watch the sixth stroke. it is the largest movement in the character, and it carries the weight like a foot set well forward. the upper part should be small and upright, and the legs wide. in running script the last stroke is often left open, with no hook, and the brush leaves the paper on its way to the next character.

68 · the fighter without anger. one good at being an officer is not martial. / one good at fighting is not angry. / one good at beating an enemy does not engage. / one good at using people goes below them. / this is called the de of not contending. / this is called the strength of using people. / this is called pairing with heaven: / the ridgepole of the ancients. four sentences have one frame: 善…者不…, “the one good at … does not …”. an officer with no martial show; a fighter with no anger; a victor who does not close with the enemy; and, with a change at the end, a user of people who goes below them. the fourth breaks the pattern of “not” and gives a positive act, and so it carries the weight. then three names for all four: the de of not contending, the strength of using people, and pairing with heaven, the ridgepole of the ancients. the passage has forty-three characters, three end rhymes, no image from nature, and no sage. it is a military saying that has been turned. read the enemy as that which you fight in yourself: a habit, a fear, a thought that returns. the usual method is martial. you make a show of resolve, you grow angry at the fault, you wrestle with it, and you stand above it as a judge. the passage reverses each step. no show: a quiet intention is enough. no anger: rage at oneself is still rage, and it feeds what it attacks. no engaging: a thought that is not fought has nothing to push against. and go below: ask the habit what it is for, as one asks a person. this is not surrender. it is the power of not pulling, and it works on the inside as it does on the field. the fourth line is the centre of the passage for anyone who directs others. english hears “using people” as a fault; the chinese means the art of bringing each person’s ability into play, and it says that the art has one condition: be under them. in practice: ask before you tell; give credit away; let the expert be more expert than you in the room. liu bang is the model. he named three men who were better than he was, and he won an empire. the first three lines apply as well. a leader who needs to look strong, who decides in anger, or who must win each argument is not yet skilled. wang bi gives the price: their strength stays with them. every fighting art of east asia teaches these four lines with the body. a tense, fierce stance is slow; the master stands as if nothing were about to happen. anger lifts the breath into the chest and narrows the eyes, and the angry one can be led by the nose. to not engage is the principle of the soft arts: do not meet force with force; be absent from the place where the blow lands. and go below: sink the centre under the partner’s centre, and their strength becomes yours to turn. the old reading of 武 as “stop the weapon” is the motto of many schools. try one thing: when someone pushes, in word or with a hand, breathe out and let the weight drop before you answer. do the two experiments of the practice note: find the first heat of anger, and ask from below. then look back over one conflict of the past month and test it against the four lines. did you make a show? was there heat? did you close with the other person, point against point? did you stand above? mark each with yes or no. then imagine the same hour with one “yes” removed, only one, and see how the rest would have gone. the passage calls this skill, 善, and skill comes from repetition.

善: good, or good at. four lines begin with 善. in english “good” is first a moral word: a good man keeps the commandments. 善 has that sense, but when it stands before a verb it means “good at”, skilled, as a good swimmer is good. the four people in this passage are experts. the text does not say that a kind soldier refuses to fight. it says that the best soldier has a quality that the second-best does not expect. chinese thought does not separate the two senses as sharply as english does: goodness is a kind of skill, and real skill has something good in it. passage 27 uses the same form for a traveller, a speaker, and a locksmith: the one who is good at walking leaves no tracks. in each case mastery is shown by a thing that is absent. english “one” stands for 者, “the one who”.

士: from chariot to study. 士 is a hard word to render because the class changed under it. in the early zhou the 士 were the lowest rank of the nobility: trained men who fought from chariots for their lords. by the warring states, armies were huge and made of drafted farmers, the old houses had fallen, and the 士 had become men of skill with no fixed master: officers, clerks, strategists, travelling persuaders, and swordsmen. confucius and his pupils were 士. for the next two thousand years the word meant the scholar-official. the shuowen glosses 士 as 事也, “one who serves”. here it is still military, and wang bi glosses it so: 士，卒之帥也, “a 士 is a leader of foot soldiers”. legge’s verse hides the rank. the first line is then about the whole class that read this book: how should a man of arms and service carry himself?

武: stop the dagger-axe. the shuowen does not define 武 in its own words. it quotes a king: 楚莊王曰：“夫武，定功戢兵。故止戈爲武。” “king zhuang of chu said: the martial settles the victory and puts weapons away. so 止, ‘to stop’, and 戈, ‘dagger-axe’, make 武.” the story is in the zuozhuan. in 597 bce chu had beaten jin, and an officer urged the king to pile up the enemy dead as a monument. the king refused, and gave this reading of the character. modern scholars read the old graph in another way: 止 is a foot, and the picture is a man who marches with a weapon (see the plate). wang bi explains 武 here as a fault of manner: 尚先陵人也, “to prize being first and to bully others”. the passage and the king agree: the summit of the martial is that no weapon moves.

怒: the general’s anger. 不怒, “not angry”, was the hard-won lesson of the age’s strategists. the sunzi warns: 主不可以怒而興師，將不可以慍而致戰, “a ruler may not raise an army from anger; a general may not give battle from resentment”. the reason follows: anger can turn back to joy, but a destroyed state cannot be restored, and the dead cannot be brought to life. the same book lists anger as a weakness to use in the enemy: if he is quick to anger, provoke him. an angry commander can be led. wang bi gives the laozi’s reason: 後而不先，應而不唱，故不在怒, “behind and not ahead, answering and not calling the tune; so anger has no place”. the graph is 心, heart, under 奴, a slave. the shuowen says 奴 gives only the sound. readers have always seen more.

不與: two words, no object. 善勝敵者不與 ends on 與, which most often means “with” or “to give”. as a verb it is “to be with, to join, to take part”. so the line says only: “does not with”. with what? the chinese leaves the place empty, and that is the meaning: there is no point of contact. wang bi fills it in: 不與爭也, “does not contend with them”. others understand “does not join battle”. english must supply an object, and “engage” is our choice. the thought was at home among the military writers. the sunzi says that to win a hundred battles is not the highest skill; to make the enemy’s army yield with no battle is the highest. the laozi’s line is shorter and stranger. it does not describe a clever victory. it describes someone who cannot be found to fight.

用人: “using people”. in english, to use a person is an offence; the philosopher kant made it the mark of wrong action. 用人 has no such sound. it is the plain chinese term for appointing, employing, and directing people, and it was the first art of a ruler: to know whom to put where. 用 is “function”, the word of passage 11, where the use of a pot is at its hollow. to 用 a person is to bring that person’s function into play. we keep “using” so that the surprise of the line can be felt. the one who is best at it is under the people used. legge’s verse says that men’s “wills he bends”. the chinese says nothing of wills, and nothing bends. the strength stays where it was, in the people, and is given.

為之下: the peasant who won. 為之下 is “acts as their below”: takes the lower place toward them, as the sea does toward the rivers in passage 66. chinese history has a famous case. liu bang was a minor local officer with no great skill in war. in 202 bce he defeated xiang yu, the best fighter of the age, and founded the han dynasty. sima qian reports his own account of it at a banquet. in planning, he said, i am not the equal of zhang liang; in supply, i am not the equal of xiao he; in battle, i am not the equal of han xin. these three are great men, and i was able to use them: 吾能用之. xiang yu had one adviser and could not use him. under the early han, the laozi became a book of the court.

不爭之德: a power, not a virtue. 德 is rendered “virtue” by legge and many after him, and then 不爭之德 becomes the virtue of not striving: a good habit, like patience. 德 is larger. it is the power that a person has by being in line with the dao, the quality that moves others with no push. so the phrase names a force: the power of not contending. 爭 is, in the shuowen, 引也, “to pull”: two hands on one thing. the four masters of the first lines each refuse a pull: the show of force, the heat of anger, the clash, the high place. because they do not pull, nothing pulls against them. the phrase is one of a family in the book: water does not contend (8); heaven’s way does not contend and is good at winning (73). we leave de in chinese.

德, 力, 極: three rhymes. the last three lines each begin 是謂, “this is called”, and in the received text each ends on a rhyme: 德, 力, 極. in the old sound system the three belong to one group (the 職 group), with a short, stopped ending. mandarin has lost it: de, li, ji. heard in the old way, the close is three quick beats, like a drum. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to differ in the middle line. they read 是謂用人, “this is called using people”, with no 之力, “the strength of”. their line is shorter, and the claim is plainer: going below is what the use of people is. the received text adds 力, strength, the word that a military reader wanted to hear, and it tells him where strength comes from. legge heard the rhymes and put the whole passage into english verse.

配天: a seat beside heaven. 配 is “to pair, to be the mate of”. 配天 is a term of the state religion of zhou. when the king sacrificed to heaven, a founding ancestor was set beside heaven to receive the offering with it; he was “paired with heaven”. a hymn of the book of songs praises the first ancestor of zhou in these words: 思文后稷，克配彼天, “accomplished lord millet, able to be the pair of that heaven”. another says that the house of shang, before it lost the people, 克配上帝, “could be the pair of the lord on high”. so the phrase gives the highest rank that the ritual had. the passage gives it to a person defined by four refusals, the last of which is to go below others. english “matching heaven” or “like heaven” makes it a comparison. it is a seat.

極: the ridgepole. 極 has 木, wood, at the left, and the shuowen defines it with a builder’s word: 棟也, “the ridgepole”, the highest beam of a house, on which the roof rests. from there it means the highest point of anything, the limit, the pole: 北極 is the north pole, and 太極, the “great ridgepole”, became the name of the first principle in later thought. 古之極 is “the ridgepole of antiquity”: the utmost that the ancients reached. the line can be cut in two ways. one: “this is called pairing with heaven; it is the utmost of the ancients”. two, with no pause: “this is called matching the utmost of heaven and of antiquity”. we take the first. other passages use the word for a limit that no one knows (58, 59). what holds up the roof of your house?

a military saying, turned. passages 68 and 69 are a pair, and both speak the language of the camp. the period had a class of military experts, later called 兵家, the school of arms. their books, the sunzi first among them, taught rulers how to win at least cost. they and the laozi share words and a world: deception of form, the weak that beats the strong, the victory with no battle. some later readers took the laozi itself as a book of war; a tang officer, wang zhen, wrote a commentary to present it so to his emperor. the passage is better read the other way. it takes the soldier’s own measure, which is skill, and shows that the highest skill has no warlike sign. then it leaves the camp and ends at the altar of heaven.

wang bi: strength that will not serve. wang bi’s comments on this passage are short, like the lines. the longest is on the fourth: 用人而不為之下，則力不為用也. “use people and do not go below them, and their strength will not be of use to you.” read the grammar: 力不為用, “the strength does not act as use”. the people still have their strength. it does not turn into function for the one above. this is exact. a person who is commanded gives obedience, which is the least that a person has. a person who is met from below gives judgment, invention, and care, which cannot be ordered. wang bi sees the line as a law of energy and adds no praise of humility. where in your work is strength present and not in use?

legge in ballad metre. here legge does something rare for him: he translates in rhymed verse, because the chinese rhymes. the cost is high. his first line is “he who in (tao’s) wars has skill”. the bracket makes the war a spiritual one, the christian soldier’s fight; the chinese has a real officer. 不武 becomes “assumes no martial port”, and “port” is an old word for bearing that was needed for the rhyme. 不與 becomes “keeps from his foes apart”. the last three lines are given as sayings in quotation marks. for 配天古之極 he has “like heaven’s his ends, / no sage of old more bright”, and neither the ritual seat nor the ridgepole is left. it is a victorian hymn on the passage. read it for its sound, and then count the chinese: forty-three characters.

find the first heat. anger has a first sign in the body, and it comes before any thought of being wronged: heat in the face or chest, a tight jaw, a breath that stops high. today, in one disagreement, look for that sign. you do not have to stop the anger. note only where the sign is, and let one full breath go out before you speak. see what the delay changes. the second experiment is for a moment when you need something from another person. before you ask, put yourself below: ask what they see, what they would do, what they need for the work. then say what you need. wang bi says that strength will not serve the one who stays above. find out if he is right.

勝 and 不爭: a contest with no pull. the pair here is contending and not contending, with above and below beside it. the passage does not refuse the contest. its people are an officer, a fighter, a victor, and a user of others, and each is called 善, good at the work. the fight still happens, and the enemy is still beaten, 勝. what is removed is the pull: the martial show, the anger, the clash, the high seat. so 不爭 is not the opposite of winning here. it is the manner in which the skilled one wins. a one-sided reading goes two ways. one hears a refusal of all fighting, and loses the soldier. one hears a trick for victory, and loses the last lines, which end at heaven and not at the enemy’s camp. the preference for the low and the cool corrects a world of generals who prized display. it also turns: the one who goes below is given the strength of others and stands, for a time, above.

the one who fights well does not fight from anger.. the one who fights well does not fight from anger. do you agree? recall a conflict that you entered hot and one that you entered cool. what was done with anger in your first home? what do you do with it now? take the opposite: anger is the proper answer to a wrong, and a fighter with none does not care enough. what in you says yes to that? when another person stays calm in a quarrel with you, what do you feel toward them? what does that tell you?

the one who is good at bringing out the strength of others places themselves below those others.. the one who is good at bringing out the strength of others places themselves below those others. who has brought out your strength? where did that person stand in relation to you? is it hard for you to have someone in the room who is better than you are? where does that come from? hold the other view: people work best under a firm hand from above. when has that been true for you, as leader or as led? does “going below” feel to you like strength or like loss of standing? why might that be worth knowing?

武 a foot and a dagger-axe. two parts are joined in this character. the long slanting stroke with its hook and dot, and the horizontal at the top, are 戈, the dagger-axe: a blade set crosswise on a long shaft, the common weapon of bronze age china. the shuowen calls 戈 a level-headed halberd and says it is a picture. the lower left is 止. the shuowen explains 止 as a base, and adds 故以止爲足, “so 止 is used for the foot”; the early graph is commonly explained as a footprint. a foot that is planted is a foot that has stopped, so 止 came to mean “to stop”. now the character can be read in two ways. read 止 as “stop”: stop the dagger-axe. that is king zhuang’s reading, and xu shen liked it so much that he made 武 one of his two examples of 會意, “joined meanings”: 比類合誼，以見指撝，“武、信”是也. his other example is 信, a person beside a word: trust. read 止 as “foot”: a foot beside a weapon, a man on the march. most modern scholars think that this was the first sense. the character has held both for two and a half thousand years. kings took it as a title, like king wu, who conquered shang; the partner word is 文, pattern and culture. later 武術, 武士, and 武俠 all carry it. the first line of this passage sides with the king of chu. eight strokes. first a short horizontal at the upper left. second a long horizontal that rises to the right: the cross of the weapon. then the foot, in four strokes: a vertical, a short horizontal to its right, a shorter vertical at the left, and a base stroke that rises to the right. the seventh stroke is the great one: it starts high, comes down in a long slant to the lower right, and ends in a hook that turns up. watch it. it is the shaft of the dagger-axe and the spine of the character; all the rest leans on it. the eighth stroke is the dot at the upper right. teachers warn pupils here: 戈 alone has a stroke that falls to the left across the shaft, and in 武 that stroke is absent. if you add it, the character is wrong. the weapon in 武 is a stroke short.

配 beside the wine jar. the left side is 酉, and it is a picture of a jar: a narrow neck, a wide body, and lines for the liquid or the bands. the shuowen ties it to the season: 八月黍成，可爲酎酒, “in the eighth month the millet is ripe and can be made into strong wine”. 酉 marks the words of fermenting and drinking: 酒, wine, with water added at the left; 醉, drunk; 醒, to become sober, to wake; 酬, to pour in return, to repay; and 醫, a doctor, since wine was a medicine. it is also the tenth of the twelve branches, the hour of the evening. the right side of 配 is now written 己, and the shuowen takes it as the sound and defines the whole as 酒色也, “the colour of wine”. the early forms are commonly explained differently: a person who kneels beside the jar. from that scene, it is thought, comes the main sense: to stand by, to be the partner of, to match. 配 is to mate, to blend, to fit one thing to another; 妃, a consort, is defined in the shuowen as 匹也, “a mate”, and has the same right-hand part. in the ancestral rite, wine was the offering, and the ancestor who was paired with heaven received it at heaven’s side. the character keeps the jar. ten strokes: seven for the jar, three for its partner. the jar: a horizontal across the top; the left side; the top and right side in one stroke with a corner; then, inside, a short stroke that falls to the left and a short vertical that bends at its foot; then a horizontal inside, and the base. keep the jar tall and narrow, because it must give room to its neighbour. then the right side: a horizontal that turns down at a corner; a short horizontal that closes it; and last a long stroke that goes down, bends, runs to the right along the base, and ends in a hook that turns up. watch the last stroke: it reaches under the right half like a mat. the two halves should stand level, like two persons at one table. neither is the larger.

69 · the guest at war. those who use arms have a saying: / “i do not dare to be the host; i am the guest. / i do not dare to advance an inch; i go back a foot.” / this is called marching ranks that are not there, / baring an arm that is not there, / pulling at an enemy who is not there, / gripping a weapon that is not there. / no disaster is greater than to take the enemy lightly. / to take the enemy lightly is nearly to lose my treasures. / so when raised armies meet, / the one who grieves wins. the passage has three parts. first a proverb of the camp, in a general’s voice: be guest and not host; give a foot sooner than take an inch. then a gloss on it in four phrases of one shape, each a military act with its object removed: ranks, arm, enemy, weapon. then a warning and a verdict. the warning has two forms in the tradition: do not take the enemy lightly, or, in the older copies, fear to have no enemy at all. either way the treasures of passage 67 are at stake. the verdict is that when armies are raised on both sides, the side that grieves wins. passage 68 gave four portraits; this passage puts the same person in the field. take the war as the one inside. a person who works on the mind often plays host: sets the agenda, attacks the fault, advances on the goal. the proverb says: be the guest in your own house. let what arises be the host for a while, and do not gain an inch on it. then the four phrases describe attention with no stance: it moves and has no fixed line; it is ready and shows no arm. the older reading of the warning is the deepest for this use. the disaster is to have no opponent left, a self so sure that nothing stands against it. and the close: the one who can grieve for what is lost in each inner victory is the one who comes through. read 主 and 客 in a negotiation, a market, or a quarrel between teams. the host’s instinct is to set terms and move first. the proverb advises the guest’s place: answer, and yield ground that costs little. the four “without” phrases describe a party that gives the other side nothing to push against: no drawn line, no show of strength, no named enemy, no weapon in the hand. the warning then turns on the strong. in the reported silk reading the great disaster is to be without a rival. a firm, a state, or a leader with no real opposition loses three things in order: care for people, restraint, and the habit of not going first. mencius says that such a state perishes. who is still able to tell you no? the proverb is a rule of the soft fighting arts. do not lead; receive. when the partner advances an inch, go back a foot, and their force falls into the space. teachers of taijiquan describe a skilled body in the words of the four phrases: the stance is no stance, the arm does not announce itself, and the partner reaches for a centre and finds none. the warning matters on the mat too: to take the other lightly is how the stronger one gets hurt. and the last line is known to anyone who has trained for years. the dangerous partner is not the furious one. it is the calm one who would be sorry to hurt you. stand, let the arms hang, and feel how much readiness needs no raised hand. try entering as a guest in one live conflict. then take the two versions of the warning as two questions for the evening. first, the received text: whom or what did i take lightly today? a risk, a rival, a person’s feelings? second, the older text: where am i without a match? in what room does no one oppose me, and what has that done to my tenderness, my restraint, my place in the line? the second question is harder. the passage calls its answer the greatest disaster, and it calls the feeling that guards against it 哀.

用兵有言: a soldier’s proverb. the passage begins with a quotation. 用兵 is “to use arms”, the common phrase for making war, and 有言 is “there is a saying”. so the first two lines are not the laozi’s own words. they come from the camp, from the oral lore of commanders, and we do not have their source. this is how much of the book was made: a saying that was already in use is set down, and then a comment follows it, here with 是謂, “this is called”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to add 曰, the mark of quotation, after 言. where the quotation ends is an editor’s choice; old chinese texts had no quotation marks. we close it after the inch and the foot. the “i” is therefore a general. listen to what a general of that age is made to say first: 不敢, “i do not dare”.

主 and 客: host and guest. the military writers used 主 and 客 as technical terms. the 客, the guest, is the army that has entered another state’s land; the 主, the host, defends at home. the sunzi speaks of “the way of being a guest”: go in deep. a text of sun bin, found in a han tomb in 1972, has a chapter on the division between guest and host. in that sense the guest is the invader, and the saying would be strange. so most readers take the words here in their plain social sense. a host arranges and decides. a guest waits to be shown a seat, eats what is served, and makes no demands. the old heshang gong commentary takes 主 as the one who moves first. the saying puts a guest’s manners into a campaign: i do not begin; i answer.

寸 and 尺: measures of the body. 寸 and 尺 are usually rendered “inch” and “foot”, and both systems come from the body. the shuowen says that a 寸 is the distance from the wrist to the place where the pulse beats; doctors still call that place 寸口, “the inch-mouth”. ten 寸 make one 尺, and the dictionary adds: 周制，寸、尺、咫、尋、常、仞諸度量，皆以人之體爲法, “in the zhou system all these measures took the human body as their rule”. a warring states 尺 was about 23 centimetres. the saying gives up ten to avoid taking one. later chinese made a proverb with the same two words and the opposite sense: 得寸進尺, “get an inch and advance a foot”, said of a greedy person. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write the verb “go back” with a loan graph: 不敢進寸而芮尺.

行無行: one graph, two words. 行無行 has the same character at both ends. the first is xing, “to walk, to march”. the second is hang, “a row”, and in an army a rank or a battle line; wang bi notes it: 行，謂行陳也, “行 means the battle array”. the shuowen gives the walking sense: 人之步趨也, “the stepping and hurrying of a person”. the early graph is commonly explained as a crossroads. so the phrase reads “to march a no-rank”: to move as an army moves, and to show no formation. three more follow in the same form, a verb, 無, and the verb’s natural object. english cannot make a noun out of “no rank”, so we write “ranks that are not there”. the chinese is quicker and odder. it is a soldier’s joke: all the drill of an army, done with nothing.

攘臂: the sleeves go up. 攘臂 is a set phrase: to push the sleeves up the arms, as a man does before a fight or hard work. the robes of the time had long, wide sleeves, and a bare forearm was a clear signal. the laozi has used the picture once before, as a joke against the confucians. in passage 38 the man of highest ritual acts, and no one responds; 則攘臂而扔之, “then he bares his arms and drags them to it”. the same two verbs, 攘 and 扔, stand side by side here. that is the sign of force: the arm shown, the other person pulled. in this passage each verb is emptied. 攘無臂: the gesture of baring, and no arm appears. a threat needs something to show. what do you show before you have said a word?

扔無敵 or 乃無敵: a list, or a result. 扔 today means “to throw away”. its old sense is different: the shuowen says 因也, “to follow on, to hold to”, and in passage 38 it is to pull a person along. so 扔無敵 is “to pull at a no-enemy”: to close with an opponent and find no one. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to have another order and another word: 攘无臂，執无兵，乃无敵矣. in their text the third phrase comes last, and its first graph is 乃, “and so, then”, with no hand beside it: “bare no arm, grip no weapon, and so there is no enemy”. then the list has three items and a conclusion. the one who shows no form of attack has no opponent. the received text made four matching phrases. the silk reading also prepares the next line, where the same two words return as a warning.

wang bi: no one to stand against. wang bi reads the four phrases as one condition: 言以謙退哀慈，不敢為物先，用戰猶行無行，攘無臂，執無兵，扔無敵也，言無有與之抗也. “it says: with modesty, withdrawal, grief, and tenderness, not daring to be ahead of things, one’s use of battle is like marching with no ranks, baring no arm, gripping no weapon, pulling at no enemy. it says that no one stands against such a one.” the strategists had a similar idea and used it as a method. the sunzi says that the height of forming troops is to arrive at no form; then the deepest spy cannot see in. in the sunzi, formlessness hides a blow. wang bi’s list of causes is different: modesty, withdrawal, grief, tenderness. those are not ways to hide. is there a difference, in practice, between no form and nothing to hide?

輕敵 or 無敵: the great variant. the received text says 禍莫大於輕敵: “no disaster is greater than to take the enemy lightly”. 輕 is “light”; the shuowen says it is first a light chariot, a fast one. to 輕 an enemy is to think little of him and to go to war easily. this is sound advice, and any general would agree. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to say something much stranger: 禍莫大於无適，无適近亡吾寶矣. their 適 writes the word 敵. “no disaster is greater than to have no enemy; to have no enemy is close to the loss of my treasures.” 無敵 is “without a match”, the boast of a power that no one can oppose. in this reading the worst thing that can happen to you is to be unrivalled. see what wang bi’s own comment shows. which line would a ruler rather have in his copy?

wang bi read “no enemy”. our chinese text is the one printed with wang bi’s commentary, and it says 輕敵. his comment does not fit it. he writes: 言吾哀慈謙退，非欲以取强，無敵於天下也。不得已而卒至於無敵，斯乃吾之所以為大禍也. “it says: my grief, tenderness, modesty, and withdrawal are not from a wish to gain strength and be without a match in the world. if against my will i come at last to be without a match, this is what i count as the great disaster.” he quotes the close as 幾亡吾寶, with 亡 and not 喪. so the text on his desk, in the 240s ce, had 無敵, as the silk texts are reported to have. later copyists changed the line above his comment and left the comment. mencius gives the political sense: a state with no rival states and no outside troubles will perish.

喪吾寶: to lose as one loses the dead. 吾寶 is “my treasures”, and wang bi says which: 寶，三寶也, the three of passage 67, which are tenderness, spareness, and not daring to go ahead of the world. a war taken up lightly, or a power with no rival, destroys exactly these three. the verb is 喪. it is the word for a funeral and for the loss of kin: the shuowen says 亾也。从哭从亾, “to lose; from 哭, to wail, and 亾, gone”. english “lose” is what one does with keys. 喪 has weeping in the graph. so the line prepares the last one. the speaker fears a loss that must be mourned, and then says that the mourner wins. the first treasure, 慈, is also what makes mourning possible. a side that has thrown tenderness away has no one to grieve for.

抗兵相加: when the sides are equal. wang bi glosses the two verbs: 抗，舉也；加，當也, “抗 is to raise; 加 is to face, to be matched against”. so 抗兵相加 is “raised armies set against each other”: the moment when two forces stand ready. 抗 also means “to oppose as an equal”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to have other wording: 故稱兵相若，則哀者勝矣. 稱兵 is “to raise troops”, and 相若 is “alike, equal to each other”. “when the forces raised are equal, the one who grieves wins.” this is a more exact claim, and a more modest one. it does not say that grief beats a larger army. it says that when numbers and weapons balance, something else decides, and that thing is not rage or the love of battle. passage 68 has just said that the good fighter is not angry. this line says what the good fighter is.

哀: mourning, not pity. 哀 is the grief of a funeral. the shuowen defines it with 閔, and defines 閔 as 弔者在門也, “the mourner who has come to the gate”. it is the word in the rites for the wailing of the bereaved. translators often soften it. legge writes “he who deplores (the situation)”, as if the general regretted an unpleasant duty. others write “compassion”. the text has already said what it means. in passage 31, when many have been killed, one weeps for them with 哀 and grief, and a victory is observed with the rites of a funeral. so 哀者 is the side that mourns before the battle, for its own dead and for the others. wang bi explains why it wins: such people 相惜, “spare and value one another”, and do not run after gain or away from harm.

legge’s helpful brackets. legge turns “those who use arms” into one person: “a master of the art of war has said”. the proverb of the camp becomes a quotation from an author. he then explains host and guest inside the lines: “the host (to commence the war)”, “the guest (to act on the defensive)”. this is one of the two readings, fixed in brackets. in the four “without” phrases he changes the order and has the general prepare to fight “where there are no ranks”, “no arms to bare”: the ground is empty, where the chinese empties the army. near the end he adds the object that wang bi supplied: “(the gentleness) which is so precious”, with his own word for 慈 from passage 67. for 哀者 he has “he who deplores (the situation)”. a victorian officer deplored. a zhou mourner wailed at the gate.

enter as a guest. choose one conflict that is alive for you now: a dispute at work, an old argument at home. the next time it opens, try the two halves of the saying. first, be the guest. do not set the terms, the place, or the first topic. let the other person be host in their own matter, and answer what is said, not what you prepared. second, when you feel the wish to press a small advantage, a point scored or a slip of theirs, give back a foot: say what is true in their case. watch the four signs in yourself: the line you have drawn up, the sleeve that goes up, the hand that reaches, the weapon that you hold ready. before all this, ask the last line’s question. if you won, what would be lost, and would you mourn it?

進 and 退, 主 and 客: a step back inside a fight. the saying sets host against guest (主, 客) and advance against retreat (進, 退), and each time it takes the second. this is not a rule that retreat is good. the speaker is one who uses arms, and the passage ends with a side that wins. the step back is a move inside a fight. it gives a foot where it could take an inch, and it lets the other side spend its force. the pairs also depend on each other. there is no guest with no host, and no going back with no one who comes on. and they turn: in the military books the guest is the army that has gone deep into another’s land. the preference corrects an age that honoured the first strike. a step back made from fear, or from contempt, is a different act; the passage calls taking the enemy lightly the great disaster. what makes a step back strong?

in a conflict it is safer to answer than to begin, and to give ground than to take it.. in a conflict it is safer to answer than to begin, and to give ground than to take it. is this your way or its reverse? think of your last quarrel: who moved first? what did giving ground mean where you grew up: good sense, or weakness? take the opposite: the one who moves first sets the terms, and ground given is ground lost. stay with it. what feelings come with the thought of the first step? when you step back, is it room given, or a wish to avoid the meeting? what do you think of people who do not step back?

when two matched forces meet, the side that grieves is the side that wins.. when two matched forces meet, the side that grieves is the side that wins. does this seem true to you, or only fine-sounding? what would it mean in a dispute that you know? have you won something and felt no grief for what it cost the other side? have you lost to someone who was sorry to win? hold the other view: grief weakens the hand, and the one who wants it more wins. where did you learn that? what do you do with sorrow in a conflict: show it, hide it, turn it to anger?

to take an opponent lightly is the greatest danger, since it costs what one holds most dear.. to take an opponent lightly is the greatest danger, since it costs what one holds most dear. whom or what do you take lightly at present? what makes you sure? where in your life does no one oppose you? what has that done to your care and your restraint? take the opposite: respect for the opponent turns into fear, and fear loses. is that your experience? think of a person who still opposes you. what do you owe to that person?

哀 a mouth inside the robe. take the character 衣, a garment. the shuowen calls it a picture and explains the word by its sound: 依也, “that which one leans on”; the upper part is the collar, and the lower strokes are the two sides of a robe that fold across each other. now open the robe and put something inside. chinese makes several characters in this way. with 中, “middle”, inside: 衷, an inner garment, and so one’s inmost feelings. with 果, “fruit”, inside: 裹, to wrap. with 口, a mouth, inside: 哀. the shuowen says 从口衣聲: the mouth gives the meaning, and 衣 gives the sound. in the old language 衣 and 哀 were close in sound; both belong to one old rhyme group (the 微 group). but the picture is hard to resist: a mouth that cries out from inside the clothes. and the clothes of grief were a great matter. for a parent, a child wore a robe of coarse, unhemmed hemp, called 衰 (cui), and that word too is written with the garment: the shuowen explains 衰 as a rain cloak of straw. the shuowen glosses 哀 as 閔, “the mourner at the gate”. so the character holds the sound of a wail and the dress of the one who wails. this is the word that the passage gives to the winning side. nine strokes. a dot at the top, then a long horizontal: the lid of the character and the collar of the robe. then the mouth in three strokes: left side, top and right side with one corner, base. it sits close under the horizontal, small and square. then the lower robe in four strokes: a stroke that falls far to the left; a vertical that ends in a hook to the right; a short stroke that falls to the left; and last a long stroke to the right that is pressed wide and then lifted. watch the sixth and the ninth strokes. they open to the left and right like a robe that falls from the shoulders, and the mouth is held between them. if the mouth is too large, the character shouts. a good hand keeps it small and lets the two long strokes carry the feeling.

兵 two hands on an axe. the shuowen gives this character in one line: 械也。从廾持斤，并力之皃. “a weapon. from 廾, two hands, that hold 斤, an axe; the look of strength joined together.” the upper part of the modern form is the axe, reshaped; the two strokes at the foot are what is left of the two hands. 斤 is a woodman’s tool; the shuowen says 斫木也, “to chop wood”. it is in 斧, an axe; 析, to split wood; 匠, a craftsman, of whom the shuowen says that the axe is “that with which vessels are made”; and 新, “new”, which the shuowen explains as the taking of wood. the two hands, 廾, are in 戒, “to be on guard”: two hands that hold a dagger-axe; and in 弄, “to play with”: two hands that hold jade. so a 兵 is at first a tool gripped hard. the word then moved outward in rings: a weapon; the man who carries it; an army; war itself. this passage uses three of the rings: 用兵, to make war; 執無兵, to grip no weapon; 抗兵, armies raised. in chinese chess the humblest piece is the 兵. the saying of the first line asks the user of arms to hold them as a guest holds a cup in another’s house. seven strokes. first a stroke that sweeps from right to left across the top, almost flat. second a vertical that comes down from under its left end. third a short horizontal that starts from the vertical. fourth a short vertical at the right, which closes the upper shape. fifth the long horizontal: the widest stroke, on which the upper part stands. then the two hands: a stroke that falls to the left, and a stroke or long dot that falls to the right. watch the long horizontal. it must be level and firm, like the shaft that the hands hold, and the last two strokes spread under it like feet set apart. in seal script the two hands are still clear, one at each side, with the fingers up. the clerical script of the han cut them down to two short strokes.

客 a foot arrives under a roof. the top is 宀, a roof with its ridge and two eaves; it marks houses and what happens in them, as in 家, 室, 安, and 宿. under the roof is 各. the shuowen takes 各 as the sound and defines 客 as 寄也, “to lodge with another”. but look at 各 itself. its lower part is 口, here an opening, the entrance of a dwelling. its upper part, 夂, is commonly explained as a foot that points downward: a foot that comes toward the entrance. the shuowen’s own note keeps the motion: 夊者，有行而止之, “a walking that is brought to a stop”. so 各 is an arrival, and scholars take it as the first way of writing a word for “to come, to arrive”. put a roof over an arrival, and you have a guest. the foot is the part to remember. a guest is the one who has come from outside, who does not own the roof, and who will go. the same 各 gives its sound to 路, a road; 落, to fall; 格, a frame; and 洛, the river luo. in passage 35 music and good food make the passing guest, 過客, stop. here the general chooses to be the guest: under another’s roof, and careful where the feet go. nine strokes. the roof first: a dot at the top centre; a short vertical dot at the left; then a long horizontal that turns down at its right end in a short hook. under it, the foot: a stroke that falls to the left; then a short horizontal that turns and falls to the left in one movement; then a long stroke to the right, which crosses the second and is pressed wide at its end. last the mouth, in three strokes: left side, top and right side, base. watch the long stroke to the right, the sixth. it reaches out from under the eaves, wider than the roof, and it gives the character its ease. the roof must be broad but light, and the mouth small and firm at the foot. if the roof is heavy, the guest looks shut in.

70 · jade under coarse cloth. my words are very easy to know, / very easy to walk. / under heaven no one can know them, / no one can walk them. / words have an ancestor. / deeds have a lord. / just because this is not known, / i am not known. / those who know me are few; / and so i am precious. / so the sage wears coarse cloth / and holds jade in the bosom. the passage is short and has three movements. a complaint: my words are very easy to know and to walk, and no one can do either. a reason: words have an ancestor and deeds a lord, and because that is not known, the speaker is not known. a turn: the knowers are few, so the value is high. then a picture that closes it: the sage in coarse cloth with jade inside the robe. the verbs 知 and 行 carry the first half; 知 comes five times in forty-seven characters. the tone is the lonely one of passage 20, where the speaker is dull and alone among bright people. here there is no sadness in the last line. it ends on jade. the teaching is easy because it asks for nothing new. one does not need to go out of the door, as wang bi says. that which knows these words is already here, before any effort, and it is nearer than the thoughts about it. that is also why no one can find it: the mind looks for something to grasp and admire, and this has no outside. it wears coarse cloth. the plain fact of being aware does not look like a treasure, so attention passes over it for brighter things. the jade is against the skin and cannot be seen by the one who carries it, only felt. the practice is small: stop looking outward for a moment and feel what is already held. two lessons, and they pull in different ways. the first is about speech. words have an ancestor: a leader’s sayings should descend from one source, so that people can predict the tenth from the first nine. if each statement is made for its occasion, people know the words and cannot know the person. the second is about display. the age of this text was a market for talent, as ours is, and the rule of a market is to be seen. the sage does not advertise. worth is carried inside, and the outside is plain enough that anyone can come near. do not make this a strategy of hidden advantage. the jade is not a card held back for the right moment. it is what the person is made of. the picture in the last line is a posture. coarse cloth on the outside: the surface of the body is ordinary and relaxed, the face is not arranged, and nothing is held up for others to see. jade in the bosom: at the centre of the chest something is quiet, cool, and dense. the movement arts say the same in their own terms: soft outside, firm inside; the appearance of an old farmer, the root of a tree. try it while you walk. let the shoulders and face be common, and put attention on a small, smooth weight behind the breastbone. then notice the first line again. to walk this is very easy. you were walking already. keep one thing unshown today. then test the passage’s claim that words have an ancestor. write down three things that you often say: to your children, to your team, to yourself. under each, write the saying that it comes from, and under that one, its parent, until you reach a sentence that has nothing behind it. that sentence is your 宗. see if you would be willing for people to know it. then look at the lord of your deeds in the same way: for three things you did today, ask who gave the order.

吾言: a voice that hides. this is one of the few passages with an “i”. chinese has two common words for it, and both are here: 吾 for “i, my” at the head of a clause, and 我 for “me” as an object and for stress. who speaks? the han historian sima qian wrote the first life of laozi, about 100 bce, and he already had little to go on. he says of him: 以自隱無名為務, “he made it his task to hide himself and be without a name”. in his story an old archivist leaves the declining court of zhou, writes five thousand characters at the request of a border guard, and is not seen again. modern scholars doubt most of this. yet it fits the voice of this passage: a speaker who expects not to be known, and who does not raise the voice.

wang bi: why easy, why impossible. wang bi gives four short reasons, one for each clause. 可不出戶窺牖而知，故曰甚易知也。無為而成，故曰甚易行也。 “it can be known with no going out of the door and no looking through the window; so it says ‘very easy to know’. it is done by not-forcing; so it says ‘very easy to walk’.” then: 惑於躁欲，故曰莫之能知也。迷於榮利，故曰莫之能行也。 “they are confused by restless desire; so it says ‘no one can know it’. they are lost in glory and profit; so it says ‘no one can walk it’.” his first reason quotes passage 47. for wang bi the difficulty is not in the teaching. nothing is hidden and nothing is hard. it is easy as stopping is easy, and a person who is running finds stopping the hardest thing.

行: to walk is to practise. 行 is “to walk”, and by extension “to carry out, to practise”. english splits these and so loses an image that runs through the whole book: 道 is a road, and a road is for walking. we keep “walk”. the pair 知 and 行, knowing and doing, became one of the long debates of chinese thought; this passage is an early place where they stand side by side. other passages answer it. the best officer hears of the dao and works hard to walk it (41). the great road is very level, and people love the side paths (53). and passage 78 repeats the complaint in almost the same words: no one under heaven does not know it, and no one can walk it. there the trouble is only in the doing. here even the knowing fails. which is your case?

宗: words have a family shrine. 宗 is a roof, 宀, over 示, an altar. the shuowen says 尊祖廟也, “the temple where the ancestors are honoured”. from the temple the word means the ancestor, the main line of descent, and the head of a clan. so 言有宗 does not say that the words have a “principle” or a “system”. it says that they have an ancestor: they descend from one source, as the members of a clan descend from one founder, and they can be traced back. passage 4 uses the word for the dao: deep, like the 宗 of the ten thousand things. a reader of the time lived inside a lineage and knew its shrine. to such a reader the claim is plain. these sayings are not loose remarks. they are kin. know the ancestor, and you will know each of them by the family face.

君: deeds have a lord. 君 is a ruler. the shuowen: 尊也。从尹。發號，故从口, “the honoured one. from 尹, to govern; he gives out commands, and so the graph has 口, a mouth”. the upper part, 尹, is commonly explained as a hand that holds a staff. 事有君: deeds have a lord, one thing that directs all the rest. with 宗, the pair covers the two orders of zhou life, the family and the court. wang bi makes both cosmic: 宗，萬物之宗也。君，萬物之主也, “the ancestor is the ancestor of the ten thousand things; the lord is the master of the ten thousand things”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to have the two words in the other places: 言有君，事有宗, “words have a lord; deeds have an ancestor”. the exchange is easy because the two images do one job. what rules your acts, and what do your words come from?

夫唯無知: whose not-knowing?. 夫唯無知，是以不我知 has no subject in its first half, and english must choose one. reading one, which we render: because people have no knowledge of this, the ancestor and the lord, they do not know me. wang bi and legge take it so. reading two: because i am 無知, “without knowledge”, i am not known. 無知 is a state that the book praises: the sage keeps the people 無知 and without desire (3), and asks whether one can care for the state, govern the people, and be 無知 (10). on that reading the speaker is not known because there is nothing clever to notice. the second half has a point of grammar: in a negative sentence a pronoun object goes before the verb, so “not know me” is 不我知, “not-me-know”. in chinese the 我 sits inside the not-knowing, surrounded by it.

希: rare, and hard to hear. 希 means “few, rare, thin”. in this book it is first a word of sound. that which is listened for and not heard is named 希 (14). to speak rarely is self-so (23). the great tone has a 希 sound (41). few in the world reach the teaching without words (43). so when the speaker says 知我者希, “those who know me are 希”, a reader of the whole book hears more than a number. the speaker is faint, as the dao is faint: at the edge of what the ear can catch. the line is not quite a complaint. it names the reason. a thing that is like the dao will be as hard to hear as the dao. the later graph 稀, with grain at the left, is used for “sparse”; the shuowen has that graph, defined as “thin”.

則我者貴: two readings and a price. the received line is 則我者貴, and 則 can be two words. as “then”: “then i am one who is precious”. as a verb, “to take as a model”: “those who model themselves on me are honoured”, or “are rare”. with 者, strict grammar favours this reading, parallel to 知我者. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to settle it with a shorter line: 則我貴矣, “then i am precious indeed”. wang bi reads the same way: 知我益希，我亦無匹, “the fewer who know me, the more i am without a match”. look at 貴. the shuowen defines it by the market: 物不賤也, “a thing that is not cheap”, and the graph has 貝, a cowrie, at its foot. it is the logic of price: what is rare is dear. there is dry humour in it. this book tells rulers not to prize rare goods (3, 64). now the speaker is one.

聖人: from “i” to “the sage”. in the last line the “i” is gone and 聖人 takes its place, as if the speaker stepped back to describe a type. “sage” needs a warning. a 聖人 is not a saint with a halo, and not only a wise man. the shuowen defines 聖 as 通也, “open all the way through”, and the graph has an ear in it: a person whose hearing reaches. elsewhere in the book the 聖人 is the model ruler. here the picture is a person of no rank at all, dressed as a labourer. this is the tension of the word in the laozi: the one most fit to be at the centre is the one whom no one notices. chinese has no “he” here. we keep “the sage” and do not add a pronoun.

褐: what the poor wore. 褐 has 衣, a garment, at the left. the shuowen gives two senses: 編枲韤, “socks plaited of hemp”, and 一曰粗衣, “also: coarse clothing”. it was cloth of rough hemp or animal hair, undyed and brownish, and in modern chinese the word is the name of the colour brown. in the warring states it was a mark of class. the rich wore silk and fur. mencius describes the followers of a teacher who held that all should farm: several dozen men, 皆衣褐, “all dressed in 褐”. and a “man in loose 褐” is his phrase for a nobody whom a brave man does not fear to face. 被, “to wear”, is to have a thing thrown over the shoulders. so the sage looks like a field hand. legge adds “(a poor garb of)”. the chinese reader needed no bracket.

玉: the jade that confucius would sell. jade was the most valued substance in ancient china, above gold. it is hard, cool, and faintly bright, and it cannot be cast or forged, only ground slowly with sand. the confucian classics made it the image of a gentleman’s character and say that he does not put it off without cause. he wore it in strings at the belt, where it could be seen and heard as he walked. this passage puts the jade inside the clothes. the analects has the other side. a pupil asks: here is a fine piece of jade; do you lock it in a box, or look for a good price and sell it? confucius answers: 沽之哉！沽之哉！我待賈者也. “sell it! sell it! i am one who waits for a buyer.” for a man who offered his jade and paid for it, see the story of mr. he. the two teachers agree that they hold jade. what do you do with yours?

懷: against the skin. 懷 is the bosom, and in early dress it is an exact place. a robe was wrapped across the chest and tied with a belt, so that a pouch formed above the belt, between cloth and body. people carried letters, food, and money there; a mother carried a small child. to 懷 a thing is to keep it in that fold. from this the word means to cherish, to long for, and to carry a child in the womb. english “carries in his heart” makes the jade a feeling. “at the centre” makes it an idea. the chinese is physical: stone against skin, kept warm by the body, with nothing to show outside. wang bi reads the two halves so: 被褐者，同其塵，懷玉者，寶其真也, “wearing coarse cloth: to be one with the dust; holding jade: to treasure what is genuine”.

to be known: the market for men. 知, “to know”, had a special weight for the class that read this book. the 士 of the warring states lived by being known. a man of ability travelled from court to court and tried to make a ruler see his worth; if he was “known”, he was employed and fed, and his family rose. great lords kept guests by the thousand. the loyalty went both ways. a famous retainer of the time said: 士為知己者死, “a man of service dies for the one who knows him”. so 不我知, “i am not known”, was the worst report that a 士 could make of his life, and confucius had to tell his pupils not to grieve over it. the speaker here states it calmly and draws a different sum: few know me, so the price is high. the jade is not for sale.

the jade that no one saw. raw jade is found inside a rough stone, and from outside the two look the same. han fei tells the best-known story about it. a man of chu named he found such a stone and offered it to his king. the king’s jade worker said: it is a stone. the king had he’s left foot cut off for fraud. he offered it to the next king, and lost the right foot. under a third king he sat at the foot of the mountain and wept for three days, and said that he did not weep for his feet. he wept because a treasure was called a stone and an honest man a liar. the king had the stone cut, and it was the finest jade in the world. the story is about not being known. the sage of this passage is the stone that does not go to court.

legge’s signet. legge’s last line reads: the sage “wears (a poor garb of) hair cloth, while he carries his (signet of) jade in his bosom”. the first bracket explains; the second invents. a signet is a seal of office, the sign of a rank that could be shown at need. with it the sage becomes a prince in disguise, like a king in a european tale who walks among the poor. the chinese has only 玉, jade, with no shape and no office. for 宗 and 君 he writes “an originating and all-comprehending (principle)” and “an authoritative law”: two metaphors from family and court become two abstractions of his century’s philosophy. and “hair cloth” brings in the hair shirt of the christian penitent. the sage’s cloth is not a penance. it is what was on the peg.

one thing unshown. today, do one good thing or have one good thought, and show it to no one. do not mention it, do not hint, and do not post it. keep it as the sage keeps the jade: inside the robe. then watch the mind for the rest of the day. it will look for a way to be known: a casual remark, a tone of voice. notice how strong the pull is, and what you believe would be added if someone knew. tomorrow, try the other half. wear the coarse cloth: in one meeting, let a point of yours go without your name on it, or let someone else explain what you know well. ask afterward what was lost. the passage says that the price went up.
