易 and 莫能, 褐 and 玉: easy, and out of reach. the first four lines hold a pair in its sharpest form: very easy, and no one can. the text does not solve it. both are said of the same words. wang bi puts the difficulty in the hearers, but the passage leaves the two statements side by side. a second pair closes it: coarse cloth outside and jade inside, the plain and the precious on one body. a third joins them: few and dear, 希 and 貴. a one-sided reading makes the speaker a hidden superior and the world a crowd of fools. that misses the dependence. the jade is dear because few know it, so the world’s not-knowing is part of its price. and cloth with no jade is only cloth. the preference for the plain outside answers a market where worth was shown and sold. it also turns: coarse cloth that is worn in order to be noticed is one more display.

what is asked is very easy to know and to do, and still no one under heaven does it.. what is asked is very easy to know and to do, and still no one under heaven does it. is there something in your own life that is easy to know, easy to do, and not done? name it. what stands between the knowing and the doing: desire, hurry, the wish for something more impressive? take the opposite: what matters is hard, and what is easy cannot be worth much. where did you learn to trust the difficult? if the important thing were simple and already at hand, what would you lose? what effort would have nowhere to go?

worth does not need to be seen; it can be carried inside under a plain surface.. worth does not need to be seen; it can be carried inside under a plain surface. do you believe this, or do you feel that worth unseen is worth lost? what did being noticed mean when you were young? what did being passed over mean? hold the other side for a while: a gift is for use, and to hide it is pride or fear. which word fits you more? when you keep something unshown, is it jade against the skin or a card held back? what do you think of people who show everything?

懷 tears kept in the robe. at the left stands 忄, the form that 心, the heart, takes at the side of a character. it marks feelings: 情, 性, 恨, 悅. the right side is 褱, and it is a small scene. its outer frame is 衣, a robe, which has been opened: the collar is at the top and the skirts are at the foot. between them are two things. the flat box with two short lines inside is 目, an eye, turned on its side. under the eye are a short vertical and four dots. the eye with these drops is the old graph 眔, and it is commonly explained as an eye that sheds tears. the shuowen takes it as the sound part of 褱 and defines 褱 with a word for holding a thing against the body. so the whole of the right side is: weeping, held inside the robe. then the heart was added at the left to make 懷, which the shuowen defines as 念思也, “to think of with longing”. the meaning has a clear line: to hold against the chest, to hold in the feelings, to cherish, to miss someone; and of a mother, to carry a child. the same right side gives the sound to 壞, “to fall into ruin”, with 土, earth. the mainland short form 怀 keeps the heart and replaces all the rest with 不, “not”. in this passage the thing in the bosom is jade. nineteen strokes. the heart at the side: a dot at the left, a dot at the right, then a long vertical between them. then the right side from the top: a dot and a horizontal, which are the collar. the eye in five strokes: the left side; the top and right side with one corner; two short verticals inside; the base. then the tears: a short vertical, a dot at the left, a small rising stroke under it, a short stroke that falls to the left, and a dot, both at the right. then the skirts of the robe in four strokes: a long stroke that falls to the left; a vertical with a hook to the right; a short stroke to the left; and the final long stroke to the right. the eye and its drops must stay small. the tang monk huaisu, 懷素, the master of wild cursive, had this character as the first of his name.

玉 three stones on a cord. three horizontal lines and one vertical through them: the shuowen says 象三玉之連，丨其貫也, “it shows three pieces of jade joined; the vertical is the cord through them”. jade was drilled and threaded, and it was worn and given in strings. that early graph looks almost the same as 王, “king”, and for centuries scribes told the two apart only by the spacing of the lines. the dot was added later to mark the jade. the side form never took the dot, so wherever you see 王 at the left of a character, it is jade and no king: 珍, precious; 理, to work jade along its veins, and so “pattern, reason”; 玩, to handle and enjoy; 環, a ring. the shuowen says that 寶, treasure, has it under a roof, and that 弄, “to play with”, is two hands that hold it: 从廾持玉. the simplified 国, “state”, even puts jade inside the border. jade is not a jewel in the western sense. it does not sparkle. it is valued for a dense, soft light, a cool touch, and a clear note when struck, and writers found in it the qualities of a person: warm and firm, and with flaws that are not hidden. here the sage holds it where no one sees. the king has four strokes. the jade has five: the king, and one small thing kept at the side. five strokes. the first horizontal, short. the second horizontal, shorter or equal, set a little nearer the first than the last. then the vertical, straight through the centre from the first line to where the base will be. then the long base horizontal, which is the widest stroke and carries the others. last the dot. it sits at the right, in the space between the second line and the base, and it falls to the right. watch the dot. it is written last and is the lightest stroke, and it changes the character’s whole meaning. if it is too large, it crowds the lower room; if too far out, it leaves the character. in seal script there is no dot, and the three lines are evenly spaced, like three discs on a string.

71 · to know not-knowing. to know not-knowing: the highest. / not to know knowing: a sickness. / just because the sickness is taken as a sickness, / by this there is no sickness. / the sage is free of sickness: / because the sage takes the sickness as a sickness, / by this free of sickness. twenty-eight characters, and only eleven different ones. the first line sets two short phrases against each other: 知不知 is the highest; 不知知 is a sickness. the words are the same and their order is reversed, and the grammar leaves each open to several readings. the rest of the passage turns on one word used as verb and as noun: 病病, to take the sickness as a sickness. the sentence is given twice, once for anyone and once for the sage, inside the frame 夫唯 … 是以. the passage has no image and no example. it is the nearest thing in the book to a formula, and it follows passage 70, where the speaker was not known. the usual mind treats not-knowing as a hole to be filled fast, with a guess, a label, or an opinion. this passage calls the hole the highest place. before a thought names what is here, there is a moment of open, awake not-knowing; contemplative traditions in many countries point to it, and some call it “don’t-know mind”. the sickness is to cover that moment with a claim and then forget that one did so. the medicine is not a new state. it is to notice the covering as it happens: to 病 the 病. that is why the sage is not ill. the sage does not lack the habit; the habit is seen each time. what is it like, now, not to know what the next moment is? a person with authority is paid to know, and so the sickness of this passage is an illness of leaders. the symptoms are familiar: the confident forecast, the quick diagnosis of a person, the meeting in which no one says “we do not know”. the duke of cai is the pattern: he took the doctor’s report as an attack on his standing. the passage offers no technique for better knowledge. it offers a habit: treat your own certainty as the first thing to examine. in practice, a leader who says “i don’t know” early makes it safe for others to bring bad news while it is still in the skin. wang bi’s sentence is a good one for a wall: knowing is not enough to be given the charge. the body knows the difference between the two lines. when you hold a view that you cannot support, something tightens: the jaw, the belly, the voice goes a little higher. that tension is the 病 in its plain sense, a small distress. when you admit that you do not know, there is first a drop, and then the breath goes lower and the shoulders come down. the movement arts train this. a student who is sure what the partner will do next is hit. a student who stands in not-knowing, ready and without a plan, can answer what comes. old medicine made the same point about health: the patient who feels the early ache and calls it by its name is already on the way to being well. say “i don’t know” three times today, and name one fault at the moment it acts. in the evening, take a sheet of paper and write at the top one matter that you are sure of: about your work, a person, or yourself. under it write what you have in fact seen, in plain sentences, and under that what you have added. do not try to reach doubt. only look at the join between the two parts. the first line of the passage calls that look the highest thing. the confucian sentence would have you correct the page. the laozi asks you to be at ease with how much of it is blank.

知不知: three characters, four sentences. 知不知 is “know, not, know”. classical chinese has no “that”, no “and yet”, and no marks to show where a clause ends, so the three characters can be at least four english sentences. one: to know that one does not know. this is the common reading. two: to know, and to hold it as not-knowing; legge takes this one, “to know and yet (think) we do not know”. three: to know not-knowing, with 不知 as a noun: to be at home in the state where nothing is grasped. four: to know the things that cannot be known, and to stop there. the zhuangzi points at the third and fourth: 知止其所不知，至矣, “knowing that stops at what it does not know has arrived”. our rendering keeps the three words in their order and lets the readings stay open. which did you hear first?

上 or 尚, and one more 不. the received text ends the first line with 上, “above, the highest”. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write 尚, “esteemed, the best”, and add the particle 矣: 知不知，尚矣. the two graphs were used for each other, and the sense is the same. the second line is the real difference. silk a is reported to read 不知不知，病矣: “not to know not-knowing is the sickness”. the received text has one 不 fewer: 不知知, “not to know knowing”, which most readers take as “not to know, and to think one knows”. with the silk reading the two lines mirror each other exactly: know your not-knowing, the best; fail to know your not-knowing, the sickness. a single small negative, lost or added by a copyist, turns a clear statement into a puzzle. many readers have learned from the puzzle.

wang bi: knowing cannot bear the weight. wang bi’s whole comment on this passage is one sentence: 不知知之不足任則病也. “not to know that knowing is not enough to be relied on: that is the sickness.” his reading of 不知知 is neither of the usual two. for him the fault is not ignorance, and it is not false confidence about some fact. it is trust in knowing as such: the belief that knowledge can carry the load of a life or a state. 任 is “to bear, to be given a charge”. knowing is a useful servant, and it cannot be given the charge. this fits passage 65, where he calls rule by cleverness a spiral of tricks. it also turns the first line: the highest thing is to know what knowing cannot do.

病: worse than ill. chinese has two old words for sickness. 疾 is an illness that strikes; the shuowen gives its sound part as 矢, an arrow. 病 is heavier: the shuowen says 疾加也, “an illness that has grown worse”. the frame on the upper left of both, 疒, is the sign of sickness; the shuowen says it shows a sick person who leans on a support (see the plate). 病 also has wider senses that the passage uses. it is a defect or flaw in a thing. it is distress. and as a verb it is “to be troubled by, to count as a fault”. confucius uses the verb in a line that speaks to passage 70: the noble person 病 his own lack of ability, and does not 病 the fact that others do not know him. english “disease” covers the first sense only.

病病: verb and noun in one graph. the passage has twenty-eight characters, and eight of them are 病. in 病病 the two are different parts of speech. the first is a verb: “to sick”, that is, to treat as sickness, to feel as a defect. the second is its object. classical chinese can use almost any word of quality in this way: 貴 it, “to hold it dear”; 輕 it, “to take it lightly”. english cannot repeat one word and must choose a verb: “recognize”, “be distressed by”, “take as”. each choice loses the sound. to a chinese ear the line is nearly a tongue-twister, bing bing … bu bing, and the joke carries the teaching: the cure is made of the same stuff as the illness, turned on itself. passage 72 does this again with 厭, and passage 64 with 欲不欲 and 學不學.

夫唯 … 是以: the book’s hinge. 夫唯 x，是以 y: “it is just because of x that y”. this small frame is one of the signatures of the laozi, and it nearly always holds a reversal. just because the sage does not stay in the work, the work does not leave (2). just because water does not contend, it is without blame (8). just because it does not fill itself, it can wear out and be renewed (15). just because there is no knowing, i am not known (70). just because one does not press, one is not detested (72). here: just because one takes the sickness as a sickness, one is not sick. 唯 is first a word of the mouth; the shuowen defines it as 諾也, “to answer yes”. the frame is a yes to something small that turns out to be the whole cause. english “only” hides how much weight it bears.

a sentence said twice. the received text says the same thing twice: 夫唯病病，是以不病, and then, of the sage, 以其病病，是以不病. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to have it once: 是以聖人之不病，以亓病病也，是以不病. “so the sage’s not being sick is by taking the sickness as sickness; and so there is no sickness.” the general sentence with 夫唯 is absent. it is possible that an early reader wrote a short explanation beside the line and that a copyist later took it into the text. it is also possible that the fuller form was a chant, said twice for memory. the effect differs. the reported silk version is one closed circle. the received text first gives the rule to everyone and then shows the sage inside it. in our rendering the two stanzas keep the echo. read them aloud once.

聖人: not the one who is never ill. “the sage” is our word for 聖人, and it should not be heard as “saint” or as “perfect being”. the shuowen defines 聖 as 通也, “open all the way through”, and the graph has an ear in it. this passage shows what the openness is for. the sage is not free of the sickness because some special nature keeps it away. the text gives the cause, 以其, “by this”: the sage takes the sickness as a sickness. so the fault does arise in the sage. it is seen as it arises, and a fault that is seen cannot do its work in the dark. the difference between the sage and others is not in what happens. it is in the speed and honesty of the recognition. chinese has no “he” here, and we repeat “the sage”.

confucius drew a line; laozi distrusts the pen. the analects has a famous sentence on the same matter. confucius says to a rash pupil: 知之為知之，不知為不知，是知也. “to take what you know as known, and what you do not know as not known: this is knowing.” it is a rule of honest accounts. there are two columns, and each item goes in the right one. the laozi’s first line can be read as agreeing with it. but the weight is elsewhere. confucius trusts the columns; a careful person can keep them. the laozi suspects the “known” column itself. in this book the people are best with little cleverness (3, 65), learning is to be reduced each day (48), and the one who knows does not speak (56). the highest state is not a full and accurate ledger. it is to know one’s way about in 不知. for the greek parallel, see socrates.

not the same as socrates. western readers think at once of socrates, who said at his trial that he was wiser than others in one small thing: he did not think that he knew what he did not know. the two lines are near in time and in wording. they differ in use. for socrates, to know one’s ignorance is a beginning. it clears away false belief so that the search for a true definition can start, and the search is the good life. ignorance is a lack to be reduced by questions. in the laozi, 不知 is not only a lack. it is a place where one can stand, and the sage lives there. there is no promise that the not-knowing will be filled. the greek puts down his false knowledge to seek the true. the chinese text asks whether you can stay with empty hands, and be well.

the duke who was not ill. han fei tells a story in his notes on the laozi. the doctor bian que saw duke huan of cai and said: you have an illness in the skin; if it is not treated it will go deeper. the duke said: i have no illness. when the doctor had gone he added: doctors like to treat the healthy and take the credit. ten days later the illness was in the flesh; then in the gut. on the second and third visits the duke did not answer. at the fourth visit bian que looked and turned away, because it was in the bone marrow. five days later the duke fell ill, and he died. the oldest medical classic says that the sage treats what is not yet ill. the duke’s first illness was slight. his second was that he could not 病 it. is there an early sign that you have declined to see?

legge’s “(think)”. legge fills the open grammar with one bracketed word, used twice: “to know and yet (think) we do not know is the highest (attainment); not to know (and yet think) we do know is a disease.” his “think” turns the first line into a virtue of modesty: the person really knows, and humbly supposes otherwise. that is one of the four readings, and the one most at home in a victorian classroom. “attainment” is also his: a rung on a ladder of achievement. for 病病 he writes “being pained at (the thought of) having this disease”, which keeps the two senses apart, pain and disease, and loses the repeated word. he renders 病 as “disease” throughout, a term of the hospital. the chinese word also means a flaw in a pot or an argument.

three times “i don’t know”. today, catch three moments in which you are about to speak with more certainty than you have: an opinion on the news, a judgment of a person’s motive, an answer to a child. in each, say the plain words: “i don’t know.” say them with no apology and no hurry to add what you do know. then stay in the gap for one breath. notice the feeling in the body. for most people it is a small alarm, as if something had been lost. that alarm is the place where the passage points. the second half of the practice is the verb 病: once today, when you see a fault of your own in action, name it at once, to yourself or aloud: “that was vanity”, “that was fear”. do not add blame. the naming is the treatment.

知 and 不知, 病 and 不病: each inside the other. two pairs make the whole passage: knowing and not-knowing (知, 不知), sickness and freedom from sickness (病, 不病). neither pair is sorted into good and bad. not-knowing appears on both sides of the first line: once inside the high thing and once inside the sickness. what differs is whether it is known. so the high thing is still a knowing; the text does not praise ignorance. the second pair is tied closer still. the way to 不病 goes through 病: one must take the sickness as a sickness. health here is not the absence of the fault. it is the fault seen. a one-sided reading says “not-knowing is best” and makes a new certainty of it. that is 不知知 again, the sickness in fresh clothes. the preference corrects an age, and a kind of mind, that is paid to be sure. can a person be sure of their not-knowing, and be well?

to know that one does not know is high; to take not-knowing for knowledge is a sickness.. to know that one does not know is high; to take not-knowing for knowledge is a sickness. do you agree? when did you last say “i do not know” and mean it? what did not-knowing cost you at school, at work, at home? what did it cost the adults around you to admit it? take the other view: a person must commit to a judgment, and too much “i do not know” is a way to hide. where is that true of you? what do you feel toward people who are very sure? toward people who are seldom sure? which of the two are you afraid to be?

a fault that is seen as a fault has already lost its hold.. a fault that is seen as a fault has already lost its hold. is this so in your experience? name a fault that you see clearly and that still acts. how were faults met where you grew up: named, punished, hidden, laughed at? hold the opposite: seeing is not enough, and a fault yields to effort and correction. stay with that. does it tire you or steady you? which is more natural to you, to look at a fault or to set about fixing it? what might the other way know?

病 the sickbed and the third stem. every character for illness in chinese lies under one frame: 疒. you see it in 疾, illness; 痛, pain; 療, to treat; 瘦, thin; 癌, cancer. the shuowen explains it: 倚也。人有疾病，象倚箸之形, “to lean. when a person is ill; it shows the form of leaning on something”. the oracle-bone forms are commonly explained as a person who lies on a bed, with the bed drawn standing on its end and small drops beside the body. the two short strokes at the left of the modern frame are commonly taken as what remains of the bed’s legs. inside the frame, 病 has 丙. the shuowen gives it as the sound: 从疒丙聲. 丙 is the third of the ten heavenly stems, the signs by which days were counted, and the shuowen places it in the south, where all things are complete and bright. in the scheme of the five phases this stem belongs to fire. many readers have therefore seen a fever on the bed. that is a pleasant aid to memory; the dictionary claims only the sound, and 丙 gives the same sound to 柄, a handle, and 炳, bright. the word itself means an illness that has become grave, and then any flaw or distress. the character for the healer, 醫, has an arrow inside it and a wine jar under it; the shuowen says that wine is that by which sickness is treated. this passage offers a different medicine: the word 病 itself, used as a verb. ten strokes. the frame first: a dot at the top; a horizontal under it; then a long stroke that starts at the left end of the horizontal and falls far down to the left. then the two small strokes on the outside of that long one: a dot, and below it a short stroke that rises to the right. then 丙 inside: a horizontal; a vertical at the left; the top and right side in one stroke that turns down and ends in a hook; and inside these a stroke that falls to the left and a last dot to the right. watch the long third stroke. it is the back of the frame, and it must curve away so that the inside has room. a frame of this kind covers two sides only, top and left. the lower right is open, and a calligrapher lets the inner part stand a little out of it.

知 an arrow beside a mouth. the left side is 矢, an arrow. the shuowen calls it the arrow of bow and crossbow and says that the graph shows 鏑栝羽之形, “the form of the head, the notch, and the feathers”. the right side is 口, a mouth. the shuowen’s entry for the whole is short: 詞也。从口从矢, “a word of speech. from mouth and arrow”. it does not say why. the usual explanation, made famous by the qing scholar duan yucai, is speed: one who knows a thing speaks of it at once, and the word leaves the mouth like an arrow. others think of aim: to know is to hit the mark. both are later readings of an old graph, so hold them lightly. the same arrow is in 疾, illness, under the sickness frame: an illness that strikes fast, and the old word also means “swift”. so the two key words of this passage, 知 and 病, have relatives that share an arrow. add 曰, “to speak”, now written like 日, beneath 知 and you have 智, “cleverness”; early manuscripts did not separate the two, and the laozi distrusts the second. note what the picture leaves out. it has no eye and no heart. in this graph knowing is a thing said: quick, aimed, and gone from the bow. the passage asks for the knowing that can stay on the string. eight strokes: five for the arrow, three for the mouth. the arrow: a short stroke that falls to the left; a short horizontal that starts under it; a longer horizontal below; then a long stroke that falls to the left through both; and last a dot to the right. when 矢 stands alone, its final stroke is a long sweep to the right. here it is pulled in to a dot, to make room for its neighbour. this is a rule of the regular script: a part at the left gives way. then the mouth: left side, top and right side with one corner, base. watch its height. the mouth is set low, level with the foot of the arrow and well under its head, so that the character leans forward a little. if the mouth is as tall as the arrow, the character goes stiff.

72 · when fear runs out. when the people do not fear what is to be feared, / the great dread arrives. / do not cramp the place where they dwell. / do not press down on that by which they live. / only because there is no pressing, / there is no loathing. / so the sage / knows the self and does not show the self; / cares for the self and does not set a high price on the self; / and so leaves that, takes this. the passage moves from a state to a self. it begins with a law of politics in eight characters: when the people no longer fear the fearsome, the great dread comes. two prohibitions follow, in the form of orders to a ruler: do not cramp where they live, and do not press on what they live by. a hinge sentence turns on one graph: no pressing, and so no loathing. then 是以, “for this reason”, the passage names the sage, and the subject changes to four small phrases about 自, the self: know it, do not show it; care for it, do not price it high. it ends with the book’s formula of choice. the claim is in the order: public oppression has a private root. read the people as the body and its plain needs, as the heshang gong commentary does, and the ruler as the will. a hard will governs the body by threat: work or be ashamed, perform or be nothing. for a time the body fears and obeys. then one day it does not fear, and the great dread arrives as collapse, illness, or a sudden refusal to go on. the middle lines are the remedy. do not crowd the heart; leave it room. do not press on the life; let it have sleep, food, and slow hours. wang bi says: do not be weary of your own stillness. the last lines name the cause of the tyranny: a self that must be seen and priced drives its own body like a conscript. authority that rests on fear is a loan against a limited account. each threat that is carried out, each rule with a penalty, draws on it. when people have nothing more to lose, or simply stop caring, the fear is spent, and what follows is not calm. it is the event of 209 bce on some scale: the resignation, the strike, the quiet sabotage. the passage gives two plain tests of a leader, and both can be checked: housing and livelihood, or in modern terms the space and time that people have, and their pay and load. then it looks for the root in the leader’s own self-regard. rising titles and visible importance at the top are paid for lower down. the sage’s way is cheap for everyone: self-knowledge costs the people nothing. pressure and disgust are bodily facts, and the passage uses one word for both. something that presses on the chest makes the breath short, and the body turns away from it. a person who has been crowded for a long time, at a desk, in a house, or in a marriage, shows it in the shoulders. the two orders of the passage can be given to one’s own body. give the dwelling room: let the chest open and the belly be soft, so that the breath has a wide house. do not press on the life: stop a little before the limit, in work and in exercise. movement teachers say seventy parts in a hundred. what is not pressed does not come to hate the practice, and it will come back tomorrow. ask “where do i press?” and lift one pressure for a day, with no announcement. then try the four phrases of the close as a short review in the evening. self-knowing: name one true thing that you noticed about yourself today. self-showing: recall one moment in which you arranged how you looked to others. self-care: name one thing that you did to keep your life in good order. self-price: recall one moment in which you needed to count for more than the person beside you. two of the four are “this”, and two are “that”. the passage says which to leave and which to take.

畏: a ghost’s head and a tiger’s claws. 畏 is fear of something greater than oneself: awe, dread, deep respect. the shuowen builds it from two terrors: 从甶，虎省。鬼頭而虎爪，可畏也. “from 甶, a ghost’s head, and a reduced 虎, tiger. a ghost’s head and a tiger’s claws: this is to be feared.” modern scholars commonly read the oldest forms as a figure with a great mask-like head that holds a stick. in both readings the fear is of a power that is not quite human. the book uses the word with care. the masters of old were wary, as if they 畏 their neighbours on all sides (15). the second-best ruler is one whom the people 畏 (17). and passage 74 asks: when the people do not 畏 death, why threaten them with death? fear is a store that a ruler can spend, and it has a bottom.

畏 and 威: fear and the fearsome. the first line has two words that are one. 畏 (wei) is “to fear”. 威 (wei) is “that which makes one fear”: awe, majesty, the power to punish. they differ only in tone in modern speech, and scholars take them as two forms of one old root, the feeling and its cause. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to write a single graph for all of them: 民之不畏畏，則大畏將至矣, “when the people do not fear the fearsome, the great fearsome is about to arrive”. the received text gave the noun its own character. so the line is tighter in chinese than any english can be: wei, wei, wei. the ruler’s 威 exists only as the people’s 畏. it is not a thing that the ruler has. when the fear stops, the majesty is gone at the same moment, and something else comes in the gap.

wang bi: the great dread is collapse. what is 大威, “the great dread”? the line has been read as a moral for the people: if they do not fear what they should, disaster comes; legge takes it so. most chinese commentators read it as a warning to the ruler, and the next lines, which are prohibitions addressed to the one with power, support them. wang bi describes the sequence: 威不能復制民，民不能堪其威，則上下大潰矣，天誅將至. “the power can no longer control the people, and the people can no longer bear the power; then above and below break apart completely, and heaven’s punishment is about to arrive.” his verb 潰 is used of a dike that bursts. some modern readers make the line a promise: when people lose their fear, true authority arrives. the lines that follow do not support them. see how it happened in 209 bce.

209 bce: equally death. the legalist state ruled by 威. its theorists held that a ruler has two handles, reward and punishment, and that penalties must be so heavy that no one dares to offend. qin united china on this plan in 221 bce. twelve years later, a party of nine hundred conscripts on their way to a frontier post was stopped by rain. under qin law the penalty for late arrival was death. one of them, chen sheng, a hired farmhand, put the case to the others in words that sima qian records: 今亡亦死，舉大計亦死，等死，死國可乎. “now if we run we die, and if we rise we die. it is equally death. shall we die for a state?” they rose. within three years the empire was gone. the law had spent all the fear there was. passage 74 states the principle; this passage names the result.

狎, 狹, 閘: three graphs for one squeeze. the received text has 狎. the shuowen explains that graph through a dog: 犬可習也, “a dog that can be made familiar”. from it comes the sense “to be too familiar with, to treat with easy contempt”. so one reading is: do not treat their homes with contempt. the heshang gong edition writes 狹, “narrow”: do not make their dwellings narrow, and most readers think that this is the word meant. the mawangdui silk texts are reported to have a third graph: 毋閘亓所居. the shuowen says of 閘: 開閉門也, “to open and shut a gate”; here it is read as shutting in. the three share a sound and an idea, which is to crowd people where they live. the readings differ in the picture: a ruler who walks through homes as he likes, walls that close in, or a gate shut from outside.

其所居, 其所生: whose house, whose life?. 其 is “their” or “its” or “one’s”, and the chinese does not say whose. the political reading, which we render, takes it as the people’s: their dwellings, and their living, which means their fields, grain, and labour. a state presses on these with taxes, forced work, and war, and passage 75 says so plainly. two old commentators read the line inwardly. wang bi: 清靜無為謂之居，謙後不盈謂之生, “clear stillness and not-forcing are what is called the dwelling; modesty, the rear place, and not being full are what is called the life”. for him these belong to the ruler, who leaves them at his peril. the heshang gong commentary takes the dwelling as the heart, where the spirit lives, and the life as the vital essence. so the same eight characters are a law for a state and a rule for a body. both squeeze the same way.

不厭 … 不厭: the same four characters. 夫唯不厭，是以不厭. the two halves end in the same two characters, and the sense depends on hearing two different words in them. the graph 厭 wrote two words. one is “to press down”, later written 壓; the shuowen defines 厭 as 笮也, “to press”. the other is “to be full of, to be sick of, to loathe”; the silk texts are reported to write that one 猒, which the shuowen defines as “to have eaten one’s fill”. most readers take the line so: only because the ruler does not press (ya), the people do not loathe (yan). the mawangdui silk texts are reported to keep one graph for all three places: 毋猒亓所生。夫唯弗猒，是以不猒. english cannot do it. we write “pressing” and “loathing” and lose the echo. in chinese the weight above and the disgust below are one word seen from two sides.

wang bi: do not loathe yourself. wang bi reads the pair in another way, and it is worth setting beside the usual one. on the first 不厭 he writes: 不自厭也, “it is not to 厭 oneself”. on the second: 不自厭，是以天下莫之厭, “one does not 厭 oneself, and so no one in the world 厭 one”. he adds 自, “self”, to the first half. for him the line is about the ruler’s relation to the ruler’s own dwelling and life, the stillness and modesty named in his earlier comment. a ruler who is not weary of these, who does not press and crowd them out of himself, is a ruler of whom the world does not weary. the outer result follows the inner habit. this reading prepares the last lines, which have 自 four times. are you weary of your own quiet?

聖人: the ruler with no display. we write “the sage” for 聖人. the word does not mean a saint or a holy man, and it means more than a wise one. the shuowen defines 聖 as 通也, “open all the way through”; the graph has an ear in it. in this passage the sage is the answer to a political problem. the first lines describe rule by dread and its end. then 是以, “for this reason”, the sage does two things and refuses two things, and all four concern the self. the claim is that the state’s pressure on the people begins in the ruler’s view of the ruler: display and high self-price above become weight below. chinese has no pronoun here. we write “the self” four times, where a smoother english would say “himself”, and the stiffness is the cost of adding no “he”.

自知: not the greek “know thyself”. 自知 is “self-know”, and a western reader hears the motto of the temple at delphi. the greek command told a mortal to know his limits before the gods, and later philosophy made it a call to examine the soul by reason. the laozi’s 自知 is neither a humbling nor an inquiry. passage 33 gives the contrast: 知人者智，自知者明, “to know others is cleverness; to know oneself is light”. knowing others is a skill that one uses on them. knowing oneself is a clarity, the word 明, and it has no object to work on. here it is set against 自見, self-display. the same light either stays in and makes things clear or is turned outward to be looked at. the sage has the first and so has no need of the second. 自 is, in the shuowen, a picture of the nose.

見: to see, to be seen. 見 is an eye on a pair of legs; the shuowen says 視也。从儿从目, “to look. from a person and an eye”. read jian, it is “to see”. read xian, it is “to appear, to show”, the sense later written 現. chinese uses one graph for the act and for its reverse. 自見 is then “to show oneself”, and inside it is “to see oneself”: the person who displays is the one who is always looking at the self as others might. passage 22 says that one who does not show the self is bright; passage 24 says that one who shows the self is not bright. wang bi ties it to the first line: the sage does not display what the sage knows 以光耀行威, “so as to dazzle and to work 威”. display is a small form of dread.

自愛: care, not self-esteem. 自愛 looks like the modern phrase “self-love”, and modern psychology would hear self-esteem. christian moral writing, on the other side, made self-love the root of sin. neither fits. 愛 in early chinese is to care for a thing and so to be sparing of it, to be unwilling to waste it; it can mean “to grudge”. passage 44 uses it so: 甚愛必大費, “great attachment is sure to cost dear”. to 自愛 is to take care of one’s life as a careful person takes care of a tool or a field: not to spend it on show. passage 13 says that the world can be entrusted to one who cares for the body as for the world. the second half then makes sense: this care does not raise one’s price. one looks after the self and does not admire it.

自貴: an age of rising titles. 貴 is “costly” and “of high rank”. 自貴 is to set one’s own price high, to make oneself grand. the period gave clear cases. the zhou house had one king, and the heads of states were dukes and marquises. in the 4th century bce they began, one after another, to call themselves 王, king. in 288 bce the rulers of qin and qi went a step further and took the title 帝, a word for a high god, as emperor of the west and emperor of the east; qin kept it for about two months, and qi for two days. each rise in title came with larger palaces, tombs, and armies, and the cost fell on the dwellings and livelihoods of the people. wang bi sums it up: 自貴則物狎厭居生, “when one sets oneself high, the dwelling and the life are crowded and pressed”. self-price above is paid for below.

去彼取此: that, and this. 去彼取此, “leave that, take this”, closes three passages of the book in the same four characters: 12, 38, and 72. 彼 is “that”, the thing over there; 此 is “this”, the thing at hand. in passage 12, “that” is the eye and its colours, and “this” is the belly. in passage 38, “that” is the thin flower of ritual and foresight, and “this” is the thick fruit. here “that” is self-display and self-price, and “this” is self-knowing and self-care. each time the choice is for the near, the inner, and the plain over the far, the shown, and the fine. the formula is nearly a gesture: a hand that points away and then at the chest. in modern mandarin 去 and 取 are near-homophones, qu and qu. this is a modern likeness only; the old sounds were not close.

legge turns it on the people. legge reads the whole first half as advice to the people about their own conduct. “when the people do not fear what they ought to fear, that which is their great dread will come on them.” the words “ought to” are his. then the two prohibitions become: “let them not thoughtlessly indulge themselves in their ordinary life; let them not act as if weary of what that life depends on.” the ruler who cramps and presses has left the passage, and a careless populace has taken his place. this is a preacher’s reading, a sermon on reverence and sober living for a congregation. it could be defended from the grammar, since 其 names no owner. but most chinese readers, wang bi among them, heard a warning addressed upward. a victorian missionary did not expect a sacred book to threaten the governing class.

where do i press?. each person has some small realm: a household, a team, a class, a child. today, look for the two acts that the passage forbids. to cramp the dwelling: do i enter another person’s space, time, or attention as i please? a child’s room, a colleague’s evening, a partner’s silence? to press on the living: do i load people with more than their means, in work, in demands, in my moods? look for the sign that the passage names, which is 厭, the loathing that answers pressure. it is quiet at first: a slow reply, eyes that go down. then turn to the last lines. when i press, is it because i am showing myself to someone? choose one pressure and take it off for a day. tell no one that you did.

彼 and 此: twins, not strangers. the passage ends on a pair, that and this (彼, 此), and it fills each side with two things: self-showing and self-pricing there; self-knowing and self-caring here. look at how near the two sides are. all four begin with 自, the self. to know the self and to show the self share one graph for seeing. to care for the self and to set a price on it are both forms of regard. “that” is not a foreign vice. it is “this”, turned outward for an audience. the opening has the same shape: the people’s fear and the ruler’s fearsomeness are one word, and when the small fear runs out the great dread arrives. the text does choose, and the choice answers an age of rising titles. it also turns. self-knowledge that is spoken of with pride has become display. self-care that counts its own worth has become a price. where is the line in you today?

rule by fear lasts until the fear runs out, and then something worse arrives.. rule by fear lasts until the fear runs out, and then something worse arrives. have you seen this in a family, a workplace, or a country? what arrived when the fear ended? where do you rule by a kind of fear, over others or over your own body? who ruled you that way? take the opposite view: with no fear of consequences, people and habits run loose. how much do you believe that? what in you stopped fearing some time ago? did you notice when it happened?

it is enough to know and care for oneself, with no need to be seen or highly priced.. it is enough to know and care for oneself, with no need to be seen or highly priced. is it enough for you? in what room is it hardest? when did you first learn that you had to be seen in order to count? hold the other side: a self that is not shown is not shared, and to ask a fair price is self-respect. what is true in that? what do you think of people who display themselves? is any part of that judgment a wish?

people come to loathe what presses on them; where nothing presses, nothing is loathed.. people come to loathe what presses on them; where nothing presses, nothing is loathed. what presses on you at present, and what do you feel toward it? whom do you press: a child, a colleague, your own body? would they say so? take the opposite: pressure is how people grow, and those who are not pressed stay small. which pressures in your past do you thank? how do you tell the pressure that forms a person from the pressure that makes a person turn away?

威 the mother-in-law. the word for awe and majesty, for the dread power of kings and armies, has a woman in the middle of it. look inside the frame: 女, a woman. the frame around and over her is 戌, which is at first a weapon, a broad axe on a shaft; the long slanting stroke with its hook is the same one that you see in 戈, the dagger-axe. the shuowen’s definition is a surprise: 姑也。从女从戌。漢律曰：“婦告威姑。” “the husband’s mother. from 女 and 戌. the han statutes say: ‘a wife reports to the 威姑.’” so for xu shen the first meaning of 威 is a person: the mother-in-law, the 威姑 or “awesome mother” of the legal phrase. a bride in early china left her own family and entered her husband’s house, and there she was under the daily command of his mother. the dictionary takes that as the home of the word. modern scholars read the picture more simply: a woman under a weapon, and so fear, and that which causes it. other characters keep the weapon 戌: 滅, to put out, to destroy, which is the shuowen’s own gloss for 戌; and 咸, “all”. do not confuse 戌 with 戍, to guard a frontier, or 戊, a heavenly stem. the passage uses 威 for the state’s terror. the character remembers that awe is first learned at home. who was the first person that you feared? nine strokes. first a horizontal across the top. second a long stroke that starts under its left end and falls in a curve to the lower left: the outer wall. third a short horizontal inside. then the woman in three strokes: one that goes down to the left and turns back to the right; one that falls to the left across it; and a short horizontal that rises a little. the seventh stroke is the great slanting hook: it starts above the top line, comes down through it to the lower right, and turns up. the eighth is a stroke that falls to the left across the hook. the ninth is a dot at the upper right. watch the woman. she must be written small and a little low, so that the long hook can pass over her. the two long strokes, the second and the seventh, lean apart and hold her between them.

畏 a ghost’s head, a tiger’s claws. the top looks like 田, a field. it is not a field. the shuowen names it 甶 and says 鬼頭也。象形, “a ghost’s head; a picture”. compare 鬼, a ghost: the same square head on a kneeling body. the shuowen explains 鬼 with a pun: 人所歸爲鬼, “that to which a person returns (歸) is a ghost (鬼)”. the dead were not gone. they had gone home, and they could send illness or blessing. under the head in 畏 the shuowen sees the claws of a tiger, and it gives the whole in one phrase: 鬼頭而虎爪，可畏也, “a ghost’s head and a tiger’s claws: to be feared”. the ghost was the worst thing unseen and the tiger the worst thing seen. the oldest forms are commonly explained otherwise, as a great-headed figure that holds a stick or weapon: perhaps a masked exorcist. both give fear a face. 畏 is not fright at a noise. it is the steady dread of a power, and it shades into respect: 敬畏 is reverence, and the analects says that the noble person has three things that he 畏. as a sound part it is in 喂, to feed, to call out; 偎, to nestle against; and 猥, low, vulgar. in the first line of this passage, the fear of the people is the ruler’s whole stock of power. nine strokes. the head first, in five: the left side; the top and right side in one stroke with a corner; a horizontal inside; a vertical inside; and the base that closes the box. then a long horizontal under the head, wider than the head on both sides. then the claws: a vertical that ends in a hook rising to the right; a short stroke that falls to the left; and last a long stroke to the right, pressed wide and lifted. watch the long horizontal, the sixth stroke. it divides the character like a shoulder line, with the square head above and the open limbs below. the head must be small and firm. the last stroke reaches far out to the right and gives the figure its movement. in seal script the lower part is curved like a hooked hand.

厭 dog meat under a cliff. this character is a stack of four small pictures. take the inside first: 猒. its right side is 犬, a dog. its lower left, written like 月, is 肉, meat. the shuowen joins these two as 肰 and defines it: 犬肉也, “dog meat”, a common food of the time. the same pair, with fire beneath, is 然, “to burn”, the second half of 自然. the upper left of 猒 the shuowen gives as 甘, “sweet, good to eat”, a mouth with something in it. together: 猒，飽也, “to have eaten one’s fill”. the first idea is a pleasant one, a full stomach after good meat. but fullness turns. one who has had enough has soon had too much, and so the word came to mean “to be sick of, to loathe”. now put 厂 over it. the shuowen says 厂 is a cliff with an overhang, under which people can live. with the cliff on top, the shuowen defines 厭 as 笮也, “to press down”. later writers divided the senses among new graphs: 壓, with earth, to press; 饜, with food, to be sated; and 魘, with a ghost, a nightmare, the ghost that presses on a sleeper. in this passage one graph does two jobs in four characters: the weight that comes down, and the disgust that comes up. fourteen strokes. the cliff first: a horizontal across the top, then a long stroke that falls from its left end to the lower left. under this roof, the left column: a small box in four strokes (left side; top and right side; a short line inside; the base), and under it the meat in four strokes (a left side that curves out a little; the top and right side with a hook; a short line inside; a second short line under it). then the dog at the right: a horizontal; a long stroke that falls to the left through it; a long stroke to the right; and last the dot at the upper right. watch the proportions. the long left stroke of the cliff must lean well out, so that all three inner parts fit under it. the dog’s last sweep runs out from under the cliff to the right, and the character is open on that side.

73 · heaven’s wide net. courage in daring: killing. / courage in not daring: life. / of these two, / sometimes benefit, sometimes harm. / what heaven hates: / who knows the reason? / so even the sage finds it hard. / the way of heaven: / it does not contend, and is good at winning; / does not speak, and is good at answering; / does not summon, and things come of themselves; / slack, and good at planning. / heaven’s net is wide, wide. / its mesh is loose, / and it loses nothing. the passage has three parts. first, a pair of lines as short as a law: courage that goes into daring ends in 殺; courage that goes into not daring ends in 活, a word with water in it. the text does not say who kills or who lives; see the two readings. second, a question: heaven has dislikes, and who knows the reason? third, four matched lines on the way of heaven, each built as “not this, and yet good at that”: no contest and it wins, no speech and it answers, no summons and things come, a slack belt and good plans. the close is a picture from fishing: a net that is wide, with an open mesh, that lets nothing slip. the objects are a weapon, a stream, a mouth that calls, a sash, and knotted cord. the courage that the passage prefers is hard to see from outside, because nothing happens. a sharp reply is not sent. a decision that would feel strong is left for a day. the text calls this 不敢 and insists that it is 勇: the same rise of breath, turned the other way. it then removes the comfort of a rule. the careful do not always gain; the line allows that, and the next line says that nobody knows heaven’s reasons. so the restraint cannot be a strategy to get a safe result. it rests on something else: a trust that the net is roomy, and that one does not have to seize each thing to keep it. the slack belt comes before the good plan in the sentence. it may also come first in the body. read with the active sense of 殺, the first lines speak to anyone who can end things: a post, a project, a person’s place in a group. to be brave in daring is to cut fast and call it strength. to be brave in not daring is harder, because the leader then carries the open problem and the doubt of others. the four lines on heaven describe an authority that most leaders do not trust: it does not contend, does not announce, does not summon. wang bi’s key is position: stay low, and people bring you what you need to know. the net gives the measure for rules. the states of that age drew their nets of law tighter each generation. a wide mesh is not neglect if the leader in fact loses no one. three words here are body words. 勇 is breath, by the shuowen’s own definition. 活 is the sound of water that runs. 繟 is a belt let out. together they describe a state that a martial artist will know: the breath is full, the joints are not locked, the waist is loose. a fighter who is brave in daring commits the whole weight and can be led past the centre. one who is brave in not daring keeps the root and lets the other come: 不召而自來. the good response, 應, is a match in timing and not a second attack. stand with the knees soft. let the belly out against the belt. feel how much wider the field of attention becomes when the middle of the body is not held. a river does not argue with a rock and is past it. spring does not announce a date and the buds answer. no one summons the swallows or the wheat. these are the four lines on heaven, seen in a year. the last image needs a longer look. a fishing net with a wide mesh lets the small fish go and the water pass; that is why it can be drawn through the sea at all, and why there are fish next year. a net that held everything could not be lifted. the text says that heaven’s net is of the open kind, and still nothing is outside it. an ecologist might say the same in other words: no act leaves the system. the result may arrive late and far from the place where the act was done. find one moment today when you feel the surge to act boldly: to send the message, to correct someone, to close a question. notice the breath; that is 勇. do not hold the surge down. give it the other direction for one hour: be brave enough to not do the thing yet. while you wait, loosen something at your waist, the belt or only the muscles, and breathe into the space. after the hour, look at the matter again. sometimes you will act, and the act will be cleaner. sometimes the matter will have come to you in a new form. do not expect a reward each time; the passage does not promise one. afterwards, read how legge turned the first line into a rule for criminals, and ask what he was afraid of.

勇: courage is breath. the shuowen gives 勇 a definition of one word: 气也, “it is breath”. 气 is the old way to write 氣: the breath, the vapour that rises, the force that moves a body. so courage is not first a moral quality. it is a surge in the chest. the graph has 力, strength, below, and 甬 above for the sound. the line does not praise this surge and does not blame it. it asks where the surge goes: into 敢, daring, or into 不敢, not daring. the second is still 勇. passage 67 gives the source that the laozi trusts: 慈故能勇, “from care comes the ability to be brave”. where in your body do you feel the breath rise before a bold act?

不敢 is not fear. english hears “not daring” as weakness. the chinese phrase 不敢 has a different history. it was the polite word of a person who knows the limits of a position: “i would not presume”. the laozi makes it a discipline. the sage helps the ten thousand things to be as they are 而不敢為, “and does not dare to act on them” (64). one of the three things that the speaker holds dear is 不敢為天下先, “not daring to go ahead of all under heaven” (67). the soldier says 不敢為主, “i do not dare to be the host”, the one who starts the fight (69). in each place the speaker has the power to act and holds it back. that takes 勇. the line says so in plain words: courage in not daring. what english word would you use for a restraint that needs more nerve than the act?

killed, or killing?. 則殺 is two characters: “then, kill”. chinese verbs have no passive form, and the line names no victim. most readers, wang bi among them, hear the passive: the person who is brave in daring gets killed, and the careful person lives. but 殺 and 活 can also be active. then the line is about a person who holds power over others, a judge or a ruler: the one who is brave in daring kills; the one who is brave in not daring lets live. this second reading leads straight into the next passage, with its executioner and its question about who may kill. our rendering uses the bare nouns “killing” and “life”, so that both readings stay open. english had to drop the verb to do it.

wang bi: a death that is one’s own. wang bi’s notes on the first two lines are short. on the first: 必不得其死也, “such a one will surely not get their own death”. on the second: 必齊命也, “such a one will surely complete the allotted span”. the phrase 不得其死 comes from passage 42: 強梁者不得其死, “the violent and strong do not get their own death”. the idea behind it is old and strange to us. each life has a death that belongs to it, at the end of its 命, its allotted time. to die by the sword or the law is to lose that death. so for wang bi the first line is not about a reward for caution. it is about whether a person arrives at the end that was theirs. what would it mean to you to “get your own death”?

活: the sound of running water. the word for “to live” in this line is not the usual 生, to be born and grow. it is 活, and the shuowen does not define it as life at all. it says 水流聲, “the sound of water that flows”. the left side is 氵, water. to be 活 is to move like a stream: the modern word 活潑, lively, keeps the sense. a modern collated edition of the mawangdui silk texts prints 栝 here, a graph with the same sound-part and a tree in place of the water; such loans by sound are common in early manuscripts. set the two verbs of the opening lines side by side. 殺 has a weapon in it. 活 has water in it. five passages later, water becomes the open subject (78). did the text choose this word for life by accident?

或…或…: which one gains?. 或利或害 is four characters: “some gain, some harm”. 或 means “one of them, someone”, and also “sometimes, perhaps”. the first reading sorts the two kinds of courage: one of the two benefits, and the other harms. wang bi reads it so: 俱勇而所施者異, “both are courage, but where it is applied differs”. the second reading is less tidy: of these two, each sometimes gains and sometimes harms. the bold person sometimes wins. the careful person sometimes dies. that reading fits the next line better, because the next line is a question with no answer: who knows why heaven hates what it hates? our rendering says “sometimes” and does not say which of the two does which, so both readings stay open. the text may give a rule in line two and take the certainty back in line four.

a heaven with dislikes. 惡 is read wu here: to hate, to find foul. read e, the same graph means “bad”. so 天之所惡 is “that which heaven hates”. 天 is hard to carry into english. it is the sky over the fields. for the early zhou kings it was also the power that gave and removed the right to rule. modern versions often write “nature” and make the line a statement about physical law. the missionaries wrote “heaven” and heard their god. the chinese word is neither a mechanism nor a person. it has no voice, no face, and no book of rules, and still it has a grain: some things go against it. then comes the honest part. 孰知其故: who knows the cause? the text claims that heaven has dislikes and admits that no one can read them. can you act well without the reason?

a line that came from elsewhere. 是以聖人猶難之, “so even the sage finds it hard”, stands also in passage 63, word for word. there it ends a teaching on doing hard things while they are still easy. here it sits between a question about heaven and a description of heaven’s way. the line is reported to be absent from both mawangdui silk texts; a modern collated edition of them goes from 孰知其故 straight to 天之道. most scholars think that a later copyist added it, perhaps from a note in a margin. we keep it because our pinned text has it, and because the addition is not foolish. some reader, long ago, came to “who knows the reason?” and wanted to say: no one, not even the sage, and so the sage is careful. 聖人 is not a saint. it is a person whose hearing is attuned, and here, one who knows the limit of that hearing.

one graph for battle and for ease. the received text says 不爭, “does not contend”, a favourite phrase of the book (8, 22, 66, 68, 81). a modern collated edition of the mawangdui silk texts prints a different graph: 不彈而善勝. most editors read 彈 here as a loan for 戰, battle: “does not fight, and is good at winning”. that is the language of the generals. the sunzi says that the highest skill is 不戰而屈人之兵, “to bend the other side’s army without battle”. three lines later the collated text prints the same graph again: 彈而善謀, where our text has 繟然, “slack”. look at the three characters: 戰, 彈, 繟. all contain 單, which gave the sound. a scribe who wrote by ear used one graph for two words: for the thing that heaven does not do, and for the manner in which it does everything.

應: an answer without words. 應 (ying) is to answer, as an echo answers a shout. the shuowen defines it with one word, 當: to match, to meet exactly. so the line does not say that heaven replies in some secret language. it says that heaven does not speak and the fit still comes: seed and season, act and result. wang bi explains: 順則吉，逆則凶, “go with it and things turn out well; go against it and they turn out badly”. confucius said nearly the same thing, in one of the places where the two traditions touch: 天何言哉, “what does heaven ever say? the four seasons run, the hundred things are born.” english “answer” suggests a message. 應 is nearer to the way a valley returns a sound, or a body returns to balance.

wang bi: stay low, and things come home. 召 is a court word: to summon. a ruler summons a minister; a lord summons troops. the shuowen builds it from 口, a mouth. heaven does not do this, and still everything arrives. wang bi’s comment is six characters: 處下則物自歸, “keep to the low place and things return of themselves”. he reads the line through passage 66, where the rivers and the sea are kings of a hundred valleys because they lie below them. 歸 is a warm word: to go home, as a bride goes to her new house. so the picture is not of a force that pulls. it is of a place that is low and open enough to be a home. english needs a subject for “come”; our “things” is wang bi’s 物. the word for “come” has its own story.

來: wheat that heaven sent. 來, “to come”, began as a picture of a wheat plant. the shuowen tells the story: the zhou people received a fine wheat as a gift; the graph shows its awns; and 天所來也，故爲行來之來, “it is what heaven made come, so the graph serves for the ‘come’ of coming and going”. modern scholars say more simply that the picture of wheat was borrowed for a word with the same sound. the plant itself got a new graph, 麥, which is 來 with a foot below it. either way, an early reader of 不召而自來 saw a stalk of grain in the last word. nobody summons wheat. a farmer prepares the ground and waits, and it comes.

繟: a belt let out. 繟 (chan) is a rare word, and the shuowen defines it by an object: 帶緩也, “a belt that is slack”. the left part is 糸, silk thread; the right part, 單, gives the sound. so the way of heaven, at the moment when the text calls it a good planner, is pictured as a sash that hangs loose. other old editions write other words in this place: 坦, level and at ease, or 默, silent. the collated silk text has a loan graph. the body sense of 繟 is the most exact. a person who plans from fear pulls the belt tight: jaw, shoulders, belly. wang bi describes heaven’s kind of planning as 安而不忘危, “at rest, and not forgetful of danger”. loosen your own belt one notch, in fact or in thought. does your next plan change?

網: knotted cord, for fishing. the oldest form of this word is 网, a picture: a frame with crossed cords inside. the shuowen gives its origin: 庖犧所結繩以漁, “what paoxi knotted from cord, to fish with”. paoxi, or fuxi, is the first culture hero; in the book of changes he looks at the patterns of heaven and earth and then makes nets for hunting and fishing. so the net is the first tool, older than the plow. it is a tool for catching. modern versions that write “network” turn it into a web of links, which is a twentieth-century picture. the line keeps the hunter’s sense and then changes it in two ways: this net is very wide, and its mesh is open. who, or what, is the catch?

恢恢: a word said twice. 恢 means large, with room in it; the shuowen says simply 大也, “great”. said twice, 恢恢 is not “very large”. doubled words in old chinese are sound-pictures. they give the feel of a thing, as english does with “far, far away”. the best-known use outside this line is in the zhuangzi. cook ding explains how his knife stays sharp after nineteen years: the joints of the ox have gaps, the blade has no thickness, and so 恢恢乎其於遊刃必有餘地矣, “how roomy! there is surely space to spare for the blade to play”. so 恢恢 is the roominess that lets a thing move without a cut. heaven’s net is roomy in that way. say hui hui aloud, slowly. the sound has the breadth that it names.

疏: to let through. 疏 is “sparse, wide apart”: the holes of this net are large. the shuowen gives the root sense: 通也, “to let pass, to go through”. the word is used for the work of clearing a blocked river so that it runs. in later chinese it also means “distant” (of kin) and “careless”. so the text says a hard thing about heaven’s net: it is made mostly of openings. a tight net is what a nervous ruler wants, with a rule for every case. this one lets almost everything through, and the next three characters say that it loses nothing. how can both be true? one answer: it does not need to stop a thing to hold it. the fish is still in the sea.

a proverb for the guilty. 天網恢恢，疏而不失 became one of the best-known sayings in chinese. in everyday use the last word changed to 漏, “to leak”: 疏而不漏. people say it when a criminal is caught after many years: heaven’s net is wide, but nothing leaks through. it is a proverb about justice, and it has comforted the wronged for two thousand years. the older word is quieter. 失 is to lose, to let slip; the shuowen defines it as 縱, “to let go”, and files it under 手, the hand. 不失 is “does not let slip”. this can be the grip of a judge. it can also be the hold of a net under a fall, or of a mother’s hand. the passage began with killing and with what heaven hates, so the hard sense is present. which sense do you hear at the end?

laws cast in bronze. the first lines enter a debate of the age: how much should a state kill? in 536 bce the minister zichan of zheng had a penal code cast in bronze, the first written law that the chinese record names. a statesman of jin wrote to protest: when people know the written rules, they will lose respect and contend over every point. in 513 bce jin cast its own code on an iron vessel, and confucius is said to have objected. over the next centuries the states built finer and tighter nets of law, with death for many offences; the legalists made this a theory. against that background, heaven’s net with its loose mesh is an argument. the next passage continues it: a ruler who kills in place of the great executioner cuts their own hand.

legge fills in the crime. legge’s first sentence has two sets of brackets. the daring is “(to do wrong, in defiance of the laws)”, and the not-daring is “(to do so)”. the chinese has none of this. he turned an open line about two directions of courage into a line about criminals and law-abiding subjects, the reading that a victorian magistrate would expect. then he gives the heaven line as a rhymed couplet: “when heaven’s anger smites a man”. 惡 is dislike. it became anger, and it gained a verb, “smites”, from the english bible. the wonder in the chinese is that heaven hates and no one knows why. in legge the wonder is why a certain man was struck. he also makes the sage unsure “(as to what to do in the former case)”. read his version beside the characters and count the brackets.

敢 and 不敢: one breath, two directions. 此兩者, “these two”, names the pair: 敢, daring, and 不敢, not daring. the text does not set courage against cowardice. both sides are 勇; one breath goes two ways. each side needs the other. not daring has meaning only where daring is possible, and a bold act is clean only in a person who could also have held back. the pairs that follow turn the same way: 殺 and 活, 利 and 害. the opening lines lean toward not daring. the lean corrects an age that paid for boldness with heads. it is not a rule. 或利或害 can say that each side sometimes gains and sometimes harms, and the next line admits that nobody knows the reason. restraint also turns. held as a habit, it becomes a refusal to act when the hour needs the act. a reader who takes only one side loses the question: where does the breath go now?

holding back from a bold act can take as much courage as the act itself.. holding back from a bold act can take as much courage as the act itself. does this match what you have seen? recall one time when not acting was the braver thing, and one time when it was only fear. who taught you which of the two counts as courage: a parent, a team, a workplace? what did they call the person who waited? take the other side for a while: the bold act is the honest one, and waiting is a way to hide. what do you feel in the chest when you say that? when you judge someone as reckless, or as timid, what in yourself are you looking at?

nothing has to be seized or forced, because in the end nothing slips through the wide net.. nothing has to be seized or forced, because in the end nothing slips through the wide net. do you trust this? name one thing in your life that you believe would be lost if you stopped holding it tight. where does your answer come from? think of a time when something did slip away, and nobody caught it. now hold the opposite: the mesh is loose, and things are lost for good unless someone acts. stay there for a minute. is the feeling fear, or energy, or both? which picture do you live by on most days? what does it cost you, and what does it spare you?

nobody can know why some acts end well and others badly; even the wisest person finds it hard.. nobody can know why some acts end well and others badly; even the wisest person finds it hard. is that true in your experience, or do you think that results can mostly be explained? think of a good outcome that you count as earned. how much of it can you in fact account for? try the opposite view: there is a reason for each result, and a careful person can find it. what does that view give you? what weight does it put on you? which is harder for you to live with: a world with reasons that you failed to read, or a world that gives none?

網 three layers of a net. this character was built in three steps, and you can still see each one. step one is the picture 网: a frame with crossed cords inside. the shuowen says 下象网交文, “the lower part shows the crossed pattern of a net”, and credits the tool to the first sage, paoxi. step two: writers added 亡 inside the frame to mark the sound, and got 罔. but 罔 was soon borrowed for other words of the same sound: “to have none”, “to deceive”. step three: to make the net a net again, they added 糸, silk thread, on the left: 網. so the full character says “thread”, then “net”, then how to pronounce it. in 1956 the simplified script went back to step one, 网. now meet the family. as the top part of a character the net is flattened to 罒. the shuowen explains 羅 as a net of silk for birds. it explains 買, to buy, as a net over 貝, a cowrie shell: to net a profit at the market. and it says that 罪 was first a bamboo fish trap; the qin chose it for “crime”, because the old graph 辠 looked too much like 皇; commentators add that 皇 was the first emperor’s new title. since then, crime has been written with the net. the proverb about heaven’s net and the guilty was waiting in the script. fourteen strokes. the silk comes first, in six: a stroke that falls left and turns back; a second one below it; a dot that ties the twist; then three small dots in a row at the foot. keep this side narrow; it is the cord, and the net needs the room. stroke seven is the left wall of the frame. stroke eight makes the top and the right wall in one movement and ends in a hook. watch that corner: the brush stops, sets its shoulder, and comes down. inside, a dot and a short slash lean together; then a level line; then the three strokes of 亡, a dot, a level line, and an angle that closes the bottom. in seal script the inside was a true mesh of crossed lines. clerical script made it an abbreviation, and the eye still reads “net”.

勇 breath over sinew. two parts, one above the other. below is 力, strength. the shuowen calls it 筋也, sinew, and says the graph shows a sinew’s form; many modern scholars see in the oldest forms a digging tool like a plow, though this is debated. either way it is the force of a body at work. you know it from 男, a man: 田 field over 力, and the shuowen says 言男用力於田也, “it means that a man uses strength in the field”. above is 甬 (yong), which gives the sound. it is commonly explained as a picture of a bell with its handle; the shuowen gives a different account, of plants that burst into flower. the same part carries the same sound into 通 (to pass through), 桶 (a bucket), 踊 (to leap), and 涌 (to well up, of water). look at that list: things that rise or push through. sound-parts were often chosen with an ear for sense. now the surprise. the shuowen defines 勇 as 气, breath. and the dictionaries record an old variant that sets 心, the heart, in place of 力. so the tradition wrote courage two ways: as a rising over muscle, and as a rising over the heart. the laozi asks only which way it goes: into daring, or into not daring. nine strokes. the top begins with a short level stroke that turns and falls left, then a dot under it: a small cap. then the box: the left side down; the top and right side in one stroke with a corner; two short level lines; and an upright through the middle. seven strokes so far, and they should sit compact and a little narrow. now 力, in two strokes that decide the character. stroke eight goes right, turns the corner, falls with a slight lean, and ends in a hook to the left. stroke nine is the long sweep down to the lower left; it starts above the horizontal and passes through it. let it run out to a point. the box stays still, and the last stroke moves. a good writer makes the whole character lean forward a little, like a person about to step.

74 · the great carpenter’s axe. the people do not fear death. / how, then, frighten them with death? / suppose the people were made to fear death always, / and those who do the irregular: / i could seize them and kill them. / who would dare? / there is always the one in charge of killing, who kills. / to kill in the place of the one in charge of killing: / this is called hewing in the place of the great carpenter. / hew in the place of the great carpenter, / and seldom is the hand not hurt. the passage moves from a market square to a workshop. it opens with a fact and a question: the people do not dread death, so how can death frighten them? then a ruler’s voice tries the opposite case: suppose they always feared it, and i seized and killed each person who did the odd thing; who would dare? no answer follows. the text changes scene. killing has its own officer, the one in charge of killing. to kill in that officer’s place is to take the axe from the great carpenter and hew in the master’s place. the last line is dry: seldom is the hand not hurt. the passage holds a ghost’s head with tiger claws, a hawk’s stare, shackles, an office title, a heavy axe, and one cut hand. it is the third of four passages on fear and death. each person has a small ruler inside who governs by threat. it says: if you fail, you are worthless; if you rest, you will fall behind. the method works for a time. then a day comes when the threat has been used too often, and the inner people do not fear it. nothing moves. the passage describes this exactly: 民不畏死，奈何以死懼之. its second half offers a different trust. results have their own officer. an act that goes against the grain of things meets its end without a second punishment from you. to add self-hatred to a mistake is to hew in the place of the great carpenter. the mistake is seldom corrected by it, and the hand is hurt. can you leave a fault to its own result, and only watch? a leader who governs by fear needs the fear to stay fresh. each use spends some of it. the first line marks the point where it is all spent. in the text’s own world that point brought down a dynasty. the second half gives a more exact warning than “do not be harsh”. it names a fault of role: 代, to act in another’s place. many of the results that a leader wants to impose already have an agent: the response of colleagues, as wang bi says, or the plain result of the work, or a fair process that exists for the purpose. when the leader takes that work over in person, the anger of the punished and the fear of the watchers attach to the leader. shang yang died under his own law. ask before a hard act: whose axe is this? hold an axe once, if you can, or a heavy kitchen cleaver. the tool has its own line of fall. a trained hand lifts it and then mostly lets it go; the weight does the work, and the other hand stays outside the line. an untrained hand pushes the blade, corrects it in the air, and brings the free hand in to steady the wood. that is where the cut comes from. the zhuangzi’s carpenter whirls the axe until it makes a wind and removes a speck from a nose. the mastery is a relaxed arm and an exact stop. the verb 執, to seize, is the opposite body state: the fist closed, the forearm hard. a closed fist cannot feel where the edge is. notice your own grip the next time you use a knife. in a forest nothing is executed and everything dies. death has its seasons and its agents: frost, age, the hawk, the fungus that takes a tree which has finished. this is one old reading of the one in charge of killing: the standing order by which each thing reaches its term. people who take this office over, with good intentions, have often cut their own hand. they kill the wolves, and the deer strip the hillsides. they poison the insects, and the birds go. the passage does not say that nothing should ever be cut. a carpenter fells trees. it says that the cut is a master’s work, and that the master is already at the bench. what in your garden, or your care, would you leave to the frost? today, catch one threat that you make. it may be to a child, a colleague, or yourself: “if this happens again, then…”. do not judge it. ask the first question of the passage: does the other person still fear this? if the threat has been made many times, the honest answer is often no. then ask the second question: is this my axe? try, once, to name the natural result and step back from the role of the one who delivers it. say what will follow from the act, and do not say what you will do to the person. afterwards read legge’s version, with its capital “one”, and compare it with the plain job title in the chinese.

畏: a ghost’s head, a tiger’s claws. the shuowen explains 畏 as a monster. its definition is 惡也, “to find hateful”, and then it reads the picture: 鬼頭而虎爪，可畏也, “the head of a ghost and the claws of a tiger: a thing to dread”. the top part, now written like 田, a field, is for the shuowen the head of a spirit of the dead; the same head is the top of 鬼, ghost. so 畏 is not ordinary fear. it is the dread felt before a power that is not human: the dead, a great lord, heaven. confucius used the word for the three things that a noble person holds in awe. now read the first line again. the people do not 畏 death. the greatest of the powers has lost its ghost head for them. what has to happen to a people before that is true?
