two fears, three deaths, five killings. the first sentence uses two words for fear. the people do not 畏 death: 畏 is dread and awe, a lasting attitude. the ruler wants to 懼 them: 懼 is fright, and here it means “to cause fright”. the shuowen builds 懼 from 心, heart, and 瞿, and it defines 瞿 as 鷹隼之視也, “the stare of a hawk or falcon”: two eyes above a bird. so 懼 is the wide-eyed start of a creature that sees the hawk. a state can produce that start with an execution in the market. it cannot produce awe. count also the heavy words. 死, death, comes three times in the first sixteen characters. 殺, to kill, comes five times in the passage. no other passage of the book says it so often. in 常有司殺者殺 two 殺 stand back to back: the first ends a title, and the second is the verb. the sound of the text is a drum.

the logic that ended qin. the first line was tested in history. the state of qin united china in 221 bce with the strictest laws of the age. in 209 bce a group of conscripts was held up by rain on the way to a frontier post. under qin law the penalty for late arrival was death. their leader, chen sheng, put the case to them, as the historian sima qian records it: 今亡亦死，舉大計亦死, “now, to run away is death, and to start a great plan is also death”. they rose. within three years the dynasty was gone. a law that kills for everything leaves nothing to fear. the next passage gives the laozi’s own account of why a people comes to this point: those above them take too much, and so they take death lightly (75).

three “ifs” in the collated silk text. the received text has two steps: the people do not fear death; but suppose they always did. a modern collated edition of the mawangdui silk texts has three, each with 恆, “constantly” (our text writes 常; see the note on the taboo in passage 1). first: 若民恆且不畏死，奈何以殺懼之也, “if the people constantly do not fear death, how frighten them with killing?” second: 若民恆是畏死, if they constantly do fear it, then “i” may kill the offender, and who will dare? third: 若民恆且必畏死，則恆有司殺者, “if the people constantly and surely fear death, then there is constantly one in charge of killing”. the third step is absent from our text. (our 若使 may also be a plain “if”: “if the people always feared death”.) it ties the two halves of the passage together. where death is truly feared, the office of killing is already filled, and the ruler does not need to take it.

wang bi on 奇, the odd. wang bi comments on only one word of the first sentence: 詭異亂群謂之奇也, “the devious and strange, that which disturbs the group, is called 奇”. the shuowen gives the plain sense: 異也。一曰不耦, “different; another explanation: not paired”, an odd number. so 為奇者 are “those who do the odd thing”. it is not a word for a crime that a code lists. it is whatever does not match. that makes it a dangerous word in a ruler’s mouth, because the ruler decides what matches. the laozi uses it elsewhere without blame: 以奇用兵, “use the irregular to use weapons” (57), and 正復為奇, “the regular turns again into the irregular” (58). the state prizes in a general the same quality that it kills in a subject.

who says “i”?. 吾, “i”, speaks in a number of passages of this book. only here does it have a sword. the speaker can seize and kill. so the voice is a ruler’s, or the voice of a teacher who speaks as a ruler for one sentence to try the thought. 得 is “to get to, to have the chance”; our “could” follows it. the sentence is a trial in thought. suppose the method works: fear is constant, and i remove each person who steps out of line. the voice asks a question, and then it does not answer. it turns away to speak of the executioner and the carpenter. english needs a “them” after “seize” and after “kill”, twice; the chinese has one 之 for both. notice how quickly the “i” leaves the passage after this line. it does not return.

執: the arrest inside “to hold”. 執 is the common classical word for “to hold, to grasp”. here it has its first sense. the shuowen defines it as 捕罪人也, “to arrest an offender”. its left part is, for the shuowen, a thing 所以驚人, “used to terrify people”; the early forms are commonly explained as a pair of shackles, with a kneeling person whose hands are in them. the same part stands in 報, which the shuowen defines as passing sentence on an offender. so when the laozi says elsewhere 執者失之, “the one who grasps loses it” (29, 64), an early reader could see the fetters in the verb. to grasp a thing is to put it under arrest. here the ruler dreams of that grip on a whole people.

dare to do what?. 孰敢 is two characters: “who dares?” the verb has no object. the usual reading supplies one from the line before: who would dare to do the irregular thing? then the sentence is the ruler’s boast, and the rest of the passage answers it. a second reading takes the question another way: seize them and kill them, and who would dare to do that? then the doubt is already inside the ruler’s sentence. the second reading has a witness in the passage before this one, which opened with the same verb: 勇於敢則殺, courage in daring ends in killing (73). there the one who dares is the one near the blade. our rendering leaves the object out, as the chinese does. which question do you hear?

who is in charge of killing?. 司殺者 is “the one who has charge of killing”. 司 is an office word. zhou and warring states governments were full of such titles: 司馬, in charge of horses, the minister of war; 司寇, in charge of bandits, the minister of justice; 司空, in charge of works. so the phrase sounds like a post in a ministry. the text does not say who holds it. three answers are old. it is heaven, whose wide net loses nothing. it is death itself, which comes to each person at the due time. or it is the proper officer of the law, and the warning is to a ruler who kills by personal will, outside the process. wang bi gives a fourth answer. english versions that write “the executioner” or “one who presides” have already chosen. the chinese gives a job title and leaves the desk empty.

wang bi: the executioner is everyone. wang bi’s comment on the last lines does not mention heaven. he writes: 為逆，順者之所惡忿也；不仁者，人之所疾也。故曰，常有司殺也。 “one who acts against the order is the thing that those who go with the order hate and resent. one who is without humaneness is the thing that people detest. so the text says: there is always one in charge of killing.” for wang bi the standing executioner is the common feeling of the people. a person who does real harm is already surrounded: neighbours turn away, help stops, the group closes. the ruler does not need to add a blade to this, and a ruler who does so takes on a hatred that was not aimed at the ruler before. does a group that you know punish in this way, without any officer?

代: to take another’s turn. 代 is written with 亻, a person, and 弋, which gives the sound. the shuowen defines it in one word: 更也, “to change over”, as when one watchman relieves the next. from this come the later senses “a generation” and “a dynasty”: each takes the place of the one before. in this passage the word comes three times in the last two sentences, and it carries the charge. the ruler is not accused of cruelty. the ruler is accused of substitution: of standing at another’s post and doing another’s work. the zhuangzi uses the same word for the same fault: even if the cook does not keep the kitchen in order, the priest does not step over the ritual vessels 而代之, “and take the cook’s place”. what work do you do that is in fact someone else’s turn?

the carpenter who did not hurt the nose. 匠 is a woodworker, and 大匠 is the master of the craft. under the han the title of the director of palace building works contained these two characters. the zhuangzi tells of such a master, carpenter shi. a man of ying had a speck of plaster on the tip of his nose, as thin as a fly’s wing, and asked the carpenter to cut it off. 匠石運斤成風, “carpenter shi whirled his axe until it made a wind”, and hewed. the plaster was gone and 鼻不傷, “the nose was not hurt”. the story uses the two key words of our last line: 斲, to hew, and 傷, to hurt. that is what the great carpenter’s stroke is like. it removes exactly what must go and touches nothing else. now put the same axe in the hand of a person who has only watched.

斲: the axe at work. 斲 (zhuo) is to hew: to shape timber with blows of an edged tool. the shuowen defines it by another axe word, 斫, and files it under 斤. 斤 is the tool itself; the shuowen says 斫木也。象形, “it chops wood; a picture”. it was an axe or an adze, with a heavy head on a bent handle, swung toward the worker’s own feet and hands. this is not carving with a knife at a bench. a beam is squared by a row of full blows, each a finger’s width from the last. the skill is in the stop. later 斤 was borrowed for a unit of weight, the catty, and most readers now know only that sense. the tool is still inside 斧 (axe), 析 (to split wood), and 匠 (the carpenter).

the lawmaker’s hand. 希有不傷其手 is a craftsman’s understatement: “seldom is there one who does not wound the hand”. the age gave examples. shang yang rebuilt the state of qin in the fourth century bce on rewards, registers, and harsh punishments, with whole groups of households liable for one member’s offence. when his patron died in 338 bce he fled. an innkeeper refused him a bed, because lord shang’s own law punished anyone who lodged a traveller without papers. he was caught, and his body was torn apart by chariots. li si, the minister who helped the first emperor apply the same method to all of china, was cut in two in the market in 208 bce. the laozi may be older or younger than shang yang; scholars do not agree on its date. the carpenter’s proverb did not need to wait for him.

four passages on fear and death. passages 72 to 75 stand together and speak to each other. 72 begins 民不畏威，則大威至: when the people do not dread authority, a greater dread arrives. 73 sets courage in daring against courage in not daring, and ends with heaven’s net, wide and with a loose mesh, that loses nothing. 74, this one, asks what use it is to threaten death, and warns against killing in another’s place. 75 gives the cause: the people starve and take death lightly because those above them consume too much. read in a row, the four make one argument about the limits of fear as a tool of rule. they share words: 畏 in 72 and 74, 敢 and 殺 in 73 and 74, 死 in 74 and 75, 民 in three of the four. read alone, each one sounds like a proverb. in sequence they sound like a case brought before a ruler.

legge’s capital o. legge writes: “there is always one who presides over the infliction death”. the capital letter is his. for a missionary of 1891 the reader could supply only one name for that one. the chinese 司殺者 has no capital, no “one”, and no “he”; it is a job title. legge also turns 為奇者, “those who do the odd thing”, into “those who do wrong”, so that the ruler’s targets are plainly guilty. and he softens the ruler’s act with “put them to death”, the language of a court, where the chinese has the bare 殺, kill. with these three changes the passage becomes a sermon: leave judgment to god. that reading is possible. but the text chose a workshop for its picture, and not a throne room.

whose axe is this?. the next time you are about to punish, ask the carpenter’s question first. the punishment may be small: a cold reply, a public correction, the removal of a task from someone who failed at it. before you act, ask three things. is this my post, or do i stand in for someone or something else: the group, the rules, the plain result of the person’s own act? has the result perhaps already arrived without me? and where is my hand in relation to the edge? you do not have to decide against acting. a carpenter does hew. the passage only says that the one who takes the tool from the master is seldom unhurt. notice, a day later, where the cut went.

畏 and 不畏: fear spends itself. the passage stands on two cases: 民不畏死, the people do not fear death, and 常畏死, they fear it constantly. the pair is 畏 and 不畏, dread and its absence. the ruler of the middle lines wants one side only: constant fear. the text shows why that side cannot be held alone. fear needs something to lose. when threat takes that thing away, fear turns into its opposite, and the people of the first line are the result. passage 72 says it in one sentence: 民不畏威，則大威至, when the people do not dread authority, a greater dread arrives. so each side makes the other. the text does not rank them. fearlessness is not praised here as courage; it is a symptom. dread is not praised as order; it is the thing that a threat uses up. a second pair stands under this one: 奇, the odd, and its unnamed partner 正, the regular, which turn into each other. who decides which is which?

fear that is used too often stops working, and people with nothing left to lose cannot be threatened.. fear that is used too often stops working, and people with nothing left to lose cannot be threatened. have you seen this happen, in a family, a school, a job, or in the way you speak to yourself? which threats were used on you when you were young? which of them still work, and which wore out? take the other side: a firm threat, kept fresh and carried out, is what holds people and habits in line. say it as if you believed it. what in you agrees? what does your answer show about how much you trust people, or yourself, to act well without fear?

results have their own agent, and whoever steps in to deliver the punishment in person is usually the one hurt.. results have their own agent, and whoever steps in to deliver the punishment in person is usually the one hurt. do you believe that wrong acts meet their result without your help? what evidence do you have, for and against? recall a time when you punished someone, in a small way or a large one. where did the cut land? now the opposite: if you do not act, nobody will, and the harm goes on. stay with that. is there anger in it, or duty, or a wish to be the one who sets things right? whose work do you most often take over? what would you have to feel if you left it to them?

匠 an axe in its box. two parts, and the shuowen names both: 从匚从斤, “from 匚 and from 斤”. 匚 is a box seen from the side, open to the right; the shuowen calls it 受物之器, “a vessel that receives things”. 斤 is the axe, and the shuowen adds a line of pure workshop sense: 斤，所以作器也, “the axe is that with which vessels are made”. so 匠 is an axe in its box, and the definition is 木工也, a worker in wood. now follow the axe through its family. the shuowen explains 兵, weapon or soldier, as two hands that hold a 斤. it explains 析, to split, as 木 wood and 斤. for 所, now the common word for “place”, it gives 伐木聲也, “the sound of felling trees”, and quotes the book of odes; the word was borrowed for its sound. 新, new, is defined as 取木也, “to take wood”; the firewood sense is now written 薪, with grass on top, and the old graph was left with “new”: fresh-cut. 斧, the usual word for axe, sets 父, father, on top for the sound. look how much of daily language was cut with this tool. the last line of the passage uses the verb that belongs to it, 斲, which has the same 斤 on its right side. the carpenter keeps the axe in a box. who taught you where to keep yours? six strokes, and the order is the lesson. stroke one is the lid of the box, a level line. then the brush leaves the box unfinished and writes the whole axe inside it: a short flat stroke that falls left, the blade; a longer one that falls left below it; a level line; an upright. only then does stroke six close the box: down the left side, a firm turn at the corner, and along the bottom, a little past the lid above. this rule holds for all characters of this frame: the contents go in before the box is shut. watch the turn in the last stroke. in regular script the brush lifts slightly, sets down again, and moves right with even weight. in seal script the frame was a smooth curve, like bent wood.

畏 ghost head, tiger claws. cover the lower half and you see 田, a field. that is an accident of later writing. the shuowen calls this top part 甶 and defines it as 鬼頭也, “the head of a ghost”: the large, strange head of a spirit of the dead. you can find the same head, with one small stroke above it, at the top of 鬼, ghost; the shuowen says of that word 人所歸爲鬼, “that to which a person returns is called 鬼”. below the head, in 畏, the shuowen sees what is left of 虎, tiger: 鬼頭而虎爪，可畏也, “a ghost’s head and a tiger’s claws: a thing to dread”. modern scholars read the oldest forms a little differently, commonly as a ghost-headed figure that holds a rod or weapon. both readings agree on the main point: 畏 is a picture of the thing feared, and the thing is not human. compare 懼, the passage’s other word for fear, which shows the one who is afraid: a heart, and the two wide eyes of a bird. and compare the field that is a real field: 男, a man, is 田 over 力, strength; the shuowen says a man uses strength in the field. the same square shape is a ghost’s face in one character and a farm in the other. a reader has to learn, for each one, what stands behind the square. nine strokes. the head takes five: the left side down; the top and right side in one stroke with a corner; the inner level line; the inner upright; the base that shuts it. make the head wide and not tall. stroke six is a long level line under it, wider than the head, like shoulders. the last three strokes are the claws. stroke seven goes straight down from the line and flicks up to the right at its foot. stroke eight is a short slash that falls left from the right side. stroke nine is the long pressing stroke to the lower right: the brush starts light, grows heavy, and lifts to a point. that last stroke carries the weight of the whole character. in clerical script it flares into a broad tail.

司 a ruler in the mirror. the shuowen says something unusual about this character: 从反后, “it is 后 turned around”. put the two side by side: 后 and 司. each has a mouth, 口, and one level stroke, under a cover; in 后 the cover opens to the right, and in 司 it opens to the left. for the shuowen 后 is the sovereign who 施令以告四方, “issues orders to inform the four quarters”: a figure with a mouth that gives commands. 司 is the mirror image, and its definition is 臣司事於外者, “a minister who manages affairs outside”, away from the court. so the lord faces one way and speaks; the officer faces the other way and carries the word out. modern scholars think that in the oldest writing the two were often one graph written in either direction. the shuowen’s reading is still a good way to remember them, and it shows how a han scholar thought about office: an officer is a ruler reversed. the family is large. 詞, a word or phrase, has 言, speech, beside 司. 伺, to watch and wait on, adds a person. 飼, to feed animals, adds food. in each, someone attends to a charge. in this passage the charge is killing, and the text asks the ruler to respect the officer’s desk. five strokes. the first is the cover and it does most of the work: a level line to the right, a firm corner, a long fall with a slight lean inward, and a hook to the left at the foot. give it height; the rest lives under it. stroke two is a short level line, set high and not touching the right wall. then the mouth, in three: the left side down; the top and right side with a corner; the base. keep the mouth small and to the left, so that white space stays between it and the hook. that open space is the character’s balance. in running script the level line and the mouth often flow together in one turning movement, and the hook becomes a quick return of the wrist.

75 · those above eat. the people starve. / those above them eat so much in grain tax: / that is why they starve. / the people are hard to govern. / those above them have their doings: / that is why they are hard to govern. / the people take death lightly. / those above them seek life’s thickness: / that is why they take death lightly. / only the one who does nothing for the sake of life / is worthier than prizing life. three sentences with one frame, then a fourth that breaks it. the people starve: those above them eat so much grain tax. the people are in disorder: those above them have their doings. the people hold death light: those above them pile life thick. each sentence returns to its first words, like a door that shuts. the last sentence changes the subject from classes to a kind of person: the one with no doing for life’s sake is worth more than prizing life. the things in the passage are a failed harvest, a mouth, a measure of grain, a light chariot, a mountain, and a cowrie shell. the passage ends the group that began at 72, and it answers the first line of 74: this is why the people do not fear death. read the three sentences as a map of one person. there is a part that rules: the planner, the one with ambitions for this life. there is a part that is ruled: the body, the plain energies of the day. when the planner takes too much, the body starves: of sleep, of unclaimed time. when the planner has many projects, the body becomes hard to govern: it stalls, it falls ill, it does the opposite. when the planner reaches for a thicker life, something below begins to hold life cheap, and takes risks or goes numb. the last line points past the usual cure. the usual cure is to prize life more: more care, better habits. the text says that there is something better, a living that is not a project at all. it does not explain how. it only says that such a one is worth more. the passage is the plainest statement of responsibility in the book. wang bi’s summary is “it comes from above”. when a group is poor in something, ask first what the top takes: salary is the obvious thing, and time, credit, and attention are the larger ones. when a group is hard to lead, count the initiatives; 有為 includes good ideas. when people stop caring whether they stay or go, look at how richly the leaders live in comparison. the figures of one farm in wei show how small the margin below can be while those above see only a fair tithe. the frame of the sentences gives the discipline: start with the people, go up to yourself for the cause, and come back down to check the result. try the exercise once with a real complaint. a body can be over-governed. the person who diets by rule, trains by plan, tracks sleep, and takes ten supplements is “seeking life’s thickness”. the early daoists knew this type well, and so does passage 50, where those who live life too thickly walk toward the place of death. the practices that later grew from this book go the other way. the breath is not driven; it is left to become fine by itself. the posture is not held up by will; the weight is given to the ground. in such practice the body becomes easy to “govern” at the moment when the governor stops having plans for it. sit for five minutes and do nothing for the sake of your health. do not improve the breath. notice whether the body takes this as neglect or as relief. a field has a simple law: it can give only what grew. a tax in grain is a claim on a living system, and the system has a floor. the seed for next year, the food of the people who work the land, the fodder of the ox: when the claim goes below that floor, the yield of every later year falls. li kui’s sum is an early piece of ecology in this sense; it finds the floor by counting. the first line of the passage sees the same thing from below. the shuowen’s 饑 is a year when the grain does not ripen. the passage adds a second kind of failed harvest: the grain ripens, and it does not reach the mouths of the growers. any system where the top feeds on the base has this limit. a forest shows the other pattern: the canopy drops its leaves to feed the roots. at one meal today, trace the food upward and downward. downward: who grew it, carried it, cooked it? upward: who takes a share of the price on the way, and are you, in other parts of your life, one of those who take a share of the work of others? do not turn this into guilt; the passage is a diagnosis and gives no sentence. then make one small change in the direction of the last line. find one thing that you do purely “for the sake of life”, to thicken it: an upgrade, a precaution, an extra. leave it out for one day and watch what the day is like. if you like, compare the three versions of the third sentence: ours, the collated silk text, and legge.

饑: when the grain does not ripen. chinese has two old words that english gives as “hunger”, and they sound the same. 飢 is the hunger of a body; the shuowen defines it as 餓, to starve. 饑, the word in our text, is larger. the shuowen says 穀不孰爲饑, “when the grain does not ripen, that is called 饑”. it is a failed harvest, a famine year; the dictionary has a second word, 饉, for a year when the vegetables fail. famine in this sense comes from heaven: drought, flood, locusts. the line takes this word and gives it a human cause. the grain ripened, and the people starve. a modern collated edition of the mawangdui silk texts writes the famine word in the opening clause and the body word in the conclusion: 是以飢. so the event of the first clause becomes the empty belly of the last.

wang bi: it comes from above. the text does not say “the ruler”, “the lords”, or “the government”. it says 其上, “their above”: whoever stands over them. the word is a direction, and it covers the king, the minister, the tax officer, and the landlord in one stroke. wang bi sums up the whole passage in a sentence: 言民之所以僻，治之所以亂，皆由上不由其下也，民從上也。 “it says: the reason why the people go crooked, and the reason why order turns to disorder, both come from above and do not come from those below. the people follow those above.” this is a hard rule for anyone who leads. it removes the usual excuse, that the people are lazy or lawless by nature. wang bi served at a court. he knew who would read the sentence.

食稅: to eat the tax. the verb is 食, to eat. tax was paid in grain, so the phrase is nearly literal: those above eat the tax. the people and their superiors eat from one harvest, and the text counts only one thing, 多, how much goes up. the picture was common in the age. an old song in the book of odes speaks to a tax-taker as to a rat: 碩鼠碩鼠，無食我黍, “big rat, big rat, do not eat my millet”. mencius told a king to his face: there is fat meat in your kitchen and there are fat horses in your stable, and the people have the look of hunger; 此率獸而食人也, “this is to lead on beasts to eat people”. english “consume” or “levy” makes the act clean. the chinese keeps the mouth in it.

稅: grain, measured out. 稅 has 禾, the grain plant, on the left; the shuowen defines it as 租, rent on a field. the word marks a change in how states lived. under the old zhou system, as later writers describe it, farmers worked a lord’s plot beside their own. in 594 bce the chronicle of lu records three words: 初稅畝, “for the first time, a tax by the acre”. from then on a state measured each field and took a share of what grew. the fair share in confucian memory was one part in ten. a lord of lu complained that two parts in ten were not enough for him, and a disciple of confucius answered: 百姓足，君孰與不足, “if the hundred families have enough, with whom will the ruler lack?” armies of the warring states ate from this tax.

a farmer’s accounts, about 400 bce. li kui, a minister of the state of wei, worked out the budget of an ordinary farm, and the han history preserves his sum. one man with a family of five works a hundred mu of land. in a normal year it yields 150 measures of grain. the tithe takes 15. the family eats 90. the 45 that remain are sold; after the costs of the village rites and of clothing, the year ends 450 coins short. sickness, funerals, and extra levies are not yet counted. this is the tax at its fair rate, in a good year, by a government’s own figures. li kui wanted the state to buy and sell grain so that such families would survive. now add a war, a new palace, or a bad harvest, and read the first line of the passage again.

a proof that closes like a trap. the first three sentences have one frame. 民之 x: the people’s x. 以其上…: because of their above. 是以 x: for this reason, x. each sentence ends with the two characters that it began with: 饑…饑, 難治…難治, 輕死…輕死. the form is that of a court argument, and it leaves no gap for a second cause. in each sentence 民 comes first and 上 comes in the middle, so the eye moves from the people up to their rulers and back down to the people. three times the result lands where it started. the frame also hides a climb: hunger, then disorder, then contempt for death. that last step is the opening of the passage before this one: 民不畏死. so this passage gives the cause of that one, after the fact. what, in the fourth sentence, breaks the frame?

hard to govern, or simply not in order. 治 has water on its left. the shuowen records it only as the name of a river; it is commonly explained as the work of managing water, with dikes and channels, and from that the work of putting a state in order. a well-governed state is one where things flow in their beds. 難治, “hard to govern”, appears also in passage 65, and there the cause is the people’s cleverness. here the cause is above. a modern collated edition of the mawangdui silk texts reads differently in this sentence: 百姓之不治也, “the hundred families are not in order”. in that version the people are not “hard” for someone. they are in disorder, a plain state of affairs. the received wording looks at them from the ruler’s chair. which sentence would a farmer have said?

有為: the opposite of wu wei. 有為 is “to have doing”. it is the exact opposite of the book’s most famous term, 無為, “to be without doing”: to act without force, and without a project laid over things. so the second sentence is a technical one. the people are hard to govern because their rulers govern: plan, order, reform, build, mobilise. english versions say “interfere” or “meddle”, which makes the fault a bad habit. the chinese is neutral and wider. it includes the well-meant programme. a modern collated edition of the mawangdui silk texts has one more word: 有以為, “have something that they act for”, a purpose behind the doing. passage 38 uses the same phrase to mark the line between the highest 德 and the lower kinds. passage 57 gives the other side: 我無為而民自化, “i am without doing, and the people change of themselves”.

輕: a light chariot. 輕 has 車, a cart, on its left, and the shuowen defines it as 輕車也, “a light chariot”: the fast war vehicle with little armour. from that came “light” in every sense, and “to treat lightly”. 輕死 is to hold death as a light thing. the phrase sounds brave, and soldiers were praised for it. the text uses it as a symptom. a people that takes death lightly will rebel, rob, or enlist; it has nothing heavy to hold it down. the book likes this pair of weights. 重為輕根, “the heavy is the root of the light” (26). the good small state of passage 80 is one where the people 重死, “take death heavily”, and so do not move far away. light death and thick life stand in one line here. what makes a life heavy enough to keep?

who seeks the thick life?. our pinned text reads 以其上求生之厚: because those above them seek life’s thickness. the third sentence then matches the first two, and the rulers’ luxury is the cause. a modern collated edition of the mawangdui silk texts has no 上 here: 以亓求生之厚也, “because of their seeking life’s thickness”. the standard wang bi and heshang gong editions also lack it. the 上 of our pinned text is reported from the fu yi edition, and wang bi’s own comment, “it comes from above”, supports it. then “their” points back to the people. they themselves strain after a rich living, take risks for it, and so hold death cheap. legge translated a text of this kind. scholars are divided. some think that a later editor added 上 to make three matched sentences. others think that an early scribe dropped it. both versions lead to the same last line, because the last line is not addressed to a class. whoever makes life into a thing to be piled up, above or below, is the one it speaks of.

厚: thick as a mountain. 厚 is thickness. the shuowen defines it by the largest thick thing it knows: 山陵之厚也, “the thickness of mountains and hills”. the cliff sign 厂 is at its upper left. from this come the senses rich, generous, heavy, lavish. 生之厚 is “the thickness of life”: layers of food, cloth, servants, and tonics. the same phrase is in passage 50, in a darker place. three people in ten, it says there, move from life toward the place of death. why? 以其生生之厚, “because they live life so thickly”. the word is not always blame. passage 55 praises one who holds 德 thickly, 含德之厚, and compares that person to a newborn child. so thickness is good in what you are and dangerous in what you add. modern versions that write “security” or “survival” miss the point: the fault is excess, and fear is not mentioned.

無以生為: six ways to fail in english. the phrase has four characters: 無 (without), 以 (taking, by means of), 生 (life), 為 (doing, making). word for word: “without taking life as a doing”. one reading: the person who does not act for the sake of life, who has no project called “my life”. a second: the person who does not make something of life, does not work it up. a third, closer to the ruler: one who does not use the living of others as material. all three are in the chinese. english must add a subject, “the one who”, because the chinese has only 者, a marker that turns the phrase into “such a one”. note what the phrase does not say. it does not say “despise life” or “give life up”. the person still lives. only the 為, the forced doing on top of life, is absent.

貴生: a slogan of the age. 貴生, “to prize life”, was the name of a teaching. its best-known voice was yang zhu, of the fourth century bce. mencius attacked him in a famous line: he would not pull out one hair to benefit the whole world. yang zhu’s own writings are lost. the teaching survives in a compendium made in qin about 239 bce, which has a chapter with this title; it says that a wise person will not harm the body for a throne. that was a serious position in an age that spent lives freely, and it is close to parts of the laozi (13, 44). so the last line makes a fine distinction inside its own camp. to prize life is good. to have no need to prize it is better, because the one who prizes a thing begins to guard it, feed it, and fear for it. is that distinction real in your experience?

賢 and 貴: two words with money in them. look at the bottom of 賢 and of 貴. both stand on 貝, the cowrie shell, which the early chinese used as money; the shuowen says 古者貨貝, “the ancients used shells as goods”. 貴 is defined as 物不賤也, “a thing that is not cheap”: dear, costly, and so honoured. 賢 is defined as 多才, “with much ability”; many scholars think that the first sense was “with much wealth”, and that the word then moved from rich to able to good. with 於 after it, 賢 makes a comparison: “worth more than”. so the closing line can be heard in the language of a market: the one who does nothing for life’s sake is worth more than pricing life high. the passage began with grain that was taken. it ends by asking what a life is worth, and it uses the words of the people who did the taking.

legge’s “superiors” and their “agency”. legge’s first sentence is strong: the people starve “because of the multitude of taxes consumed by their superiors”. “consumed” keeps part of the eating. his second sentence shows a scholar who is uneasy. 有為 becomes “the (excessive) agency of their superiors (in governing them)”, with two sets of brackets. a victorian who believed in good government could not write that government as such was the cause; he added “excessive”. in the third sentence he follows the editions that have no 上, and he makes the people the ones who labour “in seeking for the means of living”. that turns thick living into bare survival, and the rulers leave the sentence. his last line advises us “to leave the subject of living altogether out of view”. it is the calm of a study. the chinese is nearer to the field.

look one level up. take one complaint that you have about people in your care or under your direction: children, a team, students, tenants. write it in the frame of the passage. “they are …” on the first line. then, before any other cause, try the second line as the text gives it: “because the one above them …”, and put yourself there. what do you eat that they have grown? time, attention, credit, the pleasant tasks? what do you do, 有為, that makes them hard to lead? fill in the line even if you do not believe it. then read the three lines aloud. the passage does not claim that this is always the whole truth. it claims that it is the first place to look, and the last place where those above usually look.

輕 and 厚: light death, thick life. the third sentence joins two weights: 輕死, death held light, and 生之厚, life piled thick. they are one fact seen from two ends. where life is made thick in one place, it grows thin in another, and there death weighs little. the same holds for the pair that frames all three sentences, 上 and 民, above and below: each is defined by the other, and the harvest is one. the last line favors doing nothing for the sake of life over prizing life. that preference corrects an age, and a class, that thickened life at the cost of others. it is not contempt for life. it also turns. the person who drops the project of life stands close to the people who take death lightly, and the passage treats their lightness as a symptom. passage 80 wants death to be heavy again. so light and heavy trade places from line to line. which of the two do you carry now?

when the people below are hungry, unruly, or careless of life, the first cause is in those above them.. when the people below are hungry, unruly, or careless of life, the first cause is in those above them. do you agree? test it on a group where you are below, and then on a group where you are above. which is easier for you to say: “they are the problem”, or “i am”? where did you learn that reflex? hold the opposite for a few minutes: people answer for their own state, whoever leads them. what is true in that? what does it protect you from? look at where you blame upward and where you blame downward. do the two match the places where you have power?

the more those in charge plan, reform, and manage, the harder the people become to lead.. the more those in charge plan, reform, and manage, the harder the people become to lead. where have you watched this happen? where have you watched the reverse: a group that drifted because no one gave direction? when something goes wrong near you, is your first move to do more? who showed you that move? try the opposite on: good order needs active hands, and to leave things alone is neglect. how does your body respond to that sentence? what would you learn about yourself if you did less for one week and things went well?

a life that is guarded and thickened as a project is worth less than a life that is simply lived.. a life that is guarded and thickened as a project is worth less than a life that is simply lived. is this so for you? list what you do purely to make your life longer, safer, or fuller. what is under that effort: an illness in the family, a lean time, a fear of missing something? now take the other side: life is the one thing you have, and to prize and protect it is plain good sense. let that be right for a while. what relaxes, and what tightens? think of someone who takes great care of their life, and someone who takes none. which one annoys you more? what might that say?

食 a lid over the grain. 食 is the noun “food” and the verb “to eat”, and in this passage it is what rulers do to the tax. the shuowen takes the character apart as 亼 over 皀. 皀 is its word for 穀之馨香, “the fragrance of grain”: a vessel with good grain inside, and at the foot a spoon to take it up. 亼, the roof shape at the top, means “to bring together”; the shuowen says it gives the sound, and adds that some read the two parts together as one meaning. modern scholars commonly explain the whole graph as one picture: a food vessel on a stand, heaped with cooked grain, with its lid above. both accounts agree that the character shows grain that is ready to eat. that matters in this passage, where food and tax are the same substance. as the left side of other characters it becomes 飠, and the family is large: 飯 (cooked grain; a meal), 飽 (full; the shuowen says 猒, satisfied), 養 (to feed and so to rear, with 羊, sheep, for the sound), 餘 (plenty; what is left over), 飢 and 餓 (hunger). and 饑, the famine of the first line, is 食 with 幾 beside it for the sound; 幾 by itself means “how much?” or “almost”. the passage puts 饑 and 食 a few characters apart: the people’s famine, and the eating above. they share the same vessel. who lifts the lid? nine strokes. the first two are the lid: a long stroke that falls to the left and a long one that presses out to the right, meeting at the peak. make them wide; everything else sits under this roof. stroke three is a small dot under the peak. stroke four makes the top and the right side of the vessel in one movement with a corner. strokes five and six are the two short level lines inside. stroke seven comes down the left side and, at the foot, flicks up to the right; this lift joins the vessel to its base. stroke eight is a short slash to the left, and stroke nine is a last press to the lower right. in clerical script the two roof strokes spread like wings. when 食 stands at the left as 飠, the final press shrinks to a dot, to make room for its neighbour.

稅 grain handed over. on the left is 禾, the grain plant. the shuowen calls it 嘉穀, “the fine grain”, and notes that it sprouts in the second month and ripens in the eighth; the top stroke of the graph, bent to the left, is the heavy ear that hangs down. in north china this was millet. you meet 禾 in 秋 (autumn; in its modern shape, grain and fire), 種 (seed), 私 (private; the shuowen says it first named a kind of grain), 利 (gain; in its modern shape, grain and a knife), 和 (harmony, where 禾 gives the sound), and 租 (rent on a field). on the right is 兌 (dui), which gives the sound. the shuowen defines 兌 as 說, and it carries a group of senses: to loosen, to exchange, to be pleased. it is the sound-part of 說 (to explain; in old texts also “to be glad”), 脫 (to shed, to take off), 銳 (sharp), and 悅 (glad). so 稅 is grain plus a word that sounds like “take off”. scholars do not all agree that the sense of 兌 plays a part here, and the safe statement is that it marks the sound. still, an early reader saw grain and a shedding. tax was the part of the harvest that came off the top. the shuowen’s definition is one word, 租. the passage’s definition is one verb: it is what those above eat. the first chinese record of such a tax is three characters long. twelve strokes: five for the grain, seven for the right side. 禾 begins with the ear, a short stroke that falls from right to left, almost flat. then a level line; then the upright stalk through it; then a slash to the lower left and a dot to the lower right, the leaves. on the left side of a character the last stroke of 禾 is always a dot and never a long press, so that the plant does not push into its neighbour. now 兌: two short strokes at the top that lean toward each other; the mouth 口 in three strokes; and below it two legs, a slash to the left and then a stroke that goes down, bends, runs right, and ends in an upward hook. that final hook is the longest line in the character and balances the tall stalk on the other side.

賢 the shell under “worthy”. the lower half is 貝, a cowrie. the shuowen says it is 海介蟲, “a shelled creature of the sea”, and tells its history in a line: the ancients used shells as money and treasured the tortoise; the zhou had coins; the qin abolished shells and used cash. the script kept what the market dropped. almost every word about value stands on this shell. 財 is wealth, 人所寶也, “what people treasure”. 貨 is goods. 買 is to buy and 賣 is to sell. 賤 is cheap, and the shuowen says 賈少也, “the price is low”. 貧, poor, is 分 over 貝, and the shuowen reads it as it looks: 財分少也, “wealth, divided, is little”. 賞 is a reward. 貴 is dear. the upper half of 賢 is 臤, which the shuowen defines as 堅, firm, and it adds: 古文以爲賢字, “the old script used this as the character 賢”. so the first way to write “worthy” was “firm”: a hand, 又, beside 臣, a servant. the shell came later. you can see 臤 again in 堅 (hard: firm earth) and 緊 (tight: firm thread). 賢 is then a firm servant with a shell: able, and also rich in means. the laozi distrusts the word: 不尚賢, “do not exalt the worthy” (3). here it uses it only to compare, and the thing that it rates higher has no price. fifteen strokes. first 臣, in six: a level line at the top; a short upright under it; a level stroke that turns down at a corner; a short level line inside; a second short upright; and last the long stroke that goes down the left side and turns along the bottom, as in a box that is shut after it is filled. keep it narrow. then 又, in two: a level stroke that turns and falls left, and a long press to the right that crosses it. these two parts share the upper half and must leave each other room; 又 sits a little lower and reaches out. then the shell, in seven: the left side; the top and right side with a corner; a level line inside; a second; a third that closes the box; a slash to the left; and a dot to the right. the feet should spread just wider than the box.

76 · soft alive, stiff dead. a person, alive, is soft and weak; / dead, hard and strong. / the ten thousand things, the grasses and trees, / alive, are soft and tender; / dead, dry and withered. / so the hard and strong are the company of death; / the soft and weak are the company of life. / for this reason / an army that is strong does not win; / a tree that is strong meets the axe. / the strong and great take the place below; / the soft and weak take the place above. the passage is a proof from the hand, in four steps. step one: touch a person. alive, the body is soft and weak; dead, it is hard and stiff. step two: touch a plant. alive, it is soft and tender; dead, it is dry wood. step three, the rule, perhaps an old saying: hardness belongs to death’s company, softness to life’s. step four applies the rule to the two things that the age admired most, a strong army and a tall tree: the first does not win, and the second is cut down. the close turns the tree into a diagram: thick trunk below, soft twigs above. the key word 強 comes five times. the evidence is all physical: skin, a shoot, a dry stick, an axe. no abstraction is needed, and the text uses none. apply the test to the mind. a living view can be bent and comes back; it can take a question. a dead view is hard: it cannot be touched without a crack, and so it has to be defended. most of us carry some of each. the hard ones feel like our strength, and they are often the positions we are most proud of. the passage suggests that they are the parts that have already stopped. this is uncomfortable, and the text does not soften it: 弱 is “weak”, the word that no one wants. to let a fixed opinion become tender again is to feel, for a while, without defence. that feeling is the brittle softness of a new shoot. the passage counts it as the sign of life. where are you certain in a way that cannot bend? the fourth step speaks to those who build strong things: 兵強則不勝, a strong army does not win. wang bi’s reason is that everything else comes to hate it; the fall of the strongest house in jin was the textbook case. an organisation is strong in this fatal sense when it cannot bend: its rules have no exceptions, its plans admit no doubt, its leader is never wrong. such a group wins for a while and then meets the one situation that its strength does not fit. the last line gives a design. put what is strong and large underneath, as support: the trunk, the budget, the firm commitments. put what is soft at the top and the edge, where the group meets the weather: the people who listen and adjust. most organisations do the reverse. they put the hardest person at the front. this is the passage that the soft martial arts took as their own, and 柔道 carries its first adjective in its name. the body lesson is exact. a stiff arm gives the partner a handle: the force goes straight through it to your centre. a soft arm gives nothing to push on, and it can still feel. softness here is the state in which you get the most information, because a tense muscle is numb. age is partly a slow rehearsal of the corpse: joints lose range, the breath grows shallow, the face sets. practice works against this by wetting and bending, and not by forcing. test it with your hand. the infant of passage 55 is the model: bones weak, sinews soft, and a grip that does not let go. walk in a wood after a storm. the trunks that lie on the ground are mostly the big, rigid ones; some texts of this passage say outright that the strong tree breaks. the grass under them is flat and will stand again by evening. the woodcutter makes the same choice as the wind: the straight tree is cut first. a living tree keeps its soft parts where the growth is: the tips of twigs and roots, and a thin wet layer under the bark. the heartwood that gives the trunk its strength is dead cells. so the tree itself has the arrangement of the last line: the strong and great below and within, the soft and weak above and outside. water is the test in each case. green wood is half water, and the shuowen’s word for death is to run dry. two passages later the book makes water its direct subject. twice today, do the hand test. once on your own body: find one place that is hard without reason and let it go soft for three breaths. once on your thinking: find one opinion that you hold stiffly and say aloud the best point on the other side, as if you meant it. notice the moment of feeling undefended; it is short. then look at one strong thing that you admire, a tree, a building, an institution, and ask where its softness is and whether it has kept any. if you want a companion text, read legge’s version and mark each place where he chose a gentler english word than the chinese gives. ask whether his choices are themselves soft, or only polite.

生: alive, or at birth?. 人之生也 is “a person’s 生”. 生 is to be born, to grow, and to be alive; chinese does not divide these. legge chose “at his birth”. then the line sets a newborn beside a corpse, the two ends of a life. that reading has support in passage 55, where the infant’s bones are weak and its sinews soft, 骨弱筋柔, and its grip is firm. our “alive” takes the wider sense: at any age, the living body gives under the hand, and the dead one does not. the chinese has both at once, and with them a third thought: softness is greatest at the start and is lost by degrees. on that reading we stiffen all our lives. english also needs a body word that the chinese leaves out. the line does not say “body”. it says 人, a person: the whole person is soft or hard.

柔: wood that bends and comes back. 柔 has 木, a tree, at its foot. the shuowen defines it as 木曲直也, “wood that can be made crooked and straight”. this is green wood, the kind that a wheelwright bends over a fire into a rim; a related word, 煣, with fire added, means exactly that work. so 柔 is not the softness of a cushion, which only gives way. it is the softness of a young branch: it gives way, keeps its fibre, and returns. english “soft” loses the return. “supple” and “pliant” keep it and lose the tenderness. the word became the name of a whole method. passage 36 says that the soft and weak overcome the hard and strong, and two thousand years later japanese teachers named their arts with this character: 柔術 and 柔道.

weak has to stay weak. 弱 is “weak”. modern versions often change it to “flexible”, “yielding”, or “receptive”, words that a reader can accept as praise. the chinese word is not polite in that way. the shuowen glosses it 橈, “bent”, like a thing that cannot hold itself up, and sees in the graph the fine hair of an animal. it is the word for a small state, a sick man, a child. the laozi chose it on purpose and repeats it: 弱者道之用, “weakness is how dao works” (40); nothing in the world is softer and weaker than water (78). the teaching is harder than “be flexible”. it says that the quality that we fear and hide is on the side of life. notice your own first response to the word “weak”. is that response soft, or hard?

死: to run dry. the shuowen defines death with a water word: 死，澌也，人所離也, “死 is 澌; it is that from which the person departs”. 澌 is water that runs out to the last drop. the graph, the shuowen says, joins 歺, broken bone, and 人, a person. so death, in the dictionary’s picture, is a drying and a leaving: the moisture goes, and the person steps away from the bones. this fits the passage closely. its second sentence ends with 枯槁, dried and withered, and its proof is the difference between wet wood and dry. life here is not a spirit that is added to matter. it is the wetness and bend of the matter itself. the word for “to live” in passage 73, 活, is the sound of running water by the same dictionary’s account.

堅強: now a compliment. 堅 is hard like packed earth; the graph has 土, earth, at its foot, and the shuowen defines it by 剛, the hardness of metal. 強 is strong. together, 堅強, they are in this passage the mark of a corpse. a modern chinese reader meets a shock here that an english reader cannot feel. in today’s language 堅強 (jianqiang) is a warm word: “be strong”, said to a friend in grief or to a child who has fallen. it means resilient, brave. the laozi’s phrase for the dead body has become the phrase for courage. the modern use is not wrong; languages move. but the old line still asks its question of the new word. when you tell someone to be 堅強, what do you ask them to stop feeling?

強, five times. the passage has fifty-eight characters, and among its words of quality 強 is the one that returns most: 堅強, 堅強, 兵強, 木強, 強大. each time it stands on the losing side. the book is not simple about this word. elsewhere it gives 強 a good sense by turning it inward: 自勝者強, “one who overcomes the self is strong” (33), and 守柔曰強, “to keep to the soft is called strong” (52). it also warns that the violent and strong do not get their own death (42). so the laozi has two strengths. one is the strength that shows, in a jaw, an army, a trunk. the other has no outward form and is found by keeping to the soft. only the first is “the company of death”. english has one word for both, and so has the chinese; the reader has to hear which is meant.

脆: soft and easy to snap. legge wrote “soft and brittle”, and the pair looks odd in english, where brittle things are hard. the chinese word explains it. the shuowen enters 脆 under its older form 脃 and defines it 小耎易斷也, “small, soft, and easily broken”. it has 月, flesh, on the left. this is the nature of a new shoot or a bean sprout: full of water, tender, and crisp. you can snap it with two fingers. the modern language keeps both sides, in 脆弱, fragile, and in the word for crisp food. so the line admits something that praise of softness usually leaves out. the living thing is easy to damage. passage 64 says the same of affairs: 其脆易泮, “while a thing is tender it is easy to break up”. life is on the side of what can be hurt.

枯槁: the other dry wood. 枯 and 槁 both have 木, a tree, on the left, and both mean dried-out wood; the shuowen defines the one by the other. 枯 has 古, “old”, as its sound-part, and a learner can remember it as old wood. the pair sets a trap for readers of the other great daoist book. in the zhuangzi a master sits so still that his student asks: can the body really be made like 槁木, withered wood, and the heart like dead ashes? there the dry tree is praise: a mind in which the usual sap of want and fear has stopped. in the laozi the dry tree is only dead. the two books do not disagree about practice. the zhuangzi’s sitter is not rigid; he has let go so fully that nothing in him pushes back. from outside, deep ease and death can look alike. how do you tell them apart in a person?

“so it is said”: a proverb inside. our text joins the conclusion with one word, 故, “so”. a modern collated edition of the mawangdui silk texts has two: 故曰, “so it is said”. that small word 曰 changes the status of the next lines. they are a quotation. the author did not invent “the hard and strong are the company of death”; it was a saying, and the passage is built to lead up to it. the collated silk text also has a longer soft side: 柔弱微細，生之徒也, “the soft, weak, minute, and fine are the company of life”, and it repeats the four words in the last line. 微 and 細 are words for the very small. they widen the claim from the pliant to the slight: what is too small to notice is also on life’s side. the received text dropped them, perhaps to make the two halves match. the collated text also has two more characters in the first line, 亓死也恆仞堅強; editors read them as a word for a body stretched stiff.

徒: those who walk behind. 徒 first meant to go on foot. from that came foot soldiers, as against the men in chariots; then the followers of a lord or a teacher; then “people of a kind”. confucius uses it for his own students, and for “the kind of people one can live among”. so 死之徒 is “those who go on foot behind death”: its followers, its troop. legge’s “concomitants” turns a crowd into an abstract noun. the phrase is from passage 50, which counts heads: 生之徒十有三，死之徒十有三, “the company of life, three in ten; the company of death, three in ten”. there the two companies are sets of people. here they are qualities, and the picture still holds: hardness walks in death’s train. with a military word in the middle of the passage, the next line about armies does not come from nowhere.

wang bi: what all things hate. why does a strong army not win? one could give a tactical answer: it grows proud, slow, and predictable. wang bi gives a different one: 强兵以暴於天下者，物之所惡也，故必不得勝。 “one who uses a strong army to do violence in the world is the thing that all others hate. so such a one will surely not get the victory.” his reason is the reaction of everything else. strength that shows itself gathers enemies, as the house of zhi learned. the phrase 物之所惡 echoes the question of passage 73, where heaven has things that it hates and no one knows the reason. here a reason is given. note also that the chinese says 不勝, “does not win”, and wang bi says 不得勝, “does not get to win”. he does not say that the army loses each battle. it fails to get what a victory is for.

the strongest house in jin. the warring states period is often dated from one lesson in strength. in the fifth century bce the great state of jin was run by a few noble houses. the strongest by far was the house of zhi, under zhi bo. he demanded land from the others. han and wei gave way. zhao refused, and zhi bo led all three armies against the zhao city of jinyang and turned a river into it. the city was near its end when a zhao envoy went by night to han and wei and said: when we are gone, you are next. they turned the water on zhi bo’s camp. in 453 bce his house was destroyed and his skull, the histories say, was lacquered as a cup. han, wei, and zhao divided jin. readers of this passage in that age knew the story as we know our own wars.

木強則兵: one line, four endings. the last character of this line differs from text to text. our pinned text has 兵: weapon, soldier. as a verb it gives “a strong tree is taken with the blade”; the shuowen’s own picture of 兵 is two hands that hold an axe, so our “meets the axe” stays close to the graph. wang bi’s note fits it: 物所加也, “it is what things are laid on”. the heshang gong text has 共; legge followed it, read it as 拱, to circle with the arms, and wrote of a tree that fills the outstretched arms and invites the feller. a modern collated edition of the mawangdui silk texts prints 木強則恆; the two manuscripts are reported to differ here, and the reading is disputed. and when the liezi and the huainanzi quote the saying, they give 木強則折, “a strong tree breaks”: the stiff trunk in a storm. blade, embrace, or wind. the tree’s end is the one fixed point.

the straight tree is cut first. the tree that suffers for its strength became a theme of the zhuangzi. a proverb there says 直木先伐，甘井先竭, “the straight tree is the first to be felled; the sweet well is the first to be drained”. in its stories a carpenter walks past a huge oak without a look, because its wood is useless: boats made of it sink, coffins rot, doors sweat sap. the oak comes to him in a dream and says that uselessness is what let it grow so large. the laozi’s line is shorter and less playful. it does not recommend that you be useless. it states a fact of the timber trade: the trunk that is hard, thick, and straight is the one that the axe is for. what in you is good timber, and who has noticed?

wang bi: it is a tree. 強大處下，柔弱處上: the strong and great are placed below; the soft and weak are placed above. many readers hear a promise that the ranks of society will be reversed, and english readers hear the verse about the meek who inherit the earth. wang bi reads no such promise. his two notes are among the shortest in his commentary. on “below”: 木之本也, “this is the root and trunk of the tree”. on “above”: 枝條是也, “this is the branches and twigs”. the line still describes the tree of the line before. the thick, hard part is at the bottom. the part that moves in the wind, puts out leaves, and takes the light is at the top. it is a description of how a living thing is arranged. whether it is also a statement about rank, the reader must decide. the book often praises the low place (8, 66), and here the low place holds the hard part. “below” and “above” are two positions in one tree, and neither is a prize.

the arts named “soft”. the thought of this passage became a way to train the body. in japan, schools of unarmed fighting took the name 柔術 (jujutsu), “the technique of 柔”, and in 1882 kano jigoro named his reform of them 柔道 (judo), “the way of 柔”. the character is the 柔 of our first line. in china the writings on taijiquan, set down in the nineteenth century, are full of the passage’s terms; one of them says 極柔軟，然後極堅剛, “be soft to the limit, and after that hard to the limit”. that sentence goes a step that the laozi does not go. it makes softness the road to a better hardness. the passage itself promises no such return. it says only where life is. does softness need to be justified by the strength that it produces?

legge’s “man”, and a tree in brackets. legge begins “man at his birth is supple and weak; at his death, firm and strong”. “supple” and “firm” are kinder than the chinese: 柔 and 堅 can bear them, but they hide the rhyme of ideas with the tree that follows. “man” and “his” are english; 人 is a person of either sex. his tree line is the most interesting. he writes that a strong tree “will fill the out-stretched arms, (and thereby invites the feller.)” the brackets hold his own explanation. he was translating a text with 共, and the chinese gave him only “a strong tree, then: arms around it”; the feller is his. it is a good guess, and it agrees in the end with the 兵 of our text. his “concomitants of death” for 死之徒 is the latin of a lecture hall. the chinese has people on foot.

the proof is in the hand. the passage argues from touch, so test it by touch. press the pad of your thumb into the muscle of your forearm. it gives, and when you let go it returns: that is 柔. bend a green twig and a dry one. then find the places where you are, at this moment, 堅強 without need. the usual ones are the jaw, the tongue against the palate, the shoulders, the hands, the belly. in each, something is braced against a blow that has not come. let one of them go soft and see what feeling was held under it. often it is a small fear. the passage does not ask you to be limp. a living branch is not limp. it asks on which side of the line each part of you now stands.

柔弱 and 堅強: the twig and the trunk. the passage sets 柔弱, soft and weak, against 堅強, hard and strong, and ties them to a second pair, 生 and 死. it plainly favors the soft. the preference is a correction. the age admired the strong army and the tall tree, and the text points at what that admiration does not see. it is not a rule for all time. the soft side turns: the tender shoot is easy to snap, and green wood that lives becomes trunk. the hard side has its work too. the last lines do not remove the strong and great. they give it a place, below, where it carries the twigs; a tree with no heartwood does not stand. elsewhere the book calls keeping to the soft a kind of strength. so the two depend on each other in one body. a reader who hears only “soft good, hard bad” will miss where hardness belongs, and the moment when softness has become limp.

what is soft and weak belongs to life, and what is hard and strong belongs to death.. what is soft and weak belongs to life, and what is hard and strong belongs to death. do you accept this? where does your own experience support it, and where does it refuse? what were you told about weakness as a child? who was called weak, and what happened to them? stand on the other side: hardness is what kept you alive and upright when things were bad, and softness was a luxury. give that view its full weight. what does it remember? notice which word you would less like to hear said of you: “hard” or “weak”. what does that choice guard?

the strong army does not win, and the strong tree is the one that gets cut.. the strong army does not win, and the strong tree is the one that gets cut. think of a strong thing that you have seen fall: a company, a body, a marriage, a state. did its strength play a part? now think of a strong thing that lasted. what does the passage leave out? where are you strong in a way that others can see? has that drawn the axe, or kept it away? if strength both protects and exposes, how do you decide where to show it? what old lesson makes that decision for you?

in a living thing the hard and great part sits below, and the soft part is on top.. in a living thing the hard and great part sits below, and the soft part is on top. look at how you are arranged. what do you put in front when you meet people: the firm part or the tender part? where did that order come from? what happened, once, when the soft part was in front? reverse it in thought: let what is firm in you hold you up from below, unseen, and let what is soft meet the day. what do you expect to happen? is that expectation a memory?

弱 two bows that bend. the character is one shape written twice. each half has 弓 above, which today is the graph for a bow, and two short strokes below. the shuowen explains it so: 上象橈曲，彡象毛氂橈弱也, “the upper part pictures a thing bent and curved; the lower strokes picture fine hair, bent and weak”. and why two? 弱物并，故从二, “weak things go side by side, so it is doubled”. that last sentence is a small piece of observation: the weak are found together, like reeds. modern scholars discuss the early forms and do not agree; some see two bows with loose strings or ornaments. the bow reading is useful for a learner even if it is not certain, because the bow is the origin of the opposite word. the shuowen’s proper graph for “strong” is 彊, defined as 弓有力也, “a bow that has force”. so in the old script both strong and weak are said with a bow: one that is drawn tight, one that curves and gives. the next passage opens with a bow that is being strung. look also at the double form itself. chinese often doubles a graph for “many”: 林, a grove, from two 木. here the doubling means something else: what is weak does not stand alone. the laozi says weakness is how dao works. the character adds: and it works in company. ten strokes: five, and the same five again. the bow takes three. a short level stroke that turns down at a corner; a second level stroke; then one long line that goes down, turns right, turns down again, and hooks to the left. that third stroke has two corners and a hook, and the brush should pause at each. then two small strokes under the hook: a dot, and a stroke that rises to the right. now write the whole thing again beside it. the skill is in making twins that are not identical. a good hand writes the left one narrower and a little higher, the right one broader with a stronger hook, so that the pair leans together. in cursive script each bow becomes one turning line, like a ribbon let fall.

柔 a spear on a tree. below is 木, a tree. the shuowen says of it 冒地而生, “it pushes up through the ground and grows”, and that the lower part of the graph shows roots. above is 矛, a spear; the shuowen describes a long one, set upright on a war chariot. so the character for “soft” is a weapon on top of a tree. the spear is there for its sound: the two words belong to one old rhyme group, the one that the tradition calls 幽, and you can hear the same sound-part in 茅 (mao), thatch grass. that is the dictionary’s whole account: 从木矛聲. the meaning comes from the tree. the definition is 木曲直也, “wood that can be bent and straightened”. a second-century reader thought at once of the craftsman who steams and bends green wood; add the fire sign and you get 煣, that very work, and with the hand sign 揉, to rub and knead. with the foot sign it is 蹂, to trample. the family all work a thing until it gives. there is a quiet irony in the graph for a reader of this passage. the hardest object of the age, the spear point, sits in the character and has no say in the meaning. the living wood under it decides. that is very nearly what the passage claims of armies and trees. nine strokes, five for the spear and four for the tree. the spear begins with a short level stroke that turns and falls left, then a dot under it. the third stroke is a longer level line that ends in a small downward hook. the fourth comes down through it and hooks left at the foot: the shaft. the fifth is a slash to the lower left. keep these five compact; they are the upper third. then the tree. a long level line, the widest in the character. an upright through its middle. then the two great strokes that give the character its life: a sweep to the lower left and a press to the lower right. they must open like branches under weight, light at the start and full at the end. if these two are stiff, the character contradicts its meaning.

強 the insect that means strong. look at the right side, at the bottom: 虫, the sign for insects, worms, and snakes. what is it doing in the word for “strong”? the shuowen answers plainly. 強 is 蚚也, the name of an insect, commonly said to be a weevil that lives in grain: 从虫弘聲, “from 虫, with 弘 for the sound”. the word “strong” had its own graph, 彊, which the shuowen defines as 弓有力也, “a bow that has force”; its right side shows fields with boundary lines, and it also wrote the word for a border, now 疆. but 彊 took many strokes, and 強 had the same sound. writers borrowed the insect, and in time the borrowed graph won. so each time this passage says “strong”, the brush writes a bow, 弓, and a bug. the bow on the left is real history: strength was first the pull of a bow. the upper right part, written 厶 here and 口 in the common variant 强, is what is left of 弘, which the shuowen calls the sound of a bowstring. read the passage with this in mind: 堅強, 兵強, 木強, 強大. the great word of the generals is written with a small soft creature that eats stored grain from inside. the scribes did not mean a joke. the laozi would have enjoyed it. eleven strokes. the bow on the left takes three, as in 弱: a level stroke with a corner, a second level stroke, and the long line with two corners and a hook. make it tall and narrow. on the right, first the small upper part in two strokes: a line that falls left and turns back to the right, and a dot. then the insect in six: the left side of its box; the top and right side with a corner; the base; an upright through the middle that runs below the box; a rising stroke to the right; and a final dot. that last dot sits at the lower right corner and steadies the whole. the left side is all bends and the right side is small pieces. the variant 强, with 口 on top, is the standard form in mainland china today.

77 · stringing the bow. the way of heaven: / is it not like the stringing of a bow? / the high is pressed down, / the low is lifted. / what has more than enough is reduced; / what has not enough is mended. / the way of heaven / takes from what has more than enough / and mends what has not enough. / the way of people is not so. / it takes from those who have not enough / to offer up to those who have more than enough. / who can have more than enough / and offer it to all under heaven? / only one who has dao. / so the sage acts and does not lean on it, / finishes the work and does not stay in it: / has no wish to show worth. the passage opens with a question about a tool: is the way of heaven not like the stringing of a bow? four short clauses describe the act. the high tip is pressed down and the low one lifted; the part with too much is reduced and the part with too little is mended. then the rule is stated twice, once for heaven and once, reversed, for people, who take from the poor and lift it up to the rich. a question follows: who can hold a surplus and offer it to the world? the answer is short: one who has dao. the close describes that person with an old refrain: acts without leaning on the act, finishes and leaves, shows no worth. the things in the passage are a bow, leftover food, a foot, a patched robe, and three hands that hold up a tray. the bow can be read as one person. each of us has parts that stand too high: the skill we are known for, the opinion we repeat, the story of what we have done. and each has parts that hang low, unfed: a talent that was dropped, a grief that was not given time. the human way, inside, is to keep serving the high tip. we give more hours to what already has our regard and take them from what is already poor. heaven’s way would press the first down a little and lift the second. the last lines name the hardest piece of this. not to show worth means that even the inner audience is dismissed. wang bi says why it is hard: each of us has a self, and from inside that self, “mine” weighs more. every organisation has a bow in it, and by default it is strung the human way: the best-funded unit gets the next budget, the person with the most credit gets the next opportunity, the customer who pays most gets the most care. the sociologists call this the matthew effect. the passage asks a leader to see it as a choice and to do the archer’s work: press down what stands high, starting with the leader’s own share, and lift what hangs low. note the word for the low side: mend, not “add”. it means close attention to the place of the tear. the last lines then guard against the usual failure of generous leaders, which is to keep an account of their generosity. in an age that paid for merit by the head, the text asks for work that leaves no claim. stringing a composite bow is a whole-body act. the archer steps through the bow, sets one tip against the foot or the thigh, and bends the limbs back with the hips. strength in the arms alone will not do it, and force at one point will twist the limb and ruin years of work. the ends must come level together. a body is strung in the same way. where the shoulders ride high, press them down; where the chest has sunk, lift it; where one leg takes all the weight, share it. no part is removed. the tension that was badly spread is spread well, and the body that was a curled stick becomes something that can send an arrow. stand, and find your own high tip and low tip. then note: 張 is stringing, and the shot is another word. heaven’s way of levelling can be watched in an afternoon. water leaves the high ground and gathers in the low. heat moves from the warm stone to the cool air until they match. a hill is worn down grain by grain and the valley fills. the moon that is full begins to wane on the next night. no judge does this, and nothing is punished; the high place only has more to give off. living systems add a second movement, and it is the one that the passage calls mending: a forest closes a gap where a tree fell, and skin closes a cut. against these stands the pattern that people make, in which what is large draws more to itself. the text does not say that this is unnatural in every sense. it says that it is ours, and so it can be done differently. do the archer’s check today with one real thing: find a place where you have more than enough and a person or a part of your life that has too little of the same thing, and move some across. keep the three rules of the last lines. do not lean on it: make no claim from it later. do not stay in it: leave when it is done. do not show it: tell no one. if that seems easy, try the same with praise. the next time credit comes to you that also belongs to others, press that high tip down at once and lift theirs. then read legge’s sentence on the human way, with its “he” and “his own”, and ask why he needed a single guilty man.

聖人: not a saint. 聖人 is “the sage” by custom, and the english word misleads. this is not a saint: there is no holiness here and no reward after death. it is not only a wise man either. the graph has 耳, an ear, and the shuowen defines the word as 通, “to pass through, to reach”: a person whose hearing is open, and who leads by that attunement. in this passage the attunement has a plain form: the sage hears where there is too much and where too little, and moves the surplus.

天之道: the book’s closing theme. the phrase 天之道, “the way of heaven”, is rare in the first seventy passages. it closes passage 9, and passage 47 says that one can see it without looking out of the window. then, in the book’s last pages, it comes in four of the last nine passages: heaven’s way does not contend and wins (73); it is like a bow being strung (77); it has no favourites (79); it benefits and does not harm (81, the last line but one of the whole book). only here is it set against 人之道, the way of people, as its opposite. the mawangdui silk texts place passages 80 and 81 earlier, and their book begins with the part on 德; so there this group, up to passage 79, ends the first half. in both orders, a reader who has followed many passages on rule, war, and hunger is given this measure at the close: look at what heaven does with a surplus.

張弓: to string, not to shoot. english versions often say “bending a bow” or “drawing a bow”, and the reader sees an archer who takes aim. the shuowen is exact about bow words, and it gives another picture. 張 is 施弓弦也, “to put the string on a bow”. to draw the bow for a shot is a different word, 引, 開弓也, “to open the bow”. to take the string off is 弛, 弓解也, “the bow released”. so 張弓 is the act before any arrow: the bow is made ready. the old phrase 一張一弛, “now strung, now unstrung”, used of the rule of the sage kings, keeps the pair. some commentators do read our line as aiming: aim too high, lower it. the stringing reading explains the next two lines better, as the shape of the bow shows.
