a bow that curves the wrong way. the bow of the warring states was not a bent stick. it was a composite: the manual of the royal workshops lists six materials, 幹、角、筋、膠、絲、漆, a wooden core, horn, sinew, glue, silk, and lacquer, each to be gathered in its own season, and a good bow took years to finish. unstrung, such a bow curls forward, away from the archer; its tips point the wrong way. to string it, the archer braces it against the body and bends the whole thing back through itself. the tip that stands high is pressed down, the tip that hangs low is brought up, and the string is slipped on. in one movement the two ends are brought level. 高者抑之，下者舉之 describes that movement. nothing is cut off the bow, and nothing is added. its own tension is redistributed until it can work.

餘 and 足: leftovers and a foot. the two measures of the passage are homely words. 有餘 is “to have 餘”. 餘 has 食, food, on its left, and the shuowen defines it as 饒, plenty: it is the food that is left after everyone has eaten. 不足 is “not 足”. 足 is a foot; the shuowen says 人之足也。在下, “a person’s foot; it is at the bottom”. how a foot came to mean “enough” is not certain, and the word may simply have been borrowed for its sound. the book has made much of it already: 知足者富, “one who knows what is enough is rich” (33); 知足不辱, “know what is enough and meet no disgrace” (44). so the passage does not speak of rich and poor as classes or as sums of money. it speaks of the table after the meal, and of whether there was enough to stand on.

損 and its lost partner 益. 損 is to lessen; the shuowen says 減也. its fixed partner in old chinese is 益, to add. the two are a pair of hexagrams in the book of changes, numbers 41 and 42, and the old commentary on them is political: 損下益上, “take from below and add above”, is the figure of loss, and 損上益下，民說无疆, “take from above and add below, and the people’s joy has no limit”, is the figure of gain. the laozi uses the pair twice: things are sometimes increased by being reduced (42); learning adds each day, and dao takes away each day (48). in our passage the received text puts 補, to mend, where a reader expects 益. a modern collated edition of the mawangdui silk texts has the expected word in the summary line: 損有餘而益不足. an educated reader heard the two hexagrams either way.

補: to mend a robe. 補 has 衤, the sign for clothing, on its left. the shuowen defines it 完衣也, “to make a garment whole”: to put a patch on. so heaven’s way with those who lack is described in a word from the sewing basket. the choice is worth a moment. to add, 益, is neutral: one pours more in. to mend supposes that the thing was whole once and has a tear. it also supposes close work, a hand that goes to the exact place of the damage with a piece cut to fit. the surplus is “reduced”, an act of quantity; the lack is “mended”, an act of care. our rendering keeps “mend” for this reason, though “supplement” is the usual english. what in your reach has a tear and not a shortage?

the way of people: fields without end. 人之道則不然: “the way of people, however, is not so.” what follows is the sharpest social sentence in the book: people take from those who lack and offer it up to those who have extra. the age gave the evidence. once land could be bought and sold and taxed by the acre, it gathered in few hands. a han scholar described the result under qin: 富者田連阡陌，貧者亡立錐之地, “the fields of the rich run on from path to path, and the poor have no ground in which to stand an awl”. the landless then paid half their crop as rent. a note on our english: 者 in these lines can be “what” or “who”. we write “what” for heaven’s lines and “those who” for the human lines. the chinese does not change the word. it is the same mark for a bow tip and for a hungry family.

“to him that hath”. a western reader knows the human way from another book. the gospel of matthew says: to everyone who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away. in 1968 the sociologist robert merton named the pattern after that verse, the “matthew effect”: fame brings more fame, capital brings more capital. modern economics often describes this as a law of nature, like compound interest. the laozi sorts things the other way around. gathering to the top is 人之道, the way that people make. the levelling is 天之道, what heaven does: water runs down, the full moon wanes, the high tip of the bow comes down. so the text denies that concentration is natural. which of the two ways do you take, without thinking, to be the way things are?

奉: hands that lift upward. 奉 is not “to give”. the shuowen defines it 承也, “to hold up, to receive from above”, and builds it from hands: 从手从廾, one hand and then a pair of hands, with a sound-part on top. it is the gesture of a servant who lifts a tray to a lord, with both hands and a lowered head. the word was used for tribute, for an order received from a king, and, with 亻 added, for an official’s salary: 俸. so the direction is fixed: 奉 goes up. in the human way, the poor hold up their little to the rich, as a tenant brings rent to the hall. then the text asks its question with the same verb and a new direction: who can 奉 a surplus to 天下, to all under heaven? the one with extra is asked to stand in the servant’s posture, and the whole world sits in the lord’s seat.

offered to the world, or to heaven?. the received text asks: 孰能有餘以奉天下, who can have a surplus and offer it to all under heaven? a modern collated edition of the mawangdui silk texts has a longer question with a different receiver: 孰能有餘而有以取奉於天者, “who can have a surplus and have the means to take from it and offer it up to heaven?” in that version the surplus is not handed to the people directly. it is given back to 天, to the power whose way is to level, as one returns a loan. the practical result may be the same. the posture differs. in the received text the one with dao is a giver, and can be thanked. in the collated silk text that person only passes back what was never owned, and no one is in debt. the collated silk text also ends the answer with 乎, a particle of doubt: “only one who has dao, perhaps?”

有餘, 有道: two kinds of having. the verb 有, to have, comes five times in the passage. four times its object is 餘, surplus. the fifth time, in the answer to the question, its object is 道: 唯有道者, “only one who has dao”. the line sets the two havings side by side. one kind of having can be counted, stored, taken, and offered. can dao be had in that way? the first passage of the book said that it cannot even be named. so 有道 must mean something else: to be in the way, to have it as one has a habit or a native language. such a having does not grow less when it is used. that may be why its owner can let the other kind go. the phrase 有道者 comes also in passages 24 and 31, both times for one who refuses to stay with excess.

wang bi: each one has a self. why is the human way the reverse of heaven’s? wang bi’s answer is not greed. he writes: 如人之量，則各有其身，不得相均。如惟無身無私乎，自然然後乃能與天地合德。 “by the human measure, each one has a self of their own, and so they cannot be made level with each other. only one who is without self and without private interest, and is so of itself, can then join in 德 with heaven and earth.” 身 is the body and the self that goes with it. heaven can level because it has no body to feed first. a person looks out from one place, and from that place “mine” weighs more. wang bi does not call this a sin. he calls it a measure, 量, a limit of capacity. the passage’s sage is one in whom that measure has widened. is levelling possible for a being with a body?

a refrain comes back. 為而不恃, “acts and does not lean on it”, is a refrain of the book. it stands in passage 2 of the sage, in passage 10 of the dark 德, and in passage 51 of dao itself, which gives life to the ten thousand things and does not own them. 功成而不處 is close to a line in passage 2 as well. 恃 is to lean on something as a support; the shuowen says 賴也, to depend on. so the phrase does not mean “acts without hope of reward”. it means that the sage does not rest any weight on what was done: no claim, no standing derived from it. here the refrain has a new task. it follows a passage on surplus, and it shows what a surplus of merit would be. a person who leans on past deeds holds a store of credit. the sage keeps none.

功: merit, counted in heads. 功 joins 工, work, and 力, strength, and the shuowen gives it a public sense: 以勞定國也, “by toil to make the state secure”. it is the word for service that earns a reward. in the warring states the reward became a system. the state of qin had a ladder of some twenty ranks, and a soldier climbed it by 軍功, merit in war, which the law measured in the heads of enemy soldiers. one head brought one rank, with land and servants attached. other states had similar schemes. a man’s 功 was thus his capital, entered in a register and paid out for life. against this background 功成而不處, “the work is finished and one does not stay in it”, is not mild advice about modesty. it asks a person to walk away from the one account that the age honoured.

wang bi: unseen, in order to level. the last clause is 其不欲見賢. 其 is a particle of mood here, close to “surely”. 見 is read xian, “to show”, and not jian, “to see”: the sage does not wish to let worth be seen. wang bi connects this to the whole passage: 是以聖人不欲示其賢以均天下, “so the sage does not wish to display their worth, in order to make the world level”. his point is fine. visible excellence is itself a height. if the sage stood out, people would look up, rank themselves, and strive; the sage would have “more than enough” of regard. so the sage presses that high tip down. wang bi describes the result with a phrase from passages 4 and 56: 和光同塵, softening the glare and becoming one with the dust. 賢 is a money word by origin, with a shell in it (see passage 75). not to show it is to keep one’s wealth out of the market.

legge’s “superabundance”. legge gives 有餘 as “superabundance” four times. the latin word has six syllables and no table in it; the chinese is “having leftovers”. for the bow he writes that what was high “is brought low”, and what was low “is raised up”. these are the cadences of the english bible, where valleys are exalted and the mighty are put down, and they turn a craftsman’s movement into a judgment. his brackets are honest: “(the method of)”, “(part of the bow)”, “(so heaven)”. the sharpest change is in the human way. legge makes it one man’s sin: “he takes away from those who have not enough to add to his own superabundance”. the chinese has no “he” and no “his own”. it describes an order of things in which everyone takes part, including those who 奉, who hold up the tribute with their own hands.

find one high tip. take stock as the archer does, by looking for what stands too high and what hangs too low. money is one case, and often not the first. where do you have 有餘 today? perhaps time on one day of the week, or attention, or knowledge that a younger colleague lacks, or simply room in the house. and who near you is at 不足 in the same thing? choose one pair. then move a little from the high to the low, and do it in the manner of the last lines: do not announce it, do not keep a count, and do not return to see how grateful the person is. notice what the giving feels like when no credit is stored. the text’s word for that kind of giving is 奉: both hands, from below.

高 and 下, 有餘 and 不足: one bow. two pairs run through the passage: 高 and 下, high and low, and 有餘 and 不足, surplus and lack. a bow has two tips, and neither is the wrong one. high is high only against low, and a surplus is measured by the lack beside it. heaven’s way does not prefer the low to the high. it moves between them until the bow can work. the movement does not stop: the tip that was lifted will stand high and be pressed in its turn. passage 2 said it first: 高下相傾, high and low lean on each other. the text does set 天之道 over 人之道. that preference corrects an order in which the full grow fuller. it is not a rule that having is bad. the question asks 孰能有餘, who can have a surplus and offer it; without a high tip there is nothing to give. a reading that only blames the rich misses this. a strung bow is also unstrung in its time.

the natural way takes from what has too much and gives to what has too little.. the natural way takes from what has too much and gives to what has too little. is this what you see when you look at the world? give one case for it and one against. which did your family hold to be natural: that things even out, or that the strong gather more? how was it said at the table? take the other side for a while: gathering to the top is the real law, and levelling is a wish. what comes with that view: relief, anger, shame, a kind of pride? your answer may follow the tip of the bow on which you stand. are you the high one or the low one, and in what?

left to themselves, people take from those who lack and hand it up to those who already have more.. left to themselves, people take from those who lack and hand it up to those who already have more. do you take part in this? follow one thing that you gave this week, time or praise or money, and see whether it went up or down. why is it easier to give to those who already have? what do you hope to receive from them? suppose the opposite were true of people: that their first movement is to share downward. can you find that movement in yourself? when was it last free to act? what do you judge in the rich, or in the poor, that you would not like to find in yourself?

work that is truly finished is left behind, with no claim made and no worth shown.. work that is truly finished is left behind, with no claim made and no worth shown. can you do something well and not want it seen? recall the last time, and how long the silence lasted. what did recognition mean where you grew up? was it rare, or cheap, or a condition of being loved? argue the other side: to be seen for good work is fair, and it shows others what is possible. hold that for a while. does it feel like an excuse or like a truth? which do you fear more: to be overlooked, or to be found wanting when you are looked at? how does that fear shape what you show?

張 the bow made ready. on the left is 弓, a bow, and it is still a picture: the bent stave with its grip, seen from the side. the shuowen sums up the weapon in four words, 以近窮遠, “from near at hand, to reach the far”. on the right is 長, which gives the sound; alone it means long (chang) or elder, to grow (zhang). the early forms of 長 are commonly explained as a person with long hair, and long hair meant long years. the shuowen’s definition of 張 is exact: 施弓弦也, “to put the string on the bow”. everything else that the word means comes from that moment. a strung bow is stretched, so 張 is to stretch and to spread: a net, a sail, a banner. it is to open wide: the eyes, the mouth. passage 36 uses it so: 將欲歙之，必固張之, “what is to be closed must first be opened wide”. it became the counting word for flat things that are spread out, a sheet of paper, a table, a bed, and for bows themselves. it is one of the most common family names in china, and tradition explains the name by an ancestor who made bows. the sound-part has its own family: the shuowen defines 帳, a tent, by this very word, 張也, a thing stretched; and 漲 is water that swells. in all of them something is pulled out to its working size. the passage chooses the first sense: a bow made ready, and not yet a shot. eleven strokes: three for the bow, eight for 長. the bow is the same on every page: a level stroke with a corner, a second level stroke, then the long line that goes down, turns twice, and ends in a hook to the left. keep it narrow, on the left third. now 長. a short level stroke at the top; an upright that hangs from its left end; two more short level strokes to the right of the upright; then a long level line under all of them, the widest in the character. from that line the brush goes down and flicks up to the right; then a short slash to the left; then the final press to the lower right, long and open. watch that last stroke. the bow on the left is coiled, and this stroke on the right is released, like a string that has been let go.

補 a patch on a robe. the left side is 衤, the form that 衣 takes beside another part. 衣 is clothing, and the shuowen says of it 上曰衣，下曰裳, “the upper garment is 衣, the lower is 裳”. the early graph is commonly explained as a robe seen from the front, with its collar and its two crossed lapels. the right side, 甫 (fu), gives the sound; the same part gives the sound in 捕 (to catch) and 鋪 (to spread out). the shuowen’s definition of 補 is 完衣也, “to make a garment whole”. so this is the plain verb for sewing a patch on a worn place. from there it widened: to repair a wall, to fill a vacant post, to make up a shortage, to nourish a weak body; chinese medicine still calls a tonic a 補 medicine. look at the clothing family, because cloth words hide in unexpected places. 初, “beginning”, is 衣 and 刀, a knife, and the shuowen explains it: 裁衣之始也, “the start of cutting out a garment”. every beginning, in chinese, is the first cut into whole cloth. 裁, to cut cloth, also means to decide. 裏, the lining, means “inside”, and 表, the outer garment, means “surface”. a language that thinks with cloth knows that things are cut, sewn, worn through, and mended. the passage says that heaven mends. it began the world with a cut, 初, and it keeps the needle. twelve strokes: five for the clothing sign, seven for 甫. begin with a dot at the top left. the second stroke goes right, turns, and falls away to the left. the third is an upright from the turning point. the fourth is a short slash to the left and the fifth a small dot to the right, tucked close; these two are the lapels. note that the clothing sign has two small strokes here; the sign for spirits and altars, 礻, has only one, and learners often confuse the pair. now the right side: a level line; the left upright of the frame; the top-and-right stroke with its corner and a hook at the foot; two short level lines inside; then a long upright through the centre, from above the first line to the base. last, a dot at the upper right. the centre upright must be truly vertical. it is the needle of the character.

奉 three hands under a gift. the modern shape hides its parts, so begin with the shuowen: 从手从廾，𡴀聲, “from a hand, and from a pair of hands, with 𡴀 for the sound”. 廾 is two hands held up side by side. you can see it at the foot of 兵, where two hands hold an axe, and of 弄, to play with, where they hold a piece of jade. in 奉 the writers were not content with two. they added a third hand below, the 手 that is now the three strokes at the bottom. the top three level strokes and the two great sweeping strokes are what regular script made of the sound-part and the pair of hands. the definition is 承也: to bear up, to receive respectfully. and 承 itself is defined by 奉; its old form is commonly explained as hands that lift a kneeling figure. so the picture is of a thing held up from below, by more hands than are needed, toward someone higher. the family keeps the gesture. 捧 adds yet another hand: to carry in both palms. 俸 adds a person: a salary, the grain that the state hands to its officers. 棒 adds wood: a staff. the top of 奉 looks like the top of 春 (spring), 泰 (peace), and 奏 (to present); regular script merged several different old forms into this one shape, so the likeness proves nothing about meaning. in the passage the gift goes up from the poor. then the text turns the same hands toward the world. eight strokes. three level lines first, from the top down. they are not equal: the first is of middle length, the second slightly shorter, the third the longest, and each rises slightly to the right. then the two sweeping strokes. the fourth stroke starts above the first line, passes down through all three, and falls far out to the lower left. the fifth starts at the third line and presses out to the lower right, thin at first and broad at the end. these two make a roof, and it must be wide enough to shelter what is below. under it: two short level lines, the lower one longer, and a final upright through both that runs down to a point. in clerical script the right-hand sweep ends in a heavy flared tail, and the character looks like a figure with its arms raised.

78 · the dirt of the state. under heaven nothing is softer and weaker than water, / yet for attacking the hard and strong / nothing can beat it: / there is nothing to put in its place. / weak overcomes strong, / soft overcomes hard. / under heaven no one does not know this; / no one can walk it. / so a sage has said: / “to take on the dirt of the state / is to be called lord of the altars of soil and grain. / to take on the state’s ill omens / is to be king of all under heaven.” / straight words seem turned around. the passage has two halves and a last line. the first half is about water: nothing is softer or weaker, and nothing is better at the assault on hard things, because nothing can take its place. then the general rule, weak over strong and soft over hard, with a dry remark: everyone knows it and no one can walk it. the second half is a rhymed saying about rulers. to receive the state’s dirt is to be lord of its altars; to receive its ill omens is to be king. the link between the halves is not stated. it is in the image: water runs to the lowest place and takes everything that is washed down. the ruler is that low water. the last line, straight words seem turned around, comments on this passage and on the book. everyone knows, no one can walk it. why not? because to be soft and low in fact, and not only in theory, one must receive what the low place receives. in a person this is the material that the mind sends away: shame, failure, the envy that one denies, the old injury. the usual inner government is hard: it keeps a clean image by pushing the dirt out, onto others or out of sight. the verse describes another government. the one who can take the dirt into awareness and hold it, without washing it off and without drowning in it, becomes master of the whole inner state, because nothing in it is any longer in exile. this is not redemption. the mud is not turned into gold. it settles. still water with silt at the bottom is clear at the top. the verse is the book’s shortest definition of legitimacy. authority belongs to the one who receives what the group cannot bear to hold: its failures and its bad luck. court language already said so in its forms, since rulers called themselves the orphan and the grainless; the text asks that the form be filled. the model is king tang in the mulberry grove: the guilt of the ten thousand regions rests on me. note the two levels. to take the dirt, the internal faults, makes one fit to lead a group. to take the ill omens, the blows from outside that are no one’s fault, makes one fit for more than a group. note also what the modern phrase “taking responsibility” leaves out: the ruler in the verse does not resign afterwards. try the low place once before you judge the idea. water’s way of attack is a lesson in contact. it does not strike a wall. it leans on it with its whole weight, finds each crack, and stays. in the soft martial arts this is called sticking and following: the hand rests on the partner’s arm, heavy and without force, and goes where the arm goes. the partner pushes and meets nothing hard; the pressure only arrives somewhere else. to do this the body must receive. a push is taken in through the arms, down the spine, and into the ground, as a low field takes rain. the beginner’s body refuses and braces; that is 剛. stand with a partner and let them push your shoulder slowly. do not resist and do not collapse. let the push drain through you to your feet. everyone knows this, and to do it takes years. a gorge is the plain proof of the first lines. a river with no edge cut it through rock, and it used the rock’s own grit as its teeth. water does this by being what nothing can replace: it keeps its nature at every point, and it never stops arriving. the second half of the passage is also in the landscape. follow any stream down and you reach a marsh, a delta, a lake bed. all the dirt of the country ends there: silt, leaves, the waste of towns. these low, muddy places are the most fertile ground on earth, and the early states of china grew on river silt. the saying in the zuo chronicle puts the ruler beside the marsh for this reason. in the living world, to receive the dirt is the start of soil. the first altar of a state was a mound of earth. use water today as a teacher, twice. first, with the hands: when you wash something, watch what the water does. it does not scrub. it takes the dirt into itself and carries it down, and the thing is clean because the water agreed to be dirty. second, with people: be the low place once. when a small blame is in the air and looking for someone, receive it, even if only a tenth of it is yours, and say nothing in your defence. feel how much effort the usual defence costs. in the evening, read the last line again, 正言若反, and pick one sentence from this book that sounded upside down when you first met it. does it still seem reversed? then compare the saying with legge’s hymn stanza.

聖人: not a saint. 聖人 is “the sage” by custom, and the english word misleads. this is not a saint: there is no holiness here and no reward after death. it is not only a wise man either. the graph has 耳, an ear, and the shuowen defines the word as 通, “to pass through, to reach”: a person whose hearing is open, and who leads by that attunement. here a sage is quoted on what makes a ruler. for early readers the sages were first of all the kings of old, and the saying that follows is about one of their acts.

水: the level. the shuowen does not define water as wet. its definition is one word: 凖也, “it is the level”. water is the thing that finds the horizontal, and builders used a trough of it to set a line true. this fits the passage before this one, where heaven’s way is to bring the high down and the low up. the dictionary then reads the graph: 象眾水並流，中有微陽之气也, “it pictures many waters that flow side by side, with a faint breath of yang in the middle”. the centre line of 水 is the current; the strokes at the sides are the waters that join it. water has been the book’s teacher since passage 8: the highest good is like water, which benefits all things and stays in the places that people despise. here the lesson is the last one, and the hardest: what water’s low place means for a ruler.

攻: water at the walls. 攻 is the word for an assault on a fortified place; the shuowen says 擊也, to strike. for a reader of the warring states, “water attacks the hard and strong” was also a report of events. cities had walls of rammed earth, and generals learned to turn rivers against them. in 453 bce zhi bo led a river into jinyang until the people hung their cooking pots from the rafters. in 279 bce the qin general bai qi dug a channel and drowned the chu city of yan. in 225 bce wang ben of qin breached the dikes above daliang, the capital of wei; after three months the walls dissolved and the state was at an end. the sunzi notes dryly: 以水佐攻者強, “those who use water to support an attack are strong”. so the soft thing was a siege engine. the passage knows this and goes past it.

易: replace, change, or easy?. 其無以易之 turns on 易, a word with three senses. wang bi takes “to replace”: 以，用也。其，謂水也。言用水之柔弱，無物可以易之也。 “以 means to use. 其 refers to water. the line says: for the use of water’s softness and weakness, there is no thing that can take its place.” we follow him. a second sense is “to change”: nothing can alter water. cut it, block it, boil it, and it comes back as itself. this reading explains the victory: the attacker that cannot be changed outlasts the wall that can. a third sense is “easy”, and a few readers take the line so: water treats nothing as easy. a modern collated edition of the mawangdui silk texts begins the clause with 以, “because”, which makes it plainly the reason for the lines before. all three senses belong to one word, and the calligraphy plate for 易 below tells its story.

four words, re-paired. the first sentence joins the qualities in two compounds: 柔弱, soft-weak, and 堅強, hard-strong. the second sentence takes them apart and sets them in single combat: 弱 against 強, 柔 against 剛. 剛 is new. it is the hardness of metal; the shuowen defines it as 彊斷也, “to cut through by force”, and the graph has 刂, a knife, on its right. with 柔 it makes one of the great pairs of chinese thought: in the book of changes, 剛 and 柔 are the names of the unbroken and the broken line. a modern collated edition of the mawangdui silk texts has a different first clause: 水之勝剛, “water’s overcoming of the hard”. there the image stays on the surface for one more line. passage 36 gives the same thought in four characters: 柔弱勝剛強. the saying was already old, and that is the point of the next line.

莫, four times: no one, nothing. the passage is built on 莫, “none”. nothing is softer than water. nothing can beat it. no one does not know. no one can do it. the graph began as a picture of dusk; the shuowen says 日且冥也。从日在茻中, “the sun about to go dark: a sun in the middle of tall grass”. it was borrowed for the negative, and a new graph, 暮, was made for the evening. the third and fourth 莫 make the most honest sentence in the book: 莫不知，莫能行. everyone knows; no one can walk it. 行 is to walk, to put the feet on the road. passage 70 said the same of the whole teaching: my words are very easy to know and very easy to walk, and no one under heaven can know them or walk them. why is this knowledge so hard to walk? the quotation that follows gives the reason: the price is dirt.

a verse inside the prose. 聖人云, “a sage has said”. the author steps back and quotes; the same formula introduces a saying in passage 57. the four lines that follow are a small poem, and they rhyme. in the sound system reconstructed for old chinese, 垢 and 主 end in the same rhyme, the group that the tradition calls 侯, and 祥 and 王 share another, the group called 陽. modern mandarin has lost the first pair (gou, zhu) and kept the second (xiang, wang). so dirt rhymes with lord, and ill omen rhymes with king. the ear joins what the mind keeps apart. the verse is probably older than the book: a court saying about what makes a ruler, which the author found and set here as the answer to “no one can walk it”. the chinese has no “a” or “the”, so 聖人 can also be “the sages”.

受: from hand to hand. 受 is to receive. the shuowen defines it as 相付也, “to hand over to one another”, and builds it from two hands, one above and one below, with a reduced 舟, boat, between them for the sound. the early forms are commonly explained as two hands and a vessel that passes from one to the other. in early writing the one graph served for giving and for getting; later a hand was added at the side for the giver’s part, 授. so 受 is not passive, like “to suffer” or “to be blamed”. it is the active half of a handing-over: someone holds out the vessel, and the ruler puts out both hands. our “take on” tries to keep that. the dirt of the state is offered every day. the verse asks who will hold out their hands for it.

垢: the ruler holds dirt in the mouth. 垢 is dirt: grime on skin, mud in water. the shuowen says 濁也, “turbid”, and the graph has 土, earth, on its left. english versions write “disgrace”, “humiliation”, or “blame”, and the link to the first half is cut. the first half is about water, and water takes the dirt: it runs to the lowest place, and everything that is washed ends in it. the verse had a known relative. in 594 bce, the zuo chronicle tells, a minister of jin quoted a saying to his lord: 川澤納汙，山藪藏疾，瑾瑜匿瑕，國君含垢，天之道也. “rivers and marshes take in filth; mountains and thickets hide harmful things; fine jade hides its flaws; the ruler of a state holds dirt in the mouth. this is heaven’s way.” the ruler is listed with the marsh. what is the “dirt” of a group that you belong to, and where does it now collect?

dirt, or insult? and a forbidden name. a modern collated edition of the mawangdui silk texts reads 受邦之詬. two words differ. first, 詬 for 垢. the two graphs share the sound-part 后 and differ in the other half: 垢 has earth, and 詬 has 言, speech. the shuowen defines 詬 as 恥, shame: it is abuse that is spoken. in the silk version the ruler takes the insults of the state: the curses of the people in a bad year. early scribes often wrote one of such a pair for the other, so we cannot be sure which word was meant. the received graph keeps the tie to water; the silk graph is closer to politics. second, 邦 for 國. both mean “state”. 邦 was the personal name of the first han emperor, liu bang, and after his reign scribes replaced it with 國 through the whole book. the same kind of taboo changed the first line of passage 1.

社稷: soil and millet. 社 is the altar of the soil, which the shuowen defines as 地主, “lord of the earth”, and 稷 is the altar of millet, which the shuowen calls 五穀之長, “the chief of the five grains”. each state had the pair, beside the ruler’s residence: an open mound of earth for the god of that land, and a place of offering to the grain that fed it. open is important. an old ritual text says that the altar of a conquered state was roofed over, so that it would no longer receive the light of heaven. to found a state was to raise these altars, and to destroy one was to cover them. so 社稷 came to mean the state itself, more than any ruler; mencius ranks the people first, the altars second, and the ruler last. 社稷主 is the one who presides at the offerings. the verse says who that is: the person who receives the dirt. soil is, after all, what the first altar is made of.

不祥, and a king in the mulberry grove. 祥 has 礻, the altar sign, beside 羊, a sheep, the animal of offering. the shuowen defines it as 福, blessing. 不祥 are the bad signs: eclipse, flood, drought, a strange birth. they were read as heaven’s warning to a state. who answers for them? the founding story of the shang dynasty gives the model. after king tang took the throne, no rain fell for years. tang went to the mulberry grove, cut off his hair, and offered himself as the victim. his prayer survives in several old books; the analects gives it so: 朕躬有罪，無以萬方；萬方有罪，罪在朕躬. “if i myself have guilt, do not hold the ten thousand regions to it. if the ten thousand regions have guilt, the guilt rests on me.” the rain came. for centuries afterwards, emperors answered a disaster with an edict that blamed themselves.

lord of one state, king of all. the verse has two steps. the one who takes the state’s dirt is 社稷主, lord of one state’s altars. the one who takes its ill omens is 天下王, king of all under heaven. in the warring states that second title was the prize of the age. seven rulers called themselves 王, and each hoped to be the one king. the books of strategy told them how: armies, alliances, grain. the verse gives another qualification, and it has nothing to do with force. the shuowen defines 王 by a word of like sound, 往: 天下所歸往也, “the one to whom all under heaven go home”. passage 66 uses the word of water: the rivers and the sea can be 王 of the hundred valleys because they lie below them. so “king” here is less a rank than a low point, where everything arrives. english “king” has a throne under it. this one has a valley floor.

orphan, widowed, grainless. the verse describes a habit that every reader of the time knew from court speech. a ruler did not say “i”. he called himself 孤, the orphan; 寡人, the lonely or deficient one; or 不穀, “the one without grain”, the unfruitful. the laozi points to this twice: these are the names that people most hate, and lords and kings take them as their titles (39, 42). so the grammar of rule already contained the idea of the verse: the highest person carries the lowest names. by the warring states the names were only etiquette, and a king who called himself “the orphan” could tax his people to starvation, as passage 75 says. the verse asks for the content behind the title. what would change if the humble words that leaders use, “i serve”, “i take full responsibility”, were taken as literal?

not a scapegoat, not “responsibility”. two western frames press on this verse, and both bend it. the first is religious: the scapegoat that carries the people’s sins into the desert, and the servant who has “borne our griefs”. in those pictures the bearer is driven out or killed, and the guilt goes away with him. the chinese ruler is not removed. he stays, and the dirt stays in him, as silt stays in a lake. nothing is redeemed. it is held. the second frame is managerial: “the leader takes responsibility”. that is an office phrase, and it is often a prelude to a statement and a clean exit. 垢 is not a statement. it is the mud itself: the failures, the hatred, the things that no one will touch. the verse does not say that taking it is noble. it says that this, and nothing finer, is what the word “lord” means.

正言若反: the book names its method. four characters close the passage: straight words, like, reversed. 正 is upright and correct, the word for a line that is true. 反 is a thing turned over; the shuowen says 覆也. the sentence is a reader’s guide to the whole book, placed three passages before the end. the weak wins. the low is king. the one who knows does not speak. each of these sounds upside down, and the text says: that is how straight speech sounds to a bent ear. two earlier lines stand behind it. 反者道之動, “turning back is the movement of dao” (40); there 反 is what dao does. and passage 41 lists a row of “seems”: the bright way seems dim, the way forward seems to go back. 若 is “seems”, and it matters. the words are not reversed. they seem so, from where we stand. what would you have to change for them to sound straight?

legge’s hymn. legge saw that the sage’s saying was verse, and he gave it rhyme and metre: “he who accepts his state’s reproach, / is hailed therefore its altars’ lord; / to him who bears men’s direful woes / they all the name of king accord.” it is an english hymn stanza. 垢, dirt, is “reproach”, a word from the psalms. 不祥, bad omens, are “men’s direful woes”, and the verb is “bears”: a nineteenth-century churchgoer hears the suffering servant at once. “king” has a capital. legge added a crowd that hails and accords; the chinese has only 是謂, “this is called”. he ends: “words that are strictly true seem to be paradoxical”, which is fair, and his “paradoxical” is greek for the same thought: against opinion. his first sentence shows less ease. for 其無以易之 he gives two readings joined by a dash, and adds “(so effectual)” in brackets.

be the low place once. in any group, some things roll downhill until they find a person: the task that no one wants, the complaint with no clear owner, the fault that belongs to everyone a little. most of us step aside by reflex. once this week, when such a thing rolls toward you, hold out your hands. say “give it to me”, or simply take it, and add no speech about it. then observe three things. first, what the others do: often the room relaxes, as ground drains when it has an outlet. second, what your body does: the pull to explain, to mention that it was not your fault. third, whether you can let the dirt settle in you without becoming dirty in your own eyes. water that takes mud is still water. do not do this every time. the verse describes a ruler, and one must know the size of one’s lake.

弱 and 強, 柔 and 剛: which one is strong?. the line names two pairs, 弱 and 強, 柔 and 剛, and joins each with 勝, to overcome. it is easy to freeze this into a rule: the weak wins. the chinese has no “always”, and the passage itself undoes the rule. water is called the weakest thing, and in the same sentence it attacks and nothing can beat it. at the moment of victory the weak one is the strong one; the pair has turned. the wall turns as well: the hard thing is the thing that breaks. water is not soft at all hours. it is ice in winter and a flood in spring. the text favors the soft side as a correction, in an age that knew the saying and still ranked by force. the second half shows the same turn in a ruler: the lowest place, which takes the dirt, is the lord’s seat. the last line names the method. 正 and 反, straight and reversed, are how each side sounds from the other.

the weak overcomes the strong and the soft overcomes the hard, as water wears down a wall.. the weak overcomes the strong and the soft overcomes the hard, as water wears down a wall. do you believe it? everyone is said to know it. do you know it in a way that changes what you do? recall a time when you gave way and it worked, and a time when you gave way and were simply run over. what made the difference? take the other side honestly: force decides, and softness wins only when force allows it. stay with that. what in your history speaks for it? if you find that you trust only one of the two, what would it cost you to grant the other its hour?

everyone knows that yielding works, and almost no one can live by it.. everyone knows that yielding works, and almost no one can live by it. name one thing that you know to be right and do not do. how long have you known it? what stands between the knowing and the doing: a fear, a habit, a picture of the person you would be if you did it? try the opposite thought: if you do not act on a thing, you do not in fact know it. is that fairer to you, or harsher?

the right to lead belongs to the one who takes the dirt and bad luck of the group.. the right to lead belongs to the one who takes the dirt and bad luck of the group. do you agree, or do you think that authority should rest on skill, or strength, or the choice of the group? when blame was in the air in your first family, where did it land? were you the one who took it, or the one who stepped aside? now hold the opposite: a person who takes on what is not theirs lets the others stay careless, and is used. what rises in you: recognition, resentment, relief? is there dirt of your own that you leave for someone else to hold? who holds it?

垢 earth beside a sovereign. two parts, side by side. on the left is 土, earth. the shuowen says of it 地之吐生物者也, “that part of the ground which puts forth living things”, and it reads the two level strokes as the surface and the depth of the ground, with the upright as a thing that comes out. on the right is 后 (hou), which gives the sound. and here a reader of this passage should stop, because 后 is a word for a ruler. the shuowen defines it as 繼體君也, “the lord who continues the line”, the sovereign who 施令以告四方, “issues commands to inform the four quarters”. it is the title in 后稷, lord millet, the ancestor of the zhou house, and later it became the word for a queen. so the character for dirt is written “earth” and “sovereign”. the dictionary treats this as sound only: 从土后聲. no one planned a meaning. but the passage says that the one who receives 垢 is lord of the altars, and the altar of the soil is a mound of 土. the graph happens to hold the whole verse. its sister 詬, with speech in place of earth, means spoken abuse; the collated silk text has that graph here. others with the same sound-part are 逅, a meeting by chance, and 姤, the hexagram of meeting. as for the meaning, the shuowen says 濁也: turbid, like water that carries earth. that is the first half of the passage in one word. nine strokes: three for earth, six for the sovereign. earth at the left is narrow: a short level line, an upright through it, and then a base stroke that does not lie flat. it rises to the right, like a flick. this is the rule for 土 on the left side; the rising stroke makes room and points to the next part. now 后. its first stroke is a short flat slash across the top, written from right to left. its second is a long slash that starts under the first and falls far to the lower left; give it a slow curve. third, a level line that starts at that long stroke and runs right. then the mouth in three strokes: left side, top and right side with a corner, base. keep the mouth small and low, under the level line. the long slash is the roof of the whole right side.

易 the lizard of change. the shuowen begins its entry with three names of one small animal: 蜥易，蝘蜓，守宮也, the lizard, the gecko, the “palace guard” that lives on house walls. then it says 象形, “a picture”: the top part is the head, and the lower strokes are the legs and tail. on this account 易, the word for change, is a lizard, an animal that tradition says changes its colour through the day, and the creature itself was later written with an insect sign added: 蜴. the shuowen then records a second opinion from a book of secret lore: 日月爲易，象陰陽也, “sun and moon make 易; it pictures yin and yang”. in the modern shape you can indeed see 日, the sun, on top, and with good will a moon below. modern scholars doubt both stories. the oldest forms are commonly explained as liquid poured from one vessel into another: an exchange. the three senses of the word follow from any of these pictures. to change. to exchange one thing for another, which is the sense that wang bi takes in this passage. and easy: what changes without resistance. the same graph names the book of changes, 易經. its family keeps the sound: 賜, to bestow, with a shell; 錫, tin, with metal; 踢, to kick, with a foot. water is the best 易 thing in the world, and the line says that nothing can 易 it. eight strokes: four above, four below. the upper part is written as 日, the sun: left side down; top and right side in one stroke with a corner; the inner level line; the base that closes it. keep it flat and compact, a little narrower than what comes next. the lower part begins with a slash that falls left from under the box. the sixth stroke is the important one: it goes right, turns a corner, comes down with a slight curve inward, and ends in a hook. inside its curve go two more slashes, parallel, both falling to the left. the three slashes must not be equal. write the first short, the second longer, the third longest, like the legs of an animal seen from the side. in cursive script the whole lower part becomes one spiral.

主 the flame in the lamp. this plain character, 王 with a dot on top, is one of the surprises of the shuowen. its definition is 鐙中火主也, “the flame in the middle of a lamp”. the lower part is the lamp: a stand with a bowl for the oil. the dot at the top is the flame, and the shuowen says that the dot is also the sound and the root of the word; it explains 丶 by itself as the mark that a reader makes at a stopping place, a small point of ink. so 主 began as the point of fire at the centre of a dark room. from there the sense grew by a clear path. the flame is what the room gathers around, so 主 is the host as against the guest, the owner as against the borrower, the lord as against the subject, and the main point as against the side issues. when the word had taken on these senses, the lamp wick got a new graph with fire added: 炷. the family shares the idea of a fixed point: 住, to stay, with a person; 柱, a pillar, with wood; 注, to pour onto one spot, with water; 駐, to halt a horse. do not confuse 主 with 王, the king, which the shuowen explains as three lines joined by one, though the two meet in this verse: 社稷主 and 天下王. the lord of the altars is, by the old picture, a small flame. a flame gives light because it accepts to burn. five strokes. first the dot: set the brush down at the top centre, press to the lower right, and lift. it should sit clear of the line below and not touch it. then three level lines and an upright, in this order: the first level line; the second, shorter; then the upright, from the first line down through the second; and last the long base, which closes the foot. space the three level lines evenly and make the base the widest. everything hangs from the dot, so its place decides whether the character stands straight; a dot too far left makes the lamp lean. in seal script the top is a small upright tongue of flame and the body below is clearly a stand with a bowl. regular script reduced the flame to one touch of the brush tip.

79 · the left tally. make peace in a great grievance, / and some grievance is sure to be left over. / how can that count as good? / so the sage holds the left tally / and makes no claim on anyone. / one with de keeps the tally; / one without de keeps the tithe. / the way of heaven has no kin. / it is always with the good person. the passage starts where a negotiation ends. a great grievance has been brought to accord, and the text observes that some of it remains, and asks how that can be called good. the answer is an object: a tally, the split bamboo contract of the age. the sage holds one half of it, the left, and presents no claim. two officers are then compared: the one with de keeps tallies, and the one without keeps the tithe. the close lifts the eyes: heaven’s way has no kin, and it is always with the good person. the things in the passage are a song for two voices, a body that turns in bed, a notched stick, a thorn over a shell, and a tax register. in the oldest manuscripts this was the last passage of a book. each of us keeps accounts. in them are the notched sticks of every wrong done to us, and we can match the notches years later. the passage does not ask us to throw the sticks away. that would be a pretence, and the residue would stay, as it stays after any made peace. it describes a different way to hold them: the tally in the hand, clear, and no demand. a claim that is not pressed stops growing. the mind is then free to do what wang bi advises and look at its own half: what did i owe, and did i pay? most grievance lives on the hope of collection. the last lines remove the helper that we hoped for. heaven has no kin: it is not on my side because i am me. three lessons for people who settle disputes. first, be modest about settlements. after a great conflict, an agreement on paper leaves a remainder, and a leader who announces that the matter is closed will meet it again. the better work is earlier: clear agreements, kept, before a grievance forms. second, the line on two officers describes two styles of authority. one keeps the record of what people have freely undertaken and trusts them to honour it. the other takes a share and looks for faults. people know very quickly which kind they work for. third, a strong position is a tally in the hand, and its best use is restraint. feng xuan burned his lord’s tallies and bought loyalty that no interest could buy. the text asks for the restraint without the calculation. the last line can be watched in any field. rain falls on the careful farmer’s land and on the careless one’s alike; that is 無親, no kin. yet the field that was dug and mulched takes the rain in, and the hard field sheds it. heaven is “with” the good farmer, and it chose no one. rivers show the first half. two streams that meet after a storm, one clear and one brown, run side by side in the same bed for a long way before they mix; the join is made at once and the accord takes miles. a broken bone knits and remains visible on a picture of the limb for life. things that are joined after a break carry the break. this is not a moral fault in them. it is why the text looks for the good before the break. do the exercise of the uncollected tally this week with one real debt of the non-money kind. hold it clearly; do not present it. beside that, do one small act of the earlier kind that wang bi points to: find an agreement that you are part of which is not clear, with a colleague, a partner, a child, and make your own half exact. say what you will do and by when. many great grievances begin as a tally that nobody cut. at the end of the week, read the last line and then sima qian’s doubt about it. do not hurry to defend the line. ask what you expect heaven to do for the good, and whether legge’s “on the side of” is your reading too.

聖人: not a saint. 聖人 is “the sage” by custom, and the english word misleads. this is not a saint: there is no holiness here and no reward after death. it is not only a wise man either. the graph has 耳, an ear, and the shuowen defines the word as 通, “to pass through, to reach”: a person whose hearing is open, and who leads by that attunement. in this passage the sage is a party to a contract, with a tally in the hand like anyone else. the difference is in what is done with it.

和: to answer in song. the first word is a musical one. the shuowen defines 和 as 相譍也, “to answer one another”: one voice sings a line and a second voice comes in on it. from that comes harmony, and from harmony, peace between people. as a verb, 和 is what a mediator does: brings two parties into tune. the text is doubtful about this work when the grievance is great. voices can be brought into tune for an afternoon. elsewhere the book prizes 和 deeply: the ten thousand things carry yin on their backs and hold yang in their arms, and the blended breath makes their 和 (42); to know 和 is called constancy (55). so the word itself is not in question. the question is whether accord can be made after the fact, by a treaty, when it was not kept before.

怨: a heart that turns in bed. 怨 is the grievance of one who has been wronged, or believes so: resentment that is kept. the shuowen defines it as 恚, hatred, and builds it from 心, the heart, with 夗 above for the sound. look up 夗 by itself and the dictionary gives a picture that is hard to forget: 轉臥也, “to turn over while lying down”. it is written with 夕, evening, and a bent figure. the shuowen does not say that this sense plays a part in 怨; it marks only the sound. but a reader of the graph sees an evening, a body that turns, and a heart under them. that is an exact description of a grudge at night. english “grievance” is a legal word, and “resentment” is latin for “feeling again”. the chinese graph shows where the feeling is felt again, and at what hour.

wang bi: the wound does not go back. why is there always a remainder? wang bi writes: 不明理其契，以致大怨已至。而德和之，其傷不復，故有餘怨也。 “one did not keep the tally clear and in order, and so a great grievance has already come. if one then uses 德 to make peace in it, the wound does not return to what it was. so there is grievance left over.” his weight is on 已, “already”. peace-making arrives after the damage, and damage of this kind does not reverse. so he moves the whole teaching to an earlier point in time: the work is to keep one’s own agreements clear, so that the great grievance never forms. this agrees with passages 63 and 64: deal with a thing while it is small; act on it before it exists. the word 餘 was “surplus” in passage 77. here the surplus is of pain.

安可以為善: an honest question. 安 is here the question word “how?”, and the line is five characters: how can [this] be taken as good? the text does not say that reconciliation is bad. it says that it cannot be called 善, the good outcome, because the residue is still in the hearts of both sides. this goes against a moral habit of english, in which “they made peace” is a happy ending. it also seems to go against the book itself. passage 63 said 報怨以德, “answer grievance with 德”, a line that confucius is said to have questioned: with what, then, will you answer kindness? the two passages can be read together. to answer a small grievance with 德 at once, before it grows, is passage 63. to arrive with good will after a great one has formed is this line, and it is too late for “good”.

契: a contract you can split. a 契 was a strip of bamboo or wood. the terms of a loan or a sale were written on it, notches were cut across its edge, and it was split down the middle. each party kept one half. when the debt came due, the halves were set side by side; if the notches met, the claim was true. the shuowen says of a related word, 券, that the two parts were cut apart with a knife along the side. such tallies were the ordinary instrument of credit in the warring states, and the state used the same device in bronze for military orders. the book of changes makes them a mark of civilisation: in high antiquity people ruled by knotted cords, and later sages replaced these with 書契, writing and tallies. the next passage of the laozi asks for the knotted cords back.

left half or right half?. which half did the creditor hold? readers have argued for two thousand years. the heshang gong commentary and many later scholars say the left: the sage is the lender who holds the proof of a claim and does not use it. but two texts of the period speak of a person who “takes the right tally” in order to press a demand, with the very verb 責. on that evidence the right half is the creditor’s and the left the debtor’s, and the sage takes the lower seat in the contract: the side that owes. a ritual text adds that one who presents grain holds the right half, and the old comment there says that the right was the side of honour. the two mawangdui silk texts are reported to disagree: silk a has 右介, the right tally, and silk b has the left, as our text does. custom may have differed from state to state. in every version the next clause is the same, and it carries the sense: no demand is made.

責: a thorn over money. 責 has 貝, the cowrie shell that was money, at its foot. the shuowen defines the word as 求也, “to demand”, and names the top part as 朿, which gives the sound. 朿 is its word for a thorn, 木芒也, the sharp point on a tree; the same part, with a knife, makes 刺, to stab. so the graph for pressing a claim is, to the eye, a thorn over a shell. the word has three senses that english keeps apart: to demand payment; to blame or reproach; and a duty, as in the modern 責任, responsibility. with a person added it is 債, debt. in chinese, then, to blame someone is to present a bill. 不責於人 can be heard both ways at once: the sage does not collect from people, and does not reproach them. is there a difference, when you reproach someone, from asking to be paid?

the man who burned the tallies. the age had a famous case of this passage in action. lord mengchang, a minister of qi about 300 bce, kept three thousand retainers and lived on loans to the people of his fief, xue. he sent a poor retainer named feng xuan to collect. feng xuan called in all the debtors, matched their tallies, and then, in the lord’s name, burned the tallies in front of them. the people shouted “ten thousand years”. mengchang was angry: where was his money? feng xuan answered that the lord’s house was full of goods and lacked one thing, 義, right dealing, and that he had bought it for him. a year later mengchang lost his post and went home to xue. the whole population came out a hundred li to meet him. the story is told as clever policy. the passage is less interested in the return.

德 in a passage about debt. we leave 德 as de. its usual english, “virtue”, was right in the old sense of that word, the power in a thing, as when a herb has virtue. in the laozi it is the inner power of a person or creature that is in accord with dao. but 德 had a second, everyday sense in this period, and a passage on tallies brings it out. a 德 was a kindness done, and so a credit: the one who received it owed something back. texts of the time speak of “claiming one’s 德” from a ruler, in the very phrase used for debts. so 有德, “to have 德”, can also be heard as “to be owed”. the line plays on this. the person with real 德 is the one who holds the proof of what is owed, the tally, and only keeps it. wang bi reads the keeping in his own way.

wang bi: mind your own half. on 有德司契 wang bi writes: 有德之人念思其契，不念怨生而後責於人也。 “the person who has 德 keeps their thought on their own tally. they do not wait until grievance has arisen and afterwards make demands on others.” and on the left tally: 左契，防怨之所由生也, “the left tally guards the place from which grievance is born”. in his reading the tally is not mainly a claim. it is a record of what was agreed, and the person with 德 studies their own half: what did i undertake? have i kept it? the attention goes to one’s own side of every agreement. the other person’s side is left to the other person. this turns the line into a daily discipline, and it explains how the sage can hold a tally for life and never press a claim: the tally was for self-examination.

徹: the tithe, or the hunt for faults. 司徹 is “to have charge of 徹”, and the word has been read in three ways. the plainest takes it as the name of the zhou land tax. mencius says: the xia took tribute, the yin took labour, and 周人百畝而徹, “the people of zhou took the 徹 on a hundred mu”, about one part in ten. then the line sets two officers side by side. one keeps tallies and waits for free payment. the other keeps the tithe and takes a fixed share, due or not, in good years and bad. trust faces extraction, and the passage joins the criticism of passages 75 and 77. wang bi reads otherwise: 徹，司人之過也, “徹 is to watch for people’s faults”. the shuowen’s root sense is 通, to go right through. others read the graph as 轍, wheel-tracks: the marks that people leave. tithe or fault, the one without 德 is busy with what others owe.

無親: heaven has no relatives. 親 is a parent, a kinsman, one’s own people. the shuowen’s gloss is 至, “to reach all the way”: those who are closest. zhou society was built on this word. fiefs went to the king’s kin; office went by lineage; and the confucians made 親親, “treating kin as kin”, the root of all goodness. to say 天道無親 is therefore a political act. heaven’s way has no family, no clan, no chosen house. the thought was older than the laozi. a saying preserved in the zuo chronicle from a lost zhou document runs: 皇天無親，惟德是輔, “august heaven has no kin; it helps only 德”. that saying had served the zhou to explain why heaven left the shang kings. passage 5 has the same coolness: heaven and earth are not humane. for whom would this line be bad news?

no favourites, yet “always with the good”?. the last two clauses seem to conflict. heaven has no favourites; and it is always 與 the good person. 與 can mean “to give to”, “to side with”, and “to be with”. if it means “to reward”, then heaven has favourites after all, the good ones. the conflict resolves when 親 and 善 are read with care. 親 is closeness by birth or tie: heaven has none of that. 善 is a way of acting, and in this book it often means “good at”: good at walking, good at closing (27). the 善人 of this passage is the one just described, who holds the tally and makes no claim. heaven’s way was said in passage 77 to take from surplus and mend lack. a person who acts so is going where heaven goes. heaven is “with” that person as a current is with a swimmer. no choice is made, and no reward is paid.

the historian’s doubt. the closing line became a proverb, and the greatest historian of china used it to ask a terrible question. sima qian (about 145–86 bce) opens his collection of biographies with bo yi and shu qi, two brothers who refused on principle to eat the grain of a new dynasty and starved on a mountain. he writes: some say 天道無親，常與善人. were bo yi and shu qi not good people? and the robber zhi killed the innocent every day and died in bed at a great age. then: 余甚惑焉，儻所謂天道，是邪非邪, “i am deeply perplexed. this so-called way of heaven: is it so, or is it not?” sima qian had himself been castrated for speaking in defence of a defeated general. he read 與 as “reward” and found the line false. does the other reading of 與 answer him, or only step around him?

once, the last line of a book. in the received order this passage is third from the end. in the mawangdui silk texts it stands at a greater place. those texts begin with the part on 德, our passages 38 to 81, and put our 80 and 81 earlier, after 66. so their first book runs out here; after the words 恆與善人 the collated silk text marks the start of the part on dao. for readers of that edition, the book of 德 ended on the line about heaven’s way. its last images were a split piece of bamboo, a tax officer, and a heaven without family. the same book opens, in our passage 38, with the highest 德 that does not act as 德. a reader who went from that opening to this close was shown what such 德 looks like in the hand: a tally that is held and never presented.

legge’s eight brackets. legge needed eight sets of brackets for this short passage, and they show where the chinese gave him less than a victorian sentence requires. the grudge remains “(in the mind of the one who was wrong)”; the chinese does not say in whose mind. the sage does not insist on the “(speedy) fulfilment” of the contract; the chinese says that the sage makes no demand, with no word about speed. 德 becomes “the attributes (of the tao)”, a phrase from theology, where god has attributes. for 徹 he writes “the conditions favourable to himself”, which is a guess. at the end, 無親 becomes “no partiality of love”. a missionary could not write that heaven has no love for its own; he wrote that its love is impartial. his last clause is exact and brave: “it is always on the side of the good man”. only “man” is added.

hold one tally, and do not present it. think of something that is owed to you. it may be money. more often it is an apology, a favour returned, an acknowledgment of work that you did. you hold your half of that tally, and the notches are clear in your mind; you can recite them. for one week, keep the tally and do not present it. do not hint at it, and do not mention it to a third person. this is not the same as forgiving the debt or pretending that it does not exist. the sage holds the tally. then do wang bi’s exercise and look at your own half of the same agreement: what did you undertake, and did you deliver it? notice at what hour the grievance comes to you. the graph 怨 suggests that it is at night.

有德 and 無德: two halves of one stick. the passage holds several pairs: 和 and 怨, accord and grievance; the left tally and the right; 有德 and 無德. the tally shows how such pairs work. it is one stick, split. a claim has no meaning without a debt, and neither half proves anything alone. the holder of one claim is a debtor in some other contract, and readers do not agree on which half the sage holds. 德 itself has two faces: an inner power, and a credit that someone owes. the text favors the keeper of the tally over the keeper of the tithe. that preference corrects an age of extraction. it is not a rule against every claim. the favored side also turns: a person who is proud of the claims not pressed keeps a second account, of merit, and collects on that. accord and grievance turn too. each made peace leaves a remainder, and the remainder is the seed of the next grievance.

after a great grievance is settled, some of it is sure to remain, so peace made afterwards is not enough.. after a great grievance is settled, some of it is sure to remain, so peace made afterwards is not enough. is this true of the peace that you have made? think of one settled quarrel and look for what is left in it. what were you taught about forgiving: that it wipes the slate, or that it does not? who taught you, and did they live by it? take the opposite view: a real reconciliation leaves nothing over, and a bond can be stronger at the mended place. have you known one such case? what did it need? which do you hold more tightly: the grievances that others have against you, or yours against them? what does each give you?

a person of inner power keeps the proof of what is owed and does not press the claim.. a person of inner power keeps the proof of what is owed and does not press the claim. could you do this with a debt that matters? what do you feel when you picture it: freedom, or the sense of being a fool? look at how debts were handled around you when you were young. were accounts kept exactly, or never spoken of? stand on the other side: to claim what is owed is self-respect, and silence teaches people to take from you. give that its due. where has it been true for you? when you do not ask, is it restraint, or fear of the answer? how do you tell the two apart?

the way of heaven has no favourites, yet it goes along with those who act well.. the way of heaven has no favourites, yet it goes along with those who act well. do you believe that acting well is met by anything at all? what have you seen? was there a favourite in your family? were you the one, or not? how does that colour what you expect from life? try the plain opposite: nothing is with anyone, and good people starve while the cruel grow old. a great historian feared so. can you still act well if that is how it is? what do you secretly expect to receive for being good? what happens in you when it does not arrive?

契 notches, a knife, and a great thing. the character has three parts, and the top two tell how a contract was made. at the upper left is 丰, three short strokes across one upright: a stick with notches cut in it. at the upper right is 刀, a knife, the tool that cut them. the shuowen treats these two together as one older graph, 㓞, the act of carving. under them is 大, “great”, which the dictionary explains as the picture of a person: 天大，地大，人亦大, “heaven is great, earth is great, and a person is also great”. the definition of the whole is 大約也, “a major agreement”. so 契 says: a great matter, settled with a knife and notches. a variant graph, 栔, has 木, wood, at the foot in place of 大. the shuowen then quotes the book of changes on the invention of writing and tallies, which replaced the knotted cords. the word spread from the object to what it does. 契 is to fit together exactly, as two halves fit: a deep friendship is 默契, a silent tally. its relatives carry the knife sense: 楔, a wedge, with wood; 鍥, to carve, with metal. the modern word for a contract is still 契約. note what this instrument assumes: two people, one object, and a future day when the halves will meet. the sage of the passage holds half of that future and does not call it in. nine strokes. the notched stick first, in four: three short level strokes from the top down, the third rising a little to the right, and then the upright through all three. keep it narrow and to the left. the knife next, in two: a stroke that goes right, turns the corner, and comes down to a hook; then a slash inside it, falling left. the stick and the knife share the upper half and must stand close without touching. then 大 below, in three: a long level line that underlines both upper parts; a slash from its centre to the lower left; and a press to the lower right. these last two open like a person’s legs and carry everything above. the upper half is small, careful cutting, and the lower half is one broad gesture. a good hand lets the difference show.

怨 evening, a bent body, a heart. the lower part is 心, the heart, and it tells you the field: this is a feeling. the heart sign is under most chinese words for states of mind: 思 (to think), 忘 (to forget), 怒 (anger), 恩 (kindness received), 悲 (grief). above it is 夗 (yuan), which gives the sound. 夗 has two halves of its own. the left is 夕, evening, the crescent moon just risen. the right is a bent or kneeling figure. the shuowen defines 夗 as 轉臥也, “to turn over while lying down”, and comments 臥有卪也, “even in lying down there is a measure”. you know this sound-part from 鴛, the mandarin duck, the bird of faithful pairs, and from 宛, to bend or wind, which the shuowen explains as grass that bends over and covers itself. the family is about curling and turning. so read 怨 from the top: evening; a body that turns; and under them the heart. the dictionary’s own definition is short, 恚也, “hatred held in”, and it does not claim that the parts make a picture. but a learner is allowed to keep a picture that fits this well. a grievance is the thing that turns us over at night. the passage says that even after peace is made, some of it is left. the body knows where. nine strokes: five above, four below. evening first: a short slash to the left; a stroke that goes right, turns, and sweeps down to the left; a dot inside. then the bent figure: a stroke that goes right, turns, and hooks; and under it a stroke that comes down, bends, runs right, and hooks upward. these two parts sit side by side and should lean toward each other a little. now the heart, wide and low, in four strokes that never touch: a dot at the left; the long lying hook, which dips like the bottom of a bowl and flicks up at the right end; a dot above the middle of the bowl; a dot at the far right. the lying hook is the hardest stroke in regular script. enter lightly, press as it curves, and hook toward the centre dot. the three dots should look as if they are in motion over still water.

責 the thorn on the shell. the lower part is 貝, the cowrie shell, which was money before metal coins, and which stands under most words of value: 財 (wealth), 貨 (goods), 買 (to buy), 貴 (dear), 貧 (poor). the upper part is now four simple strokes. the shuowen names what it was: 朿, a thorn, 木芒也, “the sharp point of a tree”, and says that it gives the sound. you can see the thorn more fully in 刺, to stab, where it stands beside a knife, and in 棗, the jujube, a thorny tree written with two of them. the definition of 責 is 求也: to demand, to seek what is due. so the word was first about payment. its other senses grew from that: to hold someone to account, to reproach, to punish, and then the duty for which one is held to account. the family is the vocabulary of obligation. 債 adds a person: a debt. 積, with grain, is to pile up; the shuowen says 聚也, to gather. 績, with thread, is spun yarn and so a record of work done. 蹟, with a foot, is a track left behind. in each, something has built up that can be counted. the passage’s sage has the shell’s worth in hand and leaves the thorn unused: 不責於人. feel the difference in your own speech between stating what is owed and pressing the point in. eleven strokes: four for the top, seven for the shell. the top begins with a level line; then a second, a little shorter; then an upright that starts above the first line and passes down through both; then a third level line, long, which the upright meets and does not cross. this long line is the lid of the character, and it should reach past the shell on both sides. the shell: its left side; its top and right side in one stroke with a corner; two short level lines inside; a third that closes the box; and then the two feet, a slash to the left and a dot to the right. keep the box tall and narrow, with even spaces. the feet spread just wider than the box and end level with each other. in running script the three top lines become one zigzag and the feet become two quick dots.

80 · the neighbour’s rooster. a small state, few people. / let there be tools for ten and for a hundred, / and let them go unused. / let the people take death as a heavy thing / and not move far away. / though there are boats and carts, / there is no occasion to ride them. / though there are armour and weapons, / there is no occasion to draw them up. / let people go back to knotted cords and use them: / find their food sweet, / their clothes beautiful, / their homes at rest, / their customs a joy. / neighbouring states look across at each other; / the sound of chickens and dogs is heard from one to the other; / and the people reach old age and death / without going back and forth. four characters set the scene: small state, few people. then a series of wishes, each marked by 使. there are tools for ten and a hundred, unused. the people hold death heavy and stay. boats and carts stand idle; armour and weapons are never drawn up. people return to knotted cords. then four short phrases, each a verb of feeling: they find sweet their food, find beautiful their clothes, rest in their homes, rejoice in their customs. the close is a long shot across a border. two states gaze at each other; chickens and dogs are heard across the line; people grow old and die and do not go back and forth. count what is present: tools, boats, carts, armour, weapons, cords, food, clothes, houses, customs, neighbours, animals. everything is present, and the passage is about what is not done with it. the passage can be read as a state of mind. the mind has its tools for ten and a hundred: plans, comparisons, the power to imagine every other life. it has boats and carts: the ability to leave any moment for another. it has armour and weapons, and it has script, the running record of who owes what. in the small state all of these remain and none is in use. what is left is the four verbs. the food is sweet, and the room is restful, because attention has stopped travelling. the far country is still there. one can see it, and even hear its roosters, and the old pull to go is quiet. this is not innocence. the text says 復, return: it is the peace of one who has been everywhere in thought and now stays. no ruler of the warring states wanted few people, and no modern institution wants to be small. the passage asks leaders to question growth as a goal, and it gives a different measure of success: do the people find their food sweet, their work and homes good, their own customs a joy? do they hold life dear enough to stay? capacity is not forbidden. the state has the machines and the arms. the art is to have them and find no occasion for them, which is harder than not having them. sima qian’s objection should be heard: as a policy imposed from above, this needs force, and then it is a prison. wang bi’s answer is that it is a demonstration and not a decree. a leader can remove the causes of flight. a leader cannot order contentment. the scale of the passage is the scale of a valley. a rooster’s call carries perhaps a kilometre in still air, and a dog’s bark a little more. within that radius a farming community can find water, fuel, soil, and seed, and it can know every tree. the graph for custom, 俗, puts a person beside a valley. each valley shapes a way of living that fits it. ecologists speak of a bioregion; the idea is close. when boats and carts are in constant use, the valley’s limits stop teaching, because whatever is short can be brought in and whatever is waste can be sent out. the two states that gaze at each other are like two watersheds on either side of a ridge: near, visible, and each complete. the line does not despise the far side. it lets it be whole. try one day within earshot, or a single hour of it if a day is not possible. if even that is hard, do only the four verbs at one meal: 甘其食. take the food that is in the house, and before you eat, look at it; then find it sweet. the grammar is exact: the sweetness is something that you do. afterwards ask the honest questions that the passage raises. would you choose this life? sima qian thought that no one would. was the hour restful, or did you feel shut in? then read the zhuangzi’s version, which places the village in the far past, and tao yuanming’s, which hides it behind a cave. three writers could not agree on where the small state is. where did you find it?

小國寡民: four characters, no verb. the passage opens with four characters and no grammar: small, state, few, people. chinese adjectives can act as verbs, so there are two ways to hear it. as a description: “a small state with few people”, the setting of what follows. as a programme: “make the state small; make the people few”. the second is a shock. it tells a ruler to shrink the two things that every ruler of the age tried to enlarge. wang bi takes the first way. many modern readers take the second. our rendering keeps the four words as a bare phrase, without a verb, so that the choice stays open. english had to add “a” and a comma. note also what 國 is: a wall and a weapon are in the graph, as the shuowen reads it. the text takes the war-state of its time and imagines it small.
