wang bi: the small state is only the example. wang bi does not read the opening as a plan to make states small. he writes: 國既小，民又寡，尚可使反古，況國大民眾乎？故舉小國而言也。 “when the state is small and the people, moreover, few, they can still be brought to return to the ancient way. how much more, then, when the state is large and the people many? so the text takes a small state as its example.” his logic is unexpected. one would think that the simple life is easier in a small place. wang bi says that a small, poor state has the least to work with, and that even there the return is possible; a great state has still more room for it. for him the passage does not describe a village that hides from the world. it is a demonstration, in the smallest case, of what any government could allow.

寡民: the one thing no king wanted. 寡 is “few”. the shuowen builds it from a roof and a word for sharing out: what is divided becomes little. it was also the ruler’s own humble name, 寡人, “the deficient one”. put the two uses side by side and you have the main anxiety of the warring states. population was power: more people meant more grain and more soldiers. king hui of liang complains to mencius: i use my whole heart for my state, and yet 鄰國之民不加少，寡人之民不加多, “the people of neighbouring states do not grow fewer, and my people do not grow more. why?” the state of qin offered land and tax relief to draw settlers from its rivals. households were registered and forbidden to leave. in this setting the two characters 寡民 reverse the whole policy of the age. the lonely one is asked to want a lonely state.

使: who is speaking, and in what mood?. 使 comes three times in the passage: 使有, 使民, 使人. it means “to cause, to make, to send”, and also “suppose that”. english must pick a mood. legge wrote “i would so order it… i would make the people”: a ruler’s voice with a plan. that adds an “i” that the chinese does not have. others write “let there be”, which sounds like a wish or a blessing. others take it as a thought: “suppose there were”. the tone of the whole passage hangs on this word. is it a blueprint, a daydream, a memory, or a mirror held up to a violent age? our “let” is the lightest option that english offers, and it still adds something. read the passage three times, once in each mood, and notice which one you believe.

什伯之器: machines, or squad weapons?. 什 and 伯 are ten and a hundred, and 器 is any made tool. there are two old readings. one: implements that do the work of ten or a hundred men, labour-saving devices. a modern collated edition of the mawangdui silk texts supports this, for it adds a word: 十百人之器, “tools of ten or a hundred people”. legge heard a third sense, men with the ability of ten or a hundred. the other reading is military. the shuowen defines 什 as 相什保也, households in tens that stand surety for each other, and in the armies of the age the squad of ten and the company of a hundred were the basic units. then 什伯之器 are the arms and gear of the levy, and the line agrees with the later one about armour that is never drawn up. on both readings the tools exist. they are not destroyed. they are left where they lie.

death made heavy again. 重死 is “to hold death heavy”. it answers passage 75 exactly, where the people 輕死, hold death light, because those above them take too much. a people that holds death light will rebel or run. a people that holds it heavy stays, because life at home is worth keeping. wang bi explains: 使民不用，惟身是寶，不貪貨賂，故各安其居，重死而不遠徙也。 “let the people have no use for such things; let them treasure only their own persons, and not covet goods. then each is at peace in the home, holds death heavy, and does not move far.” moving far was what desperate people did: they fled taxes, war, and famine. a modern collated edition of the mawangdui silk texts has no 不 here: 使民重死而遠徙. some editors read 遠 as a verb, “keep far from moving”, with the same sense; others think that a negative was lost. what makes a life heavy enough that death is heavy too?

陳: the battle line. 陳 is to set things out in rows, and in military use it is read zhen: the array, troops drawn up for battle. formation was the science of the age; an army that could hold its lines under drums and flags won. the analects has a scene with this word. duke ling of wei asked confucius about 陳, battle formations. confucius replied that he had learned about ritual vessels and had never studied the matters of armies, and he left wei the next day. the laozi’s sentence is gentler and stranger. it does not refuse the weapons, and it does not melt them down. the state keeps armour and blades, and there is 無所, “no place where, no occasion on which”, to draw them up. english “display” is too weak for the word, and “use” is too wide. a line is what never forms.

結繩: before writing. knotted cords were the record-keeping of the time before script, as the chinese remembered it. the book of changes says: 上古結繩而治，後世聖人易之以書契, “in high antiquity people knotted cords and so kept order; the sages of later ages replaced them with writing and tallies”. a large knot for a large matter, a small knot for a small one, later scholars said. the device is real: the inca ran an empire on knotted cords, the quipu, with no writing. for the laozi the cords stand for a world without documents: no registers of households, no tax rolls, no law codes, no contracts like the tally of the passage before this. they also create a problem that the text does not hide. this wish to return to a time before writing has come to us in writing. is the book a tool that hopes to be left unused, like the boats?

甘 and 美: four verbs of feeling. 甘其食，美其服: literally “sweet their food, beautiful their clothes”. the adjectives stand first and act as verbs: the people find their food sweet. this matters. the text does not say that the food is plain and that they bear it, and it does not say that the food is rich. it says nothing about the food at all. it describes a relation between people and what they have. legge could not leave it so; he added “(coarse)” food, “(plain)” clothes, “(poor)” dwellings in brackets, and made them contented peasants. the two words explain each other in the shuowen: 甘 is defined as 美, and 美 as 甘. 甘 is a mouth with something held in it. 美 is 羊 over 大, a sheep and “large”; the dictionary notes that the sheep is chief among animals for the table. both began on the tongue.

安: a woman under a roof. 安 is a roof, 宀, with 女, a woman, beneath it, and the shuowen defines it by one word: 靜也, stillness. it reads the graph as it looks: 从女在宀下, “a woman under a roof”. peace, in this picture, is a house with someone at home in it. the word is the usual chinese for safety and peace, and in the laozi it has weight: passage 35 promises 安平太, rest, evenness, and greatness, to those who go toward the great image. here it is a verb with 居, a dwelling: to be at rest in one’s home. a modern collated edition of the mawangdui silk texts has the four phrases in another order, with joy in customs third and rest at home last. in that version the list ends indoors, in stillness, before the text turns to the neighbours.

樂其俗: music in the valley. 樂 is read le, joy, and yue, music; it is one graph, and for early china one thing. the shuowen defines it as the name for all music, 五聲八音緫名, and sees in the graph drums on a wooden stand. so to 樂 one’s customs is to be glad in them, and it carries an echo of singing and drums at the village feast. 俗 is custom: the ways of a place. the shuowen says 習也, “what is practised”, and the graph is a person beside 谷, a valley, which gives the sound. a learner may notice that each valley has its people and its ways. the confucians wanted to reform local customs by ritual from the centre: 移風易俗, “shift the airs and change the customs”. the laozi’s line asks for no change. the people are to take joy in the customs they have.

望: to look for one who is away. 鄰國相望: neighbouring states “gaze toward each other”. 望 is not plain seeing. it is a long look into the distance, at a hill, at the full moon, toward a hope. the shuowen’s definition is a small story: 出亡在外，望其還也, “someone has gone away and is abroad; one looks out for their return”. so the word has longing in it. 鄰, a neighbour, is defined as 五家爲鄰, “five families make a 鄰”: the smallest unit of village life. the states of this line are close enough to be neighbours in that homely sense, and they look across at each other as people look toward someone they think of. the text gives the gaze, and it gives the hearing, and then it withholds the visit. the sentence is not cold. it may be the fullest picture in the book of being near without taking.

chickens and dogs, for two thousand years. the chickens and dogs are the sound of a settled place. a village that has them has grain to spare, and nobody there is about to flee. the phrase became a fixed expression, 雞犬相聞, for neighbours who live within earshot. its most famous return is in a short tale of about 421 ce by the poet tao yuanming. a fisherman follows a stream through peach blossom, squeezes through a cave, and finds a hidden valley: good fields, ponds, mulberry and bamboo, paths between the plots, and 雞犬相聞, chickens and dogs heard from one house to the next. the people there fled the wars of qin about six hundred years before and have never heard of the dynasties since. he leaves, and no one can find the place again. tao yuanming answers the laozi’s 使 with a story. the small state exists, and the road to it is lost.

不相往來: what kind of traffic stops?. 往來 is “going and coming”. a modern reader hears isolation: no visits, no friendship, no curiosity. that may be too private a hearing. in the language of the time 往來 was also the traffic between states, and that traffic had a character. envoys went and came to make alliances against a third party. merchants went and came with goods that created wants. armies went and came on the roads that the boats and carts used. refugees went and came. when a peasant of the warring states crossed a border, it was seldom for a holiday. read so, the last line describes two communities that need nothing from each other and fear nothing from each other. they are within hearing, and that is company enough. the line still troubles many readers, and it should. what would you lose, and what would you be spared?

the same village, in the zhuangzi. the second half of this passage stands almost word for word in the zhuangzi, in a chapter called “rifling trunks”. but there it has a date. the writer lists twelve rulers of deepest antiquity and says: 當是時也，民結繩而用之, “in that time, the people knotted cords and used them”, found their food sweet, their clothes beautiful, their customs a joy, their homes at rest; neighbouring states looked across at each other, the sounds of chickens and dogs were heard, and the people grew old and died without going back and forth. 若此之時，則至治已, “a time like that was the height of good order”. then he turns in anger on his own age, in which people crane their necks and run after any clever man. in the zhuangzi the village is a lost golden age. its order of phrases and its 雞狗 for 雞犬 agree with the collated mawangdui wording. the laozi’s version has no “in that time”. it has only 使. which is the older form, no one knows.

a historian of commerce objects. about 100 bce the historian sima qian wrote a chapter on the men who had grown rich by trade. he opened it with this passage, quoted at length: neighbouring states in sight of each other, the people content with their food, clothes, customs, and work, no traffic until death. then he gave his verdict: to make this one’s aim in recent times, one would have to stop up the eyes and ears of the people, and it could hardly be done. people’s ears and eyes want fine sounds and sights, and their mouths want the taste of meat, and no teaching will change it. the wise ruler, he says, goes along with these wants. this is the first great objection to the passage, and it comes from a serious man. he read 使 as a policy and judged that it would need force. is he right about the policy, and wrong about the mood?

not quite a utopia. western readers file this passage under “utopia”, a word that thomas more coined in 1516 from greek: no-place. the word brings a tradition with it: plato’s city, more’s island, the planned community with its laws and its founder. those are designs, and they are full of institutions. the laozi’s small state has almost none. it is defined by what is not used: tools, boats, armour, writing. a second western frame is the “noble savage”, the happy primitive of the eighteenth century. that does not fit either. these people have boats, weapons, and machines, and they have known writing; the text says 復, “return”. they are not innocent. they have what a civilisation has and do not reach for it. the nearest thing in the book is the person of passage 28, who knows the male and keeps to the female. this is the same person, as a whole society.

not at the end, in the oldest copies. we meet this passage as the last but one, a quiet picture before the book closes. the mawangdui silk texts, buried in 168 bce, have it elsewhere. there our 80 and 81 follow our 66, and then the text goes on with 67. passage 66 is the one on the rivers and the sea, which are kings of the hundred valleys because they lie low. in that order the small state comes straight after the sea’s lesson in lowness, and before the passages on care, war, and death. it is a picture in the middle of the argument, and not a farewell. a modern collated edition prints 邦 for 國 in this passage; 國 was put in later to avoid the name of the first han emperor, liu bang. someone, at some time, moved these two passages to the end. whoever did it chose a village to close the book.

legge’s “i would”. legge puts the passage in the mouth of a planner: “i would so order it”, “i would make the people”. the chinese has no “i”. he reads 什伯之器 as “individuals with the abilities of ten or a hundred men” whom the state does not employ, one of the traditional readings. he explains the knotted cords in brackets: “(instead of the written characters)”. he cannot believe that the people simply find their food sweet, and adds “(coarse)”, “(plain)”, “(poor)”, and “(simple)”: four adjectives of pity from a man of the age of progress. and for 不相往來 he writes that they should not “have any intercourse with” the neighbour. legge worked for thirty years in hong kong, a colony founded to open china to trade. he was a fair man, and praise of a life without traffic was hard for his age to hear.

one day within earshot. give the passage one day. choose a day when you can stay within the distance that a rooster’s call would carry from your door: on foot, no vehicle. leave some of your “tools for ten and for a hundred” where they lie; you know which machines do the work of a hundred people for you, and which of them you could rest. write nothing down that day. then do the four verbs, on purpose. eat one plain meal and try to find it sweet. put on ordinary clothes and find them good. sit in your own room until it is restful. do one thing that is a custom of your household or street, and enjoy it. in the evening, listen for the neighbours. you need not visit. notice what you missed, and how strongly, and what you did not miss at all.

有 and 不用: having, and not using. the passage has no named pair like soft and hard. its pair is in its grammar: 有…而不用, there are tools, and they are not used; 雖有…無所, though there are boats, there is no occasion. having and not using stand together in each sentence, and neither is given up. a people with no boats cannot choose to stay; their staying is only lack. the text needs the boat at the shore for the staying to mean anything. the close has a second pair of the same kind: near and apart. the states look across at each other and hear each other, and do not visit. a one-sided reading takes the passage as “simple good, complex bad”, or “home good, travel bad”. the characters do not say so. the lean toward staying corrects an age of forced movement: levies, flight, armies on the roads. it also turns. staying that is enforced is a prison, as sima qian saw, and a tool that is left unused for ever is no longer had.

people can find their own food sweet and their own home restful, with no need to go elsewhere.. people can find their own food sweet and their own home restful, with no need to go elsewhere. is that so for you? what in your present life do you find sweet as it is? where did you learn that the better life is somewhere else, or that it is here? who in your family left, and who stayed? take the other side: the wish to go, to see, to trade, to meet strangers is the best thing in people, and staying is a slow sleep. let that be true for a while. what wakes up? when you see someone content with little, do you feel respect, envy, or a quiet scorn? what might that feeling be about?

a good life has powerful tools and weapons at hand and finds no occasion to use them.. a good life has powerful tools and weapons at hand and finds no occasion to use them. which of your powers could you leave unused? think of a tool, a skill, or an argument that you know would win. what happens in you when you hold a capacity back: ease, or the fear that it is wasted? now the opposite: what you can do, you should do, and an unused gift is a loss to everyone. whose voice says that in your head? is your restraint a choice, or a lack of nerve? is your use of power a choice, or a habit? how would you know?

a community does well when it is small and its people are few.. a community does well when it is small and its people are few. do you agree? in which size of group have you been most yourself? what does growth mean to you: safety, proof, life itself? where does that meaning come from? hold the opposite: only large numbers and open roads bring the medicine, the music, and the stranger who changes your mind. what would you not give up? if both are true, what are you in fact choosing between?

甘 something held in the mouth. this is one of the simplest characters in the book and one of the oldest ideas. the shuowen explains it in six characters: 从口含一, “from a mouth that holds a one”. the outer shape is 口, a mouth, drawn open at the top in the modern form. the short line inside is the thing in the mouth: a bit of food that is good enough to keep there and not swallow at once. that is sweetness, shown by what the mouth does with it. the definition is 美也, “fine, good to taste”. then the shuowen adds a line that a reader of the laozi will not expect: 一，道也, “the one is dao”. the dictionary’s author lived in a world where “the one” was a name for the way, and he saw it even here, held in the mouth. take that as his piety and not as the origin of the graph. still, it suits this passage, which finds the way in a meal. the family is about taste. 甜, the modern word for sweet, adds 舌, a tongue. 旨, fine flavour, is defined by the shuowen as 美 and built from 甘. in old texts 甘 also means “willingly”: 甘心, a sweet heart, is to do a thing gladly. in the passage it is a verb: 甘其食, to find one’s food sweet. the sweetness is in the mouth that holds, and not only in the food. five strokes. first a long level line across the upper half; it is wider than everything else and gives the character its span. then two uprights, the left one first and the right one second. each starts above the level line and crosses down through it, so the top stays open. the right upright starts a little higher and stands very straight. fourth, the short level line inside, which touches both uprights: the thing in the mouth. fifth, the base, which closes the vessel. because the character is so plain, spacing is everything. the two inner spaces, above and below the short line, should be nearly equal, with the upper one a touch larger. the uprights lean very slightly toward each other at the foot, so that the shape narrows like a cup. in seal script the outline is a rounded mouth with a single dash inside, and you can see the picture at once.

國 a wall, a weapon, a piece of ground. open the outer box and look inside. the inside is 或, and the shuowen explains it part by part: 从囗从戈，以守一。一，地也, “from an enclosure and a dagger-axe, with which to guard the one; the one is the ground”. 戈 is the dagger-axe, the standard infantry weapon of the bronze age: a blade set crosswise on a long shaft. the small 口 is a walled town. the short stroke under it is land. so 或 already means a defended territory, and the shuowen defines it as 邦, a state. later this graph was borrowed for the word “perhaps, someone”, and so a second, larger wall was drawn around the whole to mark the old meaning: 國. the character now has two walls and a weapon. that is the warring state in one sign: land, a fortified centre, arms, and a frontier. the same inner part, with earth added, is 域, a territory. the simplified form 国 put 玉, jade, inside the wall; an older popular form had 王, a king. each age writes what it thinks a state holds. a modern collated edition of the mawangdui silk texts does not print this character in the passage. it has 邦, which has no weapon in it: 邑, a settlement, with a sound-part. and the passage itself goes through the graph piece by piece: a small enclosure, few people in it, and the 戈 never drawn up. eleven strokes, and the rule of the frame applies: the box is closed last. stroke one is the left wall. stroke two is the top and the right wall in one movement with a corner. now the contents. a level line, the top of the inner part. the small mouth in three strokes: left side, top and right side, base. under it a short stroke that rises to the right: the ground. then the dagger-axe: its long slanting hook, which starts high, crosses the level line, sweeps down to the right, and flicks up; a slash that crosses the hook near its foot; and a dot at the upper right. only now does stroke eleven shut the box along the bottom. the slanting hook is the life of the character. it must have room inside the walls and still look as if it could reach past them.

雞 the bird that knows the hour. the right side is 隹, a bird. the shuowen says 鳥之短尾緫名也, “the general name for short-tailed birds”, and it is a picture: a head, a body, and wing feathers shown as level strokes. its long-tailed partner is 鳥. you meet 隹 in 雀 (sparrow), 雁 (wild goose), 集 (to gather: a bird on a tree), 雙 (a pair: two birds in a hand), and 難 (difficult; first the name of a bird). the left side is 奚 (xi), which gives the sound. so the structure is plain: a bird, pronounced something like 奚. a variant form, 鷄, uses the long-tailed bird, and the simplified form is 鸡. the oldest forms of the word were simply drawings of a rooster with a comb, as far as scholars can tell; the sound-part was added later. what makes the entry worth learning is the definition: 知時畜也, “the domestic animal that knows the time”. before clocks, the rooster was the timekeeper of the house. it called the hours before dawn, and a household rose by it. an old ode has a wife say “the cock has crowed” to get her husband up. so in this passage the sound heard across the border is not noise. it is the neighbours’ morning. the two states keep the same hours and know it by ear. they need no writing for that, and no envoy. eighteen strokes: ten on the left, eight on the right. the left part has three levels. at the top, four small strokes: a short flat slash, two dots, and a short slash that leans left; they sit like a comb. in the middle, the twisted thread 幺 in three strokes: two that fall left and turn back, and a dot. at the foot, 大 in three: a level line, a slash to the left, and a press that is shortened to a dot, because the bird needs the room. then the bird, in eight: a slash; a long upright under it; a dot at the top; three level lines, one under the other; an upright that joins them; and a last level line at the foot, the longest. keep the four level lines evenly spaced. the left side is small and busy, and the right side is tall and regular.

81 · plain words, open hands. words to trust are not beautiful; / beautiful words are not to be trusted. / the good do not argue; / those who argue are not good. / those who know are not widely learned; / the widely learned do not know. / the sage does not pile up. / having already worked for others, has still more; / having already given to others, has more again. / the way of heaven / benefits and does not harm. / the way of the sage / acts and does not contend. the passage has three movements and no images from nature at all; it is the plainest page in the book. first, three mirror pairs about speech and knowledge: words to trust against beautiful words, the good against those who argue, those who know against the widely learned. second, three lines on having: the sage does not pile up; having already worked for others, has still more; having given, has more again. third, two last lines that set two ways side by side: heaven’s way benefits and does not harm; the sage’s way acts and does not contend. inside the characters there is more to see: a person beside a word, two litigants with speech between them, a heap of grain, a blade that does not cut, and two hands that pull at one thing. in the received order this is the last page. the six opening lines are a mirror for the reader who has come to the end of a wise book. by now you have collected many fine sayings. you may be able to argue for them, and you know a good deal about the text. the passage looks at exactly these three gains, beauty, argument, and breadth, and says that none of them is the thing. what is left? wang bi’s three small notes point to it: the plain stuff, the uncarved wood, the one. then the lines on giving describe what a person is like who lives from there: nothing is stored up, not even insight. an insight that is kept as a possession goes stale. used for others, it comes back larger. the last two words give the test for all of it: is there any pulling in this? the passage gives a leader three warnings and one rule. distrust the polished report and the polished speaker; the words to rely on are often clumsy. notice who wins by argument in your meetings, because skill in argument and being right are different gifts, and the age that prized debaters most was an age of ruin. prefer the person who knows the work to the bottom over the one with a wide view of everything. then the rule: do not pile up. a leader has stores of several kinds: information, credit, access, the pleasant tasks. each of them can grow when it is given away, and it often spoils when it is held. the closing pair gives the standard for every act of leading: it should benefit and not harm, and it should be done without a contest. the collated silk text says that this is simply the human way. 不爭 is a state of the body before it is a policy. 爭 is two hands on one thing, each pulling. you can feel it without any opponent: one muscle pulls against another, the will pulls against the breath, the shoulders pull up while the mind says “relax”. most effort that tires us is this inner tug. 為而不爭, to act and not contend, is movement in which nothing pulls against anything else: the push comes from the ground, passes through loose joints, and leaves through the hand. the lines on giving fit the breath. lungs do not pile up. the out-breath that empties them fully is what lets the next breath come in by itself, and the bellows of passage 5 says the same. breathe out to the end, once, and wait. the plainest words in the passage describe what the living world does every day. nothing in a forest piles up for long. a tree that holds its leaves through winter in a cold country is broken by snow; the tree that gives them all to the ground is fed by them in spring. 既以與人，己愈多: having given, it has more. the sun is the largest case: it benefits and does not harm, and it gives without a store that we can see the bottom of. a river that is dammed turns stale and fills with silt, and a river that runs stays itself. the granary is the human invention that set us apart from this, and the state grew from the granary. the passage does not ask us to burn the granary. it says that the sage does not live as one. as the last practice of the book, take one line from each movement. from the first: write or say one plain sentence that you will stand beside, and let it be less handsome than you could make it. from the second: give one thing away completely, to the end, and do not replace it at once. stay with the empty place for a day. from the third: do one piece of work today with no opponent in it at all, no rival, no deadline to beat, no earlier self to surpass. act, and do not contend. then close the book, as the passage itself advises: its words are fine, and fine words are not the point. if you open it again tomorrow, open it where the oldest copies begin, or anywhere.

聖人: not a saint. 聖人 is “the sage” by custom, and the english word misleads. this is not a saint: there is no holiness here and no reward after death. it is not only a wise man either. the graph has 耳, an ear, and the shuowen defines the word as 通, “to pass through, to reach”: a person whose hearing is open, and who leads by that attunement. this is the figure’s last appearance in the book, and the portrait is plain: no store, open hands, no contest.

信: a person beside their word. 信 is 亻, a person, beside 言, speech. the shuowen calls it a joined-meaning graph, 會意, and defines it as 誠, sincerity. the picture is easy to read: a person who stands next to what was said. so 信 is not “true” in the sense of a statement that matches a fact. it is “trustworthy”: words that someone will keep. from it come the senses “to believe”, “good faith”, and later “a letter”, words sent with a person’s name on them. the laozi uses it often and gives it weight. where good faith is not enough, there is no faith in return (17, 23). the sage keeps faith with the faithless too, and so gains 信 (49). light promises bring little trust (63). the last passage opens with it. before you weigh these words, the text says, ask the first question: can they be relied on?

a beautiful book warns against beauty. 美言不信: beautiful words are not to be trusted. the sentence is itself beautiful. it mirrors the line before it, four characters against four, and the book that it closes is one of the finest pieces of rhymed prose in chinese. the author knew this. so the first lines can be read as a warning about the book in your hands: you have enjoyed these sayings, and enjoyment is not a reason to rely on them. passage 62 has the practical side: 美言可以市, “fine words can be taken to market”; another old punctuation reads 美言可以市尊, “fine words can buy honour”. they are a currency. passage 1 began by saying that a way that can be told is not the constant dao. passage 81 ends by saying that words that please are not the ones to trust. between these two cautions stand five thousand words. is that a contradiction, or the only honest way to frame a book?

not “truth” against “beauty”. english readers hear the first lines through a famous pair. plato distrusted the poets; keats answered that beauty is truth and truth beauty. the laozi seems to take a side in that quarrel. it does not, because neither of its words means what ours do. 信 is reliability between people, and no abstract truth stands behind it. 美 is what pleases the senses: the shuowen defines it by the taste of mutton, and passage 2 says that when all the world knows the beautiful as beautiful, ugliness is already there. so the lines are practical. words that can be relied on are usually plain, because they were not shaped to please; words shaped to please were shaped for the hearer’s pleasure, and that is a different aim. passage 35 says of dao in the mouth: 淡乎其無味, “how bland; it has no taste”.

three mirrors, and a different middle. the first six lines are three mirror pairs. each pair has the form a is not b; b is not a: 信 and 美, 善 and 辯, 知 and 博. the figure closes each thought like a clasp, and it makes the lines easy to remember. a modern collated edition of the mawangdui silk texts has the pairs in another order and with one different word. it reads: 知者不博，博者不知。善者不多，多者不善, “those who know are not broad; the broad do not know. the good do not have much; those with much are not good.” there is no 辯, no arguing, in that version. in its place is 多, “much”, which leads straight into the next line: the sage does not pile up. the received text’s line about argument may come from another edition or an editor. both versions exist. the silk one makes the passage a single thought about having little.

辯: speech between two litigants. 辯 is built like a courtroom. in the middle is 言, speech. on each side stands 辛. the shuowen explains the pair 辡 as 辠人相與訟也, “two accused persons who bring suit against each other”, and it says of 辛 that it has to do with offence and punishment. then 辯 itself: 治也。从言在辡之閒, “to settle; speech placed between the two litigants”. so the word for eloquent argument began as pleading in a lawsuit. to 辯 is to make one’s case against an opponent before a judge. that is the manner that the line rejects: speech as a contest with a winner. passage 45 says 大辯若訥, “the greatest eloquence seems to stammer”. english “argue” once meant “to make clear”. the chinese word never lost the two parties and the offence.

the age of the debaters. in the fourth and third centuries bce, 辯 was a profession. rulers kept halls of scholars who argued before them; the king of qi housed hundreds at the jixia gate of his capital, with stipends and no duties except to dispute. the mohists made disputation a method with rules, to fix what is so and what is not so. the debaters around hui shi and gongsun long argued that a white horse is not a horse, and that there are moments when a flying arrow neither moves nor is at rest. travelling persuaders talked states into and out of alliances, and one speech could make a man chief minister. even mencius, who despised the trade, was accused of it and replied: 予豈好辯哉？予不得已也, “do i love disputation? i have no choice.” against this background 善者不辯 is not a remark about manners. it declines the main intellectual activity of the time, in a book that never names an opponent.

博: five cartloads of books. 博 is breadth. the shuowen says 大通也, “great and thorough reach”, and the graph has 十, ten, the complete number, at its side. for the confucians it was a duty: the noble person 博學於文, “learns broadly in the records”. the zhuangzi says of the debater hui shi that his books filled five carts, and adds that his way was crooked and his words missed the mark. books were bundles of bamboo strips then, and five carts were a great library. the laozi sets 知, knowing, against this. its own account of knowing is in two earlier lines: 其出彌遠，其知彌少, “the further one goes out, the less one knows” (47); and in learning one gains each day, in dao one loses each day (48). this is not praise of ignorance. a person can know one thing to the bottom, or many things by their surfaces. which do you do?

wang bi: three notes of four characters. wang bi’s last comments are as spare as the text. on “words to trust are not beautiful”: 實在質也, “the substance is in the plain stuff”. on “beautiful words are not to be trusted”: 本在樸也, “the root is in the uncarved wood”. on “those who know are not broad”: 極在一也, “the summit is in the one”. each note has four characters and the same frame: x is in y. he names three places where the real thing lives: 質, raw material before ornament; 樸, the uncut block, the book’s image for the unworked self since passage 15; and 一, the one of passages 22 and 39. ornament, carving, and breadth all move away from these. a young man who had read everything wrote these three lines, and he died at twenty-three. he gives no argument for them. would an argument have helped?

積: grain in a heap. 積 has 禾, the grain plant, on its left; the shuowen defines it 聚也, to gather into a heap. its right side, 責, gives the sound and is itself the word for a debt that is claimed. the first sense is the stack of sheaves and the full granary. stores were the strength of a state: the texts of the age measure a ruler by his 積, and a general by how many years of grain stand behind him. the word also had an honoured moral use. the confucian xunzi built his teaching on it: heap up earth and you make a mountain; heap up good acts and you make a sage. 聖人不積 answers both. the zhuangzi’s last chapter sums up the old master in these terms: he took having a store as not having enough. what do you keep in heaps, and against what day?

既: already done. 既以為人 is four characters: already, using, for, others. 既 marks an act as complete. most english versions write “the more the sage does for others, the more…”, a sliding scale. the chinese puts a finished act first: having already done it for others, the sage has still more. as a full verb 既 means “to use up”, as in passage 35, and some readers hear that sense here: having spent everything. the ordinary grammar of 既以 says only “having already”, and our rendering stays with it. 為 is read wei here, “for the sake of”; in the last line of the book the same graph is read wei, “to act”. 人 and 己 stand side by side: others, self. the sentence has no subject and no “he”; our english leaves a gap before “has” to keep that. and it does not say what was done or given. goods, strength, teaching, life: the line fits all of them. which did you supply as you read?

愈: the bellows returns. 己愈有, 己愈多: oneself, the more, has; oneself, the more, much. the word 愈, “more and more”, has appeared once before in the book, in the picture of the bellows: 虛而不屈，動而愈出, “empty and never exhausted; the more it moves, the more comes out” (5). there the space between heaven and earth is a bellows that gives because it is empty. here the sage is the same instrument. nothing is stored inside, and so the flow through does not stop. the claim sounds like a paradox, and people repeat it as a strategy: give, and you will get. the text does not offer that bargain. a person who gives in order to have more is still piling up, by a longer road. the line describes what is observed in one who does not pile up at all. it may be simple arithmetic of another kind: what is used for others is not lost to the user.

wang bi: what all things honour. on 聖人不積 wang bi writes: 無私自有，唯善是與，任物而已。 “the sage has no private holding of their own; gives only where it is good; and leaves things to themselves, that is all.” the middle phrase echoes the end of passage 79, where heaven’s way is always with the good. on “has still more” he adds three characters: 物所尊也, “this is what things honour”. on “has more again”: 物所歸也, “this is what things come home to”. so for wang bi the “more” is not more goods. the one who keeps nothing back is honoured by all things and becomes the place to which they return, as the sea is the place to which rivers return. 歸 is his favourite verb for this, and he used it in passage 73: stay low, and things come home. the sage’s wealth is that things return.

利: legge’s “sharpness”. legge’s last sentence begins: “with all the sharpness of the way of heaven, it injures not”. other translators write “benefits and does not harm”. both come from one word. 利 is written with 禾, grain, and 刂, a knife, and its first sense is the keen edge of a blade; the shuowen defines it as 銛, sharp. from the sharp tool that works well came “advantage, profit, benefit”. legge chose the older sense, and it gives a striking line: heaven’s way is keen and does not cut. passage 58 says the same of the sage: square and does not slice, pointed and does not stab. most readers take the later sense, as we do. the chinese does not choose. legge also wrote “sincere” for 信, which makes trust a feeling inside the speaker, and added “(in the tao)” twice. his very last words are “he does not strive”.

the sage’s way, or everyone’s?. the received text ends with 聖人之道, “the way of the sage”. a modern collated edition of the mawangdui silk texts has one word less: 人之道，為而弗爭, “the way of people: act and do not contend”. the difference is large. in passage 77, 人之道 was the bad way, the one that takes from the poor and offers to the rich, set against heaven’s way. if the silk reading is the older one, the book here gives 人之道 a second meaning: the way that people could walk. it is no longer the special path of a rare figure. it is the human way as such, restored: heaven benefits and does not harm; people act and do not contend. a later hand may have added 聖 to remove the clash with passage 77. which ending do you prefer: one that describes a sage, or one that describes you?

爭: the book’s last word. the final character of the received text is 爭, with 不 before it: not contend. the shuowen defines 爭 in one word, 引也, “to pull”, and the graph is commonly explained as two hands, one above and one below, that pull at a single object. it is a tug-of-war. the shuowen even defines 訟, a lawsuit, by this word. 不爭 runs through the whole book like a thread, and here the thread is tied off. do not exalt the worthy, and the people will not contend (3). water benefits all things and does not contend (8). because the sage does not contend, no one under heaven can contend with the sage (22, 66). it is the 德 of not contending (68). heaven’s way does not contend and is good at winning (73). and last: act, and do not contend. the book does not end on dao, or 德, or 無. it ends on a pair of hands that let go.

an ending that was made later. the historian sima qian tells that laozi wrote a book in two parts, of five thousand and some words, and went away; no one knows where he ended. for two thousand years readers have taken this passage as the farewell: a look back at the words, an open hand, and silence. the oldest manuscripts tell another story. in the mawangdui silk texts this passage is in the middle: it follows our 80, which follows our 66, and our 67 comes next. their book ends with our passage 37. the guodian bamboo slips, a century and more older, are reported to lack this passage entirely. so the “last page” is the work of an editor, perhaps of the early han. it was a wise choice. a book whose first line doubts the telling ends with a line that doubts fine words, and then stops.

one plain sentence. today, before you send a message that matters, do the test of the first line. read what you wrote and mark every phrase that is there to please, to impress, or to protect you. then ask of what remains: will i stand beside this? that is 信, the person next to the word. send the short version. later in the day, when someone says a thing that you think is wrong, try the third line once. do not argue. say what you know in one sentence, without the case for it, and stop. notice the discomfort; the urge to add a second sentence is 辯, the litigant in you. and once, give something away to the end: finish the good coffee on a guest, give the whole afternoon. see whether “has still more” is true in any sense that you can feel.

與 and 有, 人 and 己: to give and to have. the second movement rests on two pairs: 與 and 有, to give and to have, and 人 and 己, others and self. common sense makes them a scale: what goes to others leaves me. the lines join them the other way. having given, one has more. the text does not rank self below others, and it does not say that having is bad; the words that end the two lines are 有 and 多, “has” and “much”. giving needs a holder and a thing held, and the bellows gives only because air comes in again. the passage does favor the open hand over the heap. that corrects a world that measures a person by the store. it is not a rule to empty oneself. the favored side also turns: giving that keeps count is piling up by another road, and a giver who cannot receive leaves others no room to give. where do you stand in that circle today?

words that can be trusted are not beautiful, and beautiful words are not to be trusted.. words that can be trusted are not beautiful, and beautiful words are not to be trusted. do you agree? think of the person whose word you rely on most. how do they speak? have fine words ever deceived you? have you used them to cover something? what was covered? take the other side: beauty in speech is a kind of care, and a true thing that is well said reaches further. this book is itself well said. what does that do to the claim? do you distrust charm, or plainness? where did that distrust begin, and whom has it kept out?

the one who stores nothing and gives to others ends with more, not less.. the one who stores nothing and gives to others ends with more, not less. has this been true for you in any sense that you can point to? has it also been false? what do you keep in reserve: money, time, affection, knowledge? what day are you keeping it for? now hold the opposite: what you give is gone, and a person with no store is at the mercy of others. that is also experience. whose experience is it, in your family? are you easier with giving or with receiving? what does the harder one ask you to admit?

it is possible to act fully in the world and not compete with anyone.. it is possible to act fully in the world and not compete with anyone. is it? look at one piece of work that you did this week. who was the rival in it, seen or unseen? when did winning first matter to you, and what did you get for it? take the other side: contest sharpens people, and without a rival most of us do less than we can. what part of you needs the opponent? if the contest stopped, what would move you to act? does that question feel like rest, or like a threat?

辯 two litigants and a word. this is the largest character in the passage, and it is built in three columns. cover the middle and you see the same shape twice: 辛 on the left and 辛 on the right. the shuowen says that 辛 has to do with 辠, offence; modern scholars commonly explain the early graph as a blade or chisel used to mark criminals and captives. doubled, the two make 辡, and the shuowen defines it: 辠人相與訟也, “accused persons who bring suit against each other”. two parties stand face to face, each with a mark of guilt. now look at what the scribes put between them. in our character it is 言, speech: 从言在辡之閒, “speech placed between the litigants”. that is 辯, to plead, to argue a case. the frame of two litigants was used again and again, and each time the thing in the middle changes the word. with 刂, a knife, in the middle it is 辨: to cut between two, to tell apart. with 力, strength, it is 辦: to deal with a matter; the shuowen says “to apply strength”. with 糸, thread, it is 辮: to braid; the shuowen says 交也, to cross over. with 瓜, a melon, it is 瓣: the shuowen says the segments inside a melon, and now a petal. speech, a knife, strength, thread, a fruit: something is always set between two sides. the line says that the good do not stand in that frame. twenty-one strokes: seven, seven, and seven. each 辛 has a dot at the top, a level line, two small strokes that lean toward each other, two more level lines, and an upright. in the left-hand 辛 the last upright curves away to the lower left, to make room. in the right-hand 辛 it comes straight down and ends in a firm point. between them, 言 is written second: a dot, a long level line, two shorter ones, and a small mouth in three strokes. the art is in the widths. each column gets a third of the square, and each must be made narrow enough to share it; a beginner writes three full characters and the result sprawls. keep the level lines of all three parts at different heights so that they do not form bars across the whole. in running script the two litigants shrink to a few quick turns.

信 a person standing by a word. two parts, and the shuowen calls their union 會意, joined meaning: 从人从言, “from a person and from speech”. on the left is 亻, the form that 人 takes at the side: a person seen in profile, two strokes. on the right is 言. the shuowen separates 言 from its near neighbour: 直言曰言，論難曰語, “to speak straight out is 言; to discuss and dispute is 語”. the graph has 口, a mouth, at its foot, and lines above it that are commonly explained as a tongue or a flute; the shuowen names the upper part as a sound-mark. so 信 is a person, and straight speech. nothing else is in the picture: no oath, no witness, no seal. trust is only the nearness of the two. look at the family of 言, which holds most of what people do with words: 語 (to discuss), 詩 (a poem; the shuowen says 志也, what the heart is set on), 誠 (sincere; defined by 信, as 信 is defined by 誠), 訟 (a lawsuit), 說 (to explain), 謀 (to plan), 讓 (to yield). and 辯, where speech stands between two opponents. in 信 it stands beside one person. the whole first movement of the passage is in that change of position. the word later came to mean a letter and then a message. each is a word that still has its person beside it. nine strokes: two and seven. the person: a slash that falls to the lower left, and an upright that starts from the middle of the slash and stands straight. it is slim and tall, and it leans a little toward its partner. then speech. a dot at the top, set above the centre of what is to come. a long level line, the widest stroke on the right side. two shorter level lines under it, close together and of nearly equal length. then the mouth: left side, top and right side with a corner, base. the mouth is no wider than the two short lines above it. the spaces between the four level strokes must be even; this is the test of the character. the upright of the person and the stack of level lines make the whole effect, and a good hand keeps the two parts close and does not let them touch.

爭 two hands, one thing. the last character of the book is a picture of a quarrel. the shuowen’s definition is one word: 引也, “to pull”. it files the graph under 𠬪, its sign for two hands, one that reaches down from above and one that reaches up from below. in the modern shape the upper hand is the claw-like top, 爫, which you know from 受, to receive, and 采, to pick. the lower hand is the part that looks like 彐, a hand seen from the side with three fingers. the long stroke that runs down through the lower hand is commonly explained as the thing between them, the object that both are holding. so: a hand, a hand, and one thing. in 受 two hands pass an object across, and the shuowen defines it as handing over to one another. in 爭 the same two hands pull, and neither lets go. the two characters differ in what is between the hands, and in what the hands intend. the family of 爭 holds a surprise. 靜, stillness, the great word of passage 16, has 爭 on its right side as its sound-part; so has 淨, clean. the shuowen treats this as sound alone, and no one should build a theory on it. still, each time the book wrote “stillness” it wrote a quarrel beside the colour of new growth, 青. the final words are 不爭: the hands open, and the thing between them is free. eight strokes. the upper hand takes four: a short flat slash across the top, written from right to left; two dots under it, side by side; and a longer slash that falls to the left. then the lower hand. stroke five is a level line that turns a corner and comes down a short way. stroke six is a long level line that passes right through and reaches out on both sides; it is the widest stroke and the balance beam of the character. stroke seven is a short level line below it, which closes the hand. stroke eight is the upright: it starts inside the hand, runs straight down through all the level lines, and ends in a hook to the left. write it last and without hurry. it is the thing that the two hands hold, and, in the received order, the last stroke of the whole book.

the keeper of the pass. laozi kept the archives of the zhou court for many years. he watched the dynasty grow weak and its rulers quarrel, and at last he decided to leave. he set out to the west, an old man on a slow animal, and came to the hangu pass, the gate between the heartland and the wild country beyond. the keeper of the pass was a man named yin xi. later tradition says that yin xi had read the sky, seen a purple vapour drift in from the east, and known that a sage was coming. when the old traveller arrived, yin xi would not simply wave him through. "you are about to vanish from the world," he said. "before you go, make the effort to write a book for me." laozi did not trust words. when confucius had come to him with questions about the ancient sages, he had answered that those men and their bones had long since rotted away, and only their sayings were left. yet he stayed at the pass, and he wrote. the book had two parts, one on the way and one on its power, a little more than five thousand characters in all. then he handed it to the keeper, went on through the gate, and travelled west. the historian sima qian closes the account in a few plain words: nobody knows where his life ended. the book stayed behind. the man who wrote it did not. shiji 63 (biography of laozi); liexian zhuan

confucius meets a dragon. when confucius was still a young teacher, he travelled to the zhou capital to ask the archivist laozi about the rites of the ancient kings. he came with questions about ceremonies, ancestors, and the conduct of a gentleman. laozi did not answer the questions. "the people you keep quoting are gone," he said. "their flesh and their bones have rotted. all that is left of them is talk. a gentleman rides in a carriage when the times suit him; when they do not, he lets the wind roll him along like a dry weed. i have heard that a clever trader keeps his best goods out of sight, so that his stall looks bare, and that a person whose virtue is whole wears the face of a simpleton. put away that proud manner, those many wants, that eagerness and those large plans. they do your body no good. i have nothing more to say to you." confucius went back to his students and was silent for three days. at last they asked him what had happened. "birds fly, fish swim, animals run; that much i understand," he said. "for a runner you set a snare. for a swimmer you drop a line. for a flyer you shoot a corded arrow. but a dragon climbs on wind and cloud into the sky, and how it does that is beyond me. i met laozi today. he is a dragon." shiji 63; zhuangzi ch.14 (tianyun)

cook ding carves an ox. a cook named ding was taking apart an ox for lord wenhui. his hand pressed here, his shoulder leaned there, his foot planted, his knee pushed, and the hide and flesh parted with a whisper and a swish. every move of the blade kept time, like the old mulberry forest dance, like the jingshou movement of the ancient xianchi music. "ah, marvellous!" said the lord. "so this is how far skill can go?" ding laid down the knife. "what i love is the way. it is a step past skill. in my first days at this work, an ox was simply a great block of ox in front of me. three years on, i had stopped seeing it as one whole thing. today i meet it with my spirit and do not look with my eyes. the senses rest; the spirit goes where it will. i trust the grain that heaven put in the animal. i strike into the wide seams, steer through the hollow places, and go along with the way it is built. i never so much as graze a ligament, let alone a big bone. "a fine cook needs a new knife every year, because he slices. a common cook needs one every month, because he chops. my knife has served nineteen years and gone through thousands of oxen, and the edge is as keen as on the day it came off the whetstone. there are gaps at the joints, and the edge of a blade is so thin it has no thickness. put what has no thickness into what has a gap, and it moves about freely, with room to spare. "even so, when i reach a tangled place, i see that it is hard. i take care and hold myself in check. my gaze settles, my hand slows, the knife hardly moves, and the whole of it parts with a soft rush and sinks down, the way loose soil settles onto the ground. i stand there with the knife, look all around, and let the satisfaction fill me. then i clean the blade and put it away." "splendid," said lord wenhui. "listening to a cook, i have learned how to care for life." zhuangzi ch.3 (yangsheng zhu)

the butterfly dream. zhuang zhou once dreamed that he was a butterfly. in the dream there was nothing in him but butterfly: wings bright and lively, glad in his own easy freedom. the name zhuang zhou meant nothing to him. a moment later his eyes opened. the body on the mat was zhuang zhou's, stiff and startled and beyond doubt. now he could not tell. had zhuang zhou been dreaming of a butterfly? or was a butterfly at this moment dreaming of zhuang zhou? zhuangzi adds only one more remark: surely there is some boundary between the man and the butterfly. and this crossing of the boundary, he says, is what is meant by the changing of things. the story is very short, and it does not end with a lesson. it leaves the reader in the moment just after waking, when the edges of the self are still soft. the daodejing says that being and non-being give birth to each other, that long and short shape each other. here the dreamer and the dreamed do the same. zhuangzi ch.2 (qiwu lun)

the useless tree. a master carpenter named shi was on the road to the state of qi. at a place called qu yuan, “crooked shaft”, he passed the oak that served as the village shrine. it was big enough to shade several thousand oxen, and a rope around its trunk would have measured a hundred armspans. it rose high over the nearby hills before its first branch, and a dozen or so of those branches could each have been hollowed into a boat. people crowded around it as they crowd a market. the carpenter did not even glance at it and kept walking. his apprentice stared, then ran after him. "master, i have never seen such timber. why won't you look?" "enough," said shi. "it is loose, worthless wood. a boat of it would sink. a coffin of it would soon rot. doors of it would weep sap; pillars of it would fill with grubs. no one can use it, and that is why it has grown so old." that night the oak came to him in a dream. "what are you comparing me with? with trees of good grain? think of the crab-apple and the pear, the tangerine and the pomelo, and every tree that bears a crop. when harvest comes, people tear the fruit from them and treat them roughly; heavy boughs crack and thin ones are dragged down. what they are good at is exactly what hurts them, and so they are cut off halfway through the span heaven gave them. for a long, long time my whole aim has been to be of no use. only now, with death not far off, have i got there, and being of no use is what has served me best. if i had been of use, would i ever have reached this size? besides, you are a thing and i am a thing. what gives one thing the right to sort out another? you are a stray, unused man yourself, with one foot in the grave. what can you tell about a stray, unused tree?" when shi woke he told the dream. "if it wanted to be useless," asked the apprentice, "why is it the shrine?" "quiet! not a word," said shi. "it is only lodging in the shrine, to keep off those who do not understand it and would abuse it." zhuangzi ch.4 (renjian shi)

huizi's giant gourd. huizi, zhuangzi's friend and favourite opponent in argument, came to him with a complaint. "the king of wei gave me seeds for a giant gourd. i planted them, and the gourd that grew would hold five bushels. i filled it with water, but the rind was not strong enough to hold itself up. i split it to make dippers, but the halves sprawled so wide that there was nowhere to put them. big it certainly was, but useless, so i smashed it." "you just do not know how to use big things," said zhuangzi. "there was a family in song with a salve that kept hands from cracking. for generations they used it in their work of rinsing silk floss in the river. a traveller heard of it and offered a hundred pieces of gold for the recipe. the family talked it over: rinsing silk had never brought them more than a few pieces of gold, and here were a hundred pieces in a single morning. they sold. the traveller went to the king of wu, who was at war with yue, and the king made him a commander. that winter wu fought yue on the water, and with their hands unharmed by the cold, the men of wu won a great victory. the traveller was rewarded with land. "the salve was the same salve. for one man it opened the way to land and title; for the family it meant more years at the riverbank with wet silk. what made the difference was only the use it was put to. "you had a gourd that held five bushels. why didn't you lash it to yourself as a great float and drift away over the rivers and lakes? instead you fretted that it was too shallow to hold anything. your mind is still choked with tangled scrub." zhuangzi ch.1 (xiaoyao you)

the frog in the old well. the sophist gongsun long boasted that he could win any argument. prince mou of wei answered him with a story. a frog lived in a broken-down well. one day he called up to a great turtle from the eastern sea. "oh, i am happy! when i go out, i leap along the well's wooden rim. when i come in, i rest on the ledge where a brick has fallen away. when i plunge into the water, it bears me up under my arms and props my chin. when i kick into the mud, it swallows my feet to the ankles. i look around at the red wrigglers, the crabs and the tadpoles, and not one of them can do what i do. to be master of a whole pit of water, to perch over a whole sunken well: what joy could be greater? why not drop in some time and see for yourself?" the turtle tried. before his left foot was in, his right knee was already jammed. he eased himself back out and began to tell the frog about the sea. "a thousand li cannot give you its breadth. a thousand fathoms cannot reach its depth. in the days of yu, nine years in ten were floods, yet the sea did not swell. in the days of tang, seven years in eight were droughts, yet its shore did not shrink. long times and short times do not move it; heavy rain and little rain do not raise or lower it. that is the great happiness of the eastern sea." when the frog in the well heard this, he started in alarm, then shrank into himself, lost and bewildered. zhuangzi ch.17 (qiushui)

the happy fish of the hao river. zhuangzi and huizi were walking together on the bridge over the hao river. "look at the minnows," said zhuangzi. "they come out and wander about at their ease. that is what fish enjoy." "you are no fish," said huizi. "from where do you know what fish enjoy?" "and you are not me," said zhuangzi. "from where do you know that i don't know what fish enjoy?" "i am not you, so i certainly don't know what you know," said huizi. "but you are certainly not a fish. so the case is closed: you do not know the joy of fish." "then look again at your own first words," said zhuangzi. "you said, 'how can you know the joy of fish?' to put it that way, you had already granted that i knew it, and asked only how. here is how: i knew it standing on this bridge, above the hao." huizi wins the argument on logic. zhuangzi does not try to beat him on logic. he simply points back to the bridge, the water, and the small silver fish in it. knowing happens there, in the meeting, before anyone starts to argue about it. zhuangzi ch.17 (qiushui)

the death of hundun. long ago the lord of the southern sea was named shu, "swift". the lord of the northern sea was named hu, "sudden". the lord of the middle realm was named hundun, "the undivided". now and then swift and sudden came together in hundun's country, and every time he received them with great kindness. the two of them began to plan a way to pay him back. "every person has seven holes," they said to each other, "for looking and listening, for eating and breathing. this one has not a single hole. let us make him some." so each day they drilled one opening. when the seventh day came, hundun was dead. this is the last story in the inner chapters of the zhuangzi. the two visitors mean well. they want to give their friend what they themselves have: eyes and ears and a mouth, a way to take in the world in separate pieces. but hundun was whole because he was not divided. the daodejing says that the five colours blind the eye and the five tones deafen the ear. it speaks of returning to the uncarved block. hundun is that block, and kindness of the wrong kind cut it apart. zhuangzi ch.7 (ying diwang)

the yellow emperor's lost pearl. the yellow emperor went wandering north of the red water. he climbed the hill of kunlun and gazed toward the south. on the way back, he found that he had dropped his black pearl. he sent knowledge to search for it, and knowledge came back empty-handed. he sent li zhu, the man whose eyes could pick out a single hair at a hundred paces, and li zhu came back empty-handed. he sent chigou, the quarrelsome talker, and chigou came back empty-handed. finally he sent xiangwang, whose name means something like "image-gone" or "no-likeness". xiangwang came back with the pearl. "how odd," said the yellow emperor. "so it was xiangwang who could find it!" the dark pearl is the way itself: the dark, round, quiet centre of things. cleverness does not reach it. keen sight does not reach it. fine speech does not reach it. the one who finds it is the one who has no fixed shape and makes no effort to grasp. in the daodejing, the way is looked at but not seen, listened to but not heard, grasped at but not caught. its finder must be the same. zhuangzi ch.12 (tiandi)

the old man at the frontier loses his horse. near the northern frontier lived an old man who was skilled in reading the signs of things. one day, for no reason, his horse ran away into the lands of the northern tribes. his neighbours came to console him. "how do you know this is not a blessing?" said the old man. some months later, the horse came home, and it brought a fine horse of the northern breed with it. the neighbours came to congratulate him. "how do you know this is not a misfortune?" said the old man. now the family had good horses, and the old man's son loved to ride. he fell from the new horse and broke his thigh bone. the neighbours came to console him. "how do you know this is not a blessing?" said the old man. a year later the northern tribes invaded across the frontier. every able-bodied young man took up a bow and went to fight. near the frontier, nine men out of ten died. because the son was lame, he did not go, and father and son both survived. the huainanzi ends: blessing turns into disaster, and disaster into blessing. their changes have no end, and their depths cannot be measured. the daodejing says the same thing in fewer words: misfortune is what fortune leans on; fortune is where misfortune hides. huainanzi ch.18 (renjian xun)

zhuangzi drums on a basin. zhuangzi's wife died. huizi came to pay his respects and found zhuangzi squatting with his legs flung out, thumping on a pot and singing. huizi was shocked. "this woman lived with you for years, raised your children and aged at your side. dry eyes at her death i could perhaps forgive. a song and a drummed-on basin go far past that." "you are wrong," said zhuangzi. "when she had just died, how could i alone feel nothing? but then i looked back to where she began. in the beginning she had no life. and not only no life: no shape. and not only no shape: no breath. somewhere in that dim, formless drift, something shifted and there was breath. the breath shifted and there was a shape. the shape shifted and there was a living person. now one more shift has carried her to death. it is like spring giving way to summer, autumn to winter: the seasons simply moving on. "right now she sleeps, stretched out quietly, in the great room of heaven and earth. for me to follow her with loud wailing would only prove that i had grasped nothing of how our lives are allotted. that is why i gave up weeping." the daodejing says that all things flourish and each returns to its root. returning to the root is called stillness. zhuangzi drums because he has seen the root. zhuangzi ch.18 (zhile)

the turtle in the mud. zhuangzi sat fishing on the bank of the pu river. two senior officers arrived, sent ahead by the king of chu. "his majesty," they said, "would like to burden you with his whole kingdom." zhuangzi kept his eyes on the line and did not turn around. "i am told," he said, "that chu owns a holy turtle that died three thousand years ago. the king keeps it wrapped in a cloth, inside a basket, high up in the hall of his ancestors. tell me: if that turtle had been asked, would it have chosen to die so that its bones could be treasured? or to stay alive, trailing its tail through the mud?" "it would sooner stay alive," said the two officers, "trailing its tail through the mud." "then off you go," said zhuangzi. "i too will keep trailing my tail through the mud." the daodejing asks: which is dearer, your name or your life? which is worth more, your life or your goods? the officials offer a place in the temple. zhuangzi chooses the river, the pole, and the mud. zhuangzi ch.17 (qiushui)

three in the morning. a man who kept monkeys was sharing out acorns. "three in the morning," he announced, "and four in the evening." the monkeys flew into a rage. "very well," he said. "four in the morning and three in the evening." the monkeys were overjoyed. the acorns had not changed, and neither had their number. only the monkeys' feelings had changed, and the keeper simply went along with them. zhuangzi tells this little tale in the middle of a long argument about right and wrong, this and that. people wear out their minds trying to prove that things are one, he says, and do not see that they were the same all along. that is what he calls "three in the morning". the sage, by contrast, lets right and wrong settle into harmony and rests on what he calls the potter's wheel of heaven, turning evenly. he lets both sides walk their road. the daodejing's sage has no fixed heart of his own; he takes the heart of the people as his heart. the monkey keeper is a small, comic version of that sage. he does not win the argument. he feeds the monkeys. zhuangzi ch.2 (qiwu lun)

the gamecock like wood. ji xingzi was raising a fighting cock for the king. after ten days the king asked whether the bird was ready. "not yet. it is all empty swagger and trusts its own temper." ten days later the king asked again. "not yet. it still answers every noise and jumps at every shadow." ten more days passed, and the king asked again. "not yet. it still glares and puffs itself up." after ten more days the king asked once more. "nearly. another cock can crow at it now and nothing in it stirs. from across the yard you would take it for a bird carved out of wood. its power is whole. no strange cock will dare to take it on; they will turn tail and flee." the daodejing says that the best warrior is not warlike, the best fighter is not angry, and the one who best defeats an enemy does not engage him. ji xingzi's cock wins without fighting because it has stopped wanting to fight. what frightens the others is not its fury but its stillness. zhuangzi ch.19 (dasheng); parallel in liezi ch.2 (huangdi)

the swimmer at luliang falls. confucius was gazing at the falls of luliang. the water dropped thirty fathoms, and its foam ran on for forty li; no turtle, crocodile or fish could swim in it. yet he saw a grown man go into the water. thinking the man was in some trouble and meant to end his life, confucius sent his students running along the bank to pull him out. a few hundred paces downstream the man climbed out on his own, shook his loose hair, and strolled along the dike singing. confucius hurried after him. "i took you for a ghost, but now i see you are a man. tell me, is there some method to treading water like that?" "no, no method. i set out from where i was, i grew up along with what i am, and i let it all come out as it was bound to. i go down with the whirl as it sinks and come up with the boil as it rises. i keep to the way of the water and add nothing of my own. that is how i tread it." "what do you mean, set out from where you were, grow up with what you are, come out as you were bound to?" "i was born among the hills and was at ease in the hills: that is where i set out. i grew up by the water and became at ease in the water: that is what i am. i do it without knowing why i do it: that is what was bound to be." nothing in the world is softer or weaker than water, says the daodejing, yet nothing is better at attacking the hard and strong. the swimmer does not fight that power. he goes with it. zhuangzi ch.19 (dasheng); parallel in liezi ch.2 (huangdi)

wheelwright bian and the duke's book. duke huan sat reading in the upper hall. in the courtyard below, the wheelwright bian was shaping a wheel. bian set down his mallet and chisel, climbed the steps, and asked, "may i ask whose words my lord is reading?" "the words of the sages," said the duke. "are those sages living?" "they have been dead a long time." "then what my lord is reading is nothing but the leftover mash of the ancients." the duke flushed. "i am reading, and a wheel-maker presumes to comment? explain yourself and you may live. fail, and you die." "i can only judge by my own trade," said bian. "when i cut a spoke hole, if i work it slowly, the joint goes in easily but will not grip. if i work it fast, it grips but will not go in. it has to be neither too slow nor too fast. my hands find that point and my heart agrees with them. no words of mine can carry it, and yet the work has its exact rule all the same. i cannot make it clear to my own son, and my son cannot receive it from me. that is why i am seventy and still carving wheels. the ancients took what could not be handed down into the grave with them. so what my lord is reading is only their leftover mash." the daodejing begins: the way that can be spoken is not the constant way. bian says the same from the wheelwright's bench. zhuangzi ch.13 (tiandao)

woodworker qing carves a bell stand. qing the woodworker carved a frame to hang bells from. when it was done, people who saw it were startled; it looked like the work of ghosts or gods. the marquis of lu came to see it and asked, "what art did you use to make this?" "i am a craftsman. what art would i have? still, there is one thing. when i am about to make a bell frame, i take care not to squander my breath and energy. i fast, to quiet my heart. after three days of fasting, i no longer dare to think of praise, prizes, rank or pay. after five days, i no longer dare to think of being admired or blamed, of being skilful or clumsy. after seven days, i suddenly forget that i have four limbs and a body at all. by then my lord's court has stopped existing for me. my skill draws into one point, and everything outside that could unsettle me melts away. "after that i walk up into the wooded hills and study each tree as it has grown by itself. when i meet a trunk whose shape is already right, the finished frame shows itself to me inside it, and i start cutting. when no tree is right, i leave it. so heaven is joined to heaven. if my frames seem to come from spirits, that may be the reason." the daodejing speaks of returning to the uncarved block, pu. qing does carve, but only after he has become uncarved himself, and only along the shape the tree already holds. zhuangzi ch.19 (dasheng)

the peach blossom spring. in the taiyuan years of the jin dynasty, a fisherman from wuling rowed up a stream and lost track of how far he had gone. suddenly he came upon a grove of peach trees in blossom. for several hundred paces along both banks there were no other trees. fragrant grass grew fresh and lovely, and petals drifted down everywhere. at the end of the grove the stream began at a hill. in the hill was a small opening, and light seemed to come through it. he left his boat and went in. at first the passage was so narrow that only one person could pass. after some dozens of steps, it opened out into bright, level land. there were neat houses, good fields, pretty ponds, mulberry and bamboo. paths crossed between the fields, and he could hear chickens and dogs from one farm to the next. men and women worked in the fields. the old people and the children were all at ease and content. the villagers were astonished to see him. they took him home and killed a chicken for dinner. their ancestors, they said, had fled the turmoil of the qin age with their wives, children and neighbours, and had never gone out again. they had not heard of the han dynasty, let alone the wei and the jin. when he told them, they sighed. after some days he left. they asked him not to tell anyone outside. he marked his route carefully and reported to the governor. but when men went to look, they could not find the way again. no one ever has. tao yuanming, taohua yuan ji (c. 421 ce)

bian he's uncut jade. a man of chu named bian he found an uncut stone of jade in the chu mountains. he presented it to king li. the king had his jade worker look at it, and the jade worker said, "it is only a stone." the king thought bian he was trying to cheat him, and had his left foot cut off. when king li died and king wu came to the throne, bian he presented the stone again. again the jade worker said, "it is only a stone." again the king thought he was a cheat, and had his right foot cut off. when king wu died and king wen came to the throne, bian he took the stone in his arms and wept at the foot of the chu mountains. he wept for three days and three nights, until his tears were gone and blood came instead. the king heard about this and sent someone to ask him why. "many men in the world have lost their feet. why do you weep so bitterly?" "i do not weep for my feet," said bian he. "i weep because a precious jade is called a stone, and an honest man is called a cheat." the king had the jade worker cut and polish the stone, and a great treasure appeared inside it. it was named the jade of master he. the daodejing says: those who know me are few. so the sage wears coarse cloth and carries jade inside it. hanfeizi ch.13 (he shi)

jiufang gao chooses a horse. duke mu of qin said to bo le, the famous judge of horses, "you are growing old. is there anyone in your family i could send to find horses?" "a good horse can be known by its form, its bones, and its muscles," said bo le. "but a horse that is the best under heaven seems to vanish, to leave no dust and no tracks. my sons have small talent. they can tell a good horse, but not the best. but i have a friend, a man who gathers firewood and sells vegetables, called jiufang gao. in horses he is not below me." the duke sent jiufang gao out. three months later he returned. "i have found one, in shaqiu." "what kind of horse?" "a mare, and yellow." the duke sent for it. it was a stallion, and black. he was displeased and called bo le. "your friend cannot even tell colour or sex. what can he know about horses?" bo le gave a long sigh. "has he really come so far? then he is ten thousand times better than me. gao is watching the hidden springs of the animal. he holds on to the fine part and lets the rough part go; he keeps his eyes on what counts and lets the rest slip by unnoticed. the way gao judges a horse reaches past horses altogether." when the horse arrived, it was indeed the best horse under heaven. the daodejing says: the great image has no shape. the greatest skill seems clumsy. liezi ch.8 (shuofu); a parallel in huainanzi ch.12 calls the judge jiufang yin
