the man of song pulls up his sprouts. there was a man of the state of song who worried that his young grain was not growing fast enough. so one day he went into his field and pulled each sprout up a little, to help it grow. he came home worn out and said to his family, "i am exhausted today. i have been helping the sprouts grow." his son ran out to the field to look. all the sprouts had withered. this story comes from mencius, not from a daoist book, but daoist readers have always loved it. mencius uses it to warn against two mistakes. some people neglect what they are growing and do not weed it at all. others are impatient and pull at it. the second mistake, he says, does more harm than the first. the daodejing warns about the same impatience. one who stands on tiptoe does not stand firm. one who takes long strides does not walk far. the world is a sacred vessel that cannot be forced: whoever acts on it ruins it, whoever grasps it loses it. a tree you can barely put your arms around grew from a tiny shoot, and it grew at its own pace. mencius 2a:2

the sacrificial ox. king wei of chu heard that zhuang zhou was a man of great ability. he sent messengers with rich gifts to invite him to become chief minister. zhuang zhou laughed and said to the messengers, "a thousand pieces of gold is a great fortune. a minister's rank is a high honour. but have you never seen the ox they offer at the suburban sacrifice? for years it eats the best fodder. then they hang patterned silks on it and lead it into the great temple. when that day comes it would happily be some stray little pig nobody wants, but by then there is no way back. "go away quickly. do not dirty me. i would rather play and enjoy myself in a muddy ditch than be held in check by a ruler of a state. i will never take office, all my life. i will live as i please." the daodejing warns: to fill a hall with gold and jade is to be unable to guard it. to be rich and honoured and proud is to invite disaster. when the work is done, step back: that is the way of heaven. the ox in silk and the turtle in the box tell the same story. zhuangzi always chose the mud. shiji 63 (biography of zhuang zhou); zhuangzi ch.32

the old man's shoe. zhang liang had tried to kill the first emperor of qin, and he had failed. he changed his name and hid in the town of xiapi. one day, on a bridge there, an old man in coarse cloth walked up, let his shoe fall under the bridge on purpose, and said, "boy, go down and fetch my shoe." liang was stunned. he wanted to hit him. but the man was old, so he forced his anger down, climbed down, and brought the shoe. "put it on me," said the old man. liang had already fetched it, so he knelt and put it on the foot that was held out. the old man laughed and walked off. he went about one li and came back. "the boy can be taught. meet me here in five days, at dawn." liang came at dawn. the old man was there already, and angry. "you make a date with an old man and arrive after him? five days from now, come earlier." liang came at cockcrow. again the old man was there first. "late again? five more days." this time liang went before midnight. after a while the old man arrived, and he was pleased. "this is how it should be." he handed over a book. "read this and you will be a teacher of kings. in thirteen years you will see me in jibei. the yellow stone at the foot of mount gucheng is me." he left and was not seen again. at daylight liang looked at the book. it was taigong's art of war. he read and recited it constantly, and he became the strategist who helped to found the han. thirteen years later he found a yellow stone at the foot of mount gucheng, and he kept it as a treasure. the daodejing says: to keep to the soft is called strength. shiji 55 (hereditary house of the marquis of liu)

the king who tasted gall. king fuchai of wu broke the army of yue. king goujian of yue was left with five thousand men, shut in on mount kuaiji. his adviser fan li said, "send humble words and rich gifts. if wu refuses, offer yourself." so the minister zhong went to the wu camp. he moved forward on his knees, struck his head on the ground, and said, "goujian asks to be your servant, and his wife to be your maid." the wu minister wu zixu warned his king against it. but zhong secretly brought beautiful women and treasures to the grand steward of wu, and wu let yue live. goujian went home. he hung a gall bladder by his seat. he looked up at it when he sat and when he lay down, and he tasted it when he ate and drank. "have you forgotten the shame of kuaiji?" he said to himself. he worked in the fields with his own hands, and his wife wove the cloth. he ate no meat and wore no second colour. he bowed to able men, gave to the poor, mourned the dead, and shared the labour of the common people. wu grew proud and marched north to contend with the great states. yue struck from behind. after twenty-two years of planning, yue had fuchai shut in on mount gusu, and now his envoy came forward on his knees. goujian could hardly bear to refuse. fan li beat the drum and sent the troops forward. fuchai covered his face and killed himself. the daodejing says: a small state that puts itself below a great state takes the great state. shiji 41 (hereditary house of goujian, king of yue)

fan li leaves at the height. fan li served king goujian of yue for more than twenty years. together they destroyed the state of wu, and goujian became the chief of the lords. fan li held the title of supreme general. at that moment he left. he took a boat out to sea and did not come back. from the state of qi he sent a letter to his old colleague, the minister zhong. "when the birds are all shot, the good bow is put away. when the hare is dead, the hound is cooked. the king has a long neck and a mouth like a beak. a man can share trouble with him, but not ease. why do you not go?" zhong read the letter and stayed. he only said that he was ill and stopped going to court. someone told the king that zhong was planning a revolt. the king sent him a sword, and zhong killed himself. in qi, fan li took a new name and farmed by the sea with his sons. in a few years his property was worth hundreds of thousands. the people of qi made him chancellor. he sighed. "at home, a thousand in gold. in office, the rank of chancellor. for a commoner this is the top. to hold an honoured name for long brings no good." he gave back the seal and shared out his wealth among friends and neighbours. he went quietly to the town of tao, and there he traded and grew rich a second time, under the name lord zhu of tao. the daodejing says: the good one bears fruit, and stops. shiji 41 (hereditary house of goujian, king of yue)

the chancellor who changed nothing. xiao he wrote the laws of the young han empire. when he died, cao shen took his place as chancellor. years before, in qi, a teacher of the yellow emperor and laozi had told cao shen: "the way to govern values clear stillness, and the people settle of themselves." cao shen changed nothing. he kept every rule of xiao he. he chose slow, plain-spoken men as his clerks and sent away the sharp ones who wanted a name. day and night he drank good wine. officials and guests came to give him advice. he poured wine for them. when they tried to speak, he poured more, and they went home drunk with the advice unsaid. the young emperor hui was troubled. he told cao shen's son to ask his father, in private, why he did not attend to affairs. cao shen gave his son two hundred strokes. "go and wait on the emperor. the affairs of the empire are not for you to talk about." at court the emperor reproached him. cao shen took off his cap. "who is the wiser ruler, your majesty or the founding emperor?" "how could i dare to compare myself with him?" "and who is the abler man, i or xiao he?" "you do not seem to be his equal." "your majesty is right. those two settled the empire, and the laws are clear. if your majesty sits with folded hands, and we keep our posts and follow the rules without losing them, is that not enough?" "good," said the emperor. "you may rest." cao shen was chancellor for three years. the people sang that xiao he's laws were as straight as a drawn line, and that cao shen kept them, and so the people had peace. the daodejing says: i love stillness, and the people come straight of themselves. shiji 54 (hereditary house of chancellor cao)

the physician who ran away. the physician bian que came before lord huan of cai. he stood a while and said, "my lord has an illness. it lies in the pores of the skin. if it is not treated, i fear it will go deeper." "i am not ill," said the lord. when bian que had gone, he said, "doctors like to treat the healthy and take the credit." ten days later bian que came again. "the illness is in the flesh now. untreated, it will go deeper." the lord did not answer, and he was not pleased. ten days later bian que came again. "the illness is in the stomach and the bowels. untreated, it will go deeper." again the lord did not answer. ten days later bian que saw the lord from a distance. he turned around and ran. the lord sent a man to ask him why. "in the pores, hot compresses can reach an illness. in the flesh, needles can reach it. in the stomach and bowels, boiled medicines can reach it. in the marrow of the bones, it belongs to the master of fates, and nothing can be done. it is in the marrow now. so i no longer ask to treat him." five days later the lord's body began to hurt. he sent men to find bian que, but bian que had fled to qin. the lord died. the hanfeizi adds that a good doctor attacks an illness while it is still at the skin, and that the sage, in the same way, attends to things early. the hanfeizi tells it for daodejing ch.63: plan for the hard while it is easy; work on the great while it is fine as a thread. hanfeizi ch.21 (yu lao); shiji 105 tells it of a marquis huan of qi

the ivory chopsticks. zhou, the last king of shang, had a pair of chopsticks made of ivory. his kinsman jizi saw them and was afraid. jizi reasoned like this. ivory chopsticks will not be set beside bowls of baked clay. they will call for cups of jade and rhinoceros horn. ivory chopsticks and jade cups will not be used for a broth of beans and bean leaves. they will call for yak, elephant, and unborn leopard. a man who eats yak, elephant, and unborn leopard will not wear a short coat of rough cloth, and he will not eat under a roof of thatch. he will want brocade in nine layers, wide halls, and high terraces. "i fear where this ends," said jizi. "so i am afraid of where it begins." five years went by. king zhou had a garden of meat. he had the grid of hot metal for burning people. he climbed a hill of wine dregs and looked down on a pool of wine. and so he was destroyed, and shang with him. the hanfeizi says that jizi saw a pair of ivory chopsticks and knew from them the ruin of the whole realm. then it quotes the daodejing: to see the small is called clear sight. hanfeizi ch.21 (yu lao)

three years for one leaf. a man of song carved a paper mulberry leaf out of ivory for his lord. the work took him three years. the leaf was perfect. the stalk and the veins were thick in one place and thin in another, as they are in a living leaf. it had the fine hairs and the soft shine. when it was mixed in with real mulberry leaves, nobody could pick it out. for this feat the man was given a salary from the state of song. liezi heard about it. he said, "if heaven and earth took three years to finish one leaf, there would be very few things with leaves." the hanfeizi tells the story to explain a line of the daodejing. a person who does not ride on what heaven and earth supply, it says, and loads everything on one body, is doing the work of that one leaf. grain that is sown in winter: even hou ji, the first farmer, could not make it thrive. a great crop in a rich year: even a slave cannot spoil it. with the strength of one person, hou ji is not enough. following what is so of itself, a slave is more than enough. the hanfeizi caps the story with a line of daodejing ch.64: to assist the self-so of the ten thousand things, and not dare to act. hanfeizi ch.21 (yu lao); liezi ch.8 (shuofu) has the same story with a leaf of jade

the crowd behind nanrong chu. nanrong chu was no longer young, and his mind gave him no peace. his teacher gengsang chu could not help him, and sent him south to laozi. he packed his grain and walked for seven days and seven nights. laozi looked at him. "have you come from gengsang chu?" "yes." "then why have you brought so many people with you?" nanrong chu was startled and looked behind him. nobody was there. "you do not understand what i mean?" said laozi. nanrong chu hung his head in shame. then he looked up and sighed. "now i have forgotten my answer, and so i have lost my question as well." after a while he found it again. "if i do not know things, people call me a fool. if i do know things, the knowing brings grief to my own body. if i am not kind, i hurt others. if i am kind, i hurt myself. how can i get out of this?" he stayed in the guest house for ten days and worked on himself, and then he came back, still unhappy. so laozi gave him the rule for guarding life. "can you hold the one in your arms? can you not lose it? can you stop? can you let go of others and look for it in yourself? can you be a baby? a baby howls all day and its throat is not hoarse. that is harmony at its peak. it clenches its fist all day and the hand does not cramp. it stares all day and the eyes do not blink. it walks and does not know where to. it rests and does not know what for. it goes along with things and shares the same current. that is the rule for guarding life." zhuangzi ch.23 (gengsang chu)

the straw dogs after the rite. confucius was travelling west to the state of wei. his student yan yuan asked the music master jin, "what do you think of my master's journey?" "a pity," said master jin. "your master will come to a dead end." "why?" "before the straw dogs are set out for the offering, they are kept in a basket and wrapped in embroidered cloth. the priest fasts before he carries them in. after the offering, people who walk by tread on their heads and backs, and the grass cutters pick them up to light the cooking fire. that is all. if someone puts them back in the basket, wraps them in embroidery again, and lives and sleeps beneath them, he gets no good dreams. he gets nightmares. your master has gathered up the straw dogs that the old kings set out long ago. he and his students live and sleep beneath them. "on water, nothing is better than a boat. on land, nothing is better than a cart. a boat goes well on water, but push it on land and in a lifetime it will not move a few feet. are the old days and today not like water and land? "the beauty xi shi had a pain in her chest and frowned at her neighbours. an ugly woman of the village saw this and thought it lovely. she went home, pressed her hands to her chest, and frowned at everyone. the rich shut their gates and stayed in. the poor took their wives and children and ran. she knew that the frown was beautiful. she did not know what made it beautiful." the daodejing says: heaven and earth treat the ten thousand things as straw dogs. zhuangzi ch.14 (tianyun)

the vessel that tips when full. confucius visited the ancestral temple of duke huan of lu. he saw a vessel there that sat at a slant. "what vessel is this?" he asked the keeper of the temple. "it is the vessel that sits at the right of the seat," said the keeper. "i have heard of it," said confucius. "empty, it leans. half full, it stands straight. full, it turns over." he looked at his students. "pour water into it." the students ladled water in. when the vessel was half full, it stood straight. when it was full, it turned over and spilled everything. when it was empty, it leaned again. confucius sighed. "ah! is there anything that is full and does not turn over?" his student zilu said, "may i ask: is there a way to hold fullness?" "sharp wits and wide knowledge: guard them with dullness. achievements that cover the world: guard them with yielding. courage that shakes the age: guard it with caution. wealth that reaches the four seas: guard it with modesty. this is called the way of ladling out and making less." the huainanzi closes with a line of the daodejing: whoever keeps this way does not want to be full. xunzi ch.28 (youzuo); retold in huainanzi ch.12 (daoying xun), which ends with daodejing ch.15

the minister who turned his carriage. lin xiangru was a man of low birth. he faced down the king of qin twice and saved the honour of zhao, and the king of zhao ranked him above the old general lian po. lian po was furious. "i am the general of zhao. i have taken cities and won battles in the field. xiangru has only worked his tongue, and he sits above me. i am ashamed to be below him. when i meet him, i will humiliate him." xiangru heard this. after that he said he was ill on court days, so that the two would not have to dispute their places. once, when he was out, he saw lian po far off, and he turned his carriage aside and hid. his retainers were ashamed. "we left our families to serve you because we admired your high spirit. now you hide from a man of your own rank. a common man would be ashamed of this. we ask to leave." xiangru stopped them. "which is more terrible, general lian or the king of qin?" "the king of qin." "i shouted at the king of qin in his own court and shamed his ministers. would i fear general lian? but i think of this. strong qin does not dare to send troops against zhao for one reason: the two of us are here. if two tigers fight, both will not come out alive. i do this because i put the danger of the state first and a private grudge after." lian po heard what he had said. he bared his shoulders, tied a rod of thorn on his back, and came to xiangru's gate to ask for punishment. the two became friends unto death. the daodejing says: because the sage does not contend, no one under heaven can contend with the sage. shiji 81 (biographies of lian po and lin xiangru)

the lord father at shaqiu. king wuling of zhao was a strong king. he put his soldiers into the short coats of the northern riders and taught them to shoot from horseback, and he won wide lands. then, in the twenty-seventh year of his rule, while he was still alive and well, he gave the throne to a young son. he called himself the lord father. he meant to be free to lead the army. he was a restless man. once he dressed as his own envoy and rode into qin to take a look at its king. the king of qin thought that this envoy did not carry himself like any man's servant, and sent riders after him. the lord father was already through the pass. he had an elder son, zhang, whom he had passed over. at court he saw his elder son, downcast, bow down to the boy king, and he pitied him. he thought of cutting the state in two. he could not decide. on a visit to shaqiu, zhang rose in revolt and lost. he fled to his father's lodge, and his father let him in. the king's ministers surrounded the lodge and killed zhang. then they were afraid. if they lifted the siege, the lord father would destroy them. so they kept it. they called to the people inside: "the last one out dies." everyone came out. the lord father could not get out, and he had no food. he took sparrow nestlings from their nests and ate them. after more than three months he starved to death in the palace at shaqiu. the hanfeizi says: the state is a ruler's baggage wagon, and the lord father left his while he lived. the daodejing asks: how can the lord of ten thousand chariots take the body lightly before all under heaven? shiji 43 (hereditary house of zhao); hanfeizi ch.21 (yu lao) uses him to explain daodejing 26

the general and the thief. zifa, a general of chu, liked to seek out men who had a skill. a man of chu came to see him. "i hear that you look for men of skill. i am a thief. i would like to serve as one of your soldiers, with my skill." zifa hurried out to meet him. his sash was not tied and his cap was not straight, and he received the man with full courtesy. his attendants objected. "a thief robs the whole world. why treat him with respect?" "this is not something for you to judge," said zifa. not long after, qi raised an army and attacked chu. zifa led the defence, and three times his troops were pushed back. the able officers of chu used up all their plans, and the army of qi only grew stronger. the thief came forward. "i have a small skill. let me use it for you." "go," said zifa, and he did not ask what the man meant to do. that night the thief took down the bed curtain of the qi general and brought it back. zifa sent it across with a message: "one of our men went out for firewood and found the general's curtain. we return it." the next night the thief brought the general's pillow. zifa sent it back. the night after, he brought the general's hairpin. zifa sent it back. the army of qi was badly shaken. the general said to his officers, "if we do not leave today, i fear that chu will take my head." he turned his army around and went home. the huainanzi says that no skill is too slight; it depends on how a ruler uses it. then it quotes the daodejing: the not-good person is the good person's material. huainanzi ch.12 (daoying xun)

the robber's five virtues. people guard against thieves who cut open trunks, feel in bags, and break into chests. they tie the cords tight and make the bolts and clasps firm. the world calls this wisdom. then a great thief comes. he puts the chest on his back, lifts the trunk, shoulders the bag, and runs. his one fear is that the cords and clasps will not hold. the state of qi was once like a well-tied chest. its villages were in sight of one another. its temples, its districts, and its laws all followed the pattern of the sages. then one morning tian chengzi killed the lord of qi and stole the state. he stole the wise laws along with it. people called him a robber, but he lived as safely as the sage kings, and his house held qi for generations. a follower of the bandit zhi once asked him, "does a robber also have a way?" "where can anyone go without a way?" said zhi. "to guess what is stored inside a house: that is sageliness. to go in first: that is courage. to come out last: that is duty. to know if the job can be done or not: that is wisdom. to divide the loot in equal shares: that is humaneness. nobody in the world has become a great robber without all five." the chapter draws its own conclusion. a man who steals a belt hook is put to death. a man who steals a state becomes a lord, and humaneness and duty are then found at his gate. the daodejing says: the more laws and orders are displayed, the more thieves and bandits there are. zhuangzi ch.10 (quqie)

zengzi kills the pig. the wife of zengzi was leaving for the market. her small son followed her and cried. "go back home," she said. "when i return, i will kill a pig for you." she came back from the market, and zengzi was about to catch a pig and kill it. she stopped him. "i was only playing with the child." "a child is not someone to play with in that way," said zengzi. "a child knows nothing yet. he depends on his father and mother to learn, and he listens to what they teach. if you deceive him now, you teach him to deceive. when a mother deceives her son, the son does not trust his mother. that is no way to teach him." and he killed the pig and cooked it. the same chapter tells a second story. marquis wen of wei set a day to go hunting with his gamekeeper. the next day a fierce wind blew. his attendants told him to stay in. "no," said the marquis. "i will not break my word because the wind is strong." he drove the carriage himself, went out into the wind, and told the gamekeeper in person that the hunt was called off. the daodejing says: trust not enough, there: no trust, there. hanfeizi ch.32 (wai chu shuo, upper left)

no mound for the victory. in 597 bce the army of chu met the army of jin at bi, and jin was routed. the jin soldiers fought one another for places in the boats to get back across the yellow river. an officer of chu named pan dang came to king zhuang. "why does my lord not build a war monument? gather the jin dead and raise a great mound over them. i have heard that one who defeats an enemy must show it to his sons and grandsons, so that they do not forget the deeds of war." "this is not something that you understand," said the king. "look at the written character for war. it is made of 'stop' and 'spear'." the zuozhuan gives his words as 止戈為武. "war is for seven things: to forbid violence, to put away weapons, to keep what is great, to settle the work, to give the people rest, to bring the many into accord, and to make wealth grow. i have caused the bones of the men of two states to lie in the open. that is violence. i have shown my weapons to frighten the lords. that is not putting weapons away. of the seven, i have not one. what would i show to my sons and grandsons? "in old times the wise kings struck down the disrespectful. they took the worst of them and buried them under a mound as a great punishment. here there is no criminal. these people all gave their loyalty and died for their lord's command. how can i make a mound of them?" he made an offering to the river. he built a shrine to his forefathers and reported there that the task was done. then he went home. the daodejing says: a battle won: observe it with the rites of mourning. zuozhuan, duke xuan, year 12

lin hui drops the jade. confucius said to zisang hu, "i was driven out of lu twice. in song they cut down the tree where i sat. in wei they wiped out my footprints. i was in want in shang and zhou, and surrounded between chen and cai. and through all these troubles my kin have grown more distant and my friends and followers have drifted away. why is that?" "have you not heard about the man of jia who fled?" said zisang hu. "his name was lin hui. he threw away a disc of jade worth a thousand in gold, put his baby on his back, and ran. someone asked him, 'did you think of the price? a baby is worth little. did you think of the burden? a baby is a great burden. why throw away the jade and carry the baby?' lin hui said, 'the jade and i were joined by profit. this child and i are joined by heaven.' "things that profit joins throw one another away when trouble presses. things that heaven joins hold on to one another when trouble presses. the friendship of a noble person is bland, like water. the friendship of a small person is sweet, like new wine. the bland one grows close. the sweet one breaks off." "i accept the teaching with respect," said confucius. he walked home slowly and at ease. he gave up his studies and put away his books. his students no longer bowed before him, and their love for him grew. the daodejing says: the dao, as it comes out of the mouth: bland! it has no flavor. zhuangzi ch.20 (shanmu)

xu you refuses the world. the sage king yao wanted to hand all under heaven to the hermit xu you. "the sun and moon are up," said yao, "and the torch is still burning. is it not hard for the torch to give light? the rain falls in its season, and a man is still carrying water to the fields. is that not wasted work? if you took the throne, the world would be in order. yet i still sit in the seat. i look at myself and see what i lack. please take the world." "you govern the world," said xu you, "and the world is already governed. if i took your place now, would i do it for the name? the name is the guest of the real thing. shall i be a guest? "the wren nests in the deep forest and uses no more than one branch. the mole drinks at the river and takes no more than a bellyful. go home, my lord, and rest. i have no use for the world. "the cook may not be keeping his kitchen in order. even so, the priest and the stand-in for the dead do not step over the wine jars and the meat stands to do his work for him." the daodejing says: once the names are there, it is time to know where to stop. zhuangzi ch.1 (xiaoyao you)

late is death, revolt is death. in the seventh month of 209 bce, nine hundred poor men were called up to guard the frontier at yuyang. on the march they camped at daze village. heavy rain fell, the road was cut, and they saw that they could not reach the post by the set day. under the law of qin, all who came late were to lose their heads. two of the squad leaders, chen sheng and wu guang, talked it over. "if we run, we die. if we start a great undertaking, we die. death either way. why not die for a state of our own?" they prepared the men. they wrote "chen sheng will be king" in red on a piece of silk and put it in the belly of a fish that the soldiers bought for dinner. at night wu guang hid by a shrine near the camp, lit a fire, and called out like a fox: "great chu will rise. chen sheng will be king." in the morning the soldiers pointed at chen sheng and whispered. then wu guang provoked one of the officers, who was drunk, into flogging him. the officer drew his sword. wu guang took it and killed him. chen sheng helped, and they killed both officers. they called the men together. "you have all met with this rain, and you are all late. the late lose their heads. and even if you are spared, six or seven of every ten frontier guards die. if a brave man dies, let it be for a great name. are kings and lords, generals and ministers, a breed apart?" the shiji gives this last line as 王侯將相寧有種乎. "we accept your command," said the men. within three years qin had fallen. the daodejing says: the people do not fear death. how, then, frighten them with death? shiji 48 (hereditary house of chen she)

feng xuan burns the tallies. lord mengchang of qi kept many guests in his house. the people of his fief, xue, owed him money. he asked which of his guests could keep accounts and collect the debts. a poor guest named feng xuan signed his name. feng xuan asked, "when the debts are all in, what shall i buy with the money?" "look at what my house has little of," said the lord. feng xuan drove to xue. he had the officials call in everyone who owed money, and each debtor brought his half of the tally to be matched. when all the tallies were matched, feng xuan stood up. he declared, as if by the lord's order, that the debts were a gift to the people. then he burned the tallies. the people shouted, "ten thousand years!" he drove straight back. the lord was surprised at his speed. "are the debts collected? what did you buy?" "you told me to look at what your house has little of. your palace is piled with treasure, and your stables are full. what your house has little of is right dealing. so i bought right dealing for you." "how does one buy that?" "you have only this small xue, and you do not care for its people as your children. you treat them as a merchant treats a market. i gave them the debts and burned the tallies." the lord was not pleased. "enough, sir." a year later the king of qi dismissed him, and he went to xue. he was still a hundred li away when the people came out to meet him on the road, the old on their arms and the children by the hand. he turned to feng xuan. "today i see what you bought for me." the daodejing says: the sage holds the left tally and makes no claim on anyone. zhanguo ce, stratagems of qi 4; shiji 75 tells it differently, calls him feng huan, and has him burn only the tallies of those too poor to pay

jie zhitui asks for nothing. chong'er, a prince of jin, lived in exile for nineteen years. a few men followed him through all of it. when he came home and ruled as duke wen, he rewarded those who had gone with him. jie zhitui had gone with him. he said nothing about a reward, and no reward came to him. jie zhitui said to his mother, "of the old duke's sons, only our lord is left. heaven has not ended the line of jin, so there had to be a ruler. who else could it be? heaven set him up. yet these gentlemen think it was their own strength. to steal a person's goods is called robbery. what is it, then, to take the work of heaven and call it one's own? i find it hard to live among them." "why not ask as well?" said his mother. "if you die like this, whom will you blame?" "to copy a fault that i have condemned would be worse. and i have spoken with resentment. i will not eat his food." "then at least let him know. what of that?" "words are the ornament of the body. my body is about to go into hiding. why ornament it? that would be to seek notice." "can you really be like this?" said his mother. "then i will go into hiding with you." they went away and lived hidden until they died. the duke looked for him and could not find him. he set aside the fields of mianshang in his name. "let this record my fault," he said, "and honour a good man." later tellings add a forest fire that the duke lit to drive him out. the zuozhuan does not have it. the daodejing says: the work is complete; it does not name it "mine". zuozhuan, duke xi, year 24

the gardener and the well-sweep. zigong, a student of confucius, was travelling through the country south of the han river. he saw an old man at work in a vegetable garden. the old man had dug a sloping tunnel down to his well. he went in, came out with a jar of water in his arms, and poured it on the beds. he puffed and strained, and for all his labour very little was done. "there is a machine for this," said zigong. "in one day it waters a hundred beds. it takes little strength and does a great deal. would you not like one, sir?" the gardener looked up. "how does it work?" "it is a wooden arm, heavy at the back and light at the front. it lifts the water as if it were pulling it out, so fast that it seems to boil over. it is called a well-sweep." the gardener's face flushed with anger. then he laughed. "i heard this from my teacher. where there are machines, there will be machine business. where there is machine business, there will be a machine heart. with a machine heart in the chest, what is pure and plain is no longer whole. then the spirit does not settle, and what has an unsettled spirit, the dao does not carry. it is not that i do not know of your machine. i would be ashamed to use it." zigong was abashed. he looked down and gave no answer. he walked on, pale and not himself, and he had gone thirty li before he recovered. the daodejing says: the more craft and skill people have, the more strange things arise. zhuangzi ch.12 (tiandi)

wash your bowl, have some tea. in tang times the chan master congshen lived at a temple in zhaozhou, and people called him by the name of the place. a monk came to him and said, "i have only just entered the monastery. i beg the master to teach me." "have you eaten your rice gruel?" said zhaozhou. "i have eaten." "then go and wash your bowl." the record says that the monk understood something. another time, zhaozhou asked a monk who had just arrived, "have you been here before?" "i have been here." "go and have some tea." he asked the second the same question. "i have not been here." "go and have some tea." later the prior of the temple came to him. "to the one who had been here, you said, 'go and have some tea.' to the one who had not been here, you also said, 'go and have some tea.' why?" "prior!" called zhaozhou. "yes?" said the prior. "go and have some tea." zhaozhou gives no explanation. the daodejing says: the dao, as it comes out of the mouth: bland! it has no flavor. wumenguan (the gateless barrier), case 7; the tea story is in the chan records of zhaozhou congshen (wudeng huiyuan)

king tai leaves bin. long before the house of zhou ruled, its ancestor king tai lived with his people in the land of bin. the di tribes raided them. king tai gave the di furs and silk. the raids did not stop. he gave them dogs and horses. the raids did not stop. he gave them pearls and jade. the raids did not stop. he called the elders together. "what the di want is our land. i have heard that a ruler does not harm people with the thing that is meant to feed them. why should you worry about having no lord? i am going to leave." in the zhuangzi he says more. "to live beside a man's older brother and have the younger brother killed, to live beside a father and have his son killed: i cannot bear it. stay here, all of you, and do your best. what difference is there between being my subjects and being subjects of the di?" he took his staff and left bin. he crossed mount liang and settled at the foot of mount qi. the people of bin said, "this is a humane man. we must not lose him." mencius says that they followed him like a crowd on its way to market. in the zhuangzi they go after him in an unbroken line. a new state grew up under mount qi, and from it, generations later, came the kings of zhou. the daodejing says: all under heaven are glad to push the sage forward and do not tire. mencius 1b:15; also told in zhuangzi ch.28 (rangwang)

fish and rocks. 魚石圖 bada shanren (zhu da) qing dynasty, 1699 a tall scroll: a heavy rock hangs at the top, and below it a few tiny minnows dart in empty space near another rock. bada shanren's tiny minnows dart beneath a heavy rock. fish should not leave the deep water. the rock at the top seems about to fall. below it, a few tiny minnows, each only a flick or two of ink, dart through open space. bada shanren was a member of the ming royal family who became a monk after the dynasty fell; his fish and birds often look sideways at the world. chapter 36 says the soft and weak overcome the hard and strong. fish should not leave the depths; the sharp tools of a state should not be shown. notice how much empty paper surrounds the minnows. they are safe there, as fish are safe in deep water.

bamboo slips from a chu tomb. 楚簡 unknown scribes eastern zhou dynasty, 4th to 3rd century bce narrow strips of dark bamboo lie side by side, each written with a column of small characters. bamboo slips from a chu tomb, the kind of writing material on which the earliest daodejing copies survive. the sage holds the left half of the tally and does not press for payment. look at the narrow strips laid side by side, each with a single column of small characters. contracts and debts in ancient china were often written on split tallies; each side kept half. the oldest known manuscripts of laozi, found at guodian in 1993, were written on slips like these. chapter 79 says after a great quarrel is settled, some resentment always remains. so the sage holds the left half of the tally but makes no demands on others. the way of heaven has no favourites; it is always with the good. notice the patient handwriting.

bell (zhong) with dragons and spirals. 甬鐘 unknown zhou bronze caster late western zhou dynasty, c. 850 to 771 bce a bronze bell with a long shaft, rows of raised knobs and a curved, cut-away rim. a zhou ritual bell, silent in times of mourning. laozi says a victory should be marked with the rites of mourning. this bell was struck at sacrifices and court rites nearly three thousand years ago. look at the rows of knobs, the curved rim, the dragons in low relief. in zhou mourning, such bells were taken down and fell silent: the absence of music marked a funeral. chapter 31 says weapons are instruments of ill omen; a gentleman uses them only when he must, and values calm. a victory is not beautiful. those who rejoice in killing cannot win the world. after a battle, the dead should be mourned and the victory treated as a funeral. imagine the hall after a victory with this bell left unstruck.

zhuangzi dreaming of a butterfly. 莊周夢蝶 lu zhi ming dynasty, mid-16th century a man sleeps on a flat rock under a willow; two small butterflies drift in the air above him. lu zhi paints zhuangzi asleep on a rock while two butterflies drift above him. which one is dreaming? the sleeper lies flat and heavy on the rock; the butterflies are almost nothing, two flicks of the brush in the air. heavy and light, solid and empty, waking and dreaming: the painting is built on pairs, like this chapter. laozi says that beautiful and ugly, long and short, high and low give rise to each other. notice how the willow strands hang down toward the sleeper while the butterflies rise. nothing here wins. each thing is itself only because the other is there. stay with the empty air between the man and the insects.

old plum (from miscellaneous paintings album). 古梅 chen hongshou ming to qing dynasty, mid-17th century an album spread: a few lines of calligraphy on the left, a gnarled old plum branch with small blossoms on the right. an old plum branch, gnarled and spare, still flowers. in caring for people and serving heaven, nothing is better than frugality. the branch is crooked and rough, with only a few blossoms. chen hongshou leaves most of the leaf empty. old plum trees were admired in china because they bloom in the cold, on wood that looks dead. chapter 59 says in governing people and serving heaven, nothing is better than frugality. being frugal means preparing early; it builds up virtue. this is called deep roots and firm stem, the way to long life and lasting vision. look at the thin branch holding its flowers.

diagram of the golden elixir: three, five, one. 金丹三五一圖 chen zhixu yuan dynasty, 14th century five small numbered circles, one to five, set in a cross and joined in pairs by curved lines, under the title 金丹三五一圖. a yuan daoist diagram joins five numbered circles into one. later daoists read chapter 42's counting of one, two and three into their own number lore. chen zhixu drew this for inner alchemy, the daoist practice of refining body and spirit. look at the five small circles marked one to five, set in a cross, and the curved lines that join them in pairs around the five at the centre. the pairs each make five, and the fives join into one. it is not a picture of chapter 42, but it grows from it. the chapter says the dao gives birth to one, one to two, two to three, and three to the ten thousand things; they carry shade on the back and hold sun in the arms, and the surging breath makes their accord. follow the lines back to the centre.

children playing on a winter day. 冬日嬰戲圖 attributed to su hanchen song dynasty, 12th century a girl bends toward a kitten while trailing a peacock-feather lure for her small brother, beneath flowering plum and camellia. a girl and her small brother play with a cat under winter blossoms. the sage treats all people as his children. the children wear fine clothes. the girl bends toward a kitten while she trails a peacock-feather lure behind her, and her small brother reaches for the feathers. plum and camellia bloom against the cold. chapter 49 says the sage has no fixed heart of his own; he takes the hearts of the people as his heart. he is good to the good and also good to those who are not good. in the world he is calm and unbiased; the people turn their eyes and ears to him, and he treats them all as children. notice how gently the girl attends to the smallest creature.

confucius meeting laozi. 孔子見老子 anonymous han artisans eastern han dynasty a wide rubbing: rows of small figures, with confucius and laozi meeting in the middle register. a han rubbing of confucius visiting laozi to ask about the rites. laozi says ritual is the thin husk of loyalty. look for the two figures facing each other in the centre of the band. around them stand students and attendants, all in the formal pose of a meeting. the story was popular on han tomb carvings: the great teacher of ritual coming to learn from the archivist of zhou. chapter 38 says high virtue is not conscious of itself, and so it has virtue. when the way is lost, virtue appears; then benevolence, then righteousness, then ritual, which is the thin edge of loyalty and the beginning of disorder. the great person stays with the fruit, not the flower.

portrait of confucius as teacher. 先師孔子行教像 after wu daozi stele after a tang dynasty design (8th century); later rubbing a black-and-white rubbing of confucius standing in long robes with hands folded, under a title in large characters. a rubbing of confucius the great teacher. when the great way is forgotten, benevolence and righteousness are preached. this image was carved in stone after a design by the tang painter wu daozi, then printed by pressing paper on the stone and rubbing it with ink. look at the dignified figure, the folded hands, the long robe. confucius taught benevolence, rightness and ritual. chapter 18 makes a sharp point: these virtues are named and taught only when the way has already been lost. when families quarrel, people praise filial children. the chapter is not mocking confucius. it asks what kind of world needs such teachers. notice the solemn weight of the portrait.

bowl, ding ware. 定窯碗 ding kilns, hebei song dynasty, 12th century a plain, creamy white stoneware bowl. a plain white ding ware bowl. taste the tasteless; do great things while they are small. the bowl has no painted decoration, only the soft cream of its glaze and the line of its rim. song connoisseurs loved ding ware for exactly this restraint. chapter 63 says: act without acting, work without working, taste the tasteless. handle the difficult while it is easy; do the great while it is small. all difficult things in the world start from easy ones. the sage never tries to do great things, and so achieves greatness. look at the simple curve of the bowl. nothing here is hard, and nothing is missing.

tripod cauldron (ding). 鼎 unknown shang bronze caster late shang dynasty, 13th to 11th century bce a bronze three-legged cauldron with two upright handles and a decorated band, in a museum case. the ding was the symbol of rule in ancient china. laozi calls the world a sacred vessel that cannot be grabbed. look at the solid legs, the raised handles, the band of masks around the belly. ding cauldrons held offerings, and to own the great ding meant to own the kingdom. chapter 29 warns those who want to take the world and work on it: all under heaven is a spirit vessel. who works on it ruins it; who grips it loses it. things sometimes lead and sometimes follow. notice that this vessel is meant to be filled, carried with care and used in ritual, not seized.

residents on the outskirts of dragon abode. 龍宿郊民圖 attributed to dong yuan five dynasties, 10th century soft green hills curve around a broad river; boats and tiny villagers gather on the shore. in this scroll attributed to dong yuan, soft hills curve around a wide river. the way in the world is like streams flowing to rivers and the sea. follow the river from the far distance toward the shore, where boats gather and people wait. the hills are round and gentle, painted in long, soft strokes. chapter 32 says the way, constant and nameless, is like the uncarved block. if rulers could keep it, all things would come of themselves, and the sweet dew would fall without being commanded. the way in the world is like small streams flowing into the rivers and the sea. notice how every line in this landscape leads toward the water.

riverbank. 溪岸圖 attributed to dong yuan five dynasties, 10th century a tall, dark scroll of a winding river and wind-blown water, with a pavilion on the bank and mountains above. in this scroll attributed to dong yuan, the river winds left and right. the great way flows everywhere. trace the water from the top of the scroll to the bottom. it turns this way and that, wind-blown, never in a straight line. mountains, a house and trees all lean along its course. chapter 34 says the great way flows everywhere, to the left and to the right. all things depend on it, and it does not refuse them. it completes its work and claims nothing. because it never makes itself great, it can be great. let your eye drift with the current.

sitting alone by a stream. 臨流獨坐圖 attributed to fan kuan northern song dynasty, 11th century tall, dark mountains rise above a stream; a small figure sits alone on the bank near the bottom. a small figure sits alone beside a stream under dark mountains. one who knows himself is enlightened. find the seated figure near the bottom. he looks out at the water, his back to the high cliffs. he is not climbing or travelling. chapter 33 says: one who knows others is clever; one who knows himself is enlightened. one who conquers others is strong; one who conquers himself is mighty. one who knows when he has enough is rich. stay with the man by the stream. the great mountain behind him does not distract him. what is he looking at?

travelers among mountains and streams. 谿山行旅圖 fan kuan northern song dynasty, c. 1000 a huge mountain wall fills the top of a tall scroll; a thin waterfall falls on the right; tiny travellers with mules pass along the bottom. fan kuan's mountain fills the sky; the travellers below are almost too small to see. something formless existed before heaven and earth. stand back and let the great mountain wall press toward you. then search the bottom edge for the travellers and their mules, tiny and patient. the waterfall on the right is a single white thread. chapter 25 speaks of something formed in chaos before heaven and earth, silent and empty, standing alone and unchanging. we call it the way, or great. humans follow earth, earth follows heaven, heaven follows the way, the way follows what is so of itself. this painting places people inside that order, small but walking.

pictures of tilling and weaving. 御製耕織圖 jiao bingzhen (designs), zhu gui (blocks) qing dynasty, 1696 farm families in thatched houses bow and make offerings after the harvest; bare winter trees behind. farm families give thanks after the harvest. people starve when those above eat too much in taxes. this print comes from a set of pictures of farming and weaving made for the kangxi emperor in 1696. look at the families bowing in the yard, the thatched roofs, the bare trees. the grain on which the empire lived came from houses like these. chapter 75 says the people starve because those above them eat too much in grain tax. they are hard to govern because those above them have their doings. they take death lightly because those above them seek life’s thickness. look at the humble offering, and ask who should be giving thanks to whom.

gu wine vessel. 觚 unknown shang bronze caster late shang dynasty, 13th to 11th century bce a tall, slender bronze cup with a wide trumpet mouth, a narrow waist and a decorated base, on a museum plinth. the gu is a wine vessel whose use is its hollow. its mouth flares wide, and its centre is mostly air. follow the outline from the wide mouth down to the narrow waist and out again to the base. the bronze is only a thin skin around an empty column. three thousand years ago this cup held offerings for ancestors. chapter 4 says the way is empty, yet using it never fills it up; it is deep, like the ancestor of the ten thousand things. imagine looking down into the gu from above: a dark round hole with no bottom you can see. the shape is useful because it holds back from being solid.

early spring. 早春圖 guo xi northern song dynasty, 1072 twisting mountains and gnarled trees rise in mist; streams and small figures appear in the lower corners. guo xi's mountains seem to stir as spring begins. the way gives birth; virtue nourishes. the whole scroll twists upward like steam: rocks curl, trees reach, mist lifts. look at the fishermen and travellers in the lower corners, small signs of human life waking up with the season. chapter 51 says the way gives birth to all things, virtue nourishes them, matter shapes them, circumstances complete them. the way gives birth and does not possess; it acts and does not rely; it raises and does not rule. this is called mysterious virtue. spring does all its work and asks nothing in return.

daruma. 達磨 hakuin ekaku edo period, 18th century a huge, glaring face of bodhidharma drawn in thick ink strokes, with one sweeping black stroke for the robe and a large inscription above, mounted as a hanging scroll. hakuin's bodhidharma stares out with wide eyes but does not move. the best warrior is not warlike. this huge face is made of a few thick, wet strokes; the robe is one bold sweep. the inscription above says, roughly, "point straight at the human heart; see your nature and become buddha." bodhidharma's stare is fierce, yet he sits completely still. chapter 68 says the best warrior is not warlike, the best fighter is not angry, the best winner does not engage. this is the virtue of not contending. compare the gamecock in zhuangzi that became like wood. see the story "the gamecock like wood".

battle at the bridge. 橋上交戰 anonymous tomb artisans eastern han dynasty, 2nd century a long black rubbing crowded with chariots, horses and soldiers fighting on and around an arched bridge. a han stone shows chariots fighting on a bridge. where armies camp, thorns and brambles grow. this rubbing comes from a family shrine of the second century. look along the long band: horses rearing, chariots crowded on the arch of the bridge, soldiers in the water below. it is energetic and full of noise. chapter 30 advises those who help rulers with the way not to use force. where armies have stayed, thorns grow; after a great war, bad years follow. gain your goal, and stop. do not boast. look at how the fighters are packed so tightly they can hardly move. look again at the han battle on the bridge. military strategists say: i would rather be the guest than the host. this time, notice the moments of retreat in the crowd: horses turning, figures falling back toward the river. chapter 69 quotes the strategists: i do not dare to be the host; i am the guest. i do not dare to advance an inch; i go back a foot. this is called marching ranks that are not there, baring an arm that is not there. no disaster is greater than to take the enemy lightly. when raised armies meet, the one who grieves wins. look for the stillness hidden inside the struggle.

bronze model chariot. 銅車馬 unknown han bronze caster eastern han dynasty, 1st to 3rd century a small bronze two-wheeled chariot with spoked wheels and a seated driver, behind a bronze horse. a han model chariot: thirty spokes share one hub, and the wheel turns because the hub is empty. look at the wheels. the spokes run inward to the hub, and the axle passes through the hole at its centre. without that hole there would be no wheel, only a heavy disc. chapter 11 uses three images: the empty hub of a cart, the hollow of a clay pot, the open space of a door and window. what is there gives benefit; what is not there gives use. this little bronze cart was buried with its owner. even in the tomb, it shows how emptiness makes things move. the sage travels all day without leaving the baggage cart. heaviness is the root of lightness. look again at this little bronze cart. it is a light escort chariot, not the heavy baggage wagon of the chapter, but it shows the same thing: its wheels can turn because the box sits firmly on the axle. chapter 26 says heaviness is the root of lightness, and stillness is the ruler of agitation. the sage travels all day and never leaves his heavy carts behind; even with splendid views, he stays calm and apart. notice the weight in the bronze, the low centre of gravity, the steady horse. a light, restless ruler loses his root. a grounded one can move far.

night-shining white. 照夜白圖 attributed to han gan tang dynasty, c. 750 a white horse tied to a black post rears and pulls against its tether, eyes wide; seals and inscriptions crowd around it. the emperor's horse strains against its post, eyes rolling. one who stands on tiptoe is not steady. night-shining white was the favourite horse of the tang emperor xuanzong. the painting, attributed to han gan, shows it tied to a black post, rearing, nostrils wide. all that strength goes nowhere. chapter 24 says one who stands on tiptoe does not stand firm; one who takes long strides does not go far; one who shows off is not seen clearly. look at the stamps and inscriptions crowding around the horse: centuries of owners added their seals. the horse is famous and still tied. compare its tense body to the calm line of the post.

mirror with deities, chariot, and the white tiger. 神人車馬畫像鏡 unknown han bronze caster eastern han dynasty, 2nd century the decorated back of a round bronze mirror: a central knob, seated deities, a chariot and a tiger in relief. a han bronze mirror: its polished face is gone, but its back shows the cosmos. can you clean the dark mirror so that no stain remains? this is the back of the mirror. the other side was once polished bronze. start at the central knob, then circle outward past the seated deities, the chariot and the tiger, to the plain rim. everything turns around a still centre. chapter 10 asks a series of questions: can you embrace the one without letting go, soften your breath like an infant, polish the dark mirror until it has no flaw? the mirror was an image for the mind in early china. it reflects everything and keeps nothing.

pictorial stone: queen mother of the west, chariot, hunt. 畫像石 anonymous han artisans eastern han dynasty, 1st to 2nd century a carved stone slab in three bands: seated figures at top, a chariot and attendants in the middle, hunters with nets and animals below. a carved han stone in three balanced bands: deities, a chariot, a hunt. the way of heaven is like stretching a bow: lower the high, raise the low. read the slab from top to bottom. the upper band shows seated figures of the spirit world; the middle a chariot and attendants; the lowest a hunt, with nets, a leashed animal and running game. high and low, spirits and hunters, are held in one balanced frame. chapter 77 says the way of heaven is like drawing a bow: the high end is pulled down, the low end raised; what has too much is reduced, what has too little is filled. the way of people is different: they take from those who lack to give to those who have more. look for balance in the bands.

shide (from the pair hanshan and shide). 拾得 indara (yintuoluo) yuan dynasty, 14th century a ragged, laughing monk with a broom, drawn in a few loose ink strokes on pale paper. shide, the ragged temple sweeper, looks like a fool. chapter 41 says the bright way seems dark and the purest white seems soiled. indara drew shide with a few loose, almost careless strokes. the broom, the tattered robe and the open mouth are all you need. hanshan and shide were tang dynasty eccentrics who lived at a temple, wrote poems on rocks and laughed at monks and officials alike. chapter 41 says the bright way seems dark, high virtue seems like a valley, the purest white seems soiled, and the great image has no shape. people who see only rags and a broom laugh. look at the joy in this ragged figure. shide in rags, with his broom, looks like nobody. the sage wears coarse cloth and carries jade inside it. look again at this ragged figure. nothing about him announces wisdom: a torn robe, a broom, a grin. shide and his friend hanshan lived at a tang temple, swept floors, wrote poems on rocks, and were taken for madmen. chapter 70 is laozi speaking about himself: my words are very easy to know and very easy to practise, yet no one in the world can know them or practise them. those who know me are few, and that makes me precious. so the sage wears coarse cloth and carries jade inside it. see the story "bian he's uncut jade".

the sound of spring in a lonely valley. 幽谷春聲 hongren qing dynasty, 1661 a tall, pale landscape of angular rock faces, thin bare trees and a small stream winding down through a quiet valley. hongren's valley is pale and still, with a thin stream running down its centre. the valley spirit does not die. start at the top among the angular rocks and follow the stream downward. the forms are drawn in thin, dry lines with almost no shading, so the whole valley feels open and clean. chapter 6 speaks of the valley spirit and the mysterious female, the root of heaven and earth, which goes on and on and is never used up. a valley is a low, receiving place. everything flows into it. notice that the painting has no strong focus; your eye keeps sinking toward the low, quiet centre, as water does.

dwelling in the fuchun mountains (detail). 富春山居圖 huang gongwang yuan dynasty, 1348 to 1350 a long, pale scroll of riverbanks, pines and low hills, drawn in dry, light brushstrokes. huang gongwang's long scroll of quiet hills shows people living by the river. i do nothing, and the people transform themselves. the brushwork is dry and light; nothing shouts. follow the riverbank, the pines, the small houses. huang gongwang worked on this scroll for several years, adding a little at a time when the mood came. chapter 57 says the more prohibitions there are, the poorer the people; the more sharp weapons, the more trouble; the more laws, the more thieves. so the sage says: i do nothing, and the people change by themselves. i love stillness, and they become upright. look at how the painting seems to unroll on its own.

auspicious cranes. 瑞鶴圖 attributed to emperor huizong (court painting) northern song dynasty, 1112 white cranes circle in a deep blue sky above the roof of a palace gate. cranes circle the palace gate in a painting from emperor huizong's court, a sign of good fortune. fifteen years later his dynasty fell. the blue is intense, the cranes elegant, the roof precise. it bears the name of an emperor who loved art and luxury and kept painters at his court. in 1127 his capital fell to invaders and he died a captive. chapter 53 says the great way is very level, but people love side paths. the court is very fine, the fields full of weeds, the granaries empty; people wear rich clothes and carry sharp swords, eat and drink too much, have more wealth than they need. this is called robbery. look at the beauty, and remember the fields.

listening to the qin (detail). 聽琴圖 attributed to emperor huizong northern song dynasty, early 12th century under a pine, a man in a dark robe plays a qin on a low table; an official in green looks up, another in red bows his head. under a pine, a man plays the qin while two officials listen. music and good food make travellers stop; the way has no flavour. the player sits with his head bowed toward the strings. the listener in green lifts his head and looks up and away; the one in red bows his head. a small incense burner stands on a stand. chapter 35 says music and fine food make passing travellers stop, but the way, when spoken, is bland and has no flavour. look at it and it is not enough to see; listen and it is not enough to hear; use it and it never runs out. the qin's music was quiet and plain. notice the stillness of the three men.

bi disc. 玉璧 liangzhu culture carver neolithic, c. 2500 bce a flat round jade disc with a hole in the centre, mottled brown and green. a jade bi disc, a treasure offered to heaven. better than jade and fine horses is to sit still and offer the way. look at the round disc with its round hole. bi discs were laid in tombs and offered in rituals to heaven. they were among the most precious things a ruler could give. chapter 62 says the way is the hidden treasure of all things. when a new emperor is crowned, rather than offering a jade disc followed by a team of four horses, it is better to sit still and offer this way. why did the ancients value it? because with it, those who seek will find, and those who err are forgiven.

cong. 玉琮 liangzhu culture carver neolithic, c. 2500 bce a tall, dark green jade tube, square outside and round inside, divided into stacked sections. the cong is round inside and square outside, a joining of heaven and earth. everything that attains the one is whole. look at the tall, dark green tube. the outer corners are square; the hole through its centre is round. in early china, round stood for heaven and square for earth. chapter 39 says that in ancient times, heaven attained the one and became clear, earth attained the one and became steady, valleys attained the one and became full. the ruler takes the lowly as his root. do not wish to jingle like jade; be rough like stone. notice that this jade is not glittering. it is plain, heavy and quiet.

seeking the dao in the autumn mountains. 秋山問道圖 attributed to juran five dynasties to northern song, 10th century rounded hills covered with soft hemp-fibre strokes; a small thatched hut sits in a fold near the middle. juran's title says it all: seeking the dao in the autumn mountains. find the small hut in the fold of the hills. the hills are built from long, soft strokes like hemp fibres, rounded and calm. near the middle there is a small hut where two figures sit and talk. that is the seeking. everything around them is mountain, mist and pine. chapter 21 says we can know the beginning of all things only through this hidden essence, which is very real and can be trusted. juran does not paint the answer. he paints the long walk up and the quiet conversation. let your eye climb slowly, as if you were going to join them.

a deep valley conceals a monk's home. 深谷隱僧家圖 kuncan qing dynasty, 17th century a tall, crowded mountain landscape; a small dwelling sits hidden deep among folds of rock and trees. kuncan hides a monk's house deep in the folds of the mountain. find it, and notice how much the valley protects it. this painting is crowded where hongren's is bare. rock, trees and mist press in from all sides. take your time to find the small dwelling tucked into the hollow. once you see it, the whole mountain seems to curve around it like a cupped hand. the valley in chapter 6 is not empty for its own sake. it gives shelter and gives birth. kuncan was a buddhist monk who lived in mountain temples; he knew what it is to be held by a landscape. let your eye rest in the hollow. a dwelling hidden deep in the mountains, far from clever government. the ancients did not make people sharp but kept them simple. look again for the little house in the folds of rock. it is protected, unseen, not displayed. chapter 65 says those who practised the way in ancient times did not use it to make the people clever, but to keep them simple. people are hard to govern when they have too much cunning. governing by cleverness harms the state; governing without it blesses the state. this is deep and far-reaching virtue; it turns things around and leads back to great harmony. notice how far the house is from any road.

laozi riding an ox (paintings after ancient masters). 老子騎牛 chen hongshou ming dynasty, before 1652 an old man in white robes rides a dark ox past bamboo, holding a scroll; rocks and a stream lie below. laozi rides slowly past bamboo on his ox. i have three things to treasure: tenderness, spareness, and not daring to go ahead of the world. chen hongshou gives laozi a gentle, slightly strange face and a calm ox. he sits loosely, in no hurry, as if the road will wait. bamboo bends behind him. chapter 67 is one of the few places where the speaker says "i" so plainly: i have three things to treasure; i hold them and keep them safe. the first is tenderness, the second is spareness, the third is not daring to go ahead of the world. tenderness makes courage possible. look at the old man's relaxed hands. nothing about him pushes forward.

laozi riding an ox. 老子騎牛圖 zhang lu ming dynasty, early 16th century an old man with a high bald head sits on an ox, holding a scroll and looking up; the ox steps forward with lowered horns. zhang lu's laozi rides away on his ox, looking up from his book. true words are not beautiful; beautiful words are not true. the old man's head is high and bald; his eyes are lifted, perhaps to the sky, perhaps to the road ahead. the ox steps forward with lowered horns. zhang lu paints with quick, rough strokes, nothing polished. chapter 81 is the last chapter: true words are not beautiful; good people do not argue; those who know are not learned. the sage does not hoard. the more he does for others, the more he has; the more he gives, the more he gains. laozi leaves, and the book stays. see the story "the keeper of the pass".

a solitary temple amid clearing peaks. 晴巒蕭寺圖 attributed to li cheng northern song dynasty, 10th to 11th century a pagoda and temple buildings stand in the middle ground below a great central peak; travellers and inns appear at the foot. the great peak behind the temple has stood for ages. it lasts because it does not live for itself. the composition is built on a strong central axis: the mountain at the top, the pagoda below it, the inns and travellers at the bottom. everything is arranged in layers that rise slowly. yet the peak does nothing. it gives shade, holds water, shelters the temple, and asks for nothing. chapter 7 says heaven and earth endure because they do not live for themselves; the sage puts himself last and so finds himself first. notice how the temple stands lower than the peak and the travellers lower still, and how calm this order feels.

returning herdsman in snow. 雪中歸牧圖 li di southern song dynasty, 12th century a herdsman hunched against the cold rides a water buffalo under a bare, snowy tree, holding out a stick with two pheasants hanging from it. a herdsman rides home on his buffalo through snow. show plainness, embrace the uncarved block, have few desires. the herdsman is bundled against the cold and hunched forward. he holds a stick out in front of him, with two pheasants hanging from its tip. the buffalo lowers its head and plods. a bare, snow-laden tree leans over them. nothing here is clever. chapter 19 says to cast off sageliness and cleverness, and the people will benefit a hundred times; show the plain silk, hold the uncarved block, reduce the self, lessen desire. li di's buffalo and rider move as one, at their own pace. look at the soft grey of the snowy sky and the patient walk home.

five horses (first section). 五馬圖 li gonglin northern song dynasty, c. 1090 a dappled horse drawn in fine, plain ink lines stands quietly beside its groom. li gonglin's horse stands calmly with its groom. when the world has the way, horses fertilise the fields. li gonglin drew this horse with fine, plain ink lines and almost no colour. the animal is quiet and powerful. the groom holds the reins loosely. chapter 46 says when the world has the way, fast horses are sent back to haul dung in the fields. when the world lacks the way, war horses are bred on the frontier. no disaster is greater than not knowing what is enough. look at the horse's calm eye and soft stance. it is not running anywhere. this is a horse at peace.

wind in pines among a myriad valleys. 萬壑松風圖 li tang northern song dynasty, 1124 dense pines and dark rock fill the scroll; a stream runs through the valley below sharp peaks. li tang fills the scroll with pines and valleys. know the male, keep to the female; be a valley for the world. the painting is dense and dark: strong peaks above, deep pines below, a stream running through the gorge. let your eye drop down from the heights to the low places, where water collects and the wind moves in the pines. chapter 28 says: know the white, keep to the black; know honour, keep to humility; be a valley for the world, and constant virtue will be enough. you will return to the uncarved block. notice how the valley floor, not the peak, holds the life of this picture.

immortal in splashed ink. 潑墨仙人 liang kai southern song dynasty, 13th century an album spread: on the right a big-bellied immortal made of broad, wet ink strokes; on the left an inscription. liang kai's immortal stumbles forward, belly out, eyes squinting. everyone else is bright; i alone am dull. look at how the body is made: a few broad, wet sweeps of ink, with only tiny fine strokes for the face. the figure seems about to fall over or burst out laughing. chapter 20 is the most personal chapter of the daodejing. others are busy and festive, says the speaker; i alone am drifting, like a baby that has not yet smiled. others have more than enough; i alone seem to have lost something. yet i value being fed by the mother. notice how happy this foolish figure looks.

li bai strolling and chanting. 李白行吟圖 liang kai southern song dynasty, 13th century a poet in a long robe, drawn in a few quick lines, walks with his head tilted back on blank paper. the poet li bai, who had both favour and disgrace at court, walks off alone. liang kai needs only a few lines. count the strokes. the robe is one long sweep; the head a few quick touches. li bai looks up as he walks, chanting a poem to himself. he served at the tang court, was praised, then sent away. chapter 13 says that favour and disgrace are both alarming, because both depend on others. the person who values his own body as much as the whole world can be trusted with the world. liang kai himself is said to have walked away from the song painting academy. his li bai belongs to nobody. notice how much blank paper surrounds him.

fish swimming amid falling flowers (detail). 落花遊魚圖 attributed to liu cai northern song dynasty, late 11th to early 12th century goldfish and carp swim among water plants under drifting blossoms. goldfish turn and drift among the plants. govern a great state as you cook a small fish: gently, and not too much stirring. look at how each fish moves in its own direction, some up, some down, all at ease. nothing disturbs the water. chapter 60 begins with a famous image: govern a great state as you would cook a small fish. stir it too much and it falls apart. when the world is governed by the way, even the spirits lose their power to harm. let your eye drift with the fish. the painter has not crowded them or ordered them in lines. each finds its own place.

listening to the wind in the pines. 靜聽松風圖 ma lin southern song dynasty, 1246 a scholar sits at the foot of a tall, twisting pine, one arm resting on a root, looking calmly outward; a servant stands nearby. a scholar sits under a pine and listens to the wind. without going out the door, one can know the world. the man sits at the foot of the pine, one arm resting on a root, looking calmly out to the right. above him, the trunk twists high into the scroll. a stream runs nearby. he is not travelling or studying. he is listening. chapter 47 says: without going out the door, know the world; without looking out the window, see the way of heaven. the further you go, the less you know. imagine the sound the scholar hears. let the painting go quiet in your mind until only the wind in the pines is left.

waves of the autumn flood (water album). 秋水迴波 ma yuan southern song dynasty, early 13th century even rows of small curling waves cover the leaf like woven cloth, with a title in the upper corner. ma yuan's autumn water spreads in endless small waves. nothing in the world is softer than water, yet nothing is better at wearing down the hard. look at the patient rhythm of the waves, row after row, like woven cloth. no single wave is strong. yet the whole surface moves with great power. chapter 78 says nothing under heaven is softer or weaker than water, yet for attacking the hard and strong nothing can surpass it, because nothing can take its place. everyone knows that the weak overcome the strong and the soft overcome the hard, yet no one can practise it. straight words seem crooked. let your eye ride the waves to the far edge.

clouds rising from the green sea (water album). 雲生蒼海 ma yuan southern song dynasty, early 13th century long, slow swells of sea across the bottom of the leaf, with mist rising into blank golden silk above. long swells of the sea under rising mist. rivers and seas rule a hundred valleys because they lie lower. the waves here are broad and slow, rolling across the bottom of the leaf. above them, cloud rises into empty golden silk. all the water in the world ends here. chapter 66 says rivers and seas can be kings of the hundred valleys because they are good at staying low. so the sage, wishing to be above the people, speaks humbly; wishing to lead them, walks behind. he is on top, and the people do not feel his weight. let your eye sink to the bottom of the painting and rest.

walking on a mountain path in spring. 山徑春行 ma yuan southern song dynasty, c. 1190 to 1225 a scholar walks along a path at the lower left under willow branches; a servant follows with a qin; one bird perches, another flies; the right side is open space with a short poem. ma yuan's scholar strolls along a spring path. a good walker leaves no tracks. the walker is at the lower left, sleeves loose, brushing past willow branches. a servant follows with a qin. one bird perches on a willow twig; another takes flight. the rest of the leaf is open space with a short poem. nothing is forced. chapter 27 says a good traveller leaves no tracks, a good speaker makes no slips, a good counter needs no tally. the sage is always good at saving people, so no one is thrown away. look at how lightly the figure moves into the empty right side of the painting, as if he will leave no mark there.

boundless expanse of the yangzi (water album). 長江萬頃 ma yuan southern song dynasty, early 13th century an album leaf filled edge to edge with a fine net of curling ink waves on golden silk. ma yuan's waves fill the whole leaf with a soft, even net. water benefits all things and does not compete. look closely at a single wave: one curling line that rises, folds over, and passes its motion to the next. no wave is larger or more important than its neighbours. then step back and see the whole yangzi spread out flat and wide. chapter 8 says the highest good is like water. it nourishes everything, does not contend, and settles in low places that people dislike. ma yuan has painted nothing but water, yet the page feels alive. let your breathing follow the rhythm of the lines.

scholar viewing a waterfall. 觀瀑圖 ma yuan southern song dynasty, c. 1190 to 1225 a square album leaf: a scholar sits on a rock under a leaning pine and gazes at a waterfall pouring from the cliff. a scholar watches a waterfall pour through the rocks. the softest thing in the world rides over the hardest. find the white line of water falling from the cliff, then the scholar on the rock, quiet and attentive. the pine leans across the leaf. chapter 43 says the softest thing in the world overcomes the hardest; what has no substance enters where there is no gap. from this i know the value of non-action. few in the world reach the teaching without words. the scholar does not speak. he watches water do what it has always done: wear away stone by never stopping.

the yellow river breaches its course (water album). 黃河逆流 ma yuan southern song dynasty, early 13th century heavy, churning waves curl and break into foam across the whole album leaf. ma yuan's yellow river throws up foam and spray. a whirlwind does not last all morning. watch the big waves rise and crash, then notice the smaller ones already settling at the edges. ma yuan's brush moves fast here, with heavy, curling lines. chapter 23 says that to speak little is natural. a whirlwind does not last all morning; a downpour does not last all day. if even heaven and earth cannot keep up such force for long, how much less can people? let the noise of the painting rise in you, and then let it fall. look at the calmer water at the edges.
