jar with spiral designs. 彩陶罐 majiayao culture potter neolithic, c. 3300 bce a round-bellied clay jar with a narrow neck, painted with bold black spirals that swirl around its body. a potter shaped this jar more than five thousand years ago. the clay makes the walls; the empty inside makes it useful. follow the black spirals around the belly of the jar. they swirl and turn, almost like water. the painted surface is lovely, but think about the inside, which you cannot see. that hidden space is why the jar was made. it held grain, or water, or seeds for the next year. chapter 11 says we shape clay into a vessel, and it is the empty space inside that makes it work. the spirals turn around a hollow centre, just as the chapter turns around its central idea.

calligraphy in cursive script. 草書 mi fu northern song dynasty, late 11th century lines of quick, flowing cursive characters in black ink on tan paper, with red seals. mi fu's cursive looks careless and spills across the page. the greatest skill seems clumsy. look at one character and you may not recognise it. the strokes run together, thicken, thin out, and rush on. mi fu was a master of every script, yet in his cursive writing he lets the brush seem almost out of control. chapter 45 says great completion seems incomplete, yet its use is never exhausted. great fullness seems empty. great straightness seems bent; great skill seems clumsy; great eloquence seems to stammer. follow one line from top to bottom without trying to read it. feel the speed and the pauses.

cloudy mountains. 雲山圖 attributed to mi youren southern song dynasty, 12th century a horizontal scroll of soft, rounded hills and clumps of trees half dissolved in mist, painted in wet dots of ink. these hills, attributed to mi youren, are only half there; mist takes away their edges. look for the place where ink stops and nothing begins. the painter built these mountains from soft, wet dots laid side by side, so that no line ever closes a shape. find one hilltop and try to say where it ends. you cannot. the trees dissolve in the same way. the painting lives in the passage between named things and the unnamed mist that holds them. chapter 1 calls this the gate of all mysteries: the nameless and the named come out together and differ only in name. let your eye rest in the grey spaces. they are not gaps in the picture. they are the picture's source.

dragon (from dragon and tiger). 龍 attributed to muqi fachang southern song dynasty, 13th century a dark hanging scroll in which a dragon's head and claws half appear through swirling cloud and mist. this dragon, attributed to muqi, comes and goes in the clouds. the way is elusive and vague, and yet within it there is an image. give your eyes time. at first the scroll looks like dark fog. then a head appears, a claw, a curl of body, and they fade again into the mist. the painter used soft, wet ink that leaves no hard edges. chapter 21 says the way is shadowy and indistinct, yet within it there is form; dark and obscure, yet within it there is essence. the dragon was an old chinese image for what cannot be pinned down. confucius used it for laozi himself. watch for the moment when the dragon disappears.

tiger (from dragon and tiger). 虎 attributed to muqi fachang southern song dynasty, 13th century a tiger crouches low in long grass, its body drawn in soft, wet ink; its striped tail curls along the bottom. this tiger, attributed to muqi, crouches in the grass. one who cares well for life meets no tiger on the road. look first at the eyes, then at the soft, wet ink of the body. the tiger is powerful but not attacking. chapter 50 says among those who go out into life and into death, some are companions of life, some companions of death. those who care well for life walk without meeting rhinoceros or tiger. their bodies offer no place for the claw or the horn. why? because they have no place of death. look at the tiger. it is not looking for you.

the rongxi studio. 容膝齋圖 ni zan yuan dynasty, 1372 a few thin trees and an empty pavilion on a near bank, wide blank water, and low hills on the far shore; long inscriptions above. ni zan paints an empty pavilion between two shores. attain the summit of emptiness; hold fast to stillness. the picture has three parts: a near bank with thin trees and an empty hut, a wide band of blank water, and low hills far away. no person is present. ni zan used dry, light ink and almost no colour. chapter 16 asks us to reach complete emptiness and keep deep stillness, and to watch the ten thousand things rise and return to their root. let your eye rest in the empty water. it is the centre of the painting. the hut waits there, like a mind with nothing in it, ready to receive.

ox and herdsman both forgotten (ten oxherding pictures, no. 8). 人牛俱忘 attributed to tensho shubun muromachi period, 15th century an empty circle drawn on old, stained paper. nothing is inside it. the eighth of the ten oxherding pictures is an empty circle. in pursuing the way, one loses a little every day. in the earlier pictures of this series, a herdsman searches for an ox, catches it, tames it, rides it home. then, in the eighth, both the ox and the man are gone. only the circle remains. chapter 48 says those who study gain more every day; those who follow the way lose more every day. lose and lose again, until you reach non-action. do nothing, and nothing is left undone. look into the circle. there is nothing to find there, and nothing missing.

the peach blossom spring. 桃花源圖 traditionally attributed to qiu ying ming dynasty, 16th century a long blue-green handscroll section: a stream, trees and a small boat near a hidden valley. a fisherman finds a hidden valley where people have lived in peace for centuries. small country, few people. follow the stream into the scroll as the fisherman did. blue-green hills and blossoming trees close around the water. chapter 80 imagines a small state with few people. they have tools but do not use them, boats and carts but do not ride them, weapons but do not display them. they find their food sweet, their clothes beautiful, their homes peaceful, their customs pleasant. neighbouring villages are so close that they can hear each other's roosters and dogs, yet people grow old and die without visiting. see the story "the peach blossom spring".

circle, triangle, square. ○△□ sengai gibon edo period, c. 1819 to 1828 three bold ink shapes, a square, a triangle and a circle, overlapping in a row beside a column of cursive writing. sengai's square, triangle and circle lean on each other. each shape is clear only because the others are next to it. read the shapes from left to right, then from right to left. the square is firm and closed; the triangle points; the circle opens. they overlap, so that one stroke belongs to two shapes at once. sengai never explained the picture, and that is part of its humour. chapter 2 says that the sage teaches without words and lets things arise without claiming them. the brush here does the same. look at the dry, broken edges of the ink: the shapes are not perfect, and they do not try to be.

splashed-ink landscape. 破墨山水圖 sesshu toyo muromachi period, 1495 wet blots and washes of ink suggest a rock, a tree, a tavern flag and faint peaks; very little is drawn with lines. sesshu's splashed ink barely forms a picture. look at it and you do not quite see it. at first there are only blots and washes of grey. slowly a rock appears, then a tree, then the roof of a small house with a flag, then mountains so pale they seem breathed onto the paper. nothing is outlined. chapter 14 describes the way as what you look at and do not see, listen to and do not hear, grasp and do not catch. it is shape without shape, image without thing. let your eyes go soft. the painting comes and goes, as the chapter says the way does.

huike offering his arm to bodhidharma. 慧可斷臂圖 sesshu toyo muromachi period, 1496 bodhidharma sits facing a cave wall, drawn in a pale outline; behind him the monk huike holds out his severed arm. huike cuts off his arm to show bodhidharma he is sincere. to know not-knowing: the highest. bodhidharma sits facing the cave wall, drawn in a pale, firm outline. he does not turn. behind him, huike holds out his arm, his face tense. sesshu painted this at seventy-six. the story says huike asked to have his mind put at rest, and bodhidharma said, "bring me your mind." huike said, "i have searched, and i cannot find it." chapter 71 says: to know not-knowing is the highest; not to know knowing is a sickness. look at the great blank face of the wall.

autumn and winter landscapes. 秋冬山水圖 sesshu toyo muromachi period, 1470s two hanging scrolls side by side: on the left a winter scene with a sharp vertical line of cliff and a small temple; on the right an autumn shore. in sesshu's winter landscape a sharp line of cliff cuts down through cold air. the ancient masters were careful, as if crossing a winter stream. look at the left scroll first. a single dark stroke runs down the middle like a crack in ice. beside it, a tiny temple and a figure with a hat move through the snow. everything is still and alert. chapter 15 says the ancient masters were hesitant, as if crossing a stream in winter; watchful, as if they feared their neighbours; simple, like uncarved wood; open, like a valley; murky, like muddy water. then turn to the autumn scroll on the right, softer and wider. both seasons ask for the same attention.

landscape with man crossing a bridge. attributed to shen zhou ming or qing dynasty an album leaf: a man with his hands in his sleeves crosses a small bridge toward a cottage among pines; a boy carrying a qin follows. a man crosses a little bridge toward his cottage, a boy with a qin behind him. do not crowd people's dwellings; do not weary their lives. the cottage sits among pines; the hills are soft and rounded. the walker moves slowly, hands in his sleeves, and a boy follows with a qin. the leaf is attributed to shen zhou, who spent most of his life in the countryside near suzhou and refused official posts. chapter 72 says when people do not fear authority, something terrible will come. do not narrow where they live; do not oppress their livelihood. if you do not oppress them, they will not tire of you. the sage knows himself but does not display himself. look at the small, safe world this man is walking into.

returning home (album leaf). 歸棹 shitao qing dynasty, c. 1695 a man sits in a small boat on blank water; reeds at the bottom, soft hills at the top, red seals in the corner. shitao's traveller sits in a small boat on blank water, going home. know the child; return to the mother. the painting is mostly empty. the man in the boat sits quietly; reeds lean at the bottom, a few soft hills appear far above. chapter 52 says the world has a beginning, which is its mother. knowing the mother, you know the child; knowing the child, return to the mother, and to the end of your life you will be safe. block the openings, close the doors, and you will not be worn out. see the small and call it clear. the boat is moving home. let it.

dunhuang star chart (north polar region). 敦煌星圖 unknown astronomer tang dynasty, c. 700 hand-drawn constellations as dots joined by lines, around the north pole, with notes in chinese. a tang dynasty star chart from dunhuang maps the sky around the pole. heaven's net is vast; its mesh is wide, yet nothing slips through. look at the dots and lines: each group is a constellation, carefully named. this chart, made around 700 ce, is one of the oldest star maps in the world. the stars seem scattered and far apart, yet they turn together around the still pole, night after night. chapter 73 says the way of heaven does not contend yet wins well, does not speak yet answers well, is not summoned yet comes, is calm yet plans well. heaven's net is wide and loose, yet nothing is lost. look at the spaces between the stars.

children at play in an autumn garden. 秋庭戲嬰圖 attributed to su hanchen song dynasty, 12th century under a tall garden rock and autumn flowers, two children bend over a round stool, absorbed in a game. two children bend over their game in an autumn garden, in a painting attributed to su hanchen. one who holds virtue fully is like a newborn child. look past the tall garden rock and the flowers to the children at the round stools. their heads are close together. they do not notice anything else. chapter 55 says one rich in virtue is like a newborn. wasps and snakes do not bite it; wild beasts do not attack it. its bones are soft, its muscles weak, yet its grip is firm. it cries all day and does not grow hoarse: its harmony is perfect. notice how relaxed the children's bodies are, and how completely they attend.

children at play (album leaf). 嬰戲圖 attributed to su hanchen song dynasty, 12th century two small children by a flowering plant: one stands reaching toward a butterfly, the other sits with a round fan and looks up. two small children play beside a flowering plant, one reaching toward a butterfly. can you soften your breath and become like a child? watch the children. the one on the left stands and stretches a hand toward a butterfly above the plant; the one on the right sits on the ground with a round fan and looks up at his playmate. they are absorbed and do not know they are being looked at. this leaf, attributed to su hanchen, catches their round bodies and quick attention exactly. chapter 10 asks whether you can concentrate your breath until it is as soft as an infant's. the children here do not try to be soft. they simply are. their whole being goes into one small, fluttering thing.

river chart of heaven and earth. 天地自然河圖 zhao huiqian ming dynasty, c. 1370 a black-and-white circle split into two swirling halves, each with a small dot, ringed by the names of the eight trigrams. one of the earliest printed yin-yang swirls, from about 1370. returning is the movement of the way. look at the black and white halves turning around each other. each carries a small dot of the other. around the circle are the names of the eight trigrams. zhao huiqian called this the river chart of heaven and earth. chapter 40 is very short: returning is the movement of the way; weakness is the use of the way. the ten thousand things are born from being, and being is born from non-being. follow the curve with your eye. it never stops; it always comes back.

pine trees (left screen). 松林圖屏風 hasegawa tohaku azuchi-momoyama period, late 16th century a six-panel folding screen of pine trees in mist, painted in pale and dark ink, with much of the paper left empty. tohaku's pines appear and disappear in fog. the way does nothing, yet nothing is left undone. this is one screen of a pair. stand back. the pines seem to come forward and sink back as mist moves through them. some are painted with dark, fast strokes; others are only a breath of grey. much of the screen is empty paper. chapter 37 says the way never acts, yet nothing is left undone. if rulers could hold to it, all things would transform themselves. without desire there is stillness, and the world settles of itself. let your eye stay in the fog between the trees.

ge zhichuan moving his dwelling. 葛稚川移居圖 wang meng yuan dynasty, c. 1360s a tall mountain scroll in red, green and blue; tiny figures with an ox cross a bridge toward a house in the hills. the daoist ge hong moves his family into the mountains, leaving office behind. when the work is done, step back. find the tiny figures crossing the bridge at the lower left: ge hong with his household and an ox. then follow the path upward into the folds of green and blue mountain, where the house waits. wang meng crowds the scroll with texture and colour, but the story at its heart is a quiet withdrawal. chapter 9 warns that filling a hall with gold and jade means you cannot guard it, and that pride in wealth invites disaster. withdraw when the work is done: that is the way of heaven. the travellers do not look back.

a thousand li of rivers and mountains (detail). 千里江山圖 wang ximeng northern song dynasty, 1113 a detail of brilliant blue and green mountain peaks along a river, with an inscription at the top. wang ximeng's blue and green peaks are dazzling. laozi warns that the five colours can blind the eye. this is a small part of a huge scroll painted by a young court artist in 1113. the mineral blues and greens are brilliant even after nine hundred years. let yourself enjoy them. then notice the pull they have on you, the wish to see more and more. chapter 12 says the five colours blind the eye, the five tones deafen the ear, and the chase drives the heart wild. the sage cares for the belly, not the eye. close your eyes for a moment after looking. what stays with you?

solitary walker in autumn. 秋林獨步 wen zhengming ming dynasty, 1554 a tall ink scroll of bare autumn trees; birds rise above them, and a single figure walks along a path below. a lone figure walks under bare autumn trees. a journey of a thousand li begins beneath your feet. find the small walker at the bottom of the scroll. above him, tall bare trees rise and birds lift into the air. wen zhengming painted this in 1554, when he was in his eighties. chapter 64 traces three big things back to something tiny: the tree too wide to hug to a shoot, the nine-tiered terrace to baskets of earth, the long road to the ground under one foot. look at the walker's next step. the whole journey is there.

the seven junipers. 七檜圖 wen zhengming ming dynasty, 1532 a horizontal ink painting of old, twisted juniper trunks and branches knotted together across the paper. wen zhengming's ancient junipers are twisted and knotted. bent, they stay whole. these trees stood in a garden in suzhou and were already old when wen zhengming drew them. trace one trunk and you lose it among the others. every branch bends, forks, turns back. yet the trees are full of life. chapter 22 begins: bent, then whole; crooked, then straight; hollow, then full; worn, then new. a straight tree is cut for timber. a crooked one is left to grow. let your eye follow the knots without trying to straighten them. ancient junipers, shaped by centuries of weather rather than by any carpenter. whoever cuts in place of the master carpenter rarely escapes hurting his hand. follow one knotted trunk through the tangle. no human tool made these shapes; wind, frost, drought and time did. chapter 74 says: the people do not fear death. how, then, frighten them with death? there is always the master executioner, heaven itself, who decides when things end. to kill in its place is like hewing wood in place of the master carpenter: few who try it escape cutting their own hands. look at how these trees were left to the great carpenter, and how strange and alive its work is.

old trees by a cold waterfall. 古木寒泉圖 wen zhengming ming dynasty, 1531 twisted old trees and pale rocks at the lower left; a thin waterfall falls between distant cliffs; two small figures stand at the bottom. old trees twist beside a cold waterfall. living things are soft and supple; dead things are hard and dry. look at the trees: some branches still bend and leaf; others are stiff and broken. far off, between the cliffs, a thin waterfall slides down without end. two small figures stand at the bottom, listening. chapter 76 says people are soft and weak when born, hard and stiff when dead. plants are tender and supple when alive, dry and brittle when dead. so the hard and strong are companions of death; the soft and weak are companions of life. a rigid army is defeated; a rigid tree is cut. compare the water to the dead wood.

fisherman. 漁父圖 wu zhen yuan dynasty, 1342 a tall scroll: trees on a near bank, a small fishing boat on calm water, distant hills and a poem at the top. a fisherman floats on calm water, far from court. which is dearer, fame or your life? the boat is very small. above it, a poem by the painter praises the fisherman's life. wu zhen was a yuan dynasty recluse who painted fishermen again and again; for him, the fisherman meant a person who has chosen freedom over office. chapter 44 asks: fame or the self, which is dearer? the self or possessions, which is more? gain or loss, which harms more? one who knows what is enough is not disgraced; one who knows when to stop is not in danger. look at the stillness of the water.

twin pines. 雙松圖 wu zhen yuan dynasty, 1328 two tall pines with twisting trunks stand together in the foreground; a stream and hills lie behind them. two old pines stand together, deeply rooted. what is well planted cannot be uprooted. follow each trunk down to the ground. the roots grip the earth; the branches twist but hold. behind them, a stream and soft hills. wu zhen painted this in 1328. chapter 54 says what is well planted is not uprooted, what is well embraced does not slip away. cultivate it in yourself, and virtue is real; in your family, and it is abundant; in your village, and it lasts long. look at how the two trees lean together. they are rooted, and they are companions.

pure and remote view of streams and mountains (detail). 溪山清遠圖 attributed to xia gui southern song dynasty, early 13th century ink cliffs with pines lean over open water; much of the paper is left blank as mist. this scroll, attributed to xia gui, leaves most of the paper blank. the empty space works like the bellows in this chapter: it gives, and it is never used up. look at how much is not painted. cliffs and pines crowd one side, and everything else is mist and water. yet the blank paper does not feel weak; it gives the rocks their weight and the trees their reach. chapter 5 says heaven and earth are like a bellows: empty but not exhausted; the more it moves, the more comes out. breathe slowly while you look. let the empty part of the picture breathe with you. the painting does not favour any one thing. rock, tree and fog are all simply allowed.

twelve views from a thatched hut (detail). 山水十二景 xia gui southern song dynasty, early 13th century a low bank with a few trees and tiny figures at the far left, and wide, empty mist across the rest of the silk. xia gui puts a few trees and tiny figures on a low bank and leaves the rest as mist. nothing here asks for attention. look first at the left edge, where the trees and the little figures sit. then let your eye travel right across the wide, golden emptiness. there is no palace, no treasure, nothing to compete for. chapter 3 advises not to praise the clever or prize rare goods, so that people are not stirred to quarrel or steal. the sage empties hearts and fills bellies. this painting feels like that kind of life: modest, settled, with plenty of room to breathe. the mist is not a lack. it is the quiet in which the small scene can rest.

fishermen's evening song (detail). 漁父圖 xu daoning northern song dynasty, c. 1049 steep, narrow peaks rise above a wide river; small fishing boats float on the water below. fishermen work the river under huge peaks. no ruler appears; the people live their lives and say, "we did this ourselves." find the small boats near the bottom. then let your eye climb the narrow, steep mountains that rise like folded curtains. the fishermen are tiny, but the painting belongs to them. nobody commands them. chapter 17 says the best rulers are those the people barely know exist. when the work is done, the people say it happened by itself. xu daoning painted this around 1049, and it has the quiet of evening. listen for the song in the title. it is the people's song, not the court's.

emperor taizong receiving the tibetan envoy. 步輦圖 attributed to yan liben tang dynasty design, 7th century (probably a song copy) court ladies carry emperor taizong in a litter under fans; three men, one in red, stand before him with folded hands. the tang emperor receives an envoy from tibet. a great state should be like the low place where rivers meet. on the right, the emperor sits in a litter carried by court ladies. on the left, an official in red, the tibetan envoy and an interpreter stand with hands folded. this meeting led to a marriage alliance. chapter 61 says a great state is the low reach of the river, where all under heaven meets: the female of all under heaven. by stillness the female always gets the better of the male, and takes the place below. a great state gains small states by lowering itself. notice the tension: the emperor is raised up and carried, while the envoy stands. the painting shows tang power. the chapter asks the powerful to do the opposite, and to take the lower place.

yin xi, keeper of the pass. 尹喜 unknown ming woodblock artist (in hong zicheng's xianfo qizong) ming dynasty, c. 1602 a woodblock print of a robed man with a long beard reading an open book beside a low table with an incense burner, under willow branches. yin xi, the keeper of the pass, reads the book laozi left behind. notice that he holds the text, but the author is gone. begin with the open book in yin xi's hands, then let your eye move out to everything that is not the book: the willow, the incense smoke you cannot see, the white page around him. the printer used only black lines, and most of the paper stays empty. this is the first scene in the life of the daodejing: a reader alone with words that point beyond themselves. the opening chapter warns that the way which can be spoken is not the constant way. yin xi seems to know this. he reads slowly, as if listening for what the words cannot hold.

man and horse. 人馬圖 zhao mengfu yuan dynasty, 1296 a groom in a red-brown robe stands calmly beside a pale horse with a dark mane. a groom stands calmly beside his horse. misfortune is what fortune leans on; fortune is where misfortune hides. the man and the horse stand side by side, neither leading. zhao mengfu painted this in 1296. he was a descendant of the song royal house who served the mongol emperors, a choice that brought him both honour and criticism. chapter 58 says misfortune is where good fortune rests; good fortune is where misfortune hides. who knows where it ends? there is no fixed right. look at the calm face of the groom. he does not know whether this horse will bring good or bad luck. see the story "the old man at the frontier loses his horse".

the pleasures of fishes (detail). 魚樂圖 zhou dongqing yuan dynasty, 1291 a large carp curves upward among water plants; a smaller fish swims nearby on pale silk. zhou dongqing's carp turn among water plants, free and at ease. one who knows does not speak. this scroll is called the pleasures of fishes, after the story of zhuangzi and huizi on the bridge over the hao river. look at the big carp curving upward, its body light in the water. the plants move with the current. chapter 56 says one who knows does not speak; one who speaks does not know. stop the openings, blunt what is sharp, untie what is divided, temper the light, join the dust. this is called the dark sameness. the fish are not explaining their joy. see the story "the happy fish of the hao river".

kitchen scene with a butcher. 庖廚圖 anonymous carvers; said to be han dynasty said to be han dynasty (206 bce–220 ce) a carved figure works at a hanging carcass while another robed figure stands watching. a kitchen relief, said to be han, of a butcher at the carcass. what has no substance enters where there is no gap. the commons file calls this cook ding, from the zhuangzi. that is not confirmed: han tombs often show kitchen scenes, and this may be one of many. look anyway at the butcher bent to the hanging carcass and the robed figure who watches. in the zhuangzi story, the cook's blade stays keen because it moves through the spaces between the joints. passage 43 says: what has no substance enters where there is no gap. find the gaps in the carving itself: between the two figures, under the beam. see the story "cook ding carves an ox". a butcher's skilled, dangerous work. hew in the place of the great carpenter, and seldom is the hand not hurt. look at how the worker braces against the weight, and at the hand close to the blade. cutting was a trade, learned over years. passage 74 says: to kill in the place of the one in charge of killing is called hewing in the place of the great carpenter, and seldom is the hand not hurt. the passage is about a ruler who takes death into his own hands. the image keeps it bodily: a blade in the wrong hands cuts its holder. this relief is said to be han, and its source is not confirmed.

laozi on his buffalo, followed by a disciple. 老子騎牛 unknown chinese painter qing dynasty, 18th century (as reported) a white-bearded old man in pink robes rides a black water buffalo; a boy in green walks beside him carrying a gourd on a staff. laozi on his buffalo, a boy with a gourd beside him. those who know me are few; and so i am precious. this is laozi as later tradition pictured him: the white beard, the high bald head, the slow water buffalo, a young follower with a gourd on his staff. look at how plain the journey is. no banners, no escort. in passage 70 the words speak of themselves: they are easy to know and easy to walk, and yet no one under heaven walks them. so the sage wears coarse cloth and holds jade in the bosom. the painting is reported as 18th-century chinese; its collection is not known. see the story "bian he's uncut jade".

spring plowing (landscape album in various styles). 四季山水圖冊 zha shibiao qing dynasty, 1684 an album leaf in light ink and colour: thatched farmhouses among round willow trees on low banks, with a small boat on the calm water between them. farmhouses sit among willows on a quiet river delta in spring. “empty the heart, fill the belly.” start at the cluster of thatched roofs near the top, then follow the banks down and to the right. zha shibiao painted this album at sixty-eight, and he made the willows with quick, wet strokes, so each tree is a round puff of blue-green ink. there is no hero in this picture and no grand peak. the water in the middle is bare paper. nothing here is hard to get, and nothing is on show. the passage gives the sage’s way of ordering: “empty the heart, fill the belly, weaken the will, strengthen the bones.” this leaf looks like that kind of place: fed, quiet, and without much to want.

ding ware bowl of the xing type with bi-disc foot. unknown artist five dynasties, 907–60 a shallow, wide bowl with an ivory-white glaze and a flat foot, photographed against a dark grey ground. a plain white bowl from the gongxian kilns, made for drinking tea. “dao is an empty bowl. use it, and perhaps it does not fill.” look first at the inside of the bowl, which you can only half see. the potter gave it a wide, low rim and no decoration at all: only a smooth ivory glaze over a white body. the museum says bowls of this kind were used for tea and were traded as far as samarra. its use is in the hollow, not in the clay. the passage begins, “dao is an empty bowl. use it, and perhaps it does not fill.” let your eye rest on the curve where the light falls into the bowl. that open space is what the bowl gives.

dog. 狗 unknown artist eastern han dynasty, 25–220 ce a glazed earthenware dog sits on its haunches with its long neck raised, its ears up and its mouth open. a glazed clay dog from the eastern han, with its head up and its mouth open. “they treat the ten thousand things as straw dogs.” start with the open mouth and the pricked ears, then follow the long neck down to the folded legs. the potter shaped it with a light, humorous hand, and the lead glaze runs over it like brown honey. clay animals like this one were often placed in han tombs. a straw dog, too, was a thing made for a rite: honoured during the rite, then put aside. the passage says heaven and earth “treat the ten thousand things as straw dogs.” this dog is not straw, but it asks the same question. what is a made thing worth after its use is over?

yoro waterfall in mino province (tour of the waterfalls in various provinces). katsushika hokusai edo period, c. 1833 a tall woodblock print: a white waterfall drops in blue lines down a green cliff to a pool, where small travellers in wide hats rest by the rocks. hokusai’s yoro falls drops straight down to the low pool, where travellers stop to rest. “it stays in the place the crowd hates, and so it is near to dao.” begin at the top of the falls and let your eye drop with the water, line by line, to the foam at the bottom. hokusai printed the fall as a column of separate blue strokes, so it looks both still and moving. at its foot, small figures in wide hats rest, and one carries a load. everything in the picture leans toward the low pool. that is where the water goes, and where people come to drink and rest. the passage says water “stays in the place the crowd hates, and so it is near to dao.” it does not contend; it only keeps going down.

windy landscape with sailboat. unknown artist muromachi period, mid-1400s a tall, pale ink painting: a small house and pine trees on a bank at lower left, a sail on open water, and a faint mountain in the distance. a retired official’s small house by the water faces one distant sail. “the work carried through, the body steps back: the way of heaven.” start at the small house in the lower left, half hidden by bent pines. then cross the wide, empty water to the sail, and go on to the faint mountain at the top. the museum describes the house as the retreat of an official who has left government service. the painter used very little ink; most of the scroll is mist and bare paper. nothing here is filled to the brim. the passage ends, “the work carried through, the body steps back: the way of heaven.” this painting shows what stepping back can look like: a small roof, some wind, and a lot of room.

old trees by a wintry brook. 古木寒泉圖 wen zhengming ming dynasty, 1551 a tall, narrow scroll: two gnarled old trees stand over a thin stream among rocks, with an inscription and a wide pale sky above. wen zhengming painted these bare old trees over a cold stream in his eighties. “wary, as if crossing a river in winter.” start at the twisted trunks near the bottom and follow the small stream as it winds between the rocks. wen zhengming painted the bark with dry, broken strokes, so the trees look worn but still standing. above them is a wide field of empty paper and his small, careful inscription, which says he painted it playfully, in his eighties. the passage pictures the officers of old as “wary, as if crossing a river in winter,” and “solid, like uncarved wood.” these trees have both: the caution of great age and the plain strength of wood that no one has shaped.

returning home. unknown artist muromachi period, mid-1500s an ink landscape: a boat comes toward a small pavilion under a tall pine and jagged cliffs, with misty water and far peaks behind. a small boat comes home to a pavilion below a pine and jagged cliffs. “each go home again to the root.” find the small boat near the shore at the bottom, then the pavilion it is heading for under the leaning pine. behind them the cliffs rise in sharp, dark strokes, and behind the cliffs the mist takes everything away. the scroll carries a seal of the monk-painter shokei, but the museum says the seal was added later, so the painter is unknown. the passage watches the ten thousand things rise and then “each go home again to the root.” here the journey is almost over. look at how much of the scroll is still water and haze: the return happens in stillness.

river village: fisherman’s joy. 江村漁樂圖 zhao mengfu yuan dynasty, c. 1302–3 a round fan painting on silk: tall trees on a flat river shore, small fishing boats on the water, and blue-green hills behind. on zhao mengfu’s round fan, fishermen work a flat river below blue hills. “the hundred families all say: ‘we are so of ourselves.’” begin with the tall trees on the right, then move left across the flat, shining water where small boats drift. zhao mengfu filled the far hills with blue and green mineral colour, an old style that he used here on a small fan. no ruler, palace, or soldier appears. the fishermen get on with their day. the passage praises the ruler whom those below only know is there. when the work is done, “the hundred families all say: ‘we are so of ourselves.’” in this village the order is so light that you cannot see who keeps it.

budai. 布袋 jonan etetsu muromachi period, late 1400s an ink painting of the fat, smiling monk budai, who carries a big cloth sack on a stick over his shoulder, below a long inscription. budai, the wandering monk with a cloth sack, grins below a long inscription. “mine is the heart of a fool!” start with the round, smiling face, then follow the loose robe down to the bare feet and across to the huge sack. the zen monk jonan etetsu painted budai with soft grey washes and a few fast, dark lines. in chan legend, budai was a wandering monk said to carry all he owned in one bag. he looks clumsy, and he does not seem to care. the speaker of this passage stands apart from the merry crowd: “mine is the heart of a fool! murky, murky.” budai’s grin shows that foolishness from the outside: no plan, no rank, no home to go to.

river village in a rainstorm. 江村風雨圖 lu wenying ming dynasty, c. 1480–1507 a dark silk scroll: slanting bands of rain sweep across trees bent by wind above a riverside village and small boats. wind and slanting rain lash a river village in lu wenying’s scroll. “a sudden rain does not last the day.” start with the pale diagonal streaks at the upper left and follow them down across the bent trees to the roofs at the bottom. lu wenying, a court painter of the hongzhi era, laid the rain over the silk in pale washes, so the whole picture leans one way. the village has gone indoors. the storm looks total, but the passage reminds us: “a whirlwind does not last the morning; a sudden rain does not last the day.” even heaven and earth cannot keep it up. look again at the boats tied by the shore. they are waiting, not fighting.

streams and mountains without end (detail). 溪山無盡 unknown artist late northern song to jin dynasty, 1100–1150 a detail of a long handscroll on dark silk: wooded hills and rocky masses rise and fall along a river, with small paths and houses among them. in this detail of a long silk handscroll, hills and streams run on past both edges. “great means passing on. passing on means far. far means turning back.” pick any small path or roof and follow it until it goes behind a ridge. a handscroll is unrolled a little at a time, so the land seems to have no first or last mountain. here you see one section only. the unknown painter built the hills from many small brushstrokes and darker trees, with river and mist between them. the passage tries to name the thing born before heaven and earth, and says: “great means passing on. passing on means far. far means turning back.” the scroll moves the same way: on, then far, then around again.

snow landscape. 雪中山水図 yosa buson edo period, mid-1770s a tall painting of snow-covered mountains and trees in grey ink, with a small roofed retreat half buried in white at the centre. buson’s snow covers mountains, trees, and a small scholar’s retreat, and no path shows. “good walking leaves no rut or footprint.” start at the small roof in the middle, then look for the path that led to it. there is none to see. yosa buson, famous as a poet, left the snow as bare paper and painted grey sky around it, so the white seems to glow. the museum notes warm red undertones under the grey, and birds come down into the trees. the passage opens, “good walking leaves no rut or footprint.” whoever lives here came and went without a mark. let your eye travel the same way, lightly, from roof to peak and back.

playing the qin in a secluded valley. 幽壑鳴琴圖 wen zhengming ming dynasty, 1548 a tall scroll of steep, layered cliffs in light colour, with pines and a waterfall running down a deep ravine to a stream at the bottom. wen zhengming’s deep ravine gathers cliffs, pines, and falling water into one long valley. “be the valley of all under heaven.” start at the stream at the bottom of the scroll, then climb the ravine, past the waterfall and the pines, to the peaks. wen zhengming stacked the rocks in many layers of pale ochre and blue, so the valley is a long, narrow gap that holds everything else. his poem on the scroll answers the old song of the pine wind with a tune on the qin. the passage asks us to “be the valley of all under heaven” and to go “back again to the uncarved wood.” the low, open place collects the water, the sound, and the people.

square wine container (fangyou). unknown artist shang dynasty, c. 1250–1046 bce a square bronze ritual wine vessel with a lid and a curved handle, covered with crested birds and spiral patterns, green with age. a shang bronze ritual vessel for wine, cast with crested birds. “all under heaven is a spirit vessel. it cannot be worked on.” start at the small knob on the lid and follow the edges down to the base. every face of this bronze is cast with crested birds against a dense ground of fine spirals, and the green crust is three thousand years of age. it was made for ritual, not for daily pouring. a vessel like this is handled with care, never hammered into a new shape. the passage says, “all under heaven is a spirit vessel. it cannot be worked on. who works on it ruins it.” the design was set once, in the mould. nothing on it can change now without breaking it.

ceremonial dagger-axe with animal masks (ge). 饕餮紋玉戈 unknown artist shang dynasty, c. 1600–1050 bce a pale jade blade shaped like a dagger-axe, with a pointed tip, a central ridge, and a small carved animal mask near the hole at its base. a shang jade blade in the shape of a bronze weapon, made for ceremony. “fruit, and no forcing.” start at the point and slide back along the ridge to the carved mask and the small hole where it was once tied. the museum says this jade copies the shape of bronze dagger-axes, the weapon of its time, and that jade could only be worked slowly with abrasive sand. a blade made so slowly was most likely never meant to strike. the shape of a weapon became a sign of rank and rite. the passage warns against forcing the world with weapons: “where an army has camped, thorn and bramble grow.” here the weapon’s shape remains, and its force is gone.

sword. unknown artist han dynasty, 206 bce–220 ce a straight bronze sword with a ring at the end of its hilt and a narrow guard, green with corrosion, standing upright on a dark ground. a plain bronze sword from the han dynasty, its blade dulled by age. “weapons are tools of ill omen, not a gentleman’s tools.” look at the ring at the top of the hilt, then follow the blade down to its point. there is no inlay and no gold, only bronze dulled to green and brown. the museum record gives little more than a name and a date, and that silence suits it. the passage says, “fine weapons are tools of ill omen,” and asks that even a battle won be met “with the rites of mourning.” it also says: “win, and do not find it beautiful.” let the long, narrow form stand alone in the dark. it asks to be understood, not admired.

river and mountains on a clear autumn day (detail). 江山秋霽圖 dong qichang ming dynasty, c. 1624–27 a detail of an ink handscroll: rounded, folded hills run diagonally across pale paper, with groves of trees and open water below. dong qichang’s folded hills run down toward open water. “a likeness for dao in all under heaven: streams and valleys, and the river and the sea.” start at the top left, where the hills begin, and follow their folds down to the right, past the groves, to the water at the edge. dong qichang set the landscape on a diagonal and built it from dry, repeated strokes, a way of painting that recalls older masters. his inscription names huang gongwang as his model. look at how the hills spill into flat ground and then into water. the passage ends: “a likeness for dao in all under heaven: streams and valleys, and the river and the sea.” everything in this detail runs down to the low, open place.

poet and recluse hanshan. unknown artist ming dynasty, 1400s a dark silk painting of the poet hanshan with wild hair and a loose pale robe, standing alone under overhanging branches. the hermit poet hanshan stands alone in a loose robe, his hair wild. “one who knows the self is bright.” start with the face under the mass of black hair, then follow the pale robe down to the feet. hanshan, the cold mountain poet of the tang, is said to have lived alone among cliffs and to have written his poems on rocks and trees. here he stands against dark branches and holds his sleeve close, as if the wind is strong. the painter is unknown. no one in the scene judges him. the passage says, “one who knows others is clever. one who knows the self is bright.” hanshan is not trying to be seen.

nine dragon pool. 九龍潭圖 mei qing qing dynasty, 1690s a tall scroll: a white waterfall winds down a mountain in many curves between soft grey rocks, past a small pine and autumn trees. mei qing’s waterfall at huangshan bends left and right through nine pools. “the great dao floods, oh: it can go left and right.” begin at the top, where the water first shows as a white ribbon, and follow it down, curve by curve, to the bottom. mei qing probably sketched this fall at huangshan in 1690, at about sixty-eight. the museum says it has nine bends, each with a green pool. he left the water as bare paper and shaped it only with the rocks around it. the passage says, “the great dao floods, oh: it can go left and right.” the water here does just that. it fills each pool and moves on, and it never calls the pools its own.

tea bowl (jian ware). unknown artist song dynasty, 12th century a deep, dark brown tea bowl with fine streaks in its glaze like hare’s fur and a small unglazed foot. a song tea bowl from fujian with a dark glaze called hare’s fur. “the dao, as it comes out of the mouth: bland! it has no flavor.” start at the rim, where the glaze thins to brown, then look down into the dark centre. the fine streaks, called hare’s fur, come from iron in the glaze. bowls like this were made in fujian for whisked tea in the song dynasty. the bowl does not call for attention; you have to come close to see the streaks at all. the passage sets music and cakes, which stop the passing guest, against the dao: “bland! it has no flavor.” then it adds, “use it: not enough to end it.” the bowl waits, empty, for something plain.

a pair of carp. unknown artist joseon dynasty (1392–1910) a tall korean ink painting: two carp, one above the other, turn in grey water near rocks and water plants. two carp turn in deep water in a korean ink painting. “fish must not slip out of the deep.” start with the upper carp, its body curved and its tail up, then drop to the second fish near the rocks. the painter used soft grey washes for the water and darker ink for scales and fins, so the fish seem to move inside the water, not on the paper. neither fish breaks the surface. the passage moves from the soft and weak that overcome the hard and strong to this: “fish must not slip out of the deep.” in the deep, a fish is safe and free; out of it, it is lost. the plain grey around them is their shelter.

scholar reclining and watching rising clouds. 坐看雲起圖 ma lin southern song dynasty, c. 1256 a round fan painting on silk: a scholar lies on a rock at the water’s edge at lower left, looking across a wide, empty space to a faint peak. ma lin’s scholar lies by the water and watches clouds rise out of empty space. “having is born from not-having.” find the small reclining scholar at the lower left, then follow his gaze across the empty silk to the faint peak and the clouds that form near it. ma lin painted this fan in reply to a couplet by wang wei that emperor lizong wrote out: walk to where the water ends, then sit and watch the clouds rise. almost the whole fan is empty, and the clouds come out of that emptiness. the passage says, “turning back is the movement of the dao,” and “having is born from not-having.” the scholar has reached the end of the water and turned to watch.

haboku (flung-ink) landscape. shugetsu tokan muromachi period, c. 1510 an ink painting of splashes and quick strokes: a dark, blurred mass of trees and rocks rises from a low shore, with a few dark marks for boats or stones. shugetsu’s flung ink makes a landscape out of blots and a few quick strokes. “the great image is without shape.” start with the darkest blot in the centre and try to decide what it is: trees, a cliff, a roof? then look at the small dark marks on the shore below it. shugetsu used the haboku, or flung-ink, method, which hides a planned composition inside what looks like chance. the museum says the brush here carries the painter’s state of mind in one moment. most of the paper is left blank. the passage lists things that seem their opposite and ends with this: “the great image is without shape.” the painting gives a landscape without fixing a single line.

mirror with images of daoist deities. unknown artist eastern han dynasty, 2nd or 3rd century ce the back of a round, dark bronze mirror, with a central knob surrounded by rings of small seated figures, animals, and patterned bands. the back of an eastern han bronze mirror: one knob at the centre, then rings of deities and beasts. “the dao gives birth to one. one gives birth to two.” start at the knob in the centre, then move outward ring by ring. around the knob, small bosses divide the field; between them sit figures that the museum calls daoist deities, with beasts among them. bands of pattern close the circle at the edge. the polished face, on the other side, once showed whoever held it. the back reads like a map of how many things come from one centre. the passage says, “the dao gives birth to one. one gives birth to two. two gives birth to three. three gives birth to the ten thousand things.” read the rings in that order.

gazing at a waterfall. 観瀑図 soami muromachi period, early 1500s an ink landscape: two figures stand on a railed terrace under a twisted pine, looking toward a thin waterfall that falls through mist at the left. two men on a terrace watch a thin waterfall pour through mist. “the softest thing under heaven gallops over the hardest thing under heaven.” start with the two men at the railing, then follow their gaze to the waterfall at the far left, a pale strip of water between dark rocks. soami built the scene from soft washes and a few hard, dry strokes for the rocks and the pine. the museum links the subject to li bai’s poem on gazing at the waterfall on mount lu. water is soft, yet it has cut this whole gorge. the passage says, “the softest thing under heaven gallops over the hardest thing under heaven.” the men stand still; the water does the work.

the hermit xu you resting by a stream. 箕山高隱圖 dai jin ming dynasty, 1400s a tall silk scroll: a man in a short robe sits at ease below overhanging pines and steep cliffs, near a small stream. xu you, who refused a throne, rests by a stream under cliffs and pines. “know enough: no disgrace. know to stop: no danger.” look for the small seated figure near the bottom, then climb through the pines to the high cliffs. dai jin shows xu you in a labourer’s short robe, his belly showing, one arm on a raised knee. in the old story, the sage-emperor yao offered him the throne; he refused it and went to farm on mount ji. the passage asks, “name or body: which is nearer?” xu you chose the body and the stream. his ease shows the end of the passage: “know enough: no disgrace. know to stop: no danger. then it can last long.”

crackle-glazed bowl. unknown artist goryeo dynasty, 1100s a wide, shallow celadon bowl in pale grey-green, its glaze covered with a fine web of cracks. a korean celadon bowl, its green glaze crazed with fine cracks. “great completion seems chipped; its use does not wear out.” start at the rim, then let your eye wander over the web of fine lines in the glaze. cracks like these form as glaze and clay shrink at different rates while they cool. to a careless eye they look like damage; to a potter they are part of the surface. the museum says everyday bowls like this were often placed in goryeo tombs. the passage opens, “great completion seems chipped; its use does not wear out.” this bowl is whole and still able to hold. its flaws are where the light catches.

farming and herding buffalo in summer. kano hideyori muromachi to momoyama period, mid- to late 1500s a pale ink landscape: willows and low banks along a wide river, with small farmers in the fields and water buffalo wading near the shore. farmers and water buffalo work the fields by a summer river. “when the world has dao, running horses are turned back to dung the fields.” start at the willows on the right, then look along the banks for the small figures and the buffalo at work. kano hideyori painted with light ink and a few touches of colour, and he left the river wide and calm. the museum says scenes like this were linked with the ideal of a prosperous realm. no animal here is going to war. the passage says, “when the world has dao, running horses are turned back to dung the fields.” the animals in this scroll pull, wade, and graze. that is what enough looks like.

scholar reading in a thatched hut by a waterfall (paintings after ancient masters). chen hongshou ming dynasty, before 1652 an album leaf: a huge pine with blue-green needles leans over a thatched hut among rocks, with a seated scholar inside and a far lake behind. in chen hongshou’s album leaf, a scholar sits in a thatched hut under a great pine. “without going out of the door, know the world.” look first for the hut, half hidden under the pine, and the scholar seated inside it. then look up at the fan of needles, drawn one cluster at a time, and out to the lake and the far shore at the top. chen hongshou painted in a deliberately old-fashioned, very precise way, with rocks like stacked blocks. the whole world seems to arrive at the hut while the reader stays put. the passage says, “without going out of the door, know the world. without peeping through the window, see heaven’s way.” he sits still; the view comes to him.

covered jar (hu). 鎏金错银壶 unknown artist eastern zhou dynasty, warring states period, late 4th/3rd century bce a pear-shaped bronze jar with a lid topped by small animals, its body covered in swirling patterns of inlaid silver and bands of gilding. a warring states bronze jar, gilded and inlaid with silver swirls. “glutted with drink and food, with goods in surplus.” start with the small animals on the lid, then let the silver spirals pull your eye around the body. the bronze is inlaid with strands of silver and gilded in bands: a luxury for a noble house of the warring states. it is beautiful, and it is also a sign of how much that house could take. the passage describes a court swept clean while the fields are weedy and the granaries empty. its people wear patterned silks, “glutted with drink and food, with goods in surplus. this is called the robbers’ boast.” look again at the gold.

water village (detail). 平橋遠水 wen boren ming dynasty, 1570 a detail of a pale ink handscroll: bare trees and a few houses on low marshy banks, with flat water and a line of soft mountains behind. a quiet village on low marshland, from wen boren’s handscroll. “tend it in the village: its de then lasts.” start with the gnarled tree at the right, then move left across the low banks and the houses among the bare trees. wen boren painted this scroll in the autumn of 1570 with pale, dry ink. the museum notes that paths and bridges cross the land, but only two people appear in the whole scroll. it looks calm, almost too calm. the passage moves outward from the body to the household, the village, and the state: “tend it in the village: its de then lasts.” here nothing is torn out. the houses stay where they were set up.

playing with an infant. 嬰戲圖 unknown artist qing dynasty, qianlong reign, 1736–95 a colour woodblock print: two young women in long robes reach toward a small child who stands on a bench between them, wearing a red bib. two women play with a small child in a qing colour woodblock print. “one who holds de within, thick and deep, is like a red child.” start with the child at the top centre, standing with arms out, then look at the two women whose hands reach toward him. the printer used firm black outlines and flat areas of blue, orange, and red. prints like this were sold in the cities of jiangnan and hung on walls. the baby is the still point; the adults move around him. the passage says that one who holds de “is like a red child,” with “bones weak, sinews soft, yet the grip is firm.” look at how steadily the child stands on the bench.

bodhidharma. 菩提達磨図 unkei eii muromachi period, early to mid-1500s an ink painting of the monk bodhidharma from the chest up, with large eyes, a heavy beard, and a robe drawn in a few broad strokes, below an inscription. unkei eii’s bodhidharma looks out in silence, wrapped in a few broad strokes of robe. “one who knows does not speak.” start with the eyes, wide and steady, then let your gaze drop to the robe, which is only a few thick strokes of ink. bodhidharma is said to have brought chan to china in the early 500s. in one story he met emperor wu, saw that the emperor did not understand, and simply left. here his mouth is closed. the painter gives most of the paper to empty space and a short inscription. the passage begins, “one who knows does not speak. one who speaks does not know.” notice how much this face says without a word.

returning peasants in a spring evening. tao hong ming dynasty, early 1600s an album leaf on silk: bare trees on a flat plain by a shallow stream, with a few farmers walking home and birds flying in the pale sky. farmers walk home past bare trees at the start of the farming year. “i have no business, and the people grow rich of themselves.” look for the small figures walking among the trees on the right, then follow the shallow stream back to the hills and the line of birds in the sky. tao hong painted early spring with thin washes and a few touches of green. the museum reads the scene as hope for a good harvest. no official stands over these farmers, and no notice is posted. the passage says, “i do not force, and the people change of themselves,” and “i have no business, and the people grow rich of themselves.” the order here comes with the season, not by command.

old pine tree (detail). 畫松圖 wen zhengming ming dynasty, late 1530s a detail of an ink handscroll: the twisted trunk and long branches of an old pine reach across pale paper, covered with clusters of needles. wen zhengming’s old pine twists across the scroll, bent but deeply rooted. “this is called deep roots and a firm taproot.” start where the thick trunk enters at the left and follow it as it turns, splits, and reaches to the right. wen zhengming made the bark from pale washes and the needles from quick, dark strokes, so the tree feels both heavy and alive. his inscription likens the branches to a dragon’s whiskers. a pine like this grows slowly and spends little. the passage praises “the farmer’s sparing” and ends: “this is called deep roots and a firm taproot: the way of long life and lasting sight.” see how far the branches reach from one root you cannot see.

tripod cauldron (ding). 鼎 unknown artist shang dynasty, 1200–1100 bce a bronze tripod cooking vessel with two upright handles, a round bowl decorated with a band of masks, and three straight legs. a shang bronze ding, a cooking vessel for offerings of grain and meat. “ruling a great state is like the cooking of a small fish.” start at the two upright handles on the rim, then drop to the band of masks and the three firm legs. the museum says ding were made in sets of different sizes and used to offer grain and meat to the spirits of the ancestors. a small fish in a pot like this falls apart if you stir it too much. the passage says, “ruling a great state is like the cooking of a small fish,” and then speaks of ghosts whose spirit-force does not harm people. this vessel joins both worlds: the kitchen and the rite.

traveling in autumn mountains (landscape album in various styles). zha shibiao qing dynasty, 1684 an album leaf: a traveller on a donkey and a porter with a carrying pole cross a flat shore, below tall autumn trees with red leaves and a cliff. a traveller on a donkey and his porter set out under autumn trees. “a journey of a thousand li begins under the foot.” start with the rider and the porter at the left, small and just setting out. then follow the empty, level shore toward the trees and the far water. zha shibiao used light, wet strokes and touches of red for the autumn leaves. the long road ahead is mostly blank paper. the passage says, “a tree that fills the arms’ embrace is born from the tip of a hair,” and “a journey of a thousand li begins under the foot.” the whole trip still lies ahead. all the rider can take is the next step.

fishermen-hermits in stream and mountain. 溪山漁隱圖 zhao yong yuan dynasty, 1300s a tall silk scroll: tall trees on a rocky near shore, small houseboats with fishermen on the water, and low wooded hills across the river. zhao yong’s fishermen sit low in their boats between two shores. “the river and the sea can be kings of the hundred valleys.” start with the tall trees on the near bank, then find the small houseboats at the left, where fishermen hold short rods. across the water, low hills fade into the distance. zhao yong, son of zhao mengfu, used the southern plan of two shores divided by a river. the water fills the middle of the painting and lies below everything else. the passage says the river and the sea rule the hundred valleys “because they are good at being below them.” the fishermen also keep low and quiet, and nobody contends with them.

monk mending clothes in the morning sun. 朝陽補綴図 unknown artist nanbokucho period, c. 1350 a tall ink painting: a monk sits on the ground at the bottom and holds up his robe to mend it, below a few hanging branches. a monk holds his old robe up to the morning light and mends it. “the second is spareness.” look for the monk at the bottom, raising his robe toward the light to find the hole. the painter used a few pale lines for the body and one heavy black stroke for the cloth. above him, most of the scroll is bare paper and a few branches. the museum says the scene shows the zen ideal of practice in every moment, even the plain ones. the passage names three treasures: tenderness, spareness, and “not daring to go ahead of the world.” to mend instead of replace is spareness. notice how calm the work looks.

dagger-axe (ge). unknown artist shang dynasty, 1600–1046 bce a bronze dagger-axe blade, wide and pointed, green and silver with corrosion, with a patterned tang at the right. a bronze dagger-axe from the shang, its blade worn green and silver. “i do not dare to advance an inch; i go back a foot.” start at the point and move back along the blade to the patterned tang, where it was once bound to a wooden shaft. blades like this were used widely in shang warfare, swung on a long handle. corrosion has turned the edge to patches of green and silver. it no longer cuts. the passage quotes a saying of those who use arms: “i do not dare to be the host; i am the guest. i do not dare to advance an inch; i go back a foot.” it ends: “the one who grieves wins.” hold that line next to this blade.

farmer returning home in autumn. 秋景色帰農夫図 yosa buson edo period, 1781 a tall silk scroll: a farmer on a plank bridge waves at a crow on his load of grain while his water buffalo wades a stream below pines and misty hills. buson’s farmer shoos a crow from his grain while his buffalo wades the stream. “the people starve. those above them eat so much in grain tax.” start with the farmer on the plank bridge, then the crow, then the buffalo in the water below. the museum says the farmer is scolding a crow that came to eat his grain. buson kept it light, with tall pines and soft hills in mist. still, the subject is a small harvest and a hungry bird. the passage puts it plainly: “the people starve. those above them eat so much in grain tax: that is why they starve.” here, at least, the farmer guards what he grew. see how little there is to guard.

bamboo in the wind. 風竹圖 puming (xuechuang) yuan dynasty, 1300s an ink painting on silk: thin stalks of bamboo with dark, pointed leaves bend in the wind above a rock, with orchids at their foot. the monk puming painted bamboo that bends in the wind and does not break. “the soft and weak are the company of life.” start at the rock at the bottom, then follow the thin stalks upward as they curve to the left. puming, a monk in suzhou, painted each leaf with one stroke, pressing and lifting the brush so that the leaf narrows to a point. the museum notes that bamboo does not break under snow or wind. it bends, and then it stands again. the passage says, “a person, alive, is soft and weak; dead, hard and strong,” and “a tree that is strong meets the axe.” the bamboo lasts because it gives way.

waterfall and rocks. tsubaki chinzan edo period, 1847 an album leaf in ink: a waterfall runs down between high, folded cliffs with pines to a pool among rounded rocks. in tsubaki chinzan’s album leaf, a waterfall cuts down through folded cliffs. “under heaven nothing is softer and weaker than water.” start at the inscription at the top left, then move across to the cliffs and down the fall to the rocks in the pool. tsubaki chinzan made this leaf after the styles of the chinese painter zhai dakun, and he copied zhai’s inscriptions too. the cliffs are built from many dry, folded strokes; the water is only the paper left white between them. yet it is the water that has shaped the rock. the passage says, “under heaven nothing is softer and weaker than water, yet for attacking the hard and strong nothing can beat it.”

new year’s day in a village at stone lake. 石湖村舍 li shida ming dynasty, 1609 an album leaf in ink and light colour: a farmhouse among bare willows, with guests coming over a small bridge and boys in the courtyard. guests come to a village farmhouse to greet the elders on new year’s day. “their homes at rest, their customs a joy.” start with the house in the centre, then find the guests on the bridge and the boys in the yard. the museum says the boys are lighting firecrackers, servants beat a gong at the gate, and inside the hosts offer hot wine. li shida drew the willows bare, with a quick, scratchy line. this village is small and complete. the passage imagines such a place, where people “find their food sweet, their clothes beautiful, their homes at rest, their customs a joy,” and the sound of chickens and dogs carries from one village to the next.

poem by wang wei in the cursive script style. 王維詩 song lizong (emperor lizong) southern song dynasty, 1256 a round silk fan with two columns of large cursive characters, a seal, and a small signature, mounted on white paper. emperor lizong wrote out ten characters from a poem by wang wei on this round fan. “words to trust are not beautiful.” start at the top of the right column and read down, then the left: ten characters in two lines. emperor lizong wrote out a couplet by the tang poet wang wei about walking to where the water ends and watching the clouds rise. ma lin painted the other half of this fan. the brush moves fast, but the characters stay plain and open, with wide space around them. the passage begins, “words to trust are not beautiful,” and says the sage “does not pile up.” ten characters are enough here. notice what is left unsaid around them.

peach blossom spring. 桃花源圖 cai jia qing dynasty, 1763 misty peaks above a hidden valley of fields, houses, and blossoming trees; a small boat waits at the mouth of a cave in the cliff; old pines in the foreground. a hidden valley of farms and blossom, reached through a cave. though there are boats and carts, there is no occasion to ride them. start at the old pines at the bottom, then find the cave in the cliff on the right: a small boat waits in its mouth. that is how the fisherman in tao yuanming's story came in, and why no one could find the way again. above it the valley opens: fields, a cluster of roofs, trees in blossom, a lone figure by the water. passage 80 pictures such a place: a small state, few people, homes at rest, and boats that no one needs to ride. cai jia hides the entrance and gives the valley most of the paper. see the story "peach blossom spring".

the wheelwright's hand. zhuangzi, ch. 13 (tian dao, the way of heaven) 得之於手而應於心，口不能言，有數存焉於其間 the hand gets it and the heart answers. the mouth cannot say it. yet there is a knack in there. wheelwright bian tells a duke that the book in his hands is the dregs of dead men. his proof is his own trade. cut the wheel too slowly and the fit is loose. cut too fast and it jams and will not go in. the right speed lives in his hand, and he cannot give it even to his son. the laozi opens with the same wall: 道可道，非常道. zhuangzi turns the wall into a workshop. the way that cannot be said is not far off or misty. it is as close as a skill. what do your hands know that you could not write down?

words run out. yijing, xici (great treatise), part 1 書不盡言，言不盡意。 writing does not exhaust speech. speech does not exhaust meaning. the great treatise agrees with the first line of the laozi, and then takes a different road. if words fall short, it says, the sages set up images to carry the whole meaning: the broken and unbroken lines of the hexagrams. the laozi offers no such tool. it says 名可名，非常名 and leaves the reader at the gate. so two old books meet the same limit. one builds a system of pictures to get past it. the other keeps pointing at the limit itself. notice that the laozi also thinks in images: valley, water, gate, infant. is an image a kind of word, or something else?

the gate of illusion. cao xueqin, story of the stone, ch. 1 and ch. 5 (gate of the great-void illusion land) 假作真時真亦假，無為有處有還無。 when false is taken for true, true is also false. where nothing is made into something, something turns back to nothing. this couplet hangs on the stone arch of 太虛幻境, the great-void illusion land. a dreamer reads it in chapter 1 and the boy baoyu reads it again in chapter 5. its second line plays with the same pair as this passage: 有 and 無, having and not-having. the laozi says 有無相生, each gives birth to the other. cao xueqin makes the same turn sound like a warning. the laozi is calm about the pair. the novel is sad about it, because its people love what is 有 and will lose it. note one more trick. the characters 無為 sit inside the line, but here they do not mean wu wei. they mean 'nothing is taken as'. does the echo of the phrase still ring?

born and dying together. zhuangzi, ch. 2 (qi wu lun, making things equal) 方生方死，方死方生，方可方不可 at the moment of birth, dying. at the moment of dying, birth. at the moment of yes, no. the laozi says the opposites lean on each other: long and short, high and low, before and after. zhuangzi pushes harder. he takes the two heaviest pairs, life and death, right and wrong, and says they also arise together. each 'that' comes out of a 'this'. then he draws a conclusion the laozi leaves quiet: the sage does not walk down either side, and 'lights things up by heaven' instead. the laozi's sage also steps back, into 無為之事 and 不言之教. zhuangzi shows what the step feels like from inside. it feels like no longer needing to win the argument.

the void as the way. musashi, book of five rings, void scroll (空之巻) 空を道とし、道を空とみる所也。 take the void as the way, and see the way as void. musashi's last scroll is one page long, and this is its last line. the laozi says 道沖, the dao is empty like a bowl, and use does not fill it. musashi's 空 is a buddhist word, but he gives it a soldier's test. the true void is not confusion. it comes when the clouds of doubt clear after long training. so the two texts agree that the center is empty, and they differ on the road. the laozi's emptiness is there from the start, 'ancestor of the ten thousand things'. musashi's emptiness is earned, morning after morning. is emptiness something found or something made?

straw dogs, before and after. zhuangzi, ch. 14 (tian yun, the turning of heaven) 夫芻狗之未陳也，盛以篋衍，巾以文繡 before the straw dogs are set out, they lie in a basket, wrapped in embroidered cloth. the laozi names straw dogs, 芻狗, and does not explain them. zhuangzi does. before the rite, the straw dogs are kept in a box under fine cloth, and the priest fasts before he touches them. after the rite, people walk on their heads, and the grass-cutters burn them for cooking. nobody hates them. their hour is over. this makes 天地不仁 less cold than it sounds in english. heaven and earth are not cruel. they do not cling. zhuangzi then uses the image as a joke on confucius, who drags old rites into a new age and sleeps under yesterday's straw dogs. what are you still wrapping in embroidered cloth?

the clean white ground. cao xueqin, story of the stone, ch. 5 (last song of the dream suite, birds each fly to the wood) 好一似食盡鳥投林，落了片白茫茫大地真乾淨。 it is just like birds that fly to the wood when the food is gone. what is left is a wide white ground, truly clean. in a dream, the boy baoyu hears a suite of songs that tell the end of his family before it happens. this is the close of the coda. the officials fall, the rich lose their gold, each debt is paid, and then the stage is bare. the picture is the laozi's 天地不仁 seen from inside a great house. heaven and earth treat the jia family as straw dogs: honored for a season, then let go. the novel does not call this cruel. it says 乾淨, clean. the laozi says the space between heaven and earth is like a bellows, empty and never used up. can a bare ground be a comfort?

the field that bears. yijing, hexagram 2 kun (the receptive), tuan commentary 至哉坤元，萬物資生，乃順承天。 how complete is the source in kun! the ten thousand things take their birth from it, and it follows and receives heaven. the laozi's 谷神, the valley spirit, is called 玄牝, the dark female, and her gate is the root of heaven and earth. the yijing has its own great female: 坤, six broken lines, the earth. both give birth without effort and are never used up. but look at the difference in rank. in the yijing commentary, kun 'follows and receives heaven'. she is second. in the laozi, the dark female is first; heaven and earth come out of her gate. the laozi takes the receiving side and puts it at the root of everything. that was a bold move in a world that ranked heaven over earth.

set out last, arrive first. sunzi, art of war, ch. 7 (jun zheng, armies contending) 後人發，先人至，此知迂直之計者也。 set out after the other and arrive before the other. this is to know the plan of the crooked and the straight. the laozi says the sage puts the self behind and so comes to the front: 後其身而身先. sunzi has almost the same words about a march. take the long road, bait the enemy off the short one, start late, arrive first. the grammar is alike and the heart is not. sunzi's general goes behind as a plan, in order to be first. the laozi's sage goes behind because there is no private end to push: 以其無私. then the text adds a line that sounds like sunzi after all: 'so the private end is fulfilled'. is the laozi teaching selflessness, or the deepest strategy? the passage does not let you settle.

water takes the vessel's shape. musashi, book of five rings, earth scroll (地之巻), outline of the water scroll 水は方圓の器にしたかひ、一てきとなり、さうかひとなる。 water follows the square or round vessel. it becomes one drop, and it becomes the wide blue sea. musashi names his second scroll after water and says: make the heart into water. his reason is close to 上善若水. water has no shape of its own, so no shape defeats it. but see what each writer does with this. the laozi praises water because it goes to the low places that people hate, and so it does not contend: 不爭. musashi praises water because it fits any enemy and any ground, and so it wins. one man reads water as humility. the other reads it as readiness. both are true of water. which one do you see first?

the army shaped like water. sunzi, art of war, ch. 6 (xu shi, empty and full) 夫兵形象水，水之行，避高而趨下 the form of an army is like water. water in its course avoids the high and hurries to the low. this is the closest that sunzi comes to the laozi's own words. water runs from the high place to the low. an army should run from the enemy's full place to the empty one. the chapter goes on, in the edition used here: 'an army has no fixed force and no constant form'. the laozi's water also 'dwells in places the crowd dislikes'. for the laozi the low place is good in itself, near to the dao. for sunzi the low place is the gap in a wall. the same image serves peace in one book and attack in the other. this is why the two books are so often read together, and why they should not be mixed up.

water in the pit. yijing, hexagram 29 kan (the pit, water doubled), tuan commentary 水流而不盈，行險而不失其信。 water flows on and does not fill up. it goes through danger and stays true. the yijing sees water in a darker place than the laozi does. hexagram 29 is water over water, a pit inside a pit. it is the sign of danger. yet the comment finds the same virtue that the laozi finds. water keeps moving and never fills to the brim, and it stays true in a bad place. the laozi's list of water's goods includes 言善信, 'in speech, good at being true'. the yijing uses the same word, 信, for water in the gorge. so the laozi's gentle water has already been through the pit. the softness is not innocence.

the moon when full. cao xueqin, story of the stone, ch. 13 (qin keqing's ghost warns wang xifeng) 月滿則虧，水滿則溢 the moon when full will wane. water when full will spill. a young wife of the jia house dies in the night, and her spirit comes to the family's sharpest manager with two old sayings. the house has been bright for a hundred years, she says. buy farmland around the ancestral graves now, and put the family school there. land kept for the sacrifices is not seized even when a house is condemned. this is the laozi's 持而盈之，不如其已 put to work in a household budget. the ghost does not ask for retreat from the world. she asks for a plan that expects the turn. xifeng admires the speech and does nothing. the novel is, in one way, the story of that advice not taken. what would you set aside if you believed the moon was full?

the dragon too high. yijing, hexagram 1 qian (the creative), top line and its image comment 亢龍有悔，盈不可久也。 the dragon that has gone too high has regret. what is full cannot last. the first hexagram tells the life of a dragon in six lines. it hides, appears, leaps, flies; in the third line a person toils all day in its place. the sixth line is the surprise. the dragon climbs past its place and there is regret. the comment gives the reason in four characters, and the key word is 盈, full, the same word the laozi uses here. the laozi says: when the work is done, step back; this is heaven's way, 功遂身退，天之道. the yijing gives no advice at the top line. it only shows what happens to those who stay. read the two together and the laozi sounds less like a moral and more like weather.
