leave at the top, then start again. wing reads the full vessel as a cycle of growth and decline. fullness must turn, so a person who stays after success will feel the fall. wing gives a psychological cause: when you identify with an achievement, inner growth stops. the advice has two halves. withdraw when the work is done. then go to the next task, lightly, with no load of status or property. our page stays closer to the images of brim and blade. wing's addition, that retirement is a move to new work and not an end, is worth keeping.

breath and soul, or inner balance?. wing reads the six questions as tests of balance between two sides of a person: aggressive drive, and the spontaneous need to belong. a person who joins the two keeps the influence that wing calls "intellectual gravity". a note links ch'i to tai chi. our page reads the same questions as bodily practice: the soul held to the one, the breath made soft as an infant's, the dark mirror washed. we think the chinese speaks of a real body. wing's reading is a fair translation of that practice into the language of character.

make an absence and let the world fill it. hub, pot, and room all work because of the part that is not there. wing takes one more step and turns the observation into a method. in any event, wing says, the tao is the missing part that drives the change. so a person can create a felt absence on purpose: leave a role open, a question unanswered, a space unfilled. natural forces then move to close the gap. this is a typical wing move, from image to technique. our page stays with the three objects, but the technique is a fair experiment for a reader.

the belly as the intuitive centre. wing treats this passage as control of input. a flood of colour, sound, flavour, and speed blunts insight, and a hunger for rare goods bends judgement. wing cites the old commentator wang bi on belly and eye: one takes things in and is fed, the other is ruled by outside things. wing then reads the belly as the centre, the seat of the intuitive mind. a paradox closes the note: strong desires leave a person few options, and a person tied to little is free to experience everything. our page keeps the belly as a belly.

"expanding identification". this is one of wing's key terms. praise and blame both tie a person to the small self, because both depend on the judgement of others. reduce that dependence, wing says, and identity begins to reach outward until it takes in the world. only such a person is fit to guide it. our page reads the passage through 身, the body, which the chinese repeats six times, and through the two opposite ways to read the last lines. wing's term names something our reading shares: care that does not stop at one's own skin.

trace events to their start. wing finds this passage especially hard to enter, since it describes the tao by what the senses cannot find. the tao shows itself only in effects: in ideas, events, and social change. wing then makes the closing lines practical. follow any event back to its beginning. follow your own existence back as well, to reach the intuitive mind. from there a person can foresee outcomes. wing adds a thought from quantum physics: the observer helps to form what is observed. our page reads the last image as a thread to hold, with no promise of control.

muddy water is reality itself. for wing the muddy water is not a problem to solve. it is how reality looks from inside. a person who settles into its unity begins to see the pattern, and can then guide it with moves so steady that nothing resists. wing reads the old masters' caution as stored advantage: force that stays in reserve. the closing advice is the most useful part. be a channel and not a storehouse; a person who stays unfilled is renewed. our page gives more room to the seven wary similes, such as the walker on winter ice.

hidden power is usable power. wing turns the ranking of rulers into a working method. heavy leaders go against nature. the best leader holds back, sets direction indirectly, chooses words with care, and trusts people. the people then feel that the result is their own, and wing observes that they also produce more. the striking claim is about the leader: the less visible the power, the more of it can be used. wing's short formula is to guide and not to rule. our page adds the textual history of the first line, which wing does not discuss.

instinct first, morality as repair. wing reads this passage as a defence of human instinct. people are good by nature. talk of morality becomes loud only where a society is already corrupt, talk of duty where family ties are false, and patriotism where a nation is split. for wing these are repairs invented by the intellect, and virtue that is enforced injures the instinct it tries to replace. wing adds a warning for seekers: people who read their own experience through a borrowed system are lost as well. our page sets the lines against the confucian vocabulary that they answer.

the crowd as a shared mind. wing hears an accomplished taoist in this passage and takes it as a call to think alone: leave the crowd, drop dogma, trust direct experience. wing renders the crowd with a term close to jung's collective unconscious. the independent person does not simply escape that shared mind. such a person adds to it, and looks ahead to where evolution points. our page hears something wing passes over: doubt and loneliness in the speaker's voice. the two readings fit together. independence has a cost, and the passage admits it.

a thought experiment before the big bang. wing rates this passage very highly. the tao here is like the field of a magnet: nobody sees it, and everybody can see what it moves. wing calls it a force that carries information, and claims that the trends of a culture follow the same laws as physical forces. then comes an exercise. picture matter and energy as one thing before the universe began. go behind even that picture, to a creative state outside time and space. the cosmology is of its decade. as a meditation prompt for the haze and the seed in this passage, it still works.

"intellectual gravity". wing coins this phrase for the pull that a collected person has on events. the argument is one of cause and effect. an open grab for position is a cause, and its effect cannot be controlled. a person who does not display, justify, or boast keeps energy inside, and gains weight. events then bend toward that person. wing says that outcomes in society, as in physics, depend on how this weight is spread among the people involved. our page keeps the older image: bent, and so whole.

power over others as hidden slavery. a squall is over before noon. wing draws a rule from it: violent effort stops soon and calls up a reaction that cancels it. only an attitude that a person can hold for years changes anything. wing then gives the clearest definition of the book's key word. "power" means independence and freedom inside one's own life. it does not mean command of other people, which wing regards as a concealed form of bondage for the one who commands. a larger mind makes a deeper change, since people become what they believe.

groups correct the show-off. wing files this passage under organizations and reads it as group psychology. a group behaves like a system that balances itself. members who push for attention, play two sides, or boast set off a strong reaction, and the group pulls them down. wing adds a diagnostic use. excess and redundancy in any situation are signs that it is unstable and will decline fast. the wise member notices the signs and leaves quietly. our page stays with the body image of a person on tiptoe, who cannot stand for long.

four forces and one substance. wing reads the opening lines as cosmology in the modern sense. they describe a state in which matter and energy were not yet separate, and wing compares it with the search of physicists for one interaction at the origin. the four known forces, wing says, appeared in the first instant, and the tao is their action, in the cosmos and in society alike. the ruler stands among the four great things because a leader can see those laws at work in people. our page uses such parallels only as open metaphor, and ends on 自然, "so of itself".

ten thousand chariots, in modern terms. the chinese speaks of a lord with ten thousand war chariots. wing stops to make the number felt. for an ancient reader, that was a force past imagining, and wing compares it with nuclear power in the 1980s. the comparison gives weight to the plain advice of the passage. a person who holds that much force must not be light or restless, since the whole organization rests on the leader's centre. wing sets a portrait of the qianlong emperor near the passage as a model of the serious, educated ruler.

the "light" as information. wing reads this passage as an account of how knowledge moves between people. the best systems hold with no extra force, like a knot that needs no rope. they rest on free, creative action and a feel for human need. the wise person wastes nobody, and so passes on what wing calls the "light": information that guides evolution. the fresh point is about the teacher. an uninformed person needs a model, and the person who serves as the model gains energy and insight from that role. both sides change.

the leader as a reservoir. wing makes this passage a portrait of the leader as connector. such a leader knows the strong side and stays on the quiet side. the leader then becomes a low place, like a reservoir, where the talents of separate people collect and are exchanged. wing adds a physics parallel. four forces hold matter together, and a leader who binds people into one effort does similar work in society. infant, limitless, and uncarved block are, for wing, three pictures of one whole before division. our page keeps the hen and the valley as images.

a passage for the adviser. most readers take this passage as a warning to rulers. wing notices that the chinese addresses the person who assists a ruler, and builds the reading on that. an adviser has a duty to restrain. large bodies cannot stop their own motion, and an organization that confuses defence with attack uses up its resources until its people go hungry. wing adds a point about the adviser's own mind: time spent on aggressive plans narrows it, until it can no longer see where society is going. stop at the result, and take nothing more.

a sharp mind is also a weapon. wing widens the meaning of "weapon". an army counts, and so does a keen mind or a smart plan, at the moment a person uses it to force another person. all of these are necessary evils at best. wing's rule is that force adds to personal power only when its user regrets it. a leader's visible sorrow over a conflict also calms disputes inside the organization. wing treats the funeral lines as later commentary that entered the text. our page keeps them and reads the mourning rite as the centre of the passage.

too much structure suits machines. wing reads the warning about names as a warning about organization charts. a leader who defines every role and rule builds a place fit for machines. people who are held in fixed roles stop creating, and a body that is fully systematized is closed to evolution; wing says it moves toward extinction. with simple, loose management, people look at the goal and not at the method, and they have nothing to resent. the reading is narrow beside the chinese, which also has sweet dew and rivers. as management advice it has aged well.

how the small defeats the large. wing gives this passage a strategic reading with two parts. first, the strongest position carries the most risk. an organization is most exposed when it is overextended and pleased with its own praise and profit. advantages that stay hidden last longer, since they provoke nobody; fish do not survive out of deep water. second, the opening lines become a method for a small body that faces a large one. do not resist. yield, and feed the excess of the large body until it overreaches. our page also shows how legalist writers used these lines.

reversal as electrical charge. wing explains the turning of the way with the language of charge. yin and yang are negative and positive states. an extreme is a state that carries too much charge, so it is unstable and starts to move toward its opposite. in society the same law appears as cycles of easy and hard, active and passive. the practical result is moderation: a person who avoids extremes and stays receptive moves with the main forces. the physics is loose, but the picture of an overcharged state makes the short chinese text easy to remember.

many problems end when nobody fights them. wing reads the soft thing that enters where there is no gap as a rule of least effort. most difficulties, wing argues, are born from reactions to something larger. remove the aggression and many of them leave. when action is truly needed, the lightest touch works best, because it does not create a second set of problems. wing adds two remarks that lift the reading above technique. to leave things alone is a kind of freedom. it also takes courage, because the pressure to act is strong.

let things pass through. wing's commentary here is unusually blunt about people who live only to collect. the argument under the bluntness is worth keeping. hoarding trains the mind to see reality as fixed, and a fixed view cannot grow. a person with few needs is mobile and independent. wing describes a flow: release what you hold, and more comes in and moves on through your life. to need less also brings a person nearer to the self. our page reads the three opening questions, name or body, body or goods, as real questions with no easy answer.

cold and heat. wing reads the two short lines near the end in a way we have not seen elsewhere. "cold" is taken as lifeless matter, which needs vigorous work before it becomes a tool. "heated" is taken as the human being, who needs a calm centre. our page reads the lines as two plain facts about a body: restless movement beats cold, and stillness beats heat. from there the chinese steps to its last words, clear and still. wing's version is inventive. we think the plain reading prepares the ending better.

observation that does not disturb. wing joins the daily loss of this passage to the observer problem in physics. a person who acts in order to learn something changes the scene, so what comes back is a record of reactions to the actor. fixed ideas distort in a second way, since they freeze a world that arrives as possibility and change. the ideal observer has cleared those ideas and does not interfere. what that person receives is clean, in wing's account, and it refines intuition. passage 47 has a matching note: hold still, and the inner world can mirror the outer one.

trust as chemistry. why answer distrust with trust? wing gives a chemist's reason. an extreme is neutralized only by its opposite, as in a chemical reaction. aggression that meets aggression grows; aggression that meets its opposite loses its charge. wing calls this ability to neutralize extremes the highest power, because it changes the other person from inside and leaves peace behind. wing also reads the wise person's lack of a fixed mind as a practical matter: belief systems distort incoming information. our page keeps the image of the hundred clans and their one heart.

thirteen, or three in ten?. the number phrase 十有三 can be read two ways. wing takes it as thirteen and explains the thirteen as the senses and their openings. a person who limits what leaves through them builds up vital energy and has no weak place for harm to enter. this follows an old reading that goes back to han fei. our page takes the phrase as "three in ten" and reads the first half as a count of people: three hold to life, three to death, three move toward death by living too thickly. both readings end with the same picture: no place for the horn.

hold a picture of the unit at its best. the passage climbs from self to family, community, state, and world. wing turns the climb into an exercise. for each scale, form a clear mental image of how that unit works at its best: no contention, mutual support, a pleasing social life. the image shows the pattern under the unit. wing goes further and claims that an ideal held firmly in a developed mind pulls reality toward it, for later generations as well. our page reads the same lines through the ancestral sacrifice that does not stop.

a title the chinese does not supply. wing's title for this passage names non-contention, and the commentary explains the infant's safety that way: the infant attacks nothing, so nothing attacks the infant. adults can use the same method against social danger. the chinese of this passage does not contain 不爭, the phrase for "not contending". our page reads the infant through the body: soft bones and a firm grip, a full store of essence, a cry all day with no hoarse throat. the safety comes from wholeness. wing's point and ours meet in the last lines, where forced strength grows old fast.

wait, and the schemers show themselves. wing reads the small fish as advice for an uncertain period. a delicate situation falls apart under too much handling. when no easy and elegant solution exists, wait and watch. wing then gives the ghost lines an organizational sense. when a leader brings the tao into the affairs of a group, matters become clear to everybody. self-serving plans become obvious and lose their effect, and a group that does not fear manipulation works well. before the passage, wing places a portrait of the first tang emperor, presented as a reformer.

service as the source of power. wing treats this passage as diplomacy and then widens it. the strong side should take the low place. that stance looks weak, yet it has the strength of generosity, and the small side has nothing to resent. each side has a real need: the large one to gather and support, the small one to serve a wider public. wing holds that the rule applies at every scale, from two people to two nations, and closes with a reversal of the usual link between ruling and serving.

king yu and the flood. before this passage wing tells the legend of yu, who tamed the great floods. earlier efforts had built dikes against the rivers. yu dredged channels instead, so that the water could reach the sea by its own course. he worked for thirteen years and, the legend says, passed his own door three times without going in. the pairing is deliberate. wing's commentary describes influence that goes to the point of least resistance, follows that point as it moves, and never meets a large problem head on. yu is the picture of it.

feel where events begin. wing reads this long passage as a theory of timing. forceful action meets an equal counter-force, which either cancels the actor or spoils the situation. the skilled person works at the origin, when a situation is small, simple, and least reactive. two conditions follow. one must learn to sense the place and time where things start, an instinct that desire and dogma block. one must also hold a position from which to guide events through to the end, since many efforts fail near completion. our page keeps the tree, the tower, and the first step under the foot.

a democratic ideal, early. wing calls this passage a democratic ideal and remarks that it suits the present better than the age that produced it, twenty-five centuries ago. the leader identifies fully with the people, so their interests become the leader's interests. wing stresses the test in the text: neither words nor actions may show any sense of being above others. support given to such a leader lasts, because nobody feels the weight. our page reads the image first: the sea rules a hundred valleys by lying below them.

too large to think. wing reads the odd opening as a paradox with a purpose. whatever the mind can fully hold becomes small and manageable, and the manageable is no source of real power. the tao is too large for that, and the effort to think it anyway is itself a source of strength. wing then calls the three treasures the emotional base of the whole method: feelings, not rules. compassion comes first because it gives foresight and vision, and so the compassionate leader prevails. our page stays with the three treasures as things held and guarded.

a contest of ideas. wing moves this military passage from the battlefield to the mind. conflict between ideologies is a normal part of social change. ideas pushed by aggression meet direct resistance, and both sides escalate. ideas offered by indirect means enter and stay. that is why, on wing's reading, the saying prefers a long retreat to a short advance. the side that is able to grieve over the conflict is the more evolved side, and its ideas win in the end. wing notes the author's fear that escalation destroys the three treasures of passage 67.

who is speaking?. wing holds that the "i" of this passage is the tao itself, and that the first readers were rulers and their scholars, the only people in early china who could read. the jade under coarse cloth becomes strategy: keep an advantage inside a plain exterior. our page hears a human voice, close to the lonely speaker of passage 20, who complains that easy words find no takers. we read the jade as worth that needs no display. wing's point about audience is a good reminder that the book was written for people with power.

the net as a field of law. wing reads heaven's wide net as a boundless field of physical law. every act, thought, and event falls inside it. nothing escapes notice, and nature answers each extreme with precision. from this wing draws a calm conclusion, not a threatening one: nature's way is both the standard of conduct and the easiest road, so the person who copies it meets the least resistance. our page keeps the doubt in the middle of the passage, where the text asks who knows why heaven dislikes a thing.

adapt or go extinct. wing reads soft and stiff through evolution. the universe changes, so whatever adapts survives. fixed beliefs, fixed habits of food or thought, and fixed responses lead toward extinction; the same situation at a later time may need a new answer. flexibility, wing adds, sharpens instinct and lengthens life. the last line of wing's version carries an echo of the bible verse about the meek. the page before shows a painting of bamboo under snow, which the caption presents as a sign of long life and responsive strength.

one balancing law at three scales. wing tests the bow image at three levels. in ecology, a species that grows too dominant is brought down, and fragile ones find support. in the atom, a particle with excess charge seeks its opposite and settles. in society, people who dominate raise a common wish to cancel them, and people in need raise a wish to help. the wise person works with this tendency: a modest position draws energy toward itself. wing notes, as the chinese does, that human habit runs the other way and takes from those who have little.

two kinds of blame. wing separates the two burdens named near the end of this passage. disgrace is error that arises inside the group. misfortune arrives from outside. a leader who accepts the first can lead the group. a leader who accepts the second believes in a duty to foresee, and can lead far beyond the group. in both cases the leader behaves as water does: no edge, no fixed form, and so nothing for a blow to land on. wing argues that taking responsibility steadies a position and does not weaken it.

the creditor's chance. wing reads the tally as a study of the stronger party in any obligation. that party has the duty to prevent leftover resentment. a claim that is pressed returns later as trouble. a claim that is held lightly creates gratitude and shapes a future that suits the giver. wing adds a practical consolation: if the other side fails, the giver has learned the right partner and the right time for an agreement. before the passage stands a portrait page on king wen, who by tradition studied the book of changes in prison.

a small state, or any organization?. wing translates 國 as "organization" throughout, on the ground that the character shows bounded, defended land. so this passage becomes a model for a self-sufficient unit of any size: a family, a business, a nation. a good unit gives each member health, education, and recreation, and satisfied members stay loyal. our page keeps the small state and its strange details: unused tools, knotted cords, a neighbour's rooster heard across the border. we read a wish more than a plan. wing's question still stands: what would make people glad to stay?

hoarding information breaks the flow. wing closes the book with a law of flow. the wise person does not store up; the more that person gives, the more passes through. wing extends the list of things that should not be hoarded from goods to services and to information, and calls any such hoard a dangerous imbalance, for the holder first of all. the earlier lines become three qualities to protect: reality without decoration, good work that needs no defence, and knowledge that reaches inward. it is a fitting last note for a book about influence without possession.

she unnames them. short-story ursula k. le guin 1985 eve gives the animals' names back, and then her own. without the names, the wall between her and the animals falls, and she finds that she must now speak slowly and with care. the story shows the passage's pair: the named world of the ten thousand things, and the nameless that was there before it. le guin later made her own english version of the daodejing.

the snow man. poem wallace stevens 1921 a listener stands in a winter landscape and adds no feeling of their own to it. the poem asks for a mind that sees only what is there, and also the nothing that is there. this is close to the passage's 'always without wanting, to watch its fineness'. the wanting mind sees the edges of things; the still mind sees what is before the edges.

on exactitude in science. short-story jorge luis borges 1946 an empire makes a map as large as the land itself, point for point. the map is useless, and later generations leave it to rot in the desert. the one-paragraph story shows by contrast what the passage's first lines say: a way that is fully told, and a name that is fully given, are not the constant thing that they describe.

arrival. film denis villeneuve 2016 a linguist learns a written language of circles that has no before and after. as she learns its names, she starts to see time in a different way. the film can be read as a picture of 'named: the mother of the ten thousand things': a naming system makes a world. the film also shows that something larger stays outside every such system.

the left hand of darkness. novel ursula k. le guin 1969 an envoy visits a world where people are not fixed as male or female. he learns a local verse in which light and darkness are the two hands of one body, and he draws the yin-yang sign for his friend. the novel shows the passage's claim that the two sides of a pair give birth to each other. a person who keeps only one side misunderstands both.

both sides, now. song joni mitchell (first recorded by judy collins) 1967 the singer looks at clouds, at love, and at life, each from two opposite sides. she then says that she still does not know the thing itself. the song does not choose a winning side. it is close to the passage: the beautiful and the ugly arrive together, and a view from one side is only half of a pair.

inside out. film pete docter (pixar) 2015 joy tries to keep sadness away from a girl's memories, and the girl's inner world starts to break. the repair comes when joy sees that the happy memories were made together with the sad ones. the film shows 'there, already, is the not-good' as a fact of the heart: the two sides complete each other, as hard and easy do.

eye of the beholder (the twilight zone). episode rod serling 1960 doctors try to repair a woman's face so that she looks like everyone else. at the end the viewer sees the faces, and the judgment of beautiful and ugly turns over. the episode shows the passage's first lines. when all under heaven agree on what is beautiful, that same agreement makes the ugly, and it makes an outcast.

the gods must be crazy. film jamie uys 1980 a glass bottle falls from an aircraft into a kalahari band that owns almost nothing. the bottle is useful, and there is only one. for the first time the people feel envy and anger. one man walks to the edge of the world to throw the bottle away. the comedy shows 'not prizing goods hard to get' with one object.

a diamond is forever. ad frances gerety, n. w. ayer & son, for de beers 1947 this advertising line taught several generations that a marriage needs a diamond. it made a stone into a good that is hard to get and that must be shown. it is the passage turned around: 'showing what can be desired' as a planned trade. the passage says that such showing puts the people's heart in disorder.

harrison bergeron. short-story kurt vonnegut 1961 a future state makes all people equal by force. strong people carry weights, and clever people hear loud noises that break their thoughts. the story is a warning about one reading of this passage. 'not exalting the worthy' and 'weaken the will' become cruel when a clever ruler forces them. the passage ends with not-forcing.

the lathe of heaven. novel ursula k. le guin 1971 a quiet man has dreams that change the world. his doctor uses the dreams to repair the world: war, crowding, race. each repair makes a worse problem. the doctor is one of the passage's 'clever ones' who dare to act. the dreamer wants only to stop forcing. le guin took the title from the zhuangzi and several chapter mottoes from daoist texts.

mad men. tv matthew weiner 2007 the series follows people in a 1960s advertising agency. their work is to show what can be desired, and the best of them know that the want never ends. their own lives show the cost: restless hearts in full houses. the series is a long picture of the opposite of 'empty the heart, fill the belly'.

being there. film hal ashby; novel by jerzy kosinski 1979 chance is a gardener with no plans and no opinions. powerful people meet him and hear deep advice in his plain words about plants. they pour their meaning into him, and he does not fill. the film is a comedy, and it also shows the passage's image: an empty bowl that people use again and again.

columbo. tv richard levinson and william link 1968 the detective wears an old raincoat, forgets his pencil, and praises the suspect's fine house. he blunts his own sharpness and tempers his own light, and proud people stop guarding themselves. then he unties the knot. the series shows four lines of the passage as a working method: blunt, untie, temper, join the dust.

spirited away. anime hayao miyazaki 2001 no-face is a spirit with a mask and nothing inside. in the greedy bathhouse he tries to fill the emptiness: he makes gold, eats food, and then eats workers, and he only gets larger and sadder. away from the bathhouse he is quiet and useful. he shows the passage by contrast: an emptiness that people try to fill, and an emptiness that people leave open.

i'm nobody! who are you?. poem emily dickinson 1891 the speaker is glad to be nobody, and finds a second nobody to share the secret. to be somebody looks to her like a loud and public job. the short poem has the mood of 'tempering the light, joining the dust'. the passage's dao is also hard to see: 'it seems, perhaps, to be there'.

straw dogs. film sam peckinpah 1971 peckinpah took the film's title from this passage. a mild scholar in an english village is pushed until he kills the men who attack his house. the film reads 'straw dogs' in a dark way: people are things to be used and thrown away. the passage itself says less than this. it says that heaven and earth do not take sides.

straw dogs: thoughts on humans and other animals. book john gray 2002 the philosopher john gray takes his title from this passage. he argues that humans are one animal among the others, and that the world has no special plan for them. the book is a modern, sharp version of the first four lines: heaven and earth are not humane, and they do not treat people as an exception.

the open boat. short-story stephen crane 1897 four men from a sunk ship row a small boat toward the shore. one of them sees that the sea is not cruel and not kind. it does not see him at all. then the men look after each other. the story shows 'heaven and earth are not humane' without despair: the sea treats all four men the same.

grizzly man. film werner herzog 2005 timothy treadwell lived among alaskan bears and believed that they knew and loved him. a bear killed him. herzog, who made the film from treadwell's own tapes, says that he sees in the bears' faces only a search for food. the film puts two views side by side, and herzog's view is the passage's first line.

princess mononoke. anime hayao miyazaki 1997 deep in a forest lives a spirit that gives life and takes life with each step. people cut off its head to own its power, and the land starts to die. when the head is returned, green comes back over the burned hills. the film shows a source that is used and does not wear out, and that does not die.

always coming home. novel ursula k. le guin 1985 the book collects the songs, stories, and customs of a people who live in a place that they call the valley. they do not conquer and they do not build empires. descent runs through the mother's house. the book can be read as a long picture of a culture built on the passage's images: the valley and the female root.

the force that through the green fuse drives the flower. poem dylan thomas 1933 one hidden force pushes the flower up, moves the water, and moves the speaker's own blood. the same force also brings each of them to an end. the poem does not name the force. it is near to the passage's thin thread that 'seems to be there', the root from which all things come, and which use does not exhaust.

moana. film ron clements and john musker (disney) 2016 an island goddess is the source of all life in the sea. a hero steals her heart to give its power to people, and a slow rot spreads from island to island. a girl returns the heart, and life returns. the film shows the 'root of heaven and earth' as female, quiet, and generous. it also shows the cost when people try to own the root.

it's a wonderful life. film frank capra 1946 george bailey gives up his travels, his college, and his own plans, each time for other people. he thinks that he has put his life behind him and lost it. on one night the whole town comes to carry him. the film shows the passage's turn: he 'puts the body behind, and the body is in front'.

ikiru. film akira kurosawa 1952 a city clerk learns that he will soon die. he spends his last months pushing one small playground through the offices, and he takes no credit. after his death other men claim the work. the people of the district know who did it. he is 'without the private', and so the one thing that was his own is completed.

the picture of dorian gray. novel oscar wilde 1890 a young man wishes that his portrait will grow old in his place. he then lives only for his own pleasure and his own face. he keeps his body and loses everything else, and at the end he loses the body too. the novel is the opposite path to the passage: he lives for himself, and so he does not last.

groundhog day. film harold ramis 1993 a proud weatherman must live the same day again and again. first he uses the day for himself, and it does not end. later he spends each day on the people of the town and asks for nothing. only then does the next morning come. the film shows that the private is completed when a person stops living for the private.

longstreet. tv stirling silliphant (with bruce lee) 1971 bruce lee plays a martial-arts teacher in this detective series. he tells his blind student to be without a fixed form, like water, which takes the shape of any cup. lee repeated the idea in a 1971 television interview with pierre berton. the lesson is the passage in a fight: water does not contend, and so nothing can block it.

bitter work (avatar: the last airbender). episode aaron ehasz (writer); michael dante dimartino and bryan konietzko (series creators) 2006 iroh teaches his nephew to turn lightning aside. he learned the method by watching waterbenders: do not block the force, but give it a path through the body and out. zuko's own anger is what keeps him from making lightning. the episode shows water as a teacher of those who use force.

bridge over troubled water. song simon & garfunkel (written by paul simon) 1970 the singer offers to go down low so that a tired friend can cross over. the singer asks for nothing and does not compete for notice. the song takes the passage's side of the high and low pair. its help comes from the low place, as water benefits the ten thousand things 'in the place the crowd hates'.

siddhartha. novel hermann hesse 1922 after years as a monk and then as a rich merchant, siddhartha becomes a ferryman's helper. the old ferryman has a low station and few words, and he has learned all that he knows from the river. siddhartha learns to listen to the water too. the novel shows the passage's claim that the low place is near to dao.

there will be blood. film paul thomas anderson 2007 an oil man says that he has a competition in him and that he wants no one else to succeed. he takes what is under other people's land and wins every contest. he ends alone in a large house, with a dead man on the floor. the film shows the cost of the opposite of water: contending in all things.

citizen kane. film orson welles 1941 kane fills a palace with statues and goods from all over the world. many of them stay in their boxes. he dies alone there, and workers burn the things that nobody wants. the film is a full picture of two lines of the passage: 'gold and jade fill the hall: no one can guard them.'

ozymandias. poem percy bysshe shelley 1818 a traveller finds two stone legs and a broken face in an empty desert. the words on the base tell the mighty to look at the king's works and despair. no works are left. the poem shows the passage's line on those who are 'rich, high in rank, and proud': the pride itself carries the ruin.

breaking bad. tv vince gilligan 2008 a teacher starts to make drugs to leave money for his family. he soon has more than they can ever spend, and he does not stop, because he wants to be the best at it. the pile of money in a storage room is the passage's vessel filled to the brim. 'better to have stopped' is the whole story.

one last time (hamilton). song lin-manuel miranda 2015 george washington tells hamilton that he will not seek another term. he wants the country to learn how to go on without him. hamilton argues, and then he writes the farewell. the song shows the passage's last lines as a public act: 'the work carried through, the body steps back.'

the great gatsby. novel f. scott fitzgerald 1925 gatsby builds a great house, fills it with guests and shirts and music, and holds it up as an offer to one woman. he cannot stop at enough, because the display is the point. when he dies, almost no guest comes to the funeral. the novel shows a hall filled with gold and jade that no one guards.

kung fu panda. film mark osborne and john stevenson (dreamworks) 2008 a soft, round panda is chosen over five hard fighters. the secret scroll that all of them want is a blank, shining surface that shows the reader's own face. the old tortoise master tells the teacher to stop controlling. the film plays with several of the passage's questions: softness like an infant, a clear mirror, and raising without ruling.

the prophet. book kahlil gibran 1923 in the part about children, the prophet tells parents that their children come through them and do not belong to them. parents can give love and a house, but not their own thoughts. he compares the parent to a bow and the child to an arrow. this is the passage's 'giving life, not owning; raising, not ruling' in a much-loved modern form.

finding nemo. film andrew stanton (pixar) 2003 a father fish has lost almost all his family, and he holds his last son so tightly that the son swims away to prove himself. the father crosses the sea to find him. at the end the father must let the son go into danger and trust him. the film is one long answer to 'raising, not ruling'.

if you love somebody set them free. song sting 1985 the song says that love is not possession, and that a person cannot keep another person like a thing in a box. sting wrote it partly as an answer to his own earlier hit about watching a lover. its plain message is the passage's 'giving life, not owning', moved from the parent and the ruler to the lover.

4′33″. music john cage 1952 a player sits at the instrument for three movements and plays no note. the piece is a frame with nothing in it, and the room fills it: rain, coughs, chairs, breath. cage was drawing on zen buddhism and the chinese i ching at the time. the piece does for music what the passage does for the wheel: the use is 'right at its nothing'.

think small. ad doyle dane bernbach (helmut krone, julian koenig), for volkswagen 1959 a very small picture of a car sits on a page that is almost all white space. other car advertisements of the time filled every corner. this one made readers stop and look, and it changed the trade. the empty paper does the work. it is the passage's clay vessel in print: the gain is in what is there, and the use is in what is not.

portal. game valve 2007 the player has one tool, and the tool makes holes. every wall, floor, and gap in the test rooms is solved by an opening, not by a thing. the player learns to see a room by its empty places. the game is a modern exercise in the passage's third image: 'cut doors and windows to make a room.'

late spring. film yasujiro ozu 1949 a daughter must marry and leave her father. on their last trip, at night, the camera leaves her face and rests on a vase in a dim room. nothing happens in the shot. viewers have argued about it for decades, because the empty shot holds the feeling of the whole film. the nothing gives the use.

hills like white elephants. short-story ernest hemingway 1927 a man and a young woman wait for a train and talk about drinks and hills. they never name the thing that they are deciding. the story is built around that hole, as a wheel is built around its hub. the reader feels the weight because of what is absent from the page.

fifteen million merits (black mirror). episode charlie brooker and konnie huq 2011 people live in small rooms whose walls are screens. they ride exercise bicycles to earn credits, and they must pay to skip the advertisements. when one man shouts the truth on a talent show, his anger becomes a new programme. the episode shows the five colors and the five notes at full strength, and the blind eye and deaf ear that result.

wall-e. film andrew stanton (pixar) 2008 on a starship, people float in chairs with a screen in front of each face and a drink in each hand. they have not seen the pool beside them or the person next to them. a small robot knocks one screen away, and a woman looks up. the film shows the passage's eye that is blind from too much colour.

infinite jest. novel david foster wallace 1996 at the centre of this long novel is a film that is so pleasing that viewers cannot stop watching, and they die in front of it. around it are people caught by drugs, sport, and television. the novel takes the passage's warning to its limit: what feeds only the eye can make the heart 'break out in madness'.

(i can't get no) satisfaction. song the rolling stones 1965 the singer hears a radio voice and a television man who tell him what to want and how his shirts must look. he tries and tries, and no satisfaction comes. the song is a complaint from inside the world of the passage's first five lines. more notes and more colours leave the ear and eye more hungry.

walden. book henry david thoreau 1854 thoreau lives for two years in a small house that he built beside a pond. he counts the cost of his beans and his nails, and he asks what a person needs. he drops the rest as weight. the book is an american trial of 'for the belly, not for the eye': he leaves that and takes this.

nosedive (black mirror). episode charlie brooker, rashida jones, michael schur; directed by joe wright 2016 every meeting ends with a score from one to five, and the score decides a person's house, seat, and friends. a woman with a good score lives in fear of each small look, and then she falls. the episode shows the passage's first line in full: getting favor startles her, and losing favor startles her.

sunset boulevard. film billy wilder 1950 a star of silent films lives in a decaying house with her old pictures. she waits for the public's love to return. favor once made her great, and so she could not live when it left. the film shows why the passage says that 'favor makes the lower one': the one who receives favor depends on the one who gives it.

bojack horseman. tv raphael bob-waksberg 2014 a former television star wins new praise, a mistaken oscar nomination, and a new series. none of it calms him, and each loss of praise breaks him again. the series is a long study of the self that favor and disgrace both startle. it is the 'great trouble' that the passage ties to having a self to defend.

if—. poem rudyard kipling 1910 a father lists for his son the marks of a steady person. one line is the passage in small: to meet triumph and disaster 'and treat those two impostors just the same'. kipling asks for a stiff will. the passage goes one step further: it says that favor and disgrace are equally a start of fear.

mushishi. manga yuki urushibara 1999 ginko walks from village to village and studies mushi: forms of life near the source of all life, which most people cannot see, hear, or hold. he does not kill them when he can avoid it. he learns how they move and helps people live beside them. the series gives a quiet picture of 'the shape of no shape'.

star wars. film george lucas 1977 an old teacher tells a farm boy about a field that surrounds and joins all living things. the boy cannot see it. he hits the target only when he switches off his targeting computer and trusts the force. writers have often compared the force with daoist ideas of dao and qi. the scene fits 'looked at, not seen'.

solaris. novel stanisław lem 1961 scientists have studied a living ocean on a far planet for a hundred years. they have filled libraries with names and theories, and they still do not know what it is or if it knows them. the novel is a long form of one line of the passage: these things 'cannot be questioned to the end'.

the little prince. novel antoine de saint-exupery 1943 a fox teaches a small prince a secret about the things that matter most: the eye cannot see them. the pilot who tells the story learns that a desert is beautiful because a well is hidden in it. the book gives children the passage's first claim, that the real thing is looked at and not seen.

mister rogers' neighborhood. tv fred rogers 1968 fred rogers changes his shoes slowly, feeds the fish, and lets a long silence stay in the programme. he does not hurry a child's question. television around him became louder and faster for thirty years, and he did not. the programme shows the passage's question about muddy water that comes clear slowly, through stillness.

kiki's delivery service. anime hayao miyazaki 1989 a young witch works hard at her delivery job and then loses the power to fly. a painter friend tells her about her own blocks: she stops trying, walks, sleeps, and waits. kiki rests, and the power returns when it is needed. the film shows both of the passage's questions: stillness that clears, and movement that brings back life.

seven samurai. film akira kurosawa 1954 the leader of the seven is an old soldier who has lost many battles. he is watchful at every door, plain in his manner, and slow to speak. the best swordsman of the group is the quietest man in it. the film gives faces to the passage's list: 'wary, as if crossing a river in winter'.

zen and the art of motorcycle maintenance. book robert m. pirsig 1974 the narrator describes the moment when a mechanic is stuck on a screw that will not turn. he says that the stuck moment is not a failure. the mechanic must stop, look at the machine with no plan, and wait for the mind to settle. this is the passage's muddy water, cleared through stillness, in a workshop.

spring, summer, fall, winter... and spring. film kim ki-duk 2003 a small temple floats on a lake. a boy grows up there, leaves in passion, returns in guilt, becomes the old monk, and receives a new boy. each season of the film is one age of his life. the film is buddhist, and it shows the passage's line with great calm: things 'each go home again to the root'.

turn! turn! turn!. song pete seeger; recorded by the byrds 1965 seeger set to music the list of paired seasons from the book of ecclesiastes: a time to be born and a time to die, to plant and to pull up. the byrds made it a hit. the song watches things rise and go back, as the passage does, and it does not call one half of each pair good.

four quartets. poem t. s. eliot 1943 across four long poems eliot looks for a still point in the middle of the turning world. he ends with the thought that all our searching will bring us back to the place where we started, and that we will know it for the first time. the poems are christian. their shape is the passage's: emptiness, stillness, and return.

outer wilds. game mobius digital 2019 the player explores a small solar system for twenty-two minutes. then the sun dies, and the same morning starts again. nothing can stop the ending. the player can only watch, learn, and at last accept it beside a camp fire. the game teaches the passage's skill: 'i, by this, watch the return.'

the lion king. film roger allers and rob minkoff (disney) 1994 a father shows his son that lions eat the antelope, and that dead lions become the grass that the antelope eat. the son runs from his place in this circle, and the land goes grey under a ruler who only takes. the land turns green when the son returns. the film shows return to the root, and the 'wild rising' of those who do not know it.

the man who planted trees. short-story jean giono 1953 a shepherd plants one hundred acorns each day in a dry, empty valley. he does this for decades and tells nobody. water returns, and then villages and families. officials come to protect what they call a natural forest. this is the passage's last line almost word for word: the people say that it happened of itself.

mary poppins. film robert stevenson (disney); books by p. l. travers 1964 a nanny arrives in an unhappy house. she gives few orders and no reasons. by the end the father has mended a kite and taken his children to the park, and he believes that the change is his own. the family does not see her leave. she is the passage's highest kind of leader: the work is done, and she is not in it.

12 angry men. film sidney lumet; written by reginald rose 1957 eleven jurors vote guilty. the twelfth does not say that the accused is innocent. he asks questions, and he lets each man find his own doubt. at the end the jurors go their own ways, and almost no names are known. the film shows leading with few and costly words, so that each person says: i came to this myself.

nineteen eighty-four. novel george orwell 1949 the ruler's face is on every wall, and his screens watch every room. the state trusts no one, and so no one can trust the state or each other. the novel shows the third rank in the passage's list, the ruler whom people fear. it also shows the two lines on trust: where trust is not given, there is none.

the remains of the day. novel kazuo ishiguro 1989 an english butler has given his whole life to perfect, loyal service. his lord was a friend to the nazis in the 1930s, and the butler did not let himself see it. his loyalty is real, and it is also a sign that the house had gone wrong. the novel shows the passage's last pair: a dark house, and a loyal minister.

the handmaid's tale. novel margaret atwood 1985 a new state speaks all day about virtue, duty, and family. it has fixed greetings, uniforms, and public prayers. behind the words the leaders break their own rules. the novel shows the passage's second pair: when cleverness comes out, there is 'the great fabrication'. loud right conduct is a sign that the way is lost.

succession. tv jesse armstrong 2018 four adult children compete for their father's company. they say 'i love you' and 'family first' most often when they are about to betray each other. the series shows the passage's third pair. when the six kin are out of tune, speeches about devoted children and tender parents appear. in a family that is in tune, nobody needs the speeches.

the dark knight. film christopher nolan 2008 a city's courts and police have failed. so the city has a masked hero, and it puts its hope in a brave prosecutor. the film is honest about this: a city that needs such men is a sick city, and the hero wants a day when he is not needed. this is the passage's logic of the loyal minister in a disordered state.

the tao of pooh. book benjamin hoff 1982 hoff uses a. a. milne's bear to explain daoist ideas to western readers. pooh is his example of pu, the uncarved wood: plain, not clever, and for that reason able to do what rabbit and owl cannot. the book is a direct, popular reading of this passage's last lines, and many readers first met the daodejing through it.

simple gifts. song joseph brackett (shaker song) 1848 this shaker dance song begins: 'tis the gift to be simple, 'tis the gift to be free'. it says that a person who has come down to the right place will not be ashamed to bow and to bend. aaron copland later used the tune. the song shares the passage's trust in the undyed and the uncarved.

perfect days. film wim wenders 2023 a man in tokyo cleans public toilets with great care. he owns a few cassettes, some paperbacks, and some young trees. he photographs the light in the leaves at lunch. the film watches his days and does not explain him. it is a modern picture of 'less of what is private, fewer wants', with its sadness left in.

fight club. film david fincher; novel by chuck palahniuk 1999 an office worker hates his furniture catalogue life. he and a new friend throw away comfort and profit, and men follow them. the plain life soon becomes rules, uniforms, a leader, and bombs. the film is a warning about this passage read with force: 'cut off' and 'throw away' become a new cleverness, with no uncarved wood to fasten to.

the big lebowski. film joel and ethan coen 1998 the dude has no job, no plan, and a dressing gown. the men around him are sharp and busy: a rich man, a soldier, artists, criminals. all of them have a use. he drifts through their plots, 'swaying, like the sea', and at the end he is the only one who is unchanged. the film is a comic portrait of the passage's speaker.

bartleby, the scrivener. short-story herman melville 1853 a clerk in a wall street office answers each request with the words 'i would prefer not to'. he does not argue, and he does not leave. the busy lawyers cannot place him or use him. bartleby is a darker brother of the passage's speaker: 'i alone am a block', alone among people who all have their use.

i just wasn't made for these times. song the beach boys (brian wilson and tony asher) 1966 the singer looks for a place where he fits and for people who will stay with his ideas, and he does not find them. the music is rich, and the voice is alone in it. the song has the passage's central feeling: the crowd is merry and has more than enough, and 'i alone seem to have lost it'.

(sittin' on) the dock of the bay. song otis redding and steve cropper 1968 a man has left his home and crossed the country. he sits at the water and watches the ships and the tide. he will not do what people tell him to do, and nothing changes. the song stays in the passage's mood of drift and adds no moral: 'drooping, as with no home to go to'.

lost in translation. film sofia coppola 2003 two americans cannot sleep in a tokyo hotel. around them are parties, game halls, and bright signs, and they feel no part of it. the film does not cure them. it lets them be dim together for a few days. it shows the passage's contrast between the bright, sharp crowd and the one who is 'dusk, dusk'.

stalker. film andrei tarkovsky 1979 a guide leads two men into a closed zone. it is wet, green, and unclear, and no straight path is safe in it. the men are told that a room at the centre gives a person's deepest wish. the film never proves it. it shows the passage's claim: within the dim and flickering there is something very real. the guide also speaks a prayer that follows the daodejing on softness.

tomorrow never knows. song the beatles (lennon–mccartney) 1966 john lennon took the words from a 1964 guide to psychedelic experience that was based on the tibetan book of the dead. the song tells the listener to stop thinking and float into a shining emptiness. one drone, tape loops, and a far voice make the sound itself dim and flickering. within it, the song says, there is something to know.

close encounters of the third kind. film steven spielberg 1977 after a light passes over his truck, a man has a shape in his mind that he cannot name. he builds it from shaving foam, potatoes, and mud. his family thinks that he is ill. the shape is a real mountain. the film is a story of the passage's sequence: first dim, then an image, then a thing, then a proof.

blowup. film michelangelo antonioni 1966 a photographer enlarges a picture of a park and thinks that he sees a body in the leaves. he enlarges again, and the image becomes grain. the film leaves the question open. it explores the same ground as the passage, from the side of doubt: how a person knows that 'within it there is a thing' when the image is only flickering.

anthem. song leonard cohen 1992 cohen tells the listener to stop waiting for a perfect offering. in the song's best-known image, every thing has a break in it, and the break is where the light enters. the song does not praise damage and does not hide it. it joins the two sides, as the passage does: 'bent, then whole.' 'hollow, then full.'

the velveteen rabbit. book margery williams 1922 an old toy horse explains to a new toy rabbit how a toy becomes real. it happens slowly, when a child loves the toy for a long time. by then the fur is rubbed off and the joints are loose. the story is the passage's fourth line told for children: 'worn, then new.'

little miss sunshine. film jonathan dayton and valerie faris 2006 a family of people who have each failed drives a broken van to a child beauty contest. the father sells a plan for winners. they lose the contest badly, on a stage, together, and they drive home whole for the first time. the film shows the passage's turn: when they stop contending, nobody can defeat them.

celeste. game maddy thorson and noel berry (maddy makes games) 2018 a young woman climbs a mountain, and a dark copy of herself tries to stop her. she fights the copy, and she falls to the bottom. she climbs again only after she stops the fight and takes that part of herself with her. the game makes the player feel 'crooked, then straight' in the hands.

all things must pass. song george harrison 1970 harrison's song says that a sunrise does not last all morning and a cloudburst does not last all day. he took these images from timothy leary's poem version of this chapter of the daodejing, as harrison himself said. the song is this passage in popular music: hard weather passes of itself, and so does grief.

nothing gold can stay. poem robert frost 1923 in eight short lines frost says that the first green of spring is gold, and that it holds for only an hour. leaf follows leaf, and dawn goes down to day. the poem has the passage's sparse words and its plain law. if heaven and earth cannot keep a high moment up, a person cannot.

the red turtle. film michael dudok de wit 2016 a man is thrown onto an empty island. he fights it and tries three times to escape. then he stops, and he lives a whole life there. a great wave destroys the forest, and the forest grows again. the film has no spoken words. it shows 'sparse words: so of itself', and a man who becomes one with his place.

uncut gems. film josh and benny safdie 2019 a new york jeweller bets, borrows, and talks without stopping for two hours of film. each win is put on a larger bet. he tries to keep a whirlwind going for the whole day. the film shows by contrast the passage's weather: if even heaven and earth cannot keep a squall up, a man cannot.

the emperor's new clothes. short-story hans christian andersen 1837 an emperor loves fine dress and loves to be seen in it. two cheats sell him cloth that does not exist, and he walks through the town in nothing. a child says so. the tale is the passage's third line in one picture: 'one who shows the self is not bright.' the show hides nothing, and all people see it.

you're so vain. song carly simon 1972 the singer describes a man who walks into a party as if he is boarding a yacht, and who watches himself in the mirror while he dances. he will also believe that this song is about him. the song is a light picture of the passage's self-display, and of why other people 'loathe' it.

the office (uk). tv ricky gervais and stephen merchant 2001 a paper company manager tells a camera crew that he is a great leader, a comedian, and a friend to his staff. the staff look at the floor. the more he praises himself, the less merit anyone sees. the series is the passage's middle lines made into comedy: 'one who boasts has no merit.'

black swan. film darren aronofsky 2010 a ballet dancer wants to be perfect in a double role. she pushes her body and mind past what they can hold, and she breaks on the night of her triumph. the film shows the passage's first line as a life: a person can go up on tiptoe for one moment, but cannot stand there.

one-punch man. manga one; redrawn by yusuke murata 2009 saitama can defeat any enemy with one hit. he has a low hero rank, a cheap apartment, and almost no fame, and he lets other heroes take the credit. around him, heroes fight for rank and for a good image. the comedy puts the passage's two kinds side by side: the one who shows the self, and the one who does not.

2001: a space odyssey. film stanley kubrick 1968 a black slab appears before humans exist, and the film never says what it is. kubrick gives it no name and almost no words. a man follows it farther than anyone has gone, and he comes back toward the earth as a child. the film's shape is the passage's: great, passing on, far, and 'far means turning back'.

the last question. short-story isaac asimov 1956 across billions of years, people ask a growing computer whether the running-down of the universe can be reversed. the stars go out. people merge with the machine. at the far end of everything, the answer comes, and it is a beginning. the story can be read with the passage's line that what goes far turns back.

phoenix. manga osamu tezuka 1967 tezuka's life work jumps between japan's far past and the far future, and each book moves closer to the present. an undying bird watches people grasp at long life, die, and come back in new forms. in one book all life ends and slowly starts again. the series shows something that 'goes all round and is not in danger'.

everything. game david oreilly 2017 the player can become any thing in the game: a bear, a stone, a galaxy, a grain of pollen. the player moves up and down in scale, and the largest level leads back into the smallest. recorded talks by alan watts play during the game. it lets the player try the passage's chain: person, earth, heaven, dao.

the tree of life. film terrence malick 2011 the film puts one texas family of the 1950s next to the birth of stars, seas, and the first animals. a mother's whispered questions go out to something that she cannot name. the film does not rank the small story below the large one. like the passage, it sets the person, the earth, and heaven in one line.

the unbearable lightness of being. novel milan kundera 1984 the novel opens with a question about the pair of weight and lightness: which one is good? one man keeps his loves light and free. one woman carries hers as a heavy fate. kundera shows the cost and the gift of each side. the book is a modern study of the passage's first line: 'heavy is the root of light.'

the lord of the rings. novel j. r. r. tolkien 1954 sam gamgee carries the pack: the rope, the salt, and the cooking pots, almost to the mountain. he is slow, plain, and steady, and the quest fails without him. frodo has the great task, and sam is its root. tolkien gives a face to the passage's traveller who 'does not leave the baggage wagons'.

marie antoinette. film sofia coppola 2006 a young queen fills her days at versailles with cakes, shoes, cards, and parties. the film stays inside the bright rooms with her, and the hungry country is far away, until a crowd is at the gate. it shows the passage's warning to the lord who is light before all under heaven: 'the root is lost'.

like a rolling stone. song bob dylan 1965 the singer speaks to a woman who was rich and well taught, and who laughed at people below her. now she has no home and no direction, and she must deal with people whom she did not see before. the song asks her how that feels. it is the passage's last pair: light, and the root is lost.

death stranding. game hideo kojima (kojima productions) 2019 the player is a porter who walks across a broken country with cargo on his back. the whole game is the load: how to stack it, balance it, and keep it dry. a player who runs light and fast falls. the game lets a person feel the passage's first line in the body: the heavy is the root of the light.

the gleaners and i. film agnes varda 2000 varda films people who pick up what others leave: potatoes after the harvest, food from market bins, broken clocks and dolls. some do it from need and some from choice. she films her own old hands too, as one more found thing. the documentary shows the passage's promise: 'there is no discarded thing', and no discarded person.

les miserables. novel victor hugo 1862 a bishop gives a bed to a released convict whom every inn has refused. the convict steals his silver. when the police bring the man back, the bishop says that the silver was a gift and adds two candlesticks. the man's whole later life grows from this. the bishop is 'good at coming to people's aid', and so no person is discarded.

lilo & stitch. film chris sanders and dean deblois (disney) 2002 stitch is a failed experiment that was made to destroy, and his makers want to lock him away. lilo is a lonely girl whom the other children avoid. her small, broken family takes him in, with the rule that nobody is left behind. the film shows the passage from the side of those whom others discard.

good will hunting. film gus van sant; written by matt damon and ben affleck 1997 a cleaner at a university is a mathematical genius, and he hits people and pushes help away. five therapists give up. the sixth stays, and the work with the young man also opens the therapist's own closed grief. the film shows the passage's pair: the teacher and the material need each other, and each must be prized.

shoplifters. film hirokazu kore-eda 2018 a poor group in tokyo lives as a family. no one in it is related by law: an old woman, a couple, a runaway, a boy, and a small girl whom they find cold on a balcony. each of them was left by someone. the film asks who is skilled at keeping people, and it complicates the passage's 'no discarded person'.

the left hand of darkness. novel ursula k. le guin 1969 the people of the planet gethen are male and female in one body, by turns. the envoy from earth must drop his habit of ranking the two sides. the novel shows the first pair of this passage: know the cock, keep to the hen. le guin later made her own english version of the tao te ching, and the book uses light and shadow as a second pair.

orlando: a biography. novel virginia woolf 1928 orlando lives for centuries, first as a man and then as a woman, and stays one person. the change takes nothing away. orlando knows the male side from inside and then keeps to the female side. the book can be read as a picture of holding both sides of the first pair, with no side made the lesser.

the little prince. novel antoine de saint-exupery 1943 a pilot who has learned the adult world of numbers and rank meets a child who sees plain things as they are. the pilot does not forget what he knows. he goes back to the child's sight and keeps it. this is the movement the passage names three times: know the high side, keep to the low side, and go back again to the infant.

fight club. film david fincher (film); chuck palahniuk (novel) 1999 men who feel small build a club and then an army on hardness only. they know the cock and throw the hen away. the result is not strength. the result is a mind split in two and a city in danger. the film shows the cost of holding one side of the pair and refusing the other.

the lathe of heaven. novel ursula k. le guin 1971 george orr's dreams change the real world. his doctor uses the dreams to repair the world: no war, no hunger, no crowding. each repair brings a worse harm. this is the passage as a story: the world is a spirit vessel, and who works on it ruins it. le guin took the title from the zhuangzi and put daoist lines at the head of chapters.

the lord of the rings. novel j. r. r. tolkien 1954 the ring gives the power to order the whole world. every strong person who grips the ring is ruined by it, even those who want to do good. the wise refuse to take the ring at all. the story shows the two lines at the center of the passage: who works on it ruins it, and who grips it loses it.

nausicaa of the valley of the wind. anime hayao miyazaki 1984 kingdoms want to burn a poison forest and take control of the land. nausicaa learns that the forest is cleaning the earth by its own slow process. the people who try to fix the world by force bring disaster. she watches, follows, and does not grip. the film shows a world that cannot be worked on.

jurassic park. film steven spielberg (film); michael crichton (novel) 1993 a rich man makes a living world and believes he can manage every part of it with fences and computers. the creatures do not stay in the plan. some go ahead and some follow, as the passage says of all creatures. the park fails in one night. the grand plan is the thing that the sage puts away.

everybody wants to rule the world. song tears for fears 1985 the song names the common wish to take the world and hold it. the bright tune carries a warning: the control does not last, and the wish itself wears people down. it gives the mood of the first line of the passage, the wanting to take all under heaven, and it shows why the sage puts the grand away.

ozymandias. poem percy bysshe shelley 1818 a traveller finds the broken statue of a king who boasted of his works. the boast is still cut in the stone, and sand is all around. shelley's line is short: "nothing beside remains." the poem shows the last line of the passage. a creature at full strength then grows old, and force that took the strong place does not keep it.

grave of the fireflies. anime isao takahata (film); akiyuki nosaka (story) 1988 two children try to stay alive in japan in the last months of the war. no battle is on screen for long. the film shows what comes after the armies: burned towns and no food. it is the passage's own image. where an army has camped, thorns grow, and after a great host there are years of hunger.

where have all the flowers gone?. song pete seeger and joe hickerson 1955 the song moves in a circle: flowers, young women, young men, soldiers, graves, and flowers again. each verse asks the same question of the next thing; joe hickerson's later verses, added in 1960, close the circle. war is not shown as an event that ends. war is shown as business that comes back, which is the third line of the passage.

seven samurai. film akira kurosawa 1954 farmers hire seven fighters to stop a band of robbers. the fighters do the work because there is no other choice, and four of them die. at the end the farmers sing and plant rice. the leader says that the victory belongs to the farmers. the film shows fruit, and stop: the result, with no pride and no strong place taken.

munich. film steven spielberg 2005 a team is sent to kill the men behind an attack. each killing is answered by a new killing, and new men take the place of the dead. the leader ends with fear and no rest. the film shows the line that such business likes to come back. force does not stop at its fruit here, and so it has no end.

all quiet on the western front. novel erich maria remarque 1929 a german schoolboy goes to the trenches with his class, and the class dies around him. the teachers at home speak of glory. the soldiers see only the dead. the novel treats every battle as a funeral, for both sides. that is the rule of the passage: mourn the many killed, and hold the victory with the rites of grief.

dulce et decorum est. poem wilfred owen 1920 owen describes a gas attack and one man who does not get his mask on in time. then he turns to the people at home who call death in war sweet and fitting. he calls that saying a lie. the poem is the passage's warning in a soldier's voice: do not find victory beautiful.

unforgiven. film clint eastwood 1992 an old gunman takes one more job. a young man who admired killers kills for the first time and is sick with it. the old man tells him plainly how heavy a killing is. the western usually finds the gun beautiful. this film refuses to. it shows weapons as tools of ill omen, used with no delight.

apocalypse now. film francis ford coppola 1979 an officer plays opera from helicopters during an attack and speaks with joy about the smell of napalm after a morning airstrike. further up the river, a colonel has made killing his whole world. the film shows the person the passage warns of: one who finds victory beautiful and delights in killing. that person loses everything the heart was set on.

spec ops: the line. game yager development 2012 the game looks like a common military shooter. then it makes the player see the people the player has killed, and it does not let the player feel like a hero. the win at the end feels like a loss. the game can be read as the passage's rule turned on its own kind: win, and do not find it beautiful.

masters of war. song bob dylan 1963 the singer speaks to the people who make weapons and sell them, and who stay far from the dead. he does not accept their reasons. the song puts the passage's first line in a modern voice. fine weapons are tools of ill omen, and one who has the dao does not stay with them.

the tao of pooh. book benjamin hoff 1982 hoff uses the bear from a. a. milne's stories to explain the uncarved wood, the word pu in this passage. pooh is simple and small. the clever animals fail, and things come to pooh of themselves. the book names the daodejing as its source. it is a light and direct picture of the thing that no one can make a servant.

being there. film hal ashby (film); jerzy kosinski (novel) 1979 chance is a gardener with no name in the world and no plan. rich and powerful people meet him and hear deep counsel in his plain talk about plants. they come to him as guests. no one can use him, because he wants nothing. the film can be read as a comedy about the uncarved wood among lords and kings.

a wizard of earthsea. novel ursula k. le guin 1968 in earthsea, to know the true name of a thing is to have power over it. the young wizard ged uses names to show his strength and lets a shadow into the world. his teachers tell him that a wizard must know when not to act. the novel shows the passage's turn: once the names are there, know where to stop.

on exactitude in science. short-story jorge luis borges 1946 the mapmakers of an empire make larger and larger maps. at last they make a map as large as the empire itself. the map is of no use, and it rots in the desert. in one paragraph, borges shows cutting and naming that does not know where to stop.

ikiru. film akira kurosawa 1952 a city clerk learns that he will die soon. he sees that he has not lived. he stops trying to please his office and puts his last strength into one small playground. he dies on its swing. the children use the playground after him. the film shows the last line of the passage: one who dies and is not lost.

groundhog day. film harold ramis 1993 a weatherman lives the same day again and again. first he uses what he learns about other people to trick them. that is the clever side of the first pair. it gets him nothing. the day ends only after he has changed himself. the film moves from knowing others to knowing the self, and from force to the strength of self-mastery.

if—. poem rudyard kipling 1910 the poem is one long sentence of conditions. each condition is a victory over the self: keep calm, wait, lose and start again, hold on. nothing in the list is a victory over another person. it can be read next to the second pair of the passage. one who overcomes others has force, and one who overcomes the self is strong.

mad men. tv matthew weiner 2007 don draper reads other people very well, and he sells them their own wishes. he does not know himself. he lives under another man's name. he wins account after account and it is not enough. the series shows a man who has the first half of each pair in the passage, the clever half and the forceful half, and lacks the second.

the giving tree. book shel silverstein 1964 a tree gives a boy its fruit, then its branches, then its trunk, and asks for nothing. the tree does not act the lord over the boy. readers do not agree about the book. some see pure giving, and some see a boy who only takes. the two readings fit the passage: the things lean on it and live, and it does not name the work "mine".

the man who planted trees. short-story jean giono 1953 a shepherd plants acorns, one hundred each day, in dry hills, for decades. he tells no one. forests grow, streams run again, and villages fill with people. the people do not know who did it, and he does not say. the story shows the middle of the passage: the work is complete, and it does not name the work "mine".

my neighbor totoro. anime hayao miyazaki 1988 a large forest spirit lives next to two girls whose mother is sick. the spirit gives them shelter in the rain, helps their seeds grow, and sends help when one girl is lost. the spirit gives no orders and asks for no thanks. it is great, and it can be named among the small. the film shows power that feeds and does not rule.

the truman show. film peter weir 1998 a television producer has given one man a whole town, food, weather, and a wife. the producer watches from the false sky and says he knows what is best for the man. he clothes and feeds, and he does act the lord. the man walks out through a door in the sky. the film shows the opposite of the passage, and its failure.
